The lack of vasa vasorum makes the abdominal aorta a 'watershed' for nutrition.
Atherosclerotic plaques act as a barrier to diffusion.
This metabolic stress leads to medial thinning.
Structural failure follows the loss of smooth muscle and elastic tissue.
microReview: No vasa vasorum in infrarenal media + atherosclerosis = medial starvation = aneurysm.
examinerTraps: The examiner might suggest 'increased pressure' is the only reason; however, the lack of vasa vasorum is the key anatomical vulnerability.
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow...
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes an aneurysm caused by the seeding of an arterial wall by a circulating microorganism, typically seen in the setting of infective endocarditis?

explanations.a: Berry aneurysms are congenital saccular aneurysms in the Circle of Willis.
explanations.b: A mycotic aneurysm is an aneurysm resulting from an infection of the vessel wall, often from an infected embolus (e.g., in endocarditis) or direct extension.
explanations.c: Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms are small microaneurysms in the basal ganglia associated with chronic hypertension.
explanations.d: Fusiform describes a shape (circumferential), not an etiology.
explanations.e: Dissecting aneurysm is an older, slightly inaccurate term for aortic dissection.

ankiCards: A(n) {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm is caused by infection weakening the vessel wall.
The term 'mycotic' is a misnomer because most of these aneurysms are {{c1::bacterial}}, not fungal.
A common source for mycotic aneurysms is {{c1::infective endocarditis}}.
The primary mechanism of a mycotic aneurysm is an {{c1::infected embolus}} lodging in the wall.
Mycotic aneurysms carry a high risk of {{c1::rupture}} and sepsis.
keyPoints: Mycotic aneurysms are infectious in origin.
Common pathogens include Staphylococcus and Streptococcus species.
Destruction of the media by inflammation causes the dilation.
They can occur in any artery, including the aorta and cerebral vessels.
The term was coined by Osler.
microReview: Infection + Vessel wall destruction = Mycotic Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Don't assume 'mycotic' means fungal; in pathology board questions, it almost always refers to a bacterial infection of the arterial wall.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 58-year-old woman with polycystic kidney disease (PKD) presents to the emergency department with the sudden onset of the 'worst headache of her life.' On physical examination, she has neck stiffness. Which of the following is the most likely location of the vascular abnormality responsible for her symptoms?

explanations.a: Bleeding in the basal ganglia is typical of hypertensive intraparenchymal hemorrhage (Charcot-Bouchard).
explanations.b: Berry aneurysms (saccular aneurysms) occur at branch points in the Circle of Willis, with the anterior communicating artery being the most common site. They are associated with PKD.
explanations.c: Aneurysms here would cause chest pain, not a sudden severe headache.
explanations.d: The middle meningeal artery is involved in epidural hematomas, usually following trauma.
explanations.e: While aneurysms can occur here, the anterior circle (like the A-com) is more frequent for subarachnoid hemorrhage.

ankiCards: {{c1::Berry (saccular)}} aneurysms are found in the Circle of Willis.
The most common site for a Berry aneurysm is the {{c1::anterior communicating}} artery.
Berry aneurysms are associated with {{c1::Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD)}}.
Rupture of a Berry aneurysm causes {{c1::subarachnoid}} hemorrhage.
Risk factors for Berry aneurysm rupture include {{c1::hypertension}} and smoking.
keyPoints: Berry aneurysms are due to a congenital defect in the tunica media.
They are not present at birth but develop over time.
ADPKD and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome are classic associations.
Presentation is 'thunderclap headache'.
Diagnosis is typically confirmed by CT or lumbar puncture (xanthochromia).
microReview: PKD + Sudden worst headache = Ruptured Berry Aneurysm in the Circle of Willis.
examinerTraps: Differentiate the location: Charcot-Bouchard (basal ganglia/HTN) vs. Berry (Circle of Willis/PKD).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture...
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Syphilitic aortitis leads to the formation of aneurysms in the ascending aorta primarily through which of the following mechanisms?

options.a: Obstruction of the vasa vasorum by endarteritis obliterans
options.b: Direct invasion of the tunica intima by Treponema pallidum
options.c: Formation of intimal plaques containing cholesterol crystals
options.d: Genetic mutation in the fibrillin-1 protein
options.e: Autoimmune destruction of the elastic lamina

explanations.a: Tertiary syphilis causes 'endarteritis obliterans' of the vasa vasorum, leading to ischemic injury of the aortic media and subsequent weakening (aneurysm).
explanations.b: While the spirochetes are present, the damage is mediated by the ischemic effect of the vasa vasorum destruction, not direct intimal invasion.
explanations.c: Cholesterol plaques are the hallmark of atherosclerosis, which typically affects the abdominal aorta.
explanations.d: This is the mechanism for Marfan syndrome.
explanations.e: Syphilis is an infectious, not a primary autoimmune, process.

ankiCards: Tertiary syphilis involves the {{c1::ascending}} aorta.
The hallmark of syphilitic aortitis is {{c1::endarteritis obliterans}} of the vasa vasorum.
Syphilitic involvement of the aorta results in a {{c1::'tree-bark'}} appearance of the intima.
The dilation of the aortic root in syphilis can lead to {{c1::aortic valve insufficiency}}.
Ischemia of the media in syphilis causes loss of {{c1::elastic}} fibers.
keyPoints: Syphilitic (luetic) aneurysms are now rare due to antibiotics.
The 'tree-barking' is due to scarring from the ischemic media.
The dilation often involves the aortic valve ring (aneurysm of the aortic root).
The resulting aortic regurgitation leads to 'cor bovinum' (massive heart).
Death usually occurs from heart failure or rupture.
microReview: Syphilis = Endarteritis of vasa vasorum = Medial ischemia = Ascending Aortic Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Atherosclerosis is rare in the ascending aorta; if an aneurysm is there, think HTN, Marfan, or Syphilis.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture...
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following is a classic complication of an abdominal aortic aneurysm where a piece of the mural thrombus breaks off and occludes a distal vessel, leading to 'blue toe syndrome'?

explanations.a: Aortic dissection is a separate process of blood tearing through the media, though it can coexist with an aneurysm.
explanations.b: Aneurysms often contain mural thrombi (due to stagnant/turbulent flow). These can embolize distally, causing ischemia in the lower extremities (blue toe syndrome).
explanations.c: Erosion refers to the aneurysm wearing away adjacent structures like vertebrae, but it doesn't cause distal ischemia.
explanations.d: Compression of adjacent structures (e.g., ureters) is possible but doesn't cause blue toes.
explanations.e: Rupture causes massive retroperitoneal hemorrhage and shock.

ankiCards: Aneurysms often contain a {{c1::mural thrombus}} due to turbulent blood flow.
{{c1::Embolization}} of a thrombus from an AAA can cause 'blue toe syndrome'.
The triad of a ruptured AAA is {{c1::hypotension}}, {{c2::flank/back pain}}, and a {{c3::pulsatile mass}}.
AAAs can cause {{c1::hydronephrosis}} by compressing the ureters.
{{c1::Atherosclerotic}} debris can also embolize from an aneurysm.
keyPoints: Stagnant flow in the 'pouch' of the aneurysm promotes clotting.
Distal embolization is a common reason for foot ischemia in these patients.
AAAs can also rupture into the peritoneal cavity or retroperitoneum.
Large AAAs can obstruct branch vessels (e.g., iliac, mesenteric).
Surgical intervention targets both rupture risk and embolic risk.
microReview: AAA + Mural Thrombus + Embolism = Distal Ischemia (Blue Toe).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'Blue Toe Syndrome' (micro-emboli) with 'Acute Limb Ischemia' from a large saddle embolus from the heart.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively... or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 65-year-old man presents with persistent hoarseness and a brassy cough. A chest X-ray shows a mass in the mediastinum, and subsequent CT reveals a 6 cm aneurysm of the aortic arch. Which of the following mechanisms is the most likely cause of his specific symptoms?

options.a: Compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve
options.d: Obstruction of the superior vena cava

explanations.a: Thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAA) can compress the left recurrent laryngeal nerve as it loops around the arch, leading to hoarseness.
explanations.b: Rupture would cause sudden collapse and death, not chronic hoarseness.
explanations.c: Syphilis causes TAA, but the question asks for the 'mechanism of the symptoms', which is compression.
explanations.d: SVC syndrome causes facial swelling and venous distention, not typically isolated hoarseness.
explanations.e: Subclavian thrombosis would cause arm ischemia.

ankiCards: Thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAA) can compress the {{c1::recurrent laryngeal}} nerve.
Compression of the {{c1::esophagus}} by a TAA can cause dysphagia.
TAAs can compress the {{c1::trachea}} or mainstem bronchus, leading to respiratory distress.
The most common risk factor for a non-genetic Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm is {{c1::hypertension}}.
Bone pain from a TAA is usually caused by {{c1::erosion}} of the ribs or vertebrae.
keyPoints: TAAs often present with 'mass effect' symptoms.
Hoarseness is a classic sign of arch involvement.
Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) occurs from esophageal compression.
Pain is usually substernal or back pain.
Aortic root dilation can lead to heart failure via valve incompetence.
microReview: Thoracic Aneurysm + Hoarseness = Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve compression.
examinerTraps: Is the question asking for the *cause* of the aneurysm (HTN/Syphilis) or the *cause* of the symptom (Compression)? Read carefully.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture...
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old male with a history of HIV (CD4+ count 150/mm³) presents with multiple, painless, violaceous macules and plaques on his lower extremities and hard palate. Biopsy of a skin lesion reveals proliferation of spindle cells forming slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells. Which of the following infectious agents is most likely responsible for the pathogenesis of these lesions?

explanations.a: Human herpesvirus 6 is primarily associated with roseola infantum and is not implicated in vascular tumorigenesis.
explanations.b: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent for Kaposi sarcoma, which presents as spindle cell proliferations in immunocompromised patients.
explanations.c: Epstein-Barr virus is linked to various lymphomas (e.g., Burkitt) and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, but not vascular tumors.
explanations.d: Cytomegalovirus can cause retinitis or colitis in AIDS patients but does not typically cause cutaneous vascular tumors.
explanations.e: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can look similar clinically, but the histopathology would show a neutrophilic infiltrate rather than the characteristic spindle cells of Kaposi sarcoma.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is associated with infection by {{c1::HHV-8}}.
The histological hallmark of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells with slit-like vascular spaces}}.
The four clinical forms of Kaposi Sarcoma are {{c1::Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated}}.
In AIDS-associated Kaposi Sarcoma, lesions are often found on the {{c1::skin, mucous membranes (palate), and GI tract}}.
Wait, what is the characteristic inflammatory cell seen in Bacillary Angiomatosis vs Kaposi Sarcoma? {{c1::Neutrophils vs. Mononuclear cells/lymphocytes}}.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8.
AIDS-associated KS is the most common HIV-related malignancy.
Histology shows spindle cells, slit-like spaces, and extravasated RBCs.
Classic KS usually involves older men of Mediterranean or Eastern European descent.
Endemic African KS is often aggressive and involves lymph nodes in children.
microReview: Kaposi sarcoma is a borderline malignant vascular tumor strongly associated with HHV-8. Diagnosis is confirmed by finding spindle cells and slit-like vascular channels on biopsy.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Kaposi Sarcoma (HHV-8, spindle cells, lymphocytic infiltrate) with Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella, lobular capillary proliferation, neutrophilic infiltrate).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with an exquisitely painful, small (5 mm), bluish nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. She notes that the pain is often triggered by exposure to cold. Histological examination of the excised lesion reveals aggregates of uniform, rounded cells surrounding thin-walled vascular channels. From which of the following cell types does this tumor originate?

explanations.a: While present in the tumor's vessels, endothelial cells are not the specific cells of origin for the characteristic uniform rounded 'glomus' cells.
explanations.b: Pericytes are related but are specifically associated with hemangiopericytomas, not the thermoregulatory glomus bodies.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) arise from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, which is an arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts produce collagen but do not form the characteristic nest-like structures seen in glomus tumors.
explanations.e: Schwann cells form nerve sheaths; while these lesions are painful, the tumor itself is not of neural origin.

ankiCards: A glomus tumor is typically found in the {{c1::subungual (under the nail)}} region.
The clinical triad of a glomus tumor includes pain, tenderness, and {{c1::sensitivity to cold}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle cells}} of the glomus body.
Histology of a glomus tumor shows uniform cells surrounding {{c1::vascular channels}}.
Glomus bodies are specialized {{c1::arteriovenous anastomoses}} involved in thermoregulation.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign, exquisitely painful tumors.
The classic location is the subungual region (under fingernails).
They are sensitive to cold temperatures.
Cell of origin: Modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
Treatment is simple excision.
microReview: Subungual pain + Cold sensitivity = Glomus Tumor. Originates from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
examinerTraps: A glomus tumor is different from a 'glomus jugulare tumor' (a paraganglioma); examiners may use the term 'glomangioma' as a synonym for glomus tumor.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular tumors are categorized by their clinical behavior. Which of the following is classified as an intermediate-grade (borderline) vascular neoplasm?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are strictly benign tumors.
explanations.b: Angiosarcomas are highly malignant tumors with poor prognosis.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are benign lesions.
explanations.d: Kaposi sarcoma is classified as an intermediate-grade (borderline) neoplasm because it is locally aggressive and has potential for metastasis, but lacks the extreme atypia of angiosarcomas.
explanations.e: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign, often reactive, lobular capillary hemangioma.

ankiCards: Kaposi sarcoma is categorized as a(n) {{c1::intermediate-grade (borderline)}} tumor.
Angiosarcoma is categorized as a(n) {{c1::malignant}} vascular tumor.
Hemangiomas and Glomus tumors are categorized as {{c1::benign}} vascular tumors.
{{c1::Angiosarcoma}} is a highly lethal malignant vascular tumor.
Vascular tumors of {{c1::intermediate}} grade are locally aggressive but less metastatic than sarcomas.
keyPoints: Benign: Hemangioma, Glomus tumor.
Intermediate (Borderline): Kaposi sarcoma, Hemangioendothelioma.
Malignant: Angiosarcoma.
Classification is based on potential for local recurrence and metastasis.
Kaposi sarcoma clinical progression varies by subtype (e.g., indolent classic vs aggressive AIDS).
microReview: Understanding the spectrum of vascular tumors: Benign (hemangiomas), Intermediate (Kaposi), Malignant (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: Kaposi sarcoma is often mistaken for a 'fully malignant' sarcoma due to its name, but it is technically classified as borderline/intermediate in most pathology grading systems.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... 518 Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... 520 Malignant Tumors... 522
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with several rapidly enlarging, ill-defined, violaceous skin nodules on her left arm. She has a history of radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer 10 years ago, followed by chronic lymphedema of that arm. Biopsy reveals highly atypical endothelial cells forming irregular, anastomosing vascular channels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and usually presents in HIV patients; it does not typically arise specifically from chronic lymphedema.
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy) is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious lesion caused by Bartonella and seen in immunocompromised patients, not related to lymphedema.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign lesions with large blood-filled spaces, not associated with previous surgery or malignancy.
explanations.e: Lymphangiomas are benign lymphatic malformations, not malignant lesions with atypical cells.

ankiCards: {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}} refers to angiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphedema.
Angiosarcoma histological features include {{c1::atypical endothelial cells}} and anastomosing channels.
The most common sites for angiosarcoma include the {{c1::skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver}}.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride or Thorotrast}}.
Post-irradiation angiosarcoma can occur years after treatment for {{c1::breast cancer}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms.
Chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves) is a major risk factor.
Radiation therapy is another common risk factor for cutaneous angiosarcoma.
Tumors show positive staining for endothelial markers (CD31).
High mortality rate due to early metastasis.
microReview: Malignant vascular tumor (Angiosarcoma) + Chronic Lymphedema = Stewart-Treves Syndrome.
examinerTraps: Wait for the history of radical mastectomy; if it is present with new arm nodules, think Angiosarcoma, not recurrent breast cancer or lymphedema alone.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A biopsy of a red-to-purple skin nodule in an HIV-positive patient shows a lobular proliferation of capillaries, prominent edema, and a dense infiltrate of neutrophils. Warthin-Starry silver stain reveals clusters of tangled bacilli. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma does not feature a neutrophilic infiltrate or positive Warthin-Starry staining for bacilli.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation caused by Bartonella (henselae or quintana) in immunocompromised hosts, characterized by neutrophils and silver-stain positive organisms.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma is a lobular capillary hemangioma but does not contain Bartonella bacilli.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated vascular channels and lack the neutrophilic inflammatory component.
explanations.e: Strawberry (juvenile) hemangiomas are common in infants and regress spontaneously; they are not infectious.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by bacteria of the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
The characteristic inflammatory cell in Bacillary angiomatosis is the {{c1::neutrophil}}.
{{c1::Warthin-Starry}} silver stain is used to identify the organisms in Bacillary angiomatosis.
Bacillary angiomatosis occurs primarily in {{c1::immunocompromised (HIV)}} patients.
Unlike Kaposi sarcoma, Bacillary angiomatosis is treated with {{c1::antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin)}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular tumor-like lesion caused by Bartonella henselae.
It is an opportunistic infection in AIDS patients.
Microscopy: Capillary proliferation with neutrophilic inflammation.
Silver stains (Warthin-Starry) highlight the bacilli.
It can involve skin, bone, or internal organs.
microReview: Bacillary angiomatosis: HIV + Neutrophils + Bartonella + Vascular nodules.
examinerTraps: The 'vignette trap' is thinking every skin lesion in an HIV patient is Kaposi Sarcoma. Look for the mention of neutrophils or silver stain (Bartonella).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following markers is most specific for identifying the endothelial origin of a suspected poorly differentiated malignant vascular tumor?

explanations.a: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (smooth or skeletal).
explanations.b: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells (e.g., melanoma, Schwann cells).
explanations.c: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a highly specific marker for endothelial cells and is used to diagnose angiosarcomas.
explanations.d: Cytokeratins are markers for epithelial cells (carcinomas).
explanations.e: Vimentin is a non-specific marker for all mesenchymal cells.

ankiCards: The most common immunohistochemical marker for endothelial cells is {{c1::CD31}}.
Another marker used for vascular tumors is {{c1::von Willebrand factor (Factor VIII-related antigen)}}.
{{c1::Angiosarcoma}} is a malignant tumor that expresses CD31.
Desmin is used to identify tumors of {{c1::muscle}} origin.
Cytokeratin is used to identify tumors of {{c1::epithelial}} origin.
keyPoints: CD31 is the standard marker for vascular endothelium.
von Willebrand Factor is also an endothelial marker.
Identifying markers is crucial for differentiating angiosarcomas from carcinomas or melanomas.
Vascular tumors are of mesenchymal (mesodermal) origin.
CD34 is another marker but is less specific than CD31.
microReview: Endothelial cell markers: CD31 and vWF (Factor VIII). Use them to confirm vascular lineage.
examinerTraps: Vimentin is positive in vascular tumors (mesenchymal), but it's not specific because almost all sarcomas are vimentin positive.
sourceQuote: VASCULAR STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION The general architecture and cellular composition of blood vessels are comparable throughout the cardiovascular system.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 2-week-old infant is brought to the pediatrician with a bright red, raised, 'strawberry-like' lesion on the scalp. The parents report it was not present at birth but appeared shortly after. What is the most likely natural history of this lesion?

options.c: Persistence throughout adult life without change
options.d: Progressive enlargement proportional to body growth

explanations.a: Strawberry (juvenile) hemangiomas are benign and do not undergo malignant transformation.
explanations.b: Juvenile hemangiomas typically grow rapidly for a few months and then spontaneously involute (regress), usually by age 5-7.
explanations.c: Unlike port-wine stains, strawberry hemangiomas do not typically persist into adulthood.
explanations.d: They grow faster than the child initially but then shrink, unlike some vascular malformations.
explanations.e: Kasabach-Merritt syndrome (platelet sequestration) is associated with rarer vascular tumors like tufted angioma or kaposiform hemangioendothelioma, not standard strawberry hemangiomas.

ankiCards: The common name for a juvenile hemangioma is a(n) {{c1::strawberry}} hemangioma.
The clinical course of a strawberry hemangioma involves rapid growth followed by {{c1::spontaneous regression}}.
Strawberry hemangiomas are histologically classified as {{c1::capillary}} hemangiomas.
By age 7, approximately {{c1::75-90}}% of strawberry hemangiomas have regressed.
In contrast to juvenile hemangiomas, {{c1::port-wine stains (nevus flammeus)}} usually persist and thicken.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry) are extremely common in infants.
They are benign capillary hemangiomas.
Natural history: Grow rapidly -> Plateau -> Regress.
Complete regression is the rule, not the exception.
No treatment is usually required unless they obstruct vision or the airway.
microReview: Strawberry Hemangioma = Newborn + Bright Red + Spontaneous regression.
examinerTraps: Confusing 'Strawberry Hemangioma' (regresses) with 'Port-Wine Stain' (persists).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old pregnant woman in her third trimester presents with a rapidly growing, friable, red pedunculated nodule on her gingiva (gums). It bleeds easily with minor trauma. She is concerned about malignancy. Which of the following is the most likely histological diagnosis?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma (granuloma gravidarum) is a lobular capillary hemangioma that frequently occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women.
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma is rare in young pregnant women and usually presents as an ill-defined bruised area, not a pedunculated gingival mass.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are found under nails and are painful, not friable gingival masses.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis presents similarly but is an infection in immunocompromised patients; this patient is healthy and pregnant.
explanations.e: Nevus flammeus is a flat birthmark (port-wine stain), not a growing pedunculated mass.

ankiCards: A pyogenic granuloma is histologically a(n) {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
When a pyogenic granuloma occurs in a pregnant woman's mouth, it is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
The typical clinical appearance of a pyogenic granuloma is a {{c1::pedunculated, red, friable (bleeds easily)}} mass.
Pyogenic granulomas are often triggered by {{c1::trauma or pregnancy}}.
Treatment for pyogenic granuloma usually involves {{c1::surgical excision}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer (it's neither pyogenic nor a granuloma).
It is a benign vascular proliferation (lobular capillary hemangioma).
Commonly occurs on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
High association with pregnancy (hormonal influence).
Highly vascular and prone to bleeding.
microReview: Gingival mass in pregnancy = Granuloma Gravidarum (Pyogenic Granuloma).
examinerTraps: The name 'Pyogenic Granuloma' suggests pus or granulomatous inflammation, but it has neither. It is a vascular tumor.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular tumors that demonstrate large, dilated, thin-walled vascular spaces filled with blood and separated by a scant connective tissue stroma are characteristic of which condition?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas have small, thin-walled capillaries, not large dilated spaces.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, blood-filled vascular spaces (caverns). They are common in the liver and brain.
explanations.c: Arteriovenous malformations contain thick-walled, abnormal arteries and veins with shunting, rather than just cavernous spaces.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis features capillary proliferation with neutrophilic infiltrates.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma features atypical cells and irregular channels, not well-defined benign dilated spaces.

ankiCards: {{c1::Cavernous}} hemangiomas consist of large, dilated vascular channels.
Cavernous hemangiomas of the liver are significant because they may be mistaken for {{c1::malignancy (metastasis)}} on imaging.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas {{c1::do not}} spontaneously regress.
Von Hippel-Lindau disease is associated with cavernous hemangiomas in the {{c1::cerebellum, brainstem, and retina}}.
A potential complication of a large cavernous hemangioma is {{c1::thrombosis}} or dystrophic calcification.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas involve large, blood-filled spaces.
They are often deep-seated (liver, CNS) compared to capillary types.
They are usually asymptomatic but can bleed or cause mass effect.
Histology: Large spaces, thin walls, scant stroma.
They do not regress spontaneously.
microReview: Cavernous = Big spaces. Capillary = Small spaces.
examinerTraps: Biopsying a hepatic cavernous hemangioma is dangerous due to the risk of severe hemorrhage.
sourceQuote: To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure and function.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old worker from a plastics manufacturing plant presents with weight loss, abdominal pain, and hepatomegaly. Imaging shows multiple hemorrhagic masses in the liver. A biopsy confirms a malignant vascular tumor. Chronic exposure to which of the following substances is the most likely risk factor?

explanations.a: Arsenic exposure is linked to hepatic angiosarcoma, but vinyl chloride is the classic association for plastic workers.
explanations.b: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and lung cancer.
explanations.c: Benzene is associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.d: Vinyl chloride (used in the PVC industry) is strongly associated with the development of hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.e: Beryllium exposure causes berylliosis (a granulomatous lung disease).

ankiCards: The classic chemical carcinogen for hepatic angiosarcoma is {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
Besides vinyl chloride, {{c1::arsenic and Thorotrast}} are risk factors for liver angiosarcoma.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is a highly {{c1::malignant/aggressive}} tumor.
Vinyl chloride is used in the manufacturing of {{c1::polyvinyl chloride (PVC)/plastics}}.
Angiosarcomas are derived from {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is rare but highly lethal.
It is strongly linked to occupational exposure to vinyl chloride.
Other exposures: Thorotrast (radiocontrast) and Arsenic.
Latent period between exposure and tumor development is usually decades.
Presents with jaundice, hepatomegaly, and liver failure.
microReview: Plastic worker + Liver masses = Hepatic Angiosarcoma (Vinyl chloride).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Hepatic Angiosarcoma (Vinyl chloride) with Hepatocellular Carcinoma (Aflatoxin, Hep B/C).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old male with a history of HIV and a CD4+ count of 120 cells/µL presents with multiple non-blanching, violaceous macules and plaques on his lower extremities. Biopsy of a lesion reveals proliferation of spindle cells forming slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells and hemosiderin deposits. Which of the following pathogens is most directly implicated in the pathogenesis of these lesions?

explanations.a: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of Kaposi sarcoma, which classically presents as spindle cell proliferation and slit-like vascular channels in immunocompromised patients.
explanations.b: HHV-6 is associated with roseola infantum and is not typically linked to vascular tumor formation.
explanations.c: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis in HIV patients; while it produces vascular lesions, the histology shows neutrophilic inflammation and lobular capillary proliferation rather than spindle cell slit-like spaces.
explanations.d: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) causes retinitis, colitis, and pneumonia in immunocompromised hosts but is not the primary driver of vascular spindle cell tumors.
explanations.e: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is associated with lymphomas (e.g., Burkitt, CNS lymphoma) and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not Kaposi sarcoma.

ankiCards: {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}} is the primary etiologic agent of Kaposi Sarcoma.
Kaposi Sarcoma histology shows {{c1::spindle cells}} forming slit-like vascular spaces.
In Kaposi Sarcoma, vascular slits often contain {{c1::extravasated RBCs}}.
The classic clinical presentation of Kaposi Sarcoma in HIV patients involves {{c1::violaceous (purple)}} skin lesions.
{{c1::Bacillary angiomatosis}} is a vascular differential for Kaposi Sarcoma caused by Bartonella species.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8.
The clinical presentation involves purple/violaceous macules, plaques, or nodules.
Four forms exist: Classic (older Mediterranean), Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
Histology: Slit-like spaces, spindle cells, and extravasated RBCs.
Treatment involves highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) and potentially chemotherapy.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = HHV-8 + Spindle Cells + Slit-like spaces + HIV/Immunosuppression.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Kaposi Sarcoma with Bacillary Angiomatosis; the latter features neutrophils and is caused by Bartonella.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. ... Vascular tumors are broadly categorized as benign, intermediate, or malignant.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following chemical exposures is most strongly associated with the development of hepatic angiosarcoma, a highly aggressive malignant tumor of the vascular endothelium?

explanations.a: Vinyl chloride exposure (used in the plastics industry) is a well-documented risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma, along with arsenic and Thorotrast.
explanations.b: Asbestos is primarily associated with mesothelioma and bronchogenic carcinoma.
explanations.c: Benzene exposure is strongly linked to acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.d: Aflatoxin B1 is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), not angiosarcoma.
explanations.e: Beryllium exposure is associated with berylliosis (granulomatous lung disease) and lung cancer.

ankiCards: The chemical {{c1::vinyl chloride}} is associated with hepatic angiosarcoma.
Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor of {{c1::vascular endothelial}} cells.
Three major risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma: vinyl chloride, {{c1::arsenic}}, and Thorotrast.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is considered {{c1::highly aggressive}} and carries a poor prognosis.
{{c1::CD31}} is a specific endothelial marker used to identify angiosarcoma.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a malignant endothelial neoplasm.
Can occur in skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Hepatic angiosarcoma risk factors: Vinyl chloride, Arsenic, Thorotrast.
Cutaneous angiosarcoma can occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
Histology: Atypical endothelial cells forming irregular vascular channels.
microReview: Hepatic Angiosarcoma = Vinyl Chloride + Arsenic + Thorotrast.
examinerTraps: Wait for the specific organ! If the question asks for lung cancer, it's asbestos; if it asks for vascular liver cancer, it's vinyl chloride.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism)
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old female presents with an intensely painful, small, subungual (under the fingernail) nodule. The pain is particularly triggered by exposure to cold temperatures. Histologic examination reveals nests of uniform, round cells surrounding small vascular spaces. These tumor cells are derived from which of the following?

explanations.a: The description fits a glomus tumor (glomangioma), which arises from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, an arteriovenous shunt involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.b: Peripheral nerve sheath cells (Schwann cells) give rise to schwannomas, which can be painful but lack the specific vascular glomus architecture.
explanations.c: Fibroblasts are involved in fibromas and fibrosarcomas, not subungual glomus tumors.
explanations.d: Skeletal muscle cells are the origin of rhabdomyomas, not small subungual vascular nodules.
explanations.e: Pericytes give rise to hemangiopericytomas (now often classified under solitary fibrous tumors), but the classic subungual round-cell nest tumor is the glomus tumor.

ankiCards: A {{c1::glomus tumor}} is a highly painful subungual vascular tumor.
Glomus tumors are derived from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells.
The classic clinical trigger for glomus tumor pain is {{c1::cold}}.
The normal glomus body is an {{c1::arteriovenous}} shunt involved in thermoregulation.
Histologically, glomus tumors show nests of {{c1::uniform, round}} cells.
keyPoints: Glomus tumor is a benign, extremely painful lesion.
Location: Most common under the fingernails (subungual).
Origin: Modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
Glomus bodies are specialized for thermoregulation.
Excusion is curative.
microReview: Glomus tumor = Painful + Subungual + Cold sensitive + Smooth muscle origin.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse glomus tumor with a glomus jugulare tumor (paraganglioma), which has a different origin.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 2-month-old female infant is brought to the pediatrician due to a rapidly enlarging, bright red, 'strawberry-like' lesion on her scalp. The lesion was not present at birth but appeared at two weeks of age. The parents are concerned about the growth. What is the most likely natural history of this lesion?

options.c: Persistent growth proportional to the child's age

explanations.a: This is a juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma. These typically grow rapidly for a few months and then spontaneously regress (involute) by early-to-mid childhood (usually by age 7).
explanations.b: Juvenile hemangiomas are benign and do not transform into malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.c: Unlike port-wine stains (Nevus flammeus), strawberry hemangiomas regress rather than growing proportionally forever.
explanations.d: Sturge-Weber syndrome is associated with port-wine stains (Nevus flammeus) in the V1/V2 distribution, not strawberry hemangiomas.
explanations.e: Since they regress spontaneously, the standard of care is usually observation unless they obstruct vital structures (e.g., the eye).

ankiCards: {{c1::Juvenile (strawberry)}} hemangiomas appear shortly after birth and grow rapidly.
Most strawberry hemangiomas {{c1::spontaneously regress}} by age 7.
The most common vascular tumor of infancy is the {{c1::hemangioma}}.
Unlike strawberry hemangiomas, {{c1::port-wine stains}} do not regress.
{{c1::Observation}} is the management of choice for most uncomplicated juvenile hemangiomas.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangioma is a very common benign tumor of infancy.
Appearance: Bright red, lobulated, elevated ('strawberry').
Natural history: Rapid growth followed by slow involution.
By age 7, 75-90% are completely regressed.
Histology: Dense packs of thin-walled capillaries.
microReview: Strawberry Hemangioma = Infancy + Rapid growth + Spontaneous regression.
examinerTraps: The examiner may try to confuse this with a 'Port-wine stain' (Nevus flammeus), which is present at birth and does NOT regress.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction... [and] Weakening of vessel walls.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old male with advanced AIDS presents with several red, friable, pedunculated skin nodules. Histology reveals a lobular proliferation of capillaries with prominent protuberant endothelial cells and an infiltrate of neutrophils. Warthin-Starry silver stain demonstrates clusters of small bacilli. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised patients caused by Bartonella species, characterized by neutrophilic infiltrates and silver-stain positive bacilli.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma shows spindle cells and slits, lacks neutrophilic infiltrates, and would not show bacteria on silver stain.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) can look similar histologically but is not associated with Bartonella bacilli or HIV-specific immunosuppression in this manner.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated vascular channels and lack the acute inflammatory/infectious features seen here.
explanations.e: Cherry angiomas are small, benign capillary proliferations common in the elderly; they do not present as friable nodules in AIDS patients.

ankiCards: {{c1::Bacillary angiomatosis}} is caused by Bartonella henselae or Bartonella quintana.
The characteristic inflammatory cell in bacillary angiomatosis is the {{c1::neutrophil}}.
{{c1::Warthin-Starry}} stain is used to visualize bacilli in bacillary angiomatosis.
Bacillary angiomatosis occurs primarily in {{c1::immunocompromised/AIDS}} patients.
The clinical appearance of bacillary angiomatosis is often {{c1::red, friable}} papules or nodules.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis: opportunistic infection in AIDS.
Caused by Bartonella (Gram-negative bacilli).
Histology: Capillary proliferation + neutrophils + nuclear atypia.
Silver stain (Warthin-Starry) identifies the organism.
Differential includes Kaposi Sarcoma (but KS is HHV-8 related and lacks neutrophils).
microReview: Bacillary Angiomatosis = AIDS + Bartonella + Neutrophils + Warthin-Starry stain.
examinerTraps: The word 'spindle cells' points to Kaposi; the word 'neutrophils' or 'bacilli' points to Bacillary Angiomatosis.
sourceQuote: Vascular Structure and Function... Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An 8-year-old girl is diagnosed with a large, fluctuant, poorly circumscribed mass in the left axilla. Imaging shows a multicystic lesion containing clear fluid but no blood. The mass is found to be composed of dilated spaces lined by endothelium and surrounded by lymphoid aggregates. This lesion is most commonly associated with which of the following conditions?

explanations.a: The description (cystic hygroma or cavernous lymphangioma) is a lymphatic malformation frequently found in the neck or axilla of children. Cystic hygromas are classic associations for Turner syndrome (45,X).
explanations.b: Marfan syndrome is associated with cystic medial necrosis and aortic dissection/aneurysms, not cystic hygromas.
explanations.c: Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) has many associations (AVSD, Hirschsprung), but cystic hygroma is more specifically linked to Turner syndrome.
explanations.d: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome involves collagen defects leading to hypermobility and vascular rupture, not lymphangiomas.
explanations.e: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) involves malformations of small blood vessels (telangiectasias), not large cystic lymphatic masses.

ankiCards: A {{c1::cystic hygroma}} is a cavernous lymphangioma typically found in the neck or axilla.
Cystic hygromas are frequently associated with {{c1::Turner syndrome}}.
Histologically, lymphangiomas contain {{c1::clear/serous}} fluid and lack red blood cells.
The presence of {{c1::lymphoid aggregates}} in the walls of cystic spaces suggests a lymphatic origin.
Cystic hygroma in a fetus may manifest as {{c1::hydrops fetalis}}.
keyPoints: Cystic hygroma is a type of cavernous lymphangioma.
Commonly found in the neck/axilla of infants/children.
Associated with Turner Syndrome (45,X).
Histology: Dilated lymphatic spaces lined by endothelium.
They are benign but can be difficult to resect due to lack of a capsule.
microReview: Cystic Hygroma = Lymphatic spaces + Turner Syndrome + Neck/Axilla.
examinerTraps: Ensure the fluid is clear; if the cystic spaces contained blood, it would be a cavernous hemangioma.
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes a 'benign, small, red, dome-shaped papule' that is extremely common on the trunk of elderly patients and increases in frequency with age?

explanations.a: Cherry angiomas (Senile angiomas) are very common benign vascular lesions that appear in middle-to-late adulthood, usually on the trunk.
explanations.b: Spider telangiectasias feature a central pulsatile arteriole with radiating capillaries; they are associated with high estrogen states (pregnancy, cirrhosis).
explanations.c: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a flat, congenital birthmark that does not present as dome-shaped papules in the elderly.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a rapidly growing, often ulcerated, friable nodule, frequently occurring after minor trauma.
explanations.e: Cavernous hemangiomas are typically larger, deeper, and less circumscribed than the small papular cherry angiomas.

ankiCards: {{c1::Cherry angiomas}} are the most common vascular tumors in elderly patients.
Cherry angiomas are benign and typically found on the {{c1::trunk/torso}}.
Unlike spider angiomas, cherry angiomas do {{c1::not}} blanch significantly with pressure.
The incidence of cherry angiomas {{c1::increases}} with advancing age.
Histologically, cherry angiomas show {{c1::capillary proliferation}} with thickened walls.
keyPoints: Cherry angioma = Senile angioma.
Extremely common, benign skin lesions.
Appearance: Small, bright red, 'cherry' like papules.
Location: Mostly on the trunk.
Clinical significance: Primarily cosmetic; no malignant potential.
microReview: Cherry Angioma = Elderly + Trunk + Benign Red Papule.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Cherry Angioma with Spider Angioma (estrogen/liver) or Hemangioma of Infancy.
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels (Fig. 11.1).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with several firm, bluish-red nodules on her left arm. She has a history of a radical mastectomy followed by radiation therapy for breast cancer 12 years ago. Since then, she has had persistent, severe lymphedema of the left upper extremity. A biopsy of a skin nodule shows poorly differentiated vascular channels with significant endothelial atypia and mitoses. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma occurring in the setting of chronic lymphedema (most classically post-mastectomy) is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome. It is an aggressive malignant endothelial tumor.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is HHV-8 related and usually presents as multiple violaceous lesions in HIV patients, not typically associated with post-mastectomy lymphedema.
explanations.c: While 'lymphangiosarcoma' was an old term for this condition, modern pathology classifies these as angiosarcomas (specifically, they are endothelial in origin).
explanations.d: Hemangioendothelioma is an intermediate-grade tumor, whereas this aggressive, atypical lesion in the setting of Stewart-Treves is a full malignancy.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are small, benign, and intensely painful; they do not arise from chronic lymphedema.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising from chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves}} syndrome.
A classic risk factor for cutaneous angiosarcoma is prior {{c1::radiation}} therapy.
Histology of angiosarcoma reveals {{c1::atypical}} endothelial cells and irregular vascular channels.
The prognosis for cutaneous angiosarcoma is generally {{c1::poor}}.
Angiosarcoma cells typically express the endothelial marker {{c1::CD31}} (or vWF).
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma: malignant, highly aggressive endothelial tumor.
Stewart-Treves syndrome: Angiosarcoma following chronic lymphedema (often post-mastectomy).
Radiation is a known secondary trigger for angiosarcoma.
Morphology: Ranges from well-formed vessels to solid sheets of spindle cells.
High mortality rate due to early metastasis.
microReview: Stewart-Treves = Chronic Lymphedema + Post-Mastectomy + Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Wait for the 10-12 year lag time. Angiosarcomas after radiation or lymphedema usually take a decade or more to develop.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular tumors are categorized as benign, intermediate (borderline), or malignant. Which of the following is considered an intermediate-grade vascular neoplasm that is locally aggressive but rarely metastasizes?

explanations.a: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is the classic example of an 'intermediate' grade vascular tumor. It is more aggressive than a hemangioma but less aggressive than an angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangioma is a benign tumor.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignant tumor.
explanations.d: Glomus tumor is a benign tumor.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious process (reactive vascular proliferation), not a neoplastic intermediate-grade tumor.

ankiCards: {{c1::Hemangioendothelioma}} is an intermediate-grade (borderline) vascular tumor.
Intermediate-grade vascular tumors are {{c1::locally aggressive}} but low-metastatic.
Angiosarcoma is considered a {{c1::high-grade/malignant}} vascular tumor.
Hemangiomas are considered {{c1::benign}} vascular tumors.
Kaposi sarcoma is generally classified as an {{c1::intermediate/borderline}} vascular neoplasm (though it can be aggressive).
keyPoints: Benign: Hemangioma, Glomus tumor, Lymphangioma.
Intermediate: Kaposi sarcoma, Hemangioendothelioma.
Malignant: Angiosarcoma.
Intermediate tumors show more cellularity and atypia than benign ones but lack the frank malignancy of sarcomas.
Clinical behavior is the defining characteristic of the grade.
microReview: Vascular Grades: Hemangioma (Benign) -> Hemangioendothelioma (Intermediate) -> Angiosarcoma (Malignant).
examinerTraps: The examiner may try to place Kaposi Sarcoma in 'malignant' or 'benign'; it is technically intermediate because it is often multicentric rather than truly metastatic.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors are broadly categorized as benign, intermediate, or malignant.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 25-year-old pregnant woman in her third trimester presents with a small, rapidly growing, red, ulcerated nodule on her gingiva (gums). It bleeds easily with minimal trauma. What is the most appropriate histological name for this lesion, often termed 'granuloma gravidarum' in this context?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma is histologically a 'lobular capillary hemangioma.' When it occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women, it is called a pregnancy tumor or granuloma gravidarum.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas involve large, blood-filled spaces and do not typically present as small, rapidly growing gingival nodules.
explanations.c: Nevus flammeus is a flat congenital birthmark.
explanations.d: Venous malformations are usually deeper, larger, and not rapidly growing friable nodules.
explanations.e: Arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) involve direct shunting between arteries and veins and are usually congenital or result from trauma.

ankiCards: The histological name for a pyogenic granuloma is {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
A pyogenic granuloma occurring on the gums of a pregnant woman is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized by {{c1::rapid}} growth and frequent bleeding.
Despite the name, pyogenic granulomas are neither {{c1::infectious}} (pyogenic) nor {{c1::granulomatous}}.
{{c1::Trauma}} is a common inciting factor for pyogenic granuloma.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is a lobular capillary hemangioma.
Clinically: Rapidly growing, red, friable (bleeds easily).
Common locations: Skin, gingiva, oral mucosa.
Association: Pregnancy (granuloma gravidarum) due to hormonal influences.
Regression: Can occur spontaneously, especially postpartum.
microReview: Pyogenic Granuloma = Lobular Capillary Hemangioma = Pregnancy + Bleeds easily + Gums.
examinerTraps: Don't let the name 'pyogenic' fool you; there is no pus or primary infection involved.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis)... [and] Weakening of vessel walls.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following is one of the two principal mechanisms that underlie vascular disease leading to clinical manifestations?

options.a: Proliferation of intimal smooth muscle cells
options.b: Weakening of vessel walls leading to dilation
options.d: Decreased wall-to-lumen ratio in muscular arteries

explanations.a: While intimal thickening is a response to injury, it is not one of the two primary umbrella mechanisms (narrowing or weakening) mentioned in the core pathology of vascular disease.
explanations.b: According to the fundamental principles of vascular pathology, the two main mechanisms are narrowing (stenosis/obstruction) and weakening of vessel walls (leading to dilation/rupture).
explanations.c: Upregulation, rather than downregulation, of metalloproteinases is often involved in the degradation of the extracellular matrix leading to aneurysms.
explanations.d: Muscular arteries typically show an increased wall-to-lumen ratio to control flow and pressure; a decrease is not a primary mechanism of systemic vascular disease.
explanations.e: While endothelial dysfunction occurs, the broad categories of disease are defined by structural failure or luminal narrowing.

ankiCards: The two principal mechanisms underlying vascular disease are narrowing (stenosis) and {{c1::weakening of vessel walls}}.
Weakening of blood vessel walls primarily leads to {{c1::dilation}} or rupture.
Narrowing of vessel lumens can occur progressively through {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Narrowing of vessel lumens can occur precipitously through {{c1::thrombosis or embolism}}.
Vascular pathology is responsible for more {{c1::morbidity and mortality}} than any other category of human disease.
keyPoints: Vascular disease is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality.
The two primary mechanisms of vascular pathology are luminal narrowing and wall weakening.
Wall weakening leads specifically to aneurysms (dilation) or rupture.
Luminal narrowing can be chronic (atherosclerosis) or acute (thrombosis).
Arterial walls are thicker than veins to accommodate higher pressure and pulsatile flow.
microReview: Vascular pathology focuses on two structural failures: obstruction (lumen closure) and structural degradation (wall thinning/dilation). Aneurysms fall into the latter category, resulting from a loss of wall integrity.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse the 'response' to injury (intimal thickening) with the 'mechanism' of disease (weakening/narrowing).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following structural characteristics explains why arterial walls are thicker than venous walls at the same level of branching?

options.a: Requirement to store large volumes of blood
options.b: Need to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher pressures
options.c: Absence of valves in the arterial system
options.d: Higher density of vasa vasorum in the media
options.e: Presence of a thicker adventitial layer

explanations.a: Veins, not arteries, act as capacitance vessels to store blood volumes.
explanations.b: Arterial walls are thicker to withstand the high-pressure, pulsatile nature of cardiac output, which is the primary functional driver for their architecture.
explanations.c: While arteries lack valves (except at the heart), this does not dictate the thickness of the muscular wall.
explanations.d: Vasa vasorum are more prominent in large elastic arteries, but their presence is a result of wall thickness (requiring nutrition), not the cause of it.
explanations.e: Veins often have a relatively thicker adventitia compared to their media; in arteries, the media is the dominant thick layer.

ankiCards: Arterial walls are thicker than veins to accommodate {{c1::pulsatile flow}} and higher blood pressures.
As arteries become smaller, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}}.
Muscular vessels exert control over blood flow and pressure by changing their {{c1::lumen diameter}}.
The architectural specializations of vessels reflect their distinct {{c1::functional roles}}.
Atherosclerosis primarily affects {{c1::elastic and muscular}} arteries.
keyPoints: Arteries have thicker walls than veins of comparable diameter.
The increased wall-to-lumen ratio in small vessels allows for blood pressure regulation.
Arterial architecture is adapted for high-pressure pulsatile flow.
Structural specialization is a hallmark of the cardiovascular system.
Venous disorders are significant, but arterial lesions are often more clinically life-threatening.
microReview: Form follows function: Arteries require high-pressure resistance and contractile capacity, necessitating thick media. Veins are low-pressure systems and require less wall structure.
examinerTraps: A common trap is stating that veins have thicker walls because they carry 'deoxygenated' blood; wall thickness is strictly a factor of hemodynamics (pressure/pulsatility).
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history presents with deep, boring mid-abdominal pain radiating to his back. Physical examination reveals a pulsatile mass palpated 2 cm above the umbilicus. A CT scan confirms a 6 cm dilation of the aorta below the renal arteries. Which underlying process is the most common contributor to this patient's condition?

explanations.a: Cystic medial degeneration is more commonly associated with thoracic aortic aneurysms and Marfan syndrome, rather than infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysms.
explanations.b: Atherosclerosis is the most common cause of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA), typically occurring in older male smokers.
explanations.c: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum is a hallmark of tertiary syphilis, which classically involves the ascending/thoracic aorta.
explanations.d: Berry aneurysms occur in the Circle of Willis and are unrelated to abdominal aortic pathology.
explanations.e: Mycotic aneurysms are caused by infection of the wall (e.g., Salmonella), which is much rarer than the atherosclerotic cause.

ankiCards: The most common site for an atherosclerotic aneurysm is the {{c1::abdominal aorta}}.
Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are typically located below the {{c1::renal arteries}}.
The major risk factor for AAA besides age and gender is {{c1::smoking}}.
Pathologically, AAA is associated with the thinning of the {{c1::tunica media}} secondary to atherosclerosis.
A pulsatile abdominal mass on exam is a classic sign of {{c1::Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm}}.
keyPoints: AAA is primarily an atherosclerotic disease.
The most common location is infrarenal (below the origin of renal arteries).
Major risk factors include male gender, smoking, and advanced age (>60).
Clinical presentation may include a pulsatile mass or back pain.
Rupture risk increases significantly when the diameter exceeds 5-5.5 cm.
microReview: AAA = Atherosclerosis + Infrarenal + Smoking. TAA = Hypertension/Connective Tissue Disease + Ascending Aorta.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the location; AAA is usually infrarenal because the aorta below the renal arteries has less vasa vasorum and higher mechanical stress.
sourceQuote: Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries... [leading to] Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following enzymatic changes is most characteristic of the pathogenesis leading to the weakening of the aortic media in aneurysm formation?

options.a: Increased expression of tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases (TIMPs)
options.d: Increased synthesis of collagen type I and III

explanations.a: Decreased, not increased, TIMP activity contributes to the imbalance that allows for matrix degradation.
explanations.b: Increased MMP activity (especially MMP-2 and MMP-9) leads to the degradation of elastin and collagen in the tunica media, which is a key step in aneurysm formation.
explanations.c: TGF-beta signaling can be abnormally high in certain connective tissue disorders (like Loeys-Dietz) that lead to aneurysms.
explanations.d: Aneurysms involve the degradation and loss of collagen and elastin, not an increase in effective synthesis.
explanations.e: Inflammatory cells (macrophages and T-cells) are actually increased in the wall of aneurysms, releasing the proteases that damage the tissue.

ankiCards: Aneurysm formation involves the {{c1::degradation}} of the extracellular matrix (ECM).
The enzymes primarily responsible for ECM degradation in aneurysms are {{c1::Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
MMPs are secreted by {{c1::macrophages}} and smooth muscle cells within the vessel wall.
An imbalance between MMPs and {{c1::TIMPs}} (Tissue Inhibitors of Metalloproteinases) leads to wall weakening.
Loss of {{c1::elastin}} in the media is a hallmark of aneurysmal dilation.
keyPoints: Aneurysms are characterized by an imbalance in matrix metabolism.
MMPs (Matrix Metalloproteinases) degrade collagen and elastin.
Chronic inflammation in the media contributes to proteolytic damage.
TIMPs normally inhibit MMPs; their relative deficiency leads to damage.
This process results in a wall that cannot withstand hemodynamic stress.
microReview: Molecular pathogenesis of Aneurysm: Inflammation -> MMP Release -> Degradation of Elastin/Collagen -> Structural Failure -> Dilation.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'Increased' vs 'Decreased'. Often, students think 'more' of anything is better, but 'Increased MMPs' is the pathological state here.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old woman with a history of untreated syphilis presents with a dry, brassy cough and difficulty swallowing. Imaging reveals a dilation of the ascending aorta with 'eggshell' calcification. Which of the following pathological mechanisms specifically explains the thoracic location of this aneurysm in the setting of her infection?

options.b: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.c: Cystic medial necrosis of the elastic fibers
options.e: Direct invasion of the intima by spirochetes

explanations.a: Atherosclerosis typically affects the abdominal aorta more severely than the ascending aorta.
explanations.b: Tertiary syphilis causes obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum in the thoracic aorta, leading to ischemic injury of the media and subsequent dilation (luetic aneurysm).
explanations.c: Cystic medial necrosis is associated with Marfan syndrome and hypertension, not typically syphilis.
explanations.d: Fibrillin-1 defects cause Marfan syndrome.
explanations.e: The spirochetes do not typically cause primary intimal invasion to form the aneurysm; the damage is mediated by the inflammatory response in the vasa vasorum (vasculitis of the small vessels supplying the aorta).

ankiCards: Syphilitic aneurysms typically involve the {{c1::ascending/thoracic}} aorta.
The underlying mechanism of syphilitic aneurysms is {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}} of the vasa vasorum.
Ischemia of the {{c1::tunica media}} leads to the weakening seen in luetic aneurysms.
A classic gross finding in syphilitic aortitis is a {{c1::'tree-bark'}} appearance of the intima.
Syphilitic aneurysms can cause narrowing of the {{c1::coronary ostia}}.
keyPoints: Thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAA) can be caused by syphilis (rare now) or hypertension.
Obliterative endarteritis results in media ischemia.
Endarteritis involves the small vessels (vasa vasorum) within the adventitia.
Luetic aneurysms often involve the aortic root, leading to aortic valve insufficiency.
Atherosclerosis is the leading cause of AAA, whereas Syphilis/Hypertension leads TAAs.
microReview: Syphilis = Endarteritis of vasa vasorum = Media ischemia = Thoracic Aneurysm. Think 'Tree-bark' appearance and Aortic insufficiency.
examinerTraps: The examiner might try to lead you toward atherosclerosis because it's the 'most common' cause of aneurysms in general, but syphilis specifically targets the thoracic vasa vasorum.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following defines a 'false' aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) compared to a 'true' aneurysm?

options.a: A wall composed of all three layers (intima, media, adventitia) that has dilated
options.b: A localized dissection where blood enters the media through an intimal tear
options.c: A collection of blood communicating with the lumen but contained by extravascular tissue
options.d: A congenital thinning of the muscular layer in cerebral vessels
options.e: A diffuse, circumferential dilation of a long segment of the artery

explanations.a: This describes a 'true' aneurysm, where the wall is intact but thinned.
explanations.b: This describes an aortic dissection, which is distinct from a pseudoaneurysm.
explanations.c: A false aneurysm is a pulsating hematoma that communicates with the vessel lumen through a hole in the wall, held in only by outer layers of the wall or surrounding tissue (like the heart or perivascular connective tissue).
explanations.d: This refers to the pathogenesis of Berry (saccular) aneurysms, which are 'true' aneurysms.
explanations.e: This describes a 'fusiform' aneurysm, which is a morphological subtype of a true aneurysm.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the arterial wall (intima, media, and adventitia).
A {{c1::false (pseudoaneurysm)}} aneurysm is a hematoma that forms outside the vessel wall but communicates with the lumen.
An example of a false aneurysm is a {{c1::ventricular rupture}} contained by the pericardium.
True aneurysms can be classified by shape as either {{c1::saccular}} or fusiform.
A {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm is a spherical outpouching involving only a portion of the vessel wall.
keyPoints: True Aneurysm: Intact (though thinned) 3-layer wall.
False Aneurysm (Pseudoaneurysm): Wall defect with extravascular hematoma.
Dissection: Blood between the layers of the vessel wall.
Saccular: One-sided 'bubble' (true aneurysm).
Fusiform: Circumferential dilation (true aneurysm).
microReview: True = 3 layers. False = Leakage held by 'fake' wall (clot/tissue). Dissection = Blood *inside* the wall layers.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse a dissection with a false aneurysm. In dissection, blood is within the media; in a false aneurysm, the blood has exited all layers but is 'walled off' by external structures.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which vessel layer is primarily responsible for maintaining the structural integrity and elastic recoil that prevents aneurysm formation?

explanations.a: The intima is primarily involved in metabolic and signaling functions, not structural strength.
explanations.b: The tunica media, composed of smooth muscle cells and elastic fibers, provides the bulk of the wall strength and elastic recoil; its degradation is the primary event in aneurysm formation.
explanations.c: The adventitia provides some support and contains nerves/vessels, but it is not the primary layer whose failure leads to dilation.
explanations.d: While the internal elastic lamina is part of the structure, the entire media's health is the deciding factor in aneurysm prevention.
explanations.e: Vasa vasorum are nutrient vessels, not structural layers.

ankiCards: The {{c1::tunica media}} is the thickest layer in large elastic arteries.
Degradation of the media leads to the clinical condition known as an {{c1::aneurysm}}.
In arteries, the ratio of wall thickness to {{c1::lumen diameter}} increases as vessels get smaller.
The cellular composition of the media consists mainly of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}}.
Structural failure of the media is the common pathway for both {{c1::aneurysms and dissections}}.
keyPoints: Tunica media is the critical structural layer.
Loss of medial smooth muscle or elastic fibers leads to dilation.
Arteries have more prominent media than veins.
In large arteries, the media requires its own blood supply (vasa vasorum).
Ischemia or proteolysis of the media are the two main pathways to failure.
microReview: Media = Strength. Damage to Media = Aneurysm. Media is thick in arteries to handle high pressure.
examinerTraps: The adventitia is actually very strong (collagen-rich), but 'structural integrity and recoil' specifically points to the elastic components of the media.
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching... allowing these muscular vessels to exert control over blood flow and pressure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 22-year-old man with very long limbs and fingers (arachnodactyly) is brought to the emergency department with sudden-onset, 'tearing' chest pain that radiates to his back. His blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg in the right arm and 140/90 mmHg in the left arm. What is the most likely microscopic finding in this patient's aorta?

options.e: Necrotizing vasculitis of the vasa vasorum

explanations.a: Atherosclerosis is a disease of older patients and is not the cause of dissection in Marfan syndrome.
explanations.b: The patient has Marfan syndrome. The underlying aortic pathology is cystic medial degeneration (also called cystic medial necrosis), which involves fragmentation of elastic fibers and accumulation of proteoglycans.
explanations.c: Granulomatous inflammation is characteristic of Giant Cell or Takayasu arteritis, not Marfan-related dissection.
explanations.d: This would suggest an acute infectious process or inflammatory aortitis.
explanations.e: This is more characteristic of systemic vasculitides like Polyarteritis Nodosa.

ankiCards: The 'tearing' chest pain radiating to the back is classic for {{c1::aortic dissection}}.
Marfan syndrome is caused by a mutation in the {{c1::Fibrillin-1 (FBN1)}} gene.
{{c1::Cystic medial degeneration}} is the histologic hallmark of Marfan-associated aortic disease.
Asymmetric blood pressures between the arms suggest a dissection involving the {{c1::aortic arch}}.
Marfan syndrome leads to increased signaling of {{c1::TGF-beta}}, which contributes to wall weakening.
keyPoints: Aortic dissection is a surgical emergency.
Marfan syndrome is a major risk factor for TAA and dissection in young patients.
The 'tearing' pain is a pathognomonic description.
Cystic medial degeneration refers to the loss of elastic tissue and gain of mucoid material.
Blood pressure discrepancy between arms indicates the dissection has impaired flow to the subclavian artery.
microReview: Marfan = Fibrillin-1 = High TGF-beta = Cystic Medial Degeneration = Dissection/Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'tearing' vs 'dull' pain. Tearing is Dissection; Boring/Dull is Aneurysm.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following is the most significant clinical consequence of an abdominal aortic aneurysm exceeding 6 cm in diameter?

explanations.a: Superior vena cava syndrome is caused by compression of the SVC, usually by lung tumors or thoracic masses, not AAAs.
explanations.b: The risk of rupture increases exponentially with size; for AAAs > 6 cm, the risk of rupture (leading to fatal hemorrhage/exsanguination) is very high.
explanations.c: While embolization of mural thrombus (Blue Toe Syndrome) can occur, the most lethal consequence of a large AAA is rupture.
explanations.d: Takayasu arteritis is an inflammatory condition (vasculitis), not a consequence of an existing aneurysm.
explanations.e: Aneurysms are structural dilations, not neoplastic growths; they do not 'become' malignant.

ankiCards: The risk of AAA rupture is directly related to the {{c1::diameter}} of the aneurysm.
An AAA greater than {{c1::5 or 6}} cm usually warrants surgical intervention.
Most AAAs are asymptomatic until they {{c1::rupture}}.
The mortality rate for a ruptured AAA is approximately {{c1::75-90}}%.
Rupture of an AAA usually occurs into the {{c1::peritoneal or retroperitoneal}} cavity.
keyPoints: Size is the best predictor of AAA rupture risk.
Rupture presents with the triad: sudden pain, hypotension, and pulsatile mass.
AAAs are often filled with mural thrombus.
Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for growth and rupture.
Surgical or endovascular repair is indicated for large or rapidly growing aneurysms.
microReview: AAA > 5cm = High risk of rupture. Triad = Pain + Hypotension + Pulsatile Mass.
examinerTraps: A common distractor is 'thrombosis of the aorta'. While mural thrombi form in almost all aneurysms, they rarely occlude the entire aorta; rupture is the primary threat.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with a 2-month history of an exquisitely painful, small, bluish-red nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. Physical examination reveals that the lesion is 4 mm in diameter and highly sensitive to cold temperature. Surgical excision is performed. Microscopic examination shows nests of uniform, round-to-oval cells surrounding thin-walled vascular channels.

explanations.a: The clinical presentation (subungual location, extreme pain, sensitivity to cold) and histology (nests of uniform cells) are classic for a glomus tumor, which arises from modified smooth muscle cells (glomus cells) of the glomus body.
explanations.b: While endothelial cells line the vascular channels within the tumor, they are not the primary neoplastic cell population in a glomus tumor.
explanations.c: Pericytes are the origin of hemangiopericytomas, which typically occur in the retroperitoneum or lower extremities, not subungually, and have a different histological pattern.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts are characteristic of fibromas or dermatofibromas, which are generally not painful and lack the characteristic glomus cell architecture.
explanations.e: Schwann cells are the origin of neurilemmomas (schwannomas); while these can be painful, they lack the specific vascular and glomus-cell histology described.

ankiCards: A subungual, exquisitely painful bluish-red nodule sensitive to cold is most likely a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
The glomus tumor arises from modified {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} of the thermoregulatory glomus body.
Histology of a glomus tumor shows {{c1::uniform round cells}} surrounding vascular channels.
Glomus tumors are most commonly found in the {{c1::subungual}} region (fingers or toes).
The glomus body is specialized for {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign, highly painful vascular neoplasms.
Classic location is subungual (under the nail).
They arise from specialized smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
Pain is often triggered by cold temperatures.
Surgical excision is curative.
microReview: Glomus Tumor: Small, painful, subungual, arises from thermoregulatory glomus bodies (modified smooth muscle).
examinerTraps: Do not confuse this with a subungual melanoma (which is usually pigmented and not specifically cold-sensitive) or a glomus jugulare tumor (which is a paraganglioma).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. . . Vascular Tumors: Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 35-year-old male with a history of HIV (CD4 count 150/mm³) presents with multiple dark purple, non-blanching macules and plaques on his lower extremities and hard palate. Biopsy reveals spindle-shaped cells, slit-like vascular spaces, and extravasated red blood cells. The pathogenesis of this condition is most closely associated with which of the following agents?

explanations.a: Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma, which presents as purple vascular lesions in immunocompromised patients.
explanations.b: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis in HIV patients, which can look similar clinically but is histologically characterized by neutrophilic infiltrates and clusters of bacteria (silver stain positive).
