explanations.c: HPV-16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx, not vascular tumors.
explanations.d: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and hairy leukoplakia, but not Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.e: CMV causes retinitis, esophagitis, and colitis in AIDS patients but is not oncogenic for vascular tissue.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is caused by {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
Histology of Kaposi Sarcoma reveals {{c1::spindle cells}} and slit-like vascular spaces.
Four clinical types of Kaposi Sarcoma are {{c1::Classic, Endemic, Iatrogenic, and AIDS-associated}}.
The most common site for Kaposi Sarcoma in AIDS patients (besides skin) is the {{c1::GI tract}} and mouth (palate).
Kaposi Sarcoma lesions are typically {{c1::non-blanching}} purple/red plaques.
keyPoints: HHV-8 is essential for the development of all forms of Kaposi Sarcoma (KS).
AIDS-associated KS is the most common HIV-related malignancy.
Histology shows slit-like spaces created by spindle cells containing RBCs.
Lesions do not blanch because blood is extravasated and within poorly formed vessels.
HAART (highly active antiretroviral therapy) can often cause regression of KS.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma: HHV-8, AIDS-defining illness, spindle cells, slit-like spaces, non-blanching purple lesions.
examinerTraps: The primary histological distractor is Bacillary Angiomatosis; look for neutrophils and Bartonella in the stem to distinguish it from KS.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease... Vascular Tumors... 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 62-year-old man who worked in a polyvinyl chloride (PVC) manufacturing plant for 30 years presents with weight loss, abdominal pain, and hepatomegaly. Imaging shows multiple hemorrhagic masses within the liver. A biopsy is performed, revealing malignant endothelial cells that are immunoreactive for CD31. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma of the liver is strongly associated with exposure to vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast. It is a highly aggressive malignancy of endothelial cells (CD31 positive).
explanations.b: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is associated with HBV/HCV and cirrhosis; it consists of malignant hepatocytes, not endothelial cells.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor, but it does not present with weight loss or aggressive growth and lacks malignant cytology.
explanations.d: Hepatic adenomas are benign and associated with oral contraceptive use, not PVC exposure.
explanations.e: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is a vascular tumor of intermediate grade, but the strong association with PVC and malignant features points to Angiosarcoma.

ankiCards: Liver angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride, arsenic, or Thorotrast}}.
The vascular marker used to identify angiosarcoma is {{c1::CD31}} (or vWF).
Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor of {{c1::endothelial cells}}.
{{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}} refers to angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy).
Angiosarcomas are highly {{c1::aggressive}} and have a poor prognosis.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a classic board association for PVC/Vinyl Chloride workers.
CD31 is a specific marker for endothelial differentiation.
The tumor is highly aggressive with frequent metastasis.
Grossly, it appears as multifocal hemorrhagic nodules.
Microscopically, it shows pleomorphic endothelial cells forming irregular channels.
microReview: Angiosarcoma: Malignant, CD31+, associated with PVC (liver) or radiation/lymphedema (skin).
examinerTraps: Be careful not to select 'Cavernous hemangioma' just because it's a vascular liver tumor; look for the 'malignant' or 'PVC' descriptors.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease... Malignant Tumors... 522.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular lesions is characterized by a rapidly growing, pedunculated red nodule on the skin or gingiva that bleeds easily and is histologically indistinguishable from a lobular capillary hemangioma?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma (granuloma pyogenicum) is a misnomer; it is neither pyogenic nor a granuloma. It is a rapidly growing capillary hemangioma often occurring after trauma or during pregnancy (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.b: Glomus tumors are small, painful subungual nodules, not typically pedunculated or found on gingiva.
explanations.c: Cystic hygromas are cavernous lymphangiomas found in the neck of infants, particularly those with Turner syndrome.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella and appears as red papules, but it is not typically pedunculated or primarily described as lobular capillary hemangioma in this context.
explanations.e: Spider angiomas are small, non-neoplastic vascular ectasias associated with hyperestrogenism (cirrhosis/pregnancy).

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is histologically a {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are often associated with {{c1::trauma}} or pregnancy.
A common site for pyogenic granuloma in pregnant women is the {{c1::gingiva}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized by {{c1::rapid growth}} and easy bleeding.
Despite its name, pyogenic granuloma is not caused by {{c1::infection}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign, exophytic vascular nodule.
It frequently ulcerates and bleeds with minimal trauma.
Common on skin, lips, and gingiva.
Called 'granuloma gravidarum' when occurring in the gums of pregnant women.
Usually regresses or requires simple curettage.
microReview: Pyogenic Granuloma: Rapidly growing, bleeds easily, gingiva/skin, lobular capillary hemangioma.
examinerTraps: The name is a trap! It is NOT a granuloma (no epithelioid histiocytes) and NOT pyogenic (no pus).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease... Vascular Tumors... 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 1-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for a bright red, raised 'strawberry-like' lesion on the left cheek. The parents report it appeared shortly after birth and has increased slightly in size. What is the most likely natural history of this lesion?

options.d: Rapid expansion leading to Kasabach-Merritt syndrome

explanations.a: Capillary (strawberry) hemangiomas are common in newborns. They grow rapidly for a few months and then usually spontaneously involute (75-90% disappear by age 7).
explanations.b: Benign capillary hemangiomas do not transform into malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.c: Unlike 'port-wine stains' (nevus flammeus), strawberry hemangiomas do not persist; they typically involute.
explanations.d: Kasabach-Merritt syndrome (consumptive coagulopathy) is associated with Tufted Angioma or Kaposiform Hemangioendothelioma, not standard capillary hemangiomas.
explanations.e: Capillary hemangiomas do not 'turn into' cavernous hemangiomas; they are distinct entities based on vessel size.

ankiCards: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are histologically {{c1::capillary hemangiomas}}.
The expected clinical course of a strawberry hemangioma is {{c1::spontaneous involution}}.
By age 7, approximately {{c1::75-90%}} of juvenile hemangiomas have regressed.
Strawberry hemangiomas are usually present at {{c1::birth}} or appear shortly after.
The most common location for capillary hemangiomas is the {{c1::skin/face/scalp}}.
keyPoints: Strawberry hemangiomas are the most common vascular tumor of infancy.
They are characterized by a 'growth phase' followed by an 'involution phase'.
Histology: closely packed capillaries with thin linings.
Treatment is usually observation (conservative) due to high regression rate.
Propranolol is sometimes used if the lesion obstructs vision or vital functions.
microReview: Strawberry Hemangioma: Benign, infant, skin, capillary-sized vessels, spontaneously regresses.
examinerTraps: Contrast this with 'Port-wine stains' (Nevus flammeus), which do NOT regress and grow with the child.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An infant girl born at 38 weeks gestation is noted to have significant swelling of the posterior neck and a webbed appearance of the neck skin. Ultrasound reveals a large, multicystic mass in the soft tissues of the neck. This finding is highly associated with which of the following chromosomal abnormalities?

explanations.a: Cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) of the neck is a classic finding in Turner syndrome (45, X). It is caused by failure of the lymphatic system to communicate with the venous system.
explanations.b: While Down syndrome has neck findings (increased nuchal translucency), the classic 'cystic hygroma' association in a girl with webbed neck is Turner syndrome.
explanations.c: Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome) presents with rocker-bottom feet and clenched fists, not typically cystic hygromas.
explanations.d: Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome) presents with midline defects like holoprosencephaly and cleft lip, not cystic hygromas.
explanations.e: 47, XXY (Klinefelter syndrome) affects males and does not present with neonatal neck masses.

ankiCards: A cavernous lymphangioma found in the neck of an infant is called a {{c1::cystic hygroma}}.
Cystic hygromas are strongly associated with {{c1::Turner syndrome}} (and Trisomy 21).
Histologically, lymphangiomas are distinguished from hemangiomas by the {{c1::absence of RBCs}} in the lumen.
Cystic hygromas are composed of large, dilated {{c1::lymphatic}} spaces.
The 'webbed neck' in Turner syndrome is the result of a regressed {{c1::cystic hygroma}}.
keyPoints: Cystic hygromas are benign lymphatic malformations.
Most common in the neck or axilla of children.
Strong association with Turner Syndrome (45, X).
Margins are poor, making surgical resection difficult.
Histology: Large spaces lined by endothelium containing proteinaceous fluid (lymph).
microReview: Cystic Hygroma: Cavernous lymphangioma, neck mass, Turner Syndrome, no RBCs in vessels.
examinerTraps: Differentiate between 'Simple lymphangioma' (small vessels) and 'Cavernous lymphangioma' (large, cystic spaces/hygroma).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease... 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An HIV-positive patient presents with several red-to-purple skin nodules. A biopsy shows proliferation of capillaries with prominent 'epithelioid' endothelial cells, neutrophilic inflammation, and granular purple material on H&E stain. Warthin-Starry silver stain is positive. What is the causative organism?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts caused by Bartonella (B. henselae or B. quintana). It features neutrophils and silver-stain-positive bacteria.
explanations.b: HHV-8 causes Kaposi Sarcoma, which lacks neutrophils and bacterial clusters on silver stain.
explanations.c: S. aureus causes pyogenic infections/abscesses but not this specific angiomatous proliferation.
explanations.d: Toxoplasma causes brain abscesses or congenital infections but not skin vascular tumors.
explanations.e: Treponema causes syphilis; while primary syphilis has a chancre, it does not present as a vascular tumor with epithelioid endothelial cells.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by {{c1::Bartonella henselae}} or quintana.
The silver stain used to identify Bartonella is {{c1::Warthin-Starry}}.
Histology of bacillary angiomatosis shows {{c1::neutrophils}} and bacterial clusters.
Bacillary angiomatosis occurs primarily in {{c1::immunocompromised/AIDS}} patients.
Treatment for bacillary angiomatosis is usually {{c1::erythromycin}} (or clarithromycin).
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis clinically mimics Kaposi Sarcoma.
It is a bacterial infection, not a true neoplasm.
Neutrophilic infiltrate is a key histological clue distinguishing it from KS.
Bartonella henselae is also the cause of Cat Scratch Disease in immunocompetent hosts.
B. quintana is transmitted by lice ('trench fever').
microReview: Bacillary Angiomatosis: Bartonella, AIDS, silver stain (+), neutrophils, vascular papules.
examinerTraps: The presence of neutrophils is the 'dead giveaway' for Bacillary Angiomatosis over Kaposi Sarcoma.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease... 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following histopathologic features is the most reliable criterion for distinguishing a cavernous hemangioma from a cavernous lymphangioma?

options.a: Presence of red blood cells in the lumen
options.c: Presence of a smooth muscle coat

explanations.a: Hemangiomas contain red blood cells within their lumens, whereas lymphangiomas contain clear, proteinaceous fluid (lymph) and are typically devoid of red blood cells.
explanations.b: Both are lined by a single layer of flattened, benign endothelial cells; thickness is not a distinguishing factor.
explanations.c: Neither typically has a significant smooth muscle coat compared to normal arteries or veins.
explanations.d: Both 'cavernous' forms have large, dilated spaces; size does not distinguish the two.
explanations.e: Neither tumor is characteristically encapsulated; they both tend to be unencapsulated.

ankiCards: The primary histological difference between hemangioma and lymphangioma is {{c1::RBCs in the lumen}}.
Lymphangiomas contain {{c1::proteinaceous fluid (lymph)}} instead of blood.
Both hemangiomas and lymphangiomas are lined by {{c1::endothelial cells}}.
Cavernous hemangiomas of the {{c1::liver}} are the most common benign liver tumors.
Cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) usually lack a {{c1::capsule}}.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors are classified by their origin (blood vs. lymph).
Hemangiomas: blood-filled spaces.
Lymphangiomas: lymph-filled spaces.
Clinical context: Hemangiomas often appear red/purple; lymphangiomas are often skin-colored or transilluminating.
Both can be capillary (small) or cavernous (large).
microReview: Hemangioma (RBCs) vs. Lymphangioma (No RBCs, protein fluid).
examinerTraps: Don't be fooled by 'endothelial lining'—both have it! The lumen content is the key.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease... Benign Tumors... 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 70-year-old woman presents with several firm, violaceous nodules on her left arm. She has a history of a radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection and radiotherapy for breast cancer 12 years ago. Since the surgery, she has had chronic, massive lymphedema of the left arm. What is the most likely diagnosis of the new skin nodules?

explanations.a: This is Stewart-Treves syndrome: angiosarcoma arising in a limb with chronic lymphedema, classically following radical mastectomy.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and typically occurs in AIDS patients or specific ethnic groups; it is not specifically linked to chronic lymphedema post-mastectomy.
explanations.c: While breast cancer can metastasize to the skin, the history of 12 years of lymphedema and the appearance of 'violaceous nodules' strongly suggests a primary vascular malignancy.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious process in immunocompromised patients and doesn't fit the clinical timeline of chronic lymphedema.
explanations.e: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign, rapid-growing lesion often related to trauma, not chronic lymphedema.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in a limb with chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
The classic clinical scenario for Stewart-Treves is {{c1::post-mastectomy}} lymphedema.
Angiosarcoma after radiation usually occurs after a latent period of {{c1::several years (e.g., 5-10)}}.
Angiosarcoma of the skin often presents as {{c1::violaceous/purple nodules}}.
Angiosarcomas have a {{c1::poor}} 5-year survival rate.
keyPoints: Chronic lymphedema is a major risk factor for cutaneous angiosarcoma.
Commonly follows radical mastectomy with lymph node dissection.
The tumor is highly invasive and spreads locally and hematogenously.
Treatment involves radical surgery, but prognosis is dismal.
Radiation therapy is also a known independent risk factor for angiosarcoma.
microReview: Stewart-Treves Syndrome: Chronic lymphedema + Post-mastectomy = Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Wait for the history of chronic lymphedema! This is the specific trigger for the Stewart-Treves association.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease... Malignant Tumors... 522.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which vascular tumor is classified as 'intermediate-grade' (borderline) because it is locally aggressive but has a low metastatic potential compared to high-grade malignancies?

explanations.a: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor. It occurs around medium and large veins; cells are epithelioid but form small vascular channels.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangioma is a strictly benign tumor with no metastatic potential.
explanations.c: Glomus tumor is a strictly benign tumor of modified smooth muscle cells.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignant tumor with very high metastatic potential.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation, not a neoplasm.

ankiCards: The classic intermediate-grade (borderline) vascular tumor is {{c1::epithelioid hemangioendothelioma}}.
Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma cells have an {{c1::epithelioid (round/cuboidal)}} appearance.
Unlike angiosarcoma, epithelioid hemangioendothelioma has a {{c1::lower}} metastatic rate.
Hemangioendotheliomas often arise around {{c1::medium or large veins}}.
Vascular tumors are grouped into {{c1::benign, intermediate, and malignant}} categories.
keyPoints: Intermediate-grade tumors have behavior between benign hemangiomas and malignant angiosarcomas.
Kaposi Sarcoma is also considered an intermediate-grade tumor.
Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is the quintessential example of this grade.
They can be locally destructive.
Clinical outcomes are variable but generally better than angiosarcoma.
microReview: Intermediate Vascular Tumors: Hemangioendothelioma, Kaposi Sarcoma.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse 'Hemangioendothelioma' with 'Hemangioma' (benign) or 'Angiosarcoma' (malignant).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease... Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... 520.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 74-year-old male smoker with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia presents for a routine physical examination. A pulsatile, expansile mass is palpated in the epigastric region. Ultrasound reveals a 5.5 cm dilation of the aorta below the level of the renal arteries. Which of the following biological processes is primarily responsible for the structural failure of the vessel wall in this patient?

options.a: Increased production of Type I collagen
options.c: Excessive degradation of the extracellular matrix
options.d: Hypertrophy of the medial smooth muscle cells

explanations.a: Increased production of Type I collagen would typically strengthen the vessel wall; aneurysms involve a net loss of connective tissue.
explanations.b: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) are typically overexpressed in aneurysms, leading to tissue degradation; decreased activity would be protective.
explanations.c: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are characterized by an imbalance where matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) derived from inflammatory infiltrates degrade elastin and collagen, weakening the wall.
explanations.d: Smooth muscle cell loss, rather than hypertrophy, is a hallmark of the thinning media seen in advanced aneurysmal disease.
explanations.e: Endarteritis of the vasa vasorum is specifically associated with syphilitic (obliterative) aortitis, which usually involves the thoracic aorta.

ankiCards: The primary mechanism of wall weakening in abdominal aortic aneurysms is the {{c1::degradation of the extracellular matrix}}.
In AAA, inflammatory cells in the plaque release {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}} which digest elastin and collagen.
Risk factors for AAA include male sex, age, and {{c1::smoking/tobacco use}}.
True or False: A true aneurysm involves all three layers of the arterial wall (intima, media, adventitia). {{c1::True}}
The most common location for an atherosclerotic aneurysm is the {{c1::abdominal aorta}}.
keyPoints: AAA is usually related to atherosclerosis and occurs most frequently in male smokers over age 50.
Pathogenesis involves chronic inflammation and ECM degradation by MMPs.
Aneurysms are defined as a permanent localized dilation of a vessel.
The abdominal aorta below the renal arteries is the most frequent site.
The main clinical risks are rupture, thrombosis, and embolism.
microReview: Aneurysms represent a failure of vascular structural integrity. AAA is predominantly atherosclerotic, occurring below the renal arteries. TAA (Thoracic) is often associated with hypertension or genetic connective tissue disorders (Marfan). Dissection is a separate process where blood enters the media through an intimal tear.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the cause of AAA (Atherosclerosis) with the cause of Aortic Dissection (Hypertension). Also, remember that AAA occurs *below* the renal arteries, while Syphilitic aneurysms occur in the *arch/thoracic* aorta.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: ... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old male with long, slender fingers, pectus excavatum, and a history of ectopia lentis is found to have a dilated aortic root on echocardiography. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the FBN1 gene. Which of the following pathophysiological mechanisms most directly leads to the vascular weakening in this condition?

options.c: Accumulation of glycosaminoglycans in the intima
options.d: Ischemic necrosis of the outer media

explanations.a: Defective collagen cross-linking is seen in Ehlers-Danlos or scurvy, but Marfan syndrome (FBN1) involves fibrillin.
explanations.b: Fibrillin-1 normally sequesters TGF-beta; its deficiency in Marfan syndrome leads to excessive TGF-beta signaling, which triggers matrix degradation and medial weakening.
explanations.c: While 'cystic medial necrosis' involves GAG accumulation, it is a downstream histologic finding rather than the primary genetic mechanism.
explanations.d: Ischemic necrosis of the media is characteristic of hypertensive damage to the vasa vasorum, not the primary mechanism of Marfan syndrome.
explanations.e: LDL deposition describes atherosclerosis, which is not the primary driver of aneurysms in Marfan syndrome.

ankiCards: Marfan syndrome is caused by a mutation in the {{c1::FBN1 (Fibrillin-1)}} gene.
In Marfan syndrome, loss of fibrillin leads to increased signaling of {{c1::TGF-beta}}.
Increased TGF-beta in the aortic wall leads to the histological appearance of {{c1::cystic medial necrosis (degeneration)}}.
The classic cardiovascular complication of Marfan syndrome is {{c1::thoracic aortic aneurysm/dissection}}.
Fibrillin-1 is a major component of {{c1::microfibrils}} in the extracellular matrix.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome involves a mutation in Fibrillin-1 on chromosome 15.
Fibrillin-1 deficiency causes dysregulation of TGF-beta signaling.
Histology shows loss of smooth muscle cells and elastic fiber fragmentation (cystic medial necrosis).
Patients have high risk for aortic root dilation and Type A dissection.
Physical findings: Arachnodactyly, lens subluxation, and mitral valve prolapse.
microReview: Marfan syndrome = FBN1 mutation -> Excess TGF-beta -> Medial weakening -> Thoracic Aneurysm/Dissection. Contrast this with Loeys-Dietz syndrome, which involves mutations in TGF-beta receptors themselves.
examinerTraps: Students often pick 'defective fibrillin' as the only answer. Modern boards focus on the 'increased TGF-beta' signaling pathway as the therapeutic target and primary driver.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following descriptions best defines a 'false' aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm)?

options.a: A localized dilation involving the intima and media only
options.b: A tear in the intima allowing blood to track between the media and adventitia
options.c: A wall defect leading to an extravascular hematoma that communicates with the lumen
options.d: A congenital thinning of the media in the Circle of Willis
options.e: An outward bulging of all three layers of the arterial wall

explanations.a: Aneurysms are categorized as true (3 layers) or false (breach of wall); a 2-layer dilation is not a standard definition.
explanations.b: This describes an aortic dissection, which is not an aneurysm in the classical sense of vessel dilation.
explanations.c: A false aneurysm is a breach in the vascular wall leading to a hematoma that is contained by extravascular connective tissue and remains in communication with the vessel.
explanations.d: This describes a 'berry' aneurysm, which is a true aneurysm.
explanations.e: This is the definition of a 'true' aneurysm.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves an intact but attenuated arterial wall (all 3 layers).
A {{c1::false (pseudoaneurysm)}} involves a defect in the wall leading to a communicating hematoma.
The two main shapes of true aneurysms are {{c1::saccular}} and {{c1::fusiform}}.
A blood-filled space within the vessel wall itself is called a {{c1::dissection}}.
{{c1::Cystic medial necrosis}} refers to the histological loss of smooth muscle and elastic tissue in the media.
keyPoints: True Aneurysm: All 3 layers (Intima, Media, Adventitia) are intact but dilated.
False Aneurysm: Wall is breached; hematoma is contained by external tissue.
Saccular: Spherical outpouching involving only a portion of the wall.
Fusiform: Circumferential, long-segment dilation.
Aortic Dissection is NOT an aneurysm; it is blood tracking within the media.
microReview: Aneurysm = Dilation. True = 3 layers. False = Breach + Hematoma. Saccular = One side. Fusiform = Entire circumference.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse 'dissection' with 'false aneurysm'. A dissection tracks *between* layers; a pseudoaneurysm tracks *through* all layers into a pocket outside the vessel.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: What is the most common cause of an aneurysm located in the abdominal aorta?

explanations.a: Cystic medial degeneration is more commonly associated with thoracic aortic aneurysms and Marfan syndrome.
explanations.b: Trauma usually causes false aneurysms (pseudoaneurysms), not the standard AAA.
explanations.c: Syphilis typically involves the thoracic aorta and is now rare in developed nations.
explanations.d: Atherosclerosis is the overwhelmingly most common cause of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms.
explanations.e: Mycotic aneurysms are caused by infection of the wall (e.g., from bacterial endocarditis) and are much rarer than atherosclerotic ones.

ankiCards: The most common cause of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA) is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
AAA is usually found between the {{c1::renal arteries}} and the {{c1::aortic bifurcation}}.
The most common cause of Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm (TAA) is {{c1::hypertension}}.
The major modifiable risk factor for AAA development and rupture is {{c1::smoking}}.
The inflammatory infiltrate in AAA is dominated by {{c1::macrophages and T cells}}.
keyPoints: Atherosclerosis leads to AAA by compromising nutrient diffusion to the media.
AAA is primarily a disease of the abdominal aorta.
Smoking is the strongest environmental risk factor.
Men are affected more than women.
Pathology shows thinning of the media secondary to intimal plaque.
microReview: AAA = Atherosclerosis (Below renals). TAA = Hypertension (Ascending/Arch). Syphilis = Vasa vasorum (Arch). Berry = Circle of Willis.
examinerTraps: The examiner might try to trick you by listing 'hypertension'. While hypertension contributes to atherosclerosis, atherosclerosis is the direct histological driver for AAA.
sourceQuote: atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 52-year-old male presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset, 'tearing' chest pain that radiates to his back between the scapulae. His blood pressure is 190/110 mmHg. A chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum. Which of the following is the most likely underlying predisposing factor for this patient's condition?

explanations.a: Hypercholesterolemia leads to atherosclerosis and AAA, but is less strongly associated with acute aortic dissection than hypertension.
explanations.b: Hypertension is the most common risk factor for aortic dissection, as it causes hyaline arteriolosclerosis of the vasa vasorum, leading to medial ischemia.
explanations.c: IV drug use is a risk factor for mycotic aneurysms due to bacteremia, not typically tearing aortic dissection.
explanations.d: ADPKD is associated with berry aneurysms of the Circle of Willis, not typically thoracic dissection.
explanations.e: Ankylosing spondylitis can cause aortitis and aortic regurgitation, but is a rare cause of acute tearing dissection.

ankiCards: The classic symptom of aortic dissection is {{c1::tearing/ripping}} chest pain radiating to the back.
The most common predisposing factor for aortic dissection is {{c1::hypertension}}.
Aortic dissection involves blood tracking through the {{c1::media (middle layer)}} of the vessel.
A {{c1::widened mediastinum}} on chest X-ray is a classic finding for aortic dissection.
Type A dissections involve the {{c1::ascending aorta}} and require surgical emergency care.
keyPoints: Aortic dissection is NOT a 'true' aneurysm; it is a longitudinal tear.
Hypertension causes medial ischemia by damaging vasa vasorum.
Stanford Type A: Ascending aorta (Emergency).
Stanford Type B: Descending aorta only (Often managed medically).
The pain is typically maximal at onset, unlike the building pain of MI.
microReview: Sudden onset + Tearing pain + Back radiation + Hypertension = Aortic Dissection. Look for unequal blood pressures in the arms as a clinical clue.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'tearing' pain. If the question says 'pulsatile mass,' think AAA. If it says 'tearing pain,' think Dissection.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following biochemical changes is most characteristic of the 'cystic medial degeneration' seen in individuals with thoracic aortic aneurysms?

options.b: Loss of elastic fibers and accumulation of proteoglycans
options.c: Transmutation of smooth muscle cells to osteoblasts
options.d: Fibrinoid necrosis of the small penetrating arterioles

explanations.a: Calcium accumulation (Mönckeberg) is a feature of medial calcific sclerosis, not cystic medial degeneration.
explanations.b: Cystic medial degeneration (or necrosis) is characterized by the fragmentation of elastic tissue and the creation of 'cysts' filled with mucoid ground substance (proteoglycans).
explanations.c: Osteoblastic transmutation is a feature of vascular calcification in chronic kidney disease, not TAA.
explanations.d: Fibrinoid necrosis is characteristic of malignant hypertension and small vessel vasculitis.
explanations.e: Intimal myofibroblast proliferation is a feature of the 'response to injury' model and intimal thickening, not medial cystic changes.

ankiCards: {{c1::Cystic medial necrosis}} is the histological hallmark of non-inflammatory medial weakening.
In cystic medial necrosis, the 'cysts' are actually pools of {{c1::proteoglycans (glycosaminoglycans)}}.
Cystic medial necrosis is commonly seen in {{c1::Marfan syndrome}} and long-standing hypertension.
The result of cystic medial necrosis is the loss of {{c1::elastic fibers}} and smooth muscle cells.
Does 'cystic medial necrosis' actually involve true necrosis? {{c1::No (it is a misnomer)}}
keyPoints: Histology: Fragmentation of elastic lamellae.
Basophilic 'ground substance' (mucoid material) fills the gaps.
Associated with both genetic (Marfan) and hemodynamic (Hypertension) stress.
Leads to thoracic aortic aneurysms and predisposes to dissection.
The term 'necrosis' is technically incorrect as overt cell death is often absent.
microReview: Cystic Medial Necrosis: No cysts, no necrosis. Just loss of elastic fibers and increase in 'gunk' (proteoglycans).
examinerTraps: The name is a misnomer—there are no true cysts or widespread necrosis. Focus on the loss of elastic tissue.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 66-year-old male presents with hoarseness and a persistent cough. Physical examination is unremarkable except for a high-pitched 'brassy' cough. A chest CT scan reveals a 6 cm aneurysm of the aortic arch. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism for his hoarseness?

options.a: Compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve
options.b: Vagal nerve stimulation from aortic stretching
options.c: Ischemic injury to the vocal cords
options.d: Erosion of the aneurysm into the trachea

explanations.a: Aneurysms of the aortic arch can compress the left recurrent laryngeal nerve as it loops under the arch, leading to vocal cord paralysis and hoarseness (Ortner syndrome).
explanations.b: Vagal nerve stimulation usually causes bradycardia or GI symptoms, not focal vocal cord paralysis.
explanations.c: Vocal cord ischemia is not a feature of aortic aneurysms; the mechanism is mechanical compression.
explanations.d: Erosion into the trachea would cause hemoptysis, which is a late and often fatal complication, rather than isolated hoarseness.
explanations.e: Phrenic nerve compression would lead to diaphragmatic paralysis and dyspnea, not hoarseness.

ankiCards: Aortic arch aneurysms can cause hoarseness by compressing the {{c1::left recurrent laryngeal}} nerve.
Thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAA) can cause difficulty swallowing by compressing the {{c1::esophagus}}.
Chest pain in TAA is often due to {{c1::erosion into bone (ribs/vertebrae)}}.
TAA can cause respiratory distress by compressing the {{c1::trachea or mainstem bronchi}}.
The aortic valve may be affected by TAA, leading to {{c1::aortic insufficiency (regurgitation)}}.
keyPoints: TAA symptoms are often due to compression of mediastinal structures.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve compression = Hoarseness.
Esophageal compression = Dysphagia.
Tracheal compression = Dyspnea/Cough.
Dilation of the aortic root can lead to valvular incompetence.
microReview: Aneurysms cause trouble in two ways: 1) Rupture/Hemodynamic collapse, 2) Mass effect (compressing neighbors). Arch = Nerve. Root = Valve. Abdomen = Mass.
examinerTraps: Hoarseness in a smoker often makes you think of lung cancer (Pancoast tumor). However, in the setting of a 'widened mediastinum' or 'aortic arch mass,' always consider the recurrent laryngeal nerve and TAA.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the pathogenesis of atherosclerotic abdominal aortic aneurysms, how does the presence of an intimal plaque primarily lead to the weakening of the underlying media?

options.a: By increasing the pressure within the vasa vasorum
options.b: By increasing the diffusion distance for nutrients and oxygen
options.c: By secreting toxins that directly kill smooth muscle cells
options.d: By stimulating the proliferation of elastic fibers
options.e: By inducing a localized hypersensitivity reaction

explanations.a: Atherosclerosis usually narrows the lumens of the vasa vasorum or blocks them, it doesn't typically increase their internal pressure.
explanations.b: The media of the abdominal aorta relies on diffusion from the lumen for oxygen and nutrients. A thick atherosclerotic plaque increases the diffusion distance, leading to medial ischemia and atrophy.
explanations.c: While cytokines are present, the primary structural failure is due to metabolic starvation (ischemia) and subsequent enzymatic degradation.
explanations.d: Aneurysms are characterized by the loss and fragmentation of elastic fibers, not their proliferation.
explanations.e: While inflammation is involved, it is a chronic innate/adaptive immune response to lipids/damage, not a classical type I-IV hypersensitivity.

ankiCards: Atherosclerotic plaques cause medial weakening by {{c1::increasing diffusion distance}} for nutrients.
The abdominal aorta is susceptible to AAA because its media is {{c1::thicker/lacks vasa vasorum}} compared to other segments.
Ischemia of the media leads to the death of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}}.
Loss of smooth muscle cells leads to reduced synthesis of {{c1::collagen and elastin}}.
True or False: Atherosclerosis is the primary cause of aneurysms in the ascending aorta. {{c1::False (Hypertension/Marfan is more common there)}}
keyPoints: Plaques act as a physical barrier to diffusion.
The outer media suffers from nutrient deprivation.
Medial thinning follows smooth muscle cell loss.
Inflammatory cells in the plaque release proteases (MMPs).
Result: Structural integrity of the wall is lost.
microReview: Atherosclerosis -> Plaque -> No oxygen/food for media -> Media gets thin and weak -> Aorta balloons out.
examinerTraps: Students often assume the plaque 'eats' the wall. It’s more accurate to say the plaque 'starves' the wall of oxygen by increasing the distance it must travel from the blood.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 40-year-old female with a history of untreated syphilis presents with chest pain. Imaging shows an aneurysm of the ascending aorta with a 'tree-bark' appearance of the intimal surface. Which of the following pathological processes is responsible for this specific finding?

options.a: Severe calcification of the internal elastic lamina
options.b: Extensive atherosclerosis of the aortic arch
options.c: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.d: Cystic medial necrosis of the descending aorta
options.e: Fungal infection of the aortic wall

explanations.a: Internal elastic lamina calcification is more typical of Mönckeberg sclerosis, which does not produce a 'tree-bark' appearance.
explanations.b: Atherosclerosis causes irregular plaques and ulcers, not the diffuse, fine wrinkling of 'tree-barking'.
explanations.c: Tertiary syphilis causes obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum. This results in ischemic injury to the aortic media, leading to scarring and contraction that wrinkles the overlying intima ('tree-barking').
explanations.d: Cystic medial necrosis is associated with Marfan and HTN; it doesn't classically produce the 'tree-bark' intimal wrinkling of syphilis.
explanations.e: Fungal (mycotic) infections cause rapid destruction and localized saccular aneurysms, not diffuse tree-barking.

ankiCards: The 'tree-bark' appearance of the aorta is classic for {{c1::syphilitic (luetic) aortitis}}.
Syphilis targets the {{c1::vasa vasorum}} of the ascending aorta.
Inflammation of the vasa vasorum in syphilis is called {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}}.
Destruction of the media in syphilis often leads to dilation of the {{c1::aortic valve ring}}.
Syphilitic aneurysms occur in the {{c1::tertiary}} stage of the disease.
keyPoints: Syphilitic aortitis involves the ascending aorta and arch.
Pathology: 'Plasma cell-rich' infiltrate around vasa vasorum.
Ischemia leads to medial scarring and loss of elastic recoil.
Intimal wrinkling (tree-barking) is due to the contraction of medial scars.
Common complication: Aortic regurgitation and heart failure (cor bovinum).
microReview: Syphilis -> Endarteritis of vasa vasorum -> Medial ischemia -> Scars -> Scars shrink -> Intima wrinkles (Tree-bark).
examinerTraps: If you see 'plasma cells' and 'aorta' in the same sentence, the answer is almost certainly Syphilis.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 70-year-old male with a known 4 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm presents with sudden onset of blue, cold, and painful toes on both feet. His pedal pulses are palpable. What is the most likely mechanism for his toe symptoms?

options.d: Compression of the common iliac veins
options.e: Acute dissection extending to the iliac arteries

explanations.a: Rupture causes hypotension and severe back pain, not isolated distal digital ischemia (blue toe syndrome).
explanations.b: Aneurysms are characterized by turbulent flow and stagnant areas, leading to the formation of mural thrombi. These thrombi or atherosclerotic debris can embolize distally, causing 'blue toe syndrome'.
explanations.c: Infection (mycotic aneurysm) would cause fever and leukocytosis, not typically bilateral cold toes.
explanations.d: Venous compression would cause edema and swelling, not cold, cyanotic toes (which is an arterial problem).
explanations.e: Dissection typically causes severe pain and absent pulses if a limb is involved; palpable pulses with distal ischemia point toward microemboli.

ankiCards: The clinical term for distal ischemia caused by microemboli from an AAA is {{c1::blue toe syndrome}}.
Mural thrombus forms in aneurysms due to {{c1::stasis and turbulence}}.
A significant risk of AAA larger than 5 cm is {{c1::rupture}}.
The triad of AAA rupture is {{c1::hypotension, back pain, and pulsatile mass}}.
Which side do AAA usually rupture into? {{c1::Retroperitoneal space}}
keyPoints: Aneurysms promote thrombosis due to Virchow's triad (stasis/turbulence).
Mural thrombus can break off (embolism).
Emboli often land in small digital arteries (Blue Toe Syndrome).
Peripheral pulses may still be present because the main artery is patent.
This is a common clinical sign of an underlying aneurysm.
microReview: AAA + Blue Toes = Mural thrombus embolization. AAA + Sudden pain/Low BP = Rupture. AAA + Fever = Mycotic.
examinerTraps: Palpable pulses might lead you to think it's not arterial. However, microemboli (trash foot) leave the main artery open while clogging the tiny ones at the end.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism)
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the categorization of vascular neoplasms, which of the following is classified as an intermediate-grade (borderline) tumor according to the clinical behavior and histological features?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are considered benign vascular tumors, characterized by small, thin-walled capillaries.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is the classic example of an intermediate-grade vascular tumor, exhibiting behavior more aggressive than benign lesions but usually less lethal than angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant vascular tumor with a poor prognosis.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are benign, highly painful tumors arising from specialized smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign vascular proliferation caused by opportunistic infection with Bartonella species.

ankiCards: {{c1::Kaposi sarcoma}} is the prototype for intermediate-grade vascular tumors.
Vascular tumors are classified into {{c1::benign}}, {{c2::intermediate-grade (borderline)}}, and {{c3::malignant}} categories.
Angiosarcoma is classified as a {{c1::malignant}} vascular tumor.
Capillary hemangioma is classified as a {{c1::benign}} vascular tumor.
{{c1::Glomus tumor}} is a benign but painful tumor of smooth muscle-like cells.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors range from benign to highly malignant.
Intermediate tumors like Kaposi sarcoma are locally aggressive but have low metastatic potential compared to angiosarcoma.
Classification depends on vessel architecture and cellular atypia.
Benign tumors (e.g., hemangiomas) usually form well-defined vascular channels.
Malignant tumors (e.g., angiosarcomas) often show solid growth with minimal channel formation.
microReview: Benign: Hemangioma, Glomus tumor, Bacillary angiomatosis. Intermediate: Kaposi Sarcoma, Hemangioendothelioma. Malignant: Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Bacillary angiomatosis (infectious/benign) with Kaposi Sarcoma (viral/intermediate) despite similar clinical appearance in AIDS patients.
sourceQuote:
Vascular Tumors
Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... 518
Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... 520
Malignant Tumors... 522
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An immunohistochemical marker is requested to confirm the endothelial origin of a poorly differentiated soft tissue mass. Which of the following proteins would most specifically support a diagnosis of a vascular-derived tumor?

explanations.a: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial tissues and carcinomas.
explanations.b: Desmin is a marker for muscle tissue, both smooth and skeletal.
explanations.c: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a highly specific marker for endothelial cells and is used to identify vascular tumors like angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells, melanocytes, and Schwann cells.
explanations.e: Vimentin is a general marker for mesenchymal cells and is not specific enough for vascular endothelium.

ankiCards: The most specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial cells is {{c1::CD31}} (or von Willebrand factor).
CD31 is also known as {{c1::PECAM-1}}.
Angiosarcomas often express the endothelial marker {{c1::CD31}}.
Desmin is used to identify tumors of {{c1::muscle}} origin.
Cytokeratin is used to identify tumors of {{c1::epithelial}} origin.
keyPoints: CD31 (Platelet Endothelial Cell Adhesion Molecule) is a standard vascular marker.
Von Willebrand Factor (vWF) is another endothelial marker, though sometimes less sensitive than CD31.
Vascular tumors are mesenchymal in origin.
Poorly differentiated angiosarcomas may lack obvious vessels, requiring IHC for diagnosis.
CD34 is also expressed by endothelium but is less specific than CD31.
microReview: Endothelial markers: CD31, CD34, vWF. Epithelial: Cytokeratin. Muscle: Desmin/SMA. Neural: S100/NSE.
examinerTraps: Wait for CD31 or vWF; do not select CD34 if CD31 is an option, as CD34 is also expressed in many other mesenchymal tumors (e.g., DFSP).
sourceQuote: To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure and function.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old male presents with several enlarging, bruiselike, purple nodules on his scalp. He reports they have grown rapidly over the last 3 months and occasionally bleed. He has no history of HIV. Biopsy reveals anastomosing vascular channels lined by atypical, pleomorphic endothelial cells with frequent mitotic figures. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated vascular spaces and lack cellular atypia or frequent mitoses.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma typically involves the lower extremities or viscera and presents with spindle cells and slit-like spaces, often associated with HHV-8.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma in older adults often occurs on the scalp or face and is characterized by atypical endothelial cells and rapid growth.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a rapidly growing, pedunculated red nodule that often follows trauma and histologically resembles granulation tissue.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis presents in immunocompromised patients and shows neutrophils and bacterial clumps (Bartonella).

ankiCards: Cutaneous angiosarcoma in the elderly most commonly occurs on the {{c1::scalp}}.
Angiosarcoma is histologically characterized by {{c1::atypical/pleomorphic}} endothelial cells.
The clinical appearance of cutaneous angiosarcoma is often described as {{c1::bruiselike}} purple nodules.
Unlike hemangiomas, angiosarcomas show high {{c1::mitotic}} activity.
Angiosarcoma carries a {{c1::poor}} prognosis.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a malignant endothelial tumor.
Common sites: skin (scalp), soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Risk factors: radiation, chronic lymphedema, and chemical exposures (PVC).
Histology: poorly formed vascular channels with malignant cytology.
Aggressive behavior with high rate of metastasis.
microReview: Elderly + Scalp + Purple/Bruise lesion + Atypical Endothelium = Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: The 'bruiselike' appearance often leads to a delay in diagnosis, as it is mistaken for simple trauma in the elderly.
sourceQuote: Malignant Tumors... 522... Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction... Weakening of vessel walls.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old male with long-standing HIV infection (CD4+ count 120 cells/mm³) presents with multiple red-purple macules and plaques on his legs. Biopsy of a lesion shows spindle-shaped cells and slit-like spaces containing red blood cells. Which of the following pathogens is the primary etiologic agent of this condition?

explanations.a: HPV is associated with squamous cell carcinomas and warts, not vascular tumors.
explanations.b: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can look similar but has a different histologic profile (neutrophils/bacteria).
explanations.c: HHV-8, also known as Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent in all forms of Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.d: EBV is associated with lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
explanations.e: CMV is a common opportunistic infection in AIDS but does not cause Kaposi sarcoma.

ankiCards: The etiologic agent of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::HHV-8}}.
HHV-8 is also known as {{c1::KSHV}} (Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus).
Histology of Kaposi Sarcoma shows {{c1::spindle}} cells and slit-like spaces.
The slit-like spaces in Kaposi Sarcoma contain {{c1::red blood cells}}.
Kaposi Sarcoma is most common in patients with {{c1::HIV/AIDS}}.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
Four clinical types: Classic (older Mediterranean men), Endemic African, Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
HHV-8 infection is necessary but not sufficient for KS development.
Stages: Patch, Plaque, and Nodule.
IHC for HHV-8 LNA (latent nuclear antigen) is diagnostic.
microReview: AIDS + Purple Skin Lesions + Spindle Cells/Slits = Kaposi Sarcoma (HHV-8).
examinerTraps: Bartonella causes 'Bacillary Angiomatosis'—also in AIDS patients—but histology shows lobular proliferations with neutrophils, not spindle cell slits.
sourceQuote: Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... 520... Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 4-week-old female infant is brought to the pediatrician for a rapidly growing, bright red, raised lesion on her cheek. The lesion was not present at birth. The parents are concerned because it has doubled in size over the last two weeks. What is the most likely natural history of this lesion?

explanations.a: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are benign and do not undergo malignant transformation.
explanations.b: Juvenile hemangiomas typically grow rapidly for a few months (proliferative phase) and then slowly involute, with most regressing by age 7 to 9.
explanations.c: These lesions are known for their dynamic nature (growth then regression), not stability.
explanations.d: Capillary hemangiomas do not typically turn into cavernous hemangiomas; they are distinct types.
explanations.e: While rare 'infantile hemangiomatosis' can involve the liver, a single cutaneous lesion usually regresses locally.

ankiCards: The 'strawberry' hemangioma of infancy is also called a {{c1::juvenile}} hemangioma.
Juvenile hemangiomas usually {{c1::regress/involute}} spontaneously.
The typical age for complete regression of a juvenile hemangioma is by age {{c1::7}} to {{c2::9}}.
Histologically, juvenile hemangiomas are a subtype of {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma.
True or False: Juvenile hemangiomas are usually present at birth. {{c1::False}} (they appear shortly after birth).
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangiomas are extremely common in infants.
Clinical: 'Strawberry' appearance, bright red, lobulated.
Phases: Rapid growth (first few months) followed by slow involution.
Most disappear by early childhood without treatment.
Propranolol is sometimes used if the lesion obstructs vision or the airway.
microReview: Infant + Bright Red 'Strawberry' + Growth then Regression = Juvenile Hemangioma.
examinerTraps: The rapid growth can frighten parents into thinking it is malignant, but it is a benign 'tumor-like' proliferation.
sourceQuote: Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... 518... Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with an exquisitely painful, 5-mm subungual (under the fingernail) nodule. Which of the following cell types is the origin of this tumor?

explanations.a: While it is a vascular tumor, the primary cell of origin is not the endothelium but the surrounding support cells.
explanations.b: Pericytes are related but 'modified smooth muscle cells' is the specific description for glomus cells.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts are not the primary component of glomus tumors.
explanations.e: Lymphatic endothelium forms lymphangiomas, which are typically painless.

ankiCards: A glomus tumor is most commonly found in the {{c1::subungual}} (under nail) region.
The characteristic symptom of a glomus tumor is {{c1::exquisite pain}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells.
The glomus body is involved in the physiological process of {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Glomus tumors are {{c1::benign}} (benign/malignant).
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are small, benign, but very painful.
Location: Most common in distal digits, especially under nails.
Cells: Glomus cells are modified smooth muscle cells.
Function: They originate from the glomus body (AV shunt).
Treatment: Simple excision is curative.
microReview: Subungual + Exquisite Pain + Small Nodule = Glomus Tumor.
examinerTraps: Confusion with 'Glomus jugulare' or 'Glomus tympanicum' tumors, which are actually paragangliomas (neural crest origin), not vascular smooth muscle origin.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following environmental or chemical exposures is most strongly associated with the development of hepatic angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Asbestos is primarily associated with mesothelioma and lung cancer.
explanations.b: Vinyl chloride (used in the plastics industry) is a well-known carcinogen linked specifically to hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Aflatoxin B1 is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: Benzene is primarily linked to acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.e: Beryllium exposure causes berylliosis and is linked to lung cancer.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
{{c1::Arsenic}} is another chemical (pesticides) linked to hepatic angiosarcoma.
Vinyl chloride is used in the production of {{c1::polyvinyl chloride (PVC)}}.
{{c1::Thorotrast}} (an old radiocontrast agent) is a risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is a highly {{c1::malignant}} tumor.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is rare but highly associated with specific toxins.
Toxins include: Vinyl chloride, Arsenic, and Thorotrast.
The latency period between exposure and tumor development is often decades.
The tumor is aggressive and often fatal within a year of diagnosis.
It expresses endothelial markers like CD31.
microReview: Liver Angiosarcoma = Vinyl Chloride, Arsenic, Thorotrast.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Hepatic Angiosarcoma (Vinyl Chloride) with Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HBV/HCV/Aflatoxin).
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old woman who underwent a radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer 10 years ago presents with persistent lymphedema of her left arm. Recently, she noticed several firm, dark-blue cutaneous nodules on the lymphedematous limb. Biopsy confirms a malignant vascular tumor. What is the name of this clinical syndrome?

explanations.a: Sturge-Weber syndrome involves port-wine stains and leptomeningeal angiomas.
explanations.b: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) involves multiple small telangiectasias and AVMs.
explanations.c: Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to the development of angiosarcoma in the setting of chronic lymphedema (most commonly post-mastectomy).
explanations.d: Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome involves hemangioblastomas of the CNS and retina.
explanations.e: Kasabach-Merritt syndrome is characterized by large hemangiomas leading to platelet trapping and consumptive coagulopathy.

ankiCards: {{c1::Stewart-Treves}} syndrome is angiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphedema.
Chronic lymphedema after {{c1::mastectomy}} is the classic setup for Stewart-Treves syndrome.
The malignant tumor in Stewart-Treves syndrome is {{c1::angiosarcoma}}.
Sturge-Weber syndrome is associated with a {{c1::port-wine}} stain in the V1/V2 distribution.
{{c1::Kasabach-Merritt}} syndrome involves thrombocytopenia due to sequestration in a hemangioma.
keyPoints: Chronic lymphedema is a major risk factor for angiosarcoma.
Stewart-Treves syndrome occurs roughly 10 years after axillary dissection.
The lesions often start as bruise-like areas and progress to nodules.
Prognosis is poor even with radical amputation.
It highlights the role of impaired lymphatic drainage in local immune surveillance.
microReview: Post-Mastectomy + Lymphedema + Angiosarcoma = Stewart-Treves Syndrome.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'Chronic Lymphedema' as the trigger; if the question says 'Radiation', radiation-induced angiosarcoma is also a possibility, but Stewart-Treves is the specific name for the lymphedema association.
sourceQuote: Vascular Structure and Function... 485... Vascular Tumors... 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old pregnant woman presents with a rapidly growing, bleeding, 1-cm red pedunculated nodule on her gingiva. Histological examination shows a proliferation of capillaries with intermingled edema and inflammatory cells, resembling granulation tissue. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas are deeper, larger, and don't typically grow rapidly on the gingiva during pregnancy.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) often occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum) and grows rapidly.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor with marked atypia, not common on the gingiva of young patients.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are subungual and painful, not gingival.
explanations.e: Nevus flammeus is a flat 'birthmark' (port-wine stain), not a pedunculated nodule.

ankiCards: A pyogenic granuloma on the gingiva of a pregnant woman is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are histologically similar to {{c1::granulation tissue}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are often {{c1::pedunculated}} (attached by a stalk).
The most common symptom of a pyogenic granuloma (besides the mass) is {{c1::bleeding/ulceration}}.
True or False: Pyogenic granulomas are infectious in origin. {{c1::False}} (despite the name).
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer (it's neither pyogenic nor a granuloma).
It is a form of capillary hemangioma.
Commonly follows minor trauma or occurs during pregnancy.
Histology: Lobular arrangement of capillaries with inflammation.
Treatment is surgical excision; they can recur if not fully removed.
microReview: Pregnancy + Bleeding Gingival Nodule + Granulation-like tissue = Pyogenic Granuloma.
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic granuloma' is a trick; it is actually a vascular lesion, not an infection or a granulomatous process.
sourceQuote: Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... 518... Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In patients with AIDS, a vascular proliferation occurs that histologically demonstrates lobular clusters of infant-type capillaries, prominent neutrophils, and clusters of purple granular material (demonstrated as bacilli on silver stain). What is the causative organism?

explanations.a: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, which lacks neutrophils and bacterial clusters on silver stain.
explanations.b: Bartonella henselae (or Bartonella quintana) causes Bacillary Angiomatosis, which is characterized by neutrophil-rich vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts.
explanations.c: MAC causes systemic infection but not this specific vascular tumor-like lesion.
explanations.d: S. aureus causes abscesses, not organized vascular proliferations.
explanations.e: Toxoplasma causes CNS or ocular lesions, not cutaneous vascular lesions.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
The two species of Bartonella causing bacillary angiomatosis are {{c1::B. henselae}} and {{c2::B. quintana}}.
Histology of bacillary angiomatosis shows vascular proliferation with {{c1::neutrophils}} and bacteria.
The stain used to see Bartonella in bacillary angiomatosis is the {{c1::Warthin-Starry}} (silver) stain.
Bacillary angiomatosis is primarily seen in patients with {{c1::HIV/AIDS}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis is an opportunistic infection mimicking a vascular tumor.
B. henselae is typically transmitted by cats (cat-scratch disease in healthy hosts).
B. quintana is typically transmitted by human body lice.
Unlike KS, bacillary angiomatosis responds to antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin).
It can involve the skin, bone, or internal organs (peliosis hepatis).
microReview: AIDS + Vascular Lesion + Neutrophils + Warthin-Starry positive = Bacillary Angiomatosis.
examinerTraps: Bacillary angiomatosis and Kaposi sarcoma can look identical clinically. You must look for neutrophils/bacteria (BA) vs. spindle cells/slits (KS) on histology.
sourceQuote: VASCULAR TUMORS... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... 518... Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following fundamental mechanisms is primarily responsible for the development of aneurysmal dilation and potential rupture in the vascular wall?

explanations.a: Intimal thickening is a stereotyped response to injury that usually leads to stenosis, not dilation.
explanations.b: Weakening of the vessel wall is one of the two principal mechanisms underlying vascular disease that leads specifically to dilation (aneurysm) or rupture.
explanations.c: Endothelial activation is involved in recruitment of inflammatory cells but is not the primary structural failure mechanism for aneurysms.
explanations.d: This is a normal physiological function of elastic arteries, not a pathologic mechanism.
explanations.e: Hypertrophy, particularly of the media in hypertension, is a response to pressure but does not inherently define the weakening required for an aneurysm.

ankiCards: The two principal mechanisms underlying vascular disease are narrowing/obstruction and {{c1::weakening of vessel walls}}.
Vessel wall weakening primarily leads to {{c1::dilation (aneurysm)}} or rupture.
Vascular narrowing can be progressive, such as in {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Vascular narrowing can be precipitous, such as in {{c1::thrombosis or embolism}}.
The architectural difference between arteries and veins allows arteries to accommodate {{c1::pulsatile flow}}.
keyPoints: Vascular disease morbidity and mortality is higher than any other category.
Two main pathologies: stenosis/obstruction and wall weakening.
Weakening of walls leads to aneurysms.
Dilation is a result of structural integrity failure.
Atherosclerosis and hypertension are major contributors to wall weakening.
microReview: Vascular pathology is driven by either luminal obstruction or structural failure of the wall. Aneurysms fall under the latter, where the media is compromised, leading to permanent dilation.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse intimal thickening (which narrows the lumen) with medial weakening (which widens the vessel).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male with a 40 pack-year smoking history is diagnosed with an abdominal aortic aneurysm. The pathogenesis involves the degradation of the extracellular matrix. Which of the following protein families is most directly responsible for the destruction of elastic fibers in the aortic media in this patient?

explanations.a: Caspases are involved in apoptosis, which may play a minor role, but the primary matrix destruction is enzymatic.
explanations.b: Selectins are adhesion molecules involved in leukocyte rolling.
explanations.c: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), produced by macrophages and smooth muscle cells, are the primary enzymes that degrade elastin and collagen in aneurysmal walls.
explanations.d: cGMP is a secondary messenger for vasodilation, not a structural enzyme.
explanations.e: PDGF is involved in smooth muscle cell migration and intimal thickening, not matrix degradation.

ankiCards: The degradation of the extracellular matrix in aneurysms is primarily mediated by {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
In abdominal aortic aneurysms, the inflammatory infiltrate typically produces enzymes that degrade {{c1::elastin and collagen}}.
The most significant modifiable risk factor for abdominal aortic aneurysm is {{c1::smoking}}.
Aneurysms in the abdominal aorta are most commonly located below the {{c1::renal arteries}}.
Loss of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} in the media contributes to the weakening of the aortic wall.
keyPoints: MMPs are central to the pathogenesis of aneurysms.
Chronic inflammation leads to connective tissue remodeling.
Elastin degradation is a hallmark of medial weakening.
Smoking increases MMP expression and decreases tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs).
Most AAAs are associated with atherosclerosis.
microReview: AAA is a balance of matrix synthesis and degradation. In aneurysms, increased MMP activity (often from macrophages) outweighs TIMP activity, leading to destruction of the structural elastin/collagen framework.
examinerTraps: Be careful not to select 'Selectins' or other inflammatory markers that recruit cells; the question asks for the protein family 'directly responsible for destruction'.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old man presents with a deep, boring pain in his abdomen that radiates to the lower back. Physical examination reveals a large, pulsatile mid-abdominal mass. Imaging confirms an aneurysm of the abdominal aorta. Which of the following is the most likely location of this lesion relative to other vascular structures?

options.a: Between the diaphragm and the celiac artery
options.b: Superior to the origin of the renal arteries
options.c: Inferior to the renal arteries and superior to the iliac bifurcation
options.d: Within the common iliac arteries exclusively
options.e: In the ascending portion of the aortic arch

explanations.a: This is a rare location for an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA); most are infrarenal.
explanations.b: Suprarenal AAAs are much less common than infrarenal ones.
explanations.c: The vast majority of abdominal aortic aneurysms occur between the renal arteries and the bifurcation of the aorta.
explanations.d: While AAAs can extend into the iliacs, they do not originate exclusively there in the context of a mid-abdominal mass.
explanations.e: This describes a thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA), not an abdominal one.

ankiCards: The most common site for an atherosclerotic aneurysm is the {{c1::abdominal aorta}}.
Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAAs) are usually located {{c1::below/infrarenal}} the renal arteries.
A pulsatile abdominal mass is a classic clinical finding for {{c1::abdominal aortic aneurysm}}.
The two most important causes of aortic aneurysms are {{c1::atherosclerosis}} and {{c2::hypertension}}.
The risk of rupture of an AAA is directly related to its {{c1::diameter}}.
keyPoints: AAAs are most common in men and smokers.
Location is typically infrarenal.
Presentation can be asymptomatic or include abdominal/back pain.
Atherosclerosis is the dominant predisposing factor for AAA.
Bifurcation of the aorta is the distal limit for most AAAs.
microReview: AAA: 60+ male, smoker, infrarenal, atherosclerotic. If it's suprarenal, think of other etiologies or genetic syndromes, though atherosclerosis can still be involved.
examinerTraps: The most common location is specifically *below* the renal arteries, which is a high-yield 'always' or 'usually' in board exams.
sourceQuote: Aneurysms and Dissection... many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old male is evaluated for tall stature, long fingers (arachnodactyly), and high-arched palate. He is found to have a dilation of the ascending aorta. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in a gene encoding a glycoprotein that acts as a scaffold for elastin. Defective signaling of which of the following cytokines is most implicated in this patient's vascular pathology?

explanations.a: TNF is a pro-inflammatory cytokine but not the primary driver of Marfan-related aortic disease.
explanations.b: IL-1 is involved in acute inflammation.
explanations.c: In Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1 mutation), there is increased TGF-β signaling, which contributes to the weakening of the aortic wall by inducing metalloproteinase activity and reducing matrix integrity.
explanations.d: IFN-γ is involved in macrophage activation in atherosclerosis and vasculitis.
explanations.e: VEGF is involved in angiogenesis, not the structural breakdown of the aortic media.

ankiCards: Marfan syndrome is caused by mutations in the {{c1::FBN1 (Fibrillin-1)}} gene.
Defective fibrillin leads to excessive signaling of {{c1::TGF-β}} in the vessel wall.
Excessive TGF-β signaling in Marfan syndrome leads to {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
Thoracic aortic aneurysms are most commonly associated with {{c1::hypertension}} and genetic syndromes like Marfan.
Loeys-Dietz syndrome is caused by mutations in {{c1::TGF-β receptors}}.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome: Fibrillin-1 mutation.
TGF-β overactivity is the secondary pathogenic mechanism.
Leads to thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAA).
Histology: Cystic medial degeneration (loss of SMCs and elastic fibers).
Clinically: Arachnodactyly, lens luxation, aortic root dilation.
microReview: TAA in a young person = Genetic (Marfan/Loeys-Dietz). TAA in an older person = Hypertension. AAA = Atherosclerosis. Syphilitic Aneurysm = Vasa Vasorum destruction.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'TGF-beta'—it's the common pathway in several genetic aortic syndromes (Marfan, Loeys-Dietz).
sourceQuote: Aneurysms and Dissection... Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm... Aortic Dissection
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old woman with a history of poorly controlled hypertension presents with sudden onset 'tearing' chest pain that radiates to her back. Blood pressure is 180/110 mmHg. A CT scan shows an intimal tear in the ascending aorta with blood entering the media. Which of the following is the most likely underlying histologic finding in the aortic wall?

explanations.a: Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis involves calcification of the media but does not predispose to dissection.
explanations.b: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum is seen in tertiary syphilis.
explanations.c: Cystic medial degeneration (or 'medial mucoid degeneration') is the most common predisposing histologic change in the aorta that leads to dissection, characterized by elastic fiber fragmentation and accumulation of proteoglycans.
explanations.d: Granulomatous inflammation is characteristic of Giant Cell or Takayasu arteritis.
explanations.e: Fibrinoid necrosis is typical of malignant hypertension in small arterioles, not the large aorta.

ankiCards: The most common risk factor for aortic dissection is {{c1::hypertension}}.
The classic clinical presentation of aortic dissection is {{c1::sudden, tearing/ripping chest pain}}.
Histologically, aortic dissection is associated with {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
Aortic dissection involves blood tracking into the {{c1::media}} of the vessel.
Stanford type A dissections involve the {{c1::ascending aorta}}.
keyPoints: Aortic dissection is not a 'true' aneurysm but often associated with similar wall weakness.
Hypertension causes hyaline arteriolosclerosis of vasa vasorum, leading to medial ischemia.
Cystic medial degeneration: loss of elastic tissue, 'cysts' filled with mucoid material.
Tearing pain radiating to the back is the pathognomonic symptom.
Type A is a surgical emergency; Type B can often be managed medically.
microReview: Dissection: Hypertension -> Vasa vasorum narrowing -> Medial ischemia -> Cystic medial degeneration -> Intimal tear -> Media cleavage by high-pressure blood.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'Aneurysm' with 'Dissection'. Aneurysms are dilations; dissections are 'tunnels' within the wall. However, they share the 'wall weakening' mechanism.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following defines a 'false aneurysm' (pseudoaneurysm)?

options.a: Dilation involving all three layers of the arterial wall
options.b: A localized spherical outpouching of the wall
options.c: A wall defect leading to an extravascular hematoma that communicates with the intravascular space
options.d: A longitudinal tear in the media allowing blood to form a second channel
options.e: A circumferential dilation of the entire vessel segment

explanations.a: This describes a 'true' aneurysm.
explanations.b: This describes a 'saccular' aneurysm, which is a type of true aneurysm.
explanations.c: A false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) is a breach in the vascular wall leading to an extravascular hematoma that freely communicates with the intravascular space ('pulsating hematoma').
explanations.d: This describes an aortic dissection.
explanations.e: This describes a 'fusiform' aneurysm, which is a type of true aneurysm.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true aneurysm}} involves all three layers of the vessel wall (intima, media, adventitia).
A {{c1::false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm)}} is an extravascular hematoma communicating with the vessel.
Saccular aneurysms are {{c1::spherical}} outpouchings.
Fusiform aneurysms are {{c1::circumferential}} dilations.
A classic cause of a pseudoaneurysm is a {{c1::femoral artery catheterization}} complication.
keyPoints: True aneurysm: intact but thinned wall (all layers).
False aneurysm: wall is breached; contained by perivascular tissue.
Dissection: blood enters the wall itself.
AAA and Berry aneurysms are 'true' aneurysms.
Pseudoaneurysm is often traumatic or post-procedural.
microReview: True = 3 layers. False = 0 layers (just a hole and a clot). Dissection = between layers.
examinerTraps: Careful with 'saccular' vs 'false'. Saccular is still a true aneurysm because the wall is intact.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the context of vascular structure and function, why does atherosclerosis preferentially affect elastic and muscular arteries rather than veins?

options.b: Veins have higher wall thickness-to-lumen ratios
options.c: Arteries are subjected to higher pulsatile pressures and shear stress
options.d: Arteries contain more valves that trap cholesterol
options.e: Veins lack smooth muscle cells in their media

explanations.a: Veins have an intima; it is simply thinner than in arteries.
explanations.b: Arteries have a higher ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter compared to veins.
explanations.c: Arterial walls are thicker to accommodate higher blood pressures and pulsatile flow; this mechanical stress contributes to the endothelial injury that initiates atherosclerosis.
explanations.d: Veins have valves, but they do not trap cholesterol to cause atherosclerosis.
explanations.e: Veins contain smooth muscle cells, though the media is much less organized than in arteries.

ankiCards: Atherosclerosis affects mainly {{c1::elastic and muscular arteries}}.
Arterial walls are thicker than veins to accommodate {{c1::pulsatile flow}}.
The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter is higher in {{c1::arteries}}.
Arterial muscular vessels exert control over {{c1::blood flow and pressure}}.
Structural specializations of vessels reflect their distinct {{c1::functional roles}}.
