keyPoints: Arteries handle high pressure; veins handle high volume.
Mechanical stress is a key driver of arterial pathology.
Atherosclerosis is an arterial disease.
Arterial media is thicker to withstand systole.
Vessel architecture determines the distribution of disease.
microReview: Robbins emphasizes that structure reflects function. The thick, muscular/elastic walls of arteries are necessary for high pressure but also make them targets for atherosclerosis and subsequent aneurysmal weakening.
examinerTraps: A common distractor is saying veins 'lack' a layer. They have the same layers, just in different proportions.
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures. ... atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 50-year-old male with untreated HIV and a history of syphilis presents with a barking cough and difficulty swallowing. Imaging reveals an aneurysm of the ascending aortic arch. Pathological examination of the aorta would most likely show which of the following?

options.b: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.c: Giant cell granulomas in the media
options.d: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis of the renal vessels
options.e: Fatty streaks within the thoracic aorta

explanations.a: Egg-shell calcification is more characteristic of silicosis (lymph nodes) or advanced atherosclerosis (but not specific to syphilis).
explanations.b: Tertiary syphilis causes obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum, leading to ischemic injury of the aortic media and 'tree-bark' appearance (syphilitic aortitis).
explanations.c: Giant cell granulomas are seen in Giant Cell Arteritis, not typically syphilis.
explanations.d: This is a feature of benign hypertension.
explanations.e: Fatty streaks are the earliest lesions of atherosclerosis, not the cause of syphilitic aneurysms.

ankiCards: Syphilitic aneurysms typically involve the {{c1::ascending aorta / arch}}.
The underlying mechanism of syphilitic aortitis is {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}} of the vasa vasorum.
Medial ischemia in syphilis leads to a {{c1::tree-bark}} appearance of the intima.
Aneurysms of the aortic arch can cause {{c1::respiratory distress}} or difficulty swallowing due to compression.
The vasa vasorum are the {{c1::vessels of the vessels}} that supply the outer media.
keyPoints: Syphilis = Ascending aorta (AAA is usually atherosclerosis).
Mechanism: Ischemia of the media.
Histology: Plasma cell-rich infiltrate around vasa vasorum.
Gross: Tree-barking due to scarred intima.
Clinical: Can lead to aortic valve insufficiency.
microReview: Syphilis attacks the vasa vasorum. No blood to the media -> Media dies -> Wall weakens -> Aneurysm forms in the high-pressure thoracic region.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the location; Syphilis = Thoracic (ascending). Atherosclerosis = Abdominal (infrarenal).
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the 'mycotic aneurysm'?

options.a: An aneurysm caused by a fungal infection exclusively
options.b: An aneurysm resulting from the weakening of the wall by a bacterial infection
options.c: A dilation resulting from a congenital medial defect
options.e: An aneurysm occurring in the setting of IgG4-related disease

explanations.a: Despite the name 'mycotic', most are actually bacterial (e.g., from endocarditis).
explanations.b: A mycotic aneurysm refers to an infection in the wall of an artery, leading to its weakening and dilation. Most are bacterial.
explanations.c: This describes a 'berry' aneurysm (though their exact congenital nature is debated).
explanations.d: This is a false aneurysm.
explanations.e: This describes 'inflammatory AAA'.

ankiCards: A {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm is caused by infection of the arterial wall.
The most common source of infection for a mycotic aneurysm is {{c1::infective endocarditis}} (septic emboli).
Mycotic aneurysms are most often caused by {{c1::bacteria}} rather than fungi.
Infection weakens the wall by inducing {{c1::suppurative inflammation}} and tissue destruction.
Mycotic aneurysms can lead to rapid {{c1::rupture}} and sepsis.
keyPoints: Mycotic = Infectious (usually bacterial).
Sources: Embolization (endocarditis), extension of adjacent abscess, or direct seeding.
Results in wall destruction.
Emergency due to risk of rupture and systemic infection.
Can occur in any artery.
microReview: Don't let the name 'mycotic' fool you; it's a historical term. Think 'Infected Aneurysm'. Bacteria eat the wall, wall blows out.
examinerTraps: Trap: 'Mycotic means fungal'. In pathology, it usually refers to any infected aneurysm.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 64-year-old male with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia presents with sudden, severe abdominal pain and hypotension. On examination, he is diaphoretic and has a rigid abdomen. If his condition is due to the rupture of an abdominal aortic aneurysm, which of the following is the most likely diameter of the aneurysm prior to rupture?

explanations.a: Aneurysms less than 4 cm have a near-zero risk of rupture.
explanations.b: Aneurysms between 3-4 cm are monitored but rarely rupture.
explanations.c: Risk begins to increase but is still relatively low (1% per year).
explanations.d: The risk of rupture increases significantly once the diameter exceeds 5 to 6 cm, making this the threshold for surgical intervention.
explanations.e: This is not even considered an aneurysm (dilation must be >50% of normal diameter).

ankiCards: The risk of AAA rupture is minimal if the diameter is less than {{c1::4}} cm.
Surgical intervention for AAA is generally recommended when the diameter reaches {{c1::5 or 5.5}} cm.
The clinical triad of AAA rupture is {{c1::abdominal/back pain}}, {{c2::hypotension}}, and a {{c3::pulsatile mass}}.
Mortality for AAA rupture and emergency surgery is approximately {{c1::50}}%.
AAA rupture usually occurs into the {{c1::retroperitoneum}} or peritoneal cavity.
keyPoints: Size is the best predictor of rupture risk.
Growth rate > 0.5 cm in 6 months is also a red flag.
Rupture is a surgical emergency.
Screening is recommended for male smokers over 65.
Hypertension and smoking are the key drivers of expansion.
microReview: AAA management: < 5 cm = Watch and wait (control BP/stop smoking). > 5.5 cm = Operate (Endovascular or Open repair).
examinerTraps: Remember 5 cm is the magic number for 'dangerous'. Below that, the risk of surgery often outweighs the risk of rupture.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male presents with a large, ill-defined, violaceous plaque on his scalp that has been slowly enlarging over the past four months. He initially thought it was a bruise from a minor head injury, but the area began to ulcerate and bleed. Biopsy of the lesion reveals highly pleomorphic endothelial cells forming irregular, anastomosing vascular channels that dissect through the dermal collagen. Which of the following immunohistochemical markers would most specifically confirm the lineage of these neoplastic cells?

explanations.a: Cytokeratin 7 is a marker for epithelial cells and carcinomas, not vascular tumors.
explanations.b: CD31 (platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule) is a highly specific marker for endothelial cells and is used to identify vascular tumors like angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (smooth and skeletal), not endothelial cells.
explanations.d: S100 is used to identify neural crest-derived cells, such as melanocytes or Schwann cells.
explanations.e: HMB-45 is a marker for melanoma, which can present as a dark cutaneous lesion but lacks vascular channel formation.

ankiCards: Cutaneous angiosarcoma in the elderly most commonly occurs on the {{c1::scalp}}.
The most specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial differentiation is {{c1::CD31}}.
Angiosarcomas are characterized histologically by {{c1::anastomosing vascular channels}} lined by atypical cells.
Unlike benign hemangiomas, angiosarcomas exhibit significant {{c1::cellular pleomorphism}} and mitotic activity.
Risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma include exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}} or arsenic.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor of endothelial cells.
Cutaneous angiosarcoma frequently affects the face and scalp of elderly individuals.
Histology shows irregular vascular spaces lined by atypical, pleomorphic endothelial cells.
Vascular markers like CD31 and von Willebrand factor (vWF) are diagnostic.
Aggressive behavior with poor prognosis is characteristic of these tumors.
microReview: Vascular tumors are categorized as benign (hemangioma), intermediate (Kaposi sarcoma), or malignant (angiosarcoma). Angiosarcomas are identified by atypical endothelial cells and markers such as CD31.
examinerTraps: A common trap is mistaking a scalp angiosarcoma for a simple bruise (ecchymosis) in an elderly patient due to its initial appearance.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors... Malignant Tumors... Angiosarcoma... CD31 (platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule) and von Willebrand factor (vWF) are commonly used as markers of endothelial cell differentiation.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old male with a history of untreated HIV infection presents with multiple reddish-purple macules and plaques on his lower extremities and oral mucosa. Histological examination shows spindle-shaped cells, slit-like vascular spaces containing red blood cells, and prominent inflammatory infiltrates. The pathogenesis of this condition is primarily linked to which of the following agents?

explanations.a: HPV-16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas, not vascular tumors.
explanations.b: EBV is associated with lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
explanations.c: HHV-8 (also known as KSHV) is the causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma, which presents as spindle-cell vascular tumors in immunocompromised patients.
explanations.d: CMV causes retinitis or colitis in AIDS patients but not vascular tumors.
explanations.e: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which mimics Kaposi sarcoma clinically but is bacterial in origin and lacks the characteristic spindle cells.

ankiCards: The causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}.
The histological hallmark of Kaposi Sarcoma includes {{c1::slit-like}} vascular spaces.
Kaposi Sarcoma is classified as an {{c1::intermediate}}-grade (borderline) vascular tumor.
In AIDS patients, Kaposi Sarcoma is an {{c1::AIDS-defining}} illness.
Unlike angiosarcomas, Kaposi Sarcoma is driven by {{c1::viral-encoded}} oncogenes.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is an intermediate-grade neoplasm caused by HHV-8.
Four clinical variants exist: Classic (elderly Mediterranean), Endemic (African), Iatrogenic (transplant), and AIDS-associated.
Histology: Spindle cells, extravasated RBCs, and slit-like vascular spaces.
Most common sites include skin, lymph nodes, and GI tract.
Highly sensitive to antiretroviral therapy in HIV patients.
microReview: HHV-8 infects endothelial cells, leading to the development of Kaposi sarcoma, characterized by spindle cells and slit-like spaces. This is distinct from Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella), which shows neutrophils.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse KS with Bacillary Angiomatosis; while both present with red/purple nodules in HIV, KS has spindle cells and slit-like spaces, while Bacillary Angiomatosis has neutrophilic inflammation and Bartonella organisms.
sourceQuote: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV8) and is the most common neoplasm in patients with AIDS.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 25-year-old female presents with an extremely painful, 4-mm, firm, red-blue nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. The pain is particularly exacerbated by exposure to cold. Histological examination reveals a tumor composed of specialized smooth muscle cells surrounding vascular channels. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are painless and usually occur in the skin of infants.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, highly painful tumors arising from the glomus body (a thermoregulatory structure) and are characteristically subungual.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas are larger, deep-seated vascular masses that are usually not painful.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation in immunocompromised patients.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor that is usually larger, infiltrative, and occurs in older adults.

ankiCards: A painful subungual red-blue nodule is characteristic of a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
Glomus tumors arise from specialized smooth muscle cells of the {{c1::glomus body}}.
The glomus body's physiological function is {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors consist of nests of uniform cells surrounding {{c1::vascular channels}}.
Pain in a glomus tumor is often triggered by {{c1::cold}} exposure.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but extremely painful.
Classically located in the subungual region (under the fingernail).
Arise from glomus bodies involved in thermoregulation.
Histology: Small, uniform cells (glomus cells) resembling smooth muscle.
Treatment is simple surgical excision.
microReview: Painful subungual tumor = Glomus tumor. Derived from smooth muscle cells involved in temperature control. Distinct from hemangiomas which are generally painless.
examinerTraps: Wait for the keyword 'painful' and 'subungual'. Hemangiomas are almost never described as exquisitely painful or sensitive to cold.
sourceQuote: Glomus Tumor (Glomangioma) is a benign, exquisitely painful tumor arising from specialized smooth muscle cells of the glomus bodies, arteriovenous structures involved in thermoregulation.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 3-week-old infant is brought to the pediatrician due to a bright red, raised 'strawberry-like' lesion on the chest that has appeared since birth. The mother is concerned as it seems to be growing slightly. The physician reassures her that the lesion will likely enlarge for a few months and then regress spontaneously by age seven. Which of the following describes the most likely histology of this lesion?

options.a: Large, dilated vascular spaces filled with blood and separated by connective tissue
options.b: Nests of uniform cells surrounding thermoregulatory vascular bodies
options.c: Thin-walled capillaries with scant stroma, lined by a single layer of endothelial cells
options.d: Proliferation of spindle cells with slit-like spaces and extravasated erythrocytes
options.e: Atypical endothelial cells forming irregular channels dissecting through collagen

explanations.a: This describes cavernous hemangiomas, which do not typically regress spontaneously.
explanations.b: This describes a glomus tumor, which is painful and subungual.
explanations.c: This describes a capillary hemangioma (strawberry hemangioma), the most common vascular tumor of infancy.
explanations.d: This describes Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.e: This describes angiosarcoma.

ankiCards: The common name for a juvenile capillary hemangioma is a {{c1::strawberry}} hemangioma.
Juvenile capillary hemangiomas typically {{c1::regress}} spontaneously by early childhood.
Histology of a capillary hemangioma shows {{c1::thin-walled capillaries}} lined by a single layer of endothelium.
Capillary hemangiomas are the most common vascular tumors of {{c1::infancy}}.
True or False: Strawberry hemangiomas usually require aggressive surgical excision. {{c1::False}}
keyPoints: Capillary hemangiomas are the most common benign vascular tumors.
Juvenile (strawberry) type occurs in 1 in 200 births.
They grow rapidly for a few months and then involute (75% by age 7).
Histology: Closely packed capillaries with thin walls.
Common locations: Skin, subcutaneous tissues, and mucous membranes.
microReview: Strawberry hemangioma = Capillary hemangioma of infancy. Natural history: growth followed by spontaneous regression. Histology: simple capillaries.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse capillary hemangiomas with 'port-wine stains' (Nevus flammeus). Port-wine stains are malformations that grow with the child and do not regress.
sourceQuote: Capillary hemangiomas are the most common type... Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) of the newborn skin are very common (1 in 200 births)... they nearly always regress by age 7.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old factory worker who spent 30 years in the manufacturing of polyvinyl chloride (PVC) presents with abdominal pain, weight loss, and jaundice. Imaging reveals multiple masses in the liver. A biopsy confirms a high-grade malignant vascular neoplasm. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Hepatocellular carcinoma is associated with HBV/HCV and cirrhosis, not specifically PVC.
explanations.b: Hepatic adenoma is associated with oral contraceptive use.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma of the liver is specifically associated with environmental toxins like vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor and is not associated with PVC.
explanations.e: Cholangiocarcinoma is associated with Liver Flukes and PSC, not PVC.

ankiCards: Vinyl chloride exposure is a major risk factor for hepatic {{c1::angiosarcoma}}.
Besides vinyl chloride, exposure to {{c1::arsenic}} can cause liver angiosarcoma.
Angiosarcoma is a {{c1::malignant}} neoplasm of endothelial cells.
The radioactive contrast agent formerly linked to liver angiosarcoma is {{c1::Thorotrast}}.
Liver angiosarcomas carry a very {{c1::poor}} prognosis.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare but highly aggressive malignancy.
Classic associations include Vinyl Chloride, Arsenic, and Thorotrast.
Toxins are absorbed and metabolized in the liver, leading to DNA damage in endothelial cells.
Latent period between exposure and tumor development is often decades.
Tumors are often multicentric and hemorrhagic.
microReview: PVC worker + Liver Mass + Vascular histology = Angiosarcoma. This is a classic 'occupational' cancer link in pathology.
examinerTraps: Be careful not to select Hepatocellular carcinoma just because the patient has liver masses; the PVC exposure is the 'buzzword' for angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with distinct environmental carcinogens, including arsenic... and polyvinyl chloride (PVC).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 1-year-old female with features of Turner syndrome (45,XO) is found to have a large, fluctuant, ill-defined mass in the left axilla. Imaging shows a multicystic lesion. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cystic hygromas (cavernous lymphangiomas) are common in the neck or axilla of children and are classically associated with Turner syndrome.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas are solid red masses, not large multicystic lymphatic lesions.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are small, painful subungual lesions.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a rapidly growing red nodule, often post-traumatic.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor found in older adults.

ankiCards: Cystic hygroma is another name for a {{c1::cavernous lymphangioma}}.
Cystic hygromas are characteristically associated with {{c1::Turner}} syndrome.
The most common locations for cystic hygromas are the {{c1::neck}} and axilla.
Histologically, cystic hygromas contain dilated spaces filled with {{c1::lymph}} fluid.
Cystic hygromas lack a clear {{c1::capsule}}, making surgical excision difficult.
keyPoints: Cystic hygromas are benign lymphatic malformations.
Commonly found in the neck or axilla of infants.
Strong association with chromosomal abnormalities like Turner syndrome and Down syndrome.
Composed of large, dilated lymphatic spaces lined by endothelial cells.
They can cause significant cosmetic deformity or airway obstruction.
microReview: Turner syndrome + multicystic neck/axillary mass = Cystic hygroma (lymphangioma). Lymphatic counterpart to cavernous hemangioma.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse a cystic hygroma with a branchial cleft cyst; the latter is usually unilateral and lacks the multi-cystic lymphatic histology.
sourceQuote: Cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) are typically found in the neck or axilla of children... and are common in Turner syndrome.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with a rapidly growing, pedunculated, red nodule on her gingiva that bleeds easily with minor trauma. She reports the lesion appeared two weeks ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma is malignant and does not typically occur on the gingiva of young pregnant women.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is seen in HIV patients, not healthy pregnant women.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a rapidly growing vascular lesion often appearing on the gingiva during pregnancy ('pregnancy tumor' or granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are deep, slow-growing, and not typically pedunculated or gingival.
explanations.e: Kaposi sarcoma is HHV-8 related and usually seen in the setting of immunodeficiency.

ankiCards: A 'pregnancy tumor' of the gingiva is a clinical term for a {{c1::pyogenic granuloma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized by {{c1::rapid}} growth and frequent bleeding.
Despite the name, a pyogenic granuloma is neither {{c1::pyogenic (pus-forming)}} nor a granuloma.
The histological pattern of a pyogenic granuloma is a {{c1::lobular}} capillary hemangioma.
True or False: Pyogenic granulomas often regress after pregnancy. {{c1::True}}
keyPoints: Pyogenic granulomas are benign, rapidly growing vascular nodules.
Common on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
Often follow trauma or occur during pregnancy (hormonal influence).
Histology: Lobular proliferation of capillaries with edema and inflammation.
Frequently ulcerate and bleed easily.
microReview: Rapid growth + Gingiva + Pregnancy = Pyogenic Granuloma. Not a true granuloma, but a vascular proliferation.
examinerTraps: The name is a misnomer; it's not 'pyogenic' (no pus) and it's not a 'granuloma' (no epithelioid macrophages).
sourceQuote: Pyogenic granulomas are capillary hemangiomas that manifest as rapidly growing red pedunculated nodules... they occur in the gingiva of 1% of pregnant women.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the fundamental pathological distinction between a cavernous hemangioma and a capillary hemangioma?

options.a: Cavernous hemangiomas are malignant, whereas capillary hemangiomas are benign.
options.b: Cavernous hemangiomas involve much larger, dilated vascular channels with more stroma.
options.c: Capillary hemangiomas are found only in internal organs, while cavernous are only on skin.
options.d: Capillary hemangiomas are associated with HHV-8 infection.
options.e: Cavernous hemangiomas lack an endothelial lining.

explanations.a: Both capillary and cavernous hemangiomas are benign.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are distinguished by large, dilated vascular spaces (caverns) and frequently involve deeper structures.
explanations.c: Both can be found on skin or in internal organs (liver is common for cavernous).
explanations.d: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8, not hemangiomas.
explanations.e: Both are vascular tumors and therefore must have an endothelial lining.

ankiCards: Cavernous hemangiomas are characterized by {{c1::large, dilated}} vascular channels.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas {{c1::do not}} spontaneously regress.
The most common internal organ site for a cavernous hemangioma is the {{c1::liver}}.
Cavernous hemangiomas in the CNS can be part of {{c1::von Hippel-Lindau}} disease.
The vascular spaces in a cavernous hemangioma are often filled with {{c1::thrombosis}} or calcification.
keyPoints: Hemangiomas are common benign tumors of blood-filled vessels.
Capillary hemangiomas: small vessels, thin walls, skin/mucosa.
Cavernous hemangiomas: large spaces, thick stroma, deep tissues/organs.
Cavernous types are more likely to require treatment because they don't regress and can be destructive.
Liver hemangiomas are usually discovered incidentally on imaging.
microReview: Capillary = Small vessels (strawberry). Cavernous = Large vessels (can be in liver/brain). Both are benign.
examinerTraps: A common mistake is thinking all hemangiomas regress like the 'strawberry' type. Cavernous hemangiomas are generally permanent and can enlarge.
sourceQuote: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, dilated vascular channels... they are more infiltrative and frequently involve deep structures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following syndromes is characterized by the development of multiple hemangioblastomas in the cerebellum and retina, as well as an increased risk for renal cell carcinoma?

explanations.a: Sturge-Weber involves port-wine stains (nevus flammeus) and leptomeningeal angiomas.
explanations.b: Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) is an autosomal dominant disorder featuring hemangioblastomas of the CNS and retina, renal cysts, and RCC.
explanations.c: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) features multiple telangiectasias and AVMs.
explanations.d: Tuberous sclerosis involves hamartomas and angiolipomas, not hemangioblastomas.
explanations.e: NF1 involves neurofibromas and Lisch nodules.

ankiCards: Von Hippel-Lindau disease is associated with {{c1::hemangioblastomas}} in the cerebellum.
The genetic inheritance of VHL disease is {{c1::autosomal dominant}}.
Patients with VHL have a high risk of developing {{c1::renal cell}} carcinoma.
Retinal involvement in VHL typically presents as {{c1::angiomas/hemangioblastomas}}.
VHL is caused by a mutation in the {{c1::VHL}} tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3.
keyPoints: VHL is a multisystem neoplasia syndrome.
Vascular tumors (hemangioblastomas) are a core feature.
Common sites: Cerebellum, retina, and spinal cord.
Non-vascular associations: Renal cell carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.
Due to loss of VHL gene, leading to increased HIF (hypoxia-inducible factor) and VEGF.
microReview: Cerebellar hemangioblastoma + Renal Cell Carcinoma = VHL. High VEGF levels drive the vascular tumor formation.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse hemangioblastoma (VHL) with hemangioma. Hemangioblastomas are specific highly vascular CNS tumors.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors... Cavernous hemangiomas... may be a component of von Hippel-Lindau disease, where vascular neoplasms occur in the cerebellum, retina...
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 40-year-old male with a history of long-standing lymphedema in the right arm following a radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection for a rare male breast cancer 10 years ago presents with new, firm, purple-to-black skin nodules on that same arm. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Lymphangiomas are benign and usually congenital; they do not typically arise in areas of chronic lymphedema in adults.
explanations.b: Kaposi Sarcoma presents with similar purple lesions but is associated with HHV-8 and usually involves more diffuse sites or HIV status.
explanations.c: Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema, classically after radical mastectomy.
explanations.d: Basal cell carcinoma is associated with sun exposure and does not present as purple vascular nodules.
explanations.e: Pyogenic granuloma is a fast-growing red nodule usually associated with trauma, not chronic lymphedema.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves}} syndrome.
Chronic lymphedema after {{c1::mastectomy}} is the classic trigger for Stewart-Treves syndrome.
The latent period between lymphedema and angiosarcoma development is usually {{c1::10}} years or more.
Clinically, Stewart-Treves syndrome presents as multiple {{c1::violaceous/purple}} nodules.
The prognosis for angiosarcoma in Stewart-Treves syndrome is very {{c1::poor}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma can arise as a complication of chronic lymphedema.
Stewart-Treves syndrome is the eponym for post-mastectomy lymphedema-associated angiosarcoma.
The tumor is highly aggressive with a high rate of metastasis.
Early biopsy of new skin lesions in lymphedematous limbs is critical.
Pathology is identical to other angiosarcomas (atypical endothelial cells).
microReview: Post-mastectomy lymphedema + New purple nodules = Angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves). This demonstrates that chronic stasis can lead to malignancy.
examinerTraps: The examiner may describe a woman who had a mastectomy many years ago. Even if the primary cancer is 'cured', the risk of angiosarcoma remains due to the lymphedema.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas can also occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema, traditionally in the ipsilateral arm of women several years after radical mastectomy... (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the most common benign vascular tumor characterized by small, thin-walled capillaries lined by a single layer of endothelial cells, typically occurring in the skin or mucous membranes?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are the most common type of hemangioma; they consist of closely packed thin-walled capillaries, usually involving the skin or oral mucosa.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated vascular channels and are often deeper or involve internal organs like the liver.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are small, painful lesions arising from specialized smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, not primarily capillaries.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor of endothelial cells, not a benign tumor.
explanations.e: Kaposi sarcoma is an intermediate-grade neoplasm caused by HHV-8, characterized by slit-like spaces rather than organized capillaries.

ankiCards: The most common benign vascular tumor involving skin/mucosa is the {{c1::capillary hemangioma}}.
Histologically, {{c1::capillary hemangiomas}} are composed of thin-walled capillaries lined by a single layer of endothelium.
The 'strawberry' hemangioma of the skin in infants is a subtype of {{c1::capillary hemangioma}} (specifically juvenile hemangioma).
{{c1::Cavernous hemangiomas}} are characterized by large, blood-filled vascular spaces and are frequently associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease when in the CNS.
True or False: Capillary hemangiomas have a high risk of malignant transformation. {{c1::False}}
keyPoints: Capillary hemangiomas are common benign neoplasms of capillaries.
They typically involve the skin, subcutaneous tissues, or mucous membranes.
They are composed of thin-walled capillaries with scant stroma.
Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are extremely common in newborns and often regress by age 7.
Most hemangiomas are stable and do not become malignant.
microReview: Hemangiomas are divided into capillary (small vessels) and cavernous (large vessels). Capillary types include juvenile/strawberry (infants) and pyogenic granulomas (trauma/pregnancy).
examinerTraps: Do not confuse 'capillary hemangioma' with 'bacillary angiomatosis,' which is caused by Bartonella infection but looks similar histologically.
sourceQuote:
Vascular tumors
Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... 518
Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... 520
Malignant Tumors... 522
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 58-year-old male presents with a three-month history of a painful, small (5 mm), firm, red-blue nodule located under the fingernail of his right index finger. The pain is intense and paroxysmal, triggered specifically by exposure to cold. Histological examination shows aggregates of specialized cells surrounding vascular spaces. What is the cell of origin for this lesion?

explanations.a: Endothelial cells line the vascular spaces but are not the primary neoplastic component of a glomus tumor.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a thermoregulatory arteriovenous anastomosis.
explanations.c: Fibroblasts are found in the stroma but do not form the characteristic nests of cells seen in glomus tumors.
explanations.d: Pericytes are the origin of hemangiopericytomas, which are distinct from glomus tumors.
explanations.e: Lymphatic endothelium is the origin of lymphangiomas, which are usually painless and not subungual.

ankiCards: A painful, subungual, red-blue nodule sensitive to cold is characteristic of a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle cells}}.
The specialized structure involved in glomus tumors is the {{c1::glomus body}}, used for thermoregulation.
The classic clinical triad for a glomus tumor includes: paroxysmal pain, localized tenderness, and {{c1::cold sensitivity}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors show nests of {{c1::glomus cells}} (round, uniform cells) surrounding vascular channels.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but extremely painful.
They are most commonly found in the distal digits, especially subungual (under nails).
Derived from smooth muscle cells of the thermoregulatory glomus body.
Pain is often triggered by cold temperatures.
Excision is curative.
microReview: Glomus tumor = Subungual + Cold pain + Smooth muscle origin.
examinerTraps: Wait for the 'cold sensitivity' or 'subungual' keyword. If the lesion is painless, think hemangioma; if painful, think glomus tumor.
sourceQuote:
Vascular tumors
Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... 518
Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... 520
Malignant Tumors... 522
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 64-year-old man who worked in a chemical plant for 30 years producing polyvinyl chloride (PVC) presents with abdominal distension and jaundice. Computed tomography reveals multiple ill-defined, hemorrhagic masses within the liver. Biopsy shows malignant spindle cells forming irregular vascular channels that express CD31. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Hepatic adenomas are benign and usually associated with oral contraceptive use, not PVC exposure.
explanations.b: Hepatocellular carcinoma is associated with HBV/HCV and cirrhosis, but PVC is a specific risk factor for angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma of the liver is strongly associated with exposure to vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor; it is typically asymptomatic and not associated with PVC.
explanations.e: Kaposi sarcoma is an intermediate-grade tumor associated with HHV-8, usually in the setting of immunosuppression.

ankiCards: Liver angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride (PVC)}}, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
The vascular marker often expressed by angiosarcomas is {{c1::CD31}} (or von Willebrand factor).
Angiosarcomas are histologically characterized by {{c1::malignant endothelial cells}} forming irregular vascular channels.
The prognosis of hepatic angiosarcoma is generally {{c1::poor/grave}}.
Besides the liver, angiosarcomas commonly occur in the {{c1::skin, breast, and soft tissue}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are highly malignant endothelial neoplasms.
Specific environmental carcinogens (vinyl chloride) target the liver.
CD31 is a specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial differentiation.
They are characterized by aggressive local invasion and frequent metastasis.
Histology shows pleomorphic malignant cells with high mitotic activity.
microReview: Vinyl chloride exposure + CD31 positive + Liver mass = Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Ensure you distinguish between vinyl chloride (angiosarcoma) and aflatoxin B1 (hepatocellular carcinoma).
sourceQuote:
Vascular tumors
Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... 518
Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... 520
Malignant Tumors... 522
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following pathogens is most directly implicated in the pathogenesis of the multifocal vascular neoplasm that presents as purple-to-brown skin plaques in patients with untreated Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS)?

explanations.a: HPV is associated with squamous cell carcinomas and warts, not vascular tumors.
explanations.b: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which mimics Kaposi sarcoma clinically, but is bacterial, not viral.
explanations.c: HHV-8 (also known as KSHV) is the causative agent of all forms of Kaposi sarcoma (KS).
explanations.d: EBV is associated with lymphomas (e.g., Burkitt) and nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
explanations.e: CMV causes opportunistic infections in AIDS but is not the primary driver of Kaposi sarcoma.

ankiCards: The virus associated with Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is {{c1::HHV-8}} (or Kaposi Sarcoma Herpesvirus).
Kaposi Sarcoma is classified as a {{c1::vascular}} tumor of intermediate-grade malignancy.
In the histology of KS, characteristic {{c1::slit-like}} vascular spaces are seen containing red blood cells.
The four clinical forms of KS are: Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and {{c1::AIDS-associated}}.
AIDS-associated Kaposi Sarcoma is the most common {{c1::HIV-associated malignancy}} worldwide.
keyPoints: HHV-8 encodes viral proteins that mimic host cytokines and promote angiogenesis.
KS lesions progress through three stages: patch, plaque, and nodule.
Histology shows spindle-shaped endothelial cells and extravasated RBCs.
Classic KS is usually indolent and involves the distal lower extremities of older Mediterranean men.
AIDS-associated KS can involve the skin, lymph nodes, and viscera (GI tract, lungs).
microReview: HHV-8 + Slit-like spaces + AIDS patient = Kaposi Sarcoma.
examinerTraps: A common distractor is Bartonella henselae; remember that KS is viral (HHV-8) and bacillary angiomatosis is bacterial.
sourceQuote:
Vascular tumors
Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... 518
Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... 520
Malignant Tumors... 522
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 3-week-old female infant is brought to the pediatrician for a rapidly growing, bright red, raised lesion on her cheek. The lesion was not present at birth. The parents are concerned about its appearance. What is the most appropriate management based on the natural history of this condition?

options.d: Wide local excision with lymph node biopsy

explanations.a: Surgery is generally avoided for juvenile hemangiomas unless they obstruct vital structures (e.g., vision) because they usually regress.
explanations.b: Chemotherapy is for malignant tumors; this is a benign juvenile hemangioma.
explanations.c: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas grow rapidly for a few months but usually regress spontaneously by age 7.
explanations.d: Wide local excision is for malignancies; strawberry hemangiomas are benign.
explanations.e: The lesion is not infectious; antibiotics have no role.

ankiCards: A 'strawberry' hemangioma in an infant is also known as a {{c1::juvenile}} hemangioma.
The clinical course of a juvenile hemangioma involves rapid growth followed by {{c1::spontaneous regression}}.
Spontaneous regression of strawberry hemangiomas occurs in approximately {{c1::75-90}}% of cases by age 7.
Unlike some other vascular anomalies, juvenile hemangiomas are typically {{c1::not}} present at birth.
If treatment is required for a strawberry hemangioma (e.g., visual obstruction), {{c1::propranolol}} is often the first-line therapy.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangiomas are extremely common skin tumors in infants.
They are characterized by a 'strawberry' appearance (bright red, lobulated).
They arise shortly after birth (within weeks).
The histological feature is a proliferation of thin-walled capillaries.
Expectant management (observation) is the standard of care for most cases.
microReview: Strawberry hemangioma = Infant + Rapid growth + Spontaneous regression by age 7.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse this with a 'Port-wine stain' (Nevus flammeus), which is present at birth and does not regress.
sourceQuote:
Vascular tumors
Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... 518
Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... 520
Malignant Tumors... 522
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 42-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer underwent a radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection and radiotherapy six years ago. She now presents with several persistent, enlarging, violaceous skin nodules on her right arm, which has chronic lymphedema. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to the development of angiosarcoma in the setting of chronic lymphedema (often post-mastectomy).
explanations.b: Sturge-Weber syndrome involves port-wine stains and leptomeningeal angiomatosis; it is a congenital neurocutaneous disorder.
explanations.c: Von Hippel-Lindau is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by hemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinomas, and pheochromocytomas.
explanations.d: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) involves telangiectasias of skin and mucous membranes.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is a bacterial infection seen in immunocompromised patients, not typically associated with chronic lymphedema.

ankiCards: The development of angiosarcoma in an arm with chronic lymphedema following mastectomy is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves}} syndrome.
Chronic lymphedema is a major risk factor for the development of cutaneous {{c1::angiosarcoma}}.
The typical latency period between mastectomy/lymphedema and the onset of Stewart-Treves syndrome is about {{c1::10}} years.
Stewart-Treves syndrome skin lesions typically appear as {{c1::violaceous/purple}} nodules or plaques.
The prognosis for Stewart-Treves syndrome is generally {{c1::poor}} due to early metastasis.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a rare but fatal complication of chronic lymphedema.
It was historically common after radical mastectomy (Stewart-Treves).
The pathogenesis involves localized immune dysfunction in the lymphedematous limb.
The tumors are highly aggressive and often multifocal.
Radiotherapy (post-mastectomy) also independently increases the risk of angiosarcoma.
microReview: Post-mastectomy lymphedema + Violaceous nodules = Stewart-Treves (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: The examiner might just list 'Angiosarcoma' as an option; Stewart-Treves is the specific eponym for this clinical scenario.
sourceQuote:
Vascular tumors
Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... 518
Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... 520
Malignant Tumors... 522
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old male with advanced HIV (CD4+ count < 50 cells/µL) presents with numerous friable, red-purple, dome-shaped papules on his skin. A biopsy shows a vascular proliferation with prominent neutrophils and nuclear dust (leukocytoclastic debris). Warthin-Starry silver stain reveals clusters of tangled bacilli. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?

explanations.a: Bartonella quintana (and B. henselae) causes bacillary angiomatosis in HIV patients, characterized by neutrophilic inflammation and positive silver stains.
explanations.b: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, which lacks the prominent neutrophilic infiltrate and silver-staining bacteria seen here.
explanations.c: S. aureus causes pyogenic infections but not this specific form of angiomatosis.
explanations.d: T. pallidum (syphilis) is silver-stain positive but causes endarteritis and different clinical lesions (chancre, rash).
explanations.e: MAC causes systemic infection in AIDS but does not cause primary vascular skin tumors.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by bacteria of the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
Histologically, bacillary angiomatosis is distinguished from Kaposi sarcoma by the presence of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
The silver stain used to identify Bartonella in tissue is the {{c1::Warthin-Starry}} stain.
Bartonella henselae is typically transmitted by {{c1::cats (cat-scratch)}}, while B. quintana is transmitted by {{c1::lice}}.
Bacillary angiomatosis is treated with antibiotics, such as {{c1::erythromycin or doxycycline}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis occurs in immunocompromised individuals.
It manifests as vascular skin lesions that clinically mimic Kaposi sarcoma.
Histology shows vascular proliferation with neutrophilic infiltrates and bacteria.
Host cells (endothelium) are stimulated to proliferate by bacterial proteins.
Identification of the bacilli on silver stain is diagnostic.
microReview: HIV + Silver stain positive bacilli + Neutrophils = Bacillary angiomatosis (Bartonella).
examinerTraps: The histological presence of neutrophils is the 'key' to differentiating this from Kaposi sarcoma (which has lymphocytes/plasma cells).
sourceQuote:
Vascular tumors
Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... 518
Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... 520
Malignant Tumors... 522
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which vascular lesion is described as a 'polypoid, red, friable nodule' that often occurs on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa, frequently follows trauma, and is histologically identical to an exuberant granulation tissue response?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are broader, not typically polypoid or ulcerated, and do not resemble granulation tissue as closely as pyogenic granulomas.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granulomas (lobular capillary hemangiomas) are polypoid vascular lesions that often ulcerate and bleed, resembling granulation tissue.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas are deeper, non-polypoid, and consist of large vascular spaces.
explanations.d: Cystic hygroma is a cavernous lymphangioma found in the neck, not a small polypoid nodule.
explanations.e: Spider telangiectasias are non-neoplastic vascular dilations associated with hyperestrinism.

ankiCards: The clinical term for a lobular capillary hemangioma that resembles granulation tissue is {{c1::pyogenic granuloma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are often found in the {{c1::oral mucosa/gingiva}} of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum).
Despite the name, pyogenic granulomas are neither {{c1::pyogenic (pus-forming)}} nor true granulomas.
A common history for a pyogenic granuloma involves minor {{c1::trauma}}.
True or False: Pyogenic granulomas tend to bleed easily upon minor contact. {{c1::True}}
keyPoints: Pyogenic granulomas are benign, rapidly growing vascular lesions.
They are often pedunculated/polypoid and frequently ulcerated.
Histology shows a lobular proliferation of capillaries with edema and inflammation.
The gingival lesion in pregnancy is called a 'granuloma gravidarum.'
Surgical curettage or excision is the usual treatment.
microReview: Pyogenic granuloma = Granulation tissue-like + Bleeds easily + Pregnancy/Trauma.
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic granuloma' is a misnomer; look for 'granulation tissue' in the description.

stem: A newborn girl is found to have a large, soft, fluctuant mass on the left side of her neck. Physical exam shows no other abnormalities. Imaging reveals a multi-loculated cystic lesion that transilluminates. What chromosomal abnormality is most commonly associated with this specific vascular malformation?

explanations.a: Trisomy 21 (Down Syndrome) is associated with endocardial cushion defects and duodenal atresia, not typically cystic hygromas.
explanations.b: Cystic hygromas (cavernous lymphangiomas) of the neck are classically associated with Turner Syndrome (45,X).
explanations.c: Trisomy 18 (Edwards Syndrome) is associated with rocker-bottom feet and micrognathia.
explanations.d: 47,XXY (Klinefelter Syndrome) presents in males after puberty with hypogonadism.
explanations.e: Deletion 22q11 (DiGeorge/Velocardiofacial syndrome) involves thymic aplasia and conotruncal heart defects.

ankiCards: A cavernous lymphangioma occurring in the neck of an infant is called a {{c1::cystic hygroma}}.
Cystic hygromas are most commonly associated with {{c1::Turner Syndrome}} (monosomy X).
The fluid within a cystic hygroma is {{c1::lymphatic}} fluid, often described as serous or proteinaceous.
The classic physical exam finding for a cystic hygroma is that the mass {{c1::transilluminates}}.
Cystic hygromas in the neck are caused by failure of the {{c1::lymphatic}} system to communicate with the venous system.
keyPoints: Cystic hygroma is a type of cavernous lymphangioma.
Typically located in the neck or axilla.
Composed of large, dilated lymphatic spaces lined by endothelium.
Associated with Turner Syndrome (45,X) and Trisomy 21.
Surgical removal is difficult as they lack a capsule and interdigitate with tissue.
microReview: Neck mass in newborn + Transillumination + 45,X = Cystic hygroma (Lymphangioma).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse cystic hygroma (lymphatic) with a branchial cleft cyst (epithelial/embryological remnant).

Malignant Tumors... 522

stem: Vascular ectasias are not true neoplasms but rather permanent dilations of pre-existing vessels. Which of the following conditions is characterized by a 'port-wine stain' in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve and is associated with ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomas?

explanations.a: Osler-Weber-Rendu involves hereditary telangiectasias, not port-wine stains.
explanations.b: Sturge-Weber syndrome (Encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) features a port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) and leptomeningeal vascular malformations.
explanations.c: Von Hippel-Lindau features hemangioblastomas but not the trigeminal port-wine stain.
explanations.d: Maffucci syndrome involves multiple hemangiomas and enchondromas.
explanations.e: Klippel-Trenaunay involves port-wine stains but typically on the extremities with limb overgrowth, not the trigeminal distribution.

ankiCards: The eponym for encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis is {{c1::Sturge-Weber}} syndrome.
Sturge-Weber syndrome is associated with a facial birthmark known as a {{c1::port-wine stain}} (or nevus flammeus).
The neurological complications of Sturge-Weber syndrome include {{c1::seizures}}, mental retardation, and glaucoma.
The genetic basis of Sturge-Weber syndrome is a somatic mutation in the {{c1::GNAQ}} gene.
Skull X-ray in Sturge-Weber syndrome may show 'tram-track' {{c1::calcifications}} in the cortex.
keyPoints: Sturge-Weber is a sporadic neurocutaneous disorder.
The facial port-wine stain follows the V1/V2 trigeminal distribution.
Leptomeningeal angiomas can lead to brain calcification and seizures.
Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) does not regress with age.
GNAQ gene mutation is the current molecular understanding.
microReview: Port-wine stain (V1/V2) + Seizures + Brain calcification = Sturge-Weber.
examinerTraps: Wait for the trigeminal nerve mention. If the port-wine stain is on the body, it may be Klippel-Trenaunay or simple nevus flammeus.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with an extremely painful, 4-mm, blue-red nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. The pain is sharp and paroxysmal, often triggered by exposure to cold. Histological examination reveals branching vascular channels separated by aggregates of specialized smooth muscle cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, exquisitely painful tumors arising from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, commonly found in the subungual region.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella infection and usually presents as red papules in immunocompromised patients, not subungual painful nodules.
explanations.c: Kaposi sarcoma presents as purple-red patches or plaques, often related to HHV-8, and is not typically localized to the subungual space with paroxysmal cold-induced pain.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant endothelial tumor that typically affects the scalp or skin of elderly patients, or occurs post-radiation, and lacks glomus cell morphology.
explanations.e: Strawberry (juvenile) hemangiomas are common in infants and typically regress by early childhood; they are not characterized by exquisite subungual pain in adults.

ankiCards: A subungual, exquisitely painful blue-red nodule triggered by cold is characteristic of a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
The glomus tumor arises from specialized {{c1::smooth muscle}} cells of the glomus body.
Vascular tumors of {{c1::intermediate}} grade include Kaposi sarcoma and hemangioendothelioma.
The glomus body is involved in the physiological process of {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors show branching vascular channels separated by aggregates of {{c1::glomus}} cells.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign neoplasms.
They are most common in the distal digits, especially under nails.
They are highly sensitive to temperature changes (cold).
The origin is the glomus body, an arteriovenous anastomosis.
Morphology shows nests of specialized glomus cells (modified smooth muscle).
microReview: Benign vascular tumors (hemangiomas, glomus tumors) are well-differentiated; malignant ones (angiosarcoma) are poorly differentiated and aggressive.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse glomus tumors with 'glomus jugulare' (paragangliomas) which are neuroendocrine in origin.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions. Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteri
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An 42-year-old male with a history of HIV infection and a CD4 count of 150 cells/mm³ presents with multiple violaceous, non-blanching macules and plaques on his lower extremities. Biopsy reveals proliferation of spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces containing red blood cells, and prominent inflammatory cells. Which of the following pathogens is the primary driver of this neoplastic process?

explanations.a: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent for all forms of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.b: EBV is associated with various lymphomas (e.g., Burkitt, CNS lymphoma) but not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.c: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can clinically mimic Kaposi sarcoma but has different histology (neutrophils and bacterial clusters).
explanations.d: HPV-16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx, not vascular tumors.
explanations.e: CMV can cause retinitis or colitis in AIDS patients but does not cause Kaposi sarcoma.

ankiCards: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is strongly associated with infection by {{c1::Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}.
The spindle cells in Kaposi sarcoma are derived from {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
Histology of KS shows {{c1::slit-like}} vascular spaces and extravasated red blood cells.
The most common form of KS in the United States is {{c1::AIDS-associated}} (Epidemic) KS.
Classic (European) Kaposi sarcoma typically occurs on the {{c1::lower extremities}} of older men.
keyPoints: KS is a low-grade vascular malignancy.
HHV-8 is the essential viral cofactor.
Three stages: Patch, Plaque, and Nodule.
Histology features slit-like spaces and spindle cells.
It is one of the AIDS-defining illnesses.
microReview: Slit-like spaces + Spindle cells + HHV-8 = Kaposi Sarcoma.
examinerTraps: Candidates often confuse Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella) with Kaposi Sarcoma (HHV-8). Look for 'neutrophils' in histology to favor Bartonella.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism)
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 58-year-old male presents with a enlarging, tender, ill-defined red mass on his scalp. He mentions the lesion started as a small bruise-like area six months ago but has since become ulcerated. Biopsy shows highly pleomorphic, malignant endothelial cells forming irregular vascular channels that infiltrate the dermis. Immunohistochemical staining is positive for CD31. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma is a malignant vascular tumor that most commonly occurs in the skin of the head and neck in older adults. CD31 is a specific marker for endothelial differentiation.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign, rapidly growing red pedunculated nodule (lobular capillary hemangioma), not a pleomorphic infiltrative malignancy.
explanations.c: Glomus tumor is a small, benign, exquisitely painful nodule, typically subungual, and lacks the pleomorphism seen here.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign lesions composed of large, dilated vascular spaces; they are not pleomorphic or infiltrative.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign vascular proliferation caused by Bartonella in immunocompromised hosts, showing neutrophils rather than malignant pleomorphism.

ankiCards: A malignant vascular tumor occurring on the scalp of elderly patients is likely {{c1::angiosarcoma}}.
{{c1::CD31}} (or vWF) is a reliable immunohistochemical marker for angiosarcoma.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
Angiosarcomas can occur in the arm following long-term chronic lymphedema, a condition known as {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
Histology of angiosarcoma shows {{c1::pleomorphic}} endothelial cells forming irregular channels.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is highly aggressive with a poor 5-year survival rate.
Most common cutaneous site is the scalp of the elderly.
Can be induced by radiation or chronic lymphedema.
Liver angiosarcoma risk factors: Vinyl chloride, arsenic, Thorotrast.
CD31 and CD34 are common endothelial markers.
microReview: Elderly patient + Scalp mass + Malignant endothelial cells = Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'CD31' or 'Factor VIII' to confirm vascular origin in an undifferentiated tumor.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure and function.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 25-year-old pregnant woman presents with a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated nodule on her gingiva that bleeds easily with minor trauma. The lesion appeared during her second trimester. Which of the following is the most likely pathological diagnosis?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a benign vascular lesion that often occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum). It is characterized by rapid growth and easy bleeding.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are deeper, larger, and more stable lesions; they do not typically present as a rapidly growing 'pregnancy tumor' on the gingiva.
explanations.c: Cystic hygromas are cavernous lymphangiomas typically found in the neck of infants, often associated with Turner syndrome.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are small, painful subungual nodules, not bleeding gingival masses in pregnancy.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a malignant, aggressive tumor of the elderly, not a benign reactive-like lesion of pregnancy.

ankiCards: The 'pregnancy tumor' occurring on the gingiva is histologically a {{c1::pyogenic granuloma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized by {{c1::rapid}} growth and a tendency to bleed.
Histologically, pyogenic granulomas are considered {{c1::lobular capillary hemangiomas}}.
Pyogenic granulomas often regress {{c1::spontaneously}} postpartum.
The most common location for pyogenic granulomas is the {{c1::skin}} or gingiva.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is neither pyogenic (pus-forming) nor a true granuloma.
Associated with trauma or pregnancy.
Presents as a red, pedunculated, friable mass.
Microscopy shows proliferating capillaries with edema and inflammation.
Surgical excision or observation (if pregnancy-related) are options.
microReview: Gingival mass + Pregnancy + Bleeding = Pyogenic Granuloma (Granuloma Gravidarum).
examinerTraps: Do not be misled by the name; it does not contain pus or granulomatous inflammation.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following immunohistochemical markers is most specific for identifying the endothelial origin of a poorly differentiated malignant tumor?

explanations.a: CD31 (Platelet Endothelial Cell Adhesion Molecule, PECAM-1) is a transmembrane glycoprotein highly expressed on endothelial cells and is a standard marker for vascular tumors like angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells and carcinomas.
explanations.c: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells (melanoma, Schwann cells).
explanations.d: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (skeletal, smooth, cardiac).
explanations.e: Chromogranin is a marker for neuroendocrine cells.

ankiCards: The most specific marker for endothelial cells used in immunohistochemistry is {{c1::CD31}}.
VWF (von Willebrand Factor) is also known as {{c1::Factor VIII}}-related antigen.
CD31 and {{c1::CD34}} are both used to identify vascular tumors.
Poorly differentiated angiosarcomas may require {{c1::immunohistochemistry}} for diagnosis.
Desmin positivity in a spindle cell tumor suggests a {{c1::muscle}} origin.
keyPoints: CD31 is the standard endothelial marker.
CD34 is also common but less specific (found in other mesenchymal cells).
Factor VIII-related antigen (vWF) is specific but sometimes less sensitive in poorly differentiated tumors.
Markers help distinguish angiosarcoma from melanoma or spindle cell carcinoma.
Identification of Weibel-Palade bodies on EM is the gold standard but rarely used.
microReview: CD31 = Endothelium = Vascular tumor identification.
examinerTraps: The examiner may list CD34, which is often positive, but CD31 is generally considered more specific for endothelial differentiation in the context of malignancy.
sourceQuote: To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure and function.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 64-year-old male former industrial worker presents with weight loss, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain. Imaging reveals multiple hemorrhagic masses in the liver. His occupational history is notable for long-term exposure to vinyl chloride in a plastics manufacturing plant. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare but well-recognized complication of exposure to vinyl chloride, arsenic, or Thorotrast. It is highly aggressive.
explanations.b: Hepatocellular carcinoma is more commonly associated with HBV, HCV, or cirrhosis, though vinyl chloride is a known carcinogen, angiosarcoma is the classic association with PVC monomers.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor and is usually asymptomatic; it is not associated with vinyl chloride.
explanations.d: Hepatic adenoma is associated with oral contraceptive use or anabolic steroids.
explanations.e: Focal nodular hyperplasia is a benign, non-neoplastic liver lesion characterized by a central stellate scar.

ankiCards: Exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}} is a classic risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma.
Other risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma include {{c1::arsenic}} and Thorotrast.
The most common benign tumor of the liver is the {{c1::cavernous hemangioma}}.
Angiosarcoma of the liver has a {{c1::poor}} prognosis.
Thorotrast is a discontinued {{c1::radioactive}} contrast medium once linked to liver angiosarcoma.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is linked to specific chemical exposures.
Vinyl chloride monomer (PVC industry) is the classic board association.
Thorotrast (thorium dioxide) was a historical cause.
Presentation includes RUQ pain and liver failure.
Hemorrhagic appearance on imaging/gross specimen is common.
microReview: Vinyl chloride + Liver mass + Aggressive course = Hepatic Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse vinyl chloride (angiosarcoma) with aflatoxin B1 (hepatocellular carcinoma).
sourceQuote: Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A newborn female is found to have a large, soft, fluctuant mass on the left side of her neck. Ultrasound confirms a multi-loculated fluid-filled structure. Genetic testing reveals a 45,X karyotype. What is the most likely classification for this vascular abnormality?

explanations.a: Cystic hygromas (cavernous lymphangiomas) are benign lymphatic malformations typically found in the neck or axilla of infants. They are strongly associated with Turner syndrome (45,X).
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas are small blood vessel proliferations, not large multi-loculated lymphatic masses.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are small painful subungual lesions in adults.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious process in immunocompromised adults.
explanations.e: Sturge-Weber syndrome is characterized by a port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) in the V1/V2 distribution, not a cystic neck mass.

ankiCards: Cystic hygromas of the neck in a neonate are associated with {{c1::Turner syndrome}}.
Histologically, cystic hygromas are classified as {{c1::cavernous lymphangiomas}}.
Cystic hygromas are found most commonly in the {{c1::neck}} or axilla.
The fluid within a cystic hygroma is typically {{c1::lymphatic}} fluid.
In Turner syndrome, cystic hygromas are often associated with {{c1::webbing}} of the neck.
keyPoints: Cystic hygromas are benign but can be large and disfiguring.
They consist of massively dilated lymphatic spaces.
Strong association with chromosomal aneuploidy (Turner, Down syndrome).
Neck mass + 45,X = Cystic Hygroma.
Surgical removal is difficult as they lack a capsule.
microReview: Neck mass + Turner Syndrome (45,X) = Cystic Hygroma.
examinerTraps: Candidates might pick 'hemangioma' for any vascular mass, but 'multi-loculated fluid-filled' in the neck specifically points to cystic hygroma (lymphangioma).
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels (Fig. 11.1).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 2-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for a bright red, 'strawberry-like' raised lesion on the forehead. The mother reports it was not present at birth but appeared at age 2 weeks and has grown rapidly. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

explanations.a: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas typically grow rapidly for a few months and then slowly involute. Most (75-90%) completely regress by age 7.
explanations.b: Surgical excision is usually avoided unless the lesion obstructs vision or the airway, as spontaneous regression is the rule.
explanations.c: Chemotherapy is used for malignant tumors, not benign juvenile hemangiomas.
explanations.d: Radiation is not indicated and carries significant risk for the infant.
explanations.e: Cryotherapy is generally not the first-line treatment for these lesions due to the high likelihood of spontaneous involution.

ankiCards: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas typically regress by age {{c1::7}}.
Strawberry hemangiomas are common in {{c1::infants}} (1 in 200 births).
The clinical appearance of a juvenile hemangioma is a {{c1::bright red}} raised lesion.
Unlike some other malformations, strawberry hemangiomas appear {{c1::after}} birth.
Histologically, juvenile hemangiomas are composed of {{c1::capillary}} sized vessels.
keyPoints: Strawberry hemangiomas are capillary hemangiomas of infancy.
Characterized by a growth phase followed by an involution phase.
Management is usually 'watchful waiting'.
Propanolol is sometimes used for problematic lesions (near the eye).
They are benign neoplasms.
microReview: Infant + Red strawberry lesion + Rapid growth then regression = Juvenile Hemangioma.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse strawberry hemangioma (regresses) with a Port-wine stain (does not regress and grows with the child).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction... Weakening of vessel walls.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is best categorized as which of the following based on its clinical behavior?

explanations.a: Hemangioendotheliomas, specifically the epithelioid type, are considered intermediate-grade tumors. Their behavior is between benign hemangiomas and highly malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.b: While it is less aggressive than angiosarcoma, it is more aggressive than a benign hemangioma.
explanations.c: It is not as aggressive as angiosarcoma, which is the truly malignant counterpart.
explanations.d: It is a true neoplasm, not a reactive hyperplasia (like pyogenic granuloma).
explanations.e: It is a neoplasm, not a hamartoma (a disorganized mass of tissue native to the site).

ankiCards: Hemangioendothelioma is considered a(n) {{c1::intermediate}}-grade vascular tumor.
In epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, the cells look like {{c1::epithelial}} cells.
Vascular tumors are graded as {{c1::benign, intermediate, or malignant}}.
The behavior of intermediate-grade tumors is {{c1::unpredictable}} but generally less aggressive than angiosarcoma.
Kaposi sarcoma is another example of a(n) {{c1::intermediate}}-grade vascular tumor.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors represent a spectrum from benign to malignant.
Hemangioendotheliomas occur in adults around medium and large veins.
Clinical course is variable; some metastasize in up to 20% of cases.
They can mimic carcinomas due to their epithelioid appearance.
Vascular origin is confirmed by CD31.
microReview: Epithelioid Hemangioendothelioma = Intermediate grade.
examinerTraps: Grading is key: Hemangioma (Benign), Hemangioendothelioma/Kaposi (Intermediate), Angiosarcoma (Malignant).
sourceQuote: The general architecture and cellular composition of blood vessels are comparable throughout the cardiovascular system.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 38-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of epistaxis and iron deficiency anemia. Physical exam reveals multiple 1- to 2-mm ruby-red blanching macules on his lips, tongue, and fingertips. He states his father and brother have similar findings. What is the name of this autosomal dominant condition?

explanations.a: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by malformed dilated capillaries (telangiectasias) and AVMs in the skin, mucous membranes, and internal organs.
explanations.b: Sturge-Weber syndrome involves a facial port-wine stain and leptomeningeal angiomatosis, but not systemic telangiectasias and epistaxis.
explanations.c: Von Hippel-Lindau involves hemangioblastomas of the CNS/retina and renal cell carcinoma, not mucosal telangiectasias.
explanations.d: NF1 is characterized by neurofibromas and cafe-au-lait spots.
explanations.e: Tuberous sclerosis presents with angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum) and cortical tubers, not bleeding telangiectasias.

ankiCards: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) is also known as {{c1::Osler-Weber-Rendu}} syndrome.
HHT is inherited in an {{c1::autosomal dominant}} pattern.
Common symptoms of HHT include recurrent {{c1::epistaxis}} and GI bleeding.
Mutations in the {{c1::TGF-beta}} signaling pathway are implicated in HHT.
HHT can lead to the formation of {{c1::arteriovenous malformations (AVMs)}} in the lungs or liver.
keyPoints: HHT involves widespread telangiectasias and AVMs.
Mucocutaneous lesions are characteristic (lips, tongue).
Chronic bleeding often leads to iron deficiency anemia.
Complications include high-output heart failure from AVMs.
Clinical diagnosis relies on the Curaçao criteria (Epistaxis, Telangiectasias, Visceral lesions, Family history).
microReview: Epistaxis + Telangiectasias + Autosomal Dominant = HHT.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'ruby-red' spots of HHT with 'cherry hemangiomas' (benign age-related lesions) or 'petechiae'.
sourceQuote: Arterial wall thickness gradually diminishes as the vessels become smaller, but the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 3-month-old male infant is brought to the clinic by his mother who is concerned about a bright red, raised 'strawberry-like' lesion on the child's cheek that has grown rapidly over the last month. On examination, the lesion is soft and blanches slightly with pressure. The physician informs the mother that the lesion is likely to regress spontaneously by age 7. What is the most likely histological finding in this lesion?

options.a: Cavernous blood-filled spaces with thick fibrous walls
options.b: Dilated lymphatic channels lined by simple squamous epithelium
options.d: Malignant spindle cells with slit-like vascular spaces
options.e: Modified smooth muscle cells in a perivascular arrangement

explanations.a: This describes a cavernous hemangioma, which are usually deeper, larger, and do not regress as predictably as the juvenile variety.
explanations.b: This describes a lymphangioma, which is characterized by the absence of red blood cells in the channels.
explanations.c: This is the classic description of a juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma, the most common vascular tumor of infancy.
explanations.d: This describes Kaposi Sarcoma, which is an intermediate-grade malignancy associated with HHV-8.
explanations.e: This describes a glomus tumor (glomangioma), which is a painful subungual tumor, not a strawberry hemangioma.

ankiCards: The most common vascular tumor of infancy is the {{c1::juvenile (strawberry)}} hemangioma.
Juvenile hemangiomas typically {{c1::regress}} spontaneously by early childhood.
Histologically, juvenile hemangiomas consist of thin-walled {{c1::capillaries}} with scant stroma.
The clinical appearance of a juvenile hemangioma is a {{c1::bright red}} ('strawberry') skin lesion.
Unlike cavernous hemangiomas, juvenile hemangiomas are composed of {{c1::small/capillary-sized}} vessels.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangiomas are common in newborns (1 in 200 births).
They grow rapidly for several months before beginning to fade.
Complete regression occurs in 90% of cases by age 7.
Histology shows closely packed, thin-walled capillaries.
They are benign and usually managed expectantly.
microReview: Juvenile Hemangioma = Infancy + Strawberry appearance + Rapid growth followed by regression + Capillary-sized vessels.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse with Cavernous Hemangioma, which involves large, deep vascular channels and rarely regresses.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... 518... Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) are extremely common... nearly always regress by age 7.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 42-year-old male with a history of HIV and a CD4+ count of 150 cells/mm³ presents with multiple painless, purple-to-red macules and plaques on his lower extremities and hard palate. Biopsy of a plaque reveals proliferation of spindle-shaped cells forming slit-like spaces containing extravasated red blood cells. Which of the following infectious agents is the primary driver of this pathology?

explanations.a: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can look similar but histologically shows neutrophilic infiltrates and bacterial clusters.
explanations.b: HHV-8 (also known as KSHV) is the causative agent of all forms of Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.c: HPV-16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas, particularly of the cervix and oropharynx.
explanations.d: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.e: CMV causes opportunistic infections in AIDS patients but does not cause vascular tumors.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is caused by {{c1::Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}.
Histology of Kaposi Sarcoma shows {{c1::spindle cells}} and slit-like vascular spaces.
Common locations for Kaposi Sarcoma in AIDS patients include the skin and the {{c1::hard palate (or GI tract)}}.
Kaposi Sarcoma lesions often contain {{c1::extravasated}} red blood cells and hemosiderin.
The four clinical forms of Kaposi Sarcoma are Classic, Endemic, Transplant-associated, and {{c1::AIDS-associated}}.
keyPoints: HHV-8 is essential for the pathogenesis of Kaposi Sarcoma (KS).
KS is an intermediate-grade neoplasm of endothelial cells.
AIDS-associated KS is the most common HIV-related malignancy.
Spindle cells are the diagnostic cell type in the late stage.
Lesions do not typically blanch because blood is trapped in tissue slits.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = HIV/AIDS + HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Slit-like spaces + Purple plaques.
examinerTraps: Differentiating KS from Bacillary Angiomatosis: KS has spindle cells and slit spaces; Bacillary Angiomatosis has neutrophils and Bartonella organisms.
sourceQuote: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8 and is highly associated with AIDS.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following markers is most specific for identifying the endothelial origin of a poorly differentiated malignant vascular tumor such as an angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Cytokeratins are markers for epithelial cells (carcinomas).
explanations.b: Vimentin is a general marker for mesenchymal cells and is not specific for endothelium.
explanations.c: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a highly specific marker for endothelial cells and is used to confirm the diagnosis of angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells (melanoma, Schwann cells).
explanations.e: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (leiomyosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma).

ankiCards: The endothelial-specific marker used to identify angiosarcomas is {{c1::CD31 (or PECAM-1)}}.
Another marker used for vascular tumors is {{c1::von Willebrand factor}}.
Angiosarcomas are {{c1::malignant}} neoplasms of endothelial cells.
