explanations.e: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which clinically mimics Kaposi sarcoma but is a bacterial infection characterized by neutrophilic infiltrates rather than spindle cells.

ankiCards: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
The histological hallmark of Kaposi sarcoma involves {{c1::spindle cells}} and slit-like vascular spaces.
{{c1::Epidemic (AIDS-associated)}} Kaposi sarcoma is the most common HIV-related malignancy.
Unlike Kaposi sarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis features a prominent {{c1::neutrophilic}} infiltrate.
The four forms of Kaposi sarcoma are Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and {{c1::Epidemic (AIDS-associated)}}.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a low-grade malignant vascular tumor.
HHV-8 is the essential cofactor in KS pathogenesis.
Histology shows spindle cells, slit-like spaces, and extravasated RBCs.
KS is common in AIDS patients with low CD4 counts.
Bacillary angiomatosis is a key differential but is bacterial (Bartonella).
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma: HHV-8, Spindle cells, Slit-like spaces, AIDS-defining. Bacillary Angiomatosis: Bartonella, Neutrophils, immunocompromised.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Kaposi Sarcoma (HHV-8) with Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella); both present as purple skin lesions in HIV, but histology (spindle cells vs neutrophils/bacteria) distinguishes them.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism)
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male with a history of chronic lymphedema following a radical axillary lymph node dissection 12 years ago presents with several firm, enlarging, dark-blue nodules on his upper arm. Biopsy confirms a malignancy of endothelial origin. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma (specifically Stewart-Treves syndrome) is a malignant vascular tumor that arises in the setting of chronic lymphedema, often post-mastectomy.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors are benign, painful subungual lesions arising from specialized thermoregulatory glomus bodies.
explanations.c: Hemangiopericytoma is a rare tumor arising from pericytes, now often reclassified as solitary fibrous tumors.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign, rapidly growing capillary hemangioma, often occurring on the skin or gingiva.
explanations.e: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign lesions characterized by large, blood-filled vascular spaces and are not associated with chronic lymphedema.

ankiCards: {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}} refers to angiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphedema.
Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor of {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
The classic marker for endothelial differentiation is {{c1::CD31 (or vWF)}}.
Angiosarcomas of the liver are associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride, arsenic, or Thorotrast}}.
Chronic lymphedema post-mastectomy is a risk factor for {{c1::angiosarcoma}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is highly aggressive and carries a poor prognosis.
Stewart-Treves syndrome occurs in lymphedematous limbs.
Common sites include skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Immunohistochemistry usually shows CD31 positivity.
Hepatic forms are linked to specific chemical carcinogens.
microReview: Malignant vascular tumors = Angiosarcoma. High-yield associations: Chronic lymphedema, radiation, vinyl chloride (liver).
examinerTraps: Angiosarcomas may initially look like simple bruises (ecchymoses), leading to a delay in diagnosis until they form firm nodules.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following immunohistochemical markers is most specific for identifying a tumor as being of endothelial origin?

explanations.a: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a highly specific marker for endothelial cells and is used to confirm the diagnosis of vascular tumors like angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells, used to diagnose carcinomas.
explanations.c: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (skeletal, smooth, and cardiac).
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells, including melanocytes and Schwann cells.
explanations.e: Vimentin is a non-specific marker for mesenchymal cells and is present in many different types of sarcomas and normal tissues.

ankiCards: The most specific marker for endothelial cells is {{c1::CD31}}.
CD31 is also known as {{c1::PECAM-1}}.
Besides CD31, {{c1::Von Willebrand Factor (vWF)}} is another endothelial marker.
Vimentin is a marker for {{c1::mesenchymal}} cells.
Cytokeratin markers are used for {{c1::epithelial/carcinoma}} diagnosis.
keyPoints: Endothelial markers are essential for classifying poorly differentiated vascular tumors.
CD31 is the gold standard immunohistochemical stain.
Factor VIII-related antigen (vWF) is also used but can be less sensitive.
Vascular tumors arise from the mesenchymal lineage but require specific markers for subtype identification.
IHC helps distinguish angiosarcomas from carcinomas.
microReview: Vascular Marker: CD31/PECAM-1. Muscle Marker: Desmin. Nerve Marker: S100. Epithelial Marker: Cytokeratin.
examinerTraps: Vimentin is often positive in vascular tumors because they are mesenchymal, but it is not specific enough to diagnose them as 'vascular'.
sourceQuote: The general architecture and cellular composition of blood vessels are comparable throughout the cardiovascular system.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old female in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated mass on her gingiva. It bleeds easily with minor trauma. Histological examination shows a proliferation of capillaries with associated edema and an inflammatory infiltrate. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a benign, rapidly growing lesion often found on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.b: Glomus tumors are extremely painful and typically found under the fingernails, not the gingiva.
explanations.c: Capillary hemangiomas are common benign tumors but do not typically present as rapidly growing pedunculated masses in response to pregnancy hormones.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is associated with Bartonella infection in immunocompromised hosts.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant, aggressive tumor and is histologically characterized by significant atypia and necrosis, not simple capillary proliferation.

ankiCards: A pyogenic granuloma on the gingiva of a pregnant woman is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are histologically {{c1::lobular capillary hemangiomas}}.
Pyogenic granulomas frequently {{c1::bleed}} with minor trauma.
True or False: Pyogenic granulomas are actually granulomas. {{c1::False}} (they are vascular proliferations).
Treatment for pyogenic granuloma usually involves {{c1::surgical excision}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is neither pyogenic nor a granuloma.
Commonly occurs on the skin, lips, or gingiva.
Strong association with pregnancy and trauma.
Rapid growth phase followed by stabilization.
Microscopically resembles exuberant granulation tissue.
microReview: Pregnancy + Gingival mass = Pyogenic Granuloma (Granuloma Gravidarum).
examinerTraps: Don't be fooled by the name 'pyogenic'—it doesn't mean there is an infection or pus formation.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 10-year-old child presents with a large, ill-defined mass on the side of the neck. Imaging suggests a multicystic lesion that is not connected to the venous system. The mass is excised, and pathology reveals large, dilated spaces lined by a single layer of endothelium and containing proteinaceous fluid with few lymphocytes. This lesion is most strongly associated with which of the following conditions?

explanations.a: The description matches a cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma), which is classically associated with Turner syndrome (45,XO) and Down syndrome.
explanations.b: Down syndrome can be associated with cystic hygroma, but Turner syndrome is the more classic board association for neck masses of this type.
explanations.c: Marfan syndrome is associated with cystic medial necrosis and aortic aneurysms, not cystic hygromas.
explanations.d: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) features multiple telangiectasias and AVMs.
explanations.e: Sturge-Weber syndrome features a port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) and leptomeningeal angiomas.

ankiCards: A {{c1::cystic hygroma}} is a cavernous lymphangioma typically found in the neck/axilla.
Cystic hygromas are associated with {{c1::Turner}} syndrome.
Histologically, lymphangiomas contain {{c1::proteinaceous fluid (chyle/lymph)}} and no RBCs.
Cystic hygromas are difficult to excise because they lack a {{c1::capsule}}.
Unlike hemangiomas, lymphangiomas lack {{c1::red blood cells}} in the vessel lumens.
keyPoints: Cystic hygroma is a type of cavernous lymphangioma.
Commonly found in the neck or axilla of children.
Strong association with chromosomal aneuploidies (Turner Syndrome).
Histology: Dilated lymphatic channels lined by endothelium.
Infiltrative growth makes complete surgical removal difficult.
microReview: Cystic Hygroma = Lymphatic tumor + Neck + Turner Syndrome.
examinerTraps: Wait to see if the fluid contains RBCs. If it does, it's a cavernous hemangioma; if it's clear/proteinaceous, it's a lymphangioma.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with an exquisitely painful, small, firm, blue nodule under the nail of her index finger. The pain is triggered by cold temperature. Histology shows aggregates of specialized smooth muscle cells surrounding vascular channels. These cells originate from which of the following structures?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) arise from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.b: Pericytes are found in many vessels and give rise to hemangiopericytomas, but specifically subungual painful tumors are glomus tumors.
explanations.c: Endothelial progenitor cells give rise to most vascular tumors, but glomus tumors are unique in their smooth muscle origin.
explanations.d: Hassall corpuscles are found in the thymus.
explanations.e: Merkel cells are cutaneous neuroendocrine cells; they are not vascular.

ankiCards: A {{c1::glomus tumor}} is an exquisitely painful subungual tumor.
Glomus tumors arise from the {{c1::glomus body}}, which is involved in {{c2::thermoregulation}}.
The cells in a glomus tumor are modified {{c1::smooth muscle}} cells.
The classic triad for glomus tumor includes pain, tenderness, and sensitivity to {{c1::cold}}.
Histology of a glomus tumor shows nests of uniform round cells around {{c1::vascular channels}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but clinically distressing due to pain.
Most common location is the subungual (under nail) region.
Pain is often paroxysmal and triggered by cold.
Origin: Modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
Excision is curative.
microReview: Painful subungual nodule + Cold sensitivity = Glomus Tumor (Smooth muscle origin).
examinerTraps: The pain is the key giveaway. Most other benign vascular tumors (like hemangiomas) are painless.
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic due to a large, purple 'birthmark' covering the left side of his face in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve. The parents report that the child has recently had several seizures. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head shows an ipsilateral leptomeningeal angioma. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) is characterized by a facial port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) in the V1/V2 distribution and ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomas, often leading to seizures and glaucoma.
explanations.b: Von Hippel-Lindau disease features hemangioblastomas (CNS and retina), renal cell carcinoma, and pheochromocytoma.
explanations.c: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu) presents with skin/mucosal telangiectasias and AVMs, but not a large V1-distrubuted port-wine stain.
explanations.d: Neurofibromatosis type 1 features café-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules.
explanations.e: Tuberous sclerosis features ash-leaf spots, angiofibromas, and shagreen patches, as well as hamartomas like giant cell astrocytomas.

ankiCards: Sturge-Weber syndrome is associated with a {{c1::port-wine stain (nevus flammeus)}}.
The facial lesion in Sturge-Weber syndrome usually follows the distribution of the {{c1::trigeminal (CN V)}} nerve.
CNS involvement in Sturge-Weber consists of {{c1::leptomeningeal angiomas}}.
Common complications of Sturge-Weber include {{c1::seizures}}, mental retardation, and glaucoma.
The port-wine stain in Sturge-Weber syndrome is usually {{c1::ipsilateral}} to the brain lesion.
keyPoints: Sturge-Weber syndrome is a congenital (non-hereditary) disorder.
Caused by a somatic mutation in the GNAQ gene.
Classic triad: Facial port-wine stain, leptomeningeal angioma, glaucoma.
Port-wine stains do not regress (unlike strawberry hemangiomas).
Seizures often begin in infancy or early childhood.
microReview: Port-wine stain + CN V distribution + Seizures = Sturge-Weber Syndrome.
examinerTraps: Ensure the port-wine stain is in the V1/V2 distribution. Isolated nevus flammeus is common; it's the CNS/eye involvement that makes it Sturge-Weber.
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A biopsy of a skin lesion in an HIV-positive patient shows a proliferation of capillaries with prominent 'epithelioid' endothelial cells, a dense neutrophilic infiltrate, and nuclear dust (leukocytoclasis). Warthin-Starry silver stain reveals clusters of tangled bacilli. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella bacteria (henselae or quintana) and is characterized by capillary proliferation with neutrophils and visible bacilli on silver stain.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is viral (HHV-8) and lacks the neutrophilic infiltrate and bacterial organisms.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignancy with marked cytologic atypia and does not feature bacteria.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granulomas are benign lesions that do not contain Bartonella organisms.
explanations.e: Cherry hemangiomas are common benign senile vascular lesions without inflammation or infection.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
The silver stain used to identify Bartonella is {{c1::Warthin-Starry}}.
Histologically, bacillary angiomatosis features an infiltrate of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
{{c1::Bacillary angiomatosis}} is the main infectious differential for Kaposi Sarcoma.
In bacillary angiomatosis, Bartonella henselae is typically transmitted by {{c1::cats (cat scratch disease)}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis occurs in immunocompromised individuals.
Clinically mimics Kaposi sarcoma (red/purple papules).
Histology: Lobular vascular proliferation with neutrophils.
Diagnosis: Warthin-Starry silver stain shows bacilli.
Treatment: Erythromycin or doxycycline (curable, unlike KS).
microReview: HIV + Vascular lesion + Neutrophils + Silver stain (+) = Bacillary Angiomatosis.
examinerTraps: The primary trap is confusing this with Kaposi Sarcoma. Look for the presence of neutrophils and the result of the silver stain.
sourceQuote: Vascular structural specializations reflect distinct functional roles.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old worker at a plastics manufacturing plant for 30 years presents with weight loss and abdominal pain. Imaging shows multiple hemorrhagic masses within the liver. Biopsy shows an aggressive malignancy with malignant endothelial cells lining large, irregular vascular channels. Long-term exposure to which of the following substances is the most likely risk factor?

explanations.a: Exposure to vinyl chloride (used in PVC production) is a classic risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and lung cancer.
explanations.c: Benzene is associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.d: Aflatoxin B1 (from Aspergillus) is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), not angiosarcoma.
explanations.e: Beryllium exposure causes berylliosis (granulomatous lung disease) and is associated with lung cancer.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is linked to exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}} and {{c2::arsenic}}.
Vinyl chloride is used in the manufacturing of {{c1::polyvinyl chloride (PVC)}}.
Angiosarcoma cells are positive for the endothelial marker {{c1::CD31}}.
The prognosis for hepatic angiosarcoma is generally {{c1::poor/grave}}.
Unlike HCC, hepatic angiosarcoma arises from {{c1::endothelial cells}}, not hepatocytes.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare but highly lethal tumor.
Occupational exposure (vinyl chloride) is a major board association.
Arsenic (pesticides) and Thorotrast (radiocontrast) are other classic causes.
The tumor is highly invasive and often multicentric.
Distinguish from HCC (epithelial) by histology and IHC.
microReview: Vinyl chloride / Arsenic + Liver mass = Hepatic Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse hepatic angiosarcoma with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). HCC is associated with HBV/HCV and Aflatoxin; Angiosarcoma is associated with Vinyl Chloride.
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 2-week-old infant is brought in for a bright red, raised, 'strawberry-like' lesion on the scalp that appeared several days after birth. The parents are concerned about its growth. What is the most likely natural history of this lesion?

options.b: Growth proportional to the child's height
options.e: Rapid expansion leading to high-output heart failure

explanations.a: Infantile (strawberry) hemangiomas are extremely common, grow rapidly for a few months, and then typically involute spontaneously by age 7 to 9.
explanations.b: This describes a nevus flammeus (port-wine stain), which grows with the child.
explanations.c: Benign infantile hemangiomas do not transform into malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.d: This describes cavernous hemangiomas or port-wine stains, which do not regress.
explanations.e: While very large hemangiomas can theoretically cause heart failure (Kasabach-Merritt syndrome), most strawberry hemangiomas follow a benign course of regression.

ankiCards: A {{c1::strawberry (infantile)}} hemangioma is a common benign tumor of infancy.
Strawberry hemangiomas typically appear {{c1::after birth}} and grow rapidly.
The majority of strawberry hemangiomas {{c1::involute/regress}} spontaneously by early childhood.
Strawberry hemangiomas are histologically {{c1::capillary}} hemangiomas.
Unlike strawberry hemangiomas, port-wine stains {{c1::do not}} regress.
keyPoints: Infantile hemangiomas are the most common tumor of infancy.
Usually single, but can be multiple.
Natural history: Rapid growth -> plateau -> involution.
Most disappear by age 7; 90% by age 9.
Usually managed with observation unless they obstruct vision or airway.
microReview: Strawberry hemangioma = Infant + Rapid growth + Spontaneous regression.
examinerTraps: Distinguish between 'strawberry' (regresses) and 'port-wine' (permanent/grows with child) hemangiomas.
sourceQuote: Arterial wall thickness gradually diminishes as the vessels become smaller, but the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old male with advanced HIV (CD4+ count 85 cells/mm³) presents with multiple painless, dark purple, maculopapular lesions on his lower extremities and hard palate. Skin biopsy reveals sheets of spindle-shaped cells forming slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated erythrocytes. Which of the following is the most likely causative agent for this patient's condition?

explanations.a: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised patients, which presents with similar red/purple nodules, but histologically shows lobular capillary proliferation with neutrophils and nuclear atypia, not slit-like spaces.
explanations.b: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of Kaposi sarcoma. The histology of slit-like spaces and spindle cells is pathognomonic.
explanations.c: Human papillomavirus 16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx, not vascular tumors.
explanations.d: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with various lymphomas (e.g., Burkitt, CNS lymphoma) and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, but not vascular spindle-cell tumors.
explanations.e: Cytomegalovirus can cause retinitis or colitis in AIDS patients but does not drive the formation of vascular neoplasms.

ankiCards: The causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
The histological hallmark of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells with slit-like vascular spaces}}.
The classic clinical presentation of AIDS-associated Kaposi Sarcoma involves {{c1::purple skin nodules and oral lesions}}.
Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by {{c1::Bartonella species}} and mimics Kaposi Sarcoma.
The presence of {{c1::extravasated red blood cells}} is a common histological finding in Kaposi Sarcoma.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor caused by HHV-8.
It manifests in four forms: Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
Histology shows spindle cells, slit-like spaces, and prominent extravasated RBCs.
Oral involvement (palate) is highly suggestive of the AIDS-associated form.
Treatment involves HAART (highly active antiretroviral therapy) for HIV-related cases.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma (HHV-8) presents as purple plaques/nodules. Histology: Spindle cells and slit-like vascular channels. Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella) presents similarly but has neutrophilic inflammation.
examinerTraps: Distinguishing Kaposi Sarcoma from Bacillary Angiomatosis. Look for the presence of neutrophils (Bartonella) vs. spindle cells and slit-like spaces (HHV-8).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular tumors is characterized as a benign, exquisitely painful subungual lesion arising from modified smooth muscle cells involved in thermoregulation?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are common skin/mucosal lesions but are generally painless and composed of small vessels.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, blood-filled spaces and are typically asymptomatic, often occurring in the liver.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign but very painful tumors arising from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, usually found under the fingernails.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a rapidly growing red nodule on skin or gingiva that bleeds easily; it is not specifically subungual or characteristically painful in this manner.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor, usually occurring in older adults on the head and neck; it does not arise from glomus bodies.

ankiCards: The cell of origin for a Glomus tumor is the {{c1::modified smooth muscle cell}}.
A painful tumor found specifically under the fingernails is most likely a {{c1::Glomus tumor}}.
Glomus bodies are specialized vascular structures involved in {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Is a Glomus tumor benign or malignant? {{c1::Benign}}.
Glomus tumors present with the clinical triad of paroxysmal pain, localized tenderness, and {{c1::sensitivity to cold}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors arise from specialized arteriovenous shunts (glomus bodies).
They are benign but clinically significant due to intense pain.
Location is classically subungual (under the nail bed).
The glomus body's physiological role is thermoregulation via blood flow control.
Histology shows nests of uniform round cells surrounding vascular channels.
microReview: Glomus tumor: Painful, subungual, modified smooth muscle cells (glomus cells). Benign.
examinerTraps: Confusing Glomus tumor with a subungual melanoma. Glomus tumors are exquisitely painful and usually small/red-blue, while melanoma is often pigmented and painless.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with several enlarging, poorly defined, violaceous nodules on her left arm. Ten years ago, she underwent a radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection and radiotherapy for breast adenocarcinoma. Since then, she has had persistent, severe lymphedema of the left arm. What is the most likely diagnosis for the new skin lesions?

explanations.a: Cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) are typically congenital and found in the necks of children, not arising from adult lymphedema.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation in HIV patients, not associated with chronic lymphedema.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy) is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome. It is a highly aggressive malignant vascular tumor.
explanations.d: Hemangiopericytoma (now often classified under solitary fibrous tumors) arises from pericytes and does not show this specific association with chronic lymphedema.
explanations.e: Blue rubber bleb nevus syndrome involves multiple cavernous hemangiomas, usually in the GI tract and skin; it is not related to lymphedema.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising from chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
Angiosarcomas are often positive for the endothelial marker {{c1::CD31}}.
Classic risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma include {{c1::Vinyl chloride}}, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
Angiosarcoma is a {{c1::malignant}} vascular tumor.
Radiotherapy is a known risk factor for the development of {{c1::Angiosarcoma}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms.
Stewart-Treves syndrome occurs in the setting of chronic lymphedema.
Common sites include skin (head/neck), breast, and liver.
They carry a poor prognosis due to high rates of local recurrence and metastasis.
Endothelial markers (CD31, vWF) help confirm the diagnosis.
microReview: Angiosarcoma: Malignant, associated with chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves), radiation, or specific chemicals (liver). High mortality.
examinerTraps: The examiner might offer 'Recurrent Breast Cancer' as a distractor. While possible, the combination of chronic lymphedema and new violaceous nodules strongly points toward Stewart-Treves (Angiosarcoma).
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels... arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 1-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for a rapidly growing, bright red, raised 'strawberry' lesion on the scalp. The parents are concerned about its appearance. Which of the following best describes the most likely natural history of this lesion?

options.a: Permanent persistence with growth proportional to the child
options.b: Malignant transformation into angiosarcoma by age 5
options.d: Progressive infiltration into the underlying skull

explanations.a: Port-wine stains (nevus flammeus) grow with the child and do not regress, but strawberry hemangiomas do.
explanations.b: Strawberry hemangiomas are benign and do not undergo malignant transformation.
explanations.c: Juvenile (strawberry) capillary hemangiomas are very common in newborns, grow rapidly for a few months, and then usually regress completely by age 7 to 9.
explanations.d: These lesions are superficial and do not typically invade bone or deep structures.
explanations.e: They do not 'transform' into cavernous hemangiomas, which have distinct histology (larger, deeper vascular spaces).

ankiCards: A strawberry hemangioma is histologically a {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma.
The typical natural history of a juvenile hemangioma is {{c1::spontaneous regression}}.
The age range for regression of strawberry hemangiomas is usually {{c1::5 to 9}} years.
Strawberry hemangiomas are {{c1::benign}} vascular tumors.
The location of a strawberry hemangioma is most commonly the {{c1::skin (head/neck)}}.
keyPoints: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are the most common vascular tumor of childhood.
They are capillary hemangiomas by histology.
Rapid growth occurs in the first few weeks/months of life.
Regression is expected (75-90% by age 7).
Reassurance is the first-line management unless the lesion obstructs vision or airway.
microReview: Strawberry Hemangioma: Benign, infant, capillary type, regresses spontaneously.
examinerTraps: Confusing the strawberry hemangioma (regresses) with the Port-wine stain (permanent/nevus flammeus). Port-wine stains are associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome.
sourceQuote: The general architecture and cellular composition of blood vessels are comparable throughout the cardiovascular system. However, structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which endothelial cell marker is most useful for identifying poorly differentiated vascular tumors, such as high-grade angiosarcomas, during immunohistochemical staining?

explanations.a: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells and carcinomas.
explanations.b: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells (melanoma, Schwann cells).
explanations.c: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a highly specific marker for endothelial cells and is used to identify the vascular origin of poorly differentiated tumors.
explanations.d: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (skeletal, smooth, or cardiac).
explanations.e: Vimentin is a general marker for mesenchymal cells but is not specific to endothelial cells.

ankiCards: The most specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial cells is {{c1::CD31}}.
Another name for CD31 is {{c1::PECAM-1}}.
Angiosarcomas will typically stain positive for {{c1::CD31 or von Willebrand factor}}.
CD31 is used to differentiate vascular tumors from {{c1::carcinomas or melanomas}}.
Which marker is used to identify epithelial origin? {{c1::Cytokeratin}}.
keyPoints: CD31 (Platelet Endothelial Cell Adhesion Molecule) is expressed on all endothelial cells.
It is the 'gold standard' marker for vascular neoplasms.
Angiosarcomas may lose other markers but usually retain CD31.
Von Willebrand Factor (vWF) is also used but can be less sensitive in poorly differentiated cases.
Vascular tumors are mesenchymal in origin (Vimentin positive).
microReview: Marker for Vascular Tumors: CD31. Used for Angiosarcoma identification.
examinerTraps: Don't pick Vimentin; while it is positive in vascular tumors, it's also positive in almost all sarcomas. CD31 is specific to the 'vessel' part.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use presents with a rapidly growing, painful, red nodule on his right index finger. The lesion bleeds profusely with minor trauma. Histological examination shows a pedunculated mass with a lobulated proliferation of capillaries separated by edematous stroma. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis presents with similar vascular nodules but usually multiple lesions in an immunocompromised host, caused by Bartonella.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a rapidly growing, often pedunculated, red nodule on skin or gingiva that bleeds easily. The description is classic.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are very painful and subungual but do not typically bleed easily or appear pedunculated.
explanations.d: Kaposi sarcoma usually presents as multiple purple plaques/macules, not a single pedunculated bleeding nodule.
explanations.e: Nevus flammeus is a flat, birthmark-like vascular ectasia (e.g., port-wine stain).

ankiCards: A rapidly growing, bleeding red nodule on the skin or gingiva is a {{c1::pyogenic granuloma}}.
Is a pyogenic granuloma truly pyogenic (infectious)? {{c1::No (it is a misnomer)}}.
Pyogenic granuloma is histologically a {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are frequently associated with {{c1::trauma or pregnancy}} (granuloma gravidarum).
A common clinical feature of pyogenic granuloma is that it {{c1::bleeds easily}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign vascular lesion.
It is neither pyogenic (pus-forming) nor a true granuloma.
Commonly occurs after minor trauma or on the gingiva during pregnancy.
Histology: Lobulated capillary proliferation with edematous stroma.
Treatment is usually surgical excision or curettage.
microReview: Pyogenic Granuloma: Red, pedunculated, bleeds easily, lobular capillary proliferation. Associated with trauma/pregnancy.
examinerTraps: The name 'Pyogenic' implies infection and 'Granuloma' implies granulomatous inflammation; both are incorrect. It is a vascular tumor.
sourceQuote: Vascular Structure and Function... structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following conditions is characterized by a permanent vascular ectasia that presents at birth, typically on the face, and follows the distribution of the trigeminal nerve, often associated with leptomeningeal angiomas?

explanations.a: Spider telangiectasia consists of a central arteriole with radiating vessels, often associated with hyperestrogenism (pregnancy, cirrhosis).
explanations.b: Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) involves multiple small malformations of skin and mucous membranes, but not a large facial stain in a trigeminal distribution.
explanations.c: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a vascular ectasia. When it occurs in the V1/V2 distribution of the trigeminal nerve and is associated with CNS vascular malformations, it is called Sturge-Weber syndrome.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are deeper, blood-filled masses, not flat facial ectasias.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious lesion in HIV patients.

ankiCards: The clinical name for a port-wine stain is {{c1::nevus flammeus}}.
Sturge-Weber syndrome triad: Port-wine stain, {{c1::leptomeningeal angioma}}, and glaucoma.
Does a nevus flammeus regress spontaneously? {{c1::No}}.
The facial port-wine stain in Sturge-Weber syndrome follows the distribution of the {{c1::trigeminal nerve}}.
Nevus flammeus is categorized as a vascular {{c1::ectasia}} (not a true neoplasm).
keyPoints: Nevus flammeus is a congenital vascular ectasia (dilation).
Unlike strawberry hemangiomas, they do not regress and grow with the child.
Sturge-Weber syndrome involves V1/V2 distribution.
Associated with seizures, intellectual disability, and glaucoma.
Histology shows dilated dermal capillaries.
microReview: Nevus Flammeus: Port-wine stain. Permanent. Sturge-Weber = V1/V2 trigeminal + brain angiomas.
examinerTraps: Wait to see if the question mentions trigeminal distribution or regression. If it regresses, it's a strawberry hemangioma. If it's permanent and trigeminal, it's nevus flammeus.
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels... arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 52-year-old male with long-standing cirrhosis secondary to chronic hepatitis C presents with numerous small, red lesions on his chest and back. The lesions have a central red dot with fine, radiating vessels that blanch upon pressure. What is the underlying pathophysiological mechanism for these specific skin findings?

options.d: Loss of smooth muscle innervation in small arterioles
options.e: Congenital malformation of the capillary bed

explanations.a: Bartonella quintana causes bacillary angiomatosis, not spider telangiectasias.
explanations.b: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, which presents as nodules or plaques, not radiating telangiectasias.
explanations.c: Spider telangiectasias (spider angiomas) are associated with high estrogen levels. In cirrhosis, the liver cannot metabolize estrogen, leading to its accumulation and subsequent vascular dilation.
explanations.d: The dilation is hormonal, not due to primary autonomic neuropathy.
explanations.e: These are acquired lesions, not congenital.

ankiCards: Spider telangiectasias are commonly associated with the state of {{c1::hyperestrogenism}}.
Two common conditions associated with spider angiomas are {{c1::pregnancy and cirrhosis}}.
Do spider telangiectasias blanch when the central vessel is pressed? {{c1::Yes}}.
The 'spider' appearance is caused by radiating {{c1::capillaries/vessels}} from a central arteriole.
The location of spider telangiectasias is usually restricted to the {{c1::superior vena cava distribution (face, neck, chest)}}.
keyPoints: Spider telangiectasias are acquired vascular ectasias.
The central core is a small spiral arteriole.
Pathogenesis: High estrogen levels cause vasodilation.
Seen in liver failure (poor metabolism) and pregnancy (high production).
They are benign but serve as a clinical marker for underlying systemic disease.
microReview: Spider Angioma: Central arteriole, radiating legs, blanches. Caused by high estrogen (Cirrhosis/Pregnancy).
examinerTraps: Spider telangiectasias must be distinguished from the telangiectasias of Osler-Weber-Rendu, which are hereditary and found on mucous membranes (tongue, lips) and cause bleeding.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An autopsy performed on a 50-year-old male who died of unrelated causes reveals a well-circumscribed, 2-cm, dark-red, spongy mass in the right lobe of the liver. Histology shows large, dilated, blood-filled vascular spaces separated by thin fibrous stroma. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma is an infiltrative, malignant tumor with significant atypia, not a circumscribed spongy mass.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas involve small, narrow vascular channels, not large cavernous spaces.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas are the most common benign tumors of the liver. They are often incidental findings and consist of large, blood-filled spaces.
explanations.d: Hepatic adenomas are composed of hepatocytes, not vascular spaces.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is usually multiple small nodules in immunocompromised patients, not a large solitary hepatic mass.

ankiCards: The most common benign tumor of the liver is the {{c1::cavernous hemangioma}}.
Histology of cavernous hemangioma shows {{c1::large blood-filled spaces}} separated by fibrous stroma.
Are cavernous hemangiomas usually symptomatic? {{c1::No (incidental finding)}}.
A potential complication of a large cavernous hemangioma is {{c1::thrombosis or rupture}} (though rare).
How do cavernous hemangiomas differ from capillary hemangiomas? {{c1::Vessel size (large vs small channels)}}.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are common in the liver and spleen.
They are benign and usually asymptomatic.
Grossly, they appear as 'spongy' red-blue masses.
On imaging, they show peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill-in.
Biopsy is usually avoided due to the risk of hemorrhage.
microReview: Hepatic Cavernous Hemangioma: Most common benign liver tumor. Spongy, large blood spaces. Incidental.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse cavernous hemangioma with angiosarcoma. In the liver, angiosarcoma is rare and associated with toxic exposures, while cavernous hemangioma is extremely common and benign.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 35-year-old male with AIDS presents with fever and multiple red-to-purple skin papules. A biopsy of one lesion reveals a vascular proliferation with prominent, 'epitheloid' endothelial cells and an infiltrate of neutrophils. Warthin-Starry silver stain demonstrates clusters of small bacilli. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma does not show a neutrophilic infiltrate or positive Warthin-Starry staining for bacteria.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella species in immunocompromised patients. The histology shows vascular proliferation, neutrophils, and the bacteria are visible on Warthin-Starry stain.
explanations.c: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a vasculitis, not a vascular tumor, and involves granulomas and necrosis.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor with marked atypia and is not associated with Bartonella infection.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are painful subungual lesions, not associated with AIDS or bacteria.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by {{c1::Bartonella (henselae or quintana)}}.
The histological feature that distinguishes Bacillary Angiomatosis from Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::neutrophilic infiltrate}}.
The stain used to identify Bartonella in tissue is {{c1::Warthin-Starry (silver stain)}}.
Bacillary angiomatosis is most commonly seen in {{c1::immunocompromised/AIDS}} patients.
Does Bacillary angiomatosis respond to antibiotics? {{c1::Yes (e.g., erythromycin)}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis mimics Kaposi Sarcoma clinically.
It is an opportunistic infection, not a true primary neoplasm.
Causative organisms: B. henselae (cats) or B. quintana (lice).
Pathology: Proliferation of capillaries with 'epitheloid' endothelial cells and neutrophils.
Diagnosis: Warthin-Starry silver stain shows organisms.
microReview: Bacillary Angiomatosis: Bartonella, AIDS, Warthin-Starry+, Neutrophils. Treatable with antibiotics.
examinerTraps: The presence of 'neutrophils' in a vascular tumor vignette for an AIDS patient is the strongest clue for Bacillary Angiomatosis over Kaposi Sarcoma.
sourceQuote: VASCULAR STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION: The general architecture and cellular composition of blood vessels are comparable throughout the cardiovascular system.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular pathologies typically manifest through two primary pathological mechanisms. Which of the following processes characterizes the underlying mechanism responsible for the formation of an aneurysm?

options.a: Precipitous luminal obstruction by embolic debris
options.b: Progressive stenosis due to cholesterol deposition
options.c: Weakening of the vessel wall leading to dilation
options.d: Hypertrophic remodeling of the tunica media
options.e: Endothelial cell apoptosis causing capillary leak

explanations.a: This describes embolic obstruction, which leads to ischemia or infarction, not the dilation seen in aneurysms.
explanations.b: This describes the mechanism of atherosclerosis and stenosis, which restricts blood flow rather than causing wall dilation.
explanations.c: Aneurysms occur when the structural integrity of the vessel wall is compromised, leading to permanent abnormal dilation or rupture.
explanations.d: Hypertrophic remodeling is more characteristic of the response to hypertension, which may eventually lead to narrowing rather than aneurysmal dilation.
explanations.e: Endothelial apoptosis and capillary leak describe inflammatory or microvascular pathologies, not the macro-vascular structural failure seen in aneurysms.

ankiCards: The two principal mechanisms underlying vascular disease are narrowing (stenosis) and {{c1::weakening of vessel walls}}.
Weakening of vessel walls in vascular disease leads to either {{c1::dilation}} or rupture.
Aneurysms are primarily the result of the {{c1::weakening}} of vessel walls.
Vascular stenosis can occur progressively via {{c1::atherosclerosis}} or precipitously via thrombosis.
In contrast to veins, arterial walls are thicker to accommodate {{c1::pulsatile flow}} and higher pressures.
keyPoints: Vascular disease morbidity is primarily driven by luminal obstruction or wall weakening.
Weakening of the vessel wall is the fundamental mechanical failure in aneurysm formation.
Aneurysms can lead to rupture, a life-threatening complication.
Pathogenesis involves structural degradation of the tunica media or adventitia.
Dilation is a progressive process once wall integrity is lost.
microReview: Aneurysms result from structural failure. While narrowing (stenosis) limits blood flow, weakening allows the vessel to expand under pressure, potentially leading to rupture. This is distinct from obstructive processes like thrombosis or embolism.
examinerTraps: Atherosclerosis is a major *cause* of the wall weakening that leads to an aneurysm, but the *mechanism* of the aneurysm itself is the wall weakness/dilation, not the stenosis.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: A 67-year-old male presents for a routine physical examination. He has a 40-pack-year smoking history and long-standing hypertension. During palpation of the abdomen, a prominent, pulsatile mass is noted at the level of the umbilicus. Imaging reveals a localized 5.5 cm dilation of the infrarenal aorta. Which of the following is the most likely primary contributor to this patient's condition?

explanations.a: Cystic medial degeneration is more commonly associated with thoracic aortic aneurysms and Marfan syndrome, rather than infrarenal abdominal aneurysms.
explanations.b: Atherosclerosis is the most common cause of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA), particularly in older male smokers.
explanations.c: Tertiary syphilis classically causes obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum in the ascending/thoracic aorta, not the infrarenal abdominal aorta.
explanations.d: While certain vasculitides like Takayasu can affect the aorta, they are less common causes of infrarenal pulsatile masses in elderly smokers than atherosclerosis.
explanations.e: Fibromuscular dysplasia typically affects the renal or carotid arteries and results in stenosis ('string of beads'), not large abdominal aortic aneurysms.

ankiCards: The most common cause of an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
A pulsatile abdominal mass in an elderly smoker is highly suggestive of {{c1::abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA)}}.
AAA usually occurs at the {{c1::infrarenal}} level of the aorta.
Risk factors for AAA include smoking, male sex, and {{c1::hypertension}}.
The anatomical distribution of atherosclerosis mainly involves {{c1::elastic and muscular}} arteries.
keyPoints: Atherosclerosis involves the elastic and muscular arteries.
Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are frequently associated with atherosclerosis.
Smoking is a major modifiable risk factor for AAA.
A pulsatile mass is a classic clinical finding for AAA.
AAA commonly occurs between the renal arteries and the aortic bifurcation.
microReview: Atherosclerosis weakens the media by inducing inflammation and obstructing the diffusion of nutrients from the lumen to the vessel wall, leading to the infrarenal dilation known as an AAA.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the location; AAA is usually infrarenal (atherosclerosis-related), while TAA (Thoracic) is often associated with hypertension or Marfan syndrome (cystic medial necrosis).
sourceQuote: atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: Which layer of the arterial wall is most critical in maintaining structural integrity against high pulsatile pressures and is the primary site of structural failure in aneurysm formation?

explanations.a: The intima is the innermost layer involved in signaling and atherosclerosis initiation, but it does not provide the primary structural strength of the vessel.
explanations.b: The internal elastic lamina is a thin layer separating the intima and media; it is not the main structural component.
explanations.c: The tunica media, composed of smooth muscle cells and elastic fibers, provides the tensile strength and elasticity needed to withstand blood pressure; its degradation is central to aneurysm formation.
explanations.d: The external elastic lamina is a boundary layer between the media and adventitia, providing some support but less than the bulk of the media.
explanations.e: The adventitia contains collagen and the vasa vasorum, providing external support, but the media's elastic properties are what primarily resist the pulsatile pressure of the heart.

ankiCards: Arterial walls are thicker than veins to accommodate {{c1::pulsatile flow}}.
The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}} as arteries become smaller.
Muscular vessels exert control over blood flow and {{c1::pressure}}.
The layer responsible for the tensile strength of the artery is the {{c1::tunica media}}.
Aneurysms involve the {{c1::weakening}} of the vessel wall layers.
keyPoints: Arteries have thicker walls than veins of the same level.
Media thickness correlates with the pressure the vessel must withstand.
Aneurysms represent a failure of the media's structural components.
Elasticity in large arteries allows for pulsatile flow dampening.
Muscular arteries regulate peripheral resistance and pressure.
microReview: The tunica media is the 'workhorse' of the arterial wall. In aneurysms, the loss of smooth muscle cells and degradation of elastic fibers within the media lead to the characteristic bulge.
examinerTraps: A common trap is assuming the adventitia is the strongest layer because it is the outermost; however, the media provides the primary resistance to pulsatile arterial pressure.
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: The stereotyped response to vascular injury, which may paradoxically contribute to vessel wall weakening or narrowing depending on the stimulus, is characterized by which of the following cellular events?

options.c: Intimal thickening via smooth muscle cell migration

explanations.a: Endothelial cells may become activated, but hypertrophy is not the hallmark of the stereotyped injury response.
explanations.b: While medial thinning occurs in aneurysms, the 'stereotyped response to injury' specifically refers to intimal changes.
explanations.c: Intimal thickening is the universal, stereotyped response of the vessel wall to any insult, involving smooth muscle cell migration from the media to the intima and extracellular matrix synthesis.
explanations.d: Adventitial degradation is associated with aneurysm expansion but is not the defined 'stereotyped response to injury'.
explanations.e: Internal elastic lamina fragmentation (not duplication) is often seen in injury, but intimal thickening is the primary proliferative response.

ankiCards: The stereotyped response to vascular injury is {{c1::intimal thickening}}.
Intimal thickening involves the migration of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} from the media to the intima.
Following injury, smooth muscle cells in the intima synthesize {{c1::extracellular matrix}}.
Vascular injury response is a common feature in both {{c1::atherosclerosis}} and hypertensive vascular disease.
Aneurysms involve wall {{c1::weakening}}, whereas stenosis involves luminal {{c1::narrowing}}.
keyPoints: Intimal thickening is the standard response to any vascular insult.
Smooth muscle cells change from a contractile to a synthetic phenotype.
This process can lead to luminal narrowing.
Injury can be mechanical (stent), chemical (hyperlipidemia), or hemodynamic (hypertension).
The resulting 'neointima' lacks the same regulatory properties as the original intima.
microReview: Whenever an artery is injured, smooth muscle cells migrate from the media into the intima and proliferate, creating a 'neointima'. This is the basic pathophysiology behind both atherosclerosis and the restenosis that follows balloon angioplasty or stenting.
examinerTraps: Students often confuse 'injury response' (which is proliferative/thickening) with 'aneurysm pathogenesis' (which is degradative/thinning). Intimal thickening is the repair attempt.
sourceQuote: Intimal Thickening: A Stereotyped Response to Vascular Injury
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: A 54-year-old female with a history of uncontrolled hypertension for 20 years presents with sudden-onset, 'tearing' chest pain that radiates to her back. Blood pressure is 190/110 mmHg. An urgent CT angiogram shows a longitudinal intraluminal tear in the ascending aorta, creating a false lumen. Which of the following best describes the fundamental pathological event occurring in this patient?

options.a: Dilation of all three layers of the vessel wall
options.b: Focal rupture of the tunica adventitia
options.c: Separation of the laminar planes of the media by blood
options.e: Autoimmune destruction of the internal elastic lamina

explanations.a: This describes a true aneurysm, not a dissection. Dissection involves blood entering the wall, not just a dilation.
explanations.b: Rupture of the adventitia would lead to exsanguination into the mediastinum or pericardium, not a false lumen.
explanations.c: Aortic dissection occurs when blood enters the media through an intimal tear and cleaves the laminar planes of the media.
explanations.d: While atherosclerosis can cause aneurysms, 'tearing' pain and a 'false lumen' are the hallmarks of aortic dissection, which is primarily associated with hypertension and medial weakness.
explanations.e: This describes certain types of vasculitis (like Giant Cell Arteritis), not the mechanical failure of a dissection.

ankiCards: Aortic dissection is characterized by the separation of the {{c1::media}} layers by blood.
The most common risk factor for aortic dissection is {{c1::hypertension}}.
A clinical hallmark of aortic dissection is sudden-onset {{c1::tearing}} chest pain.
In a dissection, blood enters through an intimal tear to form a {{c1::false lumen}}.
Dissection is distinct from an aneurysm because it involves {{c1::splitting of the wall}} rather than just dilation.
keyPoints: Aortic dissection is not a 'true' aneurysm but a separate pathological entity.
Hypertension is the leading risk factor for dissection.
The 'false lumen' is created within the tunica media.
Classic presentation: sudden, tearing pain radiating to the back.
Proximal (Type A) dissections are surgical emergencies.
microReview: Dissection = Blood *between* layers (usually media). Aneurysm = Dilation of *all* layers. Hypertension causes the medial degeneration (ischemia of the media due to vasa vasorum hyaline thickening) that predisposes to the tear.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Aortic Dissection with Aortic Aneurysm. While they share risk factors like hypertension, dissection involves the creation of a new channel (false lumen) within the media.
sourceQuote: Aneurysms and Dissection
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: Which of the following classes of blood vessels is the primary site for the development of atherosclerotic-related aneurysms?

explanations.a: Arterioles are the primary site of blood pressure regulation and are affected by hyaline or hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis, but not large aneurysms.
explanations.b: Capillaries consist only of an endothelial layer and basement membrane; they do not develop aneurysms or atherosclerosis.
explanations.c: Venous disorders are mentioned as 'not inconsequential,' but veins do not develop atherosclerosis or high-pressure aneurysms.
explanations.d: Atherosclerosis predominantly affects elastic and muscular arteries (e.g., aorta, iliacs), which are the main sites for aneurysmal dilation.
explanations.e: Post-capillary venules are the main site of leukocyte extravasation in inflammation, not atherosclerosis or aneurysms.

ankiCards: Atherosclerosis affects mainly {{c1::elastic and muscular}} arteries.
The primary mechanism of vascular disease involving narrowing is {{c1::stenosis}}.
Arterial walls are thicker to accommodate {{c1::higher blood pressures}}.
The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter is highest in {{c1::muscular}} vessels.
Vascular pathology is responsible for more {{c1::morbidity and mortality}} than any other disease category.
keyPoints: Atherosclerosis is a disease of large (elastic) and medium (muscular) arteries.
Aneurysms are most common in the aorta (elastic) and its major branches.
The structure of the vessel determines its susceptibility to specific diseases.
Venous walls are thinner because they operate under lower pressure.
Elastic arteries damp the pulsatility of cardiac output.
microReview: The high pressure and specific flow dynamics of elastic and muscular arteries make them the targets for atherosclerosis, which weakens the underlying media, paving the way for aneurysm formation.
examinerTraps: Be careful with 'arterioles' vs 'arteries'. Atherosclerosis is an *artery* disease. Arteriolosclerosis (hyaline/hyperplastic) is an *arteriole* disease associated with hypertension and diabetes.
sourceQuote: atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: A 72-year-old man with a long history of tobacco use presents to the emergency department with sudden, severe abdominal and back pain, followed by a brief loss of consciousness. On arrival, his blood pressure is 80/50 mmHg. Examination reveals a large, tender, pulsatile abdominal mass. What is the most immediate life-threatening complication of this patient's suspected diagnosis?

options.e: Compression of the inferior vena cava

explanations.a: While mural thrombi often form in aneurysms, embolization causes limb ischemia, not the acute hypotension seen here.
explanations.b: Renal artery stenosis causes hypertension, not the acute catastrophic shock described.
explanations.c: Rupture of an AAA leads to massive retroperitoneal or intraperitoneal hemorrhage and is the primary cause of death in these patients.
explanations.d: A mycotic aneurysm (infected) is possible but the presentation of shock and a pulsatile mass in a smoker points toward a classic AAA rupture.
explanations.e: Compression of the IVC can cause leg edema but is not an immediate cause of fatal hemorrhagic shock.

ankiCards: The most serious complication of an abdominal aortic aneurysm is {{c1::rupture}}.
Aneurysmal rupture leads to massive {{c1::hemorrhage}}.
The triad of AAA rupture is hypotension, back pain, and a {{c1::pulsatile mass}}.
Mural thrombi in aneurysms can lead to {{c1::embolization}}.
Aneurysms represent a failure of the vessel wall resulting in {{c1::dilation}}.
keyPoints: Aneurysm rupture risk is directly proportional to its diameter.
Rupture often presents as a surgical emergency with shock.
Smoking is the strongest predictor of aneurysm growth and rupture.
Aneurysms commonly contain mural thrombus due to turbulent flow.
Mortality for a ruptured AAA is extremely high (>50%).
microReview: Once an aneurysm dilates beyond a certain point (typically >5cm), the wall stress increases significantly (LaPlace's Law), leading to the catastrophic 'weakening' and 'rupture' mentioned in the text.
examinerTraps: The presence of a mural thrombus is common in AAA, but the *sudden shock* specifically indicates rupture, not embolism.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: Which structural specialization allows muscular arteries to effectively exert control over blood flow and systemic blood pressure?

options.a: Presence of a thick internal elastic lamina
options.b: High ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter
options.c: Densely packed vasa vasorum in the media

explanations.a: While present, the thickness of the elastic lamina alone doesn't grant the control over pressure that the muscular media provides.
explanations.b: The text states that the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases in smaller muscular vessels, allowing them to control flow and pressure.
explanations.c: Vasa vasorum are found in the adventitia and outer media of large elastic arteries (like the aorta) but are less prominent in smaller muscular arteries.
explanations.d: Intimal fibroblasts are associated with pathological injury responses, not normal hemodynamic control.
explanations.e: Arteries do not have valves; valves are a characteristic of veins and lymphatics.

ankiCards: Arteries have a higher ratio of wall thickness to {{c1::lumen diameter}} as they get smaller.
Muscular arteries exert control over {{c1::blood flow}} and pressure.
Structural specializations of vessels reflect their distinct {{c1::functional roles}}.
Unlike arteries, veins have {{c1::thinner}} walls at the same level of branching.
Many vascular disorders have characteristic {{c1::anatomic distributions}}.
keyPoints: Vessel architecture matches functional requirements.
Thick walls in arteries handle high pressure and pulsatile flow.
The wall-to-lumen ratio is critical for the resistance-vessel function.
Pathology is often vessel-type specific.
Smooth muscle in the media is the effector of vessel diameter control.
microReview: The geometry of muscular arteries (thick media relative to a small lumen) allows for significant changes in resistance with even minor smooth muscle contraction, thus regulating blood pressure.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'elastic' arteries (aorta) which dampen pulsatility, with 'muscular' arteries (small-medium) which regulate resistance and pressure.
sourceQuote: the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing these muscular vessels to exert control over blood flow and pressure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: In the context of vascular structure and pathology, why are the most clinically significant lesions found in arteries rather than veins?

options.a: Arteries lack the protective intimal layer found in veins
options.b: Venous walls are thicker and more resistant to structural failure
options.c: Arteries are subjected to higher pressures and pulsatile flow
options.d: Veins possess higher concentrations of smooth muscle in the media
options.e: Arterial endothelial cells have lower regenerative capacity

explanations.a: Both arteries and veins have an intima; arteries are actually more structurally robust.
explanations.b: The text explicitly states that arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins to accommodate higher pressures.
explanations.c: The high-pressure environment of the arterial system (pulsatile flow) predisposes arteries to significant lesions like atherosclerosis and aneurysms.
explanations.d: False; arteries have significantly more smooth muscle in the tunica media than veins.
explanations.e: There is no evidence that arterial endothelium regenerates less effectively; the pathology is driven by hemodynamic and metabolic stress.

ankiCards: The most clinically significant vascular lesions involve {{c1::arteries}}.
Arterial walls are thicker than veins to handle {{c1::pulsatile flow}}.
Venous disorders are described as {{c1::not inconsequential}} but less significant than arterial ones.
Vascular pathology causes more {{c1::morbidity}} than any other disease category.
Structure and composition of vessels are {{c1::comparable}} but specialized throughout the system.
keyPoints: Arteries operate under high mechanical stress.
Pressure differences dictate the difference in wall thickness between arteries and veins.
Pulsatile flow requires the elastic properties of large arteries.
Morbidity is higher in arterial disease due to ischemia and rupture risk.
Aneurysms are essentially a phenomenon of the high-pressure arterial system.
microReview: The arterial system's high pressure is a 'double-edged sword': it is necessary for perfusion but creates the mechanical stress that drives atherosclerosis and aneurysm formation.
examinerTraps: A common mistake is thinking veins are more prone to pathology because they are 'weaker' (thinner). However, the *significant* morbidity comes from the arterial side due to the pressures involved.
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: Which of the following describes the difference between progressive narrowing and precipitous obstruction of a vessel lumen as discussed in the pathogenesis of vascular disease?

options.a: Narrowing is caused by thrombi; obstruction is caused by atherosclerosis
options.b: Narrowing is caused by atherosclerosis; obstruction is caused by thrombosis
options.c: Narrowing is caused by wall dilation; obstruction is caused by wall thinning
options.d: Narrowing is always inflammatory; obstruction is always traumatic
options.e: Narrowing is reversible; obstruction is always permanent

explanations.a: This is inverted; atherosclerosis is typically a slow, progressive process.
explanations.b: Atherosclerosis causes progressive narrowing (stenosis), while thrombosis or embolism causes sudden, precipitous obstruction.
explanations.c: Dilation and thinning refer to aneurysms, not the mechanisms of luminal narrowing.
explanations.d: Atherosclerosis has inflammatory components, but thrombosis is not necessarily traumatic (it's often a complication of plaque rupture).
explanations.e: Neither is strictly reversible in most clinical contexts, and obstruction (like a clot) can be lysed by medication.

ankiCards: Progressive narrowing of vessel lumens is often caused by {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Precipitous obstruction of vessel lumens is caused by {{c1::thrombosis or embolism}}.
Two mechanisms of vascular disease: narrowing/obstruction and {{c1::weakening of walls}}.
Vascular pathology is responsible for more {{c1::mortality}} than any other disease category.
Aneurysms belong to the category of {{c1::weakening}} of vessel walls.
keyPoints: Atherosclerosis is the prototype of progressive luminal narrowing.
Thrombosis and embolism are mechanisms of acute vascular occlusion.
Luminal obstruction leads to downstream ischemia.
Vascular wall weakening leads to aneurysms and rupture.
The clinical presentation (chronic vs. acute) depends on the speed of the obstruction.
microReview: Vascular disease is simple at its core: the pipe either gets clogged (stenosis/obstruction) or the pipe bursts (weakening/aneurysm). Atherosclerosis can actually lead to both.
examinerTraps: Note that atherosclerosis can cause *both* progressive narrowing (by growing the plaque) and sudden obstruction (if the plaque ruptures and triggers a thrombus).
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism)
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: A 42-year-old male with a history of poorly controlled HIV (CD4+ count of 120 cells/mm³) presents with multiple, painless, violaceous macules and plaques on his lower extremities and hard palate. A biopsy of a skin lesion shows proliferation of spindle-shaped cells forming slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells. Which of the following infectious agents is the primary driver of this patient's pathology?

explanations.a: HHV-6 is associated with Roseola infantum, not vascular tumors.
explanations.b: HHV-8 (also known as KSHV) is the causative agent of Kaposi sarcoma, which presents as violaceous lesions in immunocompromised patients, characterized by spindle cells and slit-like vascular spaces.
explanations.c: EBV is associated with various lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, but not vascular tumors.
explanations.d: CMV causes retinitis and colitis in HIV patients but does not lead to primary vascular neoplasms.
explanations.e: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can look similar clinically but is characterized by neutrophilic infiltrates and the presence of bacteria on Warthin-Starry stain, rather than the spindle cells of Kaposi sarcoma.

ankiCards: Kaposi sarcoma is strongly associated with infection by {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
The histological hallmark of Kaposi sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells}} forming {{c2::slit-like}} vascular spaces.
The four clinical forms of Kaposi sarcoma are {{c1::Classic (European)}}, {{c2::Endemic (African)}}, {{c3::Transplant-associated}}, and {{c4::AIDS-associated}}.
In Kaposi sarcoma, slit-like spaces typically contain {{c1::extravasated red blood cells}}.
Immunohistochemical staining for {{c1::LANA-1}} can confirm the presence of HHV-8 in Kaposi sarcoma lesions.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma is a borderline/intermediate vascular tumor caused by HHV-8.
It manifests in four clinical settings: Classic, Endemic, Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
Malignant cells are spindle-shaped and derived from endothelial cells.
The hard palate and lower extremities are common sites of involvement.
Histology shows slit-like spaces with RBCs and hemosiderin deposits.
microReview: Kaposi sarcoma = HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Slit-like spaces. Bacillary angiomatosis = Bartonella + Neutrophils + Warthin-Starry stain.
examinerTraps: Confusing Bacillary angiomatosis (bacterial) with Kaposi sarcoma (viral); both occur in AIDS but histology differs significantly.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors... can be benign (e.g., hemangioma), intermediate (e.g., Kaposi sarcoma), or highly malignant (e.g., angiosarcoma).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 35-year-old female presents with an exquisitely painful, small (5 mm), red-blue nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. The pain is particularly triggered by exposure to cold temperatures. Which of the following is the most likely cell of origin for this lesion?

explanations.a: Fibroblasts are the origin of fibromas, not painful subungual vascular lesions.
explanations.b: While it is a vascular lesion, the specific glomus tumor arises from the specialized contractile cells, not standard endothelium.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, which is a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.d: Pericytes are the origin of hemangiopericytomas, which are typically larger and not characteristically subungual and cold-sensitive.
explanations.e: Lymphatic endothelium gives rise to lymphangiomas, which are painless and usually occur in the neck or axilla.

ankiCards: A {{c1::glomus tumor}} is an exquisitely painful subungual vascular tumor.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle cells}} of the glomus body.
The classic location for a glomus tumor is the {{c1::subungual (under the nail)}} region.
Pain in a glomus tumor is often triggered by {{c1::cold}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors show nests of {{c1::uniform round cells}} surrounding vascular spaces.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but extremely painful.
They occur most commonly in the distal digits, especially subungual.
They originate from the glomus body (thermoregulatory A-V shunt).
Cells are specialized, modified smooth muscle cells.
Excision is usually curative.
microReview: Painful subungual nodule + cold sensitivity = Glomus Tumor (Smooth muscle origin).
examinerTraps: Choosing endothelial cell as the origin because it is a vascular tumor; glomus tumors are unique for their smooth muscle origin.
sourceQuote: Glomus tumors... are very painful tumors that arise from specialized smooth muscle cells of glomus bodies, arteriovenous structures involved in thermoregulation.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with several firm, enlarging, dark red to purple nodules on her right arm. Ten years prior, she underwent a radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection and radiotherapy for breast adenocarcinoma. She has had persistent lymphedema of the right arm since the surgery. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is HHV-8 related and usually associated with HIV or classic elderly European presentations, not chronic lymphedema.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is infectious (Bartonella) and seen in immunocompromised states.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma occurring in the setting of chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy) is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome. It is a highly malignant tumor.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign, stable lesions, not aggressive nodules arising in lymphedema.
explanations.e: Pyogenic granulomas are small, fast-growing benign polyps of the skin or oral mucosa, often related to trauma or pregnancy.

ankiCards: {{c1::Angiosarcoma}} is a malignant vascular tumor associated with chronic lymphedema.
The development of angiosarcoma in a post-mastectomy lymphedematous arm is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
Risk factors for angiosarcoma include {{c1::radiation}}, {{c2::vinyl chloride}}, and {{c3::arsenic}}.
Angiosarcomas are immunohistochemically positive for the endothelial marker {{c1::CD31}}.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is specifically associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignant endothelial neoplasm.
Stewart-Treves syndrome is angiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphedema.
Commonly involves the skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Histology shows pleomorphic malignant cells forming irregular vascular channels.
Poor prognosis with high rates of metastasis.
microReview: Post-mastectomy + Lymphedema + New skin nodules = Stewart-Treves (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: Assuming the new nodules are metastatic breast cancer; in the setting of long-term lymphedema, angiosarcoma must be suspected.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas... can also occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema, classically in the ipsilateral arm of women who have undergone radical mastectomy.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An infant is born with a bright red, 'strawberry-like' raised lesion on the scalp. The parents are concerned as the lesion grows rapidly during the first few months of life. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this lesion?

explanations.a: Surgical excision is unnecessary and can cause scarring; these lesions usually regress.
explanations.b: Wide margins are for malignant tumors; this is a benign juvenile hemangioma.
explanations.c: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas characteristically grow for a few months and then spontaneously involute by age 7 to 10.
explanations.d: Chemotherapy is not indicated for benign hemangiomas.
explanations.e: Radiation is contraindicated due to the risk of secondary malignancies in children.

ankiCards: The common name for a juvenile hemangioma is a {{c1::strawberry}} hemangioma.
Juvenile hemangiomas usually {{c1::regress/involute}} spontaneously by age 7.
Histologically, juvenile hemangiomas are classified as {{c1::capillary}} hemangiomas.
True or False: Most strawberry hemangiomas require surgery. {{c1::False}}
The growth phase of a strawberry hemangioma occurs in the {{c1::first few months}} of life.
keyPoints: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are very common in newborns.
They are a subtype of capillary hemangioma.
Clinical course: Rapid growth followed by gradual involution.
75% completely disappear by age 7.
Conservative 'watch and wait' management is standard.
microReview: Infant + Strawberry lesion = Juvenile hemangioma = Regression expected.
examinerTraps: Suggesting aggressive treatment (surgery/laser) immediately; unless it obstructs vision or airway, observation is correct.
sourceQuote: Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) of the skin of newborns... grow rapidly for a few months but then fade and eventually regress.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old man who works in a chemical plant producing polyvinyl chloride (PVC) presents with abdominal pain and weight loss. Imaging reveals multiple mass lesions in the liver. A biopsy confirms a malignancy of the endothelial cells. Which of the following exposures is most likely responsible for this condition?

explanations.a: Arsenic is a risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma, but the plant worker's specific link is to PVC/Vinyl chloride.
explanations.b: Aflatoxin B1 is associated with Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC), not angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Vinyl chloride (monomer used in PVC production) is a classic occupational risk factor specifically linked to hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: Thorotrast (a radioactive contrast medium) was used historically and causes angiosarcoma, but is not used in modern industrial plants.
explanations.e: Benzene is associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), not vascular tumors.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is linked to the industrial chemical {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
Two other chemical/radiological agents linked to hepatic angiosarcoma are {{c1::arsenic}} and {{c2::Thorotrast}}.
Angiosarcomas are often immunohistochemically positive for the marker {{c1::CD31}} (vWF is also common).
The cell of origin in angiosarcoma is the {{c1::endothelial cell}}.
Hepatic angiosarcoma has a {{c1::poor}} prognosis.
