explanations.e: Spider telangiectasias are non-neoplastic dilations of arterioles, common in pregnancy, but are flat and 'spider-like'.

ankiCards: {{c1::Pyogenic granuloma}} is a rapidly growing, bleeding vascular nodule often found on the gingiva of pregnant women.
When found in the gingiva of a pregnant woman, a pyogenic granuloma is called a {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
True/False: Pyogenic granulomas are associated with infection and pus formation. {{c1::False (the name is a misnomer)}}.
The clinical appearance of a pyogenic granuloma is often a {{c1::pedunculated}} red mass.
Pyogenic granulomas are histologically a form of {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granulomas are misnamed; they are neither pyogenic (pus-forming) nor granulomatous.
They often regress spontaneously or after pregnancy.
Extensive edema and acute/chronic inflammation are seen histologically.
They bleed easily due to high vascularity and thin overlying epithelium.
Surgical excision is sometimes required if they do not involute.
microReview: Pyogenic granuloma = Gingiva/Skin + Pregnancy/Trauma + Rapid growth + Bleeding + Capillary proliferation.
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic' implies infection, but it is actually a purely vascular/neoplastic process.
sourceQuote: Pyogenic granulomas are capillary hemangiomas that manifest as rapidly growing red pedunculated nodules... they occur in the gingiva of 1% of pregnant women.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 5-year-old boy is evaluated for seizures and intellectual disability. On examination, a large, flat, purple-red 'port-wine stain' is noted on the right side of his face in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve. Imaging of the brain reveals ipsilateral leptomeningeal venous angiomas. Which of the following syndromes is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Osler-Weber-Rendu involves hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasias of the skin and mucous membranes, not port-wine stains.
explanations.b: Von Hippel-Lindau involves hemangioblastomas of the cerebellum and retina, and renal cell carcinomas.
explanations.c: Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) is characterized by a facial port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) and leptomeningeal angiomas.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation in AIDS patients.
explanations.e: Stewart-Treves syndrome is angiosarcoma arising in a limb with chronic lymphedema.

ankiCards: The port-wine stain in Sturge-Weber syndrome is a form of {{c1::nevus flammeus}}.
Sturge-Weber syndrome involves vascular malformations in the distribution of the {{c1::trigeminal}} nerve.
A port-wine stain that grows with the child and does not regress is called a {{c1::nevus flammeus}}.
Patients with Sturge-Weber often present with seizures and {{c1::intellectual disability/mental retardation}}.
The brain lesions in Sturge-Weber syndrome are {{c1::leptomeningeal}} venous angiomas.
keyPoints: Nevus flammeus is the most common form of vascular ectasia.
Ordinary birthmarks (faded nevi) usually regress; port-wine stains do not.
Port-wine stains thicken the skin and do not fade with time.
Sturge-Weber is a rare congenital disorder, not inherited (somatic mutation in GNAQ).
Skull X-rays may show 'tram-track' calcifications in the brain.
microReview: Port-wine stain + Trigeminal distribution + Seizures + Brain angiomas = Sturge-Weber Syndrome.
examinerTraps: Differentiate simple 'nevus flammeus' (birthmark) from the syndromic 'Sturge-Weber'.
sourceQuote: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) ... in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve may be a component of the Sturge-Weber syndrome.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Malignant vascular tumors, such as angiosarcomas, are distinguished from their benign counterparts by several histological features. Which of the following findings is most characteristic of a malignant vascular neoplasm?

options.a: Lack of endothelial cell CD31 expression
options.c: Presence of a dense fibrous capsule
options.d: Prominent cellular atypia and frequent mitoses
options.e: Fluid-filled spaces devoid of red blood cells

explanations.a: Most angiosarcomas still express CD31, as it is a marker of their endothelial origin.
explanations.b: Well-formed loops are characteristic of benign hemangiomas, not malignant tumors.
explanations.c: Angiosarcomas are typically infiltrative and lack a capsule.
explanations.d: Like most malignancies, angiosarcomas show nuclear pleomorphism, high mitotic rates, and disordered growth (anastomosing channels).
explanations.e: Spaces without RBCs are characteristic of lymphangiomas, not angiosarcomas (which are typically very hemorrhagic).

ankiCards: The most common sites for cutaneous angiosarcoma are the {{c1::scalp and face}} of elderly adults.
Angiosarcomas have a high {{c1::mitotic}} rate compared to hemangiomas.
Histologically, angiosarcomas form irregular, {{c1::anastomosing}} vascular channels.
Survival for angiosarcoma is poor, with 5-year rates around {{c1::30}}%.
Vascular tumors that are intermediate in grade (like KS) are called {{c1::borderline}} tumors.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas can arise from either blood or lymphatic vessels.
They are highly aggressive and locally invasive.
Risk factors include radiation, chronic lymphedema, and certain chemicals.
They can range from highly differentiated (vessel-forming) to undifferentiated (solid).
Metastasis occurs early and widely.
microReview: Malignant vascular tumors = Infiltration + Atypia + Mitoses + CD31 positive.
examinerTraps: A common trap is assuming malignant tumors 'lose' all their markers; angiosarcomas usually retain CD31.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas... show all degrees of differentiation, from highly plausible vascular channels to quite wild, fleshy, and solid tumors without obvious vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular pathology is responsible for significant human morbidity and mortality. According to the foundational principles of vascular disease, what are the two principal mechanisms that underlie these pathological processes?

options.a: Lumen narrowing and vessel wall weakening
options.d: Pulsatile flow reduction and venous stasis

explanations.a: The text explicitly states that narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens and weakening of vessel walls leading to dilation or rupture are the two principal mechanisms.
explanations.b: While medial calcification (Monckeberg) occurs, it is not listed as one of the two principal mechanisms of vascular disease.
explanations.c: Vasospasm is a reactive process and coagulation is a consequence, but they are not the primary underlying structural mechanisms defined.
explanations.d: These are hemodynamic consequences rather than the underlying structural mechanisms of vascular pathology.
explanations.e: Pathology typically involves intimal thickening and medial weakening, not adventitial thickening and intimal atrophy.

ankiCards: The two principal mechanisms of vascular disease are narrowing/obstruction and {{c1::weakening}} of vessel walls.
Narrowing of vessel lumens can occur progressively through {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Narrowing of vessel lumens can occur precipitously through {{c1::thrombosis or embolism}}.
Weakening of vessel walls typically leads to vessel {{c1::dilation or rupture}}.
Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity than any other category of {{c1::human disease}}.
keyPoints: Vascular disease is a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality.
Two main structural mechanisms: obstruction and weakening.
Obstruction can be chronic (atherosclerosis) or acute (thrombosis).
Wall weakening results in aneurysms or dissections.
Arterial lesions are generally more clinically significant than venous ones.
microReview: Vascular disease mechanisms center on lumen diameter (obstruction) and structural integrity (weakening/dilation).
examinerTraps: Students often confuse the 'consequence' of a disease (like ischemia) with the 'mechanism' (obstruction). Focus on the structural change described in the text.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Arterial walls are structurally specialized compared to venous walls at the same level of branching. Which of the following best describes the physiological justification and structural adaptation seen in arteries to manage systemic circulation?

options.a: Thicker walls to accommodate higher pressures and pulsatile flow
options.b: Higher density of vasa vasorum in the intima to prevent ischemia
options.c: Absent adventitial layer to allow for rapid transmural gas exchange
options.d: Decreased wall-to-lumen ratio in smaller vessels to reduce resistance
options.e: Presence of valves to prevent retrograde flow during diastole

explanations.a: Arterial walls are thicker than veins at the same level to handle the pulsatile flow and higher pressures of the arterial system.
explanations.b: Vasa vasorum are located in the adventitia and outer media, not the intima.
explanations.c: Arteries possess a well-developed adventitia; gas exchange occurs in capillaries, not muscular arteries.
explanations.d: As arteries become smaller, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter actually increases to exert better control over pressure.
explanations.e: Valves are characteristic of the venous system and lymphatics, not the arterial system.

ankiCards: Arterial walls are {{c1::thicker}} than corresponding veins at the same level of branching.
Arteries are thicker to accommodate {{c1::pulsatile flow}} and higher pressures.
As arteries become smaller, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}}.
Structural specializations in vessels reflect distinct {{c1::functional roles}}.
The increased wall-to-lumen ratio in small muscular vessels allows them to control {{c1::blood flow and pressure}}.
keyPoints: Arterial walls are thicker than venous walls.
Adaptation is required for high-pressure pulsatile flow.
Smaller vessels have a higher wall-to-lumen ratio.
Wall thickness allows for better vasomotor control.
Anatomic distribution of diseases often follows vessel types.
microReview: Structure follows function: high pressure requires thick walls (arteries), while low pressure/storage allows for thinner walls (veins).
examinerTraps: A common mistake is thinking the wall-to-lumen ratio decreases as vessels get smaller; it actually increases to provide mechanical resistance.
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male with a 50-pack-year smoking history presents for a routine physical examination. Deep palpation of the abdomen reveals a non-tender, pulsatile mass approximately 5 cm in diameter located superior to the umbilicus. He is asymptomatic. Which of the following underlying mechanisms is the most likely primary contributor to the development of this condition?

options.a: Matrix metalloproteinase-mediated degradation of the media
options.b: Cystic medial necrosis due to fibrillin-1 mutations
options.c: Chronic inflammatory destruction of the vasa vasorum
options.d: Endothelial cell loss due to chronic hyperglycemia
options.e: Congenital thinning of the internal elastic lamina

explanations.a: The clinical picture describes an Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA). AAA pathogenesis is primarily linked to atherosclerosis and an imbalance in collagen/elastin turnover mediated by MMPs.
explanations.b: This describes Marfan syndrome, which typically causes Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms in younger patients.
explanations.c: This describes the mechanism of tertiary syphilis, which affects the thoracic aorta.
explanations.d: Hyperglycemia contributes to microvascular disease (hyaline arteriolosclerosis), not typically the primary driver of large aneurysms.
explanations.e: This is the mechanism associated with Berry (saccular) aneurysms in the Circle of Willis.

ankiCards: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are most commonly associated with {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
The primary site for AAA is between the {{c1::renal arteries}} and the aortic bifurcation.
{{c1::Smoking}} is the strongest environmental risk factor for AAA.
Wall weakening in AAA is caused by {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
MMPs in the aortic wall degrade {{c1::elastin and collagen}}.
keyPoints: AAA is usually infra-renal and supra-bifurcation.
Atherosclerosis is the major risk factor/association.
Proteolytic degradation of the extracellular matrix is key.
MMPs are produced by inflammatory cells in the plaque.
Risk of rupture increases significantly above 5 cm diameter.
microReview: AAA = Older smokers + Atherosclerosis + MMP-mediated ECM degradation + Infra-renal location.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse the location: AAA is almost always infra-renal. If the stem mentions the chest or ascending aorta, think Marfan/Syphilis/HTN instead.
sourceQuote: Aneurysms and Dissection... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following descriptions accurately distinguishes a 'true' aneurysm from a 'false' aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm)?

options.a: A true aneurysm involves all three layers of the arterial wall
options.b: A false aneurysm is always caused by a congenital defect
options.c: A true aneurysm is characterized by an extravascular hematoma
options.d: A false aneurysm only involves the intimal and medial layers
options.e: A true aneurysm is defined by a longitudinal tear in the media

explanations.a: A true aneurysm involves an intact (though thinned) arterial wall containing all three layers: intima, media, and adventitia.
explanations.b: False aneurysms are usually acquired, often from trauma or iatrogenic injury (e.g., post-catheterization).
explanations.c: An extravascular hematoma that communicates with the lumen is the definition of a false aneurysm.
explanations.d: A false aneurysm does not involve the layers of the wall as a containing structure; it is a hematoma contained by extravascular tissue.
explanations.e: A longitudinal tear in the media describes an aortic dissection, not a true aneurysm.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the vessel wall.
A {{c1::false (pseudoaneurysm)}} is a breach in the wall leading to an extravascular hematoma.
Aneurysms can be {{c1::saccular}} (spherical) or {{c1::fusiform}} (circumferential).
The two main shapes of true aneurysms are {{c1::saccular and fusiform}}.
An aortic dissection occurs when blood enters the {{c1::media}} through an intimal tear.
keyPoints: True aneurysm: Intact 3-layer wall.
False aneurysm: Hematoma communicating with lumen (post-trauma).
Saccular: Focal outpouching.
Fusiform: Uniform circumferential dilation.
Dissection: Blood between layers (not a 'true' aneurysm).
microReview: True = 3 layers. False = Leak/Hematoma. Dissection = Split wall.
examinerTraps: The examiner might call a 'dissection' an 'aneurysm'. While often grouped together, they are distinct processes; a dissection is not necessarily a dilation.
sourceQuote: Aneurysms and Dissection... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old female with a history of tall stature, long fingers, and mitral valve prolapse presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset, severe, tearing chest pain radiating to her back. Her blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg. Which histological finding in the aortic wall is most characteristic of her underlying condition?

options.a: Fragmented elastic fibers and cystic spaces filled with proteoglycans
options.b: Extensive atherosclerotic plaques with calcification of the media
options.c: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.d: Granulomatous inflammation with giant cells in the media
options.e: Fibrinoid necrosis of the small penetrating arterioles

explanations.a: The patient has Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1 mutation), which leads to cystic medial necrosis (degeneration), characterized by elastic fiber fragmentation and mucoid material accumulation.
explanations.b: Atherosclerosis is the primary cause of AAA, not the thoracic complications of Marfan syndrome in a young patient.
explanations.c: This describes syphilitic aortitis, which also affects the thoracic aorta but has a different histological presentation.
explanations.d: This describes Giant Cell Arteritis or Takayasu Arteritis.
explanations.e: This is typical of malignant hypertension in small vessels, not the aorta.

ankiCards: {{c1::Marfan syndrome}} is a common cause of thoracic aortic aneurysms in young adults.
Marfan syndrome involves a mutation in the {{c1::fibrillin-1}} gene.
The histological hallmark of Marfan-related aortic disease is {{c1::cystic medial necrosis (degeneration)}}.
Cystic medial necrosis involves the loss of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} and elastic fibers.
The 'cystic' spaces in medial degeneration are filled with {{c1::proteoglycans}}.
keyPoints: Marfan Syndrome: Fibrillin-1 mutation, TGF-beta signaling overactivity.
Leads to cystic medial necrosis (not true necrosis, but degeneration).
Predisposes to Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm (TAA) and Dissection.
Classic presentation: Young patient, tearing chest pain, Marfanoid habitus.
Histology: Fragmented elastin, pooled mucoid material.
microReview: Marfan = Fibrillin = Weak Media = Tearing pain/TAA.
examinerTraps: The term 'Cystic Medial Necrosis' is a misnomer (there are no actual cysts or necrosis), so 'Medial Degeneration' is the more modern and accurate term often used in exams.
sourceQuote: Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm... Aortic Dissection
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: The pathogenesis of an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is closely linked to the failure of which structural component due to chronic inflammation?

explanations.a: The media provides the structural strength of the aorta. Its destruction (loss of smooth muscle and elastic fibers) is the central event in aneurysm formation.
explanations.b: While the internal elastic lamina is damaged, it is the overall loss of medial integrity that leads to dilation.
explanations.c: The basement membrane relates to endothelial stability but not the tensile strength of the large vessel wall.
explanations.d: The adventitia contains the vasa vasorum but is not the primary layer whose failure results in the uniform dilation seen in AAA.
explanations.e: Endothelial junctions control permeability but do not prevent the mechanical dilation of the vessel wall.

ankiCards: The primary layer of the vessel wall affected in aneurysm formation is the {{c1::media}}.
{{c1::Atherosclerosis}} causes the media to thin by obstructing the diffusion of oxygen.
Atherosclerotic plaques increase the {{c1::diffusion distance}} from the lumen to the media.
Ischemia of the media leads to the loss of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}}.
Aneurysms occur when the mechanical integrity of the {{c1::media}} is compromised.
keyPoints: The media is the primary structural layer of the artery.
Atherosclerosis causes intimal thickening, creating a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
The resulting medial ischemia leads to cell death and atrophy.
Inflammatory infiltrates in the plaque release proteases (MMPs).
The combination of ischemia and proteolysis weakens the wall.
microReview: AAA Pathogenesis = Atherosclerosis → Intimal thickening → Medial Ischemia → Medial Weakening → Dilation.
examinerTraps: Examiners may ask if 'intimal thickening' causes the aneurysm. It 'initiates' the process of ischemia, but the aneurysm itself is a failure of the 'media'.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 75-year-old male with long-standing hypertension presents with sudden, excruciating 'tearing' chest pain that radiates through to the middle of his back. He is diaphoretic, and his blood pressure is 180/110 mmHg. A CT scan shows a double lumen in the ascending aorta. What is the most likely initiating event of this condition?

explanations.a: Aortic dissection is initiated by an intimal tear that allows blood to enter and cleave the media, creating a false lumen (double lumen on CT).
explanations.b: Vasa vasorum obstruction is more associated with the chronic medial weakening of syphilitic aortitis, not the acute tear of dissection.
explanations.c: While atherosclerosis is common in these patients, a dissection is specifically initiated by an intimal tear, often in an area without plaques.
explanations.d: Syphilis causes aneurysms but is less commonly associated with acute dissection compared to hypertension.
explanations.e: Dilation of the ring is a consequence of TAA, not the cause of an acute dissection.

ankiCards: Aortic dissection is characterized by blood entering the {{c1::media}} of the vessel.
The most common risk factor for aortic dissection is {{c1::hypertension}}.
Dissection usually originates with an {{c1::intimal tear}}.
The 'double lumen' on imaging is a classic sign of {{c1::aortic dissection}}.
Dissections can occur without an obvious intimal tear due to bleeding from the {{c1::vasa vasorum}}.
keyPoints: Dissection: Cleavage of the media by pressurized blood.
Primary risk factor: Hypertension (men 40-60) and Marfan (younger).
Classic symptom: Tearing chest pain radiating to the back.
Major complication: Rupture into the pericardium (tamponade).
Often classified by the Stanford (A vs B) or DeBakey systems.
microReview: Aortic Dissection = HTN + Intimal Tear + Media Cleavage + Tearing pain.
examinerTraps: A common trap is confusing 'atherosclerosis' as the main cause of dissection. In reality, hypertension is the primary driver; atherosclerosis may actually 'protect' against dissection by scarring the media and preventing the tear from spreading.
sourceQuote: Aortic Dissection... blood splits the laminar planes of the media to form a blood-filled channel within the aortic wall.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the mechanism by which hypertension causes the 'weakening of vessel walls' that leads to thoracic aortic aneurysms?

options.a: Narrowing of the vasa vasorum lumen leading to medial ischemia
options.b: Direct enzymatic lysis of the basement membrane by renin
options.c: Decreased production of TGF-beta in the aortic wall
options.d: Calcification of the internal elastic lamina

explanations.a: In the thoracic aorta, hypertension causes hyaline thickening of the vasa vasorum, which reduces blood flow to the outer media, causing ischemia and subsequent wall weakening.
explanations.b: Renin acts on angiotensinogen in the blood, not through direct enzymatic lysis of vessel walls.
explanations.c: Increased (not decreased) TGF-beta signaling is often associated with medial weakening in conditions like Marfan syndrome.
explanations.d: Medial calcification (Monckeberg) doesn't typically cause aneurysmal dilation.
explanations.e: Adventitial changes are secondary and do not define the wall-weakening mechanism.

ankiCards: Thoracic aortic aneurysms are most commonly associated with {{c1::hypertension}}.
Hypertension causes ischemic injury to the media by affecting the {{c1::vasa vasorum}}.
The vasa vasorum supply the {{c1::outer}} half of the aortic media.
In TAA, the media shows loss of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} and elastic tissue.
Narrowing of the vasa vasorum in HTN leads to {{c1::medial degeneration}}.
keyPoints: Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm (TAA) etiology differs from AAA.
HTN is the leading cause of TAA.
HTN induces vasa vasorum narrowing → medial ischemia.
Medial ischemia → loss of SM cells and elastic fibers.
This process is known as 'medial degeneration'.
microReview: TAA = HTN → Vasa Vasorum ischemia → Medial Degeneration. AAA = Atherosclerosis → MMPs → ECM degradation.
examinerTraps: Acknowledge the difference: AAA = Atherosclerosis (mostly). TAA = Hypertension (mostly).
sourceQuote: Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm... Hypertension is the most common cause.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old male with a history of intravenous drug use presents with fever and a painful, rapidly enlarging lump in his right groin. On exam, the lump is pulsatile and warm. Blood cultures are positive for Staphylococcus aureus. This lesion is most accurately classified as which of the following?

explanations.a: A mycotic aneurysm is an aneurysm resulting from an infection of the arterial wall, often by bacteria (e.g., S. aureus) during sepsis or from IV drug use.
explanations.b: Berry aneurysms are small congenital saccular aneurysms in the Circle of Willis.
explanations.c: While it may be saccular in shape, 'mycotic' specifically defines the infectious etiology which is the most accurate classification here.
explanations.d: Dissecting aneurysms (dissections) involve blood splitting the media; this is an infection of the wall.
explanations.e: An AV fistula is a connection between an artery and a vein, not a localized infected dilation.

ankiCards: Infection of an arterial wall leading to aneurysm is called a {{c1::mycotic aneurysm}}.
Common causes of mycotic aneurysms include {{c1::infective endocarditis}} and septicemia.
A mycotic aneurysm can result from the direct {{c1::extension}} of a nearby infection.
The term 'mycotic' refers to the {{c1::shape}} or infection, not necessarily a fungal cause.
Mycotic aneurysms often lead to rapid wall destruction and {{c1::rupture}}.
keyPoints: Mycotic aneurysm = Infected aneurysm.
Most are bacterial (despite the name 'mycotic').
Origins: Embolization of vegetation (Endocarditis), extension of abscess, or IV drug use trauma.
Rapid destruction of the media by the inflammatory process.
High risk of hemorrhage and sepsis.
microReview: Fever + Pulsatile mass + S. aureus = Mycotic Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Students often assume 'mycotic' means fungal. In medical board exams, mycotic aneurysms are almost always bacterial (Staph/Salmonella) unless specified otherwise.
sourceQuote: Infection of a major artery can weaken its wall, giving rise to a mycotic aneurysm.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 64-year-old female presents with multiple cutaneous, violaceous nodules on her right arm. She underwent a radical mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer 12 years ago, which was followed by chronic, non-pitting edema of the extremity. Biopsy of a nodule shows malignant cells forming irregular vascular channels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma can arise in the setting of chronic lymphedema, a condition known as Stewart-Treves syndrome, typically occurring years after radical mastectomy.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and usually presents in HIV patients or specific elderly populations; it is not typically linked to chronic post-mastectomy lymphedema.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign vascular proliferation caused by Bartonella infection in immunocompromised hosts, characterized by neutrophils and bacteria on histology.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are small, exquisitely painful benign tumors typically found under the fingernails, arising from glomus bodies.
explanations.e: Capillary hemangiomas are benign proliferations of thin-walled capillaries, often presenting in infancy and regressing spontaneously.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema (e.g., post-mastectomy) is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
The most common immunohistochemical marker used to identify the endothelial origin of an angiosarcoma is {{c1::CD31::marker}}.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is specifically associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride::chemical}}.
Unlike benign hemangiomas, angiosarcomas show histological evidence of {{c1::atypical endothelial cells}} and irregular vascular channels.
Stewart-Treves syndrome typically develops {{c1::10 or more}} years after a radical mastectomy.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a malignant endothelial neoplasm with a high mortality rate.
Chronic lymphedema is a major risk factor for cutaneous angiosarcoma.
Other risk factors include radiation therapy and chemical exposures (vinyl chloride, arsenic).
Histology shows pleomorphic, malignant endothelial cells.
The clinical presentation usually involves enlarging, multinodular red-purple skin lesions.
microReview: Angiosarcoma is an aggressive malignancy of endothelial cells. In the clinical context of post-mastectomy lymphedema, it is termed Stewart-Treves syndrome. It must be differentiated from benign lesions by its cytological atypia and invasive growth patterns.
examinerTraps: The examiner often uses the history of radiation or mastectomy to lead you toward a recurrence of breast cancer; however, the presence of purple skin nodules in a lymphedematous limb specifically points to angiosarcoma.

bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 34-year-old man with advanced HIV infection presents with multiple reddish-purple macules on his lower extremities. A biopsy of one of the lesions reveals a proliferation of spindle-shaped cells and slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells. Which of the following is the primary driver of this patient's condition?

explanations.a: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which looks similar clinically but histologically shows neutrophils and lacks the characteristic spindle cells of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.b: HHV-8 (also known as KSHV) is the causative agent of all forms of Kaposi sarcoma, including the AIDS-related type described here.
explanations.c: HPV-16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx, not vascular tumors.
explanations.d: CMV can cause retinitis or colitis in HIV patients but is not oncogenic for vascular tissue.
explanations.e: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not Kaposi sarcoma.

ankiCards: The classic histological feature of Kaposi Sarcoma is the presence of {{c1::spindle cells}} and slit-like spaces.
Kaposi Sarcoma is caused by {{c1::HHV-8}}.
The cell of origin for Kaposi sarcoma is thought to be the {{c1::vascular or lymphatic endothelial cell}}.
Clinically, Kaposi Sarcoma lesions often follow the {{c1::Langer's lines}} (skin tension lines).
The presence of {{c1::extravasated red blood cells}} and hemosiderin is a common histological finding in Kaposi sarcoma.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma is a low-grade malignant proliferation of endothelial cells.
Four clinical variants exist: Classic (European), Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
HHV-8 DNA is found in virtually all KS lesions.
Spindle cells are the diagnostic cell type on microscopy.
Lesions can involve the skin, mucous membranes, and viscera (GI tract, lungs).
microReview: Kaposi sarcoma is an opportunistic malignancy in AIDS patients driven by HHV-8. Key histological identifiers are spindle cells and slit-like vascular spaces.
examinerTraps: Bacillary angiomatosis (caused by Bartonella) is the most common clinical mimic of Kaposi Sarcoma. Look for 'neutrophils' or 'coccobacilli' to pick Bartonella; look for 'spindle cells' or 'slit-like spaces' to pick HHV-8.

bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 41-year-old woman presents with severe, paroxysmal pain in her right thumb, which is aggravated by exposure to cold water. On physical examination, a small, 4-mm, slightly blue nodule is seen beneath the nail bed. This tumor likely originates from which of the following cell types?

explanations.a: Pericytes are found in many vascular structures, but the specific cells of the glomus body are considered specialized smooth muscle cells.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.c: Endothelial cells line the tumor's vascular spaces, but the characteristic neoplastic component is the glomus cell.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts are not the primary neoplastic component of a glomus tumor.
explanations.e: Schwann cells are the origin of schwannomas, which can be painful but do not typically present as subungual vascular-appearing nodules sensitive to cold.

ankiCards: A glomus tumor is most commonly found in the {{c1::subungual}} region (under the nail).
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells.
The classic clinical triad for glomus tumors includes point tenderness, paroxysmal pain, and {{c1::cold hypersensitivity}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors show nests of uniform, round cells surrounding {{c1::vascular channels}}.
The glomus body is an {{c1::arteriovenous anastomosis}} involved in thermoregulation.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign and exquisitely painful.
They are most common in the distal digits, particularly subungual.
They originate from the glomus body (thermoregulatory structure).
Cells are round, regular, and immunohistochemically positive for smooth muscle actin.
Excision is usually curative.
microReview: A painful subungual blue nodule is a glomus tumor until proven otherwise. It is a benign tumor of specialized smooth muscle cells.
examinerTraps: The examiner may describe the pain as 'neuropathic' to tempt you to pick a nerve tumor (like a schwannoma), but the subungual location and cold sensitivity are pathognomonic for a glomus tumor.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism) • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 27-year-old pregnant woman presents with a rapidly growing, bleeding, red nodule on her gums. She is currently in her second trimester. The lesion is 1 cm in diameter and pedunculated. Histology shows a lobulated proliferation of capillaries with associated edema and acute inflammation. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor with significant atypia, not a rapidly growing pedunculated gingival mass in a pregnant woman.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious process in immunocompromised hosts, not typically associated with pregnancy-related gingival lesions.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a common benign vascular lesion that often occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated vascular spaces and are typically deeper or internal (e.g., in the liver), not pedunculated gingival lesions.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are small, painful, and subungual, not rapidly growing gingival masses.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is histologically a {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
The common site for pyogenic granuloma in pregnant women is the {{c1::gingiva}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized by {{c1::rapid}} growth and a tendency to bleed.
The term 'pyogenic granuloma' is a misnomer because the lesion is neither {{c1::pyogenic (purulent)}} nor a true {{c1::granuloma}}.
Treatment for pyogenic granuloma usually involves {{c1::surgical excision}} or waiting for postpartum regression.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granulomas are benign, reactive vascular lesions.
They commonly occur on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
Pregnancy is a major predisposing factor (granuloma gravidarum).
Histology: Proliferation of capillaries arranged in lobules, often with overlying ulceration.
They can regress spontaneously or require simple excision.
microReview: A rapidly growing, bleeding gingival mass in a pregnant patient is a pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma). Despite the name, it is not an infection or a granulomatous process.
examinerTraps: Do not be fooled by the word 'granuloma' in the name; it does not contain epithelioid histiocytes or giant cells. Also, do not confuse it with bacillary angiomatosis, which looks similar but occurs in HIV patients.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism) • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old male presents with dull right upper quadrant pain and significant weight loss. He worked in a plastic manufacturing plant for 30 years, with frequent exposure to vinyl chloride monomers. Imaging shows multiple hemorrhagic masses in the liver. A biopsy is performed, and immunohistochemistry is positive for CD31. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Vinyl chloride exposure is a classic, high-yield risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma, a malignant tumor of endothelial cells (CD31 positive).
explanations.b: Hepatocellular carcinoma is associated with cirrhosis, Hepatitis B/C, and aflatoxin, but not specifically with vinyl chloride.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangioma is a benign, common incidental finding in the liver; it does not cause rapid weight loss or relate to chemical exposure.
explanations.d: Hepatic adenoma is associated with oral contraceptive use or anabolic steroids.
explanations.e: Focal nodular hyperplasia is a benign reactive process characterized by a central stellate scar.

ankiCards: Three specific exposures linked to hepatic angiosarcoma are {{c1::vinyl chloride}}, {{c1::arsenic}}, and {{c1::Thorotrast (thorium dioxide)}}.
CD31 (platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule) is a marker for {{c1::endothelial cells}}.
Angiosarcoma of the liver has a {{c1::poor}} prognosis.
Vinyl chloride is specifically associated with the manufacture of {{c1::polyvinyl chloride (PVC)}}.
Unlike hepatocellular carcinoma, angiosarcomas do not usually produce {{c1::alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)}}.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare but highly aggressive malignancy.
Occupational exposure to vinyl chloride is the most classic association.
CD31 and von Willebrand factor (vWF) are useful IHC markers.
The tumor often presents late with liver failure or hemoperitoneum.
The malignant cells line pre-existing vascular channels or form new ones.
microReview: Hepatic angiosarcoma + Vinyl Chloride is a classic USMLE association. CD31 positivity confirms the vascular nature of the malignant cells.
examinerTraps: The examiner might offer 'Hepatocellular Carcinoma' as a distractor for any liver mass; look specifically for the chemical exposure history (vinyl chloride, arsenic, or thorium dioxide) to select angiosarcoma.

bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 4-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for a bright red, raised 'strawberry-like' lesion on the forehead. The mother reports it appeared at 2 weeks of age and has grown since. Which of the following is the most likely natural history for this lesion?

options.d: Progressive growth causing local bone erosion
options.e: Systemic spread to the liver and lungs

explanations.a: Strawberry (capillary) hemangiomas are benign and do not undergo malignant transformation.
explanations.b: These lesions typically do not persist for life; they usually involute.
explanations.c: Capillary (juvenile/strawberry) hemangiomas usually grow for a few months and then spontaneously regress, typically by age 7 to 9.
explanations.d: Unlike some aggressive tumors, capillary hemangiomas do not typically erode bone.
explanations.e: These are localized benign lesions and do not metastasize.

ankiCards: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are histologically classified as {{c1::capillary}} hemangiomas.
The natural history of a strawberry hemangioma involves rapid growth followed by {{c1::spontaneous regression/involution}}.
By age 7, approximately {{c1::75}}% of strawberry hemangiomas have disappeared.
Strawberry hemangiomas are usually present at {{c1::birth or shortly after}}.
A deeper, less circumscribed vascular lesion in an infant that does not regress is often a {{c1::cavernous}} hemangioma (or vascular malformation).
keyPoints: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are the most common tumor of infancy.
They are benign capillary proliferations.
Clinically, they appear as bright red, lobulated masses.
They occur in about 1 in 200 births.
Management is usually observation due to high rates of spontaneous regression.
microReview: Infant + red strawberry lesion = Capillary hemangioma. Key concept: They grow initially then disappear by school age.
examinerTraps: Confusion with 'Port-wine stains' (Nevus flammeus), which are vascular ectasias that *do not* regress and may grow with the child.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism) • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular tumors is characterized by large, dilated, blood-filled vascular spaces separated by a modest connective tissue stroma, and is the most common benign tumor of the liver?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas consist of small, thin-walled capillaries, not large cavernous spaces.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated vascular channels. They are the most common benign liver tumors and can also occur in the skin or CNS.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is malignant and characterized by atypia and infiltrative growth, not well-defined benign spaces.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are small, solid-appearing nests of cells, not large dilated spaces.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is a lobular capillary proliferation associated with infection.

ankiCards: The most common benign tumor of the liver is the {{c1::cavernous hemangioma}}.
Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated, {{c1::blood-filled}} spaces.
In the CNS, cavernous hemangiomas are associated with the {{c1::von Hippel-Lindau}} disease (though more often hemangioblastomas).
A major clinical risk of large cavernous hemangiomas in the liver is {{c1::thrombosis}} or rarely rupture, but they are usually asymptomatic.
Unlike strawberry hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas usually {{c1::do not}} regress.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, thin-walled vascular channels.
They are often sharply circumscribed.
They are the most common benign primary tumor of the liver.
They are usually asymptomatic and found incidentally on imaging.
Biopsy of a suspected hepatic cavernous hemangioma is generally avoided due to the risk of hemorrhage.
microReview: Cavernous hemangiomas are 'caverns' of blood. Most common benign liver tumor. Does not regress. Contrast with 'Capillary' hemangiomas (small vessels).
examinerTraps: An incidental liver mass found on CT is usually a cavernous hemangioma. The trap is to over-investigate or biopsy it, which can cause significant bleeding.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism) • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An immunocompromised patient presents with multiple red-to-purple skin papules. Histology shows a lobular proliferation of capillaries with prominent 'hobnail' endothelial cells, an infiltrate of neutrophils, and granular purple material representing clusters of bacteria. What is the most likely causative organism?

explanations.a: Bartonella henselae (or B. quintana) causes bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised hosts, characterized by capillary proliferation and neutrophilic inflammation.
explanations.b: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, which features spindle cells and usually lacks the prominent neutrophilic infiltrate and bacteria seen here.
explanations.c: S. aureus causes pyogenic infections (abscesses, impetigo) but not this specific type of vascular tumor-like proliferation.
explanations.d: T. pallidum causes syphilis; while it involves vascular walls (endarteritis), it does not produce these angiomatous lesions.
explanations.e: CMV does not cause vascular proliferations.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by bacteria of the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
Histologically, bacillary angiomatosis features a {{c1::neutrophilic}} infiltrate, which helps distinguish it from Kaposi sarcoma.
The granular purple material seen on H&E stain in bacillary angiomatosis represents {{c1::bacteria/clusters of Bartonella}}.
To visualize Bartonella in tissue, a {{c1::Warthin-Starry}} silver stain is used.
Bacillary angiomatosis is primarily seen in {{c1::immunocompromised/HIV}} patients.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis is an opportunistic infection inducing vascular proliferation.
Causative agents: Bartonella henselae (cats) or Bartonella quintana (lice).
Commonly involves skin, but can involve bone or liver (peliosis hepatis).
Antibiotic treatment (e.g., erythromycin) leads to regression.
Histology: Proliferating capillaries with atypia, but accompanied by neutrophils and bacteria.
microReview: Bacillary angiomatosis = Bartonella + HIV + skin nodules. It is a vascular proliferation that mimics Kaposi sarcoma but is treated with antibiotics.
examinerTraps: The examiner will often present an HIV patient with purple skin lesions to make you think 'Kaposi'. You must look for 'neutrophils' or 'bacteria' in the biopsy description to choose Bacillary Angiomatosis instead.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism) • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following markers is the most specific immunohistochemical stain for identifying the endothelial cell origin of a poorly differentiated malignant vascular tumor?

explanations.a: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a transmembrane glycoprotein expressed on endothelial cells and is a highly sensitive and specific marker for vascular tumors.
explanations.b: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells (carcinomas).
explanations.c: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (myogenic tumors).
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells (melanoma, schwannoma).
explanations.e: Chromogranin is a marker for neuroendocrine cells.

ankiCards: The most specific vascular endothelial marker used in pathology is {{c1::CD31}}.
Another marker for endothelial cells, besides CD31, is {{c1::von Willebrand factor (vWF)}} (or Factor VIII-related antigen).
{{c1::ERG}} is a nuclear marker that is also highly specific for endothelial differentiation.
Malignant vascular tumors are collectively known as {{c1::angiosarcomas}}.
Poorly differentiated angiosarcomas may resemble carcinomas but will be negative for {{c1::cytokeratin}}.
keyPoints: Immunohistochemistry is essential for the diagnosis of vascular tumors.
CD31 is the gold standard endothelial marker.
vWF is also used but can be less sensitive in poorly differentiated tumors.
CD34 is often positive in vascular tumors but is less specific (also found in many other sarcomas).
Markers help distinguish angiosarcoma from other high-grade sarcomas and carcinomas.
microReview: CD31 = Endothelium. This is the single most important IHC marker for vascular tumors in Step 1 level exams.
examinerTraps: Vimentin is often mentioned as a marker for sarcomas, but it is very non-specific. CD31 is the specific answer for vascular origin.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism) • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 5-year-old child presents with a large, flat, purple-red birthmark on the left side of his face following the distribution of the trigeminal nerve. The child has a history of seizures and intellectual disability. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Sturge-Weber syndrome is characterized by a port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) in the V1/V2 distribution, leptomeningeal angiomas, and seizures.
explanations.b: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) features multiple telangiectasias of the skin and mucous membranes and AVMs.
explanations.c: von Hippel-Lindau disease is associated with hemangioblastomas of the CNS/retina and renal cell carcinoma.
explanations.d: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is characterized by cafe-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules, not port-wine stains.
explanations.e: Tuberous sclerosis features ash-leaf spots, angiofibromas, and hamartomas.

ankiCards: The clinical name for the birthmark in Sturge-Weber syndrome is {{c1::nevus flammeus (or port-wine stain)}}.
Sturge-Weber syndrome involves vascular malformations in the distribution of the {{c1::trigeminal (CN V)}} nerve.
The intracranial vascular lesion in Sturge-Weber syndrome is called a {{c1::leptomeningeal angioma}}.
Sturge-Weber syndrome is caused by a somatic mutation in the {{c1::GNAQ}} gene.
Patients with Sturge-Weber syndrome often have 'tram-track' calcifications on brain imaging due to {{c1::cortical calcification}}.
keyPoints: Sturge-Weber is a non-hereditary phakomatosis.
Classic triad: Port-wine stain, leptomeningeal angioma, and glaucoma/seizures.
The port-wine stain is a form of vascular ectasia (permanent dilation of pre-existing vessels).
The mutation is somatic (not germline).
Ipsilateral glaucoma is a common complication.
microReview: Sturge-Weber = Port-wine stain (CN V) + Brain Angioma + Seizures. It's a vascular anomaly syndrome, not a true neoplastic process, but tested alongside vascular tumors.
examinerTraps: Make sure to distinguish 'Port-wine stain' (fixed, does not regress) from 'Strawberry hemangioma' (regresses).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism) • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular pathology is responsible for significant human morbidity. Which of the following describes one of the two principal mechanisms underlying most clinically significant vascular diseases?

options.a: Increased vascular wall compliance and elastic recoil
options.b: Narrowing or complete obstruction of vessel lumens
options.c: Proliferation of the adventitial layer in large arteries
options.d: Decrease in the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter
options.e: Enhanced nutrient diffusion across the endothelial barrier

explanations.a: Vascular disease is typically associated with decreased compliance and wall weakening, not increased recoil.
explanations.b: One of the two primary mechanisms of vascular disease is narrowing (stenosis) or obstruction, either progressively (atherosclerosis) or precipitously (thrombosis/embolism).
explanations.c: Pathology usually involves intimal thickening or medial weakening rather than adventitial proliferation.
explanations.d: In muscular vessels, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter typically increases to maintain control over flow, whereas dilation (aneurysm) involves weakening.
explanations.e: Vascular pathology usually involves barriers to diffusion (e.g., intimal thickening) rather than enhanced diffusion.

ankiCards: The two principal mechanisms underlying vascular disease are {{c1::narrowing/obstruction}} and {{c2::weakening of vessel walls}}.
Narrowing of a vessel lumen can occur progressively through {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Precipitous obstruction of a vessel lumen is often caused by {{c1::thrombosis or embolism}}.
Weakening of vessel walls typically leads to {{c1::dilation (aneurysm)}} or {{c2::rupture}}.
In the cardiovascular system, arterial walls are {{c1::thicker}} than corresponding veins to accommodate higher pressures.
keyPoints: Stenosis and wall weakening are the two major pathways of vascular disease.
Stenosis can be chronic (atherosclerosis) or acute (thrombosis).
Wall weakening leads to aneurysms or dissections.
Arteries have thicker walls than veins to handle pulsatile, high-pressure flow.
Vascular structure reflects functional roles; structural failure results in clinical disease.
microReview: Vascular diseases generally fall into two categories: obstructive (stenosis) or structural failure (dilation/rupture). Atherosclerosis is a prime example of both, as it causes luminal narrowing and can also weaken the underlying media, leading to aneurysms.
examinerTraps: A common trap is confusing the clinical manifestation (e.g., ischemia) with the underlying mechanism (e.g., stenosis/obstruction).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which structural adaptation allows muscular arteries to exert maximal control over blood flow and pressure compared to elastic arteries?

options.a: Presence of an external elastic lamina only
options.b: Decreased ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter
options.c: Increased ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter
options.d: Absence of smooth muscle cells in the media
options.e: Uniform thickness across all levels of branching

explanations.a: Muscular arteries have both internal and external elastic laminae, but this is not the primary reason for flow control.
explanations.b: A decreased ratio is characteristic of veins or dilated vessels, not high-resistance muscular arteries.
explanations.c: As vessels become smaller, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing muscular vessels to exert finer control over flow and pressure.
explanations.d: The media of muscular arteries is primarily composed of smooth muscle cells to facilitate vasoconstriction.
explanations.e: Arterial wall thickness diminishes as vessels branch, rather than remaining uniform.

ankiCards: As arterial vessels become smaller, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}}.
The increased thickness-to-lumen ratio in muscular arteries allows for control of {{c1::blood flow and pressure}}.
Arterial walls are thicker than veins because they accommodate {{c1::pulsatile flow}} and {{c2::higher pressures}}.
Atherosclerosis affects mainly {{c1::elastic and muscular}} arteries.
Small muscular arteries and arterioles are the primary sites of {{c1::peripheral resistance}}.
keyPoints: The vessel wall architecture is specialized based on functional requirements.
Muscular arteries have a high wall-to-lumen ratio for hemodynamic regulation.
Arteries must withstand higher pressures than veins, necessitating thicker walls.
Vessel structural integrity is vital for preventing aneurysmal dilation.
Resistance is primarily regulated at the level of arterioles and small muscular arteries.
microReview: While large elastic arteries (aorta) handle volume, smaller muscular arteries regulate pressure. The relatively thick muscular wall compared to the lumen size allows these vessels to effectively constrict and modulate systemic vascular resistance.
examinerTraps: Students often think larger vessels have more 'control' over pressure because of their size; in reality, smaller vessels with higher wall-to-lumen ratios are the primary regulators.
sourceQuote: Arterial wall thickness gradually diminishes as the vessels become smaller, but the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing these muscular vessels to exert control over blood flow and pressure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 70-year-old male with a 50-pack-year smoking history and hypertension presents with deep, boring mid-abdominal pain. Physical examination reveals a pulsatile mass palpated between the xiphoid process and the umbilicus. A CT scan confirms a 6.0 cm infrarenal aortic dilation. Which of the following is the most significant contributor to the pathogenesis of this condition?

options.a: Congenital deficiency in type III collagen
options.b: Cystic medial degeneration from Marfan syndrome
options.c: Degradation of the media by matrix metalloproteinases
options.d: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.e: Intimal thickening reducing media nutrient supply

explanations.a: Type III collagen deficiency is associated with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, not typical atherosclerotic AAAs.
explanations.b: Marfan syndrome typically causes thoracic aortic aneurysms rather than infrarenal AAAs.
explanations.c: In abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAAs), chronic inflammation in the atherosclerotic plaque leads to the release of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) that degrade the elastin and collagen in the media.
explanations.d: This describes tertiary syphilis, which affects the ascending aorta, not the infrarenal aorta.
explanations.e: While intimal thickening occurs, the active destruction of the media by inflammatory enzymes (MMPs) is the primary driver for AAA dilation.

ankiCards: The most common cause of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms (AAA) is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
The inflammatory response in AAA leads to the release of {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
MMPs in AAA primarily degrade {{c1::elastin and collagen}} in the media.
The majority of AAAs are located {{c1::infrarenal}} (relative to the renal arteries).
The two major risk factors for AAA are {{c1::smoking}} and {{c2::male gender}}.
keyPoints: AAA is primarily an atherosclerotic disease.
Involves all three layers of the vessel wall (true aneurysm).
Usually occurs in males, smokers, and individuals over 60.
Pathogenesis involves chronic inflammation and proteolytic media destruction.
Most AAAs are found between the renal arteries and the aortic bifurcation.
microReview: AAA is a classic example of vessel wall weakening. Atherosclerosis induces an inflammatory infiltrate (macrophages/T-cells) in the media. These cells produce MMPs that chew through the structural proteins (elastin/collagen), leading to gradual thinning and expansion of the aortic wall under systemic pressure.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the location of AAA (infrarenal) with TAA (ascending/thoracic). TAA is more associated with hypertension and Marfan; AAA is more associated with atherosclerosis and smoking.
sourceQuote: Aneurysms and Dissection... Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following best defines a 'false' aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm)?

options.a: A focal dilation involving all three layers of the arterial wall
options.b: A tear in the intima that allows blood to create a second lumen
options.c: A wall defect leading to an extravascular hematoma communicating with the lumen
options.d: A uniform, symmetrical dilation involving a long segment of the vessel
options.e: A congenital thinning of the media in the Circle of Willis

explanations.a: This defines a true aneurysm.
explanations.b: This describes an aortic dissection, which is not a true aneurysm.
explanations.c: A false aneurysm is a breach in the vascular wall leading to an extravascular hematoma that freely communicates with the intravascular space ('pulsatile hematoma').
explanations.d: This describes a fusiform true aneurysm.
explanations.e: This describes a berry aneurysm, which is a type of true saccular aneurysm.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves an intact but attenuated arterial wall (all three layers).
A {{c1::false (pseudoaneurysm)}} is a defect in the vascular wall leading to an extravascular hematoma.
The hematoma in a pseudoaneurysm must {{c1::communicate}} with the intravascular space.
A {{c1::dissection}} occurs when blood enters the wall of the artery through an intimal tear.
Saccular aneurysms are {{c1::spherical}} out-pouchings involving only a portion of the vessel wall.
keyPoints: True aneurysms involve intima, media, and adventitia.
False aneurysms are essentially contained hematomas outside the vessel wall.
Aortic dissection is often incorrectly called an 'aneurysm' by patients but is a separate process.
Fusiform aneurysms are circumferential; saccular aneurysms are localized.
Common causes of pseudoaneurysms include trauma and post-catheterization complications.
microReview: Distinguish between True (all layers), False (hole in wall + hematoma), and Dissection (blood between layers). Clinically, a pseudoaneurysm often presents as a pulsatile mass following arterial trauma or surgery.
examinerTraps: A common distractor is equating 'dissection' with 'aneurysm'. While they often coexist, a dissection is a cleavage of the media, not necessarily a dilation of all three layers.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... Aneurysms and Dissection
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old woman with tall stature, long tapering fingers, and high-arched palate presents with sudden onset of severe, sharp chest pain. Blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg. An echocardiogram shows dilation of the proximal ascending aorta. What is the most likely microscopic finding in the aortic wall?

options.a: Extensive intimal calcification and cholesterol clefts
options.b: Cystic medial degeneration with loss of smooth muscle cells
options.c: Giant cell granulomatous inflammation of the media
options.d: Fibrinoid necrosis of the small vasa vasorum
options.e: Dense fibrous scarring of the adventitia

explanations.a: This describes atherosclerosis, which is rare in a 28-year-old and typically affects the abdominal aorta.
explanations.b: Marfan syndrome (suggested by the phenotype) leads to cystic medial degeneration (or necrosis), characterized by loss of smooth muscle cells and fragmentation of elastic fibers, predisposing to thoracic aortic aneurysms.
explanations.c: This describes Giant Cell Arteritis, usually seen in patients over 50.
explanations.d: This is seen in some vasculitides or malignant hypertension.
explanations.e: This is seen in tertiary syphilis (endarteritis obliterans leads to scarring) or retroperitoneal fibrosis.

ankiCards: {{c1::Marfan syndrome}} is a common genetic cause of Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (TAA).
The histological hallmark of Marfan-associated TAA is {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
Cystic medial degeneration involves the loss of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} and fragmentation of {{c2::elastic fibers}}.
TAA often involves the {{c1::ascending}} aorta.
Patients with Marfan syndrome have a mutation in the {{c1::FBN1 (fibrillin-1)}} gene.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome is a major risk factor for thoracic aneurysms and dissections.
Pathology shows accumulation of mucoid material (cystic medial degeneration).
The ascending aorta is the most common site due to high wall stress.
Clinical presentation often includes aortic insufficiency or dissection.
Contrast with AAA: TAA is more likely genetic/hypertensive; AAA is atherosclerotic.
microReview: Cystic medial degeneration isn't actually 'cystic' but describes the appearance of pale, mucoid-filled spaces in the media where elastic tissue has failed. This weakens the vessel significantly against systolic pressures.
examinerTraps: The examiner might provide a young patient with Marfan-like features; always look for 'cystic medial necrosis' or 'degeneration' as the histological answer.
sourceQuote: Aneurysms and Dissection... Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm... Aortic Dissection
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: How does advanced atherosclerosis contribute to the formation of an aneurysm in the abdominal aorta?

options.a: By increasing the thickness of the media via smooth muscle hyperplasia
options.b: By causing ischemia of the inner media through increased diffusion distance
options.c: By promoting the synthesis of cross-linked collagen in the adventitia
options.d: By direct viral infection of the endothelial cells
options.e: By inducing a shift from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism in the intima

explanations.a: Atherosclerosis causes medial thinning and atrophy, not hyperplasia.
explanations.b: Atherosclerotic plaques in the intima increase the diffusion distance for oxygen and nutrients from the lumen to the media, causing ischemic atrophy and weakening of the vessel wall.
explanations.c: Atherosclerosis leads to degradation of structural proteins, not beneficial synthesis of cross-linked collagen.
explanations.d: Atherosclerosis is an inflammatory/metabolic process, not a viral infection.
explanations.e: While metabolic shifts occur, the primary structural failure is due to media ischemia and inflammatory degradation.

ankiCards: Atherosclerosis increases the {{c1::diffusion distance}} from the lumen to the media.
Ischemia of the media in atherosclerosis leads to {{c1::atrophy and weakening}}.
The loss of {{c1::elastic}} tissue in the media predisposes the vessel to dilation.
Atherosclerotic aneurysms most commonly occur in the {{c1::Abdominal Aorta}}.
The inflammatory response to plaque involves {{c1::macrophages}} releasing proteolytic enzymes.
keyPoints: Atherosclerosis is the leading cause of AAA.
Plaque acts as a physical barrier to nutrient diffusion.
The underlying media undergoes pressure-induced atrophy and ischemic damage.
Inflammatory cells in the plaque release MMPs that degrade the extracellular matrix.
Thinning of the media makes the wall unable to resist normal blood pressure.
microReview: Atherosclerosis causes aneurysms via two paths: 1) physical barrier to nutrients (diffusion) leading to medial necrosis, and 2) recruitment of inflammatory cells that actively secrete elastases and collagenases.
examinerTraps: A common mistake is thinking the aneurysm is caused by high pressure 'pushing' the plaque; it's actually the weakening of the wall *under* the plaque.
sourceQuote: Atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 65-year-old male with a history of syphilis is found to have a dilated ascending aorta on a chest radiograph. If this patient develops an aneurysm, which of the following is a characteristic complication unique to this location and etiology?

explanations.a: This is a complication of an abdominal aortic aneurysm.
explanations.b: Claudication is caused by peripheral artery disease or iliac involvement in AAA.
explanations.c: Syphilitic (luetic) aneurysms typically involve the ascending aorta. The resulting dilation of the aortic root can stretch the aortic valve ring, leading to valvular insufficiency.
explanations.d: This results from mesenteric ischemia, often associated with AAA or embolism.
explanations.e: Blue toe syndrome is caused by microemboli from an atherosclerotic plaque, usually in the abdominal aorta.

ankiCards: Syphilitic aneurysms primarily affect the {{c1::ascending aorta (and arch)}}.
The hallmark of syphilitic aortitis is {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}} of the vasa vasorum.
Dilation of the aortic root in syphilis leads to {{c1::aortic valve insufficiency}}.
Syphilitic aneurysms are a manifestation of {{c1::tertiary}} syphilis.
The 'tree-bark' appearance of the aorta is seen in {{c1::syphilitic aortitis}}.
keyPoints: Syphilis targets the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta.
Ischemia of the outer media leads to scarring and loss of elastic tissue.
The resulting aneurysm is usually saccular or fusiform.
Aortic regurgitation is a frequent and serious clinical consequence.
This etiology has become much rarer with effective antibiotic treatment.
microReview: Syphilis causes 'endarteritis obliterans' of the vasa vasorum. Since the ascending aorta is thick and relies heavily on these vessels for nutrition, it suffers the most. The resulting scarring (tree-barking) and dilation often involve the aortic valve annulus.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'obstructive' nature of endarteritis (vasa vasorum) with the 'dilatory' nature of the resulting aortic aneurysm.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the shape of a true aneurysm that involves a circumferential, symmetrical dilation of a long vascular segment?

explanations.a: Saccular aneurysms are spherical out-pouchings involving only a portion of the vessel wall.
explanations.b: Berry aneurysms are a specific type of small saccular aneurysm.
explanations.c: Fusiform aneurysms are circumferential and symmetrical dilations of a long segment.
explanations.d: Dissection is not a shape of an aneurysm but a process of intramural hematoma formation.
explanations.e: Mycotic refers to an infected aneurysm, not a specific shape.

ankiCards: A {{c1::fusiform}} aneurysm is a circumferential, symmetrical dilation.
A {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm is a focal, spherical out-pouching.
Aneurysms are defined as permanent dilations of {{c1::all three layers}} of the wall.
{{c1::Mycotic}} aneurysms result from infection of the arterial wall.
Fusiform aneurysms are common in the {{c1::abdominal aorta}}.
keyPoints: Fusiform = long, symmetrical, circumferential.
Saccular = localized, pouch-like.
Both are 'true' aneurysms if all wall layers are involved.
Shape helps determine the risk of thrombus (saccular has higher stasis).
AAA is most commonly fusiform.
microReview: Remember: Fusiform = 'F' for 'Full circle' (circumferential). Saccular = 'S' for 'Sac' (pouch). Most AAAs are fusiform, while Berry aneurysms are saccular.
examinerTraps: Be careful not to select 'dissecting' as an aneurysm shape; it is a clinical event where blood splits the media.
sourceQuote: Aneurysms and Dissection... Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm... Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 58-year-old male with long-standing, poorly controlled hypertension presents with the sudden onset of 'tearing' back pain. His blood pressure is 210/120 mmHg. A CT scan shows a longitudinal cleavage of the aortic media by a column of blood. Which of the following is the most likely initial trigger for this event?

options.c: Septic embolization to the vasa vasorum
options.e: Cystic medial necrosis of the adventitia

explanations.a: Atherosclerosis actually inhibits dissection by causing medial scarring, which prevents the cleavage of layers.
explanations.b: The classic trigger for aortic dissection is an intimal tear, which allows high-pressure blood to enter and cleave the media.
explanations.c: This describes a mycotic aneurysm, not a dissection.
explanations.d: Inflammation is generally minimal in the acute phase of dissection; the primary issue is structural failure/tearing.
explanations.e: Cystic medial necrosis occurs in the media, not the adventitia.

ankiCards: The major risk factor for aortic dissection is {{c1::hypertension}}.
Aortic dissection typically begins with an {{c1::intimal tear}}.
The blood in a dissection travels within the {{c1::media}} layer of the vessel.
A 'double-barrel' aorta occurs when blood {{c1::re-enters}} the true lumen.
Type A dissections involve the {{c1::ascending}} aorta and are surgical emergencies.
keyPoints: Aortic dissection is distinct from a true aneurysm.
Hypertension is the most common predisposing factor.
The blood tracks between the middle and outer thirds of the media.
Clinical presentation is sudden, excruciating, 'tearing' pain.
Complications include cardiac tamponade and major branch obstruction.
microReview: Aortic dissection requires: 1) medial weakness (often from HTN-induced hyaline arteriolosclerosis of vasa vasorum) and 2) a trigger (intimal tear). Once the blood enters the media, it creates a 'false lumen'.
examinerTraps: Students often pick atherosclerosis as the cause of dissection because it causes so many other vascular issues. In fact, atherosclerosis is relatively protective against dissection because the associated scarring 'staples' the layers together.
sourceQuote: Aneurysms and Dissection... Aortic Dissection
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which property of arterial walls allows them to handle higher blood pressures and pulsatile flow compared to veins at the same level of branching?

options.a: Presence of valves to prevent backflow
options.b: Thicker walls relative to the lumen
options.c: Higher proportion of skeletal muscle fibers
options.d: Absence of an internal elastic lamina

explanations.a: Valves are a feature of veins, not arteries.
explanations.b: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher pressures.
explanations.c: Arterial walls contain smooth muscle, not skeletal muscle.
explanations.d: Arteries have a prominent internal elastic lamina; veins have a much less distinct one.
explanations.e: Veins have a larger total cross-sectional area and hold more blood volume (capacitance).

ankiCards: Arterial walls are {{c1::thicker}} than veins at the same level of branching.
Arteries accommodate {{c1::pulsatile}} flow and high pressures.
The structural specialization of vessels reflects their {{c1::distinct functional roles}}.
Veins have {{c1::thinner}} walls and larger lumens than arteries.
Vascular structure is comparable throughout the system but specialized in {{c1::specific types}} of vessels.
keyPoints: Vessel structure follows function.
Arteries are high-pressure conduits; veins are low-pressure reservoirs.
Wall thickness is the primary structural adaptation to pressure.
Aneurysms represent a failure of this structural adaptation.
Different vessels are susceptible to different pathologies (e.g., atherosclerosis in elastic arteries).
microReview: The thicker media in arteries provides the structural integrity needed to withstand the high shear stress and hydrostatic pressure of the arterial system. When this media is compromised (by MMPs or ischemia), an aneurysm forms.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'capacitance' (veins) with 'pressure resistance' (arteries).
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male presents for a routine physical examination. He has a 40-pack-year smoking history and long-standing hypertension. On abdominal palpation, a non-tender, pulsatile mass is noted at the level of the umbilicus. Imaging reveals a 5.2 cm dilation of the infrarenal abdominal aorta. Which of the following is the most likely primary pathological process responsible for this finding?

options.b: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.c: Chronic inflammation and degradation of the extracellular matrix
options.d: Congenital defect in the arterial media
options.e: Necrotizing granulomatous inflammation of the vessel wall

explanations.a: Cystic medial degeneration is the hallmark of Marfan syndrome and typically affects the ascending/thoracic aorta, not the infrarenal aorta.
explanations.b: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum is the mechanism behind syphilitic (luetic) aneurysms, which also preferentially affect the thoracic aorta.
explanations.c: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are primarily driven by atherosclerosis and a chronic inflammatory response in the media that leads to the degradation of elastin and collagen by matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs).
explanations.d: Congenital defects are more commonly associated with berry aneurysms in the circle of Willis, not large abdominal aneurysms in elderly smokers.
explanations.e: Necrotizing granulomatous inflammation is characteristic of vasculitides like Giant Cell Arteritis, which do not typically present as an isolated infrarenal pulsatile mass.

ankiCards: The most common location for an atherosclerotic aneurysm is the {{c1::infrarenal}} abdominal aorta.
The two principal mechanisms underlying vascular disease are narrowing of lumens and {{c1::weakening of vessel walls}}.
Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are most frequently associated with the risk factor of {{c1::smoking/atherosclerosis}}.
Pathogenesis of AAA involves the overactivity of {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
A pulsatile abdominal mass in an older male smoker is highly suggestive of {{c1::abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA)}}.
keyPoints: Vascular disease involves either luminal narrowing or wall weakening.
AAA is typically infrarenal and associated with atherosclerosis.
Inflammatory infiltrates in the media lead to ECM degradation.
Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for AAA.
MMPs (Matrix Metalloproteinases) play a central role in wall thinning.
AAAs are more common in men and usually occur after age 50.
microReview: Aneurysms represent a 'weakening of vessel walls' as opposed to the 'narrowing' seen in occlusive disease. AAA is defined by a 50% increase in diameter, usually infrarenal, and is driven by atherosclerotic inflammation. Thoracic aneurysms often have genetic or hypertensive roots (cystic medial necrosis).
examinerTraps: Do not confuse the location of Syphilitic aneurysms (Thoracic) with Atherosclerotic aneurysms (Abdominal). Also, remember that while hypertension is a risk factor for both, smoking is more specifically linked to AAA.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following biochemical changes is most consistently observed in the vessel wall during the formation of an aneurysm resulting from the 'weakening of vessel walls' mechanism?

options.a: Increased expression of tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs)
options.c: Increased degradation of elastin and collagen
options.d: Accumulation of glycosaminoglycans in the adventitia
