options.e: Enhanced cross-linking of collagen by lysyl oxidase

explanations.a: TIMPs inhibit the degradation of the matrix; their decreased (not increased) activity contributes to aneurysm formation.
explanations.b: MMP production is increased, not decreased, leading to the breakdown of structural proteins.
explanations.c: The fundamental biochemical failure in aneurysms is the imbalance between matrix synthesis and degradation, specifically the loss of elastin and collagen in the media.
explanations.d: Glycosaminoglycan accumulation (cystic medial degeneration) occurs in the media, not the adventitia, and is more specific to thoracic aneurysms.
explanations.e: Lysyl oxidase cross-links collagen, strengthening the wall; its deficiency (e.g., in lathyrism or Menkes disease) would lead to weakening.

ankiCards: The imbalance favoring {{c1::degradation}} over synthesis of ECM leads to aneurysm formation.
Proteolytic enzymes that degrade collagen in aneurysms are called {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
Loss of the structural protein {{c1::elastin}} allows for the initial dilation of the vessel wall.
The inflammatory cells in an aneurysm wall secrete {{c1::cytokines}} that stimulate MMP production.
{{c1::TIMPs}} are the endogenous molecules that normally counteract MMP activity in the vascular wall.
keyPoints: Aneurysms involve an imbalance in ECM metabolism.
Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) are upregulated.
TIMPs (inhibitors) are often downregulated.
Loss of elastin leads to permanent dilation.
Loss of collagen leads to eventual rupture.
microReview: Vascular wall integrity depends on the balance of the extracellular matrix (ECM). When inflammatory cells (macrophages/T-cells) infiltrate the media, they release MMPs that chew through collagen and elastin, causing the 'weakening' described in the text.
examinerTraps: The trap is thinking synthesis is the problem; the problem is usually accelerated degradation or inadequate repair of the existing matrix.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old male with a history of joint hypermobility and unusually long limbs presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset, 'tearing' chest pain radiating to his back. A CT scan confirms an aortic dissection. Histological examination of the aortic wall would most likely show which of the following?

options.a: Atheromatous plaque with a fibrous cap
options.b: Fragmentation of elastic fibers and mucoid material
options.d: Fibrinoid necrosis of the small vasa vasorum
options.e: Intimal thickening with smooth muscle cell migration

explanations.a: Atheromatous plaques are the hallmark of atherosclerosis and AAA, but the patient's age and phenotype suggest Marfan syndrome/cystic medial necrosis.
explanations.b: This describes cystic medial degeneration (also called cystic medial necrosis), the characteristic histological finding in Marfan-associated thoracic aortic disease.
explanations.c: Transmural inflammation with giant cells describes Giant Cell Arteritis.
explanations.d: Fibrinoid necrosis of vasa vasorum is not a standard finding in aortic dissection related to connective tissue disease.
explanations.e: Intimal thickening is a stereotyped response to vascular injury (as mentioned on page 488) but doesn't explain the dissection in this clinical context.

ankiCards: The histological hallmark of Marfan-associated aortic disease is {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
Cystic medial degeneration involves the fragmentation of {{c1::elastic}} fibers.
Marfan syndrome is caused by a mutation in the {{c1::FBN1 (Fibrillin-1)}} gene.
Weakening of the {{c1::media}} allows the formation of an intimal tear and subsequent dissection.
Excessive {{c1::TGF-beta}} signaling is implicated in the pathogenesis of Marfan syndrome aneurysms.
keyPoints: Aortic dissection is often preceded by medial weakness.
Cystic medial degeneration is characterized by lack of inflammation.
The media shows 'cysts' filled with amorphorous ground substance (glycosaminoglycans).
Marfan syndrome involves Fibrillin-1 mutations.
TGF-beta dysregulation contributes to matrix failure.
microReview: While AAA is inflammatory and atherosclerotic, thoracic dissections in young patients are usually non-inflammatory and genetic. The 'weakening' here is due to defective structural proteins (fibrillin) or defective signaling (TGF-beta) leading to cystic medial degeneration.
examinerTraps: Wait for the age. Elderly + Dissection = Hypertension-induced. Young + Dissection = Marfan or Ehlers-Danlos.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following definitions correctly distinguishes a 'true' aneurysm from a 'false' aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm)?

options.a: A true aneurysm involves only the intima, while a false aneurysm involves all three layers.
options.b: A true aneurysm involves an attenuated but intact arterial wall, while a false aneurysm is a wall defect leading to an extravascular hematoma.
options.c: A true aneurysm is always caused by atherosclerosis, while a false aneurysm is always caused by trauma.
options.d: A true aneurysm is cylindrical in shape, while a false aneurysm is always saccular.
options.e: A true aneurysm only occurs in arteries, while a false aneurysm only occurs in veins.

explanations.a: The opposite is true: a true aneurysm involves all three layers (intima, media, adventitia).
explanations.b: This is the classic definition. A true aneurysm is bounded by all three layers of the vessel wall. A false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) is a breach in the wall where the hematoma is contained by extravascular connective tissue.
explanations.c: Aneurysms have many etiologies (congenital, mycotic, syphilitic); they are not defined strictly by the cause.
explanations.d: True aneurysms can be saccular or fusiform (cylindrical).
explanations.e: While much rarer, both can technically occur in both systems, though they are clinically significant in the arterial system.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the arterial wall.
A {{c1::false}} aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) results from a wall defect leading to a hematoma contained by extravascular tissue.
A {{c1::dissection}} occurs when blood enters the wall of the artery as a hematoma between its layers.
Aneurysms can be classified by shape as either {{c1::saccular}} or fusiform.
A {{c1::fusiform}} aneurysm involves circumferential dilation of a long vascular segment.
keyPoints: True aneurysm: all 3 layers intact but dilated.
False aneurysm: wall breach with external containment.
Dissection: blood between wall layers.
Saccular: spherical outpouching of one portion of the wall.
Fusiform: symmetric circumferential dilation.
microReview: Understanding the architectural definition of an aneurysm is key. 'Weakening' can result in a true ballooning of all layers, or a 'rupture' that is barely contained (false aneurysm).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse a dissection with a pseudoaneurysm. In dissection, blood is *inside* the wall layers; in pseudoaneurysm, blood has *exited* the wall and is contained by surrounding tissue.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following best describes a 'mycotic' aneurysm?

options.a: An aneurysm caused specifically by a fungal infection of the vessel wall.
options.b: An aneurysm resulting from an infection that weakens the arterial wall.
options.c: A congenital aneurysm located in the distal lower extremities.
options.d: An aneurysm caused by the deposition of immune complexes.
options.e: A complication of long-term tobacco use in young men.

explanations.a: Despite the name 'mycotic', most are actually bacterial (e.g., from endocarditis).
explanations.b: A mycotic aneurysm is any aneurysm resulting from an infection (bacterial, fungal, etc.) that causes wall destruction.
explanations.c: This describes a location, but mycotic aneurysms can occur anywhere (brain, aorta, visceral).
explanations.d: This describes immune-complex vasculitis.
explanations.e: This describes Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans).

ankiCards: A {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm is caused by infection weakening the vessel wall.
The term 'mycotic' is a misnomer because most such aneurysms are {{c1::bacterial}}.
Common sources of mycotic aneurysms include {{c1::infective endocarditis}}.
Infection can reach the wall via hematogenous seeding or direct extension from an {{c1::adjacent}} abscess.
A mycotic aneurysm is a form of '{{c1::weakening}}' of the vessel wall.
keyPoints: Mycotic aneurysms are infectious in origin.
Usually bacterial (Staph, Strep, Salmonella).
They can lead to rapid rupture due to suppurative necrosis.
Often originate from septic emboli (endocarditis).
Represent a localized form of infectious vasculitis.
microReview: Infection causes 'weakening' through direct tissue destruction by microbial enzymes and the host inflammatory response (neutrophils), leading to 'dilation or rupture' as noted in the intro text.
examinerTraps: The word 'mycotic' refers to the mushroom-like shape observed by early pathologists, not necessarily a fungal etiology.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 52-year-old female presents with a 'worst headache of my life' and neck stiffness. A lumbar puncture shows xanthochromia. A CT angiogram reveals an aneurysm at the junction of the anterior communicating artery and the anterior cerebral artery. This type of aneurysm is most commonly associated with which of the following conditions?

explanations.a: Berry aneurysms (saccular aneurysms of the circle of Willis) are associated with ADPKD and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
explanations.b: Syphilis affects the thoracic aorta, not the cerebral vessels.
explanations.c: Cystic fibrosis has no specific association with berry aneurysms.
explanations.d: SLE causes vasculitis but is not a primary driver of berry aneurysms.
explanations.e: Diabetes is a risk factor for atherosclerosis and AAA, but not specifically berry aneurysms.

ankiCards: {{c1::Berry}} aneurysms are small, saccular dilations in the cerebral circulation.
The most common site for a berry aneurysm is the {{c1::anterior}} communicating artery.
Rupture of a berry aneurysm leads to {{c1::subarachnoid}} hemorrhage.
Berry aneurysms are associated with {{c1::ADPKD}}.
Berry aneurysms occur due to a {{c1::congenital}} defect in the media at vessel bifurcations.
keyPoints: Berry aneurysms are saccular.
Located at branch points in the Circle of Willis.
Lack of internal elastic lamina or smooth muscle at the site.
Strong association with ADPKD.
Clinical presentation: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (Thunderclap headache).
microReview: Cerebral berry aneurysms are 'weakening of vessel walls' due to structural gaps in the media. Unlike AAA, they are not primarily atherosclerotic, though hypertension increases their risk of rupture.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'tearing' pain of aortic dissection with the 'thunderclap' headache of subarachnoid hemorrhage from a berry aneurysm.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Pathologically, what is the 'stereotyped response' of the vascular wall to injury that often precedes or accompanies the development of luminal narrowing in the early stages of atherosclerosis?

explanations.a: Medial thinning is more characteristic of advanced aneurysms, not the initial response to injury.
explanations.b: The text (page 488) explicitly states that intimal thickening is the 'stereotyped response to vascular injury.'
explanations.c: Adventitial fibrosis can occur in chronic stages but is not the primary stereotyped response.
explanations.d: Endothelial dysfunction occurs, but 'intimal thickening' is the structural response mentioned.
explanations.e: Vasa vasorum proliferation occurs in advanced plaques (neovascularization), but isn't the 'stereotyped response'.

ankiCards: The stereotyped response to vascular injury is {{c1::intimal thickening}}.
In response to injury, {{c1::smooth muscle}} cells migrate from the media to the intima.
Migrated smooth muscle cells in the intima produce {{c1::extracellular matrix}}.
Intimal thickening can lead to the {{c1::narrowing}} of vessel lumens.
Vascular injury causes endothelial {{c1::dysfunction}} as an early event.
keyPoints: Intimal thickening is a universal response to injury.
Involves smooth muscle cell recruitment.
Resulting neointima does not contract like normal media.
Contributes to luminal stenosis.
Distinct from the wall weakening that leads to aneurysms.
microReview: The chapter contrasts two mechanisms: narrowing (via intimal thickening/atherosclerosis) and weakening (leading to aneurysms). While they often coexist in AAA, the 'stereotyped response' specifically refers to the neointimal formation.
examinerTraps: The trap is confusing the 'response to injury' (which narrows) with the 'mechanism of aneurysm' (which widens).
sourceQuote: Intimal Thickening: A Stereotyped Response to Vascular Injury
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 75-year-old male with a history of untreated syphilis presents with a barking cough and difficulty swallowing. Imaging shows a massive dilation of the ascending aorta. The wall of the dilated segment shows 'tree-barking' on its internal surface. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism for the weakening of the vessel wall in this patient?

options.a: Medial ischemia due to narrowing of the vasa vasorum
options.b: Genetic mutation in the fibrillin-1 protein
options.c: Cholesterol cleft accumulation in the intima
options.d: Infection of the endothelium by Treponema pallidum
options.e: Autoimmune destruction of the internal elastic lamina

explanations.a: Tertiary syphilis causes obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum, leading to ischemia of the outer media and subsequent 'weakening' and dilation.
explanations.b: This is Marfan syndrome.
explanations.c: This describes atherosclerosis, which usually spares the ascending aorta compared to the abdominal aorta.
explanations.d: The damage is caused by the immune response to the spirochetes in the vasa vasorum, not direct endothelial infection.
explanations.e: This is more characteristic of Giant Cell Arteritis.

ankiCards: Syphilitic aneurysms typically affect the {{c1::ascending/thoracic}} aorta.
The specific lesion in syphilis is {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}} of the vasa vasorum.
Ischemia of the media leads to the '{{c1::tree-bark}}' appearance of the intima.
Syphilitic involvement of the aortic root often causes {{c1::aortic valve insufficiency}}.
The 'tree-barking' appearance is due to {{c1::contraction}} of fibrous scars in the wall.
keyPoints: Syphilitic aneurysms are now rare.
Target the vasa vasorum of the thoracic aorta.
Medial scarring (ischemic) leads to wall weakening.
Dilation of the root can lead to valvular reflux.
Respiratory distress/dysphagia results from local compression.
microReview: Vascular wall weakening in syphilis is an indirect result of microvascular obstruction (vasa vasorum), causing a 'starvation' of the outer aortic media, leading to loss of elastic tissue and subsequent aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Remember: Atherosclerosis = Abdominal; Syphilis = Ascending/Thoracic.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history and long-standing hypertension presents for a routine physical examination. On abdominal palpation, a non-tender, pulsatile mass is noted at the level of the umbilicus. Ultrasound reveals a 4.5-cm dilation of the infrarenal aorta. Which of the following is the most likely underlying pathologic mechanism responsible for this finding?

options.b: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.d: Congenital defect in the tunica media
options.e: Infectious destruction of the arterial wall

explanations.a: Cystic medial degeneration is more commonly associated with thoracic aortic aneurysms, particularly in patients with Marfan syndrome or other connective tissue disorders.
explanations.b: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum is the hallmark of tertiary syphilis, leading to thoracic (specifically ascending) aortic aneurysms, not infrarenal aneurysms.
explanations.c: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAAs) are most frequently associated with atherosclerosis; the plaque impairs nutrient diffusion to the media, leading to secondary ischemia and wall weakening.
explanations.d: Congenital defects in the tunica media (like those in the Circle of Willis) lead to berry aneurysms, not typically large abdominal aortic aneurysms.
explanations.e: Infectious (mycotic) aneurysms are caused by seeding of the vessel wall by bacteria (e.g., from endocarditis), but they are less common than atherosclerotic aneurysms in this demographic.

ankiCards: The most common cause of an abdominal aortic aneurysm is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Abdominal aortic aneurysms are typically located {{c1::infrarenal::relation to renal arteries}}.
Atherosclerosis causes AAA by inducing {{c1::ischemia}} of the inner tunica media.
Major risk factors for AAA include {{c1::smoking}} and male gender.
The clinical presentation of a pulsatile, mid-abdominal mass suggests {{c1::Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA)}}.
keyPoints: Aneurysms represent a localized permanent dilation of a blood vessel.
Atherosclerosis is the primary driver of abdominal aortic aneurysms.
The infrarenal aorta is the most common site for atherosclerotic aneurysms.
The media becomes weakened due to reduced nutrient diffusion across the thick atherosclerotic intima.
AAA is often asymptomatic until rupture or found incidentally.
microReview: Aneurysms involve weakening of the vessel wall. AAA is usually atherosclerotic and infrarenal, whereas Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm (TAA) is often hypertensive or associated with connective tissue disorders.
examinerTraps: A common mistake is confusing the mechanism of TAA (HTN/medial degeneration) with AAA (Atherosclerosis). Also, do not confuse AAA with aortic dissection; AAA is a true aneurysm involving all three layers.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following cellular processes is most critical in the progressive weakening of the aortic wall during the formation of an aneurysm?

options.a: Increased deposition of type IV collagen
options.b: Proteolytic degradation of the extracellular matrix
options.c: Hyperplasia of the smooth muscle cells in the media
options.e: Proliferation of endothelial cells in the intima

explanations.a: Collagen deposition (fibrosis) typically strengthens tissues; however, in aneurysms, the structural collagen is degraded rather than effectively replaced.
explanations.b: The imbalance between matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs) leads to the breakdown of elastin and collagen, weakening the vessel wall.
explanations.c: Smooth muscle cells in the media actually undergo apoptosis or phenotypic change in aneurysms, leading to thinning of the wall, not hyperplasia.
explanations.d: While glycosaminoglycan accumulation occurs in cystic medial necrosis, the primary destructive force in most aneurysms is the loss of existing structural proteins.
explanations.e: Intimal thickening/proliferation is a response to injury, but it is the loss of medial integrity that allows for aneurysmal dilation.

ankiCards: The enzymes primarily responsible for degrading the aortic ECM in aneurysms are {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
Aneurysm formation is characterized by an imbalance between MMPs and {{c1::TIMPs}}.
The loss of {{c1::elastin}} in the media leads to the characteristic dilation of aneurysms.
Increased inflammatory infiltrates in the vessel wall contribute to aneurysm formation by releasing {{c1::cytokines/proteases}}.
Weakening of vessel walls in aneurysms leads to either {{c1::dilation}} or {{c1::rupture}}.
keyPoints: Aneurysm pathogenesis involves a shift in extracellular matrix metabolism.
Chronic inflammation leads to increased protease activity (MMPs).
Elastin degradation reduces the elastic recoil of the vessel.
Medial thinning is a hallmark of true aneurysms.
Genetic factors can predispose individuals by affecting collagen/elastin synthesis.
microReview: Aneurysms = Wall weakening. Mechanism = Inflammation + Proteolysis (MMPs > TIMPs) + Medial ischemia.
examinerTraps: Watch for options suggesting vessel wall thickening; while the intima may thicken due to atherosclerosis, the actual media of an aneurysm is thinned and weak.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular pathology resulting in the weakening of vessel walls is classified as one of the two principal mechanisms underlying vascular disease. What is the most immediate clinical consequence of this specific mechanism?

explanations.a: Lumen narrowing is the consequence of the first mechanism mentioned (obstruction), not weakening.
explanations.b: Weakening of the vessel wall directly leads to dilation (aneurysm) or rupture.
explanations.c: Thrombosis is a consequence of narrowing or endothelial injury, not necessarily wall weakening itself, though it can occur secondarily in an aneurysm.
explanations.d: Ischemic necrosis is the end-result of obstruction or rupture, but not the immediate anatomic change of weakening.
explanations.e: Intimal thickening is a response to injury, whereas weakening refers to medial and adventitial failure.

ankiCards: Two principal mechanisms of vascular disease are narrowing/obstruction and {{c1::weakening}} of vessel walls.
Vessel wall weakening leads to {{c1::dilation}} or rupture.
Narrowing of vessel lumens can occur progressively through {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Narrowing of vessel lumens can occur precipitously through {{c1::thrombosis/embolism}}.
The general architecture of blood vessels is comparable, but walls are thicker in {{c1::arteries}} than veins.
keyPoints: Vascular disease mechanisms: Obstruction and Weakening.
Weakening = Aneurysm / Rupture.
Obstruction = Stenosis / Ischemia.
Arterial walls accommodate higher pressures than venous walls.
The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases in smaller muscular vessels.
microReview: The source identifies two modes of disease: 1. Stenosis/Obstruction (narrowing) and 2. Weakening (dilation/rupture).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'response to injury' (intimal thickening) with the 'mechanism of disease' (weakening).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old female presents with sudden onset of severe, 'tearing' chest pain radiating to her back. She has a history of joint hypermobility and mitral valve prolapse. Her blood pressure is 110/60 mmHg in the right arm and 85/50 mmHg in the left arm. What is the most likely pathological finding in the aortic wall of this patient?

options.b: Medial layer fragmentation and mucoid pooling

explanations.a: Giant cell arteritis involves granulomatous inflammation, usually in the elderly, affecting the temporal artery.
explanations.b: This describes cystic medial necrosis (degeneration), which is the classic finding in Marfan syndrome leading to aortic dissection.
explanations.c: Neutrophilic infiltration of the adventitia is more characteristic of infectious processes or acute vasculitis.
explanations.d: Atherosclerosis is more common in older patients and usually leads to AAA, not dissection in a 32-year-old.
explanations.e: Fibrinoid necrosis is a feature of malignant hypertension or certain vasculitides, not Marfan-related dissection.

ankiCards: The classic histological finding in Marfan-related aortic disease is {{c1::cystic medial necrosis}}.
Cystic medial necrosis involves the accumulation of {{c1::glycosaminoglycans (mucoid material)}}.
Unequal blood pressures between arms in a patient with chest pain suggests {{c1::Aortic Dissection}}.
Cystic medial necrosis leads to the loss of {{c1::elastic fibers}} in the media.
The 'tearing' chest pain radiating to the back is a classic symptom of {{c1::Aortic Dissection}}.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome is a leading cause of cystic medial necrosis in young patients.
Cystic medial necrosis involves elastin fragmentation.
Aortic dissection involves a tear in the intima followed by blood entering the media.
This process is a form of wall weakening/failure.
Dissection can occur without a pre-existing aneurysm, but both share wall weakening mechanisms.
microReview: Marfan = Fibrillin-1 mutation = Weakened ECM = Cystic Medial Necrosis = Risk for TAA and Dissection.
examinerTraps: Aortic dissection is often triggered by hypertension, but in young patients with syndromic features, the primary defect is in the vessel wall structure (weakening).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old male with a history of syphilis presents with symptoms of hoarseness and a persistent cough. Imaging shows a 'tree-barking' appearance of the ascending aorta. This appearance is most directly caused by which of the following?

options.c: Accumulation of lipids in the media

explanations.a: Intimal tears are the primary event in dissection, not the cause of the 'tree-barking' surface.
explanations.b: In tertiary syphilis, obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum causes medial ischemia; the resulting death of medial cells and subsequent scarring (fibrosis) creates a wrinkled, 'tree-bark' appearance.
explanations.c: Lipids accumulate in the intima (atherosclerosis), not the media, in the context of aneurysms.
explanations.d: While syphilis is bacterial, the damage is immune-mediated and ischemic due to vessel involvement (vasa vasorum), not direct endothelial colonization.
explanations.e: This is an acquired condition, not congenital.

ankiCards: The 'tree-barking' appearance of the aorta is associated with {{c1::Tertiary Syphilis}}.
Tertiary syphilis affects the aorta by causing {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}} of the vasa vasorum.
Medial ischemia in syphilitic aortitis leads to {{c1::scarring/fibrosis}}.
Syphilitic aneurysms most commonly affect the {{c1::ascending}} aorta.
Aneurysms caused by syphilis are a result of {{c1::weakening}} of the vessel wall.
keyPoints: Syphilitic aortitis involves the vasa vasorum.
Vasa vasorum endarteritis leads to medial starvation and atrophy.
The loss of medial support causes the aorta to dilate (aneurysm).
Scarring of the intima over the damaged media produces the 'tree-bark' texture.
This is a classic cause of Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm (TAA).
microReview: Syphilis -> Vasa Vasorum destruction -> Medial ischemia -> Medial Weakening -> TAA.
examinerTraps: Atherosclerosis typically spares the ascending aorta; if an aneurysm is found there, think syphilis (historical/classic) or hypertension/connective tissue disease.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which vessel layer is most specifically compromised in the development of a true aneurysm, regardless of the etiology?

explanations.a: The adventitia provides some support, but it is not the primary structural layer whose failure leads to dilation.
explanations.b: The tunica media contains the elastin and smooth muscle necessary for structural integrity; its weakening is the core requirement for aneurysm formation.
explanations.c: The intima is the innermost layer and often shows changes (like atherosclerosis), but intimal failure alone does not cause dilation; media failure does.
explanations.d: The internal elastic lamina is a component, but the entire media is typically involved in the weakening process.
explanations.e: The external elastic lamina is part of the media/adventitia border, but the medial integrity is the primary factor.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the vessel wall.
The tunica {{c1::media}} is the layer primarily responsible for the structural strength of the artery.
Loss of {{c1::smooth muscle}} cells in the media contributes to wall weakening.
In a pseudoaneurysm, the wall is composed of {{c1::extravascular hematoma/connective tissue}}.
Vascular pathology in hypertension often involves changes in the {{c1::small muscular}} arteries.
keyPoints: Aneurysms require medial weakness.
True aneurysms involve Intima, Media, and Adventitia.
The media provides elastic recoil and tensile strength.
Arteries have thicker walls than veins to handle pressure.
Degradation of the medial ECM is a common pathway in all aneurysms.
microReview: Mechanism of aneurysm = Media weakening. Types = True (3 layers) vs False (hematoma).
examinerTraps: Pseudoaneurysms (False aneurysms) do not involve all layers; they are leaks contained by perivascular tissue.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old male with poorly controlled hypertension presents to the emergency department with sudden, excruciating back pain and fainting. His blood pressure is 70/40 mmHg. A bedside ultrasound shows a large amount of free fluid in the peritoneal cavity and a dilated abdominal aorta. What is the most likely immediate outcome of the vascular mechanism involved?

explanations.a: Stenosis refers to narrowing; while it can occur in atherosclerosis, the patient's presentation (hypotension, free fluid) indicates a leak or burst.
explanations.b: The patient is presenting with a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm, which is the catastrophic consequence of vessel wall weakening.
explanations.c: Intimal thickening is a chronic, stereotyped response to injury, not an acute life-threatening event.
explanations.d: Vascular remodeling is a long-term adaptation to pressure or flow changes.
explanations.e: Thrombotic occlusion would lead to distal ischemia (e.g., cold limb), not hypotension and peritoneal fluid.

ankiCards: The triad of hypotension, back pain, and a pulsatile mass suggests {{c1::AAA rupture}}.
AAA rupture usually leads to hemorrhage into the {{c1::peritoneum}} or retroperitoneal space.
The risk of rupture for an aneurysm increases as the {{c1::diameter}} increases.
Aneurysms >{{c1::5.5}} cm in men are usually considered for surgical repair.
The principal mechanism of AAA rupture is {{c1::weakening}} of the vessel wall.
keyPoints: Rupture is the most feared complication of an aneurysm.
Mortality for ruptured AAA is extremely high (up to 90%).
Hypertension and smoking are major modifiable risk factors for rupture.
Rupture occurs when wall stress exceeds wall strength.
Free fluid on ultrasound in a patient with an aneurysm and shock is a rupture until proven otherwise.
microReview: Aneurysm + Shock + Back Pain = Rupture. This is the endpoint of the 'Weakening' mechanism.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the pain of 'dissection' (tearing, often thoracic) with 'rupture' (excruciating, often abdominal/back with shock).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the relationship between arterial wall structure and the hemodynamic forces it must withstand?

options.a: Arterial walls are thinner than veins to allow for better gas exchange.
options.b: The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter decreases in smaller vessels.
options.c: Arterial walls are thicker than veins to accommodate higher blood pressures.
options.d: Arterial walls rely primarily on the intima for structural support.
options.e: Veins have a higher ratio of muscle to lumen diameter than arteries.

explanations.a: Arteries are thicker than veins; only capillaries are thin enough for gas exchange.
explanations.b: The ratio actually increases in smaller muscular vessels to allow for better control of flow and pressure.
explanations.c: As stated in the source text, arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher pressures.
explanations.d: The media, not the intima, provides the primary structural support.
explanations.e: Arteries have a much higher ratio of muscle to lumen than veins.

ankiCards: Arterial walls are thicker than venous walls to accommodate {{c1::higher blood pressures}}.
As arteries become smaller, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}}.
Arteries accommodate {{c1::pulsatile}} flow.
Smaller muscular vessels exert control over blood flow and {{c1::pressure}}.
Most clinically significant vascular lesions involve {{c1::arteries}}.
keyPoints: Structure reflects function in the vascular system.
Arteries are high-pressure conduits; veins are low-pressure reservoirs.
Arterial wall thickness diminishes as vessels get smaller, but the relative thickness increases.
Specific diseases have characteristic anatomic distributions based on vessel type.
Atherosclerosis mainly affects elastic and muscular arteries.
microReview: Arteries = Thick walls, high pressure, muscular. Veins = Thin walls, low pressure, valves.
examinerTraps: Wait for the 'ratio' trap—as vessels get smaller (arterioles), the absolute thickness decreases, but the thickness *relative* to the lumen increases.
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Aneurysms can be classified as 'mycotic' when they result from which of the following processes?

options.c: Infection of the vessel wall by various microbes

explanations.a: Despite the name 'mycotic,' these aneurysms can be caused by bacteria (like Salmonella) or fungi.
explanations.b: MMPs are involved in the common pathway of all aneurysms, but 'mycotic' specifically implies an infectious origin.
explanations.c: A mycotic aneurysm is an aneurysm arising from an infection in the arterial wall, often due to septic emboli or direct extension.
explanations.d: This describes vasculitis, not a mycotic aneurysm.
explanations.e: This describes Ehlers-Danlos or Marfan syndrome.

ankiCards: A {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm is caused by infection of the vessel wall.
A common source of mycotic aneurysms is {{c1::infective endocarditis}} (septic emboli).
The term 'mycotic' refers to the {{c1::appearance}} (mushroom-like) or historical confusion, not just fungal infections.
Mycotic aneurysms are a form of vessel wall {{c1::weakening}}.
A common bacterial cause of mycotic aneurysms in the aorta is {{c1::Salmonella}}.
keyPoints: Mycotic aneurysms are infectious in origin.
They can lead to rapid dilation and rupture.
They often occur at sites of pre-existing atherosclerotic damage.
Sources: Septic emboli, adjacent infection, or direct inoculation.
They are 'true' aneurysms if the infection destroys the wall allowing dilation of the layers.
microReview: Mycotic Aneurysm = Infectious weakening. Not always fungal; usually bacterial (Staph, Strep, Salmonella).
examinerTraps: The term 'mycotic' is a misnomer; it sounds like it's only fungi, but it's any infection causing wall weakening.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Which of the following describes the category of vessels most commonly affected by atherosclerosis?

explanations.a: Capillaries and venules are too small and lack the media structure where atherosclerosis typically develops.
explanations.b: As stated in the source, atherosclerosis mainly affects elastic (e.g., aorta) and muscular (e.g., coronary) arteries.
explanations.c: Veins are rarely affected by atherosclerosis because of their low-pressure environment.
explanations.d: Lymphatics are involved in lymphedema and inflammation, not atherosclerosis.
explanations.e: Atherosclerosis affects large and medium arteries; 'small arterioles' are the site of hyaline or hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis.

ankiCards: Atherosclerosis affects mainly {{c1::elastic}} and muscular arteries.
The most common site for an atherosclerotic aneurysm is the {{c1::Abdominal Aorta}}.
Vascular lesions in the {{c1::arteries}} are more clinically significant than those in veins.
Two mechanisms of vascular disease: {{c1::narrowing}} and weakening.
Atherosclerosis is a {{c1::progressive}} cause of vessel lumen obstruction.
keyPoints: Vascular disease is a leading cause of death.
Atherosclerosis targets high-pressure arterial systems.
Elastic arteries: Aorta, carotid, iliac.
Muscular arteries: Coronary, renal.
Atherosclerotic plaques cause both narrowing and wall weakening.
microReview: Atherosclerosis = Elastic/Muscular arteries. Leads to Ischemia (narrowing) or Aneurysm (weakening).
examinerTraps: Don't say 'all vessels' are affected by atherosclerosis. It is strictly an arterial disease.
sourceQuote: atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old female presents with several rapidly growing, ill-defined, purplish-red skin nodules on her left arm. She has a history of breast cancer 8 years ago, treated with a radical mastectomy and adjuvant radiotherapy. Physical examination reveals significant chronic lymphedema of the left upper extremity. A biopsy of a skin lesion shows atypical, pleomorphic endothelial cells forming irregular vascular channels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are benign lesions composed of small, thin-walled capillaries and do not show pleomorphism or association with chronic lymphedema.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors are benign, highly painful tumors arising from specialized smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, usually found under the fingernails.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a malignant vascular tumor that can arise in the setting of chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome) or following radiation therapy, both of which are present in this patient.
explanations.d: Kaposi sarcoma is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor caused by HHV-8, typically presenting as multiple purple patches or nodules, but is not specifically linked to post-mastectomy lymphedema.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign vascular proliferation caused by Bartonella species in immunocompromised patients, appearing histologically as neutrophilic infiltrates and clusters of bacteria.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema post-mastectomy is known as {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
The characteristic histological finding in angiosarcoma involves atypical {{c1::endothelial cells}} forming irregular channels.
Common environmental risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma include {{c1::vinyl chloride}}, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
Vascular tumors expressing {{c1::CD31}} (PECAM-1) confirm their endothelial origin.
Post-irradiation angiosarcoma typically occurs {{c1::several years (e.g., 5-10)}} after radiotherapy.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are highly malignant tumors of vascular endothelium.
Clinical risk factors include chronic lymphedema, radiation, and specific chemical exposures.
Stewart-Treves syndrome refers specifically to lymphangiosarcoma following radical mastectomy.
Histology shows high mitotic activity and marked cellular pleomorphism.
Prognosis is generally poor due to early local invasion and metastasis.
microReview: Angiosarcoma is the aggressive end of the vascular tumor spectrum. Look for a history of radiation or chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Stewart-Treves syndrome with Kaposi sarcoma; both present with purple lesions, but the clinical context of mastectomy/lymphedema points to Angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors... Malignant tumors... Angiosarcomas are malignant vascular neoplasms that range from highly differentiated tumors... to wildly proliferating... tumors.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A research scientist is studying the pathogenesis of a vascular tumor frequently observed in patients with Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS). The study focuses on a specific viral protein that induces the expression of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and creates an inflammatory milieu. Which infectious agent is the primary driver of this neoplastic process?

explanations.a: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not primary vascular tumors.
explanations.b: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of all forms of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.c: CMV can cause retinitis or colitis in AIDS patients but is not oncogenic for vascular tumors.
explanations.d: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which is a reactive vascular proliferation, not a true neoplastic malignancy driven by viral proteins.
explanations.e: HPV is associated with squamous cell carcinomas, particularly of the cervix and oropharynx.

ankiCards: The virus associated with Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is {{c1::Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}.
HHV-8 is also referred to as {{c1::KSHV (Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus)}}.
The four clinical forms of Kaposi Sarcoma are Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and {{c1::AIDS-associated}}.
The pathognomonic cell in Kaposi Sarcoma histology is the {{c1::spindle cell}}.
HHV-8 induces vascular proliferation primarily by stimulating {{c1::VEGF}}.
keyPoints: HHV-8 is essential but not sufficient for the development of Kaposi Sarcoma.
KS is classified as an intermediate-grade (borderline) vascular tumor.
Histology often shows slit-like spaces containing red blood cells.
AIDS-associated KS is the most common HIV-associated malignancy worldwide.
Treatment involves highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) to restore immune function.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = HHV-8 + Spindle cells + AIDS/Immunosuppression.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'Bartonella' in questions about HIV and vascular lesions; if the lesion has neutrophils and bacteria (Warthin-Starry stain), it's Bacillary Angiomatosis, not KS.
sourceQuote: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV8) and is highly associated with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old male presents with an exquisitely painful, 5-mm, firm, blue-colored nodule located under the fingernail of his right index finger. The pain is triggered by cold temperature and touch. Which of the following cell types is the origin of this tumor?

explanations.a: Endothelial cells form the lining of vessels in hemangiomas, but not the specialized glomus body tumor.
explanations.b: Pericytes are the origin of hemangiopericytomas, which are distinct from glomus tumors.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts are the source of fibromas, which are not typically subungual or temperature-sensitive.
explanations.e: Lymphatic cells form lymphangiomas, which are usually painless and found in the neck or axilla.

ankiCards: Glomus tumors most commonly occur in the {{c1::subungual (under nail)}} region.
The clinical triad of a glomus tumor includes pain, tenderness, and {{c1::sensitivity to cold}}.
Glomus tumors arise from the {{c1::glomus body}}, which regulates temperature.
Histologically, glomus tumors consist of nests of uniform cells surrounding {{c1::vascular channels}}.
The cells of origin for glomus tumors are modified {{c1::smooth muscle}} cells.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but extremely painful.
The subungual location is classic for board exams.
They are small, usually less than 1 cm in diameter.
Excision is curative.
The cells are alpha-smooth muscle actin positive.
microReview: Painful + Subungual + Cold sensitive = Glomus Tumor (Smooth muscle origin).
examinerTraps: The examiner may describe the pain as 'paroxysmal' or 'lancinating' to mimic a nerve tumor, but the location and vascular appearance are key.
sourceQuote: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, exquisitely painful tumors arising from specialized smooth muscle cells of the glomus bodies.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated 1-cm lesion on her gingiva. The lesion bleeds easily with minor trauma. She states it appeared two weeks ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: While a capillary hemangioma is a broad category, pyogenic granuloma is the specific term for this rapidly growing, pedunculated variant often found on gingiva.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are deeper, less well-circumscribed, and consist of large blood-filled spaces; they do not typically present as pedunculated gingival masses.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a benign, fast-growing vascular lesion often occurring on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa, frequently associated with pregnancy (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a malignant, poorly circumscribed lesion, not a small pedunculated nodule in a young pregnant woman.
explanations.e: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a flat, congenital vascular ectasia, not a growing mass.

ankiCards: A pyogenic granuloma occurring in the gingiva of a pregnant woman is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Despite the name, pyogenic granulomas are neither {{c1::infectious (pyogenic)}} nor {{c1::granulomatous}}.
Histologically, pyogenic granuloma is a variant of {{c1::capillary hemangioma}}.
The most common clinical locations for pyogenic granuloma are the {{c1::skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized by rapid growth and {{c1::easy bleeding}} (friability).
keyPoints: Pyogenic granulomas are benign, lobulated capillary hemangiomas.
They often follow minor trauma.
Pregnancy-associated lesions may regress spontaneously postpartum.
Histology shows proliferating capillaries with edema and an inflammatory infiltrate.
Surgical excision or curettage is the standard treatment if they don't regress.
microReview: Pregnancy + Gingiva + Bleeding mass = Pyogenic Granuloma.
examinerTraps: The name 'Pyogenic Granuloma' is a misnomer; it is not caused by pus-forming bacteria and does not show granulomas on histology.
sourceQuote: Pyogenic granulomas are capillary hemangiomas that manifest as rapidly growing red pedunculated nodules on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An HIV-positive patient with a CD4+ count of 150 cells/µL presents with multiple red-to-purple skin papules. A biopsy is performed, and a Warthin-Starry silver stain reveals clusters of tangled bacilli. Which of the following histopathological features would most reliably distinguish this condition from Kaposi sarcoma?

options.d: Presence of red blood cell extravasation

explanations.a: Both conditions involve endothelial cell proliferation.
explanations.b: Slit-like spaces are more characteristic of Kaposi Sarcoma, but 'distinguishing' based on neutrophils is a higher yield pathognomonic feature for Bacillary Angiomatosis.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is characterized by a prominent neutrophilic infiltrate, while Kaposi sarcoma typically shows a lymphocytic infiltrate or lacks significant acute inflammation.
explanations.d: RBC extravasation is common in both vascular lesions.
explanations.e: CD31 is a pan-endothelial marker and would be positive in both vascular lesions.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by bacteria of the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
The stain used to visualize the organisms in bacillary angiomatosis is the {{c1::Warthin-Starry (silver)}} stain.
Unlike Kaposi Sarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis lesions contain numerous {{c1::neutrophils}}.
The two species responsible for bacillary angiomatosis are B. henselae and {{c1::B. quintana}}.
Bacillary angiomatosis is treated with {{c1::erythromycin (or doxycycline)}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis is a reactive vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts.
It can mimic Kaposi Sarcoma clinically.
B. henselae is typically transmitted by cat scratches.
B. quintana is transmitted by human body lice.
Identification of bacteria is key to diagnosis.
microReview: Bacillary Angiomatosis = Bartonella + Neutrophils + HIV. Treat with antibiotics.
examinerTraps: Both KS and Bacillary Angiomatosis occur in HIV patients. Look for the 'Warthin-Starry' or 'neutrophils' hint to choose Bacillary Angiomatosis.
sourceQuote: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts... caused by opportunistic gram-negative bacilli of the Bartonella family.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular lesions is a common component of von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease, often occurring in the cerebellum or retina?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are common in skin but not the hallmark of VHL in the CNS.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are common in the liver but not the primary CNS lesion of VHL.
explanations.c: Hemangioblastomas are highly vascular tumors that are a characteristic feature of VHL disease, specifically in the cerebellum, retina, and spinal cord.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a malignancy not associated with the VHL germline mutation.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are peripheral subungual lesions unrelated to VHL.

ankiCards: The vascular tumor associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease is {{c1::hemangioblastoma}}.
Hemangioblastomas in VHL disease are most commonly found in the {{c1::cerebellum (or retina)}}.
VHL disease is caused by a mutation in the {{c1::VHL}} gene on chromosome {{c2::3}}.
The VHL protein normally targets {{c1::HIF-1α (Hypoxia Inducible Factor)}} for degradation.
Patients with VHL are also at high risk for {{c1::Renal Cell Carcinoma}} (clear cell type).
keyPoints: Hemangioblastomas are benign but can cause mass effect in the CNS.
VHL is an autosomal dominant condition.
Loss of VHL function leads to constitutive HIF activation and VEGF overproduction.
Retinal hemangioblastomas can lead to vision loss.
Diagnosis involves imaging and genetic testing.
microReview: VHL = Hemangioblastoma (CNS/Retina) + Renal Cell Carcinoma + Pheochromocytoma.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse hemangioblastoma with hemangioma. Hemangioblastoma is a specific entity associated with VHL.
sourceQuote: Cavernous hemangiomas... also are a component of von Hippel-Lindau disease, where vascular neoplasms occur in the cerebellum, brain stem, [and] retina.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 1-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for a bright red, raised, 'strawberry-like' lesion on his cheek. The mother noticed it shortly after birth, and it has grown slightly since then. What is the most appropriate management for this lesion?

options.d: Wide local excision with lymph node biopsy

explanations.a: Surgery is avoided as these usually regress and surgery might cause scarring.
explanations.b: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are extremely common in infants; they typically grow rapidly for a few months and then regress spontaneously by age 7 in the majority of cases.
explanations.c: Corticosteroids or beta-blockers are used only for complicated lesions (e.g., those obstructing vision).
explanations.d: This is a benign lesion; wide excision and lymph node biopsy are for malignancies.
explanations.e: Chemotherapy is not indicated for benign hemangiomas.

ankiCards: The most common vascular tumor of infancy is the {{c1::juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma}}.
Juvenile hemangiomas typically show a period of rapid growth followed by {{c1::spontaneous regression}}.
By age 7, approximately {{c1::75-90%}} of juvenile hemangiomas have regressed.
The histological appearance of a strawberry hemangioma is that of a {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma.
First-line medical therapy for 'problematic' strawberry hemangiomas (e.g., near the eye) is {{c1::propranolol}}.
keyPoints: Strawberry hemangiomas are bright red and lobulated.
They are present in 1 in 200 births.
Regression begins with fading color and softening of the mass.
Complete resolution is common by school age.
Complications are rare but include ulceration or visual obstruction.
microReview: Strawberry hemangioma = Infant + Rapid growth + Regression.
examinerTraps: The examiner might try to push for 'surgical excision' due to the rapid growth, but the correct answer is usually 'observation' or 'reassurance' unless it's blocking an eye or the airway.
sourceQuote: Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) of the newborn skin are very common... they grow rapidly for a few months but then fade and eventually regress.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular tumors are often classified by their clinical behavior. Which of the following neoplasms is correctly matched with its clinical grade?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangioma is benign.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is classified as intermediate-grade (borderline).
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor.
explanations.d: Glomus tumor is a benign tumor.
explanations.e: Hemangioendothelioma is an intermediate-grade (borderline) tumor.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma and Hemangioendothelioma are classified as {{c1::intermediate (borderline)}} vascular tumors.
The most aggressive malignant vascular tumor is {{c1::Angiosarcoma}}.
Vascular tumors that never metastasize and are cured by excision are {{c1::benign}}.
The pan-endothelial IHC marker used to identify vascular tumors is {{c1::CD31}}.
Vascular tumors are divided into three grades: Benign, {{c1::Intermediate (Borderline)}}, and Malignant.
keyPoints: Classification is based on the likelihood of metastasis and local invasion.
Benign: Hemangiomas, Glomus tumors.
Intermediate: Kaposi Sarcoma, Epithelioid Hemangioendothelioma.
Malignant: Angiosarcoma.
Metastasis is the defining feature of the malignant category.
microReview: Benign (Hemangioma) -> Intermediate (Kaposi) -> Malignant (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: Don't classify Kaposi Sarcoma as fully malignant; it's borderline because many cases are controlled by immune restoration and don't behave like high-grade sarcomas.
sourceQuote: Vascular neoplasms are divided into three categories: (1) benign tumors... (2) intermediate-grade tumors... and (3) malignant tumors (angiosarcomas).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with a large, flat, purple-red birthmark covering the left side of his face in the distribution of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve. His parents report he recently had a seizure. An MRI of the brain shows leptomeningeal venous malformations on the ipsilateral side. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) presents with multiple small telangiectasias and bleeding, not a port-wine stain.
explanations.b: Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) is characterized by a facial port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) in the trigeminal distribution and ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomas.
explanations.c: VHL disease presents with hemangioblastomas, not a facial port-wine stain.
explanations.d: Kasabach-Merritt syndrome involves platelet sequestration in a large hemangioma, leading to thrombocytopenia.
explanations.e: Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome involves port-wine stains but typically affects the limbs with associated bone and soft tissue hypertrophy.

ankiCards: The facial birthmark associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome is a {{c1::nevus flammeus (port-wine stain)}}.
Sturge-Weber syndrome is associated with vascular malformations in the {{c1::leptomeninges}}.
Common clinical manifestations of Sturge-Weber include seizures, intellectual disability, and {{c1::glaucoma}}.
The genetic mutation associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome is a somatic mutation in {{c1::GNAQ}}.
The 'port-wine stain' in Sturge-Weber typically follows the distribution of the {{c1::trigeminal (CN V)}} nerve.
keyPoints: Sturge-Weber is a non-hereditary phakomatosis.
The port-wine stain is usually present at birth and does not regress.
Skull X-rays may show 'tram-track' calcifications of the cortex.
Ipsilateral glaucoma is a frequent complication.
The port-wine stain is a form of vascular ectasia.
microReview: Port-wine stain (CN V distribution) + Seizures + Leptomeningeal angioma = Sturge-Weber.
examinerTraps: Be careful with the name: Sturge-Weber involves a port-wine stain (ectasia), not a strawberry hemangioma.
sourceQuote: Nevus flammeus in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve is a component of the Sturge-Weber syndrome... associated with venous angiomatous masses in the leptomeninges.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following environmental exposures is most strongly linked to the development of hepatic angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Aflatoxin B1 is a major risk factor for Hepatocellular Carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Vinyl chloride (used in plastic manufacturing), arsenic (pesticides), and Thorotrast (a legacy radiocontrast agent) are the classic risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Benzene exposure is primarily linked to acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.d: Asbestos exposure is linked to mesothelioma and lung cancer.
explanations.e: Coal dust is linked to coal worker's pneumoconiosis, not vascular tumors.

ankiCards: Three classic exposures linked to hepatic angiosarcoma are vinyl chloride, arsenic, and {{c1::Thorotrast}}.
Vinyl chloride is a chemical used in the production of {{c1::polyvinyl chloride (PVC)}} plastics.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is a {{c1::malignant}} tumor of endothelial cells.
Unlike hemangiomas, hepatic angiosarcoma is highly {{c1::aggressive/invasive}}.
Thorotrast was a radioactive contrast agent containing {{c1::thorium dioxide}}.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma has a long latency period (decades after exposure).
It is rare but highly lethal.
Diagnosis is often late as symptoms are non-specific (jaundice, weight loss).
IHC shows expression of CD31 and von Willebrand factor.
Occupational safety regulations have decreased vinyl chloride-related cases.
microReview: Angiosarcoma (Liver) = Vinyl Chloride / Arsenic / Thorotrast.
examinerTraps: Distinguish between 'vinyl chloride' (Angiosarcoma) and 'Aflatoxin' (Hepatocellular Carcinoma). Both affect the liver but have different origins.
sourceQuote: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with distinct environmental carcinogens, including arsenic... Thorotrast... and vinyl chloride.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 34-year-old male with a history of HIV and a CD4+ count of 120 cells/mm³ presents with multiple non-blanching, painless, purple-to-red plaques on his lower extremities and hard palate. A biopsy of one skin lesion reveals a proliferation of spindle-shaped cells forming slit-like spaces containing erythrocytes, along with a chronic inflammatory infiltrate. Which of the following is the most likely causative agent for these findings?

explanations.a: HHV-8, also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the etiologic agent for Kaposi Sarcoma, which presents as purple plaques and contains spindle cells with slit-like vascular spaces.
explanations.b: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised patients, but it is characterized by neutrophilic infiltrates and lobular capillary proliferation, not spindle cells with slit-like spaces.
explanations.c: EBV is associated with various lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not primary vascular tumors like Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.d: CMV can cause retinitis or colitis in AIDS patients but does not cause primary cutaneous vascular tumors.
explanations.e: HPV is associated with warts and various squamous cell carcinomas, not vascular spindle-cell neoplasms.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is caused by the infection of {{c1::Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}.
The histological hallmark of Kaposi Sarcoma is the presence of {{c1::spindle cells}} and {{c2::slit-like spaces}} containing RBCs.
In AIDS patients, Kaposi Sarcoma frequently involves the skin and the {{c1::hard palate/GI tract}}.
Unlike bacillary angiomatosis, Kaposi Sarcoma is characterized by a {{c1::lymphocytic}} rather than neutrophilic infiltrate.
HHV-8 is also associated with {{c1::Primary Effusion Lymphoma}}.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8.
Epidemic KS is the most common AIDS-associated malignancy.
Histology shows sheets of spindle cells and slit-like vascular channels.
Clinical presentation involves purple/red macules, plaques, or nodules.
Extracutaneous involvement commonly includes the oral cavity and GI tract.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = HIV + Purple plaques + HHV-8 + Spindle cells with slit-like spaces.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Kaposi Sarcoma (HHV-8, spindle cells, lymphocytic) with Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella, neutrophils, Warthin-Starry positive).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A skin biopsy from a patient with HIV showing vascular proliferation is stained with a Warthin-Starry silver stain, revealing numerous clusters of bacilli. Histological examination shows a prominent neutrophilic infiltrate and capillary proliferation with 'epithelioid' endothelial cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella species and is histologically characterized by capillary proliferation, epithelioid endothelial cells, and a striking neutrophilic infiltrate; the bacteria are visible on silver stain.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma shows spindle cells and slit-like spaces, typically lacks neutrophils, and is not caused by bacteria.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignancy with pleomorphic cells and does not feature clusters of bacilli.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a lobular capillary hemangioma often following trauma or pregnancy; it lacks the specific bacterial clusters seen in bacillary angiomatosis.
explanations.e: Glomus tumor arises from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body and is typically found subungually.

ankiCards: The causative agent of bacillary angiomatosis is {{c1::Bartonella (henselae or quintana)}}.
Bacillary angiomatosis is histologically characterized by an infiltrate of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
The silver stain used to identify Bartonella in bacillary angiomatosis is the {{c1::Warthin-Starry}} stain.
Bacillary angiomatosis endothelial cells are described as having an {{c1::epithelioid}} appearance.
Treatment for bacillary angiomatosis usually involves {{c1::erythromycin/antibiotics}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts.
Caused by Bartonella henselae (cat scratch) or Bartonella quintana (trench fever).
Histology: Proliferating capillaries with neutrophils and nuclear dust.
Diagnosis: Warthin-Starry stain demonstrates bacteria.
Clinical: Red/purple papules resembling Kaposi Sarcoma.
microReview: Bacillary Angiomatosis = HIV + Bartonella + Neutrophils + Warthin-Starry stain.
examinerTraps: Wait for the stain or the cell type: neutrophils favor Bacillary Angiomatosis; spindle cells favor Kaposi.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 42-year-old female presents with an exquisitely painful, 5-mm, firm, red-blue nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. She notes the pain is particularly intense when her hand is exposed to cold water. The tumor likely originates from which of the following cell types?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) arise from the specialized, modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, which is involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.b: Endothelial cells line the vascular spaces but are not the primary proliferating cell in a glomus tumor.
explanations.c: Pericytes are found around capillaries, but the glomus cell is specifically a modified smooth muscle cell of the glomus body.
explanations.d: Schwann cells form the myelin sheath of nerves; tumors of these cells are neuromas or schwannomas, which don't present this way.
explanations.e: Fibroblasts produce collagen; fibromas or dermatofibromas are typically not subungual or cold-sensitive.

ankiCards: A glomus tumor is most commonly found in the {{c1::subungual (under nail)}} region.
The characteristic symptom of a glomus tumor is intense pain triggered by {{c1::cold}}.
Glomus tumors arise from modified {{c1::smooth muscle}} cells.
The glomus body's physiological function is {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Glomus cells are histologically seen as small, uniform, round cells surrounding {{c1::vascular channels}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumor (Glomangioma) is a benign, extremely painful tumor.
Classic location: Subungual (under the fingernail).
Derived from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
Pain is often paroxysmal and triggered by cold temperature.
Histology: Branching vascular channels separated by aggregates of glomus cells.
microReview: Glomus tumor = Subungual + Extremely Painful + Cold sensitivity + Smooth muscle origin.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse 'Glomus tumor' (glomangioma) with 'Glomus jugulare' (a paraganglioma).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 62-year-old male presents with weight loss, abdominal pain, and jaundice. Imaging reveals multiple ill-defined, hemorrhagic masses within the liver. Biopsy shows highly pleomorphic, malignant cells expressing CD31. History reveals long-term occupational exposure to industrial chemicals. Which of the following exposures is most likely associated with this malignancy?

explanations.a: Hepatic angiosarcoma is strongly associated with exposure to vinyl chloride (used in PVC production), arsenic, and Thorotrast.
explanations.b: Aflatoxin B1 is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), which arises from hepatocytes, not endothelial cells.
explanations.c: Beryllium is associated with lung cancer and berylliosis (granulomatous disease).
explanations.d: Carbon tetrachloride is a hepatotoxin causing centrilobular necrosis and fatty change, but not specifically angiosarcoma.
explanations.e: Benzene is most closely linked to acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}, {{c2::arsenic}}, and Thorotrast.
Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor of {{c1::endothelial cells}}.
A useful immunohistochemical marker for angiosarcoma is {{c1::CD31 (or vWF)}}.
The prognosis for angiosarcoma is generally {{c1::poor}}.
Vinyl chloride is used in the manufacturing of {{c1::polyvinyl chloride (PVC)}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a rare, highly malignant vascular tumor.
Hepatic angiosarcoma has specific chemical associations (Vinyl chloride, Arsenic).
Tumor cells express endothelial markers like CD31.
Often presents with non-specific symptoms until late stages.
Grossly appears as multifocal, hemorrhagic, necrotic masses.
microReview: Angiosarcoma = Malignant Endothelium + CD31 positive + Vinyl Chloride association.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse angiosarcoma (CD31+) with hepatocellular carcinoma (AFP+).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 1-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for a bright red, raised, 'strawberry-like' lesion on the left cheek. The mother states it was not present at birth but appeared at 2 weeks of age and has grown rapidly. Which of the following is the most likely natural history of this lesion?

options.b: Rapid growth with potential for metastasis

explanations.a: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are common in infants; they grow rapidly initially but the vast majority (75-90%) regress spontaneously by age 7.
explanations.b: These are benign lesions; they do not metastasize.
explanations.c: They typically regress rather than persist unchanged.
explanations.d: Benign hemangiomas do not typically transform into malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.e: A port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) is a separate entity that does not grow rapidly after birth and does not regress.

ankiCards: The most common vascular tumor of infancy is the {{c1::juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma}}.
Strawberry hemangiomas typically appear {{c1::shortly after birth (first few weeks)}}.
The natural history of a strawberry hemangioma is {{c1::spontaneous regression}}.
By age 7, approximately {{c1::75-90%}} of strawberry hemangiomas have regressed.
Histologically, strawberry hemangiomas are classified as {{c1::capillary}} hemangiomas.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangiomas are extremely common (1 in 200 births).
Rapid growth phase followed by gradual involution.
Usually located on the skin or mucous membranes.
They are benign capillary proliferations.
Treatment is usually observation unless they obstruct vital functions (e.g., vision).
microReview: Strawberry hemangioma = Infant + Rapid growth + Spontaneous involution.
examinerTraps: Differentiate from Port-wine stains (Nevus flammeus), which are flat and do not regress.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 50-year-old male is found to have multiple large, blood-filled vascular spaces in the liver during an incidental ultrasound. These spaces are lined by a single layer of endothelium and separated by thin fibrous stroma. Which of the following conditions is most closely associated with similar lesions in the cerebellum and retina?

explanations.a: Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is characterized by cavernous hemangiomas (hemangioblastomas) in the cerebellum, retina, and brainstem, as well as visceral cysts and renal cell carcinoma.
explanations.b: Sturge-Weber syndrome involves a facial port-wine stain and leptomeningeal venous malformations, not typically discrete cavernous hemangiomas of the liver/cerebellum.
explanations.c: Tuberous sclerosis is associated with angiolipomas and cardiac rhabdomyomas, not cavernous hemangiomas.
explanations.d: NF1 is associated with neurofibromas and Lisch nodules, not primarily vascular hemangiomas.
explanations.e: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) features multiple small telangiectasias, not large cavernous hemangiomas.

ankiCards: Cavernous hemangiomas in the CNS and retina are characteristic of {{c1::Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL)}} disease.
Histology of cavernous hemangiomas shows {{c1::large, blood-filled spaces}} separated by fibrous stroma.
The most common internal organ involved by cavernous hemangiomas is the {{c1::liver}}.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas {{c1::do not}} spontaneously regress.
VHL disease is caused by a mutation in the {{c1::VHL}} tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas involve larger, deeper vascular channels than capillary types.
They are usually sharply circumscribed but not encapsulated.
In the liver, they are often incidental findings.
CNS/Retinal involvement suggests Von Hippel-Lindau disease.
Clinically significant if they cause mass effect or rupture (rare).
microReview: Cavernous hemangioma = Large vascular spaces + Liver + VHL association (CNS/Retina).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse cavernous hemangioma (benign) with angiosarcoma (malignant, pleomorphic).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 26-year-old female in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with a rapidly growing, 1-cm, pedunculated red mass on her gingiva. The lesion is friable and bleeds easily with minor trauma. She reports it appeared suddenly two weeks ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma (granuloma gravidarum in pregnancy) is a lobular capillary hemangioma that often occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women and is known for rapid growth and easy bleeding.
explanations.b: While it is histologically a form of capillary hemangioma, 'pyogenic granuloma' is the specific clinical name for this presentation.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are painful and subungual; they do not typically occur on the gingiva.
explanations.d: Angiosarcomas are rare, malignant, and usually occur in older adults or at sites of prior radiation, not as a sudden pregnancy-associated gingival mass.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is associated with HIV and Bartonella infection, not typically pregnancy.

ankiCards: A pyogenic granuloma occurring on the gingiva of a pregnant woman is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are histologically {{c1::lobular capillary hemangiomas}}.
Despite the name, pyogenic granulomas are neither {{c1::pyogenic (infectious)}} nor {{c2::granulomatous}}.
The clinical appearance of a pyogenic granuloma is a {{c1::pedunculated red mass}} that bleeds easily.
Many pregnancy-related pyogenic granulomas will {{c1::regress/resolve}} after delivery.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign, rapid-growing vascular lesion.
Commonly involves skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
Frequently associated with trauma or pregnancy.
Histology shows exuberant granulation-tissue-like capillary proliferation.
Surface is often ulcerated and bleeds easily (friable).
microReview: Pyogenic granuloma = Pregnancy/Trauma + Gingiva + Rapidly growing red nodule + Bleeds easily.
examinerTraps: Ignore the name 'pyogenic' and 'granuloma'—it's a hemangioma, not an infection or a true granuloma.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A researcher is studying a group of vascular tumors. To confirm the endothelial origin of a poorly differentiated spindle cell malignancy, which of the following immunohistochemical markers would be most useful and specific?

explanations.a: CD31 (Platelet Endothelial Cell Adhesion Molecule) is a highly specific marker for endothelial cells and is used to identify tumors of vascular origin like angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells and carcinomas.
explanations.c: S100 is a marker for cells of neural crest origin, such as melanocytes and Schwann cells.
explanations.d: Desmin is a marker for myogenic (muscle) cells.
explanations.e: Vimentin is a marker for all mesenchymal cells; while positive in vascular tumors, it lacks specificity as it is positive in almost all sarcomas.

ankiCards: The most common marker used to identify vascular differentiation in tumors is {{c1::CD31}}.
Another marker for endothelial cells besides CD31 is {{c1::von Willebrand factor (Factor VIII-related antigen)}}.
CD31 is also known as {{c1::PECAM-1}}.
In angiosarcoma, tumor cells will stain positive for {{c1::CD31}}.
Malignant vascular tumors that look like spindle cells must be differentiated from {{c1::fibrosarcomas or leiomyosarcomas}} using CD31.
keyPoints: Immunohistochemistry is essential for diagnosing poorly differentiated vascular tumors.
CD31 is the most specific and widely used endothelial marker.
vWF (Factor VIII) is also used but can be less sensitive in poorly differentiated cases.
Endothelial markers help differentiate angiosarcoma from other spindle cell sarcomas.
CD34 is another marker but is less specific than CD31.
microReview: Vascular tumor marker = CD31 (PECAM-1) or vWF.
examinerTraps: Vimentin is always positive in sarcomas but is never the 'best' answer for specificity.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with several firm, violaceous nodules on her right arm. She has a history of a radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer 12 years ago, which was followed by chronic, severe lymphedema of the right upper extremity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for the new skin lesions?

explanations.a: The development of angiosarcoma (specifically lymphangiosarcoma) in the setting of chronic lymphedema following mastectomy is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and usually occurs in different clinical contexts (classic, endemic, or AIDS-related).
explanations.c: Lymphangiomas are benign proliferations, typically present from birth; they do not typically arise de novo as malignant nodules in adults.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis requires Bartonella infection and immunosuppression; it is not linked to post-mastectomy lymphedema.
explanations.e: Glomangiomas are benign, painful, subungual tumors.

ankiCards: Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to the development of {{c1::angiosarcoma}} in a limb with chronic lymphedema.
Stewart-Treves syndrome is most classically seen after {{c1::radical mastectomy}} with lymph node dissection.
