The duration of lymphedema before the onset of angiosarcoma in Stewart-Treves is usually {{c1::10 or more}} years.
The skin lesions in Stewart-Treves syndrome usually appear as {{c1::purple/violaceous nodules}}.
Angiosarcoma in the setting of Stewart-Treves syndrome has a {{c1::poor}} prognosis.
keyPoints: Chronic lymphedema is a major risk factor for cutaneous angiosarcoma.
Stewart-Treves syndrome occurs after axillary node dissection for breast cancer.
The tumor arises from lymphatic or blood vessel endothelium.
Presents as multiple cutaneous nodules on the lymphedematous arm.
Highly aggressive with a high rate of metastasis.
microReview: Post-mastectomy lymphedema + Skin nodules = Stewart-Treves Syndrome (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse this with recurrent breast cancer; the purple color suggests a vascular origin (Angiosarcoma).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 5-year-old child presents with a large, flat, purple area on the left side of his face that has been present since birth and has grown proportionately with the child. The lesion follows the distribution of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve. This finding is most strongly associated with which of the following?

explanations.a: A facial port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) in the trigeminal distribution is a hallmark of Sturge-Weber syndrome, which is associated with ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomas, seizures, and glaucoma.
explanations.b: Large hemangiomas (not port-wine stains) in infants can rarely cause high-output heart failure, but it is not the primary association for this lesion.
explanations.c: Visceral cysts are associated with Von Hippel-Lindau disease, which features cavernous hemangiomas, not port-wine stains.
explanations.d: Nevus flammeus is an ectasia, not a true neoplasm, and has no significant risk of malignant transformation.
explanations.e: Hemorrhagic telangiectasias are small punctate lesions associated with Osler-Weber-Rendu, not large facial port-wine stains.

ankiCards: A port-wine stain in the V1/V2 trigeminal distribution is associated with {{c1::Sturge-Weber}} syndrome.
Sturge-Weber syndrome involves {{c1::leptomeningeal}} angiomas on the same side as the facial lesion.
Clinical complications of Sturge-Weber syndrome include {{c1::seizures}}, mental retardation, and glaucoma.
Unlike a strawberry hemangioma, a port-wine stain {{c1::does not}} regress with age.
A port-wine stain is technically classified as a vascular {{c1::ectasia}} (dilation), not a true tumor.
keyPoints: Nevus flammeus (Port-wine stain) is a common form of vascular ectasia.
Usually present at birth and persists throughout life.
Sturge-Weber syndrome: Port-wine stain + Leptomeningeal angiomatosis.
Follows the distribution of the trigeminal nerve.
Associated with intellectual disability, seizures, and hemiparesis.
microReview: Port-wine stain + Trigeminal distribution + Seizures = Sturge-Weber Syndrome.
examinerTraps: Port-wine stains grow *with* the child, whereas strawberry hemangiomas grow *faster* then disappear.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 6-month-old male infant is brought to the pediatrician for a bright red, raised, lobulated skin lesion on his right cheek. The parents state the lesion appeared shortly after birth, grew rapidly for four months, but has recently begun to flatten and fade in color. Physical examination reveals a 2-cm diameter, compressible, strawberry-like plaque. What is the most likely natural history of this lesion?

explanations.a: The description matches a juvenile (capillary) hemangioma, also known as a strawberry hemangioma. These are extremely common in infancy, grow rapidly during the first few months, and then undergo spontaneous regression in the vast majority of cases by age 7.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas are benign lesions and do not transform into malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.c: Unlike cavernous hemangiomas or port-wine stains, strawberry hemangiomas typically involute and do not persist unchanged throughout life.
explanations.d: Capillary hemangiomas are localized cutaneous or mucosal lesions; systemic involvement is rare and not characteristic of the strawberry subtype.
explanations.e: Surgical excision is usually avoided as most lesions regress spontaneously; intervention is only needed if the lesion obstructs vision or the airway.

ankiCards: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas typically {{c1::regress}} spontaneously by early childhood.
The characteristic appearance of a strawberry hemangioma is a {{c1::bright red, lobulated, raised}} plaque.
Capillary hemangiomas are composed of thin-walled capillaries with {{c1::scant}} stroma.
True or False: Capillary hemangiomas are malignant. {{c1::False}}
The rapid growth phase of a juvenile hemangioma occurs during {{c1::infancy}}.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangiomas are also called strawberry hemangiomas.
They are the most common vascular tumor of infancy.
They occur in the skin, scalp, and mucous membranes.
Growth is rapid for a few months followed by involution.
By age 7, 75-90% of these lesions have completely regressed.
microReview: Benign vascular tumors (hemangiomas) are classified by vessel size (capillary vs. cavernous). Capillary hemangiomas (strawberry type) are infantile and regress, whereas cavernous hemangiomas are deeper, larger, and do not regress spontaneously.
examinerTraps: Students often confuse the 'strawberry hemangioma' of infancy (regresses) with the 'cherry angioma' of the elderly (increases with age).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An HIV-positive patient with a CD4+ count of 150 cells/mm³ presents with multiple purple-to-red skin nodules on the lower extremities. Biopsy of a lesion shows spindle-shaped cells with slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells. Which of the following pathogens is the primary driver of this neoplastic process?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is an intermediate-grade vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8 (also known as KSHV). It is highly associated with AIDS and presents as spindle cells forming slit-like spaces.
explanations.b: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can look similar to KS clinically but is characterized by neutrophilic infiltrates and reactive vascular proliferation rather than spindle cell neoplasia.
explanations.c: HPV-16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx, not vascular tumors.
explanations.d: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.e: CMV causes retinitis and colitis in immunocompromised patients but is not oncogenic for vascular tissue.

ankiCards: The causative agent of Kaposi sarcoma is {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
The classic histologic finding in Kaposi sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells}} with slit-like vascular spaces.
{{c1::AIDS-associated}} Kaposi sarcoma is the most common HIV-related malignancy.
Unlike Kaposi Sarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis is caused by {{c1::Bartonella}} species.
The red/purple color of Kaposi sarcoma lesions is due to {{c1::extravasated RBCs}} and hemosiderin.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
HHV-8 is the essential co-factor for all forms of KS.
Four forms: Classic (older Mediterranean), Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
Histology: Spindle cells, slit-like spaces, and plasma cell infiltrates.
Lesions do not blanch perfectly because blood is outside the vessels.
microReview: Vascular tumors range from benign hemangiomas to intermediate Kaposi Sarcoma to malignant Angiosarcoma. HHV-8 infection of endothelial cells leads to the characteristic spindle cell proliferation in KS.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Kaposi Sarcoma (HHV-8, spindle cells) with Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella, neutrophils). They look identical on gross exam.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with an exquisitely painful, small, firm, blue-tinged nodule located under the fingernail of her index finger. The pain is triggered by cold exposure. Histologic examination of the lesion reveals aggregates of specialized smooth muscle cells surrounding vascular channels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: A glomus tumor (glomangioma) is a highly painful benign tumor arising from the specialized smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, which is involved in thermoregulation. They are classicially subungual (under the nail).
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas are painless and typically found on the skin of the head or neck in infants.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a malignant, aggressive tumor that rarely presents as a small, isolated, painful subungual nodule.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is seen in immunocompromised patients and presents as multiple red papules, not a single painful subungual nodule.
explanations.e: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a flat, non-painful birthmark consisting of dilated vessels.

ankiCards: A {{c1::Glomus tumor}} is a benign, exquisitely painful tumor found under the fingernails.
Glomus tumors arise from the {{c1::glomus body}}, which regulates temperature.
The characteristic cells in a glomus tumor are {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells.
Glomus tumors are triggered to cause pain by {{c1::cold}} exposure.
The classic triad for a glomus tumor is paroxysmal pain, localized tenderness, and {{c1::cold sensitivity}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but very painful.
Most common location is subungual (under the nail bed).
Derived from smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
Glomus bodies are arteriovenous anastomoses.
Excision is curative.
microReview: Subungual pain = Glomus tumor. It is a benign vascular lesion derived from thermoregulatory glomus bodies, distinct from endothelial-derived hemangiomas.
examinerTraps: Wait for the 'pain' and 'subungual' clues. Most other vascular tumors are painless.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with several firm, violaceous nodules on her left arm. She has a history of a radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection and radiotherapy for breast cancer 12 years ago. Since the surgery, she has had persistent, severe lymphedema of the left arm. What is the most likely diagnosis of these new nodules?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma can occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema, a condition known as Stewart-Treves syndrome. This classically occurs in the arm following radical mastectomy and lymph node dissection.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is HHV-8 related and usually presents in HIV patients or specific elderly populations; it is not specifically associated with post-mastectomy lymphedema.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign lesions that do not typically arise de novo in areas of chronic lymphedema.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a rapidly growing red nodule, often on the gingiva or fingers, associated with trauma or pregnancy.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts.

ankiCards: {{c1::Angiosarcoma}} is a malignant vascular tumor associated with chronic lymphedema.
Stewart-Treves syndrome is angiosarcoma occurring after {{c1::radical mastectomy}}.
The prognosis for cutaneous angiosarcoma is generally {{c1::poor}}.
Common risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma include {{c1::vinyl chloride}} and arsenic.
Angiosarcoma cells stain positive for the endothelial marker {{c1::CD31}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms.
They are aggressive with a high mortality rate.
Cutaneous angiosarcoma is associated with chronic lymphedema.
Radiation therapy is also a risk factor for subsequent angiosarcoma.
They can also occur in the liver or heart (right atrium).
microReview: Malignant vascular tumors (Angiosarcomas) are rare but deadly. Remember the 'V-A-T' mnemonic for liver angiosarcoma (Vinyl chloride, Arsenic, Thorotrast) and Stewart-Treves for the arm.
examinerTraps: The examiner may mention breast cancer history. Don't assume recurrence of the breast adenocarcinoma; the violaceous nodules in a lymphedematous limb are a red flag for angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 30-year-old male with advanced HIV presents with numerous small, red, papular skin lesions. Histology shows a proliferation of capillaries with prominent 'epithelioid' endothelial cells, a dense neutrophilic infiltrate, and granular purple material. Warthin-Starry silver stain highlights pleomorphic bacilli. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised individuals caused by Bartonella henselae or Bartonella quintana. The hallmark is the neutrophilic infiltrate and the presence of bacteria on silver stain.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma lacks a neutrophilic infiltrate and will not show bacilli on silver stain; it shows spindle cells and extravasated RBCs.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign lobular capillary hemangioma usually following trauma, not specifically associated with HIV or silver-staining bacilli.
explanations.d: Glomus tumor is a painful subungual lesion of smooth muscle, not an infectious vascular proliferation.
explanations.e: Cherry angiomas are benign senile vascular lesions that do not show the inflammatory features of bacillary angiomatosis.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by bacteria of the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
In bacillary angiomatosis, the inflammatory infiltrate is primarily {{c1::neutrophilic}}.
The stain used to identify the bacilli in bacillary angiomatosis is {{c1::Warthin-Starry (silver)}}.
Bacillary angiomatosis occurs primarily in {{c1::immunocompromised/HIV}} patients.
Unlike Kaposi Sarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis is treated with {{c1::antibiotics (erythromycin)}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis mimics Kaposi sarcoma clinically.
Caused by Bartonella henselae (from cats) or B. quintana (from lice).
Histology: Lobular vascular proliferation with neutrophils and nuclear dust.
Warthin-Starry stain is diagnostic.
Effective treatment involves antibiotics, which are not used for Kaposi sarcoma.
microReview: HIV + Vascular lesions: Check histology. Spindle cells = Kaposi Sarcoma (HHV-8). Neutrophils/Bacilli = Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella).
examinerTraps: The presence of 'purple material' on H&E in these lesions is a classic clue for clusters of Bartonella bacteria.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy develops a rapidly growing, 1-cm, pedunculated red nodule on her gingiva. The lesion bleeds easily with minor trauma. She is concerned because it reached its current size in only two weeks. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma (granuloma pyogenicum) is a rapidly growing, red, often ulcerated pedunculated lesion. It is a form of lobular capillary hemangioma common on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.b: While it is a subtype of capillary hemangioma, 'pyogenic granuloma' is the specific term for this rapidly growing, ulcerated, gingival lesion.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas are deep, slow-growing, and do not typically present as small pedunculated gingival nodules.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is malignant and very unlikely to present as a self-limited gingival nodule during pregnancy.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are painful subungual lesions, not found on the gingiva.

ankiCards: A {{c1::pyogenic granuloma}} is a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated vascular nodule.
Pyogenic granulomas are common on the {{c1::gingiva/skin}}.
When occurring in pregnant women, a pyogenic granuloma is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Histologically, a pyogenic granuloma is a form of {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
True or False: Pyogenic granulomas are usually infectious. {{c1::False (they are reactive/neoplastic)}}
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is neither pyogenic (pus-forming) nor a granuloma.
It is a lobular capillary hemangioma.
Often triggered by trauma or the hormonal changes of pregnancy.
Characterized by rapid growth and easy bleeding.
Treatment is surgical excision or curettage; pregnancy lesions may regress postpartum.
microReview: Pregnancy + Red gingival lump = Pyogenic Granuloma. Despite the name, it's a vascular proliferation (hemangioma), not an infection or a granulomatous process.
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic granuloma' is a trick because it suggests infection (pyogenic) and chronic inflammation (granuloma), but it is actually a vascular tumor.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following environmental or chemical exposures is most strongly associated with the development of hepatic angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Vinyl chloride (used in the plastics industry), arsenic (pesticides), and Thorotrast (a retired radiocontrast medium) are the classic risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and lung cancer, not angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Aflatoxin B1 is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), not angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: Benzene is associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.e: Coal dust is associated with coal worker's pneumoconiosis (black lung disease).

ankiCards: Vinyl chloride exposure is associated with {{c1::angiosarcoma}} of the liver.
Three classic risks for liver angiosarcoma: Vinyl chloride, {{c1::Arsenic}}, and Thorotrast.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is a {{c1::malignant}} tumor of endothelial cells.
{{c1::Thorotrast}} was a contrast agent once used that caused hepatic angiosarcomas decades later.
Angiosarcoma is often positive for the vascular marker {{c1::CD31}}.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare, highly malignant tumor.
It has a long latency period after chemical exposure.
Vinyl chloride is the most famous chemical association.
It is distinct from hepatocellular carcinoma (epithelial) and cavernous hemangioma (benign).
Poor prognosis due to late presentation and aggressive nature.
microReview: Malignant vascular = Angiosarcoma. Liver Angiosarcoma risks = Vinyl chloride, Arsenic, Thorotrast. Skin Angiosarcoma risk = Lymphedema/Radiation.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse hepatic angiosarcoma with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). HCC is more common and linked to Hep B/C and Aflatoxin.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 22-year-old male is diagnosed with von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease after presenting with cerebellar hemangioblastoma. Which of the following vascular lesions is most commonly associated with this genetic syndrome?

explanations.a: Von Hippel-Lindau disease is characterized by cavernous hemangiomas (vascular malformations/tumors) in the cerebellum, retina, and brainstem, as well as visceral cysts and renal cell carcinoma.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors are sporadic and not part of the VHL syndrome.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious condition found in immunocompromised patients.
explanations.d: Spider telangiectasias are associated with hyperestrogenic states like pregnancy or cirrhosis.
explanations.e: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome, not VHL.

ankiCards: Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is associated with {{c1::cavernous}} hemangiomas/hemangioblastomas.
VHL commonly involves the {{c1::cerebellum/retina}}.
Patients with VHL have an increased risk of {{c1::renal cell}} carcinoma.
The VHL gene is a {{c1::tumor suppressor}} gene located on chromosome 3.
The vascular lesions in VHL are {{c1::benign}} but cause symptoms by local pressure.
keyPoints: VHL is an autosomal dominant disorder.
Involves the VHL tumor suppressor gene.
Characterized by multiple vascular tumors (hemangioblastomas).
Targets: CNS, Retina, Liver, Pancreas.
Also associated with Pheochromocytoma.
microReview: VHL = Hemangioblastomas (Cerebellum/Retina) + Renal Cell Carcinoma + Pheochromocytoma. This is a classic multi-system genetic syndrome involving vascular neoplasia.
examinerTraps: Distinguish between Sturge-Weber (Port-wine stain on face) and VHL (Internal vascular tumors).
sourceQuote: To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure and function.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with a large, flat, purple birthmark covering the left side of his face in the distribution of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve. His parents report he has had several seizures. An MRI shows leptomeningeal venous malformations on the same side as the facial lesion. What is the diagnosis?

explanations.a: Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) features a facial port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) in the V1/V2 trigeminal distribution and ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomas, which cause seizures and mental retardation.
explanations.b: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) features multiple small telangiectasias on the skin and mucous membranes, not a large port-wine stain.
explanations.c: VHL features internal hemangioblastomas and renal cell carcinoma, not facial port-wine stains.
explanations.d: Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome involves port-wine stains, but they are usually on the limbs and associated with limb overgrowth and venous malformations.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious process in HIV patients.

ankiCards: Sturge-Weber syndrome is characterized by a {{c1::port-wine stain}} in the trigeminal distribution.
The neurological feature of Sturge-Weber is {{c1::leptomeningeal}} angiomatosis.
Common clinical manifestations of Sturge-Weber include {{c1::seizures}} and glaucoma.
The port-wine stain in Sturge-Weber is a form of {{c1::nevus flammeus}}.
True or False: Sturge-Weber syndrome is usually inherited. {{c1::False (it is a sporadic mutation in GNAQ)}}
keyPoints: Sturge-Weber is a sporadic phakomatosis.
Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a vascular ectasia.
Ipsilateral brain involvement is key (leptomeningeal angioma).
'Tram-track' calcifications may be seen on brain imaging.
Clinical triad: Port-wine stain, seizures, and glaucoma.
microReview: Trigeminal port-wine stain + Seizures = Sturge-Weber. It's an ectasia of vessels, not a true neoplasm like a hemangioma.
examinerTraps: The port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) is flat and does not regress, unlike the strawberry hemangioma which is raised and regresses.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following terms describes a permanent dilation of pre-existing small vessels (capillaries, venules, or arterioles) that forms a discrete red lesion on the skin or mucous membranes?

explanations.a: Telangiectasia is the term for permanent dilation of small vessels. This includes spider telangiectasias and nevus flammeus. They are classified under 'vascular ectasias' rather than true neoplasms.
explanations.b: Stenosis refers to the narrowing of a vessel lumen, which is the opposite of dilation.
explanations.c: Thrombosis refers to the formation of a blood clot within a vessel.
explanations.d: An aneurysm is a localized dilation of an artery or the heart, usually involving larger vessels than those in telangiectasias.
explanations.e: Hemangiopericytoma is a rare tumor arising from pericytes around capillaries, not a simple dilation of vessels.

ankiCards: {{c1::Telangiectasia}} is the permanent dilation of small pre-existing vessels.
Telangiectasias are part of a group of conditions called {{c1::vascular ectasias}}.
A {{c1::spider}} telangiectasia blanches when the central core is pressed.
Telangiectasias are {{c1::not}} true neoplasms (they are dilations).
Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia is also known as {{c1::Osler-Weber-Rendu}} syndrome.
keyPoints: Vascular ectasias are not true neoplasms.
They represent dilations of existing vessels.
Nevus flammeus is the most common form of ectasia.
Spider telangiectasias often occur in high-estrogen states.
Telangiectasias can be a sign of systemic disease (e.g., Cirrhosis, CREST syndrome).
microReview: Dilation = Ectasia/Telangiectasia. Growth/Proliferation = Hemangioma. Malignant proliferation = Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse telangiectasia with hemangioma. A telangiectasia is a dilation of what is already there; a hemangioma is a new growth of vessels.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular pathology is categorized into two principal mechanisms. A 68-year-old male with a history of hypertension presents with a bulging, pulsatile abdominal mass. Which of the following pathological mechanisms best describes the primary process leading to this patient's condition?

explanations.a: This describes thrombosis or embolism, leading to acute ischemia rather than dilation.
explanations.b: This describes atherosclerosis-driven stenosis, which limits flow rather than causing vessel expansion.
explanations.c: Weakening of the vessel wall is one of the two principal mechanisms of vascular disease and is the direct cause of aneurysmal dilation or rupture.
explanations.d: Hypertrophy of the media is a response to hypertension but does not inherently cause the dilation seen in aneurysms; weakening/atrophy is more typical.
explanations.e: Endothelial transformation is involved in angiogenesis and repair but is not the primary mechanism of aneurysm formation.

ankiCards: The two principal mechanisms underlying vascular disease are narrowing/obstruction and {{c1::weakening}} of vessel walls.
Weakening of vessel walls leads to either {{c1::dilation}} or rupture.
The clinical presentation of a pulsatile abdominal mass is characteristic of an {{c1::abdominal aortic aneurysm}}.
Atherosclerosis causes progressive {{c1::luminal narrowing}} of vessels.
Precipitous obstruction of a vessel lumen is usually caused by {{c1::thrombosis}} or embolism.
keyPoints: Vascular diseases are categorized by obstruction or wall weakening.
Aneurysms represent the 'weakening' category of vascular pathology.
Arteries have thicker walls than veins to handle higher pulsatile pressures.
Dilation is the hallmark of aneurysmal disease before rupture occurs.
Pathology often localizes based on vessel type (elastic vs. muscular).
microReview: Vascular disease mechanisms: 1. Stenosis/Obstruction (Atherosclerosis/Thrombosis). 2. Weakening (Aneurysm/Rupture). Aneurysms occur when the structural integrity of the wall (elastic fibers/collagen) is compromised.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'cause' (e.g., atherosclerosis) with the 'mechanism' (e.g., wall weakening). While atherosclerosis causes narrowing, it also contributes to wall weakening by causing ischemia of the media.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which structural feature of the arterial wall is most critical in resisting the formation of aneurysms in the presence of high pulsatile blood pressures?

options.a: A high ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter
options.b: Absence of valves within the vessel lumen
options.c: Presence of a thin tunica adventitia

explanations.a: Arterial walls are thicker than veins and the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter allows them to manage high pressures; a decrease in this structural integrity leads to dilation.
explanations.b: The absence of valves is normal for arteries but does not contribute to pressure resistance in the context of aneurysm prevention.
explanations.c: A thin adventitia would actually make the vessel weaker, not more resistant to aneurysm formation.
explanations.d: Venous return is a function of the venous system and does not impact arterial wall structural resistance.
explanations.e: Endothelial permeability regulates nutrient transport but does not provide structural strength against pulsatile mechanical stress.

ankiCards: Arterial walls are {{c1::thicker}} than corresponding veins to accommodate higher pressures.
As arteries become smaller, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}}.
Muscular vessels exert control over blood flow and pressure by adjusting their {{c1::lumen diameter}}.
Structural specializations in vessels reflect their distinct {{c1::functional roles}}.
Aneurysms are more likely to occur in vessels where the {{c1::wall}} is weakened.
keyPoints: Arterial architecture is designed for pulsatile flow.
Wall thickness-to-lumen ratio is a key determinant of pressure management.
Structural failure leads to aneurysm formation.
Elastic and muscular arteries are specifically targeted by atherosclerosis.
Veins have thinner walls compared to arteries at the same level of branching.
microReview: Arteries vs. Veins: Arteries have higher wall-to-lumen ratios to withstand MAP and pulse pressure. Any degradation of this wall (e.g., Marfan, atherosclerosis) shifts the balance toward dilation (aneurysm).
examinerTraps: The examiner may focus on the endothelium, but the mechanical strength of the vessel resides in the media and its ratio to the lumen.
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures. Arterial wall thickness gradually diminishes as the vessels become smaller, but the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history and long-standing hypertension presents with sudden onset, severe mid-abdominal pain radiating to the back. Physical exam reveals a pulsatile mass and hypotension. What is the most likely underlying structural change in the vessel wall responsible for this presentation?

options.a: Hyaline deposition in the arteriolar wall
options.b: Degradation of the extracellular matrix by proteases
options.c: Hyperplastic duplication of the internal elastic lamina
options.d: Fibrinoid necrosis of the tunica media
options.e: Granulomatous inflammation of the vasa vasorum

explanations.a: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is a complication of hypertension in small vessels, not the large-scale dilation seen in AAA.
explanations.b: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are characterized by wall weakening due to chronic inflammation and protease-mediated (e.g., MMPs) degradation of the extracellular matrix.
explanations.c: Hyperplastic changes are seen in malignant hypertension (onion-skinning) rather than aneurysmal dilation.
explanations.d: Fibrinoid necrosis is characteristic of vasculitis or malignant hypertension, not standard atherosclerotic AAA.
explanations.e: This describes Takayasu or Giant Cell arteritis, which can cause aneurysms, but the clinical context (older male, smoker) strongly points to an atherosclerotic AAA.

ankiCards: The primary mechanism of an Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA) is {{c1::wall weakening}}.
AAA is often associated with the degradation of the {{c1::extracellular matrix}}.
Risk factors for AAA include {{c1::smoking}}, male sex, and advanced age.
A {{c1::pulsatile mass}} is the classic physical exam finding for AAA.
Aneurysms and dissections are both manifestations of {{c1::vascular wall}} disease.
keyPoints: AAA is the most common form of aortic aneurysm.
Atherosclerosis is a major precursor to AAA.
Wall weakening involves an imbalance between matrix synthesis and degradation.
Clinical triad of rupture: abdominal pain, hypotension, pulsatile mass.
Elastic arteries like the aorta are most susceptible.
microReview: AAA Pathophysiology: Atherosclerosis → chronic inflammation → macrophage infiltration → release of Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMPs) → elastin/collagen degradation → wall weakening → dilation.
examinerTraps: Watch for the triad: pain, hypotension, and a pulsatile mass—this indicates rupture, a surgical emergency.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes a 'constitutional' risk factor that predisposes individuals to the vascular wall injury leading to aneurysm formation?

explanations.a: Smoking is a modifiable major risk factor, not a constitutional (fixed) one.
explanations.b: Diabetes is a modifiable major risk factor.
explanations.c: Constitutional risk factors are inherent and non-modifiable; family history, age, and male gender are the primary constitutional factors for atherosclerosis and related aneurysms.
explanations.d: Lifestyle factors are modifiable.
explanations.e: Hyperlipidemia is a modifiable major risk factor.

ankiCards: Risk factors for vascular disease are divided into {{c1::constitutional}} and modifiable categories.
Name three constitutional risk factors: {{c1::Age, Gender, and Family History/Genetics}}.
Smoking and hyperlipidemia are examples of {{c1::modifiable}} risk factors.
The progression of atherosclerosis is influenced by both {{c1::genetic}} and environmental factors.
Aneurysms often develop as a late consequence of {{c1::atherosclerotic}} disease.
keyPoints: Constitutional risk factors are non-modifiable.
Genetic predisposition plays a significant role in aneurysm development.
Age is a primary constitutional risk factor (incidence increases after 50).
Gender is a factor; males are significantly more likely to develop AAA.
Identification of risk factors helps in screening for asymptomatic aneurysms.
microReview: Aneurysm risk factors mirror atherosclerosis: Non-modifiable (Age, Sex, Genetics) and Modifiable (Smoking, HTN, Lipids).
examinerTraps: The examiner often asks to distinguish between 'modifiable' and 'constitutional'. Hypertension is the most important *modifiable* risk factor for dissection; smoking is the most important for AAA.
sourceQuote: Risk Factors... Constitutional Risk Factors... Modifiable Major Risk Factors... Additional Risk Factors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old woman with exceptionally long limbs and hypermobile joints presents with a sudden 'tearing' chest pain that radiates to her back. Imaging shows a dilated ascending aorta and a longitudinal tear in the intima. Which layer of the vascular structure is primarily deficient in this patient's condition?

explanations.a: The intima is where the tear starts, but the underlying weakness that allows the aneurysm/dissection is in the media.
explanations.b: Conditions like Marfan syndrome involve cystic medial necrosis or degeneration of the tunica media, which contains the elastic fibers responsible for structural integrity.
explanations.c: The adventitia is the outer supportive layer but is not the primary site of degeneration in thoracic aortic disease.
explanations.d: While elastic fibers are involved, the pathology involves the entire media, not just the internal elastic lamina.
explanations.e: The vasa vasorum provide blood to the outer media; while they play a role in tertiary syphilis, the primary defect in Marfan is connective tissue in the media.

ankiCards: Aortic dissection involves a tear in the {{c1::intima}} followed by blood entering the media.
Cystic medial necrosis is a feature of {{c1::Marfan syndrome}}.
The tunica {{c1::media}} is the thickest layer in elastic arteries.
Thoracic aortic aneurysms are often associated with {{c1::connective tissue}} disorders.
A 'tearing' chest pain radiating to the back is classic for {{c1::aortic dissection}}.
keyPoints: Aneurysms can lead to dissections (though they are distinct entities).
The media is the site of 'cystic medial necrosis' in thoracic aneurysms.
Genetic defects in Fibrillin-1 (Marfan) weaken the media.
Ascending aorta involvement is common in non-atherosclerotic aneurysms.
Aortic dissections are a surgical emergency.
microReview: Thoracic vs Abdominal Aneurysms: AAA = Atherosclerosis/Smoking/MMPs in older men. TAA = HTN or Connective Tissue Disease (Marfan/Ehlers-Danlos) involving the tunica media.
examinerTraps: Aneurysm vs Dissection: An aneurysm is a dilation of all three layers. A dissection is a tear in the intima with blood tracking through the media. They often coexist.
sourceQuote: Aneurysms and Dissection... Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm... Aortic Dissection
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the physiological response to vascular injury, what is the 'stereotyped' cellular response that initially occurs before the development of permanent structural weakening or narrowing?

explanations.a: Medial atrophy occurs later, specifically in atherosclerosis or hypertension-related wall damage.
explanations.b: Intimal thickening is the stereotyped, generalized response of the vessel wall to almost any form of injury (e.g., trauma, inflammation).
explanations.c: Fragmentation of elastic fibers is a specific part of medial degeneration, not the general stereotyped response.
explanations.d: Adventitial fibrosis can occur but is not the primary 'stereotyped' response mentioned.
explanations.e: Endothelial injury triggers the response, but 'thickening' is the resulting stereotyped outcome.

ankiCards: The stereotyped response to vascular injury is {{c1::intimal thickening}}.
Intimal thickening involves the migration of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} into the intima.
Vascular injury triggers a {{c1::healing}} response that can lead to stenosis.
Vascular wall response to injury is a precursor to both {{c1::atherosclerosis}} and other pathologies.
Is intimal thickening a specific or non-specific response? {{c1::Non-specific (Stereotyped)}}.
keyPoints: Vascular injury results in a stereotyped intimal response.
Smooth muscle cells migrate from the media to the intima and proliferate.
The newly formed 'neointima' can eventually narrow the lumen.
This process is distinct from the wall 'weakening' seen in aneurysms.
Understanding this helps differentiate obstructive disease from dilatory disease.
microReview: Stereotyped Response: Injury → Endothelial dysfunction → Smooth muscle cell migration/proliferation → ECM deposition → Intimal thickening (neointima).
examinerTraps: The examiner may try to swap 'intimal thickening' with 'medial hypertrophy'. Intimal thickening is the response to *injury*; medial hypertrophy is usually the response to *pressure* (hypertension).
sourceQuote: Vascular Wall Response to Injury... Intimal Thickening: A Stereotyped Response to Vascular Injury
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which vessel type is primarily affected by atherosclerosis, leading to the eventual formation of large-scale aneurysms?

explanations.a: Venules are generally not affected by atherosclerosis.
explanations.b: Venous disorders are generally unrelated to the mechanisms of atherosclerosis.
explanations.c: Arterioles are affected by arteriolosclerosis (hyaline or hyperplastic) rather than classic atherosclerosis/aneurysm.
explanations.d: Atherosclerosis mainly affects elastic arteries (like the aorta) and large muscular arteries (like the coronary and renal arteries).
explanations.e: Capillaries are too small and lack the media required for the development of classic atherosclerosis or large aneurysms.

ankiCards: Atherosclerosis affects mainly {{c1::elastic}} and muscular arteries.
The aorta is a prime example of an {{c1::elastic}} artery.
Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins to accommodate {{c1::pulsatile}} flow.
Vascular disorders have characteristic {{c1::anatomic distributions}}.
Atherosclerosis is a major cause of vessel lumen {{c1::narrowing}}.
keyPoints: Vessel distribution of disease is characteristic.
Elastic arteries have the most robust architecture but are prime targets for AAA.
Large muscular arteries (e.g., iliac) can also develop aneurysms.
The aorta's role in accommodating high pressure makes it vulnerable if the wall is compromised.
Venous disorders are 'not inconsequential' but follow different mechanisms.
microReview: Elastic Arteries (Aorta, Carotid, Iliac) + Large Muscular Arteries (Coronary, Popliteal) = Main sites for Atherosclerosis. Atherosclerosis in the Aorta = Aneurysm (AAA).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse arterioles (small) with elastic/muscular arteries (large). Hypertension affects arterioles; atherosclerosis affects large/medium arteries.
sourceQuote: Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: How do the structural changes in an aneurysm compare to the structural changes in vascular stenosis regarding the outcome of the vessel lumen?

options.a: Aneurysms involve lumen narrowing; stenosis involves lumen widening
options.b: Aneurysms involve wall thickening; stenosis involves wall thinning
options.c: Aneurysms involve wall weakening and dilation; stenosis involves luminal obstruction
options.d: Aneurysms are caused by thrombosis; stenosis is caused by rupture
options.e: Aneurysms only affect veins; stenosis only affects arteries

explanations.a: This is the exact opposite of the truth.
explanations.b: Aneurysms typically involve wall thinning/atrophy (weakening), whereas stenosis can involve intimal thickening.
explanations.c: This correctly identifies the two principal mechanisms: narrowing/obstruction (stenosis) and weakening/dilation (aneurysm).
explanations.d: Thrombosis causes stenosis/obstruction; rupture is a consequence of an aneurysm.
explanations.e: Both can affect arteries, although atherosclerosis (a main cause of both) is primarily arterial.

ankiCards: Stenosis refers to the {{c1::narrowing}} of a vessel lumen.
Aneurysms result from the {{c1::weakening}} of vessel walls.
Complete obstruction of a lumen can be {{c1::precipitous}} (e.g., thrombosis).
Progressive narrowing of a lumen is typically caused by {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Weakening of a vessel wall leads to dilation or {{c1::rupture}}.
keyPoints: Narrowing vs. Weakening are the two main pathologies.
Atherosclerosis can cause both mechanisms (narrowing directly, weakening via medial ischemia).
Dilation is the visual hallmark of an aneurysm.
Obstruction results in ischemia downstream.
Rupture results in hemorrhage.
microReview: Luminal Obstruction (Atherosclerosis/Thrombus) vs. Wall Weakening (Aneurysm/Dissection). Know that they can coexist in the same patient but represent different mechanical failures.
examinerTraps: Remember that atherosclerosis causes stenosis *and* can lead to aneurysms by causing pressure-induced atrophy of the underlying media.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old male is undergoing an evaluation for chronic leg pain. An ultrasound of the abdomen incidentally reveals a 4.5 cm dilation of the infrarenal aorta. The patient has a history of poorly controlled hypertension and is a current smoker. Which of the following describes the most common clinical course for this lesion if left untreated?

options.a: Spontaneous regression with blood pressure control
options.b: Rapid transformation into a malignant vascular tumor
options.d: Conversion into a non-dilated stenotic lesion
options.e: Obliteration of the lumen by intimal thickening

explanations.a: Aneurysms do not regress; they are permanent structural failures.
explanations.b: Aneurysms are not neoplastic; they are structural/degenerative.
explanations.c: Aneurysms tend to expand over time as the wall weakens further under tension (Law of Laplace), eventually leading to rupture.
explanations.d: While atherosclerosis is present, the 'dilation' (aneurysm) is the dominant pathology and does not revert to simple stenosis.
explanations.e: While intimal thickening occurs, it does not typically 'fill' a dilated aneurysm; rather, mural thrombus often forms inside the dilated segment.

ankiCards: The clinical course of an untreated AAA is {{c1::progressive expansion}}.
The most feared complication of an abdominal aneurysm is {{c1::rupture}}.
Aneurysms are often found {{c1::incidentally}} during imaging for other reasons.
The Law of Laplace explains why larger aneurysms are more likely to {{c1::rupture}}.
Smoking is the most potent modifiable risk factor for the expansion of {{c1::AAA}}.
keyPoints: Aneurysms are often asymptomatic until rupture.
Expansion rate is monitored (e.g., surgery usually at >5.5cm).
Infrarenal location is most common for AAA.
Risk of rupture is proportional to the diameter.
Smoking cessation is critical to slow expansion.
microReview: Natural History: Formation (Atherosclerosis) → Expansion (Proteolysis/Wall stress) → Complication (Rupture/Thrombosis/Embolism).
examinerTraps: Don't assume medical management (like BP meds) will 'cure' the aneurysm. It only slows the progression; the risk of rupture remains if the diameter is large.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which component of the arterial wall is specifically thicker than in veins to accommodate higher blood pressures, and is the primary site where weakening leads to aneurysms?

explanations.a: The intima is thin and mainly composed of endothelium and a scant subendothelial layer; it is not the main pressure-bearing layer.
explanations.b: The tunica media is significantly thicker in arteries to handle pulsatile flow; loss of its structural proteins (elastin/collagen) is the defining feature of aneurysm formation.
explanations.c: The adventitia contains connective tissue and nerves/vessels but is not the layer that differentiates the thickness of arteries and veins as significantly as the media.
explanations.d: Vasa vasorum are vessels that supply the wall, not a structural layer itself.
explanations.e: The external elastic lamina is a boundary within the wall, but the media as a whole provides the thickness.

ankiCards: The tunica {{c1::media}} is thicker in arteries than in veins.
Loss of structural integrity in the {{c1::tunica media}} leads to aneurysms.
Arterial walls accommodate {{c1::pulsatile}} flow.
Wall thickness gradually {{c1::diminishes}} as vessels become smaller.
The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}} in muscular vessels.
keyPoints: Arteries are 'pressure reservoirs'.
The media contains smooth muscle and elastic fibers.
Structural specialization (thicker media) allows for pressure control.
Venous walls are thinner because they operate under low pressure.
Aneurysms represent a failure of the media's structural support.
microReview: Artery Structure: Thick Media (Elastin/Smooth Muscle) + Thick Intima (if diseased). Vein Structure: Thin Media + Larger Lumen. Aneurysm = Medial failure.
examinerTraps: If the question asks for the layer where 'atherosclerosis' starts, it's the *intima*. If it asks for the layer that 'fails' to cause an aneurysm, it's the *media*.
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 2-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician by his mother, who is concerned about a rapidly growing, bright-red, lobulated, 'strawberry-like' lesion on the child's scalp. The lesion was not present at birth but appeared at 3 weeks of age. Which of the following is the most likely natural history of this lesion?

options.c: Lifelong persistence with no size change
options.d: Rapid expansion leading to Kasabach-Merritt syndrome
options.e: Surgical excision is mandatory during infancy

explanations.a: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are extremely common in infancy; they grow rapidly for several months but typically begin to regress by age 1 to 3 years and completely disappear by age 7 in 75% to 90% of cases.
explanations.b: Hemangiomas are benign lesions; they do not transform into malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.c: Unlike port-wine stains, juvenile hemangiomas characteristically regress.
explanations.d: While large hemangiomas can cause platelet sequestration (Kasabach-Merritt syndrome), this is rare and not the typical natural history for a standard strawberry hemangioma.
explanations.e: Management is usually conservative observation because of the high rate of spontaneous regression.

ankiCards: The most common vascular tumor of infancy is the {{c1::juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma}}.
Juvenile hemangiomas characteristically undergo {{c1::spontaneous regression}} by early childhood.
A 'strawberry' hemangioma typically appears {{c1::shortly after birth (weeks)}} rather than being present at birth.
Histologically, juvenile hemangiomas are composed of {{c1::thin-walled capillaries}} with scant stroma.
Approximately {{c1::75% to 90%}} of strawberry hemangiomas regress by age 7.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangiomas are the most common vascular tumors of infancy.
They follow a predictable cycle: rapid growth followed by slow involution.
Clinically they appear as bright red, raised, lobulated masses.
Most lesions disappear entirely by age 7 without treatment.
They are categorized under benign vascular tumors.
microReview: Juvenile hemangiomas = Rapid growth then regression. Port-wine stains = Permanent/Grow with child.
examinerTraps: Confusing juvenile hemangioma with nevus flammeus (port-wine stain); port-wine stains do not regress and grow proportionately with the child.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors... Benign tumors and tumor-like conditions... Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) are extremely common... they usually regress spontaneously by age 7.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 34-year-old female presents with a small, exquisitely painful, 4-mm bluish nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. She notes the pain is particularly intense when her hand is exposed to cold water. The lesion is surgically excised. Histology is most likely to reveal a tumor derived from which of the following cell types?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, which is a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.b: While it is a vascular tumor, the characteristic cells are the specialized glomus cells (smooth muscle), not the lining endothelial cells.
explanations.c: Fibroblasts are present in the stroma but are not the neoplastic cell of origin.
explanations.d: Schwann cells would suggest a neuroma; glomus tumors are painful but not neural in origin.
explanations.e: Glomus cells are similar to pericytes but are specifically classified as modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.

ankiCards: A painful, subungual blue tumor is most likely a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
Glomus tumors arise from specialized {{c1::smooth muscle}} cells.
The primary function of the glomus body is {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Characteristic symptom of a glomus tumor is pain triggered by {{c1::cold}}.
Histology of a glomus tumor shows nests of uniform {{c1::glomus cells}} surrounding vascular channels.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign, exquisitely painful tumors.
Classically located in the subungual (under the nail) region.
Arise from glomus bodies (specialized thermoregulatory AV shunts).
Derived from modified smooth muscle cells.
Cured by simple surgical excision.
microReview: Glomus tumor = Subungual + Painful + Cold sensitive + Smooth muscle origin.
examinerTraps: Assuming all vascular tumors are endothelial in origin; glomus tumors are smooth-muscle derived.
sourceQuote: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, exquisitely painful tumors arising from specialized smooth muscle cells of glomus bodies.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An immunocompromised patient presents with multiple red, skin papules. Histologic examination shows capillary proliferation with prominent 'epithelioid' endothelial cells, nuclear atypia, and a heavy infiltrate of neutrophils. Silver stains (Warthin-Starry) reveal clusters of tangled bacilli. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts caused by opportunistic Bartonella species. Histology shows neutrophils and bacteria (visible on silver stain).
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma histology features spindle cells and slit-like spaces, lacks the neutrophilic infiltrate, and is caused by HHV-8, not bacteria.
explanations.c: Angiosarcomas are high-grade malignancies with significant pleomorphism and do not contain bacteria.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a lobular capillary hemangioma often appearing after trauma; it does not contain Bartonella bacilli.
explanations.e: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, blood-filled spaces and lack the acute inflammatory/infectious features seen here.

ankiCards: The bacteria responsible for bacillary angiomatosis are {{c1::Bartonella henselae (or quintana)}}.
A key histologic differentiator between KS and bacillary angiomatosis is the presence of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
To visualize the causative agent in bacillary angiomatosis, a {{c1::Warthin-Starry (silver)}} stain is used.
Bacillary angiomatosis primarily affects {{c1::immunocompromised (AIDS)}} patients.
Bartonella henselae is also the cause of {{c1::Cat-scratch disease}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis mimics Kaposi Sarcoma clinically but is bacterial in origin.
Caused by Bartonella henselae (cats) or Bartonella quintana (lice).
Histology: Proliferating capillaries with neutrophils and bacterial clumps.
Silver stains are essential for diagnosis.
Treated with antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin), unlike KS.
microReview: Bacillary angiomatosis = Bartonella + Neutrophils + Silver stain positive. Kaposi = HHV-8 + Spindle cells.
examinerTraps: Wait for the silver stain or neutrophil description; if these are missing but HHV-8 is mentioned, it's KS.
sourceQuote: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts caused by opportunistic gram-negative bacilli of the Bartonella family.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with several firm, enlarging, violaceous nodules on her left arm. Ten years ago, she underwent a radical mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer, which was followed by chronic, severe lymphedema of that arm. A biopsy of a nodule shows highly pleomorphic endothelial cells forming irregular vascular channels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy) is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome.
explanations.b: Lymphangiomas are benign lesions, typically present from birth, and do not show high-grade pleomorphism.
explanations.c: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and typically presents as multifocal lesions in specific populations, not specifically post-lymphedema.
explanations.d: While possible, the description of 'irregular vascular channels' and 'pleomorphic endothelial cells' specifically points to a vascular malignancy (angiosarcoma) rather than adenocarcinoma.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are small, benign, and exquisitely painful; they do not present as large nodules in a lymphedematous limb.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma occurring in the context of chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
Histology of angiosarcoma reveals {{c1::pleomorphic endothelial cells}} and {{c2::irregular vascular channels}}.
Common risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma include {{c1::vinyl chloride}}, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
Angiosarcomas are stained with the endothelial marker {{c1::CD31}}.
The prognosis for most angiosarcomas is {{c1::poor}} (5-year survival approx 30%).
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms.
Stewart-Treves syndrome: Angiosarcoma following radical mastectomy/lymphedema.
Can also occur in the skin following radiation therapy.
Highly aggressive with poor prognosis.
Marker: CD31 (endothelial cell marker).
microReview: Post-mastectomy + Lymphedema + Purple skin nodules = Stewart-Treves syndrome (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: Confusing metastatic breast cancer (adenocarcinoma) with angiosarcoma; look for 'vascular channels' or 'CD31 positive' to confirm vascular origin.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas can also occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema, classically in the ipsilateral arm several years after radical mastectomy... (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman in her third trimester presents with a rapidly growing, pedunculated red nodule on her gingiva that bleeds easily with minor trauma. She reports it appeared two weeks ago. What is the most likely pathological diagnosis?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma is a common, rapidly growing, pedunculated red nodule on skin or gingiva. When occurring in the gingiva of pregnant women, it is called a 'pregnancy tumor' (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are deeper, larger, and do not typically present as small pedunculated gingival lesions in pregnancy.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis occurs in immunocompromised individuals and is caused by Bartonella; it is not typically associated with pregnancy.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant, aggressive tumor and is much rarer than pyogenic granuloma in this clinical context.
explanations.e: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a flat, congenital birthmark, not a growing nodule.

ankiCards: A pyogenic granuloma occurring on the gingiva of a pregnant woman is known as {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are histologically a form of {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
True/False: Pyogenic granulomas are associated with an underlying bacterial infection.
{{c1::False (they are misnamed; they are not pyogenic/purulent)}}.
The clinical appearance of a pyogenic granuloma is a {{c1::pedunculated}} red nodule that bleeds easily.
Pyogenic granulomas are often preceded by {{c1::trauma}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer (neither pyogenic nor a true granuloma).
It is a lobular capillary hemangioma.
Commonly occurs on the gingiva (especially in pregnancy) or skin.
Characterized by rapid growth and easy bleeding.
Can regress spontaneously, especially after pregnancy.
microReview: Pyogenic granuloma = Gingiva + Pregnancy + Easy bleeding + Lobular capillary proliferation.
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic' suggests infection/pus, but it is actually a vascular proliferation (hemangioma).
sourceQuote: Pyogenic granulomas are capillary hemangiomas that manifest as rapidly growing red pedunculated nodules on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa... roughly 1% of pregnant women have granuloma gravidarum.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following genetic or environmental associations is correctly paired with the vascular tumor it most frequently promotes?

explanations.a: Exposure to vinyl chloride (used in plastics), arsenic (pesticides), and Thorotrast (radiocontrast) are classic well-established risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Sturge-Weber syndrome is associated with port-wine stains (nevus flammeus) in the trigeminal distribution, not glomus tumors.
explanations.c: HHV-8 is the cause of Kaposi sarcoma, not pyogenic granuloma.
explanations.d: Turner syndrome is associated with cystic hygromas (cavernous lymphangiomas) of the neck, not strawberry hemangiomas.
explanations.e: VHL gene mutations are associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease (including hemangioblastomas), while bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella infection.

ankiCards: Vinyl chloride exposure is specifically linked to {{c1::angiosarcoma}} of the {{c2::liver}}.
Arsenic and Thorotrast are known risk factors for {{c1::hepatic angiosarcoma}}.
Cystic hygroma is a feature of {{c1::Turner syndrome}}.
Port-wine stains in the V1/V2 distribution are associated with {{c1::Sturge-Weber syndrome}}.
The viral agent linked to Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::HHV-8}}.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is linked to vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
Vascular tumors often have specific syndromic or environmental associations.
Cystic hygromas are characteristic of Turner Syndrome (45,X).
Port-wine stains (Nevus flammeus) are part of Sturge-Weber syndrome.
HHV-8 is essential for the development of all types of Kaposi Sarcoma.
microReview: Vinyl chloride/Arsenic/Thorotrast -> Hepatic Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Commonly confused associations: Turner is Cystic Hygroma (lymphatic), not Hemangioma (vascular blood).
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas... Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with distinct environmental carcinogens, including arsenic... and vinyl chloride.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which histological feature most reliably distinguishes a cavernous hemangioma from a capillary hemangioma?

options.a: The diameter and thickness of the vascular channels
options.b: The presence of HHV-8 on immunohistochemistry
options.c: The degree of endothelial cell pleomorphism
options.d: The infiltration of acute inflammatory cells
options.e: The presence of Warthin-Starry positive bacilli

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas are distinguished from capillary hemangiomas by the use of large, dilated (cavernous) vascular channels, whereas capillary hemangiomas are composed of small, thin-walled capillaries.
explanations.b: HHV-8 is used to identify Kaposi sarcoma, not hemangiomas.
explanations.c: Both capillary and cavernous hemangiomas are benign and show minimal to no endothelial pleomorphism; pleomorphism is a hallmark of angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: Inflammatory infiltration is seen in pyogenic granulomas or bacillary angiomatosis, not typically in standard hemangiomas.
explanations.e: Warthin-Starry stains are used for Bartonella in bacillary angiomatosis.

ankiCards: {{c1::Cavernous}} hemangiomas consist of large, dilated vascular channels.
{{c1::Capillary}} hemangiomas are composed of small, thin-walled vessels.
Cavernous hemangiomas of the CNS are a component of {{c1::von Hippel-Lindau}} disease.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas are {{c1::less}} likely to regress spontaneously.
Cavernous hemangiomas in the liver are usually found {{c1::incidentally}}.
keyPoints: Capillary hemangioma: small vessels, skin/mucous membranes, often regress.
Cavernous hemangioma: large dilated spaces, deeper structures, usually do not regress.
Both are benign endothelial proliferations.
Both are CD31 positive.
Cavernous types can be locally destructive due to their size.
microReview: Capillary = Small/Superficial. Cavernous = Large/Deep.
examinerTraps: Mistaking cavernous hemangiomas for malignant tumors because they are larger and don't regress; however, they lack cellular atypia/mitoses.
sourceQuote: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, dilated vascular channels... Capillary hemangiomas are composed of thin-walled capillaries with scant stroma.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An infant is born with a massive, fluctuant swelling on the left side of the neck. Ultrasound shows a multiloculated cystic mass. The physician explains to the parents that this is a benign malformation of the lymphatic system. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) is a benign lymphatic malformation typically found in the neck or axilla of infants and is strongly associated with Turner syndrome.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas involve blood vessels, are usually not cystic/multiloculated, and are 'strawberry' red.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are small, painful, and subungual; they are not massive neck swellings in infants.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignancy, extremely rare in newborns.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular lesion seen in immunocompromised adults, not a congenital lymphatic malformation.

ankiCards: The term for a cavernous lymphangioma of the neck is {{c1::cystic hygroma}}.
Cystic hygromas are frequently associated with {{c1::Turner syndrome (45,X)}}.
Histologically, lymphangiomas can be distinguished from hemangiomas by the absence of {{c1::red blood cells}} in the lumina.
Cystic hygromas are most commonly found in the {{c1::neck}} or {{c2::axilla}}.
The lining of the spaces in a cystic hygroma consists of {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
keyPoints: Cystic hygromas are benign cavernous lymphangiomas.
Classic presentation: Large, soft neck mass in an infant.
Often associated with chromosomal abnormalities (Turner, Down Syndrome).
They contain proteinaceous fluid but few red blood cells.
Difficult to resect because they lack a capsule and permeate tissues.
microReview: Neck mass + Infant + Lymphatic = Cystic hygroma.
examinerTraps: Confusion with branchial cleft cysts; cystic hygromas are usually posterior to the sternocleidomastoid and are present at or shortly after birth, while branchial cysts are often lateral and present later in childhood.
sourceQuote: Cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) are typically found in the neck or axilla of children... and are common in Turner syndrome.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 70-year-old man from Eastern Europe presents with multiple red-purple skin nodules on his lower legs. He has had these for several years, and they have grown very slowly. He is otherwise healthy and HIV-negative. Which variant of Kaposi Sarcoma does this patient most likely have?

explanations.a: Classic KS occurs in older men of Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, or Eastern European descent. It is typically indolent, remains confined to the skin (lower legs), and is not associated with HIV.
explanations.b: Endemic African KS occurs in younger people in Africa and can be much more aggressive (especially the lymphadenopathic form).
explanations.c: Transplant-associated KS occurs in patients on chronic immunosuppression; this patient is healthy.
explanations.d: AIDS-associated (epidemic) KS is the most common form in the US and is associated with HIV/AIDS; this patient is HIV-negative.
explanations.e: Iatrogenic KS is essentially the same as transplant-associated KS, occurring due to medication-induced immunosuppression.

ankiCards: The most indolent form of Kaposi Sarcoma is the {{c1::Classic}} type.
Classic Kaposi Sarcoma is typically seen in {{c1::older men}} of Mediterranean/Eastern European descent.
Unlike the AIDS-associated form, Classic KS is usually limited to the {{c1::skin (distal lower extremities)}}.
All forms of Kaposi Sarcoma are caused by the virus {{c1::HHV-8}}.
The most aggressive form of KS is usually the {{c1::AIDS-associated (Epidemic)}} type.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma has four major epidemiological forms.
Classic KS: Indolent, elderly European men, skin-limited.
Endemic African KS: Prevalent in HIV-negative Africans, can be aggressive in children.
Transplant-associated: Due to T-cell immunosuppression; may regress if drugs are stopped.
AIDS-associated: Most common HIV-related tumor, involves skin and viscera.
microReview: Old man + Eastern Europe + Leg nodules = Classic KS.
examinerTraps: Assuming all KS is AIDS-related; classic KS was described long before the HIV epidemic.
sourceQuote: Classic KS... typically affects older men of Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, or Eastern European descent... The disease is usually restricted to the skin.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 34-year-old male with a history of HIV infection (CD4+ count 150/mm³) presents with multiple painless, violaceous, raised plaques on his lower extremities and hard palate. Biopsy of a skin lesion reveals a proliferation of spindle-shaped cells forming slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells. Which of the following viral agents is the most likely driver of this patient's pathology?

explanations.a: HHV-6 is associated with Roseola infantum, not vascular tumors.
explanations.b: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of Kaposi sarcoma, which presents as spindle cell proliferation and slit-like vascular spaces.
explanations.c: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, but not primary vascular tumors.
explanations.d: CMV can cause retinitis or colitis in AIDS patients but does not cause spindle cell vascular tumors.
explanations.e: HPV-16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas (cervical, oropharyngeal), not mesenchymal vascular tumors.

ankiCards: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
The histological hallmark of Kaposi sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells}} forming {{c2::slit-like spaces}}.
AIDS-related Kaposi sarcoma often presents on the {{c1::skin}} and {{c2::mucous membranes (e.g., palate)}}.
The slit-like spaces in Kaposi sarcoma typically contain {{c1::extravasated red blood cells}}.
HHV-8 infects {{c1::endothelial cells}} and promotes their transformation.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
HHV-8 is the essential oncogenic driver for all four forms of KS.
Histology shows spindle cells and slit-like vascular channels.
Common in immunosuppressed patients (AIDS, transplant).
Cutaneous lesions progress from patches to plaques to nodules.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma: HHV-8 + Immunodeficiency -> Spindle cells + Slit-like RBC-filled spaces. Most common AIDS-defining neoplasm.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Kaposi Sarcoma with Bacillary Angiomatosis; the latter is caused by Bartonella and features neutrophilic infiltrates.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors... include benign tumors and tumor-like conditions, intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors, and malignant tumors.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 42-year-old female presents with an extremely painful, 5-mm subungual nodule on her right index finger. The pain is particularly sensitive to cold temperatures. Excision of the lesion shows a nest of specialized, modified smooth muscle cells surrounding vascular channels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are common and benign but are usually painless and not subungual.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large vascular channels; they are typically deep-seated and not associated with paroxysmal pain.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are exquisitely painful, small, benign tumors arising from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, often found in subungual locations.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor, usually much larger and more invasive than a 5-mm subungual nodule.
explanations.e: Pyogenic granulomas are rapidly growing, pedunculated red nodules that bleed easily, often following trauma.

ankiCards: A painful subungual vascular tumor is likely a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle cells}}.
The thermoregulatory organ involved in glomus tumors is the {{c1::glomus body}}.
Glomus tumors are characterized by intense pain triggered by {{c1::cold}}.
The cell of origin for a glomangioma is the {{c1::glomus cell (pericyte-like)}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign and exquisitely painful.
Classic location is the distal digits, especially subungual.
They arise from the glomus body, a thermoregulatory arteriovenous shunt.
Morphology: nests of uniform 'glomus cells' around vessels.
Surgical excision is curative.
microReview: Glomus tumor: Subungual + Exquisite pain + Modified smooth muscle cells.
examinerTraps: Wait for the 'cold sensitivity' or 'painful finger' clue to distinguish glomus tumor from other hemangiomas.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... Malignant Tumors.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male who worked in a chemical plant producing plastics for 30 years presents with weight loss and abdominal pain. Imaging shows multiple poorly defined masses in the liver. A biopsy reveals malignant endothelial cells that are positive for CD31 and show marked pleomorphism. Exposure to which of the following substances is most strongly associated with this condition?

explanations.a: Aflatoxin B1 is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Vinyl chloride (used in PVC production) is a well-known risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Benzene exposure is primarily associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.d: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and bronchogenic carcinoma.
explanations.e: Beryllium exposure is associated with berylliosis (granulomatous lung disease) and lung cancer.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
Besides vinyl chloride, hepatic angiosarcoma is linked to {{c1::arsenic}} and {{c2::Thorotrast}}.
The endothelial marker used to identify angiosarcoma is {{c1::CD31}} (or vWF).
Angiosarcoma is a highly {{c1::malignant}} vascular tumor.
Morphology of angiosarcoma includes {{c1::pleomorphic endothelial cells}} forming irregular channels.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a rare, highly aggressive malignant vascular tumor.
Hepatic angiosarcoma has specific environmental triggers: Vinyl chloride, Arsenic, Thorotrast.
Tumor cells are positive for endothelial markers (CD31).
Occurs most often in older adults.
Prognosis is poor due to frequent metastasis and local invasion.
microReview: Angiosarcoma (Liver): CD31+ + Vinyl Chloride/Arsenic + Highly Malignant.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse hepatic angiosarcoma with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). HCC is associated with HBV/HCV/Cirrhosis, while angiosarcoma is associated with specific chemical exposures.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 2-week-old neonate presents with a bright red, raised, 'strawberry-like' lesion on the scalp. The parents are concerned as the lesion has grown rapidly since birth. Which of the following is the most likely natural history for this lesion?

options.e: Invariable association with internal visceral hemangiomas

explanations.a: Juvenile hemangiomas typically regress rather than grow indefinitely.
explanations.b: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are common in newborns, grow rapidly for a few months, and usually regress completely by age 7 in the vast majority of cases.
explanations.c: Hemangiomas are benign lesions and do not transform into angiosarcomas.
explanations.d: They do not remain stable; they undergo a characteristic cycle of proliferation followed by involution.
explanations.e: While some syndromes (like PHACE) exist, most strawberry hemangiomas are isolated cutaneous findings.

ankiCards: The common name for a juvenile hemangioma is a {{c1::strawberry hemangioma}}.
Strawberry hemangiomas typically {{c1::regress}} spontaneously by age 7.
Juvenile hemangiomas are histologically classified as {{c1::capillary}} hemangiomas.
Initial growth of a juvenile hemangioma is usually {{c1::rapid}}.
True/False: Strawberry hemangiomas carry a high risk of malignancy. {{c1::False}}
keyPoints: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma is extremely common in infancy.
It is a capillary hemangioma variant.
Clinical course: Rapid growth followed by gradual involution.
75% to 90% vanish by age 7.
Usually requires no treatment unless interfering with vital functions (e.g., vision).
microReview: Strawberry Hemangioma: Infant + Rapid growth + Spontaneous regression by age 7.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse with 'Port-wine stain' (Nevus flammeus), which does not regress and grows with the child.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction... Weakening of vessel walls.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 40-year-old male with poorly controlled HIV presents with several red, friable skin nodules. Biopsy shows a proliferation of capillaries with prominent 'epithelioid' endothelial cells and an infiltrate of neutrophils. A Warthin-Starry silver stain reveals clusters of small bacilli. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma shows spindle cells and slit-like spaces, not neutrophilic infiltrates or bacilli.
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignancy with marked atypia and is not associated with bacterial infection.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella species in immunocompromised hosts. Histology shows vascular proliferation with neutrophils and causative organisms visible on silver stain.
