explanations.a: Obliteration of the vasa vasorum is the hallmark of syphilitic (tertiary) aortitis, which typically affects the ascending (thoracic) aorta, not the abdominal aorta.
explanations.b: Transmural inflammation with giant cells is characteristic of Giant Cell (temporal) Arteritis, which typically involves smaller branches of the carotid artery.
explanations.c: Infection-induced destruction is characteristic of mycotic aneurysms, usually associated with septic emboli or direct bacterial seeding.
explanations.d: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are primarily driven by atherosclerosis, where the intimal plaque impairs oxygen diffusion to the media, leading to secondary medial degeneration and wall weakening.
explanations.e: Congenital defects in the media are more typically associated with 'berry' aneurysms in the Circle of Willis, rather than large abdominal aortic aneurysms.

ankiCards: The most common cause of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA) is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Abdominal aortic aneurysms are usually located {{c1::infrarenal}} (below the renal arteries).
Atherosclerosis causes AAAs by causing {{c1::medial ischemia/degeneration}} due to impaired oxygen diffusion through the intima.
The major modifiable risk factor for the development of AAA is {{c1::cigarette smoking}}.
A {{c1::pulsatile mass}} on physical exam is a classic finding for an abdominal aortic aneurysm.
keyPoints: Atherosclerosis is the dominant cause of AAA.
Smoking is the most significant clinical risk factor.
AAA typically occurs below the renal arteries and above the iliac bifurcation.
Pathogenesis involves medial thinning secondary to intimal plaque formation.
Rupture risk increases significantly once the diameter exceeds 5.0 to 5.5 cm.
Men are affected significantly more often than women.
microReview: AAA = Atherosclerosis + Infrarenal. Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm = Hypertension + Marfan + Syphilis.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the location; AAA is infrarenal, while syphilitic aneurysms are thoracic (ascending).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: Which of the following describes the fundamental morphological difference between a 'true' aneurysm and a 'false' aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm)?

options.a: A true aneurysm involves only the tunica intima, whereas a false aneurysm involves all three layers.
options.b: A true aneurysm involves an intact but attenuated arterial wall, while a false aneurysm is an extravascular hematoma communicating with the lumen.
options.c: A true aneurysm is always caused by atherosclerosis, whereas a false aneurysm is always caused by trauma.
options.d: A true aneurysm is spherical (saccular), whereas a false aneurysm is always circumferential (fusiform).
options.e: A true aneurysm never ruptures, whereas a false aneurysm is prone to immediate hemorrhage.

explanations.a: True aneurysms must involve all three layers of the vessel wall (intima, media, and adventitia), though they may be thinned.
explanations.b: This is the classic definition. A true aneurysm involves an intact arterial wall (though attenuated), whereas a false aneurysm involves a wall defect that allows blood to leak out and be contained by connective tissue.
explanations.c: While atherosclerosis is a common cause of true aneurysms, other factors like hypertension or genetics (Marfan) also contribute; false aneurysms can result from trauma, infection, or post-surgical leaks.
explanations.d: True aneurysms can be either saccular or fusiform; the shape does not distinguish true from false.
explanations.e: Both true and false aneurysms are at risk of rupture; size and pressure are the primary determinants.

ankiCards: A(n) {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the arterial wall.
A(n) {{c1::false (pseudo)}} aneurysm is an extravascular hematoma that communicates with the intravascular space through a wall defect.
An example of a false aneurysm is a leak at a {{c1::vascular graft junction}}.
True aneurysms are classified by shape as either {{c1::saccular}} or {{c1::fusiform}}.
Vascular {{c1::dissection}} occurs when blood enters the wall itself, separating the layers.
keyPoints: True aneurysms involve all layers: intima, media, and adventitia.
False aneurysms are localized hematomas contained by extravascular tissue.
True aneurysms are subdivided into saccular (outpouching) and fusiform (circumferential).
Pseudoaneurysms often occur at arterial puncture sites or graft anastomoses.
The vessel wall in a true aneurysm is attenuated but remains structurally continuous.
microReview: True = 3 layers intact but thin. False = hole in the wall + hematoma.
examinerTraps: Students often think a dissection is a type of aneurysm; while related to wall weakness, dissection is specifically blood between the layers, not an outpocketing of all layers.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: A 24-year-old male with long, slender fingers, pectus excavatum, and a high-arched palate presents with sudden onset of substernal chest pressure. Imaging reveals a dilation of the ascending aorta and aortic valve insufficiency. Which of the following proteins is likely defective in this patient?

explanations.a: Type III collagen defects are associated with Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, which can cause aneurysms but is less commonly associated with the classic skeletal features described.
explanations.b: While elastin is degraded in many aneurysms, it is not the primary genetic defect in Marfan syndrome.
explanations.c: The patient has features of Marfan syndrome (marfanoid habitus). This is caused by mutations in Fibrillin-1, which leads to cystic medial degeneration of the aorta.
explanations.d: Fibronectin is an adhesive glycoprotein not typically associated with the genetic cause of aortic aneurysms.
explanations.e: Laminin is a component of the basement membrane; defects are not the primary cause of Marfan syndrome or aortic root dilation.

ankiCards: Marfan syndrome is caused by a mutation in the {{c1::FBN1 (Fibrillin-1)}} gene.
The histological change in the aorta associated with Marfan syndrome is {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
The most common site for aneurysm in Marfan syndrome is the {{c1::ascending aorta}}.
Defective Fibrillin-1 leads to excessive signaling of {{c1::TGF-beta}} in the vessel wall.
Cystic medial degeneration is characterized by the loss of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} and the accumulation of mucoid material.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder of connective tissue.
Fibrillin-1 is essential for the structural integrity of the extracellular matrix.
Mutations lead to weakness of the aortic media (cystic medial necrosis).
Ascending aortic involvement often leads to aortic root dilation and valvular regurgitation.
TGF-beta signaling dysregulation plays a key role in the pathogenesis.
microReview: Marfan = Fibrillin-1 = Ascending Aorta = Cystic Medial Degeneration.
examinerTraps: Wait for the clinical signs (tall, long fingers) to point toward Marfan rather than simple atherosclerosis.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: Aneurysm formation is often associated with a localized imbalance in the remodeling of the extracellular matrix. Which class of enzymes is frequently found to be overexpressed, leading to the destruction of structural proteins like collagen and elastin in the arterial media?

explanations.a: Caspases are involved in apoptosis (programmed cell death), not direct degradation of extracellular matrix fibers.
explanations.b: Increased activity of Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMPs), produced by macrophages and smooth muscle cells, degrades the extracellular matrix, weakening the vessel wall.
explanations.c: Cyclooxygenases are involved in prostaglandin synthesis and inflammation but do not directly digest structural proteins.
explanations.d: Tyrosine kinases are involved in cell signaling pathways and growth factor receptors.
explanations.e: Phospholipases break down phospholipids in cell membranes, not extracellular structural proteins like collagen.

ankiCards: The enzymes responsible for degrading collagen and elastin in aneurysms are {{c1::Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
MMPs in the aortic wall are primarily secreted by {{c1::macrophages}} and smooth muscle cells.
An imbalance between MMPs and their inhibitors, {{c1::TIMPs}}, leads to aneurysm formation.
Atherosclerosis-related aneurysms involve increased expression of MMP-{{c1::9}} and MMP-{{c1::2}}.
The loss of {{c1::elastin}} in the media is a critical step in the permanent dilation of an aneurysm.
keyPoints: Vascular wall remodeling is a balance between synthesis and degradation.
In aneurysms, degradation dominates over synthesis.
MMPs (e.g., MMP-2, MMP-9) are the primary effectors of matrix destruction.
Inflammatory cells in the plaque secrete cytokines that stimulate MMP production.
Medial thinning is the structural result of this enzymatic degradation.
microReview: MMP = Matrix Destruction = Aneurysm. TIMP = Inhibition (Protective).
examinerTraps: Do not confuse MMPs with Caspases; MMPs act extracellularly, Caspases act intracellularly.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: Which of the following describes the most likely underlying pathology of a 'mycotic' aneurysm?

options.a: Fungal infection of the aortic adventitia
options.b: Infection of the arterial wall by a circulating pathogen
options.c: Medial necrosis due to chronic hypertension
options.d: Autoimmune destruction of the internal elastic lamina
options.e: Neoplastic invasion of the tunica media

explanations.a: Despite the name 'mycotic,' these aneurysms are most frequently caused by bacteria (e.g., Salmonella, Staphylococci), not necessarily fungi.
explanations.b: A mycotic aneurysm results from infection within the wall, often from septic emboli (endocarditis) or direct extension of an adjacent infection.
explanations.c: Chronic hypertension causes hyaline arteriolosclerosis or cystic medial degeneration, not mycotic aneurysms.
explanations.d: Autoimmune destruction is characteristic of vasculitides, not mycotic (infectious) aneurysms.
explanations.e: Neoplasia is a rare cause of vessel wall destruction and is not referred to as a mycotic aneurysm.

ankiCards: A(n) {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm is an aneurysm caused by an infection of the vessel wall.
The term 'mycotic' was coined by {{c1::William Osler}} to describe the mushroom-like appearance, not the etiology.
Common bacterial causes of mycotic aneurysms include {{c1::Salmonella}} and Staphylococcus.
Mycotic aneurysms often arise from {{c1::septic emboli}} in the setting of infective endocarditis.
The primary complication of a mycotic aneurysm is rapid {{c1::rupture}} due to suppuration.
keyPoints: Mycotic aneurysms are infectious in origin.
Most are bacterial (Staph, Strep, Salmonella), not fungal.
They can arise from bacteremia, septic emboli, or direct extension.
They are characterized by rapid destruction of the vessel wall and high rupture risk.
Morphology is usually saccular.
microReview: Mycotic = Infection (usually bacterial) + Wall Weakness.
examinerTraps: The term 'mycotic' is a misnomer; it almost always refers to a bacterial infection rather than a fungus.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: A 72-year-old male with a history of untreated syphilis 30 years ago presents with shortness of breath and a new-onset diastolic murmur. Imaging reveals a dilated ascending aorta and calcification of the aortic root. Which of the following is the most characteristic histological finding in this patient's aorta?

options.a: Intimal tears with false lumen formation
options.b: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.d: Severe atherosclerosis of the abdominal aorta

explanations.a: Intimal tears with false lumen formation are the hallmark of aortic dissection, not syphilitic aortitis.
explanations.b: Syphilitic (luetic) aortitis involves the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta, where obliterative endarteritis leads to ischemic injury of the media.
explanations.c: Transmural granulomatous inflammation is seen in Takayasu or Giant Cell arteritis.
explanations.d: Atherosclerosis typically affects the abdominal aorta; syphilis specifically targets the thoracic/ascending aorta.
explanations.e: Fibrinoid necrosis of small arterioles is seen in malignant hypertension or polyarteritis nodosa.

ankiCards: Tertiary syphilis classically causes aneurysms of the {{c1::ascending/thoracic}} aorta.
The specific lesion in syphilitic aortitis is {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}} of the vasa vasorum.
Ischemic injury to the aortic media in syphilis leads to a '{{c1::tree-barking}}' appearance of the intima.
Syphilitic aneurysms can cause {{c1::aortic valve insufficiency}} due to dilation of the aortic ring.
Syphilitic aortitis is a complication of {{c1::tertiary}} syphilis.
keyPoints: Syphilis (Treponema pallidum) targets the vasa vasorum in the thoracic aorta.
Obliteration of these vessels causes medial ischemia and fibrosis.
The resulting intimal scarring is termed 'tree-barking'.
Dilation of the aortic root can lead to valvular regurgitation and heart failure.
Syphilitic aneurysms are now rare due to effective antibiotic treatment.
microReview: Syphilis = Vasa Vasorum Obliteration = Ascending Aorta = Tree-barking.
examinerTraps: Syphilis affects the *ascending* aorta; Atherosclerosis affects the *abdominal* aorta.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: In the pathogenesis of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA), which of the following best describes the role of the inflammatory infiltrate found in the vessel wall?

options.a: It promotes collagen synthesis to strengthen the wall
options.b: It produces cytokines that inhibit matrix metalloproteinases
options.c: It secretes proteolytic enzymes that degrade the structural matrix
options.d: It facilitates the repair of the internal elastic lamina
options.e: It prevents the migration of smooth muscle cells to the intima

explanations.a: The inflammatory infiltrate (macrophages, T cells) in an AAA is primarily destructive, not reparative.
explanations.b: The cytokines produced (like TNF and IL-1) actually stimulate the production of MMPs, not inhibit them.
explanations.c: Chronic inflammation in the media/adventitia leads to the production of MMPs and other proteases that digest elastin and collagen, weakening the wall.
explanations.d: The inflammation contributes to the destruction of the elastic lamina rather than its repair.
explanations.e: Smooth muscle cell loss, rather than migration inhibition, is the typical finding in the media of an aneurysm.

ankiCards: The inflammatory cells most commonly found in an AAA wall are {{c1::macrophages}} and T cells.
Inflammatory cells in an aneurysm produce {{c1::cytokines}} that increase MMP activity.
Loss of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} in the media is a hallmark of aneurysm progression.
In inflammatory AAA, there is often dense periaortic {{c1::fibrosis}}.
Inflammatory AAA is sometimes considered part of the spectrum of {{c1::IgG4}}-related disease.
keyPoints: Chronic inflammation is a key driver of AAA pathogenesis.
Macrophages secrete proteases (MMPs) that degrade the ECM.
T-cell mediated responses further recruit and activate inflammatory cells.
This leads to a net loss of medial structural integrity.
A subset (Inflammatory AAA) shows extreme fibrosis and abundant plasma cells.
microReview: Inflammation = Protease Release = Wall Weakening = Dilation.
examinerTraps: Don't assume all inflammation is 'repair'; in vascular disease, chronic inflammation is usually synonymous with tissue destruction.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: Which of the following clinical conditions is most strongly associated with the development of Berry (saccular) aneurysms in the Circle of Willis?

explanations.a: ADPKD is strongly associated with Berry aneurysms due to underlying defects in the structural proteins of the arterial wall.
explanations.b: Diabetes is a risk factor for atherosclerosis and macrovascular disease but is not specifically linked to Berry aneurysms.
explanations.c: SLE is associated with vasculitis and premature atherosclerosis, but not classically with Berry aneurysms.
explanations.d: HCM is a primary disorder of cardiac muscle, not linked to cerebral vascular outpouchings.
explanations.e: PBC is an autoimmune liver disease with no significant association with Berry aneurysms.

ankiCards: Berry aneurysms are most commonly located in the {{c1::Circle of Willis}}.
The most common specific site for a Berry aneurysm is the {{c1::anterior communicating}} artery.
The most feared complication of a Berry aneurysm is {{c1::subarachnoid hemorrhage}}.
The genetic condition most associated with Berry aneurysms is {{c1::ADPKD (Polycystic Kidney Disease)}}.
Berry aneurysms occur due to a lack of {{c1::internal elastic lamina}} and smooth muscle at arterial bifurcations.
keyPoints: Berry aneurysms are saccular dilations at bifurcations of cerebral arteries.
They are not present at birth but the underlying wall defect is congenital.
Risk factors include hypertension and cigarette smoking.
ADPKD and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome are significant genetic associations.
Rupture causes a 'thunderclap headache'.
microReview: Berry Aneurysm = Circle of Willis = ADPKD = Subarachnoid Hemorrhage.
examinerTraps: Berry aneurysms are not 'congenital' in that they aren't present at birth; rather, the *defect* in the wall is congenital, and the aneurysm develops over time.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: A 52-year-old female presents with hoarseness and a persistent dry cough. Physical exam is unremarkable except for a high blood pressure of 165/95 mmHg. A chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum and a prominence of the aortic knob. A CT scan reveals a 6 cm aneurysm of the ascending aorta. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her hoarseness?

options.a: Direct invasion of the vocal cords by atherosclerotic plaque
options.b: Compression of the recurrent laryngeal nerve
options.c: Metastatic spread of a thoracic neoplasm
options.e: Ischemic stroke affecting the nucleus ambiguus

explanations.a: Atherosclerotic plaques remain within the vessel wall and do not 'invade' the vocal cords.
explanations.b: Large thoracic aortic aneurysms can compress adjacent structures; compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve leads to vocal cord paralysis and hoarseness (Ortner's syndrome).
explanations.c: While a widened mediastinum can be seen in lung cancer, the CT scan specifically identified an aneurysm, making compression the more likely cause.
explanations.d: While an aneurysm can compress the esophagus (causing dysphagia), this would not explain hoarseness.
explanations.e: While a stroke could cause hoarseness, it would likely present with other neurological deficits, and the aneurysm provides a direct mechanical explanation.

ankiCards: Thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAA) are most commonly associated with {{c1::hypertension}}.
Hoarseness in a patient with a TAA is due to compression of the {{c1::recurrent laryngeal nerve}}.
Difficulty swallowing in TAA is caused by compression of the {{c1::esophagus}}.
TAAs can cause bone pain by eroding into the {{c1::ribs or vertebral bodies}}.
The most common cause of TAA in a younger patient is {{c1::Marfan syndrome}}.
keyPoints: Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (TAAs) are often asymptomatic until they compress local structures.
Symptoms include cough (tracheal compression) and hoarseness (nerve compression).
Hypertension is the leading cause in older adults.
Cystic medial degeneration is the common histological pathway.
TAAs carry a risk of both rupture and dissection.
microReview: Thoracic Aneurysm = Compression Symptoms (Nerve/Esophagus) + Hypertension.
examinerTraps: Don't miss the mechanical/anatomical consequences of the aneurysm's size, such as nerve compression.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: The 'threshold' for surgical intervention in an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is generally a diameter of 5.0 to 5.5 cm. This clinical guideline is based on the fact that the risk of which complication increases exponentially beyond this size?

explanations.a: While mural thrombus is common in AAAs and can cause emboli, the size threshold is primarily determined by rupture risk, not embolization risk.
explanations.b: AAA and dissection are distinct pathologies; while they share risk factors, an AAA does not typically 'progress' into a dissection.
explanations.c: The risk of rupture is <1% for AAAs <4 cm, but increases to 25% per year for aneurysms >6 cm; thus, 5.0-5.5 cm is the standard intervention threshold.
explanations.d: Vasculitis is an inflammatory condition that can *cause* an aneurysm, but an aneurysm does not convert into a vasculitis.
explanations.e: A mycotic aneurysm is an infection-initiated aneurysm; a sterile atherosclerotic aneurysm does not spontaneously 'convert' into one unless bacteremia occurs.

ankiCards: The risk of AAA rupture is directly related to its {{c1::diameter/size}}.
An AAA >{{c1::5.0 to 5.5}} cm typically requires surgical or endovascular repair.
The mortality rate for a ruptured AAA is approximately {{c1::80}} to 90%.
Most AAAs are {{c1::asymptomatic}} and discovered incidentally on imaging.
The triad of ruptured AAA is hypotension, {{c1::back/flank pain}}, and a pulsatile mass.
keyPoints: Aneurysm diameter is the best predictor of rupture risk.
The Law of Laplace (Wall Tension = Pressure x Radius) explains why larger aneurysms rupture more easily.
AAAs smaller than 4 cm are usually managed with surveillance (ultrasound).
Operative mortality for elective repair is much lower (~1-2%) than for emergency rupture repair.
Cigarette smoking and hypertension contribute to faster expansion rates.
microReview: Size > 5cm = Rupture Risk >> Surgery Risk.
examinerTraps: While 'tearing back pain' is the classic description for dissection, a ruptured AAA also causes severe back pain; look for the 'pulsatile mass' to differentiate.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: Vascular disease results from two principal pathological processes. Which of the following mechanisms is primarily responsible for the development of an aneurysm?

options.a: Precipitous thrombosis resulting in luminal obstruction
options.b: Progressive narrowing of the vessel lumen via atherosclerosis
options.c: Weakening of the vessel wall leading to dilation
options.e: Intimal thickening as a response to endothelial injury

explanations.a: Sudden luminal obstruction typically results in ischemia or infarction, rather than the dilation seen in aneurysms.
explanations.b: Progressive narrowing causes stenosis and chronic ischemia; while atherosclerosis can weaken a wall, the aneurysm specifically arises from that weakness, not the narrowing itself.
explanations.c: According to general vascular pathology principles, weakening of the vessel wall is the fundamental mechanism that permits permanent dilation (aneurysm) or rupture.
explanations.d: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is a consequence of hypertension and diabetes affecting small vessels, not the mechanism for large vessel aneurysms.
explanations.e: Intimal thickening is a stereotyped healing response to injury that typically results in lumen reduction, not dilation.

ankiCards: The two principal mechanisms of vascular disease are {{c1::luminal narrowing/obstruction}} and {{c2::weakening of vessel walls}}.
A permanent dilation of a vessel wall or the heart is defined as an {{c1::aneurysm}}.
Weakening of vessel walls typically leads to two major clinical outcomes: {{c1::dilation}} or {{c2::rupture}}.
Vascular pathology in hypertension primarily affects {{c1::small}} arteries and arterioles.
Atherosclerosis affects mainly {{c1::elastic}} and {{c2::muscular}} arteries.
keyPoints: Vascular disease is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality globally.
Pathology is divided into luminal obstruction (stenosis/thrombosis) and wall weakening (aneurysm/rupture).
Aneurysms involve all layers of the arterial wall (true) or a breach in the wall (false).
Arterial walls are thicker than veins to accommodate higher pressure and pulsatile flow.
Vessel disorders have characteristic anatomic distributions based on the type of vessel affected.
microReview: Vascular pathology focuses on two themes: luminal issues (too narrow) and structural issues (too weak). Aneurysms fall into the structural category where the wall fails to contain the pressure, leading to dilation.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'cause' (e.g., atherosclerosis) with the 'mechanism' (wall weakening). While atherosclerosis causes AAA, the mechanical reason it expands is the loss of wall integrity.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: A 68-year-old male with a history of long-standing hypertension and tobacco use is found to have a 5.5 cm dilation of the infrarenal aorta. Which of the following pathological changes in the vessel wall is the most critical step in the formation of this lesion?

options.a: Increased synthesis of type I collagen in the media
options.b: Excessive degradation of the extracellular matrix by metalloproteinases
options.c: Proliferation of smooth muscle cells within the intima
options.d: Deposition of hyaline material in the arteriolar walls
options.e: Accumulation of glycosaminoglycans in the adventitia

explanations.a: Increased collagen synthesis would generally strengthen a wall; aneurysms are associated with decreased or defective collagen.
explanations.b: Aneurysm formation involves an imbalance where matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) degrade elastin and collagen, leading to structural failure of the media.
explanations.c: Smooth muscle cell proliferation in the intima (intimal thickening) is a response to injury that narrows the lumen, rather than dilating it.
explanations.d: Hyaline deposition is characteristic of hypertensive arteriolosclerosis in small vessels, not large-scale aortic aneurysms.
explanations.e: While glycosaminoglycans can accumulate in cystic medial degeneration, it typically occurs in the media, not the adventitia, and matrix degradation is the more definitive mechanism for AAA.

ankiCards: The primary pathological driver of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) is the degradation of the {{c1::extracellular matrix (ECM)}}.
A key enzyme class involved in the breakdown of aortic wall elastin and collagen is {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
In an aneurysm, the balance shifts toward {{c1::degradation}} over synthesis of structural proteins.
The most common site for an atherosclerotic aneurysm is the {{c1::abdominal aorta (infrarenal)}}.
Major risk factors for AAA include {{c1::tobacco smoking}} and {{c2::male sex}}.
keyPoints: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are most commonly associated with atherosclerosis.
Degradation of tunica media elastin and collagen is required for permanent dilation.
Inflammatory cell infiltrates in the media produce MMPs.
The infrarenal aorta is the classic location for AAA because it lacks vasa vasorum.
Expansion rate and size (>5 cm) are the best predictors of rupture risk.
microReview: AAA Pathogenesis: Atherosclerosis -> Inflammation -> MMP Activation -> Degradation of Medial Elastin/Collagen -> Wall Weakening -> Permanent Dilation.
examinerTraps: Be careful not to select 'intimal thickening'. While atherosclerosis starts in the intima, the 'aneurysm' itself is a failure of the media.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: A 72-year-old male smoker presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset, severe, tearing back pain. On physical examination, a pulsatile mass is palpated in the epigastrium. His blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of the vessel wall weakening in this patient?

options.a: Tertiary syphilis inducing endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.c: Fibrillin-1 mutation causing cystic medial degeneration
options.d: Congenital defect in the internal elastic lamina
options.e: Staphylococcus aureus infection of the vessel wall

explanations.a: Syphilitic (luetic) aneurysms typically involve the ascending thoracic aorta, not the abdominal aorta.
explanations.b: Atherosclerosis is the dominant cause of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA). The plaque compromises nutrient diffusion to the media, causing ischemia and thinning.
explanations.c: Fibrillin-1 mutations (Marfan syndrome) cause thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections in younger patients.
explanations.d: Congenital defects in the internal elastic lamina are associated with Berry aneurysms in the Circle of Willis.
explanations.e: A mycotic (infected) aneurysm could cause this, but atherosclerosis is statistically far more common in an elderly smoker with a pulsatile abdominal mass.

ankiCards: The most common cause of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA) is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
A {{c1::pulsatile abdominal mass}} on physical exam is highly suggestive of an AAA.
The triad of ruptured AAA is {{c1::hypotension}}, {{c2::flank/back pain}}, and a {{c3::pulsatile mass}}.
Atherosclerotic plaques cause medial thinning by {{c1::obstructing nutrient diffusion}} from the lumen.
AAA are most frequently located {{c1::below (infrarenal)}} the renal arteries.
keyPoints: AAA is primarily a disease of older male smokers.
Atherosclerosis causes the media to atrophy due to impaired oxygen diffusion.
Rupture is a surgical emergency characterized by sudden pain and shock.
Normal aortic diameter is approximately 2 cm; >3 cm is considered aneurysmal.
Clinical presentation of AAA is often asymptomatic until rupture or embolization.
microReview: AAA = Older patient + Smoking + Atherosclerosis + Infrarenal location. Rupture risk increases significantly once the diameter exceeds 5.0 to 5.5 cm.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse 'tearing pain' solely with aortic dissection. While classically dissection, a ruptured AAA presents with similar severe pain and is far more likely in the presence of a palpable abdominal mass.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: A 24-year-old woman is evaluated for Marfan syndrome. She is noted to have high-arched palate, arachnodactyly, and mitral valve prolapse. Echocardiography reveals dilation of the aortic root. Which of the following best describes the histological appearance of the aortic media in this condition?

options.b: Loss of elastic fibers with 'cystic' spaces filled with mucoid material
options.c: Extensive calcification within the internal elastic lamina
options.d: Replacement of the media by dense fibrous scar tissue
options.e: Focal destruction of the media by neutrophilic abscesses

explanations.a: Giant cell arteritis involves granulomatous inflammation, typically in the temporal artery or arch, not the characteristic finding in Marfan syndrome.
explanations.b: Cystic medial degeneration (or necrosis) is the hallmark of Marfan syndrome and other conditions leading to thoracic aortic aneurysms.
explanations.c: Calcification of the internal elastic lamina describes Monckeberg medial calcific sclerosis, which does not cause aneurysms.
explanations.d: Dense fibrous scarring is more typical of a healed vasculitis or the late stages of syphilitic aortitis.
explanations.e: Neutrophilic abscesses in the wall would indicate a mycotic (infectious) aneurysm.

ankiCards: The histological hallmark of Marfan-associated aortic dilation is {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
Cystic medial degeneration involves the loss of {{c1::elastic fibers}}.
The 'cystic' spaces in medial degeneration are actually filled with {{c1::glycosaminoglycans (mucoid material)}}.
The genetic defect in Marfan syndrome is in the {{c1::Fibrillin-1 (FBN1)}} gene.
Marfan syndrome primarily causes aneurysms in the {{c1::ascending thoracic}} aorta.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome leads to TGF-beta signaling dysregulation.
Defective Fibrillin-1 prevents normal sequestration of TGF-beta.
Increased TGF-beta leads to matrix degradation and elastic fiber loss.
Cystic medial degeneration is not 'true' necrosis; it's a loss of structural integrity.
Thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAA) in Marfan's often lead to aortic dissection.
microReview: Marfan = Fibrillin-1 mutation -> Increased TGF-beta -> Cystic Medial Degeneration -> Weakened Media -> Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Avoid the word 'necrosis'. While the term 'Cystic Medial Necrosis' is historical, modern pathology prefers 'degeneration' because cell death is not the primary feature; matrix loss is.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: Aneurysms are classified into 'true' and 'false' types based on the composition of their walls. Which of the following conditions is an example of a 'false' aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm)?

options.a: A fusiform dilation of the abdominal aorta in a smoker
options.b: A saccular bulge in the Circle of Willis
options.c: A collection of blood communicating with the lumen but contained only by adventitia or perivascular tissue
options.d: A localized dilation of the ascending aorta in a patient with tertiary syphilis
options.e: An outpouching of the ventricular wall following a transmural myocardial infarction

explanations.a: Fusiform AAA involve all three layers of the wall, making them 'true' aneurysms.
explanations.b: Berry aneurysms involve the vessel wall layers (though thin), classifying them as 'true' aneurysms.
explanations.c: A false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) is a wall defect that allows blood to leak out but stay contained by external connective tissue, lacking the three-layer vessel wall.
explanations.d: Syphilitic aneurysms are 'true' aneurysms as they involve dilation of the existing (though damaged) wall.
explanations.e: Post-MI ventricular aneurysms consist of the scarred heart wall layers and are considered 'true' aneurysms of the heart.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the arterial wall (intima, media, adventitia).
A {{c1::false (pseudoaneurysm)}} is a breach in the vascular wall leading to an extravascular hematoma that communicates with the lumen.
The two main shapes of true aneurysms are {{c1::saccular}} and {{c2::fusiform}}.
A {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm is a spherical outpouching involving only a portion of the vessel wall.
A {{c1::fusiform}} aneurysm is a circumferential, spindle-shaped dilation of the vessel.
keyPoints: True aneurysms: Attenuated but intact arterial wall or thinned ventricular wall.
False aneurysms: Hematoma contained by extravascular tissue (e.g., after femoral artery catheterization).
Dissection: Blood enters the wall itself, creating a false lumen between layers.
Saccular aneurysms often contain mural thrombi.
Fusiform aneurysms are most common in the abdominal aorta and iliac arteries.
microReview: True = All layers (even if thinned). False = Blood leak held by 'scab' or surrounding tissue. Dissection = Blood *inside* the wall layers.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse a 'false aneurysm' with a 'dissection'. A false aneurysm is an external hematoma; a dissection is an internal hematoma (within the media).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: Which of the following descriptions best characterizes a 'mycotic' aneurysm?

options.a: An aneurysm caused by the direct invasion of fungal hyphae into the intima
options.b: A dilation caused by an infection within the vessel wall that weakens the media
options.c: An autoimmune reaction against the elastic lamina following a viral prodrome
options.d: A congenital thinning of the vessel wall prone to secondary yeast colonization
options.e: A vessel wall weakening caused by the deposition of immune complexes

explanations.a: Despite the name, 'mycotic' aneurysms are most commonly bacterial, not fungal.
explanations.b: A mycotic aneurysm is a dilation resulting from an infection (usually bacterial) that reaches the wall via the blood (embolization) or nearby infection, destroying the media.
explanations.c: This describes a vasculitis, not the infectious destruction of a mycotic aneurysm.
explanations.d: Mycotic aneurysms are acquired through infection, not congenital.
explanations.e: Immune complex deposition is the mechanism for Small Vessel Vasculitis, not mycotic aneurysms.

ankiCards: A {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm is an aneurysm arising from infection of the arterial wall.
The most common cause of mycotic aneurysms is {{c1::bacterial}} infection (e.g., from infective endocarditis).
A mycotic aneurysm results in rapid {{c1::dilation}} and has a high risk of {{c2::rupture}}.
Infection can reach the vessel wall via the {{c1::vasa vasorum}} or by direct seeding from the lumen.
The term 'mycotic' was coined by William Osler to describe the {{c1::mushroom}}-like appearance, not the organism.
keyPoints: Mycotic aneurysms are typically bacterial (e.g., Salmonella, Bacteroides, Staph).
Commonly occur after septic emboli from infective endocarditis.
Can also occur via direct extension of a nearby suppurative process.
They carry a very high risk of rupture due to acute inflammatory destruction.
Histology shows prominent neutrophilic infiltration and necrosis.
microReview: Mycotic = Infection-induced. Wall is destroyed by bugs/inflammation. Usually bacterial. High rupture risk.
examinerTraps: The word 'mycotic' is a major trap; students often select 'fungal' when the most common causes are bacterial (Staph, Strep, Salmonella).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: A 55-year-old male with a history of untreated syphilis presents with a barking cough and difficulty swallowing. Chest X-ray shows a large, calcified dilation of the ascending aortic arch. What is the primary mechanism of the vessel wall weakening in this patient?

options.a: Direct toxic effect of Treponema pallidum on vascular smooth muscle
options.b: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.c: Atherosclerotic plaque formation in the ascending aorta
options.d: Cystic medial degeneration due to fibrillin deficiency
options.e: Deposition of amyloid light chains in the aortic media

explanations.a: Treponema does not directly kill smooth muscle; the damage is mediated by the immune response and ischemia.
explanations.b: Tertiary syphilis causes obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum, which supplies the media of the ascending aorta. This leads to medial ischemia and weakening.
explanations.c: Atherosclerosis typically spares the ascending aorta (preferring the abdominal aorta). Syphilis is the classic cause for ascending aortic aneurysms.
explanations.d: Fibrillin deficiency is Marfan syndrome, which is genetic, not infectious.
explanations.e: Amyloidosis does not typically present as large vessel aneurysms of the ascending aorta.

ankiCards: Tertiary syphilis causes aneurysms in the {{c1::ascending}} aorta.
The mechanism of syphilitic aortitis is {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}} of the vasa vasorum.
Ischemia of the aortic media in syphilis leads to a {{c1::'tree-bark'}} appearance of the intima.
Dilation of the aortic root in syphilis often leads to {{c1::aortic valve insufficiency (regurgitation)}}.
Aneurysms of the ascending aorta can compress the {{c1::esophagus}} or {{c2::recurrent laryngeal nerve}}.
keyPoints: Syphilitic (luetic) aneurysms are now rare due to antibiotic treatment.
The 'tree-bark' appearance is due to irregular scarring following medial ischemia.
These aneurysms can cause respiratory distress (tracheal compression) or dysphagia.
Aortic valve ring dilation is a common complication (cor bovinum).
Diagnosis is confirmed with serological tests for syphilis (RPR, FTA-ABS).
microReview: Syphilis -> Vasa Vasorum Endarteritis -> Medial Ischemia -> Wall Weakening -> Ascending Aortic Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: The 'tree-barking' is an *intimal* finding, but the *weakening* that causes the aneurysm is in the *media*.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: Which of the following arteries is the most common site for 'Berry' aneurysms, which are small saccular dilations associated with subarachnoid hemorrhage?

explanations.a: The middle meningeal artery is associated with epidural hematomas (trauma), not Berry aneurysms.
explanations.b: The anterior communicating artery is the most frequent site (approx. 40%) for Berry aneurysms in the Circle of Willis.
explanations.c: While aneurysms occur here, the anterior communicating artery is more common.
explanations.d: PICA aneurysms are less common than those at the anterior communicating or middle cerebral artery bifurcations.
explanations.e: The basilar artery is a less frequent site than the anterior circulation components.

ankiCards: Berry aneurysms occur at {{c1::branch points}} in the Circle of Willis.
The most common site for a Berry aneurysm is the {{c1::anterior communicating}} artery.
Rupture of a Berry aneurysm causes {{c1::subarachnoid}} hemorrhage.
Berry aneurysms are associated with {{c1::Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD)}}.
The wall of a Berry aneurysm lacks a {{c1::muscular}} layer and an {{c2::internal elastic lamina}}.
keyPoints: Berry aneurysms are not present at birth but develop due to congenital media weakness.
Cigarette smoking and hypertension increase the risk of development/rupture.
Classic presentation: 'Worst headache of my life'.
Multiple aneurysms are present in 20-30% of cases.
The majority occur in the anterior circulation.
microReview: Berry Aneurysm = Circle of Willis + ADPKD association + Subarachnoid Hemorrhage + Anterior Communicating Artery (most common).
examinerTraps: A common trap is stating Berry aneurysms are 'congenital'. While the *predisposition* (media defect) is congenital, the aneurysm itself develops over time due to hemodynamic stress.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: A 60-year-old male is diagnosed with a 4 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm. He is asymptomatic. Which of the following is the most likely consequence of the stagnant blood flow found within the aneurysmal sac?

options.e: Increased nutrient diffusion to the media

explanations.a: Aortic dissection is more commonly associated with hypertension and thoracic aneurysms, not stagnant flow in a saccular AAA.
explanations.b: Aneurysms create local stasis and turbulence, which are components of Virchow's triad, leading to the formation of mural thrombi.
explanations.c: Fistulas usually occur due to trauma or rupture into an adjacent vein, not simply from stagnant flow.
explanations.d: Aneurysms are permanent and progressive; they do not regress spontaneously.
explanations.e: Stagnant flow and mural thrombus actually *decrease* nutrient diffusion, further weakening the wall.

ankiCards: Stagnant blood flow in an aneurysm leads to the formation of a {{c1::mural thrombus}}.
A mural thrombus in an AAA can lead to distal {{c1::embolization}}.
Distal embolization from an AAA thrombus causes {{c1::'blue toe' syndrome}}.
The presence of a thrombus in an aneurysm {{c1::decreases}} oxygen diffusion to the arterial wall.
Turbulent flow in an aneurysm sac is an example of {{c1::Virchow's Triad}} in action.
keyPoints: Mural thrombi are frequently found in large AAA.
They rarely occlude the entire lumen but can embolize.
Thrombus contributes to wall weakening by causing further medial ischemia.
Aneurysms can also compress adjacent structures like the ureter.
Management for a 4 cm aneurysm is typically 'watchful waiting' with serial imaging.
microReview: AAA -> Stasis/Turbulence -> Mural Thrombus -> Potential Embolism or Medial Ischemia.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the risk of 'thrombosis' with 'dissection'. While both involve the aorta, they are distinct processes. AAA leads to thrombi; TAA/Hypertension leads to dissection.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism)
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: A 35-year-old male presents with sudden chest pain and is found to have a thoracic aortic aneurysm. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the TGF-beta receptor. Which of the following conditions is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Marfan syndrome is caused by Fibrillin-1 (FBN1) mutations, not the receptor itself.
explanations.b: Loeys-Dietz syndrome is characterized by mutations in TGF-beta receptors (TGFBR1/2) and is associated with aggressive aneurysm formation and bifid uvula.
explanations.c: Ehlers-Danlos vascular type is caused by Type III collagen mutations (COL3A1).
explanations.d: This is a lipid disorder leading to atherosclerosis, not a primary TGF-beta signaling disorder.
explanations.e: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) involves arteriovenous malformations, not aortic aneurysms.

ankiCards: {{c1::Loeys-Dietz}} syndrome is caused by mutations in TGF-beta receptors.
Clinical features of Loeys-Dietz include {{c1::aortic aneurysms}}, {{c2::bifid uvula}}, and {{c3::hypertelorism}}.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos involves a defect in {{c1::Type III Collagen}}.
TGF-beta signaling is {{c1::increased}} (overactive) in both Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes.
Patients with Loeys-Dietz are at high risk for aortic {{c1::rupture}} at smaller diameters.
keyPoints: Loeys-Dietz syndrome involves TGFBR1, TGFBR2, SMAD3, or TGFB2/3 mutations.
It is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder.
Aneurysms can occur throughout the arterial tree, not just the aorta.
Skin findings include easy bruising and translucent skin.
Aortic dissection can occur at diameters <4.0 cm, unlike in other syndromes.
microReview: TGF-beta receptor mutation = Loeys-Dietz. Fibrillin mutation = Marfan. Collagen III mutation = Vascular EDS.
examinerTraps: A common mistake is assuming 'TGF-beta' always means Marfan. Marfan involves the *protein* that holds TGF-beta (fibrillin), while Loeys-Dietz involves the *receptors* themselves.
sourceQuote: To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure and function.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: A 68-year-old female presents with a 12-year history of persistent left upper extremity swelling following a radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection for breast adenocarcinoma. Physical examination reveals several firm, bluish-red cutaneous nodules on the edematous arm. A biopsy shows pleomorphic endothelial cells forming irregular, anastomosing vascular channels with frequent mitotic figures. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma is a malignant vascular tumor that can arise in the setting of chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome), typically occurring years after radical mastectomy.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 infection and usually presents as purple patches or plaques in immunocompromised patients, not typically secondary to chronic lymphedema.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign vascular proliferation caused by Bartonella species in immunocompromised patients, characterized by neutrophilic infiltrates.
explanations.d: Hemangioendothelioma is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor that lacks the frank malignancy and high-grade pleomorphism seen in this patient's biopsy.
explanations.e: Cavernous hemangioma is a benign lesion composed of large, blood-filled spaces and would not show pleomorphism or high mitotic activity.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema is known as {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
The classic histological finding in angiosarcoma is {{c1::atypical endothelial cells}} forming {{c2::anastomosing vascular channels}}.
{{c1::Angiosarcoma}} is a malignant vascular tumor that can be induced by prior radiation therapy.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is classically associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}} or {{c2::arsenic}}.
The most common site for cutaneous angiosarcoma is the {{c1::scalp}} of elderly men.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are highly malignant tumors of endothelial cells.
Chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome) is a major risk factor for limb angiosarcoma.
The tumor expresses endothelial markers such as CD31.
Histology reveals a spectrum from well-differentiated vascular channels to solid sheets of undifferentiated cells.
Radiation therapy is a known iatrogenic cause of these tumors.
microReview: Angiosarcomas are aggressive malignancies of vascular endothelium. Key associations include chronic lymphedema, radiation, and chemical toxins (vinyl chloride). Diagnosed via IHC for CD31.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Stewart-Treves syndrome (angiosarcoma in lymphedema) with Marjolin ulcer (squamous cell carcinoma in a chronic wound/burn).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease... Vascular Tumors 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A biopsy of a purple skin lesion in a patient with late-stage HIV reveals a proliferation of spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells, and hyaline droplets. Molecular analysis is expected to show the presence of which of the following pathogens?

explanations.a: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of all forms of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.b: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can clinically mimic Kaposi sarcoma but lacks the spindle cell morphology and HHV-8 association.
explanations.c: HPV-16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx, not vascular tumors.
explanations.d: EBV is associated with various lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, but not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.e: CMV causes opportunistic infections in HIV patients but is not oncogenic for vascular tumors.

ankiCards: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is caused by infection with {{c1::Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}.
The hallmark histological feature of Kaposi sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells}} and {{c2::slit-like spaces}}.
{{c1::AIDS-associated (epidemic)}} Kaposi sarcoma is the most common HIV-related malignancy.
Unlike bacillary angiomatosis, Kaposi sarcoma has a histological infiltrate consisting primarily of {{c1::lymphocytes}}.
The four clinical forms of Kaposi sarcoma are {{c1::Classic (European)}}, {{c2::Endemic (African)}}, {{c3::Transplant-associated}}, and {{c4::AIDS-associated}}.
keyPoints: HHV-8 infects endothelial cells and induces a spindle-cell phenotype.
Slit-like vascular spaces are formed by these spindle cells.
Extravasated RBCs and hemosiderin deposits are common histological findings.
Kaposi sarcoma is not a true neoplasm in its early stages but a reactive polyclonal proliferation.
Treatment involves HAART in HIV-positive patients to restore immune function.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Slit-like spaces + Extravasated RBCs. Distinct from Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella + Neutrophils).
examinerTraps: Examiners often pit Kaposi Sarcoma against Bacillary Angiomatosis. Look for 'neutrophils' for Bartonella and 'spindle cells' for HHV-8.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease... Vascular Tumors 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular tumors is characterized by a painful, small, red-blue nodule located most commonly under the fingernails and is derived from modified smooth muscle cells?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, exquisitely painful tumors arising from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus bodies, typically in the subungual region.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granuloma is a rapidly growing pedunculated red nodule on skin or gingiva, often following trauma or during pregnancy; it is not typically subungual or derived from glomus cells.
explanations.c: Capillary hemangiomas are common benign tumors of closely packed capillaries, not specifically painful or subungual.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a large, poorly circumscribed malignancy, unlike the small, well-defined glomus tumor.
explanations.e: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a congenital capillary malformation, not a painful nodule.

ankiCards: The glomus tumor arises from {{c1::modified smooth muscle cells}} of the glomus body.
The classic location for a glomus tumor is {{c1::under the fingernails (subungual)}}.
A key clinical symptom of a glomus tumor is {{c1::exquisite pain}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors consist of specialized cells surrounding {{c1::vascular channels}}.
Unlike most vascular tumors, glomus tumors are derived from {{c1::smooth muscle}} rather than pure endothelium.
keyPoints: Glomus bodies are neuromyoarterial receptors involved in thermoregulation.
Glomus tumors are small (<1 cm) and benign.
The pain is often triggered by cold exposure.
Excision is usually curative.
They present as a blue-red nodule under the nail bed.
microReview: Glomus tumor: Subungual + Painful + Modified Smooth Muscle. High-yield for 'spot' diagnosis in clinical vignettes.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse with subungual melanoma, which is usually pigmented (brown/black) and painless.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease... Vascular Tumors 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An 18-month-old male is brought to the pediatrician for a skin lesion on his left cheek. His mother states it was a small red dot at birth, grew rapidly into a bright red, raised 'strawberry-like' mass by 6 months, and has recently begun to fade and shrink in size. Which of the following is the most likely natural history for this lesion?

explanations.a: Infantile (strawberry) hemangiomas are extremely common, grow rapidly for a few months, and then nearly always spontaneously regress by age 7 to 9.
explanations.b: Benign infantile hemangiomas do not undergo malignant transformation.
explanations.c: Unlike port-wine stains (nevus flammeus), strawberry hemangiomas do not persist; they involute.
explanations.d: These lesions regress early in childhood, long before puberty.
explanations.e: Sturge-Weber syndrome is associated with nevus flammeus in the V1/V2 distribution, not infantile hemangiomas.

ankiCards: The common name for a juvenile hemangioma of infancy is a {{c1::strawberry hemangioma}}.
Juvenile hemangiomas typically {{c1::regress spontaneously}} by age 7.
Histologically, a strawberry hemangioma is a {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma.
Infantile hemangiomas occur in approximately {{c1::1 in 200}} live births.
The growth phase of a strawberry hemangioma occurs during the {{c1::first few months}} of life.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangiomas are the most common vascular tumor of childhood.
They are characterized by a 'strawberry' appearance.
Regression rate is 50% by age 5 and 70-90% by age 7.
They consist of thin-walled capillaries with scant stroma.
Conservative management (observation) is the standard of care unless vital structures are obstructed.
microReview: Infantile Hemangioma: Grows then Goes. Very common, benign, strawberry appearance, spontaneous involution.
examinerTraps: Mistaking a 'strawberry hemangioma' (which regresses) for a 'port-wine stain' (which persists and grows with the child).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease... Vascular Tumors 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 40-year-old patient with Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is found to have multiple vascular lesions in the cerebellum and retina. These lesions are characterized histologically by large, dilated, thin-walled vascular channels separated by a scant connective tissue stroma. What is the most likely diagnosis for these specific lesions?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated vascular spaces. They are frequently found in the CNS and are a component of Von Hippel-Lindau disease.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas consist of small, tightly packed capillaries rather than the large 'cavernous' spaces described.
explanations.c: Arteriovenous malformations involve direct connections between arteries and veins without an intervening capillary bed; they are thicker-walled and more structurally complex.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are small, painful subungual nodules, not associated with VHL.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts.

ankiCards: {{c1::Cavernous hemangiomas}} are characterized by large, blood-filled vascular spaces.
Vascular lesions in the cerebellum and retina of VHL patients are often {{c1::cavernous}} hemangiomas (hemangioblastomas).
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas do not {{c1::spontaneously regress}}.
A common visceral site for cavernous hemangiomas is the {{c1::liver}}.
In the CNS, cavernous hemangiomas can cause symptoms by {{c1::compression}} or {{c2::hemorrhage}}.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are less well-circumscribed than capillary ones.
They involve large, blood-filled spaces separated by connective tissue.
Intravascular thrombosis and dystrophic calcification (phleboliths) may occur.
They are part of the VHL disease spectrum (specifically as hemangioblastomas).
In the liver, they are usually asymptomatic and found incidentally.
microReview: Cavernous Hemangioma: Big vessels, doesn't regress, VHL association (CNS/Retina), common in the liver.
examinerTraps: Linking VHL only to renal cell carcinoma and forgetting the vascular components (hemangioblastomas/cavernous lesions).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease... Vascular Tumors 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following immunohistochemical markers is the most specific and widely used to confirm the endothelial origin of a poorly differentiated malignant tumor suspected to be an angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a highly specific marker for endothelial cells and is used to identify vascular tumors like angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells (carcinomas).
explanations.c: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (rhabdomyosarcoma or leiomyosarcoma).
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells, such as melanocytes or Schwann cells.
explanations.e: Vimentin is a non-specific marker for all mesenchymal cells.

ankiCards: The most specific IHC marker for vascular endothelium is {{c1::CD31}}.
CD31 is also known as {{c1::PECAM-1}}.
Another marker for endothelial cells (though less specific than CD31) is {{c1::von Willebrand factor (Factor VIII-related antigen)}}.
Malignant vascular tumors like angiosarcoma will stain positive for {{c1::CD31}}.
The marker {{c1::CD34}} is also expressed by endothelial cells but is also found in hematopoietic stem cells.
keyPoints: CD31 is an adhesion molecule found on junctions between endothelial cells.
Confirmation of endothelial origin is crucial for diagnosing poorly differentiated angiosarcomas.
Angiosarcomas often mimic carcinomas histologically (epithelioid angiosarcoma).
Factor VIII-related antigen is another endothelial marker but is often less sensitive.
Vimentin positivity only confirms mesenchymal origin, not specific vascular origin.
microReview: Endothelial markers: CD31 (best), CD34, Factor VIII.
examinerTraps: Vimentin is often a distractor; it's positive in almost all sarcomas but isn't specific to vascular tumors.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease... Vascular Tumors 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 26-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with a rapidly growing, 1-cm, red, pedunculated lesion on her gingiva. The lesion bleeds easily with minor trauma. Histology shows a proliferation of capillaries with associated edema and an acute inflammatory infiltrate. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) often occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum). It is a rapidly growing, friable vascular nodule.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis presents similarly but is associated with Bartonella infection in immunocompromised hosts, not pregnancy.
explanations.c: Kaposi sarcoma typically presents as multiple purple patches or plaques, not a single pedunculated gingival mass.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are deeper, non-pedunculated, and don't typically grow rapidly during pregnancy.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are subungual and exquisitely painful, not gingival.

ankiCards: A pyogenic granuloma occurring in a pregnant woman is specifically called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
The characteristic clinical feature of a pyogenic granuloma is that it {{c1::bleeds easily}}.
Histologically, a pyogenic granuloma is a form of {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma.
The typical treatment for a pyogenic granuloma is {{c1::surgical excision}}.
Despite the name 'pyogenic granuloma', the lesion is neither {{c1::pyogenic (pus-forming)}} nor a {{c2::granuloma}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granulomas are misnamed; they are lobular capillary hemangiomas.
They commonly occur on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
Trauma is a frequent inciting factor.
Extensive edema and inflammatory cells are seen histologically.
In pregnancy, many regress spontaneously after delivery.
microReview: Pyogenic Granuloma: Pregnancy/Trauma + Gingiva + Bleeds easily + Capillary proliferation.
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic granuloma' is a historical misnomer; look for 'lobular capillary hemangioma' as a synonym.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease... Vascular Tumors 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following features most reliably distinguishes bacillary angiomatosis from Kaposi sarcoma in a biopsy from an HIV-positive patient?

options.e: Clinical presentation as purple skin plaques

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis is characterized by neutrophilic infiltrates and the presence of Bartonella bacteria (seen on Warthin-Starry stain), whereas Kaposi sarcoma typically has a lymphocytic infiltrate.
explanations.b: Spindle cells are characteristic of Kaposi sarcoma, not bacillary angiomatosis.
explanations.c: HHV-8 is the cause of Kaposi sarcoma; bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella.
explanations.d: Slit-like spaces are hallmark findings in Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.e: Both can present as purple skin lesions, so clinical appearance alone is not reliable for differentiation.

ankiCards: The causative agent of bacillary angiomatosis is the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
In bacillary angiomatosis, the inflammatory infiltrate is predominantly composed of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
To visualize the bacteria in bacillary angiomatosis, a {{c1::Warthin-Starry}} silver stain is used.
Bacillary angiomatosis occurs primarily in {{c1::immunocompromised/HIV}} patients.
The two species of Bartonella responsible for vascular lesions are {{c1::B. henselae}} and {{c2::B. quintana}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign opportunistic infection.
It mimics Kaposi sarcoma clinically (red/purple nodules).
Histology shows 'atypical' but benign-appearing endothelial cells.
The hallmark is the presence of clusters of neutrophils.
It responds well to antibiotic therapy (e.g., erythromycin).
microReview: Bacillary Angiomatosis: Bartonella + Neutrophils + Warthin-Starry positive. Kaposi: HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Slit spaces.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'atypical' endothelial cells in bacillary angiomatosis with the 'malignant' cells of angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease... Vascular Tumors 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old male worker at a chemical manufacturing plant is diagnosed with a rare, aggressive hepatic malignancy. He has had long-term exposure to vinyl chloride during the production of polyvinyl chloride (PVC) plastics. Which of the following is the most likely tumor?

explanations.a: Vinyl chloride exposure is a classic and highly specific risk factor for the development of hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Hepatocellular carcinoma is more commonly associated with HBV, HCV, and cirrhosis, not specifically vinyl chloride.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangioma is a benign lesion and not associated with chemical carcinogens.
explanations.d: Cholangiocarcinoma is associated with Liver Flukes and Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis, not vinyl chloride.
explanations.e: Hepatic adenomas are associated with oral contraceptive use, not industrial chemical exposure.

ankiCards: The three classic environmental triggers for hepatic angiosarcoma are {{c1::vinyl chloride}}, {{c2::arsenic}}, and {{c3::Thorotrast}}.
Angiosarcoma is a malignancy of the {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
Hepatic angiosarcoma has a very {{c1::poor}} prognosis.
Vinyl chloride is an industrial chemical used to make {{c1::PVC (polyvinyl chloride)}}.
Thorotrast, a cause of hepatic angiosarcoma, was formerly used as a {{c1::radiographic contrast agent}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma can occur in the liver, skin, soft tissue, and breast.
Vinyl chloride is the most famous occupational risk factor.
Arsenic (pesticides) is another risk factor.
Latency between exposure and tumor development can be decades.
Tumors are typically multicentric and hemorrhagic.
microReview: Hepatic Angiosarcoma risk factors: Vinyl chloride, Arsenic, Thorotrast.
examinerTraps: Wait to see 'Vinyl Chloride' before jumping to Angiosarcoma; if the patient has cirrhosis, Hepatocellular Carcinoma is more likely.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease... Vascular Tumors 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 50-year-old male presents with a port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) in the distribution of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve. He has a history of seizures and hemiparesis. Imaging reveals ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomas and 'tram-track' calcifications in the cerebral cortex. What is the name of this syndrome?

explanations.a: Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) is characterized by a facial port-wine stain, leptomeningeal angiomas, seizures, and mental retardation.
explanations.b: VHL is associated with hemangioblastomas (cavernous-like) of the cerebellum and retina, and renal cell carcinoma, but not port-wine stains.
explanations.c: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) presents with multiple small telangiectasias and bleeding, not large port-wine stains or leptomeningeal angiomas.
explanations.d: Tuberous sclerosis features ash-leaf spots and angiofibromas, not port-wine stains.
explanations.e: NF1 features café-au-lait spots and neurofibromas.

ankiCards: Sturge-Weber syndrome consists of a facial {{c1::port-wine stain}} and {{c2::leptomeningeal angiomas}}.
The classic radiographic finding in Sturge-Weber syndrome is {{c1::tram-track calcifications}}.
Sturge-Weber is caused by a somatic mutation in the {{c1::GNAQ}} gene.
The facial lesion in Sturge-Weber is usually in the distribution of the {{c1::trigeminal (CN V)}} nerve.
Nevus flammeus is a congenital vascular malformation of {{c1::capillaries}}.
keyPoints: Sturge-Weber syndrome is a phakomatosis (neurocutaneous syndrome).
It is sporadic, not inherited.
Glaucoma is a common ocular complication.
The 'port-wine stain' is a birthmark that does not regress.
Seizures are due to the underlying brain angiomas.
microReview: Sturge-Weber: Port-wine stain (V1/V2) + Leptomeningeal angioma + Tram-track calcifications + Seizures + Glaucoma.
examinerTraps: Ensure the port-wine stain is in the V1/V2 distribution; a simple port-wine stain without neurological symptoms is just a birthmark, not the syndrome.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease... Vascular Tumors 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old female presents with multiple enlarging, violaceous, firm skin nodules on her right arm. Her medical history is significant for a radical mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection 10 years ago for breast adenocarcinoma, followed by chronic, non-pitting lymphedema of the right upper extremity. A biopsy of a skin nodule reveals highly atypical endothelial cells forming irregular vascular channels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8, typically seen in immunocompromised patients, but it does not specifically correlate with long-standing post-surgical lymphedema.
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma occurring in the setting of chronic lymphedema (often post-mastectomy) is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome. It is a highly malignant tumor of endothelial cells.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts caused by Bartonella species, not associated with chronic lymphedema.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign, rapidly growing capillary hemangioma often occurring on the skin or gingiva, typically following minor trauma or during pregnancy.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are small, exquisitely painful benign tumors arising from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, usually found subungually.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema (e.g., post-mastectomy) is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
The malignant cell of origin in angiosarcoma is the {{c1::endothelial cell}}.
Vascular tumors like angiosarcoma are often positive for the immunohistochemical marker {{c1::CD31}}.
Vinyl chloride and arsenic exposure are specific risk factors for angiosarcoma of the {{c1::liver}}.
Angiosarcomas are characterized histologically by {{c1::atypical endothelial cells}} and irregular vascular channels.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignant vascular neoplasm.
Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to angiosarcoma following chronic lymphedema.
Cutaneous angiosarcomas often appear as violaceous nodules or plaques.
Markers include CD31 and von Willebrand factor.
Prognosis for angiosarcoma is generally poor due to early metastasis.
microReview: Angiosarcomas are aggressive malignant tumors of endothelial cells. Classic associations include post-mastectomy lymphedema (Stewart-Treves), radiation exposure, and chemical carcinogens (vinyl chloride for hepatic cases).
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Stewart-Treves (angiosarcoma) with Marjolin ulcer (squamous cell carcinoma in a chronic wound).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 35-year-old male presents with an extremely painful, 5-mm blue-red nodule located under his fingernail. The pain is triggered by cold exposure and pressure. Histological examination shows nests of uniform, rounded cells surrounding thin-walled vascular spaces. These cells are derived from which of the following?

explanations.a: Endothelial cells line the vascular spaces but are not the primary neoplastic cell in glomus tumors.
explanations.b: Pericytes are the cell of origin for hemangiopericytomas, which have a 'staghorn' vascular pattern, not the specific subungual presentation of glomus tumors.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors arise from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts are involved in connective tissue tumors (e.g., fibromas), not primary vascular tumors like the glomus tumor.
explanations.e: Lymphatic endothelium gives rise to lymphangiomas, which are typically painless and cystic.

ankiCards: A painful subungual vascular tumor is most likely a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells of the glomus body.
The classic triad for glomus tumors includes {{c1::paroxysmal pain}}, localized tenderness, and cold sensitivity.
Histologically, glomus tumors show nests of {{c1::uniform rounded cells}} surrounding vascular spaces.
The glomus body's physiological function is {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but exquisitely painful.
Most common location is subungual (under the nail).
Derived from thermoregulatory glomus bodies.
Pain is often disproportionate to the size of the lesion.
Excision is curative.
microReview: Glomus Tumor: Painful, subungual, modified smooth muscle cells. Hemangioma: Benign, endothelial cells. Angiosarcoma: Malignant, endothelial cells.
examinerTraps: The examiner will often emphasize 'cold sensitivity' or 'paroxysmal pain' to lead you toward a glomus tumor.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An HIV-positive patient with a CD4+ count of 150 cells/mm³ presents with multiple reddish-purple macules and plaques on his lower extremities and oral mucosa. Biopsy shows spindle-shaped cells, slit-like vascular spaces containing red blood cells, and prominent inflammatory infiltrates. This condition is most directly caused by which of the following pathogens?

explanations.a: HHV-6 is the cause of roseola infantum, not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV).
explanations.c: EBV is associated with various lymphomas (e.g., Burkitt) and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, but not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.d: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which clinically mimics Kaposi sarcoma but is histologically distinct (neutrophils present, no slit-like spaces).
explanations.e: CMV causes retinitis and colitis in AIDS patients but does not cause vascular tumors.

ankiCards: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
The histology of Kaposi sarcoma features {{c1::spindle-shaped}} cells and slit-like vascular spaces.
The four clinical forms of Kaposi sarcoma are {{c1::Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated}}.
Unlike Kaposi sarcoma, Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by {{c1::Bartonella}} species.
Kaposi sarcoma lesions typically appear as {{c1::violaceous (purple)}} macules, plaques, or nodules.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma is a spindle cell neoplasm of endothelial origin.
Highly associated with HHV-8 infection.
AIDS-associated (Epidemic) KS is the most common HIV-related malignancy.
Histology: slit-like spaces, extravasated RBCs, and spindle cells.
Lesions do not blanch under pressure.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Slit-like spaces + AIDS/Immunosuppression. Bacillary Angiomatosis = Bartonella + Neutrophils + Warthin-Starry stain.
examinerTraps: Distinguishing Kaposi sarcoma from Bacillary Angiomatosis is a high-yield 'favorite'—look for the presence of neutrophils and Bartonella (BA) versus spindle cells and HHV-8 (KS).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old female in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with a rapidly growing, painless, 1-cm red, friable nodule on her gingiva. The lesion bleeds easily with minor trauma. Histology shows a highly vascular proliferation resembling granulation tissue with an overlying thinned epidermis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated vascular channels and are usually deeper and not friable/pedunculated.
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor with significant cellular atypia; it is not typically associated with pregnancy-related gingival growth.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) often occurs in the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum) and is characterized by granulation tissue-like histology.
explanations.d: While pyogenic granuloma is a form of capillary hemangioma, 'pyogenic granuloma' is the specific clinical name for this rapidly growing, friable, often pedunculated lesion.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is associated with Bartonella infection in immunocompromised hosts, not healthy pregnant women.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma occurring in the gingiva of a pregnant woman is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum (epulis gravidarum)}}.
The histological appearance of pyogenic granuloma resembles {{c1::granulation tissue}}.
