options.b: It provides a source for systemic thromboembolism
options.c: It is pathognomonic for an underlying fungal infection
options.d: It prevents the diffusion of nutrients to the adventitia
options.e: It represents the primary site of TGF-beta production

explanations.a: Thrombus does not provide structural integrity; the vessel wall is still weakened and at risk of rupture.
explanations.b: Stasis and turbulent flow within the aneurysm lead to the formation of mural thrombi. These can embolize to distal sites (e.g., 'blue toe syndrome' in the lower extremities).
explanations.c: Laminated thrombi (Lines of Zahn) are standard features of any slow-forming thrombus in a high-flow area; they are not specific to infection.
explanations.d: The thrombus is on the luminal side; nutrients reach the adventitia via the vasa vasorum. While thrombus might slightly affect oxygen diffusion to the intima, that is not its primary clinical significance.
explanations.e: Thrombi are made of fibrin and platelets, not a primary source of TGF-beta (which is more associated with smooth muscle cells and macrophages in the wall).

ankiCards: Stasis and turbulence in an aneurysm promote the formation of {{c1::mural thrombus}}.
Embolization of a thrombus from an AAA can lead to {{c1::ischemia}} in the lower limbs.
{{c1::Lines of Zahn}} are the visible laminations in a mural thrombus.
Mural thrombi in aneurysms can partially {{c1::occlude}} the branching vessels.
The clinical significance of mural thrombus is primarily its potential for {{c1::embolization}}.
keyPoints: Aneurysms lead to abnormal blood flow (stasis/turbulence).
Mural thrombi are common in both AAA and TAA.
Distal embolization is a major complication (e.g., renal or lower limb infarcts).
Thrombus can obscure the actual size of the lumen on imaging.
The presence of thrombus does not prevent rupture of the underlying wall.
microReview: Aneurysm -> Turbulence/Stasis -> Mural Thrombus -> Embolism.
examinerTraps: A mural thrombus *narrows* the functional lumen, but the *actual* vessel wall is still dilated.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old woman with chronic hypertension presents with a sudden, 'thunderclap' headache, the worst of her life. A CT scan shows blood in the subarachnoid space. Which of the following is the most likely site of the underlying vascular lesion?

explanations.a: Aneurysms here present with chest/back pain, not a thunderclap headache.
explanations.b: The presentation (worst headache of life, subarachnoid hemorrhage) is classic for a ruptured 'berry' (saccular) aneurysm. These are most common in the Circle of Willis, with the anterior communicating artery being the most frequent site.
explanations.c: AAA presents with abdominal/back pain or shock, not subarachnoid hemorrhage.
explanations.d: Temporal arteritis affects this vessel, but it causes localized headache and visual loss, not subarachnoid hemorrhage.
explanations.e: Atherosclerotic plaques are common here, but rupture usually causes an ischemic stroke, not a subarachnoid hemorrhage.

ankiCards: Saccular aneurysms in the Circle of Willis are commonly called {{c1::berry}} aneurysms.
The most common site for a berry aneurysm is the {{c1::anterior}} communicating artery.
Rupture of a berry aneurysm causes {{c1::subarachnoid}} hemorrhage.
Berry aneurysms are associated with {{c1::Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD)}}.
Risk factors for berry aneurysm rupture include {{c1::hypertension}} and smoking.
keyPoints: Berry aneurysms are small, saccular dilations in the cerebral circulation.
They occur at branch points in the Circle of Willis.
They are caused by a congenital lack of media (muscle) at the bifurcation.
They are not present at birth but develop over time due to hemodynamic stress.
Presentation: 'Worst headache of my life' (Subarachnoid Hemorrhage).
microReview: Berry Aneurysm = Circle of Willis = Subarachnoid Hemorrhage = ADPKD connection.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse the 'congenital' nature: the *defect* is congenital, but the *aneurysm* develops later in life.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following pathogens is most strongly associated with the development of the primary vascular malignancy characterized by purplish-red skin plaques in immunocompromised patients?

explanations.a: HHV-8 is the causative agent of Kaposi sarcoma, a vascular neoplasm common in AIDS patients that manifests as red-purple skin lesions.
explanations.b: HHV-6 is associated with Roseola infantum, not vascular malignancies.
explanations.c: HPV-16 is strongly associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx.
explanations.d: CMV can cause retinitis and esophagitis in immunocompromised patients but is not the driver of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.e: EBV is associated with various lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, but not primary vascular tumors like Kaposi sarcoma.

ankiCards: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by infection with {{c1::HHV-8}}.
The most common vascular malignancy seen in AIDS patients is {{c1::Kaposi sarcoma}}.
Histologically, Kaposi sarcoma shows {{c1::spindle cells}} and slit-like vascular spaces.
HHV-8 infection of {{c1::endothelial cells}} leads to the development of Kaposi sarcoma.
In classic Kaposi sarcoma, lesions are typically found on the {{c1::lower extremities}}.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
Associated strongly with HHV-8 (KSHV).
Commonly presents in four forms: Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
Gross appearance includes patches, plaques, and nodules.
Characterized by spindle cells and extravasated red blood cells.
microReview: Kaposi sarcoma is the signature malignancy of AIDS, driven by HHV-8. It exists on a spectrum from benign-appearing patches to aggressive nodules.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8) with Bacillary angiomatosis (Bartonella), as both present with similar red-purple skin lesions in HIV patients.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following is an immunohistochemical marker specifically used to identify the endothelial origin of a suspected vascular tumor?

explanations.a: CD31 (cluster of differentiation 31), also known as PECAM-1, is a standard marker for endothelial cells and tumors derived from them.
explanations.b: CD20 is a marker for B-lymphocytes, not vascular endothelium.
explanations.c: Desmin is an intermediate filament marker for muscle cells (smooth and skeletal).
explanations.d: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells and carcinomas.
explanations.e: S-100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells, such as melanocytes and Schwann cells.

ankiCards: A specific immunohistochemical marker for vascular endothelial cells is {{c1::CD31 (or von Willebrand factor)}}.
Angiosarcomas will typically stain positive for the marker {{c1::CD31}}.
The marker {{c1::CD31}} helps differentiate vascular tumors from other spindle cell neoplasms.
{{c1::vWF (Factor VIII-related antigen)}} is another marker for endothelial differentiation.
The marker used to identify the pericytes in a glomus tumor is usually {{c1::alpha-smooth muscle actin}}.
keyPoints: CD31 is the most specific marker for endothelial differentiation.
vWF is also used but can be less sensitive in poorly differentiated tumors.
Vascular tumors include hemangiomas, lymphangiomas, and angiosarcomas.
Malignant vascular tumors (angiosarcoma) often show marked cytologic atypia.
Identifying endothelial markers is crucial for diagnosing poorly differentiated angiosarcomas.
microReview: CD31 is the gold standard IHC marker for vascular/endothelial tumors, differentiating them from epithelial or neural tumors.
examinerTraps: S-100 is often a distractor because it stains many different things, but it is not a marker for blood vessel endothelium.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old male former plastics factory worker presents with a 4-month history of weight loss, jaundice, and dull right upper quadrant pain. Imaging reveals multiple ill-defined, hemorrhagic masses within the liver parenchyma. A biopsy shows malignant spindle cells lining irregular, anastomosing vascular channels. Exposure to which of the following substances most likely contributed to this condition?

explanations.a: Vinyl chloride exposure is a well-known risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma, a rare and aggressive vascular malignancy.
explanations.b: Asbestos exposure is associated with mesothelioma and lung carcinoma, not hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Benzene is associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.d: Aflatoxin B1 is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), not angiosarcoma.
explanations.e: Naphthylamine is associated with transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
The histological feature of {{c1::anastomosing vascular channels}} lined by atypical cells is characteristic of angiosarcoma.
Vinyl chloride is used in the manufacturing of {{c1::polyvinyl chloride (PVC)}} plastics.
Angiosarcomas are most commonly found in the {{c1::skin}}, but can occur in the liver, breast, and soft tissues.
The prognosis for hepatic angiosarcoma is generally {{c1::poor/grave}}.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare, highly malignant tumor.
Classic associations: Vinyl chloride, Arsenic, Thorotrast (radiocontrast).
Tumor cells are of endothelial origin.
Often presents at an advanced stage with liver failure or hemorrhage.
Grossly appears as multifocal, hemorrhagic nodules.
microReview: Hepatic angiosarcoma = Vinyl Chloride/Arsenic/Thorotrast. High-grade endothelial malignancy with poor prognosis.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse hepatic angiosarcoma with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC); HCC is associated with Aflatoxin and Hepatitis, whereas angiosarcoma is associated with chemical/industrial exposures.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the most likely natural progression of a 'strawberry hemangioma' (juvenile hemangioma) diagnosed in a 2-month-old infant?

options.d: Systemic spread to the liver and lungs

explanations.a: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are common in newborns; they grow rapidly for a few months but typically regress spontaneously by age 7 to 9.
explanations.b: Hemangiomas are benign and do not typically progress to angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Proportional growth and lifelong persistence are more characteristic of port-wine stains (vascular malformations).
explanations.d: Benign juvenile hemangiomas do not metastasize.
explanations.e: While very large hemangiomas can theoretically cause high-output heart failure, it is not the 'most likely' natural history for a standard strawberry hemangioma.

ankiCards: The most common vascular tumor of infancy is the {{c1::juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma}}.
Strawberry hemangiomas typically {{c1::regress}} spontaneously by age 7.
Histologically, strawberry hemangiomas are composed of {{c1::thin-walled capillaries}} lined by endothelial cells.
Strawberry hemangiomas appear at birth or shortly after and grow {{c1::rapidly}}.
Complete involution of juvenile hemangiomas occurs in {{c1::75-90}}% of cases by age 7.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangiomas are extremely common in infancy (1 in 200 births).
They are bright red, lobulated, and elevated.
Phases: Rapid growth phase, plateau phase, and slow involution phase.
Histology shows packed capillaries with inconspicuous lumens.
Treatment is usually observation due to high regression rates.
microReview: Strawberry hemangioma: Newborn, grows fast, turns bright red, disappears by second grade (age 7).
examinerTraps: Confusion with Port-wine stains (Nevus flammeus), which do NOT regress and grow with the child.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old woman in her 28th week of pregnancy presents with a 1.5-cm, rapidly growing, pedunculated red nodule on her gingiva. The lesion is friable and bleeds significantly when she brushes her teeth. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma (granuloma pyogenicum) is a common, rapidly growing benign vascular lesion often found on the gingiva of pregnant women (pregnancy tumor).
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are deeper, less likely to be pedunculated/friable, and involve larger vascular spaces.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are typically found under fingernails and are extremely painful; they do not have a pregnancy association.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella and typically occurs in immunocompromised (HIV) patients.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is an aggressive malignancy that would not typically present as a focal pedunculated gingival nodule in pregnancy.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma occurring in the gingiva of a pregnant woman is often called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
The clinical appearance of pyogenic granuloma is a {{c1::pedunculated}}, red, friable nodule.
Histologically, pyogenic granuloma resembles {{c1::granulation tissue}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are associated with {{c1::trauma}} or pregnancy.
True/False: Pyogenic granulomas are neither pyogenic nor true granulomas. {{c1::True}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is a capillary hemangioma.
Common locations: Skin, gingiva, and oral mucosa.
Often follows minor trauma.
Can regress spontaneously, especially after pregnancy (granuloma gravidarum).
Surgical excision is the standard treatment if it does not regress.
microReview: Pyogenic granuloma: Red, 'bleeds like crazy', pregnancy/trauma, gingiva, looks like granulation tissue.
examinerTraps: The name 'Pyogenic granuloma' suggests infection (pyogenic) or inflammation (granuloma), but it is actually a vascular proliferation.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 40-year-old female presents with an intensely painful, 0.5-cm blue-red nodule located under the nail bed of her right index finger. Histological examination reveals nests of uniform, rounded cells surrounding small vascular spaces. These cells are most likely derived from which of the following?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors are derived from the specialized smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, which are involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.b: While the tumor contains vascular spaces, the characteristic tumor cells are perivascular glomus cells, not the lining endothelium.
explanations.c: Fibroblasts are not the cell of origin for glomus tumors.
explanations.d: Although the tumor is painful, it is not derived from nerve cells.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are related to the blood-carrying glomus bodies, not lymphatic vessels.

ankiCards: A glomus tumor is a very painful tumor located under the {{c1::fingernail (subungual)}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle cells}} of the glomus body.
The glomus body is specialized for {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Histologically, glomus cells are {{c1::round/uniform}} and surround vascular spaces.
The primary clinical symptom of a glomus tumor is {{c1::intense pain}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign.
Classic location: Subungual (under the nail).
Small, but extremely sensitive to touch and temperature.
Derived from perivascular glomus bodies.
Cured by simple excision.
microReview: Glomus tumor: Under the nail, super painful, smooth muscle origin (glomus body).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse with a subungual melanoma (which is usually dark/pigmented and not necessarily as painful) or a simple splinter.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following conditions is characterized by a benign vascular proliferation that is histologically indistinguishable from granulation tissue and often occurs after minor trauma?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma is a form of capillary hemangioma that histologically looks exactly like exuberant granulation tissue.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis also shows vascular proliferation but typically features neutrophilic infiltrates and clusters of bacteria (Bartonella).
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, blood-filled spaces, unlike the small capillaries of granulation tissue.
explanations.d: Kaposi sarcoma features spindle cells and slit-like spaces, distinct from granulation tissue.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma features high-grade cytologic atypia and complex growth patterns, unlike benign granulation-like tissue.

ankiCards: {{c1::Pyogenic granuloma}} is the vascular lesion that histologically resembles granulation tissue.
Pyogenic granulomas are often found on the {{c1::skin}} or {{c2::gingiva}}.
Trauma is a frequent inciting factor for the development of {{c1::pyogenic granuloma}}.
A pedunculated red lesion that bleeds easily after minor trauma is most likely a {{c1::pyogenic granuloma}}.
Treatment for pyogenic granuloma usually involves {{c1::excision/curettage}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granulomas are reactive, benign vascular lesions.
Histology: Proliferation of capillaries with edema and inflammation.
Common on the fingers, face, and mouth.
Often present as rapidly growing 'meat-like' nodules.
Named 'pyogenic' because they were once thought to be caused by infection.
microReview: Pyogenic granuloma = Granulation tissue look-alike. Pedunculated, bleeds easily, trauma-related.
examinerTraps: Wait for the histology: if it looks like granulation tissue but is a distinct nodule, think Pyogenic Granuloma.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 10-year-old girl with a history of Turner syndrome (45,X) presents for a routine checkup. She has a large, soft, ill-defined mass in the left supraclavicular region that has been present since birth. Transillumination of the mass is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) is a benign lymphatic malformation commonly associated with Turner syndrome and Down syndrome, typically found in the neck or axilla.
explanations.b: Strawberry hemangiomas are blood vessel tumors and do not typically transilluminate as well as cystic lymphangiomas.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are small, painful subungual lesions.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor of adults and would not be present since birth in a child.
explanations.e: Cavernous hemangiomas involve blood vessels and are usually deeper and more solid/less transilluminable than cystic hygromas.

ankiCards: Cystic hygroma is also known as a {{c1::cavernous lymphangioma}}.
Cystic hygromas are frequently associated with {{c1::Turner syndrome}}.
The most common location for a cystic hygroma is the {{c1::neck (or axilla)}}.
Histologically, cystic hygromas consist of large {{c1::lymphatic}} spaces lined by endothelium.
A neonatal neck mass that transilluminates is highly suggestive of {{c1::cystic hygroma}}.
keyPoints: Cystic hygromas are benign but can be large and difficult to resect.
They represent malformations of the lymphatic system.
Characterized by dilated lymphatic spaces separated by connective tissue stroma.
Association with chromosomal abnormalities (Turner, Trisomies 13, 18, 21).
Transillumination is a key clinical finding.
microReview: Cystic hygroma: Turner syndrome, neck mass, lymphatics, transilluminates.
examinerTraps: Ensure you distinguish between lymphangiomas (lymph) and hemangiomas (blood). Turner syndrome is the classic 'clue' for cystic hygroma.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular tumors is classified as 'intermediate-grade' (borderline), meaning it is more aggressive than a hemangioma but less malignant than an angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is defined as an intermediate-grade vascular neoplasm. It has the potential for local aggression and dissemination but is not as rapidly fatal as angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangioma is a strictly benign tumor.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignant tumor.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign capillary hemangioma.
explanations.e: Glomus tumor is a benign neoplasm.

ankiCards: Kaposi sarcoma is categorized as an {{c1::intermediate-grade (or borderline)}} vascular tumor.
The four clinical subtypes of Kaposi sarcoma are {{c1::Classic, African, Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated}}.
Intermediate-grade vascular tumors like Kaposi sarcoma show more {{c1::cellularity}} than benign hemangiomas.
{{c1::Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma}} is another example of an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
Unlike hemangiomas, intermediate tumors are often {{c1::locally invasive}}.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors are divided into Benign, Intermediate, and Malignant.
Intermediate tumors include Kaposi Sarcoma and Hemangioendothelioma.
Intermediate tumors rarely metastasize but are locally destructive.
Kaposi sarcoma involves HHV-8 in all its variants.
The 'patch' stage of KS can look very similar to a benign hemangioma.
microReview: Classification: Benign (Hemangioma), Intermediate (Kaposi, Hemangioendothelioma), Malignant (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: Don't classify Kaposi Sarcoma as 'benign' because it's slow-growing; it is 'intermediate' because of its neoplastic nature and potential to involve viscera.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with several firm, dark-purple skin nodules on her left forearm. Her medical history is significant for a radical mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection 12 years ago for breast cancer. Since the surgery, she has had persistent, severe lymphedema of the left arm. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: This is a classic case of Stewart-Treves syndrome, where angiosarcoma develops in the setting of chronic lymphedema (usually post-mastectomy).
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is HHV-8 related and not typically associated with chronic lymphedema from surgery.
explanations.c: Lymphangiomas are usually congenital and benign, not developing as nodules in an elderly woman.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts.
explanations.e: Cherry hemangiomas are small, bright red, benign papules common in the elderly but are not associated with lymphedema or malignancy.

ankiCards: The development of angiosarcoma in a limb with chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
Stewart-Treves syndrome most commonly occurs after {{c1::radical mastectomy}}.
Angiosarcomas associated with radiation therapy are often found in the {{c1::breast}}.
Histology of angiosarcoma shows {{c1::pleomorphic}} endothelial cells and irregular vascular channels.
Angiosarcomas have a very {{c1::poor}} 5-year survival rate (approx 30%).
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant endothelial tumor.
Risk factors: Chronic lymphedema, radiation, and certain chemicals (vinyl chloride).
Can occur anywhere but prefers skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Clinically begins as small, sharply demarcated red papules that become large, fleshy masses.
Metastasizes early and widely.
microReview: Stewart-Treves syndrome: Post-mastectomy + chronic lymphedema + purple nodules = Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: The examiner may describe it as 'skin nodules' to make you think of something less serious, but the history of chronic lymphedema is the 'pathognomonic' clue for angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 65-year-old male with a 40-pack-year smoking history undergoes a routine screening ultrasound which reveals a 4.2-cm focal dilation of the infrarenal aorta. The structural integrity of the vessel wall is compromised primarily due to the degradation of the extracellular matrix. Which of the following biochemical changes is most characteristic of this condition's pathogenesis?

options.b: Decreased production of transforming growth factor-beta
options.c: Excessive cross-linking of collagen type III

explanations.a: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), derived from macrophages and smooth muscle cells, degrade elastin and collagen, which is a hallmark of abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) development.
explanations.b: TGF-beta signaling is often abnormally increased in certain genetic syndromes leading to aneurysms (like Loeys-Dietz), rather than decreased in common atherosclerotic AAAs.
explanations.c: Aneurysms are characterized by a loss of collagen and elastin, not excessive cross-linking, which would typically stiffen the wall.
explanations.d: The tunica media undergoes thinning and atrophy in AAAs, not adventitial hypertrophy.
explanations.e: Lysyl oxidase is required for cross-linking; its inhibition (e.g., by lathyrism) causes aneurysms, whereas its upregulation would theoretically strengthen the wall.

ankiCards: The primary biochemical cause of wall weakening in AAA is the {{c1::increased}} activity of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs).
In the pathogenesis of AAA, macrophages in the aortic wall release {{c1::MMP-2 and MMP-9}} which degrade elastin.
{{c1::Atherosclerosis}} is the most common predisposing factor for abdominal aortic aneurysms.
Aneurysms represent a failure of {{c1::vascular wall homeostasis}} where degradation exceeds synthesis.
The thinning of the tunica {{c1::media}} is a key histological finding in most arterial aneurysms.
keyPoints: Aneurysms result from an imbalance in extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis and degradation.
Increased MMP activity (especially MMP-2 and MMP-9) is critical for ECM breakdown.
Atherosclerosis causes intimal thickening, which limits oxygen diffusion to the media.
Ischemia of the media leads to smooth muscle cell loss and wall weakening.
Chronic inflammation in the vessel wall contributes to the proteolytic environment.
microReview: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms (AAA) are typically caused by atherosclerosis and occur most frequently in male smokers over age 65. Pathogenesis involves chronic inflammation, thinning of the media, and degradation of elastin and collagen by MMPs.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse AAA (caused by atherosclerosis) with Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (TAA), which are more commonly associated with hypertension or Marfan syndrome.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset, severe, tearing back pain. He has a history of poorly controlled hypertension. On examination, he is diaphoretic with a blood pressure of 190/110 mmHg. A CT angiogram reveals a longitudinal tear in the aortic intima with blood entering the media. If this condition were to progress to involve the pericardial space, which of the following is the most likely immediate complication?

explanations.a: Rupture of an aortic dissection into the pericardial sac leads to hemopericardium and cardiac tamponade, which is the leading cause of death in these patients.
explanations.b: While dissection can involve coronary arteries (causing MI), rupture into the pericardium specifically causes tamponade.
explanations.c: Constrictive pericarditis is a chronic scarring process, not an acute result of hemorrhage.
explanations.d: Aortic dissections cause aortic regurgitation (by affecting the aortic root), not tricuspid regurgitation.
explanations.e: Ventricular septal rupture is a complication of myocardial infarction, not aortic dissection.

ankiCards: The most common cause of death from an ascending aortic dissection is {{c1::cardiac tamponade}}.
Aortic dissection involves blood tracking through the {{c1::tunica media}}.
The major risk factor for aortic dissection in older adults is {{c1::hypertension}}.
Aortic dissection is classified as {{c1::Stanford Type A}} if it involves the ascending aorta.
The classic clinical presentation of aortic dissection is {{c1::sudden, tearing chest or back pain}}.
keyPoints: Aortic dissection is not a true aneurysm but a tear in the intima.
Hypertension is the most significant risk factor for dissection.
Type A dissections (ascending aorta) are surgical emergencies.
Rupture into the pericardium causes fatal cardiac tamponade.
Cystic medial degeneration is the underlying histological change.
microReview: Aortic dissection occurs when blood separates the laminar planes of the media to form a blood-filled channel. It is distinguished from aneurysms, though it can occur within a pre-existing aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Aortic dissection is often misdiagnosed as an acute MI; however, the 'tearing' quality of pain and asymmetrical pulses should point toward dissection.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old woman is evaluated for a family history of sudden cardiac death. Physical examination shows long tapering fingers, pectus excavatum, and ectopia lentis. Genetic testing confirms a mutation in the FBN1 gene. Which of the following histopathologic features is most likely present in her proximal aorta?

options.d: Endarteritis obliterans of the vasa vasorum

explanations.a: Cystic medial degeneration, characterized by the loss of smooth muscle cells and fragmentation of elastic fibers with accumulation of proteoglycans, is classic for Marfan syndrome (FBN1 mutation).
explanations.b: Granulomatous inflammation is seen in Large Vessel Vasculitis (e.g., Takayasu or Giant Cell Arteritis).
explanations.c: Fibrinoid necrosis is typical of malignant hypertension or polyarteritis nodosa.
explanations.d: Endarteritis obliterans of the vasa vasorum is the hallmark of syphilitic (tertiary) aortitis.
explanations.e: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is a feature of small vessel disease in diabetes or benign hypertension.

ankiCards: Marfan syndrome is caused by a mutation in the {{c1::FBN1 (Fibrillin-1)}} gene.
The characteristic histological finding in Marfan-associated aneurysms is {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
Cystic medial degeneration involves the fragmentation of {{c1::elastic fibers}}.
Fibrillin-1 mutations lead to excessive signaling of {{c1::TGF-beta}}.
Patients with Marfan syndrome are at high risk for {{c1::thoracic}} aortic aneurysms.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder affecting connective tissue.
Fibrillin-1 is essential for scaffold formation for elastic fibers.
Defective fibrillin leads to dysregulated TGF-beta signaling.
Cystic medial degeneration weakens the aortic wall.
Aortic root dilation is the most common cardiovascular manifestation.
microReview: Fibrillin-1 mutations (Marfan) cause cystic medial necrosis/degeneration. This predisposes to thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections, primarily affecting the ascending aorta.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse the 'cystic' appearance with true cysts; it represents disorganized ECM and proteoglycan-filled spaces.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following descriptions best distinguishes a 'false' aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) from a 'true' aneurysm?

options.a: The wall is composed of organized thrombus and connective tissue rather than arterial layers
options.b: It involves only the intimal and medial layers of the arterial wall
options.c: It is caused by atherosclerosis rather than congenital defects
options.d: The dilation is symmetrical and involves the entire circumference of the vessel
options.e: It occurs only in the venous system rather than the arterial system

explanations.a: A false aneurysm is a pulsating hematoma whose 'wall' is formed by extravascular connective tissue or organized blood clot, not the vessel wall layers.
explanations.b: Involvement of only certain layers describes a dissection (separation of layers), whereas a true aneurysm involves all three layers.
explanations.c: Both true and false aneurysms can be caused by various factors; etiology does not define the structural classification.
explanations.d: Symmetrical involvement describes a 'fusiform' aneurysm, which is a subtype of a true aneurysm.
explanations.e: Pseudoaneurysms occur frequently in the arterial system, often following trauma or catheterization.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the arterial wall (intima, media, adventitia).
A {{c1::false (pseudoaneurysm)}} aneurysm is a wall defect leading to an extravascular hematoma communicating with the lumen.
{{c1::Fusiform}} aneurysms are circumferential and symmetrical dilations.
{{c1::Saccular}} aneurysms are spherical outpouchings involving only a portion of the vessel wall.
A pulsating hematoma after a femoral artery puncture is most likely a {{c1::pseudoaneurysm}}.
keyPoints: True aneurysms involve the intact but attenuated vessel wall (3 layers).
False aneurysms are extravascular hematomas that communicate with the intravascular space.
Saccular aneurysms are 'bubble-like' and often contain thrombus.
Fusiform aneurysms are long, tapered, and involve the whole circumference.
Trauma and infection are common causes of pseudoaneurysms.
microReview: True aneurysms (e.g., atherosclerotic AAA, syphilitic) involve all wall layers. False aneurysms (pseudoaneurysms) are hematomas contained by adventitia or perivascular tissue.
examinerTraps: Wait for the keyword 'all three layers' for true aneurysms versus 'extravascular' or 'hematoma' for pseudoaneurysms.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 54-year-old male presents with difficulty swallowing and a persistent cough. A chest X-ray shows a large mass in the superior mediastinum, and a CT scan confirms a dilated aortic arch. Serological testing is positive for Treponema pallidum. What is the primary mechanism of aneurysm formation in this patient?

options.a: Ischemia of the outer media due to obliterative endarteritis
options.b: Direct invasion of the endothelial cells by spirochetes
options.c: Autoimmune destruction of the internal elastic lamina
options.d: Degradation of the adventitia by fungal proteases

explanations.a: Tertiary syphilis causes endarteritis obliterans of the vasa vasorum, which leads to ischemic injury of the aortic media and subsequent weakening (aneurysm).
explanations.b: The damage is mediated by ischemia from vasa vasorum involvement, not direct endothelial destruction by the spirochetes themselves.
explanations.c: Autoimmune destruction is seen in vasculitides, not syphilis.
explanations.d: Fungal involvement describes a 'mycotic' aneurysm, which is unrelated to syphilis.
explanations.e: Atherosclerosis usually affects the abdominal aorta; syphilitic aneurysms classically involve the thoracic aorta.

ankiCards: Syphilitic aneurysms typically involve the {{c1::thoracic}} aorta.
The fundamental lesion in syphilitic aortitis is {{c1::endarteritis obliterans}} of the vasa vasorum.
Ischemia of the {{c1::tunica media}} in syphilis leads to 'tree-barking' of the aortic intima.
Syphilitic aneurysms can cause dilation of the aortic root, leading to {{c1::aortic valve insufficiency}}.
The 'tree-bark' appearance in the aorta is caused by {{c1::contraction of fibrous scars}}.
keyPoints: Tertiary syphilis (cardiovascular syphilis) targets the vasa vasorum.
Narrowing of vasa vasorum leads to medial necrosis and loss of elastic tissue.
The resulting dilation often involves the aortic root and arch.
Aortic insufficiency and respiratory distress (due to compression) are common complications.
Grossly, the intima shows a wrinkled 'tree-bark' appearance.
microReview: Syphilitic (Luetic) Aneurysm: Tertiary syphilis → Endarteritis obliterans of vasa vasorum → Medial ischemia → Weakened wall → Thoracic Aneurysm + Aortic Regurgitation.
examinerTraps: Syphilis = Thoracic Aorta; Atherosclerosis = Abdominal Aorta. This is a classic distinction.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Inflammatory abdominal aortic aneurysms (IAAA) represent a distinct clinical entity. Which of the following features most specifically distinguishes an IAAA from a typical atherosclerotic AAA?

options.a: Dense periaortic fibrosis with abundant IgG4-producing plasma cells
options.c: Location in the ascending thoracic aorta
options.d: Lack of association with cigarette smoking

explanations.a: Inflammatory AAAs are characterized by dense periaortic fibrosis and a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, often as part of IgG4-related disease.
explanations.b: IAAA, like typical AAAs, frequently contain mural thrombus.
explanations.c: IAAA occurs in the abdominal aorta, just like typical AAAs.
explanations.d: The inflammatory subtype still occurs mostly in older males and is often associated with smoking.
explanations.e: They do not respond to antibiotics; they are inflammatory/autoimmune in nature, not primarily infectious.

ankiCards: Inflammatory AAA (IAAA) is characterized by {{c1::dense periaortic fibrosis}}.
A subset of inflammatory AAAs are considered manifestations of {{c1::IgG4}}-related disease.
The inflammatory infiltrate in IAAA typically contains many {{c1::plasma cells}}.
IAAA usually occurs in the {{c1::abdominal}} aorta.
Clinical presentation of IAAA often includes {{c1::back pain}} and elevated inflammatory markers (ESR).
keyPoints: IAAA is a variant of AAA occurring in younger patients frequently.
It features intense inflammation and fibrosis in the adventitia and periaortic tissues.
Symptoms often include back pain and constitutional signs.
It must be differentiated from 'mycotic' (infectious) aneurysms.
IgG4-related disease is a recognized cause of the inflammatory subtype.
microReview: IAAA = Abdominal location + Dense fibrosis + Plasma cells (IgG4+). Distinguish from atherosclerotic AAA (less inflammation) and Mycotic (infectious).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'Inflammatory' with 'Infectious' (Mycotic). Inflammatory is sterile/autoimmune.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Atherosclerosis predisposes to the formation of abdominal aortic aneurysms primarily by which of the following mechanisms?

options.a: Increasing the diffusion distance for oxygen to reach the media
options.b: Directly degrading the adventitia via cholesterol crystals
options.c: Causing systemic hypertension through renal artery stenosis
options.d: Inducing a type IV hypersensitivity reaction against elastin
options.e: Promoting the calcification of the internal elastic lamina

explanations.a: Atherosclerotic plaques in the intima increase the thickness through which oxygen must diffuse to reach the media, leading to medial ischemia and atrophy.
explanations.b: Atherosclerosis is an intimal disease; it doesn't directly 'degrade' adventitia with crystals.
explanations.c: While hypertension is a risk factor, the direct localized mechanism of aneurysm formation in atherosclerosis is medial ischemia.
explanations.d: The inflammation is primarily a chronic innate and Th1-mediated response, not specifically a type IV hypersensitivity against elastin.
explanations.e: Calcification occurs but is a consequence of the disease, not the primary mechanism of wall weakening.

ankiCards: Atherosclerosis causes AAA by inducing {{c1::ischemia}} of the inner media.
The media of the aorta normally receives nutrients via {{c1::diffusion}} from the lumen and the vasa vasorum.
Medial ischemia in AAA leads to the loss of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}}.
The most common location for an atherosclerotic aneurysm is the {{c1::abdominal aorta (infrarenal)}}.
Atherosclerotic plaques increase the {{c1::diffusion distance}} for oxygen to reach the tunica media.
keyPoints: The aorta's media is relatively avascular and relies on diffusion.
Thick intimal plaques block nutrient/oxygen flow from the lumen.
Ischemic media undergoes thinning and fibrosis.
Loss of smooth muscle cells results in loss of structural support.
This is the 'two-step' process: Atherosclerosis → Medial Atrophy → Aneurysm.
microReview: Atherosclerosis → Intimal thickening → Oxygen diffusion barrier → Medial ischemia → Smooth muscle cell death → Loss of ECM synthesis → Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Atherosclerosis is the *risk factor*, but the *mechanism* is medial ischemia/atrophy.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes a 'mycotic' aneurysm?

options.a: An aneurysm resulting from the seeding of an arterial wall by an iron-deficiency state
options.b: A fungal infection of the tunica adventitia following primary skin trauma
options.c: An infection of a major artery that weakens the wall, leading to dilation
options.d: A congenital aneurysm involving the small vessels of the lungs
options.e: An aneurysm caused by the accumulation of mucopolysaccharides in the media

explanations.a: Iron deficiency has no relation to mycotic aneurysms.
explanations.b: Despite the name 'mycotic', most are bacterial (e.g., Salmonella, Staph), and seeding is usually hematogenous from endocarditis.
explanations.c: A mycotic aneurysm is any aneurysm caused by infection (bacterial, fungal, etc.) that weakens the vessel wall.
explanations.d: They are not congenital and can occur in any major artery, most commonly the aorta or cerebral vessels.
explanations.e: Accumulation of mucopolysaccharides refers to cystic medial degeneration.

ankiCards: A {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm is an aneurysm caused by an infection of the vessel wall.
Common causes of mycotic aneurysms include seeding from {{c1::infective endocarditis}}.
The most common site for a mycotic aneurysm is the {{c1::aorta}} or cerebral arteries.
Despite the name, most mycotic aneurysms are caused by {{c1::bacteria}}.
A mycotic aneurysm can lead to rapid wall destruction and {{c1::rupture/hemorrhage}}.
keyPoints: The term 'mycotic' was coined by Osler but refers to all infectious aneurysms.
Mechanism: Hematogenous seeding or direct extension of infection.
Suppurative inflammation destroys the media.
Salmonella and Staphylococcus are frequent bacterial culprits.
These are highly unstable and prone to rupture.
microReview: Mycotic Aneurysm = Infected Aneurysm. Source: Endocarditis or septicemia. Result: Wall destruction by pus/inflammation → Dilation.
examinerTraps: The term 'mycotic' often tricks students into thinking it's *only* fungal. It's any infection (usually bacterial).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 40-year-old male presents with sudden, excruciating headache ('worst of my life'). He has a history of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). Imaging reveals a subarachnoid hemorrhage. This patient's condition is most likely caused by a lesion in which of the following locations?

explanations.a: Berry aneurysms occur in the Circle of Willis and are strongly associated with ADPKD. Their rupture causes subarachnoid hemorrhage.
explanations.b: Descending thoracic aneurysms are usually related to hypertension or atherosclerosis.
explanations.c: Abdominal aneurysms are associated with smoking and atherosclerosis.
explanations.d: Common iliac aneurysms are often extensions of AAAs.
explanations.e: Ascending aortic aneurysms are associated with Marfan syndrome or hypertension.

ankiCards: Berry aneurysms are most commonly found in the {{c1::Circle of Willis}}.
The most common clinical consequence of a ruptured berry aneurysm is {{c1::subarachnoid hemorrhage}}.
Berry aneurysms are associated with {{c1::autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)}}.
Berry aneurysms are a type of {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm.
A berry aneurysm typically lacks a {{c1::tunica media}} at the site of the lesion.
keyPoints: Berry aneurysms are small, spherical dilations.
They occur at branch points in the cerebral circulation.
Risk factors include hypertension, smoking, and ADPKD.
They are developmental defects in the media of the vessel.
Presentation: 'Thunderclap' headache.
microReview: ADPKD + Worst headache = Ruptured Berry Aneurysm in Circle of Willis. This is a classic USMLE association.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the association of ADPKD with AAA; the strongest association is with cerebral (Berry) aneurysms.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 75-year-old man presents with vague abdominal pain and a pulsatile mass felt on deep palpation. An ultrasound shows a 6-cm abdominal aortic aneurysm. Which of the following is the most significant clinical risk associated with an aneurysm of this size?

options.a: Catastrophic rupture into the peritoneal cavity
options.b: Development of a primary hepatic malignancy
options.c: Acute renal failure from compression of the ureters

explanations.a: The risk of rupture increases significantly with size; for AAAs >6 cm, the annual risk of rupture is approximately 10-25%.
explanations.b: Aneurysms do not cause hepatic malignancy.
explanations.c: While aneurysms can compress structures, the most immediate life-threatening risk for a 6-cm aneurysm is rupture.
explanations.d: SVC syndrome is caused by compression of the SVC, usually by thoracic tumors or thoracic aneurysms, not AAAs.
explanations.e: Aneurysms do not regress; they generally expand over time.

ankiCards: The risk of AAA rupture is directly proportional to its {{c1::diameter}}.
AAAs greater than {{c1::5.0 to 5.5}} cm are usually managed surgically due to high rupture risk.
The classic triad of a ruptured AAA is {{c1::hypotension}}, {{c2::abdominal/back pain}}, and a {{c3::pulsatile mass}}.
Most AAAs occur {{c1::below (infrarenal)}} the level of the renal arteries.
A common complication of an aneurysm is the formation of a mural {{c1::thrombus}}.
keyPoints: Rupture risk: <4cm (0%), 4-5cm (1%), 5-6cm (11%), >6cm (25% per year).
AAA rupture is often fatal due to massive retroperitoneal or peritoneal hemorrhage.
Surgical repair (open or endovascular) is recommended for large or rapidly expanding aneurysms.
Mural thrombi in aneurysms can embolize to distal vessels (blue toe syndrome).
Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for expansion.
microReview: Size matters in AAA. >5.5cm = high risk. Triad of rupture: Pain + Hypotension + Pulsatile Mass. Management: Surgery.
examinerTraps: Wait for the size. If the question gives a size >5.5cm, the 'best next step' is usually surgical consultation/repair.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with an exquisitely painful, small, blue-red nodule located beneath the nail bed of her right index finger. She notes that the pain is often triggered by exposure to cold temperatures. On physical examination, the lesion is less than 1 cm in diameter and extremely tender to touch. Excision of the lesion is performed. Microscopic examination is expected to show nests of uniform cells surrounding branching vascular channels.

explanations.a: Endothelial cells line the vascular channels within the tumor but are not the characteristic neoplastic cell type of a glomus tumor.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) arise from the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous shunt involved in thermoregulation. The neoplastic cells are modified smooth muscle cells.
explanations.c: Fibroblasts are found in many vascular lesions but are not the primary cell of origin for a glomus tumor.
explanations.d: Pericytes are found in hemangiopericytomas, which are distinct from glomus tumors; glomus cells are specifically modified smooth muscle cells.
explanations.e: Skeletal muscle fibers are not involved in the pathogenesis of vascular tumors like glomangiomas.

ankiCards: The characteristic location of a {{c1::glomus tumor}} is the subungual region (under the fingernail).
Glomus tumors are derived from {{c1::modified smooth muscle cells}} of the glomus body.
Clinical presentation of a glomus tumor includes exquisite pain and sensitivity to {{c1::cold}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors show nests of uniform cells surrounding {{c1::vascular channels}}.
The glomus body is an arteriovenous structure involved in {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign, highly painful vascular tumors.
They most commonly occur in the distal digits, particularly subungually.
The origin is the glomus body (a thermoregulatory neuromyoarterial receptor).
Cells appear as small, uniform, round-to-oval cells in nests.
Symptoms are classically triggered by cold exposure.
microReview: Glomus tumor: painful, subungual, modified smooth muscle cells. Do not confuse with hemangiomas which are typically painless.
examinerTraps: Students often confuse the cell of origin; it is modified smooth muscle, not endothelial cells.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old male with poorly controlled HIV/AIDS (CD4 count 85 cells/mm³) presents with multiple violaceous, raised skin plaques on his lower extremities and oral mucosa. Biopsy of a skin lesion reveals spindle-shaped cells, slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells, and a chronic inflammatory infiltrate. Which of the following pathogens is the primary etiologic agent of this condition?

explanations.a: HHV-6 is the cause of roseola infantum and is not associated with Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.b: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.c: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent for all forms of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.d: CMV causes retinitis and colitis in AIDS patients but does not cause vascular tumors.
explanations.e: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can look clinically similar but is histologically distinct (neutrophilic infiltrate, not spindle cells).

ankiCards: The causative agent of Kaposi sarcoma is {{c1::Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}.
Kaposi sarcoma is histologically characterized by {{c1::spindle-shaped cells}} and slit-like vascular spaces.
The presence of {{c1::extravasated RBCs}} is a common histological finding in Kaposi sarcoma.
The four forms of Kaposi sarcoma are: Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and {{c1::AIDS-associated}}.
{{c1::Oral mucosa}} involvement is common in the AIDS-associated form of Kaposi sarcoma.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8.
Commonly presents as purple/violaceous macules, plaques, or nodules.
Spindle cells are the hallmark histological finding.
Slit-like spaces are formed by the spindle cells and contain blood.
AIDS-associated KS is the most common HIV-related malignancy.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = HHV-8 + Spindle Cells + Slit-like spaces + AIDS patient.
examinerTraps: Distinguishing KS from Bacillary Angiomatosis: KS has spindle cells/HHV8; Bacillary Angiomatosis has neutrophils/Bartonella.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 62-year-old male presents with right upper quadrant pain, weight loss, and fatigue. He worked in a plastics manufacturing plant for 35 years with significant exposure to vinyl chloride. Imaging reveals multiple ill-defined, hemorrhagic masses within the liver. A biopsy shows large, pleomorphic endothelial cells with hyperchromatic nuclei forming irregular vascular channels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Hepatocellular carcinoma is associated with HBV/HCV and cirrhosis, not specifically vinyl chloride.
explanations.b: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor associated with environmental toxins like vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas are the most common benign liver tumors and are not associated with chemical toxins.
explanations.d: Hepatic adenomas are associated with oral contraceptive use, not industrial chemical exposure.
explanations.e: Focal nodular hyperplasia is a benign regenerative response to a localized vascular abnormality, not a malignant tumor.

ankiCards: {{c1::Angiosarcoma}} of the liver is associated with exposure to vinyl chloride.
Besides vinyl chloride, hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with {{c1::arsenic}} and Thorotrast.
Histologically, angiosarcoma shows malignant {{c1::endothelial cells}} forming irregular channels.
The immunohistochemical marker for angiosarcoma is typically {{c1::CD31}}.
Angiosarcoma has a very {{c1::poor}} prognosis due to its aggressive nature.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a malignant neoplasm of endothelial cells.
Specific associations: Vinyl chloride, arsenic, Thorotrast (liver); lymphedema (skin/Stewart-Treves).
It is characterized by rapid growth and early metastasis.
Histology shows poorly formed, anastomosing vascular channels.
Nuclear atypia and frequent mitoses in endothelial cells distinguish it from hemangiomas.
microReview: Angiosarcoma: Vinyl chloride/Arsenic (Liver) or Lymphedema (Post-mastectomy skin). Marker: CD31 (Endothelial).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse hepatocellular carcinoma (linked to cirrhosis/HBV) with angiosarcoma (linked to chemical exposures).
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the diagnosis of vascular tumors, immunohistochemistry is frequently employed to confirm the cell of origin. Which of the following markers is the most specific for identifying neoplastic cells of endothelial lineage?

explanations.a: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells and carcinomas.
explanations.b: Desmin is a marker for myogenic (muscle) cells.
explanations.c: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a transmembrane glycoprotein highly expressed on endothelial cells and is a reliable marker for vascular tumors.
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells, such as melanocytes or Schwann cells.
explanations.e: HMB-45 is a specific marker for melanocytic lesions.

ankiCards: The most specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial cells is {{c1::CD31}}.
CD31 is also known as {{c1::PECAM-1}}.
In addition to CD31, {{c1::von Willebrand factor (Factor VIII-related antigen)}} can mark vascular tumors.
Vascular tumors originate from the {{c1::endothelial}} cell lineage.
{{c1::Angiosarcoma}} and other vascular malignancies will typically stain positive for CD31.
keyPoints: CD31 is the 'gold standard' marker for vascular endothelium.
Factor VIII-related antigen is another, though sometimes less sensitive, marker.
Immunohistochemistry helps differentiate poorly differentiated angiosarcoma from other sarcomas or carcinomas.
Endothelial cells line the entirety of the vascular system.
Markers are essential when vascular channels are not clearly formed morphologically.
microReview: Vascular Marker = CD31. Epithelial = Cytokeratin. Muscle = Desmin. Nerve = S100.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'CD31' in options; 'vWF' is an older but still valid alternative, but CD31 is usually the preferred board answer.
sourceQuote: To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure and function.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 2-week-old female infant is brought to the pediatrician for a bright red, raised 'strawberry-like' lesion on her scalp. The parents report it was not present at birth but appeared shortly after. The lesion has grown rapidly over the past week. What is the most likely expected clinical course for this lesion?

options.a: Persistent growth requiring immediate surgical excision
options.b: Malignant transformation into angiosarcoma in childhood
options.c: Progressive enlargement followed by spontaneous involution
options.d: Metastasis to the regional lymph nodes
options.e: Dormancy with no change in size throughout life

explanations.a: Surgery is usually avoided as these lesions typically regress on their own.
explanations.b: Strawberry (capillary) hemangiomas are benign and do not transform into malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.c: Juvenile capillary (strawberry) hemangiomas typically grow rapidly for a few months and then spontaneously regress (involute) by age 7 in the majority of cases.
explanations.d: These are benign tumors and do not metastasize.
explanations.e: These tumors follow a dynamic course of growth and regression, they do not remain dormant.

ankiCards: The common name for a juvenile capillary hemangioma is a {{c1::strawberry}} hemangioma.
Strawberry hemangiomas typically appear {{c1::shortly after birth (days to weeks)}}.
The natural history of a strawberry hemangioma involves rapid growth followed by {{c1::spontaneous involution}}.
Most strawberry hemangiomas completely regress by age {{c1::7}}.
Histologically, these consist of thin-walled capillaries with scant {{c1::stroma}}.
keyPoints: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are extremely common in infants.
They are benign capillary hemangiomas.
Clinical course: Rapid growth -> Stability -> Regression.
Often found on the head and neck.
90% regress by age 7.
microReview: Strawberry Hemangioma = Newborn + Rapid growth + Spontaneous regression. No treatment usually needed.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse with a 'Port-wine stain' (Nevus flammeus), which does NOT regress and grows with the child.
sourceQuote: Vascular structure and function characterize specific kinds of vessels... Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old male with HIV presents with several rapidly growing, red, friable nodules on his arms. Biopsy shows a proliferation of capillaries with prominent, plump endothelial cells, a dense infiltrate of neutrophils, and clusters of small purple granular bacilli on Warthin-Starry silver stain. Which organism is responsible for this condition?

explanations.a: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, which lacks the neutrophilic infiltrate and bacterial clusters seen here.
explanations.b: Bartonella henselae (and B. quintana) causes bacillary angiomatosis, which is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised patients characterized by neutrophilic inflammation and bacteria.
explanations.c: S. aureus can cause infections but not this specific pattern of neoplastic-like vascular proliferation.
explanations.d: MAI causes systemic infection and granulomas in AIDS, but not bacillary angiomatosis.
explanations.e: T. pallidum causes syphilis; the silver stain may find it, but the pathology of bacillary angiomatosis is specific to Bartonella.

ankiCards: {{c1::Bacillary angiomatosis}} is a vascular proliferation in HIV patients caused by Bartonella species.
The two main species of Bartonella causing bacillary angiomatosis are B. henselae and {{c1::B. quintana}}.
The histological differentiator for bacillary angiomatosis is a {{c1::neutrophilic}} infiltrate.
{{c1::Warthin-Starry}} silver stain is used to visualize Bartonella in tissues.
Clinically, bacillary angiomatosis can mimic {{c1::Kaposi sarcoma}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis is an opportunistic infection in immunocompromised hosts.
It causes benign-appearing but aggressive vascular proliferations.
Pathology: Proliferating capillaries, nuclear atypia (sometimes), and neutrophils.
Causative agents: Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch link) or Bartonella quintana (lice link).
Treated with antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin), unlike Kaposi sarcoma.
microReview: Red nodules in AIDS: If Spindle cells/No bacteria = Kaposi. If Neutrophils/Silver stain (+) = Bacillary Angiomatosis.
examinerTraps: The presence of 'plump endothelial cells' can trick you into thinking it's a malignancy; look for the neutrophils and bacteria.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 25-year-old pregnant woman in her third trimester develops a rapidly growing, bleed-prone, pedunculated red nodule on her gingiva. The lesion is soft and measures 1 cm. Histology shows a lobular proliferation of capillaries with surface ulceration and edema. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are similar but lack the specific 'lobular' growth pattern and clinical association with pregnancy-related gingival 'granuloma gravidarum'.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granuloma (also known as Lobular Capillary Hemangioma) often occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are painful subungual lesions, not gingival nodules in pregnancy.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated blood-filled spaces and are usually deeper/internal.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is seen in immunocompromised patients, not typically healthy pregnant women.

ankiCards: A {{c1::pyogenic granuloma}} is a rapidly growing red nodule that frequently bleeds.
Pyogenic granuloma is histologically a {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
When occurring on the gingiva of a pregnant woman, pyogenic granuloma is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are often found on the skin, gingiva, or {{c1::oral mucosa}}.
Despite the name, pyogenic granulomas are neither {{c1::pyogenic (pus-forming)}} nor true granulomas.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is a benign vascular proliferation.
Associated with trauma or pregnancy (hormonal influence).
Characterized by a lobular arrangement of capillaries.
Clinically: Friable, red, pedunculated, bleeds easily.
Usually treated by surgical excision.
microReview: Pyogenic Granuloma = Pregnancy/Gingiva + Bleeding red nodule + Lobular Capillaries.
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic granuloma' is a trap; it has nothing to do with infection (pyogenic) or granulomatous inflammation.
sourceQuote: The general architecture and cellular composition of blood vessels are comparable throughout the cardiovascular system.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A newborn is found to have a large, fluctuant mass on the lateral aspect of the neck. Transillumination of the mass is positive. Chromosomal analysis reveals a 45,X karyotype. The neck mass most likely represents which of the following vascular malformations?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are composed of small blood vessels and typically do not present as large cystic neck masses.
explanations.b: Cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) is a lymphatic malformation characteristically found in the neck or axilla, often associated with Turner Syndrome (45,X).
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are small, painful, subungual lesions.
explanations.d: AVMs are abnormal connections between arteries and veins; they are not typically transilluminating cystic neck masses in newborns.
explanations.e: Cavernous hemangiomas involve blood vessels, whereas cystic hygromas involve lymphatic channels; the latter is much more strongly associated with Turner syndrome and neck location.

ankiCards: A cystic hygroma is a type of {{c1::cavernous lymphangioma}}.
Cystic hygromas are commonly located in the {{c1::neck}} or axilla.
A classic genetic association for cystic hygroma is {{c1::Turner Syndrome (45,X)}}.
The clinical test {{c1::transillumination}} is often positive in cystic hygromas due to their fluid-filled nature.
Histologically, cystic hygromas show dilated {{c1::lymphatic}} spaces lined by endothelial cells.
keyPoints: Lymphangiomas are the lymphatic equivalent of hemangiomas.
Cystic hygroma is the most common form of cavernous lymphangioma.
It is characterized by large, dilated lymphatic spaces.
Association with chromosomal aneuploidies (Turner syndrome, Down syndrome).
Often leads to 'webbing' of the neck after regression or treatment.
microReview: Cystic Hygroma = Neck mass + Transillumination + Turner Syndrome.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse with a branchial cleft cyst; the chromosomal association (45,X) is the key differentiator here.
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular tumors is classified as an 'intermediate-grade' (borderline) neoplasm, meaning its biological behavior lies between benign hemangiomas and highly malignant angiosarcomas?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are strictly benign.
explanations.b: Hemangioendothelioma describes a group of vascular neoplasms with intermediate behavior (e.g., epithelioid hemangioendothelioma).
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are benign.
explanations.d: Angiosarcomas are high-grade malignant tumors.
explanations.e: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a vascular malformation, not a neoplasm.

ankiCards: The term for a vascular tumor with intermediate (borderline) malignancy is {{c1::hemangioendothelioma}}.
{{c1::Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma}} is a common subtype of these borderline tumors.
Borderline vascular tumors have {{c1::lower}} metastatic potential than angiosarcomas.
Histologically, hemangioendotheliomas have more {{c1::atypia}} than benign hemangiomas.
They can occur in both soft tissues and {{c1::visceral organs (like the liver)}}.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors are graded as Benign, Intermediate, or Malignant.
Benign: Hemangiomas, Glomus tumors.
Intermediate: Hemangioendotheliomas (e.g., Epithelioid, Kaposiform).
Malignant: Angiosarcoma, Kaposi Sarcoma (though KS is often considered multifocal rather than purely metastatic).
Management depends on this classification.
microReview: Intermediate Grade = Hemangioendothelioma. (Benign = Hemangioma; Malignant = Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: Be careful with the term 'endothelioma'; usually 'hemangioendothelioma' is the one used in the 'intermediate' category.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 58-year-old female who underwent a radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer 10 years ago presents with multiple enlarging, dark-purple skin nodules on her chronic lymphedematous left arm. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: While recurrent breast cancer can happen, skin nodules in a chronically lymphedematous limb are classic for the Stewart-Treves syndrome (angiosarcoma).
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma (specifically Stewart-Treves syndrome) is a known complication of long-standing chronic lymphedema, often after mastectomy.
explanations.c: Lymphangiomas are benign malformations, not typically appearing as new nodules in an adult limb.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis requires Bartonella infection and immunosuppression, not lymphedema.
explanations.e: Stasis dermatitis is a venous insufficiency issue, not a nodular neoplastic process.

ankiCards: Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to {{c1::angiosarcoma}} arising in chronic lymphedema.
Chronic lymphedema after {{c1::mastectomy}} is the classic risk factor for Stewart-Treves syndrome.
Angiosarcoma in lymphedema usually presents as {{c1::purple/red nodules}} on the skin.
The latent period between mastectomy and angiosarcoma development is typically around {{c1::10}} years.
Angiosarcoma is an aggressive malignancy of {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma can occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema.
This specific association is named Stewart-Treves syndrome.
Clinical hint: Post-mastectomy patient with arm swelling.
These tumors are highly aggressive with poor prognosis.
The presence of CD31 positivity helps confirm the endothelial origin.
microReview: Chronic Lymphedema + Skin nodules = Stewart-Treves Syndrome (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: Don't assume skin nodules on an arm post-mastectomy are always breast cancer metastasis; if lymphedema is mentioned, think angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Vascular structure and function characterize specific kinds of vessels... Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 34-year-old male with a history of poorly controlled HIV (CD4+ count 120/mm³) presents with several painless, non-blanching, violaceous plaques on his lower extremities and hard palate. Skin biopsy reveals spindle-shaped cells forming slit-like spaces containing extravasated red blood cells. Which of the following infectious agents is the most likely driver of this pathology?

explanations.a: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus, is the causative agent of all forms of Kaposi sarcoma (KS). The clinical presentation of violaceous plaques in an HIV patient with spindle cell proliferation and slit-like vascular spaces is pathognomonic for KS.
explanations.b: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised patients, which can mimic Kaposi sarcoma clinically, but histologically it features lobular capillary proliferation with neutrophils, not spindle cells with slit-like spaces.
explanations.c: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with various lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, but it is not linked to the pathogenesis of vascular tumors like Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.d: Human papillomavirus 16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx, not vascular tumors.
explanations.e: Cytomegalovirus can cause retinitis or colitis in HIV patients but does not cause primary vascular neoplasms.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is associated with which virus? {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}
The classic histological finding in Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells}} with slit-like spaces containing RBCs.
The most common site of visceral involvement in AIDS-associated Kaposi Sarcoma is the {{c1::gastrointestinal tract}}.
What is the characteristic color of Kaposi Sarcoma lesions? {{c1::Violaceous/Purple}}
Unlike bacillary angiomatosis, Kaposi Sarcoma histology typically lacks {{c1::neutrophils/Bartonella organisms}}.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a low-grade malignant vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8.
Four clinical forms exist: Classic (older Mediterranean men), Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
Histology shows spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces, and extravasated erythrocytes.
Lesions do not blanch because the blood is not contained within well-formed vessels.
HHV-8 induces endothelial cell proliferation and an inflammatory milieu.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Slit-like spaces + Violaceous lesions.
examinerTraps: Distinguishing KS from Bacillary Angiomatosis: KS has spindle cells; Bacillary Angiomatosis has neutrophils and Warthin-Starry positive bacilli.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following immunohistochemical markers is most specific for identifying tumors of endothelial cell origin, such as angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Cytokeratin 7 is a marker for epithelial cells, commonly used to identify carcinomas.
explanations.b: CD31 (platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule) is highly specific and sensitive for endothelial cells and is the gold standard for identifying vascular tumors like angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (smooth and skeletal), used in identifying leiomyosarcomas or rhabdomyosarcomas.
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells, such as melanocytes or Schwann cells.
explanations.e: Vimentin is a non-specific marker for mesenchymal cells and is present in almost all sarcomas, but it lacks specificity for endothelial differentiation.

ankiCards: The most specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial cells is {{c1::CD31}}.
Angiosarcomas are malignant tumors derived from {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
Besides CD31, another common vascular marker is {{c1::von Willebrand factor (Factor VIII)}}.
IHC marker for epithelial tumors is {{c1::Cytokeratin}}.
IHC marker for muscle tumors is {{c1::Desmin}}.
keyPoints: Endothelial markers include CD31 and CD34.
Angiosarcomas are highly aggressive malignant vascular tumors.
These tumors can occur anywhere but most commonly in skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with vinyl chloride and arsenic exposure.
Histologically, they range from well-formed vascular channels to solid sheets of undifferentiated cells.
microReview: Endothelial tumor markers: CD31 > CD34 > Factor VIII.
examinerTraps: Vimentin is often a distractor because it is positive in vascular tumors, but it is not specific as it labels all mesenchymal cells.
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 50-year-old factory worker with chronic exposure to vinyl chloride and Thorotrast is at markedly increased risk for developing a malignant neoplasm in the liver. This tumor most likely arises from which cell type?

explanations.a: Hepatocellular carcinoma arises from hepatocytes but is more strongly linked to Hepatitis B/C and cirrhosis than to vinyl chloride.
explanations.b: Cholangiocarcinoma arises from bile duct epithelium and is associated with liver flukes and primary sclerosing cholangitis.
explanations.c: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare, highly malignant tumor of endothelial cells that has a known association with vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast exposure.
explanations.d: Kupffer cells are specialized macrophages in the liver and do not give rise to angiosarcomas.
explanations.e: Stellate cells (Ito cells) are involved in liver fibrosis but are not the origin of these vascular tumors.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
Which radioactive contrast medium is associated with hepatic angiosarcoma? {{c1::Thorotrast}}.
Angiosarcomas of the liver arise from {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
Arsenic exposure is a risk factor for which vascular malignancy? {{c1::Angiosarcoma}}.
The prognosis for hepatic angiosarcoma is generally {{c1::poor}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma of the liver is the classic example of chemical carcinogenesis in vascular pathology.
Exposures: Vinyl chloride (PVC plastic industry), Arsenic (pesticides), and Thorotrast (obsolete contrast).
The latent period between exposure and tumor development can be decades.
The tumor consists of malignant endothelial cells.
It is often fatal within a year of diagnosis.
microReview: Vinyl chloride/Arsenic/Thorotrast -> Hepatic Angiosarcoma (Endothelial origin).
examinerTraps: Do not confuse hepatic angiosarcoma (endothelial) with hepatocellular carcinoma (hepatocyte).
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old female presents with a small, 0.5-cm, exquisitely painful, firm, red-blue nodule under the fingernail of her right index finger. The pain is triggered by cold exposure. Excision of the lesion shows aggregates of uniform, rounded cells surrounding branch-point vascular channels. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are common benign tumors but are typically not painful and do not have a subungual predilection.
