microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma: HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Slit-like vessels + HIV.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Kaposi Sarcoma (HHV-8) with Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella); both occur in HIV but BA has neutrophilic infiltrates and identifiable bacteria on silver stain.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors are divided into three categories: (1) benign tumors, which are common and do not metastasize; (2) intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors; and (3) malignant tumors.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents with severe, paroxysmal pain in the tip of her left ring finger. The pain is especially acute when she reaches into the freezer. On physical examination, a small, 2-mm, blue-red nodule is visible under the nail bed. Pressure on the nodule reproduces the intense pain. This lesion most likely originates from which of the following structures?

options.a: Modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body
options.b: Fenestrated endothelial cells of the dermis
options.c: Schwann cells of the peripheral nerves
options.d: Pericytes of the capillary basement membrane

explanations.a: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, exquisitely painful tumors arising from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, which is involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.b: While vascular, the primary cell of a glomus tumor is the specialized smooth muscle cell, not a simple fenestrated endothelial cell.
explanations.c: Schwannoma can be painful, but the subungual location and cold sensitivity are classic for a glomus tumor.
explanations.d: Hemangiopericytomas arise from pericytes, but they lack the classic subungual/thermoregulatory clinical presentation of glomus tumors.
explanations.e: Fibroblasts are not the origin of this vascular thermoregulatory tumor.

ankiCards: A subungual, exquisitely painful, cold-sensitive nodule is most likely a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle cells}}.
The physiological function of the glomus body is {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Glomus tumors are most commonly found in the {{c1::distal digits (fingers/toes)}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors consist of {{c1::nests/aggregates of glomus cells}} around vascular spaces.
keyPoints: Glomus tumor = Subungual location.
Classic symptom: Intense pain triggered by cold.
Origin: Modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
Appearance: Small, blue-red nodule.
Biopsy: Uniform cells in nests around vascular channels.
microReview: Glomus tumor: Subungual + Cold pain + Modified smooth muscle cells.
examinerTraps: Examiners may call them 'glomangiomas' or simply ask for the cell of origin (specialized smooth muscle).
sourceQuote: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, exquisitely painful tumors arising from specialized smooth muscle cells of glomus bodies.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old female presents with multiple dark-red, firm nodules on her right arm. She has a history of chronic lymphedema in the same arm following a radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer 15 years ago. A biopsy shows highly pleomorphic endothelial cells forming irregular, anastomosing vascular channels. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is HHV-8 related and typically involves spindle cells and slit-like spaces, not anastomosing malignant channels post-lymphedema.
explanations.b: Hemangioendothelioma is an intermediate-grade tumor, but the classic association with chronic lymphedema points specifically to angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma occurring in the setting of chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy) is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome. It is a highly aggressive malignant vascular tumor.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign lesions consisting of large, blood-filled spaces, not pleomorphic malignant cells.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts, not a malignancy related to lymphedema.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in the context of chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
Chronic lymphedema post-{{c1::mastectomy}} is a classic risk factor for Stewart-Treves syndrome.
{{c1::Angiosarcoma}} is a malignant tumor of endothelial cells.
The marker {{c1::CD31}} is highly specific for endothelial differentiation in angiosarcoma.
Angiosarcoma of the liver is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride (or arsenic)}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignant vascular tumor.
Stewart-Treves syndrome = Lymphangiosarcoma post-mastectomy.
Associated with PVC, Arsenic, and Thorotrast in the liver.
Histology: Irregular vascular channels with pleomorphic endothelium.
Prognosis is poor due to high rate of metastasis.
microReview: Post-mastectomy lymphedema + Skin nodules = Stewart-Treves (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: Wait for the keyword 'lymphedema'. If the patient is an older man with sun-damaged skin on the scalp, it's still angiosarcoma, but if it's the arm post-mastectomy, it's the classic Stewart-Treves variant.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms with a 5-year survival rate of only about 30%.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 22-year-old pregnant female presents with a rapidly growing, 1-cm, pedunculated red mass on her gingiva. The lesion is friable and bleeds significantly with minor contact. Histological examination reveals a proliferation of capillaries and extensive edema, with an inflammatory infiltrate. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: While it is a type of capillary hemangioma, the specific clinical context (pregnancy, gingiva, rapid growth) defines it as a pyogenic granuloma.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated spaces and are usually deep-seated, not pedunculated gingival masses.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (granuloma pyogenicum or lobular capillary hemangioma) is a rapidly growing, bleed-prone red nodule often found on the gums of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are painful subungual lesions, not painless friable gingival lesions.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor with significant atypia; the described lesion is benign and inflammatory in nature.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is also known as {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
A pyogenic granuloma occurring on the gingiva of a pregnant woman is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized by {{c1::rapid}} growth and frequent {{c2::bleeding (friability)}}.
Histologically, pyogenic granuloma resembles {{c1::granulation tissue}}.
True or False: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer because it is neither pyogenic (infectious) nor a true granuloma. {{c1::True}}
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign vascular lesion.
Commonly occurs on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
Strong association with pregnancy (hormonal influence).
Often regresses spontaneously or after pregnancy.
Surgical excision is sometimes required if it doesn't regress.
microReview: Pregnant gingiva + Bleeding red nodule = Pyogenic granuloma.
examinerTraps: The name is a misnomer; it is not actually caused by an infection (pyogenic) and does not show granulomatous inflammation.
sourceQuote: Pyogenic granulomas are capillary hemangiomas that manifest as rapidly growing red, pedunculated lesions on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 58-year-old man who worked in a chemical plant for 25 years is diagnosed with hepatic angiosarcoma. Exposure to which of the following substances is most likely associated with the development of this specific tumor?

explanations.a: Asbestos is primarily associated with mesothelioma and lung cancer.
explanations.b: Beryllium exposure is associated with berylliosis and lung cancer.
explanations.c: Vinyl chloride (used in PVC production), arsenic (in pesticides), and Thorotrast (radiocontrast) are classic risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: Aflatoxin B1 is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.
explanations.e: Benzene exposure is associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

ankiCards: The classic chemical exposure linked to hepatic angiosarcoma is {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
Besides vinyl chloride, exposure to {{c1::arsenic}} is also a risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma.
{{c1::Thorotrast}} is an obsolete radiocontrast agent associated with hepatic angiosarcoma.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is a tumor of {{c1::endothelial}} origin.
Unlike HCC, angiosarcoma of the liver is NOT typically related to {{c1::cirrhosis (or Hepatitis B/C)}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is the most common primary malignant tumor of the liver of vascular origin.
Exposure associations: Vinyl chloride, Arsenic, Thorotrast.
Extremely long latency period between exposure and tumor development.
Poor prognosis; often detected at advanced stages.
Differentiation is confirmed with CD31 staining.
microReview: Hepatic Angiosarcoma: PVC + Arsenic + Thorotrast.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Aflatoxin (Hepatocellular Carcinoma) with Vinyl Chloride (Angiosarcoma).
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas can also be induced by environmental carcinogens, including arsenic (used in pesticides), Thorotrast (a radioactive contrast medium), and polyvinyl chloride (a plastic).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 3-month-old infant is brought to the clinic for a bright red, slightly raised lesion on the forehead. The mother states it was not present at birth but appeared at 2 weeks of age and has grown since. The physician explains that the lesion is benign and will likely regress spontaneously by the age of 7. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is usually present at birth and does not regress; it often grows with the child.
explanations.b: Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) are common in newborns, grow rapidly for a few months, and then typically involute by age 5-7.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas are deeper, less likely to regress, and involve larger vascular channels.
explanations.d: Cherry hemangiomas are small, bright red papules that increase in number with age in adults (senile hemangiomas).
explanations.e: Spider angiomas are associated with hyperestrogenic states (e.g., pregnancy, cirrhosis) and consist of a central arteriole with radiating capillaries.

ankiCards: The most common vascular tumor of infancy is the {{c1::juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma}}.
Juvenile hemangiomas typically {{c1::regress (involute)}} spontaneously by age 7.
Unlike a port-wine stain, a strawberry hemangioma usually appears {{c1::after birth (days to weeks)}}.
Histologically, juvenile hemangiomas are a type of {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma.
Most juvenile hemangiomas are located on the {{c1::skin (face/scalp)}}.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangioma = Strawberry hemangioma.
Grows rapidly (proliferative phase) followed by slow regression (involutional phase).
Total regression occurs in 75-90% of cases by age 7.
Benign and extremely common (1 in 200 births).
Distinguished from port-wine stains which are permanent.
microReview: Strawberry Hemangioma: Newborn + Fast growth + Spontaneous regression.
examinerTraps: Often confused with 'Port-wine stains'. Port-wine stains (Nevus flammeus) do NOT regress and are present at birth.
sourceQuote: Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) of the skin of newborns are very common; they grow rapidly for a few months but then fade and regress by age 1 to 3 years.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 42-year-old HIV-positive male presents with numerous red, papular skin lesions that resemble Kaposi sarcoma. However, histological analysis shows a vascular proliferation with prominent neutrophilic infiltrates and nuclear debris. A silver stain (Warthin-Starry) identifies clusters of small, curved bacilli. What is the most likely causative organism?

explanations.a: Bartonella henselae (or B. quintana) causes bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised hosts, presenting as vascular lesions that can mimic Kaposi Sarcoma but are characterized by neutrophils and bacteria.
explanations.b: Staphylococcus aureus causes pyogenic infections (abscesses, impetigo) but not organized vascular proliferations like bacillary angiomatosis.
explanations.c: Treponema pallidum causes syphilis; while silver-stain positive, its primary vascular pathology is endarteritis obliterans, not angiomatosis.
explanations.d: Mycobacterium leprae causes leprosy with granulomatous or lepromatous inflammation, not vascular tumors.
explanations.e: Rickettsia species infect endothelial cells and cause vasculitis, but not a tumor-like proliferation.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by bacteria of the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
In bacillary angiomatosis, the vascular proliferation is accompanied by an infiltrate of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
The causative agent of bacillary angiomatosis is best visualized using a {{c1::Warthin-Starry (silver)}} stain.
Bacillary angiomatosis is primarily seen in {{c1::immunocompromised (HIV/AIDS)}} patients.
The treatment for bacillary angiomatosis is usually {{c1::erythromycin (or doxycycline)}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis mimics Kaposi Sarcoma clinically.
Histology: Capillary proliferation with 'dirty' appearance (neutrophils + bacterial clumps).
Caused by Bartonella henselae (cat scratch) or B. quintana (trench fever).
Bartonella induces endothelial proliferation via VEGF production.
Unlike KS, it is infectious and treatable with antibiotics.
microReview: Bacillary Angiomatosis: HIV + Red papules + Neutrophils + Bartonella (Silver stain).
examinerTraps: Clinical mimic of Kaposi Sarcoma. Look for the mention of 'neutrophils' or 'silver stain' to distinguish it.
sourceQuote: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts (e.g., those with AIDS) caused by opportunistic gram-negative bacilli of the Bartonella family.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old man with a family history of Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease undergoes a routine screening. Imaging reveals multiple cavernous hemangiomas in the liver and cerebellum. Which of the following is the characteristic histological feature of a cavernous hemangioma?

options.a: Large, dilated vascular spaces filled with blood
options.b: Sheets of spindled cells with slit-like spaces
options.c: Nests of uniform round cells around vessels
options.d: Atypical endothelial cells invading the dermis
options.e: Proliferation of small, tightly packed capillaries

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, dilated blood-filled channels separated by connective tissue stroma.
explanations.b: Sheets of spindled cells with slit-like spaces describe Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.c: Nests of uniform round cells are characteristic of Glomus tumors.
explanations.d: Atypical endothelial cells characterize malignant tumors like angiosarcoma.
explanations.e: Small, tightly packed capillaries describe capillary hemangiomas.

ankiCards: A vascular tumor composed of large, blood-filled spaces is a {{c1::cavernous hemangioma}}.
Cavernous hemangiomas are frequently associated with {{c1::Von Hippel-Lindau}} disease.
The most common internal organ involved by cavernous hemangiomas is the {{c1::liver}}.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas are {{c1::less}} likely to regress.
Complications of cavernous hemangiomas include {{c1::thrombosis}} and local {{c2::rupture}}.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas involve larger, deeper vessels than capillary hemangiomas.
They are often poorly circumscribed.
Clinical significance: often asymptomatic but can rupture (especially in the CNS or liver).
Part of VHL syndrome (cerebellum, brainstem, retina).
Histology: 'Cavern-like' blood-filled spaces.
microReview: Cavernous Hemangioma: Dilated spaces + Blood + Liver/CNS + VHL.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'cavernous' appearance with 'cavernous sinus thrombosis'. Also, remember they are usually NOT as well-demarcated as capillary ones.
sourceQuote: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, dilated vascular channels. Compared with capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas are more infiltrative, frequently involve deep structures, and do not regress.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following immunohistochemical markers is most specific for identifying a tumor as being of endothelial cell origin, such as in the case of a poorly differentiated angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells (carcinomas).
explanations.b: S100 is a marker for neural crest derivatives (melanoma, Schwannoma).
explanations.c: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a transmembrane glycoprotein expressed on endothelial cells and is highly specific for vascular tumors.
explanations.d: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (rhabdomyosarcoma, leiomyoma).
explanations.e: Vimentin is a non-specific marker for mesenchymal cells.

ankiCards: The most specific vascular endothelial marker used in pathology is {{c1::CD31}}.
Another marker for endothelial cells, besides CD31, is {{c1::von Willebrand factor (Factor VIII)}}.
Angiosarcomas stain positive for the endothelial marker {{c1::CD31}}.
In poorly differentiated tumors, {{c1::CD31}} helps distinguish angiosarcoma from carcinoma.
CD31 is also known as {{c1::PECAM-1}}.
keyPoints: CD31 is the gold standard IHC marker for endothelial differentiation.
Essential for diagnosing poorly differentiated angiosarcomas.
Factor VIII (von Willebrand factor) is also used but is less sensitive.
Helps differentiate vascular tumors from other spindle-cell sarcomas.
Angiosarcomas are often high-grade and pleomorphic.
microReview: Endothelial marker: CD31 (PECAM-1).
examinerTraps: Vimentin will be positive in angiosarcoma because it's a sarcoma, but it is NOT specific; CD31 is the specific choice.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas... Endothelial differentiation can be demonstrated by staining for the endothelial-specific markers CD31 or von Willebrand factor.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular ectasias are characterized by permanent dilation of preexisting small vessels. Which of the following is a classic example of a 'port-wine stain' that is associated with trigeminal nerve distribution and potential leptomeningeal angiomas?

explanations.a: Nevus flammeus is the general term for a port-wine stain, but the syndrome involving the trigeminal nerve and CNS is specifically Sturge-Weber.
explanations.b: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) involves malformations in the skin and mucous membranes but not the classic trigeminal port-wine stain.
explanations.c: Sturge-Weber syndrome involves a port-wine stain in the V1/V2 trigeminal distribution, ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomas, glaucoma, and seizures.
explanations.d: Spider telangiectasias are small, non-syndromic lesions often seen in cirrhosis.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious proliferation, not a congenital ectasia.

ankiCards: A port-wine stain in the distribution of the {{c1::trigeminal nerve}} is characteristic of Sturge-Weber syndrome.
Sturge-Weber syndrome involves the port-wine stain and ipsilateral {{c1::leptomeningeal}} angiomas.
Patients with Sturge-Weber syndrome are at high risk for {{c1::seizures (and glaucoma/mental retardation)}}.
A permanent dilation of small vessels is called a {{c1::vascular ectasia}}.
True or False: Port-wine stains (Nevus flammeus) typically regress with age. {{c1::False}}
keyPoints: Sturge-Weber syndrome is a congenital disorder (not inherited).
Clinical triad: Port-wine stain (trigeminal nerve), seizure/seizure disorder, and glaucoma.
The skin lesion is a form of nevus flammeus.
Skull X-ray may show 'tram-track' calcifications of the leptomeningeal angioma.
The 'port-wine stain' does not fade and grows with the child.
microReview: Sturge-Weber: Trigeminal port-wine stain + Leptomeningeal angioma + Seizures.
examinerTraps: The port-wine stain is called 'Nevus flammeus', but the *syndrome* is Sturge-Weber. Be careful to select the syndrome name if systemic features are mentioned.
sourceQuote: Nevus flammeus (a 'port-wine stain')... in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve is a component of the Sturge-Weber syndrome.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with an exquisitely painful, 4-mm, firm, red-blue nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. She notes that the pain is often triggered by exposure to cold temperatures. Physical examination reveals a exquisitely tender subungual mass. The lesion is excised, and histopathology shows aggregates of specialized smooth muscle cells surrounding vascular channels.

explanations.a: Endothelial cells line the vascular channels within the tumor but are not the characteristic 'glomus cells' that define this lesion.
explanations.b: Pericytes are contractile cells around capillaries, but the specific cells of origin for a glomus tumor are the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
explanations.c: A glomus tumor (glomangioma) arises from the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation. It is composed of modified smooth muscle cells.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts are found in the stroma of many vascular lesions but do not form the characteristic nests of cells seen in a glomus tumor.
explanations.e: Mast cells may be present in inflammatory backgrounds but are not the neoplastic component of vascular tumors.

ankiCards: The characteristic 'glomus cells' in a glomus tumor are derived from {{c1::modified smooth muscle cells}}.
A subungual nodule that is extremely sensitive to cold is most likely a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
The glomus body, from which glomus tumors arise, is involved in {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Glomus tumors are most commonly found in the {{c1::distal portion of the digits}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors show branching vascular channels separated by aggregates of {{c1::glomus cells}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign, highly painful tumors.
They arise from specialized thermoregulatory glomus bodies.
Classic presentation is a subungual (under the nail) location.
Pain is specifically triggered by cold exposure.
They are composed of specialized, modified smooth muscle cells.
microReview: Glomus tumors are benign but extremely painful. They arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, specifically in the subungual region of digits.
examinerTraps: Students often confuse these with subungual melanomas; however, glomus tumors are characterized by intense pain and sensitivity to cold, which is not typical for melanoma.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors are common and range from benign hemangiomas to locally aggressive but rarely metastatic (intermediate-grade) lesions to highly malignant angiosarcomas.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with multiple firm, violaceous nodules on her right arm. She has a history of radical mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer 10 years ago, followed by chronic lymphedema of the right upper extremity. A biopsy of one of the skin nodules reveals a poorly differentiated malignancy with pleomorphic endothelial cells forming irregular vascular channels.

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and typically presents as multifocal skin lesions, but not specifically in the setting of chronic post-surgical lymphedema.
explanations.b: This is the Stewart-Treves syndrome, where chronic lymphedema (often post-mastectomy) leads to the development of cutaneous angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Hemangioendothelioma is an intermediate-grade tumor that usually occurs in adults around medium and large veins; it is not the classic association with chronic lymphedema.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign vascular proliferation caused by Bartonella infection in immunocompromised patients.
explanations.e: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign, large vascular channels that do not show the malignant features described (pleomorphic endothelial cells).

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema post-mastectomy is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
Cutaneous angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor of {{c1::endothelial cells}}.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
The vascular channels in angiosarcoma are lined by {{c1::pleomorphic/atypical}} endothelial cells.
What is the classic immunohistochemical marker for angiosarcoma? {{c1::CD31}} (or vWF).
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant endothelial cell tumor.
Chronically lymphedematous limbs are a major risk factor.
It is aggressive with a poor 5-year survival rate.
Markers include CD31 and von Willebrand factor.
Can also occur after radiation therapy.
microReview: Angiosarcoma is a lethal vascular malignancy. Suspect it in older adults with history of radiation or chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves) presenting with enlarging purple skin nodules.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse with Kaposi sarcoma; Kaposi is HHV-8 related and usually less aggressive morphologically, whereas angiosarcoma is highly pleomorphic.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas are malignant vascular neoplasms that range from highly differentiated tumors that resemble hemangiomas to wildly anaplastic lesions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old male with a history of HIV (CD4+ count 120/mm³) presents with several painless, dark purple plaques on his lower legs and trunk. Biopsy of a lesion shows a proliferation of spindle cells forming slit-like spaces containing red blood cells, along with a chronic inflammatory infiltrate. Which of the following pathogens is the primary causative agent of these lesions?

explanations.a: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can look similar clinically but is histologically characterized by neutrophilic infiltrates.
explanations.b: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of all forms of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.c: HPV-16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx, not vascular tumors.
explanations.d: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.e: CMV can cause opportunistic infections in HIV patients but does not cause Kaposi sarcoma.

ankiCards: The causative agent of Kaposi sarcoma is {{c1::HHV-8}}.
Histologically, Kaposi sarcoma is characterized by {{c1::spindle cells}} and slit-like vascular spaces.
The most common form of Kaposi sarcoma in the United States is {{c1::AIDS-associated (epidemic)}} KS.
Kaposi sarcoma lesions typically appear as {{c1::purple/red}} patches, plaques, or nodules.
Unlike bacillary angiomatosis, Kaposi sarcoma has a {{c1::lymphocytic/mononuclear}} inflammatory infiltrate.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
HHV-8 is the essential cofactor in its pathogenesis.
Four types: Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and Epidemic (AIDS).
Histology: Spindle cells, extravasated RBCs, and slit-like spaces.
Lesions progress from patches to plaques to nodules.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Slit-like spaces + AIDS/Immunosuppression.
examinerTraps: A common trap is to provide 'Bartonella' as an option. Look for 'neutrophils' (Bartonella) vs 'lymphocytes/spindle cells' (KS) in the histology description.
sourceQuote: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) and is highly associated with AIDS.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 2-week-old infant is brought to the pediatrician due to a bright red, raised 'strawberry-like' lesion on his left cheek that has appeared since birth and is rapidly increasing in size. The parents are concerned about the cosmetic appearance. Which of the following is the most likely natural history of this lesion?

explanations.a: Port-wine stains (Nevus flammeus) tend to persist and grow with the child, but juvenile hemangiomas do not.
explanations.b: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are common in newborns; they grow rapidly for a few months but then almost always spontaneously involute by age 7 in the vast majority of cases.
explanations.c: Benign juvenile hemangiomas have no significant risk of malignant transformation.
explanations.d: These are superficial cutaneous lesions and do not invade deep structures like bone.
explanations.e: Surgical excision is rarely indicated because they regress spontaneously; recurrence is not the primary feature.

ankiCards: The 'strawberry hemangioma' of infancy is histologically a {{c1::capillary hemangioma}}.
Juvenile hemangiomas usually undergo {{c1::spontaneous regression}} by early childhood.
Capillary hemangiomas are composed of thin-walled capillaries with scant {{c1::stroma}}.
The peak age for involution of juvenile hemangiomas is usually around {{c1::7}} years.
A flat, permanent vascular birthmark is typically a {{c1::nevus flammeus (port-wine stain)}}.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangioma is the most common vascular tumor of infancy.
Usually 'strawberry' colored and raised.
Rapid initial growth followed by slow regression.
Histologically categorized as a capillary hemangioma.
Complete involution occurs in 75% to 90% of cases by age 7.
microReview: Juvenile hemangioma: Strawberry-like appearance, appears shortly after birth, rapid growth, followed by complete spontaneous regression in most cases.
examinerTraps: Confusing juvenile hemangioma (regresses) with nevus flammeus/port-wine stains (persists).
sourceQuote: Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) of the skin of newborns are very common (1 in 200 births)... they nearly always regress spontaneously.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 52-year-old male factory worker presents with abdominal pain and jaundice. Imaging reveals multiple masses in the liver. He has a 20-year history of occupational exposure to chemicals used in the manufacture of polyvinyl chloride (PVC) pipes. A liver biopsy shows malignant cells with endothelial markers. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Hepatocellular carcinoma is associated with HBV/HCV and cirrhosis, not specifically vinyl chloride.
explanations.b: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare but well-recognized complication of exposure to vinyl chloride, Thorotrast, or arsenic.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor but is not associated with chemical carcinogens.
explanations.d: Cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct cancer) is associated with Liver Flukes and PSC, not vinyl chloride.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is a bacterial-induced benign vascular lesion seen in immunocompromised hosts.

ankiCards: Exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}} is a known risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is a tumor of {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
Besides vinyl chloride, what radiological contrast agent is linked to angiosarcoma? {{c1::Thorotrast}}.
Is hepatic angiosarcoma benign or malignant? {{c1::Malignant}}.
What is the prognosis for hepatic angiosarcoma? {{c1::Very poor}}.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is rare but highly aggressive.
Occupational exposure to vinyl chloride is the classic risk factor.
Arsenic and Thorotrast are other known risk factors.
It originates from the endothelial lining of liver sinusoids.
Presents with nonspecific symptoms like weight loss and RUQ pain.
microReview: Hepatic Angiosarcoma = Vinyl Chloride + Arsenic + Thorotrast + Endothelial Malignancy.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'vinyl chloride' or 'PVC' in the stem—it's the classic trigger for hepatic angiosarcoma, whereas aflatoxin points to HCC.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas... can also be associated with specific environmental exposures, including carcinogens such as vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman in her third trimester develops a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated mass on her gingiva. The lesion bleeds easily with minor trauma. Histologic examination reveals a highly vascular proliferation resembling granulation tissue. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors are painful subungual nodules, not gingival masses in pregnancy.
explanations.b: While pyogenic granulomas are a subtype of capillary hemangioma, the term pyogenic granuloma (or granuloma gravidarum) specifically describes this 'granulation tissue-like' lesion.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) often occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum). It is benign and characterized by rapid growth and bleeding.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a malignant, pleomorphic tumor, not a benign 'granulation-like' lesion in a young pregnant patient.
explanations.e: Nevus flammeus is a flat birthmark (e.g., port-wine stain) present from birth.

ankiCards: A 'pregnancy tumor' of the gingiva is a form of {{c1::pyogenic granuloma}}.
The histological appearance of pyogenic granuloma resembles {{c1::granulation tissue}}.
Despite the name, pyogenic granulomas are neither {{c1::pyogenic}} (pus-forming) nor {{c1::granulomatous}}.
The most common site for a pyogenic granuloma is the {{c1::gingiva (or skin/mucosa)}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are often {{c1::pedunculated}} and bleed easily.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it's a capillary hemangioma variant.
Frequently occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum).
Exhibits rapid growth and bleeds easily.
Histology: Proliferation of capillaries with edema and inflammation.
Many spontaneously regress or fibrose (resembling a fibroepithelial polyp).
microReview: Pyogenic Granuloma: Rapidly growing red nodule, gingiva/skin, bleeds easily, pregnancy association, granulation tissue histology.
examinerTraps: The name 'Pyogenic Granuloma' is misleading because it has nothing to do with infection (pyogenic) or granulomas (macrophages). It is a vascular tumor.
sourceQuote: Pyogenic granulomas are capillary hemangiomas that manifest as rapidly growing red pedunculated lesions on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 30-year-old male with poorly controlled AIDS presents with several red papules on his arms. Biopsy shows a vascular proliferation with an infiltrate of neutrophils and nuclear debris (leukocytoclasis). Silver stain (Warthin-Starry) reveals clusters of bacilli. Which feature best distinguishes this lesion from Kaposi sarcoma?

options.e: Site of the lesion on the skin

explanations.a: Both lesions involve vascular/endothelial proliferations.
explanations.b: Both conditions occur primarily in HIV patients; this does not distinguish them.
explanations.c: While treatment differs, 'response to therapy' is a clinical outcome, not a distinguishing histological feature of the biopsy.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis features a neutrophilic infiltrate and the presence of bacteria, whereas Kaposi sarcoma features a lymphocytic infiltrate and HHV-8.
explanations.e: Both can occur at any skin site; location is not the primary differentiator.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by bacteria of the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
The inflammatory infiltrate in bacillary angiomatosis is primarily {{c1::neutrophilic}}.
The stain used to identify Bartonella bacilli in tissue is the {{c1::Warthin-Starry}} stain.
Unlike Kaposi sarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis is treated with {{c1::antibiotics}} (e.g., erythromycin).
Bacillary angiomatosis occurs most commonly in {{c1::immunocompromised/AIDS}} patients.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella henselae or quintana.
It mimics Kaposi sarcoma clinically (red-purple skin lesions).
Key histology: Neutrophils, leukocytoclastic debris, and bacilli.
Treatment is erythromycin or doxycycline.
Pathogenesis: Bartonella induces host tissues to release HIF-1α.
microReview: Bacillary Angiomatosis = Bartonella + AIDS + Neutrophils + Antibiotics. Kaposi = HHV-8 + AIDS + Spindle Cells + Lymphocytes.
examinerTraps: The examiner will often provide the clinical picture of AIDS and purple spots; you must check for the presence of neutrophils/bacilli (Bartonella) vs. spindle cells (Kaposi).
sourceQuote: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts... caused by opportunistic gram-negative bacilli of the Bartonella family.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An autopsy of a 60-year-old man who died of a stroke reveals a 3-cm, well-circumscribed, spongy, dark-red mass in the right lobe of the liver. Histologically, the lesion consists of large, dilated, blood-filled vascular spaces separated by a thin connective tissue stroma. No atypia is seen in the endothelial cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are composed of small, capillary-sized vessels, not large dilated spaces.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are the most common benign tumors of the liver, characterized by large, blood-filled 'cavernous' spaces.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is malignant and would show pleomorphism and an infiltrative growth pattern, not a well-circumscribed spongy mass.
explanations.d: Von Meyenburg complexes are bile duct hamartomas, which are small and cystic, not vascular.
explanations.e: Metastatic adenocarcinoma typically presents as multiple solid nodules, often with central umbilication, rather than a single vascular spongy mass.

ankiCards: The most common benign tumor of the liver is the {{c1::cavernous hemangioma}}.
Histologically, cavernous hemangiomas consist of {{c1::large, dilated vascular spaces}}.
Are cavernous hemangiomas usually symptomatic or asymptomatic? {{c1::Asymptomatic}}.
Cavernous hemangiomas of the CNS are associated with {{c1::von Hippel-Lindau disease}}.
Vascular spaces in a cavernous hemangioma are separated by thin {{c1::connective tissue/fibrous}} stroma.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are common, benign, and usually incidental findings.
The liver and spleen are frequent visceral sites.
They consist of large, thin-walled vascular channels.
Clinical significance: can be mistaken for more serious tumors on imaging.
They do not typically regress, unlike juvenile capillary hemangiomas.
microReview: Cavernous Hemangioma: Most common liver tumor, large dilated vessels, blood-filled, benign, usually found incidentally.
examinerTraps: A common mistake is thinking the most common liver tumor is HCC; in reality, the most common *benign* tumor is the cavernous hemangioma.
sourceQuote: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, dilated vascular channels... They are more common in the liver and the pancreas.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular tumors is classified as an intermediate-grade (borderline) neoplasm because it is more aggressive than a hemangioma but less predictably malignant than an angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign capillary hemangioma variant.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors are benign neoplasms of modified smooth muscle.
explanations.c: Hemangioendotheliomas, specifically the epithelioid type, are considered intermediate-grade/borderline vascular tumors.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade, fully malignant tumor.
explanations.e: Simple lymphangiomas are benign lymphatic proliferations.

ankiCards: Vascular tumors between benign and malignant are classified as {{c1::intermediate-grade (borderline)}}.
An example of an intermediate-grade vascular tumor is {{c1::hemangioendothelioma}}.
In epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, cells are often {{c1::cuboidal/epithelioid}} in shape.
Intermediate-grade tumors are characterized by {{c1::locally aggressive}} behavior.
Metastatic potential of hemangioendothelioma is roughly {{c1::20-30%}} (low to moderate).
keyPoints: Hemangioendothelioma is the classic 'borderline' vascular tumor.
Most occur in adults around medium and large veins.
Clinical course is highly variable.
They are locally aggressive and can occasionally metastasize.
The term 'epithelioid' refers to the appearance of the neoplastic endothelial cells.
microReview: Vascular Tumor Spectrum: Hemangioma (Benign) -> Hemangioendothelioma (Intermediate) -> Angiosarcoma (Malignant).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse hemangioendothelioma with hemangioma (benign) or angiosarcoma (highly malignant).
sourceQuote: Intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors... include Kaposi sarcoma and hemangioendothelioma.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old man with a history of radiation therapy for facial skin cancer 15 years ago presents with an enlarging, poorly defined, bruised-looking area on his scalp. Within the area, there are several firm, grey-white nodules. Biopsy shows an infiltrative growth of atypical endothelial cells forming rudimentary vascular channels. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Seborrheic keratosis is a 'stuck-on' benign epithelial lesion, not a vascular malignancy.
explanations.b: While KS can cause purple lesions, the history of prior radiation and the location on the scalp of an elderly man strongly favor cutaneous angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Cutaneous angiosarcoma commonly occurs on the face and scalp of elderly men, often associated with a history of prior radiation or chronic sun exposure.
explanations.d: Basal cell carcinoma is an epithelial tumor; it does not form vascular channels.
explanations.e: Pyogenic granuloma is a rapidly growing benign pedunculated lesion, not an infiltrative bruise-like area.

ankiCards: Cutaneous angiosarcoma most commonly affects the {{c1::scalp/face}} of elderly patients.
A known iatrogenic cause of angiosarcoma is prior {{c1::radiation therapy}}.
Angiosarcoma lesions often look like a simple {{c1::bruise}} initially.
Does angiosarcoma have a good or poor prognosis? {{c1::Poor}}.
Histologically, angiosarcomas demonstrate {{c1::atypical/pleomorphic}} endothelial cells.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma can be induced by prior radiation therapy.
The scalp/face is the most common site in the elderly.
Initially presents as asymptomatic red papules or 'bruises'.
Aggressive local invasion and early metastasis are common.
Tumor cells express CD31 and vWF.
microReview: Elderly man + Scalp + Prior Radiation + Bruise-like lesion = Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: The early stage of angiosarcoma looks like a bruise. The 'bruise' that does not go away in an elderly person's scalp is a major red flag.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas are most common in older adults; the scalp of elderly men is a common site.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes one of the two principal mechanisms underlying vascular disease, specifically leading to the formation of aneurysms?

options.e: Vessel wall response to sustained hypotension

explanations.a: This describes a mechanism of vascular disease (obstruction) but leads to ischemia, not aneurysm formation.
explanations.b: Progressive narrowing typically results from atherosclerosis and leads to downstream ischemia rather than dilation.
explanations.c: According to the fundamental principles of vascular pathology, weakening of vessel walls leads to dilation (aneurysms) or rupture.
explanations.d: Intimal thickening is a stereotyped response to injury that generally narrows the lumen.
explanations.e: Hypertension, not hypotension, is a major contributor to vessel wall stress and weakening.

ankiCards: What are the two principal mechanisms of vascular disease? {{c1::Luminal narrowing/obstruction}} and {{c2::wall weakening}}.
Weakening of vessel walls primarily leads to {{c1::dilation (aneurysm)}} or {{c2::rupture}}.
Obstruction of vessel lumens can occur progressively through {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Precipitous obstruction of vessel lumens is usually caused by {{c1::thrombosis}} or {{c2::embolism}}.
Vascular pathology is responsible for more {{c1::morbidity and mortality}} than any other category of human disease.
keyPoints: Vascular disease morbidity and mortality exceed all other disease categories.
Vessel narrowing (stenosis) leads to ischemia.
Wall weakening leads to dilation (aneurysm) or rupture.
Normal vessel structure must be understood to appreciate pathology.
Aneurysms represent a failure of the structural integrity of the vessel wall.
microReview: Vascular pathology is broadly divided into luminal obstruction (narrowing/blockage) and wall structural failure (aneurysm/rupture). Aneurysms specifically occur when the media is weakened.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse the mechanism of stenosis (narrowing) with the mechanism of aneurysm (weakening). While atherosclerosis can cause both, the physiological outcome of wall weakening is dilation.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male with a 40-pack-year smoking history is found to have a 5.5-cm pulsatile mass in the midline of his abdomen during a routine physical exam. Which of the following is the most significant biochemical mechanism contributing to the dilation of the vessel in this patient?

options.c: Degradation of elastin by macrophage-derived enzymes
options.d: Proliferation of medial smooth muscle cells
options.e: Activation of the transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) pathway

explanations.a: Decreased or defective fibrillin-1 (Marfan syndrome) causes aneurysms, not increased synthesis.
explanations.b: Increased (not decreased) expression of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) leads to ECM degradation in aneurysms.
explanations.c: In abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA), inflammatory infiltrates (macrophages) release MMPs that degrade elastin and collagen, weakening the wall.
explanations.d: Aneurysms are characterized by smooth muscle cell loss and medial thinning, not proliferation.
explanations.e: While TGF-β is involved in some genetic thoracic aneurysms (Loeys-Dietz), smoking-related AAA is primarily driven by atherosclerosis and inflammation.

ankiCards: The primary driver of connective tissue degradation in abdominal aortic aneurysms is {{c1::Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
Which cell type is the major source of MMPs in atherosclerotic aneurysms? {{c1::Macrophages}}.
Abdominal aortic aneurysms are most commonly associated with {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Aneurysm formation involves the degradation of {{c1::elastin}} and {{c2::collagen}} in the vessel wall.
Medial ischemia in AAA is often caused by the thickening of the {{c1::intima}} by atherosclerotic plaque.
keyPoints: AAA is highly associated with smoking and atherosclerosis.
Chronic inflammation in the media leads to ECM degradation.
MMPs (collagenases/elastases) play a central role in wall weakening.
Medial thinning occurs due to smooth muscle cell death.
Aneurysms >5cm have a significant risk of rupture.
microReview: AAA pathology: Atherosclerosis -> Intimal plaque -> Medial ischemia -> Inflammation -> Macrophage MMP release -> Elastin/Collagen degradation -> Wall weakening -> Dilation.
examinerTraps: Distinguish between AAA (atherosclerosis/MMPs/smoking) and Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (hypertension/Marfan/cystic medial necrosis).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old female with a history of Marfan syndrome presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset, sharp chest pain. Imaging reveals a dilation of the ascending aorta. Histological examination of the aortic wall would most likely show which of the following features?

options.a: Dense neutrophilic infiltrate in the adventitia
options.b: Fragmented elastic fibers and proteoglycan accumulation
options.c: Endarteritis obliterans of the vasa vasorum
options.d: Calcified atherosclerotic plaques within the media

explanations.a: Neutrophilic infiltrates are characteristic of infectious (mycotic) aneurysms, not Marfan syndrome.
explanations.b: Marfan syndrome leads to cystic medial necrosis, characterized by loss of smooth muscle cells, elastic fiber fragmentation, and accumulation of mucoid material (proteoglycans).
explanations.c: Endarteritis obliterans of the vasa vasorum is the hallmark of tertiary syphilis (syphilitic aortitis).
explanations.d: Atherosclerosis typically affects the abdominal aorta; Marfan syndrome targets the thoracic aorta through non-atherosclerotic medial weakening.
explanations.e: Granulomatous inflammation is characteristic of vasculitides like Giant Cell Arteritis or Takayasu Arteritis.

ankiCards: Marfan syndrome is caused by a mutation in the {{c1::FBN1}} gene which encodes {{c2::fibrillin-1}}.
The histological hallmark of aortic weakening in Marfan syndrome is {{c1::cystic medial necrosis}}.
Cystic medial necrosis involves the fragmentation of {{c1::elastic fibers}}.
Marfan syndrome primarily predisposes patients to {{c1::thoracic}} aortic aneurysms and dissection.
Aneurysms in Marfan syndrome are driven by overactivity of the {{c1::TGF-β}} signaling pathway.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome results in defective Fibrillin-1.
Fibrillin-1 deficiency leads to TGF-β dysregulation.
Cystic medial necrosis is the classic histological description.
Ascending aorta is the most common site of involvement in Marfan.
Thoracic aneurysms often present as sharp/tearing chest pain (especially if dissecting).
microReview: Marfan syndrome -> Fibrillin-1 defect -> TGF-β overactivity -> Cystic Medial Necrosis (media degeneration) -> Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'cystic medial necrosis' with actual necrosis; it refers to the loss of cells and mucoid accumulation, but true necrosis (as in an infarct) is not usually present.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following conditions is most closely associated with the development of a 'false aneurysm' (pseudoaneurysm)?

options.b: Congenital defect in the Circle of Willis
options.c: A post-myocardial infarction ventricular wall rupture contained by pericardium
options.d: Tertiary syphilis causing vasa vasorum damage
options.e: Marfan syndrome affecting the thoracic aorta

explanations.a: Atherosclerosis leads to true aneurysms, where all three layers of the vessel wall are dilated.
explanations.b: Berry aneurysms in the Circle of Willis are true aneurysms (though they lack some medial components).
explanations.c: A false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) occurs when a wall defect leads to an extravascular hematoma that communicates with the intravascular space; a contained rupture of the heart is a classic example.
explanations.d: Syphilitic aneurysms are true aneurysms caused by medial destruction.
explanations.e: Marfan syndrome causes true aneurysms through cystic medial necrosis.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the arterial wall (intima, media, and adventitia).
A {{c1::false (pseudo)}} aneurysm is an extravascular hematoma that communicates with the intravascular space.
A classic cause of a pseudoaneurysm is {{c1::trauma}} or {{c2::ventricular rupture}}.
Are berry aneurysms true or false aneurysms? {{c1::True}}.
Aortic dissection involves blood entering the {{c1::media}} to create a blood-filled channel.
keyPoints: True aneurysms involve all 3 layers: Intima, Media, Adventitia.
False aneurysms are hematomas contained by extravascular connective tissue.
Pseudoaneurysms often follow arterial punctures or trauma.
Fusiform aneurysms are symmetrical dilations.
Saccular aneurysms are spherical outpouchings.
microReview: True = 3 layers dilated. False = leak/hematoma contained by 'scab' or surrounding tissue. Dissection = blood *within* the wall layers.
examinerTraps: Students often mistake 'saccular' for 'false'. Saccular only refers to the shape; a saccular aneurysm can still be a true aneurysm if the wall layers are intact.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 52-year-old male presents with a persistent, non-productive cough and difficulty swallowing. Imaging reveals a large aneurysm of the aortic arch. Physical examination shows a wide-based gait and a positive Romberg sign. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism for his vascular lesion?

options.b: Ischemic injury to the media due to vasa vasorum endarteritis
options.d: Cystic medial degeneration from chronic hypertension
options.e: Infection of the vessel wall by Salmonella species

explanations.a: FBN1 mutations (Marfan) cause aneurysms but wouldn't typically present with neurosyphilis symptoms (gait/Romberg).
explanations.b: The patient has signs of tertiary syphilis (Tabes dorsalis). Syphilitic aneurysms occur because endarteritis obliterans of the vasa vasorum causes ischemic injury to the outer media of the aorta.
explanations.c: Atherosclerosis usually affects the abdominal aorta; thoracic arch involvement is less common and doesn't explain the neurological signs.
explanations.d: Hypertension is a major cause of thoracic aneurysms, but the clinical context strongly points to syphilis.
explanations.e: Salmonella causes 'mycotic' (infectious) aneurysms, usually in the abdominal aorta at the site of a plaque.

ankiCards: Tertiary syphilis characteristically causes aneurysms in the {{c1::thoracic/ascending}} aorta.
The pathological hallmark of syphilitic aortitis is {{c1::endarteritis obliterans}} of the {{c2::vasa vasorum}}.
Vasa vasorum damage in syphilis leads to ischemia of the aortic {{c1::media}}.
The 'tree-bark' appearance of the aorta is associated with {{c1::syphilitic aortitis}}.
Ischemic injury in the media from syphilis leads to {{c1::contraction/scarring}} of fibrous tissue.
keyPoints: Syphilitic aneurysms are now rare due to antibiotics.
Targets the vasa vasorum in the ascending aorta.
Leads to 'tree-barking' (intimal wrinkling from medial scarring).
Associated with neurosyphilis (Tabes dorsalis).
Can cause aortic valve insufficiency by dilating the aortic root.
microReview: Syphilis -> Endarteritis of vasa vasorum -> Medial Ischemia -> Destruction of elastic tissue -> Weakening -> Thoracic Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: The examiner uses neurological signs (wide gait) to lead you to the diagnosis of Syphilis, which then requires you to know the specific vascular mechanism.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: What term is used to describe an aneurysm that arises due to an infection of the arterial wall, often resulting in the destruction of the media?

explanations.a: Berry aneurysms are small, saccular congenital dilations in the brain.
explanations.b: Fusiform refers to the shape (circumferential dilation).
explanations.c: Mycotic aneurysms are caused by infection (bacterial, fungal, etc.) of the vessel wall, often following seeding from bacteremia or infective endocarditis.
explanations.d: Dissecting aneurysm (aorta dissection) is a tear in the intima leading to blood within the wall; it is not primarily infectious.
explanations.e: Saccular refers to the shape (asymmetrical outpouching).

ankiCards: A {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm is caused by the infection of a vessel wall.
The most common cause of a mycotic aneurysm is {{c1::bacteremia/infective endocarditis}}.
Does the term 'mycotic' always imply a fungal infection? {{c1::No (usually bacterial)}}.
Aneurysms caused by infection result in the rapid destruction of the {{c1::media}}.
An aneurysm that involves only a portion of the vessel wall circumference is called {{c1::saccular}}.
keyPoints: Mycotic aneurysms are infections of the wall.
Commonly result from septic emboli.
Frequently involve pathogens like Salmonella or Staphylococcus.
They can rupture rapidly due to acute suppuration.
The name is a misnomer; most are bacterial, not fungal.
microReview: Aneurysm names based on Shape: Saccular (pouch), Fusiform (spindle). Based on Etiology: Mycotic (infectious), Syphilitic, Atherosclerotic.
examinerTraps: Don't assume 'mycotic' means fungus. In vascular pathology, it simply means an infectious aneurysm.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 35-year-old male presents with the sudden onset of the 'worst headache of his life.' A CT scan reveals subarachnoid hemorrhage. Which of the following conditions is most strongly associated with the vascular abnormality responsible for this presentation?

explanations.a: Berry aneurysms (Circle of Willis) are the leading cause of subarachnoid hemorrhage and are strongly associated with ADPKD.
explanations.b: Mönckeberg sclerosis involves calcification of the media but does not typically lead to aneurysms or subarachnoid hemorrhage.
explanations.c: Giant cell arteritis affects large vessels like the temporal artery; it does not cause berry aneurysms.
explanations.d: Endocardial fibroelastosis is a restrictive cardiomyopathy of children, unrelated to cerebral aneurysms.
explanations.e: Hypersensitivity vasculitis affects small vessels (skin) and is not linked to berry aneurysms.

ankiCards: Berry aneurysms occur most frequently in the {{c1::Circle of Willis}}.
The most common site for a berry aneurysm is the {{c1::Anterior Communicating}} artery.
Berry aneurysms are associated with {{c1::Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD)}}.
Rupture of a berry aneurysm leads to {{c1::subarachnoid}} hemorrhage.
Berry aneurysms are caused by a {{c1::congenital}} defect in the vessel wall media.
keyPoints: Berry aneurysms are small and saccular.
Occur at arterial branch points.
Media is congenitally absent at these points.
ADPKD association is a classic high-yield board fact.
Ehlers-Danlos (Type IV) is another association.
microReview: Worst headache of life -> Subarachnoid Hemorrhage -> Berry Aneurysm -> Association with ADPKD.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'thunderclap headache' or 'worst headache' to trigger the thought of berry aneurysm rupture.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the anatomical distribution of vascular disorders based on vessel structure and function?

options.a: Atherosclerosis primarily affects small muscular venules
options.b: Aneurysms occur more frequently in veins due to thinner walls
options.c: Atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
options.d: Hypertension-induced injury is localized to large elastic veins
options.e: Structural specializations of capillaries prevent the formation of any pathology

explanations.a: Atherosclerosis is a disease of arteries, not venules.
explanations.b: Aneurysms are primarily arterial because high pressure is required to drive the dilation of a weakened wall.
explanations.c: The source text notes that structural specializations characterize vessels and that atherosclerosis mainly affects elastic and muscular arteries.
explanations.d: Hypertension affects arteries and arterioles, not veins (unless there is pulmonary hypertension).
explanations.e: Capillaries are subject to many pathologies, including microangiopathies, despite their lack of a media.

ankiCards: Atherosclerosis mainly affects {{c1::elastic}} and {{c2::muscular}} arteries.
Arterial walls are {{c1::thicker}} than corresponding veins to accommodate higher pressures.
As vessels become smaller, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}}.
Many vascular disorders have characteristic {{c1::anatomic distributions}} based on vessel type.
Vascular pathology in hypertension primarily affects {{c1::small arteries and arterioles}}.
keyPoints: Vessel architecture varies to reflect functional roles.
Arteries have higher pulsatile flow and pressure than veins.
Muscular arteries exert control over blood flow and pressure.
Atherosclerosis is specific to high-pressure arterial systems.
Distribution of disease is often vessel-type specific.
microReview: Pathology follows structure: Atherosclerosis (Large Arteries), Hypertension (Small Arteries/Arterioles), Aneurysms (Arteries).
examinerTraps: Don't assume thinner walls (veins) mean more aneurysms. Aneurysms require high pressure (arterial) acting on a weakened structure.
sourceQuote: Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 70-year-old male with long-standing hypertension presents with sudden, 'tearing' back pain. A CT scan shows a false lumen in the aorta. Which of the following is the most important prerequisite for this condition?

options.c: Complete occlusion of the aortic lumen

explanations.a: Inflammation is characteristic of vasculitis, not typically the initiating event of dissection.
explanations.b: Aortic dissection requires a weakened media (often from hypertension-induced cystic medial degeneration) to allow blood to cleave the wall layers.
explanations.c: Dissection involves the creation of a second lumen, not the occlusion of the primary one (though the second can compress the first).
explanations.d: This is an arterial pathology, unrelated to venous thrombosis.
explanations.e: An extravascular hematoma is the definition of a false aneurysm, whereas this describes a dissection (intramural hematoma).

ankiCards: The most common risk factor for aortic dissection is {{c1::hypertension}}.
Aortic dissection occurs when blood enters the {{c1::media}} through an intimal tear.
Does aortic dissection always involve a pre-existing aneurysm? {{c1::No}}.
The 'false lumen' in a dissection is located between the layers of the {{c1::media}}.
Hypertension leads to {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}} in the aorta.
keyPoints: Aortic dissection is not a 'true' aneurysm but is a related form of wall failure.
Hypertension is the #1 risk factor.
Presents with sudden 'tearing' or 'ripping' pain.
Requires an intimal tear and medial weakness.
Can lead to tamponade or organ ischemia.
microReview: Dissection = Tear in intima + weakness in media -> Blood splits media -> False lumen.
examinerTraps: Aortic dissection and Aortic aneurysm are different processes, though they both involve wall weakening. Dissection is blood *within* the wall; Aneurysm is dilation of *all* layers.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: What is the primary cellular change in the arterial media that contributes to the weakening and subsequent dilation in an atherosclerotic aneurysm?

options.d: Increased production of type I collagen
options.e: Proliferation of vasa vasorum into the intima

explanations.a: Endothelial hyperplasia is not a feature of aneurysm formation.
explanations.b: Atherosclerotic plaques cause ischemia of the underlying media by increasing the diffusion distance for oxygen, leading to smooth muscle cell death and thinning of the wall.
explanations.c: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in malignant hypertension and some vasculitides, not typically in chronic aneurysms.
explanations.d: Aneurysms involve the degradation of collagen (via MMPs), not a net increase that would strengthen the wall.
explanations.e: While vasa vasorum can proliferate, it does not explain the weakening as well as the loss of structural smooth muscle cells does.

ankiCards: Aneurysm formation in the abdominal aorta is often preceded by {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Atherosclerotic plaques cause the underlying media to undergo {{c1::pressure atrophy}} and {{c2::ischemia}}.
The loss of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} in the media is a key step in aneurysm development.
Atherosclerosis-induced medial thinning results in the loss of {{c1::structural integrity}}.
Abdominal aortic aneurysms typically occur {{c1::below/infra-}} the level of the renal arteries.
keyPoints: Atherosclerosis is the most common cause of AAA.
Plaque blocks nutrient diffusion to the media.
Medial smooth muscle cells die (atrophy).
The media becomes thin and ineffective at resisting pressure.
Dilation is the inevitable result of this structural loss.
microReview: Plaque -> Medial Ischemia -> SMC Death -> Medial Thinning -> Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: The examiner may try to focus on the 'plaque' itself (intima), but the *aneurysm* happens because of what the plaque does to the *media*.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old male with a history of advanced HIV infection (CD4+ count 120 cells/mm³) presents with multiple, painless, violaceous macules and plaques on his lower extremities and hard palate. Biopsy of a skin lesion reveals spindle-shaped cells forming slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells. Which of the following infectious agents is the primary driver of this patient's condition?

explanations.a: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not vascular spindle cell tumors.
explanations.b: Human herpesvirus 6 causes roseola infantum and is not linked to vascular malignancy.
explanations.c: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of all forms of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.d: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which mimics Kaposi sarcoma clinically but is characterized by neutrophilic infiltrates and clusters of bacteria, not malignant spindle cells.
explanations.e: Human papillomavirus 16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is caused by {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
The histological hallmark of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells forming slit-like spaces}}.
Classic Kaposi Sarcoma typically occurs in {{c1::older men of Mediterranean or Eastern European descent}}.
Endemic Kaposi Sarcoma is most frequently seen in {{c1::sub-Saharan Africa}}.
In Kaposi Sarcoma, vascular slits often contain {{c1::extravasated red blood cells}}.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
HHV-8 is the essential cofactor in its pathogenesis.
Four clinical subtypes: Classic, Endemic, Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
Progression occurs through patch, plaque, and nodular stages.
The hard palate is a common site for AIDS-associated Kaposi Sarcoma.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma presents as purple/red lesions. Histology: Spindle cells, slit-like spaces, RBCs. Pathogen: HHV-8.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Kaposi Sarcoma with Bacillary Angiomatosis; the latter is bacterial (Bartonella) and shows neutrophilic inflammation rather than spindle cells.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors are divided into three categories: (1) benign tumors, which are very common; (2) intermediate-grade tumors, which are locally aggressive but rarely metastasize; and (3) malignant tumors (angiosarcomas), which are rare.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Malignant vascular tumors arising in the liver are highly associated with specific environmental exposures. A 62-year-old former industrial worker who spent decades cleaning vats used for polymerization processes presents with weight loss and abdominal pain. Imaging shows multiple hemorrhagic hepatic masses. Biopsy confirms a high-grade malignancy of endothelial origin. Exposure to which of the following substances most likely contributed to this diagnosis?

explanations.a: Vinyl chloride is a well-documented risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma, often seen in industrial workers exposed during PVC production.
explanations.b: Asbestos exposure is linked to mesothelioma and bronchogenic carcinoma, not hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Beryllium exposure causes berylliosis and lung cancer.
explanations.d: Benzene exposure is associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.e: Naphthylamine is a risk factor for transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride, arsenic, or Thorotrast}}.
Angiosarcomas are malignant tumors of {{c1::endothelial cells}}.
The marker used to identify the endothelial origin of angiosarcomas is {{c1::CD31 (or vWF)}}.
Hepatic angiosarcoma has a {{c1::poor}} prognosis.
Cutaneous angiosarcoma can occur in the setting of chronic {{c1::lymphedema}} (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignant vascular tumor.
Hepatic site is linked to vinyl chloride and arsenic.
Often presents in older adults.
Markers include CD31 and von Willebrand factor.
Grossly appears as multicentric, fleshy, red-tan or gray-white nodules.
microReview: Angiosarcoma: Malignant, CD31 positive. Risk: Vinyl Chloride (Liver), Radiation (Breast/Skin), Chronic Lymphedema (Arm).
examinerTraps: Ensure distinction between benign hemangiomas (common, incidental) and angiosarcomas (rare, aggressive, toxin-linked).
sourceQuote: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with distinct environmental carcinogens, including arsenic (pesticides), Thorotrast (a radioactive contrast medium), and vinyl chloride.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated nodule on her gingiva. The lesion bleeds easily with minor trauma. Histologic examination reveals a circumscribed proliferation of capillaries with interspersed edema and an inflammatory infiltrate. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated vascular channels and do not typically present as rapidly growing pedunculated gingival masses.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors are exquisitely painful and usually occur subungually in the fingers.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (granuloma pyogenicum) is a rapidly growing capillary hemangioma that often occurs in the gingiva of pregnant women (pregnancy tumor).
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor with significant cytologic atypia and does not present as a benign pedunculated lesion in pregnancy.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis presents similarly but is seen in immunocompromised patients and caused by Bartonella.

ankiCards: A 'pregnancy tumor' in the gingiva is a form of {{c1::pyogenic granuloma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized by {{c1::rapid growth}} and a tendency to {{c2::bleed}} easily.
Histologically, pyogenic granuloma is a variant of {{c1::capillary hemangioma}}.
True or False: Pyogenic granulomas are neither pyogenic nor true granulomas. {{c1::True}}.
The most common location for pyogenic granuloma is the {{c1::gingiva (or skin/fingers)}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign vascular lesion.
Often follows trauma or occurs during pregnancy.
Histology shows lobulated capillary proliferation with edema.
Regression can occur spontaneously, especially postpartum.
Often referred to as Lobular Capillary Hemangioma.
microReview: Pyogenic Granuloma: Pregnancy/Trauma -> Gingiva -> Rapid red nodule -> Capillary proliferation.
examinerTraps: The name is a misnomer; it is not an infection (pyogenic) and does not contain granulomas.
sourceQuote: Pyogenic granulomas are capillary hemangiomas that manifest as rapidly growing red pedunculated lesions on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 34-year-old male presents with an intensely painful, 4-mm, blue-red nodule located under the fingernail of his right index finger. The pain is triggered by cold exposure. The lesion is excised, and pathology shows nests of uniform, round cells surrounding branching vascular channels. These tumor cells are likely derived from which of the following structures?

explanations.a: Endothelial cells line the vessels but do not form the specific nested round-cell pattern of this tumor.
explanations.b: Smooth muscle cells are found in vessel walls but are not the primary origin of glomus tumors.
explanations.c: Pericytes are related but are not the specific thermoregulatory structures associated with glomus tumors.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors arise from specialized arteriovenous thermoregulatory structures called glomus bodies.
explanations.e: Lymphatic valves are not involved in glomus tumor pathogenesis.

ankiCards: A painful subungual vascular tumor is most likely a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::glomus bodies}}.
Glomus bodies are specialized {{c1::thermoregulatory}} structures.
The pain in a glomus tumor is often triggered by {{c1::cold}}.
Histology of glomus tumor shows {{c1::nests of uniform round cells}} around vessels.
keyPoints: Glomus tumor (glomangioma) is benign but extremely painful.
Classic location is subungual (under the nail).
Cells are uniform, round, and resemble smooth muscle.
Pain is out of proportion to the lesion size.
Cure is achieved by simple excision.
microReview: Glomus Tumor: Finger nail + Severe pain + Cold sensitivity = Glomus body origin.
examinerTraps: Confusing glomus tumor with a simple hemangioma; the key differentiator is the intense pain and specific subungual location.
sourceQuote: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, exquisitely painful tumors arising from specialized smooth muscle cells of glomus bodies.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which clinical variant of Kaposi Sarcoma is characterized by an indolent course, occurrence in older men of Mediterranean or Eastern European descent, and remains localized to the skin without initial visceral involvement?

explanations.a: Endemic African KS occurs in younger individuals and can be much more aggressive, especially in children (lymphadenopathic form).
explanations.b: Classic Kaposi sarcoma fits the description of an indolent, cutaneous disease in older men of specific European/Mediterranean ancestry.
explanations.c: Transplant-associated KS occurs due to T-cell immunosuppression and often regresses if immunosuppression is reduced.
explanations.d: AIDS-associated KS is the most common HIV-related malignancy and frequently involves viscera early.
explanations.e: Iatrogenic KS is another term for transplant-associated or medication-induced immunosuppression variants.

ankiCards: The four variants of Kaposi Sarcoma are {{c1::Classic, Endemic, Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated}}.
Classic Kaposi Sarcoma is typically {{c1::indolent}}.
Classic Kaposi Sarcoma is most common in {{c1::older men of Mediterranean/Eastern European descent}}.
Classic Kaposi Sarcoma is generally {{c1::not}} associated with HIV infection.
Wait-and-watch or local therapy is often sufficient for the {{c1::Classic}} variant of KS.
keyPoints: Classic KS is the 'original' description of the disease.
Strongly associated with HHV-8 but not HIV.
Presents as multiple red-purple skin plaques/nodules on distal lower extremities.
Visceral involvement is rare (less than 10%).
The disease course is very slow, and patients usually die of other causes.
microReview: Classic KS = Old Mediterranean Men + Leg lesions + HHV-8 + Indolent.
examinerTraps: The examiner may try to link all KS to HIV; remember that Classic and Endemic types can occur in HIV-negative patients.
sourceQuote: Classic Kaposi sarcoma... occurs in older men of Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, or Eastern European descent... typically an indolent course.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 10-month-old infant is brought to the clinic due to a large, bright red, 'strawberry-like' lesion on the scalp. The parents report it was a tiny red dot at birth but grew rapidly over several months. On examination, it is soft and blanches slightly. What is the most likely natural history of this lesion?

options.c: Permanent persistence and growth with the child
options.e: Progression to a high-flow arteriovenous malformation

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are benign and almost never undergo malignant transformation.
explanations.b: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are very common in infants; they grow rapidly but typically undergo spontaneous regression by age 5-7.
explanations.c: These lesions do not persist permanently; 75-90% are gone by age 7.
explanations.d: Strawberry hemangiomas are capillary, not cavernous; they do not 'become' cavernous.
explanations.e: Hemangiomas are low-flow lesions and do not transform into high-flow AVMs.

ankiCards: A 'strawberry hemangioma' of infancy is technically a {{c1::juvenile capillary hemangioma}}.
The natural history of juvenile hemangiomas involves {{c1::rapid growth}} followed by {{c2::spontaneous regression}}.
Most juvenile hemangiomas regress by age {{c1::7}}.
Juvenile hemangiomas are composed of {{c1::closely packed capillaries}}.
Histologically, these lesions show {{c1::thin-walled capillaries}} with scant stroma.
keyPoints: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are extremely common neonatally.
Incidence: 1 in 200 births.
Often multiple.
Growth occurs in the first few months.
Regression starts by age 1-3 years.
microReview: Strawberry Hemangioma: Baby + Rapid growth + Scalp/Face -> Spontaneous regression.
examinerTraps: Avoid recommending aggressive surgery or radiation; the standard of care is often observation due to high regression rates.
sourceQuote: Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) of the newborn skin are very common (1 in 200 births)... they grow rapidly for a few months but then fade and regress by age 1 to 3 years.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Cystic hygromas are large, dilated lymphatic spaces typically found in the neck or axilla of infants. These lesions are frequently associated with which of the following chromosomal abnormalities?

explanations.a: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is associated with AV canal defects, not specifically cystic hygromas.
explanations.b: 47, XXY (Klinefelter syndrome) is associated with male hypogonadism.
explanations.c: Cystic hygroma is a hallmark finding in Turner syndrome (45, X) due to abnormal lymphatic development.
explanations.d: Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome) is associated with rocker-bottom feet and micrognathia.
explanations.e: Deletion 22q11 (DiGeorge syndrome) is associated with interrupted aortic arch and truncus arteriosus.

ankiCards: A cystic hygroma is a type of {{c1::cavernous lymphangioma}}.
Cystic hygromas are most commonly located in the {{c1::neck (or axilla)}}.
Cystic hygroma in a fetus is highly associated with {{c1::Turner syndrome (45,X)}}.
