Histologically, lymphangiomas lack {{c1::red blood cells}} in their lumens.
Lymphangiomas are lined by {{c1::endothelial cells}}.
keyPoints: Cystic hygromas are benign but can be large and disfiguring.
Characterized by massively dilated lymphatic spaces.
They occur in the neck, axilla, or retroperitoneum.
Associated with Turner Syndrome and some trisomies.
Difficult to resect completely because they lack a capsule.
microReview: Cystic Hygroma: Infant + Neck mass + 45,X (Turner) = Lymphangioma.
examinerTraps: Confusing lymphangioma with cavernous hemangioma; check the lumen for RBCs (present in hemangioma, absent in lymphangioma).
sourceQuote: Cystic hygromas (cavernous lymphangiomas) occur in the neck or axilla of children and are often associated with Turner syndrome.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the 'patch' stage in the morphological progression of Kaposi Sarcoma?

options.a: Large, fleshy masses with widespread hemorrhage
options.b: Raised, purple, firm plaques with dermal spindle cells
options.c: Flat, red-to-pink macules with dilated vascular spaces lined by thin endothelium
options.d: Ulcerated nodules with high mitotic activity and necrosis
options.e: Deep, infiltrative tumors with abundant slit-like spaces

explanations.a: This describes the nodular or late stage of KS or potentially angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: This describes the plaque stage of KS.
explanations.c: The patch stage consists of flat macules that appear histologically as dilated, irregular vascular spaces lined by inconspicuous endothelial cells.
explanations.d: This describes advanced nodular KS.
explanations.e: Infiltrative tumors with slit-like spaces define the nodular stage.

ankiCards: The three stages of Kaposi Sarcoma evolution are {{c1::patch, plaque, and nodule}}.
In the patch stage of KS, vascular spaces are lined by {{c1::thin/inconspicuous}} endothelium.
Extravasated RBCs and hemosiderin-laden macrophages are seen in the {{c1::plaque (and nodular)}} stage.
The stage of KS showing sheets of spindle cells is the {{c1::nodular}} stage.
Mitotic figures and 'hyaline globules' are most common in the {{c1::nodular}} stage of KS.
keyPoints: KS progression is predictable: Patch -> Plaque -> Nodule.
Patch: Macular, looks like granulation tissue.
Plaque: Elevated, more spindle cells, slit-like spaces.
Nodule: Fleshy, spindle cell sheets, hemorrhage.
Markers of KS cells include CD31 and podoplanin.
microReview: KS Stages: Patch (Flat/Vessels) -> Plaque (Raised/Spindle cells) -> Nodule (Tumor/Sheets).
examinerTraps: The patch stage can be misdiagnosed as simple granulation tissue because it lacks the classic spindle cell sheets seen in the nodular stage.
sourceQuote: Lesions typically progress through three stages: patches, plaques, and nodules... Patches are red-to-purple macules; histologically, they show dilated vascular spaces lined by endothelial cells.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with several dark-purple, firm skin nodules on her left arm. Ten years ago, she underwent a radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection and radiation for breast cancer. Since the surgery, she has had chronic, massive lymphedema of that arm. What is the most likely diagnosis for these new skin nodules?

explanations.a: While possible, the history of chronic lymphedema specifically points to a secondary vascular malignancy.
explanations.b: Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema, classically after radical mastectomy.
explanations.c: Lymphangiomyomatosis is a rare lung disease involving smooth muscle-like cells.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is infectious and seen in the immunocompromised, not specifically linked to lymphedema.
explanations.e: Cavernous lymphangiomas are benign congenital lesions, not aggressive nodules appearing in an adult.

ankiCards: Stewart-Treves syndrome is defined as {{c1::angiosarcoma}} arising in chronic {{c2::lymphedema}}.
The classic clinical scenario for Stewart-Treves is post-{{c1::mastectomy (with lymph node dissection)}}.
Angiosarcomas are {{c1::highly}} aggressive malignancies.
Angiosarcoma cells are stained by the vascular marker {{c1::CD31}}.
Five-year survival for angiosarcoma is approximately {{c1::30}}%.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a malignant endothelial tumor.
Risk factors: Radiation, chronic lymphedema, chemical toxins.
Most commonly affects skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Lymphedema-associated angiosarcoma usually occurs ~10 years post-surgery.
Poorly defined, hemorrhagic nodules are characteristic.
microReview: Stewart-Treves: Post-mastectomy + Lymphedema + Purple nodules = Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: The nodules can be mistaken for simple bruising or radiation dermatitis; however, their persistence and growth in a lymphedematous limb are highly suspicious.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcoma can also occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema, typically in the ipsilateral arm several years after radical mastectomy... (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 50-year-old patient presents with multiple cutaneous lesions that are histologically indistinguishable from Kaposi Sarcoma, appearing as capillary proliferations with prominent epithelioid endothelial cells and neutrophilic infiltrates. The patient is HIV-positive. Warthin-Starry silver stain of the biopsy shows clusters of tangled bacilli. Which organism is responsible for this condition?

explanations.a: HHV-8 causes Kaposi Sarcoma, but KS does not contain bacterial clusters on Warthin-Starry stain.
explanations.b: MAC causes systemic infections but not this specific vascular proliferation.
explanations.c: Bartonella henselae (or B. quintana) causes bacillary angiomatosis, which mimics KS but is treated with antibiotics (erythromycin).
explanations.d: Tropheryma whipplei causes Whipple disease, characterized by PAS-positive macrophages in the GI tract.
explanations.e: Treponema pallidum causes syphilis; while it involves vessels (endarteritis), it does not cause vascular tumors.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by {{c1::Bartonella henselae (or B. quintana)}}.
The histological stain used to see Bartonella is {{c1::Warthin-Starry (silver stain)}}.
Bacillary angiomatosis is primarily seen in {{c1::immunocompromised (HIV)}} patients.
Unlike Kaposi Sarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis contains prominent {{c1::neutrophils}}.
The drug of choice for bacillary angiomatosis is {{c1::erythromycin (or doxycycline)}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation, not a true neoplasm.
Caused by opportunistic Bartonella infection.
Induces host HIF-1α, which stimulates VEGF production.
Clinically mimics Kaposi Sarcoma (red/purple skin nodules).
Microscopy shows 'nuclear dust' (neutrophilic debris) and bacteria.
microReview: Bacillary Angiomatosis: HIV + Red nodules + Neutrophils + Silver stain (Bartonella).
examinerTraps: Look for 'neutrophils' or 'silver stain/bacilli' in the stem to differentiate from Kaposi Sarcoma.
sourceQuote: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts... caused by opportunistic gram-negative bacilli of the Bartonella family.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history and long-standing hypertension presents for a routine physical examination. On palpation of the abdomen, a prominent, pulsatile mass is felt at the level of the umbilicus. He is asymptomatic, and his blood pressure is 155/95 mmHg. Imaging confirms a 5.2 cm dilation of the infrarenal abdominal aorta. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism responsible for the development of this condition?

options.b: Infiltration by inflammatory cells and proteolytic degradation
options.d: Mutation in the TGF-β receptor signaling pathway
options.e: Deposition of hyaline material in the arteriolar wall

explanations.a: Cystic medial degeneration is more commonly associated with thoracic aortic aneurysms, particularly in the setting of connective tissue disorders like Marfan syndrome, rather than infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysms.
explanations.b: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are primarily driven by atherosclerosis and chronic inflammation. Inflammatory cells (macrophages and lymphocytes) infiltrate the vessel wall, releasing matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) that degrade elastin and collagen, weakening the wall.
explanations.c: Endarteritis of the vasa vasorum is the hallmark of tertiary syphilis, which classically leads to thoracic (ascending) aortic aneurysms, not infrarenal aneurysms.
explanations.d: Mutations in the TGF-β signaling pathway are associated with Loeys-Dietz syndrome, which typically presents with thoracic aneurysms and arterial tortuosity.
explanations.e: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is a feature of benign hypertension typically seen in small arteries and arterioles, not large elastic arteries like the aorta.

ankiCards: The primary mechanism of abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) involves the degradation of {{c1::elastin and collagen}} by matrix metalloproteinases.
Risk factors for AAA include smoking, male sex, and {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
The most common location for an abdominal aortic aneurysm is {{c1::infrarenal}}.
A pulsatile abdominal mass in an older male smoker is highly suggestive of {{c1::abdominal aortic aneurysm}}.
Aneurysms result from the {{c1::weakening}} of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture.
keyPoints: AAA is most common in male smokers over age 60.
The infrarenal aorta is the most common site due to reduced vasa vasorum in this segment.
Inflammatory infiltrates lead to increased proteolytic activity (MMPs).
Surgical repair is typically indicated when the diameter exceeds 5.0–5.5 cm.
Atherosclerosis is the major predisposing factor for AAA.
microReview: Aneurysms involve all three layers of the vessel wall (true) or a hematoma communicating with the lumen (false). AAA is primarily an atherosclerotic and inflammatory process of the infrarenal aorta.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse the mechanism of AAA (inflammation/MMPs/atherosclerosis) with Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (cystic medial degeneration/syphilis/Marfan).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following fundamental structural characteristics explains why arterial walls are thicker than corresponding venous walls at the same level of branching?

options.a: Higher density of vasa vasorum in the tunica media
options.b: Requirement to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher pressures
options.c: Presence of a thicker tunica adventitia in arteries
options.d: Absence of valves to prevent retrograde flow
options.e: Higher concentration of myofibroblasts in the intima

explanations.a: Veins actually tend to have more vasa vasorum deeper in their walls compared to arteries because venous blood is deoxygenated and under low pressure.
explanations.b: As specified in the principles of vascular structure, arterial walls are thicker to accommodate the high-pressure pulsatile flow generated by the heart.
explanations.c: In many vessels, especially large veins like the vena cava, the tunica adventitia is actually the thickest layer; in arteries, the media is usually most prominent.
explanations.d: Valves are a feature of veins, but their presence does not dictate the relative thickness of the arterial wall compared to the venous wall.
explanations.e: The intima is normally thin; a high concentration of cells there usually indicates a pathologic response to injury (intimal thickening).

ankiCards: Arterial walls are thicker than veins to accommodate {{c1::pulsatile flow}} and high pressures.
As arteries become smaller, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}}.
The two principal mechanisms of vascular disease are narrowing and {{c1::weakening of walls}}.
In terms of architecture, the arterial wall layer that is most prominent is the {{c1::tunica media}}.
Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity than any other {{c1::category of human disease}}.
keyPoints: Arteries have thicker walls than veins for pressure management.
Wall thickness to lumen diameter ratio increases in smaller muscular arteries.
The tunica media contains the smooth muscle and elastic fibers essential for vascular tone.
Vascular disease involves either luminal obstruction or wall weakening.
Structural specializations of vessels reflect their distinct functional roles.
microReview: The cardiovascular system requires specialized vessel structures; arteries are built for pressure (thick media), while veins are built for volume/capacitance (thinner walls, valves).
examinerTraps: The examiner may suggest that veins have thicker walls because they carry more volume; however, arteries always have thicker walls to resist bursting under high systolic pressure.
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following mechanisms is defined by a complete obstruction of a vessel lumen that occurs precipitously, rather than progressively?

explanations.a: Atherosclerosis is a progressive narrowing of the vessel lumen over years or decades.
explanations.b: Intimal thickening is a stereotyped response to vascular injury that occurs over time as cells migrate and proliferate.
explanations.c: Vessel obstruction can occur progressively (atherosclerosis) or precipitously (thrombosis or embolism).
explanations.d: Cystic medial necrosis leads to wall weakening and dilation (aneurysm), not acute luminal obstruction.
explanations.e: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is a slow, progressive thickening of arteriolar walls in the setting of chronic hypertension or diabetes.

ankiCards: Precipitous obstruction of a vessel lumen is usually caused by {{c1::thrombosis or embolism}}.
Progressive narrowing of a vessel lumen is classically caused by {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
The two mechanisms of vascular disease are {{c1::narrowing/obstruction}} and wall weakening.
Weakening of vessel walls leads to either {{c1::dilation or rupture}}.
The architectural layer responsible for controlling flow and pressure in muscular vessels is the {{c1::tunica media}}.
keyPoints: Vascular diseases are categorized by obstruction or wall weakening.
Precipitous events (thrombosis) cause acute ischemia.
Progressive events (atherosclerosis) cause chronic ischemia.
Wall weakening results in aneurysms or dissections.
Aneurysms can lead to rupture, a life-threatening complication.
microReview: Vascular pathology causes morbidity through two main pathways: lumen narrowing (ischemia) and wall weakening (aneurysms/dissection).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'progressive' nature of the underlying plaque with the 'precipitous' nature of the superimposed thrombus.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism)
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of severe chest pain that radiates to her back between the shoulder blades. She is 6 feet 2 inches tall with long, slender fingers and a history of joint hypermobility. Physical examination reveals a high-arched palate and pectus excavatum. An urgent echocardiogram shows a dilated ascending aorta and a thin intimal flap. Which of the following is the most likely biochemical defect in this patient?

explanations.a: Type I collagen defects cause Osteogenesis Imperfecta (brittle bones, blue sclera), not typically aortic root dilation.
explanations.b: The patient has Marfan syndrome (tall stature, arachnodactyly, aortic root dilation). This is caused by mutations in Fibrillin-1, a scaffold for elastin, leading to cystic medial degeneration.
explanations.c: Lysyl oxidase deficiency (or copper deficiency) can lead to Menkes disease or impaired cross-linking, but is not the classic cause of Marfanoid habitus.
explanations.d: Type III collagen deficiency is seen in Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. While it causes arterial rupture, Marfan syndrome (Fibrillin-1) is the classic association for this phenotype.
explanations.e: LDL receptor defects cause familial hypercholesterolemia, leading to premature atherosclerosis and AAA, not the Marfanoid phenotype seen here.

ankiCards: Marfan syndrome is caused by a mutation in {{c1::Fibrillin-1}}.
The classic aortic pathology in Marfan syndrome is {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
Thoracic aortic aneurysms in young patients often suggest {{c1::Marfan syndrome}}.
Aortic dissection is characterized by an {{c1::intimal flap}} on imaging.
The scaffolding protein essential for elastic fibers in the aorta is {{c1::fibrillin}}.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome causes thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections.
Cystic medial degeneration involves the loss of smooth muscle and elastic fibers.
Fibrillin-1 mutations lead to excessive TGF-β signaling.
Clinical signs include arachnodactyly, tall stature, and lens luxation.
The ascending aorta is the most common site for aneurysms in Marfan patients.
microReview: Marfan syndrome (Fibrillin-1) and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (Collagen) are the two major genetic connective tissue disorders leading to aneurysms/dissections.
examinerTraps: Distinguish between AAA (atherosclerosis-driven, older smokers) and TAA/Dissection (genetic/hypertension-driven, often younger in genetic cases).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old male is found to have a fusiform dilation of the abdominal aorta. Histological examination of the wall would likely show that the lesion involves which of the following layers of the vessel?

explanations.a: Isolated intimal lesions are typical of early atherosclerosis, not true aneurysms.
explanations.b: Adventitia only would not constitute a true aneurysm, which involves the entire wall structure.
explanations.c: A true aneurysm must involve all three layers of the vessel wall.
explanations.d: By definition, a 'true' aneurysm involves an intact but attenuated wall consisting of all three layers: intima, media, and adventitia.
explanations.e: A true aneurysm must include the intima as the innermost boundary of the dilated lumen.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the arterial wall.
A {{c1::false (pseudoaneurysm)}} aneurysm is a wall defect leading to an extravascular hematoma.
Aneurysms are classified by shape into {{c1::saccular and fusiform}}.
Fusiform aneurysms involve {{c1::circumferential}} dilation of the vessel.
Saccular aneurysms are {{c1::spherical}} outpouchings involving only a portion of the vessel wall.
keyPoints: True aneurysms: Intima + Media + Adventitia.
Pseudoaneurysm: Extravascular hematoma communicating with the lumen.
Fusiform: Symmetric dilation.
Saccular: Asymmetric, pouch-like.
Atherosclerosis is the most common cause of AAA.
microReview: True aneurysms (AAA, saccular berry) involve all wall layers. False aneurysms (pseudoaneurysms) are actually organized hematomas leaking through a wall defect.
examinerTraps: Be careful with 'Dissection'—it is not an aneurysm (dilation) but blood tracking *within* the wall layers.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following classes of vessels is characterized by the highest ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter, primarily to exert control over blood pressure and flow?

explanations.a: Large elastic arteries have thick walls, but their lumens are also very large, keeping the ratio lower than in resistance vessels.
explanations.b: Veins have thin walls and large lumens, resulting in a low ratio.
explanations.c: As arterial wall thickness diminishes in smaller vessels, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter actually increases, allowing muscular control of pressure.
explanations.d: Capillaries consist only of an endothelial layer and basement membrane, lacking a muscular wall.
explanations.e: Post-capillary venules are thin-walled and primarily involved in nutrient exchange and leukocyte extravasation.

ankiCards: The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}} as arteries become smaller.
Resistance to blood flow is primarily controlled by {{c1::arterioles}}.
Small muscular vessels exert control over {{c1::blood flow and pressure}}.
Elastic and muscular arteries are the main targets of {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Structure-function specialization means arterial walls are {{c1::thicker}} than venous walls.
keyPoints: Arteries are thicker than veins.
Arterioles have the highest wall-to-lumen ratio.
This structure allows for high resistance (TPR control).
Atherosclerosis affects elastic and muscular arteries preferentially.
Vascular pathology is vessel-type specific.
microReview: The high wall-to-lumen ratio of arterioles makes them the primary site of total peripheral resistance (TPR) and blood pressure regulation.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'thickest wall' (Aorta) with 'highest wall-to-lumen ratio' (Arterioles).
sourceQuote: Arterial wall thickness gradually diminishes as the vessels become smaller, but the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing these muscular vessels to exert control over blood flow and pressure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the categorization of vascular disease, which of the following is the most clinically significant mechanism leading to morbidity and mortality?

options.c: Vascular wall weakening and luminal narrowing

explanations.a: While common and 'not inconsequential', venous disorders are less significant than arterial lesions.
explanations.b: Lymphatic disorders cause morbidity but are not the leading cause of vascular-related mortality.
explanations.c: The two principal mechanisms underlying the most significant vascular diseases are luminal narrowing (stenosis/obstruction) and wall weakening (dilation/rupture).
explanations.d: Myocardial vasospasm (Raynaud phenomenon equivalent) is specific and less common than general atherosclerosis.
explanations.e: Most vascular tumors are benign (e.g., hemangiomas) and do not represent the bulk of vascular morbidity.

ankiCards: The leading category of human disease causing morbidity and mortality is {{c1::vascular pathology}}.
Two principal mechanisms of vascular disease: {{c1::narrowing}} and {{c1::weakening}}.
Atherosclerosis primarily causes {{c1::narrowing/stenosis}}.
Aneurysms primarily result from wall {{c1::weakening}}.
The most clinically significant vascular lesions involve {{c1::arteries}}.
keyPoints: Vascular pathology is the top cause of human mortality.
Arterial lesions are more significant than venous ones.
Obstruction can be acute (thrombosis) or chronic (atherosclerosis).
Wall weakening leads to rupture (emergency).
Structure dictates which vessels are affected by which diseases.
microReview: Vascular pathology = Obstruction (ischemia/infarction) OR Weakening (aneurysm/rupture). Arteries are the high-stakes players.
examinerTraps: The examiner may list venous disease as the most common; while common, it is rarely the most 'clinically significant' in terms of mortality compared to arterial disease.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 75-year-old male with long-standing poorly controlled hypertension dies from a massive intra-abdominal hemorrhage. Autopsy reveals a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm. Which of the following describes a key step in the pathogenesis of the aneurysm wall weakening?

options.c: Loss of smooth muscle cells due to chronic ischemia of the media
options.e: Transformation of endothelium into smooth muscle cells

explanations.a: Aneurysms involve the degradation and loss of elastin, not increased synthesis.
explanations.b: MMP activity is increased, not suppressed, leading to matrix degradation.
explanations.c: Atherosclerotic thickening of the intima increases the diffusion distance for oxygen, leading to ischemia of the inner media. This causes smooth muscle cell loss and wall weakening.
explanations.d: The adventitia does not typically hypertrophy; the entire wall usually becomes attenuated and thin.
explanations.e: Endothelium does not transform into smooth muscle; rather, smooth muscle cells migrate into the intima in response to injury.

ankiCards: Atherosclerosis causes medial ischemia by increasing the {{c1::diffusion distance}} for oxygen.
Aneurysm formation is associated with the {{c1::loss}} of smooth muscle cells in the media.
Inflammatory cells in AAA secrete {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
The infrarenal aorta is susceptible to AAA because it has fewer {{c1::vasa vasorum}}.
Hypertension contributes to aneurysms by increasing {{c1::wall stress}}.
keyPoints: Medial ischemia is a core driver of AAA.
Ischemia results from thickened intima (atherosclerosis).
Smooth muscle cell loss leads to structural failure.
Proteolytic enzymes (MMPs) degrade the extracellular matrix.
Hypertension exacerbates the wall weakening.
microReview: AAA Pathogenesis: Atherosclerosis -> Intimal thickening -> Medial Ischemia -> Smooth Muscle Death + MMP-driven Elastolysis -> Wall Weakening -> Dilation.
examinerTraps: Watch for 'increased collagen'—while some scarring occurs, the net effect is a loss of structural integrity (elastin degradation).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old man with a history of Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) presents to the emergency department with the 'worst headache of his life.' Physical examination shows nuchal rigidity. A CT scan of the head reveals blood in the subarachnoid space. This patient's condition is most likely caused by which type of aneurysm?

explanations.a: Fusiform aneurysms are usually larger and found in the aorta or iliac arteries, not the Circle of Willis.
explanations.b: Saccular (berry) aneurysms are the most common cause of non-traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage and are strongly associated with ADPKD.
explanations.c: Mycotic aneurysms result from infection of the vessel wall, typically from septic emboli.
explanations.d: Aortic dissection (sometimes called a dissecting aneurysm, though technically different) involves a tear in the intima, not a saccular outpouching.
explanations.e: A false aneurysm is a pulsating hematoma; berry aneurysms are true aneurysms.

ankiCards: Berry aneurysms are most commonly found in the {{c1::Circle of Willis}}.
The most common site for a berry aneurysm is the {{c1::anterior communicating}} artery junction.
ADPKD is a major risk factor for {{c1::saccular (berry)}} aneurysms.
Subarachnoid hemorrhage presents classically as a {{c1::'thunderclap' headache}}.
Berry aneurysms lack a {{c1::tunica media}} at the site of the lesion.
keyPoints: Berry aneurysms are saccular.
Associated with ADPKD, Ehlers-Danlos, and hypertension.
Occur at branch points in the Circle of Willis.
Rupture causes subarachnoid hemorrhage.
They are 'true' aneurysms but lack internal elastic lamina/media at the neck.
microReview: Saccular (Berry) Aneurysm + ADPKD = Subarachnoid Hemorrhage. These are small, spherical, and occur in the cerebral circulation.
examinerTraps: The 'dissecting aneurysm' label is often used colloquially for aortic dissection, but berry aneurysms are saccular and true.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the difference between a true aneurysm and a false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm)?

options.a: True aneurysms involve only the intima; false involve all layers.
options.b: True aneurysms are always fusiform; false are always saccular.
options.c: True aneurysms have an intact attenuated wall; false involve a wall defect with an extravascular hematoma.
options.d: True aneurysms result from infection; false result from atherosclerosis.
options.e: True aneurysms are found in arteries; false are found only in veins.

explanations.a: True aneurysms must involve all three layers (intima, media, adventitia).
explanations.b: Shape (fusiform/saccular) does not determine whether an aneurysm is true or false.
explanations.c: A true aneurysm is a dilation where all layers are present (though potentially thin). A false aneurysm is a leak through the wall that is contained by extravascular tissue (e.g., pericardium or fascia).
explanations.d: Atherosclerosis and infection can both cause true or false aneurysms.
explanations.e: Both types can be found in arteries, though arterial pseudoaneurysms are a common complication of vascular procedures.

ankiCards: A {{c1::pseudoaneurysm}} is a hematoma that communicates with the intravascular space.
A {{c1::true}} aneurysm has an attenuated but intact arterial wall.
A common cause of pseudoaneurysm is {{c1::trauma or vascular intervention}}.
Ventricular rupture post-MI contained by pericardium is a {{c1::false}} aneurysm.
Aneurysms and dissections are both results of {{c1::vascular wall}} pathology.
keyPoints: True aneurysm = 3 layers.
False aneurysm = leak + contained hematoma.
False aneurysms are often called pseudoaneurysms.
Common after femoral artery catheterization.
Rupture risk depends on size and wall tension (Laplace Law).
microReview: True = Dilation of all wall layers. False = Hole in the wall with a pocket of blood on the outside.
examinerTraps: An aortic dissection is sometimes confused with a pseudoaneurysm; however, dissection is blood *between* layers, not a pocket *outside* all layers.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 74-year-old male of Mediterranean descent presents with several asymptomatic, slowly enlarging, purple-red macules and plaques on his lower extremities. He has no significant history of immunosuppression. A skin biopsy reveals a proliferation of spindle cells forming slit-like spaces containing red blood cells, accompanied by a chronic inflammatory infiltrate. Which of the following infectious agents is most likely associated with this patient's condition?

explanations.a: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with various lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, but not vascular tumors like Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.b: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent in all forms of Kaposi sarcoma, including the classic European form described here.
explanations.c: Cytomegalovirus is a common opportunistic infection in immunocompromised patients but does not cause primary vascular neoplasms.
explanations.d: Human papillomavirus 16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx.
explanations.e: Hepatitis C virus is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma and mixed cryoglobulinemia, not spindle-cell vascular tumors.

ankiCards: Classic (European) Kaposi sarcoma is most common in elderly men of {{c1::Mediterranean}} descent.
The causative agent for all forms of Kaposi sarcoma is {{c1::Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}.
Histologically, Kaposi sarcoma presents as {{c1::spindle}} cells with slit-like spaces containing {{c2::red blood cells}}.
Kaposi sarcoma in AIDS patients is often more {{c1::aggressive}} than the classic form.
The slit-like vascular spaces in Kaposi sarcoma are created by proliferating {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma is a borderline (intermediate) vascular tumor.
Four clinical forms exist: Classic, Endemic African, Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
HHV-8 is the essential cofactor for development.
Classic form is typically indolent and localized to the skin of the lower extremities.
Biopsy shows spindle-shaped cells and extravasated erythrocytes.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Slit-like RBC spaces. Classic form = Older Mediterranean men. AIDS form = Most common HIV-related malignancy.
examinerTraps: The examiner may confuse Kaposi sarcoma with Bacillary Angiomatosis; look for 'spindle cells' and 'HHV-8' for KS, vs 'neutrophils' and 'Bartonella' for BA.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors are common and range from benign hemangiomas to intermediate-grade (borderline) lesions to highly malignant angiosarcomas.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A pathology resident is reviewing a slide of a vascular lesion. The specimen shows thin-walled, dilated vascular channels filled with blood and separated by a scant connective tissue stroma. The resident notes that these lesions do not typically regress and can occur in deep visceral organs. What is the most likely classification of this lesion?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas consist of small, thin-walled capillaries and often spontaneously regress, unlike cavernous types.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated vascular channels (caverns). They are frequently deep-seated, do not regress, and can be part of Von Hippel-Lindau disease.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granulomas are lobular capillary hemangiomas that often occur on the gingiva or skin and are prone to bleeding.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious-induced vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts, characterized by neutrophils and bacteria.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are small, painful lesions arising from modified smooth muscle cells, usually subungual.

ankiCards: {{c1::Cavernous}} hemangiomas are composed of large, blood-filled vascular spaces.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas frequently involve {{c1::deep visceral}} organs (e.g., liver).
Cavernous hemangiomas of the cerebellum or retina are associated with {{c1::Von Hippel-Lindau}} disease.
Histologically, cavernous hemangiomas show channels separated by {{c1::connective tissue}} stroma.
Do cavernous hemangiomas typically regress spontaneously? {{c1::No}}.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are large, blood-filled spaces.
They are more likely than capillary hemangiomas to occur in the liver or CNS.
Clinically significant if they compress structures or rupture (especially in the brain).
Vascular channels are separated by fibrous stroma and lined by flat endothelium.
They do not undergo spontaneous regression.
microReview: Cavernous = Large vessels, deep/visceral, no regression. Capillary = Small vessels, skin, frequent regression.
examinerTraps: Watch for the mention of the liver or brain; these are classic sites for cavernous hemangiomas that may cause secondary complications.
sourceQuote: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, dilated vascular channels... they are more frequently deep-seated than capillary hemangiomas.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following cell types serves as the origin for the exquisitely painful, small, blue nodules typically found under the fingernails?

explanations.a: While present in the vessel lining, endothelial cells are not the primary proliferating cell in a glomus tumor.
explanations.b: Pericytes are associated with hemangiopericytomas (now classified differently) but not the painful subungual glomus tumor.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts produce collagen but are not the source of these vascular-derived tumors.
explanations.e: Adipocytes are the source of lipomas, which are painless fat tumors.

ankiCards: Glomus tumors arise from the {{c1::glomus body}}, which regulates temperature.
The specific cell of origin for a glomus tumor is the {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cell.
A classic clinical location for a glomus tumor is the {{c1::subungual (under nail)}} region.
Glomus tumors are characterized by the symptom of {{c1::exquisite pain}}.
The color of a glomus tumor nodule is typically {{c1::blue}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but very painful.
Most common in the distal portion of digits, particularly under the nails.
The glomus body is an arteriovenous shunt.
Histology shows nests of uniform round cells (glomus cells).
Excision is curative.
microReview: Glomus tumor = Subungual + Extreme Pain + Modified Smooth Muscle cells.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse this with a subungual melanoma (which is usually pigmented and painless) or a simple hematoma (trauma history).
sourceQuote: Glomus tumors... arise from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 26-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated mass on her gingiva that bleeds easily with minor trauma. The lesion appeared two weeks ago. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor, usually occurring in older adults, and is not associated with pregnancy.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granuloma (granuloma gravidarum when in pregnancy) is a lobular capillary hemangioma that often presents on the gingiva of pregnant women.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella infection and occurs in immunocompromised individuals, not typically healthy pregnant women.
explanations.d: Kaposi sarcoma presents as purple macules/plaques, not a rapidly growing pedunculated bleeding gingival mass.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are painful subungual lesions, not gingival masses.

ankiCards: A pyogenic granuloma occurring in a pregnant woman's gingiva is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
The histologic term for pyogenic granuloma is {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized by {{c1::rapid}} growth and frequent {{c2::bleeding}}.
Are pyogenic granulomas actually infections (pyogenic)? {{c1::No}}.
The most common location for a pyogenic granuloma is the {{c1::gingiva (or skin/mucosa)}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is neither pyogenic (pus-forming) nor a granuloma.
It is a capillary hemangioma that presents as a polypoid red mass.
Associated with pregnancy due to hormonal changes affecting vascularity.
Often regresses or fibroses after delivery.
Requires excision if it does not regress or is bothersome.
microReview: Pregnancy + Gingival Red Mass + Bleeding = Pyogenic Granuloma (Granuloma Gravidarum).
examinerTraps: The name 'Pyogenic' is a distractor; it does not imply an infectious or purulent process.
sourceQuote: Pyogenic granulomas... occur as rapidly growing red, pedunculated lesions on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa; they bleed easily and are often ulcerated.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In an HIV-positive patient, a vascular skin lesion is noted that histologically resembles Kaposi sarcoma but also contains prominent neutrophilic infiltrates and clusters of tangible bacteria (visualized by silver stain). What is the primary mechanism of this tumor's induction?

options.b: Direct infection of endothelial cells by HHV-8
options.c: Induction of host VEGF by Bartonella species
options.d: Genetic mutation in the MYC oncogene

explanations.a: Chronic lymphedema is the mechanism for Stewart-Treves syndrome (angiosarcoma), not bacillary angiomatosis.
explanations.b: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, which lacks the bacteria and heavy neutrophilic infiltrate seen here.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella henselae or Bartonella quintana, which induce host cells to produce VEGF, stimulating vascular proliferation.
explanations.d: MYC mutations are associated with Burkitt lymphoma or secondary angiosarcoma (post-radiation), not bacillary angiomatosis.
explanations.e: Polyvinyl chloride (PVC) exposure is a risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma.

ankiCards: {{c1::Bacillary angiomatosis}} is a vascular proliferation caused by Bartonella bacteria in immunocompromised hosts.
The two main species causing bacillary angiomatosis are {{c1::B. henselae}} (cat scratch) and {{c2::B. quintana}} (trench fever).
Unlike Kaposi sarcoma, Bacillary angiomatosis histology features an infiltrate of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
Bartonella species induce vascular growth by stimulating the production of {{c1::VEGF}}.
Bacteria in bacillary angiomatosis are best visualized using a {{c1::Warthin-Starry (silver)}} stain.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis mimics Kaposi sarcoma clinically but is bacterial in origin.
It occurs in immunocompromised (e.g., AIDS) patients.
B. henselae is transmitted by cats; B. quintana by human body lice.
Key histology: Capillary proliferation, neutrophils, and nuclear dust.
Treatment involves antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin), unlike KS.
microReview: AIDS + Vascular lesion + Neutrophils + Bartonella (Silver stain) = Bacillary Angiomatosis.
examinerTraps: Clinically, KS and BA look nearly identical (purple skin nodules in HIV). The presence of neutrophils or the response to antibiotics differentiates BA from KS.
sourceQuote: Bacillary angiomatosis... is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts... caused by opportunistic gram-negative bacilli of the Bartonella family.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Large, cavernous lymphatic spaces that are typically located in the neck or axilla of infants and are strongly associated with Turner syndrome are known as:

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas involve blood vessels, not lymphatic channels, and are usually skin-colored or red.
explanations.b: Cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) is a lymphatic malformation commonly found in the neck of infants and is a classic association with Turner syndrome (45,XO).
explanations.c: Simple lymphangiomas are smaller, superficial lymphatic collections, not the large cystic masses seen in Turner syndrome.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious blood vessel proliferation.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a malignant blood vessel tumor of older adults.

ankiCards: A cavernous lymphangioma located in the neck is commonly called a {{c1::cystic hygroma}}.
Cystic hygromas are frequently associated with the chromosomal abnormality {{c1::Turner syndrome (45,XO)}}.
Histologically, cystic hygromas are composed of massively dilated {{c1::lymphatic}} spaces.
Cystic hygromas are lined by a thin layer of {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
The margins of cystic hygromas are typically {{c1::poorly}} defined, making surgical resection difficult.
keyPoints: Cystic hygromas are benign but can be large and disfiguring.
Common locations: Neck, axilla, or retroperitoneum.
They contain serous or chylous fluid.
Presence in a fetus often suggests a karyotype abnormality (Turner Syndrome).
They are the lymphatic equivalent of cavernous hemangiomas.
microReview: Infant + Neck Mass + Lymphatic spaces + Turner Syndrome = Cystic Hygroma.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse with a branchial cleft cyst (lateral neck, but different histology/origin) or a thyroglossal duct cyst (midline).
sourceQuote: Cystic hygromas (cavernous lymphangiomas)... are typically found in the neck or axilla of children and are sometimes associated with Turner syndrome.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with several firm, violaceous nodules on her left arm. She has a history of a radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer 10 years ago, which was complicated by persistent, severe lymphedema. A biopsy of the skin nodules shows highly pleomorphic endothelial cells forming irregular vascular channels. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and usually presents in different clinical contexts (elderly Mediterranean or AIDS).
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infection-related benign proliferation in immunocompromised individuals.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma occurring in the setting of chronic lymphedema post-mastectomy is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome.
explanations.d: Hemangiopericytoma is a rare tumor of myofibroblast-like cells, not primarily an endothelial malignancy in this context.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are small, benign, and exquisitely painful; they do not arise from chronic lymphedema.

ankiCards: The development of angiosarcoma in the setting of chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves}} syndrome.
Angiosarcomas are highly {{c1::malignant}} tumors of endothelial cells.
A common historical risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma is exposure to {{c1::Polyvinyl chloride (PVC)}}.
Post-mastectomy patients with chronic {{c1::lymphedema}} are at risk for cutaneous angiosarcoma.
Histologically, angiosarcomas exhibit endothelial {{c1::pleomorphism}} and irregular vascular channels.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms.
Older adults are most commonly affected.
Sites: Skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Risk factors: Radiation, chronic lymphedema, PVC, Arsenic, Thorotrast.
Very aggressive with a poor 5-year survival rate.
microReview: Chronic Lymphedema (Post-mastectomy) + Purple Arm Nodules = Stewart-Treves Syndrome (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: The time frame is important; angiosarcoma usually occurs years (10+) after the mastectomy/lymphedema onset.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas can also occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema, classically in the ipsilateral arm of women who have undergone radical mastectomy... (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following immunohistochemical markers would be most useful in confirming the endothelial origin of a poorly differentiated malignant tumor suspected to be an angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells (carcinomas).
explanations.b: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a specific marker for endothelial cells and is used to identify vascular tumors, including angiosarcomas.
explanations.c: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (leiomyosarcoma or rhabdomyosarcoma).
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells (melanoma, Schwannoma).
explanations.e: CD45 is a leukocyte common antigen (lymphoma).

ankiCards: {{c1::CD31}} is a specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial cells.
Besides CD31, {{c1::von Willebrand factor (vWF)}} is another marker for vascular tumors.
Angiosarcomas are malignant tumors derived from {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
In well-differentiated angiosarcomas, the cells form {{c1::vascular channels}}.
In poorly-differentiated angiosarcomas, the cells appear {{c1::epithelioid or spindle-shaped}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas can be difficult to distinguish from carcinomas if poorly differentiated.
CD31 is the most reliable vascular marker.
Tumor cells are highly atypical and mitotically active.
They can occur anywhere but prefer skin and liver.
Metastasis occurs early, often to the lungs.
microReview: Endothelial Marker = CD31 or vWF.
examinerTraps: Be careful with 'vimentin'—it's a general mesenchymal marker, so while positive in angiosarcoma, it's not specific to endothelial cells.
sourceQuote: The endothelial nature of the proliferating cells can be demonstrated by staining for endothelial-specific markers such as CD31 or von Willebrand factor.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Exposure to which of the following environmental toxins is most specifically associated with the development of hepatic angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Aflatoxin B1 is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Vinyl chloride (PVC precursor), Thorotrast (radiocontrast), and Arsenic are the classic three risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Benzene is associated with acute myeloid leukemia.
explanations.d: Beryllium is associated with berylliosis and lung cancer.
explanations.e: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and lung cancer.

ankiCards: Three specific exposures linked to hepatic angiosarcoma are {{c1::Arsenic}}, {{c2::Thorotrast}}, and {{c3::Vinyl chloride}}.
Arsenic exposure often comes from {{c1::pesticides}}.
Vinyl chloride is an intermediate in the production of {{c1::plastics (PVC)}}.
Thorotrast was a historical {{c1::radiographic contrast agent}}.
Is hepatic angiosarcoma more common in males or females? {{c1::Males}}.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare but highly lethal malignancy.
Long latency period (decades) between exposure and tumor development.
Vinyl chloride exposure occurs in the plastic industry.
Presents with weight loss, abdominal pain, and hepatomegaly.
Most patients die within a year of diagnosis.
microReview: Hepatic Angiosarcoma = Vinyl Chloride + Arsenic + Thorotrast.
examinerTraps: Ensure you distinguish between Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HBV, HCV, Alcohol, Aflatoxin) and Hepatic Angiosarcoma (PVC, Arsenic).
sourceQuote: Hepatic angiosarcomas are associated with distinct environmental carcinogens, including arsenic... Thorotrast... and polyvinyl chloride.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A neonate is born with a bright red, raised 'strawberry-like' lesion on the cheek. Over the first few months, the lesion grows slightly in proportion to the child. What is the most likely long-term outcome for this lesion without any medical intervention?

options.d: Rapid spread to internal visceral organs
options.e: Development of a painful subungual nodule

explanations.a: Benign infantile hemangiomas do not transform into malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.b: While some hemangiomas persist, the classic 'strawberry' (juvenile) hemangioma typically regresses.
explanations.c: Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) are very common in newborns, grow for a few months, and then nearly always spontaneously regress by age 7.
explanations.d: This is a benign localized lesion, not a metastatic or invasive malignancy.
explanations.e: This describes a glomus tumor, which is unrelated to neonatal strawberry hemangiomas.

ankiCards: The common name for a juvenile hemangioma is a {{c1::strawberry}} hemangioma.
Strawberry hemangiomas are histologically classified as {{c1::capillary}} hemangiomas.
By what age do the majority of juvenile hemangiomas regress? {{c1::7 (or 5-9 years)}}.
What is the frequency of juvenile hemangiomas in newborns? {{c1::1 in 200}}.
Do juvenile hemangiomas require aggressive surgical treatment? {{c1::No (usually observation)}}.
keyPoints: Infantile (juvenile) hemangioma is the most common vascular tumor of childhood.
Usually appears shortly after birth.
Grows rapidly during the first few months (proliferative phase).
Involution begins around age 1-2.
Complete regression occurs in 75-90% of cases by age 7.
microReview: Strawberry Hemangioma = Newborn + Rapid Growth + Spontaneous Regression by age 7.
examinerTraps: The examiner may ask about management; the answer is usually 'observation' or 'reassurance' because they regress naturally.
sourceQuote: Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) of the skin of newborns are very common... they grow rapidly for a few months but then fade and typically regress by age 1 to 3 years... with 90% disappearing by age 7.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the core underlying mechanism by which vascular wall weakness leads to the formation of a true aneurysm?

options.a: Transmural inflammation leading to luminal narrowing
options.b: Focal discontinuity in the internal elastic lamina
options.c: Involvement of all three layers of the arterial wall
options.d: Extravasation of blood into a peri-arterial hematoma
options.e: Intimal thickening in response to hypertension

explanations.a: Luminal narrowing is characteristic of stenosis or atherosclerosis, whereas aneurysms involve dilation due to wall weakening.
explanations.b: Focal discontinuity in the internal elastic lamina is specifically associated with berry aneurysms, but the general definition of a true aneurysm involves the intactness of the wall layers.
explanations.c: A true aneurysm is defined as a localized permanent dilation of a blood vessel that involves all three layers (intima, media, and adventitia).
explanations.d: Extravasation of blood into a hematoma that communicates with the vessel but is contained by extravascular tissue defines a false (pseudo) aneurysm.
explanations.e: Intimal thickening is a stereotyped response to vascular injury that usually results in luminal narrowing, not dilation.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true aneurysm}} involves all three layers of the arterial wall.
A localized permanent dilation of a vessel is termed an {{c1::aneurysm}}.
The two principal mechanisms of vascular disease are {{c1::narrowing}} and {{c1::weakening of vessel walls}}.
A {{c1::false aneurysm}} (pseudoaneurysm) is a wall defect leading to an extravascular hematoma.
Dilation of an artery to more than {{c1::1.5}} times its normal diameter is typically used to define an aneurysm.
keyPoints: Aneurysms represent a weakening of the vessel wall.
True aneurysms involve the intima, media, and adventitia.
Vascular diseases typically manifest as either stenosis or dilation.
Pseudoaneurysms do not involve all three layers of the vessel wall.
Aneurysms are categorized by shape into saccular or fusiform.
microReview: Aneurysms are permanent dilations. True aneurysms involve all layers; false aneurysms are hematomas communicating with the lumen. The primary drivers are atherosclerosis and hypertension which weaken the media.
examinerTraps: Students often confuse 'dissection' with 'aneurysm'. A dissection involves blood entering the wall itself, while an aneurysm is a dilation of all wall layers.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the pathogenesis of abdominal aortic aneurysms, the degradation of which structural component of the media is primarily mediated by matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) derived from macrophages?

explanations.a: Type IV collagen is a component of basement membranes, not the primary structural protein providing recoil in the large elastic arteries.
explanations.b: Elastin degradation in the media, driven by MMPs (like MMP-2 and MMP-9) and other proteases, is the critical event in the weakening of the aortic wall leading to AAA.
explanations.c: Laminin is a glycoprotein of the basal lamina and is not the primary target of degradation in aneurysmal dilation.
explanations.d: Heparan sulfate is a proteoglycan involved in the extracellular matrix but does not provide the structural integrity that prevents aneurysm formation.
explanations.e: Fibronectin is involved in cell adhesion; its degradation is secondary to the loss of the structural scaffolding provided by elastin and collagen.

ankiCards: The primary structural protein degraded in the media during AAA formation is {{c1::elastin}}.
Inflammatory cells in an aneurysm wall secrete {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
Increased expression of {{c1::MMP-9}} by macrophages is strongly associated with AAA.
Weakening of the aortic media leads to {{c1::fusiform}} dilation in the abdomen.
Atherosclerosis causes AAA by increasing the {{c1::diffusion distance}} from the lumen to the media, causing ischemia.
keyPoints: AAA is characterized by chronic inflammation of the media.
Proteolytic enzymes (MMPs) destroy elastin and collagen.
The loss of elastin leads to the initial dilation.
Atherosclerosis is the most common predisposing factor for AAA.
Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for AAA development.
microReview: AAA Pathogenesis: Atherosclerosis → Intimal thickening → Media ischemia → Inflammation → MMP release → Elastin/Collagen degradation → Wall weakening → Dilation.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse the 'ischemia' of the media in AAA (caused by atherosclerosis) with 'vasa vasorum obliterans' seen in syphilitic thoracic aneurysms.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old male with a 50-pack-year smoking history and hypertension presents to the emergency department with sudden, severe mid-abdominal pain radiating to his back. On physical examination, a pulsatile mass is felt above the umbilicus. His blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg. What is the most likely pathological process occurring in this patient's aorta?

options.a: Intimal tear leading to a false lumen
options.b: Transmural rupture of a fusiform dilation
options.c: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.d: Cystic medial degeneration of the ascending aorta
options.e: Granulomatous inflammation of the aortic arch

explanations.a: This describes an aortic dissection, which typically presents with tearing chest pain radiating to the back and involves the thoracic aorta more frequently than the abdominal aorta.
explanations.b: The patient presents with the classic triad of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA): sudden severe pain, a pulsatile mass, and hypotension. AAA are typically fusiform.
explanations.c: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum is the mechanism for syphilitic (tertiary syphilis) aneurysms, which usually affect the thoracic aorta.
explanations.d: Cystic medial degeneration is common in Marfan syndrome and affects the ascending aorta/thoracic region, not usually the abdominal region in an older smoker.
explanations.e: Granulomatous inflammation of the aortic arch describes Takayasu arteritis, which affects younger females and presents with 'pulseless disease'.

ankiCards: The classic triad of AAA rupture is {{c1::abdominal/back pain}}, {{c2::pulsatile mass}}, and {{c3::hypotension}}.
AAAs are most commonly located between the {{c1::renal arteries}} and the {{c2::iliac bifurcation}}.
The risk of AAA rupture increases significantly when the diameter exceeds {{c1::5.0 to 5.5}} cm.
The primary risk factor for the development of AAA is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Smoking increases the risk of AAA expansion by {{c1::increasing MMP activity}}.
keyPoints: AAA is usually asymptomatic until rupture.
Rupture risk is size-dependent.
Most AAAs occur below the level of the renal arteries.
The presence of a mural thrombus is common in AAAs.
Sudden death is a frequent outcome of AAA rupture.
microReview: AAA clinical features: Older male, smoker, atherosclerosis. Location: Infrarenal. Presentation: Asymptomatic or pulsatile mass. Rupture: Hypotension, pain, shock. High mortality.
examinerTraps: Wait for the blood pressure. If the BP is high and the pain is tearing, think dissection. If BP is low and there is a pulsatile abdominal mass, think AAA rupture.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Deficiency in the signaling of which growth factor pathway is most closely associated with the development of familial thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections (TAAD)?

explanations.a: VEGF is involved in angiogenesis and permeability, not the structural maintenance of the aortic media.
explanations.b: Dysregulation of the TGF-β signaling pathway (either through mutations in receptors like TGFBR1/2 or SMAD proteins) leads to defective elastin and collagen synthesis, causing thoracic aortic aneurysms.
explanations.c: PDGF is involved in smooth muscle cell migration and proliferation but is not the primary pathway associated with TAAD syndromes.
explanations.d: FGF is involved in wound healing and angiogenesis; it is not the primary driver of medial degeneration in the aorta.
explanations.e: EGF is involved in cell growth and differentiation; it is not linked to the pathogenesis of aortic aneurysms.

ankiCards: Mutations in {{c1::TGF-β}} signaling are linked to Loeys-Dietz syndrome and thoracic aneurysms.
In Marfan syndrome, defective {{c1::Fibrillin-1}} leads to increased bioavailable {{c2::TGF-β}}.
The structural weakening in the media of thoracic aneurysms is called {{c1::cystic medial necrosis (or degeneration)}}.
Cystic medial necrosis is characterized by the loss of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} and accumulation of mucoid material.
Unlike AAA, thoracic aortic aneurysms are more commonly associated with {{c1::hypertension}} and genetic connective tissue disorders.
keyPoints: TGF-β signaling regulates extracellular matrix production.
Excessive TGF-β signaling leads to media weakening in Marfan syndrome.
Loeys-Dietz syndrome involves mutations in TGF-β receptors.
Thoracic aneurysms can cause aortic valve insufficiency.
Genetic causes of TAAD often involve the contractile apparatus of smooth muscle (e.g., ACTA2).
microReview: Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (TAA): Often genetic (Marfan, Loeys-Dietz) or due to HTN. Mechanism: Cystic medial necrosis. Key Pathway: TGF-β dysregulation. Clinical: Respiratory distress, dysphagia, or aortic root dilation.
examinerTraps: A common trap is assuming all aneurysms are caused by atherosclerosis. While AAA is largely atherosclerotic, TAA is more frequently linked to HTN and genetic defects in TGF-β/fibrillin.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which vessel type is the primary site for the development of 'Berry' aneurysms?

options.c: Arteries of the Circle of Willis

explanations.a: The descending aorta is the site for atherosclerotic or hypertensive aneurysms, but not berry aneurysms.
explanations.b: The infrarenal aorta is the primary site for abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA).
explanations.c: Berry aneurysms are small, saccular dilations occurring at the branch points of the Circle of Willis in the cerebral circulation.
explanations.d: Popliteal aneurysms are peripheral aneurysms, often associated with AAAs, but are not 'berry' type.
explanations.e: The SMA can develop mycotic aneurysms, but berry aneurysms are specifically cerebral.

ankiCards: Berry aneurysms are most commonly found in the {{c1::Circle of Willis}}.
The most common specific site for a berry aneurysm is the junction of the {{c1::anterior communicating}} artery.
Rupture of a berry aneurysm causes {{c1::subarachnoid}} hemorrhage.
Berry aneurysms are associated with {{c1::Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD)}}.
Unlike aortic aneurysms, berry aneurysms are often caused by {{c1::congenital}} defects in the arterial media.
keyPoints: Berry aneurysms are saccular.
They occur at bifurcations.
They lack a media layer at the site of the protrusion.
Clinical presentation: 'Worst headache of my life' (thunderclap headache).
Associated with Ehlers-Danlos and ADPKD.
microReview: Berry Aneurysm: Small saccular dilation at Circle of Willis branch points. Cause: Congenital media defect + HTN. Risk: Subarachnoid hemorrhage. Associated with ADPKD.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse berry aneurysms with Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms. Charcot-Bouchard occur in small perforating vessels (like lenticulostriate) and lead to intraparenchymal (not subarachnoid) hemorrhage.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old female presents with a persistent dry cough and difficulty swallowing. Imaging reveals a large dilation of the ascending aortic arch. Histological examination of the aortic wall shows obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum with a surrounding plasma cell-rich infiltrate. What is the most likely underlying etiology?

explanations.a: Hypertension causes hyaline arteriolosclerosis or cystic medial necrosis, not obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum.
explanations.b: Tertiary syphilis (luetic aneurysm) targets the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta, leading to ischemic injury of the media and a 'tree-bark' appearance of the intima.
explanations.c: Marfan syndrome involves cystic medial necrosis due to fibrillin mutations, without the specific plasma cell-rich endarteritis of the vasa vasorum.
explanations.d: Giant cell arteritis is a granulomatous vasculitis; while it can cause aneurysms, the specific description of obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum is classic for syphilis.
explanations.e: S. aureus would cause a mycotic aneurysm, which is usually a rapid destruction of the wall with neutrophils and abscess formation.

ankiCards: Syphilitic aneurysms characteristically involve the {{c1::ascending}} aorta.
The histological hallmark of syphilitic aortitis is {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}} of the vasa vasorum.
The 'tree-bark' appearance of the aorta in syphilis is due to {{c1::intimal scarring}}.
Ischemia of the {{c1::media}} in syphilis leads to the loss of elastic tissue.
Syphilitic aortitis often leads to dilation of the {{c1::aortic valve ring}}, causing insufficiency.
keyPoints: Luetic (syphilitic) aneurysms are now rare due to antibiotics.
They predominantly affect the thoracic aorta.
Media ischemia results from vasa vasorum narrowing.
Contraction of fibrous scars leads to intimal wrinkling (tree-barking).
Plasma cells are the characteristic inflammatory cell seen.
microReview: Syphilitic Aneurysm: Tertiary syphilis → vasa vasorum endarteritis → media ischemia → wall weakening → thoracic aneurysm + aortic regurgitation.
examinerTraps: If the stem mentions 'plasma cells' in the aortic wall, syphilis should be at the top of the differential.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which physiological factor explains why atherosclerosis primarily predisposes to Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms (AAA) rather than Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (TAA)?

options.a: The abdominal aorta lacks vasa vasorum in its media
options.b: The thoracic aorta has a higher concentration of matrix metalloproteinases
options.c: The abdominal aorta has a thicker intima that prevents oxygen diffusion
options.d: The thoracic aorta is subjected to higher pulsatile pressures
options.e: The abdominal aorta contains more elastic fibers than the thoracic aorta

explanations.a: The abdominal aorta is unique because its media is relatively avascular and lacks vasa vasorum. It depends on diffusion from the lumen. Atherosclerotic plaques increase this diffusion distance, causing medial ischemia and weakening.
explanations.b: MMPs are actually the effectors of damage in the abdominal aorta once inflammation starts; they are not inherently higher in the thoracic aorta.
explanations.c: Atherosclerosis creates a thick intima, but the reason it causes *ischemia* specifically in the abdominal media is the lack of a secondary blood supply (vasa vasorum) in that segment.
explanations.d: While true, higher pressure is a risk for dissection and TAA, but does not explain why atherosclerosis specifically targets the abdominal portion for aneurysms.
explanations.e: The abdominal aorta actually has *fewer* elastic fibers and more smooth muscle compared to the thoracic aorta, making it less resilient to wall stress.

ankiCards: The abdominal aortic media receives nutrients via {{c1::diffusion}} from the lumen.
The lack of {{c1::vasa vasorum}} in the infrarenal aorta makes it vulnerable to atherosclerotic ischemia.
Atherosclerotic plaques increase the {{c1::diffusion distance}} for oxygen to reach the media.
Media ischemia in the abdominal aorta leads to {{c1::smooth muscle cell}} death.
The {{c1::infrarenal}} aorta is the most common site for atherosclerotic aneurysms.
keyPoints: Atherosclerosis is the major cause of AAA.
AAA is usually infrarenal.
Oxygen diffusion is impaired by intimal plaque.
Nutrient deprivation leads to medial thinning.
Inflammation follows, further weakening the wall.
microReview: AAA and Atherosclerosis: Plaque → thickened intima → increased diffusion distance → media ischemia (no vasa vasorum in abdomen) → media atrophy → aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the mechanisms: Syphilis attacks the vasa vasorum (thoracic), while atherosclerosis blocks diffusion to a media that already lacks vasa vasorum (abdominal).
sourceQuote: Atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 34-year-old male with a history of intravenous drug use presents with a fever and a painful, rapidly enlarging mass in his right groin. An ultrasound reveals a localized dilation of the femoral artery with evidence of an adjacent abscess. What is the most appropriate term for this type of aneurysm?

explanations.a: Berry aneurysms are non-infectious congenital saccular dilations in the brain.
explanations.b: A mycotic aneurysm is an aneurysm resulting from an infection that weakens the vessel wall. In IV drug users, this often occurs from seeding of the wall during bacteremia or from adjacent infection.
explanations.c: Luetic aneurysms are caused specifically by syphilis and affect the aorta, not peripheral arteries in the groin.
explanations.d: A dissection is a longitudinal cleavage of the wall layers, not a localized infectious dilation.
explanations.e: Fusiform refers to the shape (circumferential), but 'mycotic' describes the essential infectious pathology presented.

ankiCards: A {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm is caused by infection of the arterial wall.
The most common cause of a mycotic aneurysm is {{c1::infective endocarditis}} (septic emboli).
In IV drug users, mycotic aneurysms often occur due to {{c1::direct inoculation}} or bacteremia.
Common organisms in mycotic aneurysms include {{c1::Salmonella}} and {{c2::Staphylococcus}}.
A mycotic aneurysm can lead to rapid {{c1::rupture}} and sepsis.
keyPoints: Mycotic aneurysms are not necessarily fungal (the term is historical).
They can arise from septic emboli or direct extension of an abscess.
They are usually saccular.
The vessel wall is destroyed by inflammatory cell proteases.
Risk factors include immunosuppression and IV drug use.
microReview: Mycotic Aneurysm: Infection (bacterial/fungal) → Wall destruction → Dilation. Sources: IE (emboli), Bacteremia, Extension from local abscess. Danger: Rapid expansion and rupture.
examinerTraps: The term 'mycotic' is a trick; it sounds like it must be fungal, but it is most often bacterial (e.g., S. aureus or Salmonella).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes a 'false aneurysm' (pseudoaneurysm)?

options.a: A dilation involving only the intima and media
options.b: A blood-filled space between the layers of the media
options.c: A hematoma that communicates with the intravascular space
options.d: A symmetrical dilation of the entire vessel circumference
options.e: A localized outpouching of the adventitia only

explanations.a: A true aneurysm must involve all three layers. There is no standard aneurysm involving only two.
explanations.b: This describes an aortic dissection (an intramural hematoma).
explanations.c: A false aneurysm is a breach in the vascular wall leading to an extravascular hematoma that freely communicates with the intravascular space (often contained by fibrous tissue).
explanations.d: This describes a fusiform true aneurysm.
explanations.e: The adventitia alone cannot contain the pressure; a false aneurysm is typically contained by extravascular connective tissue or a thrombus.

ankiCards: A {{c1::false aneurysm}} is a pulsatile hematoma communicating with the vessel lumen.
A common cause of a pseudoaneurysm is {{c1::iatrogenic trauma}} (e.g., femoral artery catheterization).
Unlike a true aneurysm, a pseudoaneurysm does not have {{c1::vessel wall layers}} as its boundary.
A post-myocardial infarction {{c1::ventricular aneurysm}} is an example of a false aneurysm if the wall has ruptured.
A {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm is a true aneurysm that only involves a portion of the wall circumference.
keyPoints: True aneurysms have an intact (but thinned) wall.
False aneurysms are 'contained ruptures'.
Trauma and vasculitis are common causes of pseudoaneurysms.
Clinically, they present as pulsatile masses with a 'to-and-fro' bruit.
Management often involves compression or surgical repair.
microReview: Aneurysm Types: True (Intima+Media+Adventitia intact), False (Wall breach, extravascular hematoma), Dissection (Blood between media layers).
examinerTraps: Examiners often use 'trauma' or 'post-catheterization' to lead you toward a false aneurysm.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Cystic medial necrosis, a common histological finding in thoracic aneurysms, is primarily characterized by which of the following alterations?

options.a: Extensive calcification of the internal elastic lamina
options.b: Accumulation of basophilic ground substance in the media
options.d: Replacement of smooth muscle with dense collagenous scar
options.e: Fibrinoid necrosis of the small vasa vasorum

explanations.a: Calcification of the elastic lamina is seen in Monckeberg medial sclerosis, not cystic medial necrosis.
explanations.b: Cystic medial necrosis involves the loss of smooth muscle cells and the fragmentation of elastic fibers, with the resulting gaps filled by glycosaminoglycan-rich 'mucoid' material (basophilic ground substance).
explanations.c: Despite the name 'necrosis', there is typically no cell death associated with acute inflammation or liquefaction.
explanations.d: Scarring would imply healing; in cystic medial necrosis, the structural integrity is lost without effective replacement by strong collagen.
explanations.e: Fibrinoid necrosis is characteristic of malignant hypertension or vasculitis, not the chronic degenerative change of cystic medial necrosis.

ankiCards: {{c1::Cystic medial necrosis}} is the characteristic lesion in Marfan-related aneurysms.
The 'cysts' in cystic medial necrosis are actually pools of {{c1::glycosaminoglycans (mucoid material)}}.
Medial degeneration leads to the fragmentation of {{c1::elastic fibers}}.
Cystic medial necrosis is also seen in patients with chronic {{c1::hypertension}}.
The term 'necrosis' in cystic medial necrosis is a misnomer because {{c1::inflammation}} is usually absent.
keyPoints: Cystic medial necrosis weakens the aortic root.
It is found in Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos.
It predisposes to both aneurysms and dissections.
The aortic wall becomes thin and 'tissue-paper' like.
Smooth muscle cell drop-out is a key feature.
microReview: Cystic Medial Necrosis: Non-inflammatory. Features: Elastic fiber fragmentation + loss of smooth muscle + mucoid material accumulation. Result: Medial weakening → Thoracic Aneurysm/Dissection.
examinerTraps: The name 'necrosis' is very misleading. There is no actual 'necrosis' (cell death by injury) in the classical sense, and certainly no 'cysts' (epithelial-lined spaces). It is just mucoid degeneration.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 2-month-old female infant is brought to the pediatrician for a bright red, raised, lobulated lesion on her left cheek. The mother states the lesion was small at birth but has grown rapidly over the last month. On examination, the lesion is soft, blanches partially with pressure, and measures 2 cm in diameter. Which of the following is the most likely long-term outcome for this lesion?

explanations.a: The description is classic for a juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma, which typically grows rapidly for several months and then undergoes spontaneous regression by age 7 to 9.
explanations.b: Juvenile hemangiomas are benign and do not undergo malignant transformation.
explanations.c: Unlike cavernous hemangiomas or port-wine stains, strawberry hemangiomas almost always regress rather than persist.
explanations.d: While very large internal hemangiomas (like in the liver) can cause high-output heart failure, a small 2 cm cutaneous lesion does not.
explanations.e: Hemangiomas are benign tumors and do not metastasize.

ankiCards: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas typically {{c1::regress}} spontaneously by age 7.
The clinical course of a strawberry hemangioma involves rapid growth followed by {{c1::involution}}.
{{c1::Hemangioma}} is the most common tumor of infancy.
The histological appearance of a juvenile hemangioma shows a high density of {{c1::capillaries}}.
True/False: Strawberry hemangiomas require immediate surgical excision. {{c1::False}}
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangiomas are the most common vascular tumors of infancy.
They typically present as bright red 'strawberry' lesions on the skin.
The natural history involves a 'proliferative phase' followed by a 'regressive phase'.
Histologically, they consist of thin-walled capillaries with scant stroma.
Management is usually conservative observation.
microReview: Juvenile hemangioma = Strawberry appearance + Infancy + Spontaneous regression.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse this with a Nevus Flammeus (port-wine stain), which does NOT regress and is associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 35-year-old male with a history of HIV and a low CD4+ T-cell count presents with multiple purple-to-red papules and plaques on his lower extremities and oral mucosa. A biopsy shows proliferation of spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces containing red blood cells, and a chronic inflammatory infiltrate. Which of the following infectious agents is the primary driver of this pathology?

explanations.a: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent in all forms of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.b: HHV-6 is associated with Roseola infantum, not vascular tumors.
explanations.c: CMV can cause opportunistic infections in HIV patients but does not cause Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.d: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.e: HPV-16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx.

ankiCards: The causative agent of Kaposi sarcoma is {{c1::HHV-8}}.
Kaposi sarcoma is characterized histologically by {{c1::spindle cells}} and slit-like vascular spaces.
The most common form of Kaposi sarcoma in the United States is the {{c1::AIDS-associated}} type.
