Kaposi sarcoma lesions typically appear as {{c1::purple/red}} plaques or nodules.
In AIDS-associated Kaposi sarcoma, the most common site of extra-cutaneous involvement is the {{c1::gastrointestinal tract}} or lymph nodes.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8.
Four clinical variants exist: Classic (older Mediterranean men), Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
Spindle cells are the diagnostic cell type in the late stage.
Vascular spaces are 'slit-like' and lack a well-defined basement membrane.
HHV-8 infects endothelial cells and promotes angiogenesis and cell survival.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = HHV-8 + HIV/AIDS + Spindle cells + Slit-like spaces.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'slit-like spaces' to confirm KS over bacillary angiomatosis, which features neutrophilic inflammation.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following immunohistochemical markers is most specific for identifying the cell of origin in a malignant vascular tumor such as angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a marker for endothelial cells and is used to confirm the vascular nature of poorly differentiated tumors.
explanations.b: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (skeletal or smooth).
explanations.c: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells, such as melanocytes or Schwann cells.
explanations.d: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells and carcinomas.
explanations.e: CD45 (LCA) is a marker for hematopoietic cells (leukocytes).

ankiCards: The endothelial marker used to diagnose angiosarcoma is {{c1::CD31}}.
{{c1::vWF (von Willebrand Factor)}} is another marker for endothelial cells, though often less sensitive than CD31.
Angiosarcomas are malignant tumors of {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
CD31 stands for {{c1::Platelet Endothelial Cell Adhesion Molecule-1}}.
In poorly differentiated angiosarcoma, {{c1::CD31}} helps distinguish it from carcinoma.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are aggressive malignant endothelial neoplasms.
CD31 is the most reliable marker for endothelial differentiation.
Tumors can occur in the skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with vinyl chloride and Thorotrast exposure.
Histology ranges from recognizable vascular channels to undifferentiated sheets of pleomorphic cells.
microReview: Angiosarcoma = Malignant Endothelium = CD31 positive.
examinerTraps: The examiner might offer 'Factor VIII' as a marker; while true, CD31 is usually the preferred diagnostic answer in modern pathology.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with an intensely painful, 4-mm, blue-red nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. The pain is triggered by cold exposure and local pressure. The lesion is surgically excised. From which of the following cell types is this tumor most likely derived?

explanations.a: A glomus tumor (glomangioma) arises from the specialized smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, which are involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.b: Skeletal muscle cells are not found in the glomus body.
explanations.c: While glomus tumors are vascular-associated, the primary neoplastic component is the glomus cell (modified smooth muscle), not the endothelium.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts produce collagen; they are not the cell of origin for glomus tumors.
explanations.e: Schwann cells form the myelin sheath of nerves; they are not the origin of glomus tumors.

ankiCards: The triad of a glomus tumor includes: subungual location, extreme pain, and {{c1::sensitivity to cold}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells.
The specialized structure involved in thermoregulation that gives rise to glomus tumors is the {{c1::glomus body}}.
The most common location for a glomus tumor is {{c1::subungual (under the nail)}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors show nests of small, uniform round cells surrounding {{c1::vascular channels}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but extremely painful.
They are derived from modified smooth muscle cells of the thermoregulatory glomus bodies.
The subungual (under the nail) location is a classic clinical 'buzzword'.
Surgical excision is curative.
Cells are typically small, round, and uniform ('monomorphic').
microReview: Glomus tumor = Subungual + Extreme Pain + Smooth Muscle origin.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse this with a subungual melanoma, which is usually painless and pigmented (dark brown/black).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old male with advanced AIDS presents with several dozen red, friable, dome-shaped papules on his trunk and arms. He recently adopted several kittens from a local shelter. Skin biopsy shows a vascular proliferation with prominent neutrophilic infiltrates and granular purple material. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of these lesions?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella henselae (often from cat scratches) or Bartonella quintana. It presents as vascular lesions in immunocompromised patients.
explanations.b: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, which lacks the prominent neutrophilic infiltrate and bacterial clusters seen in bacillary angiomatosis.
explanations.c: S. aureus causes pyogenic infections (abscesses, impetigo) but not vascular tumors.
explanations.d: T. pallidum causes syphilis, which has a different clinical presentation (chancre, rash).
explanations.e: Aspergillus is a fungus that causes angioinvasive disease but not these specific papular vascular proliferations.

ankiCards: {{c1::Bacillary angiomatosis}} is a vascular proliferation in AIDS patients caused by Bartonella species.
The neutrophilic infiltrate in bacillary angiomatosis helps distinguish it from {{c1::Kaposi sarcoma}}.
The stain used to visualize Bartonella in bacillary angiomatosis is the {{c1::Warthin-Starry}} silver stain.
Bartonella henselae is typically transmitted via {{c1::cats (cat scratch)}}.
First-line treatment for bacillary angiomatosis involves antibiotics like {{c1::erythromycin}} or doxycycline.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis is an opportunistic infection, not a true neoplasm.
It mimics Kaposi sarcoma clinically (red-purple papules).
Histology shows lobular capillary proliferation and neutrophils.
Granular purple material on H&E represents clusters of bacteria.
It can involve internal organs like the liver (peliosis hepatis).
microReview: Bacillary Angiomatosis = HIV + Cats + Bartonella + Neutrophils.
examinerTraps: The main distractor is Kaposi Sarcoma. Look for 'neutrophils' or 'Warthin-Starry stain' to pick Bartonella/Bacillary Angiomatosis.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A newborn is found to have a large, soft, fluctuant mass on the left side of the neck that transilluminates on physical exam. Imaging confirms a multi-loculated cystic lesion. Chromosomal analysis of the infant is performed. Which of the following is the most likely karyotype associated with this finding?

explanations.a: A cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) of the neck is a classic finding in Turner syndrome (45,X).
explanations.b: Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) is associated with heart defects and duodenal atresia, but less specifically with cystic hygromas than Turner syndrome.
explanations.c: Edwards syndrome (Trisomy 18) is associated with clenched fists and rocker-bottom feet.
explanations.d: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is not typically associated with cystic hygroma.
explanations.e: While a cystic hygroma can occur in a normal karyotype, the 'most likely' association in board exams for a neonatal neck mass is Turner syndrome.

ankiCards: A cystic hygroma is a type of {{c1::lymphangioma}}.
The most common site for a cystic hygroma is the {{c1::neck (or axilla)}}.
Cystic hygroma of the neck is strongly associated with {{c1::Turner syndrome}}.
Histologically, lymphangiomas consist of dilated spaces lined by {{c1::endothelial}} cells and containing proteinaceous fluid.
The absence of {{c1::red blood cells}} in the lumina helps distinguish lymphangioma from hemangioma.
keyPoints: Cystic hygromas are benign lymphatic malformations.
They typically present at birth in the neck or axilla.
They are composed of large, dilated lymphatic spaces.
Associated with Turner Syndrome (45,X) and Trisomy 21.
They are often difficult to resect due to lack of encapsulation.
microReview: Cystic Hygroma = Neck Mass + Transillumination + Turner Syndrome (45,X).
examinerTraps: The mass 'transilluminates' because it is fluid-filled; solid tumors like a teratoma or neuroblastoma would not.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy develops a rapidly growing, 1-cm, red pedunculated nodule on her gingiva. It bleeds easily with minimal trauma (e.g., tooth brushing). A biopsy reveals a circumscribed proliferation of capillaries arranged in lobules, accompanied by edema and an acute inflammatory infiltrate. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnosis?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a common benign lesion that often occurs on the gingiva, especially in pregnant women ('granuloma gravidarum').
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, blood-filled spaces and are usually deep-seated, not pedunculated bleeding gingival nodules.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor with significant atypia; it is rare on the gingiva and not associated with pregnancy.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are subungual and extremely painful; they do not present as gingival nodules.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis occurs in immunocompromised individuals and is caused by Bartonella infection.

ankiCards: A pyogenic granuloma occurring in the gingiva of a pregnant woman is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Despite its name, a pyogenic granuloma is neither {{c1::infectious (pyogenic)}} nor a {{c2::granuloma}}.
The histological synonym for pyogenic granuloma is {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized clinically by rapid growth and {{c1::easy bleeding}}.
The treatment for a persistent pyogenic granuloma is {{c1::surgical excision}} (or regression after pregnancy).
keyPoints: Pyogenic granulomas are misnamed; they are lobular capillary hemangiomas.
They occur frequently after minor trauma to the skin or oral mucosa.
Pregnancy is a major risk factor (hormonal influence).
They present as a 'raspberry-like' red nodule.
Spontaneous regression can occur post-partum.
microReview: Pyogenic granuloma = Pregnancy + Gingiva + Bleeds easily.
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic granuloma' is a historical misnomer. Don't look for granulomas or pus on the pathology report.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with several firm, dark blue-purple nodules on her left arm. She has a history of a radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection and radiotherapy for breast cancer 10 years ago. Since that surgery, she has had persistent, non-pitting swelling of the left arm. What is the most likely diagnosis for the new skin nodules?

explanations.a: The development of angiosarcoma in the setting of chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy) is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and usually occurs in different clinical settings (HIV or elderly Mediterranean men).
explanations.c: Cystic hygromas are congenital lymphatic malformations found in children.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign lesions and do not typically arise in the setting of chronic lymphedema.
explanations.e: Glomangiomas are benign glomus tumors, which are small and painful, not widespread nodules in lymphedematous limbs.

ankiCards: {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}} refers to angiosarcoma arising in a limb with chronic lymphedema.
Chronic lymphedema following {{c1::radical mastectomy}} is the classic precursor to Stewart-Treves syndrome.
Cutaneous angiosarcoma can also be induced by prior {{c1::radiation}} therapy.
Angiosarcoma is a highly {{c1::aggressive}} tumor with a poor 5-year survival rate.
The characteristic skin lesions of Stewart-Treves are {{c1::purple/bruise-like}} nodules or plaques.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma can be secondary to chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves).
It can also be induced by radiation or chemical toxins (vinyl chloride).
Histology shows malignant endothelial cells forming irregular channels.
It is an extremely aggressive malignancy.
Clinical appearance often mimics a simple 'bruise' in the early stages.
microReview: Post-Mastectomy Lymphedema + New Purple Nodules = Stewart-Treves (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: The examiner may describe the lesions as 'bruises' that don't heal. This is a red flag for angiosarcoma in the correct clinical context.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular tumors are categorized into benign, intermediate-grade (borderline), and malignant. Which of the following neoplasms is correctly classified as an intermediate-grade vascular tumor?

explanations.a: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is the classic example of an intermediate-grade (borderline) vascular tumor, with clinical behavior between benign hemangiomas and malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are entirely benign.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is highly malignant.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are benign.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious reactive process, not a primary neoplastic grade.

ankiCards: An example of an intermediate-grade (borderline) vascular tumor is {{c1::epithelioid hemangioendothelioma}}.
Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma cells often show characteristic {{c1::cytoplasmic vacuoles}} (intracytoplasmic lumina).
Intermediate-grade tumors are characterized by being locally {{c1::aggressive}} but having low metastatic potential.
The cell of origin for epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is the {{c1::endothelial}} cell.
True/False: All vascular tumors are either clearly benign or clearly malignant. {{c1::False}}
keyPoints: Vascular tumors form a spectrum of malignancy.
Benign: Hemangiomas, Glomus tumors.
Intermediate (Borderline): Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, Kaposi Sarcoma (often placed here, though HHV-8 driven).
Malignant: Angiosarcoma.
Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma cells resemble epithelial cells but are CD31 positive.
microReview: Intermediate Grade Vascular Tumor = Epithelioid Hemangioendothelioma.
examinerTraps: Kaposi Sarcoma is sometimes listed as intermediate, but Epithelioid Hemangioendothelioma is the classic 'borderline' textbook example.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 30-year-old male is diagnosed with multiple large, cavernous hemangiomas within the cerebellum and retina. He is also found to have a renal cell carcinoma. Which of the following genes is likely mutated in this patient?

explanations.a: Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is characterized by hemangioblastomas (a type of vascular tumor) in the cerebellum and retina, along with renal cell carcinoma.
explanations.b: APC mutation causes Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP).
explanations.c: RB1 mutation causes retinoblastoma.
explanations.d: TP53 mutation causes Li-Fraumeni syndrome.
explanations.e: NF1 mutation causes Neurofibromatosis type 1.

ankiCards: Von Hippel-Lindau disease is caused by a mutation in the {{c1::VHL}} gene.
VHL disease is characterized by {{c1::hemangioblastomas}} of the cerebellum and retina.
Patients with VHL disease have an increased risk of {{c1::renal cell carcinoma}}.
Cavernous hemangiomas of the liver and brain can also be seen in {{c1::VHL}} or as sporadic lesions.
The VHL protein is involved in the degradation of {{c1::Hypoxia Inducible Factor (HIF)}}.
keyPoints: VHL is a tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3.
Cavernous hemangiomas (and hemangioblastomas) are part of the VHL spectrum.
Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, blood-filled vascular spaces.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous ones do not spontaneously regress.
In the CNS, they can lead to hemorrhage or mass effect symptoms.
microReview: VHL = Cerebellar/Retinal Hemangioblastomas + Renal Cell Carcinoma + VHL gene.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse hemangioblastoma (VHL) with capillary hemangioma (infancy) or cavernous hemangioma (liver/brain).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the fundamental mechanical failure in the development of a true aneurysm?

options.a: Disruption of the internal elastic lamina only
options.b: Dilation of the vessel involving all three layers of the wall
options.c: Accumulation of blood within the media through an intimal tear
options.d: Extravascular hematoma communicating with the intravascular space
options.e: Focal thinning of the adventitia while the intima remains intact

explanations.a: Disruption of only the internal elastic lamina is a feature of various vascular injuries but does not define an aneurysm, which requires full-thickness wall involvement or weakening.
explanations.b: A true aneurysm is defined as a permanent dilation of an artery that involves all three layers of the arterial wall (intima, media, and adventitia).
explanations.c: This describes an aortic dissection, where blood enters the media; it is not a true aneurysm, although it is often discussed in the same category.
explanations.d: This describes a false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm), where the vessel wall is breached and the hematoma is contained by extravascular connective tissue.
explanations.e: Aneurysms involve weakening or thinning of the media primarily; the adventitia alone thinning would not typically result in the characteristic permanent dilation without medial involvement.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true aneurysm}} involves all three layers of the arterial wall: intima, media, and adventitia.
A {{c1::false aneurysm}} (pseudoaneurysm) is an extravascular hematoma that communicates with the intravascular space.
The two main shapes of aneurysms are {{c1::saccular}} and {{c2::fusiform}}.
{{c1::Fusiform}} aneurysms are characterized by circumferential, symmetrical dilation of the vessel.
An {{c1::aortic dissection}} occurs when blood enters the wall of the artery as a hematoma dissecting between its layers.
keyPoints: Aneurysms are localized abnormal dilations of blood vessels.
True aneurysms involve the intima, media, and adventitia.
Pseudoaneurysms result from a wall defect leading to an external hematoma.
Saccular aneurysms involve only a portion of the wall circumference.
Fusiform aneurysms involve the entire circumference of the vessel segment.
microReview: Aneurysms are classified as true (all 3 layers) or false (breach in wall with contained hematoma). They are further classified by shape into saccular (bubble-like) or fusiform (spindle-shaped).
examinerTraps: Do not confuse an aortic dissection (blood within the media) with a true aneurysm (dilation of all three layers).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... Aneurysms and Dissection
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which molecular mechanism is most critical in the pathogenesis of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) leading to the degradation of the extracellular matrix?

options.b: Excessive deposition of type III collagen
options.c: Inhibition of the TGF-beta signaling pathway
options.e: Activation of the protein C pathway

explanations.a: Abdominal aortic aneurysms are characterized by an imbalance where matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), often derived from macrophages, degrade elastin and collagen in the media.
explanations.b: The pathogenesis involves the degradation of collagen and elastin, not the excessive deposition of healthy collagen.
explanations.c: TGF-beta signaling is often actually implicated in vessel wall maintenance; its dysregulation (often overactivity in Marfan syndrome) contributes to aneurysms, but MMP activity is the direct degradative mechanism in AAA.
explanations.d: Increased, not reduced, elastase activity from inflammatory cells contributes to the breakdown of the elastic lamellae.
explanations.e: The protein C pathway is involved in anticoagulation and is not a primary driver of the structural degradation of the aortic wall.

ankiCards: The degradation of {{c1::elastin}} and collagen in AAA is primarily mediated by {{c2::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
In AAA, the inflammatory infiltrate in the media is predominantly composed of {{c1::macrophages}} and lymphocytes.
The most important modifiable risk factor for AAA is {{c1::cigarette smoking}}.
AAA typically occurs in the aorta {{c1::below}} the level of the renal arteries.
MMP-{{c1::9}} and MMP-{{c2::2}} are the specific gelatinases frequently implicated in aneurysm formation.
keyPoints: Chronic inflammation leads to the release of degradative enzymes.
Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) are key drivers of ECM remodeling.
Loss of smooth muscle cells and elastic fibers weakens the media.
Atherosclerosis is a major precursor to AAA formation.
AAA risk is higher in males, smokers, and those over age 65.
microReview: AAA pathogenesis is a balance between ECM synthesis and degradation. Inflammatory cells (macrophages) secrete MMPs that digest the structural proteins of the media, leading to wall thinning.
examinerTraps: Watch for options suggesting 'increased collagen synthesis'—while some compensatory synthesis occurs, the net effect is massive degradation.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... Atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 69-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history and hypertension presents for a routine physical examination. On abdominal palpation, a pulsatile mass is felt at the level of the umbilicus. He is asymptomatic. An ultrasound confirms a 5.2 cm dilation of the infrarenal aorta. What is the most likely primary underlying pathological process responsible for this finding?

explanations.a: Cystic medial degeneration is more commonly associated with thoracic aortic aneurysms and connective tissue disorders like Marfan syndrome.
explanations.b: Atherosclerosis is the dominant cause of abdominal aortic aneurysms, as it causes intimal thickening that limits oxygen diffusion to the media, leading to secondary medial ischemia and weakening.
explanations.c: Syphilitic (luetic) aneurysms typically involve the ascending aorta and the aortic arch, not the infrarenal abdominal aorta.
explanations.d: Mycotic aneurysms are caused by infection (e.g., Salmonella) and usually present with fever and rapid expansion, which is less likely in this asymptomatic screening finding.
explanations.e: While certain vasculitides (like Takayasu) can involve the aorta, they typically affect younger patients and present with systemic inflammatory symptoms.

ankiCards: The most common cause of abdominal aortic aneurysm is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
The classic clinical triad of a ruptured AAA is {{c1::sudden severe pain}}, {{c2::hypotension}}, and a {{c3::pulsatile mass}}.
AAA is usually located {{c1::infrarenal}} (relative to the renal arteries).
The risk of AAA rupture increases significantly when the diameter exceeds {{c1::5.0 to 5.5}} cm.
Screening for AAA is recommended for men aged {{c1::65–75}} who have ever smoked.
keyPoints: AAA is primarily an atherosclerotic disease.
Smoking is the strongest risk factor.
Atherosclerosis causes medial ischemia by increasing the diffusion distance for oxygen.
Most AAAs are asymptomatic until they rupture or cause distal embolization.
Infrarenal location is characteristic of atherosclerotic aneurysms.
microReview: Elderly male smoker with a pulsatile abdominal mass = AAA. Pathogenesis = Atherosclerosis leading to medial atrophy and weakening.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the location; AAA is infrarenal/atherosclerotic; Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm (TAA) is often associated with hypertension or Marfan.
sourceQuote: Atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries... Aneurysms and Dissection
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following descriptions best distinguishes a saccular aneurysm from a fusiform aneurysm?

options.a: Saccular aneurysms involve a tear in the intima, while fusiform involve all layers
options.b: Saccular aneurysms are spherical outpouchings of a portion of the wall, while fusiform involve the whole circumference
options.c: Saccular aneurysms are always infected (mycotic), while fusiform are always atherosclerotic
options.d: Saccular aneurysms only occur in the brain, while fusiform only occur in the aorta
options.e: Saccular aneurysms contain a thrombus, while fusiform aneurysms never contain thrombi

explanations.a: Both saccular and fusiform are 'true' aneurysms involving all layers. A tear in the intima is characteristic of a dissection.
explanations.b: This is the classic morphological distinction: saccular is a focal outpouching (often containing thrombus), while fusiform is a symmetrical, circumferential dilation.
explanations.c: While mycotic aneurysms are often saccular, not all saccular aneurysms are infected (e.g., berry aneurysms). Fusiform aneurysms are common in atherosclerosis but can occur in other conditions.
explanations.d: Saccular aneurysms (like berry aneurysms) are common in the brain, but can occur anywhere (e.g., in the aorta). Fusiform aneurysms are common in the aorta but not exclusive to it.
explanations.e: Both types of aneurysms frequently contain mural thrombi due to stasis and turbulent flow.

ankiCards: A {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm is a discrete outpouching (5 to 20 cm) that may contain a mural thrombus.
A {{c1::fusiform}} aneurysm is a circumferential dilation up to 20 cm in diameter and long sections of the vessel.
Mural thrombi in aneurysms can lead to {{c1::embolization}} to distal organs.
True aneurysms are defined by the involvement of the {{c1::intima, media, and adventitia}}.
Shape-based classification (saccular vs. fusiform) does not necessarily imply a specific {{c1::etiology}}.
keyPoints: Saccular = spherical/asymmetric outpouching.
Fusiform = spindle-shaped/circumferential dilation.
Both are 'true' aneurysms.
Stasis within the aneurysm predisposes to mural thrombus.
Thrombi can embolize, causing distal ischemia.
microReview: Morphology: Saccular (focal bubble) vs. Fusiform (uniform tube expansion). Both risk rupture and thrombosis.
examinerTraps: The examiner might try to link 'saccular' exclusively to 'berry' aneurysms in the Circle of Willis, but they can occur in the aorta too.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... Aneurysms and Dissection
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which vessel layer is primarily affected by the 'ischemic' damage caused by advanced atherosclerosis, directly leading to the formation of an aneurysm?

explanations.a: The intima is where the atherosclerotic plaque forms. While it thickens, the 'weakening' that leads to aneurysm happens in the layer beneath it.
explanations.b: The internal elastic lamina is a barrier between the intima and media; its degradation is part of the process, but the bulk of the wall's structural integrity lies in the media.
explanations.c: Atherosclerotic plaques in the intima increase the diffusion distance for oxygen from the lumen to the media. This leads to medial ischemia, atrophy, and loss of smooth muscle cells, which weakens the wall.
explanations.d: The external elastic lamina is at the border of the media and adventitia; its damage is secondary to the primary medial weakening.
explanations.e: The adventitia contains the vasa vasorum which supplies the outer portion of the media. In the abdominal aorta (which has few vasa vasorum), the media is particularly dependent on luminal diffusion.

ankiCards: In atherosclerosis, the {{c1::intima}} thickens, which increases the {{c2::diffusion distance}} for oxygen to the media.
Medial {{c1::ischemia}} leads to the death of smooth muscle cells and weakening of the vessel wall.
The abdominal aorta is particularly susceptible to AAA because it has fewer {{c1::vasa vasorum}} than the thoracic aorta.
{{c1::Atherosclerosis}} is the most common cause of aneurysms in the abdominal aorta.
Loss of smooth muscle cells in the media is a hallmark of {{c1::aneurysm}} formation.
keyPoints: Medial weakening is the prerequisite for aneurysm.
Atherosclerosis causes 'starvation' of the media.
Abdominal aorta relies heavily on luminal diffusion for nutrition.
Medial atrophy results in loss of elastic recoil.
The wall thins and dilates under systolic pressure.
microReview: Atherosclerosis -> Thick Intima -> Impaired Oxygen Diffusion to Media -> Medial Ischemia/Atrophy -> Weak Wall -> Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Students often think atherosclerosis 'eats' the wall from the outside; actually, it creates a diffusion barrier on the inside that starves the media.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis)... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old woman with a family history of sudden death presents with sudden onset of 'tearing' chest pain radiating to her back. Her blood pressure is 110/60 mmHg in the right arm and 80/40 mmHg in the left arm. A CT scan shows a longitudinal intramural hematoma. What is the most likely microscopic finding in her aortic wall?

explanations.a: Atherosclerosis is more common in older patients with AAA, not young patients with thoracic dissection.
explanations.b: In young patients with aortic dissection (often associated with Marfan syndrome or other connective tissue disorders), the characteristic microscopic finding is cystic medial degeneration (loss of smooth muscle and elastic tissue with accumulation of mucoid material).
explanations.c: Giant cell inflammation is seen in Temporal Arteritis or Takayasu Arteritis, which typically present with pulse deficits or jaw claudication, not acute dissection vignettes.
explanations.d: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis affects small vessels (capillaries/venules), not the aorta.
explanations.e: Fibrinoid necrosis is a feature of malignant hypertension or certain vasculitides in small arteries, not typically the aorta in this clinical context.

ankiCards: The most common predisposing factor for aortic dissection in older adults is {{c1::hypertension}}.
The most common predisposing factor for aortic dissection in young adults is {{c1::Marfan syndrome}} (or connective tissue disorders).
{{c1::Cystic medial degeneration}} is characterized by the fragmentation of elastic tissue and the creation of proteoglycan-filled spaces.
Aortic dissection pain is classically described as {{c1::tearing}} or {{c2::ripping}}.
A difference in {{c1::blood pressure}} between arms is a clinical clue for aortic dissection.
keyPoints: Aortic dissection is not a true aneurysm but a related catastrophic event.
Cystic medial degeneration involves loss of medial structural integrity.
Young patients often have a genetic basis (FBN1 mutation).
Hypertension is the major risk factor in non-genetic cases.
The 'double barrel' aorta refers to a second false lumen created by the dissection.
microReview: Young + Tearing Chest Pain + BP discrepancy = Aortic Dissection. Micro: Cystic Medial Degeneration. Major risk: Hypertension (older) or Marfan (young).
examinerTraps: Note that 'cystic medial necrosis' is an older term for 'cystic medial degeneration'—there is no actual 'necrosis' occurring.
sourceQuote: Aneurysms and Dissection... Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm... Aortic Dissection
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Syphilitic (luetic) aneurysms are historically significant causes of thoracic aortic dilation. What is the specific mechanism by which Treponema pallidum leads to this condition?

options.a: Direct invasion and destruction of the endothelial cells
options.b: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.c: Deposition of immune complexes in the adventitia
options.d: Production of bacterial elastases that degrade the media
options.e: Formation of intimal granulomas that obstruct flow

explanations.a: The bacteria do not primarily target the endothelium; they target the small vessels supplying the aorta.
explanations.b: Tertiary syphilis causes an obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta. This leads to ischemic injury of the outer media, causing weakening and 'tree-barking' of the intima.
explanations.c: Syphilitic aortitis is a delayed-type hypersensitivity/inflammatory response, not primarily an immune complex disease.
explanations.d: Treponema pallidum does not produce potent extracellular elastases; the damage is secondary to ischemia from vascular supply compromise.
explanations.e: While gummas (granulomas) occur in syphilis, the aortic damage is due to the endarteritis of the vasa vasorum, not obstructive intimal granulomas.

ankiCards: Syphilitic aneurysms typically involve the {{c1::ascending}} aorta.
The characteristic 'tree-bark' appearance of the aorta in syphilis is due to {{c1::intimal scarring}} secondary to medial ischemia.
Tertiary syphilis leads to {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}} of the vasa vasorum.
Syphilitic aortitis can lead to dilation of the aortic root, causing {{c1::aortic valve insufficiency}} (regurgitation).
The vasa vasorum are small vessels located in the {{c1::adventitia}} that supply the outer media.
keyPoints: Syphilis targets the vasa vasorum.
Ischemia of the outer media leads to weakening.
This typically results in Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm (TAA).
Aortic regurgitation is a common complication.
Distinctive 'tree-bark' intimal appearance.
microReview: Syphilis -> Vasa Vasorum Endarteritis -> Medial Ischemia -> TAA + Tree-bark Intima + Aortic Regurgitation.
examinerTraps: Syphilis = Thoracic (Ascending); Atherosclerosis = Abdominal (Infrarenal).
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 75-year-old male with a history of poorly controlled hypertension presents to the emergency department with acute, excruciating back pain and fainting. His blood pressure is 70/40 mmHg. Physical examination reveals a large, tender, pulsatile mass in the abdomen. Which complication of his condition is most likely responsible for his current presentation?

options.a: Occlusion of the mesenteric arteries by a mural thrombus
options.c: Compression of the ureters leading to hydronephrosis
options.d: Infection of the aneurysm by circulating bacteria

explanations.a: While mural thrombi can cause embolization and occlusion, it would present with bowel ischemia, not usually acute shock and a tender mass.
explanations.b: The triad of sudden severe back/abdominal pain, hypotension (shock), and a pulsatile mass is classic for AAA rupture into the peritoneal or retroperitoneal space.
explanations.c: Compression of adjacent structures (like ureters or vertebrae) can cause chronic pain or hydronephrosis, but not acute hemodynamic collapse.
explanations.d: A mycotic (infected) aneurysm might present with pain and a mass, but the sudden hypotension suggests rupture.
explanations.e: Dissection is a separate pathological process (blood between layers), whereas a pulsatile mass in an elderly man is much more likely an atherosclerotic AAA that has now ruptured.

ankiCards: The classic triad of AAA rupture is {{c1::pain}}, {{c2::hypotension}}, and a {{c3::pulsatile mass}}.
AAA rupture can occur into the {{c1::peritoneal}} cavity or the {{c2::retroperitoneum}}.
The risk of AAA rupture is most closely related to the {{c1::size (diameter)}} of the aneurysm.
Operative mortality for ruptured AAA is approximately {{c1::50}}%.
AAAs greater than {{c1::5.5}} cm are usually managed surgically or endovascularly.
keyPoints: Rupture is the most feared complication of AAA.
It presents as a surgical emergency with shock.
Mortality is extremely high if not treated immediately.
Pain often radiates to the back or flank.
Size is the best predictor of rupture risk.
microReview: Aneurysm complications: Rupture (shock/death), Embolization (distal ischemia), Compression (ureters/bone), Thrombosis (occlusion).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the pain of dissection (tearing) with the pain of AAA rupture (sudden, severe, often associated with shock).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes a 'false aneurysm' (pseudoaneurysm)?

options.a: A localized dilation of the aorta that includes the intima and media only
options.b: A tear in the intima that allows blood to create a channel in the media
options.c: A defect in the vascular wall leading to an extravascular hematoma that communicates with the intravascular space
options.d: A congenital thinning of the arterial wall found in the Circle of Willis
options.e: A spindle-shaped dilation that involves the entire circumference of the vessel

explanations.a: A true aneurysm must involve all three layers. There is no standard 'true' aneurysm involving only two.
explanations.b: This is the definition of an aortic dissection.
explanations.c: A false aneurysm is not a true dilation of the wall but a hole in the wall (e.g., from trauma or catheterization) where blood is contained by surrounding tissue/clot.
explanations.d: This describes a 'berry' aneurysm, which is a true saccular aneurysm.
explanations.e: This describes a fusiform aneurysm, which is a type of true aneurysm.

ankiCards: A {{c1::false aneurysm}} results when a wall defect leads to an extravascular hematoma.
A common cause of a femoral artery false aneurysm is {{c1::arterial catheterization}}.
Unlike a true aneurysm, a pseudoaneurysm's 'wall' is often just {{c1::clotted blood}} and connective tissue.
{{c1::Trauma}} and infection are common causes of pseudoaneurysms.
Pseudoaneurysms can be distinguished from true aneurysms using {{c1::ultrasound}} (Doppler showing flow into the sac).
keyPoints: True = all layers intact but dilated.
False = wall breached, hematoma contained.
Common after cardiac catheterization (femoral artery).
Risks include rupture and infection.
Treatment may involve thrombin injection or surgical repair.
microReview: Pseudoaneurysm = Hole in wall + 'pulsatile hematoma'. It is 'false' because the actual vessel wall layers do not form the sac.
examinerTraps: The examiner may use the term 'pulsatile hematoma'—this is synonymous with a pseudoaneurysm.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: What is the most common site for an atherosclerotic aneurysm?

explanations.a: The ascending aorta is more commonly involved in hypertensive or syndromic (Marfan) aneurysms/dissections.
explanations.b: The aortic arch is less common than the abdominal aorta for atherosclerotic aneurysms.
explanations.c: The abdominal aorta (specifically between the renal arteries and the bifurcation) is the most frequent site for atherosclerotic aneurysms.
explanations.d: Iliac arteries are often involved by extension from the abdominal aorta, but they are not the most common primary site.
explanations.e: Popliteal aneurysms are the most common peripheral aneurysms, but less common than AAA.

ankiCards: The most common site of an atherosclerotic aneurysm is the {{c1::abdominal aorta}}.
AAA usually occurs {{c1::distal}} to the origin of the renal arteries.
AAA usually occurs {{c1::proximal}} to the bifurcation of the iliac arteries.
The major risk of AAA is {{c1::rupture}} into the retroperitoneal space.
Mural thrombi in AAA are frequent due to {{c1::turbulent}} blood flow.
keyPoints: AAA is the most common aneurysm.
Location: Infrarenal abdominal aorta.
Etiology: Mostly atherosclerosis.
Pathology: Medial thinning.
Complication: Mural thrombus and rupture.
microReview: Most common aneurysm = Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA). Most common cause = Atherosclerosis. Most common location = Infrarenal.
examinerTraps: Don't pick 'thoracic aorta' just because it's larger; the abdominal portion is much more prone to atherosclerosis-induced weakening.
sourceQuote: Atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries... Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm... Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 64-year-old male presents with a 3-month history of fatigue, weight loss, and upper abdominal discomfort. Physical examination reveals hepatomegaly. His medical history is significant for 25 years of employment in a factory manufacturing polyvinyl chloride (PVC). Imaging shows multiple poorly defined, hemorrhagic masses within the liver. Biopsy demonstrates malignant spindle-shaped cells that are positive for CD31 and factor VIII-related antigen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Hepatic hemangiomas are benign, common, and usually well-circumscribed cavernous spaces, not malignant spindle-cell tumors associated with PVC.
explanations.b: Hepatocellular carcinoma is a tumor of hepatocytes, usually associated with cirrhosis or HBV/HCV, and does not typically express endothelial markers like CD31.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma of the liver is a highly aggressive malignant vascular tumor associated with exposure to arsenic, Thorotrast, and polyvinyl chloride (PVC).
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation seen in immunocompromised patients caused by Bartonella infection, not industrial toxins.
explanations.e: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 and typically involves the skin or GI tract in AIDS patients, rather than appearing as primary liver masses related to PVC.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma of the liver is associated with exposure to {{c1::polyvinyl chloride (PVC)}}, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
The immunohistochemical marker most specific for endothelial differentiation in vascular tumors is {{c1::CD31}}.
Hepatic angiosarcoma presents histologically with {{c1::malignant spindle cells}} forming irregular vascular channels.
The prognosis for patients diagnosed with hepatic angiosarcoma is generally {{c1::poor/aggressive}}.
Unlike benign hemangiomas, angiosarcomas demonstrate {{c1::marked cellular atypia}} and mitoses.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a malignant neoplasm of endothelial cells.
Specific risk factors include PVC, arsenic, and Thorotrast (liver) and chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
Markers include CD31 and von Willebrand factor (Factor VIII-related antigen).
Histology shows pleomorphic spindle cells and rudimentary vascular spaces.
These tumors are highly aggressive with high mortality rates.
microReview: Angiosarcoma: Malignant. CD31+. Risk: PVC/Arsenic (Liver), Radiation (Breast), Lymphedema (Arm).
examinerTraps: Do not confuse PVC (Angiosarcoma) with Aflatoxin (Hepatocellular carcinoma) as environmental liver carcinogens.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with an exquisitely painful, small, bluish nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. The pain is particularly triggered by exposure to cold temperatures. Histological examination reveals nests of uniform, specialized smooth muscle cells surrounding vascular channels. From which of the following cell types does this tumor originate?

explanations.a: Endothelial cells line the vascular spaces but are not the primary proliferating cell type in this specific painful subungual lesion.
explanations.b: Pericytes are contractile cells around capillaries, but the glomus tumor is specifically derived from the glomus body's smooth muscle cells.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) arise from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized thermoregulatory organ.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts produce collagen and are seen in fibromas, but they do not form the characteristic nests of cells seen in glomus tumors.
explanations.e: Lymphatic endothelium would suggest a lymphangioma, which is usually painless and not found in a subungual distribution.

ankiCards: The classic triad for a glomus tumor is {{c1::pain}}, {{c1::subungual location}}, and {{c1::sensitivity to cold}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle cells}} of the glomus body.
The glomus body is involved in the physiological process of {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Histology of a glomus tumor shows uniform cells surrounding {{c1::vascular channels}}.
Clinically, glomus tumors appear as small, {{c1::bluish}} nodules.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but extremely painful.
Commonly found in distal digits, specifically subungual.
Derived from neuromyoarterial glomus bodies.
Cells are uniform, round, and specialized smooth muscle.
Surgical excision is curative.
microReview: Glomus tumor: Painful, subungual, cold-sensitive. Origin: Modified smooth muscle cells of glomus body.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'cold sensitivity' or 'pain' to distinguish a glomus tumor from a simple subungual hematoma or hemangioma.
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels (Fig. 11.1).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An HIV-positive patient with a CD4+ count of 150/mm³ presents with multiple purple-to-red macules and plaques on the lower extremities and trunk. Biopsy reveals slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells and spindle-shaped cells. Which of the following pathogens is the primary causative agent in the pathogenesis of this condition?

explanations.a: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which looks similar clinically but histologically shows neutrophils and clusters of bacteria (Warthin-Starry stain).
explanations.b: HHV-8 (also known as KSHV) is the definitive cause of Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) across all clinical variants (AIDS-associated, classic, endemic, and transplant-associated).
explanations.c: CMV is common in HIV patients but causes retinitis or colitis, not vascular tumors like KS.
explanations.d: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.e: HPV is associated with squamous cell carcinomas and warts, not vascular lesions.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is caused by {{c1::Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}.
The characteristic histological feature of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::slit-like}} vascular spaces.
In Kaposi Sarcoma, vascular spaces are often filled with {{c1::extravasated red blood cells}}.
Kaposi Sarcoma is most commonly seen in the setting of {{c1::HIV/AIDS}} with low CD4 counts.
Biopsy of Kaposi Sarcoma shows proliferation of {{c1::spindle}} cells.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
HHV-8 viral proteins dysregulate the cell cycle (e.g., v-cyclin).
Four clinical types: Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
Histology: Slit-like spaces, spindle cells, hemorrhage, and hyaline droplets.
Treatment involves HAART for HIV-associated cases.
microReview: KS = HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Slit-like spaces + RBC extravasation.
examinerTraps: Distinguish KS from Bacillary Angiomatosis: KS has spindle cells and slit-like spaces; Bacillary Angiomatosis has neutrophils and 'bush-like' bacterial clusters.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following immunohistochemical markers is most useful for confirming the endothelial origin of a poorly differentiated malignant tumor suspected of being an angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells and carcinomas, not vascular endothelium.
explanations.b: S100 is used for melanoma and neural crest-derived tumors, not vascular lesions.
explanations.c: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a transmembrane glycoprotein expressed on endothelial cells and is a highly sensitive and specific marker for vascular tumors.
explanations.d: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (smooth or skeletal), not endothelial cells.
explanations.e: CD45 (LCA) is a marker for leukocytes and lymphomas, not vascular cells.

ankiCards: The marker {{c1::CD31}} is highly specific for confirming the endothelial origin of a tumor.
Another name for the CD31 marker is {{c1::PECAM-1}}.
Besides CD31, {{c1::Factor VIII-related antigen (vWF)}} can also identify endothelial cells.
Poorly differentiated angiosarcomas may mimic carcinomas but lack {{c1::cytokeratin}} expression.
{{c1::CD34}} is another vascular marker, though less specific than CD31.
keyPoints: CD31 is the gold standard immunohistochemical marker for endothelium.
Angiosarcomas can be so poorly differentiated they look like carcinomas; markers are essential.
CD31 facilitates the diagnosis of malignant vascular tumors.
Factor VIII-related antigen is another option but often less sensitive in high-grade tumors.
Endothelial markers help differentiate angiosarcoma from spindle cell melanoma (S100+).
microReview: Vascular Markers: CD31, CD34, vWF/Factor VIII.
examinerTraps: Examiners might list CD34; while CD34 is present in vessels, it is also in many other mesenchymal tumors, making CD31 the 'better' choice for endothelial specificity.
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 35-year-old patient with AIDS presents with skin lesions that appear histologically as a lobular proliferation of capillaries with prominent, 'epithelioid' endothelial cells, accompanied by a heavy infiltrate of neutrophils and nuclear dust (leukocytoclasis). Silver stain (Warthin-Starry) reveals clusters of bacilli. This condition is most likely caused by which mechanism?

options.b: Opportunistic infection by a gram-negative Proteobacterium
options.c: Radiation-induced DNA damage to endothelial cells
options.e: Autosomal dominant mutation in the VHL gene

explanations.a: This describes Kaposi Sarcoma (HHV-8), which does not show bacteria on silver stain.
explanations.b: The diagnosis is Bacillary Angiomatosis, caused by Bartonella henselae or Bartonella quintana, which are gram-negative Proteobacteria.
explanations.c: Radiation-induced damage is a risk factor for angiosarcoma, not bacillary angiomatosis.
explanations.d: Chronic lymphedema leads to Stewart-Treves syndrome (angiosarcoma), not an infectious vascular proliferation.
explanations.e: VHL mutations lead to cavernous hemangiomas and hemangioblastomas, not lesions with neutrophils and bacilli.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by the organism {{c1::Bartonella}} (species henselae or quintana).
The stain used to visualize the bacilli in bacillary angiomatosis is the {{c1::Warthin-Starry (silver)}} stain.
Histologically, bacillary angiomatosis features a prominent infiltrate of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
Clinically, bacillary angiomatosis can mimic {{c1::Kaposi Sarcoma}} in HIV patients.
Bartonella quintana is classically associated with the vector {{c1::human body lice}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary Angiomatosis is an infectious mimic of vascular tumors.
Occurs primarily in immunocompromised (AIDS) patients.
Induced by Bartonella species (Henselae - cats; Quintana - lice).
Histology: Lobular capillary proliferation, epithelioid endothelium, neutrophils.
Responds to antibiotic treatment (e.g., erythromycin).
microReview: Bacillary Angiomatosis: Bartonella + Neutrophils + Silver stain positive. Kaposi: HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Silver stain negative.
examinerTraps: The presence of neutrophils is the key histological 'clue' to differentiate Bacillary Angiomatosis from Kaposi Sarcoma, which typically lacks a significant neutrophilic infiltrate.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism)
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A newborn girl is noted to have a large, fluctuant mass on the left side of her neck that transilluminates on physical examination. Genetic testing reveals a 45,X karyotype. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for the neck mass?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas (strawberry) are common in infants but are typically solid, bright red cutaneous lesions, not large fluctuant neck masses.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas can occur in the neck but are not the classic association with Turner syndrome.
explanations.c: Cystic hygroma (a form of cavernous lymphangioma) is characteristically found in the neck/axilla of infants and is strongly associated with Turner syndrome (45,X).
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are small, painful subungual lesions, not large neonatal neck masses.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor of older adults or those with specific exposures; it is not seen as a congenital neck mass.

ankiCards: Cystic hygroma is a type of {{c1::cavernous lymphangioma}}.
Cystic hygroma is frequently associated with the chromosomal abnormality {{c1::Turner syndrome (45,X)}}.
A key physical exam finding of a cystic hygroma is that it {{c1::transilluminates}}.
The most common location for a cystic hygroma is the {{c1::neck (or axilla)}}.
Histologically, lymphangiomas contain spaces filled with fluid that lacks {{c1::red blood cells}}.
keyPoints: Lymphangiomas are benign lymphatic analogs of hemangiomas.
Cystic hygromas are cavernous lymphangiomas occurring in the neck.
Associated with Turner Syndrome and Down Syndrome.
They are poorly circumscribed, making surgical excision difficult.
Spaces are lined by endothelium and contain proteinaceous lymph fluid.
microReview: Turner Syndrome + Neck Mass + Transillumination = Cystic Hygroma.
examinerTraps: Ensure you distinguish lymphangioma from hemangioma by the content of the vessels: lymphangiomas lack RBCs in the lumens.
sourceQuote: To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure and function.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old male with a known history of von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is found to have a vascular lesion in the cerebellum. Which of the following histological features is most characteristic of the vascular tumors typically associated with this genetic syndrome?

options.a: Small, thin-walled capillaries with scant stroma
options.b: Large, dilated vascular channels separated by connective tissue stroma
options.c: Slit-like spaces with spindle cells and RBC extravasation
options.e: Malignant endothelial cells with high mitotic activity

explanations.a: This describes a capillary hemangioma, whereas VHL is more often associated with cavernous-type vascular lesions or hemangioblastomas.
explanations.b: VHL is associated with cavernous hemangiomas (and hemangioblastomas) which consist of large, dilated (cavernous) vascular spaces.
explanations.c: This describes Kaposi Sarcoma, which is not associated with VHL.
explanations.d: This describes a glomus tumor, which is not associated with VHL.
explanations.e: This describes angiosarcoma, which is not associated with VHL.

ankiCards: Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is associated with {{c1::cavernous}} hemangiomas of the cerebellum and retina.
VHL is an autosomal {{c1::dominant}} disorder.
Besides vascular tumors, VHL is associated with {{c1::renal cell carcinoma}}.
A {{c1::cavernous}} hemangioma consists of large, dilated vascular channels.
In VHL, cavernous hemangiomas can also be found in the {{c1::liver/pancreas}}.
keyPoints: VHL disease involves the VHL tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3.
Associated with Hemangioblastomas (CNS/Retina) and Cavernous Hemangiomas.
Cavernous hemangiomas have large, blood-filled spaces.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous ones are often deep-seated.
Clinical risk: Intracranial hemorrhage or mass effect.
microReview: VHL: Chromosome 3, RCC, Hemangioblastoma, Cavernous Hemangiomas.
examinerTraps: VHL is specifically chromosome 3. Don't confuse with NF1 (17) or NF2 (22).
sourceQuote: Arterial wall thickness gradually diminishes as the vessels become smaller, but the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An infant is born with a bright red, raised 'strawberry-like' lesion on the scalp. The parents are concerned as the lesion grows rapidly over the first few months of life. However, by age 5, the lesion has significantly regressed and faded. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas are deeper, do not usually regress spontaneously, and lack the bright red 'strawberry' appearance.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granulomas are rapidly growing pedunculated lesions that often bleed and follow trauma; they do not typically undergo spontaneous involution over years.
explanations.c: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma is a very common capillary hemangioma of infancy that grows rapidly and then almost always involutes by age 7.
explanations.d: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a flat lesion that does not regress; it grows with the child.
explanations.e: Spider angiomas are small, central arterioles with radiating vessels, often associated with hyperestrogenic states (pregnancy, cirrhosis).

ankiCards: The common name for a juvenile hemangioma is a {{c1::strawberry}} hemangioma.
Juvenile hemangiomas are histologically classified as {{c1::capillary}} hemangiomas.
Most juvenile hemangiomas {{c1::involute/regress}} by age 7.
Juvenile hemangiomas occur in approximately 1 in {{c1::200}} births.
A port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) {{c1::does not}} regress with age, unlike a strawberry hemangioma.
keyPoints: Juvenile (Strawberry) hemangioma: Benign, very common in skin.
Rapid growth phase followed by spontaneous regression.
Composed of thin-walled capillaries with minimal stroma.
Clinical appearance: Raised, bright red, lobulated.
Treatment: Observation (propranolol may be used if obstructing vision).
microReview: Strawberry Hemangioma: Newborn + Rapid growth + Regresses by age 7.
examinerTraps: Differentiating from Port-Wine Stain: Strawberry hemangiomas are raised and regress; Port-Wine stains are flat and persist/thicken.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman presents with a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated nodule on her gingiva that bleeds easily with minor trauma. Histologically, the lesion shows a circumscribed proliferation of capillaries arranged in lobules, often with overlying ulceration. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma is a malignant, poorly circumscribed lesion, not a benign pedunculated gingival mass.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is seen in immunocompromised patients and caused by Bartonella, not healthy pregnant women.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (Lobular Capillary Hemangioma) frequently occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum) and is characterized by rapid growth and bleeding.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are painful subungual lesions, not gingival nodules.
explanations.e: Cavernous hemangiomas are deeper, non-pedunculated, and don't typically appear suddenly on the gingiva during pregnancy.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is neither {{c1::pyogenic}} (infectious) nor a {{c1::granuloma}} (histologically).
The gingival form of pyogenic granuloma in pregnancy is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Histologically, pyogenic granuloma is a {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
Clinically, pyogenic granulomas are often {{c1::pedunculated}} and bleed easily.
Pyogenic granulomas often develop following {{c1::trauma}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign, polypoid capillary hemangioma.
Often occurs in skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
Strong association with pregnancy (hormonal influence).
Histology: Lobular arrangement of capillaries with edema/inflammation.
May regress after pregnancy or require simple excision.
microReview: Pyogenic Granuloma: Pregnancy + Gingiva + Bleeds easily + Lobular capillaries.
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic granuloma' is a classic distractor—remember it is actually a vascular tumor (lobular capillary hemangioma).
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels (Fig. 11.1).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for evaluation of a large, flat, purple birthmark covering the right side of his face in the distribution of the ophthalmic and maxillary branches of the trigeminal nerve. He has also had two recent seizures. MRI shows leptomeningeal venous malformations on the ipsilateral side. This clinical constellation is most consistent with which of the following?

explanations.a: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) presents with multiple small telangiectasias and epistaxis, not a large facial port-wine stain.
explanations.b: Sturge-Weber syndrome features a facial port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) in the V1/V2 distribution, ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomas, and seizures.
explanations.c: VHL involves cavernous hemangiomas and RCC but not facial port-wine stains.
explanations.d: NF1 features café-au-lait spots and neurofibromas, not vascular port-wine stains.
explanations.e: Tuberous sclerosis features ash-leaf spots and angiofibromas, but not the classic V1/V2 port-wine stain/leptomeningeal angioma combo.

ankiCards: Sturge-Weber syndrome is associated with a facial birthmark called a {{c1::port-wine stain (nevus flammeus)}}.
The port-wine stain in Sturge-Weber syndrome usually follows the distribution of the {{c1::trigeminal (CN V)}} nerve.
Sturge-Weber syndrome involves ipsilateral {{c1::leptomeningeal}} angiomas.
Common CNS symptoms of Sturge-Weber include {{c1::seizures}} and mental retardation.
A port-wine stain {{c1::does not}} spontaneously regress.
keyPoints: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a common ectasia/vascular malformation.
Most are ordinary birthmarks; those in V1/V2 distribution suggest Sturge-Weber.
Sturge-Weber involves GNAQ gene mutations.
Radiology clue: 'Tram-track' calcifications on CT/MRI of the brain.
Glaucoma is a common ocular complication of Sturge-Weber.
microReview: Sturge-Weber: Port-wine stain (V1/V2) + Seizures + Leptomeningeal angioma.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'CN V distribution' or 'seizures' to link a simple port-wine stain to the full Sturge-Weber syndrome.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the anatomical characteristic of a 'true' aneurysm?

options.a: A breach in the vascular wall leading to an extravascular hematoma communicating with the intravascular space
options.b: An attenuated but intact arterial wall or thinned ventricular wall involving all three layers
options.c: A longitudinal tear within the tunica media resulting in a blood-filled channel
options.d: A localized dilation of a vein following the destruction of the tunica adventitia
options.e: An accumulation of atherosclerotic plaque causing luminal narrowing and wall rigidity

explanations.a: This describes a false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm), where a wall defect leads to a hematoma contained by extravascular tissue.
explanations.b: A true aneurysm involves all three layers of the arterial wall (intima, media, and adventitia) or the thinned wall of the heart.
explanations.c: This describes an aortic dissection, which is distinct from an aneurysm although they often coexist.
explanations.d: Aneurysms specifically refer to arterial or cardiac dilations; venous dilations are typically referred to as varicosities.
explanations.e: This describes the process of atherosclerosis and stenosis, which is a different mechanism of vascular disease than aneurysm formation.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true aneurysm}} involves all three layers of the arterial wall (intima, media, and adventitia).
A {{c1::false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm)}} is a breach in the vascular wall leading to an extravascular hematoma.
The two principal mechanisms of vascular disease are {{c1::narrowing (stenosis)}} and {{c2::weakening of walls}}.
Saccular aneurysms are {{c1::spherical}} outpouchings involving only a portion of the vessel wall.
Fusiform aneurysms represent {{c1::circumferential}} dilations of a long vascular segment.
keyPoints: True aneurysms involve all layers of the vessel wall.
Aneurysms can be classified as saccular or fusiform.
Pseudoaneurysms result from a wall defect rather than wall expansion.
Weakening of vessel walls leads to dilation or rupture.
Aneurysms are common in the abdominal aorta and iliac arteries.
microReview: Aneurysms are localized abnormal dilations of blood vessels or the heart. They are categorized as true (involving all layers) or false (extravascular hematoma). Common causes include atherosclerosis (AAA) and hypertension (TAA).
examinerTraps: Do not confuse a false aneurysm with a true aneurysm; the key is whether all three vessel layers are present and intact in the dilated segment.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture. To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the pathogenesis of abdominal aortic aneurysms, which of the following biochemical processes is primarily responsible for the degradation of the extracellular matrix within the tunica media?

options.b: Inhibition of lysyl oxidase by copper deficiency
options.c: Activation of the caspase-dependent apoptotic pathway
options.e: Decreased production of transforming growth factor-beta

explanations.a: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), especially MMP-2 and MMP-9 produced by macrophages, degrade elastin and collagen, weakening the aortic wall.
explanations.b: Lysyl oxidase is required for collagen cross-linking; while its inhibition causes lathyrism, it is not the primary driver of typical AAA.
explanations.c: While smooth muscle cell loss occurs, the hallmark of AAA is the enzymatic degradation of the structural matrix.
explanations.d: This is characteristic of cystic medial degeneration, often seen in thoracic aneurysms or Marfan syndrome, rather than the inflammatory/atherosclerotic AAA.
explanations.e: TGF-beta signaling is often increased or dysregulated in genetic syndromes leading to aneurysms, rather than decreased in standard AAA.

ankiCards: The degradation of {{c1::elastin and collagen}} in the media is the hallmark of AAA pathogenesis.
{{c1::Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}} are the enzymes primarily responsible for matrix degradation in AAA.
MMP-2 and {{c1::MMP-9}} are specifically implicated in the expansion of abdominal aortic aneurysms.
The inflammatory infiltrate in AAA typically consists of {{c1::macrophages}} and T cells.
Atherosclerosis causes AAA by increasing the {{c1::diffusion distance}} from the lumen to the media, leading to ischemia.
keyPoints: AAA is characterized by chronic inflammation and matrix degradation.
MMPs are upregulated and tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs) are downregulated.
Elastin loss is a critical early event in wall weakening.
Ischemia of the inner media occurs due to thickened atherosclerotic plaque.
Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for AAA.
microReview: Pathogenesis of AAA involves: 1) Inflammation, 2) Degradation of ECM by MMPs, 3) Loss of SMCs due to ischemia, and 4) Weakening of the wall leading to progressive dilation.
examinerTraps: Differentiate between the mechanism of AAA (MMPs/inflammation) and TAA/Marfan (Cystic medial degeneration/TGF-beta signaling).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture. To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male smoker with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia presents for a routine physical examination. On abdominal palpation, a non-tender, pulsatile mass is felt at the level of the umbilicus. Imaging confirms a 5.5 cm dilation of the infrarenal aorta. What is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?

explanations.a: Cystic medial degeneration is more commonly associated with thoracic aortic aneurysms and connective tissue disorders.
explanations.b: Endarteritis of the vasa vasorum is the classic lesion of tertiary syphilis, leading to thoracic (obliterative) aortitis.
explanations.c: Atherosclerosis is the dominant cause of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA), typically occurring in males, smokers, and the elderly.
explanations.d: Congenital medial defects are associated with berry aneurysms in the Circle of Willis.
explanations.e: Mycotic aneurysms are caused by seeding of the vessel wall by bacteria (e.g., Salmonella) or fungi, usually presenting with fever and pain.

ankiCards: The most common site for an atherosclerotic aneurysm is the {{c1::abdominal aorta}}.
The major risk factors for AAA are {{c1::male sex}} and {{c2::smoking}}.
AAA are typically located {{c1::infrarenal}} (below the renal arteries).
The diameter threshold for significantly increased rupture risk in AAA is {{c1::5.5}} cm.
A pulsatile abdominal mass is the classic clinical finding for an {{c1::abdominal aortic aneurysm}}.
keyPoints: AAA is primarily a disease of older men who smoke.
Most AAA are located between the renal arteries and the iliac bifurcation.
Atherosclerosis compromises nutrient diffusion to the media.
Clinical presentation is often asymptomatic until rupture.
Rupture risk increases exponentially with aneurysm diameter.
microReview: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA): Elderly male smoker + Pulsatile mass + Infrarenal location + Atherosclerosis as the primary driver.
examinerTraps: Patients with AAA often have generalized atherosclerosis; however, the 'pulsatile mass' is the giveaway for the aneurysm itself, not just peripheral artery disease.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture. To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the role of the vasa vasorum in the development of syphilitic (luetic) aneurysms?

options.a: Proliferation of vasa vasorum leading to intra-mural hemorrhage
options.b: Obliterative endarteritis leading to ischemic injury of the tunica media
options.c: Aneurysmal dilation of the vasa vasorum causing compression of the adventitia
options.d: Embolic occlusion of the vasa vasorum by bacterial vegetations
options.e: Suppurative inflammation of the vasa vasorum leading to abscess formation

explanations.a: Intra-mural hemorrhage is a feature of aortic dissection, not the primary mechanism of syphilitic aortitis.
explanations.b: Tertiary syphilis causes obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum, which supplies the outer media of the thoracic aorta. This leads to medial ischemia and scarring (tree-barking).
explanations.c: The vasa vasorum undergo narrowing and occlusion, not dilation.
explanations.d: This describes a mycotic aneurysm mechanism, not the chronic vasculitis of syphilis.
explanations.e: Syphilitic aortitis is characterized by plasma cell-rich inflammation and scarring, not acute suppurative abscesses.

ankiCards: Syphilitic aneurysms typically involve the {{c1::thoracic}} aorta.
The underlying lesion in syphilitic aortitis is {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}} of the vasa vasorum.
Ischemic injury in syphilitic aortitis leads to the loss of {{c1::elastic fibers}} in the media.
The 'tree-bark' appearance of the aortic intima is characteristic of {{c1::syphilitic (luetic) aortitis}}.
Syphilitic aneurysms can lead to {{c1::aortic valve insufficiency}} due to dilation of the aortic root.
keyPoints: Tertiary syphilis targets the vasa vasorum.
Medial ischemia leads to scarring and loss of elasticity.
Contraction of fibrous scars produces the 'tree-bark' intimal appearance.
Syphilitic aneurysms are usually thoracic (ascending aorta).
Death often results from heart failure due to aortic regurgitation.
microReview: Syphilitic Aneurysm: Tertiary syphilis -> Obliterative endarteritis of vasa vasorum -> Medial ischemia -> Weakened thoracic aorta -> Tree-barking and dilation.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'plasma cells' or 'tree-barking' in the vignette to confirm syphilis over atherosclerosis.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture. To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old male with a history of tall stature, long fingers (arachnodactyly), and ectopia lentis presents with sudden-onset chest pain. Echocardiography reveals a dilated aortic root and mitral valve prolapse. What histological change is most likely present in this patient's aortic media?

explanations.a: Atherosclerosis is rare in a 24-year-old and typically affects the abdominal aorta.
explanations.b: Granulomatous inflammation is characteristic of Giant Cell Arteritis or Takayasu Arteritis.
explanations.c: Cystic medial degeneration (characterized by elastic fiber fragmentation and mucoid material accumulation) is the classic finding in Marfan syndrome.
explanations.d: This would indicate acute infectious aortitis or a mycotic aneurysm.
explanations.e: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis affects small arteries and arterioles in the setting of hypertension or diabetes.

ankiCards: {{c1::Marfan syndrome}} is caused by mutations in the FBN1 gene encoding fibrillin-1.
The histological hallmark of aortic weakness in Marfan syndrome is {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
Cystic medial degeneration involves the accumulation of {{c1::glycosaminoglycans (mucoid material)}}.
Excessive signaling of {{c1::TGF-beta}} contributes to the pathogenesis of Marfan-associated aneurysms.
Aortic {{c1::dissection}} is a common and lethal complication of aneurysms in Marfan syndrome.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome involves FBN1 mutations.
Fibrillin deficiency leads to dysregulated TGF-beta signaling.
Histology shows loss of elastic fibers and 'cysts' of mucoid ground substance.
Aneurysms typically occur in the ascending aorta (thoracic).
Patients are at high risk for aortic dissection.
microReview: Marfan Syndrome: Fibrillin-1 mutation -> High TGF-beta -> Cystic Medial Degeneration -> Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm/Dissection.
examinerTraps: The term 'cystic' is a misnomer; there are no true epithelial-lined cysts, just pools of mucoid material.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture. To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following is the most common cause of a mycotic aneurysm?

options.a: Direct invasion of a vessel by a contiguous suppurative process
options.b: Tertiary syphilitic infection of the vasa vasorum
options.c: Hematogenous seeding of the vessel wall during septicemia
options.d: Type III hypersensitivity reaction to viral antigens
options.e: Autoimmune destruction of the elastic lamina

explanations.a: While this can occur, hematogenous seeding is more common as a source for mycotic aneurysms.
explanations.b: Syphilis causes luetic aneurysms via a specific vasculitis mechanism, not 'mycotic' (infectious) seeding in the traditional sense.
explanations.c: Mycotic aneurysms result from the infection of a major artery, most often via hematogenous seeding of bacteria (e.g., from infective endocarditis).
explanations.d: This describes the mechanism of certain vasculitides like Polyarteritis Nodosa.
explanations.e: This describes autoimmune vasculitis, not an infectious (mycotic) process.

ankiCards: A {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm is an aneurysm caused by an infection in the vessel wall.
The most common cause of mycotic aneurysms is {{c1::hematogenous seeding (septicemia)}}.
Common organisms in mycotic aneurysms include {{c1::Salmonella}} and Staphylococcus.
Mycotic aneurysms often originate from {{c1::infective endocarditis}}.
The primary danger of a mycotic aneurysm is {{c1::rupture}} and fulminant sepsis.
keyPoints: The term 'mycotic' refers to any infectious aneurysm (not just fungal).
They can arise from embolization of a septic thrombus.
The vessel wall is weakened by the inflammatory response to the infection.
Bacteremia/Sepsis is the typical precursor.
Management requires intensive antibiotics and often surgical excision.
microReview: Mycotic Aneurysm = Infected Aneurysm. Source: Endocarditis or Sepsis. Result: Rapid wall destruction and high risk of rupture.
examinerTraps: Don't be fooled by the word 'mycotic'; the majority are bacterial, not fungal.
