examinerTraps: Aneurysms can cause ischemia in two ways: by the aneurysm itself obstructing a branch (like the renal artery) or by a piece of the thrombus breaking off and traveling downstream (embolism).
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively... or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism)
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old male with a history of hypertension presents with hoarseness and a persistent cough. A chest CT reveals a 7-cm aneurysm of the aortic arch. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism by which this aneurysm is causing his symptoms?

options.a: Infection of the recurrent laryngeal nerve
options.b: Compression of the recurrent laryngeal nerve

explanations.a: There is no evidence of infection in this presentation; symptoms are due to local mass effect.
explanations.b: Thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAA) can compress mediastinal structures. Compression of the recurrent laryngeal nerve leads to hoarseness.
explanations.c: Embolism causes ischemia, not usually gradual hoarseness and cough.
explanations.d: Rupture would cause catastrophic collapse and hemothorax, not chronic cough and hoarseness.
explanations.e: While TAA can cause stroke via embolism, this doesn't explain the local symptoms of cough and hoarseness.

ankiCards: Thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAAs) can cause hoarseness by compressing the {{c1::recurrent laryngeal}} nerve.
TAAs can cause difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) by compressing the {{c1::esophagus}}.
TAAs can cause respiratory distress by compressing the {{c1::trachea}} or bronchus.
Persistent cough in TAA is often due to pressure on the {{c1::trachea}}.
TAAs are most commonly associated with {{c1::hypertension}} and connective tissue disorders.
keyPoints: TAAs manifest primarily through symptoms of mass effect.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve compression -> Hoarseness.
Esophageal compression -> Dysphagia.
Tracheal compression -> Cough/Dyspnea.
Rib or vertebral erosion can cause localized bone pain.
microReview: TAA Symptoms: Respiratory (cough/wheeze), Esophageal (dysphagia), Nerve (hoarseness), Cardiac (aortic regurgitation/CHF), and Bone (pain from erosion).
examinerTraps: The examiner may use 'hoarseness' to lead you toward laryngeal cancer; always look for the 'widened mediastinum' or 'aortic arch' description to pivot to TAA.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 1-month-old infant is brought to the clinic for a bright red, raised skin lesion on the cheek that has been increasing in size since birth. The parents are concerned about its appearance. Histology of a similar lesion would show a collection of small, thin-walled capillaries. What is the most likely clinical course for this lesion?

options.a: Aggressive local invasion and frequent metastasis
options.b: Rapid growth followed by spontaneous regression
options.c: Lifelong persistence with proportional growth to the child
options.e: Association with underlying CNS vascular malformations

explanations.a: Aggressive invasion is characteristic of malignant tumors like angiosarcoma, not juvenile hemangiomas.
explanations.b: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas typically grow rapidly for several months and then begin to regress by age 1 to 3, usually disappearing by age 7.
explanations.c: Proportional growth is more characteristic of vascular malformations (like nevus flammeus) rather than juvenile hemangiomas.
explanations.d: Juvenile hemangiomas are benign and do not typically transform into malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.e: While some vascular lesions like port-wine stains are associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome, strawberry hemangiomas are generally isolated and benign.

ankiCards: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas typically {{c1::regress}} spontaneously by age 7.
The histological hallmark of juvenile hemangioma is a collection of small, thin-walled {{c1::capillaries}}.
Juvenile hemangiomas are characterized by {{c1::rapid growth}} in the first few months of life.
True/False: Juvenile hemangiomas have a high risk of malignant transformation. {{c1::False}}.
Juvenile hemangiomas are most commonly found in the {{c1::skin}} of infants.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangiomas are the most common vascular tumor of infancy.
They are characterized by a 'strawberry-like' appearance.
Natural history involves an initial proliferative phase followed by involution.
Histologically, they are capillary hemangiomas.
Most lesions do not require treatment due to spontaneous regression.
microReview: Juvenile Hemangioma: Common in newborns, grows fast, then disappears. Capillary-sized vessels. Benign.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse strawberry hemangiomas (which regress) with port-wine stains (which persist).
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors ... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions ... 518
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old male presents with multiple painful, red-purple nodules on his fingers, particularly under the fingernails. Biopsy of a nodule reveals a tumor composed of specialized smooth muscle cells involved in thermoregulation. From which of the following structures do these tumor cells most likely derive?

options.c: Modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body

explanations.a: Pericytes are involved in hemangiopericytomas, not glomus tumors.
explanations.b: Endothelial cells would characterize hemangiomas or lymphangiomas, but the glomus tumor is specifically derived from the glomus body's smooth muscle.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) arise from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, an arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.d: While many tumors arise from mesenchymal cells, the glomus tumor has a specific cell of origin (glomus cell).
explanations.e: Schwann cells are the origin of neurofibromas or schwannomas, which can also be painful but have different histology.

ankiCards: Glomus tumors are most commonly found in the {{c1::subungual}} (under the nail) region.
The primary clinical symptom of a glomus tumor is {{c1::pain}}.
Glomus tumors derive from modified {{c1::smooth muscle}} cells.
The glomus body's physiological function is {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
On histology, glomus cells are described as {{c1::round}} cells in nests.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are exquisitely painful benign tumors.
They are most common in the distal digits, especially subungual.
Derived from glomus bodies (neuromyoarterial apparatus).
Histology shows nests of uniform round cells surrounding vascular channels.
Excision is curative.
microReview: Glomus Tumor: Painful, under the nail, derived from thermoregulatory glomus bodies (modified smooth muscle).
examinerTraps: The pain is the key clinical clue; most other benign vascular tumors (like capillary hemangiomas) are painless.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors ... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions ... 518
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old male with a history of HIV (CD4+ count 150/mm³) presents with several dark purple, non-blanching macules and plaques on his lower extremities and hard palate. A biopsy of a skin lesion shows spindle-shaped cells, slit-like vascular spaces, and extravasated red blood cells. Infection with which of the following agents is most likely responsible for these findings?

explanations.a: HPV-16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas, not vascular tumors.
explanations.b: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can look similar clinically but has different histology (neutrophilic infiltrate, no spindle cells).
explanations.c: Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.d: CMV is common in HIV patients (retinitis, colitis) but does not cause Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.e: EBV is associated with B-cell lymphomas (e.g., Burkitt) and oral hairy leukoplakia, but not KS.

ankiCards: The causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}.
Kaposi Sarcoma histology shows {{c1::spindle}} cells and slit-like vascular spaces.
The non-blanching purple lesions of Kaposi Sarcoma are due to {{c1::extravasated RBCs}}.
In the US, Kaposi Sarcoma is most commonly associated with {{c1::AIDS (Epidemic KS)}}.
The hard {{c1::palate}} is a common intraoral site for Kaposi Sarcoma.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8.
There are four forms: Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
Histology: Spindle cells, slit-like spaces containing RBCs, and hemosiderin staining.
Clinical: Purple/red patches, plaques, or nodules that do not blanch.
HHV-8 infects endothelial cells and induces a proliferative state.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma: HIV + HHV-8 + Spindle cells/Slit spaces + Purple plaques.
examinerTraps: Differentiating KS from Bacillary Angiomatosis: KS has spindle cells; Bacillary Angiomatosis has neutrophils and bacteria (Warthin-Starry stain positive).
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors ... Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors ... 520
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 62-year-old male who worked for 30 years in a chemical plant manufacturing polyvinyl chloride (PVC) presents with abdominal pain and weight loss. Imaging reveals multiple mass lesions in the liver. A biopsy confirms a malignant mesenchymal tumor that stains strongly for CD31. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Hepatocellular carcinoma is an epithelial tumor (keratin positive), not a mesenchymal tumor staining for CD31.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor, but the history of PVC exposure and malignant description point to angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a highly malignant vascular tumor associated with exposure to vinyl chloride (PVC), arsenic, and Thorotrast. CD31 is a specific endothelial marker.
explanations.d: Hepatoblastoma is the most common liver tumor in children, not adults with chemical exposure.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are usually small, benign, and found in distal extremities, not the liver.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride (PVC)}}.
{{c1::CD31}} is a specific immunohistochemical marker for vascular endothelial cells.
Besides PVC, arsenic and {{c1::Thorotrast}} are risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma.
Angiosarcomas are malignant tumors of {{c1::endothelial}} cell origin.
Angiosarcomas have a {{c1::poor}} prognosis due to aggressive local invasion and metastasis.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are high-grade malignant vascular tumors.
Common locations: Skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Environmental toxins (PVC, Arsenic) are linked specifically to the liver variant.
CD31 (PECAM-1) and von Willebrand factor are key diagnostic markers.
They are highly aggressive with a poor 5-year survival rate.
microReview: Angiosarcoma: Malignant, CD31+, associated with PVC/Arsenic (liver) or radiation (breast).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse CD31 (vascular) with CD3 (T-cell) or CD30 (Reed-Sternberg).
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors ... Malignant Tumors ... 522
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old female presents with a rapidly growing, pedunculated red lesion on her gingiva that bleeds easily. She is currently in her second trimester of pregnancy. The lesion is about 1 cm in diameter and has a 'raspberry-like' appearance. Which histological description most accurately matches this lesion?

options.a: Nests of uniform glomus cells around vascular channels
options.b: Proliferation of capillaries organized into lobules with edema and inflammation
options.c: Large, dilated vascular spaces filled with blood and separated by connective tissue
options.d: Atypical endothelial cells forming irregular, anastomosing channels
options.e: Spindle cells with slit-like spaces and hemosiderin deposits

explanations.a: This describes a glomus tumor.
explanations.b: This describes a pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma), which frequently occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.c: This describes a cavernous hemangioma.
explanations.d: This describes an angiosarcoma.
explanations.e: This describes Kaposi Sarcoma.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is histologically a {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas that occur on the gingiva of pregnant women are called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
The clinical appearance of a pyogenic granuloma is often described as {{c1::raspberry-like}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are known for growing {{c1::rapidly}} and bleeding easily.
True/False: Pyogenic granuloma is an infection-induced granulomatous process. {{c1::False}} (It is a hemangioma).
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is neither pyogenic nor a granuloma.
It is a lobular capillary hemangioma.
Often follows trauma or occurs during pregnancy.
Commonly involves skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
Typically treated with surgical excision or curettage.
microReview: Pyogenic Granuloma: Pedunculated, bleeding, red bump. Pregnancy association. Lobular capillaries histologically.
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic granuloma' is a trick; look for 'lobular capillary hemangioma' in histology options.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors ... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions ... 518
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular lesions is most likely to be associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease when found in the cerebellum or retina?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are common skin/mucosal lesions, not the specific hallmark of VHL in the CNS.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas occur in the CNS but are more commonly associated with CCM (cerebral cavernous malformation) genes rather than VHL.
explanations.c: Hemangioblastomas are the classic highly vascular tumors found in the cerebellum and retina of patients with von Hippel-Lindau disease.
explanations.d: Angiosarcomas are malignant and not a typical feature of VHL.
explanations.e: Lymphangiomas involve lymphatic vessels and are not CNS tumors associated with VHL.

ankiCards: {{c1::Hemangioblastoma}} is the characteristic vascular tumor of von Hippel-Lindau disease.
In VHL, hemangioblastomas are typically found in the {{c1::cerebellum}} and retina.
Von Hippel-Lindau disease is caused by a mutation in the {{c1::VHL}} tumor suppressor gene.
Patients with VHL also have an increased risk of {{c1::renal cell carcinoma}}.
Hemangioblastomas are composed of capillary-sized vessels and vacuolated {{c1::stromal}} cells.
keyPoints: VHL disease (Chromosome 3p) involves VHL gene mutations.
VHL gene product is involved in the degradation of Hypoxia-Inducible Factor (HIF).
HIF accumulation leads to excessive VEGF production.
Hemangioblastomas are the result of this uncontrolled angiogenesis.
Associated with polycythemia due to ectopic erythropoietin.
microReview: VHL: Hemangioblastoma (Cerebellum/Retina) + Renal Cell Carcinoma + Pheochromocytoma.
examinerTraps: Confusion between hemangioma (benign skin) and hemangioblastoma (VHL-associated CNS tumor).
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors ... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions ... 518
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An 8-year-old boy presents with a large, ill-defined, soft tissue swelling on the left side of his neck. The mass is painless, fluctuates in size during upper respiratory infections, and has been present since birth. Transillumination of the mass is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) is a common congenital malformation typically found in the neck or axilla of children, often associated with Turner syndrome.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas are usually smaller, solid, and bright red if superficial, not large cystic transilluminating masses.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are small, painful, and subungual, not large neck masses.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis presents with multiple red-purple nodules in immunocompromised patients.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor of older adults, not a transilluminating congenital mass.

ankiCards: A cavernous lymphangioma in the neck of an infant is commonly called a {{c1::cystic hygroma}}.
Cystic hygromas are frequently associated with {{c1::Turner syndrome}} (45,X).
The clinical finding of {{c1::transillumination}} helps differentiate cystic hygromas from solid masses.
Lymphangiomas are composed of spaces lined by endothelium that lack {{c1::red blood cells}}.
Unlike hemangiomas, lymphangioma spaces contain {{c1::proteinaceous fluid (lymph)}}.
keyPoints: Lymphangiomas are benign lymphatic analogs of hemangiomas.
Simple (capillary) vs Cavernous (cystic hygroma).
Cystic hygromas occur in the neck or axilla.
They are characterized by large, dilated lymphatic spaces.
Commonly associated with chromosomal abnormalities (Turner, Down).
microReview: Cystic Hygroma: Neck mass + Turner syndrome + Transilluminates + Lymphatic origin.
examinerTraps: The key differentiator from hemangiomas is the absence of RBCs in the vascular spaces.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors ... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions ... 518
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 70-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer treated with a radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection 10 years ago presents with several firm, blue-black nodules on her chronically swollen left arm. Biopsy reveals a poorly differentiated malignancy with endothelial markers. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Adenocarcinoma would show glandular structures and keratin staining, not endothelial markers.
explanations.b: Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to the development of angiosarcoma in the setting of chronic lymphedema, typically following radical mastectomy.
explanations.c: Classic KS occurs in older men of Mediterranean/Eastern European descent, usually on the legs, not in an arm with chronic lymphedema.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is infectious and occurs in immunocompromised patients.
explanations.e: Melanoma would stain for S100 or HMB-45, not endothelial markers like CD31.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
The most common clinical scenario for Stewart-Treves is post-{{c1::mastectomy}} lymphedema.
Chronic {{c1::lymphedema}} is the primary risk factor for the development of angiosarcoma in this syndrome.
Angiosarcomas are characterized by {{c1::atypical}} endothelial cells.
The latency period for Stewart-Treves syndrome is often {{c1::10}} years or more.
keyPoints: Stewart-Treves syndrome: Chronic lymphedema -> Angiosarcoma.
Lymphedema is often due to lymph node dissection for breast cancer.
Presents as cutaneous nodules or bruises on the lymphedematous limb.
Highly aggressive malignancy.
Histology shows malignant endothelial cells forming poorly defined channels.
microReview: Stewart-Treves: Post-mastectomy + Chronic lymphedema + Arm Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Don't assume any skin nodule after breast cancer is recurrence; if it's on a lymphedematous arm, think Angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors ... Malignant Tumors ... 522
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A patient presents with multiple small, dilated permanent vascular channels in the skin and mucous membranes. This condition, known as Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome, is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. What is the clinical significance of these lesions in the gastrointestinal tract?

options.a: High risk of transformation into angiosarcoma
options.b: Significant risk of serious gastrointestinal bleeding
options.c: Formation of large cystic masses that obstruct the lumen

explanations.a: These lesions (telangiectasias) are benign malformations and do not transform into malignancy.
explanations.b: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) is characterized by telangiectasias that can rupture, causing nosebleeds (epistaxis) or severe GI bleeding.
explanations.c: The lesions are small ectasias, not large obstructing masses.
explanations.d: Telangiectasias persist and often increase in number with age; they do not regress.
explanations.e: HHV-8 is associated with Kaposi Sarcoma, not HHT.

ankiCards: Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia is also known as {{c1::Osler-Weber-Rendu}} syndrome.
The inheritance pattern of Osler-Weber-Rendu is {{c1::autosomal dominant}}.
A common presenting symptom of HHT is recurrent {{c1::epistaxis}} (nosebleeds).
The vascular lesions in HHT are called {{c1::telangiectasias}}.
Internal lesions in HHT can lead to {{c1::gastrointestinal}} bleeding or iron deficiency anemia.
keyPoints: Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT) is a systemic vascular malformation.
Affects skin, mucous membranes, and internal organs (lungs, liver, brain).
Complications include AV malformations (AVMs).
Clinically: Epistaxis, GI bleed, and telangiectasias on lips/tongue.
Diagnosis is based on the Curacao criteria (epistaxis, telangiectasias, visceral lesions, family history).
microReview: Osler-Weber-Rendu: AD inheritance + Telangiectasias + Bleeding (Nose/GI) + AVMs.
examinerTraps: Confusing HHT with simple spider angiomas (associated with liver cirrhosis/estrogen).
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors ... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions ... 518
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following histopathological features most reliably distinguishes a malignant angiosarcoma from a benign cavernous hemangioma?

options.a: The presence of red blood cells within vascular spaces
options.b: A single layer of flattened endothelial cells
options.c: Marked cytologic atypia and high mitotic activity
options.d: The presence of a fibrous capsule surrounding the lesion

explanations.a: Both benign and malignant vascular tumors usually contain blood.
explanations.b: Flattened, innocuous endothelium is a feature of benign hemangiomas; malignant tumors show plump, atypical cells.
explanations.c: Angiosarcomas exhibit prominent cytologic atypia, pleomorphism, and brisk mitotic activity, which are absent in benign cavernous hemangiomas.
explanations.d: Neither typically has a true capsule; hemangiomas are well-circumscribed but angiosarcomas are infiltrative.
explanations.e: Both tumors are of endothelial origin and will stain for vWF, so this does not distinguish between them.

ankiCards: Unlike hemangiomas, angiosarcomas show marked endothelial {{c1::atypia}}.
Angiosarcomas are characterized by {{c1::infiltrative}} growth rather than being well-circumscribed.
A high {{c1::mitotic}} rate is indicative of malignancy in vascular tumors.
Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, {{c1::dilated}} blood-filled spaces.
Vascular tumors of both benign and malignant grades stain for {{c1::CD31}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma: Atypical cells, mitoses, irregular channels, infiltrative.
Cavernous Hemangioma: Large channels, flat endothelium, well-defined.
Both express CD31 and vWF.
Malignant lesions often lack the organized structure of benign ones.
Clinical context (age, location, risk factors) aids the diagnosis.
microReview: Benign vs Malignant Vascular: Malignant has atypia, mitoses, and infiltrative borders.
examinerTraps: Don't use 'presence of blood' or 'vWF staining' to distinguish; they are shared features of almost all vascular tumors.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors ... Malignant Tumors ... 522
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 42-year-old male with a history of HIV (CD4+ count: 120 cells/mm³) presents with several painless, purple-to-red plaques on his lower extremities. Biopsy reveals proliferation of spindle cells forming slit-like vascular spaces filled with erythrocytes. Which of the following infectious agents is the primary driver of this patient's condition?

explanations.a: HHV-8, also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of Kaposi sarcoma, which classically presents as purple plaques and histology showing spindle cells and slit-like vascular spaces.
explanations.b: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can mimic Kaposi sarcoma clinically but is characterized by neutrophilic infiltrates and clusters of bacteria (visualized on Warthin-Starry stain).
explanations.c: CMV is a common opportunistic infection in HIV patients but typically causes retinitis, esophagitis, or colitis rather than vascular skin tumors.
explanations.d: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and primary CNS lymphoma in HIV patients, not vascular spindle-cell tumors.
explanations.e: HPV is associated with squamous cell carcinomas and warts, not vascular endothelial neoplasms.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is caused by {{c1::HHV-8}} infection.
The histological hallmark of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells}} forming slit-like spaces.
Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by {{c1::Bartonella}} species and mimics Kaposi Sarcoma.
In HIV patients, purple skin plaques with slit-like vascular spaces suggest {{c1::Kaposi Sarcoma}}.
Kaposi Sarcoma lesions are often {{c1::painless}} and purple/red.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a borderline vascular tumor caused by HHV-8.
KS is the most common neoplasm in AIDS patients.
Histology shows spindle cells, slit-like spaces, and extravasated RBCs.
Clinical presentation includes cutaneous plaques, nodules, and visceral involvement.
Distinction from bacillary angiomatosis is critical via histology (neutrophils in BA vs. spindle cells in KS).
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = HIV/HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Slit-like spaces. Bacillary Angiomatosis = Bartonella + Neutrophils + Warthin-Starry positive.
examinerTraps: A common trap is confusing Kaposi Sarcoma with Bacillary Angiomatosis; look for 'neutrophilic infiltrate' or 'spindle cells' to differentiate.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors are divided into benign (e.g., hemangiomas), intermediate-grade (e.g., Kaposi sarcoma), and malignant (e.g., angiosarcoma).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular tumors is characterized by extreme exquisite pain, typically occurring under the fingernails, and arises from modified smooth muscle cells of a specialized thermoregulatory structure?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors are benign, highly painful tumors arising from the glomus body (a thermoregulatory neuromyoarterial apparatus), most commonly found in the subungual region.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granulomas are rapidly growing red nodules on skin or oral mucosa, often associated with trauma or pregnancy, but are not characteristically subungual or exquisitely painful.
explanations.c: Capillary hemangiomas (like strawberry hemangiomas) are benign childhood tumors that typically regress and are not associated with intense localized pain.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignant tumor of the endothelium, usually seen in older adults, and is not specifically subungual or glomus-derived.
explanations.e: Hemangioendothelioma is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor with varied presentations, but does not fit the subungual/painful glomus description.

ankiCards: A painful, subungual vascular tumor is likely a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::smooth muscle}} cells of the glomus body.
The specialized thermoregulatory structure involved in glomus tumors is the {{c1::glomus body}}.
Exquisite sensitivity to {{c1::cold}} or touch is common in glomus tumors.
Glomus tumors are {{c1::benign}} neoplasms.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign.
Most common location: subungual (under the nail).
Key clinical symptom: Exquisite pain.
Derived from specialized smooth muscle cells (glomocytes).
Part of the thermoregulatory apparatus.
microReview: Subungual + Painful = Glomus Tumor (Smooth muscle origin).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse glomus tumors with 'glomus jugulare' (a paraganglioma); in vascular pathology, focus on the painful nail bed lesion.
sourceQuote: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, exquisitely painful tumors arising from specialized smooth muscle cells of glomus bodies.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 65-year-old worker at a chemical manufacturing plant with 30 years of exposure to vinyl chloride presents with jaundice and hepatomegaly. Imaging identifies multiple ill-defined, hemorrhagic masses in the liver. Which of the following immunohistochemical markers would most likely be positive in these neoplastic cells?

explanations.a: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a specific marker for endothelial cells. Given the history of vinyl chloride exposure and liver masses, the diagnosis is hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells and would be positive in carcinomas, not vascular tumors.
explanations.c: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells (e.g., melanoma, Schwannomas), not endothelial cells.
explanations.d: HepPar-1 is a marker for hepatocellular carcinoma, but the exposure to vinyl chloride specifically increases the risk for angiosarcoma.
explanations.e: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells, whereas angiosarcoma is endothelial in origin.

ankiCards: Exposure to vinyl chloride and arsenic is associated with {{c1::hepatic angiosarcoma}}.
The endothelial marker {{c1::CD31 (or vWF)}} is used to identify angiosarcomas.
Angiosarcoma is a {{c1::malignant}} tumor of the vascular endothelium.
Post-mastectomy lymphedema is a risk factor for cutaneous {{c1::angiosarcoma}}.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is a highly {{c1::aggressive}} neoplasm.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms.
Chemical risk factors: Vinyl chloride, arsenic, Thorotrast.
Environmental/Medical risk factors: Radiation, chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
CD31 is a highly specific marker for vascular differentiation.
These tumors are aggressive with a poor prognosis.
microReview: Vinyl Chloride/Arsenic/Lymphedema -> Angiosarcoma (CD31 positive).
examinerTraps: Wait for the specific chemical exposure; vinyl chloride is the classic trigger for hepatic angiosarcoma in board exams.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms... specific associations include vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with a rapidly growing, 1-cm, pedunculated, red nodule on her gingiva. The lesion bleeds easily with minor trauma. Histology shows a proliferation of capillaries with interspersed inflammatory cells and edema. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a benign, rapidly growing red nodule common in the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, blood-filled vascular spaces and are usually deep-seated and not pedunculated or gingival in this fashion.
explanations.c: Kaposi sarcoma presents as purple plaques/nodules, typically in the setting of immunodeficiency, and has different histology (spindle cells).
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is associated with Bartonella in immunocompromised patients, not typically healthy pregnant women.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are exquisitely painful and usually subungual, unlike the friable gingival mass described.

ankiCards: A 'pregnancy tumor' of the gingiva is most often a {{c1::pyogenic granuloma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are {{c1::benign}} vascular proliferations.
Histologically, pyogenic granuloma is a form of {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma.
The clinical appearance of pyogenic granuloma is a {{c1::red/friable}} nodule.
Pyogenic granulomas often recur if not {{c1::completely}} excised.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer (neither pyogenic nor a true granuloma).
Highly vascular and friable (bleeds easily).
Common on skin and oral mucosa.
Associated with pregnancy and trauma.
Histology: Lobular capillary proliferation.
microReview: Pregnancy + Gingiva + Red friable nodule = Pyogenic Granuloma (Lobular capillary hemangioma).
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic granuloma' is a trap; it is actually a vascular lesion, not an infection or a granulomatous process.
sourceQuote: Pyogenic granulomas are capillary hemangiomas that manifest as rapidly growing red pedunculated lesions on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following characteristics best distinguishes a cavernous hemangioma from a capillary hemangioma?

options.a: The presence of large, dilated vascular channels
options.b: The clinical tendency to spontaneously regress
options.c: The proliferation of small, thin-walled vessels
options.d: The absence of any association with genetic syndromes

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas are characterized by large, dilated blood-filled spaces, whereas capillary hemangiomas involve small, tight vascular channels.
explanations.b: Capillary (infantile) hemangiomas often spontaneously regress; cavernous hemangiomas usually do not.
explanations.c: Small, thin-walled vessels are characteristic of capillary hemangiomas, not cavernous ones.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are associated with Von Hippel-Lindau disease (especially in the CNS), so they do have genetic associations.
explanations.e: Both are benign tumors with negligible malignant potential.

ankiCards: {{c1::Cavernous}} hemangiomas have large, dilated vascular spaces.
{{c1::Capillary}} hemangiomas are composed of small, thin-walled vessels.
Which hemangioma type is associated with Von Hippel-Lindau? {{c1::Cavernous}}.
{{c1::Capillary (Strawberry)}} hemangiomas of infancy usually regress spontaneously.
Hemangiomas are {{c1::benign}} tumors of blood vessels.
keyPoints: Hemangiomas are the most common tumors of infancy.
Capillary: Small vessels, skin/mucous membranes, often regresses.
Cavernous: Large channels, deeper tissues, no regression.
Cavernous hemangiomas of the CNS are a feature of VHL disease.
Kasabach-Merritt syndrome involves platelet sequestration in large hemangiomas.
microReview: Capillary = Small/Tight. Cavernous = Large/Dilated (Think: Cavern = Big).
examinerTraps: Don't assume all hemangiomas regress; only the infantile/strawberry (capillary) type typically does.
sourceQuote: Cavernous hemangiomas are distinguished by the formation of large, dilated vascular channels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An 8-year-old boy presents with a bright red, slightly raised 'strawberry' lesion on his cheek. His mother states it appeared shortly after birth and grew rapidly for several months but has recently started to fade and shrink. What is the most likely natural history of this lesion?

options.a: Complete regression by age 7 in most cases

explanations.a: Infantile (strawberry) hemangiomas are extremely common, grow rapidly for a few months, and then typically regress completely by age 7 to 9.
explanations.b: Benign infantile hemangiomas do not transform into malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.c: These lesions characteristically regress rather than persist or dilate progressively.
explanations.d: While Kasabach-Merritt syndrome (coagulopathy) can occur with large hemangiomas, it is not the 'most likely' natural history for a standard strawberry hemangioma.
explanations.e: Strawberry hemangiomas are typically isolated skin lesions and not markers for visceral malignancy.

ankiCards: Strawberry (infantile) hemangiomas typically {{c1::regress}} by age 7.
Strawberry hemangiomas appear {{c1::shortly after birth}}.
The histological type of a strawberry hemangioma is {{c1::capillary}}.
Initial growth of a strawberry hemangioma is usually {{c1::rapid}}.
Strawberry hemangiomas are the most common tumors of {{c1::infancy}}.
keyPoints: Infantile hemangiomas are capillary hemangiomas.
Appearance: Bright red, lobulated (strawberry).
Incidence: 1 in 200 births.
Phases: Rapid growth followed by slow involution.
Management: Usually observation, though beta-blockers (propranolol) can be used if they interfere with function.
microReview: Infant + Strawberry lesion = Capillary hemangioma (Regresses by age 7).
examinerTraps: Wait for 'strawberry' or 'regresses'—this differentiates infantile capillary hemangiomas from port-wine stains (Nevus flammeus), which do not regress.
sourceQuote: Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) are common... they grow rapidly for a few months but then fade and regress.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A patient with long-standing lymphedema of the right arm following a radical mastectomy 12 years ago develops multiple, rapidly enlarging, violaceous skin nodules. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: This clinical scenario describes Stewart-Treves syndrome, where chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy) leads to the development of cutaneous angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is HHV-8 mediated and typically associated with HIV or classic Mediterranean elderly males, not post-mastectomy lymphedema.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious process (Bartonella) and does not typically arise in the setting of chronic lymphedema.
explanations.d: Lymphangiomas are benign lymphatic malformations, usually congenital, not aggressive nodules appearing years after surgery.
explanations.e: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign and do not appear as aggressive nodules in a lymphedematous limb.

ankiCards: {{c1::Angiosarcoma}} can arise in the setting of chronic lymphedema.
The eponymous name for post-mastectomy angiosarcoma is {{c1::Stewart-Treves}} syndrome.
Angiosarcoma of the arm often follows a {{c1::radical mastectomy}} due to lymphedema.
Cutaneous angiosarcomas appear as {{c1::violaceous/purple}} nodules.
The prognosis for Stewart-Treves angiosarcoma is {{c1::poor}}.
keyPoints: Stewart-Treves syndrome: Lymphedema -> Angiosarcoma.
Commonly occurs in the arm after axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer.
Latency period is typically about 10 years.
Malignant endothelial cells are the cell of origin.
Highly lethal and aggressive tumor.
microReview: Mastectomy + Lymphedema + Purple nodules = Angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves).
examinerTraps: The examiner might try to lead you toward lymphangioma because of the 'lymph' in lymphedema, but the appearance of new nodules years later is a classic malignancy sign.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas can also occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema, classically in the ipsilateral arm of women who have undergone radical mastectomy.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Sturge-Weber syndrome is characterized by a port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve. What is the classic intracranial vascular abnormality associated with this syndrome?

explanations.a: Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) classically features a facial port-wine stain and ipsilateral leptomeningeal venous angiomas.
explanations.b: Berry aneurysms are associated with ADPKD and Ehlers-Danlos, not Sturge-Weber.
explanations.c: While AVMs are vascular abnormalities, the specific finding in Sturge-Weber is a venous angioma/capillary malformation of the meninges.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas of the cerebellum/retina are features of Von Hippel-Lindau disease.
explanations.e: Sinus thrombosis is a vascular complication but not the primary malformation of Sturge-Weber syndrome.

ankiCards: Sturge-Weber syndrome involves a {{c1::port-wine stain}} in the V1/V2 distribution.
The intracranial lesion in Sturge-Weber is a {{c1::leptomeningeal angioma}}.
Sturge-Weber syndrome is often associated with {{c1::seizures}} and glaucoma.
Port-wine stains (nevus flammeus) {{c1::do not}} regress over time.
The distribution of the skin lesion in Sturge-Weber follows the {{c1::trigeminal}} nerve.
keyPoints: Sturge-Weber syndrome: Port-wine stain + Leptomeningeal angioma.
Clinical triad: Facial angioma, intellectual disability, and seizures.
The 'port-wine stain' is a form of nevus flammeus.
Unlike strawberry hemangiomas, port-wine stains grow with the child and don't regress.
Ipsilateral glaucoma is a common ocular complication.
microReview: Sturge-Weber = Port-wine stain (V1/V2) + Brain angioma + Seizures.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the VHL cerebellar hemangioblastoma with the Sturge-Weber leptomeningeal angioma.
sourceQuote: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a component of the Sturge-Weber syndrome... associated with leptomeningeal venous angiomas.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular ectasias are not true neoplasms but rather permanent dilations of preexisting vessels. Which of the following conditions is characterized by spider telangiectasias specifically associated with hyperestrogenic states?

explanations.a: Liver cirrhosis leads to impaired metabolism of estrogen. Excess estrogen causes spider telangiectasias (spider angiomas) on the skin.
explanations.b: Diabetes is associated with microangiopathy but not specifically hyperestrogenic spider telangiectasias.
explanations.c: CKD can cause various skin changes (e.g., uremic frost) but not spider telangiectasias.
explanations.d: Hypothyroidism is associated with myxedema, not telangiectasias of this type.
explanations.e: SLE is associated with a malar rash, but not spider telangiectasias linked to estrogen.

ankiCards: Spider telangiectasias are associated with {{c1::hyperestrogenic}} states.
The most common clinical cause of spider telangiectasias is {{c1::liver cirrhosis}}.
Spider telangiectasias blanch when the {{c1::center}} is pressed.
Estrogen-related vascular ectasias are also seen in {{c1::pregnancy}}.
Vascular ectasias are {{c1::permanent dilations}} of vessels, not true neoplasms.
keyPoints: Telangiectasias are a form of vascular ectasia.
Spider telangiectasias: Central red papule with radiating 'legs'.
Pathogenesis: High estrogen levels (cirrhosis, pregnancy).
Clinical test: Blanching when the core is compressed.
They are benign but serve as clinical markers for underlying disease.
microReview: Cirrhosis/Pregnancy -> High Estrogen -> Spider Angioma.
examinerTraps: Spider telangiectasias are often grouped with vascular tumors in textbooks, but they are 'ectasias' (dilations), not true tumors (proliferations).
sourceQuote: Spider telangiectasias... are particularly common in hyperestrogenic states such as pregnancy or liver cirrhosis.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 35-year-old male with poorly controlled AIDS presents with numerous red, papular skin lesions and fever. A biopsy reveals vascular proliferation with a dense neutrophilic infiltrate. Warthin-Starry silver stain demonstrates clusters of small bacilli. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella henselae or quintana in immunocompromised patients. It presents with vascular lesions containing neutrophils and bacteria (visible on Warthin-Starry stain).
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is also common in AIDS, but it shows spindle cells and slit-like spaces without neutrophilic infiltrates or bacteria.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign capillary proliferation, but the systemic symptoms (fever) and Warthin-Starry findings point toward an infectious cause like Bartonella.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignancy with marked cytological atypia, which is not described here.
explanations.e: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large dilated channels and would not show an acute inflammatory infiltrate or bacteria.

ankiCards: The causative agent of bacillary angiomatosis is {{c1::Bartonella}}.
Unlike Kaposi sarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis has a {{c1::neutrophilic}} infiltrate.
The silver stain used to find Bartonella is {{c1::Warthin-Starry}}.
Bacillary angiomatosis is most commonly seen in {{c1::immunocompromised/AIDS}} patients.
Erythromycin or doxycycline are used to treat {{c1::bacillary angiomatosis}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis: Bartonella + AIDS.
Key histology: Vascular proliferation + Neutrophils + Nuclear dust.
Warthin-Starry stain is positive for bacilli.
Clinical mimic of Kaposi Sarcoma.
Constitutional symptoms (fever, weight loss) are common.
microReview: Bartonella + AIDS + Neutrophils = Bacillary Angiomatosis.
examinerTraps: Wait for the Warthin-Starry result; if positive, it's Bacillary Angiomatosis, not Kaposi Sarcoma.
sourceQuote: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts... caused by opportunistic gram-negative bacilli of the Bartonella family.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents for a routine physical examination. He is asymptomatic, but physical examination reveals a pulsatile mid-abdominal mass felt just above the umbilicus. Ultrasound reveals a 4.5 cm focal dilation of the abdominal aorta. Which of the following is the most likely primary underlying mechanism responsible for this patient’s condition?

options.a: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.b: Atherosclerotic destruction of the vessel media
options.c: Cystic medial necrosis due to genetic deficiency
options.e: Transmural necrotizing inflammation of the vessel wall

explanations.a: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum is the hallmark of tertiary syphilis, which typically leads to thoracic aortic aneurysms, not abdominal.
explanations.b: Atherosclerosis is the dominant cause of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA). Plaque formation impairs nutrient diffusion to the media, leading to wall weakening and dilation.
explanations.c: Cystic medial necrosis is associated with Marfan syndrome and typically affects the ascending (thoracic) aorta rather than the abdominal aorta.
explanations.d: Hypertensive hyaline arteriolosclerosis affects small arteries and arterioles, not the large elastic arteries like the aorta.
explanations.e: Transmural necrotizing inflammation is characteristic of Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN), a small-to-medium vessel vasculitis, not AAA.

ankiCards: The most common cause of an abdominal aortic aneurysm is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are typically located {{c1::infrarenal}}.
The primary mechanism of wall weakening in AAA is {{c1::destruction of the media}} secondary to atherosclerotic plaque.
A pulsatile mid-abdominal mass is the classic clinical sign for {{c1::abdominal aortic aneurysm}}.
The greatest risk factor for the development and progression of AAA is {{c1::smoking}}.
keyPoints: AAA is primarily associated with atherosclerosis.
The media is weakened by impaired oxygen diffusion through atherosclerotic plaques.
AAAs are most commonly found between the renal arteries and the iliac bifurcation.
Smoking is the most significant modifiable risk factor.
Complications include rupture, thrombosis, and embolism.
microReview: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA): Older male smokers, infrarenal location, atherosclerotic etiology, presents as pulsatile mass or back pain if leaking.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse AAA with Aortic Dissection. Dissection is primarily driven by hypertension and cystic medial necrosis, whereas AAA is driven by atherosclerosis.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following biochemical changes within the aortic wall is most critical in the pathogenesis of progressive aortic wall weakening and aneurysm formation?

options.b: Decreased expression of transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β)
options.c: Increased deposition of type I collagen in the media
options.d: Inhibition of elastase activity by alpha-1 antitrypsin
options.e: Activation of the tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs)

explanations.a: MMPs, produced by inflammatory cells within the plaque, degrade elastin and collagen in the media, leading to structural failure of the vessel wall.
explanations.b: Increased (not decreased) TGF-β signaling is often implicated in genetic forms of aneurysm like Marfan or Loeys-Dietz syndrome, causing defective matrix assembly.
explanations.c: Aneurysm formation is associated with the loss or degradation of collagen and elastin, not an increase in healthy structural collagen.
explanations.d: Alpha-1 antitrypsin inhibits elastase; its deficiency leads to tissue destruction. In aneurysms, the balance shifts toward excessive elastase/protease activity.
explanations.e: TIMPs inhibit MMPs. In aneurysms, the ratio of MMPs to TIMPs is increased, favoring matrix degradation over preservation.

ankiCards: The biochemical hallmark of aneurysm formation is the degradation of {{c1::elastin and collagen}}.
Enzymes that degrade the extracellular matrix in aneurysms are called {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
In aneurysms, there is an {{c1::increased}} ratio of MMPs to TIMPs.
Chronic inflammation in the vessel wall leads to the recruitment of {{c1::macrophages}}, which secrete MMPs.
The structural integrity of the aorta depends on the {{c1::media}} layer.
keyPoints: Aneurysm pathogenesis involves a dynamic imbalance in matrix remodeling.
Increased matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) activity is a key driver.
Degradation of tunica media components (elastin/collagen) leads to wall thinning.
Inflammatory cells (macrophages/T-cells) facilitate this proteolytic environment.
Matrix degradation overcomes the buffering capacity of TIMPs.
microReview: Wall weakening = Proteolysis > Matrix Synthesis. Key players: MMP-2, MMP-9, and macrophage-derived elastases.
examinerTraps: Watch for 'increased' vs 'decreased'. The examiner may flip MMP and TIMP roles; remember MMPs 'Munch' the matrix.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following defines a 'true aneurysm' as opposed to a 'false aneurysm' (pseudoaneurysm)?

options.a: A hematoma that forms between the tunica media and tunica adventitia
options.b: A wall defect that allows blood to communicate with the extravascular space
options.c: A dilation that involves all three layers of the arterial wall
options.d: A tear in the tunica intima that creates a false lumen
options.e: A localized dilation caused by a focal bacterial infection

explanations.a: This describes a dissection, where blood tracks between layers, not a true aneurysm.
explanations.b: This describes a false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm), where a wall defect leads to an extravascular hematoma contained by connective tissue.
explanations.c: A true aneurysm is defined by the involvement of all three layers (intima, media, and adventitia) in the outward bulging.
explanations.d: This is the definition of an aortic dissection, which is distinct from a true aneurysm.
explanations.e: This describes a mycotic aneurysm, which is a subtype based on etiology, but it can be either true or false depending on the wall structure.

ankiCards: A true aneurysm must involve {{c1::all three}} layers of the vessel wall.
A pseudoaneurysm is an extravascular {{c1::hematoma}} that communicates with the lumen.
The three layers of the arterial wall are the {{c1::intima, media, and adventitia}}.
In an aortic dissection, blood enters the {{c1::media}} through an intimal tear.
A saccular aneurysm is a {{c1::spherical}} dilation of only a portion of the vessel wall.
keyPoints: True aneurysm: Involves Intima, Media, and Adventitia.
False aneurysm (Pseudoaneurysm): Extravascular hematoma communicating with lumen.
Dissection: Blood enters the wall itself, separating layers.
Saccular vs. Fusiform: Descriptive shapes of true aneurysms.
Congenital vascular anomalies are usually true aneurysms (e.g., Berry).
microReview: True = 3 layers (Full wall). False = Hole in wall + contained blood. Dissection = Blood between layers.
examinerTraps: Candidates often confuse pseudoaneurysms with saccular aneurysms. Saccular is a 'true' aneurysm involving all layers, just on one side; pseudoaneurysm is a 'false' aneurysm because the wall is actually ruptured.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old tall, thin male presents with sudden, sharp chest pain. On physical exam, he has long, slender fingers and high-arched palate. Imaging reveals dilation of the aortic root. Histologic examination of a similar case would most likely show which of the following?

options.c: Fragmentation of elastic fibers in the media
options.e: Fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel wall

explanations.a: Medial calcific sclerosis (Mönckeberg) involves calcification of the media but usually does not cause aneurysms or affect the aortic root in this manner.
explanations.b: This describes atherosclerosis, which is the primary cause of AAA in elderly patients, not aortic root dilation in young Marfan patients.
explanations.c: Fragmentation of elastic fibers (cystic medial necrosis) is the classic histologic finding in Marfan syndrome leading to thoracic aortic aneurysms.
explanations.d: Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis is a result of malignant hypertension and affects small vessels, not the aorta.
explanations.e: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in vasculitides or malignant hypertension, not typically in genetic aortic root dilation.

ankiCards: Marfan syndrome is caused by a mutation in the {{c1::FBN1 (Fibrillin-1)}} gene.
The histologic term for elastic fiber fragmentation in the aortic media is {{c1::cystic medial necrosis}}.
Marfan syndrome primarily causes aneurysms in the {{c1::ascending/thoracic}} aorta.
Excessive {{c1::TGF-beta}} signaling is a key pathway in Marfan-related vascular disease.
Clinical features of Marfan include {{c1::ectopia lentis}}, arachnodactyly, and tall stature.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome involves Fibrillin-1 mutations.
Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm (TAA) is the most life-threatening complication.
Cystic medial necrosis: Loss of smooth muscle and elastic tissue fragmentation.
Unlike AAA, TAA is often due to genetic defects or hypertension.
Dilation starts at the aortic root (sinus of Valsalva).
microReview: Marfan/TAA: Genetic (FBN1), Cystic medial necrosis (no real cysts), aortic root dilation, risk of dissection.
examinerTraps: The term 'cystic medial necrosis' is a misnomer; there is neither inflammation ('necrosis') nor true 'cysts'. It refers to the empty-looking spaces where elastic tissue has failed.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old male with a history of untreated tertiary syphilis is found to have an aneurysm. Which part of the aorta is most likely involved, and what is the characteristic gross appearance of the intima?

explanations.a: Syphilitic aneurysms typically occur in the thoracic aorta, not the abdominal aorta.
explanations.b: Tertiary syphilis causes obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum in the thoracic aorta. Ischemia of the media leads to scarring and a 'tree-bark' appearance of the intima.
explanations.c: Abdominal aorta is the site of atherosclerotic aneurysms, and 'onion-skin' refers to hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis.
explanations.d: While the thoracic aorta is the correct site, 'onion-skin' is the wrong descriptor for the intimal surface in syphilis.
explanations.e: 'String-of-pearls' is characteristic of Fibromuscular Dysplasia or Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN), not syphilis.

ankiCards: Syphilitic aneurysms are caused by {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}} of the vasa vasorum.
The vasa vasorum are most prominent in the {{c1::thoracic}} aorta.
The characteristic intimal appearance of a syphilitic aneurysm is {{c1::tree-barking}}.
Syphilitic aneurysms can lead to {{c1::aortic valve insufficiency}} due to dilation of the aortic ring.
The vasa vasorum supply blood to the {{c1::outer media}} of large arteries.
keyPoints: Tertiary syphilis (Treponema pallidum) affects the vasa vasorum.
Endarteritis leads to medial ischemia and fibrosis.
Contraction of fibrous scars results in the 'tree-bark' intimal look.
Thoracic location is classic (ascending aorta/arch).
Aortic root dilation may cause massive cardiac hypertrophy ('cor bovinum').
microReview: Syphilis -> Vasa Vasorum Endarteritis -> Medial Ischemia -> Thoracic Aneurysm + Tree-barking.
examinerTraps: Candidates often confuse the 'tree-barking' of syphilis with the plaques of atherosclerosis. Tree-barking is due to medial scarring and thinning, not lipid deposition.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes a 'mycotic aneurysm'?

options.a: An aneurysm caused by a fungal infection specifically
options.b: An aneurysm caused by any infected thrombus or embolus
options.c: A pseudoaneurysm resulting from direct trauma to the vessel
options.d: A congenital dilation of the vessels in the Circle of Willis
options.e: A dilation resulting from a genetic defect in collagen synthesis

explanations.a: Despite the name 'mycotic' (suggesting fungus), most are actually bacterial in origin.
explanations.b: Mycotic aneurysms result from the weakening of the vessel wall by an infectious process, usually from a seeded septic embolus or adjacent infection.
explanations.c: Direct trauma results in a traumatic pseudoaneurysm, not a mycotic aneurysm.
explanations.d: This describes a Berry aneurysm, which is usually developmental/congenital, not mycotic.
explanations.e: Genetic defects cause syndromes like Ehlers-Danlos or Marfan, not mycotic aneurysms.

ankiCards: A {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm is an aneurysm caused by an infection in the wall.
The most common cause of a mycotic aneurysm is {{c1::infective endocarditis}} (septic embolization).
Despite the name, most mycotic aneurysms are caused by {{c1::bacteria}}.
Mycotic aneurysms carry a high risk of {{c1::rupture}} due to rapid wall destruction.
{{c1::Salmonella}} is a specific organism known to cause mycotic aneurysms of the aorta.
keyPoints: Mycotic aneurysms = Infection-induced wall weakening.
Term is a misnomer (usually bacterial, not fungal).
Can result from septic emboli (endocarditis) or extension of adjacent sepsis.
Rapidly progressive and prone to rupture.
Treatment requires both antibiotics and often surgical intervention.
microReview: Mycotic Aneurysm: Infection (Endocarditis) -> Vessel Wall destruction -> Dilation.
examinerTraps: Don't pick 'fungal' just because of the name. If the options distinguish between bacterial and fungal, bacteria (like S. aureus or Salmonella) are more common.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old female with a history of Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) and poorly controlled hypertension presents to the emergency department with the 'worst headache of her life.' CT scan shows subarachnoid hemorrhage. Which type of aneurysm is most likely responsible?

explanations.a: Atherosclerotic aneurysms typically involve the aorta or iliac arteries, not the cerebral circulation.
explanations.b: Syphilitic aneurysms involve the thoracic aorta.
explanations.c: Berry aneurysms are small, saccular dilations in the Circle of Willis, strongly associated with ADPKD and hypertension; their rupture causes subarachnoid hemorrhage.
explanations.d: Mycotic aneurysms can occur in the brain but are associated with fever and endocarditis, not specifically ADPKD.
explanations.e: Aortic dissection ('dissecting aneurysm') causes chest/back pain, not subarachnoid hemorrhage.

ankiCards: Berry aneurysms are most commonly located in the {{c1::Circle of Willis}}.
The most common specific site for a Berry aneurysm is the {{c1::anterior communicating artery}}.
{{c1::ADPKD}} is the classic genetic condition associated with Berry aneurysms.
Rupture of a Berry aneurysm leads to {{c1::subarachnoid}} hemorrhage.
Berry aneurysms lack a tunica {{c1::media}} at the site of the bulge.
keyPoints: Berry aneurysm = Small saccular dilation in cerebral vessels.
Associated with ADPKD, Ehlers-Danlos, and Coarctation of the aorta.
Hypertension is a major risk factor for rupture.
Presentation: 'Thunderclap' headache.
Location: Branch points in the Circle of Willis.
microReview: ADPKD + Headache = Berry Aneurysm / Subarachnoid Hemorrhage.
examinerTraps: Be careful with the term 'dissecting aneurysm'. It is an older, technically incorrect term for aortic dissection. Dissections are not true aneurysms.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following clinical factors is the most accurate predictor of the risk of rupture for an abdominal aortic aneurysm?

options.b: The total length of the aneurysm
options.c: The maximum diameter of the aneurysm
options.e: The severity of lower extremity claudication

explanations.a: While hypertension increases stress, the diameter is the standardized metric used for surgical decision-making.
explanations.b: The length of the aneurysm does not correlate as strongly with wall tension (Law of Laplace) as the diameter does.
explanations.c: According to the Law of Laplace, wall tension is proportional to the radius. Rupture risk increases significantly once the diameter exceeds 5.0–5.5 cm.
explanations.d: Mural thrombus is common in AAAs but is not a reliable predictor of rupture risk compared to size.
explanations.e: Claudication indicates peripheral artery disease, which shares risk factors with AAA but does not predict rupture.

ankiCards: The most important predictor of AAA rupture is the {{c1::diameter}}.
The risk of AAA rupture increases significantly when the diameter is greater than {{c1::5 or 5.5}} cm.
According to the Law of Laplace, wall tension increases as the {{c1::radius/diameter}} increases.
The yearly risk of rupture for an AAA > 6 cm is approximately {{c1::10-25}}%.
Surgical intervention is generally recommended for AAAs larger than {{c1::5.5}} cm in men.
keyPoints: Rupture risk is size-dependent.
Law of Laplace: Tension = (Pressure × Radius) / Wall Thickness.
Threshold for surgery is usually 5.5 cm (men) or 5.0 cm (women).
Small aneurysms (<4 cm) have near-zero annual rupture risk.
Rapid expansion (>0.5 cm in 6 months) is also an indication for surgery.
microReview: AAA Rupture Risk: Size (Diameter) > 5.5 cm = High Risk.
examinerTraps: The examiner may suggest mural thrombus is protective or a risk factor; while it can cause emboli (Blue Toe Syndrome), it is the diameter that dictates rupture risk.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 70-year-old male with a known 6-cm abdominal aortic aneurysm presents with sudden onset severe back pain, hypotension, and a palpable abdominal mass. What is the most likely complication occurring?

options.a: Aortic dissection into the iliac arteries
options.b: Acute thrombosis of the aneurysm lumen
options.d: Embolization of mural thrombus (Blue Toe Syndrome)
options.e: Compression of the inferior vena cava

explanations.a: Aortic dissection is a different pathological entity, usually involving the thoracic aorta, though it can extend abdominaly. However, the triad of pain, hypotension, and mass strongly suggests AAA rupture.
explanations.b: Thrombosis would more likely cause acute limb ischemia, not a triad including hypotension and a pulsatile mass.
explanations.c: The clinical triad of sudden severe pain, hypotension, and a pulsatile mass is pathognomonic for AAA rupture.
explanations.d: Embolization causes localized ischemia in the feet, not systemic hypotension.
explanations.e: Compression of the IVC would cause lower extremity edema, not acute hypotension and severe back pain.

ankiCards: The classic triad of AAA rupture is {{c1::pain, hypotension, and a pulsatile mass}}.
AAA rupture most commonly occurs into the {{c1::retroperitoneal}} space or peritoneal cavity.
The mortality rate for a ruptured AAA is approximately {{c1::80-90}}%.
Aneurysms can cause {{c1::compression}} of adjacent structures like the ureter or vertebrae.
Mural thrombus in an aneurysm can lead to {{c1::distal embolization}}.
keyPoints: AAA Rupture Triad: Hypotension, back pain, pulsatile mass.
Rupture can be catastrophic (peritoneal) or somewhat contained (retroperitoneal).
Aneurysms often contain mural thrombus due to stasis/turbulence.
Erosion into adjacent vertebrae can cause chronic pain.
Obstruction of branch vessels (renal, mesenteric) can lead to organ ischemia.
microReview: AAA Rupture: Elderly smoker + Hypotension + Back Pain + Mass = Emergency Surgery.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the pain of rupture with the pain of dissection. Rupture pain is often in the back/flank and associated with shock; dissection pain is 'tearing' and moves.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which structural specialization of the arterial wall primarily accounts for why large elastic arteries like the aorta are the most common site for aneurysm formation compared to smaller muscular arteries?

options.a: Thicker tunica intima with higher cellularity
options.b: Presence of vasa vasorum in the outer media
options.c: Higher proportion of smooth muscle cells in the media
options.d: Absence of an external elastic lamina

explanations.a: The intima is normally thin; thickening is a response to injury, not a structural reason for aneurysm predilection.
explanations.b: Large arteries have a media so thick that it cannot be nourished by luminal diffusion alone. They require vasa vasorum. These vessels are susceptible to endarteritis (syphilis) or compression by plaques (atherosclerosis), leading to medial ischemia.
explanations.c: Smaller muscular arteries actually have a higher ratio of smooth muscle to provide vascular tone; large arteries are more 'elastic'.
explanations.d: Large elastic arteries have multiple elastic laminae rather than just one external elastic lamina.
explanations.e: Most arteries have continuous endothelium; this does not explain the site-specific predilection for aneurysms.

ankiCards: The vessels that supply the outer portion of the media in large arteries are the {{c1::vasa vasorum}}.
The inner half of the aortic media is nourished by {{c1::diffusion}} from the lumen.
Atherosclerosis causes AAA by increasing the {{c1::diffusion distance}} from the lumen to the media.
The high {{c1::elastic}} content of the aorta allows it to handle pulsatile flow.
{{c1::Ischemia}} of the media is the common pathway for wall weakening in both AAA and syphilitic aneurysms.
keyPoints: Large arteries (Aorta) rely on vasa vasorum for medial nutrition.
Atherosclerotic plaques block luminal diffusion to the media.
Syphilis attacks the vasa vasorum directly.
Both lead to medial ischemia and weakening.
The aorta's high pressure (systolic) provides the force for dilation.
microReview: Vasa Vasorum: Essential for thick walls (Aorta) -> Vulnerable point for ischemia -> Medial weakening -> Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Students often think aneurysms are an 'intimal' disease because atherosclerosis starts there. Aneurysms are fundamentally a 'medial' disease (weakening of the structural layer).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 34-year-old male with a history of advanced HIV infection (CD4+ count 85/mm³) presents with several painless, non-blanching, violaceous macules and plaques on his lower extremities and hard palate. Biopsy of a skin lesion reveals a proliferation of spindle-shaped cells forming slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells. Which of the following infectious agents is the most likely driver of this patient's pathology?

explanations.a: Human herpesvirus 6 is the causative agent of Roseola infantum, not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.b: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the definitive etiologic agent for all forms of Kaposi sarcoma, including the AIDS-associated (epidemic) form described.
explanations.c: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with various lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, but not vascular tumors like Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.d: Cytomegalovirus can cause retinitis or colitis in HIV patients but does not cause spindle-cell vascular proliferations.
explanations.e: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can mimic Kaposi sarcoma clinically, but the histology shows lobular capillary proliferation with neutrophils, not the slit-like spindle cell spaces characteristic of Kaposi sarcoma.

ankiCards: The infectious agent most strongly associated with Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
The classic histological finding in Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells}} forming {{c2::slit-like vascular spaces}}.
Kaposi Sarcoma in HIV patients typically presents as {{c1::violaceous/purple}} macules or plaques.
Besides the skin, Kaposi Sarcoma frequently involves the {{c1::gastrointestinal tract}} and the {{c2::oral cavity (palate)}}.
The spindle cells in Kaposi Sarcoma are of {{c1::endothelial}} origin.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a low-grade malignant vascular tumor caused by HHV-8.
Epidemic KS is the most common AIDS-associated malignancy.
Histology features spindle cells, slit-like spaces, and extravasated RBCs.
Clinical presentation involves purple-red skin plaques or nodules.
KS must be differentiated from Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella) via histology.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is an endothelial neoplasm. There are four types: Classic (older Mediterranean men), Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and Epidemic (AIDS). All are linked to HHV-8. Histologically, look for spindle cells and 'slit-like' spaces with RBCs. Clinically, it presents as cutaneous or mucosal violaceous lesions.
examinerTraps: The most common trap is confusing Kaposi Sarcoma with Bacillary Angiomatosis. Both occur in HIV patients. Look for 'neutrophils' and 'Bartonella' in the vignette for Bacillary Angiomatosis; look for 'spindle cells' and 'HHV-8' for Kaposi.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old female presents with a small, 0.5 cm, exquisitely painful nodule located beneath the nail bed of her right index finger. The pain is triggered by cold temperature and touch. A biopsy reveals a tumor composed of nests of uniform, rounded cells surrounding branching vascular channels. What is the cell of origin for this lesion?

explanations.a: While this is a vascular tumor, the specific glomus cells are not endothelial cells.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) arise from specialized, modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, an arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.c: Fibroblasts are not the primary component of glomus tumors.
explanations.d: Pericytes are related to Hemangiopericytomas (now often classified under solitary fibrous tumors), but glomus cells are specifically modified smooth muscle.
explanations.e: Lymphatic endothelium forms lymphangiomas, which are typically painless and not subungual.

ankiCards: The most common location for a Glomus tumor is the {{c1::subungual (under nail)}} region.
The classic clinical triad for a Glomus tumor includes {{c1::paroxysmal pain}}, {{c2::point tenderness}}, and {{c3::cold sensitivity}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells.
The function of the normal glomus body is {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors show nests of {{c1::uniform round cells}} around vascular spaces.
keyPoints: Glomus tumor is a benign, extremely painful lesion.
Typically occurs in the distal digits, especially under the nail bed.
Arises from glomus bodies (specialized AV shunts).
Microscopy shows 'glomus cells'—uniform, round cells with scant cytoplasm.
Surgical excision is curative.
microReview: Painful subungual nodule = Glomus Tumor. Origin = Modified smooth muscle cells of the thermoregulatory glomus body. Pain is characteristic and often triggered by cold.
examinerTraps: The examiner may try to lead you toward a 'glomus jugulare' tumor or other paragangliomas; however, the subungual location and cold-induced pain are pathognomonic for a glomus tumor.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An 82-year-old male presents with a large, rapidly enlarging, ill-defined bruise-like lesion on his scalp. He reports the area has begun to bleed spontaneously and has developed ulcerations. Biopsy shows highly pleomorphic, malignant endothelial cells forming irregular, anastomosing vascular channels that infiltrate the dermis. Immunohistochemical staining is positive for CD31. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign, pedunculated red nodule common in the gingiva or skin, usually small and not malignant.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign lesions consisting of large, blood-filled spaces; they do not show pleomorphic cells or aggressive infiltration.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a malignant vascular tumor that most commonly affects the scalp and face of elderly individuals. It is characterized by pleomorphic endothelial cells and CD31 positivity.
explanations.d: Kaposi sarcoma typically presents as violaceous plaques/nodules and is associated with HHV-8; the histology (slit-like spaces) differs from the pleomorphic channels of angiosarcoma.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign bacterial-induced lesion (Bartonella) seen in immunocompromised patients, characterized by capillary proliferation with neutrophils.

ankiCards: The most common site for cutaneous angiosarcoma is the {{c1::scalp/face}} of {{c2::elderly}} patients.
A key immunohistochemical marker for angiosarcoma is {{c1::CD31 (or vWF)}}.
Angiosarcoma of the liver is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}, {{c2::arsenic}}, or {{c3::Thorotrast}}.
Angiosarcoma arising in a limb with chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
Histologically, angiosarcoma is characterized by {{c1::pleomorphic endothelial cells}} forming {{c2::anastomosing channels}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade, malignant endothelial neoplasm.
Cutaneous forms usually occur on the head/neck of the elderly.
Poor prognosis due to early metastasis.
CD31 is a specific marker for endothelial differentiation.
Associated with radiation or chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves).
microReview: Elderly patient + Scalp 'bruise' that won't go away + CD31 positivity = Angiosarcoma. This is an aggressive cancer of the blood vessels.
examinerTraps: Wait for the mention of 'CD31' or 'vWF' to confirm endothelial origin. Do not confuse a 'scalp bruise' in an elderly person with a simple hematoma if the description mentions pleomorphism or CD31 positivity.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular tumors are categorized into benign, intermediate, and malignant grades. A specific vascular lesion is noted for its tendency to occur in the liver or spleen, consisting of large, dilated, blood-filled vascular spaces lined by a single layer of flattened endothelium and separated by a thin connective tissue stroma. Which of the following best describes this lesion?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas consist of small, thin-walled capillaries, often in the skin of infants (strawberry hemangiomas).
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are characterized by large, dilated vascular spaces. They are the most common benign tumor of the liver and can also occur in the spleen.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are small, painful, and typically found subungually.
explanations.d: Hemangioendotheliomas are intermediate-grade tumors with features between benign hemangiomas and malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious process characterized by lobular capillary proliferations, not large cavernous spaces.

ankiCards: The most common benign tumor of the liver is the {{c1::cavernous hemangioma}}.
Cavernous hemangiomas consist of {{c1::large, dilated vascular spaces}}.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas are often {{c1::deep-seated (visceral)}}.
The endothelial lining of a cavernous hemangioma is {{c1::flattened/thin}}.
A potential complication of large cavernous hemangiomas is {{c1::thrombosis}} or {{c2::calcification (phleboliths)}}.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign but can be large and involve viscera.
They are the most common primary tumor of the liver.
They do not typically regress (unlike infantile capillary hemangiomas).
Histologically: large blood-filled spaces with thin septa.
Often discovered incidentally on imaging.
microReview: Cavernous hemangioma = Big spaces (caverns). Capillary hemangioma = Small spaces (capillaries). Both are benign.
examinerTraps: A common trap is asking about biopsy of a liver cavernous hemangioma; biopsy is generally avoided due to the high risk of hemorrhage.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Infantile 'strawberry' hemangiomas are common vascular lesions that appear shortly after birth. Which of the following is the most characteristic clinical course for these lesions?

options.c: Rapid growth followed by spontaneous regression
options.e: Permanent persistence as a port-wine stain

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are entirely benign and do not transform into angiosarcomas.
explanations.b: They do not grow steadily; they have a distinct proliferative and regressive phase.
explanations.c: Strawberry hemangiomas (juvenile capillary hemangiomas) typically grow rapidly for several months and then spontaneously regress by age 7 to 9 in the majority of cases.
explanations.d: Surgical excision is usually avoided unless the lesion obstructs a vital function (e.g., vision) because of the high likelihood of spontaneous regression.
explanations.e: Port-wine stains (nevus flammeus) are malformations that persist and grow with the child, unlike strawberry hemangiomas.

ankiCards: Strawberry hemangioma is also known as {{c1::juvenile capillary hemangioma}}.
