Smoking is a major modifiable risk factor for the development of AAA.
The most frequent location for AAA is between the renal arteries and the aortic bifurcation.
microReview: Aneurysms represent a failure of vascular structural integrity. True aneurysms involve all three layers of the vessel wall. In the abdominal aorta, atherosclerosis prevents oxygen diffusion to the media, while inflammatory cells secrete MMPs that digest the extracellular matrix, causing progressive thinning and dilation.
examinerTraps: A common trap is confusing the pathogenesis of AAA (atherosclerosis/MMPs) with thoracic aortic aneurysms (hypertension/vasa vasorum ischemia) or Marfan syndrome (TGF-beta signaling defects).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old male with tall stature, exceptionally long fingers, and a history of ectopia lentis is diagnosed with a 4.5 cm dilation of the ascending aorta. Which of the following mechanisms is the most likely cause of this patient's vascular pathology?

options.a: Defective cross-linking of collagen by lysyl oxidase
options.b: Inappropriate activation of transforming growth factor-beta signaling
options.c: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.d: Replacement of the media with dense fibrous scar tissue
options.e: Scurvy-related deficiency in hydroxylation of proline residues

explanations.a: Lysyl oxidase defects are associated with Menkes disease or lathyrism, not the standard presentation of Marfan syndrome.
explanations.b: In Marfan syndrome, mutations in fibrillin-1 lead to an inability to sequester TGF-beta, resulting in excessive TGF-beta signaling which triggers matrix degradation and medial weakening.
explanations.c: Obliterative endarteritis is the classic description for syphilitic (tertiary) aneurysms of the ascending aorta.
explanations.d: Aneurysms involve the loss of elastic tissue and thinning, rather than replacement by dense fibrous scarring, which would typically stiffen the vessel.
explanations.e: Proline hydroxylation deficiency (Vitamin C deficiency) causes capillary fragility and bruising but not typically large vessel aneurysms of the ascending aorta.

ankiCards: The mutation in Marfan syndrome involves the {{c1::FBN1 (Fibrillin-1)}} gene.
Fibrillin-1 mutations in Marfan syndrome lead to increased activity of {{c1::TGF-beta}}.
Cystic medial degeneration is a histological feature often seen in {{c1::thoracic aortic aneurysms}}.
The classic ocular finding associated with the vascular risks of Marfan syndrome is {{c1::ectopia lentis (lens dislocation)}}.
In Marfan syndrome, the weakening of the aortic wall typically occurs in the {{c1::ascending aorta/aortic root}}.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder of connective tissue.
The aortic root is the most common site of life-threatening dilation in Marfan patients.
Fibrillin-1 normally sequesters TGF-beta; its deficiency leads to excess TGF-beta bioavailability.
Excess TGF-beta signaling promotes the production of MMPs and medial destruction.
Pathology often shows 'cystic medial degeneration' (fragmentation of elastic fibers).
microReview: Thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAA) are often linked to genetic conditions. Marfan syndrome (Fibrillin-1) and Loeys-Dietz syndrome (TGF-beta receptor mutations) both highlight the critical role of the TGF-beta pathway in maintaining the aortic wall's structural integrity.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Fibrillin-1 (Marfan) with Type III Collagen (Ehlers-Danlos vascular type), although both can cause aneurysms.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes a 'false aneurysm' (pseudoaneurysm)?

options.a: A localized dilation involving all three layers of the arterial wall
options.b: A longitudinal tear in the media allowing blood to create a second lumen
options.c: A spherical dilation involving only the intimal and medial layers
options.d: A wall defect leading to an extravascular hematoma that communicates with the intravascular space
options.e: An abnormal communication between an artery and a vein bypassing capillaries

explanations.a: This describes a true aneurysm (e.g., atherosclerotic or syphilitic).
explanations.b: This describes an aortic dissection.
explanations.c: Aneurysms typically involve the weakening of the entire wall; a dilation of only inner layers would not maintain structural integrity.
explanations.d: A false aneurysm is a breach in the vascular wall leading to an extravascular hematoma contained by extravascular connective tissue that still communicates with the lumen.
explanations.e: This describes an arteriovenous fistula.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the arterial wall (intima, media, and adventitia).
A {{c1::false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm)}} is a breach in the wall leading to a hematoma contained by extravascular tissue.
A {{c1::dissection}} occurs when blood enters the wall of the artery through an intimal tear.
Saccular aneurysms are {{c1::spherical}} in shape and involve only a portion of the vessel wall.
Fusiform aneurysms are characterized by {{c1::circumferential}} dilation of the vessel.
keyPoints: Aneurysms are classified as true or false based on the involvement of the vessel wall layers.
True aneurysms involve the intima, media, and adventitia (or the attenuated wall of the heart).
False aneurysms are essentially contained hematomas communicating with the vessel lumen.
Common causes of false aneurysms include trauma and myocardial rupture following an infarct.
Dissections are not aneurysms by definition, though they involve wall structural failure.
microReview: Understanding the nomenclature is vital. True aneurysms (saccular or fusiform) involve the anatomical layers of the vessel. False aneurysms (pseudoaneurysms) are essentially 'leaks' that have been walled off by external fibrous tissue.
examinerTraps: The term 'dissecting aneurysm' is technically a misnomer; 'aortic dissection' is the correct term because the vessel is not necessarily dilated initially.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 64-year-old woman with a history of intravenous drug use presents with fever and back pain. Imaging reveals a 3 cm saccular dilation of the superior mesenteric artery. Blood cultures are positive for Salmonella species. Which of the following terms best describes this vascular lesion?

explanations.a: Berry aneurysms are small, saccular dilations typically found in the Circle of Willis, associated with subarachnoid hemorrhage.
explanations.b: Dissecting aneurysms (dissections) involve blood tearing through the media, not primarily an infectious process.
explanations.c: Fusiform describes a shape (circumferential), whereas this lesion is described as saccular and is caused by infection.
explanations.d: A mycotic aneurysm is an aneurysm caused by the infection of an arterial wall, often resulting from bacteremia (e.g., from endocarditis or IV drug use).
explanations.e: Syphilitic aneurysms occur in the tertiary stage of syphilis and typically involve the ascending aorta due to vasa vasorum damage.

ankiCards: An aneurysm caused by infection of the arterial wall is called a {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm.
Mycotic aneurysms can result from {{c1::septic embolization}} (e.g., from infective endocarditis).
The most common shape for an aneurysm involving only a portion of the wall circumference is {{c1::saccular}}.
Salmonella and Staphylococcus are common organisms associated with {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysms.
Mycotic aneurysms are dangerous because they can lead to rapid expansion and {{c1::rupture/sepsis}}.
keyPoints: Mycotic aneurysms are infections of the vessel wall.
They can arise from embolization of a septic thrombus, extension of an adjacent infection, or direct seeding during bacteremia.
The name 'mycotic' is a misnomer, as most are bacterial, not fungal.
These aneurysms are often saccular and prone to rupture.
Common complications include abscess formation and systemic sepsis.
microReview: Infection can weaken the arterial wall through inflammatory destruction. While 'mycotic' implies fungus, the term is used for any infected aneurysm. These require aggressive antibiotic therapy and often surgical intervention.
examinerTraps: A common mistake is thinking 'mycotic' only refers to fungi. In pathology, 'mycotic aneurysm' almost always refers to a bacterial infection of the wall.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the development of an abdominal aortic aneurysm, what is the primary consequence of extensive intimal atherosclerosis on the underlying tunica media?

options.a: Hypertrophy of the medial smooth muscle cells
options.b: Increased oxygen diffusion to the outer media
options.c: Ischemic atrophy and loss of smooth muscle cells
options.d: Metaplasia of the endothelium into squamous cells

explanations.a: The media thins and atrophies in AAA; it does not undergo hypertrophy.
explanations.b: Atherosclerotic plaques actually increase the diffusion distance, decreasing oxygen delivery to the media.
explanations.c: Extensive atherosclerosis increases the diffusion distance from the lumen to the media, leading to ischemic injury, atrophy, and loss of the smooth muscle cells that maintain the ECM.
explanations.d: Endothelial metaplasia is not a feature of aneurysm formation.
explanations.e: While calcification (dystrophic) occurs in atherosclerosis, the primary cause of wall weakening is the loss of medial integrity, not osteoblastic transformation.

ankiCards: In AAA, atherosclerosis impairs the diffusion of {{c1::oxygen/nutrients}} to the arterial wall.
The result of chronic ischemia to the tunica media in AAA is {{c1::atrophy/smooth muscle loss}}.
Thinning of the tunica media leads to {{c1::weakening}} of the vessel wall and dilation.
The two major risk factors for AAA are {{c1::smoking}} and {{c1::hypertension}}.
AAAs are usually located {{c1::below}} the level of the renal arteries.
keyPoints: The aorta relies on diffusion from the lumen for the inner media and vasa vasorum for the outer media.
Atherosclerotic plaques act as a barrier to diffusion.
Medial ischemia leads to smooth muscle cell death.
Loss of smooth muscle cells results in decreased collagen and elastin synthesis.
This structural failure is the prerequisite for aneurysmal dilation.
microReview: Aneurysms in the abdominal aorta are fundamentally 'atherosclerotic aneurysms.' The plaque causes structural failure by choking off the blood supply to the media and by inciting an inflammatory response that digests the wall.
examinerTraps: Be careful: while hypertension is a risk factor for both, it is the *primary* driver for TAA and dissection, whereas atherosclerosis is the *primary* driver for AAA.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism)
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 75-year-old male with a history of abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) presents with sudden onset of cold, painful, and pulseless right lower extremity. He has no history of atrial fibrillation. What is the most likely source of the occlusion in his leg?

options.a: Atherosclerotic plaque rupture in the femoral artery
options.b: Embolization of a mural thrombus from the aneurysm
options.c: Paradoxical embolus via a patent foramen ovale
options.d: Septic embolus from an unrecognized endocarditis
options.e: Venous thrombosis with phlegmasia cerulea dolens

explanations.a: While possible, the presence of a known AAA makes embolization of its contents a more classical board-style association.
explanations.b: Aneurysms often contain mural thrombi due to stasis and turbulent flow. These thrombi can embolize distally, causing acute limb ischemia.
explanations.c: Paradoxical emboli require a right-to-left shunt and a venous source (DVT), which is less likely than a local aortic source in this patient.
explanations.d: There is no mention of fever or valvular disease to suggest endocarditis.
explanations.e: The presentation (cold, pulseless) describes arterial occlusion, not venous disease.

ankiCards: Aneurysms promote thrombus formation due to {{c1::stasis/turbulent flow}}.
The term for a thrombus attached to the wall of a dilated vessel is a {{c1::mural thrombus}}.
A common clinical complication of AAA, besides rupture, is distal {{c1::embolization}}.
The 'trash foot' syndrome is caused by {{c1::microemboli}} from an upstream aneurysm or plaque.
AAAs greater than {{c1::5 or 5.5}} cm are generally considered at high risk for rupture.
keyPoints: Aneurysms alter hemodynamics, leading to blood stasis and turbulence.
Stasis and endothelial injury fulfill parts of Virchow's triad, leading to mural thrombi.
Mural thrombi can friably break off and embolize.
Embolization can lead to acute limb ischemia or 'blue toe syndrome'.
AAAs are often asymptomatic until they rupture or embolize.
microReview: Aneurysms aren't just about 'bursting.' They are also major sources of thromboembolism. The stagnant flow in the 'pouch' of the aneurysm allows for layering of thrombus (Lines of Zahn), which can then travel downstream.
examinerTraps: Often students only think of AAA as a rupture risk (sudden death). Remember that distal ischemia (embolism) and pressure on adjacent structures (ureters, vertebrae) are also key complications.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the shape of an aneurysm that involves a long, circumferential segment of the aorta?

explanations.a: Berry aneurysms are small and saccular, not long or circumferential.
explanations.b: Dissection is a tear, not a shape classification of a localized dilation.
explanations.c: Fusiform aneurysms are characterized by a symmetrical, circumferential dilation along a long segment of the vessel.
explanations.d: Mycotic refers to the etiology (infection), not the shape.
explanations.e: Saccular aneurysms are 'pouch-like' and only involve a portion of the vessel wall circumference.

ankiCards: A {{c1::fusiform}} aneurysm is a circumferential dilation of a long vascular segment.
A {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm is a localized out-pouching involving only part of the wall.
True aneurysms are classified by shape into {{c1::saccular}} and {{c1::fusiform}}.
Fusiform aneurysms are most commonly found in the {{c1::abdominal aorta}}.
Saccular aneurysms are often seen in the {{c1::cerebral}} circulation (e.g., Berry aneurysms).
keyPoints: Aneurysms are morphologically classified as saccular or fusiform.
Saccular aneurysms are spherical and measure 5-20 cm in diameter.
Fusiform aneurysms vary in diameter and length.
The shape does not necessarily correlate with the underlying cause.
Both shapes represent a 'true' aneurysm if all three layers are involved.
microReview: Morphology helps describe the lesion but doesn't define the pathology. Fusiform looks like a spindle; Saccular looks like a sac. Both are 'true' if the wall layers are intact (though thinned).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'fusiform' with 'dissection'. Dissection refers to the splitting of the wall, while fusiform refers to the external shape of the dilation.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... Arterial wall thickness gradually diminishes as the vessels become smaller.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old male with untreated syphilis (Stage 3) presents with a brassy cough and difficulty swallowing. Imaging shows a massive dilation of the ascending aorta with 'eggshell' calcification. Which of the following is the primary histological finding expected in the vasa vasorum of this patient's aorta?

explanations.a: Aschoff bodies are pathognomonic for rheumatic heart disease.
explanations.b: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in malignant hypertension or certain vasculitides (like PAN).
explanations.c: Giant cell arteritis involves the larger branches of the carotid, not typically the vasa vasorum in syphilis.
explanations.d: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is a feature of benign hypertension, affecting small vessels like those in the kidney.
explanations.e: Syphilitic (luetic) aortitis is characterized by obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum, leading to ischemic injury of the aortic media and subsequent aneurysm.

ankiCards: Tertiary syphilis classically affects the {{c1::ascending}} aorta.
The vascular lesion in syphilis is caused by {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}} of the vasa vasorum.
Ischemia of the aortic media in syphilis leads to {{c1::tree-barking}} appearance of the intima.
A common complication of syphilitic aortitis is {{c1::aortic valve insufficiency (regurgitation)}}.
Syphilitic aneurysms are less common today due to effective {{c1::antibiotic (penicillin)}} therapy.
keyPoints: Syphilis (Treponema pallidum) causes tertiary cardiovascular complications.
The target is the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta.
Inflammation leads to luminal narrowing of the vasa vasorum (endarteritis).
Medial ischemia leads to the destruction of elastic tissue and fibrosis.
The resulting 'tree-bark' appearance is due to irregular intimal scarring over the weakened media.
microReview: Syphilitic aneurysms are the classic 'ascending' aortic pathology caused by infection-induced ischemia. The destruction of the media can also dilate the aortic valve ring, causing massive heart failure from regurgitation.
examinerTraps: Remember the location: Syphilis = Ascending/Arch; Atherosclerosis = Abdominal. They are almost never swapped in board questions.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following genetic syndromes is specifically associated with mutations in the TGF-beta receptor and presents with aggressive aortic aneurysm formation and bifid uvula?

explanations.a: Alport syndrome involves Type IV collagen mutations and affects kidneys, ears, and eyes.
explanations.b: EDS Vascular type involves Type III collagen (COL3A1) mutations.
explanations.c: Loeys-Dietz syndrome is caused by mutations in TGF-beta receptors (TGFBR1/2) and is characterized by arterial tortuosity, aneurysms, and a bifid uvula.
explanations.d: Marfan syndrome is due to Fibrillin-1 mutations; while it involves TGF-beta signaling, it does not typically present with a bifid uvula.
explanations.e: Williams syndrome is associated with elastin deletions and supravalvular aortic stenosis, not aneurysms.

ankiCards: Loeys-Dietz syndrome is caused by mutations in {{c1::TGF-beta receptors}}.
A clinical hallmark of Loeys-Dietz syndrome, besides aneurysms, is a {{c1::bifid uvula}}.
In contrast to Marfan, Loeys-Dietz aneurysms are often more {{c1::aggressive/rupture at smaller sizes}}.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos (Type IV) is caused by a defect in {{c1::Type III collagen}}.
Overactive {{c1::TGF-beta}} signaling is a common pathway in several syndromic aneurysms.
keyPoints: Loeys-Dietz syndrome is a relatively recently recognized connective tissue disorder.
It shares features with Marfan but has distinct physical findings (bifid uvula, hypertelorism).
Aneurysms in LDS can occur throughout the arterial tree, not just the aorta.
The underlying defect is in the TGF-beta signaling pathway (TGFBR1, TGFBR2, SMAD3).
These patients require very close monitoring because of the high risk of early rupture.
microReview: Syndromic aneurysms usually involve the TGF-beta pathway or collagen/elastin synthesis. LDS is the 'aggressive' cousin of Marfan, often requiring earlier surgical intervention.
examinerTraps: Many students select Marfan for any 'tall person with an aneurysm.' Look for clues like 'bifid uvula' or 'skin hyperelasticity' to differentiate LDS or EDS.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which layer of the vessel wall is primarily responsible for the structural integrity and tensile strength that prevents aneurysm formation?

explanations.a: The endothelium is a single layer of cells responsible for signaling and barrier function, not structural strength.
explanations.b: The internal elastic lamina is a thin layer between the intima and media, but the bulk of strength comes from the media itself.
explanations.c: The adventitia provides some support and contains the vasa vasorum, but the media is the primary pressure-bearing layer.
explanations.d: The intima is thin and is the site where atherosclerosis begins, but it does not provide tensile strength.
explanations.e: The tunica media, containing smooth muscle cells and elastic fibers (especially in elastic arteries like the aorta), provides the structural integrity required to withstand pulsatile pressure.

ankiCards: The bulk of the aortic wall's tensile strength is provided by the {{c1::tunica media}}.
Aneurysms occur when the {{c1::extracellular matrix (ECM)}} of the media is degraded.
Smooth muscle cells in the media synthesize {{c1::collagen and elastin}}.
Arterial walls are thicker than veins because they must accommodate {{c1::higher/pulsatile}} pressures.
A deficiency in {{c1::Vitamin C}} can lead to weakened vessel walls due to poor collagen cross-linking.
keyPoints: The tunica media is the thickest layer in large arteries.
It is composed of concentric layers of smooth muscle and elastic lamellae.
The balance of collagen (strength) and elastin (recoil) is maintained by smooth muscle cells.
Pathological processes like inflammation or ischemia disrupt this balance.
Loss of the media's structural components is the final common pathway for all aneurysms.
microReview: Think of the media as the 'muscle and spring' of the artery. When the muscle dies (ischemia) or the springs are cut (MMPs), the artery can no longer resist the internal blood pressure and it bulges out (aneurysm).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'site of injury' (Intima in atherosclerosis) with the 'site of structural failure' (Media in aneurysms).
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a 40-pack-year smoking history and long-standing hypertension. During a routine physical examination, a prominent pulsatile mass is palpated in the midline of the abdomen, superior to the umbilicus. Imaging reveals a 5.5-cm dilation of the abdominal aorta below the renal arteries. Which of the following pathogenetic mechanisms is primarily responsible for the structural failure of the vessel wall in this patient?

options.a: Excessive production of type I collagen by myofibroblasts
options.b: Intimal thickening due to smooth muscle cell migration
options.d: Granulomatous inflammation of the vasa vasorum
options.e: Congenital deficiency in the fibrillin-1 gene

explanations.a: Increased collagen production typically occurs during vessel repair or scarring (intimal thickening) rather than the wall weakening seen in aneurysms.
explanations.b: Intimal thickening is a stereotyped response to vascular injury (e.g., atherosclerosis) but does not explain the dilation or wall thinning characteristic of aneurysms.
explanations.c: The pathogenesis of abdominal aortic aneurysms involves an imbalance between synthesis and degradation of the extracellular matrix, characterized by increased matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) that degrade elastin and collagen.
explanations.d: Granulomatous inflammation of the vasa vasorum is characteristic of syphilitic (tertiary) aortitis, which typically affects the thoracic aorta, not the abdominal aorta.
explanations.e: Fibrillin-1 mutations cause Marfan syndrome, which leads to cystic medial degeneration and thoracic aortic aneurysms, not primarily atherosclerotic abdominal aneurysms.

ankiCards: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are most commonly associated with {{c1::atherosclerosis}} and smoking.
The primary biochemical cause of wall weakening in AAA is the increased expression of {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
AAA usually occurs between the {{c1::renal arteries}} and the {{c1::iliac bifurcation}}.
A significant risk factor for the rupture of an AAA is a diameter greater than {{c1::5 cm}}.
The two principal mechanisms underlying vascular disease are stenosis and {{c1::weakening of vessel walls}}.
keyPoints: Aneurysms represent a weakening of the vessel wall leading to dilation.
Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) derived from macrophages play a critical role in degrading the aortic wall ECM.
Tobacco use is the most significant modifiable risk factor for AAA development.
Most AAAs are located below the origin of the renal arteries.
Clinical presentation often involves an asymptomatic pulsatile abdominal mass.
Rupture risk increases significantly with the size of the aneurysm (cutoff typically >5 or 5.5 cm).
microReview: Aneurysms are localized abnormal dilations of blood vessels. AAA is the most common type, driven by atherosclerosis and chronic inflammation that recruits macrophages. These cells release MMPs, which degrade the structural integrity of the media (elastin and collagen), leading to progressive dilation.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse the location: Syphilitic aneurysms occur in the thoracic aorta due to vasa vasorum damage, while atherosclerotic aneurysms (AAA) occur in the abdominal aorta due to oxygen diffusion limitations in the thickened intima.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following best distinguishes a 'true aneurysm' from a 'false aneurysm' (pseudoaneurysm)?

options.a: A true aneurysm involves only the tunica intima and media, while a false aneurysm involves all three layers.
options.b: A true aneurysm is always fusiform, whereas a false aneurysm is always saccular.
options.c: A true aneurysm involves an intact attenuated arterial wall, whereas a false aneurysm is an extravascular hematoma communicating with the lumen.
options.d: A true aneurysm is caused by atherosclerosis, while a false aneurysm is exclusively caused by trauma.
options.e: A true aneurysm involves the venous system, whereas a false aneurysm involves the arterial system.

explanations.a: A true aneurysm must involve all three layers of the vessel wall (intima, media, and adventitia).
explanations.b: Both true and false aneurysms can vary in shape; shape does not define the histological classification.
explanations.c: This is the classic definition: a true aneurysm is bounded by all three layers of the vascular wall (though they may be thinned), while a false aneurysm is a breach in the wall where the 'wall' of the dilation is actually clotted blood and connective tissue.
explanations.d: While trauma is a common cause of false aneurysms, they can also be caused by infections or post-surgical complications; true aneurysms can be congenital or caused by various pathologies.
explanations.e: Aneurysms predominantly affect arteries, but both true and false types can occur in the arterial system.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the arterial wall (intima, media, adventitia).
A {{c1::false}} aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) is an extravascular hematoma that communicates with the intravascular space.
A {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm is a spherical outpouching involving only a portion of the vessel wall.
A {{c1::fusiform}} aneurysm is a circumferential dilation of a long vascular segment.
Vascular wall weakening leads to {{c1::dilation}} or rupture.
keyPoints: True aneurysms involve an intact (though thinned) wall containing all three layers.
False aneurysms result from a wall breach leading to a hematoma contained by extravascular tissue.
Atherosclerotic and congenital aneurysms are typically 'true'.
Post-catheterization femoral artery dilations are often 'false' aneurysms.
Dissection occurs when blood enters the wall itself, creating a false lumen.
microReview: Aneurysms are categorized by the composition of their 'wall'. If the wall contains the original (albeit remodeled) histological layers of the vessel, it is true. If the wall is formed by external connective tissue or hematoma, it is false.
examinerTraps: The examiner may describe a pulsatile mass after a procedure (like a femoral poke); this is almost always a pseudoaneurysm, not a true aneurysm.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old woman with tall stature, long tapering fingers, and high-arched palate presents with sudden onset of severe chest pain radiating to her back. Physical examination reveals a diastolic murmur heard best at the right sternal border. An echocardiogram shows dilation of the proximal ascending aorta. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cellular defect leading to this condition?

options.a: Defective cross-linking of collagen by lysyl oxidase
options.b: Abnormal folding of a glycoprotein that scaffolds elastin
options.c: Inability to neutralize elastase in the lungs
options.d: Excessive accumulation of low-density lipoproteins in the media
options.e: Autoimmune destruction of the internal elastic lamina

explanations.a: Lysyl oxidase deficiency is associated with Menkes disease or lathyrism, not the phenotype described.
explanations.b: The patient has Marfan syndrome, caused by mutations in Fibrillin-1. Fibrillin-1 is a glycoprotein that serves as a scaffold for elastin and regulates TGF-beta signaling. Defective fibrillin leads to cystic medial degeneration.
explanations.c: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency leads to inability to neutralize elastase, causing emphysema, not typically Marfan-like aortic dilations.
explanations.d: This describes atherosclerosis, which is the primary cause of abdominal, not thoracic, aneurysms in young patients with Marfan-like features.
explanations.e: This describes Giant Cell Arteritis, which typically affects older individuals and different vessel distributions.

ankiCards: Marfan syndrome is caused by a mutation in the {{c1::FBN1}} gene.
The FBN1 gene encodes the protein {{c1::fibrillin-1}}.
Thoracic aortic aneurysms in Marfan syndrome are characterized histologically by {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
Fibrillin-1 mutations lead to increased signaling of the growth factor {{c1::TGF-beta}}.
Weakening of vessel walls in the ascending aorta can lead to {{c1::aortic dissection}}.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome is a major cause of thoracic aortic aneurysms in young patients.
The genetic defect is in Fibrillin-1 (FBN1).
Histology shows 'cystic medial degeneration' (loss of smooth muscle and elastic tissue with mucoid material accumulation).
Clinical signs include arachnodactyly, ectopia lentis, and aortic root dilation.
Dilated aortic roots can lead to aortic valve insufficiency (diastolic murmur).
microReview: Marfan syndrome involves a mutation in Fibrillin-1, which normally sequesters TGF-beta. Excessive TGF-beta activity and loss of the elastin scaffold cause the tunica media to lose its elastic fibers, resulting in cystic medial necrosis and thoracic aneurysms.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'thoracic' vs 'abdominal'. Marfan usually involves the thoracic (ascending) aorta. Smoking/atherosclerosis usually involves the abdominal aorta.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: ... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following bacterial pathogens is most frequently associated with the development of a 'mycotic aneurysm' secondary to infective endocarditis?

explanations.a: E. coli is a rare cause of mycotic aneurysms compared to Gram-positive cocci.
explanations.b: B. fragilis is an anaerobe and is not a common cause of mycotic aneurysms.
explanations.c: Mycotic aneurysms result from infection of a vessel wall. The most common cause is embolization of a septic thrombus from infective endocarditis, frequently involving S. aureus or Viridans streptococci.
explanations.d: Treponema pallidum causes syphilitic aortitis (obliterative endarteritis), which is distinct from the acute suppurative infection known as a mycotic aneurysm.
explanations.e: M. tuberculosis causes granulomatous inflammation; while it can involve vessels, it is not the classic cause of 'mycotic aneurysms'.

ankiCards: A {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm is an aneurysm caused by an infection of the vessel wall.
The most common mechanism for a mycotic aneurysm is {{c1::septic embolization}} (often from endocarditis).
Despite the name, most mycotic aneurysms are {{c1::bacterial}} in origin.
Common organisms in mycotic aneurysms include {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}} and Salmonella.
Mycotic aneurysms represent a form of vessel wall {{c1::weakening}} due to inflammation/suppuration.
keyPoints: The term 'mycotic' is a misnomer; most are bacterial.
Infection can arrive via septic emboli, extension from adjacent infection, or direct seeding during bacteremia.
The wall is weakened by inflammatory destruction and abscess formation.
They are highly prone to rapid rupture.
Salmonella can seed pre-existing atherosclerotic plaques to cause mycotic aneurysms.
microReview: Mycotic aneurysms occur when an infection (usually bacterial) destroys the vessel wall. This can happen when a piece of a heart valve vegetation (S. aureus) breaks off and lodges in a distant artery, or when bacteria like Salmonella infect an already damaged (atherosclerotic) aorta.
examinerTraps: Don't pick 'fungal' just because it says 'mycotic'. It’s an old term for any infectious aneurysm.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: ... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Syphilitic aneurysms are distinct from atherosclerotic aneurysms in both location and mechanism. Which of the following pathological findings is most characteristic of the cardiovascular involvement in tertiary syphilis?

options.a: Accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages in the tunica intima
options.b: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.c: Cystic medial necrosis without inflammatory infiltrate
options.d: Transmural necrotizing vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis
options.e: Aneurysmal dilation of the distal abdominal aorta

explanations.a: This describes atherosclerosis, which primarily affects the abdominal aorta.
explanations.b: Tertiary syphilis causes an obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum in the thoracic aorta. This leads to ischemic injury of the media and subsequent 'tree-barking' appearance and dilation.
explanations.c: Cystic medial necrosis is characteristic of Marfan syndrome and hypertension, but it typically lacks the intense plasma cell-rich inflammatory infiltrate seen in syphilis.
explanations.d: This describes Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN), a medium-vessel vasculitis.
explanations.e: Syphilis characteristically affects the thoracic (ascending/arch) aorta, whereas atherosclerosis characteristically affects the abdominal aorta.

ankiCards: Syphilitic aortitis involves the {{c1::thoracic}} aorta.
The mechanism of injury in syphilitic aortitis is obliterative endarteritis of the {{c1::vasa vasorum}}.
The gross appearance of the aortic intima in syphilis is often described as {{c1::tree-barking}}.
Ischemic injury to the media in syphilis leads to replacement of elastic tissue with {{c1::fibrous scar}}.
Syphilitic aneurysms can cause {{c1::aortic valve}} insufficiency by dilating the aortic ring.
keyPoints: Tertiary syphilis targets the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta.
Endarteritis leads to medial ischemia and loss of elastic fibers.
The result is a weakened wall and 'tree-bark' appearance due to irregular scarring.
These aneurysms often involve the aortic root, causing valvular regurgitation.
Plasma cell-rich infiltrates are seen on histology.
microReview: Syphilitic (Luetic) aortitis occurs in tertiary syphilis. The spirochetes cause inflammation of the small vessels (vasa vasorum) that supply the outer half of the aortic wall. Without blood supply, the media undergoes destruction, leading to a weakened, dilated thoracic aorta.
examinerTraps: Syphilis = Thoracic/Vasa Vasorum. Atherosclerosis = Abdominal/Intimal plaque.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: ... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old male with a history of polycystic kidney disease presents to the emergency department with the 'worst headache of my life.' He has no history of trauma. A CT scan of the head shows blood in the subarachnoid space. This patient's condition is most likely caused by an aneurysm in which of the following locations?

explanations.a: Aneurysms here cause chest pain or dissection, not subarachnoid hemorrhage.
explanations.b: Abdominal aortic aneurysms present with abdominal or back pain.
explanations.c: The patient has a classic presentation of a ruptured berry (saccular) aneurysm. These are common in the Circle of Willis (especially the anterior communicating artery) and are associated with Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD).
explanations.d: Iliac aneurysms do not cause subarachnoid hemorrhage.
explanations.e: Popliteal aneurysms are the most common peripheral aneurysms but do not involve the cerebral circulation.

ankiCards: Berry aneurysms are most commonly found in the {{c1::Circle of Willis}}.
Berry aneurysms are associated with the genetic condition {{c1::ADPKD (Polycystic Kidney Disease)}}.
Rupture of a berry aneurysm causes {{c1::subarachnoid}} hemorrhage.
Berry aneurysms are a type of {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm.
The most common site for a berry aneurysm is the {{c1::anterior communicating}} artery.
keyPoints: Berry aneurysms are small, spherical dilations in cerebral vessels.
They occur at branch points in the Circle of Willis.
Associated with ADPKD and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Clinical presentation of rupture: 'Thunderclap headache'.
Unlike AAA, they are not primarily caused by atherosclerosis.
microReview: Berry aneurysms represent a congenital or acquired weakness in the arterial media at branch points. ADPKD is a high-yield association. Rupture leads to subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), often visualized as blood in the cisterns on CT.
examinerTraps: Associating ADPKD with 'kidney failure' only. Remember the vascular association with Berry aneurysms.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: ... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes a 'fusiform' aneurysm?

options.a: A spherical outpouching involving only a portion of the vessel wall
options.b: A longitudinal tear in the intima allowing blood to enter the media
options.c: A circumferential, symmetric dilation of a long segment of a vessel
options.d: An extravascular hematoma communicating with the lumen
options.e: A small dilation (<1 cm) typically involving the cerebral arteries

explanations.a: This describes a saccular aneurysm.
explanations.b: This describes an aortic dissection.
explanations.c: Fusiform aneurysms are characterized by diffuse, circumferential dilation of a long vascular segment.
explanations.d: This describes a false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm).
explanations.e: This describes a berry aneurysm (which is a subtype of saccular aneurysm).

ankiCards: A {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm is a localized spherical outpouching.
A {{c1::fusiform}} aneurysm is a circumferential dilation of a long segment.
Aneurysms are classified by {{c1::shape}} and size as either saccular or fusiform.
Both saccular and fusiform aneurysms can be {{c1::true}} aneurysms.
Vascular structure involves the intima, {{c1::media}}, and adventitia.
keyPoints: Classification of aneurysms is based on shape (saccular vs. fusiform).
Saccular: involves only a portion of the wall (bubble-like).
Fusiform: involves the entire circumference.
AAA are often fusiform.
Saccular aneurysms are common in the brain (berry) and can contain thrombus.
microReview: Shape matters for classification: Saccular (pouch) vs. Fusiform (spindle/circumferential). Both represent 'weakening of vessel walls' leading to dilation.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'fusiform' with 'dissection'. Dissection is a process (blood in wall), fusiform is a shape.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: ... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the development of atherosclerotic abdominal aortic aneurysms, the inflammatory response is characterized by the infiltration of several cell types. Which of the following cells is the primary source of the enzymes that degrade the elastic fibers of the aortic media?

explanations.a: Neutrophils are involved in acute inflammation, but the chronic remodeling of an aneurysm is driven by other cells.
explanations.b: Plasma cells are prominent in syphilitic aortitis, not the primary drivers of AAA ECM degradation.
explanations.c: In AAA, macrophages are recruited to the media and secrete matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), such as MMP-2 and MMP-9, which digest elastin and collagen.
explanations.d: NK cells are not the primary drivers of ECM remodeling in aneurysms.
explanations.e: Platelets are involved in thrombosis within the aneurysm but not the degradation of the media.

ankiCards: In AAA, {{c1::macrophages}} secrete MMPs that degrade the media.
The two most important MMPs in aneurysm pathogenesis are MMP-{{c1::2}} and MMP-{{c1::9}}.
ECM degradation in aneurysms targets {{c1::elastin}} and collagen.
Inflammation in the aortic wall is a key step in {{c1::aneurysm}} formation.
The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter is {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} in smaller muscular arteries.
keyPoints: Chronic inflammation is central to AAA pathogenesis.
Macrophages are the dominant inflammatory cell in the aneurysm wall.
MMP-2 and MMP-9 (gelatinases) are highly expressed.
Loss of elastin leads to the initial dilation; loss of collagen leads to rupture.
Atherosclerosis causes the intima to thicken, starving the media of oxygen.
microReview: AAA is an inflammatory disease. Macrophages produce MMPs which 'eat' the vessel wall's structural proteins. This happens in the abdominal aorta because it already has fewer vasa vasorum than the thoracic aorta, making it more vulnerable to ischemia when intimal plaques form.
examinerTraps: The examiner may try to swap 'MMPs' with 'TIMPs'. TIMPs (Tissue Inhibitors of Metalloproteinases) normally *prevent* aneurysms.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: ... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old male with a history of severe atherosclerosis presents with sudden, excruciating back pain and hypotension. On physical examination, he is diaphoretic, and a large, tender, pulsatile mass is felt in the abdomen. Which of the following is the most likely immediate complication causing this patient's clinical state?

options.a: Embolization of an atheromatous plaque to the kidneys
options.c: Occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery
options.d: Compression of the inferior vena cava

explanations.a: While atheroembolism can occur, it causes 'blue toe syndrome' or renal failure, not sudden hypotension and excruciating back pain.
explanations.b: This patient has the classic triad of a ruptured AAA: sudden severe pain, hypotension, and a pulsatile mass. Rupture typically occurs into the retroperitoneum or the peritoneal cavity.
explanations.c: Mesenteric ischemia causes abdominal pain, but not usually a tender pulsatile mass or sudden massive hypotension like a rupture.
explanations.d: Compression of the IVC can cause leg edema but not acute hypotension and back pain.
explanations.e: Aortocavitary fistulas occur in the heart (e.g., following endocarditis), not the abdominal aorta.

ankiCards: The classic triad of AAA rupture is {{c1::hypotension}}, {{c1::back/abdominal pain}}, and a {{c1::pulsatile mass}}.
Most AAA ruptures occur into the {{c1::retroperitoneum}}.
Mortality for a ruptured AAA is approximately {{c1::90}}%.
Aneurysms can also lead to {{c1::thrombosis}} due to stasis within the dilated segment.
Vascular pathology is responsible for more {{c1::morbidity}} and mortality than any other disease category.
keyPoints: Rupture is the most feared complication of AAA.
Rupture risk is proportional to the diameter of the aneurysm.
Symptoms of rupture include sudden pain and shock.
The abdominal aorta is the most common site for atherosclerotic aneurysms.
Mural thrombus often forms inside aneurysms due to turbulent flow.
microReview: When an AAA ruptures, it is a surgical emergency. The weakening of the vessel wall reaches a breaking point, and blood escapes. This most commonly happens when the aneurysm is >5cm in diameter.
examinerTraps: Atheroembolism vs. Rupture. Rupture = Shock/Pain. Embolism = Ischemia in distal organs (toes/kidneys).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: ... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the cardiovascular system, which vessel wall layer is primarily responsible for providing the structural strength and elasticity that is lost during aneurysm formation?

explanations.a: The intima is the innermost layer consisting of endothelium; it does not provide primary structural strength.
explanations.b: The internal elastic lamina separates the intima and media, but the bulk of the strength resides in the media itself.
explanations.c: The tunica media contains the smooth muscle cells and the extracellular matrix (elastin and collagen) required for vessel integrity. Its destruction is the hallmark of aneurysm formation.
explanations.d: The adventitia provides some support and contains nerves/vessels, but it is not the primary layer whose failure leads to the initial dilation in 'true' aneurysms.
explanations.e: The vasa vasorum are small vessels that supply the outer wall; their destruction causes medial damage, but they aren't the structural layer themselves.

ankiCards: The {{c1::tunica media}} is the vascular layer most affected in aneurysm formation.
Structural strength in the aorta is provided by {{c1::elastin}} and collagen in the media.
Loss of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} in the media contributes to wall weakening.
In smaller vessels, the ratio of {{c1::wall thickness}} to lumen diameter is higher.
Arterial walls are {{c1::thicker}} than corresponding veins.
keyPoints: The tunica media is the 'working' structural layer of the artery.
Aneurysms involve the degradation of the medial ECM.
Smooth muscle cell loss is a common feature in aneurysmal walls.
The media of the abdominal aorta is naturally thinner and has fewer vasa vasorum than the thoracic aorta.
Weakening of the media leads to dilation under physiological blood pressure.
microReview: Aneurysm = Medial Failure. Whether it's from MMPs (AAA), ischemia (Syphilis), or genetic defects (Marfan), the tunica media is the layer that gives way.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the *layer that fails* (media) with the *layer where the trigger is* (intima in atherosclerosis or adventitia in syphilis).
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with multiple firm, violaceous nodules on her right upper extremity. She has a history of a radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection and radiotherapy for breast adenocarcinoma 12 years ago. Since that time, she has suffered from persistent, non-pitting edema of the right arm. Biopsy of a nodule reveals a poorly differentiated malignancy with pleomorphic endothelial cells forming irregular vascular channels that express CD31. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and typically presents in immunocompromised patients; it does not specifically arise in the setting of chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy) is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome. It is an aggressive malignant tumor of endothelial cells.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign vascular proliferation caused by Bartonella infection in immunocompromised hosts, characterized by neutrophilic infiltrates.
explanations.d: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor, but the clinical history of chronic lymphedema and radiation strongly points to angiosarcoma.
explanations.e: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign lesions composed of large, blood-filled vascular spaces; they do not present as enlarging malignant nodules post-irradiation.

ankiCards: The development of angiosarcoma in a limb with chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
Vascular tumors that are poorly differentiated and express the marker {{c1::CD31}} are most likely angiosarcomas.
{{c1::Angiosarcoma}} is a malignant vascular tumor associated with prior radiation therapy.
Chronic lymphedema is a major risk factor for the development of {{c1::angiosarcoma}}.
Angiosarcomas of the liver are classically associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are highly malignant endothelial neoplasms.
Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to angiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphedema.
Common risk factors include radiation, lymphedema, and chemical carcinogens.
CD31 (PECAM-1) is a specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial differentiation.
These tumors have a poor prognosis due to early local invasion and metastasis.
microReview: Angiosarcoma = Malignant + CD31 positive + Radiation/Lymphedema history.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Stewart-Treves (angiosarcoma) with Kaposi Sarcoma (HHV-8); the context of mastectomy and lymphedema is the giveaway.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 35-year-old male with a history of untreated HIV infection presents with multiple reddish-purple macules and plaques on his lower extremities and oral mucosa. Histological examination of a skin biopsy reveals spindle-shaped cells, slit-like vascular spaces containing red blood cells, and a chronic inflammatory infiltrate. What is the primary etiologic agent responsible for this patient's condition?

explanations.a: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can look similar clinically but shows neutrophilic inflammation and is caused by bacteria, not a virus.
explanations.b: Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of all forms of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.c: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not vascular tumors.
explanations.d: HTLV-1 is associated with adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma.
explanations.e: CMV can cause opportunistic infections in HIV patients but does not cause Kaposi sarcoma.

ankiCards: The causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}.
Kaposi Sarcoma histology is characterized by {{c1::spindle}} cells and slit-like vascular spaces.
The four clinical forms of Kaposi Sarcoma are {{c1::Classic, Endemic, Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated}}.
Unlike bacillary angiomatosis, Kaposi Sarcoma usually lacks a {{c1::neutrophilic}} infiltrate.
The most common form of Kaposi Sarcoma in the United States is the {{c1::AIDS-associated}} type.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma is a low-grade malignant vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8.
Spindle cells are the hallmark histological finding.
HHV-8 encodes viral proteins that interfere with p53 and RB pathways.
Commonly involves the skin, but can also affect mucous membranes and viscera.
AIDS-associated KS is the most common HIV-associated malignancy.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = Spindle cells + Slit-like spaces + HHV-8 + HIV/AIDS.
examinerTraps: The examiner might offer Bartonella as an option; distinguish them by the inflammatory cell type (neutrophils in Bartonella vs. lymphocytes in KS).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 29-year-old female presents with an exquisitely painful, 4-mm, blue-red nodule located under the fingernail of her left index finger. The pain is triggered by cold exposure and pressure. If the lesion is excised, the tumor cells would most likely demonstrate differentiation toward which of the following?

explanations.a: While it is a vascular lesion, the specific cells of a glomus tumor are not simple endothelial cells but rather modified contractile cells.
explanations.b: Hemangiopericytomas arise from pericytes, but the subungual painful nodule is the classic presentation for a glomus tumor.
explanations.c: A glomus tumor (glomangioma) arises from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, which is a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.d: Skeletal muscle differentiation is characteristic of rhabdomyomas/rhabdomyosarcomas, not subungual painful nodules.
explanations.e: Fibroblastic tumors are not typically subungual and exquisitely sensitive to cold.

ankiCards: A painful subungual vascular tumor is most likely a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells.
The specialized thermoregulatory structure involved in glomus tumors is the {{c1::glomus body}}.
Clinical pain in glomus tumors is often triggered by {{c1::cold}}.
Glomus tumors are typically located in the {{c1::distal digits (fingertips/subungual)}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign, extremely painful neoplasms.
Classically found in the subungual region (under the nail).
Derived from glomus bodies (specialized thermoregulatory AV shunts).
Histology shows nests of uniform 'glomus cells' surrounding vascular channels.
Excision is curative.
microReview: Glomus Tumor = Subungual + Extreme Pain + Cold sensitivity + Smooth muscle origin.
examinerTraps: Thinking all vascular tumors are 'endothelial' in origin—glomus tumors are the exception, arising from the smooth muscle portion of the AV shunt.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An infant is born with a bright red, raised 'strawberry-like' lesion on the scalp. The lesion was not present at birth but appeared within the first week of life. It grew rapidly over the next three months but has recently remained stable. What is the most appropriate management strategy for this lesion based on its natural history?

explanations.a: Surgical excision is unnecessary as the vast majority of these lesions regress on their own.
explanations.b: Cryotherapy is generally not indicated for benign infantile hemangiomas.
explanations.c: Chemotherapy is used for malignancies, not benign capillary hemangiomas of childhood.
explanations.d: Infantile (strawberry) hemangiomas typically grow for several months and then begin to regress; 75-90% are completely gone by age 7.
explanations.e: Embolization is used for large arteriovenous malformations, not simple capillary hemangiomas.

ankiCards: The common 'strawberry hemangioma' of infancy is histologically a {{c1::capillary hemangioma}}.
Infantile hemangiomas usually undergo {{c1::spontaneous regression}} by age 7.
The clinical term for a capillary hemangioma that appears shortly after birth is a {{c1::strawberry}} hemangioma.
During the involution phase of a hemangioma, the vessels are replaced by {{c1::fibrous connective tissue}}.
Infantile hemangiomas occur in approximately {{c1::1 in 200}} live births.
keyPoints: Capillary hemangiomas are the most common type of vascular tumor.
Juvenile (infantile) type is very common in the skin of newborns.
They follow a predictable course: rapid growth followed by slow involution.
Histologically they are composed of thin-walled capillaries with scant stroma.
Management is almost always conservative (observation).
microReview: Strawberry Hemangioma = Newborn + Rapid growth + Spontaneous involution by school age.
examinerTraps: Don't jump to 'surgery' for a lesion that looks scary to parents; the hallmark of the strawberry hemangioma is its natural regression.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular lesions is characterized by a rapidly growing, pedunculated red nodule on the skin or gingival mucosa that bleeds easily and is histologically described as a lobular capillary hemangioma?

explanations.a: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a flat, permanent ectasia, not a pedunculated nodule.
explanations.b: Spider telangiectasias are small, non-palpable radial arrays of vessels, often associated with hyperestrogenic states.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (granuloma pyogenicum) is a misnomer; it is neither pyogenic nor a granuloma, but a lobular capillary hemangioma that often follows trauma or occurs during pregnancy (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, deep vascular channels and are not usually pedunculated or 'granuloma-like' on the surface.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis presents similarly but is infectious (Bartonella) and usually occurs in immunocompromised patients.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is histologically a {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
A pyogenic granuloma occurring in the gingiva of a pregnant woman is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Despite its name, pyogenic granuloma is not caused by {{c1::infection/pus (pyogenic)}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are known for their tendency to {{c1::bleed}} easily with minor trauma.
The treatment of choice for a pyogenic granuloma is {{c1::surgical excision/curettage}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granulomas are benign vascular polyps.
They frequently occur on the gingiva, fingers, or face.
They are associated with pregnancy and trauma.
Histology shows proliferating capillaries with interspersed edema and inflammatory cells.
They represent a form of exuberant granulation tissue.
microReview: Pyogenic Granuloma = Red nodule + Bleeds easily + Pregnancy/Trauma + Capillary proliferation.
examinerTraps: The name 'Pyogenic Granuloma' is a trap because it suggests an infection or a granulomatous process (like TB), but it is actually a vascular tumor.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 52-year-old male is undergoing an abdominal CT scan for suspected nephrolithiasis. The scan incidentally reveals a well-circumscribed, 3-cm hyperechoic mass in the right lobe of the liver. The patient is asymptomatic and has no history of liver disease. What is the most likely histological finding if this mass were to be biopsied?

options.a: Solid sheets of pleomorphic cells with high mitotic activity
options.b: Large, dilated vascular channels filled with blood and separated by connective tissue stroma
options.c: Small, thin-walled capillaries arranged in a lobular pattern
options.d: Slit-like spaces lined by spindle cells with HHV-8 positivity
options.e: Endothelial-lined spaces surrounded by concentric layers of glomus cells

explanations.a: This describes a malignancy, such as angiosarcoma, which would typically be symptomatic or have different imaging features.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are the most common benign tumors of the liver and consist of large, blood-filled vascular spaces.
explanations.c: This describes a capillary hemangioma, which is more common in the skin and less common as a large incidental liver mass in an adult.
explanations.d: This describes Kaposi sarcoma, which rarely presents as an isolated incidental liver mass in an asymptomatic patient.
explanations.e: This describes a glomus tumor, which is typically found in the distal extremities, not the liver.

ankiCards: The most common benign tumor of the liver is the {{c1::cavernous hemangioma}}.
Histologically, cavernous hemangiomas consist of {{c1::large, dilated}} vascular spaces.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas are usually {{c1::sharply defined/circumscribed}} but deep-seated.
A potential complication of very large cavernous hemangiomas in children is {{c1::Kasabach-Merritt syndrome (platelet sequestration)}}.
Vascular spaces in cavernous hemangiomas are separated by {{c1::connective tissue}} stroma.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, blood-filled spaces.
They are frequently incidental findings in the liver or CNS.
They do not regress spontaneously (unlike infantile capillary hemangiomas).
Clinical significance is usually related to potential rupture or pressure effects.
In the brain, they can cause seizures or focal neurological deficits.
microReview: Cavernous Hemangioma = Large spaces + Liver (most common benign tumor) + Connective tissue stroma.
examinerTraps: The incidental nature of the finding is key; most cavernous hemangiomas require no treatment.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old male with advanced AIDS (CD4 count 45 cells/mm³) presents with fever and multiple skin papules that resemble pyogenic granulomas. Biopsy shows a proliferation of small capillaries with prominent epithelioid endothelial cells and a dense neutrophilic infiltrate. Warthin-Starry silver stain reveals clusters of small bacilli. What is the most likely pathogen?

explanations.a: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, which lacks the neutrophilic infiltrate and bacterial clusters seen here.
explanations.b: Bartonella henselae (or B. quintana) causes bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised patients, characterized by vascular proliferation and neutrophilic inflammation.
explanations.c: MAC usually causes systemic symptoms and lymphadenopathy with granulomas, not vascular skin lesions.
explanations.d: S. aureus causes pyogenic infections (abscesses), not organized vascular tumors.
explanations.e: T. pallidum causes syphilis, which has different cutaneous manifestations (chancre, rash) and different silver stain morphologies.

ankiCards: {{c1::Bacillary angiomatosis}} is a vascular proliferation in HIV patients caused by Bartonella.
The histological hallmark of bacillary angiomatosis that distinguishes it from KS is a {{c1::neutrophilic}} infiltrate.
The silver stain used to visualize Bartonella bacilli is the {{c1::Warthin-Starry}} stain.
Bartonella henselae is typically transmitted to humans via {{c1::cats (cat scratch)}}.
Bartonella quintana is typically transmitted to humans via {{c1::human body lice}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis is an opportunistic infection in the immunocompromised.
It mimics Kaposi sarcoma clinically but is bacterial in origin.
The lesion is a reactive vascular proliferation, not a true neoplasm.
Histology shows 'epithelioid' endothelial cells and neutrophils.
Treatment involves antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin) rather than chemotherapy.
microReview: Bacillary Angiomatosis = HIV + Red papules + Neutrophils + Bartonella (Warthin-Starry +).
examinerTraps: Differentiating between KS and Bacillary Angiomatosis: KS = Spindle cells/Lymphocytes; Bacillary = Neutrophils/Silver stain positive bacilli.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes a vascular malformation that is present from birth, grows proportionately with the child, and is a characteristic component of Sturge-Weber syndrome when located in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve?

explanations.a: Spider telangiectasias are acquired and associated with high estrogen (e.g., cirrhosis), not congenital syndromes like Sturge-Weber.
explanations.b: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a congenital capillary malformation. When it involves the V1/V2 distribution of the trigeminal nerve, it is associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome.
explanations.c: Strawberry (infantile) hemangiomas are not typically present at birth and usually regress; port-wine stains are permanent.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are deeper and more mass-like, not a flat 'stain' or ectasia.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are small, painful nodules of the digits, not facial stains.

ankiCards: The clinical term for a permanent facial capillary malformation is {{c1::nevus flammeus (port-wine stain)}}.
Sturge-Weber syndrome involves a port-wine stain in the distribution of the {{c1::trigeminal (CN V)}} nerve.
Sturge-Weber syndrome is associated with vascular malformations of the {{c1::leptomeninges}}.
Unlike strawberry hemangiomas, port-wine stains {{c1::do not}} regress over time.
Common complications of Sturge-Weber syndrome include {{c1::seizures, mental retardation, and glaucoma}}.
keyPoints: Nevus flammeus is a form of vascular ectasia (dilation of pre-existing vessels).
Ordinary 'birthmarks' (e.g., 'salmon patch') usually fade; port-wine stains thicken and darken.
Sturge-Weber syndrome is also called encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis.
It is caused by a somatic mutation in the GNAQ gene.
The leptomeningeal angioma in Sturge-Weber can lead to calcifications ('tram-track' on CT).
microReview: Nevus Flammeus = Port-wine stain + Trigemincal distribution + Sturge-Weber + GNAQ mutation.
examinerTraps: The distinction between 'ectasia' (dilation) and 'neoplasia' (new growth). Port-wine stains are ectasias.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old male with a history of chronic arsenic exposure and previous work in a plastic manufacturing plant (vinyl chloride exposure) presents with weight loss, abdominal pain, and jaundice. Imaging shows several hemorrhagic masses within the liver. Which cell of origin is most likely for this patient's suspected malignancy?

explanations.a: Hepatocellular carcinoma is associated with HBV/HCV and cirrhosis, not specifically vinyl chloride.
explanations.b: Cholangiocarcinoma is associated with PSC and liver flukes.
explanations.c: Hepatic stellate (Ito) cells are involved in fibrosis, but do not give rise to this malignant vascular tumor.
explanations.d: The patient likely has hepatic angiosarcoma, a malignant tumor of the vascular endothelial cells associated with vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
explanations.e: Kupffer cells are hepatic macrophages and are not the origin of angiosarcomas.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast}}.
Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor of {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
The prognosis of hepatic angiosarcoma is very {{c1::poor}}.
The latency period between chemical exposure and development of hepatic angiosarcoma is usually {{c1::several decades}}.
On histology, angiosarcomas show cells that are {{c1::pleomorphic}} and form irregular channels.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are rare but highly lethal.
They exhibit aggressive local invasion and high rates of metastasis.
Liver angiosarcoma is a classic 'occupational' cancer example.
Environmental toxins (Arsenic, Vinyl Chloride) are specific risk factors.
CD31 staining confirms the endothelial origin.
microReview: Hepatic Angiosarcoma = Vinyl Chloride/Arsenic + Endothelial origin + CD31 positive + Poor prognosis.
examinerTraps: Vascular tumors of the liver: Benign = Cavernous hemangioma; Malignant = Angiosarcoma (look for toxin history).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu disease) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by malformations of capillaries and veins. What is a common and often presenting clinical symptom of this condition?

explanations.a: Claudication is a sign of arterial narrowing, not telangiectasia.
explanations.b: Osler-Weber-Rendu disease often presents with spontaneous epistaxis (nosebleeds) due to telangiectasias in the nasal mucosa.
explanations.c: Thrombophlebitis is inflammation/clotting of a vein, not a primary feature of HHT.
explanations.d: Raynaud phenomenon is a vasospastic disorder, not related to HHT malformations.
explanations.e: Painful subungual nodules describe glomus tumors.

ankiCards: Osler-Weber-Rendu disease is inherited in an {{c1::autosomal dominant}} pattern.
A frequent presenting symptom of Osler-Weber-Rendu is {{c1::epistaxis (nosebleeds)}}.
Telangiectasias in HHT are commonly found on the {{c1::skin, mucous membranes (lips/tongue), and GI tract}}.
A dangerous complication of HHT is the development of {{c1::arteriovenous malformations (AVMs)}} in the lungs or brain.
The primary defect in HHT involves the {{c1::TGF-beta}} signaling pathway.
keyPoints: HHT is a systemic vascular dysplasia.
Clinical triad: Telangiectasias, recurrent epistaxis, and family history.
Lesions consist of dilated capillaries and veins (ectasias).
Internal AVMs can lead to shunting and high-output heart failure.
Risk of paradoxical emboli or brain abscesses due to pulmonary AVMs.
microReview: Osler-Weber-Rendu = Autosomal Dominant + Epistaxis + Telangiectasias (lips/tongue) + AVMs.
examinerTraps: Be aware that these patients can present with iron deficiency anemia due to chronic GI bleeding from telangiectasias.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old female presents with multiple, enlarging, ill-defined violaceous nodules and plaques on her left upper extremity. She has a history of a radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection and radiotherapy for breast cancer 12 years ago. Since the surgery, she has had persistent, severe lymphedema of the left arm. A biopsy of one of the nodules reveals atypical spindle cells forming slit-like vascular spaces. Which of the following markers would most likely be positive in the neoplastic cells?

explanations.a: Desmin is a marker for myogenic differentiation; it would not be the primary marker for a tumor of endothelial origin.
explanations.b: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a highly specific marker for endothelial cells and is used to confirm the diagnosis of vascular tumors like angiosarcoma, which this patient has (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
explanations.c: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells, such as melanocytes or Schwann cells, not vascular endothelium.
explanations.d: Cytokeratin 7 is a marker for epithelial cells and would be used to identify metastatic breast carcinoma, but the morphology described (slit-like vascular spaces) points to a vascular origin.
explanations.e: HMB-45 is a marker for melanocytic differentiation and would be positive in melanoma, not angiosarcoma.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma following chronic lymphedema is known as {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
The most specific immunohistochemical marker for vascular endothelial tumors is {{c1::CD31}}.
Angiosarcomas are often associated with prior exposure to {{c1::radiation}} or certain chemicals like vinyl chloride.
Microscopic appearance of angiosarcoma typically shows {{c1::atypical endothelial cells}} forming irregular vascular channels.
Classic history for Stewart-Treves syndrome involves a post-mastectomy patient with {{c1::chronic lymphedema}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms.
Stewart-Treves syndrome refers specifically to angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema.
The tumor presents as enlarging cutaneous nodules, often starting as bruise-like lesions.
Endothelial markers include CD31 and von Willebrand factor (vWF).
These tumors are highly aggressive and carry a poor prognosis.
microReview: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignancy of endothelial cells. In the clinical context of chronic lymphedema (post-lymphadenectomy), it is called Stewart-Treves syndrome. Key markers are CD31 and vWF. Distinguish from Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8) and metastatic carcinoma.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Stewart-Treves with recurrent breast cancer; the morphology of vascular slits and the specific endothelial marker CD31 differentiate them.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors are divided into three categories: (1) benign (e.g., hemangiomas), which are common and usually cured by excision; (2) intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors (e.g., Kaposi sarcoma), which are locally aggressive but have low metastatic potential; and (3) malignant tumors (e.g., angiosarcomas).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An HIV-positive patient presents with several dark-purple, non-blanching macules on the lower extremities and hard palate. Histological examination reveals sheets of spindle cells, slit-like spaces containing erythrocytes, and a prominent inflammatory infiltrate. The pathogenesis of this condition is most strongly linked to which of the following mechanisms?

options.b: Inactivation of the VHL tumor suppressor gene
options.c: Dysregulation of cytokine production by HHV-8
options.d: Somatic mutation in the GNAQ gene
options.e: Exposure to thorium dioxide contrast media

explanations.a: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can mimic Kaposi sarcoma clinically, but the mechanism is bacterial infection, not viral oncogenesis.
explanations.b: VHL mutations are associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease and hemangioblastomas, not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.c: Kaposi Sarcoma is caused by Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), which encodes proteins that interfere with cell cycle control and promote angiogenesis through cytokine dysregulation.
explanations.d: GNAQ mutations are typically found in Sturge-Weber syndrome and port-wine stains, not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.e: Thorotrast (thorium dioxide) is a historical risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma, not cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma.

ankiCards: The causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::HHV-8}} (KSHV).
Kaposi Sarcoma is histologically characterized by {{c1::spindle cells}} and slit-like vascular spaces containing {{c2::red blood cells}}.
The most common site of visceral involvement in AIDS-associated Kaposi Sarcoma is the {{c1::gastrointestinal tract}}.
In contrast to bacillary angiomatosis, Kaposi Sarcoma usually lacks a prominent {{c1::neutrophilic}} infiltrate.
The four clinical forms of Kaposi Sarcoma are {{c1::Classic, Endemic African, Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated}}.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
HHV-8 is the essential cofactor in all forms of KS.
KS cells are thought to be of lymphatic endothelial origin.
The 'slit-like' spaces are diagnostic hallmarks.
AIDS-associated KS is the most common HIV-related malignancy.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma: HHV-8+, spindle cells, RBCs in slits. Bacillary Angiomatosis: Bartonella+, neutrophils, clusters of bacteria (Warthin-Starry stain). Both appear in HIV patients.
examinerTraps: The examiner may provide a description of bacillary angiomatosis (neutrophils present) to distract from Kaposi sarcoma (lymphocytes/plasma cells present). Look for HHV-8 as the primary driver.
sourceQuote: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV8) and is highly associated with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old female presents with an exquisitely painful, 4-mm, firm, red-blue nodule located under the nail bed of her right index finger.
