microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = HIV/Immunosuppression + Purple plaques + Spindle cells + HHV-8.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Kaposi Sarcoma with Bacillary Angiomatosis; look for 'spindle cells' for KS versus 'neutrophils and silver-staining bacteria' for Bartonella.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with an exquisitely painful, small, firm, blue-tinged nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. She notes that the pain is often triggered by exposure to cold temperatures. The tumor is thought to arise from the specialized neuromyoarterial apparatus involved in thermoregulation. These cells are most likely derived from which of the following?

explanations.a: The glomus tumor (glomangioma) arises from the glomus body, a specialized thermoregulatory organ. The neoplastic cells (glomus cells) are modified smooth muscle cells.
explanations.b: Endothelial cells line the vascular spaces within the tumor, but the 'glomus cells' themselves—which comprise the bulk of the tumor—are smooth muscle derivatives.
explanations.c: Schwann cells are the origin of nerve sheath tumors (schwannomas), which can be painful but do not typically present as subungual vascular nodules.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts are responsible for collagen production; they are not the specific cells of origin for the glomus tumor.
explanations.e: While pericytes are related to the vasculature (e.g., in hemangiopericytomas), the glomus cells specifically are modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.

ankiCards: A small, blue, exquisitely painful subungual tumor is likely a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
Glomus tumors arise from the {{c1::glomus body}}, which is involved in {{c2::thermoregulation}}.
The cell of origin for a glomus tumor is the {{c1::modified smooth muscle cell}}.
A classic clinical trigger for glomus tumor pain is {{c1::cold exposure}}.
Unlike hemangiomas, glomus tumors are typically {{c1::very painful}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but extremely painful.
Typical location: distal portion of digits, especially under the fingernails.
Histology: nests of uniform, round, 'monotonous' glomus cells surrounding vascular channels.
Origin: modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus apparatus.
Clinical triad: paroxysmal pain, localized tenderness, and cold hypersensitivity.
microReview: Glomus tumor = Subungual + Extreme Pain + Cold sensitivity + Smooth muscle origin.
examinerTraps: Examiners often contrast the 'exquisite pain' of a glomus tumor with the 'painless' nature of most other vascular tumors like hemangiomas.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with several firm, violaceous nodules on her left arm. She has a history of a radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection and radiotherapy for breast cancer 12 years ago. Since that time, she has had persistent, severe lymphedema of the left upper extremity. A biopsy of one of the nodules shows malignant endothelial cells forming irregular, anastomosing vascular channels. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: This patient has Stewart-Treves syndrome, where chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy) predisposes to the development of cutaneous angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and typically occurs in HIV patients or specific elderly populations, not usually as a complication of chronic lymphedema.
explanations.c: Hemangioendothelioma is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor, but the clinical context of chronic lymphedema and malignant features points specifically to angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: Lymphangiomas are benign malformations of lymphatic vessels, usually congenital, not aggressive nodules appearing after cancer treatment.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation in immunocompromised patients caused by Bartonella species.

ankiCards: Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to {{c1::angiosarcoma}} arising in the setting of {{c2::chronic lymphedema}}.
The classic clinical scenario for Stewart-Treves is a patient post-{{c1::mastectomy}} with axillary dissection.
Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor of {{c1::endothelial cells}}.
Vascular markers used to identify angiosarcoma include {{c1::CD31}} and {{c2::von Willebrand factor (vWF)}}.
Risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma include exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}, {{c2::arsenic}}, and {{c3::Thorotrast}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a highly aggressive malignant vascular tumor.
In the skin, it can be associated with radiation or chronic lymphedema.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is linked to specific chemical carcinogens.
Histology shows poorly formed, anastomosing vascular channels with cytologic atypia.
The 5-year survival rate is generally poor due to early metastasis.
microReview: Post-mastectomy lymphedema + Purple skin nodules = Stewart-Treves (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: Do not mistake the purple nodules of angiosarcoma for simple bruising or recurrence of the breast carcinoma; the specific link to lymphedema is the key diagnostic clue.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An infant is born with a bright red, slightly raised 'strawberry' lesion on the scalp. The parents are concerned as the lesion grows rapidly over the first few months of life. However, the pediatrician reassures them that the lesion is likely to undergo spontaneous regression. This lesion is most accurately classified as which of the following?

explanations.a: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma is extremely common in infants, grows rapidly for a few months, and usually involutes by age 7.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated vascular channels and are often deeper and less likely to spontaneously regress than the capillary-sized vessels of the juvenile type.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a rapidly growing red nodule that often bleeds and is frequently associated with trauma or pregnancy; it does not usually regress spontaneously.
explanations.d: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a flat, permanent vascular malformation that does not regress and grows proportionately with the child.
explanations.e: Spider telangiectasias are small, central arterioles with radiating capillaries, often associated with hyperestrogenic states (e.g., cirrhosis), not infant birthmarks.

ankiCards: The common name for a juvenile hemangioma is a {{c1::strawberry}} hemangioma.
Juvenile hemangiomas typically {{c1::regress/involute}} spontaneously by age 7.
Histologically, juvenile hemangiomas are a form of {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma.
Unlike a port-wine stain, a strawberry hemangioma is {{c1::raised/elevated}}.
{{c1::Nevus flammeus}} is the medical term for a 'port-wine stain'.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangiomas are the most common vascular tumors of infancy.
They occur in 1 in 200 live births.
Phases: Rapid proliferation followed by slow involution.
Complete regression occurs in 90% of cases by age 7.
No treatment is usually required unless they obstruct vision or the airway.
microReview: Infant + Strawberry lesion + Rapid growth then regression = Juvenile Hemangioma.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'Strawberry hemangioma' (regresses) with 'Port-wine stain' (permanent).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 42-year-old male with poorly controlled HIV presents with multiple red, friable, dome-shaped skin papules and fever. A skin biopsy shows a lobular proliferation of capillaries lined by protuberant epithelioid endothelial cells, accompanied by a prominent neutrophilic infiltrate and granular purple material. Warthin-Starry silver stain reveals clusters of bacilli. What is the most likely pathogen responsible for these lesions?

explanations.a: Bartonella quintana (and B. henselae) causes bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised hosts, characterized by vascular proliferation and a neutrophilic infiltrate.
explanations.b: HHV-8 causes Kaposi Sarcoma, which has a spindle-cell morphology and lacks the prominent neutrophilic infiltrate and silver-staining bacilli found in bacillary angiomatosis.
explanations.c: S. aureus causes pyogenic infections (abscesses, impetigo) but not organized, lobular vascular tumors.
explanations.d: M. leprae causes leprosy, characterized by granulomatous inflammation and nerve involvement, not acute vascular proliferation.
explanations.e: T. pallidum causes syphilis; while it involves vessels (endarteritis obliterans), it does not present as these specific angiomatous papules.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by bacteria of the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
In bacillary angiomatosis, the inflammatory infiltrate is predominantly composed of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
The stain used to visualize the causative organisms in bacillary angiomatosis is the {{c1::Warthin-Starry (silver)}} stain.
Unlike Kaposi Sarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis is treated with {{c1::antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin/doxycycline)}}.
Bartonella quintana is often transmitted by {{c1::human body lice}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis occurs primarily in immunocompromised (AIDS) patients.
It can involve skin, bone, or visceral organs.
Histology: Proliferation of capillaries with 'epithelioid' endothelial cells.
Key diagnostic feature: Clusters of Tangled bacilli on silver stain.
Clinical mimic: Kaposi Sarcoma (but KS is viral and treated differently).
microReview: AIDS + Red papules + Neutrophils + Silver-staining bacilli = Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella).
examinerTraps: The presence of 'neutrophils' is the histological smoking gun that differentiates Bacillary Angiomatosis from Kaposi Sarcoma (which is usually paucicellular or has lymphocytes).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old male who formerly worked in a factory manufacturing polyvinyl chloride (PVC) pipes for 20 years presents with weight loss, abdominal pain, and jaundice. Imaging shows multiple ill-defined masses in the liver. A liver biopsy demonstrates highly atypical spindle cells lining irregular, blood-filled spaces that appear to be 'tagging' onto the pre-existing hepatic sinusoids. Which immunohistochemical marker would most likely be positive in these malignant cells?

explanations.a: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a specific marker for endothelial cells. Since this patient likely has hepatic angiosarcoma (linked to PVC exposure), the malignant cells will express endothelial markers.
explanations.b: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells (e.g., carcinomas), not vascular/endothelial tumors.
explanations.c: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (skeletal or smooth), not endothelial cells.
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells (melanoma, schwannoma) and chondrocytes.
explanations.e: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is a marker for hepatocellular carcinoma, but the histology (vascular spaces/spindle cells) and PVC exposure point to angiosarcoma.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is classically associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
{{c1::CD31}} is a reliable immunohistochemical marker for endothelial differentiation.
Exposure to the radioactive contrast agent {{c1::Thorotrast}} increases the risk of hepatic angiosarcoma.
The prognosis for hepatic angiosarcoma is generally {{c1::very poor}}.
Angiosarcoma cells may show a '{{c1::sinusoidal growth pattern}}' in the liver.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a malignant neoplasm of endothelial cells.
Risk factors: Arsenic (pesticides), Thorotrast, Vinyl chloride (PVC).
IHC markers: CD31, vWF (von Willebrand factor), and CD34.
Clinical presentation: Often advanced at diagnosis with hepatomegaly and jaundice.
Morphology ranges from well-differentiated vascular channels to solid undifferentiated sheets.
microReview: PVC/Arsenic/Thorotrast + Liver vascular tumor + CD31+ = Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: A common trap is to offer Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). While PVC exposure can increase liver cancer risk, the specific 'vascular' and 'spindle cell' description strongly mandates choosing Angiosarcoma over Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 19-year-old female presents with recurrent, heavy nosebleeds (epistaxis) and several small, red, blanching spots on her lips, tongue, and fingertips. Her father and paternal grandmother had similar symptoms. This patient is at significantly increased risk for which of the following complications due to her underlying condition?

explanations.a: This is Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia). It is characterized by telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations (AVMs), which commonly occur in the lungs, brain, and liver.
explanations.b: Aortic dissection is associated with Marfan syndrome or hypertension, not Osler-Weber-Rendu.
explanations.c: Atherosclerosis is a common vascular disease but is not the primary clinical concern in Osler-Weber-Rendu.
explanations.d: Giant cell arteritis is an inflammatory vasculitis of large vessels, typically in patients over 50.
explanations.e: Coarctation of the aorta is a congenital narrowing of the aorta, often associated with Turner syndrome.

ankiCards: The other name for Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia is {{c1::Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome}}.
Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome is inherited in an {{c1::autosomal dominant}} pattern.
Common clinical manifestations of HHT include {{c1::epistaxis}} and {{c2::skin telangiectasias}}.
Patients with HHT are at risk for {{c1::arteriovenous malformations (AVMs)}} in internal organs.
AVMs in the lung can cause {{c1::hypoxemia/right-to-left shunts}} or brain abscesses.
keyPoints: HHT is an autosomal dominant disorder causing malformed dilated capillaries.
Classic presentation: Epistaxis + cutaneous/mucosal telangiectasias.
Pathogenesis: Mutations in genes involved in TGF-beta signaling.
Telangiectasias are found on skin and mucous membranes of the mouth and GI tract.
Major risk: Serious hemorrhage or AVM complications (stroke, high-output heart failure).
microReview: Epistaxis + Family history + Red spots on lips = Osler-Weber-Rendu (HHT) -> Risk of AVMs.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'telangiectasia' with 'hemangioma'. Telangiectasias are permanent dilations of pre-existing small vessels, not new tumor growths.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 2-year-old girl is evaluated for a large, soft, fluctuant mass on the left side of her neck that has been present since birth. The mass transilluminates on physical exam. Imaging confirms a multi-loculated cystic lesion. Which of the following chromosomal abnormalities is most commonly associated with this specific finding?

explanations.a: The description (neck mass, cystic, transilluminates) is classic for a cystic hygroma (a type of cavernous lymphangioma), which is frequently associated with Turner syndrome (45,X).
explanations.b: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is associated with endocardial cushion defects and duodenal atresia, but not specifically cystic hygroma.
explanations.c: Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome) features rocker-bottom feet and micrognathia, but cystic hygroma is more characteristically 'Turner'.
explanations.d: 47,XXY (Klinefelter syndrome) causes testicular atrophy and tall stature, not congenital cystic neck masses.
explanations.e: Deletion 22q11 (DiGeorge syndrome) is associated with thymic hypoplasia and cardiac outflow tract defects.

ankiCards: A cystic lymphangioma found in the neck of a child is called a {{c1::cystic hygroma}}.
Cystic hygromas are most commonly associated with {{c1::Turner syndrome}}.
The presence of a cystic hygroma in a fetus may be detected on ultrasound as {{c1::increased nuchal translucency}}.
Histologically, lymphangiomas are composed of endothelium-lined spaces that lack {{c1::red blood cells}}.
Lymphangiomas contain proteinaceous fluid and often {{c1::lymphocytes}}.
keyPoints: Lymphangiomas are the lymphatic equivalent of hemangiomas.
Simple (capillary) lymphangiomas are small; cavernous (cystic) lymphangiomas are large.
Cystic hygromas occur in the neck or axilla of children.
They are not clearly demarcated and can be difficult to resect completely.
Associated with Turner Syndrome (45,X) and various trisomies.
microReview: Cystic neck mass + Child + Transilluminates = Cystic Hygroma -> Turner Syndrome.
examinerTraps: Wait for the 'transilluminates' clue—this helps distinguish a cystic vascular lesion from a solid tumor like a neuroblastoma or lymphoma.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 29-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy develops a rapidly growing, 1-cm, red, pedunculated mass on her gingiva (gums). It bleeds easily with minor trauma. The lesion is excised, and pathology reveals a circumscribed proliferation of capillaries arranged in lobules with surrounding edema. This lesion is most accurately described as which of the following?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) often occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum). It is a benign, reactive vascular lesion.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of larger vascular spaces and are typically deeper, not pedunculated bleeding nodules on the gingiva.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a malignant, highly atypical tumor; the description of a lobular, circumscribed proliferation in a pregnant woman is far more consistent with a benign pyogenic granuloma.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are small, painful, subungual nodules, not large gingival masses.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is associated with Bartonella in HIV patients, not pregnancy-related gingival growth.

ankiCards: A {{c1::pyogenic granuloma}} is a common vascular lesion on the skin or gingiva that bleeds easily.
The 'granuloma gravidarum' is a pyogenic granuloma occurring during {{c1::pregnancy}}.
Despite its name, a pyogenic granuloma is not {{c1::infectious/purulent}} and is not a true {{c2::granuloma}}.
Histologically, pyogenic granuloma is a form of {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are often associated with a history of {{c1::trauma}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is neither pyogenic (pus-producing) nor a granuloma.
It presents as a rapidly growing, red, ulcerated polyp.
High frequency of occurrence in the oral mucosa of pregnant women.
Spontaneous regression can occur after delivery, but surgical excision is often needed.
The microscopic appearance is very similar to exuberant granulation tissue.
microReview: Pregnant + Gingival mass + Bleeds easily = Pyogenic Granuloma (Granuloma Gravidarum).
examinerTraps: The name is the trap. If the examiner asks 'What characterizes this lesion?', the answer is 'Capillary proliferation'—not 'Granulomatous inflammation' or 'Suppurative infection'.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with a large, flat, purple-red area on the left side of his face following the distribution of the trigeminal nerve. His parents report that he has recently had two generalized tonic-clonic seizures. An MRI of the brain reveals an ipsilateral leptomeningeal angioma. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) is characterized by a facial port-wine stain (nevus flammeus), seizures, and leptomeningeal angiomas.
explanations.b: Von Hippel-Lindau is associated with hemangioblastomas (cerebellum/retina), renal cell carcinoma, and pheochromocytoma, but not facial port-wine stains.
explanations.c: Osler-Weber-Rendu involves multiple telangiectasias and epistaxis, not large facial port-wine stains or leptomeningeal angiomas.
explanations.d: Maffucci syndrome involves multiple hemangiomas and enchondromas.
explanations.e: Kasabach-Merritt syndrome involves a large hemangioma that sequesters platelets, leading to consumptive coagulopathy.

ankiCards: The combination of a facial port-wine stain and leptomeningeal angiomatosis is called {{c1::Sturge-Weber syndrome}}.
In Sturge-Weber, the facial port-wine stain typically follows the distribution of the {{c1::trigeminal (CN V)}} nerve.
A common neurological symptom of Sturge-Weber syndrome is {{c1::seizures}}.
A {{c1::nevus flammeus}} is the medical term for a port-wine stain.
Unlike a strawberry hemangioma, a nevus flammeus does not {{c1::regress}}.
keyPoints: Sturge-Weber syndrome is a sporadic phakomatosis.
Clinical features: Port-wine stain, glaucoma, seizures, and intellectual disability.
The port-wine stain is usually in the V1/V2 distribution of the trigeminal nerve.
Leptomeningeal angiomas can cause 'tram-track' calcifications on imaging.
Nevus flammeus consists of dilated vessels in the dermis.
microReview: Port-wine stain (V1/V2) + Seizures + Brain angioma = Sturge-Weber.
examinerTraps: Ensure you distinguish this from 'Strawberry Hemangioma'. Sturge-Weber's 'Port-wine stain' is flat and permanent, whereas 'Strawberry' is raised and regresses.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old female presents with multiple, poorly defined, purplish-red skin plaques on her left upper extremity. She has a history of a radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection and radiotherapy for breast adenocarcinoma ten years ago. Since the surgery, she has had persistent lymphedema of the left arm. A skin biopsy of a plaque shows malignant spindle cells forming irregular, anastomosing vascular channels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8, typically presenting as multiple purple skin plaques in immunocompromised patients, but not specifically associated with chronic lymphedema or post-radiation sites.
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma is a malignant vascular tumor. The presentation of a tumor in a limb with chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy) is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome. It can also be induced by prior radiation.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign vascular proliferation in immunocompromised patients caused by Bartonella species, characterized by neutrophilic infiltrates and clusters of bacteria.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign, rapidly growing capillary hemangioma that often presents as a pedunculated red nodule on the skin or gingiva, not associated with chronic lymphedema.
explanations.e: Glomus tumor is a benign, exquisitely painful tumor arising from the glomus bodies, usually found subungually (under the fingernails).

ankiCards: The development of angiosarcoma in the setting of chronic lymphedema (e.g., post-mastectomy) is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves}} syndrome.
Angiosarcoma is a malignant neoplasm derived from {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
Classic risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma include {{c1::arsenic}}, Thorotrast, and polyvinyl chloride (PVC).
Malignant vascular tumors that form irregular, anastomosing channels are characteristic of {{c1::angiosarcoma}}.
Angiosarcomas often occur in the setting of previous exposure to {{c1::ionizing radiation}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignant vascular tumor with a poor prognosis.
Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to angiosarcoma arising in the context of chronic lymphedema.
Radiation therapy is a known risk factor for cutaneous angiosarcoma.
Histologically, they show malignant endothelial cells and anastomosing vascular channels.
They can occur in any site but most commonly involve skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
microReview: Vascular tumors are categorized as benign (hemangiomas), intermediate (Kaposi sarcoma, hemangioendothelioma), and malignant (angiosarcoma). Angiosarcomas are aggressive and associated with radiation or chronic lymphedema.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Kaposi Sarcoma with Angiosarcoma. While both have spindle cells and vascular channels, Kaposi is HHV-8 related, while Angiosarcoma in a post-mastectomy patient is Stewart-Treves syndrome.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors... Malignant Tumors... Angiosarcoma is a malignant vascular tumor... Although most commonly in the skin, soft tissues, breast, and liver.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following immunohistochemical markers is the most specific for identifying the endothelial origin of a poorly differentiated vascular neoplasm?

explanations.a: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells and carcinomas.
explanations.b: Vimentin is a non-specific marker for mesenchymal cells and is present in many tumors.
explanations.c: CD31 (Platelet Endothelial Cell Adhesion Molecule, PECAM-1) is highly specific for endothelial cells and is used to confirm the vascular nature of a tumor.
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells, melanocytes, and Schwann cells.
explanations.e: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (both smooth and skeletal).

ankiCards: The most specific vascular endothelial marker used in immunohistochemistry is {{c1::CD31}}.
Besides CD31, another marker for endothelial cells is {{c1::von Willebrand factor}} (or Factor VIII).
Endothelial cells line the interior of {{c1::blood}} and lymphatic vessels.
Vimentin is a marker for {{c1::mesenchymal}} cells but is not specific to endothelium.
In poorly differentiated angiosarcomas, {{c1::CD31}} helps distinguish them from other spindle cell sarcomas.
keyPoints: CD31 is the gold standard immunohistochemical marker for endothelial differentiation.
Vascular tumors derive from endothelial cells (blood or lymphatic).
Marker identification is crucial in poorly differentiated malignancies.
CD34 and Factor VIII are also used but CD31 is generally preferred for specificity.
Angiosarcomas may resemble carcinomas but will be CD31 positive and Cytokeratin negative.
microReview: Endothelial markers: CD31 (PECAM-1), CD34, von Willebrand Factor. Epithelial: Cytokeratin. Muscle: Desmin/Actin. Neural: S100.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'most specific'—while CD34 is common in vascular tumors, it is also expressed in many other mesenchymal tumors, making CD31 the more specific choice for endothelium.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors... Endothelial cells can be identified by the presence of von Willebrand factor or CD31.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old male with a history of advanced HIV (CD4 count 85/mm³) presents with multiple raised, red-to-purple, non-blanching papules on his legs and trunk. Biopsy reveals a proliferation of spindle-shaped cells, extravasated red blood cells, and slit-like vascular spaces. Which of the following infectious agents is the primary driver of this pathology?

explanations.a: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which looks similar but histologically shows neutrophilic inflammation and bacteria, not spindle cells and slit-like spaces.
explanations.b: Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma, which presents with spindle cells and slit-like vascular spaces.
explanations.c: HIV is the underlying cause of the immunosuppression but is not the direct transforming agent of the vascular cells in Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.d: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not vascular tumors.
explanations.e: CMV causes opportunistic infections in AIDS (retinitis, colitis) but not vascular neoplasms.

ankiCards: The virus associated with all forms of Kaposi sarcoma is {{c1::HHV-8}}.
Histologically, Kaposi sarcoma is characterized by {{c1::spindle}} cells and slit-like spaces containing RBCs.
The most common form of Kaposi sarcoma in the US is the {{c1::AIDS-associated}} (epidemic) form.
Kaposi sarcoma is classified as an {{c1::intermediate}} grade (borderline) vascular tumor.
The presence of extravasated {{c1::red blood cells}} and hemosiderin is a common histological finding in Kaposi sarcoma.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is an HHV-8 mediated neoplasm.
It is most common in AIDS patients (epidemic KS).
Histology: Proliferating spindle cells, slit-like spaces, and extravasated RBCs.
Treatment in HIV patients often involves starting antiretroviral therapy (ART).
The lesions are typically multifocal and can involve the skin, viscera, and mucous membranes.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = Spindle cells + Slit-like spaces + HHV-8. Bacillary Angiomatosis = Neutrophils + Bartonella + Capillary proliferation.
examinerTraps: Do not choose Bartonella just because the patient has HIV; the key differentiator is the histology (spindle cells vs. neutrophils).
sourceQuote: Kaposi Sarcoma... HHV-8 is the etiologic agent... lesions are characterized by a proliferation of spindle cells... creating slit-like spaces.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with an exquisitely painful, small (4 mm), blue-red nodule located under the nail of her right index finger. The pain is particularly severe when the finger is exposed to cold. A biopsy shows a cluster of specialized smooth muscle cells surrounding vascular channels. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are painless and common in skin/mucous membranes, but not specifically subungual or cold-sensitive.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, blood-filled spaces and are typically deeper and painless.
explanations.c: Glomus tumor (glomangioma) is a benign, very painful tumor arising from the glomus body. Its classic location is subungual, and it is sensitive to cold/touch.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a large, aggressive malignancy, not a small, localized subungual painful nodule.
explanations.e: Epithelioid hemangiendothelioma is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor that typically occurs around medium-to-large veins, not subungually.

ankiCards: A glomus tumor arises from the specialized smooth muscle cells of the {{c1::glomus body}}.
The classic clinical triad for a glomus tumor is {{c1::pain}}, sensitivity to cold, and localized tenderness.
The most common location for a glomus tumor is the {{c1::subungual}} (under the nail) region.
Histologically, glomus tumors consist of nests of uniform {{c1::glomus}} cells surrounding vascular channels.
Glomus tumors are {{c1::benign}} (benign/malignant) neoplasms.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are exquisitely painful benign lesions.
They arise from cells involved in thermoregulation (glomus bodies).
Characteristic subungual location.
Histology: Uniform glomus cells (modified smooth muscle) in rows/clusters.
Excision is curative.
microReview: Glomus tumor: Subungual, painful, cold-sensitive, modified smooth muscle cells.
examinerTraps: Commonly confused with subungual melanoma; however, melanoma is usually painless and pigment-based, while glomus tumor is vascular and painful.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Glomus tumor (glomangioma) is a benign but exquisitely painful tumor arising from specialized smooth muscle cells... most commonly in the distal portion of the digits, especially under the fingernails.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 2-week-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for a rapidly growing, bright red, 'strawberry-like' birthmark on the face. The lesion is soft and elevated. The mother is concerned about its growth. Which of the following is the most likely clinical course for this lesion?

explanations.a: Juvenile hemangiomas are benign and do not progress to malignancy.
explanations.b: This describes a 'port-wine stain' (nevus flammeus), not a strawberry hemangioma.
explanations.c: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas typically grow rapidly for a few months and then spontaneously involute (regress) by age 7 to 9 in most cases.
explanations.d: Surgery is avoided because of the high rate of spontaneous regression.
explanations.e: These are superficial and do not typically invade bone.

ankiCards: The common name for a juvenile hemangioma is a {{c1::strawberry}} hemangioma.
Juvenile hemangiomas are typically present at birth or appear within {{c1::weeks}} of life.
The vast majority of juvenile hemangiomas {{c1::regress}} (regress/persist) by early childhood.
Histologically, juvenile hemangiomas are classified as {{c1::capillary}} hemangiomas.
Approximately 75% to 90% of juvenile hemangiomas have regressed by age {{c1::7}}.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangiomas are the most common vascular tumor of infancy.
They are classified as capillary hemangiomas.
Growth is rapid initially, followed by a plateau.
Spontaneous involution is the hallmark clinical feature.
They are entirely benign.
microReview: Juvenile (Strawberry) Hemangioma: Newborns, grows fast then goes away (regression by age 7). Capillary-sized vessels.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse this with a 'Port-wine stain' (Nevus flammeus). Port-wine stains grow with the child and do not regress.
sourceQuote: Juvenile hemangioma (strawberry hemangioma) of the skin of newborns is very common... They grow rapidly for a few months but then spontaneously involute.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 25-year-old pregnant woman in her third trimester presents with a rapidly growing, painless, 1 cm red nodule on her gingiva. The lesion bleeds easily with minor trauma. Histologic examination shows a polypoid proliferation of capillaries with prominent edema and acute and chronic inflammation. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas involve large vascular spaces and are not typically polypoid gingival masses in pregnancy.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granuloma (granuloma pyogenicum) is a rapidly growing capillary hemangioma that often occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women (epulis gravidarum).
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a malignant, aggressive tumor and would not present as a classic 'pregnancy tumor' of the gingiva.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is associated with HIV and Bartonella infection.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are found under the nails and are painful; this lesion is painless and gingival.

ankiCards: A pyogenic granuloma occurring on the gingiva during pregnancy is called {{c1::epulis gravidarum}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are histologically a form of {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma.
Despite its name, a pyogenic granuloma is not {{c1::infectious}} or a true granuloma.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized by a {{c1::polypoid}} (shape) appearance.
Treatment for a pyogenic granuloma usually involves {{c1::surgical excision}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign vascular lesion.
Commonly occurs on skin or gingival mucosa.
Often triggered by trauma or pregnancy (hormonal influence).
Histology: Lobular capillary proliferation with inflammation and edema.
Often bleeds easily because of high vascularity.
microReview: Pyogenic granuloma: Pregnancy, gingiva, bleeds easily, capillary hemangioma subtype.
examinerTraps: The name is a misnomer; it is neither pyogenic (pus-forming) nor a granuloma. It is a vascular tumor.
sourceQuote: Pyogenic granuloma... present as rapidly growing red, pedunculated nodules on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa... pregnancy-associated pyogenic granuloma is called an epulis gravidarum.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 40-year-old male with von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease undergoes imaging that reveals multiple large, cavernous, blood-filled vascular spaces in the cerebellum and liver. These lesions are composed of large, dilated vascular channels separated by a modest connective tissue stroma. Which tumor type is most characteristic of these findings?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas consist of small, thin-walled capillaries, not large dilated spaces.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, dilated vascular channels. They are frequently found in the liver and CNS and are associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease.
explanations.c: Cystic hygromas are lymphatic malformations, usually found in the neck of infants (Turner syndrome).
explanations.d: Angiosarcomas are malignant with atypia; the description here is of benign dilated spaces.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis involves capillary-like proliferations in HIV patients.

ankiCards: Cavernous hemangiomas are associated with {{c1::von Hippel-Lindau (VHL)}} disease.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas involve {{c1::large}} vascular spaces.
The most common visceral organ involved in cavernous hemangiomas is the {{c1::liver}}.
Intracerebral cavernous hemangiomas are clinically significant because they can cause {{c1::hemorrhage}} or pressure symptoms.
Histologically, cavernous hemangiomas are separated by a {{c1::connective tissue}} stroma.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign but can be locally destructive due to size.
They are composed of large, blood-filled vascular channels.
They do not regress spontaneously (unlike juvenile capillary hemangiomas).
Commonly found in the liver, spleen, and CNS.
Association with VHL disease (cerebellar hemangioblastomas/angiomas).
microReview: Cavernous = Big spaces, don't regress, Liver/CNS, VHL association. Capillary = Small spaces, some regress, Skin.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'large' vs 'small' vascular spaces. Large = Cavernous. Small = Capillary.
sourceQuote: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, dilated vascular channels... they are more frequently involved in deep structures... and do not spontaneously regress.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which vascular tumor is categorized as an 'intermediate-grade' (borderline) neoplasm because it is more aggressive than a hemangioma but less predictably malignant than an angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Glomus tumor is a benign vascular tumor.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangioma is a benign vascular tumor.
explanations.c: Kaposi sarcoma and Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma are classified as intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignant tumor.
explanations.e: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a vascular ectasia (malformation), not a true neoplasm.

ankiCards: Kaposi sarcoma is classified as an {{c1::intermediate}} grade vascular tumor.
Another example of an intermediate-grade vascular tumor is {{c1::epithelioid hemangioendothelioma}}.
Intermediate-grade tumors are often called {{c1::borderline}} tumors.
Unlike hemangiomas, intermediate tumors are locally {{c1::aggressive}}.
Malignant vascular tumors are exemplified by {{c1::angiosarcoma}}.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors are graded as Benign, Intermediate, or Malignant.
Intermediate tumors include Kaposi Sarcoma and Epithelioid Hemangioendothelioma.
They are locally aggressive but have lower metastatic potential than angiosarcomas.
Hemangiomas are benign and never metastasize.
Angiosarcomas are highly malignant and frequently metastasize.
microReview: Grading: Benign (Hemangioma), Intermediate (Kaposi), Malignant (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: Be careful—Kaposi is often thought of as a 'cancer' in AIDS, but in pathology grading, it is 'intermediate' because it is not as universally fatal/aggressive as angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A biopsy of a red, friable skin papule in an AIDS patient shows a proliferation of capillaries with plump endothelial cells and an infiltrate of neutrophils. Special stains (Warthin-Starry) reveal clusters of bacilli. This condition is caused by an organism that also causes which of the following?

explanations.a: Syphilis is caused by Treponema pallidum.
explanations.b: The diagnosis is Bacillary Angiomatosis, caused by Bartonella henselae or Bartonella quintana. Bartonella henselae is also the cause of cat-scratch disease.
explanations.c: Lyme disease is caused by Borrelia burgdorferi.
explanations.d: Tuberculosis is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
explanations.e: Bacillary dysentery is caused by Shigella species.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by bacteria of the {{c1::Bartonella}} genus.
The histological stain used to visualize the bacteria in bacillary angiomatosis is the {{c1::Warthin-Starry}} stain.
The inflammatory cell type characteristic of bacillary angiomatosis (distinguishing it from KS) is the {{c1::neutrophil}}.
Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis and {{c1::cat-scratch}} disease.
Bartonella quintana causes bacillary angiomatosis and {{c1::trench}} fever.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis is a bacterial-induced vascular proliferation.
Occurs primarily in immunocompromised (AIDS) patients.
Caused by Bartonella henselae (cats) or B. quintana (lice).
Histology: Capillary proliferation + neutrophils + bacteria (visible on silver stain).
Differentiated from Kaposi Sarcoma by the presence of neutrophils and bacteria.
microReview: Bartonella = Bacillary Angiomatosis (AIDS) and Cat Scratch Disease (Immunocompetent). Silver stains (Warthin-Starry) positive.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'Bacillary' in Bacillary Angiomatosis with 'Bacillary Dysentery' (Shigella) or 'Acid-fast bacilli' (TB).
sourceQuote: Bacillary angiomatosis... is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts caused by opportunistic gram-negative bacilli of the Bartonella family.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Exposure to which of the following environmental toxins is most strongly associated with the development of hepatic angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Aflatoxin is associated with Hepatocellular Carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Vinyl chloride (used in the plastics industry) is a classic chemical carcinogen associated with hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Asbestos is associated with Mesothelioma and Lung Cancer.
explanations.d: Benzene is associated with Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML).
explanations.e: Beryllium is associated with Berylliosis (granulomatous lung disease) and lung cancer.

ankiCards: The industrial chemical most associated with liver angiosarcoma is {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
The pesticide component associated with liver angiosarcoma is {{c1::arsenic}}.
Hepatic angiosarcoma has a very {{c1::poor}} prognosis.
Angiosarcomas of the liver are highly associated with specific {{c1::environmental}} carcinogens.
The contrast medium previously associated with hepatic angiosarcoma is {{c1::Thorotrast}}.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is rare but highly associated with specific toxins.
Toxins: Vinyl chloride, Arsenic, Thorotrast.
Angiosarcoma is a malignancy of endothelial cells.
It often presents late with liver failure or abdominal pain.
PVC (polyvinyl chloride) workers were historically at risk due to vinyl chloride monomer exposure.
microReview: Hepatic Angiosarcoma toxins: VAT (Vinyl chloride, Arsenic, Thorotrast).
examinerTraps: Aflatoxin/Hepatitis B are for Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC). Vinyl chloride/Arsenic are for Angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcoma... hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with distinct environmental carcinogens, including arsenic, Thorotrast, and vinyl chloride.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old woman presents with several firm, violaceous nodules on her left upper extremity. She has a history of a radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection and radiotherapy for breast cancer 12 years ago. Since that time, she has had persistent, non-pitting edema of the left arm. A biopsy of one of the nodules reveals poorly formed vascular channels lined by atypical, pleomorphic endothelial cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 and typically presents in immunocompromised patients; it does not usually arise specifically from chronic lymphedema.
explanations.b: This clinical scenario (Stewart-Treves syndrome) describes angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema, often after radical mastectomy and lymph node dissection.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella infection and is characterized by neutrophilic infiltrates and capillary proliferation, not malignant endothelial atypia.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign lesions characterized by large, dilated vascular spaces and lack the cellular atypia and pleomorphism seen in this malignant tumor.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are small, painful, benign tumors typically found under the fingernails, arising from specialized smooth muscle cells of glomus bodies.

ankiCards: {{c1::Stewart-Treves}} syndrome refers to the development of angiosarcoma in the setting of chronic lymphedema.
Malignant vascular tumors that stain for the endothelial marker {{c1::CD31}} are most likely angiosarcomas.
Angiosarcomas are most commonly associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}} or {{c2::Thorotrast}} in the liver.
Histologically, {{c1::angiosarcoma}} shows atypical endothelial cells and poorly formed vascular channels.
Long-term post-mastectomy {{c1::lymphedema}} is a major risk factor for cutaneous angiosarcoma.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor of endothelial cells.
Chronic lymphedema is a classic precursor to cutaneous angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves Syndrome).
Histological features include pleomorphic cells and rudimentary vascular channels.
CD31 is a specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial differentiation.
Prognosis is generally poor due to aggressive local invasion and early metastasis.
microReview: Vascular tumors range from benign hemangiomas to highly malignant angiosarcomas. Angiosarcoma is distinguished by malignant atypia and an association with environmental toxins or chronic lymphedema. Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and has different clinical contexts.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Stewart-Treves (Angiosarcoma from lymphedema) with Marjolin ulcer (Squamous cell carcinoma from chronic wounds/burns).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An HIV-positive patient with a CD4+ count of 150/mm³ presents with multiple reddish-purple skin macules and plaques. Biopsy of a lesion shows proliferation of spindle-shaped cells, slit-like vascular spaces, and extravasated red blood cells. Which of the following pathogens is the primary driver of this neoplastic process?

explanations.a: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi Sarcoma-Associated Herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.b: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which clinically mimics Kaposi sarcoma but is characterized by neutrophilic inflammation and is treatable with antibiotics.
explanations.c: HPV-16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas (cervical, anal, oropharyngeal), not vascular tumors.
explanations.d: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and hairy leukoplakia, but not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.e: CMV can cause opportunistic infections in HIV patients (retinitis, colitis) but is not the oncogenic driver of Kaposi sarcoma.

ankiCards: The causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::HHV-8 (or KSHV)}}.
Kaposi Sarcoma histology is characterized by {{c1::spindle}} cells and slit-like vascular spaces.
{{c1::Extravasated RBCs}} and hemosiderin deposits are commonly seen in Kaposi Sarcoma lesions.
The AIDS-defining vascular malignancy is {{c1::Kaposi Sarcoma}}.
Unlike bacillary angiomatosis, Kaposi Sarcoma histology shows a lack of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
keyPoints: HHV-8 is required for the development of all forms of Kaposi Sarcoma.
The tumor involves spindle cells of endothelial/mesenchymal origin.
Clinical forms include Classic, Endemic (African), Iatrogenic, and AIDS-associated.
Slit-like spaces containing RBCs are a hallmark histologic finding.
Treatment involves HAART (in AIDS patients) and sometimes chemotherapy or local excision.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a spindle-cell tumor driven by HHV-8. In the context of AIDS, it is one of the most common malignancies. Histology is the definitive way to distinguish it from the infectious mimic, bacillary angiomatosis.
examinerTraps: The examiner may present a biopsy showing 'neutrophilic infiltrate' to lead you toward Bacillary Angiomatosis instead of Kaposi Sarcoma.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old man presents with an exquisitely painful, 5-mm, blue-red nodule located under the fingernail of his right index finger. Histological examination shows aggregates of specialized glomus cells surrounding vascular channels. These cells are derived from which of the following cell types?

explanations.a: While the tumor contains vascular channels, the characteristic glomus cells themselves are not endothelial.
explanations.b: Glomus cells are specialized, modified smooth muscle cells found in the glomus body, an arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.c: Pericytes are found in hemangiopericytomas; while related to smooth muscle, they are not the specific cell of origin for glomus tumors.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts produce collagen and are not the primary component of a glomus tumor.
explanations.e: Skeletal muscle is not involved in the formation of vascular glomus bodies.

ankiCards: Glomus tumors are most commonly located in the {{c1::subungual}} region (under the nail).
The clinical hallmark of a glomus tumor is that it is {{c1::exquisitely painful}}.
Glomus cells are modified {{c1::smooth muscle}} cells.
The physiological function of the glomus body is {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
On histology, glomus tumors show nests of {{c1::round, uniform}} cells around vascular spaces.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but extremely painful.
They arise from the glomus body (a thermoregulatory AV shunt).
Classic location is the subungual (under nail) area of fingers.
Cells are uniform, round, and derived from smooth muscle.
Surgical excision is curative.
microReview: Pain + Subungual + Vascular nodule = Glomus tumor. This is a recall-heavy topic focusing on the modified smooth muscle origin of the glomus body cells.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse a 'Glomus tumor' (vascular) with a 'Glomus jugulare tumor' (paraganglioma).
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 1-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician by his mother, who is concerned about a rapidly enlarging bright red, raised 'strawberry-like' lesion on the infant's scalp. The lesion was not present at birth. The physician informs the mother that the lesion is likely to grow for several more months and then gradually disappear. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas (juvenile/strawberry hemangiomas) are common in newborns, grow rapidly, and usually regress spontaneously by age 7.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of larger vascular channels, are more deep-seated, and do not typically regress spontaneously like strawberry hemangiomas.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma is a rapidly growing red nodule that often bleeds and is common on skin/gingiva; it usually requires excision and doesn't follow the 'grow-then-regress' infant pattern.
explanations.d: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a flat, permanent vascular malformation that does not regress.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor, extremely rare in infants, and would not be expected to regress.

ankiCards: The common name for a juvenile capillary hemangioma is a {{c1::strawberry}} hemangioma.
Juvenile hemangiomas usually undergo {{c1::spontaneous regression}} by age 7.
A port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) {{c1::does not}} regress with age.
Capillary hemangiomas are composed of thin-walled capillaries with {{c1::scant}} stroma.
The most common benign vascular tumor of infancy is the {{c1::capillary (strawberry) hemangioma}}.
keyPoints: Strawberry hemangiomas are very common in early infancy.
They typically appear shortly after birth and enlarge over several months.
Spontaneous regression occurs in the vast majority (75-90%) of cases by early childhood.
No treatment is usually required unless they obstruct vision or the airway.
Histology shows closely packed capillaries lined by normal-appearing endothelium.
microReview: Juvenile capillary hemangioma = bright red, raised, grows then regresses. Port-wine stain = flat, does not regress. Knowing the natural history is key for management questions.
examinerTraps: The trap is choosing 'excise' or 'biopsy'—the correct management for a strawberry hemangioma is observation due to likely regression.
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels... Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old male with a history of occupational exposure to vinyl chloride for 20 years presents with fatigue and abdominal distension. Imaging reveals multiple mass lesions within the liver. Biopsy shows malignant spindle cells forming irregular vascular channels that express CD31. What is the most likely mechanism of oncogenesis in this patient?

options.c: Viral-mediated inhibition of the p53 tumor suppressor

explanations.a: Bartonella leads to bacillary angiomatosis, which is an infectious proliferation, not a malignant transformation associated with vinyl chloride.
explanations.b: Vinyl chloride and Thorotrast are known chemical carcinogens that cause DNA damage specifically leading to hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: While HHV-8 inhibits p53 in Kaposi sarcoma, angiosarcoma induced by vinyl chloride is a chemical-related mutagenic process.
explanations.d: Congenital cavernous hemangiomas are benign and not related to industrial chemical exposure.
explanations.e: Autoimmune mechanisms characterize vasculitides, not malignant vascular tumors like angiosarcoma.

ankiCards: Exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}} is a major risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma.
{{c1::Thorotrast}} (a former contrast agent) is historically associated with hepatic angiosarcoma.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor of {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
The vascular marker {{c1::CD31}} (PECAM-1) is positive in angiosarcoma.
Unlike hemangiomas, angiosarcomas exhibit significant {{c1::cellular atypia}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is the classic example of a chemically induced vascular malignancy.
Vinyl chloride is used in the plastics (PVC) industry.
The liver is the primary site for chemically induced angiosarcoma.
These tumors are aggressive and often metastatic at the time of diagnosis.
CD31 is the gold-standard IHC marker for confirming endothelial origin.
microReview: Vinyl chloride + Liver mass + Malignant vessels = Hepatic Angiosarcoma. This is a high-yield 'occupational pathology' association.
examinerTraps: The examiner may mention 'PVC' instead of 'vinyl chloride'—ensure you recognize the association between plastic manufacturing and this specific tumor.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular lesions is most likely to be associated with Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease and presents as a benign, but potentially space-occupying, lesion in the cerebellum or retina?

explanations.a: Hemangioblastomas are highly vascular tumors characteristic of Von Hippel-Lindau disease, most commonly found in the cerebellum and retina.
explanations.b: Lymphangiomas are benign malformations of lymphatic vessels and are not specifically associated with VHL.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor and not part of the VHL syndrome spectrum.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are subungual painful tumors and not associated with VHL.
explanations.e: Capillary hemangiomas are common skin/liver lesions but are not the specific CNS/retinal lesion found in VHL.

ankiCards: Von Hippel-Lindau disease is associated with {{c1::hemangioblastomas}} of the cerebellum and retina.
The VHL gene is a tumor suppressor located on chromosome {{c1::3}}.
Besides vascular tumors, VHL disease increases the risk of {{c1::renal cell carcinoma}} (clear cell).
{{c1::Hemangioblastomas}} are benign but can cause symptoms due to local compression in the CNS.
VHL disease also presents with {{c1::pheochromocytomas}}.
keyPoints: VHL is an autosomal dominant syndrome.
Hemangioblastoma is the hallmark vascular tumor of VHL.
Cerebellar lesions can cause ataxia and hydrocephalus.
Retinal lesions can lead to hemorrhage and vision loss.
Screening for RCC and pheochromocytoma is mandatory in these patients.
microReview: VHL = Hemangioblastoma (CNS/Retina) + Renal Cell Carcinoma + Pheochromocytoma. This link between vascular tumors and genetics is very common in board exams.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Hemangioblastoma (VHL) with Hemangioma (generic) or Hemangiopericytoma.
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels... Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 31-year-old pregnant woman presents with a rapidly growing, painless, red, pedunculated nodule on her gingiva that bleeds easily with minor trauma. She is in her second trimester. The physician explains that the lesion is a reactive proliferation of capillaries and is likely to regress after delivery. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a benign, fast-growing vascular lesion often found on the gums of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is infectious (Bartonella) and usually occurs in immunocompromised individuals, not typically as a pregnancy-related gingival nodule.
explanations.c: Kaposi sarcoma presents as purple macules/plaques in HIV/immunocompromised patients and is not associated with pregnancy-related hormonal changes.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor that would not be expected to be pedunculated, rapidly growing on the gingiva, or regress after delivery.
explanations.e: Cavernous hemangiomas are deeper, larger vascular lesions that do not typically present as pedunculated gingival 'granulomas' that bleed easily.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer because it is neither {{c1::pyogenic}} (pus-forming) nor a {{c2::granuloma}}.
The 'pregnancy tumor' of the gingiva is histologically a {{c1::pyogenic granuloma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized by proliferation of {{c1::capillaries}} and edema.
A key clinical feature of pyogenic granuloma is that it {{c1::bleeds easily}}.
Treatment for pyogenic granuloma usually involves {{c1::surgical excision}} (if it doesn't regress post-partum).
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is an acquired, benign vascular lesion.
It is often triggered by trauma or hormonal changes (pregnancy).
The most common site is the gingiva (gums).
Despite the name, it is a form of capillary hemangioma, not a granulomatous infection.
Histology shows lobules of capillaries in an edematous stroma.
microReview: Gingival mass + Pregnancy + Bleeding = Pyogenic Granuloma. This is a 'misnomer' favorite of examiners.
examinerTraps: The name 'Pyogenic Granuloma' is a trap; it does not contain granulomas and isn't caused by pyogenic bacteria.
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels (Fig. 11.1).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following clinical features distinguishes a cavernous hemangioma from a capillary hemangioma?

options.a: Propensity for spontaneous regression in childhood
options.b: Association with the skin and mucous membranes only
options.c: Involvement of deep-seated structures like the liver and brain
options.d: Presence of highly atypical endothelial cells on histology

explanations.a: Capillary (strawberry) hemangiomas regress; cavernous hemangiomas rarely do.
explanations.b: Both can involve skin, but cavernous hemangiomas are more famous for involving deep organs.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas are typically larger, less well-circumscribed, and more frequently involve deep structures like the liver, brain, or viscera.
explanations.d: Atypical endothelial cells are a feature of angiosarcoma, not benign hemangiomas.
explanations.e: HHV-8 is associated with Kaposi sarcoma, not cavernous hemangiomas.

ankiCards: {{c1::Cavernous}} hemangiomas consist of large, dilated vascular channels.
The most common benign tumor of the liver is the {{c1::cavernous hemangioma}}.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas involve {{c1::deep}} structures.
CNS cavernous hemangiomas can cause {{c1::seizures}} or hemorrhage.
On histology, cavernous hemangiomas show vascular spaces separated by {{c1::connective tissue}} stroma.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are larger and deeper than capillary hemangiomas.
They are the most common benign tumor of the liver.
In the brain, they are called 'cavernomas' and can be symptomatic.
They do not spontaneously regress (unlike strawberry hemangiomas).
They can be part of Lindau disease (but VHL is more specific to hemangioblastomas).
microReview: Capillary = Small vessels, superficial, regresses. Cavernous = Large vessels, deep organs, does not regress.
examinerTraps: The examiner might try to confuse 'Cavernous Hemangioma' of the liver (benign) with 'Hepatic Angiosarcoma' (malignant). Check for atypia vs. simple dilated channels.
sourceQuote: For example, arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching... many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the clinic for a routine check-up. She has a large, flat, purple-red birthmark covering the right side of her face in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve. Her parents report that she recently had a seizure. What is the most likely diagnosis associated with these findings?

explanations.a: Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) is characterized by a facial port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) in the V1/V2 distribution, ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomas, and seizures.
explanations.b: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) presents with telangiectasias on the skin and mucous membranes and epistaxis, not facial port-wine stains.
explanations.c: VHL presents with hemangioblastomas (CNS/Retina), not port-wine stains.
explanations.d: Tuberous sclerosis presents with ash-leaf spots and angiofibromas, not port-wine stains.
explanations.e: NF1 presents with cafe-au-lait spots and neurofibromas, not port-wine stains.

ankiCards: Sturge-Weber syndrome is characterized by a facial {{c1::port-wine stain}} (nevus flammeus).
The facial lesion in Sturge-Weber syndrome usually follows the distribution of the {{c1::trigeminal}} nerve.
Ipsilateral {{c1::leptomeningeal}} angiomas in Sturge-Weber syndrome can cause seizures.
A port-wine stain is a type of {{c1::vascular malformation}}.
Sturge-Weber syndrome is associated with a mutation in the {{c1::GNAQ}} gene.
keyPoints: Sturge-Weber syndrome is sporadic, not inherited.
The port-wine stain is present at birth and does not regress.
Neurological complications include seizures, intellectual disability, and hemiparesis.
Glaucoma is a common ophthalmic complication.
Skull X-ray may show 'tram-track' calcifications of the gyri.
microReview: Facial Port-Wine Stain + Seizures = Sturge-Weber. The lesion is a capillary malformation (nevus flammeus).
examinerTraps: Wait for the trigeminal distribution—a random hemangioma on the arm is not Sturge-Weber.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by malformations of capillaries and veins. Which of the following is the most common clinical presentation of this condition?

explanations.a: Recurrent epistaxis (nosebleeds) is the most common presenting symptom due to telangiectasias of the nasal mucosa.
explanations.b: Subungual pain is characteristic of glomus tumors, not HHT.
explanations.c: Lymphedema is associated with Stewart-Treves syndrome or Milroy disease, not HHT.
explanations.d: While HHT can have hepatic AVMs, hepatomegaly is not the most common presenting symptom.
explanations.e: Scalp nodules (like strawberry hemangiomas) are not a feature of HHT.

ankiCards: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia is also known as {{c1::Osler-Weber-Rendu}} syndrome.
The most common symptom of HHT is recurrent {{c1::epistaxis}}.
HHT is inherited in an {{c1::autosomal dominant}} fashion.
Telangiectasias in HHT are commonly found on the {{c1::skin}} and {{c2::mucous membranes}}.
A major risk in HHT patients is the development of {{c1::arteriovenous malformations (AVMs)}} in the lungs, brain, or liver.
keyPoints: HHT involves mutations in TGF-beta signaling pathway genes (ENG, ACVRL1).
Clinical triad: telangiectasias, recurrent epistaxis, and a family history.
Telangiectasias are small, dilated blood vessels near the surface of the skin/mucosa.
AVMs in the lung can lead to right-to-left shunts and paradoxical emboli.
Management focuses on controlling bleeding and screening for AVMs.
microReview: HHT = Epistaxis + Telangiectasias + AVMs. It is a disorder of vascular wall formation.
examinerTraps: The examiner might link HHT to 'iron deficiency anemia' due to chronic GI bleeding or epistaxis—recognize the underlying vascular cause.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure and function.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes a 'true' aneurysm rather than a 'false' (pseudoaneurysm) or a dissection?

options.a: A localized hematoma that communicates with the intravascular space through a hole in the vascular wall
options.b: Dilation involving all three layers of the arterial wall or the attenuated wall of the heart
options.c: Blood entering the wall of an artery as a hematoma that dissects between its layers
options.d: A breach in the vascular wall leading to an extravascular hematoma contained by extravascular connective tissue
options.e: Fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina without any change in the external diameter of the vessel

explanations.a: This describes a false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm), such as a post-catheterization femoral artery lesion.
explanations.b: A true aneurysm involves all layers of the vessel (intima, media, and adventitia) or the heart wall (e.g., post-MI ventricular aneurysm).
explanations.c: This describes an aortic dissection, which is distinct from a true aneurysm because the blood is within the wall layers rather than a dilation of all layers.
explanations.d: This is another description of a false aneurysm, where the wall of the 'aneurysm' is actually organized thrombus and connective tissue, not vessel wall.
explanations.e: Fragmentation of the elastic lamina is a precursor to weakening but does not define an aneurysm, which requires dilation.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers (intima, media, adventitia) of the vessel wall.
A pseudoaneurysm (false aneurysm) is an extravascular {{c1::hematoma}} that communicates with the intravascular space.
Aortic {{c1::dissection}} occurs when blood enters the wall of the artery and spreads between its layers.
Two main shapes of aneurysms are {{c1::saccular}} (spherical outpouches) and {{c1::fusiform}} (circumferential).
The attenuated wall of the heart following a myocardial infarction can form a {{c1::true}} aneurysm.
keyPoints: True aneurysms involve all layers of the arterial wall.
False aneurysms are extravascular hematomas communicating with the vessel lumen.
Saccular aneurysms are discrete outpouchings often containing thrombus.
Fusiform aneurysms are diffuse, circumferential dilations.
Dissections are not synonymous with aneurysms, though they can coexist.
microReview: True aneurysms involve an intact but thinned wall (all 3 layers), whereas false aneurysms (pseudoaneurysms) involve a wall defect leading to an external hematoma. Dissection involves blood tracking between wall layers.
examinerTraps: Confusing a pseudoaneurysm (e.g., from trauma) with a true aneurysm. Remember: True = All 3 layers intact.
sourceQuote: A true aneurysm involves an intact arterial wall or an attenuated ventricular wall of the heart. In contrast, a false aneurysm (also called pseudoaneurysm) is a defect in the vascular wall leading to an extravascular hematoma.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which biochemical mechanism is primarily responsible for the weakening of the aortic wall in the pathogenesis of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA)?

options.a: Increased deposition of type I collagen in the medial layer
options.b: Decreased production of transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β)
options.c: Increased expression of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) by macrophages
options.d: Direct viral infection of smooth muscle cells causing apoptosis
options.e: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum

explanations.a: Increased collagen would typically strengthen a wall; AAA involves the degradation of collagen and elastin.
explanations.b: Increased TGF-β signaling is actually associated with some thoracic aortic aneurysms (e.g., Marfan-like syndromes), but its decrease is not the primary driver in AAA.
explanations.c: Macrophages in atherosclerotic plaques release MMPs (like elastases and collagenases) that degrade the extracellular matrix, leading to wall weakening.
explanations.d: Aneurysms are generally not caused by direct viral infections of smooth muscle cells.
explanations.e: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum is the classic mechanism for syphilitic (tertiary) aneurysms, usually in the thoracic aorta.

ankiCards: The degradation of the extracellular matrix in AAA is mediated by {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
Inflammatory cells in AAA, particularly {{c1::macrophages}}, secrete proteases that weaken the wall.
Atherosclerosis causes AAA by increasing the {{c1::diffusion distance}} from the lumen to the media, leading to ischemia.
The two most important causes of aortic aneurysms are {{c1::atherosclerosis}} and {{c1::hypertension}}.
{{c1::Atherosclerosis}} is the dominant factor in abdominal aortic aneurysms.
keyPoints: AAA is primarily driven by inflammatory remodeling.
MMPs (collagenases and elastases) degrade the structural integrity of the media.
Atherosclerosis induces medial ischemia by thickening the intima.
Genetic predispositions often involve polymorphisms in MMPs.
Chronic inflammation (macrophages/T-cells) is a hallmark of AAA pathology.
microReview: Pathogenesis of AAA: Atherosclerosis → Intimal thickening → Medial ischemia + Inflammation (macrophages) → Release of MMPs → Degradation of Elastin/Collagen → Wall Weakening → Dilation.
examinerTraps: Choosing TGF-β as the answer for AAA. TGF-β is more relevant to Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms and Marfan Syndrome.
sourceQuote: Inadequate or abnormal connective tissue synthesis... Excessive connective tissue degradation... Loss of smooth muscle cells or change in the smooth muscle cell phenotype.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male with a 40-pack-year smoking history and hypertension presents to the emergency department with sudden, severe mid-abdominal pain radiating to his back. Physical examination reveals a pulsatile, tender abdominal mass and a blood pressure of 85/50 mmHg. What is the most likely anatomical location for the lesion responsible for this presentation?

options.d: Abdominal aorta, above the renal arteries
options.e: Abdominal aorta, below the renal arteries

explanations.a: Aneurysms of the ascending aorta are more commonly associated with hypertension or Marfan syndrome, not the classic 'pulsatile abdominal mass'.
explanations.b: Aortic arch aneurysms are less common and usually present with compression of mediastinal structures.
explanations.c: Descending thoracic aneurysms do not present as an abdominal mass.
explanations.d: While AAAs can be suprarenal, the vast majority (90%+) occur below the renal arteries and above the iliac bifurcation.
explanations.e: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are typically located between the renal arteries and the bifurcation of the aorta.

ankiCards: The most common location for an atherosclerotic aneurysm is the {{c1::abdominal aorta}}.
Most AAAs occur {{c1::below}} the level of the renal arteries.
The classic triad of a ruptured AAA is {{c1::flank/back pain}}, {{c1::hypotension}}, and a {{c1::pulsatile mass}}.
The risk of AAA rupture increases significantly when the diameter exceeds {{c1::5.0 to 5.5}} cm.
The primary risk factor for the development of AAA is {{c1::smoking}}.
keyPoints: AAA is most common in male smokers over age 65.
Location: Infrarenal abdominal aorta.
Rupture presents with the 'classic triad': Pain, hypotension, pulsatile mass.
Management: Monitoring for small aneurysms, surgical/endovascular repair for those >5.5cm.
Atherosclerosis is the primary underlying pathological process.
microReview: Older male smoker + pulsatile mass + hypotension = Ruptured AAA. Location is almost always infrarenal.
examinerTraps: Mistaking AAA for a thoracic aneurysm or dissection. Thoracic aneurysms usually present with chest pain or cough/hoarseness.
sourceQuote: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAAs) occur more frequently in men and in smokers, and rarely before age 50. Atherosclerosis is a major cause... most are positioned between the renal arteries and the bifurcation of the aorta.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the histological hallmark of 'cystic medial degeneration' often seen in thoracic aortic aneurysms associated with Marfan syndrome?

options.a: Replacement of the media with dense fibrous scar tissue
options.b: Elastic fiber fragmentation and accumulation of proteoglycan-rich extracellular matrix
options.c: Large numbers of giant cells and granulomatous inflammation in the media
options.d: Extensive calcification of the internal elastic lamina (Mönckeberg sclerosis)
options.e: Neutrophilic infiltration and microabscess formation within the adventitia

explanations.a: Fibrous scarring is more typical of chronic injury or healed dissection, not the cystic medial degeneration phase.
explanations.b: Cystic medial degeneration is characterized by the loss of smooth muscle cells and the presence of 'cysts' (actually pools of basophilic ground substance/mucoid material) and fragmented elastic fibers.
explanations.c: Giant cells and granulomas are characteristic of Giant Cell Arteritis or Takayasu Arteritis, not cystic medial degeneration.
explanations.d: Mönckeberg sclerosis involves calcification of the media in muscular arteries, which is usually clinically insignificant and not associated with aneurysms.
explanations.e: Neutrophilic infiltration suggests an acute infectious (mycotic) aneurysm.

ankiCards: Cystic medial necrosis (degeneration) is the histological hallmark of {{c1::thoracic aortic aneurysms}}.
In Marfan syndrome, there is a mutation in the {{c1::FBN1 (fibrillin-1)}} gene.
Cystic medial degeneration involves the accumulation of {{c1::proteoglycans (or GAGs)}} in the media.
Mutations in {{c1::TGF-beta}} receptors can also lead to thoracic aortic aneurysms.
Loss of {{c1::elastic fibers}} in the media leads to the weakening characteristic of aneurysms.
keyPoints: Cystic medial degeneration involves elastic fiber loss.
It is commonly associated with Marfan syndrome (Fibrillin-1 mutation).
It results in 'cysts' filled with amorphic ground substance.
TGF-β signaling is often pathologically increased in these conditions.
It predisposes patients to both thoracic aneurysms and aortic dissections.
microReview: Cystic Medial Degeneration = Marfan/Hypertension/TGF-β issues → Fragmented elastic fibers + Proteoglycan 'cysts' → Weak media → Thoracic Aneurysm/Dissection.
examinerTraps: The term 'cystic medial necrosis' is a misnomer because there is actually no necrosis or true cysts; it is degeneration and mucoid accumulation.
sourceQuote: Cystic medial degeneration is characterized by the loss of smooth muscle cells, elastic fiber fragmentation, and the presence of areas of amorphous proteoglycan-rich extracellular matrix.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old female presents with difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) and a persistent dry cough. A chest CT reveals a large 6-cm aneurysm of the aortic arch. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her dysphagia?

options.a: Invasion of the esophagus by a malignant vascular tumor
options.b: Compression of the esophagus by the aneurysmal sac
