In the CNS, they can cause pressure symptoms or hemorrhage.
microReview: Large blood-filled spaces + Liver (most common) = Cavernous Hemangioma.
examinerTraps: Mistaking a hepatic cavernous hemangioma for a malignant tumor on imaging; they have a characteristic 'filling' pattern on tagged RBC scans or CT.
sourceQuote: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, dilated vascular channels... they are the most common benign tumor of the liver.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation seen in immunocompromised individuals. Histological evaluation shows capillary proliferation with prominent 'epithelioid' endothelial cells, neutrophilic infiltrates, and granular material. What is the nature of the granular material found in these lesions?

explanations.a: The 'granular material' seen in bacillary angiomatosis consists of clusters of Bartonella bacteria, which can be visualized using Warthin-Starry silver stains.
explanations.b: Immune complexes are seen in vasculitis, not typically as granular masses in this vascular tumor.
explanations.c: Amyloid would show apple-green birefringence under polarized light with Congo Red, not the granular histology of BA.
explanations.d: Calcium would appear purple/basophilic and crunchy, not granular bacterial clusters.
explanations.e: Degraded collagen (fibrinoid necrosis) is characteristic of certain vasculitides, but not BA.

ankiCards: The causative organisms of bacillary angiomatosis are {{c1::Bartonella henselae and Bartonella quintana}}.
Bacillary angiomatosis is characterized by the presence of {{c1::neutrophils}} and bacterial clusters.
To visualize the bacteria in bacillary angiomatosis, a {{c1::Warthin-Starry / silver}} stain is used.
Bacillary angiomatosis occurs primarily in {{c1::immunocompromised (AIDS)}} patients.
Bartonella henselae is typically transmitted by {{c1::cats (cat-scratch)}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis (BA) is an opportunistic infection.
B. henselae (cats) and B. quintana (lice/trench fever) are the agents.
It involves skin, bone, or internal organs.
Histology: Proliferating capillaries, epithelioid endothelium, neutrophils.
Treatment involves antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin).
microReview: AIDS patient + Red papules + Neutrophils + Bartonella = Bacillary Angiomatosis.
examinerTraps: BA can look almost identical to Kaposi Sarcoma clinically; the presence of neutrophils and the lack of HHV-8 help differentiate.
sourceQuote: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts... caused by opportunistic gram-negative bacilli of the Bartonella family.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old female presents with a cluster of painful, dark red nodules on her right arm. Ten years ago, she underwent a radical mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection for breast adenocarcinoma, which was followed by chronic, persistent lymphedema of the limb. Skin biopsy of a nodule reveals atypical, pleomorphic endothelial cells forming irregular vascular channels that infiltrate the dermis. Immunohistochemical staining is positive for CD31.

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and typically presents as purple-red patches or plaques, often in immunocompromised patients, but does not usually arise from chronic lymphedema.
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema following radical mastectomy is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome. It is a highly aggressive malignant vascular tumor characterized by pleomorphic CD31+ endothelial cells.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign vascular proliferation caused by Bartonella infection in immunocompromised hosts, characterized by neutrophils and granular material, not pleomorphic malignancy.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are benign, exquisitely painful tumors that usually occur subungually and arise from specialized glomus bodies (smooth muscle cells), not pleomorphic endothelium.
explanations.e: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign lesions composed of large, blood-filled vascular spaces and lack the cellular atypia or infiltrative growth seen in this patient.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising from chronic lymphedema (e.g., post-mastectomy) is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
The immunohistochemical marker used to identify endothelial origin in vascular tumors is {{c1::CD31::marker}}.
Angiosarcoma of the liver is classically associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride::chemical}}.
The clinical prognosis for angiosarcoma is generally {{c1::poor::good/poor}} due to early local invasion and metastasis.
Histologically, angiosarcoma is characterized by {{c1::pleomorphic}} endothelial cells forming irregular channels.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignant vascular tumor.
Stewart-Treves syndrome refers specifically to lymphangiosarcoma following chronic lymphedema.
Histology shows irregular, anastomosing vascular channels lined by atypical endothelial cells.
CD31 and vWF are positive markers for these tumors.
Risk factors include radiation, chronic lymphedema, and chemical toxins like arsenic.
microReview: Angiosarcoma: Malignant, pleomorphic cells, CD31+, associated with lymphedema (Stewart-Treves) and radiation.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Stewart-Treves (malignant, post-lymphedema) with simple lymphangiomas (benign).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. ... Vascular Tumors 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A patient with advanced HIV infection presents with multiple violaceous, raised skin plaques on the trunk and lower extremities. Biopsy reveals spindle cell proliferation with slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells. Which of the following pathogens is the primary oncogenic driver for this condition?

explanations.a: HPV-16 is primarily associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix, anus, and oropharynx.
explanations.b: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which mimics Kaposi sarcoma clinically but is a bacterial infection, not a viral malignancy.
explanations.c: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is strongly associated with Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus (KSHV).
explanations.d: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and hairy leukoplakia, but not KS.
explanations.e: CMV causes retinitis and colitis in AIDS patients but is not the driver of vascular tumors.

ankiCards: The virus etiologically linked to all forms of Kaposi sarcoma is {{c1::HHV-8}}.
The histologic hallmark of Kaposi sarcoma includes {{c1::spindle}} cells and slit-like vascular spaces.
The presence of {{c1::extravasated RBCs}} and hemosiderin is a common finding in Kaposi sarcoma lesions.
Kaposi sarcoma is an {{c1::AIDS-defining}} illness in HIV-positive patients.
The most common form of Kaposi sarcoma in the United States is the {{c1::AIDS-associated}} type.
keyPoints: HHV-8 encodes viral homologs of cyclin D and other proteins that promote cell proliferation.
KS lesions progress through three stages: patch, plaque, and nodule.
Spindle cells are the characteristic proliferative cell type in KS.
Extravasated red blood cells are typically present in the slit-like spaces.
Treatment often involves antiretroviral therapy (ART) to restore immune function.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma: HHV-8, spindle cells, slit-like spaces, extravasated RBCs, AIDS-associated.
examinerTraps: Distinguish KS (HHV-8, spindle cells) from Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella, neutrophils).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. ... Vascular Tumors 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 25-year-old male presents with an extremely painful, small, bluish nodule located under the fingernail of his left index finger. He notes that the pain is triggered by cold temperatures.

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are common benign vascular tumors but are typically not painful and not localized specifically to the subungual region.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, exquisitely painful tumors arising from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, frequently found in the subungual region.
explanations.c: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a vascular ectasia that presents as a flat, non-painful birthmark.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granulomas are rapidly growing, pedunculated red nodules, often on skin or gingiva, that bleed easily but are not classically subungual or cold-sensitive.
explanations.e: Angiosarcomas are large, aggressive, infiltrative malignant tumors, unlike the small, localized glomus tumor.

ankiCards: The subungual (under the nail) location is classic for a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells involved in thermoregulation.
A clinical feature that distinguishes glomus tumors from other vascular lesions is extreme {{c1::pain}}.
Glomus tumors are most commonly found in the {{c1::distal digits}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors show nests of uniform, round cells surrounding {{c1::vascular}} channels.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign neoplasms.
They arise from glomus bodies, which are specialized arteriovenous anastomoses.
Classic presentation: triad of paroxysmal pain, point tenderness, and cold sensitivity.
Subungual (fingernail) area is the most common site.
Excision is curative.
microReview: Glomus tumor: Subungual, painful, cold-sensitive, smooth muscle origin.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'exquisitely painful' and 'subungual'—these are the high-yield descriptors for Glomus tumors.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. ... Vascular Tumors 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular lesions is characterized by a 'strawberry' appearance at birth, rapid growth during the first few months of life, and spontaneous regression by age 7?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas involve large vascular spaces, occur deeper in tissue, and do not typically undergo spontaneous regression.
explanations.b: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are very common in infants, grow rapidly after birth, and nearly always involute by age 7-9.
explanations.c: Spider telangiectasias are small dilated vessels with a central core, often associated with hyperestrogenic states (pregnancy, cirrhosis), and do not follow the strawberry hemangioma growth pattern.
explanations.d: Nevus flammeus is a flat capillary malformation (birthmark) that typically persists throughout life and does not regress.
explanations.e: Lymphangiomas are malformations of the lymphatic system that usually persist or enlarge, requiring surgical management.

ankiCards: A strawberry-like vascular lesion in an infant that eventually regresses is a {{c1::juvenile hemangioma}}.
Juvenile hemangiomas typically undergo spontaneous {{c1::regression/involution}} by age 7.
The most common site for juvenile hemangiomas is the {{c1::skin}} (or head/neck).
In contrast to juvenile hemangiomas, {{c1::nevus flammeus}} does not regress over time.
Juvenile hemangiomas are histologically characterized as {{c1::capillary}} hemangiomas.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangiomas are the most common tumors of infancy.
They present at birth or within the first weeks of life.
The 'strawberry' moniker comes from the bright red, lobulated appearance.
Regression is the rule, usually completed by early childhood.
Treatment is usually conservative (observation).
microReview: Juvenile hemangioma: Infant, strawberry-red, rapid growth, then spontaneous regression.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse with Nevus Flammeus (port-wine stain), which does NOT regress and grows with the child.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. ... Vascular Tumors 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman in her second trimester presents with a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated mass on her gingiva. The lesion is soft and bleeds easily when she brushes her teeth. On examination, it appears as a 1-cm ulcerated nodule. If biopsied, the lesion would show a proliferation of capillaries with extensive edema and inflammatory infiltrate.

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a benign vascular lesion that often occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum) and bleeds easily.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors are painful and subungual; they do not typically present as gingival masses in pregnancy.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas are deeper, more permanent lesions and lack the rapid growth and inflammatory appearance of a pyogenic granuloma.
explanations.d: Kaposi sarcoma presents as purple plaques or nodules, often in the setting of HIV/HHV-8, and would not typically be a solitary, rapidly growing pedunculated gingival mass in a healthy pregnant female.
explanations.e: Angiosarcomas are malignant and usually occur in older patients or specific risk settings; they do not present as simple gingival 'pregnancy' nodules.

ankiCards: A rapidly growing, pedunculated red nodule on the gingiva of a pregnant woman is likely a {{c1::pyogenic granuloma}}.
Another name for a pyogenic granuloma occurring in pregnancy is {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized histologically as a proliferation of {{c1::capillaries}}.
A key clinical feature of pyogenic granuloma is that it {{c1::bleeds}} easily.
Despite its name, a pyogenic granuloma is neither {{c1::pyogenic}} (infectious) nor a {{c1::granuloma}} (histologically).
keyPoints: Pyogenic granulomas are misnamed; they are lobular capillary hemangiomas.
Commonly found on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
They are often triggered by trauma or hormonal changes (pregnancy).
They can regress spontaneously or may require simple excision.
Histology: highly vascular granulation-like tissue.
microReview: Pyogenic granuloma: Gingiva, pregnancy, bleeds easily, lobular capillary proliferation.
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic granuloma' is a misnomer; look for 'lobular capillary hemangioma' as a synonym.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. ... Vascular Tumors 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An immunocompromised patient presents with multiple skin nodules. Biopsy reveals a vascular proliferation with prominent neutrophilic infiltrates and clusters of granular purple material. Silver stains (Warthin-Starry) identify the causative organisms as small bacilli. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 and shows spindle cells, not neutrophilic infiltrates or bacteria on Warthin-Starry stain.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella species in immunocompromised patients; it features vascular proliferation with neutrophils and bacteria detectable by silver stain.
explanations.c: Cystic hygromas are lymphatic malformations typically found in the neck of children (Turner syndrome) and are not infectious.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignancy with pleomorphic cells and no bacterial involvement.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are benign smooth muscle neoplasms that are not associated with infections or immunocompromise.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by bacteria of the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
To visualize the organisms in bacillary angiomatosis, a {{c1::Warthin-Starry (silver)}} stain is used.
Histologically, bacillary angiomatosis differs from Kaposi sarcoma by the presence of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
The species causing bacillary angiomatosis from cat scratches is {{c1::Bartonella henselae}}.
Bacillary angiomatosis is primarily seen in patients who are {{c1::immunocompromised}} (e.g., AIDS).
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis is a bacterial-induced vascular proliferation.
It mimics Kaposi sarcoma clinically.
Caused by B. henselae (cat scratch) or B. quintana (trench fever/lice).
Treatment involves antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin).
Histology: proliferation of capillaries with nuclear atypia and neutrophilic inflammation.
microReview: Bacillary angiomatosis: Bartonella, AIDS, neutrophils, Warthin-Starry silver stain positive.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse with Kaposi Sarcoma. Look for 'neutrophils' and 'silver stain' to point toward Bacillary Angiomatosis.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. ... Vascular Tumors 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following chemical exposures is most strongly associated with the development of hepatic angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Benzene is classically associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.b: Asbestos exposure is the primary risk factor for mesothelioma and lung carcinoma.
explanations.c: Vinyl chloride (used in PVC production), arsenic, and Thorotrast are the classic risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: Aflatoxin B1 is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), particularly in regions with high HBV prevalence.
explanations.e: Naphthylamine exposure is linked to transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder.

ankiCards: The classic chemical associated with hepatic angiosarcoma in PVC workers is {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
In addition to vinyl chloride, the metalloid {{c1::arsenic}} is linked to hepatic angiosarcoma.
Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor of {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
{{c1::Thorotrast::radiocontrast}} is a legacy radioactive contrast agent known to cause hepatic angiosarcoma.
The organ most commonly affected by chemical-induced angiosarcoma is the {{c1::liver}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma can occur anywhere but often involves skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is rare but highly associated with specific toxins.
Vinyl chloride is the most famous industrial risk factor.
The latent period between exposure and tumor development can be decades.
Most cases are high-grade and have a very poor prognosis.
microReview: Hepatic Angiosarcoma: Vinyl chloride, Arsenic, Thorotrast, malignant endothelium.
examinerTraps: Differentiate between Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HBV, HCV, Aflatoxin) and Angiosarcoma (Vinyl chloride, Arsenic).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. ... Vascular Tumors 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 4-year-old child presents with a large, flat, dull red 'port-wine' birthmark covering the left side of his face in the distribution of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve. The parents are concerned about his recent onset of seizures. MRI reveals ipsilateral leptomeningeal vascular malformations. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) involves multiple small telangiectasias and AV malformations, not a large port-wine stain.
explanations.b: Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) features a facial nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) in the trigeminal distribution and ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomas, often leading to seizures.
explanations.c: Von Hippel-Lindau disease involves hemangioblastomas of the cerebellum and retina, as well as renal cell carcinoma, but not port-wine stains.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation seen in immunocompromised patients, not a congenital syndrome.
explanations.e: Kasabach-Merritt syndrome involves the sequestration of platelets within a large cavernous hemangioma, leading to consumptive coagulopathy.

ankiCards: The constellation of facial port-wine stain and leptomeningeal angiomatosis is {{c1::Sturge-Weber}} syndrome.
Sturge-Weber syndrome typically involves a port-wine stain in the distribution of the {{c1::trigeminal}} nerve.
A common CNS complication of Sturge-Weber syndrome is {{c1::seizures}}.
A port-wine stain is also known as {{c1::nevus flammeus}}.
Sturge-Weber syndrome is associated with a mutation in the {{c1::GNAQ}} gene.
keyPoints: Nevus flammeus is a common ectasia (port-wine stain).
Most are ordinary birthmarks, but those in the V1/V2 trigeminal distribution may indicate Sturge-Weber.
Leptomeningeal involvement can lead to mental retardation, hemiplegia, and seizures.
Radiology may show 'tram-track' calcifications in the brain.
It is a sporadic (non-inherited) condition.
microReview: Sturge-Weber: Port-wine stain (trigeminal distribution), leptomeningeal angioma, seizures, GNAQ mutation.
examinerTraps: Standard 'port-wine stains' are just nevus flammeus; it's only 'Sturge-Weber' when associated with CNS or ocular findings.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. ... Vascular Tumors 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A large, poorly circumscribed benign vascular lesion is found in the liver of an asymptomatic 45-year-old male during imaging for unrelated trauma. Histology shows large, dilated, blood-filled vascular spaces separated by a scant connective tissue stroma. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas consist of small, thin-walled capillaries, unlike the large, dilated spaces described here.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are the most common benign tumors of the liver and are characterized by large, blood-filled vascular channels.
explanations.c: Hemangioendotheliomas are intermediate-grade tumors that have features between benign hemangiomas and malignant angiosarcomas; they do not typically present as simple dilated spaces.
explanations.d: Angiosarcomas are malignant with significant cellular atypia and infiltrative growth, which is not described.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors arise from smooth muscle and are typically found in the distal extremities, not the liver.

ankiCards: The most common benign tumor of the liver is the {{c1::cavernous hemangioma}}.
Histologically, cavernous hemangiomas show large, dilated channels filled with {{c1::blood}}.
A potential complication of very large cavernous hemangiomas in infants is {{c1::Kasabach-Merritt}} syndrome.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas involve {{c1::larger/dilated}} vascular spaces.
Cavernous hemangiomas in the liver are usually found {{c1::incidentally}}.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are common and benign.
They can occur in the skin, viscera (liver is most common), or brain.
Usually asymptomatic, but can bleed or cause mass effect if very large.
They do not regress, unlike juvenile capillary hemangiomas.
Biopsy is usually avoided in the liver due to the risk of hemorrhage.
microReview: Cavernous Hemangioma: Liver (common), large blood-filled spaces, benign, incidental find.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse cavernous hemangioma with angiosarcoma in the liver; look for 'benign' and 'dilated spaces' versus 'malignant' and 'atypia'.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. ... Vascular Tumors 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the most common clinical course for a Classic (European) Kaposi sarcoma?

options.a: Highly aggressive with early visceral involvement
options.b: Indolent cutaneous lesions localized to the lower extremities
options.c: Rapidly fatal within months of diagnosis
options.d: Primarily involves lymph nodes in young African children
options.e: Requires aggressive systemic chemotherapy for survival

explanations.a: Aggressive visceral involvement is more characteristic of AIDS-associated KS, not the Classic type.
explanations.b: Classic (European) KS is an indolent disease typically seen in older men of Mediterranean or Eastern European descent, presenting as distal limb lesions.
explanations.c: The Classic form is usually chronic and rarely the cause of death.
explanations.d: Lymphadenopathic KS (African/Endemic) is the form that typically affects young children and is more aggressive.
explanations.e: Classic KS often requires only local treatment or observation because of its slow progression.

ankiCards: The 'Classic' form of Kaposi sarcoma is typically seen in older men of {{c1::Mediterranean}} descent.
Classic Kaposi sarcoma is usually {{c1::indolent/slow-growing}} in its clinical course.
In contrast to the AIDS-associated form, Classic KS is usually limited to the {{c1::skin (distal limbs)}}.
The form of KS seen in HIV-negative young African children is the {{c1::lymphadenopathic (endemic)}} form.
All forms of KS, including the Classic type, are associated with {{c1::HHV-8}}.
keyPoints: There are four major types of KS: Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
Classic KS: older men, Mediterranean/Jewish, indolent, skin-limited.
Endemic KS: African, can be indolent or aggressive (especially in children).
Transplant-associated: occurs with immunosuppression; may regress if immunosuppression is reduced.
AIDS-associated: most common in the US, very aggressive, widespread.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma Types: Classic (old men, indolent), Endemic (African), Transplant, AIDS-associated (aggressive).
examinerTraps: Don't assume all KS is AIDS-related. Classic KS is a distinct, much more indolent clinical entity.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. ... Vascular Tumors 518.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 42-year-old male with a history of advanced HIV (CD4+ count 85 cells/uL) presents with multiple non-blanching, purple-to-red plaques on his lower extremities and hard palate. Biopsy of a lesion reveals spindled-shaped cells with slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells. Immunostaining is positive for a double-stranded DNA virus. Which of the following is the most likely causative agent?

explanations.a: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.b: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) is the direct causative agent of Kaposi sarcoma, which presents as purple/red plaques in immunocompromised patients and features spindle cells with slit-like spaces.
explanations.c: Cytomegalovirus causes retinitis or colitis in AIDS patients but does not cause vascular tumors.
explanations.d: Human papillomavirus is associated with cervical cancer and warts, not vascular lesions.
explanations.e: Hepatitis B virus is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma and polyarteritis nodosa, not vascular tumors.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is caused by {{c1::Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}.
The classic histological finding in Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells with slit-like vascular spaces}}.
A red/purple vascular plaque in an HIV patient should raise suspicion for {{c1::Kaposi Sarcoma}}.
Kaposi sarcoma cells often stain positive for {{c1::CD31}} (an endothelial marker).
The four types of Kaposi Sarcoma are Classic, Endemic, {{c1::Transplant-associated}}, and AIDS-associated.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma is a malignant vascular tumor caused by HHV-8.
Most common in AIDS patients (epidemic form).
Histology shows slit-like spaces filled with RBCs and spindle-shaped endothelial cells.
HHV-8 is also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV).
It typically involves the skin, but can also involve mucous membranes and viscera.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma: HHV-8 + HIV + Spindle cells/Slit-like spaces + Purple plaques.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8) with Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella henselae), which also appears in HIV patients but features neutrophilic infiltrates.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with an extremely painful, 5-mm, bluish nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. She notes that the pain is exacerbated by cold temperatures. Excision of the lesion reveals a tumor composed of nests and aggregates of uniform cells surrounding thin-walled vascular channels. From which cell type is this tumor derived?

explanations.a: Pericytes are the origin of hemangiopericytomas, not glomus tumors.
explanations.b: While it is a vascular tumor, the primary neoplastic component is not the endothelial cell.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) arise from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts are involved in fibromas, not vascular thermoregulatory tumors.
explanations.e: Skeletal muscle cells are not part of the glomus body structure.

ankiCards: A painful subungual (under nail) vascular nodule is most likely a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle cells}}.
The normal glomus body is involved in {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Histology of a glomus tumor shows nests of cells around {{c1::vascular channels}}.
The pain in a glomus tumor is often triggered by {{c1::cold}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign and exquisitely painful.
Classic location: distal digits, especially subungual.
Arise from glomus bodies (specialized AV shunts).
Cell of origin: Specialized smooth muscle cells.
Treatment is simple surgical excision.
microReview: Glomus Tumor: Subungual + Exquisite Pain + Cold Sensitivity + Modified Smooth Muscle.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'exquisite pain' or 'subungual' to differentiate glomus tumor from simple capillary hemangiomas.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the most likely natural history of a 'strawberry' (juvenile) hemangioma appearing on the scalp of a newborn?

options.c: Initial rapid growth followed by spontaneous regression
options.d: Metastasis to the regional lymph nodes
options.e: Development of thrombocytopenia due to platelet trapping

explanations.a: Juvenile hemangiomas are benign and do not typically transform into angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Unlike port-wine stains, strawberry hemangiomas usually regress.
explanations.c: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are common in newborns; they grow rapidly for several months and then usually regress spontaneously by age 7 to 9.
explanations.d: They are benign and do not metastasize.
explanations.e: Platelet trapping (Kasabach-Merritt syndrome) is usually associated with larger, cavernous hemangiomas or tufted angiomas, not standard juvenile ones.

ankiCards: The common 'strawberry hemangioma' of infancy is histologically a {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma.
Juvenile hemangiomas usually undergo {{c1::spontaneous regression}}.
Juvenile hemangiomas are found in approximately 1 in {{c1::200}} births.
By age 7, approximately {{c1::75-90}}% of strawberry hemangiomas have regressed.
A strawberry hemangioma is also known as a {{c1::juvenile}} hemangioma.
keyPoints: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma is extremely common in infancy.
They are capillary-type hemangiomas.
Characterized by rapid growth followed by involution.
Most disappear by early childhood without treatment.
Grossly appear as bright red, lobulated masses.
microReview: Strawberry Hemangioma: Newborn + Rapid Growth + Spontaneous Regression by Age 7.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse this with a port-wine stain (Nevus Flammeus), which does not regress and grows with the child.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis)... or Weakening of vessel walls.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male with a 30-year history of working in the plastic manufacturing industry presents with jaundice, weight loss, and abdominal pain. Imaging reveals multiple ill-defined masses in the liver. Biopsy confirms a malignant vascular neoplasm. Exposure to which of the following substances is most strongly associated with this condition?

explanations.a: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and lung cancer.
explanations.b: Vinyl chloride (used in PVC production), arsenic, and Thorotrast are classic risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Aflatoxin B1 is a risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: Benzene is associated with acute myeloid leukemia.
explanations.e: While arsenic is associated with hepatic angiosarcoma, vinyl chloride is the specific association linked to the plastics/PVC industry in medical boards.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
Three major risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma are vinyl chloride, arsenic, and {{c1::Thorotrast}}.
Angiosarcomas are highly {{c1::malignant}} tumors of endothelial cells.
The endothelial marker used to identify angiosarcoma is {{c1::CD31 (or vWF)}}.
Angiosarcoma post-mastectomy and chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are aggressive malignant endothelial tumors.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is linked to specific chemical carcinogens.
Vinyl chloride exposure is classic for the plastics industry.
Poor prognosis due to early metastasis and difficulty in surgical resection.
Histology: Atypical endothelial cells forming irregular vascular channels.
microReview: Hepatic Angiosarcoma: Vinyl Chloride + Arsenic + Thorotrast + CD31 positive.
examinerTraps: Distinguish from Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC), which is associated with Hep B/C and Cirrhosis, not vinyl chloride.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An 8-year-old girl with Turner syndrome (45,XO) is evaluated for a large, soft, fluctuant mass on the left side of her neck. The mass has been present since birth and transilluminates on physical exam. What is the most likely pathological classification of this lesion?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are usually smaller, solid, and on the skin surface, not large cystic neck masses.
explanations.b: Cystic hygromas (cavernous lymphangiomas) are common in the neck or axilla and are classically associated with Turner syndrome.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are small, painful, and subungual.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation in immunocompromised patients.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor, unlikely to be a congenital transilluminating mass in a child.

ankiCards: A cystic hygroma is a {{c1::cavernous lymphangioma}}.
Cystic hygromas are frequently associated with {{c1::Turner Syndrome}}.
The classic location for a cystic hygroma is the {{c1::neck (or axilla)}}.
Cystic hygromas are composed of large, dilated {{c1::lymphatic}} spaces.
Unlike hemangiomas, the spaces in lymphangiomas lack {{c1::red blood cells}}.
keyPoints: Cystic hygromas are benign lymphatic malformations.
Often present at birth; associated with chromosomal aneuploidy.
Histology: Dilated lymphatic channels lined by endothelium.
Characterized by the absence of RBCs in the lumens.
They can be large and infiltrative, making resection difficult.
microReview: Cystic Hygroma: Turner Syndrome + Neck Mass + Lymphatic Origin + Transilluminates.
examinerTraps: Look for 'Turner syndrome' as a massive hint for cystic hygroma.
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old pregnant woman in her third trimester presents with a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated nodule on her gingiva. The lesion bleeds easily with minor trauma. Biopsy shows a circumscribed proliferation of capillaries arranged in lobules with interspersing edema and inflammatory cells. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnosis?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis presents similarly but occurs in immunocompromised individuals and is caused by Bartonella.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a common benign vascular lesion often found on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.c: Nevus flammeus is a flat birthmark (port-wine stain), not a pedunculated nodule.
explanations.d: Spider telangiectasia are small radial vessels, usually associated with hyperestrinism in cirrhosis, not pedunculated gingival masses.
explanations.e: Kaposi sarcoma is HHV-8 related and usually presents as plaques/patches in HIV patients, not a single gingival nodule in pregnancy.

ankiCards: A pyogenic granuloma is histologically a {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas that occur on the gingiva of pregnant women are called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
A key clinical feature of pyogenic granuloma is that it {{c1::bleeds easily}}.
Despite the name, a pyogenic granuloma is neither {{c1::pyogenic (infectious)}} nor a {{c1::granuloma}}.
Treatment for pyogenic granuloma is usually {{c1::surgical excision}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is a vascular proliferation.
Common on skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
Associated with pregnancy and trauma.
Often regresses or persists until excision.
Histology shows a 'lobular' arrangement of capillaries.
microReview: Pyogenic Granuloma: Pregnancy + Gingiva + Bleeds easily + Lobular Capillary Hemangioma.
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic granuloma' implies infection or granulomatous inflammation, but it is actually a vascular tumor.
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An autosomal dominant disorder characterized by multiple small aneurysmal telangiectasias of the skin and mucous membranes, which frequently results in epistaxis or gastrointestinal bleeding, is caused by mutations in genes involved in which signaling pathway?

explanations.a: Wnt/Beta-catenin is associated with colon cancer (FAP), not HHT.
explanations.b: Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome) is caused by mutations in genes (like endoglin or ALK-1) that modulate TGF-beta signaling.
explanations.c: Notch signaling is critical for vascular development but not the primary driver of HHT mutations.
explanations.d: Hedgehog signaling is associated with basal cell carcinoma.
explanations.e: While VEGF is involved in angiogenesis, the genetic defect in HHT is in the TGF-beta pathway components.

ankiCards: Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia is also known as {{c1::Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome}}.
The inheritance pattern of Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome is {{c1::autosomal dominant}}.
Classic symptoms of HHT include {{c1::epistaxis}} and GI bleeding.
HHT involves mutations in the {{c1::TGF-beta}} signaling pathway.
Major risk in HHT patients includes {{c1::arteriovenous malformations (AVMs)}} in the lungs or brain.
keyPoints: HHT is a systemic vascular dysplasia.
Presents with telangiectasias and AVMs.
Mutations involve Endoglin (ENG) or Activin receptor-like kinase 1 (ACVRL1).
Clinical triad: Telangiectasia, recurrent epistaxis, family history.
Can lead to high-output heart failure due to AVMs.
microReview: HHT: AD inheritance + Epistaxis + TGF-beta pathway + Telangiectasia.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse with simple spider telangiectasias (liver disease) or ataxia-telangiectasia.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular tumors are categorized as benign, intermediate (borderline), or malignant. Which of the following is considered an intermediate-grade vascular neoplasm?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas are strictly benign.
explanations.b: Hemangioendotheliomas (like Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma) are categorized as intermediate-grade tumors, meaning they are locally aggressive but have lower metastatic potential than angiosarcomas.
explanations.c: Angiosarcomas are high-grade malignant tumors.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are benign.
explanations.e: Cystic hygromas (lymphangiomas) are benign.

ankiCards: A {{c1::hemangioendothelioma}} is an example of an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
Unlike hemangiomas, {{c1::intermediate}} grade tumors are often locally invasive.
The most common intermediate-grade vascular tumor is {{c1::Epithelioid}} hemangioendothelioma.
{{c1::Angiosarcoma}} is the prototypical high-grade malignant vascular tumor.
Benign vascular tumors like {{c1::hemangiomas}} rarely metastasize.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors span a spectrum of behavior.
Benign: Hemangiomas, glomus tumors.
Intermediate: Hemangioendotheliomas.
Malignant: Angiosarcoma, Kaposi sarcoma.
Intermediate tumors show more cellularity and atypia than benign ones but lack the full features of malignancy.
microReview: Vascular Grades: Benign (Hemangioma) -> Intermediate (Hemangioendothelioma) -> Malignant (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: Be careful with 'Kaposi Sarcoma'—while usually aggressive, it is technically often grouped with malignant or intermediate depending on the subtype, but Hemangioendothelioma is the classic 'intermediate' answer.
sourceQuote: The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing these muscular vessels to exert control over blood flow.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old female presents with an enlarging, poorly defined, bruising area on her left arm. Ten years ago, she underwent a radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection and radiotherapy for breast cancer, resulting in chronic lymphedema of that arm. Biopsy of the skin lesion shows high-grade pleomorphic cells forming rudimentary vascular channels. Which diagnosis is most likely?

explanations.a: Lymphangiomyomatosis is a lung disease in women of childbearing age.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis requires Bartonella infection and immunocompromise.
explanations.c: This patient has Stewart-Treves syndrome: angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy).
explanations.d: Kaposi sarcoma is HHV-8 related and usually not associated with chronic lymphedema in this fashion.
explanations.e: Lymphangiomas are benign and usually congenital, not a late-onset malignancy.

ankiCards: Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to {{c1::angiosarcoma}} arising in chronic lymphedema.
The most common surgical history preceding Stewart-Treves is {{c1::radical mastectomy}}.
Histology of angiosarcoma reveals {{c1::pleomorphic endothelial cells}}.
Angiosarcoma is highly aggressive with a {{c1::poor}} 5-year survival rate.
Radiation therapy is a known risk factor for subsequent {{c1::angiosarcoma}} development.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma can occur anywhere but often involves the skin and soft tissues.
Chronic lymphedema is a major risk factor.
Often starts as small red papules or 'bruises' that expand.
Markers: CD31 and CD34 positive.
Can also occur in the heart (usually right atrium).
microReview: Stewart-Treves: Post-mastectomy + Chronic Lymphedema + Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: The lesion might look like a simple bruise initially, which delays diagnosis.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively... or precipitously.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular lesions is characterized histologically by large, dilated vascular channels filled with blood and separated by a scant connective tissue stroma, often occurring in the liver or spleen?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas have small, thin-walled capillaries, not large dilated spaces.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, blood-filled vascular spaces (caverns). They are the most common benign tumor of the liver.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors have small vessels surrounded by nests of specialized glomus cells.
explanations.d: Angiosarcomas show malignant, poorly formed vessels and nuclear atypia.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis shows capillary proliferation with neutrophilic inflammation and bacteria.

ankiCards: The most common benign tumor of the liver is the {{c1::cavernous hemangioma}}.
Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, {{c1::dilated}} vascular spaces.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas do {{c1::not}} spontaneously regress.
A clinical risk of liver cavernous hemangioma is {{c1::rupture/bleeding}} (though rare).
Biopsy of a suspected liver hemangioma is generally {{c1::avoided}} due to risk of bleeding.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign.
Most common in the liver and CNS.
Spaces are filled with blood and separated by fibrous stroma.
Usually asymptomatic and found incidentally on imaging.
Can be part of von Hippel-Lindau disease if found in the CNS.
microReview: Cavernous Hemangioma: Liver + Large Blood Spaces + Benign + Most common liver tumor.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse with 'Strawberry hemangioma' (capillary type, regresses) or 'Cystic hygroma' (lymphatic type).
sourceQuote: To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male presents to the clinic for a routine physical examination. He has a 40-pack-year smoking history and long-standing hypertension. On abdominal palpation, a non-tender, pulsatile mass is noted at the level of the umbilicus. Ultrasound confirms a 5.2-cm localized dilation of the infrarenal abdominal aorta involving all layers of the vessel wall. Which of the following is the most likely primary pathological process responsible for this finding?

explanations.a: Cystic medial degeneration is more commonly associated with thoracic aortic aneurysms in the context of Marfan syndrome, rather than the abdominal aorta.
explanations.b: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAAs) are typically true aneurysms involving all three layers, where the primary underlying mechanism is the destruction and weakening of the tunica media, often secondary to atherosclerosis.
explanations.c: While endothelial dysfunction is an early step in atherosclerosis, it is not the direct structural mechanism that leads to the weakening and dilation of the vessel wall.
explanations.d: Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis is a response to malignant hypertension affecting small vessels (arterioles), resulting in an 'onion-skin' appearance, not large-vessel aneurysms.
explanations.e: Vasa vasorum endarteritis (obliterative endarteritis) is a characteristic finding of tertiary syphilis, which primarily affects the ascending aorta rather than the infrarenal abdominal aorta.

ankiCards: The two principal mechanisms of vascular disease are narrowing/obstruction and {{c1::weakening of vessel walls}}.
A 'true' aneurysm involves {{c1::all three layers}} of the vessel wall (intima, media, and adventitia).
The most common cause of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Vascular wall weakening in aneurysms typically results from the degradation of the {{c1::tunica media}}.
{{c1::Atherosclerosis}} mainly affects elastic and muscular arteries.
keyPoints: Vascular disease arises from lumen narrowing/obstruction or wall weakening.
True aneurysms must involve the intima, media, and adventitia.
AAAs are predominantly infrarenal and associated with smoking and atherosclerosis.
Weakening of the vessel wall leads to dilation or rupture.
The tunica media's structural integrity is critical for resisting high pulsatile pressures.
Arterial walls are thicker than veins to accommodate higher blood pressures.
microReview: Aneurysms represent a failure of the structural integrity of the vessel wall. In the aorta, this usually manifests as the degradation of the media (via MMPs and inflammation in atherosclerosis or TGF-beta signaling in genetic syndromes). Abdominal sites favor atherosclerosis-driven media thinning, whereas thoracic sites favor cystic medial degeneration or syphilis.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse AAA with Aortic Dissection. Dissection involves blood tracking between layers (false lumen), whereas a true aneurysm involves the dilation of all intact layers.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following fundamental structural characteristics explains why arterial walls are significantly thicker than their corresponding venous counterparts at the same level of branching?

options.a: Higher density of vasa vasorum in the adventitia
options.b: Need to accommodate pulsatile flow and high pressure
options.c: Presence of a thicker intimal layer in arteries

explanations.a: Vasa vasorum are more numerous in veins because they carry deoxygenated blood, necessitating an external nutrient supply for the outer wall.
explanations.b: According to the principles of vascular structure, arterial walls are thicker to accommodate the high pressures and pulsatile flow generated by cardiac contraction.
explanations.c: The intima is typically the thinnest layer in a healthy vessel; the media is the layer that provides the thickness and strength to arteries.
explanations.d: Valves, not wall thickness, are the primary mechanism for preventing retrograde flow in the venous system.
explanations.e: Metabolic exchange occurs in capillaries, which are characterized by an extremely thin wall (single layer of endothelium) to facilitate diffusion.

ankiCards: Arterial walls are thicker than veins to accommodate {{c1::pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures}}.
As arteries become smaller, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}}.
Muscular vessels exert control over blood flow and pressure by adjusting {{c1::lumen diameter}}.
The architectural composition of blood vessels is comparable throughout the system, but structural specializations reflect {{c1::distinct functional roles}}.
Atherosclerosis affects mainly {{c1::elastic and muscular}} arteries.
keyPoints: Vessel architecture reflects the hemodynamic demands of the specific vascular bed.
Arteries have higher wall-to-lumen ratios as they transition to resistance vessels (arterioles).
The tunica media is the primary determinant of arterial wall thickness.
Venous systems operate under low pressure and thus require thinner walls.
Structural failure of the arterial media leads directly to aneurysm formation.
microReview: Arteries must withstand systolic pressures. Their thickness, primarily in the tunica media, allows them to maintain structural integrity. When this wall is weakened—either by intrinsic defects or extrinsic factors like atherosclerosis—the lumen dilates, forming an aneurysm.
examinerTraps: A common mistake is thinking the 'intima' is the thickest layer due to atherosclerosis. In health, the media is the thickest and most structurally significant layer in arteries.
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular pathology is categorized as a leading cause of morbidity and mortality. Which of the following is one of the two principal mechanisms identified as the basis for most clinically significant vascular disease?

options.d: Pathologic thickening of the vasa vasorum
options.e: Selective depletion of smooth muscle cells

explanations.a: Arteriovenous shunting is a vascular anomaly, but not one of the two 'principal mechanisms' of general vascular disease described in core pathology.
explanations.b: The two principal mechanisms are: 1) narrowing/obstruction (stenosis/thrombosis) and 2) weakening of walls leading to dilation/rupture.
explanations.c: Endothelial growth signaling is involved in repair, but its inhibition is not one of the two primary mechanisms of disease mentioned.
explanations.d: Vasa vasorum pathology occurs (e.g., in syphilis), but it is a specific etiology, not a broad primary mechanism.
explanations.e: Smooth muscle cell depletion is a feature of certain pathologies (like medial thinning), but it is not listed as a primary broad category.

ankiCards: The two primary mechanisms of vascular disease are lumen narrowing and {{c1::vessel wall weakening}}.
Progressive narrowing of vessel lumens is most commonly caused by {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Precipitous obstruction of vessel lumens is often caused by {{c1::thrombosis or embolism}}.
Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity than {{c1::any other category}} of human disease.
Weakening of vessel walls leads to either {{c1::dilation or rupture}}.
keyPoints: Narrowing/Obstruction is the first major mechanism of vascular disease.
Wall Weakening (leading to aneurysm/dissection) is the second major mechanism.
Atherosclerosis is the classic example of progressive narrowing.
Embolism/Thrombosis represents precipitous obstruction.
Dilation (aneurysm) and rupture are the consequences of wall weakening.
microReview: All vascular disease boils down to either the 'pipe' getting blocked (narrowing/obstruction) or the 'pipe' wall failing (weakening/dilation). Aneurysms fall into the second category.
examinerTraps: The examiner may list specific diseases (like Polyarteritis Nodosa). Remember that the 'mechanism' refers to the functional outcome (blockage or weakening).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old female with a history of tobacco use and hyperlipidemia presents with sudden, severe abdominal pain radiating to her back. She is hypotensive (BP 80/50 mmHg) and tachycardic. Physical exam reveals a large, tender, pulsatile abdominal mass. If this patient had survived, a biopsy of the affected vessel would most likely have shown which of the following?

explanations.a: Atypical lymphoid infiltrates suggest lymphoma, which does not cause acute aortic rupture.
explanations.b: This patient has a ruptured AAA. The most common underlying factor for AAA is atherosclerosis, which causes thinning of the underlying media through pressure and nutrient diffusion impairment.
explanations.c: Giant cell inflammation is typical of Temporal Arteritis or Takayasu Arteritis, which usually cause stenosis or systemic symptoms, not typically infrarenal AAA rupture.
explanations.d: Medial necrotizing vasculitis is not the standard term for the atherosclerotic weakening seen in AAA.
explanations.e: Fibrinoid necrosis is characteristic of Polyarteritis Nodosa or malignant hypertension, affecting small to medium arteries, not the aorta.

ankiCards: The classic triad of a ruptured AAA is {{c1::pain, hypotension, and a pulsatile mass}}.
Biopsy of an AAA usually shows advanced {{c1::atherosclerosis}} with medial thinning.
AAAs are most frequently found {{c1::infrarenal}}.
Sudden abdominal pain radiating to the back in an elderly smoker suggests {{c1::AAA rupture}}.
{{c1::Smoking}} is the most significant risk factor for the development of AAA.
keyPoints: AAA rupture is a surgical emergency.
Risk of rupture is directly proportional to the diameter of the aneurysm.
Atherosclerosis contributes to media weakening by obstructing nutrient diffusion from the lumen.
Most AAAs are asymptomatic until they rupture or cause mass effect.
The back pain in AAA rupture is caused by retroperitoneal hemorrhage.
microReview: In AAA, atherosclerosis 'starves' the tunica media of oxygen and nutrients (which normally diffuse from the lumen), leading to smooth muscle cell loss and ECM degradation. This weakening results in an aneurysm that can eventually rupture.
examinerTraps: Wait for the 'pulsatile mass'—it is the hallmark of AAA. If it's just 'tearing pain' without the mass, think dissection.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following changes in vessel morphology occurs as arterial branching progresses from large elastic arteries toward smaller muscular arteries and arterioles?

options.a: The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases
options.b: The total volume of the tunica adventitia decreases
options.c: The amount of elastic fibers in the media increases
options.d: The number of vasa vasorum in the wall increases
options.e: The absolute thickness of the vessel wall increases

explanations.a: While the absolute thickness of the wall decreases as vessels get smaller, the relative ratio of wall thickness to the diameter of the lumen increases, giving these vessels greater control over pressure.
explanations.b: While the adventitia may thin, it is the thickness-to-lumen ratio that is the specific structural adaptation highlighted in core pathology texts.
explanations.c: Elastic fibers decrease as you move from elastic (aorta) to muscular arteries; muscular arteries have more smooth muscle.
explanations.d: Vasa vasorum are primarily needed in very thick-walled large vessels where diffusion from the lumen is insufficient.
explanations.e: The absolute thickness decreases as the vessel size decreases; it is the *ratio* that increases.

ankiCards: Arterial wall thickness gradually {{c1::diminishes}} as vessels become smaller.
The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}} in smaller muscular vessels.
Muscular vessels exert control over {{c1::blood flow and pressure}}.
Elastic arteries transition into {{c1::muscular}} arteries.
Specific kinds of vessels are characterized by {{c1::structural specializations}} reflecting functional roles.
keyPoints: Elastic arteries (e.g., aorta) serve as conducting vessels.
Muscular arteries and arterioles serve as resistance vessels.
Higher thickness-to-lumen ratios in arterioles allow for significant blood pressure regulation.
Pathology in these layers leads to different disease states (Aneurysm vs. Hypertension).
Vascular structure is tailored to the hemodynamic environment.
microReview: Large arteries = High elastic content (to dampen pulse). Small arteries = High muscle-to-lumen ratio (to control resistance/BP). Structural weakness in the former leads to aneurysms.
examinerTraps: The 'absolute' vs 'relative' thickness trap. Arterioles are much thinner than the aorta, but compared to their own tiny hole (lumen), their walls are relatively very thick.
sourceQuote: Arterial wall thickness gradually diminishes as the vessels become smaller, but the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing these muscular vessels to exert control over blood flow and pressure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old male is diagnosed with a 'false aneurysm' (pseudoaneurysm) of the femoral artery following a cardiac catheterization. Which of the following best describes the structural characteristic of this lesion?

options.a: A focal dilation involving all three layers of the vessel wall
options.b: An extravascular hematoma that communicates with the intravascular space
options.c: A longitudinal tear in the media allowing blood to track between layers
options.d: A localized bulge consisting only of the tunica adventitia
options.e: A uniform circumferential dilation of the arterial segment

explanations.a: A focal dilation involving all three layers defines a true aneurysm (saccular).
explanations.b: A pseudoaneurysm (false aneurysm) is a collection of blood that forms outside the vessel wall, contained by surrounding connective tissue, but still communicating with the lumen.
explanations.c: Blood tracking between layers describes an aortic dissection.
explanations.d: A true aneurysm involves all layers; if only adventitia were involved, it would likely still be a type of pseudoaneurysm if the media was breached.
explanations.e: Uniform circumferential dilation describes a fusiform true aneurysm.

ankiCards: A pseudoaneurysm is an {{c1::extravascular hematoma}} communicating with the lumen.
A true aneurysm involves {{c1::all three layers}} of the vessel wall.
A {{c1::fusiform}} aneurysm is a circumferential, symmetrical dilation.
A {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm is a localized out-pouching.
Pseudoaneurysms often occur following {{c1::trauma or catheterization}}.
keyPoints: True aneurysms (saccular/fusiform) are bounded by all arterial layers.
False aneurysms result from a wall defect.
Common causes of pseudoaneurysm include trauma, infection, or iatrogenic injury.
Dissection is distinct from aneurysm (blood within the wall vs. wall dilation).
Aneurysms are classified by shape and wall involvement.
microReview: True = 3 layers intact but stretched. False = Wall punctured, blood leak contained by tissue 'scab' or adventitia.
examinerTraps: Mistaking 'saccular' for 'false'. Saccular is a 'true' aneurysm because the wall layers (though thin) are still present.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 40-year-old male with a history of Marfan syndrome presents for evaluation. Imaging reveals dilation of the aortic root and the ascending thoracic aorta. The patient is at risk for aneurysm formation due to an inherited defect in fibrillin-1. This defect primarily leads to the weakening of which vascular component?

explanations.a: Endothelial junctions relate to permeability, not the structural tensile strength needed to prevent aneurysms.
explanations.b: Fibrillin-1 mutations lead to dysregulated TGF-beta signaling and loss of elastic fibers in the tunica media (cystic medial degeneration), weakening the ECM.
explanations.c: The internal elastic lamina is a single layer; the general media ECM is the primary structural failure site in Marfan-related TAA.
explanations.d: Metabolic defects of smooth muscle cells are not the primary mechanism of Marfan syndrome.
explanations.e: While vasa vasorum issues cause syphilis-related aneurysms, they are not the primary mechanism in Marfan syndrome.

ankiCards: Marfan syndrome is associated with aneurysms of the {{c1::thoracic aorta (aortic root)}}.
The genetic defect in Marfan syndrome involves {{c1::fibrillin-1}}.
Weakening of the {{c1::tunica media}} is the hallmark of Marfan-associated aneurysms.
Cystic medial degeneration involves the loss of {{c1::elastic fibers}}.
Dysregulated {{c1::TGF-beta}} signaling is a key pathway in Marfan vascular pathology.
keyPoints: Thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAA) are often genetic (Marfan, Loeys-Dietz).
TAAs involve the ascending aorta.
Aortic root dilation can lead to aortic valve insufficiency.
Medial weakening is the common pathway for all true aneurysms.
Fibrillin is essential for the structural integrity of elastic arteries.
microReview: Marfan = Ascending Aorta = Medial Degeneration. Atherosclerosis = Abdominal Aorta = Medial Thinning.
examinerTraps: The examiner might ask for the specific protein (fibrillin) or the resulting histologic change (cystic medial degeneration).
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels... Arterial walls are thicker... to accommodate pulsatile flow.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the pathogenesis of abdominal aortic aneurysms, atherosclerosis contributes to the weakening of the arterial wall primarily through which of the following effects on the tunica media?

options.b: Increasing the diffusion distance for oxygen
options.c: Inducing hyperplasia of smooth muscle cells
options.e: Reducing the total number of vasa vasorum

explanations.a: Coagulation factors are involved in thrombosis, not the chronic structural weakening of the media.
explanations.b: Atherosclerotic plaques in the intima increase the diffusion distance for oxygen and nutrients from the lumen to the media, leading to ischemic medial necrosis and weakening.
explanations.c: Aneurysms are characterized by medial thinning and smooth muscle *loss*, not hyperplasia.
explanations.d: While intimal calcification occurs in atherosclerosis, it is the medial thinning/weakening that leads to the aneurysm.
explanations.e: Vasa vasorum actually often proliferate (neo-vascularization) in response to atherosclerotic plaques, though they remain insufficient to prevent medial ischemia.

ankiCards: In AAA, atherosclerosis causes {{c1::ischemic}} injury to the tunica media.
Atherosclerotic plaques increase the {{c1::diffusion distance}} for nutrients from the lumen.
Weakening of the media leads to vascular {{c1::dilation}}.
Atherosclerosis primarily affects {{c1::elastic and muscular}} arteries.
The result of chronic medial ischemia in the aorta is {{c1::aneurysm formation}}.
keyPoints: The media of the aorta depends partly on diffusion from the lumen.
Thick intimal plaques block this diffusion.
Resultant medial atrophy weakens the vessel wall.
Inflammatory cells in plaques also release proteases (MMPs) that degrade the ECM.
The abdominal aorta is particularly susceptible as it has fewer vasa vasorum than the thoracic aorta.
microReview: Plaque = Wall Thickening in Intima + Wall Weakening in Media. The media 'starves' because it's too far from the blood in the lumen.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'thickened wall' (due to plaque) with 'strong wall'. Aneurysmal walls are often very thin and fragile despite the presence of plaque.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which layer of the arterial wall is primarily responsible for the structural specialized role of exerting control over blood flow and pressure in muscular vessels?

explanations.a: The external elastic lamina is a boundary layer, not the primary contractile component.
explanations.b: The internal elastic lamina separates the intima from the media.
explanations.c: The adventitia contains connective tissue and vasa vasorum but does not exert active pressure control.
explanations.d: The intima is a single layer of endothelium and minimal subendothelial tissue.
explanations.e: The tunica media, composed of smooth muscle cells, is the thickest layer in arteries and is responsible for vasoconstriction/vasodilation to regulate pressure.

ankiCards: The layer of the artery containing smooth muscle is the {{c1::tunica media}}.
Muscular vessels exert control over pressure via the {{c1::ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter}}.
The thickest layer in a healthy artery is the {{c1::tunica media}}.
Vascular wall response to injury often involves the {{c1::intima}}.
Medial weakening is the root cause of {{c1::aneurysms}}.
keyPoints: The tunica media is the 'muscular' part of the artery.
Media thickness correlates with the vessel's ability to resist pressure.
Resistance to flow is regulated at the level of muscular arteries and arterioles.
Aneurysm results when the media can no longer sustain the wall tension.
Wall thickness to lumen diameter ratio is highest in resistance vessels.
microReview: Media = Muscle = Management of pressure. If the Media is messed up, you get an aneurysm (loss of structural strength) or can't control BP.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the *response* to injury (intimal thickening) with the *normal* control of pressure (medial contraction).
sourceQuote: the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing these muscular vessels to exert control over blood flow and pressure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following fundamental mechanisms is most directly responsible for the development of an abdominal aortic aneurysm in the context of atherosclerosis?

options.a: Increased synthesis of type I collagen in the adventitia
options.b: Inhibition of matrix metalloproteinases in the media
options.c: Impaired nutrient diffusion due to intimal thickening
options.d: Hyperplasia of the vasa vasorum in the media

explanations.a: Synthesis of collagen is typically decreased or disorganized, not increased, leading to wall weakening.
explanations.b: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) are usually upregulated, not inhibited, which leads to the degradation of the extracellular matrix.
explanations.c: Atherosclerotic intimal thickening increases the distance for oxygen and nutrients to diffuse from the lumen to the media, leading to medial ischemia and weakening.
explanations.d: The media of the abdominal aorta is relatively avascular; atherosclerosis compromises what little supply exists and does not typically lead to beneficial hyperplasia.
explanations.e: Pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-1, TNF) are characteristically secreted by macrophages in the plaque, promoting matrix degradation.

ankiCards: The two principal mechanisms underlying vascular disease are narrowing/obstruction and {{c1::weakening of vessel walls}}.
Weakening of vessel walls leads to two major clinical outcomes: {{c1::dilation}} or {{c2::rupture}}.
In atherosclerosis, medial weakening is often caused by impaired {{c1::nutrient diffusion}} through a thickened intima.
Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAAs) are most frequently associated with the underlying condition {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
The degradation of the extracellular matrix in aneurysms is largely mediated by {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
keyPoints: Vascular disease involves either lumen obstruction or wall weakening.
Wall weakening leads to aneurysmal dilation or rupture.
Atherosclerosis causes medial ischemia by increasing diffusion distance from the lumen.
Medial ischemia results in the loss of smooth muscle cells and elastic fibers.
Inflammatory infiltrates in atherosclerotic plaques release proteases that further degrade the matrix.
The abdominal aorta is the most common site for atherosclerotic aneurysms.
microReview: Aneurysms occur when the structural integrity of the vessel wall is compromised. In the abdominal aorta, this is most commonly due to atherosclerosis, which causes intimal thickening. This thickening acts as a barrier to the diffusion of oxygen and nutrients from the lumen to the media, leading to medial degeneration and weakening.
examinerTraps: A common mistake is thinking the vasa vasorum provides enough nutrients to the abdominal aorta; however, the distal aorta is relatively poorly supplied, making it more vulnerable to luminal diffusion issues.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipi-tously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism) • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which histological layer's degradation is the hallmark of the 'weakening of vessel walls' that directly precedes the formation of a true aneurysm?

explanations.a: The adventitia contains supportive connective tissue and vasa vasorum but its primary degradation is not the defining hallmark of early aneurysm formation.
explanations.b: The tunica media contains the smooth muscle and elastic fibers responsible for vessel recoil and strength; its degradation is the central step in wall weakening.
explanations.c: The intima is involved in atherosclerosis, but it is the secondary weakening of the media that leads to the actual aneurysm.
explanations.d: While this layer is damaged, the generalized loss of medial integrity (cystic medial necrosis or smooth muscle loss) is more critical for global wall weakening.
explanations.e: The external elastic lamina is part of the media/adventitia junction, but media loss is the primary driver.

ankiCards: The hallmark histological layer affected in the development of a true aneurysm is the {{c1::tuna media}}.
A true aneurysm involves an intact but thinned {{c1::attenuated}} wall layer.
Cystic medial degeneration involves the loss of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} and elastic tissue.
The media's strength is primarily derived from its {{c1::elastic fibers}} and collagen.
Degradation of the media leads to the mechanical failure known as {{c1::dilation}}.
keyPoints: True aneurysms involve all three layers of the vessel wall (intima, media, adventitia).
Weakening typically involves loss of smooth muscle cells from the media.
Reduced synthesis of collagen or increased degradation of elastin leads to media thinning.
Medial degeneration is often called 'cystic medial necrosis', though necrosis is not always present.
The structural failure of the media allows the high intraluminal pressure to bulge the wall.
microReview: Aneurysms represent a failure of the mechanical properties of the vessel wall. Since the tunica media provides the bulk of the tensile strength and elasticity, any process that results in medial thinning (ischemia, inflammation, or genetic defects in collagen) will lead to weakening and dilation.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse a true aneurysm (all three layers involved) with a pseudoaneurysm (a hematoma contained by extravascular tissue).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male smoker with a history of hypertension presents for a routine physical examination. On abdominal palpation, a non-tender, pulsatile mass is noted at the level of the umbilicus. Imaging reveals a 5.2 cm dilation of the infrarenal aorta. Which of the following biological processes is most likely occurring within the wall of the affected segment?

options.e: Hyaline thickening of the arteriolar walls

explanations.a: Lysyl oxidase is needed for collagen cross-linking; its deficiency, not increase, would lead to weakening.
explanations.b: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are characterized by chronic inflammatory infiltrates (macrophages, lymphocytes) that produce proteases like MMPs.
explanations.c: Smooth muscle cell apoptosis is actually increased in the media of aneurysmal walls.
explanations.d: While glycosaminoglycans can accumulate in cystic medial degeneration, 'chronic transmural inflammation' is more characteristic of the atherosclerotic AAA described.
explanations.e: Hyaline thickening is a feature of small vessel disease (arteriolosclerosis), not large vessel aneurysms.

ankiCards: The classic clinical finding for an Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA) is a {{c1::pulsatile mass}}.
The most important risk factor for AAA is {{c1::cigarette smoking}}.
AAAs are usually located below the level of the {{c1::renal arteries}}.
Inflammatory cells in an AAA secrete {{c1::proteases (or MMPs)}} that degrade the vessel wall.
AAA is primarily a complication of the condition {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
keyPoints: AAAs are most common in male smokers over age 50.
The infrarenal location is most frequent because it lacks vasa vasorum protection.
Chronic inflammation leads to elastolysis and media destruction.
Risk of rupture increases significantly once the diameter exceeds 5.0-5.5 cm.
Most AAAs are asymptomatic until they rupture or are found on exam.
microReview: This patient has a classic Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm. The underlying pathology is atherosclerosis, which triggers a chronic inflammatory response in the aortic wall. Macrophages release matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) that digest elastin and collagen, significantly weakening the media and leading to dilation.
examinerTraps: Aneurysms are often asymptomatic. The presence of pain usually suggests rapid expansion or impending rupture.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following is the most likely consequence of a persistent narrowing of the vasa vasorum in the thoracic aorta, as seen in tertiary syphilis?

explanations.a: Calcification is more characteristic of atherosclerosis rather than the specific endarteritis of syphilis.
explanations.b: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum leads to ischemic injury of the outer media, resulting in medial atrophy and scarring.
explanations.c: The adventitia becomes scarred (fibrotic), but the primary functional defect leading to aneurysm is medial atrophy.
explanations.d: Syphilitic aortitis leads to dilation (aneurysm), not stenosis of the aortic lumen.
explanations.e: Syphilis typically leads to 'tree-barking' of the intima due to underlying medial scarring, not simple subendothelial fibrosis.

ankiCards: Syphilitic (luetic) aneurysms primarily affect the {{c1::thoracic}} aorta.
The mechanism in syphilitic aortitis is the narrowing of the {{c1::vasa vasorum}}.
Ischemia of the outer media in syphilis leads to a condition called {{c1::medial atrophy}}.
The classic gross appearance of the intima in syphilitic aortitis is {{c1::tree-barking}}.
Syphilitic aneurysms can lead to death by {{c1::aortic valve insufficiency}} or rupture.
keyPoints: Tertiary syphilis causes obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum.
The thoracic aorta relies heavily on the vasa vasorum for medial nutrition.
Medial ischemia leads to the loss of elastic tissue and replacement by fibrous scars.
Scarring causes the intima to wrinkle, appearing like 'tree-bark'.
Weakening of the aortic root can lead to dilation and valvular regurgitation.
microReview: Syphilitic aortitis is a classic example of wall weakening due to nutrient deprivation. By narrowing the vasa vasorum, the spirochetes induce ischemia of the outer media. This ischemia causes the muscular and elastic components of the media to wither (medial atrophy), leading to massive dilation of the thoracic aorta.
examinerTraps: Contrast this with AAA, which is usually infrarenal and atherosclerotic. Syphilitic aneurysms are thoracic.
