examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'tree-barking' with 'fatty streaks'; tree-barking is a sign of syphilitic aortitis, while fatty streaks are early atherosclerosis.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 4-month-old male infant is brought to the pediatrician by his mother, who is concerned about a rapidly enlarging bright-red, raised lesion on the infant's left cheek. The lesion was not present at birth but appeared at age 2 weeks and has grown significantly since. On physical examination, the lesion is well-circumscribed, lobulated, and blanches partially with pressure. The physician informs the mother that the lesion is likely to spontaneously regress by age 7. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors are painful, subungual lesions arising from modified smooth muscle cells, typically seen in adults, not infants.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) are common benign tumors of infancy that appear shortly after birth, grow rapidly, and usually regress by age 7.
explanations.c: Angiosarcomas are highly malignant tumors seen primarily in older adults, often associated with radiation or chronic lymphedema.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granulomas are rapidly growing pedunculated red nodules on the skin or gingiva, often following trauma, and do not typically follow the 'grow then regress' cycle of infantile hemangiomas.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation caused by Bartonella infection, primarily seen in immunocompromised patients, not healthy infants.

ankiCards: The most common vascular tumor of infancy that typically regresses by age 7 is the {{c1::capillary (strawberry) hemangioma}}.
Capillary hemangiomas are characterized histologically by {{c1::closely packed capillaries}} with thin walls.
In contrast to port-wine stains, strawberry hemangiomas {{c1::regress}} over time.
Vascular tumors are divided into three grades: {{c1::benign}}, {{c1::intermediate (borderline)}}, and {{c1::malignant}}.
A cavernous hemangioma is often associated with {{c1::Von Hippel-Lindau}} disease when found in the cerebellum or brainstem.
keyPoints: Hemangiomas are common childhood tumors.
Strawberry hemangiomas appear shortly after birth and enlarge before regressing.
Histology shows thin-walled capillaries with scant stroma.
Classification of vascular tumors depends on endothelial differentiation and cellularity.
Most hemangiomas are localized, but they can be part of systemic syndromes.
microReview: Infantile hemangiomas follow a predictable lifecycle: proliferation followed by involution. They are benign and usually managed expectantly.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse strawberry hemangiomas with Port-wine stains (Nevus flammeus); Port-wine stains do not regress and grow proportionately with the child.
sourceQuote:
Vascular Tumors
Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions
Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors
Malignant Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old female presents with an intensely painful, small, bluish nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. She notes that the pain is triggered by exposure to cold. Histological examination reveals aggregates of specialized cells surrounding vascular spaces. From which of the following cell types does this tumor originate?

explanations.a: While endothelial cells line the vessels within the tumor, the characteristic neoplastic component is the glomus cell.
explanations.b: Pericytes are found in hemangiopericytomas, which are distinct from glomus tumors.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors arise from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts are the origin of fibromas, not glomus tumors.
explanations.e: Lymphatic endothelial cells are the origin of lymphangiomas.

ankiCards: Glomus tumors are most commonly found in the {{c1::subungual}} region (under the nail).
The clinical hallmark of a glomus tumor is {{c1::exquisite pain}}, often triggered by cold.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells.
The specialized structure involved in thermoregulation from which glomus tumors arise is the {{c1::glomus body}}.
On histology, glomus cells appear as {{c1::uniform, round}} cells surrounding vascular channels.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but extremely painful.
Classic location is subungual (under the fingernail).
Origin: Modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
Glomus bodies are neuromyoarterial receptors for temperature regulation.
Surgical excision is usually curative.
microReview: Painful subungual nodule + thermoregulation cell origin = Glomus Tumor.
examinerTraps: The examiner may try to confuse glomus tumors with 'glomus jugulare' tumors (paragangliomas); however, the subungual location and smooth muscle origin are specific for the vascular glomus tumor.
sourceQuote:
Vascular Tumors
Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions
Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors
Malignant Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old male with a history of HIV (CD4 count 150/mm³) presents with several painless, purple-to-red macules and plaques on his lower extremities and oral mucosa. A biopsy of a skin lesion shows spindle-shaped cells forming slit-like spaces containing red blood cells, along with a chronic inflammatory infiltrate. Which of the following infectious agents is the primary driver of this pathology?

explanations.a: HIV causes the immunosuppression that allows the tumor to develop, but it is not the direct oncogenic driver of the vascular proliferation.
explanations.b: HHV-8 (also known as Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus) is the causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma, which presents as vascular lesions in immunocompromised hosts.
explanations.c: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can look similar clinically but shows a neutrophilic infiltrate rather than spindle cells with slit-like spaces.
explanations.d: EBV is associated with lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not vascular tumors.
explanations.e: CMV causes retinitis and colitis in AIDS patients but not vascular skin tumors.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is strongly associated with infection by {{c1::HHV-8}}.
The characteristic histological feature of KS is {{c1::spindle cells}} forming {{c2::slit-like spaces}}.
In KS, the slit-like spaces usually contain {{c1::red blood cells}}.
The most common form of KS in the United States is {{c1::AIDS-associated (epidemic)}} KS.
Unlike KS, bacillary angiomatosis features a {{c1::neutrophilic}} inflammatory infiltrate.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a low-grade malignant vascular tumor.
HHV-8 is essential for the pathogenesis of all forms of KS.
Stages include patch, plaque, and nodular stages.
Common sites: skin, mouth, GI tract, and lymph nodes.
KS is an AIDS-defining illness.
microReview: AIDS patient + purple skin lesions + spindle cells/slits = HHV-8 associated Kaposi Sarcoma.
examinerTraps: The examiner often places HIV in the options to see if you can distinguish between the cause of immunosuppression (HIV) and the cause of the tumor itself (HHV-8).
sourceQuote:
Vascular Tumors
Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions
Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors
Malignant Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male who worked in a chemical plant for 30 years presents with weight loss and abdominal pain. Imaging reveals multiple masses in the liver. A biopsy confirms a high-grade malignant vascular tumor. Exposure to which of the following substances is most strongly associated with this specific malignancy?

explanations.a: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and lung cancer, not hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Benzene exposure is a risk factor for acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.c: Vinyl chloride (used in PVC production), arsenic, and Thorotrast are classic risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: Beryllium exposure causes berylliosis (a granulomatous lung disease) and lung cancer.
explanations.e: Aflatoxin B1 is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.

ankiCards: Three classic risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma are {{c1::vinyl chloride}}, {{c2::arsenic}}, and {{c3::Thorotrast}}.
Angiosarcoma is a {{c1::malignant}} tumor of endothelial cells.
The vascular marker {{c1::CD31}} is typically positive in angiosarcomas.
Angiosarcomas that occur in the arm after radical mastectomy are known as {{c1::Stewart-Treves}} syndrome.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is a highly aggressive tumor with a {{c1::poor}} prognosis.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is linked to specific environmental toxins (Vinyl chloride).
Cutaneous angiosarcoma can occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema.
Histology shows pleomorphic malignant cells forming irregular vascular channels.
CD31 (an endothelial marker) is used for diagnosis.
microReview: Hepatic Angiosarcoma = Vinyl Chloride / Arsenic / Thorotrast. Poor prognosis. Malignant endothelial cells.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Aflatoxin (Hepatocellular carcinoma) with Vinyl Chloride (Hepatic Angiosarcoma).
sourceQuote:
Vascular Tumors
Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions
Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors
Malignant Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following histopathological features most reliably distinguishes a cavernous hemangioma from a capillary hemangioma?

explanations.a: Both capillary and cavernous hemangiomas are benign and do not typically show endothelial atypia.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are characterized by large, dilated (cavernous) blood-filled vascular spaces, while capillary hemangiomas consist of small, thin-walled capillaries.
explanations.c: Mitotic figures are generally low in both benign hemangiomas.
explanations.d: HHV-8 is associated with Kaposi Sarcoma, not benign hemangiomas.
explanations.e: Inflammation is not a defining feature for distinguishing these two types of hemangiomas.

ankiCards: {{c1::Cavernous}} hemangiomas consist of large, dilated vascular channels.
{{c1::Capillary}} hemangiomas consist of small, closely packed, thin-walled vessels.
Cavernous hemangiomas of the liver are the most common {{c1::benign}} liver tumor.
Unlike strawberry hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas usually {{c1::do not}} spontaneously regress.
A potential complication of large cavernous hemangiomas is {{c1::thrombosis}} or consumption of platelets.
keyPoints: Capillary vs. Cavernous is based on the diameter of the vascular spaces.
Both are benign endothelial proliferations.
Cavernous hemangiomas can involve deep structures (liver, brain).
Cavernous hemangiomas are more likely to require clinical attention due to size or location.
They are usually well-circumscribed but not encapsulated.
microReview: Capillary = Small vessels. Cavernous = Large vessels. Both = Benign.
examinerTraps: The examiner may suggest 'malignant transformation' as a distractor; benign hemangiomas almost never transform into angiosarcomas.
sourceQuote:
Vascular Tumors
Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions
Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors
Malignant Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 26-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated mass on her gingiva. The lesion bleeds easily with minor trauma. The physician explains that this is a 'pregnancy tumor' and may regress after delivery. Which of the following is the most likely pathological diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cystic hygroma is a cavernous lymphangioma typically found in the neck of infants and associated with Turner syndrome.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation in immunocompromised patients.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) often occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum) and can regress postpartum.
explanations.d: Cavernous lymphangioma describes large lymphatic spaces, not the small vascular spaces and prominent inflammation of pyogenic granuloma.
explanations.e: Spider angiomas are small telangiectasias associated with high estrogen states (like pregnancy or cirrhosis) but are not pedunculated masses.

ankiCards: The clinical term for a pyogenic granuloma occurring in a pregnant patient is {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized histologically as {{c1::lobular capillary hemangiomas}}.
A key clinical feature of pyogenic granulomas is that they {{c1::bleed easily}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are often preceded by {{c1::trauma}}.
Histology of a pyogenic granuloma shows proliferating capillaries with {{c1::edema}} and {{c2::inflammation}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is neither pyogenic (pus-forming) nor a true granuloma.
It is a form of capillary hemangioma.
Commonly found on skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
Associated with pregnancy due to hormonal influences on the vasculature.
Surgical excision or curettage is the standard treatment if it doesn't regress.
microReview: Pregnancy + gingival red mass + bleeding = Pyogenic Granuloma (Granuloma Gravidarum).
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic granuloma' is a classic 'false name' trap. It is actually a vascular tumor, not a granulomatous inflammatory process.
sourceQuote:
Vascular Tumors
Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions
Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors
Malignant Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A biopsy of a cutaneous lesion in an immunocompromised patient reveals a vascular proliferation. Histology shows clusters of capillaries with prominent 'epithelioid' endothelial cells, a neutrophilic infiltrate, and granular purple material. Silver staining (Warthin-Starry) confirms the presence of bacilli. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi Sarcoma shows spindle cells, slit-like spaces, and a lymphocytic/plasma cell infiltrate, not neutrophils or bacteria.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella henselae or quintana and presents with vascular proliferation, neutrophilic inflammation, and visible bacilli on silver stain.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor with marked cellular atypia and no bacterial association.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign capillary hemangioma but lacks the specific bacterial clusters seen in bacillary angiomatosis.
explanations.e: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is an intermediate-grade tumor that lacks a neutrophilic infiltrate and bacterial clusters.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by organisms of the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
The histological hallmark that distinguishes bacillary angiomatosis from Kaposi Sarcoma is the presence of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
To visualize the bacteria in bacillary angiomatosis, a {{c1::silver (or Warthin-Starry)}} stain is used.
Bacillary angiomatosis is primarily seen in {{c1::immunocompromised/AIDS}} patients.
The source of Bartonella henselae is usually a {{c1::cat (scratch or bite)}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis mimics Kaposi Sarcoma clinically.
Caused by Bartonella henselae (cat scratch) or Bartonella quintana (body lice).
Key histology: Endothelial proliferation + Neutrophils + Bacteria.
Treatment involves antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin).
Essential to distinguish from KS because the treatments are entirely different.
microReview: AIDS + vascular skin lesion + Neutrophils + Silver stain (+) = Bacillary Angiomatosis.
examinerTraps: The presence of neutrophils is the 'giveaway' clue to distinguish this from Kaposi Sarcoma, which typically has a mononuclear infiltrate.
sourceQuote:
Vascular Tumors
Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions
Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors
Malignant Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular tumors is classified as an 'intermediate-grade (borderline)' neoplasm, meaning its behavior is between benign hemangiomas and highly malignant angiosarcomas?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors are strictly benign.
explanations.b: Cystic hygromas (cavernous lymphangiomas) are benign.
explanations.c: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is the classic example of an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
explanations.d: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a vascular ectasia (dilation), not a true neoplasm, and is benign.
explanations.e: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign neoplasms.

ankiCards: The classification of vascular tumors includes benign, {{c1::intermediate (borderline)}}, and malignant.
{{c1::Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma}} is an example of an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
Intermediate-grade tumors are characterized by {{c1::locally aggressive}} behavior but low metastatic potential compared to angiosarcomas.
{{c1::Kaposi Sarcoma}} is also often categorized as an intermediate-grade (borderline) malignancy.
The cells in an epithelioid hemangioendothelioma are {{c1::plump/cuboidal (epithelioid)}}.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors exist on a spectrum of malignancy.
Intermediate-grade tumors include Kaposi Sarcoma and Epithelioid Hemangioendothelioma.
Intermediate tumors can recur locally.
Angiosarcoma is the high-grade malignant end of the spectrum.
Hemangiomas are the benign end of the spectrum.
microReview: Classification: Benign (Hemangioma) -> Intermediate (Kaposi, Epithelioid Hemangioendothelioma) -> Malignant (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: The examiner may use 'Hemangiopericytoma' (now often classified elsewhere) or 'Epithelioid hemangioma' (benign) to confuse you with 'Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma' (intermediate).
sourceQuote:
Vascular Tumors
Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions
Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors
Malignant Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 10-year-old girl with Turner syndrome (45,X) is found to have a large, soft, fluctuant mass in the left posterior triangle of her neck. The mass transilluminates on physical exam. Imaging shows a multicystic lesion containing clear fluid but no red blood cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas contain blood and would not appear as clear-fluid multicystic masses.
explanations.b: Cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) is a common finding in the neck of children, especially those with Turner syndrome or Down syndrome.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are small, painful, and subungual; they do not present as large neck masses.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis presents as red/purple skin nodules, not large cystic neck masses.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a solid malignant tumor of adults, not a cystic lesion of childhood.

ankiCards: A cystic hygroma is a {{c1::cavernous lymphangioma}}.
Cystic hygromas are characteristically associated with {{c1::Turner}} syndrome.
Unlike hemangiomas, lymphangiomas lack {{c1::red blood cells}} in their lumens.
The classic location for a cystic hygroma is the {{c1::neck (or axilla)}}.
On physical exam, cystic hygromas often {{c1::transilluminate}}.
keyPoints: Cystic hygromas are benign lymphatic malformations.
Often present at birth or in early childhood.
Frequently associated with chromosomal aneuploidies (Turner syndrome).
They consist of large, dilated lymphatic spaces lined by endothelium.
Treatment is surgical, though they can be difficult to remove completely.
microReview: Turner syndrome + neck mass + cystic/transilluminates = Cystic Hygroma.
examinerTraps: A common trap is confusing 'cystic hygroma' with 'branchial cleft cyst'. While both appear in the neck, the association with Turner syndrome and the multicystic lymphatic nature point to cystic hygroma.

stem: Which of the following markers is most commonly used by pathologists to confirm the endothelial origin of a suspected poorly differentiated vascular malignancy?

explanations.a: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells (carcinomas).
explanations.b: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells.
explanations.c: CD31 (PECAM-1) and von Willebrand factor (vWF) are highly specific markers for endothelial cells.
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells (melanoma, Schwann cells).
explanations.e: Vimentin is a non-specific marker for all mesenchymal cells; while positive in vascular tumors, it is not specific for them.

ankiCards: The most specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial cells is {{c1::CD31}}.
Another marker used for vascular tumors is {{c1::von Willebrand factor (vWF)}}.
CD31 is also known as {{c1::PECAM-1}}.
Immunohistochemistry is essential to distinguish poorly differentiated {{c1::angiosarcomas}} from carcinomas.
Malignant vascular tumors are of {{c1::mesenchymal}} origin.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors are of mesenchymal origin.
CD31 is the most reliable marker for endothelial differentiation.
Markers are critical for diagnosing high-grade angiosarcomas.
vWF (Factor VIII-related antigen) is also used.
These markers help rule out other spindle-cell malignancies.
microReview: Endothelial Marker = CD31 / vWF.
examinerTraps: Watch for 'Vimentin'; it is positive in all sarcomas, so it won't help you specifically identify a tumor as 'vascular'.

stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with an exquisitely painful, 4-mm, firm, red-blue nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. She notes that the pain is often triggered by exposure to cold. The lesion is surgically excised, and histopathological examination reveals nests of uniform, specialized smooth-muscle cells surrounding vascular spaces. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are common benign tumors that usually occur in the skin or mucous membranes and are not typically associated with extreme pain or cold sensitivity.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, blood-filled vascular spaces and are often deep-seated; they are not typically found in a subungual location nor are they characteristically painful.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, highly painful tumors arising from the specialized smooth-muscle cells of glomus bodies, which are involved in thermoregulation. They characteristically occur in the subungual region.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a rapidly growing pedunculated red nodule, often on the gingiva or skin, which bleeds easily and is associated with trauma or pregnancy, rather than exquisite pain.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a malignant vascular tumor that typically presents as larger, poorly defined, enlarging masses, most commonly in the scalp of elderly individuals or in the setting of chronic lymphedema.

ankiCards: The most common location for a {{c1::glomus tumor}} is the subungual (under the nail) region.
Glomus tumors arise from specialized {{c1::smooth muscle}} cells involved in thermoregulation.
A painful red-blue nodule under the nail that is sensitive to cold is characteristic of a {{c1::glomus tumor (glomangioma)}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors show nests of {{c1::uniform}} cells surrounding vascular spaces.
Unlike most vascular tumors, the glomus tumor is notable for being {{c1::exquisitely painful}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign neoplasms of modified smooth muscle cells.
They are part of the 'benign tumors' category of vascular pathology.
Classical presentation is a small, painful, subungual nodule.
Symptoms are often exacerbated by cold temperature.
Surgical excision is curative.
microReview: Vascular tumors are categorized into benign (hemangiomas, glomus tumors), intermediate (Kaposi sarcoma, hemangioendothelioma), and malignant (angiosarcoma). Glomus tumors are unique for their origin from glomus bodies and their clinical symptom of intense pain.
examinerTraps: Students often confuse glomus tumors with subungual hematomas; however, the exquisite pain and sensitivity to cold, along with the histopathology of specialized smooth muscle cells, are diagnostic for glomus tumor.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old male with a history of HIV and a CD4 count of 150 cells/mm³ presents with multiple purple, maculopapular skin lesions on his lower extremities. Biopsy reveals spindle-shaped cells, slit-like vascular spaces, and extravasated red blood cells. The pathogenesis of this condition is most strongly linked to which of the following pathogens?

explanations.a: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can look similar to Kaposi sarcoma in HIV patients, but it shows neutrophils and tangential bacteria rather than spindle cells.
explanations.b: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of all forms of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.c: Human papillomavirus 16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx, not vascular tumors.
explanations.d: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and hairy leukoplakia, but not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.e: Cytomegalovirus causes opportunistic infections in HIV patients (retinitis, colitis) but is not the driver of vascular neoplasia in Kaposi sarcoma.

ankiCards: The infectious agent associated with all forms of Kaposi sarcoma is {{c1::Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}.
The characteristic histology of Kaposi sarcoma includes {{c1::spindle}} cells and slit-like vascular spaces.
In the United States, Kaposi sarcoma is most commonly seen as an {{c1::AIDS}}-defining illness.
Unlike bacillary angiomatosis, Kaposi sarcoma histology lacks {{c1::neutrophils}} and bacteria.
HHV-8 is also known as {{c1::KSHV (Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus)}}.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
HHV-8 is the essential cofactor in the pathogenesis of KS.
KS presents in four forms: Classic, Endemic African, Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
Histology shows spindle cells, slit-like spaces with RBCs, and hemosiderin staining.
KS lesions progress from patches to plaques to nodules.
microReview: Kaposi sarcoma is categorized as an intermediate-grade (borderline) tumor. It is driven by HHV-8 and often occurs in the setting of immunosuppression.
examinerTraps: Distinguishing KS from Bacillary Angiomatosis is a common board topic. KS is spindle-cell dominant and HHV-8 positive; Bacillary Angiomatosis is neutrophil-rich and caused by Bartonella.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old woman presents with several firm, enlarging, violaceous nodules on her left arm. She has a history of a radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection and radiotherapy for breast cancer 10 years ago. Since the surgery, she has had persistent, non-pitting edema of the left arm. A biopsy of one of the nodules shows malignant endothelial cells with significant atypia. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is an intermediate-grade tumor associated with HHV-8; it does not typically arise in the setting of chronic lymphedema after breast cancer treatment.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign vascular proliferation in immunocompromised patients caused by Bartonella infection.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a malignant vascular tumor. When it occurs in the setting of chronic lymphedema (often post-mastectomy), it is specifically referred to as Stewart-Treves syndrome.
explanations.d: Cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) are benign lymphatic malformations, usually present at birth, and do not show malignant atypia.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are small, benign, exquisitely painful subungual nodules, which does not match this patient's clinical presentation.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma occurring in the setting of chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
Angiosarcoma is a {{c1::malignant}} vascular tumor that can be induced by radiation.
Malignant endothelial cells in angiosarcoma typically express the marker {{c1::CD31}}.
The classic clinical setting for Stewart-Treves syndrome is years after a {{c1::mastectomy}} with lymph node dissection.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are aggressive, high-grade malignant vascular tumors.
They can occur in skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to angiosarcoma following chronic lymphedema.
Histology shows pleomorphic, malignant cells forming vascular channels.
They have a very poor prognosis with frequent metastasis.
microReview: Malignant vascular tumors (angiosarcomas) can be triggered by lymphedema, radiation, or chemical carcinogens (like vinyl chloride for the liver).
examinerTraps: Patients post-mastectomy are at risk for Stewart-Treves syndrome. Examiners expect you to link 'chronic lymphedema' + 'purple skin nodules' + 'malignant cells' to Angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular lesions is characterized as a rapidly growing, pedunculated, red skin nodule that bleeds easily, is frequently associated with trauma or pregnancy, and histologically resembles exuberant granulation tissue?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas involve large vascular channels and are often deep-seated; they are not typically pedunculated or prone to easy bleeding.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas are the most common type and consist of small capillaries; they are usually not pedunculated nor associated with 'granulation tissue' appearance.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (granuloma pyogenicum) is a benign vascular lesion that grows rapidly, bleeds easily, and histologically appears as exuberant granulation tissue.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella and occurs in the immunocompromised, showing bacterial clusters on Warthin-Starry stain.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are small, painful subungual nodules, not large bleeding pedunculated masses.

ankiCards: A pedunculated vascular nodule on the gingiva of a pregnant woman is likely a {{c1::pyogenic granuloma}}.
Histologically, a pyogenic granuloma resembles {{c1::granulation tissue}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are often triggered by {{c1::trauma}} or pregnancy.
The term 'granuloma pyogenicum' is a misnomer because it is neither {{c1::granulomatous}} nor pyogenic (pus-forming).
Pyogenic granulomas are categorized under {{c1::benign}} vascular tumors.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign vascular proliferation.
Commonly found on skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
Frequent in pregnant women ('pregnancy tumor' or granuloma gravidarum).
Usually follows minor trauma.
Bleeds easily and grows rapidly.
microReview: Benign vascular tumors like pyogenic granulomas are reactive proliferations rather than true neoplasms in many cases, often following injury.
examinerTraps: The name is misleading—it contains no granulomas and is not primarily caused by infection (pyogenic). It is purely a vascular proliferation.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 2-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for a bright red, raised 'strawberry-like' birthmark on his forehead that has been enlarging since birth. The parents are concerned about its growth. Which of the following is the most likely natural history of this lesion?

options.b: Persistent growth proportional to the child's height
options.c: Spontaneous regression by age 7 to 9 years
options.d: Life-long stability without change in size
options.e: Early dissemination to the liver and spleen

explanations.a: Infantile hemangiomas are benign and do not transform into malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.b: Unlike vascular malformations (like port-wine stains), infantile hemangiomas undergo a predictable cycle of growth followed by regression.
explanations.c: Infantile (strawberry) hemangiomas typically grow for a few months and then slowly involute, with the vast majority regressing completely by age 7 to 9.
explanations.d: These lesions are dynamic and do not remain stable; they are known for their eventual regression.
explanations.e: While cavernous hemangiomas can involve internal organs, strawberry hemangiomas are typically cutaneous and do not disseminate.

ankiCards: Infantile hemangiomas are also known as {{c1::strawberry}} hemangiomas.
The natural history of a strawberry hemangioma involves rapid growth followed by {{c1::spontaneous regression}}.
Most strawberry hemangiomas disappear by the age of {{c1::7 to 9}}.
Strawberry hemangiomas are classified as {{c1::capillary}} hemangiomas.
They are the most {{c1::common}} tumor of infancy.
keyPoints: Infantile hemangiomas are extremely common benign tumors.
They are often not present at birth but appear in the first few weeks.
Characterized by a 'strawberry-like' appearance.
Regression is the rule; treatment is only needed if obstructing vision or airway.
Histology shows closely packed thin-walled capillaries.
microReview: Vascular tumors of childhood are overwhelmingly benign. The strawberry hemangioma is the classic example of a tumor that regresses spontaneously.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse 'infantile hemangioma' (regresses) with 'port-wine stain' (grows with the child and does not regress).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 50-year-old male presents with right upper quadrant pain and weight loss. Imaging reveals multiple masses in the liver. A biopsy shows a high-grade malignant tumor forming irregular vascular channels. Further history reveals the patient worked in a plastic manufacturing plant for 30 years with chronic exposure to vinyl chloride monomers. Which of the following tumors is most likely?

explanations.a: Hepatocellular carcinoma is associated with HBV/HCV and cirrhosis, not specifically vinyl chloride, and does not form vascular channels.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign, common, and asymptomatic incidental findings, not high-grade malignancies.
explanations.c: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare, highly malignant tumor with a known association with specific carcinogens including vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
explanations.d: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor, less aggressive than angiosarcoma and not classically linked to vinyl chloride.
explanations.e: Biliary cystadenoma is a benign cystic lesion of the bile ducts, unrelated to vascular markers or vinyl chloride.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to the chemical {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
Other risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma include {{c1::arsenic}} and Thorotrast.
Vinyl chloride exposure is classically associated with the {{c1::plastic}} manufacturing industry.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is a {{c1::malignant}} vascular tumor.
The prognosis for hepatic angiosarcoma is generally {{c1::poor}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms.
Environmental toxins are significant risk factors for the hepatic variant.
Vinyl chloride is used in PVC production.
Thorotrast was a radioactive contrast agent formerly used in radiology.
Histology demonstrates atypia and vascular channel formation.
microReview: Malignant tumors (angiosarcomas) of the liver are rare but provide a classic example of chemical carcinogenesis (vinyl chloride).
examinerTraps: While Hepatocellular Carcinoma is more common, 'vinyl chloride' + 'liver mass' + 'vascular channels' is the specific triad for Angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular tumors are categorized based on their clinical behavior. Which of the following is classified as an intermediate-grade (borderline) vascular tumor, exhibiting features between benign hemangiomas and highly malignant angiosarcomas?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors are strictly benign.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is the classic example of an intermediate-grade vascular tumor. It is locally aggressive but rarely as rapidly fatal as angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granulomas are benign reactive vascular proliferations.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign lesions.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious-induced benign proliferation of blood vessels.

ankiCards: {{c1::Kaposi sarcoma}} is the most well-known intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
Intermediate-grade tumors are also described as {{c1::borderline}} tumors.
The four clinical types of Kaposi sarcoma include Classic, Endemic, Transplant, and {{c1::AIDS}}-associated.
Intermediate-grade tumors like KS are more aggressive than {{c1::benign}} hemangiomas.
Intermediate-grade tumors are less aggressive than {{c1::angiosarcomas}}.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors span a spectrum from benign to malignant.
Intermediate-grade tumors (like KS and Hemangioendothelioma) are locally invasive.
They have a low but real potential for metastasis.
Kaposi sarcoma is driven by HHV-8.
They often require management of the underlying immune state.
microReview: The classification of vascular tumors into benign, intermediate, and malignant categories is a fundamental concept in vascular pathology as listed in the chapter contents.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'intermediate' with 'metastasizing'. While they can metastasize, their hallmark is being locally aggressive yet less rapid than true sarcomas.
sourceQuote: VASCULAR TUMORS: Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... Malignant Tumors...
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following immunohistochemical markers is most specific for identifying tumors of endothelial cell origin, such as angiosarcomas or hemangiomas?

explanations.a: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells (carcinomas).
explanations.b: Vimentin is a general marker for mesenchymal cells but is not specific to endothelium.
explanations.c: CD31 (also known as PECAM-1) is highly specific for endothelial cells and is used to confirm the vascular nature of a tumor.
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells (melanoma, Schwann cells).
explanations.e: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (leiomyomas, rhabdomyosarcomas).

ankiCards: The most useful immunohistochemical marker for endothelial cells is {{c1::CD31}}.
Another name for the CD31 marker is {{c1::PECAM-1}}.
Angiosarcomas are confirmed to be vascular in origin by positive staining for {{c1::CD31 or von Willebrand factor}}.
{{c1::Cytokeratin}} would be negative in most vascular tumors as they are not epithelial.
{{c1::Desmin}} would be positive in muscle tumors but negative in pure vascular tumors.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors arise from endothelial cells.
CD31 is the gold-standard marker for endothelium.
von Willebrand Factor (vWF) is also used but can be less sensitive.
Immunohistochemistry helps differentiate poorly differentiated angiosarcomas from carcinomas.
Markers like CD34 are also used but are less specific than CD31.
microReview: Endothelial markers are essential for diagnosing poorly differentiated malignant vascular tumors.
examinerTraps: CD34 is often given as an option; while it stains endothelium, it also stains many other mesenchymal tumors (like DFSP), making CD31 the 'single best' choice for specificity.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 40-year-old male with a history of recurrent seizures and intellectual disability is found to have multiple large, blood-filled spaces in his liver on routine ultrasound. Physical exam reveals several 'port-wine' stains on his face. This patient is at high risk for which of the following vascular malformations associated with his likely genetic syndrome?

explanations.a: Ataxia-telangiectasia involves cerebellar ataxia and telangiectasias, but not port-wine stains or the seizures described.
explanations.b: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) involves multiple telangiectasias and AVMs, primarily causing epistaxis and GI bleeding.
explanations.c: von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) is associated with cavernous hemangiomas of the cerebellum and retina, as well as renal cell carcinoma, but not typically facial port-wine stains.
explanations.d: Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) is characterized by a facial port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve, ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomas, seizures, and intellectual disability.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infection, not a genetic syndrome.

ankiCards: The combination of facial port-wine stain and leptomeningeal angiomas is called {{c1::Sturge-Weber syndrome}}.
Sturge-Weber syndrome is associated with {{c1::seizures}} and intellectual disability.
A port-wine stain is also known as a {{c1::nevus flammeus}}.
Unlike strawberry hemangiomas, port-wine stains {{c1::do not}} regress spontaneously.
Cavernous hemangiomas of the CNS are a feature of {{c1::von Hippel-Lindau}} disease.
keyPoints: Sturge-Weber syndrome is a congenital vascular disorder.
It involves capillary malformations (port-wine stains).
The facial lesion usually follows the V1/V2 trigeminal distribution.
Associated with 'tram-track' calcifications on brain imaging.
Cavernous hemangiomas are distinct from port-wine stains.
microReview: Syndromic associations of vascular tumors/malformations (VHL, Sturge-Weber, Osler-Weber-Rendu) are high-yield board topics.
examinerTraps: The examiner may use 'cavernous hemangioma' in the stem to distract you toward VHL, but the 'port-wine stain' and 'seizures' are the pathognomonic keys for Sturge-Weber.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An immunocompromised patient presents with multiple red-purple skin papules. Histologic analysis shows a vascular proliferation with prominent neutrophilic infiltrates and clusters of organisms that stain positive with Warthin-Starry silver stain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma has spindle cells and minimal inflammation; it does not stain with Warthin-Starry and is caused by HHV-8.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts caused by Bartonella (henselae or quintana). It is characterized by neutrophils and bacteria visible on Warthin-Starry stain.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor with significant atypia and no bacterial association.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign malformations of large vessels, not related to infection or neutrophilic infiltration.
explanations.e: Pyogenic granuloma shows granulation tissue-like proliferation but lacks the specific bacterial clusters seen in bacillary angiomatosis.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by bacteria of the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
The silver stain used to identify Bartonella in tissue is the {{c1::Warthin-Starry}} stain.
Unlike Kaposi sarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis contains an infiltrate of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
Bacillary angiomatosis occurs primarily in {{c1::immunocompromised/AIDS}} patients.
Treatment for bacillary angiomatosis is {{c1::antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin)}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis mimics Kaposi Sarcoma clinically.
It is a benign, opportunistic infection-induced vascular lesion.
Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch) and Bartonella quintana (trench fever) are the agents.
Histology: Proliferating capillaries, nuclear atypia, and neutrophilic debris.
Key diagnostic tool: Warthin-Starry stain showing granular purple bacilli.
microReview: Distinguishing the two main vascular lesions in AIDS (KS vs. Bacillary Angiomatosis) relies on the presence of neutrophils and the Warthin-Starry stain.
examinerTraps: Wait for the histology. If the question says 'spindle cells,' pick KS. If it says 'neutrophils and silver stain,' pick Bacillary Angiomatosis.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents for evaluation of several expanding, purple-red, cutaneous nodules on her right arm. She has a surgical history of a radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection 10 years ago for breast cancer, which was followed by local radiation. Since the surgery, she has had persistent, severe lymphedema in that extremity. Biopsy of a nodule shows atypical endothelial cells forming irregular, anastomosing vascular channels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma is a malignant vascular tumor that can arise in the setting of chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome), classically after radical mastectomy and lymph node dissection. Histology reveals poorly formed, anastomosing vascular channels lined by malignant endothelial cells.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign vascular proliferation seen in immunocompromised patients caused by Bartonella species; it lacks the malignant cytologic features and history of chronic lymphedema seen here.
explanations.c: Capillary hemangioma is a benign vascular lesion common in infants; it consists of well-formed capillaries and does not present as aggressive nodules in the setting of chronic lymphedema.
explanations.d: Glomus tumor is a painful, benign vascular tumor usually located under the fingernails, derived from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
explanations.e: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 and typically presents as purple plaques/nodules in HIV-infected patients; while it involves vascular proliferation, it is not specifically associated with chronic post-mastectomy lymphedema like angiosarcoma.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema (e.g., post-mastectomy) is known as {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
The malignant cell of origin in an angiosarcoma is the {{c1::endothelial cell}}.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is classically associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}} or Thorotrast.
Histologically, angiosarcomas demonstrate malignant cells forming {{c1::anastomosing vascular channels}}.
Unlike benign hemangiomas, angiosarcomas have a {{c1::poor}} prognosis with high rates of local recurrence and metastasis.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are aggressive, malignant endothelial neoplasms.
Chronic lymphedema is a major risk factor for cutaneous angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
Radiation therapy is a known iatrogenic risk factor for subsequent vascular malignancy.
Morphology ranges from well-formed vascular spaces to solid, undifferentiated sheets.
Immunohistochemical staining for CD31 is typically positive in these tumors.
microReview: Angiosarcomas: High-grade malignancy of endothelium. Associations: Stewart-Treves (lymphedema), Vinyl chloride (liver), Radiation (skin). Markers: CD31, vWF.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Stewart-Treves syndrome (angiosarcoma) with Kaposi sarcoma; both present as purple lesions, but the clinical context of chronic lymphedema versus HHV-8/HIV is the defining differentiator.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An 8-week-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for a rapidly growing, bright red, raised lesion on his forehead. The mother states it was not present at birth but appeared at two weeks of age. The lesion is soft, blanches partially with pressure, and measures 2 cm. What is the most likely natural history of this lesion?

options.a: Distant metastasis to the lungs and liver
options.c: Persistent growth proportional to child's height

explanations.a: Benign infantile hemangiomas do not metastasize.
explanations.b: Infantile (strawberry) hemangiomas are benign and do not undergo malignant transformation into angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Unlike port-wine stains (Nevus flammeus), which grow with the child, strawberry hemangiomas typically involute.
explanations.d: Infantile (strawberry) hemangiomas typically grow rapidly for several months and then begin to regress spontaneously, usually disappearing by age 7 to 9.
explanations.e: Isolated strawberry hemangiomas are typically cutaneous and not associated with systemic CNS involvement, unlike Sturge-Weber syndrome (which is associated with port-wine stains).

ankiCards: The most common vascular tumor of infancy is the {{c1::infantile (strawberry) hemangioma}}.
Strawberry hemangiomas typically appear {{c1::after birth}} (within weeks) rather than being present at birth.
The expected clinical course of a strawberry hemangioma is {{c1::spontaneous regression/involution}}.
Strawberry hemangiomas are histologically characterized as {{c1::capillary}} hemangiomas.
Unlike strawberry hemangiomas, {{c1::cavernous}} hemangiomas are more likely to involve deep structures and do not regress.
keyPoints: Infantile hemangiomas are the most common tumors of childhood.
They are 'strawberry' in appearance: bright red, lobulated, and elevated.
Vast majority (90%) involute by age 7.
Management is usually observation unless they obstruct vision or the airway.
They are composed of thin-walled capillaries with scant stroma.
microReview: Strawberry Hemangioma: Grows rapidly then regresses. Port-wine Stain: Flat, does not regress, grows with child.
examinerTraps: A common mistake is assuming all 'birthmarks' are permanent. Infantile hemangiomas are dynamic and specifically known for their regressive phase.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old male with a history of advanced HIV (CD4+ count 85/mm³) presents with several painless, reddish-purple macules and plaques on his lower extremities and oral mucosa. Biopsy of a lesion reveals sheets of spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells, and hyaline droplets. Which of the following pathogens is the causative agent of this condition?

explanations.a: Bartonella causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can look similar clinically but histologically shows lobular capillary proliferation with neutrophils and 'dust-like' bacteria, not slit-like spaces with spindle cells.
explanations.b: CMV causes systemic infections and retinitis in HIV but is not the cause of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.c: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and hairy leukoplakia, not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.d: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of all forms of Kaposi sarcoma (KS).
explanations.e: HPV is associated with squamous cell carcinomas and warts, not vascular tumors.

ankiCards: The causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
Histology of Kaposi Sarcoma shows {{c1::slit-like}} vascular spaces and {{c2::spindle}} cells.
Extravasated {{c1::red blood cells}} and hemosiderin are commonly seen in the slit-like spaces of Kaposi Sarcoma.
Kaposi Sarcoma is often associated with the {{c1::AIDS/HIV}} epidemic.
The four clinical forms of Kaposi Sarcoma are {{c1::Classic, Endemic African, Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated}}.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma is an intermediate-grade vascular neoplasm.
HHV-8 infects endothelial cells and promotes uncontrolled proliferation.
The disease often begins as macules (patch stage) and progresses to plaques and nodules.
Common sites include skin, mucous membranes, and the gastrointestinal tract.
In AIDS-associated KS, HAART therapy often leads to lesion regression.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma: HHV-8, spindle cells, slit-like spaces, RBC extravasation, AIDS-defining illness.
examinerTraps: The examiner may provide a description of 'Bacillary Angiomatosis' (neutrophilic infiltrate) as a distractor for Kaposi Sarcoma (spindle cells). Look for the specific histologic buzzwords.
sourceQuote: Vascular Structure and Function characterizes specific kinds of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular tumors is a benign, exquisitely painful neoplasm typically found in the distal portion of the fingers, specifically under the nail bed?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor, usually large and painless in early stages, not associated with the subungual region.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign but typically larger, deeper, and non-painful; they frequently involve the liver or CNS.
explanations.c: A glomus tumor (glomangioma) is a benign but very painful tumor arising from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus bodies, which are involved in thermoregulation and are concentrated under the nails.
explanations.d: Hemangioendotheliomas are intermediate-grade tumors that can occur in various sites but do not typically present as painful subungual nodules.
explanations.e: Pyogenic granuloma is a rapidly growing red nodule on skin or gingiva that bleeds easily; it is not typically associated with exquisite pain or the subungual location.

ankiCards: A painful, red-blue tumor under the fingernail is most likely a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle cells}} of the glomus body.
The primary function of the glomus body is {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
True or False: Glomus tumors are malignant. {{c1::False}}.
Glomus tumors are histologically characterized by nests of uniform {{c1::glomus cells}} surrounding vascular channels.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are small (<1 cm) and benign.
Classic triad: Paroxysmal pain, localized tenderness, and sensitivity to cold.
Derived from the glomus body (arteriovenous anastomosis).
Surgical excision is curative.
Must be differentiated from subungual melanoma (which is pigmented and usually painless).
microReview: Glomus Tumor: Painful, subungual, smooth muscle origin, benign.
examinerTraps: Pain is the key. Most vascular tumors are painless; the glomus tumor is a notable exception frequently tested because of its specific location and symptom profile.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which vascular lesion is characterized as a large, cavernous, lymphatic-filled space, most commonly found in the neck or axilla of infants, and is strongly associated with Turner Syndrome and Down Syndrome?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas involve small blood vessels, not dilated lymphatic spaces.
explanations.b: Cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) is a lymphatic malformation typically located in the neck or axilla. It is classically associated with chromosomal aneuploidies like Turner Syndrome (45,X).
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are blood vessel tumors of smooth muscle origin, not lymphatic.
explanations.d: Hemangioendothelioma is a borderline vascular tumor of blood vessels.
explanations.e: Sturge-Weber syndrome is a constellation of findings including a port-wine stain (capillary malformation), but 'cystic hygroma' is the specific name for the lymphatic lesion described.

ankiCards: Cystic hygroma is a type of {{c1::cavernous lymphangioma}}.
Cystic hygromas are most commonly found in the {{c1::neck (or axilla)}}.
A fetus with a cystic hygroma should be evaluated for {{c1::Turner Syndrome (or Down Syndrome)}}.
Histologically, cystic hygromas consist of large, dilated spaces lined by {{c1::endothelial}} cells and containing {{c2::lymph}}.
Cystic hygromas are difficult to resect because they {{c1::lack capsules}} and infiltrate tissue.
keyPoints: Cystic hygromas are benign but can cause significant mass effect.
They are often identified on prenatal ultrasound.
Association with Turner Syndrome: Leads to webbed neck after regression.
They contain proteinaceous lymph fluid and small numbers of lymphocytes.
They are differentiated from hemangiomas by the absence of red blood cells in the spaces.
microReview: Cystic Hygroma: Neck, Lymphatic, Turner Syndrome (45,X), benign.
examinerTraps: The examiner may use 'cavernous hemangioma' as a distractor; remember that cystic hygromas contain lymph, not blood, and are specifically associated with Turner syndrome and the posterior triangle of the neck.
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old pregnant woman in her third trimester presents with a rapidly growing, pedunculated, 1 cm red nodule on her gingiva that bleeds easily with minimal trauma. She is concerned about malignancy. The lesion is excised, and pathology shows a circumscribed proliferation of capillaries with associated edema and inflammation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignancy; this lesion is benign and associated with pregnancy.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is seen in immunocompromised patients, not typically associated with pregnancy.
explanations.c: Cherry angiomas are small, stable, red papules common in the elderly, not rapidly growing pedunculated gingival masses.
explanations.d: Kaposi sarcoma is a malignancy (HHV-8) and does not typically present as a single pedunculated mass following minor trauma.
explanations.e: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a benign, fast-growing vascular lesion that often occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum). They are prone to bleeding and often follow trauma.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is actually a(n) {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
A pyogenic granuloma occurring on the gingiva of a pregnant woman is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Clinically, pyogenic granulomas are known for growing {{c1::rapidly}} and {{c2::bleeding}} easily.
True or False: Pyogenic granulomas are associated with infection and pus formation. {{c1::False}}.
The treatment for a symptomatic pyogenic granuloma is {{c1::surgical excision}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granulomas are benign vascular proliferations.
They often occur on the skin, lips, or gingiva.
Pregnancy is a major predisposing factor due to hormonal changes.
Histologically, they show a lobular arrangement of capillaries.
They are not actually pyogenic (pus-forming) or granulomatous.
microReview: Pyogenic Granuloma: Pregnancy, Gingiva, bleeds easily, benign, lobular capillaries.
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic granuloma' is a historical misnomer. Don't be fooled into thinking it's an infectious process (pyogenic) or a type of chronic inflammation (granuloma).
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old male worker at a chemical manufacturing plant presents with weight loss, abdominal pain, and jaundice. Imaging reveals multiple mass lesions in the liver. Biopsy confirms a malignant tumor of endothelial origin. Long-term exposure to which of the following substances most likely contributed to this patient's condition?

explanations.a: Aflatoxin B1 is a risk factor for Hepatocellular Carcinoma, not hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Arsenic is associated with hepatic angiosarcoma, but vinyl chloride is the classic 'industrial' association for chemical plant workers.
explanations.c: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and lung cancer.
explanations.d: Benzene is associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.e: Vinyl chloride (used in the plastics industry) is a well-documented carcinogen specifically associated with the development of hepatic angiosarcoma.

ankiCards: Exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}} is a classic risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma.
Besides vinyl chloride, exposure to {{c1::arsenic}} and {{c2::Thorotrast}} also increases risk for hepatic angiosarcoma.
Angiosarcomas of the liver are highly {{c1::aggressive/malignant}}.
The cell type that becomes malignant in hepatic angiosarcoma is the {{c1::endothelial cell}}.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is much rarer than {{c1::hepatocellular carcinoma}} but has a much stronger industrial link.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare but deadly vascular malignancy.
Industrial exposures: Vinyl chloride, arsenic, Thorotrast (radiocontrast).
Clinical presentation often involves late-stage liver failure or hemorrhage.
Histology shows malignant cells lining vascular channels or solid sheets.
It is one of the classic 'occupational' cancers in medical board exams.
microReview: Hepatic Angiosarcoma: Vinyl Chloride, Arsenic, Thorotrast. Highly malignant.
examinerTraps: Differentiating between Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) and Hepatic Angiosarcoma is key. If the vignette mentions 'vinyl chloride' or 'PVC factory,' choose angiosarcoma over HCC.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively... or precipitously.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the difference between a cavernous hemangioma and a capillary hemangioma?

options.a: Capillary hemangiomas are malignant, while cavernous are benign.
options.b: Cavernous hemangiomas involve larger, more dilated vascular channels and are less likely to regress.
options.c: Cavernous hemangiomas occur only in the skin, while capillary occur in internal organs.
options.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are caused by viruses, while capillary are genetic.
options.e: Only capillary hemangiomas are associated with Von Hippel-Lindau disease.

explanations.a: Both capillary and cavernous hemangiomas are benign.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, blood-filled vascular spaces (caverns) separated by connective tissue. They are usually deeper, involve internal organs like the liver or brain, and do not regress spontaneously like infantile capillary hemangiomas.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas frequently involve internal organs; capillary hemangiomas are most common in the skin and mucous membranes.
explanations.d: Neither is primarily caused by a virus (unlike Kaposi Sarcoma).
explanations.e: Von Hippel-Lindau is associated with hemangioblastomas (specifically in the cerebellum/retina), which are distinct from common cavernous hemangiomas.

ankiCards: {{c1::Cavernous}} hemangiomas are characterized by large, dilated, blood-filled vascular spaces.
True or False: Cavernous hemangiomas commonly undergo spontaneous regression. {{c1::False}}.
The most common benign tumor of the liver is the {{c1::cavernous hemangioma}}.
A major complication of CNS cavernous hemangiomas is {{c1::hemorrhage}}.
Cavernous hemangiomas are separated by {{c1::connective tissue/stroma}}.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign but can be locally destructive due to size.
They are often found in the liver, spleen, and CNS.
On imaging of the liver, they show peripheral enhancement with 'filling in'.
They do not have the 'strawberry' appearance or regression pattern of infantile capillary hemangiomas.
They are often asymptomatic and found incidentally.
microReview: Cavernous Hemangioma: Large channels, liver/CNS, do NOT regress, benign.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse cavernous hemangiomas with 'cavernous lymphangiomas' (cystic hygromas). Hemangiomas contain blood; lymphangiomas contain lymph.
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following conditions is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor that frequently occurs in the setting of AIDS and shows spindle cells forming slit-like spaces with extravasated red blood cells on histology?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignant tumor, not intermediate.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign infectious proliferation, not a neoplasm.
explanations.c: Glomus tumor is a benign tumor of smooth muscle origin.
explanations.d: Kaposi sarcoma is classified as an intermediate-grade (borderline) vascular tumor because it is locally aggressive and can be multifocal, but is rarely as rapidly fatal as angiosarcoma.
explanations.e: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign hemangioma.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is classified as a(n) {{c1::intermediate-grade (borderline)}} vascular tumor.
The spindle cells in Kaposi Sarcoma are infected with {{c1::HHV-8}}.
{{c1::AIDS-associated}} Kaposi Sarcoma is the most common variant in the United States.
Hyaline droplets in Kaposi Sarcoma spindle cells represent {{c1::ingested plasma proteins}}.
KS lesions typically progress through three stages: {{c1::Patch, Plaque, and Nodule}}.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma involves a characteristic spindle-cell proliferation.
The 'slit-like' spaces are diagnostic and contain erythrocytes.
Clinical variants include Classic (older Mediterranean men) and Endemic (African).
Transplant-associated KS occurs due to T-cell immunosuppression.
HHV-8 encodes viral homologues of human proteins (like Cyclin D) to drive the cell cycle.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma: HHV-8, Spindle cells, Slit spaces, Intermediate-grade.
examinerTraps: Be careful with the classification. While many think of Kaposi Sarcoma as 'cancer' (which it is), technically it is categorized as 'intermediate-grade' rather than high-grade 'malignant' in the same category as angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 19-year-old male is evaluated for recurrent headaches and vision changes. Physical exam reveals several small, bright red, flat macules on his trunk. An MRI of the brain shows a 2 cm cyst with an enhancing mural nodule in the cerebellum. Laboratory studies reveal an elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit. What is the most likely vascular tumor present in his cerebellum?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma of the CNS is extremely rare and does not typically present as a mural nodule in a cyst.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas of the CNS typically look like 'popcorn' on MRI due to blood products of different ages and do not usually cause erythrocytosis.
explanations.c: Hemangioblastoma is a highly vascular tumor associated with Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease. It classically presents in the cerebellum as a cyst with a mural nodule and can produce erythropoietin, leading to polycythemia (elevated hemoglobin).
explanations.d: Kaposi sarcoma does not typically involve the cerebellum or cause polycythemia.
explanations.e: Pyogenic granulomas are skin/mucosal lesions and do not occur in the brain.

ankiCards: A cerebellar cyst with an enhancing mural nodule is the classic radiologic description of a {{c1::hemangioblastoma}}.
Hemangioblastomas are highly vascular tumors associated with {{c1::Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL)}} disease.
Hemangioblastomas can cause secondary polycythemia by secreting {{c1::erythropoietin (EPO)}}.
Patients with VHL disease often also develop {{c1::renal cell carcinoma}} (clear cell type).
The genetics of VHL disease involve a mutation in a tumor suppressor gene on chromosome {{c1::3}}.
keyPoints: Hemangioblastoma: Benign but located in critical areas (cerebellum, retina).
VHL Association: Autosomal dominant inheritance.
Clinical signs of VHL: Hemangioblastomas, RCC, Pheochromocytomas.
Erythropoietin production by the tumor leads to elevated Hct.
Histology: Vacuolated 'foamy' stromal cells and numerous capillaries.
microReview: Hemangioblastoma: VHL, Cerebellum, EPO (Polycythemia), Cyst + Nodule.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse hemangioblastoma with hemangioma. Hemangioblastoma is a specific entity associated with VHL and erythropoietin production.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the two principal mechanisms that underlie the majority of vascular diseases resulting in significant morbidity and mortality?

options.a: Arterial spasm and venous valve insufficiency
options.b: Luminal narrowing and weakening of vessel walls

explanations.a: Arterial spasm (e.g., Raynaud's) and venous insufficiency are important but do not constitute the two primary overarching mechanisms of vascular disease defined in major pathology.
explanations.b: The two primary mechanisms of vascular disease are narrowing/obstruction (e.g., atherosclerosis, thrombosis) and weakening of the walls leading to dilation/rupture (aneurysms).
explanations.c: Endothelial activation is an early step in many processes, but adventitial hypertrophy is not a primary mechanism of systemic vascular morbidity.
explanations.d: These are specialized processes associated with specific pathologies like lymphedema or angiogenesis, not the primary mechanisms of systemic vascular disease.
explanations.e: Vascular disease typically involves intimal thickening (not thinning) and medial weakening (rather than just calcification) as the primary drivers of pathology.

ankiCards: The two principal mechanisms of vascular disease are {{c1::luminal narrowing/obstruction}} and {{c2::vessel wall weakening}}.
Vascular wall weakening primarily leads to {{c1::dilation (aneurysm)}} or {{c2::rupture}}.
Luminal narrowing in vascular disease can be progressive (e.g., atherosclerosis) or {{c1::precipitous (thrombosis/embolism)}}.
Which mechanism of vascular disease is responsible for aneurysm formation? {{c1::Weakening of vessel walls}}
Atherosclerosis primarily causes morbidity through which mechanism? {{c1::Luminal narrowing (stenosis)}}
keyPoints: Vascular pathology is a leading cause of human morbidity and mortality.
Obstruction can be progressive (atherosclerosis) or acute (thrombosis).
Wall weakening leads to permanent dilation (aneurysm) or catastrophic rupture.
Arterial lesions are generally more clinically significant than venous lesions.
The architectural response to injury often involves intimal thickening.
microReview: Vascular disease mechanisms center on 'Flow' (obstruction) and 'Integrity' (weakness/rupture).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the response to injury (intimal thickening) with the mechanism of dilation (wall weakening).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Arterial walls are generally thicker than their corresponding venous counterparts. This structural specialization primarily allows the arteries to accommodate which of the following physiological factors?

explanations.a: Arteries carry higher oxygen tension than veins; thick walls are not an adaptation to low oxygen.
explanations.b: Flow in large arteries is often turbulent or complex, especially near branch points, rather than perfectly constant and laminar.
explanations.c: Arterial walls are thicker to withstand the high, pulsatile pressures generated by cardiac contraction.
explanations.d: While the wall is metabolically active, the thickness is a mechanical adaptation, not purely a metabolic one.
explanations.e: Veins, with thinner walls and higher compliance, serve as the primary volume storage (capacitance) vessels.

ankiCards: Arterial walls are thicker than veins to accommodate {{c1::pulsatile flow}} and {{c2::higher blood pressures}}.
As arteries become smaller, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}}.
Which vessel type allows for the most control over blood flow and pressure? {{c1::Muscular (resistance) arteries}}
Veins are thinner than arteries at the same level of branching because they operate under {{c1::lower}} pressure.
Atherosclerosis predominantly affects which vessel types? {{c1::Elastic and muscular arteries}}
keyPoints: Arterial thickness is proportional to the pressure it must contain.
The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases in smaller muscular arteries.
Structural specialization reflects distinct functional roles.
Veins serve as capacitance vessels; arteries serve as resistance and distribution vessels.
Vascular disorders often have characteristic anatomic distributions based on vessel type.
microReview: Structure follows function: Thick walls = Pressure resistance; Thin walls/Valves = Capacitance/Return.
examinerTraps: Distractors often mention 'veins' having thicker walls; remember, veins are thin and floppy compared to the rigid, thick-walled arteries.
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old male with a 40-pack-year smoking history and long-standing hypertension presents with vague mid-abdominal pain. Physical examination reveals a pulsatile mass midway between the xiphoid process and the umbilicus. An ultrasound confirms a 6-cm abdominal aortic aneurysm. Which of the following is the most likely underlying pathophysiological process responsible for this finding?

explanations.a: Cystic medial necrosis (medial degeneration) is more commonly associated with thoracic aortic aneurysms, particularly in Marfan syndrome.
explanations.b: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum is a hallmark of tertiary syphilis, usually affecting the ascending (thoracic) aorta.
explanations.c: Atherosclerosis is the most common cause of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA), typically occurring infrarenally where nutrient diffusion to the media is most compromised.
explanations.d: Granulomatous inflammation is characteristic of vasculitides like Takayasu or Giant Cell Arteritis, not typical AAA.
explanations.e: Congenital medial defects are usually associated with 'berry' aneurysms in the Circle of Willis, not large abdominal aneurysms.

ankiCards: The most common cause of an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
AAA typically occurs in which location relative to the renal arteries? {{c1::Infrarenal}}
Risk factors for AAA include {{c1::male sex}}, {{c2::smoking}}, and age over 60.
The primary mechanism by which atherosclerosis causes AAA is through {{c1::ischemic thinning of the media}}.
A pulsatile abdominal mass in an older male smoker is highly suggestive of {{c1::Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA)}}.
keyPoints: AAA is primarily an atherosclerotic disease.
The infrarenal aorta is the most common site due to its reliance on luminal diffusion for medial nutrition.
Smoking is a stronger risk factor for AAA than for most other atherosclerotic manifestations.
Aneurysms >5cm in males usually require surgical intervention due to rupture risk.
Pathogenesis involves matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) activity and ECM degradation.
microReview: AAA = Atherosclerosis + Infrarenal + Smoking + Male.
examinerTraps: A common trap is confusing 'Cystic Medial Necrosis' (Thoracic) with 'Atherosclerosis' (Abdominal).
sourceQuote: Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries... [leading to] weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old tall male with long fingers and pectus excavatum is diagnosed with a thoracic aortic aneurysm. Molecular analysis reveals a mutation in the Fibrillin-1 gene. This defect leads to excessive activation of which of the following signaling pathways in the vessel wall?

explanations.a: Wnt signaling is crucial for embryogenesis and cancer, but not the primary driver of Marfan-related aneurysm.
explanations.b: Fibrillin-1 normally sequesters TGF-beta; its deficiency leads to excessive TGF-beta bioavailability, causing abnormal vascular smooth muscle cell signaling and ECM remodeling.
explanations.c: NOTCH1 mutations are associated with bicuspid aortic valve and calcific aortic stenosis, but not Marfan syndrome.
explanations.d: VEGF is involved in angiogenesis, not the weakening of the aortic media in connective tissue diseases.
explanations.e: TNF-alpha is a pro-inflammatory cytokine central to vasculitis but not the primary pathway in cystic medial degeneration.

ankiCards: In Marfan syndrome, the defect in Fibrillin-1 leads to overactivity of the {{c1::TGF-beta}} signaling pathway.
Cystic medial degeneration is characterized by the loss of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} and fragmented {{c2::elastic fibers}}.
Thoracic aortic aneurysms are most frequently associated with {{c1::hypertension}} and {{c2::connective tissue disorders (e.g., Marfan)}}.
Fibrillin-1 is a major component of {{c1::microfibrils}} in the extracellular matrix.
Excessive TGF-beta in the aortic wall leads to increased production of {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder of Fibrillin-1.
