Loss of Fibrillin-1 results in 'medial degeneration' (formerly cystic medial necrosis).
TGF-beta overactivity drives the deleterious remodeling of the aortic media.
Thoracic aneurysms can lead to aortic valve insufficiency due to root dilation.
Beta-blockers or TGF-beta inhibitors are used to slow the rate of dilation.
microReview: Marfan = Fibrillin-1 = TGF-beta overactivity = Thoracic Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Fibrillin with Fibronectin or Collagen. Fibrillin-1 is the specific protein in Marfan's.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following terms describes a localized dilation of an artery where the wall is formed by an organized hematoma that communicates with the intravascular space, rather than by all three layers of the arterial wall?

explanations.a: Saccular aneurysms are 'true' aneurysms involving all three layers (intima, media, adventitia) that bulge on one side.
explanations.b: Fusiform aneurysms are 'true' aneurysms involving all three layers with circumferential dilation.
explanations.c: Berry aneurysms are small saccular true aneurysms, usually in the Circle of Willis.
explanations.d: A pseudoaneurysm (false aneurysm) occurs when a wall defect leads to an extravascular hematoma that freely communicates with the lumen; the 'wall' is connective tissue, not vessel layers.
explanations.e: A dissection occurs when blood enters the wall itself, creating a false lumen within the media, rather than a localized bulging hematoma.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the vessel wall (intima, media, and adventitia).
A {{c1::false (pseudoaneurysm)}} involves a wall defect and an external hematoma communicating with the lumen.
An example of a false aneurysm is a {{c1::post-catheterization femoral artery hematoma}}.
{{c1::Saccular}} aneurysms are spherical dilations involving only a portion of the vessel wall.
{{c1::Fusiform}} aneurysms are circumferential dilations of a long vascular segment.
keyPoints: True aneurysms: Saccular and Fusiform.
False aneurysms: Pseudoaneurysms (contained hematomas).
True aneurysms must contain intima, media, and adventitia.
Common causes of pseudoaneurysm include trauma and vascular intervention.
Vascular dissections are distinct from both true and false aneurysms (blood within the wall layers).
microReview: True = 3 layers. False = Hematoma. Saccular = One side. Fusiform = All around.
examinerTraps: Watch for the word 'communicates'. Both dissections and pseudoaneurysms involve blood moving out of the true lumen, but pseudoaneurysms are walled off by extra-vascular tissue.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old male with untreated syphilis and a positive RPR/VDRL presents with a cough and difficulty swallowing. Imaging reveals an aneurysm of the ascending aorta and 'eggshell' calcification of the aortic root. This condition is caused by obliterative endarteritis of which of the following structures?

explanations.a: The internal elastic lamina is destroyed secondary to the ischemia, but it is not the primary site of obliterative endarteritis.
explanations.b: Tertiary syphilis causes obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum in the aortic adventitia, leading to ischemic injury of the aortic media.
explanations.c: The thoracic duct is involved in lymph drainage and is not affected by syphilitic endarteritis.
explanations.d: While the intima may show 'tree-barking' as a secondary change, the primary lesion is in the vasa vasorum.
explanations.e: Cardiac valves may be affected by the dilation (aortic insufficiency), but the endarteritis occurs in the small vessels supplying the aorta.

ankiCards: Syphilitic (luetic) aneurysms typically involve the {{c1::ascending (thoracic)}} aorta.
The hallmark pathology of syphilitic aortitis is {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}} of the vasa vasorum.
Ischemic injury to the aortic media in syphilis leads to a {{c1::'tree-bark'}} appearance of the intima.
Syphilitic aneurysms can cause narrowing of the {{c1::coronary ostia}} and aortic valve {{c2::insufficiency}}.
Which stage of syphilis is associated with aortic aneurysms? {{c1::Tertiary}}
keyPoints: Luetic (syphilitic) aneurysms are rare in the antibiotic era.
The vasa vasorum provide nutrients to the outer media of large elastic arteries.
Obliteration of vasa vasorum leads to medial atrophy and scarring.
Contraction of these scars leads to the characteristic 'tree-bark' intimal wrinkling.
The ascending aorta is most commonly affected.
microReview: Syphilis = Vasa Vasorum Obliteration = Medial Ischemia = Thoracic Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Commonly confused with AAA. Remember: Syphilis = Thoracic/Ascending; Atherosclerosis = Abdominal/Infrarenal.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following cellular changes is the most consistent and stereotyped response of the vascular wall to almost any form of injury, such as endothelial denudation or chronic hypertension?

explanations.a: Medial thinning is often a consequence of injury (like atherosclerosis) but not the stereotyped healing response.
explanations.b: Adventitial fibrosis can occur, but it is not the primary 'stereotyped' response described in vascular pathology.
explanations.c: Intimal thickening, involving smooth muscle cell migration and ECM deposition (neointima formation), is the universal response to vascular injury.
explanations.d: Endothelial injury triggers the response, but apoptosis of the endothelium is the trigger, not the constructive response itself.
explanations.e: Valvular calcification is specific to cardiac valves and is not a general vascular wall response.

ankiCards: The stereotyped response of the vascular wall to injury is {{c1::intimal thickening}}.
Cells that migrate to the intima during injury are {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} (or precursors).
Neointimal smooth muscle cells differ from medial cells as they are {{c1::proliferative}} and synthesize {{c2::extracellular matrix}}.
Does the 'neointima' usually contract like normal media? {{c1::No}}.
Vascular injury leads to the formation of a {{c1::neointima}}.
keyPoints: Vascular injury triggers a wound-healing response.
Smooth muscle cells migrate from the media to the intima.
These cells proliferate and deposit collagen/ECM.
The resulting 'intimal thickening' can lead to luminal stenosis.
This process is common to atherosclerosis, vasculitis, and physical trauma.
microReview: Vascular Injury = Smooth Muscle Migration = Intimal Thickening (Neointima).
examinerTraps: A common trap is thinking the vessel wall 'thins' as a response to injury. While it may thin in aneurysms, the active *response* is thickening.
sourceQuote: Vascular Wall Response to Injury... Intimal Thickening: A Stereotyped Response to Vascular Injury
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 70-year-old female with a history of hypertension and atherosclerosis presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset, severe 'tearing' back pain. Her blood pressure is 80/40 mmHg. Which of the following is the most likely immediate life-threatening complication of this patient's underlying vascular condition?

explanations.a: The description of 'tearing' pain and hypotension in a hypertensive patient strongly suggests aortic dissection. If the dissection involves the proximal aorta, it can rupture into the pericardial sac, causing fatal cardiac tamponade.
explanations.b: SVC syndrome is caused by external compression of the SVC (e.g., lung cancer), not by aortic dissection/aneurysm rupture.
explanations.c: Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease) is a vasculitis of small/medium vessels in young smokers, unrelated to this presentation.
explanations.d: Nutcracker syndrome is the compression of the left renal vein, which does not present with sudden tearing back pain and shock.
explanations.e: Raynaud phenomenon is a vasospastic disorder of distal digits, not a life-threatening aortic emergency.

ankiCards: The most common cause of death from aortic dissection is {{c1::rupture}} into a body cavity.
Aortic dissection rupture into the pericardial sac results in {{c1::cardiac tamponade}}.
Sudden-onset 'tearing' or 'ripping' chest pain radiating to the back is classic for {{c1::aortic dissection}}.
The major risk factor for aortic dissection is {{c1::hypertension}}.
Aortic dissections involving the ascending aorta are classified as Stanford Type {{c1::A}}.
keyPoints: Aortic dissection is not a 'true' aneurysm but a hemorrhage into the media.
Stanford Type A involves the ascending aorta and is a surgical emergency.
Stanford Type B involves only the descending aorta and is often managed medically.
Hypertension causes hyaline arteriolosclerosis of the vasa vasorum, predisposing to medial ischemia.
Tamponade is the #1 cause of death in Type A dissections.
microReview: Tearing Pain + Low BP = Aortic Dissection/Rupture. Proximal = Tamponade risk.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'Aneurysm' (dilation) with 'Dissection' (split in the wall). They are related but distinct pathological entities.
sourceQuote: Aneurysms and Dissection... Aortic Dissection [Page 507]
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vessel types primarily exerts the greatest control over systemic blood flow and blood pressure through changes in lumen diameter relative to wall thickness?

explanations.a: Elastic arteries (like the aorta) primarily dampen pulsatility rather than providing fine-tuned resistance control.
explanations.b: As vessels become smaller (muscular arteries and arterioles), the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing these vessels to act as 'resistance' vessels to control pressure.
explanations.c: Large veins are capacitance vessels with low resistance; they do not control systemic pressure in this manner.
explanations.d: Capillaries consist of a single layer of endothelium and have no muscular wall to control lumen diameter.
explanations.e: Lymphatics transport fluid and do not regulate systemic blood pressure.

ankiCards: The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}} as arteries become smaller.
{{c1::Muscular}} arteries (and arterioles) are the primary regulators of vascular resistance.
Elastic arteries are designed to accommodate {{c1::pulsatile}} flow.
Which vessel layer contains the smooth muscle cells responsible for vasoconstriction? {{c1::Tunica media}}
Atherosclerosis mainly affects {{c1::elastic}} and {{c2::muscular}} arteries.
keyPoints: Arterioles are the primary site of peripheral resistance.
Wall/Lumen ratio is key to blood pressure regulation.
Structural specialization (e.g., elastic fibers vs. smooth muscle) dictates vessel function.
Vascular pathology is often vessel-type specific.
Atherosclerosis favors larger vessels, while hypertension favors smaller resistance vessels.
microReview: Small Muscular Arteries = High Wall/Lumen Ratio = Pressure Control.
examinerTraps: Be careful: while 'arterioles' are the *most* important for resistance, 'muscular arteries' are the category provided in the text that controls flow.
sourceQuote: the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing these muscular vessels to exert control over blood flow and pressure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old male with a history of intravenous drug use presents with high fever, a new holosystolic murmur at the apex, and a painful, red, pulsatile mass in the right brachial artery. Which of the following is the most likely classification of this arterial lesion?

explanations.a: Berry aneurysms are congenital defects in cerebral vessels, not related to infection or IV drug use.
explanations.b: A mycotic aneurysm is a true aneurysm resulting from the infection of an arterial wall, often via septic emboli from infective endocarditis (common in IV drug users).
explanations.c: Syphilitic aneurysms occur in the tertiary stage of syphilis and almost exclusively involve the ascending aorta.
explanations.d: Dissection involves blood splitting the media; it is usually related to hypertension or connective tissue disease, not acute infection.
explanations.e: Atherosclerotic aneurysms typically occur in older patients in the infrarenal aorta, not as acute painful masses in the arm of a young person.

ankiCards: A {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm is an aneurysm resulting from infection of the vessel wall.
Common sources of infection for mycotic aneurysms include {{c1::septic emboli (endocarditis)}} and direct extension of nearby suppuration.
The term 'mycotic' in mycotic aneurysm usually refers to {{c1::any microbial (often bacterial)}} infection, not just fungi.
Mycotic aneurysms are characterized by rapid {{c1::dilation}} and a high risk of {{c2::rupture}}.
In IV drug users, mycotic aneurysms often follow {{c1::Infective Endocarditis}}.
keyPoints: Mycotic aneurysms are a complication of bacteremia/sepsis.
The name is a misnomer; most are bacterial, not fungal.
The infection weakens the wall, leading to rapid expansion.
Common sites include the aorta, cerebral, and mesenteric/brachial arteries.
Treatment involves antibiotics and often surgical excision.
microReview: Infection (e.g., Endocarditis) + Arterial Dilation = Mycotic Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Don't be fooled by the name 'mycotic'; the cause is usually *Staphylococcus* or *Salmonella*, not a fungus.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 3-week-old female infant is brought to the pediatrician for a bright red, raised, lobulated lesion on her left cheek that has appeared since birth. The mother notes the lesion seems to be enlarging rapidly. Physical examination reveals a 2-cm 'strawberry-like' mass that blanches slightly on pressure. Which of the following is the most likely clinical course for this lesion?

options.b: Lifelong persistence without change in size

explanations.a: Infantile capillary hemangiomas are benign and do not undergo malignant transformation into angiosarcomas.
explanations.b: These lesions are characterized by a period of rapid growth followed by regression, rather than remaining static for life.
explanations.c: Capillary (infantile) hemangiomas typically grow rapidly for several months and then spontaneously regress or involute by age 7 to 9 in the majority of cases.
explanations.d: Port-wine stains (nevus flammeus) are a different type of vascular malformation that persists and thickens over time, unlike the strawberry hemangioma.
explanations.e: Systemic arteriovenous shunts are characteristic of large cavernous hemangiomas or AV malformations, not simple capillary hemangiomas.

ankiCards: Infantile (strawberry) hemangiomas are characterized by a period of rapid growth followed by {{c1::spontaneous regression/involution}}.
A bright red, lobulated vascular lesion in a newborn that blanches is most likely a {{c1::capillary (or infantile) hemangioma}}.
True/False: Most infantile hemangiomas require immediate surgical excision. {{c1::False (most involute by age 7)}}.
Histologically, capillary hemangiomas are composed of thin-walled capillaries with {{c1::scant}} stroma.
The clinical term for a capillary hemangioma of infancy is a(n) {{c1::strawberry}} hemangioma.
keyPoints: Capillary hemangiomas are the most common type of vascular tumor.
They occur in the skin, subcutaneous tissues, and mucous membranes.
Strawberry hemangiomas of the newborn are extremely common (1 in 200 births).
Natural history involves rapid growth for several months followed by regression.
By age 7, approximately 75% to 90% of these lesions have completely disappeared.
microReview: Vascular tumors are classified as benign (hemangiomas), intermediate (Kaposi sarcoma), or malignant (angiosarcoma). Capillary hemangiomas are benign proliferations of capillaries, common in infancy, and usually regress.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'strawberry hemangioma' (capillary) with 'port-wine stain' (venous malformation). Only the former reliably regresses; port-wine stains persist and grow with the child.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors... are benign tumors and tumor-like conditions... Capillary hemangiomas are the most common type... Infantile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) of the skin of newborns are very common.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old man with a history of HIV infection (CD4+ count 150/mm³) presents with multiple painless, purple macules and plaques on his lower extremities and trunk. Biopsy of a lesion shows a proliferation of spindle cells forming slit-like spaces containing red blood cells. The pathogenesis of this condition is most directly linked to which of the following pathogens?

explanations.a: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.b: HHV-8 (also known as KSHV) is the causative agent for all forms of Kaposi sarcoma, including the AIDS-associated (epidemic) form described here.
explanations.c: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised patients, which mimics Kaposi sarcoma clinically but is histologically distinct (neutrophilic infiltrate).
explanations.d: HPV-16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx.
explanations.e: CMV can cause retinitis or colitis in AIDS patients but does not cause vascular tumors.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is caused by infection with {{c1::Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}.
The histological hallmark of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells}} forming {{c2::slit-like spaces}}.
The slit-like spaces in Kaposi Sarcoma typically contain {{c1::red blood cells (erythrocytes)}}.
{{c1::Bacillary angiomatosis}} is a vascular lesion in AIDS patients that mimics Kaposi sarcoma but is caused by Bartonella.
Kaposi Sarcoma in HIV patients is classified as {{c1::Epidemic (or AIDS-associated)}} KS.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a low-grade malignant vascular tumor caused by HHV-8.
Four forms: Classic (older Mediterranean men), Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and Epidemic (AIDS).
The spindle cells are the malignant element, likely of endothelial origin.
Histology: Slit-like vascular spaces, extravasated RBCs, and hemosiderin-laden macrophages.
In AIDS patients, KS is an AIDS-defining illness and often involves the viscera.
microReview: HHV-8 infects endothelial cells, leading to uncontrolled proliferation and inflammation. This is exacerbated by the lack of T-cell immunity in HIV/AIDS.
examinerTraps: Distinguishing KS from Bacillary Angiomatosis: KS has spindle cells and slit-like spaces; Bacillary Angiomatosis has lobular capillary proliferation and neutrophils (associated with Bartonella).
sourceQuote: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8... In the United States, it is the most common HIV-related malignancy.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with a 4-mm, exquisitely painful, firm, red-blue nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. She notes that the pain is often paroxysmal and triggered by cold exposure. Histological examination shows aggregates of specialized cells surrounding vascular channels. These cells are most likely derived from which of the following?

explanations.a: Endothelial cells line the vascular channels within the tumor but are not the source of the painful 'glomus cells'.
explanations.b: Lymphatic endothelial cells form lymphangiomas, which are typically painless and located in the neck or axilla.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, an arteriovenous structure involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts are found in the stroma but do not form the characteristic nests of a glomus tumor.
explanations.e: While the tumor is painful, it is not derived from nerve sheath cells (like a schwannoma).

ankiCards: A glomus tumor is typically found in the {{c1::subungual (under nail)}} region.
The hallmark symptom of a glomus tumor is {{c1::exquisite pain (paroxysmal)}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle cells}}.
The normal glomus body is an arteriovenous structure used for {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors show nests of {{c1::uniform round cells}} around vascular spaces.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but extremely painful.
Commonly located in the distal digits, particularly under the nails.
Derived from the glomus body (specialized AV shunt).
Excision is usually curative.
Pathology shows nests of monomorphic cells resembling smooth muscle cells.
microReview: Painful skin tumors mnemonic: 'ANGEL' - Angiomyoma, Neuroma, Glomus tumor, Eccrine spiradenoma, Leiomyoma.
examinerTraps: Wait for the 'subungual' and 'pain' cues. If it's a painless subungual blue mass, consider a subungual hematoma or melanoma.
sourceQuote: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, exquisitely painful tumors arising from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus bodies.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with several small, dark-red to purple, dome-shaped nodules on her right upper arm. Ten years ago, she underwent a radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection and radiation therapy for breast cancer. Since the surgery, her right arm has been chronically swollen. A biopsy of one of the arm nodules reveals highly atypical endothelial cells forming irregular vascular channels that infiltrate the dermis. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 and typically occurs in the setting of HIV or specific populations; it lacks the extreme cytologic atypia seen in angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign bacterial infection (Bartonella) seen in HIV patients.
explanations.c: This is Stewart-Treves syndrome, where chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy) predisposes to the development of cutaneous angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign, lack atypia, and do not typically arise in the setting of chronic lymphedema.
explanations.e: Pyogenic granulomas are rapidly growing, pedunculated benign lesions that often follow trauma; they do not show infiltrative malignant growth.

ankiCards: Chronic lymphedema post-mastectomy is a risk factor for {{c1::angiosarcoma}}.
The eponym for angiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphedema is {{c1::Stewart-Treves}} syndrome.
Angiosarcomas are histologically characterized by {{c1::highly atypical endothelial cells}}.
Besides lymphedema, angiosarcoma of the skin is also associated with previous {{c1::radiation}} therapy.
Angiosarcoma of the liver is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride (or arsenic/Thorotrast)}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms.
Older adults are most commonly affected.
They occur most frequently in the skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
They are aggressive and have a poor 5-year survival rate (approx. 30%).
They can be identified by the endothelial marker CD31.
microReview: Angiosarcoma presents as a range of histological patterns from well-formed vascular channels to solid sheets of spindle cells. CD31 is a specific marker used for diagnosis.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Stewart-Treves (angiosarcoma) with lymphedema-associated cellulitis. If the description mentions 'purple nodules' and 'atypia', think malignancy.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms... skin angiosarcomas can occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema, traditionally in the ipsilateral arm after radical mastectomy.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An infant is born with a large, soft, fluctuant mass on the left side of the neck. Physical examination also reveals a webbed neck and low-set ears. Genetic testing confirms a 45,X karyotype. The neck mass is most likely which of the following?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are composed of small blood vessels and are usually on the skin/surface, not large deep fluctuant neck masses.
explanations.b: Cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) is a benign lymphatic malformation frequently associated with Turner syndrome (45,X).
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are small, painful, and typically found under fingernails.
explanations.d: Angiosarcomas are malignant and usually occur in older adults, not as congenital neck masses.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts.

ankiCards: A cavernous lymphangioma of the neck is also known as a {{c1::cystic hygroma}}.
Cystic hygromas are frequently associated with {{c1::Turner}} syndrome.
Histologically, lymphangiomas lack {{c1::red blood cells}} in their lumens.
Turner syndrome is characterized by the karyotype {{c1::45,X}}.
Lymphangiomas are the lymphatic equivalent of {{c1::hemangiomas}}.
keyPoints: Lymphangiomas are benign lymphatic analogs of hemangiomas.
Capillary lymphangiomas occur in the skin/subcutaneous tissue.
Cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) occur in the neck or axilla of children.
They consist of large, dilated lymphatic spaces lined by endothelium.
They are often difficult to excise because they lack a capsule and permeate tissues.
microReview: Cystic hygroma + Turner Syndrome = High yield Step 1 association. Both involve abnormalities in lymphatic development or drainage.
examinerTraps: Wait for the chromosomal/phenotypic clue (webbed neck, 45,X). This distinguishes a general neck mass from a cystic hygroma.
sourceQuote: Cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) are typically found in the neck or axilla of children... and are common in Turner syndrome.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with a rapidly growing, pedunculated, red lesion on her gingiva. The lesion bleeds easily with minor trauma. Which of the following is the most likely histopathologic diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas are deeper, larger, and involve large blood-filled spaces, not typically appearing as small gingival polyps.
explanations.b: Nevus flammeus is a flat birthmark (e.g., port-wine stain).
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a common, fast-growing, friable lesion often found on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.d: Kaposi sarcoma is a malignancy related to HHV-8; it does not typically present as a single pedunculated gingival lesion in a healthy pregnant woman.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is an aggressive malignancy with significant cellular atypia, unlike the benign reactive-appearing pyogenic granuloma.

ankiCards: A pyogenic granuloma found on the gingiva of a pregnant woman is called a {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized by {{c1::rapid}} growth and frequent {{c2::bleeding}}.
Despite the name, a pyogenic granuloma is not a {{c1::granuloma (or infectious/pyogenic)}}; it is a vascular lesion.
Histologically, pyogenic granulomas resemble {{c1::granulation tissue}} (or capillary hemangioma).
Common locations for pyogenic granuloma include the {{c1::skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granulomas are capillary hemangiomas that present as rapidly growing red nodules.
They are often pedunculated and ulcerated.
They are misnamed: they are neither pyogenic (pus-forming) nor granulomatous.
The gingival version in pregnancy is common and may regress after delivery.
Treatment is usually surgical excision.
microReview: Fast-growing, bleeding, pregnant, gums = Pyogenic granuloma.
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic granuloma' is a total misnomer. It's actually a lobular capillary hemangioma.
sourceQuote: Pyogenic granulomas are capillary hemangiomas that manifest as rapidly growing red pedunculated lesions... A pregnancy tumor (granuloma gravidarum) is a pyogenic granuloma that occurs in the gingiva of pregnant women.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old man who worked in a chemical plant for 30 years producing polyvinyl chloride (PVC) presents with abdominal pain and weight loss. Imaging reveals multiple ill-defined, hemorrhagic masses within the liver. Biopsy shows highly pleomorphic, spindle-shaped cells lining irregular, slit-like vascular spaces. Immunostaining is positive for CD31. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Hepatocellular carcinoma is associated with HBV/HCV and cirrhosis, not vinyl chloride.
explanations.b: Cholangiocarcinoma is a cancer of the bile ducts, associated with PSC or liver flukes.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma of the liver is specifically associated with occupational exposure to vinyl chloride, arsenic, or Thorotrast.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are the most common benign liver tumors and do not show pleomorphic malignant cells or Slit-like spaces.
explanations.e: Focal nodular hyperplasia is a benign regenerative response to a vascular malformation, typically showing a 'central scar'.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}, {{c2::arsenic}}, and {{c3::Thorotrast}}.
The specific endothelial marker positive in angiosarcoma is {{c1::CD31}}.
Angiosarcoma is a {{c1::malignant}} tumor of the endothelium.
Vinyl chloride is used in the manufacturing of {{c1::polyvinyl chloride (PVC)/plastics}}.
Malignant spindle cells lining vascular spaces in the liver suggest {{c1::angiosarcoma}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas of the liver are rare but highly associated with specific carcinogens.
Vinyl chloride (plastic industry), Arsenic (pesticides), and Thorotrast (radiocontrast) are the classic three.
They are aggressive and often metastatic by the time of diagnosis.
Tumor cells express CD31 and von Willebrand factor.
Morphology ranges from well-differentiated vessels to undifferentiated solid masses.
microReview: Liver + Vinyl Chloride + CD31 positive = Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Don't pick Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC). While common, it doesn't have the endothelial marker CD31 or the specific 'vinyl chloride' association.
sourceQuote: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with distinct environmental carcinogens, including arsenic (pesticides), Thorotrast (a radioactive contrast medium), and vinyl chloride.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 22-year-old male with untreated AIDS presents with several skin lesions and respiratory distress. Bronchoscopy reveals violaceous endobronchial plaques. Skin biopsy shows a spindle cell proliferation. In this patient, the tumor cells most likely express which protein that drives the proliferation via autocrine and paracrine loops?

explanations.a: HER2/neu is an EGF receptor overexpressed in certain breast cancers, not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.b: HHV-8 infection in Kaposi sarcoma induces the production of VEGF and other cytokines, which promote the characteristic vascular and spindle cell proliferation.
explanations.c: BCR-ABL is found in chronic myeloid leukemia.
explanations.d: While p53 may be involved in many cancers, it is not the primary driver for the vascular proliferation in KS.
explanations.e: BRAF V600E is associated with melanoma and papillary thyroid cancer.

ankiCards: In Kaposi Sarcoma, HHV-8 induces the production of {{c1::VEGF}} which drives vascular growth.
The endobronchial plaques in an AIDS patient are a manifestation of {{c1::Kaposi Sarcoma}}.
KS cells produce {{c1::cytokines}} that promote their own growth and the growth of normal cells (paracrine).
{{c1::HHV-8}} is also known as KSHV (Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus).
The clinical stage of KS where lesions become raised and purple is the {{c1::plaque}} stage.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma cells are 'spindle cells' of endothelial origin.
HHV-8 encodes viral G-protein coupled receptors that stimulate VEGF.
The disease process involves both inflammatory and neoplastic components.
It can affect the skin, mouth, GI tract, and lungs (visceral involvement).
In AIDS, highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) can cause regression of KS.
microReview: KS Pathogenesis: HHV-8 + Immunosuppression -> Cytokines (VEGF) -> Vascular/Spindle cell proliferation.
examinerTraps: Recall that KS is not just a skin disease; in AIDS, it often involves the lungs (causing hemoptysis/distress) and GI tract.
sourceQuote: Infected cells [with HHV-8] produce several cytokines... including VEGF, which promotes both vascular proliferation and the growth of the spindle cells.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular lesions is characterized by a 'port-wine stain' appearance and is classically associated with leptomeningeal angiomatosis, seizures, and mental retardation in Sturge-Weber syndrome?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas (strawberry) usually regress and are not associated with Sturge-Weber.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are larger, deeper lesions that do not typically present as a flat port-wine stain.
explanations.c: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a form of ectasia; when found in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve, it can be part of Sturge-Weber syndrome.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor, not a congenital malformation like a port-wine stain.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are small, painful subungual nodules.

ankiCards: The medical term for a port-wine stain is {{c1::nevus flammeus}}.
Sturge-Weber syndrome involves a port-wine stain in the distribution of the {{c1::trigeminal (CN V)}} nerve.
Patients with Sturge-Weber syndrome often have {{c1::leptomeningeal}} angiomatosis.
Common CNS symptoms in Sturge-Weber include {{c1::seizures}} and mental retardation.
True/False: A standard nevus flammeus (birthmark) usually regresses spontaneously. {{c1::False}}.
keyPoints: Nevus flammeus is a congenital vascular malformation (ectasia).
The 'port-wine stain' is a special form that grows and thickens with the child.
Sturge-Weber syndrome: Port-wine stain + Ipsilateral glaucoma + Meningeal angiomas.
The meningeal angiomas are typically in the ophthalmic (V1) or maxillary (V2) distribution.
Radiology may show 'tram-track' calcifications in the brain.
microReview: Port-wine stain + Seizures = Sturge-Weber Syndrome.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'Nevus Simplex' (salmon patch/stork bite that fades) with 'Nevus Flammeus' (port-wine stain that persists).
sourceQuote: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain)... when in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve, may be associated with the Sturge-Weber syndrome.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular tumors is considered 'intermediate grade' (borderline), possessing features that fall between benign hemangiomas and highly malignant angiosarcomas?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign capillary hemangioma.
explanations.b: Hemangioendotheliomas, particularly the epithelioid type, are intermediate-grade vascular neoplasms with unpredictable behavior.
explanations.c: Cystic hygroma is a benign lymphatic malformation.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign reactive vascular proliferation caused by infection.
explanations.e: Nevus flammeus is a benign vascular ectasia.

ankiCards: {{c1::Hemangioendothelioma}} is the classic example of an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
Epithelioid hemangioendotheliomas are often found around {{c1::medium-to-large veins}}.
Intermediate-grade tumors have behavior between {{c1::benign}} hemangiomas and {{c2::malignant}} angiosarcomas.
True/False: Most patients with hemangioendothelioma die within one year. {{c1::False (most are cured by excision, but some metastasize)}}.
Histologically, hemangioendotheliomas often contain {{c1::epithelioid}} cells.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors are grouped into Benign, Intermediate, and Malignant.
Intermediate grade means they are locally aggressive but have low metastatic potential.
Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is the most common intermediate tumor.
Tumor cells are plump and cuboidal (epithelioid).
Clinical behavior is highly variable and hard to predict from histology.
microReview: Benign = Hemangioma; Intermediate = Hemangioendothelioma; Malignant = Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Note that 'Kaposi Sarcoma' is also sometimes classified as intermediate-grade (borderline) because it is usually not as aggressive as a true angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors... epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is a vascular tumor of adults occurring around medium-sized and large veins.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 64-year-old woman presents with several firm, violaceous nodules on her left arm. Ten years ago, she underwent a radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection and radiotherapy for breast adenocarcinoma. Since that time, she has had chronic, non-pitting edema of the left upper extremity. A biopsy of one of the nodules shows atypical spindle cells forming irregular, anastomosing vascular channels that dissect through the dermal collagen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are benign lesions, typically occurring in infancy, and do not present as violaceous nodules in the setting of chronic lymphedema.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors are small, painful, benign tumors typically found under the fingernails, arising from specialized smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
explanations.c: While Kaposi sarcoma presents as violaceous lesions, it is associated with HHV-8 infection and usually occurs in the setting of immunosuppression or specific ethnic predispositions, not chronic lymphedema post-mastectomy.
explanations.d: This patient has Stewart-Treves syndrome, which is the development of angiosarcoma in the setting of chronic lymphedema (most commonly post-mastectomy with lymph node dissection). Histology shows malignant endothelial cells forming anastomosing channels.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella infection in immunocompromised patients; while it forms vascular lesions, it does not fit the clinical history of chronic lymphedema and malignancy.

ankiCards: Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to {{c1::angiosarcoma}} arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema.
The most common clinical scenario for Stewart-Treves syndrome is post-{{c1::mastectomy}} with axillary node dissection.
Histologically, angiosarcoma is characterized by {{c1::anastomosing}} vascular channels lined by atypical endothelial cells.
Angiosarcoma is a {{c1::malignant}} vascular tumor with a very poor prognosis.
Besides lymphedema, angiosarcoma is associated with prior exposure to {{c1::radiation}} or chemicals like vinyl chloride.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor of endothelial cells.
Chronic lymphedema is a major risk factor for cutaneous angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
Radiation therapy for breast cancer is a known independent risk factor for chest wall angiosarcoma.
Histology demonstrates infiltrative, irregular vascular spaces with prominent cytologic atypia.
Tumor cells are typically positive for endothelial markers like CD31.
microReview: Vascular tumors range from benign (hemangioma) to intermediate (Kaposi) to malignant (Angiosarcoma). Angiosarcomas are aggressive and often associated with specific environmental triggers or chronic stasis.
examinerTraps: Students often confuse Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8) with Angiosarcoma (Chronic lymphedema/Stewart-Treves) because both present as violaceous skin lesions.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... Malignant Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old male with a history of advanced HIV (CD4+ count < 100 cells/μL) presents with multiple reddish-purple, maculopapular skin lesions on his lower extremities and trunk. Biopsy reveals proliferation of spindle-shaped cells, slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells, and hyaline droplets. Which of the following pathogens is the primary causative agent of this condition?

explanations.a: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can look similar clinically but has a neutrophilic infiltrate and different histology (no slit-like spaces).
explanations.b: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the definitive cause of all forms of Kaposi Sarcoma (KS).
explanations.c: EBV is associated with various lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, but not with vascular tumors like Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.d: CMV can cause opportunistic infections in AIDS patients but is not oncogenic for vascular endothelium in the context of KS.
explanations.e: HPV is associated with squamous cell carcinomas and warts, not vascular lesions.

ankiCards: The causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::HHV-8}} (also known as KSHV).
Kaposi Sarcoma histology is characterized by {{c1::slit-like}} vascular spaces and spindle cells.
In AIDS patients, Kaposi Sarcoma is considered an {{c1::AIDS-defining}} illness.
The reddish-purple color of Kaposi lesions is due to {{c1::extravasated}} red blood cells.
{{c1::Bartonella}} causes bacillary angiomatosis, which is the main differential for Kaposi Sarcoma.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is an intermediate-grade vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8.
There are four forms: Classic (older Mediterranean men), Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
The characteristic histological feature is spindle cells forming slit-like spaces with RBCs.
HHV-8 infects endothelial cells and induces a spindle-cell phenotype.
Diagnosis is confirmed by HHV-8 immunostaining.
microReview: When you see an HIV patient with purple skin lesions, think Kaposi (HHV-8) or Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella). Histology distinguishes them: slit-spaces for Kaposi, neutrophils/bacteria for Bacillary.
examinerTraps: Mistaking the bacterial cause (Bartonella) for the viral cause (HHV-8) in an AIDS patient with vascular skin lesions.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... Malignant Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 25-year-old man presents with an exquisitely painful, 4-mm, blue-red nodule located under the fingernail of his right index finger. He notes that the pain is often triggered by exposure to cold. The tumor most likely originates from which of the following cell types?

explanations.a: While most vascular tumors are endothelial, the glomus tumor arises from specialized smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
explanations.b: Pericytes are the origin of hemangiopericytomas, which are generally not painful subungual lesions.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors arise from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus bodies, which are specialized arteriovenous structures involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts produce collagen and are not the primary cell type in a glomus tumor.
explanations.e: Lymphatic endothelial cells form lymphangiomas, which are typically painless and not subungual.

ankiCards: A glomus tumor is most commonly found in the {{c1::subungual}} (under nail) region.
Glomus tumors are characterized by the clinical triad of pain, tenderness, and sensitivity to {{c1::cold}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells of the glomus body.
The glomus body is a specialized {{c1::arteriovenous}} anastomosis used for thermoregulation.
Histologically, glomus tumors show nests of uniform, round cells surrounding {{c1::vascular}} channels.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but extremely painful.
Classic location: distal digits, especially subungual.
Origin: Modified smooth muscle cells (glomus cells).
Function of normal glomus body: Thermoregulation.
Treatment is simple excision, which is curative.
microReview: Subungual + Exquisite pain + Blue/Red color = Glomus Tumor (Smooth muscle origin).
examinerTraps: Thinking all vascular tumors are endothelial. Glomus cells are modified smooth muscle.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the histopathological evaluation of a suspected malignant vascular tumor, which of the following immunohistochemical markers is most specific for confirming endothelial differentiation?

explanations.a: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells (carcinomas).
explanations.b: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (leio/rhabdomyosarcomas).
explanations.c: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells (melanoma, Schwannoma).
explanations.d: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a highly specific and sensitive marker for endothelial cells and is used to identify vascular tumors like angiosarcoma.
explanations.e: Vimentin is a general marker for mesenchymal cells and is not specific for endothelium.

ankiCards: The most specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial cells is {{c1::CD31}}.
CD31 is also known as {{c1::PECAM-1}} (Platelet Endothelial Cell Adhesion Molecule).
Another marker for endothelial cells (though less specific than CD31) is {{c1::von Willebrand factor}} (vWF).
Angiosarcomas will typically stain positive for the marker {{c1::CD31}}.
{{c1::Factor VIII}}-related antigen is also an older marker used for vascular tumors.
keyPoints: Endothelial markers are essential for diagnosing poorly differentiated angiosarcomas.
CD31 (PECAM-1) is the gold standard.
CD34 is also used but is less specific (it stains many mesenchymal tumors).
ERG is a newer, very sensitive nuclear marker for endothelial differentiation.
Immunohistochemistry helps differentiate vascular tumors from other spindle cell sarcomas.
microReview: Markers for Endothelium: CD31 (Best), CD34, vWF (Factor VIII), ERG.
examinerTraps: CD34 is often used, but CD31 is more specific for the endothelial lineage.
sourceQuote: Vascular Structure and Function... Vascular Tumors... Malignant Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 1-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician by his mother, who is concerned about a bright red, raised, lobulated lesion on the baby's scalp that has been growing rapidly since birth. The mother states the lesion was not present at birth but appeared at 2 weeks of age. Which of the following is the most likely clinical course for this lesion?

options.e: Systemic spread to the liver and lungs

explanations.a: Infantile (strawberry) hemangiomas are benign and do not undergo malignant transformation.
explanations.b: Strawberry (juvenile) hemangiomas typically grow rapidly for a few months and then spontaneously involute (regress) by age 5 to 7 years.
explanations.c: These lesions do not grow indefinitely; they are characterized by predictable regression.
explanations.d: While very large internal hemangiomas can rarely cause high-output failure (e.g., in the liver), a standard cutaneous strawberry hemangioma does not.
explanations.e: Hemangiomas are benign and do not metastasize.

ankiCards: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are typically {{c1::absent}} at birth but appear within weeks.
The most common clinical course for a strawberry hemangioma is {{c1::spontaneous regression}}.
Most juvenile hemangiomas completely involute by age {{c1::7}}.
Histologically, juvenile hemangiomas are a type of {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma.
A strawberry hemangioma is a {{c1::benign}} vascular tumor of childhood.
keyPoints: Strawberry hemangioma = Juvenile hemangioma.
Extremely common (1 in 200 births).
Phase 1: Rapid growth (first few months).
Phase 2: Stabilization and slow regression.
Complete involution occurs in ~90% of cases by age 7.
microReview: Infant + Red 'Strawberry' lesion + Rapid growth = Juvenile Hemangioma. Management: Observation (it will go away).
examinerTraps: Distinguishing Strawberry hemangioma (regresses) from Port-wine stain (Sturge-Weber, does not regress).
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An 18-year-old male with a history of long-standing epilepsy and intellectual disability is found to have a large, dull-red, flat 'port-wine' birthmark on the right side of his face, following the distribution of the trigeminal nerve. Radiographic imaging of the head shows tram-track calcifications in the underlying leptomeninges. This constellation of findings is associated with which of the following conditions?

explanations.a: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) involves multiple telangiectasias and AVMs, not port-wine stains and leptomeningeal angiomas.
explanations.b: Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) is characterized by a facial port-wine stain (nevus flammeus), leptomeningeal venous angiomas, seizures, and mental retardation.
explanations.c: VHL involves hemangioblastomas (CNS/Retina) and renal cell carcinoma, not port-wine stains.
explanations.d: NF1 presents with café-au-lait spots and neurofibromas, not vascular port-wine stains.
explanations.e: Tuberous sclerosis presents with ash-leaf spots and angiofibromas, but the vascular malformation described is classic for Sturge-Weber.

ankiCards: Sturge-Weber syndrome is characterized by a facial {{c1::port-wine stain}} (nevus flammeus).
The facial lesion in Sturge-Weber follows the distribution of the {{c1::trigeminal}} nerve.
Brain involvement in Sturge-Weber includes {{c1::leptomeningeal}} angiomas.
Radiology of Sturge-Weber often shows '{{c1::tram-track}}' calcifications in the cortex.
The clinical triad of Sturge-Weber includes skin lesions, {{c1::seizures}}, and intellectual disability.
keyPoints: Sturge-Weber syndrome is a sporadic neurocutaneous disorder.
The vascular lesion is a capillary malformation (Nevus flammeus).
Leptomeningeal angiomas occur ipsilateral to the skin lesion.
The 'tram-track' calcifications represent calcified gyri.
GNAQ gene mutations are often implicated.
microReview: Port-wine stain (V1/V2 distribution) + Seizures + Tram-track calcifications = Sturge-Weber.
examinerTraps: Mistaking a Port-wine stain (permanent) for a Strawberry hemangioma (regresses).
sourceQuote: Vascular Anomalies... Vascular Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old man who worked for 20 years in a chemical plant producing polyvinyl chloride (PVC) presents with abdominal pain, weight loss, and jaundice. Imaging reveals multiple mass lesions within the liver. A biopsy of a liver mass shows spindle-shaped malignant cells lining large, cavernous vascular spaces. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Hepatic adenomas are benign and usually associated with oral contraceptives or anabolic steroids, not PVC.
explanations.b: HCC is the most common primary liver cancer, but it is typically associated with cirrhosis or hepatitis, and its histology is epithelial, not vascular spindle cells.
explanations.c: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare but highly aggressive tumor associated with exposure to vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are the most common benign liver tumors and are usually asymptomatic, not presenting with weight loss and malignancy.
explanations.e: This is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor, but the specific association with vinyl chloride strongly points toward the fully malignant angiosarcoma.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
Other risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma include {{c1::arsenic}} and Thorotrast.
The malignant cells in angiosarcoma are of {{c1::endothelial}} origin.
Vinyl chloride is used in the manufacture of the plastic {{c1::PVC}}.
The prognosis for hepatic angiosarcoma is very {{c1::poor}}.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a classic board association for industrial chemical exposure.
Vinyl chloride monomers are used in plastics industries.
Latent period between exposure and tumor development is usually decades.
The tumor is aggressive with frequent metastasis.
Histology: Atypical endothelial cells, often spindle-shaped, invading liver sinusoids.
microReview: Exposure History + Liver Mass + Vascular Histology = Angiosarcoma. Key exposures: Vinyl chloride, Arsenic, Thorotrast.
examinerTraps: Confusing Cavernous Hemangioma (benign, incidental) with Angiosarcoma (malignant, symptomatic).
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Malignant Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman presents with a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated nodule on her gingiva that bleeds easily with minor trauma. The lesion appeared during her second trimester. Histological examination shows a highly vascularized proliferation of capillaries with prominent edema and inflammatory cells, resembling granulation tissue. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors are subungual and painful; they do not typically occur on the gingiva during pregnancy.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a benign, fast-growing vascular lesion often occurring on the skin or oral mucosa (gingiva), especially during pregnancy (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, blood-filled spaces and do not usually present as pedunculated, bleeding gingival masses.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor and does not typically present as a pregnancy-related gingival nodule.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is associated with Bartonella in HIV patients, not pregnancy.

ankiCards: A pyogenic granuloma that occurs on the gingiva during pregnancy is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
The clinical appearance of a pyogenic granuloma is a red, {{c1::pedunculated}} mass that bleeds easily.
Histologically, a pyogenic granuloma resembles {{c1::granulation tissue}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are essentially a type of {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma.
Despite the name, a pyogenic granuloma is neither {{c1::pyogenic}} (infectious) nor a true granuloma.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is a benign vascular neoplasm.
Commonly occurs after minor trauma.
Gingival lesions in pregnant women are common due to hormonal influences.
They can regress spontaneously after delivery or require simple excision.
Histology: Lobular arrangement of capillaries with inflammation.
microReview: Pregnant woman + Bleeding gum nodule = Pyogenic Granuloma (Granuloma gravidarum).
examinerTraps: The name 'Pyogenic Granuloma' suggests infection or granulomatous inflammation, but it is actually a vascular proliferation.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular tumors is characterized as 'intermediate-grade' (borderline) due to its locally aggressive nature and low but definite metastatic potential?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are completely benign.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are completely benign.
explanations.c: Kaposi Sarcoma is classified as an intermediate-grade (borderline) vascular tumor because its behavior ranges from indolent to locally aggressive with limited metastatic potential compared to angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade, highly malignant tumor.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are benign.

ankiCards: Vascular tumors are classified as benign, {{c1::intermediate}} (borderline), or malignant.
{{c1::Kaposi Sarcoma}} and hemangioendothelioma are examples of intermediate-grade vascular tumors.
Intermediate-grade tumors are {{c1::locally aggressive}} but have lower metastatic potential than angiosarcoma.
{{c1::Angiosarcoma}} is the prototypical high-grade malignant vascular tumor.
{{c1::Hemangiomas}} are the prototypical benign vascular tumors.
keyPoints: Tumor grading in vascular pathology is based on clinical behavior.
Benign: Hemangioma, Glomus tumor.
Intermediate: Kaposi Sarcoma, Hemangioendothelioma.
Malignant: Angiosarcoma.
Kaposi Sarcoma is the most common 'intermediate' lesion discussed.
microReview: Benign = Hemangioma; Intermediate = Kaposi; Malignant = Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Assuming Kaposi Sarcoma is a simple benign 'rash' or a highly metastatic sarcoma; it is officially borderline/intermediate.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... Malignant Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 40-year-old male with a history of poorly controlled AIDS presents with a fever and multiple friable, red-to-purple skin papules. A biopsy of a lesion is performed, and Warthin-Starry silver staining reveals clusters of small, bacilli. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 (a virus) and would not show bacilli on Warthin-Starry stain; it would also lack the neutrophilic infiltrate typical of this presentation.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella henselae or B. quintana in immunocompromised patients. It presents with vascular skin lesions and is diagnosed by seeing organisms on silver (Warthin-Starry) stain.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a malignancy of endothelium and does not contain bacterial clusters.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign reactive lesion, not specifically associated with AIDS or bacteria.
explanations.e: Cherry hemangiomas are common benign senile vascular lesions and are not associated with bacteria or fever.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by the bacteria {{c1::Bartonella}} henselae/quintana.
The specific stain used to identify Bartonella in tissue is the {{c1::Warthin-Starry}} silver stain.
Bacillary angiomatosis is a clinical mimic of {{c1::Kaposi Sarcoma}}.
Unlike Kaposi Sarcoma, Bacillary angiomatosis features a {{c1::neutrophilic}} inflammatory infiltrate.
The reservoir for Bartonella henselae is typically {{c1::cats}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis: opportunistic infection in HIV/AIDS.
Causative agents: Bartonella henselae (cat scratch) or Bartonella quintana (body lice).
Histology: Proliferation of capillaries with protuberant epithelioid endothelial cells and neutrophils.
Stain of choice: Warthin-Starry silver stain.
Treatment: Antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin), unlike Kaposi which requires antiretrovirals/chemo.
microReview: Vascular skin lesion in AIDS: If Warthin-Starry positive = Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella); If Warthin-Starry negative and slit-spaces = Kaposi (HHV-8).
examinerTraps: Choosing Kaposi sarcoma simply because the patient has AIDS, without accounting for the silver stain findings.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male presents for a routine physical examination. He has a 45-pack-year smoking history and long-standing hypertension. On abdominal palpation, a prominent, pulsatile mass is felt at the level of the umbilicus. Imaging confirms a 5.2 cm dilation of the infrarenal aorta. Which of the following is the primary underlying mechanism responsible for this patient's condition?

options.b: Inflammatory destruction of the vasa vasorum
options.c: Atherosclerosis-induced intimal thickening and impaired media nutrition
options.d: Congenital defect in the internal elastic lamina
options.e: Intimal tear leading to blood tracking within the vessel wall

explanations.a: Cystic medial degeneration is the classic mechanism for thoracic aortic aneurysms, often associated with Marfan syndrome, rather than the more common abdominal aortic aneurysm associated with atherosclerosis.
explanations.b: Destruction of the vasa vasorum is the mechanism for syphilitic (tertiary syphilis) aneurysms, which typically occur in the ascending aorta.
explanations.c: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are primarily driven by atherosclerosis. The thickened intima increases the diffusion distance for nutrients from the lumen to the media, leading to medial ischemia, atrophy, and wall weakening.
explanations.d: Congenital defects in the internal elastic lamina are the hallmark of Berry aneurysms in the Circle of Willis, not AAAs.
explanations.e: An intimal tear leading to blood tracking between the layers of the media describes an aortic dissection, which is a distinct clinical entity from a true aneurysm.

ankiCards: The most common cause of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms (AAA) is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Atherosclerosis causes AAA by increasing the {{c1::diffusion}} distance for oxygen/nutrients, leading to media ischemia.
The most common location for a clinical aneurysm caused by atherosclerosis is the {{c1::infrarenal}} abdominal aorta.
The two principal mechanisms of vascular disease are narrowing/obstruction and {{c1::weakening}} of vessel walls.
A pulsatile abdominal mass in an older male smoker is highly suggestive of {{c1::abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA)}}.
keyPoints: Atherosclerosis is the dominant risk factor for Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm.
Mechanism involves intimal plaque causing pressure-induced atrophy of the media.
Media ischemia leads to the loss of elastic fibers and wall thinning.
AAA typically occurs below the renal arteries and above the iliac bifurcation.
Rupture risk increases significantly once the diameter exceeds 5 cm.
microReview: Aneurysms involve the weakening of the vessel wall. AAAs are primarily atherosclerotic (infrarenal), whereas Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (TAAs) are often associated with hypertension or connective tissue disorders like Marfan (cystic medial necrosis).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the site: AAAs are infrarenal (atherosclerosis), while TAAs are ascending (hypertension/Marfan). Syphilitic aneurysms also favor the ascending aorta.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular pathology can be broadly categorized based on the functional integrity and structural architecture of the vessel wall. If a patient develops a hematoma that communicates with the intravascular space through a defect in the vascular wall, while the outer wall of the hematoma consists only of extravascular connective tissue, how is this lesion classified?

explanations.a: A saccular aneurysm is a 'true' aneurysm involving all three layers of the vessel wall (intima, media, adventitia).
explanations.b: A fusiform aneurysm is a 'true' aneurysm involving all three layers, characterized by circumferential dilation.
explanations.c: A false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) is a breach in the vascular wall leading to an extravascular hematoma that freely communicates with the intravascular space.
explanations.d: A dissection occurs when blood enters the wall of the artery itself, creating a false lumen between layers, typically the media.
explanations.e: Arteriovenous malformations are direct connections between arteries and veins bypassing capillaries, not related to localized wall ruptures.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the arterial wall.
A {{c1::false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm)}} is a wall defect leading to an extravascular hematoma communicating with the lumen.
A {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm is a spherical outpouching involving only a portion of the vessel wall.
A {{c1::fusiform}} aneurysm is a circumferential, spindle-shaped dilation of the vessel.
An aortic {{c1::dissection}} occurs when blood tracks between the layers of the media.
keyPoints: True aneurysms (saccular/fusiform) involve the intact attenuated vessel wall (intima, media, and adventitia).
False aneurysms (pseudoaneurysms) involve a wall defect and a hematoma bounded by extravascular tissue.
Common causes of pseudoaneurysms include trauma or femoral artery catheterization.
Dissection is not synonymous with aneurysm; it is the entry of blood into the media itself.
Understanding these categories is vital for determining the risk of rupture.
microReview: Distinguish between True Aneurysms (all 3 wall layers dilated) and False Aneurysms (rupture through the wall with contained hematoma).
examinerTraps: Wait for the description of the wall layers. If all three layers are present, it is a 'True' aneurysm regardless of shape (saccular/fusiform).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: ... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old male presents with sudden-onset, severe 'tearing' chest pain that radiates to his back. Physical exam reveals arachnodactyly, a high-arched palate, and pectus excavatum. Genetic testing confirms a mutation in a gene encoding an extracellular matrix glycoprotein. This patient's vascular condition is most likely characterized by which histological finding?

explanations.a: Vasa vasorum endarteritis (obliterative endarteritis) is typical of tertiary syphilis, which affects the ascending aorta but is not associated with Marfan syndrome.
explanations.b: Medial calcific sclerosis (Mönckeberg) involves calcification of the media in muscular arteries and does not usually lead to dissection or aneurysms.
explanations.c: Marfan syndrome (FBN1 mutation) leads to cystic medial degeneration, characterized by the loss of smooth muscle cells and elastic fibers with the accumulation of proteoglycans, predisposing to aneurysms and dissection.
explanations.d: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a small-vessel inflammatory condition, not related to large-vessel genetic weakness.
explanations.e: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is a result of chronic hypertension or diabetes in small arterioles, not the large vessels affected in Marfan syndrome.

ankiCards: Marfan syndrome is caused by a mutation in the {{c1::FBN1 (Fibrillin-1)}} gene.
The characteristic histological finding in Marfan-associated aortic disease is {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
Cystic medial degeneration involves the loss of {{c1::elastic fibers/smooth muscle cells}} and accumulation of proteoglycans.
Patients with Marfan syndrome are at high risk for thoracic aortic {{c1::aneurysm and dissection}}.
A 'tearing' chest pain radiating to the back in a tall patient with long fingers suggests {{c1::aortic dissection}}.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome results in defective Fibrillin-1, a scaffold for elastin.
This leads to weakened aortic media (cystic medial degeneration).
TGF-beta signaling is often abnormally increased in these patients.
Clinical signs: Tall stature, long limbs/fingers, lens dislocation, aortic root dilation.
This represents a 'weakening of vessel walls' mechanism of disease.
microReview: Marfan syndrome -> Fibrillin-1 defect -> Weak media (Cystic medial necrosis/degeneration) -> Thoracic aortic aneurysm/dissection.
examinerTraps: The term 'Cystic medial necrosis' is common but 'degeneration' is more accurate because there is no actual necrosis involved.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the pathogenesis of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA), which family of enzymes is most directly implicated in the degradation of the extracellular matrix within the arterial media, contributing to wall weakening?

explanations.a: Caspases are involved in apoptosis, but the primary driver of wall destruction in AAA is the enzymatic degradation of collagen and elastin.
explanations.b: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), especially MMP-2 and MMP-9, are produced by inflammatory cells in the plaque and media. They degrade elastin and collagen, leading to wall weakening.
explanations.c: COXs are involved in prostaglandin synthesis and inflammation but are not the primary enzymes degrading the structural matrix of the wall.
explanations.d: Creatine kinases are intracellular enzymes involved in energy metabolism, used clinically as markers of muscle damage.
explanations.e: Glutathione peroxidases are antioxidant enzymes that protect cells from oxidative stress but do not degrade the media.

ankiCards: The enzymes primarily responsible for degrading the aortic media in AAA are {{c1::Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
Two specific MMPs implicated in aneurysm formation are {{c1::MMP-2 and MMP-9}}.
MMPs in AAA are typically secreted by {{c1::macrophages/inflammatory cells}}.
Degradation of {{c1::elastin and collagen}} in the media leads to vascular wall weakening.
The recruitment of an {{c1::inflammatory}} infiltrate is a key step in the progression of atherosclerotic AAA.
keyPoints: AAA involves a chronic inflammatory infiltrate in the media and adventitia.
Macrophages secrete MMPs that digest the structural proteins (elastin/collagen).
This process results in a 'weakening of vessel walls' (the second mechanism in the text).
Increased MMP activity is often balanced by TIMPs (tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases).
The resulting loss of elastic recoil and tensile strength leads to dilation.
microReview: Inflammation -> Macrophages -> MMPs (2 and 9) -> Degradation of elastin/collagen -> Aortic wall weakening -> AAA.
examinerTraps: Often, they will ask for the cell type (macrophage) or the enzyme (MMP). Remember both.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following conditions is the most common cause of an aneurysm that specifically targets the ascending aorta and is associated with 'tree-barking' appearance of the intimal surface?

explanations.a: Atherosclerosis typically affects the abdominal aorta, not the ascending aorta, and does not cause tree-barking.
explanations.b: Diabetes causes hyaline arteriolosclerosis of small vessels, not large-vessel aneurysms with this morphology.
explanations.c: Tertiary syphilis causes obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum. This results in medial ischemia, scarring, and 'tree-barking' of the intima in the ascending aorta.
explanations.d: Giant cell arteritis is an inflammatory vasculitis of large vessels but is not the classic cause of 'tree-barking' aneurysms.
explanations.e: Kawasaki disease primarily causes coronary artery aneurysms in children.

ankiCards: The 'tree-barking' appearance of the aorta is a classic sign of {{c1::syphilitic (luetic)}} aortitis.
Syphilitic aneurysms occur in the {{c1::ascending}} aorta.
The underlying mechanism of syphilitic aneurysm is {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}} of the vasa vasorum.
Ischemia of the {{c1::media}} in syphilis leads to replacement with fibrous tissue (scarring).
Syphilitic aortitis can lead to dilation of the aortic valve ring, causing {{c1::aortic insufficiency/regurgitation}}.
keyPoints: Syphilitic (luetic) aneurysms are now rare due to antibiotics.
They result from the 'weakening of vessel walls' via nutrient deprivation.
Affects the vasa vasorum (the vessels of the vessels).
Media becomes thin and scarred; intima shows 'tree-barking'.
Often involves the aortic root and valve.
microReview: Syphilis -> Vasa vasorum endarteritis -> Medial ischemia -> Fibrosis/Weakness -> Ascending Aorta Aneurysm + Tree-barking.
examinerTraps: Make sure to distinguish 'tree-barking' (Syphilis) from 'fatty streaks/plaques' (Atherosclerosis).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old female with a history of Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) presents to the emergency department with the 'worst headache of her life.' CT scan shows blood in the subarachnoid space. Which of the following is the most likely location of the vascular lesion that ruptured?

explanations.a: Infrarenal aorta is the site of atherosclerotic AAAs, which would not cause a subarachnoid hemorrhage.
explanations.b: ADPKD is strongly associated with 'Berry' aneurysms in the Circle of Willis. The anterior communicating artery is the most common site of these aneurysms.
explanations.c: Ascending thoracic aorta aneurysms are associated with Marfan or hypertension, not ADPKD.
explanations.d: Common iliac artery aneurysms are usually extensions of AAAs.
explanations.e: Coronary artery aneurysms are associated with Kawasaki disease.

ankiCards: The most common type of intracranial aneurysm is the {{c1::Berry (saccular)}} aneurysm.
Berry aneurysms are most commonly found in the {{c1::Circle of Willis}}.
A condition strongly associated with Berry aneurysms is {{c1::ADPKD}}.
The rupture of a Berry aneurysm causes {{c1::subarachnoid}} hemorrhage.
Berry aneurysms occur due to a {{c1::congenital}} defect in the media/internal elastic lamina at branch points.
keyPoints: Berry aneurysms are small, saccular dilations.
They occur at arterial branch points (e.g., anterior communicating artery).
Lack of internal elastic lamina and smooth muscle at these points predisposes to dilation.
Associated with ADPKD and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Clinical presentation: 'Thunderclap' headache.
microReview: ADPKD -> Berry Aneurysm (Circle of Willis) -> Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (Thunderclap headache).
examinerTraps: Aneurysms in ADPKD occur in the brain (Berry), not the kidney, though the kidneys have cysts.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Aneurysms can sometimes be caused by the seeding of an arterial wall by a circulating microorganism, or by the extension of an adjacent suppurative process. What is the specific term for an aneurysm that arises from such an infectious etiology?

explanations.a: Berry aneurysms are congenital defects in the cerebral circulation.
explanations.b: A mycotic aneurysm is an aneurysm resulting from an infection of the vessel wall, often from bacteremia (e.g., infective endocarditis) or local infection.
explanations.c: Saccular refers to the shape of an aneurysm, not its infectious etiology.
explanations.d: Dissection involves blood entering the wall, and while it's sometimes called a 'dissecting aneurysm,' it is not necessarily infectious.
explanations.e: Cystic medial degeneration describes the histological state in Marfan, not an infection.

ankiCards: A {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm is one caused by an infection of the arterial wall.
Mycotic aneurysms often result from {{c1::bacteremia}} (e.g., from endocarditis).
Despite the name 'mycotic', these aneurysms are most often {{c1::bacterial}} in origin.
An infection can cause an aneurysm by inducing an {{c1::inflammatory}} response that weakens the wall.
Mycotic aneurysms are a form of the '{{c1::weakening of vessel walls}}' mechanism.
keyPoints: Mycotic aneuryses are infectious in origin.
Commonly follow infective endocarditis with septic emboli.
Inflammation leads to rapid destruction of the media.
They are highly prone to rupture due to acute weakening.
The term 'mycotic' is a historical misnomer; most are bacterial.
microReview: Infection + Vessel Wall Weakening = Mycotic Aneurysm. Usually bacterial, not fungal.
examinerTraps: The word 'mycotic' sounds like it must be a fungus, but in pathology, it refers to any infectious aneurysm (usually bacterial).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old female with a history of poorly controlled hypertension presents with sudden, excruciating chest pain that she describes as 'stabbing' and radiating to the neck. Her blood pressure is 190/110 mmHg. A chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum. What is the most important risk factor for the development of the underlying medial hematoma in this patient?

explanations.a: Hypercholesterolemia is the major risk factor for atherosclerosis and AAAs, but less so for aortic dissection.
explanations.b: Hypertension is the most important risk factor for aortic dissection in older adults. It causes pressure-related changes in the vasa vasorum and medial hypertrophy, predisposing to tears.
explanations.c: Smoking is a huge risk factor for AAA but is secondary to hypertension in the context of aortic dissection.
explanations.d: Diabetes is a risk factor for general vascular disease but not specifically for the mechanical medial tear of dissection.
explanations.e: Obesity is a metabolic risk factor but is not the primary driver of the medial weakening seen in dissection.

ankiCards: The single most important risk factor for aortic dissection is {{c1::hypertension}}.
Aortic dissection involves an {{c1::intimal}} tear that allows blood to enter the media.
A widened mediastinum on chest X-ray in a hypertensive patient suggests {{c1::aortic dissection}}.
Aortic dissection is distinct from a 'true' aneurysm because it creates a {{c1::false lumen}}.
The classic clinical description of aortic dissection pain is {{c1::tearing or stabbing}}.
keyPoints: Aortic dissection: Blood splits the laminar planes of the media.
Risk factors: Hypertension (older), Connective tissue disease (younger).
Classification: Stanford Type A (ascending) and Type B (descending).
Type A is a surgical emergency due to risk of tamponade.
This condition represents a specific type of wall weakness/failure.
microReview: Hypertension -> Medial hypertrophy/Vasa vasorum changes -> Media weakness -> Intimal tear -> Aortic Dissection.
examinerTraps: Atherosclerosis is actually protective against dissection because the scarring can 'glue' the layers together; hypertension is the real culprit here.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male with a 40-pack-year smoking history and long-standing hypertension presents for a routine physical examination. A pulsatile mass is palpated in the mid-abdomen. An ultrasound confirms a 5.2 cm focal dilation of the abdominal aorta. Which of the following fundamental mechanisms of vascular disease is primarily responsible for the development of this patient's condition?

explanations.a: Precipitous luminal obstruction refers to sudden blockages like thrombosis or embolism, which typically lead to ischemia rather than dilation.
explanations.b: Progressive intimal thickening is a stereotyped response to injury but usually results in stenosis or narrowing rather than the dilation seen in aneurysms.
