ankiCards: A bright red, raised vascular lesion in an infant that appears after birth is likely a {{c1::strawberry (capillary) hemangioma}}.
The common outcome for a strawberry hemangioma is {{c1::spontaneous regression}}.
Most infantile hemangiomas disappear by age {{c1::7 (or 5-9)}}.
Histologically, strawberry hemangiomas are composed of {{c1::closely packed capillaries}}.
Unlike strawberry hemangiomas, {{c1::port-wine stains (Nevus flammeus)}} do not regress and grow with the child.
keyPoints: Capillary hemangioma is the most common vascular tumor.
Infantile type is called 'strawberry hemangioma' due to its appearance.
They are characterized by a rapid growth phase followed by gradual involution.
Histology shows thin-walled capillaries with scant stroma.
Treatment is usually observation unless they obstruct vision or the airway.
microReview: Infantile hemangiomas are benign proliferations of capillaries. Their hallmark is the predictable life cycle: rapid growth after birth followed by slow regression.
examinerTraps: Confusing strawberry hemangiomas with port-wine stains (Nevus flammeus). Port-wine stains are present at birth, do not regress, and are associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular lesions is characterized histologically by a 'lobular' arrangement of proliferating capillaries and is often associated with pregnancy or minor trauma to the gingiva?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated vascular spaces, not a lobular arrangement of small capillaries.
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor with significant atypia, not a benign lobular capillary proliferation.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a rapidly growing pedunculated red nodule on the skin or gingiva, often following trauma or during pregnancy.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella and involves capillaries, but its hallmark is neutrophilic infiltrates and bacteria, not necessarily the classic clinical 'pregnancy tumor' presentation.
explanations.e: Spider angioma is a non-neoplastic vascular ectasia, not a proliferative tumor.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer because it is neither {{c1::pyogenic (pus-forming)}} nor a {{c2::granuloma}}.
The histological name for pyogenic granuloma is {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are often associated with {{c1::pregnancy}} (granuloma gravidarum) or {{c2::trauma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are classically located on the {{c1::gingiva}} or {{c2::skin}}.
The clinical appearance of a pyogenic granuloma is a {{c1::pedunculated red nodule}} that bleeds easily.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign vascular proliferation.
It grows rapidly and can bleed with minimal provocation.
Histology shows capillaries arranged in lobules separated by stroma.
It is often referred to as 'granuloma gravidarum' when occurring in the mouth of pregnant women.
Surgical excision or curettage is the standard treatment.
microReview: Pyogenic granulomas are essentially exuberant reactive vascular proliferations. They are notable for their rapid growth and tendency to bleed.
examinerTraps: The name is a trap. It sounds like an infection or an inflammatory granuloma, but it is actually a capillary hemangioma.
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old female underwent a radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer 12 years ago. She has since suffered from chronic, severe lymphedema of the left arm. Recently, she noticed several dark-purple, firm skin nodules developing on the lymphedematous limb. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: While recurrence is possible, the development of purple nodules in the setting of chronic lymphedema specifically points to a vascular malignancy.
explanations.b: Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema, typically following radical mastectomy.
explanations.c: Stasis dermatitis is a skin change due to venous insufficiency, not chronic lymphatic obstruction, and doesn't present as firm purple nodules.
explanations.d: Thrombophlebitis is inflammation of a vein due to a clot, usually presenting as a linear, tender cord.
explanations.e: Cellulitis is an acute bacterial infection of the dermis, presenting with warmth, redness, and fever, not chronic purple nodules.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
The most common cause of Stewart-Treves syndrome is lymphedema following {{c1::radical mastectomy}}.
The latent period between the start of lymphedema and the appearance of angiosarcoma is typically {{c1::many years (e.g., 10+ years)}}.
Stewart-Treves syndrome presents as {{c1::purple-red skin nodules}} or plaques.
The prognosis for Stewart-Treves syndrome is generally {{c1::poor}}.
keyPoints: Chronic lymphedema is a major risk factor for cutaneous angiosarcoma.
Radical mastectomy with axillary dissection was a common historical trigger.
These tumors are aggressive and often have already metastasized at diagnosis.
Histology shows atypical endothelial cells and irregular vascular spaces.
Prevention involves managing lymphedema effectively.
microReview: Stewart-Treves syndrome is the classic association between chronic lymphedema and angiosarcoma. It demonstrates that long-standing lymphatic stasis may be oncogenic.
examinerTraps: Don't assume any skin nodule on a post-mastectomy patient is metastatic breast cancer; the context of chronic lymphedema and the purple color should trigger the thought of angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 30-year-old male with HIV presents with multiple skin lesions. Biopsy and Warthin-Starry silver staining reveal clusters of tangled bacilli within the lesion. Which of the following cells are the primary proliferative component, and what is the organism?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation of endothelial cells caused by Bartonella species (B. henselae or B. quintana), which are identified by silver stains.
explanations.b: HHV-8 causes Kaposi Sarcoma, not bacillary angiomatosis, and it is a virus, not a silver-stainable bacillus.
explanations.c: MAI causes systemic infection but not this specific type of vascular lesion.
explanations.d: HHV-8 is associated with Kaposi Sarcoma, which does not show bacilli on silver stain.
explanations.e: While B. quintana can cause bacillary angiomatosis, the primary proliferating cell is the endothelial cell, not the pericyte.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by the bacteria {{c1::Bartonella henselae}} or {{c2::Bartonella quintana}}.
The stain used to identify Bartonella in bacillary angiomatosis is the {{c1::Warthin-Starry (silver) stain}}.
Bacillary angiomatosis is characterized by a neutrophilic infiltrate and {{c1::capillary}} proliferation.
Bacillary angiomatosis is most commonly seen in {{c1::immunocompromised (e.g., HIV)}} patients.
Clinically, bacillary angiomatosis can mimic {{c1::Kaposi Sarcoma}}.
keyPoints: Bartonella henselae is also the agent of cat-scratch disease.
Bartonella quintana is associated with 'trench fever' and is transmitted by lice.
Histologically, the lesions show lobular capillary proliferation with prominent neutrophils.
Unlike Kaposi Sarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis is treatable with antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin).
Silver stains highlight the extracellular bacteria.
microReview: Bacillary angiomatosis is an opportunistic infection that triggers endothelial proliferation. It is a critical differential for Kaposi Sarcoma in AIDS patients.
examinerTraps: The trap is confusing the clinical presentation (purple nodules in an HIV patient) with Kaposi Sarcoma. The silver stain and presence of neutrophils are the keys to identifying Bacillary Angiomatosis.
sourceQuote: Vascular Structure and Function characterizes specific kinds of vessels... Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following is the most common benign tumor of the liver, typically appearing as a well-circumscribed, red-blue, soft mass composed of large, blood-filled vascular spaces?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are composed of small, narrow vessels and are more common in the skin than the liver.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are the most common benign liver tumors. They consist of large, dilated (cavernous) blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous stroma.
explanations.c: Hepatocellular adenoma is a benign tumor of hepatocytes, not vascular spaces.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a malignant vascular tumor, not benign, and is much rarer.
explanations.e: Focal nodular hyperplasia is a regenerative response to a vascular anomaly, but it is composed of hepatocytes and bile ducts with a central scar, not large vascular spaces.

ankiCards: The most common benign tumor of the liver is the {{c1::cavernous hemangioma}}.
Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, {{c1::dilated}} blood-filled vascular spaces.
Histologically, cavernous hemangiomas show vascular spaces separated by {{c1::fibrous stroma (connective tissue)}}.
The risk of rupture for a hepatic cavernous hemangioma is generally {{c1::low}}.
On imaging, cavernous hemangiomas show {{c1::peripheral nodular enhancement}} with gradual centripetal fill-in.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are usually asymptomatic and discovered incidentally.
They can reach large sizes ('giant' hemangiomas).
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, they do not typically regress.
Biopsy is usually avoided due to the risk of hemorrhage.
They can occur in other organs, including the brain (cavernous malformations).
microReview: Cavernous hemangiomas are slow-flow vascular malformations/tumors. In the liver, they are the most frequent benign neoplasm encountered by clinicians.
examinerTraps: Be careful not to confuse hemangioma with hemangioblastoma (associated with von Hippel-Lindau) or hepatocellular carcinoma.
sourceQuote: VASCULAR STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION: The general architecture and cellular composition of blood vessels are comparable throughout the cardiovascular system.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu disease) is an autosomal dominant disorder that results in malformed dilated capillaries and veins. Patients most commonly present with which of the following clinical findings?

explanations.a: Painful subungual nodules are characteristic of glomus tumors, not HHT.
explanations.b: HHT is characterized by telangiectasias of the skin and mucous membranes (especially the mouth and nose), leading to frequent epistaxis (nosebleeds) and gastrointestinal hemorrhage.
explanations.c: Telangiectasias in HHT are benign vascular malformations, not precursors to malignancy.
explanations.d: Axillary freckling (Crowe sign) is a feature of Neurofibromatosis Type 1, not HHT.
explanations.e: Limb overgrowth is seen in Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome, which involves port-wine stains and venous malformations, not HHT.

ankiCards: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia is also known as {{c1::Osler-Weber-Rendu disease}}.
HHT is inherited in an {{c1::autosomal dominant}} pattern.
The most common initial presentation of HHT is recurrent {{c1::epistaxis (nosebleeds)}}.
HHT causes telangiectasias in the {{c1::skin}}, {{c2::mucous membranes}}, and {{c3::internal organs}}.
Internal organ complications of HHT include {{c1::arteriovenous malformations (AVMs)}} in the lungs or liver.
keyPoints: HHT involves mutations in genes involved in TGF-beta signaling (e.g., ENG, ACVRL1).
Telangiectasias are dilated vessels that can rupture easily.
Recurrent GI bleeding can lead to iron deficiency anemia.
Pulmonary AVMs can lead to right-to-left shunts and paradoxical emboli.
It is a multisystem vascular dysplasia.
microReview: Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT) is a genetic disorder of vessel wall structure. Its hallmark is mucosal telangiectasia that bleeds easily.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse HHT with Sturge-Weber syndrome (port-wine stain, leptomeningeal angioma) or von Hippel-Lindau (hemangioblastomas). The key for HHT is 'nosebleeds' and 'GI bleeds' in a family history context.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male presents with multiple rapidly enlarging, violaceous nodules on his scalp. He has a significant history of breast cancer 10 years ago for which he received extensive local radiation therapy. A biopsy of one of the scalp lesions reveals poorly defined, anastomosing vascular channels lined by atypical endothelial cells with frequent mitoses. Which of the following genetic alterations is most commonly associated with this patient's clinical presentation?

explanations.a: The patient has post-radiation angiosarcoma of the scalp. Secondary (radiation-induced) angiosarcomas are highly associated with MYC amplification, which is a key diagnostic differentiator from primary angiosarcomas.
explanations.b: BRAF V600E mutations are characteristic of melanoma and some carcinomas, but not typically associated with cutaneous angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: APC gene deletions are linked to Familial Adenomatous Polyposis and colorectal cancer, not vascular malignancies.
explanations.d: KRAS mutations are common in pancreatic, lung, and colorectal cancers, but are not the primary driver in radiation-induced vascular tumors.
explanations.e: VHL mutations are associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease and cavernous hemangiomas/hemangioblastomas, not malignant angiosarcoma.

ankiCards: Secondary angiosarcoma following radiation therapy is associated with {{c1::MYC}} amplification.
The characteristic histological feature of {{c1::angiosarcoma}} is atypical endothelial cells lining anastomosing vascular channels.
Angiosarcoma is a {{c1::malignant}} vascular tumor with a poor prognosis.
Vascular tumors of the liver, such as angiosarcoma, are associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
The immunohistochemical marker {{c1::CD31}} confirms the endothelial origin of a malignant tumor.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are highly aggressive malignant endothelial neoplasms.
Older adults are most commonly affected, often on the scalp.
Radiation-induced angiosarcoma typically occurs years after treatment for breast cancer or other malignancies.
MYC amplification is a hallmark of post-radiation angiosarcoma.
Tumor cells are immunoreactive for endothelial markers like CD31 and vWF.
microReview: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignant tumor. Risk factors include radiation, chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome), and chemicals like arsenic or vinyl chloride. Histology shows pleomorphic cells forming irregular vascular spaces.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Kaposi sarcoma with angiosarcoma; Kaposi is HHV-8 related and usually presents with spindle cells and slit-like spaces rather than the highly pleomorphic, frank malignancy of angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old male with a history of HIV (CD4+ count 150/mm³) presents with several painless, reddish-purple macules and plaques on his lower extremities and hard palate. Biopsy of a plaque reveals proliferating spindle cells, extravasated red blood cells, and slit-like vascular spaces. Which of the following pathogens is the causative agent of this condition?

explanations.a: Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent for all forms of Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.b: Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.c: Bartonella henselae causes Bacillary Angiomatosis in HIV patients, which clinically mimics KS but shows neutrophils and bacteria on Warthin-Starry stain.
explanations.d: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) causes retinitis and colitis in immunocompromised patients but is not oncogenic for vascular tumors.
explanations.e: Human Papillomavirus 16 (HPV-16) is associated with squamous cell carcinomas, particularly of the cervix and oropharynx.

ankiCards: The causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
Histology of Kaposi Sarcoma reveals {{c1::spindle cells}} and slit-like spaces containing RBCs.
The most common site for extracutaneous Kaposi Sarcoma in AIDS patients is the {{c1::gastrointestinal tract}}.
{{c1::Bacillary angiomatosis}} is the primary clinical differential for Kaposi sarcoma in HIV patients.
The treatment for AIDS-related Kaposi Sarcoma primarily involves {{c1::Antiretroviral therapy (ART)}}.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
Four clinical types: Classic (older Mediterranean men), Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
HHV-8 infects endothelial cells and promotes oncogenesis.
Spindle cells are the diagnostic histological hallmark.
Lesions progress from macules (patch) to plaques to nodules.
microReview: KS is a spindle cell tumor. Slit-like spaces contain extravasated RBCs and hemosiderin. HHV-8 is required for the diagnosis. In AIDS patients, improving immune status with ART can lead to regression.
examinerTraps: Distinguish KS from Bacillary Angiomatosis: KS has spindle cells/HHV-8; Bacillary Angiomatosis has neutrophils/Bartonella and is treatable with erythromycin.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old female presents with an intensely painful, small (5 mm), bluish-red nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. She notes the pain is often triggered by exposure to cold. Histological examination shows aggregates of specialized cells surrounding vascular channels. From which of the following cell types does this tumor most likely arise?

explanations.a: A glomus tumor (glomangioma) arises from the glomus body, which contains specialized, modified smooth muscle cells involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.b: Pericytes give rise to hemangiopericytomas, but glomus tumors specifically arise from the specialized cells of the glomus body.
explanations.c: Fibroblasts produce collagen and are involved in dermatofibromas, but not the vascular-related glomus tumor.
explanations.d: Neural crest cells give rise to many structures including melanocytes, but glomus cells are of mesenchymal/smooth muscle origin.
explanations.e: Skeletal muscle fibers are not found in the subungual region and do not form vascular tumors.

ankiCards: A painful subungual blue tumor is most likely a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
Glomus tumors arise from the {{c1::glomus body}}, which is involved in thermoregulation.
The specialized cells in a glomus tumor are modified {{c1::smooth muscle}} cells.
Glomus tumors are classically triggered by {{c1::cold}} temperature.
Glomus tumors are {{c1::benign}} vascular neoplasms.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are exquisitely painful benign lesions.
The subungual (under nail) location is the classic clinical presentation.
Pain is paroxysmal and often cold-induced.
Histology: Uniform, round 'glomus cells' in nests around vessels.
Excision is curative.
microReview: Small, painful, subungual = Glomus tumor. Origin: Thermoregulatory glomus bodies. Cells: Modified smooth muscle.
examinerTraps: Wait for the 'painful' keyword. Most vascular tumors (hemangiomas) are painless; glomus tumors and angiolipomas are the exceptions.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 27-year-old female in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated mass on her gingiva that bleeds easily with minor trauma. The lesion appeared two weeks ago. Biopsy reveals a circumscribed proliferation of capillaries with associated edema and inflammatory infiltrate. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma (granuloma pyogenicum) is a rapidly growing capillary hemangioma that often occurs on the gingiva, especially in pregnant women ('pregnancy tumor' or granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated blood-filled spaces and are usually deep-seated or in the liver, not pedunculated gingival masses.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are painful subungual lesions, not rapidly growing gingival masses.
explanations.d: Angiosarcomas are malignant and usually occur in older patients or post-radiation; they do not present as a sudden pedunculated mass during pregnancy.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella in immunocompromised patients; while it looks similar, the patient's pregnancy status makes pyogenic granuloma much more likely.

ankiCards: A 'pregnancy tumor' on the gingiva is histologically a {{c1::pyogenic granuloma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are a subtype of {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma.
Pyogenic granuloma is often triggered by {{c1::trauma}} or hormonal changes.
The clinical appearance of a pyogenic granuloma is a {{c1::pedunculated}} red mass.
Pyogenic granulomas often undergo {{c1::ulceration}} and bleeding.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer (it is neither pyogenic nor a granuloma).
It is a lobular capillary hemangioma.
Common locations: Skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
Associated with pregnancy due to hormonal influences on vasculature.
Can regress spontaneously postpartum or after trauma removal.
microReview: Rapid growth + pregnancy + gingiva = Pyogenic granuloma. Histology: Granulation-tissue-like appearance with lobulated capillaries.
examinerTraps: The name 'Pyogenic granuloma' is a trap; it has nothing to do with pus-forming bacteria or granulomatous inflammation.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 4-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for a bright red, raised 'strawberry-like' lesion on the chest. The parents state it appeared shortly after birth and has grown slightly in proportion to the child. Which of the following is the most likely natural history of this lesion?

options.d: Rapid expansion leading to Kasabach-Merritt syndrome

explanations.a: Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) are very common in infancy, grow rapidly for a few months, and then typically involute and regress spontaneously by age 5-7.
explanations.b: Juvenile hemangiomas are benign and do not undergo malignant transformation.
explanations.c: Unlike 'port-wine stains' (nevus flammeus), strawberry hemangiomas usually regress.
explanations.d: Kasabach-Merritt syndrome (consumptive coagulopathy) is associated with rare, large Tufted angiomas or Kaposiform hemangioendotheliomas, not standard strawberry hemangiomas.
explanations.e: Capillary and cavernous hemangiomas are distinct entities; one does not usually progress into the other.

ankiCards: A {{c1::juvenile (strawberry)}} hemangioma is the most common vascular tumor of infancy.
The typical natural history of a strawberry hemangioma is {{c1::spontaneous regression}}.
Strawberry hemangiomas are histologically {{c1::capillary}} hemangiomas.
90% of juvenile hemangiomas regress by age {{c1::7}}.
Unlike strawberry hemangiomas, a {{c1::nevus flammeus (port-wine stain)}} does not regress.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangiomas are 'strawberry' colored and raised.
They occur in 1 in 200 live births.
Growth phase (first few months) is followed by an involution phase.
Management is usually observation (conservative).
They are benign capillary proliferations.
microReview: Infant + Strawberry lesion = Juvenile hemangioma. Key fact: It goes away on its own.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse this with a port-wine stain. Port-wine stains are flat and grow with the child (do not regress).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following immunohistochemical markers is the most specific for identifying tumors of vascular endothelial origin, such as angiosarcomas or hemangiomas?

explanations.a: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a highly specific marker for endothelial cells and is used to confirm the vascular nature of undifferentiated tumors.
explanations.b: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (smooth and skeletal), not endothelium.
explanations.c: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells, including melanocytes and Schwann cells.
explanations.d: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells and carcinomas.
explanations.e: Chromogranin is a marker for neuroendocrine cells.

ankiCards: {{c1::CD31}} and vWF (von Willebrand Factor) are markers for endothelial cells.
The most common endothelial marker used in pathology for vascular tumors is {{c1::CD31}}.
In angiosarcoma, cells will be positive for the marker {{c1::CD31::marker name}}.
Vascular tumors express {{c1::Factor VIII}}-related antigen.
Immunohistochemistry for {{c1::CD31}} helps distinguish angiosarcoma from melanoma or carcinoma.
keyPoints: Endothelial markers include CD31, CD34, and von Willebrand Factor (vWF).
CD31 is considered the most specific among them.
vWF is also known as Factor VIII-related antigen.
Malignant vascular tumors may lose some markers but usually retain CD31.
IHC is crucial for diagnosing poorly differentiated angiosarcomas.
microReview: Identifying a vascular tumor? Look for CD31 or vWF on IHC.
examinerTraps: CD34 is also used but is less specific than CD31, as it can be found in some fibroblastic tumors and hematopoietic cells.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 10-year-old boy presents with a large, flat, purple-red birthmark on the left side of his face following the distribution of the trigeminal nerve. He also has a history of refractory seizures and developmental delay. Imaging shows leptomeningeal angiomas on the ipsilateral side. What is the name of the skin lesion described?

explanations.a: A nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a flat, congenital vascular ectasia. In the distribution of the CN V1/V2, it is associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome.
explanations.b: Spider telangiectasias are small, central arterioles with radiating vessels, often associated with hyperestrogenic states (cirrhosis, pregnancy).
explanations.c: Cherry angiomas are small, ruby-red papules that develop in adults as they age; they are not congenital or associated with Sturge-Weber.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are deeper, blood-filled masses, not flat facial 'stains'.
explanations.e: Pyogenic granulomas are acquired, pedunculated, bleeding nodules, not congenital flat stains.

ankiCards: Sturge-Weber syndrome is characterized by a {{c1::nevus flammeus (port-wine stain)}} in the CN V1/V2 distribution.
The intracranial component of Sturge-Weber syndrome involves {{c1::leptomeningeal}} angiomas.
Unlike strawberry hemangiomas, a nevus flammeus {{c1::does not}} regress with age.
The genetic basis of Sturge-Weber syndrome involves a somatic mutation in the {{c1::GNAQ}} gene.
Patients with Sturge-Weber syndrome often suffer from {{c1::seizures}}, glaucoma, and mental retardation.
keyPoints: Nevus flammeus is a form of vascular ectasia (dilation of existing vessels).
Port-wine stains grow proportionately with the child.
Sturge-Weber syndrome (Encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) is a sporadic condition.
Vascular malformations affect the skin and the brain meninges.
Radiology often shows 'tram-track' calcifications in the brain.
microReview: Port-wine stain + CN V distribution + Seizures = Sturge-Weber Syndrome. The lesion is a Nevus Flammeus.
examinerTraps: The examiner may call it a 'port-wine stain' or 'nevus flammeus'. These are the same. Do not confuse with 'nevus simplex' (salmon patch/stork bite), which is common and fades.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old male with a history of chronic alcoholism and cirrhosis presents with numerous small, red lesions on his chest. Each lesion has a central red dot with fine vessels radiating outward that blanch when pressure is applied to the center. Which of the following is the underlying mechanism for these lesions?

explanations.a: Spider telangiectasias are associated with high estrogen levels, which occur in cirrhosis because the liver cannot metabolize estrogen.
explanations.b: Chronic venous hypertension causes varicose veins and stasis dermatitis, not spider angiomas.
explanations.c: Bacterial infection (Bartonella) causes bacillary angiomatosis, which presents as nodules, not spider telangiectasias.
explanations.d: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, which presents as purple plaques/nodules.
explanations.e: Spider telangiectasias are typically acquired, not congenital malformations.

ankiCards: Spider telangiectasias are commonly seen in patients with {{c1::liver cirrhosis}} or pregnancy.
The hormonal driver for spider telangiectasias is {{c1::estrogen}}.
Applying pressure to the {{c1::center}} of a spider angioma causes it to blanch.
Spider telangiectasias are a form of vascular {{c1::ectasia}}.
In cirrhosis, the liver's failure to metabolize {{c1::estrogen}} leads to palmar erythema and spider angiomas.
keyPoints: Spider telangiectasias (spider angiomas) consist of a central, pulsatile arteriole.
They occur most commonly on the face, neck, and upper chest.
They are a classic physical exam finding in chronic liver disease.
They also occur during pregnancy due to high estrogen.
Blanching occurs because the blood flow radiates from the central feeder vessel.
microReview: Cirrhosis + 'Spider' lesions on chest = High estrogen causing vascular dilation.
examinerTraps: Blanching is the key physical exam feature. If it doesn't blanch, it's likely purpura or a different vascular tumor.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 48-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of epistaxis and multiple small, ruby-red blanching macules on his tongue, lips, and fingertips. He mentions that his father and sister have similar symptoms and frequent 'stomach bleeds.' Which of the following conditions is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Osler-Weber-Rendu disease (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by multiple telangiectasias on the skin and mucous membranes, causing bleeding.
explanations.b: Sturge-Weber involves port-wine stains and brain angiomas, not diffuse mucosal telangiectasias and epistaxis.
explanations.c: Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) presents with hemangioblastomas of the CNS and retina and renal cell carcinoma, not mucosal telangiectasias.
explanations.d: Wegener (GPA) can cause epistaxis due to necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis, but it doesn't cause diffuse blanching telangiectasias.
explanations.e: Ehlers-Danlos (vascular type) causes vessel rupture and bruising, but the specific finding of mucosal telangiectasias and autosomal dominant inheritance of bleeds fits HHT better.

ankiCards: The eponym for Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT) is {{c1::Osler-Weber-Rendu disease}}.
HHT is inherited in an {{c1::autosomal dominant}} pattern.
Major complications of HHT include epistaxis, GI bleeds, and {{c1::arteriovenous malformations (AVMs)}}.
Telangiectasias in HHT are found on the skin and {{c1::mucous membranes}}.
HHT is caused by mutations in genes involved in the {{c1::TGF-beta}} signaling pathway.
keyPoints: Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT) is a systemic vascular dysplasia.
Classic triad: Telangiectasias, recurrent epistaxis, and family history.
AVMs can occur in the lungs, liver, or brain.
TGF-beta signaling mutations (ENG or ACVRL1) are common causes.
Iron deficiency anemia often results from chronic GI loss.
microReview: Nosebleeds + Tongue spots + Family history = Osler-Weber-Rendu (HHT).
examinerTraps: Note the autosomal dominant inheritance. The presence of 'stomach bleeds' points toward internal telangiectasias/AVMs typical of HHT.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An autopsy of a 62-year-old former shipyard worker reveals a large, hemorrhagic, poorly circumscribed mass in the liver. Microscopic sections show malignant cells of endothelial origin. Which of the following environmental exposures is most strongly linked to this specific hepatic malignancy?

explanations.a: Vinyl chloride (used in PVC production), arsenic, and Thorotrast are classic risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Asbestos exposure is linked to mesothelioma and lung cancer, not hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Aflatoxin B1 is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), which arises from hepatocytes, not endothelium.
explanations.d: Benzene exposure is primarily associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.e: Beryllium exposure is associated with berylliosis and lung cancer.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
Besides vinyl chloride, {{c1::arsenic}} is a chemical risk factor for liver angiosarcoma.
Angiosarcoma cells line vascular spaces and are of {{c1::endothelial}} origin.
{{c1::Thorotrast}} is a radioactive contrast medium previously linked to angiosarcoma.
Unlike HCC, angiosarcoma of the liver does not produce {{c1::alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma of the liver is a rare but highly lethal tumor.
It has specific occupational links (PVC industry).
Latent period between exposure and tumor development can be decades.
The tumor is highly aggressive and usually multicentric.
Distinguish from HCC: Angiosarcoma is a mesenchymal tumor; HCC is epithelial.
microReview: Liver + Angiosarcoma + Exposure = Vinyl Chloride or Arsenic.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse angiosarcoma with hepatocellular carcinoma. Angiosarcoma is a vascular tumor (CD31+); HCC is from hepatocytes (AFP+).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old female presents with several firm, violaceous nodules on her right upper extremity. She has a history of a radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection and radiotherapy for breast cancer 12 years ago. Since the surgery, she has had persistent, non-pitting edema of the right arm. A biopsy of a nodule shows atypical endothelial cells forming irregular vascular channels that infiltrate the dermis. Immunohistochemical staining is positive for CD31. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8, typically presenting as purple patches or plaques in immunocompromised patients or elderly Mediterranean men, not specifically linked to chronic lymphedema.
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma can occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema, a phenomenon known as Stewart-Treves syndrome, occurring years after radical mastectomy and lymph node dissection.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is a reactive vascular proliferation seen in immunocompromised patients caused by Bartonella henselae or quintana, characterized by neutrophilic infiltrates.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are benign, exquisitely painful tumors arising from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, usually located under the fingernails.
explanations.e: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign, large, dilated vascular channels that do not show the cellular atypia or infiltrative growth seen in this patient.

ankiCards: The development of angiosarcoma in the setting of chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy) is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
Angiosarcomas are malignant vascular tumors that staining positively for the endothelial marker {{c1::CD31}}.
Risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma include exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
The histological hallmark of angiosarcoma is the presence of {{c1::atypical endothelial cells}} forming irregular vascular channels.
Unlike benign hemangiomas, angiosarcomas are characterized by {{c1::infiltrative}} growth and significant cellular pleomorphism.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor of endothelial cells.
Stewart-Treves syndrome refers specifically to angiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphedema.
Markers include CD31 and von Willebrand factor (vWF).
Cutaneous angiosarcoma often presents as enlarging, bruised-looking areas or nodules.
Five-year survival rates for these tumors are generally poor (approx. 30%).
Irradiation is a known risk factor for subsequent angiosarcoma development.
microReview: Angiosarcoma = Malignant endothelial tumor + CD31/CD34 positivity + History of Radiation/Lymphedema (Stewart-Treves) or Vinyl Chloride.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Stewart-Treves (angiosarcoma in lymphedema) with Sturge-Weber (port-wine stain/V1 distribution).

stem: A research team is investigating the pathogenesis of a vascular tumor characterized by spindle-shaped cells and slit-like spaces containing extravasated red blood cells. The tumor is found to be strongly associated with a specific gamma-herpesvirus that induces a latent infection in endothelial cells, leading to the production of pro-inflammatory and pro-angiogenic cytokines. Which virus is the primary etiologic agent?

explanations.a: HHV-6 is the cause of roseola infantum and is not associated with vascular tumors.
explanations.b: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent for all forms of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.c: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and other B-cell malignancies, but not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.d: CMV causes opportunistic infections in immunocompromised hosts but is not oncogenic for vascular tumors.
explanations.e: HBV is a risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, not vascular neoplasms.

ankiCards: The etiologic agent of Kaposi sarcoma is {{c1::Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}.
HHV-8 is also known as {{c1::KSHV (Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus)}}.
Kaposi sarcoma histology classically shows {{c1::spindle cells}} and slit-like vascular spaces.
{{c1::AIDS-associated}} Kaposi sarcoma is the most common HIV-related malignancy worldwide.
HHV-8 causes vascular proliferation by inducing {{c1::pro-angiogenic}} cytokines.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
Four clinical types: Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
HHV-8 is necessary but not sufficient for the development of KS.
Histology: Spindle cells, slit-like spaces, extravasated RBCs, and hemosiderin deposition.
KS cells are of endothelial origin (lymphatic or blood vessel).
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Slit-like spaces + Extravasated RBCs.
examinerTraps: Examiners may test the association between HHV-8 and Primary Effusion Lymphoma or Multicentric Castleman Disease, but the classic association is Kaposi Sarcoma.

stem: Which of the following cell types is the origin of a glomus tumor, a benign but exquisitely painful neoplasm typically found in the distal portion of the fingers?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.b: Pericytes are the origin of hemangiopericytomas, not glomus tumors.
explanations.c: Standard endothelial cells give rise to hemangiomas and angiosarcomas.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts give rise to fibromas or fibrosarcomas, not vascular glomus tumors.
explanations.e: Lymphatic endothelial cells give rise to lymphangiomas.

ankiCards: Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells.
A glomus tumor is most commonly found {{c1::under the fingernails (subungual)}}.
The clinical hallmark of a glomus tumor is that it is {{c1::exquisitely painful}}.
Glomus bodies are specialized {{c1::arteriovenous anastomoses}} involved in thermoregulation.
Histology of a glomus tumor shows nests of uniform {{c1::round}} cells surrounding vascular spaces.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign vascular neoplasms.
Location: Most commonly subungual (under the nail).
Symptom: Paroxysmal pain, often triggered by cold.
Origin: Smooth muscle cells of the thermoregulatory glomus body.
Morphology: Branching vascular channels separated by aggregates of glomus cells.
microReview: Glomus tumor = Subungual + Extremely Painful + Modified Smooth Muscle Cells.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse glomus tumors with 'glomus jugulare' (paragangliomas), which have different cell origins (neural crest).

stem: A 26-year-old female in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated mass on her gingiva. The mass bleeds easily with minor trauma. Histological examination shows a highly vascular proliferation resembling granulation tissue with significant edema and inflammatory infiltrate. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas occur in newborns and infants, not adults.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a common benign lesion that often occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum) and resembles granulation tissue.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated vascular spaces and are not typically pedunculated gingival masses associated with pregnancy.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a malignant, infiltrative tumor, not a localized, pedunculated, reactive-appearing mass.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is associated with HIV/immunosuppression and Bartonella infection, not pregnancy.

ankiCards: A pyogenic granuloma occurring in the gingiva of a pregnant woman is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Histologically, a pyogenic granuloma resembles {{c1::granulation tissue}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized by {{c1::rapid}} growth and a tendency to bleed easily.
The treatment of choice for a symptomatic pyogenic granuloma is {{c1::surgical excision}}.
Despite its name, a pyogenic granuloma is neither {{c1::pyogenic (pus-forming)}} nor a true granuloma.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is a lobular capillary hemangioma.
Often follows minor trauma.
Classic location: Skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
Association: Pregnancy (hormonal influence).
Regression: Can occur spontaneously, especially postpartum.
microReview: Pyogenic Granuloma = Pregnancy/Trauma + Gingiva + Granulation-tissue-like + Bleeds easily.
examinerTraps: The name is a misnomer; look for 'granulation tissue' in the description to confirm the diagnosis.

stem: An immunocompromised patient presents with multiple cutaneous red papules. Biopsy shows vascular proliferation with prominent neutrophilic infiltrates and clusters of Warthin-Starry stain-positive organisms. This condition must be distinguished from Kaposi sarcoma. What is the most likely pathogen responsible for this lesion?

explanations.a: Bartonella henselae (or B. quintana) causes bacillary angiomatosis in HIV/AIDS patients, which histologically features neutrophils and silver-staining bacteria.
explanations.b: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, which lacks the neutrophilic infiltrate and bacterial clusters seen in bacillary angiomatosis.
explanations.c: S. aureus causes pyogenic infections but not vascular proliferative lesions like bacillary angiomatosis.
explanations.d: T. pallidum causes syphilis; although it involves vessels (endarteritis), it does not cause this specific vascular tumor-like proliferation.
explanations.e: MAC causes systemic infection in AIDS patients but not vascular papules with this histology.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by bacteria of the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
Histology of bacillary angiomatosis shows vascular proliferation and an infiltrate of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
The organisms in bacillary angiomatosis are best visualized using the {{c1::Warthin-Starry (or silver)}} stain.
Bacillary angiomatosis occurs primarily in {{c1::immunocompromised/AIDS}} patients.
Distinguishing bacillary angiomatosis from Kaposi sarcoma is critical because the former is treated with {{c1::antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin)}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis (BA) is a reactive vascular proliferation.
Causative agents: Bartonella henselae (cats) and Bartonella quintana (lice).
Key histological feature: Neutrophilic microabscesses (absent in Kaposi).
Clinical: Red/purple skin papules/nodules.
Treatment: Antibiotics (macrolides).
microReview: Bacillary Angiomatosis = HIV + Bartonella + Neutrophils + Warthin-Starry (+) + Erythromycin Tx.
examinerTraps: Kaposi sarcoma and Bacillary angiomatosis look very similar clinically in AIDS patients. Look for 'neutrophils' or 'silver stain' to pick Bartonella.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following is the most likely clinical course for a 'strawberry' (juvenile) hemangioma discovered on the scalp of a 2-week-old infant?

options.b: Rapid growth followed by spontaneous regression

explanations.a: Juvenile hemangiomas are benign and do not transform into malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.b: Juvenile hemangiomas characteristically grow rapidly for several months and then spontaneously involute (regress) by age 5 to 7.
explanations.c: Persistence is not the rule; 90% regress by age 7.
explanations.d: Surgery is rarely needed because they regress naturally.
explanations.e: While multiple hemangiomas can occur, a single juvenile hemangioma typically does not 'spread' like a malignancy.

ankiCards: Juvenile hemangiomas are also known as {{c1::strawberry}} hemangiomas.
The typical natural history of a juvenile hemangioma involves {{c1::spontaneous regression}}.
Most juvenile hemangiomas have completely regressed by age {{c1::7}}.
Juvenile hemangiomas are the most common tumors of {{c1::infancy}}.
Histologically, juvenile hemangiomas are {{c1::capillary}} hemangiomas (small, thin-walled vessels).
keyPoints: Extremely common in infants (1 in 200 births).
Often multiple.
Location: Skin is most common.
Growth phase: Fast growth in the first few months.
Involutes completely in the majority of cases.
microReview: Strawberry Hemangioma = Infant + Rapid initial growth + Involutes by age 7.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse with cavernous hemangiomas, which are deeper, larger, and do not regress spontaneously.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician for evaluation of a large, flat, purple-red birthmark covering the left side of his face in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve. The parents report he has recently had two episodes of generalized tonic-clonic seizures. An MRI of the brain shows leptomeningeal angiomas on the ipsilateral side. This clinical constellation is associated with a mutation in which of the following genes?

explanations.a: VHL mutations cause von Hippel-Lindau disease, characterized by hemangioblastomas and renal cell carcinoma, not port-wine stains.
explanations.b: Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) is caused by a somatic activating mutation in the GNAQ gene.
explanations.c: TSC1/TSC2 mutations cause Tuberous Sclerosis, which features angiofibromas (not port-wine stains) and seizures.
explanations.d: NF1 causes Neurofibromatosis type 1, featuring neurofibromas and cafe-au-lait spots.
explanations.e: APC mutations are associated with Familial Adenomatous Polyposis.

ankiCards: The facial lesion in Sturge-Weber syndrome is called a {{c1::port-wine stain (nevus flammeus)}}.
The inheritance pattern of the GNAQ mutation in Sturge-Weber syndrome is {{c1::somatic (not inherited)}}.
Sturge-Weber syndrome classically involves a port-wine stain in the {{c1::V1/V2 (Trigeminal)}} distribution.
The neurological complications of Sturge-Weber syndrome include {{c1::seizures}}, mental retardation, and glaucoma.
Radiology in Sturge-Weber syndrome may show 'tram-track' {{c1::calcifications}} in the brain.
keyPoints: Sturge-Weber syndrome is a phakomatosis.
Key triad: Facial port-wine stain, leptomeningeal angioma, and glaucoma.
Gene: GNAQ (somatic activating mutation).
The port-wine stain is a form of capillary malformation (ectasia).
Seizures are due to the underlying vascular malformations in the meninges.
microReview: Sturge-Weber = GNAQ + Port-wine stain (V1/V2) + Seizures + Leptomeningeal angioma.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'seizures' or 'mental retardation' to distinguish a simple birthmark (nevus flammeus) from Sturge-Weber syndrome.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old male worker at a chemical manufacturing plant presents with abdominal pain and weight loss. Imaging reveals multiple masses in the liver. A biopsy confirms a malignant vascular tumor. The patient's occupational history reveals long-term exposure to vinyl chloride. Which molecular marker or histological feature would most likely be present in this neoplasm?

explanations.a: The patient has hepatic angiosarcoma (linked to vinyl chloride). As a vascular endothelial tumor, it expresses CD31 (PECAM-1).
explanations.b: HHV-8 is associated with Kaposi sarcoma, not hepatic angiosarcoma caused by chemical toxins.
explanations.c: Birbeck granules are found in Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
explanations.d: Psammoma bodies are found in papillary thyroid carcinoma, meningioma, and mesothelioma.
explanations.e: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived tumors (melanoma, Schwannoma) and is typically negative in angiosarcoma.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with occupational exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
Besides vinyl chloride, exposure to {{c1::arsenic}} is a risk factor for liver angiosarcoma.
Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor of {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
Most angiosarcomas are highly {{c1::aggressive}} and have a poor prognosis.
The most sensitive and specific endothelial marker for immunohistochemistry is {{c1::CD31}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma of the liver is rare but classically associated with specific toxins.
Other associations: Thorotrast (radiocontrast media).
Vinyl chloride is used in the plastics industry.
The tumor cells show marked atypia and form poorly defined vascular channels.
Metastasis occurs early, most frequently to the lungs.
microReview: Liver Angiosarcoma = Vinyl Chloride/Arsenic/Thorotrast + CD31 (+) + Highly aggressive.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse hepatic angiosarcoma (vascular) with hepatocellular carcinoma (epithelial), which is more commonly linked to HBV/HCV or cirrhosis.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Cystic hygromas are large, dilated lymphatic spaces that typically occur in the neck or axilla of children. This specific type of cavernous lymphangioma is strongly associated with which of the following chromosomal abnormalities?

explanations.a: While Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) has various anomalies, cystic hygroma is the classic association for Turner syndrome.
explanations.b: Turner syndrome (45, X) is characteristically associated with cystic hygromas of the neck, which later resolve into 'webbed neck'.
explanations.c: Klinefelter syndrome (47, XXY) is not associated with cystic hygromas.
explanations.d: Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome) features micrognathia and rocker-bottom feet, but not specifically cystic hygromas as a defining feature.
explanations.e: Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome) features midline defects like holoprosencephaly and cleft lip/palate.

ankiCards: A cavernous lymphangioma found in the neck of a child is called a {{c1::cystic hygroma}}.
Cystic hygroma is a characteristic finding in {{c1::Turner syndrome}}.
The 'webbing' of the neck in Turner syndrome is the result of a regressed {{c1::cystic hygroma}}.
Lymphangiomas are distinguished from hemangiomas by the absence of {{c1::red blood cells}} in the lumens.
Cystic hygromas are composed of massively dilated {{c1::lymphatic}} channels.
keyPoints: Lymphangiomas are the lymphatic equivalent of hemangiomas.
Cystic hygroma: Large cavernous spaces in the neck/axilla.
Often present at birth.
Boundaries are poorly defined, making surgical excision difficult.
Association: Turner syndrome (45, X) and Down syndrome.
microReview: Cystic Hygroma = Neck mass + Turner Syndrome (45, X) + Dilated lymphatics.
examinerTraps: Cystic hygromas are benign, but their size and location can cause respiratory distress in newborns.

bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 48-year-old male with a history of chronic alcohol abuse and cirrhosis presents with several small, bright red, pulsatile vascular lesions on his chest. Each lesion has a central core with small radiating vessels that blanch when pressure is applied to the center. This physical finding is most directly caused by an excess of which of the following?

explanations.a: Progesterone is not implicated in the formation of spider telangiectasias.
explanations.b: Hyperestrinism (due to the liver's inability to metabolize estrogen in cirrhosis) leads to spider telangiectasias and palmar erythema.
explanations.c: Testosterone levels are often decreased in cirrhosis, but the vascular changes are due to estrogen.
explanations.d: Excess cortisol causes striae and easy bruising, but not spider angiomas.
explanations.e: Excess aldosterone (secondary hyperaldosteronism) occurs in cirrhosis due to decreased effective circulating volume, but it causes edema/ascites, not vascular spiders.

ankiCards: The clinical name for 'spider' vascular lesions is {{c1::spider telangiectasia (or spider angioma)}}.
Spider telangiectasias in cirrhosis are caused by {{c1::hyperestrinism}}.
A spider angioma will {{c1::blanch}} when the central vessel is compressed.
Spider telangiectasias are commonly found in pregnant women and patients with {{c1::cirrhosis (liver failure)}}.
Spider telangiectasias are considered a form of {{c1::vascular ectasia}} rather than a true neoplasm.
keyPoints: Spider telangiectasia: Radial array of dilated subcutaneous arteries.
Location: Usually above the waist (face, neck, upper chest).
Pathogenesis: High estrogen levels cause vasodilation.
Clinical context: Cirrhosis, Pregnancy, or Estrogen therapy.
They are non-neoplastic vascular malformations.
microReview: Spider Angioma = Cirrhosis/Pregnancy + High Estrogen + Blanches on pressure.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse spider telangiectasias with 'spider veins' (varicose veins), which are venous and do not have a central pulsatile feeder.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old male with a history of HIV and a CD4+ count of 120 cells/mm³ presents with multiple, painless, violaceous macules and plaques on his lower extremities and hard palate. Skin biopsy reveals spindle-shaped cells forming slit-like spaces filled with red blood cells and a lymphocytic infiltrate. Which of the following pathogens is most likely associated with this patient's condition?

explanations.a: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma, which presents as violaceous lesions in immunocompromised patients.
explanations.b: Human herpesvirus 6 is the cause of roseola infantum and is not associated with vascular tumor formation.
explanations.c: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and hairy leukoplakia, but not with vascular spindle cell tumors.
explanations.d: Cytomegalovirus causes retinitis or colitis in AIDS patients but does not typically induce vascular tumors.
explanations.e: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can look similar to Kaposi sarcoma, but is a bacterial infection characterized by neutrophilic inflammation, not the spindle-cell slit-like morphology of Kaposi sarcoma.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is caused by {{c1::Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}.
The characteristic histopathologic finding in Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells}} forming {{c2::slit-like spaces}}.
Kaposi Sarcoma lesions are typically {{c1::violaceous/purple}} in color.
In AIDS patients, Kaposi Sarcoma frequently involves the {{c1::skin}}, {{c2::mucous membranes}}, and {{c3::visceral organs}}.
The inflammatory infiltrate in Kaposi Sarcoma is primarily {{c1::lymphocytic}}, whereas bacillary angiomatosis features {{c2::neutrophils}}.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8.
It is classified into four types: Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
The clinical presentation involves red-purple macules, plaques, or nodules.
Histology shows spindle cells, slit-like vascular channels, and extravasated red blood cells.
KS must be differentiated from Bacillary Angiomatosis, which is bacterial (Bartonella).
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Slit-like spaces + AIDS/Immunosuppression.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Kaposi Sarcoma (HHV-8, lymphocytes) with Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella, neutrophils). Both present with purple skin lesions in HIV patients.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors are divided into three categories: (1) benign (e.g., hemangioma), (2) intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors (e.g., Kaposi sarcoma), and (3) malignant tumors (e.g., angiosarcoma).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following cellular origins best characterizes the glomus tumor (glomangioma), a highly painful lesion typically found in the subungual region?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors arise from the specialized, modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, which are involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors do not arise from endothelial cells; endothelial cells line the vessels but do not form the bulk of the glomus tumor mass.
explanations.c: Fibroblasts are not the origin of glomus tumors; glomus cells show contractile (smooth muscle) differentiation.
explanations.d: While many tumors have mesenchymal origins, glomus tumors specifically demonstrate smooth muscle differentiation, not an undifferentiated primitive state.
explanations.e: Pericytes are related to smooth muscle but the glomus tumor is specifically linked to the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, not generic pericytes.

ankiCards: Glomus tumors are most commonly found in the {{c1::subungual (under nail)}} region.
The glomus tumor is characterized by extreme {{c1::pain/tenderness}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells.
The physiological function of the glomus body is {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
On histology, glomus cells appear as {{c1::small, uniform round}} cells.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign, exquisitely painful tumors.
They are derived from modified smooth muscle cells of glomus bodies.
The glomus body is a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis.
Commonly located under the fingernails.
Treatment is simple excision, which is curative.
microReview: Glomus tumor = Painful + Subungual + Modified smooth muscle cells.
examinerTraps: The examiner might try to confuse glomus tumors with 'glomus jugulare' or 'glomus tympanicum' (paragangliomas), which are neuroendocrine, not vascular smooth muscle.
sourceQuote: Glomus tumors are benign, exquisitely painful tumors arising from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 26-year-old female in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with a rapidly growing, friable, red-to-purple nodule on her gingiva that bleeds easily with minor trauma. The lesion is approximately 1 cm in diameter. Which of the following is the most likely histological diagnosis?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a benign, rapidly growing vascular lesion often occurring on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor, usually occurring in older adults, and would not present as a localized, benign gingival nodule in a young pregnant woman.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, blood-filled spaces and are typically deeper, less friable, and do not grow as rapidly as pyogenic granulomas.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are painful subungual lesions, not painless gingival nodules.
explanations.e: Cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) is typically found in the neck or axilla of infants and consists of lymphatic spaces, not friable vascular tissue.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is also known as {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
A pyogenic granuloma occurring in a pregnant woman's gingiva is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
The clinical hallmark of a pyogenic granuloma is that it is {{c1::friable}} and {{c2::bleeds easily}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are {{c1::benign::benign or malignant}} lesions.
Histologically, pyogenic granulomas resemble {{c1::granulation tissue}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granulomas are common, benign vascular lesions of the skin or oral mucosa.
They are characterized by rapid growth and easy bleeding.
Pregnancy is a significant risk factor (hormonal influence).
Histology shows a lobular proliferation of capillaries with edema and inflammation.
They may regress spontaneously after delivery or require excision.
microReview: Pyogenic granuloma = Pregnancy + Gingiva + Rapid growth + Bleeds easily.
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic granuloma' is a misnomer; it is neither pyogenic (pus-forming) nor a granuloma (it is a hemangioma).
sourceQuote: Pyogenic granulomas are capillary hemangiomas that manifest as rapidly growing red pedunculated lesions on the skin, gingival, or oral mucosa.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular tumors are categorized by their biological behavior. Which of the following neoplasms is classified as an intermediate-grade (borderline) vascular tumor?

explanations.a: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma and Kaposi sarcoma are the classic examples of intermediate-grade (borderline) vascular tumors.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangioma is a benign vascular tumor.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant vascular tumor.
explanations.d: Glomus tumor is a benign vascular tumor.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious reactive vascular proliferation, not a neoplastic intermediate-grade tumor.

ankiCards: The two main examples of intermediate-grade vascular tumors are {{c1::Kaposi sarcoma}} and {{c2::epithelioid hemangioendothelioma}}.
Angiosarcoma is classified as a {{c1::malignant}} vascular tumor.
Capillary hemangioma is classified as a {{c1::benign}} vascular tumor.
Intermediate-grade vascular tumors are also referred to as {{c1::borderline}} tumors.
Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma occurs in {{c1::medium-sized and large veins}}.
keyPoints: Benign: Hemangiomas, Glomus tumors.
Intermediate (Borderline): Kaposi sarcoma, Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma.
Malignant: Angiosarcoma, Hemangiopericytoma (malignant types).
Borderline tumors are locally aggressive but have lower metastatic potential than malignant ones.
Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma tumor cells are plump and cuboidal (epithelioid).
microReview: Intermediate Grade = Kaposi + Hemangioendothelioma.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'Hemangioma' (benign) with 'Hemangioendothelioma' (intermediate) or 'Angiosarcoma' (malignant).
sourceQuote: Intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors... include Kaposi sarcoma and hemangioendothelioma.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old male presents with several enlarging, ill-defined, bruiselike, reddish-purple nodules on his scalp. He has no history of trauma or radiation. Biopsy shows wildly atypical endothelial cells forming irregular vascular channels that invade the dermis. Immunohistochemical staining for CD31 is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma is a malignant vascular tumor that commonly occurs in the scalp of elderly men, characterized by atypical endothelial cells and CD31 positivity.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma presents with spindle cells and HHV-8 association; it is less likely on the scalp of an immunocompetent elderly man without other symptoms.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious proliferation found in immunocompromised hosts and shows lobular growth with neutrophils, not diffuse atypia.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign, lack atypia, and do not present as enlarging, invasive nodules in the elderly.
explanations.e: Pyogenic granulomas are benign, small, pedunculated lesions, not ill-defined invasive nodules on the scalp.

ankiCards: The most common site for cutaneous angiosarcoma is the {{c1::scalp}} of {{c2::elderly}} patients.
A specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial differentiation is {{c1::CD31 (or vWF)}}.
Angiosarcomas can be induced by chronic {{c1::lymphedema}} or prior {{c2::radiation}}.
Histologically, angiosarcoma shows {{c1::atypical/malignant}} endothelial cells.
The prognosis for angiosarcoma is generally {{c1::poor}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms.
Risk factors include older age, radiation exposure, and chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
Hepatic angiosarcoma is linked to arsenic, Thorotrast, and polyvinyl chloride (PVC).
They are highly aggressive with high metastatic rates.
CD31 is a highly specific marker for these tumors.
microReview: Angiosarcoma = Elderly scalp OR post-radiation OR PVC/Arsenic (Liver) + CD31 positive.
examinerTraps: A bruiselike appearance in an elderly patient on the scalp is often mistaken for simple trauma, delaying the diagnosis of angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Malignant tumors... Angiosarcomas are malignant vascular neoplasms that vary from highly differentiated tumors... to quite anaplastic lesions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular malformations is characterized by large, dilated vascular channels, often involving deep structures, and is a component of von Hippel-Lindau disease when located in the cerebellum or retina?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated blood-filled spaces. In von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease, cavernous hemangiomas (specifically hemangioblastomas) occur in the cerebellum and retina.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas consist of small, thin-walled capillaries and are not the characteristic lesion of VHL disease.
explanations.c: Cystic hygroma is a lymphatic malformation, not a blood vessel hemangioma.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are small, painful lesions of the extremities and are not associated with VHL disease.
explanations.e: Spider angiomas are small, non-neoplastic vascular ectasias often seen in liver cirrhosis.

ankiCards: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of {{c1::large/dilated}} vascular channels.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas {{c1::do not}} spontaneously regress.
In von Hippel-Lindau disease, vascular tumors are found in the {{c1::cerebellum}} and {{c2::retina}}.
Cavernous hemangiomas of the liver are often discovered {{c1::incidentally}} via imaging.
Vascular tumors in VHL disease are specifically termed {{c1::hemangioblastomas}}.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas involve larger, more dilated channels than capillary types.
They are often deep-seated and do not regress.
They can be part of von Hippel-Lindau disease (as hemangioblastomas).
Can occur in the liver, brain, and other viscera.
They may be locally destructive due to pressure or size but are benign.
microReview: Cavernous Hemangioma = Large spaces + No regression + VHL (Cerebellum/Retina).
examinerTraps: While both are 'hemangiomas', the capillary type is superficial/regresses, while the cavernous type is deep/persistent.
sourceQuote: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, dilated vascular channels... they are more infiltrative, frequently involve deep structures, and do not regress.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which specific vascular lesion is described as a 'strawberry hemangioma' that typically appears shortly after birth, grows rapidly for a few months, and then regresses by age 7 in the majority of cases?

explanations.a: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are very common in newborns, grow rapidly, and then almost always spontaneously involute by early childhood.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas do not regress and are composed of larger vascular spaces.
explanations.c: Port-wine stains (a form of nevus flammeus) grow with the child and do not regress; they often thicken over time.
explanations.d: Nevus flammeus (ordinary birthmark) is a vascular ectasia that typically fades (stork bite) or persists (port-wine stain), but is not a 'strawberry' hemangioma.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor of the elderly, not an infant lesion.

ankiCards: The 'strawberry hemangioma' is technically called a {{c1::juvenile}} hemangioma.
Juvenile hemangiomas typically {{c1::regress/involute}} by age 7.
A juvenile hemangioma is a type of {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma.
The clinical course of a strawberry hemangioma involves {{c1::initial rapid growth}} followed by {{c2::regression}}.
The incidence of juvenile hemangioma is approximately 1 in {{c1::200}} births.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangioma is the most common vascular tumor of infancy.
Usually occurs on the skin of the face or scalp.
They appear within the first few weeks of life.
Complete regression occurs in 75-90% of cases by age 7.
Histology shows a proliferation of thin-walled capillaries.
microReview: Strawberry Hemangioma = Juvenile = Newborn + Rapid growth + Regression by age 7.
examinerTraps: Confusing 'strawberry hemangioma' (which regresses) with 'port-wine stain' (which persists and grows with the child).
sourceQuote: Juvenile hemangioma (strawberry hemangioma) of the skin of newborns is extremely common... they usually regress spontaneously by age 7.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An HIV-positive patient presents with numerous red, skin nodules. Laboratory investigation reveals that the proliferation is caused by a gram-negative bacillus that induces host cells to release Hypoxia-Inducible Factor 1-alpha (HIF-1α). Which organism is responsible for this reactive vascular proliferation?

explanations.a: Bartonella henselae (and Bartonella quintana) causes Bacillary Angiomatosis in immunocompromised hosts by stimulating VEGF through the HIF-1α pathway.
explanations.b: Rickettsia causes vasculitis and typhus but does not typically cause localized vascular tumor-like proliferations.
explanations.c: HHV-8 causes Kaposi Sarcoma, which is a neoplasm, not a reactive bacterial proliferation.
explanations.d: Staphylococcus aureus causes pyogenic infections (abscesses), not vascular angiomatosis.
explanations.e: Treponema pallidum causes syphilis; while it involves vessels (endarteritis), it does not cause angiomatosis.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by the bacteria {{c1::Bartonella henselae}} or {{c2::Bartonella quintana}}.
The mechanism of Bartonella-induced vascular growth involves the stimulation of {{c1::VEGF}}.
Bartonella organisms are visualized on tissue sections using the {{c1::Warthin-Starry}} silver stain.
Unlike Kaposi Sarcoma, Bacillary Angiomatosis contains an infiltrate of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
Bacillary Angiomatosis is treated with {{c1::antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin)}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis is a reactive vascular proliferation, not a true neoplasm.
It occurs primarily in immunocompromised (AIDS) patients.
Caused by Bartonella species (cat-scratch disease or trench fever agents).
Histology shows lobular capillary proliferation with neutrophilic debris.
The presence of bacteria (Warthin-Starry stain) distinguishes it from Kaposi Sarcoma.
microReview: Bacillary Angiomatosis = Bartonella + Neutrophils + Warthin-Starry + AIDS.
examinerTraps: The examiner will often provide a vignette of an HIV patient and expect you to choose between HHV-8 (Kaposi) and Bartonella (Bacillary Angiomatosis) based on histology (neutrophils vs spindle cells).
sourceQuote: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts caused by opportunistic gram-negative bacilli of the Bartonella family.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old female presents with a history of radical mastectomy followed by radiation and chronic lymphedema of the right arm for the past 12 years. She now presents with several persistent, bluish-purple, firm skin nodules on that same arm. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: This is the classic presentation of Stewart-Treves syndrome, where angiosarcoma develops in the setting of chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy).
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is HHV-8 related and usually multifocal; it is not specifically associated with chronic lymphedema after surgery.
explanations.c: Lymphangiomas are benign malformations, usually congenital, and do not appear as new malignant nodules in an adult with lymphedema.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis requires Bartonella infection and immunocompromise; it is not associated with chronic lymphedema.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are small, painful subungual lesions, not large nodules in a lymphedematous limb.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
Stewart-Treves syndrome most commonly occurs after {{c1::radical mastectomy}}.
The typical latency between lymphedema and the development of angiosarcoma is about {{c1::10 years}}.
Angiosarcomas are highly {{c1::aggressive}} malignant tumors.
Histologically, angiosarcoma in Stewart-Treves syndrome shows {{c1::atypical endothelial cells}}.
keyPoints: Stewart-Treves syndrome is a specific clinical scenario for angiosarcoma.
It results from chronic lymphedema, usually post-surgical.
The nodules are often mistaken for bruises or infections initially.
Prognosis is poor due to early metastasis.
Surgical excision and radiation are the main treatments, but recurrence is common.
microReview: Post-mastectomy + Chronic Lymphedema + New purple nodules = Angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves).
examinerTraps: Wait for the 'long-term' history. If the nodules appear 1-2 years after surgery, it's more likely recurrent breast cancer. If it's 10+ years with lymphedema, think Angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas can also occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema, classically in the ipsilateral arm of women several years after radical mastectomy... (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the most likely clinical outcome for a child born with a 'stork bite' (nevus flammeus) on the nape of the neck?

explanations.a: The common 'stork bite' or 'angel kiss' (nevus flammeus) is a light pink, flat ectasia that usually fades and regresses spontaneously.
explanations.b: Nevus flammeus is a benign vascular ectasia and does not undergo malignant transformation.
explanations.c: A port-wine stain is a different, more permanent form of nevus flammeus that does not evolve from a standard stork bite.
explanations.d: Sturge-Weber syndrome is associated with port-wine stains in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve, not a simple stork bite on the neck.
explanations.e: Subungual pain is characteristic of glomus tumors, not nevus flammeus.

ankiCards: Nevus flammeus is a type of vascular {{c1::ectasia}}, not a true neoplasm.
The 'stork bite' is a nevus flammeus found on the {{c1::nape of the neck}}.
Most ordinary nevus flammeus lesions eventually {{c1::regress/disappear}}.
A port-wine stain is a {{c1::permanent}} form of nevus flammeus.
Port-wine stains in the trigeminal distribution are associated with {{c1::Sturge-Weber}} syndrome.
keyPoints: Nevus flammeus is the most common form of vascular ectasia.
It is a congenital capillary malformation.
Ordinary ones (stork bites) are flat and usually fade.
Port-wine stains are a sub-type that grow with the child and thicken.
Sturge-Weber includes port-wine stains, leptomeningeal angiomas, and glaucoma.
microReview: Nevus flammeus (Stork bite) = Benign ectasia + Fades/Regresses.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'stork bite' (common, fades) with 'port-wine stain' (permanent, syndrome-associated).
sourceQuote: Nevus flammeus, the ordinary 'birthmark', is the most common form of vascular ectasia... most ultimately regress.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)
