Muscular arteries regulate peripheral resistance.
The media's integrity is essential to prevent dilation.
Vessel architecture changes based on the hemodynamic load.
Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins.
microReview: Control of pressure and flow is a function of the smooth muscle in the media. Failure of this same layer to maintain structural integrity leads to aneurysms.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the layer that *controls* pressure (media) with the layer that *senses* it (endothelium/intima).
sourceQuote: the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing these muscular vessels to exert control over blood flow and pressure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old male with long, slender fingers and a history of lens dislocation is admitted with sudden-onset, tearing chest pain. Imaging shows a dilation of the ascending aorta. Which of the following is the most likely microscopic finding in the aortic wall?

options.a: Atherosclerotic plaque with a fibrous cap
options.c: Endarteritis obliterans of the vasa vasorum

explanations.a: Atherosclerosis is more common in the abdominal aorta of older patients, not the ascending aorta of a young patient with Marfan features.
explanations.b: Marfan syndrome leads to cystic medial degeneration (loss of smooth muscle and elastic tissue), causing thoracic aortic aneurysms.
explanations.c: Endarteritis obliterans is the hallmark of tertiary syphilis affecting the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta.
explanations.d: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis affects small vessels, not the aorta.
explanations.e: Medial calcification (Mönckeberg) usually occurs in muscular arteries and does not lead to dilation.

ankiCards: Thoracic aortic aneurysms in Marfan syndrome are caused by {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
Patients with Marfan syndrome have mutations in the {{c1::fibrillin-1}} gene.
A tearing chest pain in a patient with aortic dilation suggests {{c1::aortic dissection}}.
Weakening of the {{c1::media}} is the underlying mechanism for thoracic aneurysms.
The ascending aorta is the most common site for aneurysms related to {{c1::hypertension}} and genetic syndromes.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome is a common cause of aneurysms in the young.
Cystic medial necrosis/degeneration is the histological hallmark.
Ascending aorta is the typical site.
Tearing pain suggests dissection as a complication.
Fibrillin-1 defects lead to weakened elastic tissue.
microReview: Genetic defects in connective tissue (like Marfan) lead to medial weakening, showcasing the 'weakening of vessel walls' mechanism of vascular disease.
examinerTraps: Atherosclerosis is common for *abdominal* aneurysms; genetic or hypertensive causes are more common for *thoracic* (ascending) aneurysms.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old male with a history of poorly controlled HIV (CD4+ count 150/mm³) presents with multiple painless, reddish-purple macules and plaques on his lower extremities and oral mucosa. A biopsy of a skin lesion reveals spindle-shaped cells forming slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells. Which of the following infectious agents is most likely responsible for this patient's condition?

explanations.a: HHV-6 is associated with Roseola infantum, not vascular tumors.
explanations.b: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of Kaposi sarcoma, which presents as spindle-cell vascular proliferations in immunocompromised hosts.
explanations.c: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can look similar clinically but shows a lobular proliferation of capillaries with neutrophilic infiltrates and granular purple bacteria on Warthin-Starry stain.
explanations.d: EBV is associated with various lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, but not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.e: CMV causes retinitis and colitis in HIV patients but does not cause primary vascular neoplasms.

ankiCards: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
The histology of Kaposi sarcoma features {{c1::spindle}} cells and slit-like vascular spaces.
In AIDS patients, Kaposi sarcoma frequently involves the {{c1::skin, mucous membranes, and GI tract}}.
Kaposi sarcoma lesions usually contain extravasated {{c1::red blood cells}}.
Unlike bacillary angiomatosis, Kaposi sarcoma lacks {{c1::neutrophilic}} infiltrates.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a low-grade malignant vascular tumor caused by HHV-8.
Four clinical forms exist: Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
Histology: Spindle cells, slit-like spaces, and RBC extravasation.
It is the most common neoplasm in patients with AIDS.
Diagnosis is confirmed by histology and HHV-8 immunostaining.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma (HHV-8) presents as purple plaques/nodules. Histology: spindle cells + slit-like spaces. Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella) presents similarly but has neutrophils and bacteria.
examinerTraps: Distinguishing Kaposi sarcoma from Bacillary Angiomatosis is a common board topic. Look for 'neutrophils' or 'Warthin-Starry stain' to point toward Bartonella.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following immunohistochemical markers is the most specific and sensitive for identifying tumors of endothelial cell origin, such as angiosarcomas?

explanations.a: CD31 (platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule) is highly specific for endothelial cells and is used to identify vascular tumors.
explanations.b: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells, such as melanocytes or Schwann cells.
explanations.c: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells and carcinomas.
explanations.d: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (smooth or skeletal).
explanations.e: CD45 (LCA) is a marker for hematopoietic cells (leukocytes).

ankiCards: The most useful immunohistochemical marker for endothelial differentiation is {{c1::CD31}}.
Angiosarcomas are malignant tumors derived from {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
CD31 is also known as {{c1::PECAM-1}}.
Besides CD31, another vascular marker often used is {{c1::von Willebrand factor (vWF)}}.
In poorly differentiated angiosarcomas, {{c1::CD31}} helps distinguish them from carcinomas.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors originate from endothelial cells or supporting cells.
CD31 is the gold standard immunohistochemical marker for endothelium.
Angiosarcomas can be highly aggressive and poorly differentiated.
Angiosarcomas can occur in the skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Hepatic angiosarcomas are associated with vinyl chloride and arsenic exposure.
microReview: Endothelial markers: CD31, CD34, vWF. CD31 is highly sensitive/specific for vascular neoplasms.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse CD31 with CD3 or CD34. CD3 is for T-cells; CD34 is for hematopoietic stems and many soft tissue tumors but is less specific for endothelium than CD31.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with an exquisitely painful, 5-mm, firm, blue-tinged nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. The pain is triggered by cold exposure. A biopsy of the lesion reveals aggregates of specialized smooth muscle cells surrounding branch-like vascular channels. What is the cell of origin for this tumor?

explanations.a: Endothelial cells line the vascular spaces but are not the primary proliferating cell in glomus tumors.
explanations.b: While related, the glomus cell is specifically a modified smooth muscle cell of the glomus body, not a standard capillary pericyte.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts are not the primary component of glomus tumors.
explanations.e: Schwann cells are found in neuromas, which can be painful, but do not form the vascular aggregates seen in glomus tumors.

ankiCards: A glomus tumor is typically found in the {{c1::subungual}} region (under fingernails).
The classic symptom triad of a glomus tumor includes pain, tenderness, and sensitivity to {{c1::cold}}.
Glomus tumors arise from modified {{c1::smooth muscle}} cells of the glomus body.
The glomus body is a specialized {{c1::arteriovenous anastomosis}} involved in thermoregulation.
On histology, glomus cells appear as nests of {{c1::monomorphic round}} cells.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but extremely painful.
Location: Most common in distal digits, especially subungual.
Origin: Modified smooth muscle cells (glomus cells).
Function: Glomus bodies regulate temperature by shunting blood.
Treatment is simple surgical excision.
microReview: Painful subungual nodule + cold sensitivity = Glomus tumor. Origin = Modified smooth muscle cells.
examinerTraps: The pain is very disproportionate to the small size of the lesion. Examiners often use 'cold sensitivity' as a pathognomonic clue.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An infant is born with a bright red, raised, 'strawberry-like' lesion on the scalp. The lesion grows rapidly over the first few months of life but begins to fade and shrink by age 2. By age 7, the lesion has completely disappeared. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas are deeper, involve larger vascular channels, and rarely regress spontaneously.
explanations.b: Capillary (strawberry) hemangiomas are common in newborns, grow rapidly, and then almost always regress by age 7-9.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granulomas are rapidly growing pedunculated red nodules that often bleed and follow trauma; they do not typically regress spontaneously.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are painful subungual lesions in adults, not regressing birthmarks in infants.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor, usually in elderly adults, and does not regress.

ankiCards: A {{c1::capillary (strawberry)}} hemangioma is a common benign tumor of infancy.
Capillary hemangiomas typically {{c1::regress}} spontaneously by age 7.
The histology of a capillary hemangioma shows thin-walled {{c1::capillaries}} with scant stroma.
Strawberry hemangiomas are most frequently located on the {{c1::skin}}.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, {{c1::cavernous}} hemangiomas involve large, blood-filled spaces.
keyPoints: Capillary hemangiomas are the most common vascular tumor of infancy.
They are often called 'strawberry' hemangiomas because of their appearance.
Growth phase (first few months) followed by involution phase (years).
Most have completely regressed by age 7.
Histologically, they consist of closely packed capillaries lined by endothelial cells.
microReview: Infant + Bright red skin lesion + Spontaneous regression = Juvenile/Capillary Hemangioma.
examinerTraps: The word 'strawberry' is the classic giveaway. Don't confuse it with 'Port-wine stain' (Nevus flammeus), which does not regress and grows with the child.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Cavernous hemangiomas of the cerebellum or retina are a defining feature of which of the following autosomal dominant syndromes, also characterized by renal cell carcinomas and pheochromocytomas?

explanations.a: Sturge-Weber is characterized by port-wine stains and leptomeningeal angiomas, not VHL-associated tumors.
explanations.b: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) features multiple telangiectasias and AVMs.
explanations.c: Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease features hemangioblastomas (capillary/cavernous-like) of the CNS/retina, clear cell RCC, and pheochromocytomas.
explanations.d: NF1 features neurofibromas and Lisch nodules, not primary vascular tumors.
explanations.e: Tuberous sclerosis features facial angiofibromas and renal angiomyolipomas.

ankiCards: Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is associated with {{c1::hemangioblastomas}} of the cerebellum and retina.
The inheritance pattern of VHL disease is {{c1::autosomal dominant}}.
Patients with VHL are at high risk for clear cell {{c1::renal cell carcinoma}}.
Sturge-Weber syndrome features a {{c1::port-wine stain}} in the V1/V2 distribution.
Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome is also known as {{c1::Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT)}}.
keyPoints: VHL is caused by mutations in the VHL tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3p.
Vascular lesions in VHL are often hemangioblastomas (histologically distinct but related to vascular tumors).
Key features: Cerebellar/retinal hemangioblastomas, RCC, Pheochromocytoma.
Sturge-Weber: GNAQ mutation, port-wine stain, glaucoma.
HHT (Osler-Weber-Rendu): TGF-beta signaling mutations, epistaxis, GI bleeds.
microReview: VHL = Hemangioblastoma + RCC + Pheo. Sturge-Weber = Port-wine stain + Leptomeningeal angioma. HHT = Telangiectasia + AVMs.
examinerTraps: Carefully distinguish between 'hemangioma' and 'hemangioblastoma'; while Robbins groups them, VHL is specifically associated with hemangioblastomas.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with several enlarging, ill-defined, violaceous skin nodules on her left arm. Ten years ago, she underwent a radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection and radiation therapy for breast cancer, resulting in chronic lymphedema of the left arm. A biopsy of a nodule confirms a diagnosis of angiosarcoma. This clinical scenario is an example of which of the following?

explanations.a: Li-Fraumeni involves germline p53 mutations and multiple cancers, but isn't specific to post-lymphedema angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to the development of angiosarcoma in the setting of chronic lymphedema, classically after mastectomy.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious process in HIV patients.
explanations.d: Maffucci syndrome involves multiple hemangiomas and enchondromas.
explanations.e: Kasabach-Merritt syndrome is a consumptive coagulopathy associated with large hemangiomas.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
Stewart-Treves syndrome classically occurs after {{c1::radical mastectomy}}.
The prognosis for cutaneous angiosarcoma is generally {{c1::poor}}.
Risk factors for angiosarcoma include chronic lymphedema, {{c1::radiation}}, and certain chemicals.
Histology of angiosarcoma shows malignant {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a malignant endothelial neoplasm.
Chronic lymphedema (e.g., post-mastectomy axillary dissection) is a major risk factor.
Radiation therapy also increases the risk of local angiosarcoma.
Stewart-Treves syndrome: Lymphedema -> Angiosarcoma.
High mortality due to early metastasis.
microReview: Post-mastectomy lymphedema + New purple arm nodules = Stewart-Treves syndrome (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: The delay between the surgery/lymphedema and the cancer is usually around 10 years. Don't confuse this with simple recurrence of breast cancer.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Exposure to which of the following environmental toxins is most strongly associated with the development of hepatic angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and lung cancer.
explanations.b: Aflatoxin B1 is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Vinyl chloride (used in PVC production), arsenic, and Thorotrast are classically linked to hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: Benzene is associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.e: Beryllium is associated with berylliosis and lung cancer.

ankiCards: Three major risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma are vinyl chloride, {{c1::arsenic}}, and Thorotrast.
Vinyl chloride is a gas used in the production of {{c1::polyvinyl chloride (PVC)}}.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is a tumor of {{c1::endothelial}} cells in the liver.
Aflatoxin is associated with HCC, while vinyl chloride is associated with {{c1::angiosarcoma}}.
The latency period for chemical-induced angiosarcoma can be {{c1::decades}}.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is rare but highly lethal.
It is one of the classic examples of occupational carcinogenesis.
Arsenic (pesticides), Vinyl chloride (plastic industry), Thorotrast (old radiocontrast).
Patients often present late with abdominal pain and liver failure.
Tumor cells are CD31 positive.
microReview: Hepatic Angiosarcoma associations: Vinyl chloride, Arsenic, Thorotrast.
examinerTraps: Differentiating the causes of liver cancer: HCC (Hepatitis B/C, Alcohol, Aflatoxin) vs Angiosarcoma (Vinyl Chloride).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 10-year-old boy presents with a large, rapidly growing vascular mass on his thigh. Laboratory studies show severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count 25,000/mm³) and evidence of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. This combination of a large vascular tumor and consumptive coagulopathy is known as:

explanations.a: Sturge-Weber is a neurocutaneous disorder, not a coagulopathy.
explanations.b: Kasabach-Merritt syndrome involves platelet sequestration and consumption within a large, rapidly growing vascular tumor (usually kaposiform hemangioendothelioma).
explanations.c: Trousseau syndrome is migratory thrombophlebitis associated with malignancy (classically pancreatic).
explanations.d: Osler-Weber-Rendu features telangiectasias and bleeding but not typically localized platelet consumption.
explanations.e: Blue rubber bleb nevus syndrome involves multiple venous malformations in the GI tract and skin.

ankiCards: Kasabach-Merritt syndrome is characterized by a vascular tumor and {{c1::thrombocytopenia}}.
The pathophysiology of Kasabach-Merritt involves {{c1::platelet sequestration}} within the tumor.
The tumors most often associated with Kasabach-Merritt are {{c1::kaposiform hemangioendotheliomas}}.
Laboratory findings in Kasabach-Merritt include low {{c1::fibrinogen}} and elevated D-dimer.
Kasabach-Merritt syndrome often leads to a life-threatening {{c1::consumptive coagulopathy}}.
keyPoints: Kasabach-Merritt syndrome is a rare, life-threatening complication of certain vascular tumors.
It involves profound thrombocytopenia and consumptive coagulopathy.
Seen mostly in infants and young children.
Associated tumors: Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma and tufted angioma.
Treatment involves managing the tumor (e.g., vincristine, sirolimus) and supportive care.
microReview: Large vascular mass + Low platelets + Consumptive Coagulopathy = Kasabach-Merritt Syndrome.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse this with DIC in sepsis; while the labs look similar to DIC, the presence of a 'large vascular mass' is the trigger.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 25-year-old pregnant woman develops a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated nodule on her gingiva that bleeds easily with minor trauma. Histologically, the lesion shows a lobular proliferation of capillaries with interspersed inflammatory cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are typically birthmarks in infants, not gingival nodules in adults.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granuloma (granuloma pyogenicum) is a benign vascular lesion that commonly occurs on the gingiva (often in pregnant women, called 'pregnancy tumor' or granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are subungual and painful; they do not typically occur on the gingiva.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor with significant cytological atypia, unlike the benign look of pyogenic granuloma.
explanations.e: Kaposi sarcoma presents as purple macules/plaques in HIV patients, not a single pedunculated gingival mass.

ankiCards: A pyogenic granuloma in a pregnant woman is often called a {{c1::pregnancy tumor (granuloma gravidarum)}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are neither {{c1::pyogenic}} (infectious) nor {{c1::granulomas}} (histologically).
The clinical appearance of a pyogenic granuloma is a {{c1::pedunculated}} red nodule that bleeds easily.
Histologically, pyogenic granuloma is a {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
Preferred treatment for a pyogenic granuloma is {{c1::surgical excision}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a common benign vascular lesion of the skin and oral mucosa.
Despite the name, it is a lobular capillary hemangioma, not a granuloma.
Associated with pregnancy and trauma.
Highly vascular and friable (bleeds easily).
Can regress after pregnancy but usually requires excision.
microReview: Gingiva + Pregnancy + Bleeding nodule = Pyogenic granuloma.
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic granuloma' is a misnomer; it is neither pus-forming nor a granuloma. Examiners like to test this distinction.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the fundamental pathological distinction between a cavernous hemangioma and a capillary hemangioma?

explanations.a: Neither capillary nor cavernous hemangiomas show atypia, as both are benign.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas consist of small, thin-walled capillaries, while cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated vascular spaces.
explanations.c: HHV-8 is associated with Kaposi sarcoma, not benign hemangiomas.
explanations.d: Both are benign; the difference is morphological, not in biological potential.
explanations.e: Neither typically has a prominent inflammatory infiltrate unless ulcerated.

ankiCards: {{c1::Capillary}} hemangiomas have small, thin-walled vessels.
{{c1::Cavernous}} hemangiomas have large, dilated vascular channels.
Cavernous hemangiomas are often {{c1::deep-seated}} (e.g., in the liver).
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas rarely {{c1::regress}}.
A common complication of large cavernous hemangiomas is {{c1::thrombosis}}.
keyPoints: Hemangiomas are categorized by the size of the vascular spaces.
Capillary = Small, tight channels; Cavernous = Large, blood-filled spaces.
Cavernous hemangiomas of the liver are the most common benign liver tumor.
Cavernous hemangiomas are more likely to require intervention if they cause mass effect.
Both are lined by a single layer of normal endothelial cells.
microReview: Hemangioma types: Capillary (small/surface) vs Cavernous (large/deep). Both are benign.
examinerTraps: Don't assume 'cavernous' means more dangerous; it simply describes the architecture of the blood vessels.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular pathology is categorized by two principal mechanisms that lead to disease. One mechanism involves the narrowing or obstruction of vessel lumens. What is the second principal mechanism?

options.a: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
options.b: Excessive intimal thickening from fibroblast proliferation
options.c: Dilation of venous valves leading to retrograde flow
options.d: Hyaline deposition in the basement membrane of capillaries
options.e: Necrosis of the tunica adventitia in elastic arteries

explanations.a: The two principal mechanisms of vascular disease are lumen narrowing/obstruction and the weakening of vessel walls which results in dilation or rupture (aneurysms).
explanations.b: Intimal thickening is a response to injury, but it is not listed as one of the two primary mechanisms underlying all vascular disease in the source.
explanations.c: Venous disorders are mentioned as significant, but valve dilation is a specific feature of venous disease, not one of the two overarching principles of vascular pathology.
explanations.d: Hyaline deposition is characteristic of hypertensive vascular disease but is not a principal mechanism for general vascular morbidity/mortality.
explanations.e: The tunica media is typically the layer associated with weakening and aneurysm formation, not specifically the adventitia in this context.

ankiCards: What are the two principal mechanisms underlying vascular disease? {{c1::Narrowing/obstruction}} and {{c2::weakening of vessel walls}}.
Weakening of vessel walls primarily leads to {{c1::dilation}} or {{c2::rupture}}.
Narrowing of vessel lumens can occur progressively through {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Precipitous obstruction of a vessel lumen is usually caused by {{c1::thrombosis}} or {{c2::embolism}}.
Aneurysms fall under the pathological category of {{c1::weakening of vessel walls}}.
keyPoints: Vascular pathology is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality.
Two main mechanisms: Stenosis/Obstruction and Wall Weakening.
Obstruction can be progressive (atherosclerosis) or acute (thrombosis).
Weakening leads to dilation (aneurysm) or rupture.
Arterial lesions are generally more clinically significant than venous ones.
microReview: Vascular disease is fundamentally a problem of either 'getting blood through' (stenosis) or 'holding blood in' (weakening). Aneurysms represent the latter category.
examinerTraps: Avoid confusing a 'response to injury' (like intimal thickening) with a 'principal mechanism' of disease (like wall weakening).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Muscular vessels are characterized by a high ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter compared to elastic arteries. What is the primary functional significance of this structural adaptation in these vessels?

options.a: To exert control over blood flow and pressure
options.b: To facilitate gas exchange through the vessel wall
options.c: To prevent the formation of atherosclerotic plaques
options.d: To store potential energy during cardiac systole
options.e: To allow for the passive return of venous blood

explanations.a: The high ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter in smaller muscular vessels allows them to change their diameter significantly, thereby controlling blood flow resistance and systemic pressure.
explanations.b: Gas exchange occurs in capillaries, which have only an endothelial layer and no muscular wall.
explanations.c: Atherosclerosis actually preferentially affects muscular and elastic arteries; the wall thickness does not prevent it.
explanations.d: Storing energy during systole is a function of large elastic arteries (like the aorta), not the smaller muscular vessels.
explanations.e: Passive return is a characteristic of the venous system, which has thinner walls and lower pressure.

ankiCards: Arterial walls are {{c1::thicker}} than corresponding veins at the same level of branching.
In small muscular vessels, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}}.
The increased wall-to-lumen ratio in muscular vessels allows them to control {{c1::blood flow}} and {{c2::pressure}}.
Large vessels that accommodate pulsatile flow are classified as {{c1::elastic}} arteries.
Atherosclerosis affects which two types of arteries? {{c1::Elastic}} and {{c2::muscular}} arteries.
keyPoints: Arteries have thicker walls than veins to handle high pressure.
The wall-to-lumen ratio increases as vessels get smaller.
Muscular arteries regulate systemic vascular resistance.
Elastic arteries (like the aorta) handle pulsatile flow.
Structure reflects distinct functional roles in the vascular tree.
microReview: Vessel structure is tailored to function: large vessels manage pressure/pulsatility (elasticity), while smaller vessels manage flow/resistance (muscularity).
examinerTraps: Don't assume all arteries are the same; the wall-to-lumen ratio increases in smaller vessels, even though total wall thickness decreases.
sourceQuote: the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing these muscular vessels to exert control over blood flow and pressure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old male with a history of smoking and hypertension presents for a routine physical exam. Palpation of the abdomen reveals a prominent, pulsatile mass just above the umbilicus. Ultrasound confirms a 5.2 cm infrarenal aortic dilation. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism for this finding?

explanations.a: The clinical presentation of a pulsatile abdominal mass is classic for an Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA). Aneurysms are caused by the weakening of the vessel wall leading to dilation.
explanations.b: Stenosis refers to narrowing, which would not cause a palpable pulsatile mass/dilation; it would lead to ischemic symptoms.
explanations.c: Acute thrombosis would cause sudden distal ischemia (e.g., cold, blue legs), not a chronic pulsatile mass.
explanations.d: Intimal thickening is a response to injury (like hypertension) but is not the primary mechanism that defines an aneurysm's macroscopic dilation.
explanations.e: Vessels (except for the heart and veins) do not have valves; the tunica media provides structural integrity, not valvular function.

ankiCards: A pulsatile abdominal mass is a classic clinical sign of {{c1::Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA)}}.
The primary pathological mechanism of an aneurysm is {{c1::weakening of the vessel wall}}.
Aneurysms lead to {{c1::dilation}} or {{c2::rupture}}.
AAA is often associated with which modifiable risk factor mentioned in the text? {{c1::Atherosclerosis}} (implied by vascular disease principles).
Most aneurysms occur in {{c1::elastic}} and {{c2::muscular}} arteries.
keyPoints: AAA often presents as an asymptomatic pulsatile mass.
Pathogenesis involves loss of structural integrity of the arterial wall.
Atherosclerosis is a major precursor to AAA formation.
Weakening allows the vessel to expand under arterial pressure.
Risk of rupture increases with aneurysm diameter.
microReview: Aneurysms = Wall Weakening. Stenosis = Narrowing. Both are major vascular disease pathways.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'pulsatile' in the stem; it distinguishes a mass from a simple tumor or cyst and points directly to vascular dilation.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: ... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which property of elastic arteries, such as the aorta, is primarily responsible for maintaining continuous blood flow through the peripheral tissues during cardiac diastole?

options.a: Elastic recoil of the vessel wall
options.b: High resistance of the muscular media
options.e: Thinness of the vessel wall relative to the lumen

explanations.a: Elastic arteries contain abundant elastic fibers. They expand during systole to store energy and recoil during diastole to push blood forward, maintaining pressure.
explanations.b: High resistance is a feature of smaller muscular arteries and arterioles, not large elastic arteries.
explanations.c: Arteries do not contain valves; valves are found in veins and the heart.
explanations.d: The adventitia is mainly connective tissue and does not provide active contraction for blood propulsion.
explanations.e: Arteries have thicker walls than veins; thinness would lead to rupture under high pressure rather than flow maintenance.

ankiCards: Large arteries that accommodate pulsatile flow are known as {{c1::elastic}} arteries.
Arterial walls are {{c1::thicker}} than vein walls at the same level of branching.
The ability of the aorta to handle high pressure is due to its {{c1::thicker}} wall.
Functional specialization in vessels is reflected by their {{c1::structural architecture}}.
Atherosclerosis primarily affects {{c1::elastic}} and {{c2::muscular}} arteries.
keyPoints: Elastic arteries expand to accommodate pulsatile cardiac output.
Diastolic recoil maintains tissue perfusion.
Arteries are structurally thicker than veins to handle high pressure.
Wall composition varies based on the functional role of the vessel.
Loss of elasticity (as in aging or disease) contributes to vascular pathology.
microReview: Structure follows function: Elasticity in the aorta manages pulsatility; thickness in arteries manages pressure.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'muscular vessels' (control flow) with 'elastic vessels' (accommodate pulsatility).
sourceQuote: arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the context of the cardiovascular system, which of the following vessel types are the primary site for the development of atherosclerosis?

explanations.a: As per the classification of vascular diseases, atherosclerosis is a pathology that affects mainly the elastic and muscular arteries.
explanations.b: Arterioles are more commonly affected by hyaline or hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis; venules are not primary sites for atherosclerosis.
explanations.c: Veins and lymphatics do not develop atherosclerosis as it is an arterial disease related to high-pressure flow.
explanations.d: Capillaries lack the tunica media and intima structure required for the formation of complex atherosclerotic plaques.
explanations.e: Vasa vasorum are 'vessels of vessels' and are too small for primary atherosclerotic plaque formation.

ankiCards: Atherosclerosis mainly affects {{c1::elastic}} and {{c2::muscular}} arteries.
The most clinically significant vascular lesions involve {{c1::arteries}}.
Which category of disease is responsible for more morbidity than any other? {{c1::Vascular pathology}}.
Two mechanisms of vascular disease: {{c1::Narrowing}} and {{c2::Wall weakening}}.
Atherosclerosis can cause lumen narrowing {{c1::progressively}}.
keyPoints: Atherosclerosis is an arterial-specific disease.
It targets elastic (e.g., aorta) and muscular (e.g., coronary) arteries.
Lesions lead to progressive narrowing.
Vascular disease is the leading cause of human morbidity.
Atherosclerosis is a major cause of arterial stenosis.
microReview: If it's an artery (elastic or muscular), it's a target for atherosclerosis. If it's a vein or capillary, it's generally not.
examinerTraps: Be careful with the term 'muscular vessels'; while they include small arteries, 'muscular arteries' specifically refers to the medium-sized named arteries (like the femoral or coronary) which are prime targets for atherosclerosis.
sourceQuote: Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 64-year-old female presents with sudden, excruciating 'tearing' chest pain that radiates to her back. She has a history of poorly controlled hypertension. Her blood pressure is 180/110 mmHg. A CT scan shows an intimal tear and blood entering the media of the ascending aorta. This condition represents which primary mechanism of vascular disease?

explanations.a: The description (tearing pain, hypertension, blood in media) is classic for an aortic dissection. This falls under the category of 'weakening of vessel walls,' which leads to dilation, dissection, or rupture.
explanations.b: Dissection is an acute process involving wall structural failure, not a progressive narrowing of the lumen (stenosis).
explanations.c: While some dissections are associated with genetic conditions (like Marfan), the primary mechanism of the pathology itself is wall weakening.
explanations.d: This is an arterial pathology (aorta), not a venous obstruction.
explanations.e: Capillary changes are seen in diabetes or small-vessel disease, not in large-vessel aortic dissections.

ankiCards: Aortic dissection is classified under the mechanism of {{c1::weakening of vessel walls}}.
Dilation of a vessel wall is known as an {{c1::aneurysm}}.
Rupture of a vessel is a consequence of {{c1::wall weakening}}.
Arterial walls are thicker than veins to accommodate {{c1::pulsatile flow}}.
Pathology in high-pressure vessels most commonly involves {{c1::arteries}}.
keyPoints: Aortic dissection involves blood splitting the media.
Hypertension is a major risk factor for wall weakening.
Tearing chest pain is the classic clinical presentation.
It is a life-threatening vascular emergency.
Fits the 'weakening/dilation/rupture' category of vascular disease.
microReview: Tearing pain + High BP = Dissection. Category: Wall Weakening/Rupture.
examinerTraps: Aortic dissection is often grouped with aneurysms because both share the underlying mechanism of 'weakening of vessel walls.'
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following structural changes is most characteristic of the arterial response to chronic high blood pressure, potentially leading to increased vascular resistance?

options.a: Increased ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter
options.c: Loss of smooth muscle cells in the media
options.d: Decrease in the total number of elastic fibers

explanations.a: In response to hypertension, muscular arteries and arterioles undergo structural changes (like intimal thickening and medial hypertrophy) that increase the wall-to-lumen ratio to manage the pressure, which also increases resistance.
explanations.b: Thinning of the media is associated with aneurysm formation (weakening), not the compensatory response to hypertension.
explanations.c: Hypertension often leads to hypertrophy (increase in size/activity) of smooth muscle cells, not loss.
explanations.d: While elastic fibers may degrade in aging, the characteristic response to pressure control in muscular vessels involves wall thickening.
explanations.e: Expansion (ectasia/aneurysm) is a sign of wall failure (weakening), not the regulatory mechanism of muscular vessels.

ankiCards: The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}} as vessels become smaller.
Muscular vessels exert control over {{c1::blood flow}} and {{c2::pressure}}.
Arterial wall thickness {{c1::diminishes}} as vessels become smaller, but the wall-to-lumen ratio {{c2::increases}}.
Hypertension involves pathology in the {{c1::blood pressure regulation}} system.
Vascular wall response to injury often involves {{c1::intimal thickening}}.
keyPoints: Small arteries have the highest wall-to-lumen ratio.
This structure is optimized for resistance and pressure control.
Vessels respond to injury with stereotypic changes.
Intimal thickening is a common response to hypertension.
Structural specialization allows vessels to meet specific physiological needs.
microReview: Wall-to-lumen ratio = Control. Thickening = Response to Pressure/Injury. Dilation = Wall Failure.
examinerTraps: Be careful: Total wall thickness is greatest in the aorta, but the *ratio* of wall thickness to lumen size is greatest in small muscular arteries.
sourceQuote: Arterial wall thickness gradually diminishes as the vessels become smaller, but the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing these muscular vessels to exert control over blood flow and pressure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the 'precipitous' mechanism of vessel lumen obstruction?

explanations.a: The text defines precipitous (sudden) obstruction as being caused by thrombosis or embolism.
explanations.b: Atherosclerosis is described as a 'progressive' cause of narrowing, not precipitous.
explanations.c: Cystic medial degeneration relates to wall weakening, not lumen obstruction.
explanations.d: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is a chronic, progressive narrowing seen in hypertension/diabetes.
explanations.e: Intimal hyperplasia is a progressive response to vascular injury.

ankiCards: Obstruction of a vessel lumen that happens 'precipitously' is caused by {{c1::thrombosis}} or {{c2::embolism}}.
Obstruction of a vessel lumen that happens 'progressively' is caused by {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Narrowing of a vessel is also known as {{c1::stenosis}}.
Vascular disorders often have characteristic {{c1::anatomic distributions}}.
The most clinically significant vascular lesions involve {{c1::arteries}}.
keyPoints: Obstruction can be acute or chronic.
Acute (precipitous) = Thrombosis/Embolism.
Chronic (progressive) = Atherosclerosis.
Stenosis and Wall Weakening are the two main vascular disease paths.
Anatomical distribution is key to identifying specific vascular disorders.
microReview: Precipitous = Fast (clot). Progressive = Slow (plaque). Both lead to stenosis.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the speed of the process. Atherosclerosis is the underlying condition, but the *precipitous* event is usually the superimposed thrombus.
sourceQuote: either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism)
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Venous disorders are described as 'not inconsequential' despite arterial lesions being more clinically significant. Which of the following is a key structural difference that explains why veins are generally under lower pressure than arteries?

options.a: Venous walls are thinner than corresponding arterial walls
options.b: Veins have a higher ratio of muscle to elastic fibers
options.c: Venous lumens are significantly smaller than arterial lumens
options.d: Veins lack an endothelial lining (tunica intima)
options.e: The tunica adventitia is absent in the venous system

explanations.a: Arterial walls are thicker to accommodate high, pulsatile pressure. Venous walls are thinner because they operate under low-pressure conditions.
explanations.b: Arteries (especially muscular ones) have more muscle; veins are less muscular and more distensible.
explanations.c: Venous lumens are typically larger than arterial lumens at the same level to accommodate a higher volume of blood (capacitance).
explanations.d: All blood vessels (arteries, veins, capillaries) are lined by endothelium.
explanations.e: Veins possess all three layers (intima, media, adventitia), though they are less distinct than in arteries.

ankiCards: Arterial walls are {{c1::thicker}} than corresponding veins.
Venous disorders are described as {{c1::not inconsequential}}.
The primary role of thicker arterial walls is to handle {{c1::pulsatile flow}} and {{c2::higher pressures}}.
The architectural composition of vessels is {{c1::comparable}} throughout the system but has specializations.
Vascular pathology is responsible for more {{c1::morbidity}} and {{c2::mortality}} than any other disease category.
keyPoints: Arteries have thicker walls than veins.
Thickness is required to withstand high pressure.
Veins function as high-volume, low-pressure reservoirs.
Structural specialization reflects functional roles.
Venous disease (like varicosities or DVT) is still clinically important.
microReview: Thick wall = High Pressure (Artery). Thin wall = Low Pressure (Vein).
examinerTraps: The text notes that structural specializations 'characterize specific kinds of vessels.' Always relate wall thickness to the pressure of the system it resides in.
sourceQuote: arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which layer of the blood vessel is primarily involved in the structural 'weakening' that leads to the formation of an aneurysm?

explanations.a: The tunica media provides the structural integrity of the vessel (containing smooth muscle and elastic fibers). Weakening of this layer is the hallmark of aneurysm formation.
explanations.b: The intima is the innermost layer; while atherosclerosis starts here, the dilation (aneurysm) results from media failure.
explanations.c: The internal elastic lamina is a component, but 'weakening of the wall' refers more broadly to the medial layer's integrity.
explanations.d: Vasa vasorum nourish the outer layers; their dysfunction can lead to medial weakening, but the media itself is what weakens to form the aneurysm.
explanations.e: The endothelium is a single cell layer that does not provide structural strength against dilation.

ankiCards: Which vessel layer is responsible for structural integrity? {{c1::Tunica media}}.
Aneurysms are caused by the {{c1::weakening}} of vessel walls.
The structural architecture of vessels is characteristically {{c1::anatomic}} in distribution.
Atherosclerosis affects which vessel layers? Primarily {{c1::intima}} (leading to secondary medial changes).
Vascular disease mechanisms: 1. Narrowing 2. {{c1::Wall weakening}}.
keyPoints: The tunica media is the 'strength' layer of the artery.
Loss of medial smooth muscle or elastic tissue leads to aneurysms.
Aneurysms involve all layers of the wall (true aneurysms).
Weakening allows for permanent dilation.
Atherosclerosis can cause secondary media weakening.
microReview: Media = Strength. Weak Media = Aneurysm/Dilation.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'intimal thickening' (response to injury) with the 'wall weakening' (media failure) that leads to dilation.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 34-year-old HIV-positive male presents with multiple painless, reddish-purple macules and plaques on his lower extremities and trunk. Physical examination reveals similar lesions on the hard palate. A biopsy of a skin lesion demonstrates proliferation of spindle-shaped cells forming slit-like vascular spaces containing red blood cells. Which of the following infectious agents is the most likely driver of this pathology?

explanations.a: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which presents with similar red papules but is characterized by neutrophilic infiltrates and clusters of tangles of bacilli, not spindle-cell slit-like spaces.
explanations.b: Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma, which typically presents with the described spindle-cell morphology and slit-like vascular spaces.
explanations.c: While HIV provides the immunosuppressive environment that allows Kaposi Sarcoma to flourish, it is not the direct oncogenic driver of the vascular proliferation.
explanations.d: Epstein-Barr Virus is associated with various lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, but not with primary vascular tumors like Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.e: Cytomegalovirus can cause retinitis or colitis in immunocompromised patients but is not associated with the development of vascular skin tumors.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is associated with infection by {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
The histological hallmark of Kaposi Sarcoma consists of {{c1::spindle cells}} forming {{c2::slit-like spaces}}.
In AIDS patients, Kaposi Sarcoma often involves the skin and the {{c1::hard palate/gastrointestinal tract}}.
{{c1::Bacillary angiomatosis}} is a differential for Kaposi Sarcoma but features a prominent {{c2::neutrophilic}} infiltrate.
The most common site for 'classic' Kaposi Sarcoma (non-AIDS) is the {{c1::lower extremities}} of older men of Mediterranean descent.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a low-grade malignant vascular tumor caused by HHV-8.
The four clinical forms are Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
Morphology progresses from patches to plaques to nodules.
Histology shows spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces, and extravasated RBCs.
KS cells are thought to be derived from lymphatic endothelial cells.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Slit-like spaces + AIDS/Immunosuppression.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse KS with Bacillary Angiomatosis; look for 'spindle cells' for KS versus 'neutrophils/bacteria' for Bacillary Angiomatosis.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 62-year-old male presents with fatigue and right upper quadrant discomfort. Imaging reveals multiple ill-defined masses within the liver. History reveals chronic occupational exposure to vinyl chloride during his work in a plastics manufacturing plant. A biopsy confirms a high-grade malignant vascular neoplasm. Immunohistochemical staining for which of the following markers would most likely be positive in these neoplastic cells?

explanations.a: CD31 (platelet-endothelial cell adhesion molecule) is a highly specific marker for endothelial cells and is used to identify vascular tumors like angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells and would be positive in carcinomas, not vascular sarcomas.
explanations.c: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (smooth or skeletal) and would be positive in leiomyosarcomas or rhabdomyosarcomas.
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells (melanocytes, Schwann cells) and is not typical for vascular tumors.
explanations.e: HMB-45 is a specific marker for melanocytic differentiation and is used in the diagnosis of melanoma.

ankiCards: The vascular marker {{c1::CD31}} is used to confirm the endothelial origin of a tumor.
Liver angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}, {{c2::thorotrast}}, or {{c3::arsenic}}.
{{c1::Angiosarcoma}} is a highly malignant tumor of endothelial cells.
Angiosarcomas can occur in the skin, soft tissue, breast, and {{c1::liver}}.
A marker other than CD31 used for vascular endothelium is {{c1::von Willebrand factor (vWF) / Factor VIII}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are aggressive malignant endothelial neoplasms.
Environmental carcinogens for hepatic angiosarcoma include vinyl chloride and arsenic.
They typically present as enlarging, fleshy, red-tan to gray-white masses.
Histology ranges from well-formed vascular channels to solid sheets of undifferentiated cells.
Markers include CD31 and von Willebrand factor (vWF).
microReview: Angiosarcoma = CD31+ + Malignant endothelial cells + Carcinogen exposure (PVC/Arsenic).
examinerTraps: The liver location might tempt you toward Hepatocellular Carcinoma; however, the 'vinyl chloride' history specifically points to Angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism) • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with a small, exquisitely painful, firm blue nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. She notes that the pain is often triggered by exposure to cold temperatures. The lesion is excised. Microscopically, the tumor is composed of nests and aggregates of uniform, rounded cells surrounding thin-walled vascular channels. These cells are most likely derived from which of the following?

explanations.a: Endothelial cells line the vascular channels within the tumor, but the primary 'glomus cells' that characterize this lesion are not endothelial in origin.
explanations.b: While glomus cells are related to perivascular cells, they are specifically defined as modified smooth muscle cells of the thermoregulatory glomus body.
explanations.c: A glomus tumor arises from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.d: Schwann cells would be seen in neural tumors like schwannomas, which can be painful but lack the specific vascular glomus architecture.
explanations.e: Fibroblasts are present in many tumors but are not the characteristic cell type of a glomus tumor.

ankiCards: A {{c1::glomus tumor}} is an exquisitely painful tumor found under the fingernails.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells.
The function of the glomus body, from which these tumors arise, is {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Glomus tumors are characterized by pain sensitivity to {{c1::cold}}.
Histologically, glomus cells appear as aggregates of {{c1::uniform, round}} cells around vessels.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but very painful neoplasms.
Classic location is the subungual (under the nail) region of digits.
They arise from specialized glomus bodies (arteriovenous shunts).
Morphology: Monomorphic round cells in nests.
Excision is curative.
microReview: Glomus tumor = Subungual + Cold pain + Modified Smooth Muscle cells.
examinerTraps: The 'blue' color and 'pain' might make one think of a blue nevus or melanoma, but the specific location and cold-sensitivity are diagnostic for Glomus tumor.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated nodule on her gingiva. The lesion bleeds easily with minor trauma. Histological examination shows an exuberant proliferation of capillaries with associated edema and an acute and chronic inflammatory infiltrate, resembling granulation tissue. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are common benign tumors but typically do not grow as rapidly or present as 'granulation tissue' nodules on the gingiva during pregnancy.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated vascular channels and are often deep-seated, not superficial pedunculated gingival lesions.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a common, rapidly growing red nodule on the skin or gingiva (epulis gravidarum in pregnancy) that resembles granulation tissue.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis presents with similar lesions but occurs primarily in immunocompromised patients (e.g., HIV) and is caused by Bartonella.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are small, painful subungual lesions, not rapidly growing gingival masses.

ankiCards: A {{c1::Pyogenic granuloma}} is a rapidly growing vascular lesion often found on the gingiva of pregnant women.
The gingival form of pyogenic granuloma in pregnancy is also called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum / epulis gravidarum}}.
Histologically, a pyogenic granuloma resembles {{c1::granulation tissue}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are neither {{c1::pyogenic (pus-forming)}} nor true {{c2::granulomas}}.
Treatment for pyogenic granuloma involves {{c1::surgical excision/curettage}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is a capillary hemangioma variant.
It manifests as a pedunculated red mass that bleeds easily.
Common on skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
Frequently associated with pregnancy ('pregnancy tumor').
Spontaneous regression can occur post-partum.
microReview: Pyogenic Granuloma = Pregnancy + Gingiva + Granulation tissue-like + Bleeds.
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic granuloma' is a trap; it is actually a vascular proliferation (hemangioma), not a collection of macrophages or an infection.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following syndromes is characterized by permanent vascular dilations (telangiectasias) of the skin and mucous membranes, which can lead to clinical complications such as recurrent epistaxis or gastrointestinal bleeding?

explanations.a: Sturge-Weber syndrome involves port-wine stains in the trigeminal distribution and leptomeningeal angiomas, not systemic mucosal telangiectasias causing bleeding.
explanations.b: Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) is an autosomal dominant disorder causing malformed dilated vessels in the skin, mucous membranes, and internal organs.
explanations.c: Von Hippel-Lindau disease involves hemangioblastomas (CNS/retina) and renal cell carcinoma, not generalized telangiectasias.
explanations.d: Kasabach-Merritt syndrome is a complication of large hemangiomas involving platelet sequestration and thrombocytopenia.
explanations.e: Ataxia-telangiectasia features cerebellar ataxia, immunodeficiency, and telangiectasias, but is primarily a DNA repair defect syndrome.

ankiCards: Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome is also known as {{c1::Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT)}}.
The inheritance pattern of Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome is {{c1::Autosomal Dominant}}.
A common presenting symptom of HHT is recurrent {{c1::epistaxis (nosebleeds)}}.
HHT results from mutations in genes involved in the {{c1::TGF-beta}} signaling pathway.
HHT is characterized by telangiectasias on the skin, {{c1::lips/tongue}}, and GI tract.
keyPoints: Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome is a genetic vascular dysplasia.
Manifests as multiple small aneurysmal telangiectasias.
Sites: Skin, mucous membranes (lips, tongue, nose, GI).
Major risk: Serious bleeding from rupture of these thin-walled vessels.
Associated with mutations in endoglin or ALK-1.
microReview: Osler-Weber-Rendu = AD + Nosebleeds + Telangiectasias on lips/tongue.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the telangiectasias of HHT with 'Spider angiomas' seen in liver cirrhosis.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular tumors are often classified by their degree of differentiation and clinical behavior. Which of the following best describes the morphologic difference between a capillary hemangioma and a cavernous hemangioma?

options.a: Capillary hemangiomas lack an endothelial lining, whereas cavernous ones possess it.
options.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated blood-filled spaces separated by connective tissue stroma.
options.c: Capillary hemangiomas are always malignant, while cavernous ones are always benign.
options.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are more common in infants, while capillary hemangiomas are adult-onset.
options.e: Capillary hemangiomas are deeply infiltrative, whereas cavernous hemangiomas are encapsulated.

explanations.a: Both capillary and cavernous hemangiomas are lined by normal-appearing endothelial cells.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are distinguished by the presence of large, cavernous vascular channels, unlike the small, thin-walled capillaries of a capillary hemangioma.
explanations.c: Both types are benign vascular tumors.
explanations.d: Capillary ('strawberry') hemangiomas are very common in infants, while cavernous hemangiomas can occur at any age but are often found in internal organs in adults.
explanations.e: Both are usually well-circumscribed, though cavernous hemangiomas are frequently deeper and less circumscribed than capillary ones.

ankiCards: A {{c1::cavernous}} hemangioma consists of large, dilated vascular spaces.
A {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma consists of small, tightly packed thin-walled vessels.
Cavernous hemangiomas in the brain are clinical significant because they can cause {{c1::hemorrhage/seizures}}.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas usually {{c1::do not}} spontaneously regress.
Von Hippel-Lindau disease is associated with cavernous hemangiomas in the {{c1::cerebellum/retina/pancreas}}.
keyPoints: Hemangiomas are common benign tumors composed of blood-filled vessels.
Capillary hemangiomas are the most common type (e.g., strawberry hemangioma).
Cavernous hemangiomas involve larger, more irregular channels.
Internal organ cavernous hemangiomas (e.g., liver) are usually asymptomatic.
They are distinguished from malformations by their neoplastic growth.
microReview: Capillary = Small vessels. Cavernous = Large/Dilated vessels. Both are benign.
examinerTraps: Commonly confused: A cavernous hemangioma of the liver is the most common benign liver tumor—don't mistake it for a malignancy on imaging.
sourceQuote: To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure and function.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 74-year-old woman presents with several firm, purple-to-red nodules on her left arm. Ten years ago, she underwent a radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer, followed by radiation therapy. She has had persistent, severe lymphedema of the left arm since the surgery. A biopsy of the skin nodules shows malignant cells forming irregular vascular channels. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 and typically occurs in HIV patients or specific elderly populations, not specifically in the setting of chronic lymphedema post-mastectomy.
explanations.b: Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to the development of angiosarcoma in the setting of chronic lymphedema, most commonly following radical mastectomy.
explanations.c: Metastatic adenocarcinoma would show glandular structures and cytokeratin positivity, not vascular channels and endothelial markers.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation associated with Bartonella in immunocompromised hosts.
explanations.e: Lymphangioma circumscriptum is a benign malformation of lymphatics, not an aggressive malignant tumor with purple nodules.

ankiCards: {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}} is angiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphedema.
The most classic scenario for Stewart-Treves syndrome is post-{{c1::mastectomy}} lymphedema.
Histologically, the tumor in Stewart-Treves syndrome is an {{c1::angiosarcoma}}.
Persistent lymphedema for over {{c1::10}} years is a significant risk factor for angiosarcoma.
Angiosarcomas associated with radiation therapy typically appear within the {{c1::radiation field}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are aggressive with a poor 5-year survival (approx 30%).
Chronic lymphedema is a major predisposing factor for cutaneous angiosarcoma.
Post-mastectomy lymphedema angiosarcoma = Stewart-Treves Syndrome.
The tumor starts as small papules that coalesce into large fleshy masses.
Metastasis occurs early, often to the lungs.
microReview: Post-Mastectomy + Lymphedema + Purple Nodules = Stewart-Treves (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: Examiners may use 'Stewart-Treves' and 'Angiosarcoma' interchangeably; know that Stewart-Treves is the clinical eponym for this specific angiosarcoma context.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An 8-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for a bright red, raised 'strawberry-like' lesion on the scalp. The parents state the lesion appeared shortly after birth and has increased in size. Which of the following is the most likely natural history for this lesion?

options.c: Lifelong persistence without change in size
options.d: Systemic spread to the liver and spleen
options.e: Necessity of immediate radical surgical excision

explanations.a: Capillary (strawberry) hemangiomas are entirely benign and do not undergo malignant transformation.
explanations.b: Most juvenile (strawberry) capillary hemangiomas grow rapidly for a few months but then begin to regress, with the majority disappearing by age 7 to 9.
explanations.c: They typically do not persist throughout life; they undergo involution.
explanations.d: Capillary hemangiomas are localized benign tumors, not systemic malignancies.
explanations.e: Surgical excision is usually avoided unless the lesion interferes with vital functions (e.g., vision) because of the high rate of spontaneous regression.

ankiCards: The 'strawberry hemangioma' of infancy is histologically a {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma.
The typical natural history of a juvenile hemangioma involves {{c1::involution/regression}}.
Juvenile hemangiomas are usually present at birth or appear within the first {{c1::weeks}} of life.
By age 7, approximately {{c1::75-90%}} of juvenile hemangiomas have regressed.
Histologically, these lesions show {{c1::closely packed}} capillaries with scant stroma.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangiomas are extremely common in newborns (1 in 200).
They are also known as 'strawberry hemangiomas'.
Growth phase is followed by a slow involution phase.
They are benign and usually require only observation.
Complete regression usually leaves normal or slightly scarred skin.
microReview: Strawberry Hemangioma = Infant + Rapid growth + Spontaneous regression.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'strawberry hemangioma' (regresses) with 'port-wine stain' (grows with the child and does not regress).
sourceQuote: Arterial wall thickness gradually diminishes as the vessels become smaller, but the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing these muscular vessels to exert control over blood flow and pressure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation that can clinically mimic Kaposi sarcoma. It is specifically caused by opportunistic infections in immunocompromised individuals. What is the characteristic histological finding that distinguishes bacillary angiomatosis from Kaposi sarcoma?

options.a: Presence of spindle-shaped cells with slit-like spaces
options.b: Proliferation of capillaries with prominent neutrophilic infiltrates
options.c: Widespread necrosis and glassy hyaline globules
options.d: Lack of any endothelial cell markers (CD31 negative)
options.e: Large, dilated cavernous spaces filled with lymph

explanations.a: Spindle cells and slit-like spaces are the classic features of Kaposi sarcoma, not bacillary angiomatosis.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is characterized by a proliferation of capillaries with reactive endothelial cells and a prominent infiltrate of neutrophils and nuclear dust.
explanations.c: While necrosis can occur, it is the neutrophilic infiltrate and bacterial clusters (visible on silver stains) that are diagnostic.
explanations.d: Both are vascular tumors and should be CD31 positive.
explanations.e: Cavernous spaces filled with lymph describe a lymphangioma, not bacillary angiomatosis.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by bacteria of the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
The two main species causing bacillary angiomatosis are {{c1::B. henselae}} and {{c2::B. quintana}}.
Unlike Kaposi Sarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis contains a prominent infiltrate of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
To visualize the organisms in bacillary angiomatosis, the {{c1::Warthin-Starry (silver)}} stain is used.
The primary treatment for bacillary angiomatosis is {{c1::erythromycin / doxycycline / antibiotics}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious mimics of vascular neoplasms.
Caused by Bartonella (henselae from cats, quintana from lice).
Occurs in immunocompromised patients (AIDS).
Features: Proliferating capillaries, neutrophils, and bacterial clumps.
Responds well to antibiotic therapy.
microReview: Bacillary Angiomatosis = Bartonella + Neutrophils + Silver stain + AIDS.
examinerTraps: A common trap is to provide a vignette of an AIDS patient with skin lesions and ask for the treatment—ensure you distinguish KS (chemo/ART) from Bacillary Angiomatosis (antibiotics).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following descriptions best characterizes a 'nevus flammeus' (port-wine stain) when it occurs as part of the Sturge-Weber syndrome?

options.a: A benign neoplasm of capillaries that regresses by age 10.
options.b: A malignant vascular tumor that commonly metastasizes to the brain.
options.c: A congenital vascular ectasia that grows proportionately with the child.
options.d: A painful vascular lesion arising from modified smooth muscle cells.
options.e: A hyperplastic response to chronic infection with Bartonella.

explanations.a: This describes a juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma, which regresses. Nevus flammeus does not regress.
explanations.b: Nevus flammeus is a benign ectasia (dilation of existing vessels), not a malignancy.
explanations.c: Nevus flammeus is a form of vascular ectasia (a 'birthmark') that is present at birth and grows as the child grows, without regressing.
explanations.d: This describes a glomus tumor.
explanations.e: This describes bacillary angiomatosis.

ankiCards: A 'port-wine stain' is the clinical term for a {{c1::nevus flammeus}}.
Sturge-Weber syndrome involves a port-wine stain in the distribution of the {{c1::trigeminal (CN V)}} nerve.
Sturge-Weber syndrome is associated with vascular malformations in the {{c1::leptomeninges (ipsilateral)}}.
Unlike strawberry hemangiomas, port-wine stains {{c1::do not}} regress over time.
Complications of Sturge-Weber syndrome include seizures and {{c1::intellectual disability / glaucoma}}.
keyPoints: Nevus flammeus is a flat, congenital vascular ectasia.
Port-wine stains (large nevus flammeus) tend to thicken and darken over time.
Sturge-Weber Syndrome: Port-wine stain + venous malformations in brain/eye.
Sturge-Weber is associated with a somatic mutation in the GNAQ gene.
The 'stain' follows the ophthalmic or maxillary divisions of the trigeminal nerve.
microReview: Sturge-Weber = Port-wine stain (CN V) + Glaucoma + Epilepsy + Leptomeningeal angioma.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'Nevus flammeus' (Port-wine stain, permanent) with 'Nevus simplex' (Salmon patch, usually fades).
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels... For example, arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 64-year-old woman presents with several firm, violaceous nodules on her left upper arm. She has a history of radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection for breast adenocarcinoma ten years ago, which was followed by chronic, persistent lymphedema of the ipsilateral limb. A skin biopsy of a nodule shows malignant spindle cells forming irregular, anastomosing vascular channels. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor associated with HHV-8, typically presenting in immunosuppressed patients or as classic Mediterranean type, not specifically linked to post-surgical lymphedema.
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma can occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome), typically appearing years after radical mastectomy and lymph node dissection.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign vascular proliferation caused by Bartonella infection in immunocompromised hosts, characterized by neutrophils and bacteria on histology.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangioma is a benign vascular lesion composed of large, dilated blood-filled spaces; it does not present as malignant spindle cells or irregular channels.
explanations.e: Glomus tumor is a benign, painful tumor arising from specialized glomus bodies, typically found subungually (under the fingernails).

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma occurring in the setting of chronic lymphedema (e.g. post-mastectomy) is known as {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
The malignant vascular tumor characterized by irregular, anastomosing channels lined by atypical endothelial cells is {{c1::angiosarcoma}}.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is classically associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}, arsenic, or Thorotrast.
The immunohistochemical marker most specific for endothelial differentiation in vascular tumors is {{c1::CD31 (or von Willebrand factor)}}.
In contrast to hemangiomas, angiosarcomas exhibit significant {{c1::cytologic atypia and mitotic activity}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor of endothelial cells.
Stewart-Treves syndrome refers specifically to angiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphedema.
Common risk factors include radiation therapy and chemical toxins like vinyl chloride.
Histologically, they show irregular vascular spaces with pleomorphic cells.
Staining for CD31 or vWF confirms the endothelial origin.
Metastasis occurs early, typically via hematogenous spread.
microReview: Vascular tumors range from benign (hemangiomas) to intermediate (Kaposi sarcoma) to highly malignant (Angiosarcoma). Stewart-Treves syndrome is a high-yield clinical association involving post-mastectomy lymphedema leading to angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Stewart-Treves syndrome with Kaposi sarcoma; the former is associated with chronic lymphedema and is highly malignant, while the latter is HHV-8 driven and categorized as intermediate-grade.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors... Malignant Tumors... Angiosarcoma is a malignant vascular tumor that most commonly occurs in the skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: A 32-year-old male presents with an extremely painful, 4-mm, blue-red nodule located under the nail bed of his right index finger. The pain is triggered by cold exposure and pressure. Which of the following cells is the most likely origin of this lesion?

explanations.a: Pericytes are found in hemangiopericytomas, which are distinct from the painful subungual glomus tumors.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.c: Fibroblasts are the origin of fibromas or fibrosarcomas, which do not typically present as painful subungual vascular nodules.
explanations.d: Capillary endothelial cells form hemangiomas, which are usually not exquisitely painful or cold-sensitive.
explanations.e: Lymphatic endothelial cells form lymphangiomas, which are typically painless and not subungual.

ankiCards: A painful subungual vascular tumor is most likely a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle cells}} of the glomus body.
The classic triad of symptoms for a glomus tumor includes {{c1::paroxysmal pain}}, sensitivity to cold, and localized tenderness.
Glomus bodies are specialized {{c1::arteriovenous anastomoses}} involved in thermoregulation.
On histology, glomus tumors show nests of uniform, round cells surrounding {{c1::vascular channels}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but extremely painful.
Most common site is the subungual region (fingernails).
Origin is the glomus body (thermoregulation organ).
Cells are specialized smooth muscle, not endothelial cells.
Excision is curative.
microReview: Small, blue, exquisitely painful subungual lesion = Glomus tumor (modified smooth muscle cells).
examinerTraps: The examiner may use 'subungual' to hint at glomus tumor, but beware of 'subungual melanoma,' which is usually pigmented and not primarily characterized by paroxysmal pain.
sourceQuote: Glomus tumors... arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus bodies, specialized arteriovenous structures involved in thermoregulation.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: Which of the following describes the most likely pathogenesis of the violaceous skin lesions frequently seen in patients with advanced HIV/AIDS, characterized histologically by spindle cells and slit-like vascular spaces?

options.a: Mutation in the VHL tumor suppressor gene
options.b: Infection of endothelial cells by HHV-8
options.e: Proliferation of endothelial cells due to Bartonella henselae

explanations.a: VHL mutations are associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease, which presents with hemangioblastomas, not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8/KSHV), which induces endothelial proliferation, spindle cell morphology, and an inflammatory milieu.
explanations.c: BRAF mutations are common in melanomas, not primary vascular tumors like Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.d: GNAQ mutations are associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome and uveal melanoma.
explanations.e: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can look similar to Kaposi sarcoma clinically but is bacterial in origin and histologically distinct (neutrophils present).

ankiCards: The causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}.
The characteristic histological feature of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells}} forming slit-like spaces containing RBCs.
The four clinical types of Kaposi Sarcoma are Classic, Endemic (African), {{c1::Iatrogenic}} (transplant), and AIDS-associated.
{{c1::HHV-8}} is also known as Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus (KSHV).
Kaposi Sarcoma lesions often contain inflammatory cells and extravasated {{c1::erythrocytes}}.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma is an intermediate-grade vascular neoplasm.
HHV-8 (KSHV) is the essential etiologic factor.
