Berry aneurysms are often associated with a congenital {{c1::deficiency in the media (elastic tissue)}}.
keyPoints: Berry aneurysms are true saccular aneurysms.
They occur at vessel bifurcations.
Clinical presentation: 'Worst headache of my life' (subarachnoid hemorrhage).
Associated with Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD).
They are not present at birth but develop over time due to wall stress.
microReview: Berry Aneurysm = Circle of Willis = Branching Points = Subarachnoid Hemorrhage.
examinerTraps: ADPKD patients are classically screened for Berry aneurysms because they are a major cause of death in these patients.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... (p. 485)
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following explains why Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms (AAAs) typically occur in the infrarenal segment of the aorta?

options.a: Presence of more vasa vasorum in the abdominal media
options.b: Relatively sparse vasa vasorum in the abdominal aortic wall
options.c: Higher concentrations of elastic fibers in the distal aorta
options.d: Reduced blood pressure in the infrarenal segment
options.e: Increased thickness of the media in the abdominal segment

explanations.a: The abdominal aorta actually has fewer vasa vasorum, making the media more dependent on luminal diffusion.
explanations.b: The infrarenal aorta lacks vasa vasorum in its media; nutrient diffusion from the lumen is hindered by atherosclerosis, causing medial ischemia and weakening.
explanations.c: The distal aorta has fewer elastic fibers compared to the thoracic aorta.
explanations.d: Blood pressure is not significantly reduced in the infrarenal segment; wall stress remains high.
explanations.e: The media is thinner, not thicker, in the abdominal aorta compared to the thoracic segment.

ankiCards: The media of the infrarenal aorta is more vulnerable to weakening because it lacks {{c1::vasa vasorum}}.
Nutrients for the abdominal aortic media must arrive via {{c1::diffusion}} from the lumen.
{{c1::Atherosclerosis}} acts as a physical barrier to diffusion, starving the media of oxygen.
The abdominal aorta has less {{c1::elastic}} tissue than the thoracic aorta.
Aneurysms occur when medial degradation exceeds the wall's ability to {{c1::repair/resist stress}}.
keyPoints: The thoracic aorta is well-vascularized by vasa vasorum.
The abdominal aorta media is relatively avascular.
Atherosclerotic plaques thicken the intima and block diffusion to the media.
Medial ischemia leads to smooth muscle cell death and fibrosis.
This metabolic 'starvation' explains the predilection of AAA for the infrarenal site.
microReview: No Vasa Vasorum + Plaque Blocking Diffusion = Starved Media = AAA.
examinerTraps: Atherosclerosis causes AAAs not just by 'pressure' but by starving the media through diffusion blockage.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions. Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular pathology is categorized into two principal mechanisms of disease. Which of the following processes best describes the pathogenesis resulting in the formation of an aneurysm?

options.a: Narrowing of the vessel lumen via progressive intimal thickening
options.b: Precipitous obstruction of the vessel lumen via thromboembolism
options.c: Weakening of the vessel wall leading to dilation or rupture
options.d: Increased ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter
options.e: Stenosis caused by chronic hypertensive hyaline change

explanations.a: Intimal thickening and narrowing are characteristics of atherosclerosis and stenosis, not the primary mechanism of aneurysm formation.
explanations.b: Thromboembolism causes acute occlusion and ischemia rather than dilation or aneurysm formation.
explanations.c: Weakening of the vessel wall is one of the two primary mechanisms of vascular disease and is the direct cause of aneurysms and dissections.
explanations.d: An increased ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter is a normal structural feature of smaller muscular arteries to control blood pressure, not a pathological mechanism of aneurysm.
explanations.e: Hyaline change in hypertension leads to vessel narrowing (arteriolosclerosis), not dilation.

ankiCards: The two principal mechanisms of vascular disease are narrowing/obstruction and {{c1::weakening}} of vessel walls.
Weakening of vessel walls typically leads to {{c1::dilation}} or rupture.
Aneurysms are specifically characterized by the {{c1::dilation}} of a blood vessel.
Stenosis and obstruction are often caused by {{c1::atherosclerosis}} or thrombosis.
Arterial walls are thicker than veins to accommodate {{c1::pulsatile}} flow and higher pressures.
keyPoints: Vascular disease primarily occurs via two mechanisms: luminal narrowing/obstruction or wall weakening.
Aneurysms represent the clinical manifestation of vessel wall weakening.
Vessel wall weakening results in permanent dilation (aneurysm) or catastrophic rupture.
Atherosclerosis can contribute to both mechanisms: narrowing via plaque and weakening via medial ischemia.
The architectural response of vessels is often tailored to the local hemodynamic environment (pressure/flow).
microReview: Aneurysms involve all layers of the vessel (true aneurysm) or a breach in the wall with a hematoma (false aneurysm), stemming from structural failure of the tunica media.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse the mechanism of formation (wall weakening) with the secondary complications (luminal narrowing due to mural thrombus within the aneurysm).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male presents for a routine physical examination. He has a 40 pack-year smoking history and long-standing hypertension. Palpation of the abdomen reveals a pulsatile mass midway between the xiphoid process and the umbilicus. Imaging confirms a 5.5 cm dilation of the abdominal aorta. What is the most likely primary driving mechanism in the development of this condition?

options.b: Degradation of extracellular matrix by metalloproteinases
options.c: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.d: Congenital defect in the internal elastic lamina

explanations.a: Cystic medial degeneration is the classic cause of Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms, often seen in Marfan syndrome, rather than Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms (AAA).
explanations.b: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms are primarily driven by atherosclerosis and inflammation, where matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) from macrophages degrade the elastin and collagen in the media.
explanations.c: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum is the mechanism behind syphilitic (tertiary syphilis) aneurysms, which usually occur in the thoracic aorta.
explanations.d: Defects in the internal elastic lamina are associated with Berry aneurysms in the Circle of Willis, not AAA.
explanations.e: Vasculitis (like Polyarteritis Nodosa) can cause aneurysms in medium-sized arteries, but it is not the primary cause of atherosclerotic AAA.

ankiCards: The most common cause of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA) is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
The enzymes responsible for degrading the aortic wall in AAA are {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
AAA is typically located between the {{c1::renal}} arteries and the iliac bifurcation.
A major modifiable risk factor for AAA development is {{c1::smoking}}.
AAA characteristically presents as a {{c1::pulsatile}} abdominal mass.
keyPoints: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms (AAA) are most frequently associated with atherosclerosis.
Pathogenesis involves chronic inflammation in the media and adventitia.
Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) produced by inflammatory cells degrade structural proteins (elastin/collagen).
Smoking is the strongest environmental risk factor for AAA.
Most AAAs occur below the renal arteries and above the iliac bifurcation.
microReview: AAA = Atherosclerosis + Smoking + MMPs; TAA = Hypertension + Cystic Medial Degeneration.
examinerTraps: Atherosclerosis causes AAA not just by plaque formation, but by preventing nutrient diffusion to the media, leading to secondary medial thinning and weakening.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which structural feature of the arterial wall allows these vessels to accommodate higher pressures and pulsatile flow compared to veins at the same level of branching?

options.a: Presence of valves within the tunica intima
options.b: Higher ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter
options.c: Increased density of vasa vasorum in the media
options.e: Dominance of skeletal muscle in the tunica media

explanations.a: Valves are present in veins to prevent retrograde flow, not in arteries to accommodate high pressure.
explanations.b: Arterial walls are thicker relative to their lumen size compared to veins; this allows them to withstand and control high blood pressure and pulsatile flow.
explanations.c: While large arteries have vasa vasorum in the adventitia/outer media, it is not the feature that accommodates pulsatile flow.
explanations.d: The internal elastic lamina is usually prominent and continuous in arteries to provide recoil; it is not typically discontinuous in healthy arteries.
explanations.e: The tunica media of arteries consists of smooth muscle cells, not skeletal muscle.

ankiCards: Arterial walls are {{c1::thicker}} than veins at the same level of branching.
The {{c1::ratio}} of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases as arteries become smaller.
Arteries have thicker walls to accommodate {{c1::pulsatile}} flow.
Specific kinds of vessels have structural specializations that reflect distinct {{c1::functional}} roles.
Atherosclerosis mainly affects {{c1::elastic}} and muscular arteries.
keyPoints: Arteries have thicker walls than veins to handle higher systemic pressures.
The thickness-to-lumen ratio allows muscular arteries to regulate blood flow and pressure.
Structure reflects function: elastic arteries accommodate surge, muscular arteries distribute flow.
Vascular pathology is often vessel-type specific (e.g., atherosclerosis in elastic arteries).
Vascular architecture is generally comparable across the system but specialized at specific levels.
microReview: High pressure = Thick wall/Small lumen (Artery); Low pressure = Thin wall/Large lumen (Vein).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse arterial thickness with pathological hypertrophy; the thickness is a normal physiological adaptation to high pressure.
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old male presents with sudden-onset, severe chest pain that radiates to his back. He is 195 cm tall (6'5"), has exceptionally long fingers (arachnodactyly), and high-arched palate. Physical examination reveals a diastolic murmur at the right sternal border. If his condition is left untreated, what is the most likely histologic finding in his aortic media?

options.e: Fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel wall

explanations.a: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is a result of chronic hypertension and diabetes, affecting small arterioles, not the aortic media.
explanations.b: The patient has Marfan syndrome (tall stature, long fingers, aortic dissection). The underlying pathology is cystic medial degeneration, characterized by the loss of smooth muscle cells and fragmentation of elastic fibers with the accumulation of proteoglycan-rich extracellular matrix.
explanations.c: Transmural granulomatous inflammation is seen in Giant Cell Arteritis or Takayasu Arteritis, not Marfan syndrome.
explanations.d: Mönckeberg sclerosis involves calcification of the media in muscular arteries and is usually clinically insignificant.
explanations.e: Fibrinoid necrosis is typical of malignant hypertension or certain vasculitides (like Polyarteritis Nodosa).

ankiCards: The underlying histological change in Marfan-associated aneurysms is {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
Marfan syndrome is caused by mutations in the {{c1::FBN1 (Fibrillin-1)}} gene.
Cystic medial degeneration involves the accumulation of {{c1::proteoglycans}} in the media.
Cystic medial degeneration leads to the fragmentation of {{c1::elastic}} fibers.
The diastolic murmur in a Marfan patient suggests {{c1::aortic root}} dilation and regurgitation.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome is a major cause of thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections in young patients.
The defect is in fibrillin-1, leading to abnormal TGF-beta signaling and weakened elastic tissue.
Histology shows 'cystic medial degeneration' (also called cystic medial necrosis).
This is characterized by loss of elastic tissue and creation of 'cysts' filled with mucoid material.
Weakening of the aortic media predisposes to both aneurysm and dissection.
microReview: Marfan = Fibrillin-1 mutation -> TGF-beta signaling defect -> Cystic Medial Degeneration -> Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm/Dissection.
examinerTraps: The term 'cystic medial necrosis' is common but inaccurate because there is no actual necrosis involved; 'degeneration' is the preferred term.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following descriptions best defines a 'False Aneurysm' (pseudoaneurysm)?

options.a: A localized permanent dilation of all three layers of the arterial wall
options.b: Dilation of only the tunica intima and media through a defect in the adventitia
options.c: A collection of blood that communicates with the intravascular space through a hole in the vessel wall
options.d: Longitudinal cleavage of the aortic media by a column of high-pressure blood
options.e: Outpouching of the vessel wall caused by a congenital thinning of the muscularis

explanations.a: This is the definition of a True Aneurysm.
explanations.b: Aneurysms do not typically involve the intima/media protruding through the adventitia.
explanations.c: A false aneurysm is a pulsating hematoma that communicates with the vessel lumen through a defect in the wall, with the outer 'wall' being extravascular connective tissue, not the original vessel layers.
explanations.d: This describes an Aortic Dissection.
explanations.e: This refers to a Berry Aneurysm (a type of true aneurysm).

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the vessel wall (intima, media, adventitia).
A {{c1::false}} aneurysm is a hematoma that communicates with the intravascular space.
A {{c1::dissection}} occurs when blood enters the wall of the artery as a hematoma dissecting between its layers.
False aneurysms are often caused by {{c1::trauma}} or iatrogenic injury (e.g., catheterization).
The outer boundary of a false aneurysm consists of {{c1::extravascular}} connective tissue.
keyPoints: Aneurysms are classified as true or false based on the layers involved.
True aneurysms (e.g., atherosclerotic, syphilitic, congenital) involve the intact attenuated vessel wall.
False aneurysms (pseudoaneurysms) involve a breach in the wall with a contained hematoma.
Aortic dissection is distinct from an aneurysm, though they often coexist.
False aneurysms carry a high risk of rupture because they lack the structural support of the vessel wall.
microReview: True = All 3 layers intact; False = Breach + Hematoma; Dissection = Blood between layers.
examinerTraps: Examiners often use the term 'pseudoaneurysm' interchangeably with 'false aneurysm'. Both signify the absence of all three vascular layers in the wall of the dilation.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 52-year-old female presents with a severe headache. A CT scan of the head shows subarachnoid hemorrhage. Further history reveals she has Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD). What is the most likely location of the aneurysm that ruptured?

options.a: Abdominal aorta below the renal arteries
options.c: Anterior communicating artery of the Circle of Willis

explanations.a: Atherosclerotic AAAs occur here, but they do not cause subarachnoid hemorrhage.
explanations.b: Ascending aortic aneurysms are associated with hypertension or Marfan syndrome, not typically with ADPKD and subarachnoid hemorrhage.
explanations.c: Patients with ADPKD have a high incidence of Berry (saccular) aneurysms in the Circle of Willis, particularly at the anterior communicating artery. Rupture leads to subarachnoid hemorrhage.
explanations.d: Descending aortic aneurysms are related to atherosclerosis and hypertension.
explanations.e: Iliac aneurysms are usually extensions of AAAs.

ankiCards: Berry aneurysms are commonly located in the {{c1::Circle of Willis}}.
A common genetic condition associated with Berry aneurysms is {{c1::ADPKD}}.
Rupture of a Berry aneurysm causes {{c1::subarachnoid}} hemorrhage.
The most frequent specific site for a Berry aneurysm is the {{c1::anterior}} communicating artery.
Berry aneurysms are considered {{c1::true}} aneurysms because they involve the vessel wall (though media is thin).
keyPoints: Berry aneurysms are small, saccular dilations in the cerebral circulation.
They occur at branch points where the arterial media is congenitally weak.
ADPKD and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome are significant risk factors.
Rupture presents as a 'sudden, worst headache of life' (Subarachnoid Hemorrhage).
They are not related to atherosclerosis.
microReview: ADPKD + Headache = Ruptured Berry Aneurysm in Circle of Willis.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the association: ADPKD is associated with Berry aneurysms, NOT with Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which vascular layer is primarily affected and thinned out in the pathogenesis of an atherosclerotic Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm?

explanations.a: The intima is thickened in atherosclerosis (plaque formation), not thinned.
explanations.b: In AAA, the tunica media undergoes significant thinning and destruction of elastic fibers, which leads to the weakening and subsequent dilation of the vessel.
explanations.c: The adventitia usually shows inflammatory changes but is not the layer whose destruction primarily causes the dilation.
explanations.d: The internal elastic lamina is part of the intima/media junction but its destruction is secondary to the overall medial degeneration.
explanations.e: The vasa vasorum are the small vessels supplying the outer wall; their compromise may lead to medial ischemia, but they are not the thinned layer.

ankiCards: In AAA, the tunica {{c1::media}} undergoes significant thinning.
Atherosclerosis causes medial weakening by restricting {{c1::nutrient}} diffusion from the lumen.
Thinning of the media in AAA is accompanied by the loss of {{c1::smooth muscle}} cells.
Destruction of the media allows the aorta to {{c1::dilate}} under systemic pressure.
Most atherosclerotic aneurysms are located in the {{c1::abdominal}} aorta.
keyPoints: The tunica media provides the structural integrity of the arterial wall.
Atherosclerotic plaques in the intima increase the diffusion distance for oxygen and nutrients.
Medial ischemia leads to smooth muscle cell death and elastic fiber loss.
Chronic inflammation further degrades the media via proteases.
The resulting thinned media is unable to resist blood pressure, leading to aneurysm.
microReview: Atherosclerosis -> Intimal plaque -> Medial ischemia/inflammation -> Medial thinning -> AAA.
examinerTraps: While the *initial* pathology of atherosclerosis is in the intima, the *aneurysm* forms because of what happens to the media.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 75-year-old male with a history of untreated syphilis presents with a barking cough and difficulty swallowing. Imaging shows a massive dilation of the ascending aorta. The wall of the aorta appears 'tree-barked' on gross inspection. Which of the following is the hallmark microscopic finding of this condition?

options.b: Endarteritis obliterans of the vasa vasorum
options.d: Intimal tears with false lumen formation
options.e: Lipid-laden macrophage accumulation in the intima

explanations.a: This describes Mönckeberg sclerosis, which is unrelated to syphilis.
explanations.b: Tertiary syphilis causes obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum in the aorta. This results in ischemia of the tunica media, leading to weakening and the 'tree-bark' appearance of the ascending aorta (Syphilitic Aneurysm).
explanations.c: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in vasculitis and malignant hypertension.
explanations.d: This describes an aortic dissection.
explanations.e: This describes an early atherosclerotic lesion (fatty streak).

ankiCards: Syphilitic aneurysms typically involve the {{c1::ascending}} aorta.
The 'tree-bark' appearance in syphilis is due to {{c1::ischemic}} scarring of the media.
Syphilis affects the aorta by causing {{c1::endarteritis obliterans}} of the vasa vasorum.
Ischemia from syphilis causes the destruction of {{c1::elastic}} fibers in the media.
Symptoms of syphilitic aneurysms often arise from {{c1::compression}} of mediastinal structures.
keyPoints: Tertiary syphilis (cardiovascular syphilis) targets the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta.
Endarteritis obliterans leads to medial ischemia and scarring.
Loss of elastic support causes the vessel to dilate (aneurysm).
Grossly, the intima has a wrinkled, 'tree-bark' appearance due to underlying medial scars.
These aneurysms can cause aortic valve insufficiency by dilating the aortic ring.
microReview: Syphilis -> Vasa vasorum endarteritis -> Medial ischemia -> Ascending Aortic Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Syphilitic aneurysms are almost always in the *ascending* aorta, whereas atherosclerotic aneurysms are almost always in the *abdominal* aorta.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the development of a 'Mycotic Aneurysm', what is the underlying cause of the vessel wall weakening?

options.a: Autoimmune destruction of type IV collagen
options.b: Infection of the vessel wall by a circulating pathogen
options.c: Congenital absence of the tunica adventitia
options.d: Chronic pressure overload from systemic hypertension
options.e: Ischemic necrosis due to intimal plaque

explanations.a: Autoimmune collagen destruction is not the primary cause of mycotic aneurysms.
explanations.b: A mycotic aneurysm is an aneurysm resulting from an infection (usually bacterial, despite the name 'mycotic') that weakens the vessel wall through suppuration and inflammation.
explanations.c: Congenital absence of adventitia is not a recognized pathology for this condition.
explanations.d: Hypertension causes TAA/dissection, not specifically mycotic aneurysms.
explanations.e: This describes the mechanism of atherosclerotic AAA.

ankiCards: A {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm is caused by infection of the vessel wall.
Mycotic aneurysms can result from seeding by {{c1::bacteremia}} (e.g., from endocarditis).
Despite the name, most mycotic aneurysms are {{c1::bacterial}} in origin.
Infection leads to wall weakening through {{c1::suppurative}} inflammation.
A mycotic aneurysm is a form of {{c1::infectious}} vasculitis.
keyPoints: Mycotic aneurysms result from infection of the arterial wall.
Common origins include embolization from infective endocarditis or direct extension from an adjacent abscess.
Inflammation and bacterial enzymes destroy the media and structural proteins.
They are highly prone to rapid expansion and rupture.
They can occur in any artery, but are often found in the cerebral or visceral circulation.
microReview: Mycotic Aneurysm = Infected Aneurysm (Bacterial > Fungal).
examinerTraps: The term 'mycotic' was coined by William Osler to describe the mushroom-like appearance, but it usually refers to bacterial infections, not fungi.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old female presents with sudden, excruciating pain in her chest that she describes as 'tearing' and 'moving downward'. She has a history of poorly controlled hypertension. Her blood pressure is 210/115 mmHg. Chest X-ray reveals a widened mediastinum. What is the most likely pathological event occurring in her aorta?

options.a: Rupture of an abdominal aortic aneurysm
options.b: Dilation of all layers of the ascending aorta
options.c: Blood tracking through a medial tear in the aortic wall
options.d: Infection of the aorta by Staphylococcus aureus
options.e: Acute calcification of the aortic valve

explanations.a: AAA presents with abdominal or back pain, not tearing chest pain.
explanations.b: This describes an aneurysm; while related, it is the 'tearing' pain and 'moving' nature that specifically signal a dissection.
explanations.c: Aortic dissection occurs when blood enters a tear in the intima and tracks (dissects) through the media, creating a false lumen. This typically presents with tearing chest pain radiating to the back.
explanations.d: This would describe a mycotic aneurysm, which presents with fever and sepsis, not sudden tearing pain.
explanations.e: Aortic stenosis causes a murmur and syncope, not tearing chest pain.

ankiCards: Aortic dissection is most commonly associated with {{c1::hypertension}}.
The classic symptom of aortic dissection is {{c1::tearing}} chest pain.
In a dissection, blood tracks through the {{c1::media}} of the vessel.
A widened {{c1::mediastinum}} on X-ray is a classic finding in aortic dissection.
Stanford Type {{c1::A}} dissections involve the ascending aorta and are surgical emergencies.
keyPoints: Aortic dissection is distinct from an aneurysm but also results from wall weakening.
Hypertension is the single most important risk factor for non-genetic cases.
The process begins with an intimal tear.
Blood creates a false lumen within the media, which can rupture back into the true lumen or out of the aorta.
Major complications include tamponade, aortic insufficiency, and organ ischemia.
microReview: Hypertension + Tearing pain + Widened mediastinum = Aortic Dissection.
examinerTraps: Aneurysm and Dissection are different: Aneurysm is a dilation of all layers; Dissection is blood splitting the media.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 34-year-old male with a history of advanced HIV infection (CD4+ count 120 cells/uL) presents with several non-tender, purple-to-red macules and plaques on his lower extremities and oral mucosa. A biopsy of a skin lesion reveals spindle-shaped cells forming slit-like spaces containing extravasated red blood cells. Which of the following pathogens is the most likely causative agent of these lesions?

explanations.a: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not vascular tumors like Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.b: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the definitive causative agent of all forms of Kaposi sarcoma, including the AIDS-associated variant described.
explanations.c: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) can cause retinitis or colitis in AIDS patients but does not drive the proliferation of endothelial spindle cells.
explanations.d: Human papillomavirus 16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx, not vascular malignancies.
explanations.e: Hepatitis B virus is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma and polyarteritis nodosa, not the spindle cell vascular proliferation of Kaposi sarcoma.

ankiCards: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by infection with {{c1::Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}.
The characteristic histological finding in Kaposi sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells}} forming {{c2::slit-like vascular spaces}}.
The four clinical forms of Kaposi sarcoma are {{c1::Classic (European)}}, {{c2::Endemic (African)}}, {{c3::Transplant-associated}}, and {{c4::AIDS-associated}}.
HHV-8 belongs to the {{c1::gamma-herpesvirus}} subfamily.
Extravasation of {{c1::red blood cells}} and the presence of {{c2::hemosiderin-laden macrophages}} are common in Kaposi sarcoma lesions.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8.
It manifests as purple/red skin macules, plaques, or nodules.
Histology shows spindle cells and slit-like vascular channels.
AIDS-associated Kaposi sarcoma is the most aggressive form in the US.
HHV-8 also causes primary effusion lymphoma.
Lesions can involve the skin, mucous membranes, and viscera.
microReview: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor. In the setting of HIV/AIDS, it is an AIDS-defining illness. The underlying mechanism involves HHV-8 infection of endothelial cells, leading to uncontrolled proliferation. Biopsy is diagnostic, showing the classic 'spindle cells' and 'slit-like spaces'.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Kaposi sarcoma with Bacillary angiomatosis. While both present as red-purple skin lesions in HIV patients, Bacillary angiomatosis (Bartonella) shows a neutrophilic infiltrate, while KS shows spindle cells and minimal inflammation.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old female presents with multiple rapidly enlarging, dark-blue nodules on her right arm. She has a history of a radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection 12 years ago for breast cancer, which was followed by chronic, massive lymphedema of the same arm. A biopsy of one nodule confirms a high-grade malignant tumor of endothelial origin. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Hemangiomas are benign vascular tumors and do not arise typically in the setting of chronic lymphedema.
explanations.b: Lymphangiomas are benign malformations of lymphatic vessels, usually seen in children, not aggressive nodules in adults.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy) is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome. It is a highly aggressive malignant vascular tumor.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are small, exquisitely painful benign tumors typically found under the fingernails.
explanations.e: While Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular tumor, it is associated with HHV-8 and not specifically with chronic post-surgical lymphedema.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
The cell of origin for angiosarcoma is the {{c1::endothelial cell}}.
Angiosarcomas are most commonly found in the {{c1::skin}}, {{c2::breast}}, and {{c3::liver}}.
Environmental toxins associated with hepatic angiosarcoma include {{c1::vinyl chloride}}, {{c2::arsenic}}, and {{c3::Thorotrast}}.
Immunohistochemical markers for angiosarcoma include {{c1::CD31}} and {{c2::vWF (Factor VIII)}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms.
Stewart-Treves syndrome occurs after long-standing lymphedema.
Radiation therapy for breast cancer is also a risk factor for cutaneous angiosarcoma.
These tumors are highly aggressive with poor 5-year survival rates.
They can range from well-differentiated vascular channels to poorly differentiated sheets of pleomorphic cells.
microReview: Angiosarcoma is a rare but lethal malignancy. Look for a history of radiation (years prior) or chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves). CD31 is the classic marker. Liver involvement is classically linked to specific industrial exposures.
examinerTraps: A common trap is to confuse the 'red/blue nodules' with benign hemangiomas. Rapid growth and a background of lymphedema/radiation must trigger suspicion of angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 29-year-old female presents with a 4mm, exquisitely painful, red-blue nodule located under the nail bed of her left index finger. She notes that the pain is sharp and intensely aggravated by exposure to cold. From which of the following cell types does this neoplasm most likely originate?

explanations.a: Fibroblasts are not the cell of origin for glomus tumors.
explanations.b: While the tumor contains vascular channels, the neoplastic cells themselves are not endothelial.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) arise from the glomus body, which is composed of modified smooth muscle cells involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.d: Schwann cells give rise to neuromas or schwannomas, which can be painful but do not typically present as subungual cold-sensitive nodules.
explanations.e: Pericytes are the origin of hemangiopericytomas, which are distinct from glomus tumors.

ankiCards: Glomus tumors are most commonly located in the {{c1::subungual (under the nail)}} region.
The classic clinical triad for a glomus tumor includes {{c1::paroxysmal pain}}, {{c2::localized tenderness}}, and {{c3::cold hypersensitivity}}.
Glomus tumors originate from the {{c1::glomus body (modified smooth muscle cells)}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors show nests of {{c1::uniform round cells}} surrounding vascular channels.
Glomus tumors are {{c1::benign}} (benign/malignant).
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign and extremely painful.
They are specialized neuromyoarterial receptors.
They help regulate temperature by shunting blood.
Surgical excision is curative.
Microscopy shows rows or nests of specialized 'glomus cells'.
microReview: Think 'Glomus = Gloves/Cold'. Subungual location + extreme pain + cold sensitivity = Glomus tumor. Origin: Modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
examinerTraps: The examiner may offer 'Endothelial cells' as a distractor because it is a 'vascular' tumor. Remember that the neoplastic component is the specialized smooth muscle cell of the glomus body.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 41-year-old male with poorly controlled HIV presents with several red, friable, dome-shaped papules on his trunk. A biopsy of one lesion demonstrates a proliferation of capillaries lined by prominent, 'epithelioid' endothelial cells with atypia. There is a dense infiltrate of neutrophils and granular purple material in the interstitium. A Warthin-Starry silver stain highlights clusters of small bacilli. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma lacks neutrophilic infiltrates and is caused by HHV-8, not bacteria.
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignancy and would not show bacterial clusters on Warthin-Starry stain.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised patients caused by Bartonella henselae or Bartonella quintana, characterized by neutrophilic inflammation and positive silver stains.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a lobular capillary hemangioma often occurring after trauma or in pregnancy; it does not show clusters of bacilli.
explanations.e: Cavernous hemangioma consists of large, blood-filled spaces and is not associated with bacterial infection or 'epithelioid' endothelial atypia.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by bacteria of the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
The histological hallmark of Bacillary angiomatosis that distinguishes it from Kaposi sarcoma is the presence of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
The stain used to identify Bartonella in tissue is the {{c1::Warthin-Starry (silver)}} stain.
Bacillary angiomatosis occurs primarily in {{c1::immunocompromised (HIV/AIDS)}} patients.
The treatment for Bacillary angiomatosis is usually {{c1::erythromycin (or other antibiotics)}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis mimics Kaposi sarcoma clinically.
It is a reactive vascular proliferation, not a true neoplasm.
Bartonella henselae is often transmitted by cat scratches.
Bartonella quintana is often transmitted by human body lice.
Prompt treatment with antibiotics leads to regression.
microReview: HIV + Red Papules + Neutrophils + Bacilli (Silver stain) = Bacillary angiomatosis. It is crucial to distinguish this from Kaposi sarcoma because the treatment (antibiotics vs chemotherapy/HAART) is different.
examinerTraps: The 'atypia' in the endothelial cells can mislead students toward a diagnosis of malignancy like angiosarcoma. Focus on the Warthin-Starry stain and neutrophils.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 26-year-old pregnant woman presents with a rapidly growing, 1cm, pedunculated red mass on her gingiva that bleeds easily with minor trauma. The lesion is surgically excised. Histological examination shows a circumscribed lobular proliferation of capillaries with associated edema and acute inflammation. Which of the following is the most accurate pathological name for this lesion?

explanations.a: While it is a type of capillary hemangioma, 'pyogenic granuloma' is the specific name for this clinical presentation.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated blood-filled spaces and are usually deep-seated, not superficial pedunculated gingival masses.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (or granuloma gravidarum when occurring in pregnancy) is a lobular capillary hemangioma that presents as a rapidly growing, friable red nodule on skin or gingiva.
explanations.d: Spider angiomas are small vascular ectasias with a central feeder vessel, not large pedunculated masses.
explanations.e: Cherry angiomas are benign, small, bright red papules common in older adults, not rapidly growing gingival masses.

ankiCards: A pyogenic granuloma is histologically a {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are often associated with {{c1::trauma}} or {{c2::pregnancy (granuloma gravidarum)}}.
The most common locations for pyogenic granulomas are the {{c1::skin}}, {{c2::gingiva}}, and {{c3::oral mucosa}}.
True or False: Pyogenic granulomas are usually infectious in origin. {{c1::False}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized clinically by being {{c1::friable (bleed easily)}} and {{c2::pedunculated}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is neither pyogenic nor a granuloma.
It is a benign vascular lesion.
Regression can occur after pregnancy (granuloma gravidarum).
Histology shows lobules of capillaries separated by stroma.
Often involves the gingiva (1% of pregnant women).
microReview: Pregnant patient + Bleeding gum lesion = Pyogenic granuloma (Granuloma gravidarum). It's essentially a fast-growing hemangioma.
examinerTraps: The name 'Pyogenic granuloma' is a trick because the lesion does not typically contain pus (pyogenic) and is not a true granuloma histologically.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 52-year-old male who worked in the plastics industry for 25 years, specifically with vinyl chloride polymerization, presents with fatigue, weight loss, and jaundice. Imaging reveals multiple ill-defined, hemorrhagic masses in the liver. A biopsy shows malignant cells that express CD31. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Hepatocellular carcinoma is the most common primary liver cancer but is associated with HBV/HCV or cirrhosis, not specifically vinyl chloride, and does not express CD31 (an endothelial marker).
explanations.b: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare malignancy strongly linked to environmental toxins like vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast. It expresses the endothelial marker CD31.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas are the most common benign liver tumors and would not present as malignant masses with constitutional symptoms.
explanations.d: Hepatic adenomas are benign and associated with oral contraceptive use, not industrial chemical exposure.
explanations.e: Cholangiocarcinoma arises from bile duct epithelium and is not a vascular tumor.

ankiCards: The industrial chemical most associated with hepatic angiosarcoma is {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
CD31 is an immunohistochemical marker for cells of {{c1::endothelial}} origin.
Besides vinyl chloride, other risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma include {{c1::arsenic}} and {{c2::Thorotrast (radioactive contrast material)}}.
Hepatic angiosarcomas are histologically {{c1::highly malignant (poorly differentiated)}}.
Symptoms of hepatic angiosarcoma include {{c1::abdominal pain}}, {{c2::jaundice}}, and {{c3::weight loss}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma of the liver is a classic example of occupational carcinogenesis.
It has a very long latency period (decades) after exposure.
CD31 (PECAM-1) is highly specific for vascular tumors.
The prognosis is very poor.
Vinyl chloride is used in the production of PVC (Polyvinyl chloride).
microReview: Vinyl chloride + Liver tumor + CD31 positive = Hepatic Angiosarcoma. This is a high-yield board association.
examinerTraps: Don't pick Hepatocellular carcinoma just because the patient has a liver mass and jaundice. The specific mention of 'Vinyl Chloride' and 'CD31' is the key to identifying a vascular malignancy.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An 8-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for a bright-red, raised 'strawberry-like' lesion on his forehead that has grown since birth. The parents are concerned about the cosmetic appearance. Which of the following is the most likely natural history of this lesion?

options.b: Rapid growth followed by spontaneous regression
options.c: Lifelong persistence without change in size
options.d: Expansion proportional to the child's growth
options.e: Immediate need for radical surgical excision

explanations.a: Juvenile hemangiomas are completely benign and do not transform into angiosarcomas.
explanations.b: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are common in newborns. They typically grow rapidly for a few months and then begin to regress spontaneously, usually disappearing by age 7 to 9.
explanations.c: They do not persist lifelong; most (up to 90%) completely resolve by age 7.
explanations.d: Capillary malformations (like port-wine stains) grow proportionally with the child, but strawberry hemangiomas regress.
explanations.e: Surgical excision is rarely necessary as they regress on their own.

ankiCards: The most common variant of hemangioma in infants is the {{c1::juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma}}.
Strawberry hemangiomas are usually present at birth or appear within {{c1::the first few weeks}} of life.
The majority of strawberry hemangiomas regress by age {{c1::7}}.
The anatomical distribution of strawberry hemangiomas is most commonly the {{c1::head and neck}}.
A bright red, lobulated vascular birthmark that blanches with pressure is likely a {{c1::capillary hemangioma}}.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangiomas are extremely common (1 in 200 births).
They are benign capillary hemangiomas.
Phase 1: Rapid proliferation.
Phase 2: Slow involution.
Parents should be reassured rather than rushed to surgery.
microReview: Strawberry Hemangioma = Newborn + Rapid growth + Regression by school age. Management is usually observation.
examinerTraps: Contrast this with 'Port-wine stains' (Nevus flammeus), which do not regress and grow with the child. Strawberry hemangiomas always go away.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following immunohistochemical markers is the most specific for identifying tumors of endothelial cell origin, such as angiosarcomas?

explanations.a: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (smooth and skeletal).
explanations.b: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells (melanoma, Schwann cells).
explanations.c: CD31 (also known as PECAM-1) is a transmembrane glycoprotein expressed on endothelial cells and is a highly specific marker for vascular tumors.
explanations.d: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells (carcinomas).
explanations.e: Vimentin is a non-specific marker for mesenchymal cells.

ankiCards: CD31 is also known as {{c1::PECAM-1}}.
{{c1::CD31}} is the most specific marker for endothelial differentiation in tumors.
Factor VIII-related antigen (vWF) is another marker for {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
Angiosarcomas are CD31 {{c1::positive}}.
Glomus tumors would be positive for {{c1::smooth muscle actin (SMA)}} rather than CD31.
keyPoints: Vascular markers are used to confirm endothelial origin in poorly differentiated tumors.
CD31 is expressed at endothelial cell-cell junctions.
vWF (Factor VIII) is also used but is sometimes less sensitive.
CD34 is another marker but is less specific than CD31.
Markers help distinguish angiosarcoma from melanoma or carcinoma.
microReview: IHC markers: CD31/vWF = Vascular; Desmin = Muscle; S100 = Melanoma/Neural; Cytokeratin = Carcinoma; CD45 = Lymphoma.
examinerTraps: While Vimentin will be positive in angiosarcomas (since they are mesenchymal), it is not specific. Always choose CD31 for the most specific endothelial marker.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 75-year-old man of Mediterranean descent presents with several persistent, slow-growing, purple plaques on his distal lower extremities. He is otherwise healthy and HIV-negative. Which variant of Kaposi sarcoma does this patient most likely have?

explanations.a: AIDS-associated KS occurs in HIV+ patients and is much more aggressive and disseminated.
explanations.b: Endemic African KS occurs in younger patients (often children) and can be very aggressive, involving lymph nodes.
explanations.c: Transplant-associated KS occurs in patients on chronic immunosuppression.
explanations.d: Classic Kaposi Sarcoma typically affects older men of Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, or Eastern European descent. It is characterized by slow-growing skin lesions restricted to the lower limbs and is generally not associated with HIV.
explanations.e: Iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma is another term for transplant-associated or drug-induced KS.

ankiCards: Classic Kaposi sarcoma is most common in {{c1::older men}} of {{c2::Mediterranean}} descent.
True or False: Classic Kaposi sarcoma is usually associated with HIV. {{c1::False}}.
Classic Kaposi sarcoma is usually {{c1::indolent (slow-growing)}}.
The primary location of lesions in Classic Kaposi sarcoma is the {{c1::distal lower extremities}}.
All forms of Kaposi sarcoma are associated with {{c1::HHV-8}}.
keyPoints: Classic KS is the 'old man' variant.
It stays localized to the skin in most cases.
Surgical excision or local radiation is often sufficient.
It is rarely the cause of death.
Pathogenesis still involves HHV-8 despite lack of HIV.
microReview: Kaposi variants: Classic (Old Mediterranean men, indolent); Endemic (African, can be aggressive in kids); Transplant-associated (Immunosuppression); AIDS-associated (Most common in US, aggressive).
examinerTraps: A common mistake is thinking all Kaposi sarcoma is AIDS-related. Always check the patient's demographic and HIV status.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old male with a history of von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease undergoes routine surveillance. MRI of the abdomen reveals a 3cm, well-circumscribed, incidentally found lesion in the liver. Histology shows large, cavernous blood-filled spaces separated by a thin connective tissue stroma. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma would be poorly circumscribed, hemorrhagic, and cytologically malignant.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are the most common benign tumors of the liver. They consist of large, dilated vascular spaces. While VHL is more famously associated with hemangioblastomas (CNS/Retina), cavernous hemangiomas of the liver are also seen.
explanations.c: Capillary hemangiomas consist of small, thin-walled capillaries, not the large 'cavernous' spaces described.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are not typically found as incidental liver masses; they are painful distal extremity tumors.
explanations.e: Hemangioblastomas are the classic VHL lesion but are usually located in the cerebellum, brainstem, or retina, not the liver.

ankiCards: The most common benign tumor of the liver is the {{c1::cavernous hemangioma}}.
Histology of a cavernous hemangioma shows {{c1::large, blood-filled vascular spaces}}.
Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is associated with vascular tumors like {{c1::hemangioblastomas}} and {{c2::angiomas}}.
Complications of large cavernous hemangiomas can include {{c1::thrombosis}} or {{c2::rupture}}.
True or False: Most cavernous hemangiomas require surgical treatment. {{c1::False (most are asymptomatic)}}.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are often incidental findings.
They can reach 'giant' sizes (>5cm).
They do not undergo malignant transformation.
The vascular spaces are lined by a single layer of endothelium.
Biopsy is often avoided due to the risk of hemorrhage.
microReview: Liver + Large blood-filled spaces = Cavernous hemangioma. Most common benign liver tumor. Avoid biopsy due to bleeding risk.
examinerTraps: The inclusion of 'VHL' is a distractor to make you think of hemangioblastoma. However, the description 'cavernous blood-filled spaces' in the liver specifically defines a cavernous hemangioma.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old man presents for a routine physical examination. He has a 40-pack-year smoking history and well-controlled hypertension. On abdominal palpation, a non-tender, pulsating mass is felt in the midline above the umbilicus. Bedside ultrasound confirms a 4.5-cm dilation of the aorta. Which of the following is the most likely primary pathogenetic mechanism for this condition?

options.a: Autoimmune-mediated destruction of the vasa vasorum
options.b: Congenital deficiency in type III collagen synthesis
options.c: Cystic medial necrosis due to fibrillin-1 mutations
options.d: Ischemia-induced atrophy of the outer media
options.e: Obliterative endarteritis of the tunica adventitia

explanations.a: Autoimmune-mediated destruction is more characteristic of large-vessel vasculitides like Takayasu arteritis, not the typical pathogenesis of an atherosclerotic AAA.
explanations.b: Type III collagen deficiency is characteristic of Vascular Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome, which leads to arterial rupture but usually at a younger age and in different distributions.
explanations.c: Fibrillin-1 mutations cause Marfan Syndrome, typically associated with thoracic aortic aneurysms and cystic medial degeneration, rather than abdominal ones.
explanations.d: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are primarily driven by atherosclerosis. The thickening of the intima by plaque increases the diffusion distance for nutrients, leading to ischemia of the inner media, which subsequently weakens the wall and leads to dilation.
explanations.e: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum is the hallmark of tertiary syphilis, which characteristically affects the ascending thoracic aorta.

ankiCards: The most common cause of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms (AAA) is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Atherosclerosis causes AAA by inducing {{c1::ischemia}} of the outer media due to increased diffusion distance.
The characteristic location of an atherosclerotic AAA is {{c1::infrarenal}}.
Major risk factors for AAA include {{c1::smoking}} and male sex.
A pulsating abdominal mass in an older male smoker should raise suspicion for {{c1::Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA)}}.
keyPoints: Aneurysms represent a weakening of the vessel wall leading to dilation.
Atherosclerosis is the leading cause of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms.
The media becomes weakened due to impaired nutrient diffusion from the lumen through the thick atherosclerotic plaque.
AAAs are most frequently infrarenal and above the iliac bifurcation.
Clinical presentation often includes an asymptomatic pulsating mass or sudden catastrophic rupture.
microReview: Aneurysms involve all three layers of the vessel wall (true aneurysm). Abdominal = Atherosclerosis/Ischemia. Thoracic = Hypertension/Syphilis/Marfan.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the pathogenesis of abdominal aneurysms (atherosclerosis) with thoracic aneurysms (cystic medial degeneration or syphilis).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following best defines a 'true aneurysm' as compared to a 'false aneurysm' (pseudoaneurysm)?

options.a: A breach in the vascular wall leading to an extravascular hematoma
options.b: An attenuated but intact vessel wall involving all three tunics
options.c: A localized dissection of blood into the media layer
options.d: A dilation occurring only in the venous system
options.e: A bulging of the heart wall after a myocardial infarction

explanations.a: This describes a false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm), where a hole in the wall allows blood to collect in the extravascular space while being contained by connective tissue.
explanations.b: A true aneurysm is a localized permanent dilation of a blood vessel that involves all three layers of the wall (intima, media, and adventitia), though they may be thinned.
explanations.c: This describes an aortic dissection, where blood enters the wall itself, separating the layers.
explanations.d: Aneurysms can occur in arteries or veins, but the definition of a true aneurysm is structural, not vessel-specific.
explanations.e: While post-MI ventricular aneurysms exist, they involve cardiac muscle, not specifically the three-layered vascular wall structure described in the definition of vascular aneurysms.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the arterial wall (intima, media, and adventitia).
A {{c1::false (pseudoaneurysm)}} aneurysm is an extravascular hematoma that communicates with the intravascular space.
In a true aneurysm, the vessel wall is {{c1::attenuated (thinned)}} but intact.
Vascular dissections differ from aneurysms because blood enters the {{c1::media}} layer to create a false lumen.
A common cause of pseudoaneurysms is {{c1::trauma}} or iatrogenic injury (e.g., post-catheterization).
keyPoints: True aneurysms involve the intima, media, and adventitia.
False aneurysms are contained hematomas resulting from a wall defect.
Aneurysms are classified by shape: saccular (one-sided) or fusiform (circumferential).
Vessel wall weakening is a fundamental mechanism of vascular pathology.
The structural integrity of the media is critical to preventing aneurysm formation.
microReview: True = 3 layers. False = Hematoma. Dissection = Blood between layers.
examinerTraps: The examiner may describe a pulsatile mass after a femoral artery puncture; this is usually a pseudoaneurysm (false aneurysm), not a true one.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which specific anatomic distribution is most characteristic for aneurysms driven primarily by the modifiable risk factor of hypertension?

explanations.a: Abdominal aortic aneurysms are most strongly associated with atherosclerosis and smoking.
explanations.b: Hypertension is the most common cause of thoracic aortic aneurysms. It leads to wall stress and medial degenerative changes.
explanations.c: Coronary artery aneurysms are rare and usually associated with Kawasaki disease in children.
explanations.d: Veins typically develop varicosities, not hypertensive aneurysms.
explanations.e: Pulmonary artery aneurysms are very rare and typically associated with pulmonary hypertension or congenital defects, not systemic hypertension.

ankiCards: The most common risk factor for Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms is {{c1::hypertension}}.
The most common risk factor for Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms is {{c1::smoking/atherosclerosis}}.
Hypertension leads to thoracic aneurysms via {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
Aneurysms of the ascending aorta are specifically associated with {{c1::hypertension}} and Marfan syndrome.
Syphilitic aneurysms typically involve the {{c1::thoracic}} aorta.
keyPoints: Hypertension is a major driver of thoracic aortic aneurysms.
Atherosclerosis is the major driver of abdominal aortic aneurysms.
Vessel wall response to injury includes intimal thickening and medial degeneration.
Aneurysms represent a loss of balance between wall stress and wall strength.
Pathology often follows specific anatomic distributions based on the underlying insult.
microReview: Thoracic = HTN. Abdominal = Atherosclerosis.
examinerTraps: Atherosclerosis can occur in the thoracic aorta, but hypertension and Marfan's are much more characteristic causes for aneurysms in that specific proximal location.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old man with a family history of sudden death at an early age presents with sudden-onset, severe chest pain radiating to the back. Physical exam reveals tall stature, long spindly fingers, and pectus excavatum. A murmur of aortic regurgitation is heard. What is the most likely microscopic finding in this patient's aortic wall?

options.a: Dense neutrophilic infiltration of the adventitia
options.b: Fragmentation of elastic fibers and mucoid material accumulation
options.d: Intimal plaque with a necrotic lipid core
options.e: Small vessel vasculitis of the vasa vasorum

explanations.a: Neutrophilic infiltration is characteristic of infectious (mycotic) aneurysms or acute vasculitis.
explanations.b: This patient has Marfan syndrome. The aortic finding is cystic medial degeneration (or necrosis), characterized by loss of smooth muscle cells and elastic tissue, replaced by proteoglycans (mucoid material).
explanations.c: Granulomatous inflammation with giant cells is characteristic of Giant Cell Arteritis or Takayasu Arteritis.
explanations.d: This describes atherosclerosis, which is the primary driver of AAAs, not the thoracic complications of Marfan syndrome.
explanations.e: This is seen in tertiary syphilis (endarteritis obliterans), which also affects the thoracic aorta but is not associated with Marfanoid habitus.

ankiCards: The classic histological finding in Marfan-associated aneurysms is {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
Cystic medial degeneration involves the fragmentation of {{c1::elastic}} fibers.
Patients with Marfan syndrome are at high risk for {{c1::thoracic aortic dissection}} and aneurysms.
The genetic defect in Marfan syndrome involves the {{c1::FBN1 (Fibrillin-1)}} gene.
Cystic medial degeneration results in the accumulation of {{c1::mucoid (proteoglycan)}} material in the media.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome is a leading cause of thoracic aortic aneurysms in young patients.
The defect in fibrillin-1 leads to aberrant TGF-beta signaling and weakened ECM.
Histologically, the media shows loss of elastic lamellae (cystic medial necrosis).
Aortic root dilation often leads to aortic valve insufficiency (regurgitation).
Severe chest pain radiating to the back in this context suggests aortic dissection.
microReview: Marfan = Fibrillin-1 defect -> Medial elastic fiber fragmentation -> Aneurysm/Dissection.
examinerTraps: Don't be fooled by the term 'necrosis' in 'cystic medial necrosis'; there is actually no overt cell death/necrosis in the classic sense, just loss of structural organization.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following is an example of a mycotic aneurysm?

options.a: A dilation of the aorta caused by tertiary syphilis
options.b: An aneurysm arising from an infected embolus in infective endocarditis
options.c: A small saccular aneurysm in the Circle of Willis
options.d: A pseudoaneurysm following a gunshot wound to the leg
options.e: A fusiform aneurysm of the abdominal aorta due to smoking

explanations.a: Syphilitic aneurysms are due to endarteritis of the vasa vasorum, not primarily a fungal or bacterial infection of the wall itself (though Treponema is a bacterium).
explanations.b: A 'mycotic aneurysm' refers to any aneurysm resulting from an infection that weakens the wall, most commonly from bacterial seeding during infective endocarditis.
explanations.c: Berry aneurysms in the Circle of Willis are typically congenital or due to hypertension, not infection.
explanations.d: This is a traumatic pseudoaneurysm.
explanations.e: This is an atherosclerotic aneurysm.

ankiCards: The term 'mycotic aneurysm' refers to an aneurysm caused by {{c1::infection}}.
The most common cause of mycotic aneurysms is {{c1::infective endocarditis}} (via septic emboli).
Mycotic aneurysms are dangerous because they can lead to {{c1::rupture}} and sepsis.
Despite the name 'mycotic', most are actually caused by {{c1::bacteria}}.
Infection weakens the vessel wall by inducing an intense {{c1::inflammatory}} response.
keyPoints: Mycotic aneurysms are caused by microbial seeding of the arterial wall.
They can arise from bacteremia, septic emboli, or direct extension from an adjacent abscess.
The inflammatory response destroys the media, leading to rapid dilation.
Staphylococcus and Streptococcus are common causative organisms.
The name 'mycotic' was coined by William Osler due to their mushroom-like appearance.
microReview: Mycotic = Infection-induced wall weakening.
examinerTraps: Students often think 'mycotic' must mean 'fungal'. In pathology, it refers to any infection-driven aneurysm (usually bacterial).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the pathogenesis of abdominal aortic aneurysms, how does the presence of an atherosclerotic plaque specifically contribute to the weakening of the tunica media?

options.a: Direct mechanical erosion by calcified cholesterol crystals
options.b: Induction of smooth muscle cell hyperplasia in the media
options.c: Increase in the diffusion distance for oxygen and nutrients from the lumen
options.d: Release of growth factors that increase elastic fiber synthesis
options.e: Activation of the complement cascade in the adventitial layer

explanations.a: Crystals don't 'erode' the wall mechanically in this context; the damage is metabolic.
explanations.b: Atherosclerosis leads to smooth muscle cell *loss* (atrophy) in the media, not hyperplasia.
explanations.c: The aortic wall (especially the inner media) depends on diffusion from the lumen. Thick atherosclerotic plaques increase this distance, causing ischemic atrophy of the media.
explanations.d: Atherosclerosis actually leads to the degradation of elastic fibers by metalloproteinases.
explanations.e: While inflammation occurs, the primary driver of medial weakening in AAA is the ischemic effect of the plaque barrier.

ankiCards: Atherosclerotic plaques in the aorta cause medial {{c1::ischemia}}.
Ischemia of the media leads to the loss of {{c1::smooth muscle}} cells.
In AAA, the balance between ECM synthesis and degradation is shifted toward {{c1::degradation}}.
Inflammatory cells in the plaque release {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}} that digest the wall.
The abdominal aorta is susceptible to AAA because it has fewer {{c1::vasa vasorum}} than the thoracic aorta.
keyPoints: Atherosclerosis impairs nutrient delivery to the vessel wall.
Ischemic atrophy of the media reduces its structural integrity.
Chronic inflammation in the plaque produces proteases (MMPs).
MMPs degrade collagen and elastin in the media and adventitia.
The resulting wall thinning allows for progressive aneurysmal dilation.
microReview: Plaque = Barrier -> Ischemia -> Media Atrophy -> Dilation.
examinerTraps: The examiner may suggest that hypertension 'pushes' the wall out; while HTN contributes, the primary *pathological* change in the abdominal aorta is the atherosclerotic-mediated weakening.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old man presents with sudden, intense back pain and dizziness. His blood pressure is 80/50 mmHg, and his heart rate is 120 bpm. He has a history of smoking and high cholesterol. Physical exam shows a cold, pale right lower extremity with an absent pulse. Emergency CT shows a large retroperitoneal hematoma. What is the most common clinical complication that preceded this event in patients with this underlying vascular condition?

options.a: Congestive heart failure from chronic volume overload
options.b: Formation of a mural thrombus with distal embolization
options.c: Infection of the vessel wall by Salmonella species
options.d: Occlusion of the renal arteries by intimal hyperplasia
options.e: Rupture into the superior vena cava

explanations.a: Aneurysms do not typically cause CHF unless they involve the aortic root and cause valve regurgitation.
explanations.b: Mural thrombi frequently form in the stagnant, turbulent flow of an aneurysm. These can embolize to distal sites (e.g., the leg), causing acute ischemia, as seen in this patient's pale leg.
explanations.c: While mycotic aneurysms exist, they are not the 'most common' complication of a typical atherosclerotic AAA.
explanations.d: AAA usually occurs *infrarenally*, so renal artery involvement is less common than distal embolism.
explanations.e: AAAs rupture into the retroperitoneum or peritoneal cavity, not the superior vena cava (which is in the thorax).

ankiCards: The triad of ruptured AAA is {{c1::back/abdominal pain}}, {{c1::hypotension}}, and a {{c1::pulsatile mass}}.
Stagnant blood flow in an aneurysm leads to the formation of a {{c1::mural thrombus}}.
Distal embolization of a mural thrombus is often called '{{c1::Blue Toe}} Syndrome'.
The risk of rupture for an AAA increases significantly once the diameter exceeds {{c1::5.0 to 5.5}} cm.
Most AAAs are {{c1::asymptomatic}} until they rupture or embolize.
keyPoints: AAA complications: Rupture, Embolization, Obstruction, and Impingement.
Rupture is the most feared complication, with very high mortality.
Mural thrombi form due to Virchow’s triad (stasis and endothelial injury).
Sudden back pain + Hypotension = Ruptured AAA until proven otherwise.
Management of large aneurysms involves surgical or endovascular repair.
microReview: AAA = Embolism risk + Rupture risk (threshold ~5cm).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the pain of AAA rupture (back/flank) with the pain of aortic dissection (tearing/ripping chest pain).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the classification of vascular morphology, which term describes an aneurysm that involves only a portion of the vessel circumference and often contains a mural thrombus?

explanations.a: An AV fistula is an abnormal communication between an artery and a vein.
explanations.b: A dissection is not a true aneurysm; it is blood tracking between layers.
explanations.c: A fusiform aneurysm is a circumferential, symmetrical dilation of the vessel.
explanations.d: Saccular aneurysms are spherical outpouchings involving only a portion of the vessel wall; they often contain thrombi due to blood stasis.
explanations.e: Varicose veins are dilated, tortuous veins, usually in the legs.

ankiCards: A {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm is a localized outpouching of only part of the vessel wall.
A {{c1::fusiform}} aneurysm is a circumferential dilation of the vessel segment.
Berry aneurysms are a specific type of {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm found in the brain.
Mural thrombi are more common in {{c1::saccular}} aneurysms due to stagnant flow.
Both saccular and fusiform dilations can be {{c1::true}} aneurysms if they involve all three layers.
keyPoints: Aneurysms are categorized by macroscopic shape.
Saccular: 5-20cm, often contains thrombus.
Fusiform: Up to 20cm, involves entire circumference.
The shape does not strictly determine the underlying cause.
Both shapes represent structural failure of the tunica media.
microReview: Saccular = One side/Sac. Fusiform = All around/Spindle.
examinerTraps: A 'dissecting aneurysm' is an older, technically incorrect term. Use 'aortic dissection' instead, as it is not a true dilation of all layers.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old male with a history of untreated syphilis presents with a persistent 'brassy' cough and difficulty swallowing. Imaging reveals a dilation of the ascending aorta with extensive calcification. This patient's condition is primarily caused by which of the following?

options.a: Accumulation of LDL within the intimal layer
options.b: Destruction of the vasa vasorum in the adventitia
options.c: Genetic mutation in the TGF-beta receptor
options.d: Hypertrophy of the aortic smooth muscle cells
options.e: Septic embolization from the mitral valve

explanations.a: This is atherosclerosis, which usually spares the ascending aorta and focuses on the abdominal aorta.
explanations.b: Tertiary syphilis causes 'obliterative endarteritis' of the vasa vasorum. This leads to ischemic injury of the aortic media, resulting in scarring, loss of elasticity, and aneurysm formation (luetic aneurysm).
explanations.c: TGF-beta receptor mutations are associated with Loeys-Dietz syndrome, which also causes aneurysms, but not specifically linked to syphilis habitus.
explanations.d: Syphilis leads to smooth muscle *loss* and fibrosis (scarring), not hypertrophy.
explanations.e: This would cause a mycotic aneurysm, not the classic syphilitic aortitis.

ankiCards: Syphilitic (luetic) aneurysms primarily affect the {{c1::ascending thoracic}} aorta.
The hallmark of syphilitic aortitis is {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}} of the vasa vasorum.
Ischemia of the media in syphilis leads to a '{{c1::tree-bark}}' appearance of the intima.
Syphilitic aneurysms can cause a 'brassy' cough by compressing the {{c1::left recurrent laryngeal}} nerve.
The scarring of the aortic valve ring in syphilis leads to {{c1::aortic regurgitation}}.
keyPoints: Tertiary syphilis targets the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta.
Obliterative endarteritis leads to medial ischemia.
The resulting fibrosis causes the intima to appear wrinkled ('tree-barking').
Symptoms result from compression of mediastinal structures (esophagus, airway).
Aortic root dilation can lead to fatal heart failure due to valve insufficiency.
microReview: Syphilis = Vasa Vasorum Endarteritis -> Medial Ischemia -> Thoracic Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Atherosclerosis and Syphilis both cause medial ischemia, but the *mechanism* (plaque barrier vs. vasa vasorum obstruction) and *location* (abdominal vs. thoracic) differ.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the 'stereotyped' response of a blood vessel wall to almost any form of injury, including the stressors that lead to aneurysm formation?

options.b: Intimal thickening via smooth muscle cell migration
options.c: Medial hypertrophy with increased elastin synthesis
options.d: Necrosis of the endothelial basement membrane
options.e: Spontaneous regression of the internal elastic lamina

explanations.a: Adventitial changes occur, but they are not the 'stereotyped' response described for all vascular injury.
explanations.b: The universal response to vascular injury is intimal thickening. Smooth muscle cells migrate from the media to the intima, proliferate, and synthesize extracellular matrix.
explanations.c: Injury usually leads to medial thinning or scarring in the context of aneurysms, not hypertrophy.
explanations.d: Endothelial injury occurs, but 'necrosis of the basement membrane' is not the defined stereotyped response.
explanations.e: The internal elastic lamina is often broken or degraded, but it does not 'regress' as a programmed response.

ankiCards: The stereotyped response to vascular injury is {{c1::intimal thickening}}.
In response to injury, smooth muscle cells migrate from the {{c1::media}} to the {{c1::intima}}.
The 'neointima' consists of smooth muscle cells and {{c1::extracellular matrix}}.
Unlike normal media, neointimal smooth muscle cells are {{c1::proliferative}} and non-contractile.
Intimal thickening is a feature of both {{c1::atherosclerosis}} and hypertensive vascular disease.
keyPoints: Vascular injury triggers a wound-healing response.
Endothelial loss or dysfunction stimulates smooth muscle cell recruitment.
Recruited cells convert from a contractile to a synthetic phenotype.
The resulting intimal thickening is often irreversible.
This process can narrow the lumen or, if the media is compromised, contribute to wall weakening.
microReview: Injury -> SMC migration to Intima -> Matrix deposition -> Thickening.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'intimal thickening' (the response) with 'atherosclerosis' (a specific disease). Intimal thickening happens in many conditions (vasculitis, trauma, HTN).
sourceQuote: Intimal Thickening: A Stereotyped Response to Vascular Injury
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 34-year-old male with a history of poorly controlled HIV (CD4+ count 85/mm³) presents with several painless, dark-purple, maculopapular lesions on his lower extremities and hard palate. A biopsy of a skin lesion reveals spindle-shaped cells forming slit-like spaces containing red blood cells, accompanied by a lymphocytic infiltrate. Which of the following infectious agents is the most likely driver of this pathology?

explanations.a: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of Kaposi sarcoma, which characteristically presents with spindle cells and slit-like vascular spaces.
explanations.b: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can look similar clinically but histologically shows lobular capillary proliferation with neutrophils, not spindle cells with slit-like spaces.
explanations.c: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not primary vascular tumors.
explanations.d: Cytomegalovirus can cause opportunistic infections in HIV patients (like retinitis or colitis) but is not the driver of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.e: Human papillomavirus is associated with squamous cell carcinomas and warts, not vascular spindle cell malignancies.

ankiCards: The causative agent of Kaposi sarcoma is {{c1::Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}.
Histologically, Kaposi sarcoma shows {{c1::spindle cells}} and {{c2::slit-like spaces}} containing RBCs.
The four clinical forms of Kaposi sarcoma are Classic, Endemic African, {{c1::Transplant-associated}}, and {{c2::AIDS-associated}}.
Unlike Kaposi sarcoma, Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by the bacterium {{c1::Bartonella}}.
Kaposi sarcoma lesions in AIDS patients are most commonly found on the skin, {{c1::mucous membranes}}, and GI tract.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a low-grade malignant vascular tumor caused by HHV-8.
AIDS-associated KS is the most common HIV-related malignancy.
The classic histological hallmark is spindle cells with slit-like vascular channels.
HHV-8 encodes viral homologues of human genes that promote cell proliferation.
Differential diagnosis includes Bacillary angiomatosis, which features neutrophilic inflammation.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8. It presents as red/purple patches, plaques, or nodules. Histology: Spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces, extravasated RBCs. Four types: Classic (elderly Mediterranean), Endemic (African), Iatrogenic (transplant), and AIDS-associated (epidemic).
examinerTraps: Distinguishing KS from Bacillary angiomatosis is a high-yield 'trap'. Look for 'spindle cells' for KS and 'neutrophils' or 'Warthin-Starry stain positivity' for Bartonella.
