stem: A 22-year-old female presents with a highly painful, 4-mm, firm blue nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. The lesion is extremely sensitive to cold and pressure. If excised, this lesion would most likely be composed of cells derived from which of the following?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are exquisitely painful tumors arising from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, an arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.b: While it is a vascular tumor, the predominant cell type providing its unique character is the glomus cell (smooth muscle), not the endothelium.
explanations.c: While most tumors have mesenchymal origins, 'modified smooth muscle cells' is the specific expected answer for a glomus tumor.
explanations.d: Schwannomas are peripheral nerve sheath tumors; while they can be painful, they do not typically present as subungual blue nodules sensitive to cold.
explanations.e: Skeletal muscle is not the origin of glomus tumors; they arise from vascular thermoregulatory structures.

ankiCards: Glomus tumors are most commonly found in the {{c1::subungual (under nail)}} region.
The primary clinical symptom of a glomus tumor is {{c1::exquisite pain}} (often triggered by cold).
The cell of origin for a glomus tumor is the {{c1::modified smooth muscle cell}} of the glomus body.
A glomus tumor is also known as a {{c1::glomangioma}}.
On histology, glomus tumors show nests of {{c1::uniform round cells}} surrounding vascular channels.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but very painful.
Commonly located in distal digits, particularly subungual.
Derived from the glomus body (arteriovenous shunt for thermoregulation).
Characterized by nests of specialized glomus cells (modified smooth muscle).
Surgical excision is usually curative.
microReview: Subungual + Pain + Cold sensitivity = Glomus tumor. Cell of origin = Modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
examinerTraps: Confusing a glomus tumor with a subungual melanoma. Glomus tumors are usually small, blue, and very painful, whereas melanomas are typically pigmented streaks (melanonychia) and painless.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with several enlarging, ill-defined, violaceous skin plaques on her left arm. She has a history of a radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer 12 years ago, which was complicated by chronic, massive lymphedema of the ipsilateral arm. A biopsy of a skin plaque shows malignant endothelial cells expressing CD31. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma is a malignant vascular tumor. In the setting of chronic lymphedema following radical mastectomy, this is specifically known as Stewart-Treves syndrome.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and usually presents in immunosuppressed patients, not specifically in the setting of post-surgical lymphedema.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign bacterial proliferation (Bartonella) seen in HIV patients, not a malignancy.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign, well-circumscribed vascular malformations, not aggressive malignant plaques.
explanations.e: Lymphangiomas are benign malformations of lymphatic vessels, usually congenital, not acquired malignant lesions.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
The immunohistochemical marker most specific for endothelial origin in angiosarcoma is {{c1::CD31}} (or vWF).
Angiosarcoma is a {{c1::malignant}} neoplasm of endothelial cells.
Risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma include {{c1::vinyl chloride}}, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
The prognosis for cutaneous angiosarcoma is generally {{c1::poor}} due to early metastasis.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a highly aggressive malignant tumor of endothelial cells.
Can occur anywhere but most common in skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Stewart-Treves syndrome: Angiosarcoma following chronic lymphedema (e.g., post-mastectomy).
Markers: CD31 and Von Willebrand Factor.
Histology: Atypia, pleomorphism, and disorganized vascular channels.
microReview: Post-mastectomy + Chronic lymphedema + New purple nodules = Stewart-Treves Syndrome (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: The examiner may describe the patient as having 'massive arm swelling' instead of 'lymphedema'. Recognize this as the underlying risk factor for Stewart-Treves syndrome.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 26-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy develops a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated nodule on her gingiva (gums). It bleeds easily with minor trauma. The lesion is excised for comfort. Histology reveals a circumscribed proliferation of capillaries arranged in lobules with associated edema and inflammatory cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma (also known as lobular capillary hemangioma) is a common benign vascular lesion that often occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas are similar but typically occur in infants (strawberry hemangioma) and aren't specifically triggered by pregnancy trauma in this manner.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are painful subungual lesions, not pedunculated gingival nodules.
explanations.d: Angiosarcomas are highly malignant and would show significant cellular atypia, not a benign lobular capillary pattern.
explanations.e: Spider angiomas are small, central arterioles with radiating capillaries, often associated with high estrogen states (cirrhosis/pregnancy), but they are flat or slightly raised, not pedunculated nodules.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer because it is neither {{c1::pyogenic (pus-forming)}} nor a {{c2::granuloma}}.
Pyogenic granuloma is histologically a {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
A pyogenic granuloma occurring in the gingiva of a pregnant woman is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
The clinical hallmark of a pyogenic granuloma is that it {{c1::bleeds easily}} with minor trauma.
The most common sites for pyogenic granuloma are the {{c1::skin, gingiva, and oral mucosa}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign, pedunculated, red vascular nodule.
Commonly follows minor trauma or occurs during pregnancy.
Histology: Lobular arrangement of capillaries with inflammatory infiltrate.
Despite the name, it is not an infection or a true granulomatous process.
Usually treated by simple surgical excision.
microReview: Pregnancy + Bleeding gum nodule = Pyogenic granuloma (Lobular capillary hemangioma).
examinerTraps: The name 'Pyogenic granuloma' is a trap because there is no pus and no granulomas. Always remember it is actually a capillary hemangioma subtype.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A pathology resident is reviewing a slide of a vascular tumor. The specimen shows large, dilated vascular spaces filled with blood, separated by a modest connective tissue stroma. There is no evidence of cellular atypia or malignancy. These lesions are frequently found in the liver and spleen and may be part of von Hippel-Lindau disease. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, blood-filled vascular spaces. They are common in the liver and are associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas consist of small, thin-walled capillaries, not the large 'cavernous' spaces described.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis involves capillary proliferation and neutrophils, usually in immunocompromised hosts.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is malignant and would show significant atypia and tissue invasion.
explanations.e: Glomangiomas are specifically composed of glomus cells and are usually small and located in the digits.

ankiCards: {{c1::Cavernous hemangiomas}} are the most common benign tumors of the liver.
The most common complication of a large internal cavernous hemangioma is {{c1::spontaneous rupture (hemorrhage)}}.
Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of {{c1::large, blood-filled spaces}}.
Vascular tumors of the cerebellum and retina in von Hippel-Lindau disease are called {{c1::hemangioblastomas}}.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas {{c1::rarely}} regress spontaneously.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign but can be large and locally destructive.
Most common benign tumor of the liver.
Often discovered incidentally on imaging.
Can be part of the von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome clinical spectrum.
Histology: Large vascular channels separated by fibrous stroma; no atypia.
microReview: Large blood-filled channels + Liver/Spleen/Brain = Cavernous hemangioma.
examinerTraps: Examiners often use 'liver' as the primary location for cavernous hemangioma. Do not confuse it with hepatic angiosarcoma (which is associated with toxins like vinyl chloride).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following environmental toxins is most strongly associated with the development of hepatic angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Vinyl chloride exposure (used in the plastics industry) is a classic risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Aflatoxin B1 (from Aspergillus) is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Benzene exposure is primarily associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.d: Beryllium exposure is associated with berylliosis and lung cancer.
explanations.e: Asbestos exposure is associated with mesothelioma and lung cancer.

ankiCards: Exposure to {{c1::Vinyl chloride}} is a known risk factor for liver angiosarcoma.
The three classic toxins associated with hepatic angiosarcoma are vinyl chloride, {{c1::arsenic}}, and {{c2::Thorotrast}}.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is a {{c1::malignant}} tumor of endothelial cells.
Aflatoxin is associated with HCC, while vinyl chloride is associated with {{c1::angiosarcoma}}.
Angiosarcoma is often CD31 positive, indicating an {{c1::endothelial}} origin.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is rare but highly lethal.
Vinyl chloride is the classic occupational exposure (PVC production).
Arsenic (found in pesticides) is another chemical risk factor.
Thorotrast (a former radiocontrast agent) is a historical risk factor.
Presents with weight loss, abdominal pain, and hepatomegaly.
microReview: Plastic worker (Vinyl Chloride) + Liver mass = Hepatic Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Vascular tumors vs. Hepatocytes. HCC (Aflatoxin, Hepatitis) vs. Angiosarcoma (Vinyl Chloride, Arsenic). Know the difference.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 2-week-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for a bright red, raised 'strawberry-like' lesion on the right cheek. The parents state the lesion was not present at birth but appeared recently and is growing. Which of the following is the most likely clinical course for this lesion?

explanations.a: This is a juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma. They characteristically grow rapidly for a few months and then slowly regress, with the majority disappearing by age 7 to 9.
explanations.b: Juvenile hemangiomas are benign and do not transform into malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.c: This describes a Port-wine stain (nevus flammeus), which does not regress and may darken or thicken.
explanations.d: While ulceration can occur, it is not the typical or 'most likely' clinical course.
explanations.e: Juvenile hemangiomas are localized benign skin lesions and do not behave like metastatic malignancies.

ankiCards: Juvenile hemangioma is also known as a {{c1::strawberry}} hemangioma.
Juvenile hemangiomas typically {{c1::regress}} spontaneously by early childhood.
Histologically, juvenile hemangiomas are classified as {{c1::capillary}} hemangiomas.
Unlike strawberry hemangiomas, port-wine stains {{c1::do not}} regress.
Strawberry hemangiomas are the {{c1::most common}} vascular tumor of infancy.
keyPoints: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma is a benign capillary hemangioma.
Very common in infants (1 in 200 births).
Natural history: Rapid growth phase followed by gradual involution.
75% to 90% are gone by age 7.
Treatment is usually observation unless the lesion obstructs vision or airway.
microReview: Infant + Strawberry nodule = Juvenile hemangioma. Course = Regresses by school age.
examinerTraps: Distinguishing between Strawberry hemangioma (regresses) and Port-wine stain (grows with child, persists).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular lesions is characterized by a permanent dilation of small vessels, forming a flat, red lesion that typically follows the distribution of the trigeminal nerve and is associated with the GNAQ gene mutation?

explanations.a: Nevus flammeus (Port-wine stain) is a vascular malformation that presents as a flat, red/purple birthmark. When it follows the V1/V2 distribution of the trigeminal nerve, it may be associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome and GNAQ mutations.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas are raised, not flat, and are true neoplasms, not just dilations.
explanations.c: Spider telangiectasias are small, central arterioles with radiating vessels, usually acquired and related to hyperestrogenism.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are deep, blood-filled masses, not flat facial marks.
explanations.e: Lymphangiomas are lymphatic malformations, usually clear or pale, not red port-wine stains.

ankiCards: A port-wine stain in the V1/V2 distribution is associated with {{c1::Sturge-Weber}} syndrome.
Sturge-Weber syndrome involves port-wine stains and {{c1::leptomeningeal}} angiomas.
The gene mutation associated with port-wine stains and Sturge-Weber is {{c1::GNAQ}}.
Nevus flammeus is a {{c1::vascular malformation (ectasia)}}, not a true neoplasm.
Clinically, port-wine stains {{c1::do not}} regress and grow as the child grows.
keyPoints: Nevus flammeus (Port-wine stain) is an ectasia (dilation of existing vessels).
Most commonly on the face.
GNAQ somatic mutations are often found in these lesions.
Sturge-Weber syndrome triad: Port-wine stain, leptomeningeal angioma, glaucoma/seizures.
Radiologically, Sturge-Weber may show 'tram-track' calcifications in the brain.
microReview: Facial Port-Wine Stain + Seizures = Sturge-Weber Syndrome (GNAQ mutation).
examinerTraps: The examiner may call it 'nevus flammeus' instead of 'port-wine stain'. They are the same thing.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following histopathological features is most characteristic of a malignant vascular tumor (angiosarcoma) as opposed to a benign hemangioma?

explanations.a: Angiosarcomas are characterized by prominent cellular atypia, pleomorphism, and frequent mitoses. Hemangiomas lack these features.
explanations.b: Organized lobular patterns are characteristic of benign pyogenic granulomas.
explanations.c: Both benign hemangiomas and malignant angiosarcomas can have blood-filled spaces, so this does not differentiate them.
explanations.d: CD31 is a marker of endothelial origin and is expressed in both benign and malignant vascular tumors.
explanations.e: Malignant tumors typically have *high* mitotic rates, not an absence of them.

ankiCards: Malignant vascular tumors are called {{c1::angiosarcomas}}.
A key histological difference between hemangioma and angiosarcoma is the presence of {{c1::atypia/pleomorphism}}.
CD31 is an IHC marker for {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
Vascular tumors that are intermediate in grade (between benign and malignant) are called {{c1::hemangioendotheliomas}}.
Angiosarcomas often fail to form well-defined {{c1::vascular channels}} (they are poorly differentiated).
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is the most aggressive vascular malignancy.
Microscopically: Plump, atypical endothelial cells; multi-layering.
Poorly differentiated areas may look like undifferentiated sarcomas.
Common in elderly (skin of head/neck) or lymphedema patients.
CD31 is the most useful marker for confirming endothelial origin.
microReview: Benign = Well-formed channels, no atypia. Malignant = Atypia, pleomorphism, necrosis, invasion.
examinerTraps: Thinking CD31 only stains malignant cells. CD31 stains *all* endothelial cells, whether benign or malignant.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old male presents with a large, ill-defined mass in his deep soft tissues of the thigh. Biopsy shows cords and nests of 'epithelioid' endothelial cells with cytoplasmic vacuoles that look like 'blister-like' vascular channels. The tumor is categorized as intermediate-grade. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor characterized by endothelial cells that look epithelioid (plump/rounded) and have characteristic intracellular vascular lumens (blister cells).
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign and have thin-walled, large vessels, not epithelioid cells.
explanations.c: Kaposi sarcoma shows spindle cells and is associated with HHV-8, not an epithelioid morphology.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are small, benign, and derived from smooth muscle, not intermediate-grade epithelioid endothelial tumors.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is high-grade/malignant and usually more pleomorphic and aggressive than 'intermediate-grade'.

ankiCards: {{c1::Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma}} is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
The characteristic histology of epithelioid hemangioendothelioma includes cells with {{c1::cytoplasmic vacuoles}} (blister cells).
Intermediate-grade tumors are also referred to as {{c1::borderline}} tumors.
Epithelioid hemangioendotheliomas can occur in {{c1::soft tissue, liver, or lung}}.
Epithelioid endothelial cells are {{c1::plump/rounded}} and resemble epithelial cells.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors are graded as Benign, Intermediate (Borderline), or Malignant.
Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is the classic intermediate example.
Features 'blister-like' cells representing primitive vascular lumens.
Clinical behavior is unpredictable but generally better than angiosarcoma.
Often involves large veins or deep soft tissue.
microReview: Intermediate Grade + Epithelioid cells + Blister-like vacuoles = Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma.
examinerTraps: The term 'epithelioid' may lead you to think of a carcinoma. CD31 staining will confirm it is actually a vascular tumor.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 36-year-old male with a history of HIV and a CD4+ count of 120 cells/µL presents with multiple non-blanching, purplish-red macules and plaques on his lower extremities and hard palate. Skin biopsy reveals proliferation of spindle-shaped cells forming slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells and hemosiderin. Which of the following pathogens is the primary causative agent of these lesions?

explanations.a: HHV-8 (also known as KSHV) is the definitive causative agent of all forms of Kaposi sarcoma. It infects endothelial cells and promotes oncogenesis through viral homologs of cellular proteins.
explanations.b: HPV-16 is strongly associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix, oropharynx, and anus, not vascular tumors.
explanations.c: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and primary CNS lymphoma in HIV patients, but not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.d: CMV causes retinitis and colitis in immunocompromised patients but is not oncogenic for vascular tissue.
explanations.e: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which clinically mimics Kaposi sarcoma but is characterized histologically by neutrophilic infiltrates and clusters of bacteria rather than the spindle cell slits of Kaposi.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is caused by {{c1::Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}.
The characteristic histological feature of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells}} forming {{c2::slit-like vascular spaces}}.
Kaposi Sarcoma lesions often contain {{c1::extravasated red blood cells}} and {{c2::hemosiderin}} deposits.
The most common site for extracutaneous Kaposi Sarcoma in AIDS patients is the {{c1::gastrointestinal tract}}.
Bacillary angiomatosis is a differential for Kaposi Sarcoma but is caused by {{c1::Bartonella species}}.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a low-grade malignant vascular tumor associated with HHV-8.
AIDS-associated KS is the most aggressive form and occurs in patients with low CD4 counts.
Histology shows spindle-shaped endothelial cells and slit-like spaces.
HHV-8 is required for the development of all clinical subtypes of KS.
Clinical presentation involves purple or red plaques/nodules on the skin or mucous membranes.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Slit-like spaces + HIV. Bacillary Angiomatosis = Bartonella + Neutrophils + Warthin-Starry stain positive.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Kaposi Sarcoma with Bacillary Angiomatosis; look for neutrophils and bacteria (Bartonella) vs spindle cells and slits (KS).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... or Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 58-year-old male who worked in a polyvinyl chloride (PVC) manufacturing plant for 30 years presents with right upper quadrant pain and significant weight loss. Imaging reveals multiple ill-defined, hemorrhagic masses within the liver. Biopsy shows highly pleomorphic, malignant endothelial cells that express CD31. Which of the following exposures is most strongly linked to the development of this specific hepatic malignancy?

explanations.a: Arsenic is a known risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma, but vinyl chloride is the classic occupational association mentioned in the context of plastics manufacturing.
explanations.b: Aflatoxin B1 is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), not angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Vinyl chloride monomer (used in PVC production) is a well-established environmental carcinogen specifically linked to hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: Thorotrast (a former radiopaque contrast medium) is associated with hepatic angiosarcoma, but the patient's occupational history specifically points to vinyl chloride.
explanations.e: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and bronchogenic carcinoma, not vascular tumors.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}, {{c2::arsenic}}, and {{c3::Thorotrast}}.
The vascular-specific immunohistochemical marker for angiosarcoma is {{c1::CD31}} (or vWF).
Angiosarcoma consists of malignant {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
Cutaneous angiosarcoma can occur in the setting of chronic {{c1::lymphedema}} (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
Vinyl chloride is specifically used in the production of {{c1::polyvinyl chloride (PVC)}} plastics.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are highly malignant tumors of endothelial cells.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
These tumors are aggressive with a poor 5-year survival rate.
CD31 (PECAM-1) is a reliable marker for endothelial differentiation.
Metastases occur early, most commonly to the lungs and lymph nodes.

examinerTraps: Distinguish between Hepatocellular Carcinoma (linked to Hep B/C, Aflatoxin) and Angiosarcoma (linked to PVC, Thorotrast).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... or Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture

stem: A 29-year-old female presents with a small (5 mm), exquisitely painful, red-blue nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. She notes the pain is often triggered by exposure to cold. Histological examination reveals a tumor composed of nests of uniform, round cells surrounding small vascular channels. These cells are derived from which of the following?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) arise from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.b: Endothelial cells line the vascular spaces but are not the primary neoplastic component of a glomus tumor.
explanations.c: Pericytes are found in hemangiopericytomas, which are distinct from glomus tumors.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts are not the cell of origin for this vascular-related thermoregulatory tumor.
explanations.e: Neural crest cells give rise to many tissues but are not the specific origin of the contractile glomus cells.

ankiCards: A glomus tumor is most commonly found in the {{c1::subungual (under nail)}} region.
The hallmark symptom of a glomus tumor is {{c1::paroxysmal pain}} triggered by {{c2::cold}}.
Glomus tumors arise from the {{c1::glomus body}}, which is involved in {{c2::thermoregulation}}.
The cells of a glomus tumor are derived from {{c1::modified smooth muscle cells}}.
Histology of a glomus tumor shows uniform, round cells surrounding {{c1::vascular channels}}.

Most common location is subungual (distal digits).
Derived from specialized smooth muscle cells of glomus bodies.
The glomus body acts as an arteriovenous shunt for temperature control.

sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... or Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old female in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with a rapidly growing, bright red, 1.5-cm pedunculated lesion on her gingiva. It bleeds easily with minor trauma, such as tooth brushing. The lesion is excised, and pathology shows a circumscribed proliferation of capillaries arranged in lobules, accompanied by edema and an inflammatory infiltrate. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a benign vascular lesion that often occurs on the skin or gingiva (granuloma gravidarum) of pregnant women. It is characterized by rapid growth and easy bleeding.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated vascular channels and are usually deeper and not pedunculated or rapidly growing.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is seen in immunocompromised patients and is caused by Bartonella, not typically associated with pregnancy.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are painful and usually subungual, not found on the gingiva.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor with significant cytological atypia, unlike the benign lobular architecture of pyogenic granuloma.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is actually a {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas that occur in the gingiva of pregnant women are called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
The classic clinical presentation of pyogenic granuloma is a {{c1::rapidly growing}}, {{c2::pedunculated}} red nodule that {{c3::bleeds easily}}.
Histologically, pyogenic granuloma shows capillaries arranged in {{c1::lobules}}.
Treatment for pyogenic granuloma is usually {{c1::surgical excision}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is neither pyogenic (pus-forming) nor a granuloma.
It is a pedunculated red mass commonly on skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
Often follows trauma or occurs during pregnancy.
Histology: Lobular arrangement of capillaries with surrounding edema/inflammation.
Can regress spontaneously, especially after pregnancy.
microReview: Pregnancy + Gingival mass + Bleeding = Pyogenic granuloma (Lobular capillary hemangioma).
examinerTraps: The name is a misnomer; don't look for granulomatous inflammation (like in TB) or overt infection (pus).
sourceQuote: Two principalisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... or Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old male with a history of Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease undergoes surveillance imaging. A 3-cm, well-circumscribed mass is identified in the right lobe of the liver. Biopsy reveals large, blood-filled vascular spaces separated by a sparse connective tissue stroma. No cytological atypia is noted. This lesion is best classified as which of the following?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated (cavernous) vascular spaces. They are the most common benign tumor of the liver and are associated with VHL disease (especially in the CNS and retina).
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas involve small, thin-walled capillaries, not the large spaces described.
explanations.c: Cystic hygroma is a lymphangioma occurring in the neck or axilla of children, often associated with Turner syndrome.
explanations.d: Spider telangiectasias are small, non-neoplastic vascular ectasias, not large masses.
explanations.e: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is an intermediate-grade tumor with epithelioid cells, not benign blood-filled spaces.

ankiCards: The most common benign tumor of the liver is the {{c1::cavernous hemangioma}}.
Cavernous hemangiomas consist of {{c1::large, dilated vascular spaces}}.
VHL disease is associated with hemangiomas in the {{c1::cerebellum}}, {{c2::brainstem}}, and {{c3::retina}}.
Histologically, the vascular spaces in a cavernous hemangioma are separated by {{c1::connective tissue stroma}}.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas are usually {{c1::larger}} and {{c2::not}} circumscribed (though liver ones appear well-defined).
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign vascular tumors characterized by large blood-filled channels.
They are the most common primary tumor of the liver.
Usually asymptomatic; found incidentally on imaging.
Histology: Large vascular spaces, thin walls, no atypia.
Clinical significance: May be confused with malignancy on imaging; risk of rupture is low.
microReview: Large blood spaces + Liver + VHL association = Cavernous hemangioma.
examinerTraps: Do not biopsy suspected hepatic hemangiomas if possible, due to the risk of hemorrhage, though the question provides biopsy findings for diagnosis.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... or Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 5-year-old child presents with a large, flat, port-wine colored birthmark (nevus flammeus) on the left side of his face, following the distribution of the trigeminal nerve (V1 and V2 branches). The physician orders an MRI to screen for leptomeningeal angiomas. This constellation of findings is most consistent with which of the following conditions?

explanations.a: Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) is characterized by a port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) in the trigeminal distribution, ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomas, and often glaucoma and seizures.
explanations.b: Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) involves multiple small telangiectasias of the skin and mucous membranes and AVMs.
explanations.c: VHL disease involves hemangioblastomas (CNS/retina), renal cell carcinoma, and pheochromocytoma.
explanations.d: Maffucci syndrome involves multiple hemangiomas and enchondromas.
explanations.e: Kasabach-Merritt syndrome is a consumptive coagulopathy associated with large vascular tumors like tufted angiomas.

ankiCards: Sturge-Weber syndrome is associated with a facial birthmark called a {{c1::nevus flammeus}} (port-wine stain).
The port-wine stain in Sturge-Weber syndrome typically follows the distribution of the {{c1::trigeminal nerve}}.
Internal manifestations of Sturge-Weber include {{c1::leptomeningeal angiomas}}.
Sturge-Weber syndrome is caused by a somatic mutation in the {{c1::GNAQ}} gene.
Common complications of Sturge-Weber syndrome include {{c1::seizures}}, {{c2::hemiplegia}}, and {{c3::glaucoma}}.
keyPoints: Nevus flammeus (Port-wine stain) is a form of vascular ectasia.
Most port-wine stains are isolated, but those in the trigeminal area suggest Sturge-Weber.
Leptomeningeal angiomas can lead to mental retardation and seizures.
The classic radiologic sign is 'tram-track' calcifications in the brain.
It is a sporadic (non-inherited) condition.
microReview: Port-wine stain (Trigeminal) + Seizures + Brain calcification = Sturge-Weber syndrome.
examinerTraps: Nevus flammeus is permanent and grows with the child, unlike a 'strawberry hemangioma' which regresses.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... or Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An 82-year-old female presents with several dark red, dome-shaped papules on her trunk. They are asymptomatic and have been present for years. These lesions represent the most common vascular anomaly of the skin in adults and are characterized by a proliferation of capillaries. What is the correct term for these lesions?

explanations.a: Cherry hemangiomas (senile hemangiomas) are very common benign vascular lesions that increase in number with age. They are small, bright red, and consist of capillary proliferations.
explanations.b: Strawberry hemangiomas (juvenile hemangiomas) occur in infants and typically regress by age 7.
explanations.c: Nevus simplex (salmon patch) is a birthmark seen in newborns, often on the neck (stork bite) or forehead.
explanations.d: Spider angiomas (spider telangiectasias) have a central feeder vessel with radiating 'legs' and are associated with hyperestrogenic states (e.g., cirrhosis).
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation seen in immunocompromised hosts.

ankiCards: The most common vascular tumor of the skin in adults is the {{c1::cherry hemangioma}}.
Cherry hemangiomas typically {{c1::increase}} in number with advancing age.
Unlike juvenile hemangiomas, cherry hemangiomas {{c1::do not}} regress.
Spider angiomas blanch when the {{c1::central}} portion is compressed.
Histologically, cherry hemangiomas show proliferations of {{c1::capillaries}}.
keyPoints: Cherry hemangiomas are benign and require no treatment unless for cosmetic reasons.
They are characterized by their bright red color and small size (1-5mm).
Histology: Dilated capillaries lined by flattened endothelium.
They are distinguishable from petechiae because hemangiomas are raised and blanchable (initially).
Commonly found on the trunk and extremities.
microReview: Older adult + Red papules + Trunk = Cherry hemangioma (Benign, age-related).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Cherry hemangioma (adult) with Strawberry hemangioma (infant).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... or Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: To differentiate a poorly differentiated vascular sarcoma from other types of high-grade malignancies (such as carcinomas or melanomas), a pathologist uses immunohistochemical staining. Which of the following markers is most specific for identifying cells of endothelial origin?

explanations.a: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a transmembrane glycoprotein expressed on endothelial cells and is the most sensitive and specific marker for vascular tumors.
explanations.b: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells (carcinomas).
explanations.c: S100 is a marker for melanocytes, Schwann cells, and Langerhans cells.
explanations.d: CD45 (Leukocyte Common Antigen) is a marker for hematopoietic cells (lymphomas).
explanations.e: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (rhabdomyosarcomas or leiomyosarcomas).

ankiCards: The most specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial cells is {{c1::CD31}}.
Another marker for endothelial cells, though less specific than CD31, is {{c1::von Willebrand factor (vWF)}}.
Vascular tumors originate from {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
In angiosarcoma, malignant cells retain the expression of {{c1::CD31}}.
Factor VIII-related antigen is another name for {{c1::von Willebrand factor}}.
keyPoints: Identification of vascular origin is crucial in poorly differentiated tumors.
CD31 is the gold standard IHC marker for endothelium.
CD34 is also used but is less specific (also marks hematopoietic stems).
Endothelial markers help distinguish angiosarcoma from amelanotic melanoma or spindle cell carcinoma.
Vascular tumors can be benign (hemangioma), intermediate (Kaposi), or malignant (angiosarcoma).
microReview: Endothelial marker = CD31. Epithelial = Cytokeratin. Muscle = Desmin. Leukocyte = CD45.
examinerTraps: While CD34 is often used, CD31 is generally considered more specific for endothelial differentiation in the context of vascular tumors.
sourceQuote: To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure and function.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 62-year-old female presents with several firm, violaceous nodules on her left arm. She has a history of breast cancer treated with a radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection 12 years ago, complicated by persistent, severe lymphedema of the left arm. Biopsy of a nodule confirms an angiosarcoma. What is the name of this specific clinical presentation?

explanations.a: Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to the development of angiosarcoma (traditionally called lymphangiosarcoma) in the setting of chronic lymphedema, classically after mastectomy.
explanations.b: Li-Fraumeni syndrome is a germline TP53 mutation leading to various cancers, but not specifically associated with lymphedema.
explanations.c: Gorlin syndrome (Basal Cell Nevus Syndrome) involves multiple basal cell carcinomas and PTCH mutations.
explanations.d: Trousseau syndrome is migratory thrombophlebitis associated with malignancy (hypercoagulability).
explanations.e: Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome is hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia.

ankiCards: Stewart-Treves syndrome is the development of {{c1::angiosarcoma}} in a limb with chronic {{c2::lymphedema}}.
The classic history for Stewart-Treves syndrome is a patient who underwent a {{c1::mastectomy}} years prior.
The prognosis for angiosarcoma in Stewart-Treves syndrome is generally {{c1::poor}}.
Chronic lymphedema leads to localized {{c1::immune suppression}}, which may predispose to angiosarcoma.
Clinically, Stewart-Treves presents as {{c1::purple/violaceous nodules}} on the lymphedematous limb.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignant endothelial tumor.
It can be induced by radiation or chronic lymphedema.
Stewart-Treves syndrome is a specific eponymous association.
Lymphedema is usually the result of surgical lymph node dissection.
Treatment involves aggressive surgery (amputation) but recurrence is high.
microReview: Post-mastectomy + Chronic lymphedema + New purple nodules = Stewart-Treves (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: Wait for the long latency period; Stewart-Treves usually occurs 10+ years after the mastectomy.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... or Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular tumors is characterized as an 'intermediate-grade' (borderline) neoplasm that is more aggressive than a hemangioma but less predictably malignant than an angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is the classic example of an intermediate-grade vascular tumor. While it can be locally aggressive and systemic, it often responds to ART or local therapy and behaves less aggressively than true angiosarcomas.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors are strictly benign.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granulomas are strictly benign.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade, highly malignant tumor.
explanations.e: Capillary hemangioma is a strictly benign tumor.

ankiCards: Vascular tumors are classified as {{c1::benign}}, {{c2::intermediate (borderline)}}, or {{c3::malignant}}.
The most common intermediate-grade vascular tumor is {{c1::Kaposi sarcoma}}.
Another intermediate-grade vascular tumor is the {{c1::epithelioid hemangioendothelioma}}.
{{c1::Angiosarcomas}} are the primary malignant vascular tumors.
Benign vascular tumors like {{c1::hemangiomas}} rarely undergo malignant transformation.
keyPoints: Vascular neoplasms vary from benign to highly lethal.
Intermediate-grade tumors (like KS) are locally invasive but have lower metastatic potential than angiosarcoma.
Hemangiomas (benign) are very common and usually do not require treatment.
Malignant tumors (angiosarcoma) have a 5-year survival rate of only ~30%.
The classification is based on histological features and clinical behavior.
microReview: Benign = Hemangioma. Intermediate = Kaposi Sarcoma / Hemangioendothelioma. Malignant = Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Don't assume all 'sarcomas' have the same malignancy grade; Kaposi is specifically 'intermediate'.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following fundamental mechanisms is primarily responsible for the development of aneurysms and vascular dissections?

options.a: Increased vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation
options.b: Weakening of vessel walls leading to dilation
options.c: Precipitous complete obstruction of vessel lumens

explanations.a: Proliferation of smooth muscle cells typically contributes to intimal thickening rather than the wall weakening seen in aneurysms.
explanations.b: This is one of the two principal mechanisms underlying vascular disease and is the direct cause of aneurysms (dilation) and ruptures.
explanations.c: This describes acute thrombosis or embolism, leading to ischemia rather than aneurysm formation.
explanations.d: While atherosclerosis is a risk factor for aneurysms, the narrowing itself is a separate mechanism of vascular disease (stenosis).
explanations.e: Nitric oxide is a vasodilator; its production is generally protective against the stiffening and inflammation that lead to wall weakening.

ankiCards: The two principal mechanisms of vascular disease are narrowing/obstruction and {{c1::weakening of vessel walls}}.
Weakening of vessel walls leads to two major clinical outcomes: {{c1::dilation}} or {{c2::rupture}}.
Vascular pathology is responsible for more {{c1::morbidity}} and {{c2::mortality}} than any other disease category.
In the context of aneurysms, dilation refers to an increase in {{c1::vessel diameter}}.
Aneurysms and dissections are primarily classified under the category of {{c1::vascular wall weakening}}.
keyPoints: Vascular disease involves two main pathways: stenosis/obstruction and wall weakening.
Wall weakening is the hallmark of aneurysm formation.
Aneurysms result in localized permanent dilations of blood vessels.
Weakening can lead to life-threatening rupture.
Pathology is most significant in the arterial system.
microReview: Aneurysms represent a localized dilation of a blood vessel caused by a structural defect or weakening of the vessel wall. This contrasts with atherosclerotic stenosis, which involves narrowing of the lumen. The primary risk associated with aneurysms is rupture and hemorrhage.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse the mechanism of 'vessel narrowing' (atherosclerosis) with 'vessel weakening' (aneurysm), even though atherosclerosis can cause wall weakening.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Arterial walls are structurally thicker than their corresponding venous counterparts. Which specific layer of the arterial wall is most significantly expanded to accommodate higher pulsatile blood pressures?

explanations.a: The adventitia contains nerves and vasa vasorum but does not provide the primary structural resistance to pressure.
explanations.b: The external elastic lamina is a boundary layer but not the thickest component.
explanations.c: The tunica media, composed of smooth muscle cells and elastic fibers, is much thicker in arteries to manage high pressures and pulsatile flow.
explanations.d: The intima is a single layer of endothelial cells and subendothelial space; it is the layer that thickens during injury response.
explanations.e: The internal elastic lamina is a thin layer separating the intima from the media.

ankiCards: Compared to veins, arterial walls are {{c1::thicker}} to accommodate higher pressure.
The specific arterial wall layer that responds to pulsatile flow is the {{c1::tunica media}}.
As arteries become smaller, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}}.
Muscular vessels exert control over blood flow and pressure by adjusting the {{c1::tunica media}}.
Atherosclerosis mainly affects {{c1::elastic}} and {{c2::muscular}} arteries.
keyPoints: Arteries have thicker walls than veins to handle high pressure.
The tunica media is the thickest layer in major arteries.
Wall thickness to lumen ratio increases in smaller muscular arteries.
This structural design allows for blood flow and pressure regulation.
Vascular diseases often show characteristic anatomic distributions based on vessel type.
microReview: The arterial system is designed for high-pressure transport. The media's thickness relative to the lumen provides the structural integrity needed to prevent dilation (aneurysm) under physiological stress.
examinerTraps: Students often focus on the 'intima' because of atherosclerosis, but the structural integrity (and its failure in aneurysms) is primarily a function of the media.
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents with a deep, boring back pain. Physical examination reveals a pulsatile abdominal mass below the level of the umbilicus. Imaging confirms a 6-cm dilation of the abdominal aorta. Which of the following is the most likely primary contributor to the weakening of the vessel wall in this patient?

options.a: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.b: Chronic transmural inflammation and ECM degradation
options.d: Congenital defect in the collagen type III synthesis
options.e: Mycotic seeding of the vessel wall

explanations.a: This is the classic mechanism for syphilitic (luetic) aneurysms, which usually involve the ascending aorta.
explanations.b: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are primarily driven by atherosclerosis, which causes chronic inflammation and the release of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) that degrade the extracellular matrix (ECM).
explanations.c: Cystic medial degeneration is more commonly associated with thoracic aortic aneurysms, particularly in Marfan syndrome or hypertension.
explanations.d: This describes Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, which can cause aneurysms but is less common than atherosclerosis in an older smoker.
explanations.e: Mycotic aneurysms are caused by infection (e.g., Salmonella, Staph) rather than the chronic process typical of AAA.

ankiCards: The most common cause of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA) is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
The primary location of an AAA is usually {{c1::below}} the renal arteries.
AAA pathogenesis involves the degradation of {{c1::extracellular matrix (ECM)}} in the media.
A key clinical sign of an AAA is a {{c1::pulsatile abdominal mass}}.
Major risk factors for AAA include {{c1::male sex}}, {{c2::smoking}}, and age over 50.
keyPoints: AAA is the most common form of aortic aneurysm.
It is strongly associated with smoking and atherosclerosis.
Inflammatory infiltrates in the media lead to proteolysis.
Degradation of elastin and collagen is a critical step.
Rupture risk increases significantly once the diameter exceeds 5 cm.
microReview: In AAA, atherosclerosis causes ischemia of the inner media by increasing the diffusion distance from the lumen, while also inducing inflammation. This leads to the loss of smooth muscle cells and degradation of the ECM, resulting in wall thinning and dilation.
examinerTraps: Atherosclerosis is the 'cause' (risk factor), but the 'mechanism' of wall weakening is the enzymatic degradation of the matrix (MMPs) and chronic inflammation.
sourceQuote: atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Aneurysms are classified as 'true' or 'false' (pseudoaneurysms). Which of the following defines a true aneurysm?

options.a: A wall defect leading to an extravascular hematoma
options.b: Dilation of the vessel involving all three layers of the wall
options.c: A tear in the intima allowing blood to enter the media
options.d: A collection of blood communicating with the lumen but bounded only by adventitia
options.e: Localized narrowing followed by post-stenotic dilation

explanations.a: This describes a false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm).
explanations.b: A true aneurysm involves all layers: intima, media, and adventitia (e.g., atherosclerotic or syphilitic).
explanations.c: This describes an aortic dissection, not a true aneurysm.
explanations.d: This is a characteristic of a pseudoaneurysm, often caused by trauma or catheterization.
explanations.e: Post-stenotic dilation is a hemodynamic effect but does not define the structure of a true aneurysm.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the arterial wall.
A {{c1::false}} aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) is a wall defect leading to an extravascular hematoma.
Common examples of true aneurysms include {{c1::atherosclerotic}} and {{c2::congenital}} aneurysms.
Aortic dissection involves blood entering the {{c1::media}} through an intimal tear.
The three layers of an arterial wall are the {{c1::intima}}, {{c2::media}}, and {{c3::adventitia}}.
keyPoints: True aneurysms involve an attenuated but intact arterial wall (3 layers).
False aneurysms are hematomas that communicate with the intravascular space.
Dissection occurs when blood splays apart the laminar planes of the media.
Saccular aneurysms are spherical outpocketings.
Fusiform aneurysms involve circumferential dilation.
microReview: Understanding the structural difference between true aneurysms, pseudoaneurysms, and dissections is vital. True aneurysms (fusiform or saccular) keep the wall intact but stretched. Pseudoaneurysms represent a leak contained by extravascular tissue.
examinerTraps: Aortic dissection is often colloquially called an 'aneurysm' by patients, but pathologically it is a separate entity (separation of layers vs. dilation of all layers).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) play a critical role in the pathogenesis of aneurysms. Which of the following best describes their mechanism in this context?

options.a: Promoting the synthesis of type I collagen in the media
options.b: Degradation of elastin and collagen in the extracellular matrix
options.c: Increasing the cross-linking of elastic fibers
options.d: Inhibiting the migration of smooth muscle cells to the intima
options.e: Neutralizing the effects of Transforming Growth Factor-beta (TGF-β)

explanations.a: MMPs degrade collagen; they do not promote its synthesis.
explanations.b: MMPs (like MMP-2 and MMP-9) are upregulated in aneurysms and actively break down the structural proteins (elastin/collagen) that provide wall strength.
explanations.c: Cross-linking (via lysyl oxidase) strengthens the wall; MMPs do the opposite.
explanations.d: MMPs actually facilitate cell migration by breaking down the basement membrane/matrix, but that is not the primary mechanism of aneurysm dilation.
explanations.e: While TGF-β is involved in aneurysm signaling (especially in Marfan syndrome), MMPs do not function as direct TGF-β neutralizers.

ankiCards: {{c1::Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}} are enzymes that degrade the ECM in aneurysm formation.
Increased expression of {{c1::MMP-2}} and {{c2::MMP-9}} is seen in abdominal aortic aneurysms.
The balance between MMPs and {{c1::TIMPs}} (tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases) regulates matrix stability.
Loss of {{c1::elastin}} in the tunica media leads to the characteristic dilation of aneurysms.
Inflammatory cells in the aneurysm wall (macrophages) are the primary source of {{c1::MMPs}}.
keyPoints: Aneurysm formation is an active process of matrix remodeling.
MMPs are proteases that digest collagen and elastin.
Chronic inflammation (atherosclerosis) recruits macrophages that secrete MMPs.
A decrease in TIMPs often accompanies the increase in MMPs.
This biochemical imbalance results in a structurally incompetent vessel wall.
microReview: The structural integrity of the aorta depends on the balance of ECM production and degradation. In aneurysms, increased MMP activity (often from inflammatory cells) outweighs the stabilizing forces of collagen and elastin, leading to progressive expansion.
examinerTraps: Watch for options suggesting MMPs build the wall or that they only affect the intima; their most devastating effect is in the media.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old female with long, tapering fingers and hypermobile joints presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset chest pain radiating to her back. She is tall for her age and has a history of ectopia lentis. Which of the following is the most likely microscopic finding in her aortic wall?

options.a: Extensive calcification of the tunica media
options.b: Cystic medial degeneration with loss of elastic fibers
options.c: Transmural granulomatous inflammation with giant cells
options.e: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis of the vasa vasorum

explanations.a: Medial calcification (Monckeberg) usually does not lead to dissection or aneurysm in this clinical profile.
explanations.b: This patient has Marfan syndrome (FBN1 mutation). The characteristic aortic pathology is cystic medial degeneration (fragmentation of elastic tissue and accumulation of proteoglycans).
explanations.c: This describes Giant Cell Arteritis or Takayasu Arteritis, not Marfan syndrome.
explanations.d: This describes a mycotic aneurysm/infection.
explanations.e: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is a feature of hypertension and diabetes, primarily in small vessels, not the aorta in Marfan syndrome.

ankiCards: Marfan syndrome is caused by a mutation in the {{c1::FBN1 (Fibrillin-1)}} gene.
The characteristic aortic wall change in Marfan syndrome is {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
Marfan syndrome frequently leads to aneurysms in the {{c1::ascending/thoracic}} aorta.
Histology of cystic medial degeneration shows fragmentation of {{c1::elastic fibers}}.
Excessive {{c1::TGF-beta}} signaling is a key molecular driver in Marfan-related vascular disease.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome leads to thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAA).
Pathology involves 'cystic medial degeneration' (not actually cysts).
Loss of elastic fibers and gain of mucoid material weakens the media.
Clinical signs include arachnodactyly, tall stature, and lens luxation.
Aortic dissection is a major cause of death in these patients.
microReview: Marfan syndrome-associated aneurysms are conceptualized as a defect in structural scaffolding (fibrillin) combined with dysregulated growth factor signaling (TGF-beta), leading to a weakened media that cannot withstand hemodynamic stress.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'Cystic Medial Degeneration' with 'Atherosclerosis'. Marfan patients are young and their aneurysms are usually proximal (thoracic), whereas atherosclerotic ones are distal (abdominal).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which vessel types are the primary targets of atherosclerotic lesions that subsequently predispose to aneurysm formation?

explanations.a: Arterioles are affected by hyaline or hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis, not usually the classic large-scale atherosclerosis that leads to aneurysms.
explanations.b: Atherosclerosis involves the intima of large elastic arteries (aorta) and muscular arteries (coronary, renal), eventually weakening the underlying media.
explanations.c: Veins are rarely affected by atherosclerosis due to lower pressure environments.
explanations.d: Venules are involved in inflammation/leukocyte trafficking, not atherosclerosis.
explanations.e: Lymphatics are not involved in atherosclerotic disease.

ankiCards: Atherosclerosis primarily affects {{c1::elastic}} and {{c2::muscular}} arteries.
The arterial wall is thicker than the venous wall to accommodate {{c1::pulsatile flow}}.
The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}} as vessels become smaller.
{{c1::Atherosclerosis}} is a major risk factor for abdominal aortic aneurysms.
Many vascular disorders have characteristic {{c1::anatomic distributions}} based on vessel type.
keyPoints: Arteries and veins have comparable architecture but different thicknesses.
The aorta is the classic elastic artery.
Atherosclerosis is a disease of the arterial side of the circulation.
The structural specialization of vessels reflects their functional roles.
Vascular pathology in hypertension and atherosclerosis starts in specific vessel layers.
microReview: Aneurysms occur where hemodynamic stress is high and wall structure is compromised. Large elastic arteries like the aorta are uniquely susceptible to the wall-weakening effects of both atherosclerosis and high-pressure pulsatile flow.
examinerTraps: A common trap is including 'veins' in the answer; although veins can have disorders (varicosities), they do not develop atherosclerotic aneurysms.
sourceQuote: Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old male with untreated hypertension for 20 years presents with sudden-onset, severe 'tearing' chest pain. An urgent CT scan reveals a longitudinal intimal tear and a false lumen within the aortic media. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: AAA is usually asymptomatic until rupture and occurs below the renal arteries, not typically presenting with 'tearing' chest pain.
explanations.b: Aortic dissection is characterized by an intimal tear and blood tracking through the media, often in the setting of hypertension.
explanations.c: Berry aneurysms occur in the Circle of Willis and cause subarachnoid hemorrhage.
explanations.d: Atherosclerotic aneurysms are dilations, not 'tears' with false lumens.
explanations.e: Mycotic aneurysms result from infection and are usually smaller and more localized.

ankiCards: The classic clinical presentation of aortic dissection is {{c1::sudden, tearing chest pain}}.
The most common risk factor for aortic dissection is {{c1::hypertension}}.
Aortic dissection occurs when blood enters a tear in the {{c1::intima}}.
In a dissection, blood separates the laminar planes of the {{c1::media}}.
A {{c1::false lumen}} is created when blood tracks through the aortic wall in a dissection.
keyPoints: Aortic dissection is a medical emergency distinct from a true aneurysm.
Hypertension causes hypertrophy of the vasa vasorum, leading to medial ischemia.
The 'tearing' pain often radiates to the back between the scapulae.
Type A dissections involve the ascending aorta; Type B involve the descending.
Rupture into the pericardium (tamponade) is a common cause of death.
microReview: While both aneurysms and dissections involve wall weakness, dissection is specifically a 'splitting' of the media. Hypertension is the most common cause by inducing medial degenerative changes and stress.
examinerTraps: Aneurysm vs. Dissection: Aneurysms are dilations; dissections are separations. A patient can have both, but 'tearing' pain points specifically to dissection.
sourceQuote: Aneurysms and Dissection... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Syphilitic (luetic) aneurysms are a manifestation of tertiary syphilis. What is the specific mechanism by which Treponema pallidum infection causes the weakening of the aortic wall?

options.a: Direct invasion of the tunica intima by spirochetes
options.b: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.c: Formation of cholesterol-rich plaques in the media
options.d: Activation of the alternative complement pathway in the adventitia
options.e: Inhibition of smooth muscle cell apoptosis

explanations.a: Spirochetes are rarely found in the lesion; the damage is immune-mediated ischemia.
explanations.b: The infection causes inflammation and narrowing (obliterative endarteritis) of the vasa vasorum, which supplies the outer media of the aorta. This leads to medial ischemia and weakening.
explanations.c: This describes atherosclerosis, not syphilis.
explanations.d: Syphilis is associated with a plasma cell-rich infiltrate, not specifically an alternative complement deficiency or activation pattern.
explanations.e: Ischemia actually leads to smooth muscle cell *loss* (atrophy), not inhibition of apoptosis.

ankiCards: Syphilitic aneurysms typically involve the {{c1::ascending/thoracic}} aorta.
The mechanism in luetic aneurysms is {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}} of the vasa vasorum.
Ischemia of the {{c1::media}} in syphilis leads to a 'tree-bark' appearance of the intima.
Syphilitic aneurysms can cause dilation of the aortic valve ring, leading to {{c1::aortic insufficiency}}.
The primary cell type found in the inflammatory infiltrate of a syphilitic aorta is the {{c1::plasma cell}}.
keyPoints: Tertiary syphilis targets the vasa vasorum of the thoracic aorta.
Narrowing of vasa vasorum leads to medial atrophy.
The loss of elastic support results in massive aneurysm formation.
Contraction of fibrous scars leads to the 'tree-bark' intimal appearance.
It is much rarer now due to effective penicillin treatment of early syphilis.
microReview: Syphilis causes a 'proximal' aneurysm by starving the media of its blood supply (vasa vasorum), whereas atherosclerosis causes 'distal' aneurysms by inflammatory matrix degradation.
examinerTraps: Syphilis = Ascending Aorta (Thoracic); Atherosclerosis = Descending/Abdominal Aorta. Don't mix the locations.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following is considered a major modifiable risk factor that contributes to the pathogenesis of atherosclerotic-related aneurysms?

explanations.a: Male sex is actually a constitutional (non-modifiable) risk factor for AAA.
explanations.b: Family history is a non-modifiable constitutional risk factor.
explanations.c: Smoking is the most significant modifiable risk factor for both atherosclerosis and abdominal aortic aneurysms.
explanations.d: Age is a non-modifiable constitutional risk factor.
explanations.e: Genetic polymorphisms are non-modifiable.

ankiCards: The most important modifiable risk factor for AAA is {{c1::smoking}}.
Modifiable risk factors for atherosclerosis include {{c1::hypertension}}, {{c2::diabetes}}, and {{c3::hyperlipidemia}}.
Constitutional (non-modifiable) risk factors include {{c1::age}}, {{c2::sex}}, and {{c3::genetics}}.
AAA is much more common in {{c1::men}} than in women.
Smoking increases the rate of {{c1::aneurysm expansion}} and risk of rupture.
keyPoints: Aneurysm risk factors mirror atherosclerosis risk factors.
Smoking is more strongly linked to AAA than to coronary artery disease.
Hypertension is also a major modifiable driver.
Stopping smoking reduces the risk of aneurysm-related death.
Constitutional factors (like age >50) define the target screening population.
microReview: Risk factors for aneurysms are divided into constitutional (age, male sex) and modifiable (smoking, hypertension). Smoking is the single most important behavior-related factor for AAA development.
examinerTraps: Be careful to distinguish between 'constitutional' (non-modifiable) and 'modifiable' risk factors as the question specifically asks for modifiable.
sourceQuote: Modifiable Major Risk Factors... Constitutional Risk Factors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old female presents with a highly painful, 5-mm, firm, blue-colored nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. She notes that the pain is exquisite and triggered by cold exposure. Physical examination reveals a subungual lesion that is tender to palpation. The lesion is excised, and histology shows nests of uniform cells surrounding branching vascular channels. What is the most likely cell of origin for this patient's condition?

explanations.a: While this is a vascular tumor, the specific nests of glomus cells that characterize this painful subungual lesion are not primary endothelial cells but rather perivascular.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) arise from the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation. The tumor cells are modified smooth muscle cells.
explanations.c: Fibroblasts are found in many vascular lesions but do not form the characteristic nests of uniform 'glomus cells' seen in this diagnosis.
explanations.d: While the tumor is painful, it does not arise from Schwann cells or other nerve sheath components; the pain is thought to be mediated by the proximity of nerves to the tumor.
explanations.e: Mesenchymal cells are the distant precursors of all vascular tissues, but the specific glomus tumor is differentiated toward specialized smooth muscle.

ankiCards: A painful, blue subungual nodule is most likely a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
The glomus tumor arises from specialized {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} of the glomus body.
Glomus tumors are classically located {{c1::under the fingernails (subungual)}}.
The primary function of the normal glomus body is {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Are glomus tumors usually benign or malignant? {{c1::Benign}}
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but extremely painful.
They are commonly located in the subungual region (fingernails).
The cells of origin are modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
Pain is often paroxysmal and triggered by cold.
Histology shows uniform cells in nests around vascular spaces.
microReview: Glomus tumor = Painful subungual blue nodule = Modified smooth muscle cells (Glomus body).
examinerTraps: Do not confuse this with a subungual melanoma, which is usually pigmented (brown/black) and painless, or a subungual hematoma, which follows trauma.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male with a history of chronic lymphedema of the left upper extremity following a radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection 10 years ago presents with several firm, violaceous skin nodules on the same arm. A biopsy of one of the nodules reveals a poorly differentiated malignancy with pleomorphic endothelial cells forming irregular, anastomosing vascular channels. Immunohistochemical staining is positive for CD31. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and typically presents in AIDS patients or elderly Mediterranean men; it is not specifically linked to chronic lymphedema.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign proliferation in immunocompromised hosts caused by Bartonella infection, not a malignant vascular tumor.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy) is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome. CD31 is a specific endothelial marker.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign, large vascular spaces; they do not show the pleomorphism or anastomosing channels seen here.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are small, painful, benign lesions; they do not present as spreading violaceous nodules in a lymphedematous limb.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphedema post-mastectomy is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
The vascular marker {{c1::CD31}} (PECAM-1) is used to identify angiosarcoma.
Angiosarcoma histology is characterized by {{c1::anastomosing vascular channels}} and atypical endothelial cells.
Is angiosarcoma considered highly aggressive or indolent? {{c1::Highly aggressive}}.
Risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma include vinyl chloride and {{c1::arsenic}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a malignant endothelial neoplasm.
Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to angiosarcoma in chronic lymphedema.
CD31 (endothelial marker) is highly specific for vascular tumors.
It has a very poor prognosis with frequent metastasis.
Histology shows irregular vascular spaces with malignant cells.
microReview: Chronic lymphedema + Violaceous nodules = Stewart-Treves syndrome = Angiosarcoma (CD31+).
examinerTraps: Distinguish from Kaposi sarcoma by the clinical history (lymphedema vs. HIV) and the degree of cellular atypia (higher in angiosarcoma).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An infant is born with a bright red, raised 'strawberry' lesion on the scalp. The parents are concerned about the appearance. The physician explains that the lesion will likely grow for a few months and then regress. Which of the following is the most characteristic clinical course for this lesion?

options.d: Rapid expansion leading to heart failure
options.e: Surgical excision is mandatory within 1 month

explanations.a: Strawberry (juvenile) hemangiomas are benign and do not undergo malignant transformation.
explanations.b: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are common in newborns; they typically grow rapidly for a period and then spontaneously regress by age 7 to 9.
explanations.c: While cavernous or cherry hemangiomas might persist, the strawberry (juvenile) variant is known for self-involution.
explanations.d: While extremely large hemangiomas can cause high-output heart failure (Kasabach-Merritt), this is not the characteristic course for a standard strawberry hemangioma.
explanations.e: Excision is usually avoided because these lesions regress on their own, often with excellent cosmetic results.

ankiCards: The juvenile hemangioma is also known as a(n) {{c1::strawberry}} hemangioma.
Strawberry hemangiomas typically {{c1::regress}} by early childhood.
The age by which most strawberry hemangiomas disappear is {{c1::7-9 years}}.
Histologically, juvenile hemangiomas consist of {{c1::capillary}} sized vessels.
Is a strawberry hemangioma present at birth or shortly after? {{c1::Shortly after birth (first few weeks)}}.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangioma is a very common benign tumor of infancy.
It appears as a bright red, raised lesion (strawberry-like).
The natural history involves a growth phase followed by involution.
Vast majority regress completely by age 7.
Treatment is usually conservative (observation).
microReview: Strawberry Hemangioma = Newborn = Grow then Regress by age 7.
examinerTraps: Confusing strawberry hemangioma (regresses) with a Port-wine stain (persists and grows with the child).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction... [and] Weakening of vessel walls.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 40-year-old male with advanced AIDS presents with several red-to-purple, papular skin lesions on his trunk. He also reports fever and weight loss. A biopsy of a skin lesion reveals a proliferation of small blood vessels with prominent, plump (epithelioid) endothelial cells and an infiltrate of neutrophils. Warthin-Starry silver stain reveals clusters of tangled bacilli. What is the most likely causative organism?

explanations.a: HHV-8 causes Kaposi Sarcoma, which also presents in AIDS patients with purple lesions, but histology shows spindle cells and no bacteria on Warthin-Starry stain.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella species (B. henselae or B. quintana) in immunocompromised patients, presenting with vascular proliferation and neutrophilic infiltrates.
explanations.c: S. aureus causes pyogenic infections but not the specific vascular proliferative lesions known as bacillary angiomatosis.
explanations.d: MAI is a common infection in AIDS but causes granulomatous disease or systemic infection rather than cutaneous vascular tumors.
explanations.e: CMV causes retinitis, esophagitis, or colitis in AIDS but is not associated with cutaneous vascular proliferations.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis in AIDS patients is caused by {{c1::Bartonella henselae/quintana}}.
The stain used to identify the bacteria in bacillary angiomatosis is {{c1::Warthin-Starry}}.
Unlike Kaposi sarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis features an infiltrate of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
The endothelial cells in bacillary angiomatosis are described as {{c1::epithelioid/plump}}.
Which condition mimics Kaposi sarcoma clinically but is bacterial? {{c1::Bacillary angiomatosis}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis occurs in immunocompromised hosts (HIV/AIDS).
Caused by Bartonella henselae (cat scratch) or Bartonella quintana (body lice).
Clinically mimics Kaposi sarcoma (red/purple papules).
Histology: Capillary proliferation with neutrophils and bacterial clusters.
Diagnosis confirmed by silver stain (Warthin-Starry).
microReview: AIDS + Purple lesions + Neutrophils + Silver stain (Bartonella) = Bacillary Angiomatosis.
examinerTraps: The most common trap is confusing this with Kaposi sarcoma. Look for 'neutrophils' or 'Warthin-Starry' or 'bacteria' to pick Bacillary Angiomatosis.
sourceQuote: Vascular Structure and Function characterizes specific kinds of vessels...structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old male with a long history of industrial exposure to vinyl chloride during plastics manufacturing presents with jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. Imaging reveals multiple mass lesions in the liver. A biopsy confirms a malignant vascular tumor. This tumor is most likely to show immunoreactivity for which of the following markers?

explanations.a: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial tumors (carcinomas), not vascular tumors.
explanations.b: Alpha-fetoprotein is a marker for hepatocellular carcinoma or yolk sac tumors.
explanations.c: Vinyl chloride exposure is a classic risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma. CD31 (PECAM-1) is a marker for endothelial differentiation found in angiosarcomas.
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived tumors like melanoma or schwannoma.
explanations.e: HMB-45 is a specific marker for melanocytic tumors.

ankiCards: Exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}} or arsenic is linked to hepatic angiosarcoma.
{{c1::CD31}} is the most specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial cells.
The most common malignant tumor of the liver is metastasis, but the classic chemical-induced vascular one is {{c1::angiosarcoma}}.
Angiosarcoma is a malignancy of {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with which environmental toxin? {{c1::Arsenic (or Vinyl Chloride)}}.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is rare but highly associated with specific toxins.
Toxins include Vinyl Chloride, Arsenic, and Thorotrast.
It is a highly aggressive malignant tumor.
Endothelial markers include CD31 and von Willebrand factor.
Patients often present with liver failure or hemoperitoneum.
microReview: Vinyl chloride/Arsenic = Liver Angiosarcoma = CD31 positive.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse with Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC), which is associated with Hep B/C and Aflatoxin, not Vinyl Chloride.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A newborn female is noted to have a large, fluctuant, transilluminating mass on the left side of her neck. Physical examination also reveals a low posterior hairline and webbed neck. Chromosomal analysis shows a 45,X karyotype. The neck mass is most likely a collection of which of the following?
