A widening of the {{c1::mediastinum}} on X-ray is a sign of TAA.
Difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) in TAA is caused by compression of the {{c1::esophagus}}.
keyPoints: TAA causes: Hypertension (most common) and Marfan (genetic).
Symptoms result from compression of local structures (esophagus, recurrent laryngeal nerve).
Media weakening is the core mechanism.
TAA can lead to aortic valve insufficiency if the root is involved.
Rupture risk increases with diameter > 6 cm.
microReview: Thoracic Aneurysm = Hypertension + Medial Degeneration. Contrast this with Abdominal Aneurysm = Atherosclerosis + Smoking.
examinerTraps: Wait for the location. Ascending aorta = Hypertension/Medial degeneration. Infrarenal aorta = Atherosclerosis.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular disorders often have characteristic anatomic distributions. According to the general patterns of vascular pathology, which type of vessels are predominantly affected by atherosclerosis?

explanations.a: Atherosclerosis specifically targets large elastic arteries (e.g., aorta, carotids) and medium-sized muscular arteries (e.g., coronary, popliteal).
explanations.b: Small arteries and arterioles are more commonly affected by hypertension (arteriolosclerosis), not atherosclerosis.
explanations.c: Veins are rarely affected by atherosclerosis unless they are used as arterial grafts.
explanations.d: Capillaries and lymphatics are not sites of atherosclerotic plaque formation.
explanations.e: Arteriovenous anastomoses are not the primary target of atherosclerosis.

ankiCards: Atherosclerosis mainly affects {{c1::elastic}} and {{c1::muscular}} arteries.
The aorta is an example of a {{c1::large elastic}} artery.
Coronary and renal arteries are examples of {{c1::muscular}} arteries.
Vascular pathology distribution is determined by {{c1::structural specializations}}.
Aneurysms in elastic arteries are often related to the failure of the {{c1::tunica media}}.
keyPoints: Atherosclerosis is a disease of large and medium arteries.
It does not affect the venous system under normal conditions.
The abdominal aorta is the most common site for atherosclerotic aneurysms.
Elastic arteries have the highest concentration of elastin for compliance.
Pathology varies based on the vessel's anatomical structure.
microReview: Atherosclerosis = High pressure + Large/Medium arteries (Elastic/Muscular).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse atherosclerosis (plaques in large/medium arteries) with arteriolosclerosis (wall thickening in small arteries).
sourceQuote: Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old male presents with sudden, tearing chest pain radiating to the back. Physical examination reveals tall stature, long fingers (arachnodactyly), and high-arched palate. An echocardiogram shows dilation of the aortic root and a proximal intimal flap. Which component of the vessel wall is most likely primarily defective in this patient?

explanations.a: Tight junctions relate to permeability, not the structural strength required to prevent aneurysms.
explanations.b: This patient likely has Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1 defect). Fibrillin-1 is an extracellular matrix protein essential for elastic fiber integrity.
explanations.c: Smooth muscle cell contraction (actin/myosin) is not the primary defect in Marfan-related aortic disease, though smooth muscle loss occurs secondarily.
explanations.d: Type IV collagen is in basement membranes; Type I and III are more relevant for vessel wall strength in the adventitia/media.
explanations.e: Vasa vasorum integrity is relevant in syphilitic aortitis, not Marfan syndrome.

ankiCards: Marfan syndrome involves a defect in {{c1::fibrillin-1}}.
A common aortic complication of Marfan syndrome is {{c1::aortic dissection}} or {{c1::aneurysm}}.
The histological change in the aorta in Marfan is {{c1::cystic medial necrosis}}.
Cystic medial necrosis refers to the loss of {{c1::elastic fibers}} and {{c1::smooth muscle cells}}.
Marfan syndrome is an example of {{c1::weakening}} of the vessel wall.
keyPoints: Genetic defects in ECM (e.g., Marfan) lead to weakened media.
Weakened media allows for aneurysmal dilation or dissection.
Clinical features (tall, long fingers) suggest a systemic connective tissue disorder.
Aortic root dilation is a classic feature of Marfan.
TGF-beta signaling is often overactive in these conditions.
microReview: Marfan = Fibrillin-1 mutation = Weakened ECM = Medial failure = Aneurysm/Dissection.
examinerTraps: A common trap is choosing 'atherosclerosis' for any aneurysm. In a young patient with Marfan features, always look for genetic ECM defects.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: The progression from a normal artery to an aneurysmal dilation involves a shift in the balance of vessel wall homeostasis. Which of the following biochemical changes most directly contributes to the 'weakening of vessel walls' mentioned as a principal mechanism of disease?

options.c: Increased synthesis of tropoelastin by myofibroblasts
options.d: Decreased production of reactive oxygen species (ROS)
options.e: Inhibition of Tissue Inhibitors of Metalloproteinases (TIMPs)

explanations.a: MMPs (like MMP-2 and MMP-9) degrade collagen and elastin in the tunica media, leading to structural weakening.
explanations.b: Increased (not decreased) recruitment of monocytes/macrophages occurs, releasing the MMPs that degrade the wall.
explanations.c: Decreased (or dysfunctional) synthesis of structural proteins occurs, not increased productive synthesis.
explanations.d: ROS are usually increased in inflammatory vascular disease, contributing to wall damage.
explanations.e: While TIMP inhibition would lead to more MMP activity, 'Increased activity of MMPs' (a) is the more direct driver of the proteolysis described in aneurysms.

ankiCards: {{c1::Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMPs)}} are enzymes that degrade the aortic wall matrix.
The degradation of {{c1::elastin and collagen}} weakens the arterial media.
Inflammatory cells in an aneurysm secrete {{c1::cytokines}} that upregulate MMPs.
Aneurysms occur when the rate of matrix degradation {{c1::exceeds}} the rate of synthesis.
Genetic conditions can predispose to wall weakening by altering {{c1::ECM}} metabolism.
keyPoints: Aneurysm pathogenesis involves a balance between matrix synthesis and degradation.
Chronic inflammation leads to excessive MMP activity.
Elastin degradation is critical for the initial dilation.
Collagen degradation is critical for eventual rupture.
Tobacco smoke increases oxidative stress and inflammatory cell activity.
microReview: Aneurysm = Inflammation + MMPs > TIMPs + Degraded Elastin/Collagen.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse MMPs (which degrade the wall) with growth factors (which might attempt to repair it).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the relationship between arterial branching and the control of systemic blood pressure?

options.a: Large elastic arteries provide the greatest resistance to flow
options.b: The wall-to-lumen ratio decreases as vessels approach the capillaries
options.c: Muscular arteries and arterioles exert control over flow and pressure
options.d: Arterial walls thicken as they transition into the venous system
options.e: Vessel diameter remains constant across all branching levels

explanations.a: Large elastic arteries are for conductance and compliance, not high resistance.
explanations.b: The wall-to-lumen ratio actually increases in smaller muscular arteries and arterioles.
explanations.c: Due to their high wall-to-lumen ratio and smooth muscle content, muscular arteries and arterioles are the primary sites of resistance and pressure control.
explanations.d: Veins are thinner than arteries at the same level.
explanations.e: Vessel diameter decreases with branching, while total cross-sectional area increases.

ankiCards: Resistance to blood flow is primarily controlled by {{c1::muscular arteries and arterioles}}.
Large elastic arteries like the {{c1::aorta}} handle high pulsatile pressures.
The {{c1::tunica media}} is the layer responsible for vasoconstriction/dilation.
Small vessels have a {{c1::higher}} ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter than large vessels.
Pathology in small vessels often affects {{c1::blood pressure regulation}}.
keyPoints: Arterioles are the 'faucets' of the cardiovascular system.
Aorta acts as a pressure reservoir (Windkessel).
Wall thickness/lumen ratio is highest in resistance vessels.
Smooth muscle in the media is the effector for pressure control.
Aneurysms usually occur in elastic or muscular arteries where wall stress is high.
microReview: Resistance = Muscular Arteries/Arterioles (High Wall:Lumen). Conductance = Elastic Arteries (Aorta).
examinerTraps: Thinking the aorta provides resistance because it is 'large'. Resistance is inversely proportional to the 4th power of the radius; small vessels provide the bulk of resistance.
sourceQuote: Arterial wall thickness gradually diminishes as the vessels become smaller, but the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing these muscular vessels to exert control over blood flow and pressure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old male with a history of syphilis presents with a 'brassy' cough and hoarseness. Imaging reveals a 'tree-bark' appearance of the ascending aortic intima and a saccular aneurysm. Which histological finding in the vasa vasorum is most characteristic of this specific condition?

explanations.a: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in malignant hypertension and certain vasculitides (e.g., PAN).
explanations.b: Syphilitic (luetic) aortitis is characterized by obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum, leading to ischemia and weakening of the aortic media.
explanations.c: Atheromatous plaques are the hallmark of atherosclerosis, not syphilitic aortitis (though the 'tree-barking' is often due to secondary atherosclerosis).
explanations.d: Cystic medial necrosis is associated with hypertension and Marfan syndrome.
explanations.e: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis affects small vessels (e.g., skin capillaries) in hypersensitivity reactions.

ankiCards: Syphilitic aortitis involves the {{c1::ascending}} aorta.
The 'tree-bark' appearance of the aorta is seen in {{c1::tertiary syphilis}}.
Ischemia of the media in syphilis is caused by {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}} of the vasa vasorum.
Syphilitic aneurysms can cause {{c1::aortic valve insufficiency}} due to ring dilation.
Hoarseness in aortic aneurysms is due to compression of the {{c1::recurrent laryngeal nerve}}.
keyPoints: Syphilis targets the vasa vasorum of the thoracic aorta.
Endarteritis causes medial ischemia and scarring.
The intima develops a wrinkled 'tree-bark' appearance.
This is a rare cause of aneurysms in the antibiotic era.
Complications include root dilation and coronary ostial stenosis.
microReview: Syphilis = Ascending Aorta + Vasa Vasorum Obliteration + Medial Ischemia.
examinerTraps: Remember that syphilis preferentially affects the ascending aorta, while atherosclerosis preferentially affects the abdominal aorta.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular tumors is characterized as the most common benign variant occurring in infancy, typically presenting as a 'strawberry' lesion on the skin that regresses spontaneously by age seven?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, dilated vascular channels and are less likely to regress spontaneously compared to the capillary type.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) are the most common vascular tumors of infancy; they grow rapidly but usually regress by age 7.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are painful benign tumors arising from the glomus bodies, typically found under the fingernails, not strawberry-like lesions of infancy.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granulomas are rapidly growing pedunculated red nodules that often bleed and are associated with trauma or pregnancy, rather than being the classic infantile strawberry lesion.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation caused by Bartonella species, typically seen in immunocompromised patients.

ankiCards: What is the most common vascular tumor of {{c1::infancy}}?
Capillary hemangiomas (strawberry) usually {{c1::regress}} spontaneously by age 7.
{{c1::Cavernous}} hemangiomas involve large, blood-filled spaces and are associated with Von Hippel-Lindau disease.
A pedunculated, red, bleeding nodule on the skin or gingiva is most likely a {{c1::pyogenic granuloma}}.
Vascular tumors are divided into benign, {{c1::intermediate}}, and malignant grades.
keyPoints: Capillary hemangiomas are the most common vascular tumors in infants.
Spontaneous regression is a hallmark of strawberry (capillary) hemangiomas.
Hemangiomas are generally benign and composed of blood-filled vessels.
Vascular tumors can be classified by the size of the vessels involved (capillary vs. cavernous).
Histologically, capillary hemangiomas show closely packed thin-walled capillaries.
microReview: Benign vascular tumors (hemangiomas) are classified by vessel size. Capillary hemangiomas involve small vessels and are common in skin/mucous membranes. Cavernous hemangiomas involve larger channels and can affect deep organs like the liver.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse capillary hemangiomas with pyogenic granulomas; both are red and vascular, but pyogenic granulomas are often ulcerated and associated with trauma or pregnancy.
sourceQuote:
Vascular Tumors
Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions 518
Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors 520
Malignant Tumors 522
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 35-year-old male with advanced HIV infection presents with multiple purple-to-red macules and plaques on his lower extremities and oral mucosa. A biopsy reveals spindle-shaped cells and slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells. Which pathogen is most likely responsible for this presentation?

explanations.a: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which looks similar clinically but histologically shows neutrophilic infiltrates and clusters of bacteria (Warthin-Starry stain positive).
explanations.b: HHV-8 (also known as KSHV) is the causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma, which presents as spindle-cell vascular proliferations in HIV patients.
explanations.c: EBV is associated with lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, but not vascular tumors like Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.d: HPV is associated with warts and squamous cell carcinomas, not vascular lesions.
explanations.e: CMV causes retinitis or colitis in AIDS patients but does not drive vascular tumorigenesis.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is caused by {{c1::Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}.
The classic histologic finding in Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells}} with slit-like vascular spaces.
{{c1::AIDS-associated}} Kaposi Sarcoma is the most common HIV-related malignancy.
The characteristic skin lesions of Kaposi Sarcoma are {{c1::purple/red}} macules or plaques.
Unlike bacillary angiomatosis, Kaposi Sarcoma does {{c1::not}} respond to antibiotics.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
HHV-8 infection is necessary but not sufficient for KS development.
Epidemic KS is the form associated with HIV/AIDS.
Histology shows slit-like spaces created by malignant spindle cells.
Extravasated red blood cells are commonly seen in the tumor stroma.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a low-grade malignancy of endothelial cells. It occurs in four forms: Classic (older Mediterranean men), Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and Epidemic (AIDS). HHV-8 is the universal driver.
examinerTraps: Distinguishing KS from Bacillary Angiomatosis is common. Look for spindle cells (KS) vs. neutrophils and bacteria (BA).
sourceQuote: Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors 520... Kaposi Sarcoma is caused by HHV-8.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A newborn female is found to have a large, soft, fluctuant mass on the left side of her neck. Physical examination also reveals a webbed neck and a low posterior hairline. Imaging shows a multi-loculated cystic mass. What is the most likely diagnosis for this neck lesion?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are typically solid, bright red 'strawberry' marks on the skin surface, not deep multiloculated cystic masses.
explanations.b: Cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) is a benign lymphatic malformation often found in the neck or axilla, frequently associated with Turner syndrome (45,X).
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are small, extremely painful subungual nodules; they do not present as large neck masses in neonates.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor, usually occurring in older adults on the scalp or in the liver; it is not a neonatal cystic lesion.
explanations.e: Simple lymphangiomas are smaller, more superficial lymphatic lesions, whereas large multiloculated neck masses are specifically termed cystic hygromas.

ankiCards: {{c1::Cystic hygroma}} is a cavernous lymphangioma often found in the neck of infants.
Cystic hygromas are strongly associated with {{c1::Turner syndrome}}.
Histologically, lymphangiomas are distinguished from hemangiomas by the absence of {{c1::red blood cells}} in the lumens.
The most common location for a cystic hygroma is the {{c1::neck (or axilla)}}.
Cystic hygromas are {{c1::benign}} but can be difficult to resect due to lack of encapsulation.
keyPoints: Cystic hygromas are cavernous lymphangiomas.
Commonly associated with chromosomal aneuploidies like Turner Syndrome.
Characterized by large, dilated lymphatic spaces lined by endothelium.
They are benign but can cause local compression of neck structures.
They contain proteinaceous fluid and few lymphocytes.
microReview: Lymphatic tumors include simple lymphangiomas and cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas). Cystic hygromas occur in the neck/axilla of children and are markers for Turner syndrome or Down syndrome.
examinerTraps: The examiner uses Turner syndrome features (webbed neck) to point towards cystic hygroma, which is a classic association.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions 518
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with a small, 0.5-cm, exquisitely painful blue nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. Microscopic examination of the lesion shows nests of uniform, round cells surrounding branching vascular channels. From which specialized structure do these tumor cells originate?

options.b: Smooth muscle of the glomus body

explanations.a: Lymphatic endothelium gives rise to lymphangiomas, which are typically painless.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) arise from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.c: Pericytes give rise to hemangiopericytomas (now often classified as solitary fibrous tumors), not the classic subungual glomus tumor.
explanations.d: Vascular endothelial cells give rise to hemangiomas and angiosarcomas, but the specific 'glomus cell' is a modified smooth muscle cell.
explanations.e: Fibroblasts give rise to fibromas or fibrosarcomas, which do not show the characteristic round-cell nests of glomus tumors.

ankiCards: {{c1::Glomus tumor}} is an exquisitely painful, subungual vascular tumor.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells.
The glomus body's physiological function is {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Histology of a glomus tumor shows nests of {{c1::uniform round cells}} around vessels.
The most common location for a glomus tumor is the {{c1::distal portion of digits (subungual)}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but highly symptomatic due to pain.
Classic location is subungual (under the nail).
Arise from glomus bodies (AV anastomoses).
Tumor cells are modified smooth muscle cells, not endothelial cells.
Excision is curative.
microReview: Glomus tumors are small, red-blue, and painful. They are unique among vascular tumors because the primary cell is a modified smooth muscle cell rather than an endothelial cell.
examinerTraps: The pain is the key clinical clue. Almost all other benign vascular tumors (like hemangiomas) are painless.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions 518
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old male with AIDS presents with multiple red, papular skin lesions. Histopathology shows a vascular proliferation with prominent neutrophils and nuclear dust. Warthin-Starry silver stain reveals clusters of tangled bacilli. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi Sarcoma is HHV-8 related, shows spindle cells, and lacks the neutrophilic infiltrate and bacteria seen here.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella (henselae or quintana) and is characterized by vascular proliferation with neutrophils and visible bacilli.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignancy with significant cytological atypia, not an infectious-driven proliferation.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign reactive lesion, often following trauma, and does not contain Bartonella organisms.
explanations.e: Hemangioendothelioma is an intermediate-grade tumor with 'epithelioid' cells, not infectious bacilli.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
The stain used to identify Bartonella in bacillary angiomatosis is the {{c1::Warthin-Starry}} stain.
Unlike Kaposi Sarcoma, Bacillary Angiomatosis contains an infiltrate of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
Bacillary angiomatosis occurs primarily in {{c1::immunocompromised/AIDS}} patients.
Treatment for bacillary angiomatosis involves {{c1::antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin)}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis is an opportunistic infection.
It mimics Kaposi Sarcoma clinically (red/purple nodules).
Driven by Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch) or Bartonella quintana (trench fever).
The inflammatory response is predominantly neutrophilic.
It is a treatable condition with antibiotics.
microReview: Bacillary angiomatosis vs. Kaposi Sarcoma: Both occur in AIDS. BA = Neutrophils + Bartonella (stains silver). KS = Spindle cells + HHV-8.
examinerTraps: The examiner may omit the history of AIDS but mention the silver stain or neutrophils to differentiate from Kaposi.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions 518
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male former shipyard worker presents with right upper quadrant pain, weight loss, and jaundice. He has a history of long-term exposure to vinyl chloride in the plastics industry. Imaging shows multiple hemorrhagic masses within the liver. Biopsy reveals malignant endothelial cells with marked atypia. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Hepatic adenoma is a benign epithelial tumor associated with oral contraceptive use, not vinyl chloride.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are the most common benign liver tumors; they do not show malignant atypia or associate with vinyl chloride.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma of the liver is a highly aggressive malignancy specifically associated with exposure to vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
explanations.d: Hepatocellular carcinoma is associated with cirrhosis, Hep B/C, and aflatoxin, but not specifically with vinyl chloride in this vascular context.
explanations.e: Hemangioendothelioma is intermediate-grade; while the epithelioid type can occur in the liver, the vinyl chloride association strongly points to angiosarcoma.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}, arsenic, or Thorotrast.
Angiosarcoma is a {{c1::malignant}} tumor of endothelial cells.
The immunohistochemical marker for angiosarcoma is {{c1::CD31}}.
A patient with long-term lymphedema after mastectomy developing a vascular tumor has {{c1::Stewart-Treves}} syndrome.
The prognosis for angiosarcoma is generally {{c1::poor}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is an aggressive malignant vascular tumor.
Environmental toxins (PVC, arsenic) are major risk factors for the hepatic form.
It can occur in the skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Histology shows pleomorphic endothelial cells forming irregular vascular channels.
Malignant cells are positive for CD31 and vWF.
microReview: Angiosarcomas are high-grade. Key associations: Liver (PVC/Arsenic/Thorotrast), Skin/Arm (Post-radiation or chronic lymphedema/Stewart-Treves).
examinerTraps: Vinyl chloride is a specific buzzword for hepatic angiosarcoma. Don't be distracted by HCC.
sourceQuote: Malignant Tumors 522... Angiosarcoma
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A researcher is studying the immunohistochemical profile of various vascular neoplasms. Which of the following markers would be most helpful in confirming the endothelial origin of a poorly differentiated malignant tumor?

explanations.a: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells and carcinomas.
explanations.b: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (skeletal, smooth, cardiac).
explanations.c: CD31 (PECAM-1) and von Willebrand Factor (vWF) are specific markers for endothelial cells and are used to identify vascular tumors.
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells (melanoma, Schwann cells).
explanations.e: CD45 is the leukocyte common antigen used to identify hematopoietic cells.

ankiCards: {{c1::CD31}} is the most specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial cells.
von Willebrand Factor (vWF) is also known as {{c1::Factor VIII-related antigen}}.
Angiosarcomas are confirmed as vascular by staining for {{c1::CD31}}.
Vascular tumors arise from {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
Marker used to distinguish carcinoma from angiosarcoma is {{c1::Cytokeratin}} (positive in carcinoma).
keyPoints: CD31 is used to identify both benign and malignant vascular tumors.
Endothelial markers include CD31, CD34, and vWF.
Vascular tumors can be so poorly differentiated they look like carcinomas or sarcomas.
Staining is essential for identifying the 'slit-like' spaces as vascular.
CD31 is also known as platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule (PECAM-1).
microReview: Confirming vascular origin requires endothelial markers: CD31 and vWF. This is crucial for high-grade tumors like angiosarcoma that lack well-formed vessels.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'CD31' or 'vWF'. Sometimes 'CD34' is used, but it's less specific than CD31.
sourceQuote: Malignant Tumors 522... identification of endothelial markers such as CD31 or von Willebrand factor.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which vascular lesion is characterized as a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated nodule that frequently ulcerates and bleeds, often occurring on the gingiva of pregnant women?

explanations.a: Nevus flammeus is a flat 'birthmark' or 'port-wine stain' that does not grow as a pedunculated nodule.
explanations.b: Spider angiomas are small, non-palpable lesions with radiating vessels, common in hyperestrogenic states (cirrhosis/pregnancy), but not bleeding nodules.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (granuloma pyogenicum) is a benign, inflamed capillary hemangioma that often presents on the gingiva ('pregnancy tumor') or skin.
explanations.d: Cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) are large, deep neck masses, not small bleeding gingival nodules.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis can look similar but is specifically caused by Bartonella in immunocompromised patients, not typically pregnancy.

ankiCards: A 'pregnancy tumor' in the oral cavity is histologically a {{c1::pyogenic granuloma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized by {{c1::rapid}} growth and frequent bleeding.
Despite the name, pyogenic granuloma is neither {{c1::pyogenic (pus-forming)}} nor a granuloma.
Histologically, a pyogenic granuloma is a form of {{c1::capillary hemangioma}}.
Treatment for a pyogenic granuloma is usually {{c1::surgical excision}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it's a vascular proliferation.
Often triggered by minor trauma.
Pregnancy-associated gingival lesions often regress after delivery.
Histology shows granulation-like tissue with many capillaries.
It is a benign, reactive process.
microReview: Pyogenic granuloma = Rapidly growing, red, bleeding, pedunculated nodule. High association with pregnancy (gingiva) and trauma (fingers).
examinerTraps: The name is a trap—it does not contain granulomas and isn't caused by infection (pyogenic).
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions 518
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the clinic due to a large, flat, purple area on the right side of his face that has been present since birth and has grown proportionately with him. He also has a history of refractory seizures and hemiparesis. What is the most likely diagnosis for the cutaneous lesion?

explanations.a: Strawberry hemangiomas (capillary hemangiomas) are raised and usually regress; this lesion is flat and permanent.
explanations.b: Nevus flammeus (Port-wine stain) is a permanent vascular ectasia. When it occurs in the trigeminal distribution with seizures, it suggests Sturge-Weber syndrome.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas are typically deeper, mass-forming lesions, not flat birthmarks.
explanations.d: Spider telangiectasias are small, blanching lesions with central arterioles, not large facial stains.
explanations.e: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) presents with multiple small telangiectasias and epistaxis, not a large port-wine stain.

ankiCards: A permanent, flat, purple facial birthmark is called a {{c1::Port-wine stain (nevus flammeus)}}.
Sturge-Weber syndrome triad: Port-wine stain, {{c1::leptomeningeal angioma}}, and glaucoma/seizures.
The Port-wine stain in Sturge-Weber syndrome usually follows the {{c1::trigeminal (CN V)}} nerve distribution.
Unlike strawberry hemangiomas, port-wine stains do {{c1::not}} regress with age.
Nevus flammeus is categorized as a vascular {{c1::ectasia}} (dilation), not a true neoplasm.
keyPoints: Nevus flammeus is the 'ordinary' birthmark.
Port-wine stains are a more extensive form of nevus flammeus.
They thicken and darken over time and do not regress.
Sturge-Weber syndrome involves the brain and the skin (neurocutaneous).
Mental retardation and seizures are common in Sturge-Weber.
microReview: Vascular ectasias are dilations of pre-existing vessels. Port-wine stains (Nevus flammeus) are the classic example. Association with seizures/trigeminal distribution = Sturge-Weber Syndrome.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'strawberry' (regresses) with the 'port-wine' (permanent).
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions 518
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the 'classic' variant of Kaposi Sarcoma, distinguishing it from the 'epidemic' or AIDS-associated variant?

options.a: Highly aggressive with early visceral involvement
options.b: Occurs primarily in young children in Equatorial Africa
options.c: Presents as indolent, distal lower extremity nodules in older men
options.e: Strongly associated with organ transplantation and immunosuppression

explanations.a: This describes the epidemic (AIDS-associated) or lymphadenopathic (African) variants, not the classic form.
explanations.b: This describes the endemic African variant of Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.c: Classic Kaposi Sarcoma typically occurs in older men of Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, or Eastern European descent and is usually limited to the skin of the lower legs.
explanations.d: Classic KS is not associated with HIV, so ART is not applicable; epidemic KS is the form that responds to ART.
explanations.e: This describes transplant-associated Kaposi Sarcoma.

ankiCards: The four types of Kaposi Sarcoma are Classic, Endemic African, {{c1::Transplant-associated}}, and Epidemic (AIDS).
Classic Kaposi Sarcoma is seen in {{c1::older men}} of Mediterranean/Eastern European descent.
The clinical course of Classic KS is usually {{c1::indolent/slow-growing}}.
All forms of Kaposi Sarcoma are associated with {{c1::HHV-8}}.
Endemic African KS is often {{c1::aggressive}} and occurs in children or young adults.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma has 4 distinct epidemiological patterns.
Classic KS is largely restricted to the skin.
Endemic (African) KS is the most common tumor in Central Africa.
Transplant KS occurs due to T-cell immunosuppression.
Epidemic KS is the most common neoplasm in AIDS patients.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma: Classic (Old Mediterranean, leg), Endemic (African, aggressive), Transplant (Imunosuppression), Epidemic (AIDS). All HHV-8 positive.
examinerTraps: The examiner may ask to differentiate the populations. 'Old Mediterranean man' = Classic. 'HIV' = Epidemic.
sourceQuote: Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors 520... Classic Kaposi sarcoma... Endemic African Kaposi sarcoma... Transplant-associated Kaposi sarcoma... AIDS-associated (epidemic) Kaposi sarcoma.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Two principal mechanisms are responsible for the majority of clinically significant vascular diseases. One mechanism involves luminal narrowing or complete obstruction. According to the foundational principles of vascular pathology, what is the second primary mechanism that results in clinical disease?

explanations.a: Weakening of vessel walls is one of the two fundamental mechanisms of vascular disease, leading to dilation (aneurysm) or rupture.
explanations.b: Endothelial hypertrophy is not a primary mechanism of major vascular disease; intimal thickening is a response to injury but not the core mechanism of weakening.
explanations.c: Venous disorders usually involve valvular incompetence (e.g., varicose veins), not excessive competence.
explanations.d: While vascular tumors exist, they are not listed as one of the two principal mechanisms underlying general vascular morbidity and mortality.
explanations.e: Increased hydrostatic pressure is a consequence of disease (like heart failure) rather than a primary mechanism of vessel wall pathology itself.

ankiCards: What are the two principal mechanisms underlying vascular disease? {{c1::Narrowing/obstruction}} and {{c2::weakening of walls}}.
Vessel wall weakening leads to either {{c1::dilation}} or {{c2::rupture}}.
The most clinically significant vascular lesions typically involve {{c1::arteries}}.
Narrowing of vessel lumens can occur progressively through {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Precipitous obstruction of a vessel lumen is usually caused by {{c1::thrombosis}} or {{c2::embolism}}.
keyPoints: Vascular pathology is a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality.
The two primary drivers of disease are luminal obstruction and wall weakening.
Obstruction can be chronic (atherosclerosis) or acute (thrombosis).
Wall weakening results in aneurysms or dissections.
Arterial lesions are generally more clinically significant than venous ones.
Structural specializations in vessels reflect their specific functional roles.
microReview: Vascular disease manifests through two main pathways: either the pipe gets blocked (stenosis/thrombosis) or the pipe wall fails (aneurysm/rupture).
examinerTraps: Do not confuse the response to injury (intimal thickening) with the primary mechanisms of disease (obstruction/weakening).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: The structural integrity of the aortic wall depends on the balance between extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis and degradation. Which of the following biochemical changes is most directly associated with the wall weakening observed in abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA)?

options.a: Decreased production of reactive oxygen species
options.b: Inhibition of macrophage infiltration into the media
options.d: Enhanced synthesis of tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs)
options.e: Stabilization of the internal elastic lamina

explanations.a: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are actually increased in AAA, contributing to oxidative stress and matrix degradation.
explanations.b: AAA is characterized by increased inflammatory infiltration (macrophages and T cells), which secrete proteases.
explanations.c: Increased MMP activity (especially MMP-2 and MMP-9) leads to the degradation of elastin and collagen, weakening the media.
explanations.d: TIMPs inhibit MMPs; in AAA, the balance shifts toward MMPs, meaning TIMP activity is relatively insufficient.
explanations.e: Aneurysms are characterized by the fragmentation and loss of the elastic lamina, not its stabilization.

ankiCards: The primary enzyme class responsible for ECM degradation in aneurysms is {{c1::Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
In AAA, the balance between MMPs and {{c1::TIMPs}} is disrupted.
The two specific MMPs often overexpressed in aortic aneurysms are {{c1::MMP-2}} and {{c2::MMP-9}}.
Inflammatory cells in the aneurysm wall, such as {{c1::macrophages}}, produce proteases that degrade the media.
Degradation of {{c1::elastin}} and {{c2::collagen}} is the hallmark of aortic wall weakening.
keyPoints: AAA involves a chronic inflammatory infiltrate in the aortic wall.
Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) are the chief effectors of matrix degradation.
Atherosclerosis is a major risk factor for AAA as it compromises nutrient diffusion to the media.
The media undergoes thinning and loss of smooth muscle cells.
Aneurysm formation requires the degradation of the structural proteins collagen and elastin.
microReview: AAA = Inflammation + MMPs > TIMPs + Elastin/Collagen degradation = Wall weakening.
examinerTraps: Atherosclerosis causes AAA not just by blocking blood, but by causing medial ischemia and inflammation that degrades the wall.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history and hypertension presents for a routine physical examination. A non-tender, pulsatile mass is palpated in the midline of the abdomen at the level of the umbilicus. Imaging confirms a 5.2 cm dilation of the infrarenal aorta. What is the most likely underlying pathophysiology of this condition?

options.a: Cystic medial degeneration related to fibrillin mutations
options.c: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.d: Granulomatous inflammation of the aortic arch
options.e: Congenital defect in the internal elastic lamina

explanations.a: Cystic medial degeneration is more typical of thoracic aortic aneurysms, often associated with Marfan syndrome or hypertension.
explanations.b: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are most commonly caused by atherosclerosis, which limits nutrient diffusion from the lumen to the media, causing wall weakening.
explanations.c: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum is the hallmark of tertiary syphilis, which typically affects the ascending aorta (thoracic).
explanations.d: Granulomatous inflammation (e.g., Takayasu arteritis) affects the aortic arch and its branches, not typically the infrarenal aorta.
explanations.e: Congenital defects (like those in Berry aneurysms) involve the Circle of Willis, not the abdominal aorta.

ankiCards: The most common location for an atherosclerotic aneurysm is the {{c1::abdominal aorta}}.
The majority of abdominal aortic aneurysms are located {{c1::infrarenal}} (below the renal arteries).
The two most significant risk factors for AAA are {{c1::smoking}} and {{c2::male gender}}.
Atherosclerosis causes the media to weaken by {{c1::impeding nutrient diffusion}} from the lumen.
A {{c1::pulsatile mass}} on physical exam is a classic finding for AAA.
keyPoints: AAA is usually infrarenal and supra-iliac.
Atherosclerosis is the dominant predisposing factor for AAA.
Risk of rupture increases significantly once the diameter exceeds 5.0 - 5.5 cm.
Clinical presentation is often asymptomatic until rupture occurs.
Smoking is a stronger risk factor for AAA than for atherosclerosis in other beds.
microReview: Older male smoker + pulsatile abdominal mass = AAA. Pathogenesis = Atherosclerosis leading to medial thinning.
examinerTraps: The examiner may try to link hypertension primarily to AAA, but while relevant, atherosclerosis and smoking are more definitive for the abdominal location.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In certain genetic syndromes, such as Marfan syndrome, the development of thoracic aortic aneurysms is linked to the dysregulation of which signaling pathway?

explanations.a: The Wnt pathway is involved in development and cancer, not primarily in the weakening of the aortic media in Marfan syndrome.
explanations.b: While inflammation is involved in AAA, Marfan-related TAA is primarily a connective tissue/signaling disorder.
explanations.c: Fibrillin-1 mutations in Marfan syndrome lead to increased bioavailability of TGF-β, which induces metalloproteinase activity and matrix degradation.
explanations.d: VEGF is involved in angiogenesis, not the structural breakdown of the aortic media.
explanations.e: The CDK pathway regulates the cell cycle and is not the driver of aneurysmal dilation in Marfan syndrome.

ankiCards: Marfan syndrome is caused by mutations in the {{c1::Fibrillin-1 (FBN1)}} gene.
Fibrillin-1 mutations lead to increased signaling of {{c1::TGF-beta}}.
Increased TGF-beta signaling in the aorta leads to {{c1::elastic fiber}} fragmentation.
Loeys-Dietz syndrome involves mutations in {{c1::TGF-beta receptors}}.
The histological change in the media in Marfan syndrome is called {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder of connective tissue.
Fibrillin-1 normally sequesters TGF-β; its deficiency leads to excess active TGF-β.
TGF-β signaling increases the production of matrix metalloproteinases.
This leads to 'cystic medial degeneration' (loss of SMCs and elastic tissue).
Thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections are the leading causes of death in Marfan patients.
microReview: Marfan = Fibrillin-1 mutation -> High TGF-β -> Matrix degradation -> Thoracic Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Marfan (Fibrillin-1) with Ehlers-Danlos (Collagen Type III) as the primary cause of TGF-beta dysregulation.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes a 'false' aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm), as distinguished from a 'true' aneurysm?

options.a: A wall defect allowing blood to form an extravascular hematoma
options.b: A localized dilation involving all three layers of the vessel wall
options.c: A longitudinal tear in the media forming a second blood-filled channel
options.d: A diffuse, circumferential dilation of a long segment of the artery
options.e: An asymmetric bulging of only one side of the vessel wall

explanations.a: A false aneurysm is a breach in the vascular wall leading to an extravascular hematoma that freely communicates with the intravascular space ('pulsating hematoma').
explanations.b: This describes a 'true' aneurysm, which must involve the intima, media, and adventitia (or a thinned-out version of them).
explanations.c: This describes an aortic dissection, which is not a true aneurysm (though they can coexist).
explanations.d: This describes a 'fusiform' aneurysm, which is a subtype of a true aneurysm.
explanations.e: This describes a 'saccular' aneurysm, which is a subtype of a true aneurysm.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the arterial wall (intima, media, adventitia).
A {{c1::false}} aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) is a wall defect that results in an extravascular hematoma.
An example of a false aneurysm is a leak at a {{c1::vascular graft}} junction.
A {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm is a spherical dilation involving only a portion of the wall circumference.
A {{c1::fusiform}} aneurysm is a circumferential, spindle-shaped dilation of the vessel.
keyPoints: True aneurysms involve all layers of the vessel wall.
False aneurysms are essentially contained hematomas outside the vessel wall.
Aortic dissection involves blood entering the wall itself, separating the layers.
Saccular aneurysms are often seen in the Circle of Willis (Berry aneurysms).
Fusiform aneurysms are most common in the abdominal aorta.
microReview: True = Wall expands (all layers). False = Wall breaks (blood leaks out but is contained). Dissection = Wall splits.
examinerTraps: Aortic dissection is frequently mislabeled as an 'aneurysm' by students, but it is a separate pathological process involving a mural hematoma.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 74-year-old male with a history of poorly controlled hypertension presents with sudden, excruciating 'tearing' chest pain that radiates to his back. His blood pressure is 190/110 mmHg. A chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum. Which of the following is the most likely initiating event for this patient's condition?

options.a: Rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque in the abdominal aorta
options.b: Infection of the vessel wall by Salmonella species
options.c: An intimal tear allowing blood to enter the media
options.d: Autoimmune destruction of the internal elastic lamina
options.e: Saccular dilation of the middle cerebral artery

explanations.a: Atherosclerotic plaque rupture typically causes thrombosis or embolism, not a tearing chest pain with mediastinal widening.
explanations.b: Salmonella can cause mycotic aneurysms, but the clinical presentation of tearing pain and hypertension strongly points to dissection.
explanations.c: The patient's presentation is classic for aortic dissection, where an intimal tear allows pressurized blood to create a cleavage plane in the media.
explanations.d: This describes giant cell arteritis, which typically causes headache and jaw claudication rather than sudden tearing chest pain.
explanations.e: This describes a Berry aneurysm, which would present with a subarachnoid hemorrhage (sudden 'worst headache of life').

ankiCards: The most common risk factor for aortic dissection is {{c1::hypertension}}.
The classic symptom of aortic dissection is {{c1::sudden, tearing/ripping pain}}.
Aortic dissection occurs when blood enters a tear in the {{c1::intima}}.
The blood in a dissection creates a channel within the {{c1::tunica media}}.
A common radiographic finding in aortic dissection is a {{c1::widened mediastinum}}.
keyPoints: Aortic dissection is often a catastrophic event.
Hypertension is the most common predisposing factor in older adults.
In younger patients, connective tissue disorders (Marfan) are more common causes.
The dissection can rupture back into the lumen (double-barreled aorta) or outward (fatal hemorrhage).
Type A dissections involve the ascending aorta and are surgical emergencies.
microReview: HTN + Tearing Chest Pain + Widened Mediastinum = Aortic Dissection. Mechanism = Intimal tear.
examinerTraps: Aortic dissection is NOT always associated with an aneurysm. It can occur in an aorta of normal diameter if the media is weakened by hypertension.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: The pathogenesis of an abdominal aortic aneurysm is largely driven by a chronic inflammatory response. Which cell type is primarily responsible for secreting the elastolytic and collagenolytic enzymes that lead to medial destruction in these cases?

explanations.a: Endothelial cells line the vessel but are not the primary source of the degradative enzymes in the media of an AAA.
explanations.b: Infiltrating macrophages in the aortic wall produce matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) such as MMP-9, which are critical for the degradation of the media.
explanations.c: Eosinophils are associated with allergic reactions and some vasculitides (Churg-Strauss), but not the standard pathogenesis of AAA.
explanations.d: Platelets are involved in thrombosis but do not drive the chronic remodeling and medial weakening of the aortic wall.
explanations.e: While fibroblasts are involved in repair and fibrosis, they are not the primary drivers of the destruction seen in the inflammatory phase of AAA.

ankiCards: In AAA, {{c1::macrophages}} are the main inflammatory cells producing proteases.
The enzyme {{c1::MMP-9}} is highly expressed by macrophages in aneurysmal walls.
Chronic inflammation in AAA is often triggered by products of {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Loss of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} in the media is a common feature of aneurysm progression.
The destruction of {{c1::elastin}} allows for the initial dilation of the vessel.
keyPoints: AAA involves a transmural inflammatory infiltrate.
Macrophages and T cells are the predominant inflammatory cells.
Cytokines like TNF and IL-1 promote MMP production.
The resulting loss of elastic fibers and collagen leads to wall expansion.
Genetic factors and smoking exacerbate this inflammatory environment.
microReview: Atherosclerosis -> Macrophages -> MMPs -> Media destruction -> AAA.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'inflammation' of atherosclerosis (subendothelial) with the 'inflammation' of AAA (often transmural/medial).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 52-year-old male with a history of intravenous drug use presents with fever and a painful, rapidly enlarging mass in his right groin. On examination, the mass is pulsatile and erythematous. Blood cultures are positive for Staphylococcus aureus. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Berry aneurysms occur in the Circle of Willis and are not associated with peripheral infection or IV drug use.
explanations.b: Atherosclerotic aneurysms are usually slow-growing and non-febrile; they are not caused by acute bacterial seeding.
explanations.c: A mycotic aneurysm is an aneurysm resulting from an infection that weakens the vessel wall (often from bacteremia or septic emboli).
explanations.d: Syphilitic aneurysms typically affect the thoracic aorta and are a manifestation of tertiary syphilis, not acute staph bacteremia.
explanations.e: A dissecting hematoma (aortic dissection) is typically not associated with localized infection or peripheral pulsatile masses in the groin.

ankiCards: A {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm is caused by infection of the arterial wall.
The most common cause of mycotic aneurysms in IV drug users is {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}.
Infection can reach the vessel wall via {{c1::bacteremia}} or {{c2::septic emboli}}.
Mycotic aneurysms are characterized by {{c1::rapid growth}} and risk of rupture.
The term 'mycotic' is a misnomer, as most are {{c1::bacterial}} in origin.
keyPoints: Mycotic aneurysms result from microbial seeding of the wall.
They can occur from bacteremia, septic emboli, or adjacent abscesses.
Common organisms include Salmonella and Staphylococcus.
Inflammation leads to rapid destruction of the media and adventitia.
Patients often present with systemic signs of infection (fever, leukocytosis).
microReview: Fever + Pulsatile mass + Positive blood cultures = Mycotic Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: The term 'mycotic' sounds like 'fungal', but in pathology, it refers to any infected aneurysm, most commonly bacterial.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the effect of chronic hypertension on the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta, which subsequently predisposes to thoracic aortic aneurysms?

explanations.a: Hypertension causes narrowing, not neovascularization, of the vasa vasorum.
explanations.b: Hypertension causes hyaline arteriolosclerosis of the vasa vasorum, narrowing their lumens and causing ischemic injury to the outer media.
explanations.c: Dilation does not occur; instead, the vessels are narrowed by wall thickening.
explanations.d: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in malignant hypertension and small-vessel vasculitis, but the chronic change in vasa vasorum leading to aneurysm is hyaline thickening.
explanations.e: Arteriovenous shunts are not a feature of hypertensive changes in the vasa vasorum.

ankiCards: Hypertension leads to {{c1::hyaline}} thickening of the vasa vasorum.
Ischemia of the {{c1::outer media}} occurs when the vasa vasorum are narrowed.
Ischemic injury in the aortic media leads to the loss of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}}.
The loss of smooth muscle and elastic tissue is called {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
Cystic medial degeneration is the hallmark of {{c1::thoracic}} aortic aneurysms.
keyPoints: The thoracic aorta relies on vasa vasorum for nutrients to the outer media.
Hypertension causes 'degenerative' changes in these small supply vessels.
Ischemia leads to medial weakening and scarring.
Hypertension is the most common cause of non-genetic thoracic aortic aneurysms.
This process is distinct from the atherosclerosis that drives AAA.
microReview: HTN -> Vasa Vasorum narrowing -> Medial Ischemia -> Medial Weakening -> Thoracic Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Students often assume atherosclerosis causes all aneurysms. However, hypertension-induced vasa vasorum ischemia is the more common driver for thoracic aneurysms.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Tertiary syphilis is a classic, though now rare, cause of aneurysms. In which segment of the vascular system do these aneurysms characteristically occur?

explanations.a: Syphilitic (luetic) aneurysms characteristically involve the ascending aorta and aortic arch due to obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum.
explanations.b: Atherosclerotic aneurysms typically involve the infrarenal abdominal aorta, not syphilitic ones.
explanations.c: Common iliac involvements are usually extensions of abdominal aortic aneurysms.
explanations.d: Popliteal aneurysms are often peripheral manifestations of generalized atherosclerotic aneurysmal disease.
explanations.e: Aneurysms in the middle cerebral artery are typically 'Berry' aneurysms, which are congenital/hemodynamic, not syphilitic.

ankiCards: Syphilitic aneurysms occur in the {{c1::ascending}} aorta.
The characteristic histopathology of syphilis in the aorta is {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}}.
The vessels targeted by syphilis in the aortic wall are the {{c1::vasa vasorum}}.
Syphilitic aortitis results in a {{c1::tree-bark}} appearance of the intima.
The dilation of the aortic root in syphilis can lead to {{c1::aortic valve insufficiency}}.
keyPoints: Tertiary syphilis causes 'luetic' aortitis.
It targets the vasa vasorum, causing an inflammatory response and ischemia.
The resulting scarring causes the 'tree-bark' intimal appearance.
It primarily affects the thoracic segment (ascending/arch).
Death usually occurs from heart failure (due to aortic regurgitation) or rupture.
microReview: Syphilis -> Vasa Vasorum inflammation -> Ischemic media -> Thoracic Aneurysm + Tree-bark intima.
examinerTraps: Atherosclerosis and Syphilis both affect the aorta, but Syphilis is 'thoracic and medial/adventitial' while Atherosclerosis is 'abdominal and intimal/medial'.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old male with a history of HIV and a CD4+ count of 150/mm³ presents with several painless, dark-purple, maculopapular lesions on his lower extremities. A skin biopsy reveals proliferation of spindle cells forming slit-like spaces containing extravasated red blood cells. Which of the following infectious agents is most likely associated with this patient's condition?

explanations.a: HHV-8, also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of Kaposi sarcoma, which is characterized by spindle cells and slit-like vascular spaces.
explanations.b: HPV-16 is primarily associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx, not vascular tumors.
explanations.c: EBV is associated with various lymphomas (e.g., Burkitt) and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, but not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.d: CMV can cause retinitis and colitis in AIDS patients but does not drive the formation of these vascular lesions.
explanations.e: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised patients, which may look similar clinically but shows a neutrophilic infiltrate rather than slit-like spaces with spindle cells.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is associated with which virus? {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}
The characteristic histological feature of Kaposi Sarcoma includes {{c1::spindle cells}} and slit-like spaces.
{{c1::AIDS-associated (Epidemic)}} Kaposi sarcoma is the most common HIV-related malignancy.
In Kaposi sarcoma, the slit-like spaces typically contain {{c1::extravasated red blood cells}}.
Name the vascular tumor associated with spindle cell proliferation in HIV patients: {{c1::Kaposi Sarcoma}}
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8.
There are four clinical forms: Classic (older Mediterranean men), Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated (Epidemic).
Histology typically shows spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces, and extravasated RBCs.
It is considered an intermediate-grade (borderline) tumor.
In AIDS patients, it is the most common malignancy and often involves skin, mouth, and GI tract.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) = HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Slit-like spaces + RBCs. Bacillary Angiomatosis (BA) = Bartonella + Neutrophils + Capillary proliferation.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Kaposi sarcoma with Bacillary angiomatosis. Both occur in AIDS patients as purple skin lesions, but KS has spindle cells (HHV-8) while BA has neutrophilic inflammation (Bartonella).
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors are divided into three categories: (1) benign tumors... (2) intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors... (3) malignant tumors... Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm caused by human herpesvirus 8.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with an intensely painful, small blue nodule (5 mm) located under the fingernail of her right index finger. She notes the pain is significantly exacerbated by cold exposure. Which of the following is the most likely cellular origin of this lesion?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.b: Endothelial cells line the vascular spaces but are not the primary proliferating cell type in a glomus tumor.
explanations.c: While many tumors arise from mesenchymal cells, the specific diagnosis of glomus tumor is tied to the specialized glomus cells.
explanations.d: Lymphatic endothelial cells would characterize a lymphangioma, which is typically painless.
explanations.e: Pericytes are found in hemangiopericytomas, which are distinct from the classic subungual glomus tumor.

ankiCards: A subungual, exquisitely painful tumor sensitive to cold is likely a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells.
The glomus body is a specialized {{c1::arteriovenous anastomosis}} involved in thermoregulation.
The most common location for a glomus tumor is the {{c1::subungual (under fingernail)}} region.
True/False: Glomus tumors are malignant. {{c1::False (they are benign)}}
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign, extremely painful neoplasms.
Classically located in the distal portion of digits, especially subungual.
Arise from glomus bodies (thermoregulatory AV shunts).
Exquisite sensitivity to cold is a diagnostic hallmark.
Histologically show nests of uniform, round 'glomus cells' around vascular spaces.
microReview: Subungual + Pain + Cold Sensitivity = Glomus Tumor (Smooth Muscle Origin).
examinerTraps: Wait for the 'cold sensitivity' or 'subungual' keyword; otherwise, a blue nodule could be many things. Glomus tumors are benign, not malignant.
sourceQuote: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, exquisitely painful tumors arising from specialized smooth muscle cells of glomus bodies.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male who worked in a polyvinyl chloride (PVC) manufacturing plant for 30 years presents with weight loss, fatigue, and abdominal pain. Imaging reveals multiple mass lesions in the liver. A biopsy shows malignant cells that express CD31 and show prominent nuclear pleomorphism with irregular vascular channels. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor associated with exposure to vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast. CD31 is a specific marker for endothelial differentiation.
explanations.b: Hepatocellular carcinoma is associated with cirrhosis and hepatitis but does not express the vascular marker CD31.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas are the most common benign liver tumors and do not show malignancy or nuclear pleomorphism.
explanations.d: Hepatic adenomas are benign and associated with oral contraceptive use, not PVC exposure.
explanations.e: Cholangiocarcinoma arises from bile duct epithelium and does not present as a malignant vascular tumor.

ankiCards: The most specific immunohistochemical marker for angiosarcoma is {{c1::CD31 (or vWF)}}.
Exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride (or arsenic/Thorotrast)}} is a risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma.
Angiosarcoma is a {{c1::malignant}} neoplasm of endothelial cells.
What is the prognosis for most patients with angiosarcoma? {{c1::Poor (highly aggressive)}}
Cutaneous angiosarcoma can occur in the setting of chronic {{c1::lymphedema}} (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms.
Risk factors include vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast (for liver) and radiation (for skin).
CD31 is the classic immunohistochemical marker for vascular origin.
Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to angiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphedema (e.g., post-mastectomy).
They are highly aggressive with a poor 5-year survival rate.
microReview: Angiosarcoma = CD31+ + Vinyl Chloride + Highly Malignant Endothelium.
examinerTraps: The examiner may give the chemical exposure (vinyl chloride) and expect you to know it causes angiosarcoma specifically in the liver.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms... Hepatic angiosarcomas are associated with distinct carcinogens, including arsenic... and polyvinyl chloride.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the categorization of vascular neoplasms, which of the following is strictly classified as an 'intermediate-grade (borderline)' tumor, possessing biological behavior between benign hemangiomas and highly malignant angiosarcomas?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma and hemangioendothelioma are the classic examples of intermediate-grade vascular tumors.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign capillary hemangioma.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangioma is a benign tumor.
explanations.d: Cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) is a benign tumor of the lymphatics.
explanations.e: Glomus tumor is a benign neoplasm of specialized smooth muscle cells.

ankiCards: Name an intermediate-grade vascular tumor: {{c1::Kaposi sarcoma (or Hemangioendothelioma)}}.
True/False: Glomus tumors are intermediate-grade. {{c1::False (they are benign)}}
True/False: Angiosarcoma is intermediate-grade. {{c1::False (it is malignant)}}
The biological behavior of {{c1::intermediate-grade}} tumors is between benign and malignant.
Kaposi sarcoma is caused by which virus? {{c1::HHV-8}}
keyPoints: Vascular tumors are tiered: Benign, Intermediate, and Malignant.
Benign examples: Hemangiomas, Glomus tumors, Lymphangiomas.
Intermediate examples: Kaposi sarcoma, Hemangioendotheliomas.
Malignant examples: Angiosarcoma, Hemangiopericytoma (some forms).
Intermediate tumors are locally aggressive but have lower metastatic potential than angiosarcoma.
microReview: Benign (Hemangioma) -> Intermediate (Kaposi) -> Malignant (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'locally aggressive' with 'highly malignant'. Kaposi sarcoma rarely kills quickly through metastasis, unlike angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors... Intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors: Kaposi sarcoma and hemangioendothelioma.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 2-week-old female infant is brought to the pediatrician for a bright red, raised 'strawberry-like' lesion on her scalp that has been growing since birth. The parents are concerned about its appearance. Which of the following is the most likely natural history of this lesion?

options.c: Persistent growth proportional to the child's height

explanations.a: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are very common in newborns, grow rapidly for a few months, and then typically regress spontaneously by age 7.
explanations.b: Benign hemangiomas almost never transform into malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.c: While they grow initially, they do not grow indefinitely; they undergo involution.
explanations.d: Very large cavernous hemangiomas or hepatic hemangiomas can cause high-output heart failure, but a small scalp strawberry hemangioma does not.
explanations.e: Von Hippel-Lindau disease is associated with cavernous hemangiomas and hemangioblastomas, not the typical strawberry (capillary) hemangioma of infancy.

ankiCards: Juvenile hemangiomas are also known as {{c1::strawberry}} hemangiomas.
Strawberry hemangiomas typically {{c1::regress/involute}} by age 7.
A strawberry hemangioma is histologically a type of {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma.
At what age do most strawberry hemangiomas disappear? {{c1::7 (usually 5-7)}}
True/False: Strawberry hemangiomas require immediate surgical removal. {{c1::False (wait for regression)}}
keyPoints: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are common in newborns (1 in 200 births).
They are capillary hemangiomas.
Characterized by rapid growth followed by slow regression.
Complete involution occurs in 90% of cases by age 7.
Management is usually observational unless they obstruct vision or the airway.
microReview: Infant + Red Scalp Mass = Strawberry Hemangioma = Regresses by age 7.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse 'Juvenile' (strawberry/capillary) with 'Cavernous' hemangiomas. Cavernous ones are deeper, less likely to regress, and more likely to be part of a syndrome like VHL.
sourceQuote: Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) of the skin of newborns are very common... they grow rapidly for a few months but then fade and regressed... by age 7.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular conditions is characterized by a rapidly growing, pedunculated red nodule on the skin or gingiva, often following trauma or during pregnancy, and histologically represents a lobular capillary hemangioma?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is neither pyogenic nor a granuloma, but a lobular capillary hemangioma that often occurs on the gingiva ('pregnancy tumor').
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella and occurs in immunocompromised hosts, not typically triggered by pregnancy/trauma in healthy individuals.
explanations.c: Cystic hygromas are lymphatic malformations often found in the neck of infants.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are painful subungual lesions, not pedunculated gingival nodules.
explanations.e: Spider angiomas are non-neoplastic vascular ectasias associated with hyperestrogenic states (cirrhosis/pregnancy) but are not nodules.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is histologically a {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
A common site for pyogenic granuloma in pregnant women is the {{c1::gingiva (gums)}}.
True/False: Pyogenic granulomas contain pus. {{c1::False (misnomer)}}
The clinical appearance of a pyogenic granuloma is a {{c1::pedunculated}} red nodule.
Pyogenic granulomas often occur after minor {{c1::trauma}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma = Lobular capillary hemangioma.
Commonly occurs on skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
Associated with pregnancy ('granuloma gravidarum').
Often bleeds easily because it is highly vascular.
Despite the name, it is not an infection and not a true granuloma.
microReview: Pregnant + Gingival growth = Pyogenic Granuloma (Lobular Capillary Hemangioma).
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic' suggests infection (pus) and 'granuloma' suggests macrophages/giant cells; the trap is that it has neither. It is purely vascular.
sourceQuote: Pyogenic granulomas are capillary hemangiomas that manifest as rapidly growing pedunculated red nodules on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 26-year-old male with advanced AIDS presents with numerous red-to-purple skin papules. Biopsy shows a proliferation of capillaries with prominent 'epithelioid' endothelial cells and a dense infiltrate of neutrophils. A Warthin-Starry silver stain reveals clusters of small bacilli. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella (henselae or quintana) and is characterized by capillary proliferation with neutrophils and visible bacilli on silver stain.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma lacks neutrophils and bacilli; it shows spindle cells and slit-like spaces.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma shows high-grade malignancy and pleomorphism, not bacilli or acute inflammation.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign capillary hemangioma and is not typically associated with silver-stain positive bacilli.
explanations.e: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated blood-filled spaces and are not associated with infection.

ankiCards: {{c1::Bacillary angiomatosis}} is caused by Bartonella species in immunocompromised patients.
Histology of Bacillary Angiomatosis shows {{c1::neutrophils}} and epithelioid endothelial cells.
Which stain is used to visualize Bartonella in Bacillary Angiomatosis? {{c1::Warthin-Starry (silver) stain}}.
The causative agent of Bacillary Angiomatosis is usually transmitted by {{c1::cats}} (B. henselae) or lice (B. quintana).
Unlike Kaposi sarcoma, Bacillary Angiomatosis responds to {{c1::antibiotics}} (e.g., erythromycin).
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts.
Caused by Bartonella henselae or Bartonella quintana.
Histology: Capillaries, neutrophils, and nuclear dust.
Diagnosis: Warthin-Starry stain showing bacilli.
Important differential for Kaposi sarcoma in HIV/AIDS patients.
microReview: AIDS + Neutrophils + Silver Stain + Vascular Papules = Bacillary Angiomatosis.
examinerTraps: The most common trap is confusing this with Kaposi sarcoma. Remember: Neutrophils + Bacilli = Bacillary Angiomatosis; Spindle cells = Kaposi.
sourceQuote: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts... caused by opportunistic gram-negative bacilli of the Bartonella family.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following features best distinguishes a cavernous lymphangioma (cystic hygroma) from a cavernous hemangioma on histological examination?

options.a: Absence of red blood cells in the lumina
options.b: Presence of a thick muscular wall
options.c: Expression of CD31 by lining cells
options.d: Presence of spindle cells and slit-like spaces
options.e: Infiltration of the surrounding stroma by neutrophils

explanations.a: Lymphangiomas contain proteinaceous lymph fluid but lack red blood cells, whereas hemangiomas are filled with blood.
explanations.b: Neither cavernous lymphangiomas nor hemangiomas typically have thick muscular walls; they are thin-walled.
explanations.c: Both lymphatic and blood vessel endothelial cells can express CD31, so it does not distinguish between them well (though Podoplanin/D2-40 is more specific for lymphatics).
explanations.d: Spindle cells and slit-like spaces are characteristic of Kaposi sarcoma, not benign cavernous lesions.
explanations.e: Neutrophilic infiltration is characteristic of bacillary angiomatosis, not cavernous lymphangiomas.

ankiCards: A cystic hygroma is a type of {{c1::cavernous lymphangioma}}.
Cystic hygromas are commonly associated with {{c1::Turner syndrome}}.
The fluid inside a lymphangioma lumina typically lacks {{c1::red blood cells}}.
Where are cystic hygromas most commonly located? {{c1::Neck (or axilla)}}.
Unlike hemangiomas, lymphangiomas are filled with {{c1::lymph (proteinaceous fluid)}}.
keyPoints: Cystic hygroma is a large cavernous lymphangioma.
Typically found in the neck or axilla of children.
Associated with Turner syndrome and Down syndrome.
Histologically: Large spaces lined by endothelium, containing lymph, no RBCs.
Margins are often poorly defined, making surgical resection difficult.
microReview: Neck mass + Transilluminates + Turner Syndrome = Cystic Hygroma.
examinerTraps: Examiners often link cystic hygroma with Turner syndrome (45,X). Also, remember that 'cavernous' just means large spaces; the contents (blood vs. lymph) determine the name.
sourceQuote: Cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) are typically found in the neck or axilla of children... [they] are composed of large, dilated lymphatic spaces.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular ectasias are not true neoplasms but rather permanent dilations of preexisting vessels. Which of the following is a classic example of a 'birthmark' vascular ectasia that, if found in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve, may be associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome?

explanations.a: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a common vascular ectasia. When it occurs in the trigeminal nerve distribution, it can be part of Sturge-Weber syndrome.
explanations.b: Spider angiomas are acquired ectasias related to high estrogen levels, not congenital birthmarks.
explanations.c: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) involves multiple small malformations, not a single large 'port-wine' birthmark.
explanations.d: Capillary hemangioma is a true neoplasm (proliferation of vessels), not just an ectasia (dilation).
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation.

ankiCards: A port-wine stain is medically known as {{c1::nevus flammeus}}.
Sturge-Weber syndrome involves a nevus flammeus in the distribution of the {{c1::trigeminal (CN V)}} nerve.
Sturge-Weber syndrome includes port-wine stains, glaucoma, and {{c1::leptomeningeal angiomas}}.
Unlike strawberry hemangiomas, a nevus flammeus {{c1::does not}} regress with age.
Nevus flammeus is categorized as a vascular {{c1::ectasia}} (dilation), not a neoplasm.
keyPoints: Nevus flammeus is a 'port-wine stain'.
It is a vascular ectasia, not a neoplasm.
Sturge-Weber syndrome: Trigeminal port-wine stain + Leptomeningeal angioma + Mental retardation + Seizures + Glaucoma.
These lesions grow with the child and do not spontaneously regress.
Histologically shows dilated vessels in the dermis.
microReview: CN V distribution + Port-wine stain = Sturge-Weber syndrome risk.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse the 'strawberry hemangioma' (which regresses) with the 'port-wine stain' (which persists).
sourceQuote: Nevus flammeus (the ordinary 'birthmark') is the most common form of vascular ectasia... a port-wine stain is a special form... in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve... [associated with] Sturge-Weber syndrome.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following benign vascular tumors is most common in the liver and spleen and is characterized by the presence of large, cavernous, blood-filled vascular spaces separated by a sparse connective tissue stroma?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas are the most common benign tumors of the liver and consist of large, dilated, blood-filled spaces.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas consist of small, thin-walled capillaries and are more common in the skin or mucous membranes.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are small, painful, and typically found in the distal digits, not the liver.
explanations.d: Angiosarcomas are malignant and show nuclear atypia, unlike the benign cavernous hemangioma.
explanations.e: Hemangioendotheliomas are intermediate-grade tumors with more solid growth patterns.

ankiCards: The most common benign tumor of the liver is the {{c1::cavernous hemangioma}}.
Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large {{c1::blood-filled}} spaces.
True/False: Cavernous hemangiomas often regress spontaneously. {{c1::False (unlike capillary/strawberry ones)}}
Large cavernous hemangiomas may be complicated by {{c1::thrombosis (or calcification)}}.
In von Hippel-Lindau disease, cavernous hemangiomas occur in the {{c1::cerebellum/brainstem/retina/pancreas}}.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are common, often incidental findings.
They do not regress.
Most common in the liver and spleen.
