Histology: Large, thin-walled vascular channels filled with blood.
Clinical significance: Can be mistaken for a malignant tumor on imaging (needs centripetal enhancement on CT/MRI).
microReview: Liver Mass + Incidental + Benign = Cavernous Hemangioma.
examinerTraps: A common clinical trap is a biopsy of a suspected hepatic cavernous hemangioma, which is generally avoided due to the risk of significant hemorrhage.
sourceQuote: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, dilated vascular channels... They are more common in the liver and spleen.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male presents for a routine check-up. He has a 45 pack-year smoking history and long-standing untreated hypertension. Physical examination reveals a non-tender, pulsatile abdominal mass below the level of the umbilicus. Imaging confirms a 5.2-cm localized dilation of the infrarenal aorta. Which of the following is the most likely primary pathological mechanism responsible for this patient’s condition?

options.a: Cystic medial degeneration of the elastic tissue
options.b: Atherosclerotic remodeling of the vessel wall
options.c: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.d: Congenital defect in the media layer (berry type)
options.e: Granulomatous inflammation of the tunica media

explanations.a: Cystic medial degeneration is more characteristic of thoracic aortic aneurysms, often associated with Marfan syndrome, rather than the more common atherosclerotic abdominal aortic aneurysm.
explanations.b: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are primarily driven by atherosclerosis. The plaque compromises nutrient diffusion to the media, leading to secondary atrophy and weakening of the wall.
explanations.c: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum is the hallmark of tertiary syphilis, which typically affects the ascending (thoracic) aorta, not the infrarenal abdominal aorta.
explanations.d: Congenital defects in the media are associated with berry aneurysms in the Circle of Willis, which can lead to subarachnoid hemorrhage, but not large abdominal dilations.
explanations.e: Granulomatous inflammation of the media is characteristic of vasculitides like Giant Cell Arteritis or Takayasu Arteritis, rather than the smoking-related dilation described.

ankiCards: The most common cause of an abdominal aortic aneurysm is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
In an abdominal aortic aneurysm, the plaque causes {{c1::atrophy}} of the vessel media by blocking nutrient diffusion.
A pulsatile abdominal mass in an older male smoker is most likely an {{c1::abdominal aortic aneurysm}}.
The classic location for an atherosclerotic aneurysm is the {{c1::infrarenal}} aorta.
Two principal mechanisms of vascular disease are narrowing of the lumen and {{c1::weakening of the vessel wall}}.
keyPoints: Atherosclerosis is the dominant risk factor for AAA.
The infrarenal abdominal aorta is the most common site for AAA.
Pathogenesis involves transmural inflammation and degradation of the extracellular matrix.
Atherosclerotic plaques compromise oxygen/nutrient delivery to the tunica media.
Smoking is a major modifiable risk factor for AAA development and expansion.
microReview: Aneurysms represent a localized permanent dilation of a vessel. True aneurysms involve all three layers (intima, media, adventitia). AAAs are mostly atherosclerotic, occurring below the renal arteries and above the iliac bifurcation.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the site: AAA is usually infrarenal; syphilis-related aneurysms are usually in the ascending aorta/arch.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular wall weakening is a fundamental mechanism of disease that leads to dilation or rupture. In the pathogenesis of aortic aneurysms, an imbalance in which of the following processes is most directly responsible for the destruction of the elastic and collagenous framework of the tunica media?

options.b: Decreased production of Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF)
options.c: Increased levels of Tissue Inhibitor of Metalloproteinases (TIMPs)
options.d: Suppression of Transforming Growth Factor-beta (TGF-β) signaling
options.e: Decreased activation of the Renin-Angiotensin system

explanations.a: Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMPs) derived from inflammatory cells degrade the extracellular matrix (elastin and collagen). An excess of MMPs relative to their inhibitors (TIMPs) leads to wall weakening.
explanations.b: VEGF is primarily involved in angiogenesis and endothelial maintenance, not the direct mechanical weakening of the large artery tunica media.
explanations.c: TIMPs inhibit matrix degradation; therefore, increased levels would theoretically protect the vessel wall from aneurysm formation rather than cause it.
explanations.d: While TGF-β mutations (e.g., Loeys-Dietz syndrome) cause aneurysms, the mechanism in common aneurysms is usually characterized by matrix degradation through protease activity.
explanations.e: The Renin-Angiotensin system is often upregulated in vascular disease; decreasing it would generally be protective against hypertension and vascular remodeling.

ankiCards: Aneurysm formation is associated with an imbalance between {{c1::proteases (MMPs)}} and their inhibitors.
The enzymes responsible for degrading collagen and elastin in the aneurysm wall are {{c1::Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
Inflammatory cells in the aneurysm wall, such as {{c1::macrophages}}, are a major source of MMPs.
One of the two principal mechanisms of vascular disease involves {{c1::weakening}} of vessel walls.
Vascular wall weakening can lead to either {{c1::dilation}} or rupture.
keyPoints: Aneurysms involve remodeling of the extracellular matrix.
MMPs (e.g., MMP-2, MMP-9) are upregulated in aneurysmal tissue.
TIMPs are typically decreased or overwhelmed by MMP activity.
Inflammation plays a central role in chronic aneurysm development.
Destruction of the medial layer's structural proteins is the end-point of this imbalance.
microReview: Medial weakening occurs through matrix degradation, loss of smooth muscle cells, and ischemia of the inner media. This is often triggered by inflammation or genetic syndromes (Marfan/Loeys-Dietz).
examinerTraps: Timps are 'Inhibitors'; examiners often swap 'Increased MMPs' with 'Increased TIMPs' to trick students on the direction of the imbalance.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the 'true' definition of a pseudoaneurysm (false aneurysm) in vascular pathology?

options.a: A localized dilation involving the intima, media, and adventitia
options.b: An extravascular hematoma that communicates with the intravascular space
options.c: A circumferential dilation affecting a long segment of a large artery
options.d: Blood entering the arterial wall itself through an intimal tear
options.e: A congenital thinning of the arterial media at branching points

explanations.a: This defines a true aneurysm, where the wall of the vessel remains intact but dilated.
explanations.b: A pseudoaneurysm (false aneurysm) is a defect in the vascular wall leading to an extravascular hematoma that freely communicates with the intravascular space ('pulsating hematoma').
explanations.c: This describes a fusiform aneurysm, which is a subtype of a true aneurysm.
explanations.d: This describes an aortic dissection, which is distinct from an aneurysm (though often incorrectly called a 'dissecting aneurysm').
explanations.e: This refers to the pathogenesis of berry aneurysms (saccular aneurysms), which are true aneurysms.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true aneurysm}} involves all three layers of the arterial wall.
A {{c1::pseudoaneurysm (false aneurysm)}} is a hematoma that communicates with the vessel lumen through a wall defect.
A {{c1::fusiform}} aneurysm is a symmetrical, circumferential dilation of a vessel.
An {{c1::aortic dissection}} occurs when blood enters the wall of the artery through an intimal tear.
The two main shapes of true aneurysms are {{c1::saccular}} and fusiform.
keyPoints: True aneurysms have an intact, though thinned, vessel wall.
Pseudoaneurysms result from wall rupture (e.g., trauma or post-MI).
Saccular aneurysms are spherical out-pouchings.
Fusiform aneurysms are long, circumferential dilations.
Dissections are not true aneurysms because they involve blood between wall layers.
microReview: Classification of aneurysms is based on wall integrity (True vs False) and macroscopic shape (Saccular vs Fusiform). Pseudoaneurysms are commonly seen after arterial catheterization or ventricular rupture.
examinerTraps: Watch for 'dissecting aneurysm'—it is a misnomer; the preferred term is 'aortic dissection' and it is not a true aneurysm.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old male presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset, 'tearing' chest pain that radiates to his back. He is 6'4" tall with exceptionally long fingers and hypermobile joints. Blood pressure is 160/90 mmHg in the right arm and 130/70 mmHg in the left arm. What is the most likely microscopic finding in this patient's aorta?

options.b: Medial fragmentation and accumulation of proteoglycans
options.c: Foam cell accumulation in the subendothelial space
options.d: Calcification of the internal elastic lamina
options.e: Fibrinoid necrosis of the small vasa vasorum

explanations.a: Giant cell arteritis involves the media but usually presents in older patients with headache and jaw claudication, not acute dissection in a young patient.
explanations.b: This describes cystic medial degeneration, the hallmark of Marfan syndrome (suggested by the patient's habitus) and a major risk factor for aortic dissection.
explanations.c: Foam cell accumulation is characteristic of atherosclerosis, which is the leading cause of abdominal aortic aneurysms, not thoracic dissections in young patients.
explanations.d: Mönckeberg medial sclerosis involves calcification of the media but does not typically lead to dissection or significant luminal narrowing.
explanations.e: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in malignant hypertension or small vessel vasculitis, not typically the root cause of large vessel medial weakening in Marfan syndrome.

ankiCards: The histological hallmark of Marfan-associated aortic disease is {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
Cystic medial degeneration is characterized by the accumulation of {{c1::proteoglycans (mucoid material)}} in the media.
The defect in Marfan syndrome involves the {{c1::FBN1 (Fibrillin-1)}} gene.
Aortic dissection often presents with {{c1::tearing}} chest pain radiating to the back.
Asymmetric blood pressures between arms suggest {{c1::aortic dissection}} involving the great vessels.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome leads to cystic medial degeneration.
Cystic medial degeneration involves the loss of smooth muscle cells and elastic tissue fragmentation.
Aortic dissection is often triggered by hypertension acting on a weakened wall.
Clinical signs like tall stature and arachnodactyly suggest a connective tissue disorder.
The dissection plane usually occurs between the middle and outer thirds of the media.
microReview: Cystic medial degeneration is not 'cystic' but describes the appearance of pools of mucoid ground substance. It weakens the aorta, making it prone to dilation (aneurysm) and tearing (dissection).
examinerTraps: Don't pick 'atherosclerosis' for a Marfan patient; the pathology is 'cystic medial degeneration' (also called cystic medial necrosis).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular pathology is a major contributor to global mortality. According to the foundational mechanisms of vascular disease, which of the following clinical scenarios is the most direct consequence of vessel wall weakening?

options.b: Acute myocardial infarction due to plaque rupture
options.c: Subarachnoid hemorrhage from a berry aneurysm
options.d: Ischemic stroke from a carotid artery embolus

explanations.a: Stable angina is a result of lumen narrowing (stenosis), which is the first mechanism mentioned, not wall weakening.
explanations.b: Myocardial infarction involves acute obstruction (thrombosis/embolism), following the first mechanism of vascular disease.
explanations.c: Berry aneurysms represent a localized weakness in the vessel wall that leads to dilation and potential rupture; this is the second mechanism (weakening).
explanations.d: Embolic stroke is a consequence of narrowing or obstruction elsewhere, fitting the first mechanism.
explanations.e: Claudication is a symptom of peripheral artery disease, which is caused by atherosclerotic narrowing of the lumen (stenosis).

ankiCards: The two principal mechanisms of vascular disease are narrowing and {{c1::weakening}}.
Weakening of vessel walls typically leads to {{c1::dilation}} or rupture.
Aneurysms fall under the category of vessel wall {{c1::weakening}}.
Atherosclerosis can cause both narrowing and {{c1::weakening (via aneurysm)}} of vessels.
Acute vessel obstruction is most commonly caused by {{c1::thrombosis}} or embolism.
keyPoints: Vascular disease pathogenesis involves two main categories.
Category 1: Luminal narrowing (stenosis/obstruction).
Category 2: Structural weakening (dilation/rupture).
Aneurysms are the classic manifestation of structural weakening.
Stenosis is typically progressive (atherosclerosis) or acute (thrombosis).
microReview: Robbins defines two main pathways: 1) Stenosis/Obstruction (narrowing) and 2) Dilation/Rupture (weakening). Aneurysms represent the second pathway.
examinerTraps: The examiner might try to group atherosclerosis only with narrowing, but remember that atherosclerosis also causes aneurysms (weakening).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Tertiary syphilis is a classic cause of thoracic aortic aneurysms. The pathology begins with an inflammatory response in the vasa vasorum. Which of the following is the direct mechanism by which this infection leads to weakening of the aortic wall?

options.a: Direct bacterial invasion and lysis of the tunica intima
options.b: Ischemic injury to the outer media due to luminal narrowing of small vessels
options.c: Activation of the complement cascade on the internal elastic lamina
options.d: Deposition of immune complexes in the adventitial space
options.e: Massive hypertrophy of the smooth muscle cells in the media

explanations.a: Syphilis does not primarily destroy the intima; it targets the vasa vasorum in the adventitia and outer media.
explanations.b: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum causes ischemia of the outer media, leading to loss of smooth muscle and elastic tissue, and subsequent 'tree-bark' scarring and weakening.
explanations.c: Complement activation is more characteristic of hypersensitivity vasculitides, not the chronic obliterative process of syphilis.
explanations.d: Syphilitic aortitis is a direct result of infection/inflammation (endarteritis), not primarily a Type III hypersensitivity (immune complex) disease.
explanations.e: Syphilis leads to atrophy and scarring of the media, not hypertrophy.

ankiCards: Syphilitic aortitis involves the small vessels called {{c1::vasa vasorum}}.
The pathological process in the vasa vasorum in syphilis is {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}}.
Medial ischemia in syphilis leads to a {{c1::'tree-bark'}} appearance of the aortic intima.
Syphilitic aneurysms most commonly affect the {{c1::ascending}} aorta.
Weakness in the aortic root from syphilis can lead to the clinical complication of {{c1::aortic valve insufficiency}}.
keyPoints: Tertiary syphilis causes 'obliterative endarteritis' of the vasa vasorum.
Vasa vasorum supply the outer 2/3 of the media in large elastic arteries.
Ischemia results in medial necrosis and loss of elastic fibers.
The intima develops 'tree-barking' due to underlying medial scarring.
The resulting aneurysm can dilate the aortic valve ring.
microReview: Syphilitic (Luetic) Aortitis targets the vasa vasorum. This causes medial ischemia, weakening the wall, and leading to aneurysms typically in the thoracic segment.
examinerTraps: Syphilis causes *thoracic* aneurysms, whereas atherosclerosis causes *abdominal* aneurysms. This distinction is frequently tested.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old woman with a history of poorly controlled hypertension presents with sudden onset of severe, 'knife-like' pain in her chest and between her shoulder blades. On examination, she is tachycardic, and her pulses are diminished in the left lower extremity compared to the right. A chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum. What is the most significant risk factor for the development of this condition in this patient?

explanations.a: Diabetes is a risk factor for atherosclerosis, but hypertension is the single most important risk factor for aortic dissection.
explanations.b: Hypercholesterolemia drives atherosclerosis, which is associated with AAA, but hypertension is more critical for dissection.
explanations.c: Hypertension is the most common risk factor for aortic dissection, present in over 70% of cases. It causes hyaline arteriolosclerosis of the vasa vasorum, weakening the media.
explanations.d: Alcohol is not a primary risk factor for aortic dissection.
explanations.e: Obesity is a metabolic risk factor but is less directly linked to the mechanical shearing forces of dissection than hypertension.

ankiCards: The most common risk factor for aortic dissection is {{c1::hypertension}}.
Aortic dissection is characterized by an {{c1::intimal}} tear.
A widened mediastinum on X-ray in a patient with chest pain is highly suggestive of {{c1::aortic dissection}}.
In aortic dissection, blood tracks into the {{c1::media}} layer of the vessel wall.
The classic pain description for aortic dissection is {{c1::tearing or knife-like}}.
keyPoints: Hypertension is the number one risk factor for dissection.
Pathology involves an intimal tear followed by blood cleaving the media.
Type A dissections involve the ascending aorta; Type B do not.
Complications include cardiac tamponade and branch vessel occlusion.
The mediastinum often appears widened on imaging.
microReview: Aortic dissection is not a true aneurysm. It occurs when blood enters the media, creating a second (false) lumen. Hypertension is the dominant cause in older adults; connective tissue disease in younger ones.
examinerTraps: Students often mistake 'atherosclerosis' as the main cause of dissection, but atherosclerosis actually *protects* against the spread of a dissection by causing medial scarring.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the macroscopic morphology of an aneurysm that involves only a portion of the vessel circumference and results in a 'bubble-like' out-pouching?

explanations.a: Fusiform aneurysms involve the entire circumference of the vessel and are elongated/spindle-shaped.
explanations.b: Dissecting aneurysm is a misnomer; it refers to blood entering the media, not a specific shape of a true aneurysm.
explanations.c: Saccular aneurysms are spherical dilations that involve only a portion of the vessel wall, ranging from 5 to 20 cm in diameter.
explanations.d: A pseudoaneurysm is a wall defect (not a dilation of the wall itself) leading to a communicating hematoma.
explanations.e: Cylindrical is a descriptive term sometimes used for fusiform dilations but is not standard terminology in Robbins.

ankiCards: A {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm involves only a portion of the vessel circumference.
A {{c1::fusiform}} aneurysm involves the entire circumference of a vessel segment.
The shape of a berry aneurysm is typically {{c1::saccular}}.
AAAs are most commonly {{c1::fusiform}} in shape.
Localized permanent dilations of an artery are called {{c1::aneurysms}}.
keyPoints: Aneurysms are classified by shape into saccular and fusiform.
Saccular aneurysms are discrete out-pouchings.
Fusiform aneurysms are long, symmetrical dilations.
Morphology does not strictly dictate the underlying cause.
True aneurysms involve all layers of the vessel wall.
microReview: Morphology helps describe the aneurysm but doesn't define the etiology. Saccular = one side/bubble. Fusiform = all sides/spindle.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse shape (Saccular/Fusiform) with integrity (True/False). A saccular aneurysm can be a true aneurysm.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Mycotic aneurysms are a unique class of vascular dilations. What is the defining characteristic of this type of aneurysm?

options.a: They are caused by the growth of fungal organisms in the wall
options.b: They result from infection by any microorganism that weakens the wall
options.c: They are associated exclusively with autoimmune vasculitis
options.d: They represent a localized form of Mönckeberg medial sclerosis
options.e: They are always located in the pulmonary circulation

explanations.a: Despite the name 'mycotic,' they are most often bacterial (e.g., from infective endocarditis), not strictly fungal.
explanations.b: A mycotic aneurysm is any aneurysm caused by infection (bacterial, fungal, etc.) that weakens the vessel wall.
explanations.c: They are infectious, not autoimmune.
explanations.d: Mönckeberg sclerosis is a non-infectious calcification process.
explanations.e: They can occur anywhere, though they are common in cerebral and visceral arteries following embolization from endocarditis.

ankiCards: A {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm is one that results from infection of the arterial wall.
The most common cause of mycotic aneurysms is {{c1::bacterial}} infection (often via embolization).
The term 'mycotic' is a misnomer because most are not caused by {{c1::fungi}}.
Infection-induced weakening of the wall leads to rapid {{c1::dilation}} and high risk of rupture.
A source of infection for mycotic aneurysms is often {{c1::infective endocarditis}}.
keyPoints: Mycotic aneurysms result from infection in the arterial wall.
Pathways include septic emboli, extension from adjacent infection, or direct seeding.
Microorganisms destroy the media, leading to rapid weakening.
Staphylococcus and Streptococcus are common bacterial culprits.
They carry a high risk of rupture and sepsis.
microReview: Mycotic = Infectious. Don't be fooled by the 'fungal' root of the word. Most are bacterial. They are 'true' aneurysms if the wall dilates, but often lead to pseudoaneurysms if they rupture.
examinerTraps: The word 'mycotic' implies fungi—this is the classic 'trick' answer. Always remember they are usually bacterial.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 75-year-old male with a history of smoking and hypertension dies suddenly. Autopsy reveals a large amount of blood in the peritoneal cavity and a 7-cm infrarenal aortic dilation with a jagged wall defect. Histological examination of the aorta near the defect would most likely show which of the following?

options.a: Extensive intimal thickening and medial atrophy
options.b: Normal vessel architecture with acute neutrophilic infiltration
options.c: Primary defect in the synthesis of Type III collagen
options.d: Widespread granulomas with Langhans giant cells
options.e: Infiltration of the media by neoplastic endothelial cells

explanations.a: This patient died of a ruptured AAA. The underlying pathology is atherosclerosis, which is characterized by intimal plaques (thickening) and secondary atrophy of the underlying media.
explanations.b: Aneurysms represent chronic remodeling, not acute neutrophilic inflammation (unless it was a mycotic aneurysm, which is less likely than AAA in this demographic).
explanations.c: This describes Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (Vascular type), which is a rare cause of rupture in young patients, not the typical finding in an elderly smoker.
explanations.d: Granulomatous vasculitis (like Giant Cell Arteritis) is a specific inflammatory disease, not the standard finding in a common AAA.
explanations.e: This describes angiosarcoma, a malignant tumor, not the degenerative process of an aneurysm.

ankiCards: The most common cause of death from an abdominal aortic aneurysm is {{c1::rupture}}.
The risk of AAA rupture increases significantly when the diameter exceeds {{c1::5.5}} cm.
Intraperitoneal hemorrhage in an elderly man with a history of atherosclerosis is highly suggestive of {{c1::AAA rupture}}.
In AAA, the tunica media becomes {{c1::atrophic}} due to overlying atherosclerosis.
Vascular wall response to injury often involves {{c1::intimal thickening}}.
keyPoints: Atherosclerosis causes intimal thickening and medial thinning.
Medial atrophy leads to loss of tensile strength.
Rupture is the most lethal complication of AAA.
Rupture presents as the clinical triad: sudden pain, hypotension, and pulsatile mass.
AAA is primarily a disease of elderly male smokers.
microReview: AAA is a consequence of atherosclerosis. The plaque interferes with the nutrition of the media (which normally comes from the lumen), leading to medial cell death and matrix degradation.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'intimal thickening' (the plaque) with 'wall strengthening'. Even though the intima is thicker, the media (the structural layer) is thinner and weaker.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 34-year-old male with a history of poorly controlled HIV infection presents with multiple painless, violaceous plaques and nodules on his lower extremities and hard palate. Biopsy of a skin lesion reveals a proliferation of spindle cells forming slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells. Immunohistochemical staining is positive for human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis also occurs in HIV patients but is caused by Bartonella species and is characterized by neutrophilic infiltrates rather than HHV-8 positivity.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8, commonly presenting in AIDS patients as purple/violaceous lesions with characteristic spindle cells and slit-like spaces.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor of older adults or associated with specific toxins/radiation; it lacks the specific association with HHV-8.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a rapidly growing pedunculated red nodule, often on the skin or gingiva, that histologically resembles exuberant granulation tissue.
explanations.e: Cavernous hemangioma consists of large, blood-filled vascular spaces and is typically benign and not associated with HIV or HHV-8.

ankiCards: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by infection with {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
The histological hallmark of Kaposi sarcoma includes {{c1::spindle cells}} and slit-like vascular spaces.
The most common clinical setting for Kaposi sarcoma in the US is {{c1::AIDS-associated}}.
Unlike bacillary angiomatosis, Kaposi sarcoma biopsy shows a {{c1::lack}} of neutrophils.
Kaposi sarcoma lesions typically progress through three stages: patch, plaque, and {{c1::nodule}}.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma is a low-grade malignant vascular tumor strongly associated with HHV-8.
There are four major forms: Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
Histology shows sheets of spindle cells and slit-like spaces with red blood cells.
HHV-8 is necessary but not sufficient for the development of the tumor.
The AIDS-associated form is the most common HIV-related malignancy.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = HIV/Immunosuppression + HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Slit-like spaces + Violaceous lesions.
examinerTraps: Distinguishing Kaposi sarcoma from Bacillary angiomatosis; look for neutrophils and Bartonella (silver stain) in the latter, versus spindle cells and HHV-8 in the former.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors... are classified as benign (e.g., hemangioma), intermediate (e.g., Kaposi sarcoma), and malignant (e.g., angiosarcoma).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following environmental exposures is most strongly associated with the development of hepatic angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Aflatoxin B1 is a potent risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, not vascular angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Vinyl chloride exposure (used in the PVC plastic industry) is a classic risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Benzene is associated with acute myeloid leukemia, not primary vascular tumors of the liver.
explanations.d: Asbestos is primarily associated with mesothelioma and bronchogenic carcinoma.
explanations.e: Beryllium exposure is associated with berylliosis (sarcoid-like granulomas) and lung cancer.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
Besides vinyl chloride, hepatic angiosarcoma is also associated with {{c1::Arsenic}} exposure.
The marker {{c1::CD31}} is often used to confirm the endothelial origin of angiosarcomas.
Angiosarcomas are classified as {{c1::malignant}} vascular tumors.
The historical contrast agent associated with hepatic angiosarcoma is {{c1::Thorotrast}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are highly malignant endothelial cell neoplasms.
Hepatic angiosarcoma risk factors: Vinyl chloride, Arsenic, Thorotrast.
They can also occur in the breast following radiation therapy.
Clinical course is usually aggressive with poor long-term survival.
Tumor cells express endothelial markers such as CD31.
microReview: Angiosarcoma = Malignant + Vinyl Chloride/Arsenic/Thorotrast + CD31 positive.
examinerTraps: Confusing Vinyl Chloride (Angiosarcoma) with Aflatoxin (Hepatocellular Carcinoma).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old female in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with a rapidly growing, painless, red, pedunculated mass on her gingiva. The lesion bleeds easily with minor trauma. What is the most likely pathological diagnosis?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors are exquisitely painful, subungual nodules; they are not associated with pregnancy.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma presents as multiple violaceous lesions, usually in immunosuppressed patients, not as a solitary gingival mass in pregnancy.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (granuloma gravidarum when in pregnancy) is a benign, capillary-rich lesion that often occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a malignant, aggressive tumor that would not typically present as a localized, pedunculated gingival mass in a young healthy pregnant female.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis occurs in immunocompromised individuals and is caused by Bartonella, not typically associated with pregnancy.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is a {{c1::benign}} vascular lesion that occurs frequently on the gingiva of pregnant women.
The clinical term for a pyogenic granuloma during pregnancy is {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Histologically, pyogenic granuloma resembles {{c1::granulation tissue}}.
Pyogenic granuloma is characterized by its tendency to {{c1::bleed}} easily.
Treatment for a pyogenic granuloma is usually {{c1::surgical excision}} (or wait for postpartum regression).
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is neither pyogenic nor a granuloma.
It is a form of capillary hemangioma.
Often occurs following trauma or during pregnancy.
Common locations include skin and oral mucosa (gingiva).
Grossly appears as a 'raspberry-like' nodule.
microReview: Pyogenic Granuloma = Pregnancy/Trauma + Gingiva + Bleeds easily + Capillary proliferation.
examinerTraps: Thinking 'pyogenic' implies infection/pus; it is actually a vascular proliferation.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An exquisitely painful, small, red-blue nodule is discovered under the fingernail of a 40-year-old male. Microscopic examination shows nests of uniform, round cells surrounding branching vascular channels. From which of the following cell types does this tumor most likely originate?

explanations.a: While the tumor contains vascular channels, the characteristic round cells of a glomus tumor are not endothelial.
explanations.b: Glomus cells were historically thought to be related to pericytes, but current evidence defines them as modified smooth muscle cells.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts do not form the characteristic nests of round cells seen in glomus tumors.
explanations.e: Lymphatic endothelial cells form lymphangiomas, which are typically painless and located in the neck or axilla.

ankiCards: The classic location for a glomus tumor is {{c1::under the fingernail (subungual)}}.
Glomus tumors are derived from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells.
The primary clinical symptom of a glomus tumor is {{c1::extreme pain}}.
Glomus bodies are involved in the physiological process of {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Histology of a glomus tumor shows nests of {{c1::round}} cells surrounding vessels.
keyPoints: Glomus tumor (glomangioma) is a benign, painful tumor.
Arises from the glomus body (AV shunt).
Most common site: subungual (under nail).
Histology: Uniform cells with round nuclei, resembling smooth muscle differentiation.
Surgical excision is curative.
microReview: Glomus Tumor = Subungual + Pain + Modified Smooth Muscle + Thermoregulation.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'painful' in the stem; if it's a subungual lesion that is painful, think glomus tumor.
sourceQuote: To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure and function.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A newborn is found to have a large, soft, ill-defined mass on the left side of the neck. Transillumination of the mass is positive. Chromosomal analysis reveals a 45,X karyotype. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for the neck mass?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas (strawberry) are more superficial and typically do not present as large cystic neck masses associated with Turner syndrome.
explanations.b: Cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) is a lymphatic malformation often found in the neck of infants, frequently associated with Turner syndrome (45,X).
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are small, painful, and subungual, not large neck masses.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts.
explanations.e: Kaposi sarcoma is a malignancy associated with HHV-8, not congenital lymphatic malformations.

ankiCards: Cystic hygroma is a type of {{c1::cavernous lymphangioma}}.
Cystic hygroma is characteristically associated with {{c1::Turner syndrome}}.
The most common location for a cystic hygroma is the {{c1::neck (or axilla)}}.
On physical exam, a cystic hygroma will typically {{c1::transilluminate}}.
Histology of cystic hygroma shows dilated {{c1::lymphatic}} spaces lined by endothelium.
keyPoints: Cystic hygromas are benign lymphatic malformations.
Frequently associated with Turner syndrome (45,X) and Down syndrome (Trisomy 21).
Large, dilated lymphatic spaces lined by a thin layer of endothelial cells.
Clinical presentation: soft mass in the posterior triangle of the neck.
May cause difficulty in swallowing or breathing if large.
microReview: Cystic Hygroma = Turner Syndrome + Neck Mass + Lymphatic spaces + Transillumination.
examinerTraps: Confusing it with a branchial cleft cyst; cystic hygromas transilluminate and are associated with chromosomal abnormalities.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 58-year-old female who underwent a radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer 12 years ago presents with multiple small, firm, bluish-red nodules on her left arm. The arm has been chronically swollen since her surgery. A biopsy reveals poorly formed vascular channels lined by atypical, pleomorphic endothelial cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and usually presents in the context of AIDS or specific ethnic groups, not chronic lymphedema.
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma is the diagnosis; when it arises in the setting of chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy), it is specifically termed Stewart-Treves syndrome.
explanations.c: Lymphangiomas are benign malformations, not malignant proliferations of pleomorphic cells.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangioma is a benign vascular tumor with large blood-filled spaces, lacking the cellular atypia seen here.
explanations.e: While 'Stewart-Treves syndrome' describes the clinical scenario, 'Angiosarcoma' is the specific pathological diagnosis/tumor type. (Note: In many boards, both might be present, but Angiosarcoma is the histopathological entity requested by 'likely diagnosis' of the biopsy).

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
The most common clinical scenario for Stewart-Treves syndrome is post-{{c1::mastectomy}}.
Angiosarcomas stain positive for the endothelial marker {{c1::CD31}}.
Histology of angiosarcoma shows {{c1::atypical/pleomorphic}} endothelial cells.
Radiation therapy is a known risk factor for {{c1::angiosarcoma}} of the breast.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignant endothelial tumor.
Stewart-Treves syndrome: Angiosarcoma + Chronic Lymphedema.
Often occurs years after lymph node dissection.
Clinically appears as bruising or purple nodules.
High rate of metastasis and poor prognosis.
microReview: Angiosarcoma = Post-mastectomy + Chronic lymphedema + Stewart-Treves + CD31+.
examinerTraps: Distinguishing the syndrome name (Stewart-Treves) from the tumor name (Angiosarcoma).
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors... are classified as benign, intermediate, and malignant.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following is the most common benign vascular tumor of infancy, characteristically presenting as a 'strawberry' lesion that grows rapidly and then spontaneously regresses?

explanations.a: Cherry hemangiomas are small red papules that increase in number with age in adults; they do not regress.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large vascular spaces, often deeper, and do not typically regress spontaneously like the juvenile type.
explanations.c: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma is extremely common in newborns, grows for a few months, and then usually involutes by age 7.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granulomas are acquired lesions, often following trauma or during pregnancy, and do not follow the 'strawberry' growth/regression cycle.
explanations.e: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a malformation that grows with the child and does not regress.

ankiCards: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma typically {{c1::regresses/involutes}} by age 7.
The 'strawberry' appearance refers to the {{c1::Juvenile}} hemangioma.
Histologically, juvenile hemangioma is a type of {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma.
Unlike juvenile hemangiomas, port-wine stains {{c1::do not}} regress.
The first stage of juvenile hemangioma life cycle is {{c1::rapid growth}}.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangioma is the most common tumor of infancy.
Usually present at birth or within the first weeks of life.
Location is most often the skin of the head or neck.
Natural history: Rapid growth followed by slow involution.
Most cases require no treatment due to spontaneous regression.
microReview: Strawberry Hemangioma = Infant + Rapid Growth + Involution + Capillary.
examinerTraps: Confusing 'Cherry' (adults) with 'Strawberry' (infants).
sourceQuote: To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure and function.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the development of Kaposi sarcoma, the spindle cells are induced to proliferate primarily through the action of which of the following proteins encoded by HHV-8?

explanations.a: Tax protein is associated with HTLV-1 and adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma.
explanations.b: E6 protein is associated with high-risk HPV and cervical carcinoma (p53 degradation).
explanations.c: HHV-8 encodes a viral G-protein-coupled receptor (vGPCR) that stimulates VEGF production and spindle cell proliferation.
explanations.d: LMP-1 is an oncogenic protein associated with Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV).
explanations.e: EBN-1 is an EBV nuclear antigen associated with Burkitt lymphoma and other EBV-related diseases.

ankiCards: HHV-8 stimulates vascular proliferation by encoding a viral {{c1::GPCR (vGPCR)}}.
vGPCR in Kaposi sarcoma increases the expression of {{c1::VEGF}}.
HHV-8 is also known as {{c1::KSHV}} (Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus).
The primary cell type that proliferates in Kaposi sarcoma is the {{c1::spindle cell}}.
Kaposi sarcoma is considered an {{c1::intermediate}} grade tumor.
keyPoints: HHV-8 produces viral homologs of human genes (vGPCR, v-cyclin).
vGPCR stimulates the secretion of pro-angiogenic factors (VEGF).
Spindle cells express endothelial and smooth muscle markers.
Inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF) also play a role in the microenvironment.
The tumor is driven by a 'reactive' polyclonal proliferation that can become monoclonal.
microReview: HHV-8 + vGPCR + VEGF = Kaposi Sarcoma.
examinerTraps: The mechanism isn't just viral infection; it's the specific molecular mimicry and growth factor induction (vGPCR/VEGF).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction... and Weakening of vessel walls.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with a large, flat, purple-red birthmark on the right side of his face following the distribution of the trigeminal nerve (V1 and V2). His mother reports he recently had a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. MRI shows ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomatosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) presents with multiple telangiectasias and epistaxis, not port-wine stains.
explanations.b: Sturge-Weber syndrome is characterized by a port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) in the V1/V2 distribution, leptomeningeal angiomas, and seizures.
explanations.c: Von Hippel-Lindau is associated with hemangioblastomas (CNS/Retina), renal cell carcinoma, and pheochromocytoma.
explanations.d: NF1 is characterized by café-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules, not port-wine stains.
explanations.e: Tuberous sclerosis presents with ash-leaf spots, angiofibromas, and shagreen patches.

ankiCards: Sturge-Weber syndrome is associated with a {{c1::port-wine stain (nevus flammeus)}}.
The facial lesion in Sturge-Weber syndrome usually follows the {{c1::trigeminal (CN V)}} nerve distribution.
CNS involvement in Sturge-Weber includes {{c1::leptomeningeal angiomatosis}}.
Sturge-Weber syndrome is caused by a somatic mutation in the {{c1::GNAQ}} gene.
Common clinical complications of Sturge-Weber include {{c1::seizures}} and glaucoma.
keyPoints: Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) is a non-hereditary phakomatosis.
Nevus flammeus is the dermatological hallmark.
Ipsilateral leptomeningeal angioma can cause seizures and hemiparesis.
'Tram-track' calcifications may be seen on CT of the brain.
Associated with somatic activating mutations in the GNAQ gene.
microReview: Sturge-Weber = Port-wine stain (V1) + Seizures + Leptomeningeal angioma + GNAQ.
examinerTraps: Wait for the CNS symptoms (seizures) to distinguish a simple port-wine stain from Sturge-Weber syndrome.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 42-year-old male with advanced HIV infection presents with several red, friable, papular skin lesions. Histological examination shows a proliferation of small blood vessels with prominent epithelioid endothelial cells and an infiltrate of neutrophils. A silver stain (Warthin-Starry) reveals clusters of bacilli. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma lacks neutrophils and would not show bacilli on Warthin-Starry silver stain.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella species (henselae or quintana) and presents with vascular proliferation and neutrophilic infiltrates in HIV patients.
explanations.c: Verruga peruana is a skin manifestation of Bartonella bacilliformis (Carrion disease), usually restricted to the Andes mountains.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma does not contain bacilli and is not specifically linked to HIV/Bartonella.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor with significant atypia, not caused by bacterial infection.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by bacteria of the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
The two main species causing bacillary angiomatosis are B. henselae and {{c1::B. quintana}}.
The histological hallmark that distinguishes bacillary angiomatosis from KS is the presence of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
Bacteria in bacillary angiomatosis are visualized using the {{c1::Warthin-Starry}} silver stain.
Bacillary angiomatosis is primarily seen in {{c1::immunocompromised (HIV)}} patients.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis is an opportunistic infection.
Induces vascular proliferation that mimics Kaposi sarcoma.
B. henselae is typically transmitted by cats; B. quintana by lice.
Treatment involves antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin).
Histology: Lobular proliferation of capillaries with protuberant endothelial cells and nuclear dust from neutrophils.
microReview: Bacillary Angiomatosis = HIV + Bartonella + Neutrophils + Warthin-Starry silver stain.
examinerTraps: Confusing it with Kaposi Sarcoma; look for 'neutrophils' or 'bacilli' in the stem.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes one of the two principal mechanisms that underlie vascular disease leading to clinical manifestations like dilation or rupture?

explanations.a: While progressive narrowing (e.g., by atherosclerosis) is a principal mechanism, it results in stenosis or obstruction, not dilation or rupture.
explanations.b: Weakening of vessel walls is one of the two fundamental mechanisms of vascular disease; it specifically leads to dilation (aneurysm) or rupture.
explanations.c: The wall-to-lumen ratio actually increases in smaller muscular vessels to control pressure; it is not a primary mechanism of generalized vascular disease.
explanations.d: Endothelial hyperplasia is a response to injury but is not categorized as one of the two primary mechanisms underlying all vascular disease.
explanations.e: Failure to accommodate pulsatile flow is a consequence of arterial stiffening, but the primary mechanism for dilation/rupture is structural wall weakening.

ankiCards: The two principal mechanisms underlying vascular disease are narrowing/obstruction and {{c1::weakening of vessel walls}}.
Vessel wall weakening leads to two major clinical outcomes: {{c1::dilation}} or {{c2::rupture}}.
Progressive narrowing of vessel lumens is typically caused by {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Precipitous obstruction of vessel lumens is typically caused by {{c1::thrombosis}} or {{c2::embolism}}.
Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins to accommodate {{c1::pulsatile flow}} and higher blood pressures.
keyPoints: Vascular pathology accounts for more morbidity/mortality than any other disease category.
Mechanism 1: Luminal narrowing/obstruction (progressive or precipitous).
Mechanism 2: Wall weakening (leading to dilation or rupture).
Aneurysms result from the weakening of the vessel wall.
Atherosclerosis affects primarily elastic and muscular arteries.
microReview: Vascular disease is categorized by either luminal narrowing (causing ischemia) or wall weakening (causing aneurysms/rupture). Arteries are structurally thicker than veins to handle high-pressure, pulsatile blood flow.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse the consequences of atherosclerosis (stenosis) with the consequences of wall weakening (dilation/aneurysm). Both may coexist, but they represent distinct mechanical pathologies.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Anatomically, as arteries transition from elastic to muscular and then to smaller arterioles, how does the relationship between wall thickness and lumen diameter change, and what is the functional consequence of this change?

options.b: Ratio increases; increases control over blood flow
options.c: Ratio remains constant; maintains laminar flow

explanations.a: The ratio does not decrease; wall thickness diminishes, but the lumen diameter diminishes more significantly, increasing the ratio.
explanations.b: As vessels become smaller, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing muscular vessels to exert finer control over blood flow and pressure.
explanations.c: The ratio is not constant; the architecture changes to reflect the specialized functional roles of resistance vessels.
explanations.d: Smaller vessels with higher wall-to-lumen ratios are the primary drivers of peripheral resistance, not its reduction.
explanations.e: The arterial wall-to-lumen ratio has no direct role in facilitating venous return, which depends on valves and skeletal muscle pumps.

ankiCards: As arterial vessels become smaller, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}}.
Increasing the wall-to-lumen ratio allows muscular vessels to exert control over {{c1::blood flow}} and {{c2::pressure}}.
Arterial walls are {{c1::thicker}} than veins at the same level of branching.
Atherosclerosis mainly affects {{c1::elastic}} and {{c2::muscular}} arteries.
Distinct anatomic distributions of vascular diseases reflect structural {{c1::specializations}} of specific vessels.
keyPoints: Arterial wall thickness decreases in absolute terms as vessels get smaller.
The relative wall-to-lumen ratio increases in smaller vessels.
This structural shift supports the role of arterioles as resistance vessels.
Vascular architecture reflects functional requirements like pressure management.
Atherosclerosis is selective for specific arterial types (elastic and muscular).
microReview: While large elastic arteries (aorta) are the thickest, smaller muscular arteries and arterioles have a higher wall-to-lumen ratio. This allows them to regulate systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure effectively.
examinerTraps: Students often think 'thicker wall' means 'large artery'. While the aorta is the thickest, the *ratio* of wall to lumen is highest in smaller muscular arteries/arterioles.
sourceQuote: Arterial wall thickness gradually diminishes as the vessels become smaller, but the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing these muscular vessels to exert control over blood flow and pressure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old male with a 50-pack-year smoking history and hypertension presents for a routine physical. On abdominal palpation, a non-tender, pulsatile mass is noted at the level of the umbilicus. Imaging confirms a localized dilation of the abdominal aorta. What is the fundamental pathological mechanism responsible for this finding?

explanations.a: Thrombosis causes obstruction/narrowing, which would lead to ischemia (e.g., blue toe syndrome) rather than a pulsatile mass (dilation).
explanations.b: Intimal thickening is a stereotyped response to injury that usually leads to narrowing, not dilation.
explanations.c: Aneurysms (pulsatile masses) are caused by the weakening of the vessel wall, one of the two primary mechanisms of vascular disease.
explanations.d: Hypertrophy of the media is often a response to hypertension to strengthen the wall; its failure or replacement by fibrous tissue leads to weakening.
explanations.e: Arteriovenous shunts are abnormal connections, not localized dilations of the vessel wall itself.

ankiCards: A pulsatile abdominal mass in an elderly smoker is highly suggestive of an {{c1::Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA)}}.
The pathological hallmark of an aneurysm is the {{c1::weakening}} of the vessel wall.
The abdominal aorta is a common site for dilation due to its {{c1::elastic/muscular}} nature and susceptibility to atherosclerosis.
Vascular wall weakening leads to either {{c1::dilation}} or {{c2::rupture}}.
Most aneurysms are caused by the interplay of {{c1::atherosclerosis}} and hypertension weakening the wall structure.
keyPoints: Aneurysms are permanent localized dilations of the vessel.
They result from structural weakening of the tunica media.
Clinical presentation often involves a pulsatile mass or asymptomatic incidental finding.
Major risk factors include smoking, male sex, and advanced age.
Aneurysms fall under the 'weakening' category of vascular pathology.
microReview: Aneurysms occur when the structural integrity of the vessel wall is compromised. This weakening allows the high-pressure arterial blood to expand the vessel. This is distinct from obstructive disease (stenosis), which is the other main mechanism of vascular pathology.
examinerTraps: Do not select 'narrowing' or 'stenosis' for an aneurysm. While atherosclerosis (which causes narrowing) can *lead* to wall weakening, the aneurysm itself is a failure of the wall strength, not a blockage.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes a precipitous mechanism of vascular luminal obstruction, as opposed to the progressive mechanism typically seen in aneurysm-predisposing conditions?

explanations.a: Atherosclerosis is described as a progressive mechanism of narrowing.
explanations.b: Intimal thickening is a stereotyped, gradual response to injury.
explanations.c: Thrombosis (along with embolism) is described as a precipitous (sudden) mechanism of luminal obstruction.
explanations.d: Cystic medial necrosis is a process of wall weakening, not luminal obstruction.
explanations.e: Hyaline arteriosclerosis is a progressive narrowing of small vessels seen in hypertension/diabetes.

ankiCards: Luminal obstruction can be {{c1::progressive}} (e.g., atherosclerosis) or {{c2::precipitous}}.
Two examples of precipitous vascular obstruction are {{c1::thrombosis}} and {{c2::embolism}}.
Obstruction and wall weakening are the two main {{c1::mechanisms}} of vascular disease.
The primary outcome of wall weakening is {{c1::dilation}} or {{c2::rupture}}.
Vascular diseases are categorized based on whether they cause {{c1::narrowing}} or {{c2::weakening}}.
keyPoints: Obstruction can be slow (progressive) or fast (precipitous).
Thrombosis/Embolism = Precipitous.
Atherosclerosis = Progressive.
Both lead to ischemia/infarction.
This is distinct from the mechanism of 'weakening' which leads to aneurysms.
microReview: Understand the tempo of vascular occlusion. Chronic narrowing (atherosclerosis) allows for collateral formation; acute occlusion (thrombosis) usually leads to immediate infarction. Aneurysms are a separate mechanical category (wall failure).
examinerTraps: Ensure you distinguish between 'narrowing' (the mechanism) and 'atherosclerosis' (the specific disease). Also distinguish the speed (progressive vs. precipitous).
sourceQuote: either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism)
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Why are arterial walls structurally thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching?

options.a: To allow for higher rates of nutrient exchange
options.b: To accommodate pulsatile flow and higher pressures
options.c: To prevent the formation of atherosclerotic plaques
options.d: To facilitate the action of the skeletal muscle pump
options.e: To decrease the wall-to-lumen ratio for better flow

explanations.a: Nutrient exchange happens in capillaries, which have the thinnest walls, not thick arterial walls.
explanations.b: Arterial walls are thicker specifically to handle the high pressures and the pulsatile nature of blood ejected from the heart.
explanations.c: Thicker walls do not prevent atherosclerosis; in fact, the elastic and muscular arteries with these walls are the primary targets.
explanations.d: The skeletal muscle pump is a mechanism used by veins, which have thinner walls and valves.
explanations.e: Arteries have an increased wall-to-lumen ratio compared to veins, not a decreased one.

ankiCards: Arterial walls are thicker than veins to accommodate {{c1::pulsatile}} flow.
The thicker walls of arteries allow them to withstand higher {{c1::blood pressures}}.
Compared to veins at the same level, arteries have a {{c1::thicker}} wall.
Structural specializations in vessels reflect their distinct {{c1::functional roles}}.
Arteries exert control over blood flow and pressure via their {{c1::muscular}} walls.
keyPoints: Arteries operate under high-pressure conditions.
Pulsatile flow requires structural reinforcement (media thickness).
Veins are low-pressure capacitance vessels.
Wall thickness is proportional to the internal pressure the vessel must contain.
Aneurysms represent a failure of these thick walls to contain said pressure.
microReview: Arteries = High pressure/Pulsatile/Thick walls. Veins = Low pressure/Non-pulsatile/Thin walls. Vascular pathology often involves the breakdown of these structural adaptations.
examinerTraps: A common trap is saying arteries are thicker to 'pump' blood. Arteries don't pump; they *accommodate* and *control* flow/pressure through thickness and elastic recoil.
sourceQuote: For example, arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 65-year-old female with long-standing poorly controlled hypertension presents with sudden, catastrophic internal hemorrhage. Autopsy reveals a ruptured vessel. Which of the two principal mechanisms of vascular disease most likely preceded the rupture?

explanations.a: Narrowing leads to ischemia/starvation of tissues, not sudden rupture and hemorrhage.
explanations.b: Obstruction (thrombosis) leads to infarction/necrosis, not immediate rupture of the vessel wall.
explanations.c: Weakening of the vessel wall is the mechanism that leads to dilation (aneurysm) and eventually rupture.
explanations.d: An increased wall-to-lumen ratio is a normal adaptation in small vessels to control pressure; it is not a mechanism for rupture.
explanations.e: Endothelial activation is an early step in inflammation or atherosclerosis but is not the structural mechanism for rupture.

ankiCards: Sudden vessel rupture is the terminal event of {{c1::wall weakening}}.
The two outcomes of vessel wall weakening are {{c1::dilation}} and {{c2::rupture}}.
Hypertension is a major risk factor for weakening the walls of {{c1::elastic}} and {{c2::muscular}} arteries.
Catastrophic internal hemorrhage in a hypertensive patient often suggests a ruptured {{c1::aneurysm}}.
Weakening of vessel walls is one of {{c1::two}} principal mechanisms of vascular disease.
keyPoints: Rupture is a failure of structural integrity.
Wall weakening is the prerequisite for both aneurysms and rupture.
Chronic hypertension causes stress that contributes to wall weakening.
Aneurysms may be asymptomatic until the moment of rupture.
Hemorrhage is the clinical hallmark of vessel rupture.
microReview: When a vessel fails to maintain its structural integrity against internal pressure, it either dilates (aneurysm) or breaks (rupture). This is distinct from 'narrowing' diseases like stable angina or peripheral artery disease.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'cause' (e.g., hypertension) with the 'mechanism' (wall weakening). The question asks for the principal mechanism underlying the pathology.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the study of vascular pathology, which category of human disease is responsible for the highest levels of morbidity and mortality?

explanations.a: Infectious vasculitis is a specific sub-type but not the leading category overall.
explanations.b: The text states venous disorders are 'not inconsequential' but the most significant lesions involve arteries.
explanations.c: Vascular tumors (e.g., angiosarcoma) are rare compared to atherosclerotic/hypertensive disease.
explanations.d: Vascular pathology (as a broad category) is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
explanations.e: Lymphatic disorders (like lymphedema) cause significant morbidity but very little mortality compared to arterial disease.

ankiCards: Vascular pathology causes more morbidity and mortality than any other {{c1::category of human disease}}.
The most clinically significant vascular lesions involve {{c1::arteries}}.
Venous disorders are considered {{c1::not inconsequential}} compared to arterial ones.
The architecture of blood vessels is comparable throughout the system but has structural {{c1::specializations}}.
Two principal mechanisms underlie almost all {{c1::vascular disease}}.
keyPoints: Vascular disease is the #1 killer/cause of disability.
Arterial lesions are more significant than venous ones.
The basic structure of vessels is similar, but functions differ by site.
Most deaths from vascular disease involve the heart (coronaries) or brain (carotids/cerebral).
Understanding normal structure is essential to understanding pathogenesis.
microReview: Vascular pathology is the 'heavy hitter' in medicine. It underpins myocardial infarction, stroke, and aortic aneurysm—the leading causes of death in developed nations.
examinerTraps: The examiner may try to make you pick a specific disease like 'Atherosclerosis'. However, the broad 'category' is vascular pathology.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which vessel feature allows muscular arteries to effectively exert control over blood flow and pressure?

options.a: Thin tunica media with high elastic content
options.b: High ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter
options.d: A large lumen diameter relative to wall thickness
options.e: A single layer of endothelial cells only

explanations.a: This describes elastic arteries (like the aorta), which are designed for recoil, not fine-tuned pressure control.
explanations.b: The increased ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter in smaller muscular vessels (arterioles/muscular arteries) provides the mechanical leverage to regulate resistance.
explanations.c: Valves are found in veins and lymphatics, not muscular arteries.
explanations.d: A large lumen relative to wall thickness would describe a capacitance vessel (vein) or a dilated aneurysm, neither of which controls pressure well.
explanations.e: A single layer of endothelium only describes capillaries, which cannot constrict or dilate to control systemic pressure.

ankiCards: Muscular vessels exert control over pressure because the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}}.
The specialized roles of vessels are reflected in their {{c1::structural specializations}}.
As arteries become smaller, their absolute wall thickness {{c1::diminishes}}.
The primary control over systemic blood pressure occurs in {{c1::muscular}} vessels/arterioles.
Atherosclerosis typically spares {{c2::veins}} and affects {{c1::arteries}}.
keyPoints: Wall-to-lumen ratio is the key metric for resistance vessels.
Muscular arteries = Distribution and Resistance.
Elastic arteries = Pressure dampening (Windkessel effect).
Vessel diameter is inversely proportional to resistance (Poiseuille's Law).
Structural changes in these layers lead to pathology (e.g., hypertension).
microReview: The thicker the wall relative to the hole (lumen), the more power the muscle in that wall has to close the hole. This is why small muscular arteries/arterioles are the 'faucets' of the circulatory system.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'absolute thickness' with 'relative thickness (ratio)'. The aorta is the thickest vessel, but the arteriole has the highest wall-to-lumen ratio.
sourceQuote: the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing these muscular vessels to exert control over blood flow and pressure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following is an example of a precipitous obstruction of a vessel lumen?

explanations.a: Atherosclerosis is a progressive mechanism of narrowing.
explanations.b: Dilation is a result of wall weakening, not luminal obstruction.
explanations.c: Embolism is specifically cited as a precipitous (sudden) mechanism of complete luminal obstruction.
explanations.d: An aneurysm is a dilation caused by weakening, not an obstruction.
explanations.e: Rupture is a consequence of weakening, not an obstruction of the lumen.

ankiCards: Precipitous luminal obstruction is caused by {{c1::thrombosis}} or {{c2::embolism}}.
Progressive luminal narrowing is typically caused by {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Dilation and rupture are consequences of {{c1::weakening of vessel walls}}.
Narrowing and weakening are the two {{c1::principal mechanisms}} of vascular disease.
Venous disorders are less clinically significant than those affecting {{c1::arteries}}.
keyPoints: Obstruction = Ischemia.
Weakening = Aneurysm/Rupture.
Sudden obstruction = Embolism/Thrombosis.
Slow obstruction = Atherosclerosis.
Vascular pathology is the leading cause of death.
microReview: Obstruction and Weakening are the 'Big Two' in vascular pathology. Obstruction is further divided by speed: progressive (atherosclerosis) vs. precipitous (thrombosis/embolism).
examinerTraps: Aneurysm and Embolism are both 'precipitous' clinical events, but an Aneurysm is a *weakening* pathology, while an Embolism is an *obstructive* pathology.
sourceQuote: precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism)
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 34-year-old male with a history of HIV and a CD4+ count of 120 cells/mm³ presents with multiple, non-tender, violaceous macules and plaques on his lower extremities and hard palate. Skin biopsy of a lesion reveals sheets of spindle cells forming slit-like vascular spaces containing red blood cells and a lymphocytic infiltrate. Which of the following is the most likely causative agent associated with this patient's condition?

explanations.a: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the etiologic agent of Kaposi Sarcoma (KS), which presents as spindle cell proliferation and slit-like vascular spaces.
explanations.b: Human papillomavirus 16 is associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix and oropharynx, not vascular tumors.
explanations.c: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and hairy leukoplakia, but not KS.
explanations.d: Cytomegalovirus can cause opportunistic infections in AIDS patients (retinitis, colitis) but does not cause primary vascular tumors.
explanations.e: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised patients, which can look similar clinically but histologically shows lobular capillary proliferation and neutrophils, not spindle cell slit-spaces.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is caused by infection with {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
The histological hallmark of Kaposi Sarcoma is the presence of {{c1::spindle cells}} forming slit-like spaces.
Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by {{c1::Bartonella henselae}} and involves neutrophilic infiltrates.
Vascular tumors expressing {{c1::CD31}} confirm their endothelial origin.
Kaposi Sarcoma in AIDS patients is classified as the {{c1::epidemic}} form.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a low-grade malignant vascular tumor caused by HHV-8.
Slit-like vascular spaces and spindle cells are classic histological findings.
Epidemic AIDS-related KS is the most common HIV-associated malignancy.
Differential diagnosis for violaceous lesions in AIDS includes bacillary angiomatosis.
Bacillary angiomatosis is distinguished by the presence of neutrophils and Warthin-Starry stain positivity.
microReview: Vascular tumors range from benign hemangiomas to highly malignant angiosarcomas. Intermediate-grade tumors like Kaposi Sarcoma are often associated with viral drivers (HHV-8) and appear as spindle-cell proliferations on biopsy.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Kaposi Sarcoma with Bacillary Angiomatosis. Look for 'spindle cells' for KS and 'neutrophils/Bartonella' for BA.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An extremely painful, small (less than 1 cm), red-blue nodule is discovered under the fingernail of a 42-year-old woman. Histological examination reveals aggregates of specialized smooth muscle cells surrounding vascular channels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, exquisitely painful tumors arising from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, typically found in the subungual region.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas are common benign vascular tumors but are usually painless and occur in skin/mucosa from birth or early childhood.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor that presents as larger, poorly defined masses, not small painful subungual nodules.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a rapidly growing, pedunculated red nodule that bleeds easily, often on the gingiva or fingers, but is not characterized by glomus cells.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts caused by Bartonella, usually presenting as multiple lesions.

ankiCards: The classic location for a glomus tumor is the {{c1::subungual (under fingernail)}} region.
Glomus tumors are derived from specialized {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} of the glomus body.
A key clinical feature of glomus tumors is that they are {{c1::exquisitely painful}}.
The glomus body is involved in {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Histology of glomus tumors shows rows of {{c1::monomorphic round cells}} around vessels.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but very painful.
Most common site is the distal portion of the fingers, especially subungual.
They arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
The glomus body is a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis.
Excision is usually curative.
microReview: Small, painful, subungual blue-red nodules are almost pathognomonic for glomus tumors, characterized by glomus cells (modified smooth muscle).
examinerTraps: The examiner may describe the pain as 'paroxysmal' or triggered by temperature changes to point towards glomus tumor.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular tumors are immunohistochemically identified by the expression of markers specific to the endothelium. Which of the following proteins would most likely be detected in the malignant cells of a hepatic angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a highly specific marker for endothelial cells and is used to confirm the vascular origin of tumors like angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (smooth or skeletal), not endothelial cells.
explanations.c: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells, used to identify carcinomas.
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells, such as melanocytes and Schwann cells.
explanations.e: CD45 (Leukocyte Common Antigen) is a marker for hematopoietic cells, used to identify lymphomas.

ankiCards: The most common endothelial cell marker used in pathology is {{c1::CD31}} (or vWF).
Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor of {{c1::endothelial cells}}.
Expression of {{c1::CD31}} helps distinguish poorly differentiated angiosarcoma from carcinomas.
vWF (von Willebrand Factor) is also known as {{c1::Factor VIII-related antigen}} in IHC.
Endothelial markers help confirm the vascular nature of {{c1::intermediate and malignant}} tumors.
keyPoints: CD31 is the most reliable marker for endothelial differentiation.
vWF (Factor VIII-related antigen) is also used but is less sensitive than CD31.
Angiosarcomas are often poorly differentiated, making IHC essential.
CD31 staining highlights the cell borders of endothelial cells.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is specifically associated with vinyl chloride and arsenic exposure.
microReview: Identifying vascular tumors depends on endothelial markers; CD31 is the gold standard for confirming that spindle or pleomorphic cells are of vascular origin.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse CD31 (endothelial) with CD3 (T-cell) or CD34 (hematopoietic/vascular but less specific).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with several enlarging, ill-defined, violaceous skin nodules on her left arm. She has a history of a radical mastectomy followed by radiation therapy for breast cancer 12 years ago, which resulted in persistent, chronic lymphedema of the left upper extremity. A biopsy of a nodule shows highly pleomorphic malignant cells forming irregular, anastomosing vascular channels. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: This patient has Stewart-Treves syndrome, where chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy) predisposes to the development of angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and typically presents differently; while it can involve the arm, the history of radical mastectomy and chronic lymphedema is classic for angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign bacterial-induced lesion in immunocompromised patients, not a pleomorphic malignancy.
explanations.d: Lymphangioma is a benign malformation of lymphatic vessels, usually congenital, not a late-onset malignancy in the setting of lymphedema.
explanations.e: Stasis dermatitis relates to venous insufficiency and causes skin discoloration/scaling, not pleomorphic vascular nodules.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
Angiosarcoma is a {{c1::highly malignant}} tumor of endothelial cells.
Post-mastectomy {{c1::chronic lymphedema}} is a major risk factor for cutaneous angiosarcoma.
Histology of angiosarcoma shows {{c1::anastomosing}} vascular channels lined by atypical cells.
Exposure to {{c1::radiation}} is a risk factor for the development of angiosarcoma.
keyPoints: Stewart-Treves syndrome: Chronic lymphedema + Angiosarcoma.
Angiosarcomas are aggressive with a poor 5-year survival rate.
They can occur in the skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is linked to Vinyl Chloride, Arsenic, and Thorotrast.
Histologically, they show varying degrees of differentiation from recognizable vessels to solid sheets.
microReview: Malignant vascular tumors (angiosarcomas) often arise in specific settings: chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves), radiation, or specific chemical exposures (vinyl chloride).
examinerTraps: The examiner often uses the 'post-mastectomy arm' history to lead you to Stewart-Treves syndrome/Angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 25-year-old pregnant woman in her third trimester notices a rapidly growing, 1-cm red, pedunculated mass on her gingiva that bleeds easily with minor trauma. The lesion is excised. Which of the following histological features is most characteristic of this lesion?

options.b: Diffuse sheets of atypical spindle cells

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is characterized by a lobular arrangement of capillaries with edematous stroma, often occurring in the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.b: Diffuse sheets of spindle cells are characteristic of Kaposi sarcoma, not pyogenic granuloma.
explanations.c: Cavernous vascular spaces are found in cavernous hemangiomas, which are usually deeper, larger, and don't grow rapidly or bleed as easily as pyogenic granulomas.
explanations.d: Aggregates of glomus cells are characteristic of glomus tumors, not pyogenic granulomas.
explanations.e: Malignant pleomorphic endothelial cells are seen in angiosarcoma, which is a rare malignancy, unlike the common pyogenic granuloma.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is histologically a {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
Pyogenic granuloma frequently occurs in the {{c1::gingiva}} of pregnant women.
A common clinical feature of pyogenic granuloma is that it {{c1::bleeds easily}}.
Pyogenic granuloma is often {{c1::pedunculated}} (on a stalk).
Despite the name, pyogenic granuloma is neither {{c1::pyogenic (pus-forming)}} nor a {{c2::granuloma}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is a lobular capillary hemangioma.
Often occurs after trauma or during pregnancy.
