Classic location: gingiva, fingers, or face.
Rapid growth and bleeding are hallmarks.
Regression is possible (especially postpartum), but excision is common.
microReview: Pregnancy + gingival mass + easy bleeding = Pyogenic granuloma (Lobular capillary hemangioma).
examinerTraps: The name 'Pyogenic Granuloma' is a trap; it has nothing to do with infection or granulomatous inflammation.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular lesions is most likely to be associated with Von Hippel-Lindau disease when found in the cerebellum or retina?

explanations.a: Hemangioblastomas are highly vascular tumors characteristic of Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease, specifically in the cerebellum, retina, and brainstem.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas are common skin/liver lesions but are not the specific tumor defining VHL in the CNS.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas are associated with VHL in the liver but not typically the hallmark CNS finding compared to hemangioblastomas.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a sporadic or radiation-induced malignancy, not part of the VHL syndrome.
explanations.e: Lymphangiomas are benign malformations of lymphatics and are not associated with VHL.

ankiCards: Von Hippel-Lindau disease is associated with {{c1::hemangioblastomas}} in the cerebellum.
The gene mutated in VHL disease is a {{c1::tumor suppressor}} on chromosome 3.
Retinal {{c1::hemangioblastoma}} is a diagnostic feature of VHL disease.
VHL disease also predisposes to {{c1::renal cell carcinoma}} (clear cell type).
VHL disease is inherited in an {{c1::autosomal dominant}} pattern.
keyPoints: VHL syndrome: Hemangioblastomas (CNS/Retina) + Renal Cell Carcinoma + Pheochromocytoma.
Hemangioblastomas are benign but cause symptoms by mass effect.
The VHL protein is involved in the degradation of Hypoxia-Inducible Factor (HIF).
Cerebellar hemangioblastomas may produce erythropoietin, leading to polycythemia.
Diagnosis usually involves imaging and genetic testing.
microReview: VHL disease is a syndrome of 'V'ascular tumors (Hemangioblastoma), 'H'ematological issues (Polycythemia from EPO), and 'L'umbar/Renal issues (RCC).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'Hemangioma' (common, benign) with 'Hemangioblastoma' (VHL-associated).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 2-month-old infant is brought to the clinic with a bright red, slightly raised 'strawberry-like' lesion on the scalp. The parents state it has grown rapidly since birth. The physician advises the parents that the lesion will likely enlarge for several more months and then gradually regress. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are very common in infants, grow rapidly in the first few months of life, and typically involute completely by age 7.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large vascular channels, are often deeper, and do not typically regress spontaneously like strawberry hemangiomas.
explanations.c: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a flat, permanent vascular malformation that does not regress and grows proportionately with the child.
explanations.d: Spider angiomas are small, central arterioles with radiating capillaries, typically associated with hyperestrogenic states (e.g., pregnancy, cirrhosis), not infants.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor of older adults, not seen in infants with benign strawberry lesions.

ankiCards: The 'strawberry hemangioma' of infancy is histologically a {{c1::capillary hemangioma}}.
Juvenile hemangiomas usually undergo {{c1::spontaneous regression}} by age 7.
The rapid growth phase of juvenile hemangiomas occurs during the {{c1::first few months}} of life.
Strawberry hemangiomas are most common on the {{c1::skin (face/scalp)}}.
Unlike juvenile hemangiomas, a {{c1::port-wine stain}} (nevus flammeus) does not regress.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangioma = Strawberry hemangioma.
Extremely common: 1 in 200 births.
Natural history: Rapid growth -> Stability -> Regression.
Regression is complete in 90% of cases by age 7.
Histology: Closely packed capillaries with thin walls.
microReview: Infant + bright red 'strawberry' + rapid growth followed by predicted regression = Juvenile Capillary Hemangioma.
examinerTraps: Wait-and-see is the standard management for strawberry hemangiomas; examiners may ask for the treatment, which is usually observation.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following environmental or industrial exposures is most strongly associated with the development of hepatic angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Vinyl chloride (used in PVC production) is a well-known carcinogen specifically linked to hepatic angiosarcoma, along with arsenic and Thorotrast.
explanations.b: Asbestos is primarily associated with mesothelioma and lung carcinoma.
explanations.c: Benzene is primarily associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.d: Carbon tetrachloride causes centrilobular necrosis and fatty change in the liver, but is not a primary driver of angiosarcoma.
explanations.e: Aflatoxin B1 is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
Besides vinyl chloride, {{c1::arsenic}} is an environmental cause of hepatic angiosarcoma.
{{c1::Thorotrast}} (an old radiopaque contrast) is a historical cause of hepatic angiosarcoma.
Angiosarcomas have a very {{c1::poor}} prognosis.
Unlike hemangiomas, angiosarcomas show significant {{c1::cytologic atypia/pleomorphism}}.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare but lethal malignancy.
Occupational exposure to vinyl chloride (plastics industry) is the classic risk factor.
Arsenic (pesticides) is another risk factor.
The latent period between exposure and tumor development is usually long (years).
The tumor is aggressive and usually metastatic at discovery.
microReview: Vinyl chloride and Arsenic = Hepatic Angiosarcoma. Aflatoxin = Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
examinerTraps: Be careful to distinguish between Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) and Hepatic Angiosarcoma; the exposures are different.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 50-year-old male with a history of alcohol use disorder presents with multiple 'spider-like' vascular lesions on his chest and face. These lesions blanch when the central point is pressed. What is the underlying pathophysiology of these lesions in this patient?

explanations.a: Spider angiomas (nevus araneus) are associated with hyperestrogenic states, which occur in cirrhosis because the diseased liver cannot properly metabolize estrogens.
explanations.b: HHV-8 causes Kaposi Sarcoma, not spider angiomas.
explanations.c: Bacterial infection (Bartonella) causes bacillary angiomatosis, which presents as nodules, not blanching spider-like lesions.
explanations.d: Hypertension does not cause spider angiomas; they are related to hormonal imbalances/vasodilation.
explanations.e: Spider angiomas are acquired, not congenital malformations like Sturge-Weber syndrome.

ankiCards: Spider angiomas are associated with {{c1::cirrhosis}} and {{c2::pregnancy}}.
The mechanism for spider angiomas in liver disease is {{c1::hyperestrogenism}}.
Spider angiomas consist of a central {{c1::arteriole}} with radiating capillaries.
When the central point of a spider angioma is pressed, the lesion {{c1::blanches}}.
Spider angiomas are typically found on the {{c1::face, neck, or upper chest}}.
keyPoints: Spider angiomas are a sign of hyperestrogenism.
Common in cirrhosis and pregnancy.
They are not true neoplasms but rather vascular ectasias.
Blanching is a key diagnostic feature.
Usually disappear if the underlying hormonal state is corrected.
microReview: Cirrhosis leads to high estrogen (liver can't degrade it), which leads to spider angiomas and palmar erythema.
examinerTraps: Spider angiomas are often listed alongside 'palmar erythema' and 'gynecomastia' as signs of liver failure/hyperestrogenism.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following best describes the clinical behavior and histological classification of a Hemangioendothelioma?

explanations.a: Hemangioendotheliomas occupy an intermediate category between benign hemangiomas and highly malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.b: Hemangiomas are strictly benign, but hemangioendotheliomas have metastatic potential, even if low.
explanations.c: Angiosarcomas are the highly aggressive malignancies; hemangioendotheliomas are more indolent.
explanations.d: Hamartomatous growths describe lesions like some hemangiomas in syndromes, but not the classification of hemangioendothelioma.
explanations.e: Pyogenic granuloma is often reactive, but hemangioendothelioma is a true neoplasm.

ankiCards: Hemangioendothelioma is classified as an {{c1::intermediate-grade}} vascular tumor.
Intermediate-grade tumors are also called {{c1::borderline}} tumors.
Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is a tumor of {{c1::endothelial}} cells that look like epithelial cells.
The metastatic potential of hemangioendothelioma is {{c1::lower}} than angiosarcoma.
Vascular tumors are divided into {{c1::benign, intermediate, and malignant}} categories.
keyPoints: Hemangioendothelioma is 'borderline' (between benign and malignant).
Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is a well-known subtype occurring around medium/large veins.
Clinical behavior is variable and unpredictable.
Histology shows cords or nests of round/spindle endothelial cells.
Surgery is the primary treatment.
microReview: Vascular tumors follow a spectrum: Hemangioma (Benign) -> Hemangioendothelioma (Intermediate) -> Angiosarcoma (Malignant).
examinerTraps: The word 'endothelioma' might sound benign, but the 'intermediate' status means it can recur and occasionally metastasize.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the pathogenesis of abdominal aortic aneurysms, atherosclerosis plays a dominant role by increasing the thickness of the intima. By what mechanism does this intimal thickening primarily contribute to the weakening of the underlying media?

options.a: Direct proteolytic digestion of the internal elastic lamina by lipid-laden macrophages
options.b: Impairment of nutrient and oxygen diffusion from the lumen to the media
options.c: Mechanical compression of the vasa vasorum by the atherosclerotic plaque
options.d: Induction of smooth muscle cell hyperplasia in the tunica media
options.e: Retrograde blood flow into the media through intimal ulcerations

explanations.a: While macrophages release proteases, the fundamental issue in atherosclerotic aneurysm formation is the diffusion barrier created by the plaque.
explanations.b: The aorta's media relies on diffusion from the lumen for nutrients; a thick atherosclerotic plaque acts as a barrier, causing medial ischemia, atrophy, and wall weakening.
explanations.c: The vasa vasorum are primarily located in the outer third of the media and adventitia in the thoracic aorta; the abdominal aorta lacks them in the inner media, making it more reliant on luminal diffusion.
explanations.d: Atherosclerosis typically leads to smooth muscle cell loss and atrophy in the media, not hyperplasia.
explanations.e: This describes the mechanism of an aortic dissection rather than the pathogenesis of a true atherosclerotic aneurysm.

ankiCards: The abdominal aorta is susceptible to aneurysms because it lacks {{c1::vasa vasorum}} in its inner media.
Atherosclerotic plaques cause medial weakening by {{c1::increasing the diffusion distance}} for nutrients and oxygen.
The primary consequence of intimal thickening on the underlying media is {{c1::ischemic atrophy}}.
Two principal mechanisms of vascular disease are narrowing of lumens and {{c1::weakening of vessel walls}}.
The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter is higher in {{c1::muscular arteries}} compared to elastic arteries.
keyPoints: Atherosclerosis is the most common cause of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms (AAA).
Plaques increase diffusion distance from the lumen to the media.
Medial ischemia leads to smooth muscle cell death and extracellular matrix loss.
The abdominal aorta is more vulnerable than the thoracic aorta due to sparse vasa vasorum.
Weakening of the wall eventually results in dilation or rupture.
microReview: Aneurysms represent a failure of vascular structural integrity. In elastic arteries like the aorta, the media requires constant nutrition. Atherosclerosis creates a physical barrier (plaque), leading to medial 'starvation,' atrophy, and subsequent aneurysmal dilation.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the mechanism of AAA (atherosclerosis/ischemia) with Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (often cystic medial degeneration or syphilis).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 67-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history and hypertension presents for a routine physical examination. On palpation of the abdomen, a pulsating mass is felt at the level of the umbilicus. Imaging reveals a 5.5-cm dilation of the infrarenal aorta. Which of the following is the most likely microscopic finding in the wall of this lesion?

options.b: Endarteritis obliterans of the vasa vasorum
options.c: Extensive intimal atherosclerotic plaque with medial thinning
options.e: Fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel wall

explanations.a: This is characteristic of Giant Cell Arteritis, which typically affects the temporal artery or branches of the carotid.
explanations.b: This is the hallmark of syphilitic (tertiary) aneurysms, which usually involve the thoracic aorta.
explanations.c: The patient has classic risk factors (age, smoking, male) for an Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA), which is driven by atherosclerosis and resulting medial atrophy.
explanations.d: This is a feature of malignant hypertension affecting small arterioles, not the large aorta.
explanations.e: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in necrotizing vasculitides or malignant hypertension, not standard AAA.

ankiCards: The most common location for an atherosclerotic aneurysm is the {{c1::abdominal aorta}}.
A pulsatile abdominal mass in an older male smoker is most likely an {{c1::abdominal aortic aneurysm}}.
Most AAAs are located {{c1::infrarenal::relation to renal arteries}}.
The major risk factor for the development of AAA is {{c1::smoking}}.
Medial thinning in AAA is secondary to {{c1::atherosclerotic plaque}} formation.
keyPoints: AAA is usually infrarenal and supra-iliac.
Clinical presentation often involves a pulsatile abdominal mass.
Risk factors include male gender, smoking, and age >50.
The structural failure is due to loss of elastic fibers and smooth muscle in the media.
Surgical intervention is typically considered when the diameter exceeds 5.0-5.5 cm.
microReview: AAA is a chronic inflammatory process where atherosclerotic plaques impair the health of the tunica media. The loss of medial strength under high arterial pressure leads to the progressive 'ballooning' of the vessel.
examinerTraps: The examiner may try to distract you with 'vasa vasorum' pathology; remember that AAA is atherosclerotic, while TAA (thoracic) is more likely associated with hypertension or syphilis (obliterative endarteritis).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes a 'false aneurysm' (pseudoaneurysm)?

options.a: A localized dilation involving all three layers of the arterial wall
options.b: A longitudinal tear in the media followed by an intramural hematoma
options.c: A wall defect leading to an extravascular hematoma that communicates with the intravascular space
options.d: A congenital thinning of the muscularis at arterial bifurcations
options.e: A diffuse, circumferential dilation of a long segment of the artery

explanations.a: This defines a 'true' aneurysm (e.g., atherosclerotic or saccular).
explanations.b: This describes an aortic dissection.
explanations.c: A false aneurysm is a breach in the vessel wall that allows blood to leak out, but it is contained by the surrounding connective tissue/adventitia.
explanations.d: This describes a 'berry' (saccular) aneurysm, which is a true aneurysm.
explanations.e: This describes a fusiform aneurysm, which is a subtype of a true aneurysm.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the vessel wall (intima, media, adventitia).
A {{c1::false (pseudoaneurysm)}} aneurysm is an extravascular hematoma communicating with the lumen.
A classic cause of a pseudoaneurysm is {{c1::trauma}} or iatrogenic injury (e.g., catheterization).
A {{c1::fusiform}} aneurysm is a circumferential dilation of a vessel segment.
A {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm is a spherical outpouching involving only a portion of the vessel wall.
keyPoints: True aneurysms include the intact attenuated vessel wall.
False aneurysms are essentially contained hematomas.
Dissections occur when blood enters the wall itself, creating a false lumen.
Saccular aneurysms are common in the Circle of Willis.
Fusiform aneurysms are common in the abdominal aorta.
microReview: Differentiation between true and false aneurysms depends on the integrity of the vessel wall layers. True = all layers present; False = leak contained by extravascular tissue.
examinerTraps: Aortic dissection is often colloquially called an 'aneurysm' by patients, but pathologically it is not a true aneurysm because it involves blood dissecting between layers.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which molecular alteration is most significantly associated with the development of thoracic aortic aneurysms in patients with Marfan syndrome?

options.d: Excessive deposition of Type I collagen in the media

explanations.a: MMP activity is typically increased in aneurysms, leading to the degradation of the extracellular matrix.
explanations.b: Fibrillin-1 mutations in Marfan syndrome lead to reduced sequestration of TGF-β, causing excessive TGF-β signaling, which promotes abnormal matrix production and wall weakening.
explanations.c: Vitamin C deficiency (Scurvy) affects collagen cross-linking but is not the primary mechanism in Marfan-related TAA.
explanations.d: There is a loss of structural collagen and elastin, not an excess of functional Type I collagen.
explanations.e: Lysyl oxidase is required for cross-linking elastin/collagen; its inhibition (e.g., lathyrism) causes aneurysms, but it is not the Marfan driver.

ankiCards: Marfan syndrome is caused by a mutation in the {{c1::FBN1 (Fibrillin-1)}} gene.
The thoracic aortic weakening in Marfan syndrome is characterized by {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
Mutations in FBN1 lead to excessive {{c1::TGF-β}} signaling.
The primary structural protein affected in Marfan syndrome is {{c1::elastin}} via fibrillin scaffolding.
Loeys-Dietz syndrome involves mutations in {{c1::TGF-β receptors}}.
keyPoints: Fibrillin-1 normally sequesters TGF-β.
Excessive TGF-β signaling leads to elastic fiber fragmentation.
This process is termed 'Cystic Medial Degeneration' (formerly necrosis).
Clinically, this presents as Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm (TAA).
β-blockers or TGF-β inhibitors (losartan) are used to slow progression.
microReview: In Marfan syndrome, the vessel wall is not just 'missing' a protein; the dysregulation of growth factors (TGF-β) causes the body to actively remodel the media into a weaker, more disorganized state.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Marfan (Fibrillin-1) with Ehlers-Danlos Type IV (Type III Collagen). Both cause aneurysms but via different structural defects.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 42-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presents with a sudden, severe 'thunderclap' headache. A CT scan of the head shows subarachnoid hemorrhage. Which of the following conditions is most strongly associated with this patient's underlying vascular lesion?

explanations.a: Berry (saccular) aneurysms in the Circle of Willis are the most common cause of non-traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage and are associated with ADPKD.
explanations.b: Syphilis is associated with thoracic aortic aneurysms, not cerebral berry aneurysms.
explanations.c: Diabetes is a risk factor for atherosclerosis and small vessel disease, but not specifically for berry aneurysms.
explanations.d: Monckeberg involves calcification of the media in muscular arteries but does not cause aneurysms or hemorrhage.
explanations.e: Giant cell arteritis involves large vessel inflammation and rarely causes subarachnoid hemorrhage.

ankiCards: The most common site for berry aneurysms is the {{c1::anterior communicating artery (Circle of Willis)}}.
{{c1::Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)}} is the genetic condition most associated with berry aneurysms.
Berry aneurysms lack a {{c1::tunica media}} and an internal elastic lamina.
Rupture of a berry aneurysm causes {{c1::subarachnoid}} hemorrhage.
Risk factors for berry aneurysm rupture include hypertension and {{c1::smoking}}.
keyPoints: Berry aneurysms occur at arterial branch points.
They are 'true' aneurysms but are congenital/developmental.
Clinical hallmark: 'Worst headache of my life' (thunderclap).
Associated with ADPKD and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Histology shows absence of smooth muscle at the site of the sac.
microReview: Berry aneurysms are developmental defects where the muscular layer of the artery fails to form at branch points. Over time, high pressure causes the remaining wall to bulge and eventually rupture into the subarachnoid space.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'polycystic kidney disease' in the stem; it's a classic USMLE association for berry aneurysms.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: The inflammatory response in the wall of an abdominal aortic aneurysm is characterized by an imbalance between which of the following?

options.b: Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMPs) and Tissue Inhibitors of Metalloproteinases (TIMPs)
options.e: Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF) and Angiopoietin

explanations.a: This imbalance relates to platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction.
explanations.b: In aneurysms, increased MMP expression (from macrophages) overwhelms TIMPs, leading to the degradation of collagen and elastin in the media.
explanations.c: This relates to vascular tone and endothelial dysfunction.
explanations.d: This relates to the risk of atherosclerosis, but not the specific enzymatic destruction of the wall matrix.
explanations.e: This relates to angiogenesis.

ankiCards: In aneurysm formation, macrophages secrete {{c1::Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
MMPs contribute to the degradation of {{c1::elastin and collagen}} in the vessel wall.
The endogenous inhibitors of MMPs are called {{c1::TIMPs (Tissue Inhibitors of Metalloproteinases)}}.
Aneurysm development requires an imbalance favoring {{c1::proteolysis}} over matrix synthesis.
Common MMPs involved in AAA include {{c1::MMP-2 and MMP-9}}.
keyPoints: Chronic inflammation is a key component of AAA.
Infiltrating macrophages and T-cells produce cytokines.
Cytokines increase MMP production.
Elastin degradation is irreversible as mature elastin does not regenerate.
Loss of structural integrity leads to progressive dilation.
microReview: The vessel wall is a dynamic structure. Aneurysms occur when the 'demolition' (MMPs) exceeds the 'repair/maintenance' (TIMPs and smooth muscle synthesis), primarily due to chronic inflammation often triggered by atherosclerosis.
examinerTraps: The examiner may use 'elastases' and 'MMPs' interchangeably; both contribute to the same outcome of matrix breakdown.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with a brassy cough and difficulty swallowing. Imaging shows a dilated ascending aortic arch. His medical history is notable for a treated sexually transmitted infection twenty years ago. Physical examination reveals an 'Argyll Robertson' pupil. What is the characteristic gross appearance of the aortic intima in this condition?

options.a: Smooth, glistening surface with fatty streaks
options.e: Yellow, necrotic debris in the subendothelial space

explanations.a: This describes normal intima or early atherosclerosis.
explanations.b: This describes advanced atherosclerosis, common in AAA but less specific for the 'tree-bark' look of syphilis.
explanations.c: Syphilitic aortitis leads to obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum, causing medial ischemia and scarring, which results in a 'tree-bark' appearance of the intima.
explanations.d: This describes myxoid change seen in cystic medial degeneration.
explanations.e: This is characteristic of an atheroma.

ankiCards: Syphilitic aneurysms typically involve the {{c1::ascending aorta (thoracic)}}.
The underlying pathology of syphilitic aortitis is {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}} of the vasa vasorum.
The gross 'tree-bark' appearance of the aorta is caused by {{c1::medial scarring}}.
Syphilitic aortitis can lead to {{c1::aortic valve insufficiency}} due to dilation of the aortic root.
The organism responsible for syphilitic aneurysms is {{c1::Treponema pallidum}}.
keyPoints: Tertiary syphilis targets the vasa vasorum.
Destruction of the media results in loss of elastic support.
It typically causes Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (TAA).
Dilation of the aortic root can pull the valve cusps apart (aortic regurgitation).
The 'tree-barking' is due to contraction of fibrous scars.
microReview: Syphilis is a classic 'vasa vasorum' disease. By choking off the blood supply to the aortic media in the thoracic region, it causes massive death of the elastic tissue, leading to dilation and a scarred, wrinkled intimal surface.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'tree-bark' of syphilis with the 'onion-skinning' of hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis. One is gross, the other is microscopic.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 19-year-old college student with extremely long fingers, pectus excavatum, and joint hypermobility presents with sudden onset of tearing chest pain radiating to the back. Blood pressure is 140/90 mmHg in the right arm and 100/60 mmHg in the left arm. What is the most likely microscopic finding in the patient's aorta?

options.b: Disorganization of the media with 'cyst-like' spaces filled with proteoglycans
options.c: Severe calcification of the internal elastic lamina
options.d: Mononuclear cell infiltrates around the vasa vasorum
options.e: Lipid-filled macrophages in the subendothelial space

explanations.a: This would suggest an infectious (mycotic) process or vasculitis.
explanations.b: The patient has Marfan syndrome. The underlying defect is cystic medial degeneration, characterized by loss of smooth muscle cells and accumulation of basophilic mucoid material.
explanations.c: This describes Monckeberg sclerosis, which is not associated with Marfan or dissection.
explanations.d: This describes syphilitic aortitis.
explanations.e: This describes an early atherosclerotic lesion (fatty streak).

ankiCards: Aortic dissection involves a tear in the {{c1::intima}} allowing blood into the media.
The most common predisposing factor for aortic dissection is {{c1::hypertension}}.
In young patients, the most common cause of aortic dissection is {{c1::Marfan syndrome}}.
Cystic medial degeneration shows spaces filled with {{c1::mucoid material (proteoglycans)}}.
A difference in blood pressure between arms suggests {{c1::aortic dissection}}.
keyPoints: Aortic dissection is not a 'true' aneurysm but often associated with them.
The 'tearing' pain is classic.
Cystic medial degeneration is the histologic substrate.
Marfan syndrome (Fibrillin-1) is the classic genetic association.
The double-lumen appearance on imaging confirms the diagnosis.
microReview: Cystic medial degeneration is a misnomer; there are no 'true' cysts. Instead, the elastic tissue disappears and is replaced by a jelly-like matrix of proteoglycans, which provides no structural strength, allowing the intima to tear and the media to split.
examinerTraps: The examiner uses the BP discrepancy to lead you to 'dissection,' then asks for the 'histology' of the underlying cause (Marfan).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following is the most common clinical complication of an untreated abdominal aortic aneurysm?

options.a: Embolization of atheromatous material to distal limbs
options.b: Compression of the ureter leading to hydronephrosis

explanations.a: This occurs ('trash feet') but is less common and less immediately fatal than rupture.
explanations.b: Compression of adjacent structures can occur but is rare compared to the risk of rupture.
explanations.c: The most significant and feared complication of AAA is rupture, which leads to fatal hemorrhage.
explanations.d: Mycotic aneurysms (infected) can occur, but this is a specific subtype, not the standard complication of an atherosclerotic AAA.
explanations.e: Aneurysms do not undergo malignant transformation into angiosarcomas.

ankiCards: The risk of AAA rupture is directly related to the {{c1::diameter}} of the aneurysm.
Aneurysms greater than {{c1::5.0 - 5.5 cm}} have a high risk of rupture.
The classic triad of AAA rupture is {{c1::flank/back pain, hypotension, and a pulsatile mass}}.
AAA rupture usually occurs into the {{c1::peritoneal cavity or retroperitoneum}}.
Atherosclerosis causes AAA primarily by {{c1::thinning the media}}.
keyPoints: Rupture is the primary cause of death from AAA.
Mural thrombus often forms within the aneurysm due to stasis.
Embolism can lead to lower limb ischemia.
Pain usually precedes or accompanies rupture.
Screening with ultrasound is recommended for male smokers over 65.
microReview: AAA is a 'ticking time bomb.' As the diameter increases (Laplace's Law: Tension = Pressure x Radius), the wall tension increases while the wall strength (weakened by atherosclerosis) decreases, eventually leading to catastrophic rupture.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'thrombosis' of the aneurysm (which is common) with the most 'common clinical complication' (which is rupture if left untreated).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with an exquisitely painful, small, red-blue nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. Histological examination reveals aggregates of specialized smooth muscle cells surrounding vascular channels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are common benign tumors of thin-walled capillaries and are generally painless and found on the skin or mucous membranes.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, highly painful tumors arising from the specialized smooth muscle cells of glomus bodies, typically found in the subungual region.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised patients caused by Bartonella species, presenting as red papules, not painful subungual nodules.
explanations.d: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms that are typically large, aggressive, and occur in the skin, soft tissue, breast, or liver.
explanations.e: Pyogenic granulomas are rapidly growing pedunculated red nodules on the skin or gingiva that bleed easily; they are not specifically subungual or characteristically painful.

ankiCards: The classic location for a glomus tumor is the {{c1::subungual (under the nail)}} region.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells of the glomus body.
The primary clinical symptom of a glomus tumor is {{c1::exquisite pain}}.
Glomus bodies are involved in the physiological process of {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors show nests of cells surrounding {{c1::vascular channels/vessels}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but extremely painful.
They originate from glomus bodies, which are specialized arteriovenous anastomoses.
Most commonly occur in the distal digits, particularly under the fingernails.
Cells are modified smooth muscle cells rather than endothelial cells.
Excision is usually curative.
microReview: Glomus tumor = Painful subungual nodule + modified smooth muscle cells. Distinct from hemangiomas which are usually painless.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse glomus tumors with 'glomus jugulare' tumors (paragangliomas), which are neuroendocrine in origin.
sourceQuote: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, exquisitely painful tumors arising from specialized smooth muscle cells of glomus bodies.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 35-year-old male with advanced HIV (CD4 count < 50 cells/mm³) presents with multiple violaceous, non-blanching skin plaques and nodules on his lower extremities. Biopsy shows spindle-shaped cells forming slit-like vascular spaces containing red blood cells. What is the primary etiologic agent associated with this condition?

explanations.a: HPV-16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx, not vascular tumors.
explanations.b: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can look similar to Kaposi sarcoma clinically, but histologically shows neutrophils and bacteria (Warthin-Starry stain), not spindle cells with slits.
explanations.c: Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma in all its clinical forms.
explanations.d: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and hairy leukoplakia, but not vascular spindle-cell tumors.
explanations.e: CMV causes retinitis and colitis in HIV patients but is not oncogenic for vascular tissue.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is caused by infection with {{c1::Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}.
The histological hallmark of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells}} forming slit-like spaces.
The spaces in Kaposi Sarcoma often contain extravasated {{c1::red blood cells (erythrocytes)}}.
HHV-8 infects {{c1::endothelial cells}} and induces a proliferative state.
{{c1::AIDS-associated (Epidemic)}} Kaposi Sarcoma is the most common HIV-related malignancy.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is caused by HHV-8.
Four clinical forms: Classic (older men), Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
Histology: Spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces, extravasated RBCs, and hyaline globules.
Lesions do not blanch because blood is not contained within well-formed vessels.
Often involves skin, mucous membranes, and viscera (GI tract, lungs).
microReview: HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Slit-like spaces = Kaposi Sarcoma. Differential: Bacillary angiomatosis (neutrophilic infiltrate, Bartonella).
examinerTraps: Wait for 'spindle cells' to confirm KS; if the description emphasizes 'neutrophilic inflammation' in an HIV patient, think Bacillary Angiomatosis.
sourceQuote: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8 and is highly associated with AIDS.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 62-year-old man who worked in a chemical plant for 30 years producing polyvinyl chloride presents with fatigue, weight loss, and right upper quadrant pain. Physical examination reveals hepatomegaly. Imaging shows multiple ill-defined hemorrhagic masses within the liver. A biopsy reveals malignant endothelial cells with pleomorphic nuclei. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Hepatocellular carcinoma is associated with cirrhosis, Hep B/C, and aflatoxin, but not specifically polyvinyl chloride; it originates from hepatocytes, not endothelium.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor; it is usually asymptomatic and consists of large blood-filled spaces, not malignant pleomorphic cells.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma of the liver is a rare malignancy strongly associated with specific carcinogens: polyvinyl chloride (PVC), Thorotrast, and arsenic.
explanations.d: Hepatoblastoma is the most common liver tumor in young children (usually <3 years old), not adults with industrial exposure.
explanations.e: Hepatic adenomas are benign tumors associated with oral contraceptive or anabolic steroid use, not industrial chemical exposure.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::polyvinyl chloride (PVC)}}, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
Angiosarcomas are malignant tumors of {{c1::endothelial}} origin.
The marker {{c1::CD31}} is often positive in angiosarcomas, indicating endothelial differentiation.
Hepatic angiosarcoma has a {{c1::poor (very aggressive)}} prognosis.
Exposure to Thorotrast was a historical risk factor for {{c1::angiosarcoma}} of the liver.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are highly malignant and aggressive.
Specific risk factors for liver angiosarcoma: Polyvinyl chloride, Thorotrast, Arsenic.
Markers: CD31 and von Willebrand factor (vWF).
Commonly occurs in skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Can occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
microReview: PVC/Arsenic/Thorotrast + Liver + Malignant endothelial cells = Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: A common distractor is Hepatocellular Carcinoma. Look for the specific 'endothelial' cell type or vascular markers like CD31.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms... hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with distinct carcinogens such as arsenic, Thorotrast, and polyvinyl chloride.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy develops a rapidly growing, 1-cm red, pedunculated lesion on her gingiva. The lesion bleeds easily with minor trauma. Histological examination shows a proliferation of capillaries with associated edema and an inflammatory infiltrate resembling granulation tissue. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors are subungual and painful, not common on the gingiva of pregnant women.
explanations.b: Cystic hygromas are cavernous lymphangiomas typically found in the neck or axilla of infants, often associated with Turner syndrome.
explanations.c: Angiosarcomas are malignant and would show cellular atypia, not the benign 'granulation tissue' appearance of this lesion.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma (granuloma pyogenicum) is a benign, rapidly growing vascular lesion often occurring on the gingiva (pregnancy tumor/granuloma gravidarum) or skin.
explanations.e: Spider angiomas are small, radial arrangements of subcutaneous arteries, often seen in pregnancy or cirrhosis, but they are not pedunculated nodules.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer because it is neither {{c1::infectious/pyogenic}} nor a true {{c1::granuloma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas occurring on the gingiva of pregnant women are called {{c1::pregnancy tumors (granuloma gravidarum)}}.
Histologically, pyogenic granuloma resembles {{c1::granulation tissue}}.
A key clinical feature of pyogenic granuloma is that it {{c1::bleeds easily}} with minor trauma.
The standard treatment for a persistent pyogenic granuloma is {{c1::surgical excision/curettage}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a variant of capillary hemangioma.
Often develops after trauma or during pregnancy.
Common locations: Gingiva, fingers, face.
Appearance: Red, pedunculated, bleeds easily.
May regress spontaneously (especially post-partum) or require excision.
microReview: Pregnancy + Gingiva + Rapidly growing red nodule = Pyogenic granuloma (granuloma gravidarum).
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic granuloma' is deceptive; it doesn't contain pus and isn't a granuloma (no epithelioid macrophages).
sourceQuote: Pyogenic granulomas are capillary hemangiomas that manifest as rapidly growing red pedunculated lesions on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A newborn is found to have a large, ill-defined mass on the left side of the neck. Transillumination is positive. Genetic testing reveals a 45,X karyotype. The mass likely represents a malformation of which of the following structures?

explanations.a: Arterial malformations do not typically present as large, transilluminating cystic neck masses.
explanations.b: Venous malformations are common but cystic hygromas are specifically of lymphatic origin.
explanations.c: The clinical description of a large, cystic, transilluminating neck mass in an infant with Turner syndrome (45,X) describes a cystic hygroma, which is a cavernous lymphangioma.
explanations.d: Arteriovenous shunts (AVMs) are often high-flow and may have a thrill or bruit, unlike a cystic hygroma.
explanations.e: Capillary malformations (like port-wine stains) are superficial and flat, not deep cystic masses.

ankiCards: Cystic hygroma is a type of {{c1::cavernous lymphangioma}}.
Cystic hygromas are frequently associated with {{c1::Turner syndrome (45,X)}} and Down syndrome.
The typical location for a cystic hygroma is the {{c1::neck}} or axilla.
A clinical sign of cystic hygroma on examination is that it {{c1::transilluminates}}.
Histologically, lymphangiomas contain fluid that is {{c1::protein-rich/lymphatic}} and lacks red blood cells.
keyPoints: Cystic hygromas are benign but can be difficult to resect due to lack of encapsulation.
Strongly associated with chromosomal aneuploidies (Turner syndrome).
Occur in the neck (cervical) or axillary regions.
Histology: Large, dilated lymphatic spaces lined by endothelium.
The spaces contain pale, eosinophilic, proteinaceous fluid.
microReview: Neck mass + Turner syndrome + Transillumination = Cystic hygroma (lymphatic origin).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse with a branchial cleft cyst (also in the neck but not typically associated with Turner syndrome or large transilluminating lymphangiomatous spaces).
sourceQuote: Cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) are typically found in the neck or axilla of children and are often associated with Turner syndrome.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old woman underwent a radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer 10 years ago. Since then, she has had persistent, massive lymphedema of her left arm. Recently, she noticed several dark-red to purple cutaneous nodules developing on that arm. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: While recurrent breast cancer is possible, the presentation of new vascular-appearing skin nodules in a chronically lymphedematous limb is more characteristic of Stewart-Treves syndrome.
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma occurring in the setting of chronic lymphedema (most commonly post-mastectomy) is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome.
explanations.c: Classic Kaposi sarcoma usually presents on the lower extremities of older men of Mediterranean or Eastern European descent, not specifically in lymphedematous arms after surgery.
explanations.d: Cavernous lymphangiomas are usually congenital and present in childhood, not as new nodules in an adult.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis requires infection with Bartonella and typically occurs in immunocompromised patients; lymphedema is not a primary risk factor.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in a limb with chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
The most common cause of Stewart-Treves syndrome is lymphedema following {{c1::radical mastectomy}}.
Stewart-Treves syndrome involves a malignancy of the {{c1::vascular/endothelial}} cells.
The latency period for Stewart-Treves syndrome post-surgery is typically {{c1::10 (or more)}} years.
Cutaneous angiosarcomas first appear as small {{c1::red/purple}} papules or nodules.
keyPoints: Stewart-Treves syndrome is angiosarcoma arising from chronic lymphedema.
The classic example is post-mastectomy with axillary node clearance.
Very poor prognosis with high rates of metastasis.
Histologically shows atypical endothelial cells forming irregular vascular channels.
Markers like CD31 help distinguish it from other poorly differentiated tumors.
microReview: Mastectomy + Chronic lymphedema + New purple nodules = Stewart-Treves syndrome (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: The examiner might offer 'lymphangiosarcoma'. While descriptive, 'angiosarcoma' is the standard pathologic term used in major texts.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas can also occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema, classically in the ipsilateral arm of women several years after radical mastectomy... (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular tumors is characterized by a 'strawberry' appearance at birth or shortly thereafter, grows rapidly for several months, and then usually undergoes spontaneous regression by age 7?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas are deeper, less well-circumscribed, and do not regress as frequently as juvenile hemangiomas; they may be part of von Hippel-Lindau disease.
explanations.b: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a birthmark that does not regress; it typically grows with the child and thickens over time.
explanations.c: Juvenile hemangioma (strawberry hemangioma) is extremely common in infants, grows rapidly, and then almost always regresses (75-90% by age 7).
explanations.d: Venous malformations are permanent and do not typically undergo spontaneous regression.
explanations.e: Spider telangiectasias are small dilated arterioles, not tumors, and are usually acquired (e.g., in cirrhosis or pregnancy).

ankiCards: The common name for a juvenile hemangioma is a {{c1::strawberry}} hemangioma.
Juvenile hemangiomas typically {{c1::regress (involute)}} spontaneously by age 7.
The initial growth phase of a juvenile hemangioma occurs during the first {{c1::few months/year}} of life.
Juvenile hemangiomas are histologically classified as {{c1::capillary}} hemangiomas.
Unlike juvenile hemangiomas, port-wine stains (nevus flammeus) {{c1::do not}} regress.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangiomas are the most common vascular tumor of infancy.
Location: Skin, often on the head and neck.
Appearance: Bright red, raised, 'strawberry-like'.
Life cycle: Rapid growth followed by slow involution.
Complete regression occurs in the majority of cases by age 7.
microReview: Infant + Strawberry nodule + Regression = Juvenile (Capillary) Hemangioma.
examinerTraps: Confusing juvenile hemangioma with nevus flammeus (port-wine stain). Remember: Port-wine stains stay; Strawberries fade.
sourceQuote: Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) of the newborn skin are very common... they grow rapidly for a few months but then fade and regresses by age 1 to 3 years.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 40-year-old male with HIV presents with several bright red, skin-colored, and purple papules on his trunk. Biopsy reveals a lobular proliferation of capillaries with prominent 'epithelioid' endothelial cells, neutrophilic debris, and purple-staining granular material. Which organism is most likely responsible for these findings?

explanations.a: HHV-8 causes Kaposi Sarcoma, which histologically shows spindle cells and slits, not a neutrophilic capillary proliferation with granular bacterial clusters.
explanations.b: Bartonella henselae (or B. quintana) causes Bacillary Angiomatosis in immunocompromised patients. The granular material seen on H&E is clusters of bacteria.
explanations.c: Treponema pallidum causes syphilis; its vascular involvement is typically endarteritis obliterans, not an angiomatous proliferation.
explanations.d: S. aureus can cause pyogenic infections but not this specific angiomatous lesion with granular bacterial clusters.
explanations.e: Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) causes systemic infection and granulomas in AIDS patients, not vascular tumors.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by bacteria of the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
In bacillary angiomatosis, the histological inflammatory infiltrate is dominated by {{c1::neutrophils}}.
The 'granular purple material' seen on H&E stains in bacillary angiomatosis represents {{c1::bacteria}}.
{{c1::Warthin-Starry (silver)}} stain can be used to visualize the Bartonella organisms in tissue.
The reservoir for Bartonella henselae is the {{c1::domestic cat}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis occurs in immunocompromised (mainly HIV) patients.
Causative agents: Bartonella henselae and Bartonella quintana.
Mimics Kaposi Sarcoma clinically but is treated with antibiotics (erythromycin).
Histology: Proliferation of capillaries with epithelioid endothelium and neutrophils.
Presence of bacterial clusters is a diagnostic hallmark.
microReview: HIV + Red papules + Neutrophils + Bacteria (Bartonella) = Bacillary Angiomatosis.
examinerTraps: The clinical appearance is almost identical to Kaposi Sarcoma. The presence of neutrophils and the response to antibiotics are the key clinical discriminators.
sourceQuote: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts... caused by opportunistic gram-negative bacilli of the Bartonella family.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following conditions is a benign, permanent vascular ectasia typically appearing as a large, flat, dull-red to purple 'port-wine stain' on the face or neck that follows the distribution of the trigeminal nerve and may be associated with the Sturge-Weber syndrome?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas are raised, blood-filled masses, not flat port-wine stains.
explanations.b: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a form of vascular ectasia. When it occurs in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve, it can be part of Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis).
explanations.c: Spider telangiectasias are small, central arterioles with radiating capillaries, not large flat patches.
explanations.d: Osler-Weber-Rendu disease (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) presents with multiple small telangiectasias on the skin and mucous membranes, not a single large port-wine stain.
explanations.e: Lymphangiomas are malformations of the lymphatic system, typically appearing as cystic or papular lesions, not flat red port-wine stains.

ankiCards: A port-wine stain is also known as {{c1::nevus flammeus}}.
If a port-wine stain follows the trigeminal nerve distribution, one should suspect {{c1::Sturge-Weber}} syndrome.
The components of Sturge-Weber syndrome include port-wine stain, leptomeningeal {{c1::angiomas}}, and glaucoma.
Unlike juvenile hemangiomas, nevus flammeus {{c1::does not}} regress over time.
Nevus flammeus is categorized as a vascular {{c1::ectasia (or malformation)}} rather than a true neoplasm.
keyPoints: Nevus flammeus is the most common form of vascular ectasia.
Presents as a flat, pink to purple lesion ('port-wine stain').
Usually located on the head or neck.
Sturge-Weber syndrome: Trigeminal port-wine stain + mental retardation + seizures + ipsilateral glaucoma.
Lesions do not involute; they tend to thicken and darken with age.
microReview: Port-wine stain + Trigeminal nerve = Sturge-Weber syndrome risk.
examinerTraps: Students often confuse the terms 'hemangioma' and 'ectasia'. A port-wine stain is an ectasia (dilation of existing vessels), not a proliferation of new vessels (neoplasm).
sourceQuote: A port-wine stain is a special form of nevus flammeus... when they occur in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve, they may be associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old patient is diagnosed with Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu disease). This autosomal dominant condition is primarily characterized by malformations in which of the following?

explanations.a: Large elastic arteries are affected in conditions like Marfan syndrome, not HHT.
explanations.b: Endothelial junctions are not the primary defect in HHT.
explanations.c: Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT) is caused by mutations in genes that modulate the Transforming Growth Factor-beta (TGF-β) signaling pathway in endothelial cells.
explanations.d: Capillary basement membrane thickening is seen in diabetes, not HHT.
explanations.e: Pericyte issues are not the established molecular cause of HHT.

ankiCards: Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia is also known as {{c1::Osler-Weber-Rendu}} disease.
HHT is inherited in an {{c1::autosomal dominant}} pattern.
The clinical hallmark of HHT is telangiectasias of the skin and {{c1::mucous membranes}}.
A common presenting symptom of HHT is recurrent {{c1::epistaxis (nosebleeds)}}.
The genetic mutations in HHT affect the {{c1::TGF-β}} signaling pathway.
keyPoints: HHT is an autosomal dominant disorder of vascular development.
Characterized by multiple small aneurysmal telangiectasias.
Common sites: Nose (epistaxis), tongue, mouth, GI tract.
Serious complications: Arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) in the lung, liver, or brain.
Genes involved: Endoglin (ENG) or Activin receptor-like kinase 1 (ACVRL1).
microReview: HHT = Epistaxis + GI bleeds + Telangiectasias + TGF-β pathway mutation.
examinerTraps: A classic board question link is epistaxis + iron deficiency anemia (from GI bleeds) in a patient with red spots on their tongue.
sourceQuote: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu disease) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in genes that encode components of the TGF-β signaling pathway.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 67-year-old female presents with several firm, violaceous nodules on her right arm. She has a history of a radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection for breast adenocarcinoma 11 years ago, resulting in persistent, chronic lymphedema. A biopsy of the skin nodules reveals highly pleomorphic malignant cells forming irregular, anastomosing vascular channels. Which of the following immunohistochemical markers would most likely be positive in these malignant cells?

explanations.a: CD31 (platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule) is a highly specific marker for endothelial cells and is used to confirm the diagnosis of vascular tumors like angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells and would be positive in the original breast adenocarcinoma, but not in a primary vascular tumor.
explanations.c: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells, such as melanocytes and Schwann cells, and is negative in vascular tumors.
explanations.d: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (skeletal, smooth, and cardiac) and is not expressed by the endothelial cells of an angiosarcoma.
explanations.e: HMB-45 is a marker for melanocytic differentiation and is used in the diagnosis of melanoma.

ankiCards: The classic eponym for an angiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphedema is {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
The most specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial differentiation is {{c1::CD31}}.
Malignant vascular tumors that form irregular, anastomosing channels are called {{c1::angiosarcomas}}.
Angiosarcomas are associated with exposure to {{c1::arsenic}} and {{c2::polyvinyl chloride (PVC)}}.
Histologically, angiosarcomas show malignant {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a malignant neoplasm of endothelial cells.
Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to angiosarcoma following chronic lymphedema (e.g., post-mastectomy).
Marker CD31 or von Willebrand factor confirms endothelial origin.
Hepatic angiosarcomas are linked to PVC, Thorotrast, and arsenic.
These tumors are locally invasive and have a poor prognosis.
microReview: Angiosarcomas are aggressive malignant vascular tumors. The clinical vignette describes Stewart-Treves syndrome, where chronic lymphedema predisposes to malignant transformation of the endothelium. CD31 is the gold-standard marker.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse angiosarcoma with a recurrence of the primary breast cancer; the lymphedema history and the formation of vascular channels on biopsy point to a new primary vascular malignancy.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 42-year-old male with poorly controlled HIV presents with multiple purple, maculopapular skin lesions on his lower extremities and trunk. Histological examination of a lesion reveals a proliferation of spindle-shaped cells with numerous slit-like spaces containing extravasated erythrocytes. Which of the following pathogens is the primary driver of this neoplastic process?

explanations.a: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent for all four clinical forms of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.b: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can look similar clinically but shows a neutrophilic infiltrate rather than slit-like spaces with spindle cells.
explanations.c: HIV causes the immunosuppression that allows HHV-8 to proliferate, but HIV itself does not transform the endothelial cells.
explanations.d: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) causes retinitis or colitis in AIDS patients but does not cause vascular tumors.
explanations.e: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is associated with lymphomas (like Burkitt or DLBCL) and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not Kaposi sarcoma.

ankiCards: {{c1::HHV-8}} is the causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma.
The histological hallmark of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells}} and {{c2::slit-like spaces}} with RBCs.
Unlike Kaposi, bacillary angiomatosis is characterized by a {{c1::neutrophilic}} infiltrate.
The four types of Kaposi Sarcoma are {{c1::Classic}}, {{c2::Endemic}}, {{c3::Transplant-associated}}, and {{c4::AIDS-associated}}.
Kaposi Sarcoma lesions are typically described as {{c1::purple}} or {{c2::violaceous}}.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
HHV-8 is essential for the pathogenesis of Kaposi Sarcoma.
Slit-like vascular spaces filled with RBCs are characteristic.
AIDS-associated Kaposi is the most common HIV-related malignancy.
Lesions may involve skin, mouth, and GI tract.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is an HHV-8 driven tumor. It is classified as an intermediate tumor because it is locally aggressive but less likely to metastasize widely than angiosarcoma. Histology shows spindle cells and slit-like vascular channels.
examinerTraps: The examiner may present Bacillary Angiomatosis as a distractor. Look for 'neutrophils' or 'Warthin-Starry stain' to pick Bartonella; look for 'spindle cells' and 'slit-like spaces' to pick HHV-8.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 25-year-old male presents with an exquisitely painful, 5-mm, red-blue nodule located under the fingernail of his left index finger. The lesion is extremely sensitive to cold. Surgical excision is performed. Which of the following cell types is the origin of this tumor?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.b: While it is a vascular tumor, it does not arise from the lining endothelial cells but from the supportive muscular elements of the glomus body.
explanations.c: Hemangiopericytomas (now often classified elsewhere) arise from pericytes; glomus tumors arise specifically from glomus cells.
explanations.d: Schwann cells give rise to neuromas or schwannomas; while painful, they do not typically present as subungual vascular nodules.
explanations.e: Fibroblasts give rise to fibromas or fibrosarcomas, which lack the characteristic vascular sensitivity and subungual location of glomus tumors.

ankiCards: A painful, subungual, red-blue tumor is most likely a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle cells}}.
The glomus body is an arteriovenous anastomosis involved in {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Glomus tumors are classically located {{c1::under the fingernails}}.
Excision of a glomus tumor is usually {{c1::curative}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but extremely painful.
Classic location is subungual (under the nail).
Derived from smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
Glomus bodies regulate temperature via shunting blood.
Histology shows nests of uniform, round cells surrounding vascular spaces.
microReview: Glomus tumors are small, benign, and highly painful. Their association with the subungual region and cold sensitivity are high-yield clinical clues. They originate from smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
examinerTraps: A common mistake is thinking 'vascular tumor' always means 'endothelial cell origin'. Glomus tumors are the exception, arising from the smooth muscle of the glomus apparatus.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 30-year-old male with advanced AIDS (CD4+ count 45/mm³) presents with several friable, red, pedunculated skin papules that bleed easily. A biopsy shows a lobular proliferation of capillaries with protuberant, epithelioid endothelial cells. There is a prominent infiltrate of neutrophils and granular material. A Warthin-Starry silver stain reveals clusters of small bacilli. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella species in immunocompromised patients. It features capillary proliferation with neutrophils and visible bacteria on silver stain.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8, shows spindle cells and slit-like spaces, and lacks a neutrophilic infiltrate and bacterial organisms.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is histologically similar but is usually solitary, occurs in immunocompetent hosts, and is not associated with Bartonella.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangioma consists of large, dilated blood-filled spaces and lacks the acute inflammation and bacteria seen here.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignancy with significant atypia, which is absent in this case.

ankiCards: {{c1::Bacillary angiomatosis}} is a vascular proliferation in AIDS patients caused by Bartonella.
The histological hallmark of bacillary angiomatosis is a {{c1::neutrophilic}} infiltrate.
The stain used to identify Bartonella in tissue is the {{c1::Warthin-Starry}} silver stain.
Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by {{c1::Bartonella henselae}} or {{c2::Bartonella quintana}}.
Unlike Kaposi sarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis is treated with {{c1::antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin)}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis occurs in immunocompromised (AIDS) patients.
Caused by Bartonella henselae (cats) or Bartonella quintana (lice).
Histology: Capillary proliferation with neutrophils and nuclear dust.
Warthin-Starry stain is positive for bacilli.
Clinical presentation: Red, friable, 'juicy' nodules.
microReview: Bacillary angiomatosis is an opportunistic infection masquerading as a tumor. It mimics Kaposi Sarcoma clinically but is distinguished by the presence of neutrophils and Bartonella organisms.
examinerTraps: The presence of red nodules in an AIDS patient is a 'trigger' for Kaposi Sarcoma. Always check for the presence of neutrophils and the Warthin-Starry stain results to differentiate it from Bacillary Angiomatosis.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular tumors are classified as benign, intermediate, or malignant based on their behavior and histology. Which of the following neoplasms is correctly categorized as an intermediate-grade (borderline) vascular tumor?

explanations.a: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor that can occur around medium and large veins; its behavior is between benign hemangiomas and malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas are common benign vascular tumors.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign vascular tumors characterized by large, dilated spaces.
explanations.d: Angiosarcomas are high-grade, fully malignant vascular tumors.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are benign neoplasms of the glomus body.

ankiCards: An example of an intermediate-grade vascular tumor is {{c1::epithelioid hemangioendothelioma}}.
Kaposi sarcoma is classified as an {{c1::intermediate}}-grade vascular tumor.
{{c1::Angiosarcoma}} is the most common malignant vascular tumor.
{{c1::Hemangiomas}} are the most common benign vascular tumors.
Hemangioendotheliomas typically occur around {{c1::medium or large veins}}.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors span a spectrum: benign, intermediate, and malignant.
Intermediate tumors are locally aggressive with low metastatic potential.
Examples of intermediate tumors include Kaposi Sarcoma and Hemangioendothelioma.
Malignant tumors (Angiosarcoma) have high metastatic potential.
Benign tumors (Hemangioma) rarely recur and do not metastasize.
microReview: Understanding the classification spectrum is vital. Hemangioendothelioma and Kaposi Sarcoma sit in the middle of the 'benign-to-malignant' scale.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'cavernous hemangioma' (benign) with 'angiosarcoma' (malignant) just because cavernous hemangiomas involve deeper structures like the liver.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare but highly aggressive malignancy. In addition to radiation exposure, which of the following environmental or industrial toxins is most strongly associated with the development of this specific tumor?

explanations.a: Polyvinyl chloride (PVC), along with Thorotrast (a radioactive contrast agent no longer used) and arsenic, is a classic industrial risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and lung cancer, not vascular tumors.
explanations.c: Benzene exposure is associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.d: Aflatoxin B1 (from Aspergillus) is a risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.
explanations.e: Naphthalene is associated with cataracts and hemolytic anemia but not specifically with hepatic angiosarcoma.

ankiCards: The industrial chemical {{c1::polyvinyl chloride (PVC)}} is associated with hepatic angiosarcoma.
Arsenic exposure (e.g., in pesticides) is a risk factor for {{c1::angiosarcoma}} of the liver.
Thorotrast, a radioactive contrast medium, is linked to {{c1::hepatic angiosarcoma}}.
Angiosarcomas of the liver have a very {{c1::poor}} prognosis.
{{c1::Radiation}} therapy for breast cancer can lead to cutaneous angiosarcoma.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is linked to specific chemical exposures.
PVC (plastic industry), Thorotrast, and Arsenic are the classic triad of toxins.
Latent period between exposure and tumor development can be decades.
Angiosarcoma is CD31+.
Liver angiosarcomas are often fatal within a year of diagnosis.
microReview: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a 'sentinel' tumor for toxic industrial exposures. When you see 'liver tumor' + 'PVC/Arsenic', pick Angiosarcoma, not Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
examinerTraps: The most common liver tumor is metastasis; the most common primary liver tumor is HCC. Angiosarcoma is rare, so it is only the correct answer when specific risk factors like PVC are mentioned.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 3-week-old female infant is brought to the pediatrician by her parents because of a bright red, raised, 2-cm 'strawberry-like' lesion on her scalp. The parents report that the lesion appeared a few days after birth and has been growing slowly. What is the most appropriate next step in management based on the natural history of this lesion?

options.a: Observation, as it will likely regress spontaneously
options.b: Immediate surgical excision to prevent malignancy
options.d: Pulse-dye laser therapy for permanent removal

explanations.a: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are extremely common in infants. They typically grow rapidly for a few months and then spontaneously involute by age 7 in the vast majority of cases.
explanations.b: Surgical excision is usually unnecessary and may cause scarring; these lesions are entirely benign.
explanations.c: While beta-blockers (propranolol) or steroids are sometimes used for lesions obstructing vision or the airway, simple observation is the standard for most.
explanations.d: Laser therapy can be used for residual cosmetic issues, but observation is the first-line management for a growing lesion in a neonate.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is virtually never seen in this clinical context (neonatal scalp lesion); the diagnosis is clinical.

ankiCards: Juvenile hemangiomas are commonly called {{c1::strawberry}} hemangiomas.
Most juvenile hemangiomas {{c1::regress/involute}} by age 7.
The histology of a strawberry hemangioma shows a proliferation of {{c1::capillaries}}.
Juvenile hemangiomas are {{c1::benign}} vascular tumors.
Standard management for a non-obstructing juvenile hemangioma is {{c1::observation}}.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangioma is the most common vascular tumor of infancy.
Occurs in 1 in 200 births.
Clinical appearance: Bright red, lobulated, raised lesion.
Natural history: Rapid growth followed by slow involution.
Complications are rare unless the lesion obstructs a vital structure (e.g., eye).
microReview: Juvenile hemangiomas are benign capillary proliferations. The hallmark is 'spontaneous regression'. Medical treatment (propranolol) is only used if the lesion is life- or sight-threatening.
examinerTraps: Don't pick 'excise' for a benign infant tumor that naturally goes away. 'Observation' is the most board-appropriate answer for juvenile hemangiomas.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 22-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with a rapidly growing, 1-cm, red, pedunculated mass on her gingiva. The lesion is painless but bleeds easily when she brushes her teeth. She is concerned about cancer. A biopsy shows a highly vascular proliferation resembling granulation tissue. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma (granuloma pyogenicum) is a common, benign, pedunculated red nodule on the skin or gingiva. It is histologically similar to granulation tissue and is common in pregnant women ('pregnancy tumor').
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are usually deeper, larger, and not pedunculated or gingival-associated.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are subungual and extremely painful, unlike this gingival lesion.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis occurs in immunocompromised individuals; this patient is healthy and pregnant.
explanations.e: Kaposi sarcoma would present with multiple purple patches or nodules and HHV-8 association, rather than a single 'granulation-like' gingival mass.

ankiCards: A {{c1::pyogenic granuloma}} is a benign vascular lesion that often occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women.
The histological appearance of pyogenic granuloma resembles {{c1::granulation tissue}}.
Despite the name, pyogenic granuloma is neither {{c1::pyogenic (pus-forming)}} nor a {{c2::granuloma}}.
The common name for a pyogenic granuloma occurring in pregnancy is {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are known for their tendency to {{c1::bleed}} easily with minor trauma.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it's a capillary hemangioma.
Classic location: Gingiva (especially in pregnancy) or skin (trauma).
Histology: Lobular proliferation of capillaries with edema and inflammation.
Grossly: Pedunculated, red, friable (bleeds easily).
Many regress after pregnancy, but some require excision.
microReview: Pyogenic granuloma is a fast-growing, friable vascular lesion often triggered by hormonal changes (pregnancy) or minor trauma. It looks like 'proud flesh' or granulation tissue.
examinerTraps: The name is a trap! It contains no pus (not pyogenic) and no granulomas. It is actually a lobular capillary hemangioma.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by various tumors including renal cell carcinoma and pheochromocytoma. Which type of vascular tumor is most specifically associated with this syndrome, typically occurring in the cerebellum, retina, or brainstem?

explanations.a: Hemangioblastomas are highly vascular tumors characteristic of Von Hippel-Lindau disease. They are most commonly found in the cerebellum and retina.
explanations.b: Angiosarcomas are malignant tumors not typically associated with VHL syndrome.
explanations.c: Capillary hemangiomas are common skin/organ lesions but are not the 'classic' VHL-associated CNS tumor.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas of the CNS exist but the specific VHL-associated entity is the hemangioblastoma.
explanations.e: Lymphangiomas are benign malformations of lymphatic vessels, not specifically linked to VHL.

ankiCards: {{c1::Hemangioblastoma}} is the characteristic CNS vascular tumor in Von Hippel-Lindau disease.
VHL disease is caused by a mutation in the {{c1::VHL}} gene on chromosome {{c2::3p}}.
Besides hemangioblastomas, VHL patients often develop {{c1::Renal Cell Carcinoma}}.
Hemangioblastomas in VHL commonly occur in the {{c1::cerebellum}} and {{c2::retina}}.
The VHL protein is involved in the degradation of {{c1::Hypoxia Inducible Factor (HIF)}}.
keyPoints: VHL is a multi-system tumor syndrome.
Hemangioblastoma is a major component of the VHL clinical triad.
HIF-1alpha accumulation leads to increased VEGF and angiogenesis.
Retinal hemangioblastomas are also called 'angiomas'.
CNS hemangioblastomas can produce erythropoietin, leading to polycythemia.
microReview: VHL syndrome = Hemangioblastoma (CNS/Retina) + Renal Cell Carcinoma + Pheochromocytoma. The underlying mechanism is loss of the VHL protein, causing a 'pseudo-hypoxic' state that drives massive angiogenesis.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Hemangioblastoma (VHL) with Cavernous Hemangioma. While both are vascular, the hemangioblastoma has a specific cellular component ('vacuolated stromal cells') and a specific genetic association (VHL).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the most common histological feature of a cavernous hemangioma, distinguishing it from a capillary hemangioma?

options.a: Large, dilated vascular channels with thin walls and little stroma
options.b: Closely packed thin-walled capillaries with scant stroma
options.c: Spindle cells with slit-like spaces and hemosiderin
options.d: Nests of uniform round cells with adjacent vessels
options.e: Pleomorphic endothelial cells with prominent mitoses

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated blood-filled spaces (caverns) separated by a thin connective tissue stroma.
explanations.b: This describes a capillary hemangioma, which has small, vessel-sized channels.
explanations.c: This describes Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.d: This describes a glomus tumor.
explanations.e: This describes angiosarcoma.

ankiCards: {{c1::Cavernous}} hemangiomas have large, dilated vascular spaces compared to capillary hemangiomas.
Cavernous hemangiomas are common in the {{c1::liver}} and {{c2::brain}}.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas are {{c1::less}} likely to regress.
In the liver, cavernous hemangiomas can be mistaken for {{c1::malignant tumors (metastases)}} on imaging.
Cavernous hemangiomas of the brain are concerning because they can cause {{c1::hemorrhage}} or {{c2::seizures}}.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign but often involve deeper structures.
Most common benign tumor of the liver.
Histology: Large blood-filled spaces lined by a single layer of endothelium.
They do not spontaneously regress like juvenile hemangiomas.
Can be part of syndromes like Von Hippel-Lindau (though hemangioblastoma is more specific).
microReview: Hemangiomas are divided by the size of the vascular channels: 'Capillary' are small/tight, 'Cavernous' are large/dilated. Cavernous ones are the most common benign liver tumors.
examinerTraps: A cavernous hemangioma in the liver is often an incidental finding. Biopsying it can be dangerous due to the risk of intraperitoneal hemorrhage—imaging (MRI/CT with contrast) is usually sufficient for diagnosis.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents to the clinic for a routine physical examination.
