explanations.b: Aneurysmal dilation is a form of wall weakening, not luminal obstruction.
explanations.c: Thrombosis or embolism causes 'precipitous' (sudden) obstruction of vessel lumens.
explanations.d: This is a degenerative change in the wall leading to weakening.
explanations.e: Intimal thickening is a stereotyped response to injury that occurs over time.

ankiCards: Luminal obstruction can occur {{c1::progressively}} or {{c2::precipitously}}.
{{c1::Atherosclerosis}} is the classic example of progressive luminal narrowing.
{{c1::Thrombosis}} is a cause of precipitous luminal obstruction.
{{c1::Embolism}} is a cause of precipitous luminal obstruction.
Weakening of vessel walls leads to {{c1::dilation}} or {{c2::rupture}}.
keyPoints: Obstruction can be slow (atherosclerosis) or fast (clot).
Precipitous means sudden or steep change.
Thrombosis is a sudden luminal event.
Embolism is a sudden luminal event.
These are distinct from the 'weakening' mechanism.
microReview: Sudden blockage = Thrombosis/Embolism. Slow blockage = Atherosclerosis. Wall failure = Aneurysm/Dissection.
examinerTraps: Ensure you distinguish between the *type* of obstruction (progressive vs precipitous).
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism)
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: When considering the pathogenesis of an abdominal aortic aneurysm, which layer of the vascular wall is most likely to show the structural failure that facilitates dilation?

explanations.a: The endothelium is the inner lining; damage here leads to narrowing/thrombosis, but it doesn't provide structural strength.
explanations.b: The intima thickens in response to injury (narrowing) but isn't the primary structural support against dilation.
explanations.c: The media contains the smooth muscle and elastic fibers that provide structural integrity; its weakening leads to aneurysms.
explanations.d: The internal elastic lamina is a boundary, but the bulk of the strength is in the media.
explanations.e: Vasa vasorum nourish the outer layers but are not structural components themselves.

ankiCards: Weakening of vessel walls leads to {{c1::dilation}} or {{c2::rupture}}.
Vascular structure reflects distinct {{c1::functional roles}}.
The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter is crucial for {{c1::pressure control}}.
Arteries are thicker than veins because they handle {{c1::higher blood pressures}}.
Many vascular disorders have characteristic {{c1::anatomic distributions}}.
keyPoints: The media is the structural backbone of the artery.
Loss of elastic fibers in the media leads to aneurysm.
Weakening is one of the two core mechanisms of vascular disease.
Atherosclerosis in the intima can lead to secondary medial atrophy.
Aneurysms are essentially a failure of the wall's tensile strength.
microReview: Intima = Response to injury (thickening). Media = Structural integrity (Aneurysms). Adventitia = Support/Nourishment.
examinerTraps: Students often pick 'intima' because atherosclerosis is an intimal disease, but the *dilation* occurs because the *media* weakens.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 60-year-old patient undergoes an autopsy. The pathologist notes that the small muscular arteries in the kidneys show a significantly increased ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter compared to a healthy control. This structural adaptation is most likely an attempt to regulate which of the following?

explanations.a: Venous return is regulated by veins and the right heart, not small muscular arteries.
explanations.b: While it affects capillary pressure, the primary 'purpose' of the structural ratio mentioned is systemic regulation.
explanations.c: Small muscular vessels increase their wall-to-lumen ratio to exert control over blood flow and pressure (resistance).
explanations.d: Elastic recoil is a function of large elastic arteries like the aorta.
explanations.e: Leukocyte extravasation occurs in post-capillary venules.

ankiCards: Small muscular vessels exert control over {{c1::blood flow and pressure}}.
An increased ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter is found in {{c1::smaller}} arteries.
Vascular structure is specialized to reflect {{c1::distinct functional roles}}.
Atherosclerosis affects mostly {{c1::elastic}} and {{c2::muscular}} arteries.
Stenosis is the {{c1::narrowing}} of vessel lumens.
keyPoints: Muscular arteries are the 'faucets' of the circulatory system.
Increased thickness-to-lumen ratio provides greater contractile power.
This specialization is a response to the need for pressure control.
Vessel architecture changes along the arterial tree.
This adaptation can become pathological in hypertension.
microReview: High wall:lumen ratio = Muscular artery = Resistance control. Low wall:lumen ratio = Vein = Capacitance/Storage.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the function of large elastic arteries (conduction/recoil) with small muscular ones (resistance/control).
sourceQuote: the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing these muscular vessels to exert control over blood flow and pressure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with a 4-mm, exquisiteley painful, firm, red-blue nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. She notes that the pain is often paroxysmal and triggered by exposure to cold temperatures. Physical examination shows no other skin lesions or systemic symptoms. A biopsy of the lesion is performed, revealing aggregates of specialized cells surrounding vascular spaces.

explanations.a: Endothelial cells line all vascular tumors, but the specialized cell forming the nests in a glomus tumor is the glomus cell, which is mesenchymal.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors are benign, exquisitely painful tumors arising from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, an arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.c: Fibroblasts are present in many tumors but are not the primary cell of origin for glomus tumors.
explanations.d: While pericytes are related to vascular walls (as seen in hemangiopericytomas), they do not form the characteristic nests of a glomus tumor.
explanations.e: Skeletal muscle is not involved in the pathogenesis of vascular glomus tumors.

ankiCards: The characteristic location for a glomus tumor is {{c1::subungual (under the nail)}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells of the glomus body.
A clinical hallmark of glomus tumors is pain triggered by {{c1::cold}}.
Unlike most hemangiomas, glomus tumors are characterized by being {{c1::exquisitely painful}}.
The glomus body is an arteriovenous anastomosis involved in {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but very painful.
They typically occur in the distal portions of digits, especially subungual.
The cells of origin are glomus cells (modified smooth muscle).
The pain is often paroxysmal and temperature-sensitive.
Surgical excision is usually curative.
microReview: Glomus tumor = Subungual + Pain + Cold sensitivity + Smooth muscle origin.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse glomus tumors with glomus jugulare tumors (paragangliomas). The subungual location and cold sensitivity are diagnostic keys for the vascular glomus tumor.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors 518 / Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions 518 / Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors 520 / Malignant Tumors 522
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old male with a history of advanced HIV (CD4+ count < 100 cells/uL) presents with multiple, progressively enlarging, violaceous skin plaques on his lower extremities and trunk. Biopsy of a lesion shows spindle-shaped cells, slit-like vascular spaces containing red blood cells, and a prominent inflammatory infiltrate. The pathogenesis of this condition is most strongly linked to which of the following?

options.e: Loss of function in the VHL gene

explanations.a: UV radiation is linked to squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma, not Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.b: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is caused by Human Herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8), also known as KS-associated herpesvirus (KSHV).
explanations.c: Chronic lymphedema is a risk factor for angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves syndrome), not specifically KS.
explanations.d: Vinyl chloride is associated with hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.e: VHL mutations are associated with hemangioblastomas, not KS.

ankiCards: The causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
The most common malignancy associated with AIDS is {{c1::Kaposi Sarcoma}}.
Histologically, Kaposi Sarcoma presents with {{c1::spindle cells}} and slit-like vascular spaces.
Kaposi Sarcoma lesions are typically described as {{c1::violaceous/purple}} plaques or nodules.
HHV-8 infects {{c1::endothelial}} cells and induces them to produce pro-proliferative cytokines.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma is a low-grade malignant vascular tumor.
There are four forms: Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
All forms are linked to HHV-8 infection.
HHV-8 establishes latent infection in endothelial cells.
Treatment involves highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) for AIDS patients.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = HHV-8 + Spindle cells + AIDS/Immunosuppression + Slit-like spaces.
examinerTraps: Examiners often contrast Kaposi Sarcoma (HHV-8) with Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella). Both occur in HIV patients, but BA has a neutrophilic infiltrate and is bacterial.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors 518 / Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions 518 / Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors 520 / Malignant Tumors 522
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with several firm, dark-purple nodules on her left arm. Ten years ago, she underwent a radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection for breast adenocarcinoma, which was followed by chronic, persistent swelling of the left upper extremity. A biopsy of one of the skin nodules reveals highly pleomorphic malignant endothelial cells forming irregular, anastomosing vascular channels. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is HHV-8 related and usually presents in HIV patients; it does not typically follow chronic lymphedema.
explanations.b: This is Stewart-Treves syndrome, where chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy) predisposes the patient to cutaneous angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation caused by Bartonella.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign and do not show pleomorphic malignant cells or irregular channels.
explanations.e: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign, fast-growing inflammatory vascular lesion, often on gingiva or skin.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
Angiosarcomas are malignant tumors of {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
A common marker used to identify angiosarcoma cells is {{c1::CD31}}.
Cutaneous angiosarcoma can occur several years after {{c1::radiation}} therapy for breast cancer.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is classically associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a highly aggressive malignant vascular tumor.
The cells are pleomorphic and form irregular vascular channels.
They often occur in older adults on the scalp or in areas of chronic lymphedema.
The 5-year survival rate is generally poor due to early metastasis.
CD31 and von Willebrand factor are positive markers.
microReview: Post-mastectomy lymphedema + New purple nodules = Angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves).
examinerTraps: Do not confuse this with recurrent breast cancer. The biopsy specifically showing endothelial pleomorphism and vascular channels points to angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors 518 / Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions 518 / Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors 520 / Malignant Tumors 522
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 26-year-old woman in her second trimester of pregnancy develops a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated mass on her gingiva. The lesion is friable and bleeds easily with minimal trauma. Histological examination shows a highly vascular proliferation resembling granulation tissue with edema and an inflammatory infiltrate. What is the most appropriate name for this lesion?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are common benign tumors but the association with pregnancy and gingival location specifically describes pyogenic granuloma.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas involve larger, deeper vascular channels and are not typically pedunculated friable masses on the gingiva.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a common benign lesion that frequently occurs on the skin or oral mucosa, particularly during pregnancy (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are subungual and extremely painful, unlike the gingival mass described.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a malignancy that would show high-grade cytologic atypia, not the benign granulation-like appearance.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granulomas are often found on the {{c1::gingiva}} of pregnant women.
Histologically, pyogenic granuloma resembles {{c1::granulation tissue}}.
Another name for a pyogenic granuloma occurring in pregnancy is {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Unlike its name suggests, pyogenic granuloma is neither {{c1::pyogenic (pus-forming)}} nor a {{c2::granuloma}}.
The primary clinical characteristic of pyogenic granuloma is that it {{c1::bleeds easily (friable)}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a form of capillary hemangioma.
It presents as a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated nodule.
Commonly occurs after trauma or during pregnancy.
May spontaneously regress (especially post-partum).
Histology shows lobular arrangements of capillaries.
microReview: Pregnancy + Gingiva + Rapid growth + Bleeding = Pyogenic Granuloma.
examinerTraps: The name 'Pyogenic Granuloma' is a misnomer. It is actually a vascular lesion (hemangioma), not an infection or a granulomatous inflammation.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors 518 / Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions 518 / Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors 520 / Malignant Tumors 522
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following environmental or chemical exposures is most specifically associated with the development of a malignant vascular tumor arising in the liver?

explanations.a: Aflatoxin B1 is a potent risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Vinyl chloride (used in PVC production) is a classic chemical exposure linked to hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Ethanol is linked to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
explanations.d: Benzene is associated with acute myeloid leukemia.
explanations.e: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and lung cancer.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
Vinyl chloride is used in the manufacturing of {{c1::polyvinyl chloride (PVC)}}.
Thorotrast was a radioactive {{c1::contrast agent}} previously used in imaging that causes hepatic angiosarcoma.
Malignant endothelial cells in angiosarcoma express the marker {{c1::CD31}}.
The prognosis for hepatic angiosarcoma is very {{c1::poor}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a rare but highly fatal liver malignancy.
Specific occupational exposures (Vinyl chloride) are classic triggers.
It originates from the endothelial cells of the liver sinusoids.
Latency between exposure and tumor development is often decades.
Unlike hemangiomas, these are aggressive and invasive.
microReview: Liver vascular malignancy + PVC worker = Hepatic Angiosarcoma (Vinyl Chloride).
examinerTraps: Be careful to distinguish between hepatocellular carcinoma (liver cells) and angiosarcoma (vascular/endothelial cells).
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors 518 / Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions 518 / Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors 520 / Malignant Tumors 522
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 39-year-old male with AIDS presents with multiple red-purple skin nodules. A Warthin-Starry silver stain of a biopsy specimen reveals clusters of small bacilli. The patient reports having several kittens at home. What is the fundamental mechanism driving the vascular proliferation seen in this patient's lesions?

options.a: HHV-8 induced G-protein coupled receptor activation
options.b: Bacterial induction of host hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF-1α)
options.c: Constitutive activation of the MYC oncogene
options.d: Mutation in the VHL tumor suppressor gene
options.e: Germline mutation in the glomulin gene

explanations.a: HHV-8 mechanism applies to Kaposi Sarcoma, not Bacillary Angiomatosis.
explanations.b: In Bacillary Angiomatosis, Bartonella induces the host to produce VEGF and other factors by activating pathways like HIF-1α, leading to vascular proliferation.
explanations.c: MYC activation is seen in many cancers but is not the primary driver of this infectious vascular lesion.
explanations.d: VHL mutations drive hemangioblastomas in Von Hippel-Lindau disease.
explanations.e: Glomulin mutations are associated with familial glomus tumors.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by {{c1::Bartonella henselae}} or {{c2::Bartonella quintana}}.
The histological feature that distinguishes Bacillary Angiomatosis from Kaposi Sarcoma is a {{c1::neutrophilic}} infiltrate.
{{c1::Warthin-Starry}} silver stain is used to visualize the bacteria in Bacillary Angiomatosis.
Bacillary angiomatosis occurs primarily in {{c1::immunocompromised/HIV}} patients.
The cat-scratch disease organism, {{c1::Bartonella henselae}}, is a common cause of Bacillary Angiomatosis.
keyPoints: Bacillary Angiomatosis is an opportunistic infection in AIDS.
It presents as vascular skin lesions that mimic Kaposi Sarcoma.
Driven by Bartonella-induced angiogenesis.
Treatable with antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin).
Warthin-Starry stain is positive for bacteria.
microReview: HIV + Red nodules + Cats + Silver stain positive bacilli = Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella).
examinerTraps: Kaposi Sarcoma and Bacillary Angiomatosis look identical clinically. Look for 'neutrophils' or 'Warthin-Starry' or 'cats' in the prompt to pick Bartonella.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors 518 / Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions 518 / Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors 520 / Malignant Tumors 522
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 5-year-old child is found to have a large, deep-seated vascular lesion in the liver during an ultrasound for unrelated abdominal pain. The lesion consists of large, dilated, blood-filled vascular spaces separated by a thin connective tissue stroma. These lesions are frequently associated with Von Hippel-Lindau disease when they occur in the cerebellum. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas consist of small, thin-walled capillaries, not the large dilated spaces described.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, blood-filled vascular channels; they are common in the liver and are the vascular component of Von Hippel-Lindau disease in certain organs.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are small, painful, and subungual, not large liver masses.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a malignant, aggressive tumor with atypical cells; this describes a benign, structured lesion.
explanations.e: Hemangiopericytoma is a rare tumor of pericytes, not primarily blood-filled dilated spaces.

ankiCards: The most common benign tumor of the liver is a {{c1::cavernous hemangioma}}.
Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, {{c1::dilated}} vascular spaces.
Von Hippel-Lindau disease is associated with {{c1::hemangioblastomas}} and cavernous hemangiomas.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas are often {{c1::deep-seated}} and do not regress.
A potential complication of large cavernous hemangiomas in infants is {{c1::consumptive coagulopathy (Kasabach-Merritt syndrome)}}.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign but can be locally destructive if large.
They are sharply circumscribed.
Liver is the most common internal organ involved.
Histology: large blood-filled spaces, no atypia.
VHL association involves the cerebellum, retina, and brainstem.
microReview: Large blood spaces + Liver + VHL association = Cavernous Hemangioma.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse cavernous hemangioma with cavernous lymphangioma (hyroma). Lymphangiomas contain proteinaceous fluid (lymph), not blood.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors 518 / Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions 518 / Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors 520 / Malignant Tumors 522
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following immunohistochemical markers is most specific for identifying tumors of endothelial cell origin, such as angiosarcomas?

explanations.a: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells (carcinomas).
explanations.b: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (leiomyosarcomas, rhabdomyosarcomas).
explanations.c: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a highly specific marker for endothelial cells.
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells (melanoma, Schwannoma).
explanations.e: Vimentin is a general marker for mesenchymal cells but is not specific to endothelium.

ankiCards: The specific endothelial marker CD31 is also known as {{c1::PECAM-1}}.
Angiosarcomas can be identified by immunohistochemical staining for {{c1::CD31}} or von Willebrand factor.
Factor VIII-related antigen is another marker for {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
CD31 is used to differentiate poorly differentiated angiosarcomas from {{c1::carcinomas}}.
In Kaposi Sarcoma, the cells also express markers of the {{c1::endothelial}} lineage.
keyPoints: CD31 is the standard marker for vascular tumors.
Endothelial cells also express Von Willebrand Factor (vWF).
Vascular tumors are mesenchymal in origin (vimentin positive).
Immunohistochemistry is vital for diagnosing poorly differentiated vascular malignancies.
CD34 is also often expressed, though less specific than CD31.
microReview: Vascular origin + Immunohistochemistry = CD31.
examinerTraps: S100 or Cytokeratin are frequently used as distractors. Remember CD31 for 'Endothelial' and Desmin for 'Muscle'.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors 518 / Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions 518 / Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors 520 / Malignant Tumors 522
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An infant is born with a bright red, slightly raised, lobulated 'strawberry-like' lesion on his cheek. The lesion was not present at birth but appeared at 2 weeks of age and grew rapidly. The parents are concerned about the cosmetic appearance. What is the most likely natural history of this lesion?

explanations.a: Strawberry hemangiomas are benign and do not undergo malignant transformation.
explanations.b: Strawberry (juvenile) hemangiomas are extremely common, grow for a few months, and then typically regress spontaneously by age 5 to 7.
explanations.c: Port-wine stains (nevus flammeus) persist and darken; strawberry hemangiomas regress.
explanations.d: These are benign localized lesions and do not metastasize.
explanations.e: This association (Sturge-Weber) is characteristic of a port-wine stain in the V1/V2 distribution, not a strawberry hemangioma.

ankiCards: The strawberry hemangioma is also known as a(n) {{c1::juvenile/infantile}} hemangioma.
Most strawberry hemangiomas regress by age {{c1::7}}.
Unlike port-wine stains, strawberry hemangiomas {{c1::regress}} over time.
Strawberry hemangiomas are histologically classified as {{c1::capillary}} hemangiomas.
The prevalence of strawberry hemangiomas is approximately 1 in {{c1::200}} births.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangiomas are the most common vascular tumor of infancy.
They are often multiple.
The 'strawberry' appearance is due to the superficial capillary proliferation.
Management is usually watchful waiting due to high regression rates.
Beta-blockers (propranolol) may be used if the lesion obstructs vital functions.
microReview: Infant + Red strawberry lesion + Rapid growth = Juvenile Hemangioma (Regresses).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Port-wine stains (flat, permanent) with Strawberry hemangiomas (raised, regressing).
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors 518 / Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions 518 / Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors 520 / Malignant Tumors 522
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A child presents with a large, flat, purple-red birthmark covering the left side of his face in the distribution of the ophthalmic and maxillary branches of the trigeminal nerve. The physician orders a brain MRI to screen for associated vascular malformations. This clinical presentation is most consistent with which of the following?

explanations.a: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) involves malformations in skin and mucous membranes, causing epistaxis and GI bleeds.
explanations.b: Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) features a facial port-wine stain, leptomeningeal angiomas, and potential mental retardation and seizures.
explanations.c: VHL involves hemangioblastomas of the CNS and retina, and renal cell carcinomas.
explanations.d: NF1 features café-au-lait spots and neurofibromas, not port-wine stains.
explanations.e: Tuberous sclerosis involves angiofibromas and ash-leaf spots, not port-wine stains.

ankiCards: The facial lesion in Sturge-Weber syndrome is a(n) {{c1::port-wine stain (nevus flammeus)}}.
Sturge-Weber syndrome is associated with {{c1::leptomeningeal}} angiomas.
Patients with Sturge-Weber syndrome often have a port-wine stain in the distribution of the {{c1::trigeminal (CN V)}} nerve.
Common CNS complications of Sturge-Weber include seizures and {{c1::mental retardation}}.
Unlike strawberry hemangiomas, port-wine stains {{c1::do not}} regress.
keyPoints: Sturge-Weber syndrome is a sporadic neurocutaneous disorder.
The port-wine stain is a form of nevus flammeus.
Leptomeningeal angiomas usually occur ipsilateral to the facial lesion.
Radiology may show 'tram-track' calcifications in the brain.
Glaucoma is a common ocular association.
microReview: Port-wine stain (CN V distribution) + Brain angioma + Seizures = Sturge-Weber.
examinerTraps: The port-wine stain is flat; the strawberry hemangioma is raised. Only the port-wine stain in the trigeminal distribution is linked to Sturge-Weber.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors 518 / Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions 518 / Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors 520 / Malignant Tumors 522
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular pathology results in significant morbidity and mortality through two principal mechanisms. Which of the following describes the mechanism leading to the formation of an aneurysm?

explanations.a: Precipitous obstruction is typical of acute events like thrombosis or embolism, not aneurysm formation.
explanations.b: Progressive narrowing is a feature of atherosclerosis leading to stenosis, whereas aneurysms involve dilation.
explanations.c: Weakening of vessel walls is one of the two principal mechanisms of vascular disease, specifically leading to dilation (aneurysms) or rupture.
explanations.d: Muscular hypertrophy is a response to hypertension but is not the primary mechanism of aneurysmal dilation.
explanations.e: Endothelial proliferation is seen in healing and some tumors, but it does not cause the wall expansion seen in aneurysms.

ankiCards: The two principal mechanisms of vascular disease are narrowing/obstruction and {{c1::weakening}} of vessel walls.
Vessel wall weakening primarily leads to {{c1::dilation}} or rupture.
Aneurysms are a result of structural {{c1::weakening}} of the vessel wall.
Narrowing of vessel lumens can occur progressively through {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Narrowing of vessel lumens can occur precipitously through {{c1::thrombosis}} or embolism.
keyPoints: Vascular disease morbidity/mortality is the highest of any disease category.
Principal mechanism 1: Stenosis or complete obstruction.
Principal mechanism 2: Weakening of walls leading to dilation (aneurysm).
Stenosis can be progressive (atherosclerosis) or precipitous (thrombosis).
Normal vessel structure must be understood to appreciate pathogenesis.
microReview: Vascular pathology is categorized by either lumen restriction (stenosis/obstruction) or wall structural failure (aneurysm/rupture).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'cause' (e.g., atherosclerosis) with the 'mechanism' (e.g., weakening or narrowing). Atherosclerosis can cause both.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Arterial walls are structural specialized to accommodate specific hemodynamic requirements. Compared to veins at the same level of branching, which architectural feature is characteristic of arteries to manage higher blood pressures?

explanations.a: Arteries generally have smaller lumens than corresponding veins to maintain higher pressure.
explanations.b: Valves are a feature of veins, especially in the extremities, to prevent backflow in low-pressure systems.
explanations.c: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
explanations.d: Vasa vasorum are more prominent in the adventitia of large vessels, but wall thickness is the primary differentiator for pressure management.
explanations.e: Arteries do not have reduced intimal thickness; they have more robust media and adventitia.

ankiCards: Arterial walls are {{c1::thicker}} than corresponding veins at the same level.
Arterial structure accommodates {{c1::pulsatile}} flow and higher blood pressures.
The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}} as arteries become smaller.
Muscular vessels exert control over flow and pressure by changing their {{c1::lumen diameter}}.
Structural specializations in vessels reflect their distinct {{c1::functional roles}}.
keyPoints: Arterial walls are thicker than veins to handle high pressure.
Wall thickness to lumen ratio increases in smaller vessels.
Muscular vessels control blood pressure through diameter changes.
Structural specializations are functionally driven.
Disorders often target specific vessel types based on their anatomy.
microReview: Arteries = Thick walls, high pressure, pulsatile flow. Veins = Thin walls, low pressure, larger lumens, valves.
examinerTraps: A common mistake is thinking the ratio of wall thickness to lumen decreases in small vessels; it actually increases.
sourceQuote: For example, arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 67-year-old male with a 40-pack-year smoking history and hypertension presents for a routine physical exam. Palpation of the abdomen reveals a pulsatile mass superior to the umbilicus. A CT scan confirms a 5.5 cm dilation of the infrarenal aorta. Which of the following underlying processes is most likely responsible for the structural change in this vessel?

explanations.a: Cystic medial necrosis is more commonly associated with thoracic aortic aneurysms and Marfan syndrome.
explanations.b: Atherosclerosis is the most common cause of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA), especially in elderly male smokers.
explanations.c: Syphilitic (luetic) aneurysms typically involve the ascending aorta and are rare in the abdominal segment.
explanations.d: Congenital defects usually lead to Berry aneurysms in the Circle of Willis, not abdominal aortic aneurysms.
explanations.e: Septic embolization leads to mycotic aneurysms, which are less common than atherosclerotic AAAs.

ankiCards: The most common cause of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Atherosclerosis mainly affects {{c1::elastic}} and muscular arteries.
Classic risk factors for AAA include {{c1::smoking}} and male gender.
Abdominal aortic aneurysms are usually located in the {{c1::infrarenal}} segment.
Weakening of the vessel wall leads to {{c1::dilation}} or rupture.
keyPoints: AAA is primarily an atherosclerotic disease.
Risk factors: Male, Age >65, Smoking, Hypertension.
Usually infrarenal in location.
Presents as a pulsatile abdominal mass.
Weakening of the media allows the vessel to dilate under pressure.
microReview: AAA = Atherosclerosis + Smoking + Infrarenal. TAA (Thoracic) = Cystic Medial Necrosis + Hypertension + Marfan.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse the location: Atherosclerosis targets the abdominal aorta, whereas syphilis or Marfan syndrome targets the thoracic aorta.
sourceQuote: Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: The structural classification of blood vessels determines their susceptibility to specific pathologies. Atherosclerosis, a leading cause of aneurysmal weakening, primarily targets which specific vessel types?

explanations.a: Arterioles are more affected by hypertensive changes (hyaline/hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis) than classic atherosclerosis.
explanations.b: Venules are the site of leukocyte extravasation and are not typically affected by atherosclerosis.
explanations.c: Atherosclerosis predominantly affects large elastic arteries (aorta, carotid) and medium-sized muscular arteries (coronary, renal).
explanations.d: Veins do not develop atherosclerosis due to lower pressure and different wall composition.
explanations.e: Lymphatics are involved in fluid transport and immune cell trafficking, not atherosclerotic disease.

ankiCards: Atherosclerosis affects mainly {{c1::elastic}} and muscular arteries.
Specific kinds of vessels are characterized by structural {{c1::specializations}}.
Vascular disorders often have characteristic {{c1::anatomic distributions}}.
Elastic arteries include the {{c1::aorta}} and its major branches.
Muscular arteries include the {{c1::coronary}} and renal arteries.
keyPoints: Disease distribution is determined by vessel anatomy.
Atherosclerosis is a disease of high-pressure arterial systems.
Elastic arteries handle high volume; muscular arteries regulate flow.
Veins and capillaries are spared from atherosclerosis.
Pathology location correlates to vessel functional role.
microReview: Atherosclerosis = Elastic/Muscular Arteries. Hypertension = Arterioles. Vasculitis = Varies by vessel size.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'arterioles'—they are the target of hypertension, not atherosclerosis.
sourceQuote: Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old female with long-standing hypertension presents with sudden onset of severe, 'tearing' chest pain that radiates to her back. Blood pressure is 190/110 mmHg. A chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum. What is the most likely fundamental mechanical failure in this patient’s aorta?

explanations.a: Precipitous obstruction describes a clot (thrombosis), not the wall failure seen in dissection or aneurysm.
explanations.b: Intimal thickening is a stereotyped response to injury but doesn't cause acute tearing pain.
explanations.c: Progressive stenosis is characteristic of chronic atherosclerosis, not acute dissection.
explanations.d: Aortic dissection occurs when high pressure causes blood to enter the wall, facilitated by underlying medial weakening.
explanations.e: Decreased (not increased) vasa vasorum flow is often implicated in medial ischemia and weakening.

ankiCards: Aortic dissection is often associated with a {{c1::widened}} mediastinum on X-ray.
The clinical hallmark of aortic dissection is {{c1::tearing}} chest pain radiating to the back.
The mechanical basis for dissection/aneurysm is wall {{c1::weakening}}.
Hypertension is a major risk factor for {{c1::aortic dissection}}.
Wall weakening leads to either {{c1::dilation}} or rupture.
keyPoints: Dissection and aneurysm share the common mechanism of wall weakening.
Hypertension is the most common risk factor for aortic dissection.
Clinical presentation: Tearing pain, widened mediastinum.
Vessel wall failure leads to blood entering the media.
This is distinct from the narrowing mechanism of vascular disease.
microReview: Mechanism 1 (Narrowing) = Ischemia. Mechanism 2 (Weakening) = Aneurysm/Dissection/Rupture.
examinerTraps: Aortic dissection is not a 'true' aneurysm (which involves all three layers), but both stem from the same fundamental 'weakening' mechanism described in the text.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: As arterial diameter decreases from elastic arteries to muscular arteries, which of the following changes occurs in their architectural ratio to allow for the control of blood pressure?

options.a: Ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases
options.b: Ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter decreases
options.c: Ratio of elastic fibers to smooth muscle cells increases
options.d: Ratio of adventitia to media thickness decreases
options.e: Ratio of intima to media thickness increases

explanations.a: As vessels become smaller, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing muscular control over flow/pressure.
explanations.b: If the ratio decreased, the vessels would have less muscular power relative to their volume, hindering pressure control.
explanations.c: Muscular arteries have fewer elastic fibers than elastic arteries; the ratio of muscle to elastin increases.
explanations.d: The media is the dominant layer in muscular arteries; the ratio change of adventitia is not the primary factor in pressure regulation.
explanations.e: The intima remains a thin layer; the media becomes proportionately larger relative to the lumen in smaller arteries.

ankiCards: The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}} in smaller vessels.
Vessels that exert control over blood flow and pressure are primarily {{c1::muscular}} vessels.
Arterial wall thickness {{c1::diminishes}} as vessels become smaller, though the relative thickness compared to the lumen increases.
Control of blood flow is achieved by vessels changing their {{c1::lumen diameter}}.
Structural specializations of vessels reflect their distinct {{c1::functional}} roles.
keyPoints: Smaller vessels have a higher wall-to-lumen ratio.
This allows for effective vasoconstriction and vasodilation.
Muscular arteries are the primary 'resistance' vessels.
Architectural changes correspond to the need for pressure regulation.
Total wall thickness actually decreases in smaller vessels, even as the ratio increases.
microReview: Elastic Arteries = Volume conduction. Muscular Arteries = Flow/Pressure regulation (due to high wall:lumen ratio).
examinerTraps: The absolute wall thickness decreases in small vessels, but the 'ratio' of thickness to lumen increases. Be careful with this distinction.
sourceQuote: Arterial wall thickness gradually diminishes as the vessels become smaller, but the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing these muscular vessels to exert control over blood flow and pressure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular disease mechanisms are broadly divided into those that reduce flow and those that compromise structural integrity. Which clinical entity represents the mechanism of 'precipitous complete obstruction'?

explanations.a: Aneurysms represent wall weakening/dilation, not luminal obstruction.
explanations.b: Berry aneurysms are a form of wall weakening in the cerebral vasculature.
explanations.c: Atherosclerotic progression is described as 'progressive narrowing,' not 'precipitous complete obstruction.'
explanations.d: Embolism (and thrombosis) causes precipitous (sudden) complete obstruction of a vessel lumen.
explanations.e: Cystic medial necrosis is a histological state leading to wall weakening and aneurysms.

ankiCards: Precipitous luminal obstruction is caused by {{c1::thrombosis}} or embolism.
Progressive luminal narrowing is typically caused by {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Obstruction and weakening are the two main mechanisms of {{c1::vascular disease}}.
Narrowing is also known as {{c1::stenosis}}.
Aneurysms fall under the category of wall {{c1::weakening}}.
keyPoints: Obstruction can be gradual or sudden.
Sudden obstruction = Thrombosis/Embolism.
Gradual obstruction = Atherosclerosis.
Structural failure leads to dilation/rupture.
Dilation is the hallmark of aneurysmal disease.
microReview: Sudden = Clot (Thrombus/Embolus). Slow = Plaque (Atherosclerosis). Weak Wall = Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Atherosclerosis can lead to both progressive narrowing AND (if the plaque ruptures) precipitous thrombosis. However, the text classifies them as distinct mechanistic pathways.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism)
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old male is evaluated for chronic headaches. An MRI of the brain reveals a 4mm saccular outpouching at the junction of the anterior communicating artery and the anterior cerebral artery. This lesion is a result of structural weakness in the vessel wall. Which of the following is the most likely categorization for this finding?

explanations.a: AVMs are abnormal connections between arteries and veins, not localized wall outpouchings.
explanations.b: Berry (saccular) aneurysms occur in the Circle of Willis due to congenital media weakening, fitting the description of a structural wall weakness leading to dilation.
explanations.c: Atherosclerotic aneurysms usually occur in large vessels like the abdominal aorta, not the small arteries of the brain.
explanations.d: Mycotic aneurysms are caused by infection (e.g., endocarditis) and are less common than Berry aneurysms in this location.
explanations.e: Dissecting aneurysms involve a tear in the intima with blood tracking into the media; they are rarely 'saccular' in the brain.

ankiCards: Saccular aneurysms in the Circle of Willis are commonly called {{c1::Berry}} aneurysms.
The fundamental mechanism of aneurysm formation is vessel wall {{c1::weakening}}.
Aneurysms involve the {{c1::dilation}} or rupture of a vessel.
Berry aneurysms are often located at {{c1::branch}} points in the Circle of Willis.
Congenital defects in the {{c1::media}} are thought to underlie Berry aneurysms.
keyPoints: Berry aneurysms are saccular dilations.
Location: Circle of Willis branch points.
Mechanism: Wall weakening leading to dilation.
Complication: Subarachnoid hemorrhage.
Associated with structural wall defects.
microReview: Wall Weakening -> Dilation -> Aneurysm (AAA if aorta, Berry if brain).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'saccular' shape of Berry aneurysms with 'fusiform' shapes more common in atherosclerotic aortic aneurysms.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which category of human disease is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other, primarily due to mechanisms involving vessel narrowing or wall weakening?

explanations.a: While globally significant, infectious diseases are surpassed by vascular pathology in total morbidity and mortality.
explanations.b: The text states that vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
explanations.c: Cancer is a major cause of death, but vascular disease (heart attack, stroke, etc.) remains the leading cause.
explanations.d: Respiratory diseases are significant but do not exceed the impact of vascular conditions.
explanations.e: Metabolic syndromes often lead to vascular pathology, but the vascular lesions themselves are the direct cause of the mortality.

ankiCards: {{c1::Vascular pathology}} is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
The most clinically significant lesions involve {{c1::arteries}}.
Although less significant than arterial lesions, {{c1::venous}} disorders are not inconsequential.
The two mechanisms of vascular disease are {{c1::narrowing}} and weakening.
Understanding normal vessel structure is necessary to understand {{c1::pathogenesis}}.
keyPoints: Vascular disease is the leading cause of death globally.
Arterial lesions are more significant than venous ones.
Morbidity results from tissue ischemia or vessel rupture.
Pathology is tied to structural failure or luminal blockage.
Venous disorders (like DVT) still carry significant weight.
microReview: Vascular Disease = #1 Mortality cause. Mechanisms = Stenosis (blockage) and Weakening (dilation).
examinerTraps: Even though atherosclerosis is the 'disease', the 'category' is vascular pathology. Be precise with the question's scope.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular anatomy determines why certain diseases affect only specific regions of the circulation. Why are muscular arteries uniquely suited to exert control over blood flow and systemic blood pressure compared to larger elastic arteries?

options.a: They possess a higher density of elastic fibers in the media.
options.b: They have a greater ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter.
options.c: They are the primary site of nutrient and gas exchange.
options.d: They contain one-way valves to prevent pressure drops.
options.e: Their intima is thicker and more metabolically active.

explanations.a: Elastic fibers are more prevalent in elastic arteries (like the aorta) to dampen pulsatile flow, not in muscular ones.
explanations.b: The increased wall-to-lumen ratio in smaller muscular arteries allows their smooth muscle to effectively constrict or dilate the lumen to control pressure.
explanations.c: Nutrient exchange occurs in capillaries, which lack a muscular media.
explanations.d: Valves are found in veins, not muscular arteries.
explanations.e: Intimal thickness is not the primary factor in pressure regulation; the muscular media is.

ankiCards: Muscular vessels control blood flow by changing their {{c1::lumen diameter}}.
The wall thickness to lumen ratio {{c1::increases}} as vessels get smaller.
{{c1::Arterial}} walls are thicker than corresponding veins.
Structural specializations in vessels reflect their distinct {{c1::functional}} roles.
Atherosclerosis affects mainly {{c1::elastic}} and muscular arteries.
keyPoints: Functional roles dictate vessel structure.
High wall-to-lumen ratio = High resistance control.
Resistance vessels are mainly small muscular arteries.
Elastic vessels act as reservoirs/dampeners.
Vascular pathology is often site-specific (anatomic distribution).
microReview: Elastic Arteries = Distension/Recoil. Muscular Arteries = Resistance/Pressure control (High Wall:Lumen).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'absolute wall thickness' (highest in aorta) with 'relative wall thickness' (highest in muscular arteries/arterioles).
sourceQuote: Arterial wall thickness gradually diminishes as the vessels become smaller, but the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing these muscular vessels to exert control over blood flow and pressure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 42-year-old male presenting with advanced HIV (CD4+ count 85 cells/mm³) presents with multiple painless, purple-to-red macules and plaques on his lower extremities and oral mucosa. A biopsy of one skin lesion reveals spindle-shaped stromal cells forming slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells. Which of the following pathogens is most directly implicated in the pathogenesis of this patient's condition?

explanations.a: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised patients, which presents with similar red papules, but histology shows neutrophils and lobular capillary proliferation rather than spindle cells with slit-like spaces.
explanations.b: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma, which classically presents as purple plaques in AIDS patients with the described histology.
explanations.c: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with various lymphomas (like Burkitt's) and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, but not with primary vascular tumors like Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.d: Human papillomavirus 16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx, not vascular spindle cell lesions.
explanations.e: Cytomegalovirus can cause retinitis or colitis in AIDS patients but is not the oncogenic driver for Kaposi Sarcoma.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is caused by infection with {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
The histological hallmark of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells}} forming {{c2::slit-like}} vascular spaces.
In AIDS patients, Kaposi Sarcoma commonly presents on the {{c1::skin, mucous membranes, and GI tract}}.
Unlike bacillary angiomatosis, Kaposi Sarcoma histology lacks significant {{c1::neutrophilic}} inflammation.
The classic appearance of Kaposi Sarcoma lesions is {{c1::purple or red}} macules, plaques, or nodules.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
It is strongly associated with HHV-8 infection.
Histology shows spindle cells and slit-like spaces with extravasated RBCs.
Commonly seen in four settings: Classic (older Mediterranean men), Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
Bacillary angiomatosis is the primary differential in immunocompromised hosts.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Slit-like spaces + AIDS patient. Bacillary Angiomatosis = Bartonella + Neutrophils + AIDS patient.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Kaposi Sarcoma with Bacillary Angiomatosis; look for 'spindle cells' versus 'neutrophils' in the histology description.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors ... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions ... Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors ... Malignant Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A biopsy of a malignant, poorly circumscribed skin lesion from the scalp of an elderly man shows highly pleomorphic endothelial cells that are positive for CD31. The cells form irregular, anastomosing vascular channels. Which of the following mechanisms is the most likely driver for this aggressive neoplasm in the context of previous radiation therapy?

explanations.a: Angiosarcomas that arise secondary to irradiation (e.g., post-mastectomy radiation or on the scalp) frequently demonstrate MYC gene amplification.
explanations.b: BRAF mutations are common in melanomas, not primary vascular angiosarcomas.
explanations.c: KRAS mutations are hallmarks of pancreatic and colon cancers, not typically associated with radiation-induced angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: VHL inactivation is associated with hemangioblastomas (often in Von Hippel-Lindau disease), not angiosarcomas.
explanations.e: While TP53 mutations occur in many cancers, MYC amplification is the specific association for post-radiation angiosarcoma.

ankiCards: Secondary angiosarcomas (post-radiation) are associated with {{c1::MYC}} gene amplification.
{{c1::CD31}} is a specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial cells in angiosarcoma.
Angiosarcoma is a {{c1::malignant}} vascular tumor with a very poor prognosis.
The histological feature of angiosarcoma includes {{c1::anastomosing}} vascular channels lined by atypical cells.
Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic {{c1::lymphedema}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignant endothelial tumor.
Occurs most often in skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Environmental triggers: Arsenic, Thorotrast, Polyvinyl chloride (PVC) (especially for hepatic lesions).
Radiation is a major risk factor for cutaneous angiosarcoma.
CD31 and CD34 positivity confirms vascular origin.
microReview: Angiosarcoma: Elderly scalp or Post-mastectomy lymphedema (Stewart-Treves) or Radiation. Marker: CD31. Histology: Malignant channels.
examinerTraps: Wait for CD31 or Von Willebrand Factor positivity to confirm vascular origin before choosing Angiosarcoma over other pleomorphic sarcomas.
sourceQuote: Malignant tumors ... Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms with histology ranging from highly differentiated tumors ... to wildly anaplastic.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 25-year-old female presents with a small, exquisitely painful, 5-mm red-blue nodule under the fingernail of her right index finger. The lesion is extremely sensitive to cold and touch. This tumor most likely originates from which of the following cell types?

explanations.a: Pericytes are found in hemangiopericytomas (now classified as solitary fibrous tumors), but the classic subungual painful tumor is a glomus tumor.
explanations.b: While it is a vascular lesion, the predominant cell type in a glomus tumor is the specialized cell of the glomus body, not standard endothelial cells.
explanations.c: A glomus tumor (glomangioma) arises from the specialized smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, an arteriovenous structure involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts are not the primary cell of origin for this vascular-associated thermoregulatory tumor.
explanations.e: Lymphatic cells would form lymphangiomas, which are typically painless and not subungual.

ankiCards: A glomus tumor is characterized by being {{c1::exquisitely painful}} and located {{c2::subungually (under the nail)}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells.
The normal function of the glomus body is {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors show nests of {{c1::monomorphic round}} cells surrounding vascular spaces.
Excision of a glomus tumor is {{c1::curative}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumor is a benign, painful vascular neoplasm.
Classically located in the distal portion of digits (subungual).
Small size but outsized symptoms (pain, cold sensitivity).
Arises from glomus bodies (AV shunts).
Cell type: Modified smooth muscle cells.
microReview: Nail bed + Pain + Cold sensitivity = Glomus Tumor (modified smooth muscle cells).
examinerTraps: The examiner often emphasizes the 'pain' and 'subungual' location as pathognomonic.
sourceQuote: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, exquisitely painful tumors arising from specialized smooth muscle cells of the glomus bodies.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following liver tumors is most strongly associated with occupational exposure to vinyl chloride used in the plastic industry?

explanations.a: Hepatocellular carcinoma is associated with Hepatitis B/C and cirrhosis, not specifically vinyl chloride.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign tumor of the liver and is not linked to chemical exposures.
explanations.c: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare malignant tumor with a well-known association with vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
explanations.d: Hepatoblastoma is a childhood liver tumor not linked to adult occupational exposures.
explanations.e: Hepatic adenoma is associated with oral contraceptive use, not industrial plastic manufacturing.

ankiCards: Three specific chemicals associated with hepatic angiosarcoma are {{c1::Arsenic}}, {{c2::Thorotrast}}, and {{c3::Vinyl chloride}}.
Vinyl chloride is primarily used in the {{c1::plastics (PVC)}} industry.
Angiosarcoma of the liver is a {{c1::malignant}} neoplasm.
The latent period between exposure to vinyl chloride and development of angiosarcoma is usually {{c1::decades (long)}}.
Angiosarcoma tumor cells express the endothelial marker {{c1::CD31}}.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is highly aggressive.
Associated with occupational exposures.
Vinyl chloride exposure occurs in PVC workers.
Thorotrast (radioactive contrast) is a historical cause.
Arsenic (pesticides) is another risk factor.
microReview: PVC worker + Liver mass = Hepatic Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Vinyl Chloride (Angiosarcoma) with Aflatoxin B1 (Hepatocellular Carcinoma).
sourceQuote: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with distinct environmental carcinogens, including arsenic ... Thorotrast ... and polyvinyl chloride.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A healthy 3-week-old female infant is brought to the pediatrician by her parents who noticed a bright-red, raised, 'strawberry-like' lesion on her right cheek that has been rapidly growing since birth. Which of the following is the most likely natural history for this lesion?

explanations.a: Strawberry hemangiomas are benign and do not undergo malignant transformation.
explanations.b: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are common in newborns, grow rapidly for months, and then almost always spontaneously involute, with complete regression usually by age 7.
explanations.c: This describes a 'port-wine stain' (Nevus flammeus), which does not regress and may darken/thicken, unlike a strawberry hemangioma.
explanations.d: They are localized benign tumors and do not metastasize.
explanations.e: Surgical excision is rarely performed because they regress naturally; they do not have a high recurrence rate if removed.

ankiCards: The common name for a juvenile hemangioma is a {{c1::strawberry}} hemangioma.
Juvenile hemangiomas typically {{c1::regress/involute}} by age 7.
The growth phase of a strawberry hemangioma occurs in the {{c1::first few months}} of life.
Histologically, these are {{c1::capillary}} hemangiomas.
Unlike juvenile hemangiomas, port-wine stains {{c1::do not}} regress.
keyPoints: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma is extremely common (1 in 200 births).
Rapid early growth followed by slow involution.
80% are completely gone by age 7.
Wait-and-see management is usually preferred.
They are benign capillary-type vascular proliferations.
microReview: Infant + Red strawberry lesion = Juvenile Hemangioma = Spontaneous regression.
examinerTraps: Confusion with Nevus Flammeus (Port-wine stain). Hemangiomas grow then shrink; Nevus flammeus stays and grows with the child.
sourceQuote: Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) ... are extremely common ... they usually regress spontaneously by age 7.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An 8-year-old child presents with a large, ill-defined, spongy mass in the soft tissues of the neck. Histological examination shows large, dilated vascular spaces lined by a single layer of endothelium, filled with proteinaceous fluid but lacking red blood cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas contain large vascular spaces, but they are filled with blood (RBCs), not clear proteinaceous fluid.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas consist of small, thin-walled capillaries, not large dilated spaces.
explanations.c: Cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) typically occurs in the neck or axilla of children and consists of large, dilated lymphatic spaces filled with lymph fluid (proteinaceous, no RBCs).
explanations.d: Angiosarcomas are malignant with high atypia and RBC-filled channels, not benign fluid-filled cysts in a child.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are small, painful, and subungual, not large neck masses.

ankiCards: Cystic hygroma is the common term for a {{c1::cavernous lymphangioma}}.
Cystic hygromas are frequently associated with {{c1::Turner syndrome}}.
Unlike hemangiomas, lymphangiomas contain spaces filled with {{c1::proteinaceous/lymph}} fluid.
The most common location for a cystic hygroma is the {{c1::neck (or axilla)}}.
Histologically, cystic hygromas show dilated spaces lined by {{c1::endothelium}}.
keyPoints: Lymphangiomas are the lymphatic counterpart to hemangiomas.
Cystic hygroma is a subtype (cavernous lymphangioma).
Classically seen in the neck/axilla of infants.
Associated with chromosomal aneuploidy (e.g., Turner syndrome, Trisomies).
Benign but difficult to resect due to lack of encapsulation.
microReview: Turner syndrome / Child + Neck mass + Lymph-filled spaces = Cystic Hygroma.
examinerTraps: Check for the presence of RBCs. Hemangioma = RBCs; Lymphangioma = No RBCs (usually).
sourceQuote: Cystic hygromas (cavernous lymphangiomas) are typically found in the neck or axilla of children and rarely in the retroperitoneum.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman presents with a rapidly growing, pedunculated, red nodule on her gingiva that bleeds easily with minor trauma. She reports it appeared during her second trimester. A biopsy shows a lobulated proliferation of capillaries with extensive edema and inflammatory infiltrate. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis presents similarly but is associated with Bartonella in immunocompromised patients, not pregnancy.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a rapidly growing red nodule that often occurs on the skin or gingiva ('pregnancy tumor' or granuloma gravidarum) and bleeds easily.
explanations.c: Kaposi sarcoma is an HHV-8 associated tumor with spindle cells, not common in healthy pregnant women on the gingiva.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are deep, large-channel lesions that don't typically present as small pedunculated gingival masses.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a rare, high-grade malignancy, unlike this benign, pregnancy-associated lesion.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer because it is neither {{c1::pyogenic}} (infectious) nor a {{c2::granuloma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas that occur in the gingiva of pregnant women are called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
The clinical characteristic of pyogenic granuloma is that it {{c1::bleeds easily}}.
The histological pattern of pyogenic granuloma is a {{c1::lobular}} capillary proliferation.
Management of pyogenic granuloma involves {{c1::surgical excision/curettage}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a common benign vascular lesion.
Often follows trauma.
1% of pregnant women develop gingival pyogenic granulomas.
They can spontaneously regress after pregnancy.
The histology is essentially that of a capillary hemangioma with inflammation.
microReview: Pregnancy + Gingival mass + Bleeds easily = Pyogenic Granuloma (Granuloma gravidarum).
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic granuloma' is a trap; it has nothing to do with pus or granulomatous inflammation.
sourceQuote: Pyogenic granulomas are capillary hemangiomas that manifest as rapidly growing red pedunculated lesions on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following clinical variants of Kaposi Sarcoma is most likely to present with aggressive lymph node involvement and a lethal course in young children, predominantly in sub-Saharan Africa?

explanations.a: Chronic/Classic KS affects older Mediterranean men and is usually confined to the skin.
explanations.b: Lymphadenopathic (Endemic) KS is seen in Africa, often in HHV-8 positive children; it is aggressive, involves lymph nodes, and is frequently fatal.
explanations.c: Transplant-associated KS occurs due to immunosuppression; it can be aggressive but usually regresses if immunosuppression is reduced.
explanations.d: AIDS-associated KS is the most common form in the US but typically involves skin and viscera in adults, rather than the specific childhood lymphadenopathic African form described.
explanations.e: Iatrogenic is a synonym for transplant-associated or drug-induced KS.

ankiCards: The four variants of Kaposi Sarcoma are {{c1::Classic, Endemic, Transplant-associated, and Epidemic (AIDS)}}.
{{c1::Endemic African}} KS is the variant that often presents with aggressive lymphadenopathy in children.
Classic KS usually occurs in elderly men of {{c1::Mediterranean/Eastern European}} descent.
In {{c1::Transplant-associated}} KS, lesions may regress upon tapering of immunosuppression.
All forms of Kaposi Sarcoma are associated with the virus {{c1::HHV-8}}.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma has 4 major clinico-epidemiologic patterns.
Endemic African KS can be indolent in adults or aggressive in children.
The childhood form involves lymph nodes and has a high mortality.
AIDS-associated is the most common HIV-related malignancy.
HHV-8 infects endothelial cells and spindle cells in all variants.
microReview: Old man = Classic. African Child (Nodes) = Endemic. Transplant = Iatrogenic. AIDS = Epidemic.
examinerTraps: Don't assume all Kaposi Sarcoma is AIDS-related; the endemic African pediatric form is a distinct aggressive entity.
sourceQuote: Four forms are recognized: 1. Classic ... 2. Endemic African ... 3. Transplant-associated ... 4. AIDS-associated
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 50-year-old patient with Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is found to have a vascular tumor in the cerebellum. This tumor is histologically characterized by capillary-sized vessels separated by vacuolated 'stromal cells.' What is the diagnosis?

explanations.a: Hemangiopericytomas (solitary fibrous tumors) have a 'staghorn' vascular pattern, not associated with VHL.
explanations.b: Hemangioblastoma is the characteristic vascular tumor of VHL disease, often occurring in the cerebellum, retina, or spinal cord.
explanations.c: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is an intermediate-grade tumor often occurring in the liver or lungs, not specifically VHL.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignancy, not the typical cerebellar tumor seen in VHL.
explanations.e: Capillary hemangiomas occur in the skin/mucosa, whereas VHL involves hemangioblastomas.

ankiCards: Hemangioblastoma is associated with {{c1::Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL)}} disease.
Common locations for hemangioblastoma include the {{c1::cerebellum}} and {{c2::retina}}.
VHL disease is caused by a mutation in the {{c1::VHL}} gene on chromosome {{c2::3}}.
Histologically, hemangioblastomas contain {{c1::vacuolated stromal}} cells.
VHL disease also increases the risk of {{c1::renal cell carcinoma (clear cell type)}}.
keyPoints: VHL is an autosomal dominant syndrome.
Hemangioblastomas are the hallmark vascular tumor.
VHL protein normally degrades Hypoxia Inducible Factor (HIF).
Loss of VHL leads to increased HIF and VEGF expression.
Associated with polycythemia due to ectopic erythropoietin.
microReview: Cerebellum/Retina + VHL mutation = Hemangioblastoma.
examinerTraps: The histological 'stromal cells' are the diagnostic feature of hemangioblastoma; don't confuse them with standard endothelial cells.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors ... Hemangioblastomas are particularly common in the cerebellum and retina ... occurring in the context of von Hippel-Lindau disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old woman with a history of radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer 12 years ago presents with multiple, firm, bluish-purple skin nodules on her right arm. The arm has been chronically swollen since her surgery. What is the most likely diagnosis for these new skin lesions?

explanations.a: While recurrence is possible, the combination of chronic lymphedema and new vascular skin nodules points toward Stewart-Treves syndrome.
explanations.b: This is a classic presentation of Stewart-Treves syndrome: angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema following radical mastectomy.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis requires Bartonella infection in an immunocompromised host, which is not the primary suspect here.
explanations.d: Lymphangiomas are benign and usually congenital or childhood lesions, not new malignant nodules in an adult.
explanations.e: Kaposi sarcoma is HHV-8 related and usually presents in different distributions (AIDS/elderly), not localized to a lymphedematous limb.

ankiCards: {{c1::Stewart-Treves}} syndrome is angiosarcoma arising in a limb with chronic lymphedema.
The most common cause of Stewart-Treves syndrome is post-{{c1::mastectomy}} lymphedema.
The prognosis of angiosarcoma is {{c1::poor}}.
Angiosarcoma cells are positive for the vascular marker {{c1::CD31}}.
The latent period for Stewart-Treves syndrome is typically {{c1::many years (approx 10)}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma can be primary or secondary.
Chronic lymphedema is a major risk factor (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
Radical mastectomy with lymph node removal leads to lymphedema.
Clinically appears as bruising or nodules that eventually ulcerate.
Highly metastatic and difficult to treat.
microReview: Post-mastectomy + Chronic Lymphedema + Blue nodules = Stewart-Treves (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: The question may ask for the diagnosis or the name of the syndrome; Stewart-Treves is the name, Angiosarcoma is the pathology.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcoma can also occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema, classically in the ipsilateral arm of women several years after radical mastectomy.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 34-year-old male with a history of HIV (CD4+ count: 120 cells/µL) presents with several non-tender, reddish-purple macules and plaques on his lower extremities and oral mucosa. A biopsy of a skin lesion reveals a proliferation of spindle-shaped cells forming slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells. Which of the following infectious agents is most likely responsible for this patient's condition?

explanations.a: Human herpesvirus 6 is the causative agent of roseola infantum and is not associated with vascular tumors.
explanations.b: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of Kaposi sarcoma, which presents with spindle cell proliferation and slit-like vascular spaces.
explanations.c: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised patients; while it presents with similar red-purple lesions, the histology shows lobular capillary proliferation with neutrophils and Warthin-Starry positive bacilli, not spindle cells forming slits.
explanations.d: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with various lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, but not primary vascular tumors like Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.e: Cytomegalovirus can cause retinitis or colitis in AIDS patients but does not drive vascular endothelial oncogenesis.

ankiCards: What is the causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma? {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}
The histologic hallmark of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells}} forming slit-like vascular spaces.
The characteristic skin lesions in Kaposi Sarcoma appear as {{c1::reddish-purple}} macules, plaques, or nodules.
In contrast to bacillary angiomatosis, Kaposi sarcoma histology lacks {{c1::neutrophils}}.
Kaposi Sarcoma is categorized as a(n) {{c1::intermediate-grade (borderline)}} vascular tumor.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma is a borderline vascular tumor caused by HHV-8.
Commonly seen in immunocompromised patients, especially those with AIDS.
Histology: Spindle-shaped endothelial cells and slit-like spaces with RBCs.
Lesions can occur on skin, mucous membranes, and viscera.
HHV-8 infects endothelial cells and promotes uncontrolled growth through viral proteins.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is an HHV-8-driven neoplasm. It presents in four forms: Classic (older Mediterranean men), Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated (most common). It is distinct from bacillary angiomatosis (Bartonella-driven, neutrophilic) by its spindle cell morphology and lack of acute inflammation.
examinerTraps: Confusing Kaposi Sarcoma with Bacillary Angiomatosis is common. Look for 'spindle cells' for KS and 'neutrophils/bacilli' for Bacillary Angiomatosis.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors are divided into three categories: benign (e.g., hemangiomas), intermediate-grade (e.g., Kaposi sarcoma), and malignant (e.g., angiosarcoma).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old male presents with a 0.5-cm, exquisitely painful, firm, red-blue nodule located under the fingernail of his right index finger. Histological examination shows a well-circumscribed nest of specialized smooth muscle cells surrounding vascular channels. From which of the following structures is this tumor derived?

explanations.a: While hemangiopericytomas (now classified as solitary fibrous tumors) derive from pericyte-like cells, they are not typically exquisitely painful subungual nodules.
explanations.b: Lymphatic endothelial cells give rise to lymphangiomas, which are typically painless and transilluminate.
explanations.c: A glomus tumor (glomangioma) is a benign, exquisitely painful tumor arising from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts are not the primary cell type in vascular tumors like glomangiomas.
explanations.e: Weibel-Palade bodies are storage granules in endothelial cells; they are markers for endothelium, not the cell of origin for glomus tumors.

ankiCards: A painful subungual (under nail) red-blue tumor is most likely a(n) {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle cells}}.
The glomus body's physiological function is {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors show nests of cells surrounding {{c1::vascular channels}}.
Unlike most vascular tumors, glomus tumors are characterized by intense {{c1::pain}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign and extremely painful.
Most commonly found in the subungual region (under fingernails).
Derived from smooth muscle cells of the glomus body (thermoregulation).
Glomus bodies are specialized arteriovenous shunts.
Treatment is simple excision.
microReview: Identify the 'Triad' for Glomus tumor: 1. Subungual location, 2. Extreme pain, 3. Small blue/red nodule. Cell of origin: Modified smooth muscle.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse a glomus tumor with a subungual melanoma (which is usually pigmented and painless) or a simple hemangioma.
sourceQuote: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, exquisitely painful tumors that arise from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus bodies.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following immunohistochemical markers is most useful in confirming the endothelial origin of a poorly differentiated malignant tumor suspected of being an angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells (carcinomas).
explanations.b: Vimentin is a non-specific marker for mesenchymal cells and does not confirm endothelial differentiation.
explanations.c: CD31 (platelet-endothelial cell adhesion molecule) is a highly specific marker for vascular endothelial cells and is used to identify angiosarcomas.
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells like melanocytes and Schwann cells.
explanations.e: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (skeletal, smooth, or cardiac).

ankiCards: The specific endothelial marker used in immunohistochemistry for angiosarcomas is {{c1::CD31}}.
Angiosarcoma is a {{c1::malignant}} neoplasm of endothelial cells.
Another marker for endothelial cells besides CD31 is {{c1::von Willebrand factor}}.
CD31 is also known as {{c1::PECAM-1}}.
Poorly differentiated angiosarcomas may mimic {{c1::carcinomas}} on H&E stain.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are aggressive, malignant endothelial tumors.
CD31 is the most specific immunohistochemical marker.
Can occur anywhere but often involves skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
They may appear as innocuous red papules before becoming large, fleshy masses.
Histology ranges from well-formed vascular channels to solid sheets of pleomorphic cells.
microReview: Vascular Marker Check: CD31 (+), CD34 (+), vWF (+). These confirm endothelial origin when histology is ambiguous.
examinerTraps: CD34 is also positive in vascular tumors but is less specific than CD31 because it is expressed in many other mesenchymal tumors.
sourceQuote: Most angiosarcomas express endothelial markers such as CD31 or von Willebrand factor.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old female presents with multiple enlarging, violaceous nodules on her left arm. She has a history of a radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer 12 years ago, which was complicated by persistent, severe chronic lymphedema. A biopsy of the nodules shows a highly aggressive malignancy with pleomorphic endothelial cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious lesion in HIV patients, not associated with chronic lymphedema.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign lesions present from birth or childhood, not associated with post-surgical lymphedema.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma occurring in the setting of chronic lymphedema (often post-mastectomy) is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome.
explanations.d: Lymphangiomas are benign malformations, not aggressive malignancies with pleomorphic cells.
explanations.e: Pyogenic granulomas are benign reactive vascular proliferations often following minor trauma or pregnancy.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
The most common clinical scenario for Stewart-Treves syndrome is post-{{c1::mastectomy (with lymph node dissection)}}.
Histology of angiosarcoma shows {{c1::pleomorphic}} endothelial cells and irregular vascular channels.
Stewart-Treves syndrome typically occurs {{c1::10 or more}} years after the onset of lymphedema.
The prognosis for cutaneous angiosarcoma is generally {{c1::poor}}.
keyPoints: Chronic lymphedema is a major risk factor for cutaneous angiosarcoma.
Stewart-Treves syndrome follows radical mastectomy/axillary dissection.
Presents as multiple purple/blue skin nodules.
Highly infiltrative and metastasizes early.
5-year survival rates are low (approx. 30%).
microReview: Lymphedema + Post-Mastectomy + 10 Years + Purple Nodules = Angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves).
examinerTraps: Examiners may lead you to think it is recurrent breast cancer; look for the 'violaceous' vascular nature of the nodules and the specific history of lymphedema.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas can also occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema, classically in the ipsilateral arm of women who have undergone radical mastectomy for breast cancer.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)
