stem: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare but highly aggressive malignancy. Exposure to which of the following environmental substances is most strongly associated with the development of this specific vascular tumor?

explanations.a: Aflatoxin B1 is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Vinyl chloride (used in the plastics industry), arsenic (pesticides), and Thorotrast (radiological contrast) are classic risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Benzene exposure is primarily linked to acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.d: Asbestos exposure is linked to mesothelioma and bronchogenic carcinoma.
explanations.e: Beryllium exposure is linked to berylliosis (granulomatous disease) and lung cancer.

ankiCards: The three classic carcinogens associated with hepatic angiosarcoma are {{c1::vinyl chloride}}, {{c2::arsenic}}, and {{c3::Thorotrast}}.
Vinyl chloride is commonly used in the {{c1::plastics (PVC)}} industry.
Thorotrast was a formerly used radiological {{c1::contrast agent}} linked to angiosarcomas.
Arsenic exposure occurs via {{c1::pesticides}} or contaminated well water.
Hepatic angiosarcoma arises from the {{c1::endothelial cells}} of the liver sinusoids.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is rare but linked to specific chemical exposures.
Vinyl chloride monomer is the most high-yield association for Step 1.
Latent period between exposure and tumor development can be decades.
Tumors are highly aggressive with poor prognosis.
Must be distinguished from more common liver tumors like HCC or metastatic disease.
microReview: Chemical/Tumor associations: Vinyl chloride -> Hepatic Angiosarcoma; Aflatoxin -> HCC; Benzene -> AML; Asbestos -> Mesothelioma.
examinerTraps: The examiner might list arsenic or Thorotrast; all three are valid, but vinyl chloride is the most frequently tested industrial exposure.
sourceQuote: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with distinct environmental exposures, including arsenic (used in pesticides), Thorotrast (a radioactive contrast medium), and vinyl chloride.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 2-week-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for a bright red, raised, 'strawberry-like' lesion on the scalp. The parents state it appeared shortly after birth and has grown rapidly in size. Which of the following is the most likely natural history of this lesion?

options.a: Persistent growth requiring urgent surgical resection
options.c: Spontaneous regression by age 7 to 9 years
options.d: Development of underlying cerebral cavernous malformations
options.e: Recurrence after laser therapy in 90% of cases

explanations.a: Surgery is rarely required for juvenile hemangiomas as most regress spontaneously.
explanations.b: Juvenile hemangiomas are benign and do not undergo malignant transformation.
explanations.c: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas typically grow for a few months and then gradually regress, with the majority disappearing by age 7.
explanations.d: Strawberry hemangiomas are isolated cutaneous lesions and not associated with internal malformations like VHL or Sturge-Weber.
explanations.e: While laser therapy is an option, spontaneous regression is the expected natural history.

ankiCards: The common name for a juvenile hemangioma is a(n) {{c1::strawberry}} hemangioma.
Juvenile hemangiomas are present at birth or appear in the first {{c1::few weeks}} of life.
Most juvenile hemangiomas completely regress by age {{c1::7 (or 9)}}.
Juvenile hemangiomas are histologically classified as {{c1::capillary}} hemangiomas.
The 'strawberry' appearance is due to the proliferation of {{c1::small capillaries}}.
keyPoints: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma is extremely common in newborns.
Clinical appearance: Bright red, lobulated, raised.
Rapid growth phase followed by slow involution.
Nearly 100% of cases show some regression; 80% are gone by age 7.
Reassurance is the first-line management.
microReview: Infant + Strawberry lesion + Growth then regression = Juvenile Capillary Hemangioma.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse with a 'port-wine stain' (Nevus flammeus), which is flat and does not regress.
sourceQuote: Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) of the newborn skin are very common... they grow rapidly for a few months but then fade and eventually regress.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 25-year-old pregnant woman in her second trimester presents with a rapidly growing, pedunculated red mass on her gingiva that bleeds easily with minor trauma. Histologically, the lesion shows an exuberant proliferation of capillaries with associated edema and inflammation. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis presents similarly but occurs in immunocompromised individuals and is caused by Bartonella.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granuloma (granuloma pyogenicum) is a reactive vascular proliferation that commonly occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated vascular spaces and are not typically pedunculated rapidly growing masses on the gingiva.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor with highly atypical cells, not a benign reactive proliferation like this.
explanations.e: Spider telangiectasias are small, non-neoplastic vascular dilations associated with hyperestrogenic states (like cirrhosis), not pedunculated masses.

ankiCards: A pyogenic granuloma occurring on the gingiva of a pregnant woman is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Despite the name, pyogenic granuloma is neither {{c1::pyogenic (pus-forming)}} nor a {{c2::granuloma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized by being {{c1::pedunculated}} and bleeding easily.
Histologically, pyogenic granulomas resemble {{c1::capillary hemangiomas}} with edema.
The treatment for a bothersome pyogenic granuloma is {{c1::surgical excision}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign, reactive vascular lesion.
Often follows trauma or occurs during pregnancy.
Most common locations are gingiva, fingers, and face.
Clinically: Red, pedunculated, friable (bleeds easily).
Histology: Lobular proliferation of capillaries (lobular capillary hemangioma).
microReview: Gingival mass + Pregnancy + Bleeding = Pyogenic Granuloma (Granuloma Gravidarum).
examinerTraps: The name is a misnomer; it is not caused by infection (pyogenic) nor is it a granulomatous inflammation.
sourceQuote: Pyogenic granulomas are capillary hemangiomas that manifest as rapidly growing red, pedunculated lesions on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the fundamental pathological feature that distinguishes cavernous hemangiomas from capillary hemangiomas?

options.a: Presence of spindle cells and slit-like spaces
options.b: Size of the vascular channels and lack of circumscription
options.e: Spontaneous regression within the first decade of life

explanations.a: Spindle cells and slit-like spaces are characteristic of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, dilated vascular channels (caverns) and are often more infiltrative and less well-circumscribed than capillary hemangiomas.
explanations.c: HHV-8 is associated with Kaposi sarcoma, not cavernous hemangiomas.
explanations.d: Bartonella henselae is associated with bacillary angiomatosis.
explanations.e: Capillary hemangiomas (specifically juvenile ones) regress; cavernous hemangiomas rarely do.

ankiCards: {{c1::Cavernous}} hemangiomas are composed of large, blood-filled vascular spaces.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas frequently involve {{c1::deep visceral organs (like the liver)}}.
In the brain, cavernous hemangiomas are clinically significant because they can cause {{c1::hemorrhage}}.
Cavernous hemangiomas are a component of {{c1::von Hippel-Lindau}} disease.
Unlike juvenile hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas {{c1::do not}} spontaneously regress.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas involve large, thin-walled vascular channels.
Commonly involve the liver and CNS.
Clinically, they can cause pressure symptoms or rupture.
Distinguished from capillary hemangiomas by the diameter of the vessels.
Histology: Large spaces separated by connective tissue stroma; no regression.
microReview: Capillary = Small vessels (skin). Cavernous = Large vessels (liver/brain/deeper).
examinerTraps: If an examiner mentions a 'liver mass' incidentally found on CT that is hyper-enhancing and filled with blood, think cavernous hemangioma.
sourceQuote: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, dilated vascular channels. Compared to capillary hemangiomas, they are usually more infiltrative... and do not regress.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 4-year-old child is evaluated for developmental delay and new-onset seizures. Physical examination reveals a large, flat, purple-red patch covering the left forehead and upper eyelid in the distribution of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve. A CT scan of the head shows tram-track calcifications in the underlying cerebral cortex. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) presents with multiple small telangiectasias and epistaxis, not port-wine stains.
explanations.b: Von Hippel-Lindau is characterized by hemangioblastomas (CNS/Retina), renal cell carcinoma, and pheochromocytoma.
explanations.c: Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) is characterized by a facial port-wine stain (nevus flammeus), ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomas, seizures, and 'tram-track' calcifications.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation in immunocompromised patients.
explanations.e: Tuberous sclerosis presents with ash-leaf spots, angiofibromas, and shagreen patches, not port-wine stains.

ankiCards: Sturge-Weber syndrome is associated with a facial birthmark called a(n) {{c1::nevus flammeus (port-wine stain)}}.
The port-wine stain in Sturge-Weber typically follows the distribution of the {{c1::trigeminal (V1/V2)}} nerve.
The classic CT finding in Sturge-Weber syndrome is {{c1::tram-track calcifications}}.
Patients with Sturge-Weber syndrome are at high risk for {{c1::seizures}} and glaucoma.
Nevus flammeus is a form of {{c1::ectasia (vascular dilation)}}, not a true neoplasm.
keyPoints: Sturge-Weber syndrome is a sporadic congenital disorder.
Port-wine stain is the hallmark cutaneous finding.
Leptomeningeal venous angiomas cause underlying cortical atrophy.
Tram-track calcifications are seen on imaging due to mineral deposits in the cortex.
Port-wine stains (unlike strawberry hemangiomas) grow with the child and do not regress.
microReview: Port-wine stain + V1/V2 distribution + Seizures + Tram-track = Sturge-Weber.
examinerTraps: Wait for the trigeminal distribution. A simple nevus flammeus (birthmark) is common, but when it's in the V1/V2 area, you must suspect Sturge-Weber.
sourceQuote: Sturge-Weber syndrome... is a rare congenital disorder... associated with facial venous angiomas (port-wine stains) in the trigeminal nerve distribution.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 2-month-old infant presents with a large, soft, fluctuant mass on the left side of the neck. The mass transilluminates on physical exam. Histological evaluation shows large, dilated lymphatic spaces lined by endothelial cells and separated by an intervening connective tissue stroma containing lymphoid aggregates. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: A cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) is a benign lymphatic malformation typically found in the neck or axilla of infants and is associated with Turner syndrome.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas are blood-filled and do not typically transilluminate like lymphatic-filled spaces.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are small, painful subungual nodules, not large neck masses.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor of the elderly or those with lymphedema, not infants.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious lesion seen in HIV patients.

ankiCards: A cavernous lymphangioma in the neck of an infant is commonly called a(n) {{c1::cystic hygroma}}.
Cystic hygromas are frequently associated with {{c1::Turner syndrome}}.
The fluid inside a cystic hygroma is {{c1::lymph (chylous)}}.
A physical exam finding that helps distinguish a cystic hygroma from a solid mass is {{c1::transillumination}}.
The spaces in a lymphangioma lack {{c1::red blood cells}}.
keyPoints: Cystic hygromas are the lymphatic equivalent of cavernous hemangiomas.
Classic location: Neck (posterior triangle) or axilla.
Often found in Turner syndrome (45,X) and Down syndrome.
They can be very large and cause airway compromise.
Histology: Dilated lymphatic channels with thin walls.
microReview: Infant + Neck mass + Transilluminates + Lymphatic spaces = Cystic Hygroma.
examinerTraps: The association with Turner syndrome is a very high-yield 'second-step' question.
sourceQuote: Cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) are typically found in the neck or axilla of children and are occasionally associated with Turner syndrome.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 67-year-old male with a 45-pack-year smoking history presents for a physical examination. While palpating the abdomen, a prominent, rhythmic pulsation is noted superior to the umbilicus. An ultrasound confirms a 5.2 cm dilation of the infrarenal aorta. Which of the following biochemical processes is most central to the weakening of the aortic wall in this patient?

options.b: Decreased production of reactive oxygen species
options.c: Upregulation of tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases
options.d: Increased synthesis of type I and III collagen

explanations.a: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are characterized by an imbalance where matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) from macrophages and smooth muscle cells degrade the extracellular matrix (elastin and collagen) faster than it can be replaced.
explanations.b: Reactive oxygen species are typically increased in the setting of atherosclerosis and inflammation, contributing to wall damage, not decreased.
explanations.c: Tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs) actually protect the wall; a relative decrease in TIMP activity or an increase in MMPs leads to aneurysm formation.
explanations.d: Aneurysm formation involves the degradation of collagen and elastin; while there may be some compensatory synthesis, the net effect is a loss of structural integrity.
explanations.e: Macrophage-derived cytokines (like TNF and IL-1) are actually increased, stimulating the production of MMPs that weaken the wall.

ankiCards: The primary biochemical cause of aortic wall weakening in AAAs is an increase in {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
In AAAs, there is an imbalance between MMPs and {{c1::tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs)}}.
The most common location for an atherosclerotic aneurysm is the {{c1::infrarenal}} abdominal aorta.
Inflammatory cells in the aortic wall, specifically {{c1::macrophages}}, play a key role in ECM degradation.
Risk factors for AAA include male sex, age, and a history of {{c1::smoking}}.
keyPoints: Aneurysms represent a localized permanent dilation of a vessel.
Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) degrade elastin and collagen in the media.
Smoking is the most significant modifiable risk factor for AAA.
Atherosclerosis is the major underlying cause of abdominal aortic aneurysms.
The infrarenal location is preferred because it is distal to the renal arteries and proximal to the iliac bifurcation.
microReview: AAAs are typically found in men over 50 who smoke. The pathogenesis involves chronic inflammation, atherosclerosis, and proteolytic degradation of the tunica media. MMPs (especially MMP-2 and MMP-9) are the primary effectors of this destruction.
examinerTraps: Students often confuse the pathophysiology of AAA (atherosclerosis/MMPs) with Aortic Dissection (hypertension/cystic medial necrosis). Ensure the clinical presentation matches the mechanism.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: ... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following descriptions best distinguishes a 'true' aneurysm from a 'false' aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm)?

options.a: Involvement of all three layers of the arterial wall
options.b: Presence of an intimal tear with intramural hematoma
options.c: A localized dilation caused by a bacterial infection
options.d: A blood collection between the media and the adventitia
options.e: Formation of a communication between an artery and a vein

explanations.a: A true aneurysm involves an intact but attenuated arterial wall or thinned ventricular wall, including all three layers: intima, media, and adventitia.
explanations.b: This describes an aortic dissection, which is not a true aneurysm.
explanations.c: This describes a mycotic aneurysm, which can be either true or false depending on the wall involvement, but is defined by etiology rather than structure.
explanations.d: This describes a false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm), where a wall defect leads to an extravascular hematoma that freely communicates with the intravascular space.
explanations.e: This describes an arteriovenous fistula.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the vessel wall (intima, media, and adventitia).
A {{c1::false}} aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) is an extravascular hematoma that communicates with the lumen.
A common cause of a pseudoaneurysm is a {{c1::leak at a vascular graft junction}} or trauma.
The two main shapes of true aneurysms are {{c1::saccular}} and {{c2::fusiform}}.
A {{c1::dissection}} occurs when blood enters the wall of the artery as a hematoma between its layers.
keyPoints: True aneurysms involve the intima, media, and adventitia.
False aneurysms are bounded by extravascular connective tissue.
Saccular aneurysms are spherical outpouchings involving only a portion of the wall.
Fusiform aneurysms involve circumferential dilation of the vessel.
Pseudoaneurysms often follow trauma or catheterization procedures.
microReview: Structural integrity is the key differentiator. True = wall is intact (but thin). False = wall is breached, blood is contained by surrounding tissue.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'mycotic aneurysm' (infected) with 'pseudoaneurysm' (structural breach). A mycotic aneurysm is often a pseudoaneurysm, but the terms are not synonymous.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old male with Marfan syndrome presents for a follow-up echocardiogram. The study reveals a dilation of the ascending aorta. Histological examination of this region would most likely demonstrate which of the following pathological findings?

explanations.a: Marfan syndrome is associated with cystic medial degeneration (or necrosis), characterized by the loss of smooth muscle cells and fragmentation of elastic fibers, often seen in thoracic aortic aneurysms.
explanations.b: This is characteristic of tertiary syphilis (luetic aneurysms), which affects the vasa vasorum.
explanations.c: While common in the abdominal aorta, atherosclerosis is a less common primary cause of ascending (thoracic) aortic aneurysms compared to genetic conditions.
explanations.d: This describes conditions like Giant Cell Arteritis or Takayasu Arteritis.
explanations.e: This is seen in malignant hypertension and some small-vessel vasculitides, not typically in large vessel aneurysms.

ankiCards: The classic histological finding in Marfan-related aortic dilation is {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
Cystic medial degeneration is characterized by the loss of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} and fragmentation of {{c2::elastic fibers}}.
Marfan syndrome involves a mutation in the {{c1::Fibrillin-1}} gene.
In Marfan syndrome, there is excessive signaling of {{c1::TGF-β}} in the vessel wall.
Thoracic aortic aneurysms are most commonly associated with {{c1::hypertension}} and genetic syndromes like Marfan.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome is a leading genetic cause of thoracic aortic aneurysms.
The underlying defect involves Fibrillin-1 mutations.
TGF-beta signaling is dysregulated, leading to matrix remodeling.
Cystic medial degeneration is the descriptive term for the non-inflammatory loss of medial structural integrity.
The ascending aorta is the most common site for aneurysms in Marfan patients.
microReview: Marfan = Fibrillin-1 = TGF-beta = Cystic Medial Degeneration = Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm. This is a classic USMLE sequence.
examinerTraps: Atherosclerosis is the main cause for Abdominal Aneurysms; Hypertension and Genetic Syndromes (Marfan) are the main causes for Thoracic Aneurysms.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the development of an abdominal aortic aneurysm, which of the following cell types is most responsible for the production of the matrix metalloproteinases (MMP-2 and MMP-9) that degrade the tunica media?

explanations.a: Macrophages in the inflammatory infiltrate of an atherosclerotic plaque produce the majority of MMPs that degrade the elastic lamina and collagen in the aortic wall.
explanations.b: Endothelial cells are involved in the initiation of atherosclerosis but are not the primary source of medial-degrading MMPs in aneurysms.
explanations.c: Neutrophils are involved in acute inflammation, while the inflammation in aneurysms is typically chronic and macrophage-dominant.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts are more involved in the synthesis of the adventitial collagen and wound healing rather than the primary degradation of the media in AAAs.
explanations.e: Platelets are involved in thrombosis and release some growth factors, but they do not produce the bulk of degradative enzymes.

ankiCards: The inflammatory cell type most associated with MMP production in AAAs is the {{c1::macrophage}}.
MMP-2 and {{c1::MMP-9}} are the specific gelatinases produced by macrophages in aneurysmal walls.
The layer of the vessel wall most significantly weakened in an aneurysm is the {{c1::tunica media}}.
Proteolysis of the {{c1::extracellular matrix (ECM)}} is the hallmark of aneurysm progression.
Inflammation in AAAs is largely driven by a {{c1::chronic}} immune response.
keyPoints: Chronic inflammation is a key feature of AAA pathogenesis.
Macrophages secrete MMPs (Matrix Metalloproteinases).
Degradation of elastin leads to the loss of elastic recoil.
Degradation of collagen leads to the loss of tensile strength.
This process results in progressive vessel dilation.
microReview: AAAs are fundamentally a failure of the tunica media. Chronic inflammation (driven by atherosclerosis) recruits macrophages, which release proteases (MMPs) that eat away at the structural proteins (elastin/collagen) of the media.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse MMPs with TIMPs. MMPs 'Melt' the matrix; TIMPs 'Toughen' (inhibit melting). Aneurysms have too much MMP or too little TIMP.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Tertiary syphilis classically causes aneurysms in the ascending aorta. What is the primary mechanism by which the Treponema pallidum infection weakens the aortic wall?

options.b: Direct destruction of the intima by spirochetes
options.c: Autoimmune destruction of type III collagen
options.e: Calcification of the internal elastic lamina

explanations.a: Tertiary syphilis causes obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum (the vessels of the vessels), which leads to ischemic injury of the tunica media.
explanations.b: Spirochetes are rarely found in the lesions; the damage is secondary to the vascular supply disruption of the media.
explanations.c: While syphilis involves the immune system, it is not a primary autoimmune attack on collagen.
explanations.d: Atherosclerosis is a separate process, although syphilitic damage can predispose to 'tree-barking' of the intima which resembles severe atherosclerosis.
explanations.e: Medial calcification (Monckeberg) is a separate process unrelated to syphilis.

ankiCards: Syphilitic aneurysms typically affect the {{c1::ascending/thoracic}} aorta.
The hallmark histological finding of syphilitic aortitis is {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}}.
Syphilis targets the {{c1::vasa vasorum}}, leading to medial ischemia.
Ischemic damage to the media in syphilis leads to a {{c1::'tree-bark'}} appearance of the intima.
Syphilitic aneurysms can cause {{c1::aortic valve insufficiency}} due to dilation of the aortic root.
keyPoints: Syphilitic (Luetic) aortitis is a rare cause of aneurysm in the antibiotic era.
It specifically targets the vasa vasorum in the adventitia.
Reduced blood supply to the outer media causes smooth muscle cell death.
The resulting scarring and loss of elasticity leads to aneurysm formation.
The 'tree-bark' appearance is due to irregular intimal scarring over the damaged media.
microReview: Syphilis = Vasa Vasorum damage = Medial Ischemia = Weak Wall = Thoracic Aneurysm. Contrast this with AAA which is Atherosclerosis-driven.
examinerTraps: A common trap is to say spirochetes directly eat the aorta. They don't; they cause an inflammatory occlusion of the small nutrient vessels (vasa vasorum).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 70-year-old female with a history of severe hypertension presents with new-onset hoarseness and a persistent cough. A chest X-ray shows a large mediastinal mass. A CT scan confirms a 6.5 cm aneurysm of the aortic arch. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her hoarseness?

options.a: Compression of the recurrent laryngeal nerve
options.b: Direct invasion of the vocal cords

explanations.a: Thoracic aortic aneurysms can compress adjacent structures; compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve as it loops under the arch causes vocal cord paralysis and hoarseness.
explanations.b: Aneurysms occupy space but do not 'invade' tissues like a malignancy.
explanations.c: Aneurysms do not produce paraneoplastic hormones.
explanations.d: Rupture would present with catastrophic shock and hemothorax, not isolated hoarseness.
explanations.e: The blood supply to the larynx is not typically compromised by an aortic arch aneurysm.

ankiCards: A thoracic aortic aneurysm can cause hoarseness by compressing the {{c1::left recurrent laryngeal nerve}}.
Common symptoms of thoracic aneurysms include {{c1::cough}} (due to tracheal compression) and {{c2::dysphagia}} (due to esophageal compression).
Thoracic aortic aneurysms are most frequently associated with {{c1::hypertension}}.
Bone pain from a thoracic aneurysm is usually caused by erosion of the {{c1::ribs or vertebral bodies}}.
Dilation of the aortic root in a thoracic aneurysm can lead to {{c1::aortic valve insufficiency}}.
keyPoints: Thoracic aortic aneurysms are often asymptomatic until they compress local structures.
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve is vulnerable due to its course around the aortic arch.
Other compressive symptoms include difficulty breathing (trachea) and swallowing (esophagus).
Hypertension is the number one risk factor for thoracic aneurysms.
Rupture of a thoracic aneurysm is often fatal.
microReview: Thoracic Aneurysm symptoms = 'Mass effect' (Cough, hoarseness, dysphagia) or 'Valvular' (Heart failure from aortic regurgitation).
examinerTraps: Hoarseness in an elderly smoker often points to lung cancer, but in the context of a mediastinal mass and hypertension, an aneurysm is a high-yield differential.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the morphological appearance of a 'fusiform' aneurysm?

options.a: Circumferential dilation of a long vascular segment
options.b: A small spherical outpouching involving only one side of the wall
options.c: A collection of blood between the layers of the media
options.d: A localized breach in the wall with a pulsating hematoma
options.e: A 'berry-like' lesion occurring at vascular bifurcations

explanations.a: Fusiform aneurysms are characterized by symmetrical, circumferential dilation of a long segment of the vessel.
explanations.b: This describes a saccular aneurysm.
explanations.c: This describes an aortic dissection.
explanations.d: This describes a false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm).
explanations.e: This specifically describes a 'berry aneurysm', which is a type of saccular aneurysm common in the Circle of Willis.

ankiCards: A {{c1::fusiform}} aneurysm involves circumferential dilation of the vessel.
A {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm involves only a portion of the vessel wall and appears as an outpouching.
Fusiform aneurysms can reach up to {{c1::20}} cm in diameter.
The most common site for a fusiform aneurysm is the {{c1::abdominal aorta}}.
Aneurysms are classified by shape into {{c1::saccular}} and {{c2::fusiform}}.
keyPoints: Fusiform: Long-segment, circumferential dilation.
Saccular: Focal, bubble-like outpouching.
Both are 'True' aneurysms if all wall layers are present.
Shape does not necessarily determine the etiology (e.g., atherosclerosis can cause both).
Abdominal aortic aneurysms are frequently fusiform.
microReview: Fusiform = Football shaped (long). Saccular = Sack-like (round, one-sided).
examinerTraps: Don't assume 'saccular' only refers to Berry aneurysms in the brain; they can occur in the aorta as well.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 58-year-old male presents with sudden-onset, severe 'tearing' pain that radiates to his back. His blood pressure is 190/110 mmHg. On imaging, he is found to have an aortic dissection. While this is not a 'true' aneurysm, it shares which of the following common risk factors with thoracic aortic aneurysms?

explanations.a: Hypertension is the single most important risk factor for both aortic dissection and thoracic aortic aneurysms.
explanations.b: While related to atherosclerosis (a risk for AAA), it is not as directly linked to dissection as hypertension is.
explanations.c: Alcohol abuse is not a primary risk factor for aortic dissection.
explanations.d: Vitamin C deficiency (Scurvy) affects collagen but is not a standard cause of aortic dissection.
explanations.e: Viral infections are not known triggers for aortic dissection.

ankiCards: The most important risk factor for aortic dissection is {{c1::hypertension}}.
Aortic dissection involves blood entering the {{c1::tunica media}} through an intimal tear.
Unlike a true aneurysm, a dissection involves {{c1::separation of wall layers}}.
Risk factors shared by thoracic aneurysms and dissections include {{c1::hypertension}} and Marfan syndrome.
The 'tearing' pain of a dissection typically radiates to the {{c1::back/scapula}}.
keyPoints: Dissection is a medical emergency distinct from a stable aneurysm.
It requires an intimal tear.
Hypertension causes medial hypertrophy and ischemia, predisposing to the tear.
It creates a 'false lumen' within the vessel wall.
Can lead to sudden death via cardiac tamponade if it ruptures into the pericardium.
microReview: Aneurysm = Dilation (All layers). Dissection = Split (Between layers). Both are worsened by high pressure (Hypertension).
examinerTraps: Examiners often use 'tearing pain' and 'hypertension' to lure you into picking aneurysm when it's actually a dissection. Note the difference in the wall structure.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 'mycotic aneurysm' refers to which of the following clinical scenarios?

options.a: An aneurysm resulting from an infected vessel wall
options.b: An aneurysm caused specifically by a fungal infection
options.c: A dilation of the aorta due to cystic medial necrosis
options.d: A pseudoaneurysm following a surgical procedure
options.e: A congenital thinning of the arterial media

explanations.a: A mycotic aneurysm is any aneurysm caused by the weakening of the vessel wall due to an infection (bacterial, fungal, etc.), often from a circulating septic embolus.
explanations.b: Despite the name 'mycotic', most are actually bacterial in origin (e.g., from infective endocarditis).
explanations.c: This describes a non-infectious degenerative process.
explanations.d: Pseudoaneurysms can be mycotic if they get infected, but 'mycotic' specifically implies an infectious etiology.
explanations.e: This refers to conditions like Marfan or Ehlers-Danlos, not infection.

ankiCards: A {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm is an aneurysm caused by an infection.
Common causes of mycotic aneurysms include {{c1::septic emboli}} from endocarditis.
Most 'mycotic' aneurysms are actually caused by {{c1::bacteria}}.
Infection weakens the wall by inducing {{c1::suppurative inflammation}} and protease release.
The most common site for a mycotic aneurysm to originate from an embolus is the {{c1::cerebral}} arteries.
keyPoints: Mycotic aneurysms are infectious in origin.
The name is a misnomer; bacteria are more common than fungi.
Commonly follow infective endocarditis (septic emboli).
The infection causes rapid wall destruction.
These have a high risk of rupture due to acute inflammation.
microReview: Mycotic = Infected. It's usually from a piece of heart valve (septic embolus) getting stuck in a small vessel or seeding a large one.
examinerTraps: The name 'mycotic' sounds like fungi, but on a test, if you see 'Staph aureus infection of the aortic wall', that is a mycotic aneurysm.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old male with a history of a 5.8 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm presents with sudden onset of coldness and blue discoloration of his right great toe. No other symptoms are present. What is the most likely mechanism for this finding?

options.c: Compression of the common iliac vein
options.d: Dissection extending into the femoral artery

explanations.a: Aneurysms often contain mural thrombus (clotted blood on the wall) due to stasis and turbulent flow; these can embolize distally, causing 'blue toe syndrome'.
explanations.b: Rupture would present with shock and severe pain, not just a cold toe.
explanations.c: Venous compression would cause swelling and redness (edema), not a cold, blue 'arterial' toe.
explanations.d: While possible, mural thrombus embolization is a classic and frequent complication of established AAAs.
explanations.e: A fistula would cause high-output heart failure and a bruit, not focal distal ischemia.

ankiCards: AAAs are often filled with {{c1::mural thrombus}} due to turbulent flow.
Distal ischemia in a patient with an AAA is often called {{c1::'blue toe syndrome'}}.
Mural thrombus in an aneurysm is caused by {{c1::stasis}} and endothelial damage.
The risk of rupture for an AAA increases significantly once it exceeds {{c1::5.0 to 5.5}} cm.
Aneurysms can also present as a {{c1::pulsatile mass}} on physical exam.
keyPoints: Turbulent flow within the dilated aneurysm promotes thrombosis.
Mural thrombus can partially occlude the lumen or break off (embolize).
Emboli from an AAA typically lodge in lower extremity digital arteries.
This causes focal ischemia (blue toe) despite palpable proximal pulses.
Managing an AAA involves monitoring size to prevent rupture vs embolization.
microReview: AAA Complications: 1. Rupture (fatal), 2. Embolism (blue toe), 3. Pressure on local organs, 4. Obstruction of branch vessels.
examinerTraps: Students often focus only on 'rupture' as a complication of AAA. Embolization of the internal clot is a very common USMLE scenario.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old female presents with multiple dark red, firm nodules on her left arm. Her medical history is significant for a left-sided radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection and radiotherapy for breast cancer 12 years ago. Since the surgery, she has had chronic, persistent swelling of the left upper extremity. A biopsy of one of the nodules reveals irregular, slit-like vascular spaces lined by highly pleomorphic, mitotically active endothelial cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis presents in immunocompromised patients (e.g., HIV) as red papules but is caused by Bartonella infection and shows a neutrophilic infiltrate.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and typically presents as purple patches or plaques, often in the setting of HIV/AIDS, rather than chronic lymphedema.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma occurring in the setting of chronic lymphedema (often post-mastectomy) is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome. The histology showing atypical endothelial cells and irregular spaces is characteristic.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are small, exquisitely painful benign tumors usually found under the fingernails, derived from modified smooth muscle cells.
explanations.e: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign, large, blood-filled spaces lined by a single layer of normal endothelium, lacks the pleomorphism seen here.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma occurring in a limb with chronic lymphedema (e.g., post-mastectomy) is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves}} syndrome.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is classically associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}} or arsenic.
A vascular tumor marker that can help confirm the endothelial origin of pleomorphic cells is {{c1::CD31}}.
Angiosarcomas are characterized histologically by irregular vascular spaces lined by {{c1::atypical/pleomorphic}} endothelial cells.
What is the prognosis for most cases of cutaneous angiosarcoma? {{c1::Poor (5-year survival ~30%)}}
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a malignant endothelial neoplasm.
Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to angiosarcoma complicating chronic lymphedema.
Risk factors include radiation, chronic lymphedema, and chemical toxins (PVC, arsenic).
Most common sites are skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Histology demonstrates malignant, spindle-shaped, or epithelioid endothelial cells forming anastomosing channels.
microReview: Malignant vascular tumors (Angiosarcoma) are aggressive. Post-mastectomy patients with chronic lymphedema are at specific risk (Stewart-Treves). Histology shows high-grade atypia and irregular channels.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Stewart-Treves (angiosarcoma post-lymphedema) with Marjolin ulcer (squamous cell carcinoma in a chronic wound or burn scar).
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors include benign hemangiomas, intermediate-grade lesions (e.g., Kaposi sarcoma), and highly malignant angiosarcomas.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old male presents with a small, exquisitely painful, blue-red nodule under the fingernail of his right index finger. He reports that the pain is triggered by cold exposure. Which of the following cell types is the origin of this lesion?

explanations.a: Endothelial cells line the vascular spaces of hemangiomas, but they do not form the characteristic painful nests of a glomus tumor.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) arise from the specialized, modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, an arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.c: Pericytes are found around capillaries and are the origin of hemangiopericytomas (now often classified as solitary fibrous tumors), not glomus tumors.
explanations.d: Lymphatic endothelial cells are the origin of lymphangiomas, which are typically painless and located in the neck or axilla.
explanations.e: Fibroblasts are the origin of fibromas and fibrosarcomas, which lack the vascular thermoregulatory architecture of glomus bodies.

ankiCards: The characteristic location for a glomus tumor is {{c1::subungual (under the nail)}}.
Glomus tumors are derived from {{c1::modified smooth muscle cells}} of the glomus body.
The classic clinical triad for a glomus tumor includes pain, localized tenderness, and sensitivity to {{c1::cold}}.
A small, painful, red-blue subungual nodule is most likely a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors show nests of uniform, round cells surrounding {{c1::vascular channels}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but extremely painful.
Located primarily in the distal digits, especially subungual.
Derived from glomus bodies (thermoregulatory A-V shunts).
Classic symptom is cold hypersensitivity.
Excision is curative.
microReview: Glomus tumor = Subungual + Pain + Cold sensitivity + Smooth muscle origin.
examinerTraps: Examiners often contrast Glomus tumors with Subungual Melanoma; the latter is usually painless and pigmented (melanin), whereas glomus tumors are vascular/red-blue and painful.
sourceQuote: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, exquisitely painful tumors arising from specialized smooth muscle cells of the glomus bodies.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 35-year-old male with poorly controlled HIV (CD4+ count <100/mm³) presents with several raised, purple-to-brown plaques on his lower extremities and oral mucosa. A skin biopsy reveals proliferation of spindle-shaped cells, extravasated red blood cells, and slit-like vascular spaces. Which of the following pathogens is directly involved in the oncogenesis of this condition?

explanations.a: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis in HIV patients, which can look similar clinically but shows a neutrophilic infiltrate rather than spindle cells/slit-like spaces.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV).
explanations.c: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.d: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) causes retinitis or colitis in AIDS patients but is not oncogenic for vascular tumors.
explanations.e: HPV-16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx, not vascular tumors.

ankiCards: The causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
The histological hallmark of Kaposi Sarcoma is the presence of {{c1::spindle cells}} forming slit-like vascular spaces.
In addition to the skin, Kaposi Sarcoma commonly involves the {{c1::gastrointestinal tract}} and lymph nodes.
The characteristic skin lesion of Kaposi Sarcoma is described as a {{c1::purple/violaceous}} patch, plaque, or nodule.
HHV-8 infects {{c1::endothelial cells}} and promotes their proliferation and survival.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
Four types: Classic (older Mediterranean men), Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
HHV-8 is the essential cofactor in all forms.
Pathology: Slit-like spaces, spindle cells, prominent extravasated RBCs, and hyaline globules.
AIDS-associated KS is the most common HIV-related malignancy.
microReview: KS = HIV + HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Slit-like vascular spaces.
examinerTraps: Distinguishing KS from Bacillary Angiomatosis: KS has spindle cells (HHV-8); Bacillary Angiomatosis has neutrophils and Warthin-Starry positive bacteria (Bartonella).
sourceQuote: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8; it is most common in the setting of AIDS.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An infant is born with a bright red, slightly raised 'strawberry' lesion on the scalp. The lesion grows rapidly over the first few months of life but then begins to fade and shrink when the child is 2 years old. By age 7, the lesion has almost completely disappeared. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Port-wine stains (Nevus flammeus) are permanent and do not regress; they often grow with the child and thicken.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are deeper, larger, and involve larger vascular channels; they rarely regress spontaneously.
explanations.c: Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) are very common in infants, grow rapidly, and then characteristically regress by age 5-7.
explanations.d: Spider telangiectasias are small, central arterioles with radiating capillaries, typically associated with hyperestrogenic states (e.g., pregnancy, cirrhosis).
explanations.e: Pyogenic granulomas are rapidly growing red nodules that often bleed and follow trauma; they do not typically show the multi-year growth-regression cycle of juvenile hemangiomas.

ankiCards: The common name for a juvenile hemangioma is a {{c1::strawberry}} hemangioma.
The typical natural history of a juvenile hemangioma involves rapid growth followed by spontaneous {{c1::regression/involution}}.
By what age do most juvenile hemangiomas regress? {{c1::7 (or 5-7) years}}.
Juvenile hemangiomas are histologically classified as {{c1::capillary}} hemangiomas.
Unlike juvenile hemangiomas, a {{c1::port-wine stain (nevus flammeus)}} does not regress.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangioma is the most common vascular tumor of infancy.
Characterized by a 'strawberry' appearance.
Occurs in 1 in 200 live births.
Histology: Closely packed capillaries with thin linings.
Treatment is usually observation due to high regression rates.
microReview: Strawberry hemangioma = Infant + Rapid growth + Spontaneous regression by age 7.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse the 'strawberry' juvenile hemangioma with the 'port-wine stain'; the latter is associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome and does NOT regress.
sourceQuote: Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) of the skin of newborns are very common... they grow rapidly for a few months but then fade and eventually regress.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following chemical exposures is most strongly associated with the development of hepatic angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Aflatoxin B1 is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Vinyl chloride (used in the plastics industry), arsenic, and Thorotrast are the classic three associations for hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Benzene is associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.d: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and lung carcinoma.
explanations.e: Beryllium is associated with berylliosis (sarcoid-like granulomas) and lung cancer.

ankiCards: Vinyl chloride exposure is associated with which malignant vascular tumor? {{c1::Hepatic angiosarcoma}}.
Besides vinyl chloride, which elemental toxin is associated with hepatic angiosarcoma? {{c1::Arsenic}}.
The radioactive contrast medium previously used that caused angiosarcomas is {{c1::Thorotrast}}.
The cell of origin for hepatic angiosarcoma is the {{c1::endothelial cell}}.
Cutaneous angiosarcoma is often associated with prior {{c1::radiation}} therapy.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare, highly fatal tumor.
Strong environmental/occupational associations (PVC, Arsenic, Thorotrast).
Long latency period after exposure.
Aggressive local invasion and frequent distant metastasis.
Marker: CD31 positive.
microReview: Hepatic Angiosarcoma = PVC + Arsenic + Thorotrast + CD31.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'vinyl chloride' for angiosarcoma, but look for 'aflatoxin' if the question asks about hepatocellular carcinoma.
sourceQuote: Hepatic angiosarcomas are associated with distinct environmental carcinogens, including arsenic... and vinyl chloride.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic due to worsening seizures. On physical exam, he has a large, flat, dull-red purple patch covering the right side of his face in the distribution of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve. Imaging reveals leptomeningeal angiomas on the same side. Which of the following syndromes does this patient likely have?

explanations.a: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) presents with multiple small telangiectasias and epistaxis.
explanations.b: Von Hippel-Lindau involves hemangioblastomas (cerebellum/retina), renal cell carcinoma, and pheochromocytoma.
explanations.c: Sturge-Weber syndrome is characterized by a facial port-wine stain (nevus flammeus), ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomas, seizures, and mental retardation.
explanations.d: Kasabach-Merritt syndrome involves a large hemangioma that causes platelet sequestration and consumptive coagulopathy.
explanations.e: Stewart-Treves is angiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphedema.

ankiCards: Sturge-Weber syndrome classically presents with a facial {{c1::port-wine stain (nevus flammeus)}}.
The intracranial finding in Sturge-Weber syndrome is {{c1::leptomeningeal angiomas}}.
The facial lesion in Sturge-Weber syndrome usually follows the distribution of the {{c1::trigeminal (CN V)}} nerve.
Patients with Sturge-Weber syndrome often present with {{c1::seizures}} and intellectual disability.
What is the genetic basis of Sturge-Weber syndrome? {{c1::Somatic mutation in the GNAQ gene}}.
keyPoints: Sturge-Weber is a non-familial (sporadic) phakomatosis.
Facial port-wine stain is usually in V1/V2 distribution.
Associated with 'tram-track' calcifications on CT/MRI (cortical calcification).
May cause glaucoma due to episcleral hemangiomas.
Leptomeningeal vascular malformations lead to underlying cortical ischemia.
microReview: Sturge-Weber = Port-wine stain (CN V) + Leptomeningeal angioma + Seizures + GNAQ mutation.
examinerTraps: The facial port-wine stain is a 'nevus flammeus', which must be distinguished from 'nevus simplex' (salmon patch/stork bite), which is common and fades over time.
sourceQuote: Sturge-Weber syndrome... is a rare congenital disorder characterized by facial port-wine stains and ipsilateral venous angiomatous masses in the leptomeninges.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 42-year-old male with Advanced AIDS presents with numerous red-purple, friable, skin papules and nodules. Biopsy shows a proliferation of capillaries with prominent, protuberant epithelioid endothelial cells and an infiltrate of neutrophils. Warthin-Starry silver stain reveals clusters of tangled bacilli. What is the most appropriate management for the underlying cause of these lesions?

explanations.a: HAART is essential for HIV but does not treat the acute bacterial infection causing bacillary angiomatosis.
explanations.b: Surgical excision is not practical for numerous systemic lesions.
explanations.c: Topical retinoids can be used for localized Kaposi Sarcoma, not for bacterial infections.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella species (B. henselae or B. quintana) and responds to antibiotics like erythromycin.
explanations.e: Radiation is used for Kaposi Sarcoma, not for bacillary angiomatosis.

ankiCards: The causative organism of Bacillary Angiomatosis in HIV patients is {{c1::Bartonella (henselae or quintana)}}.
Histologically, Bacillary Angiomatosis is distinguished from Kaposi Sarcoma by the presence of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
The silver stain used to visualize Bartonella bacilli is {{c1::Warthin-Starry}}.
Bacillary angiomatosis lesions are characteristically {{c1::friable (easily bleeding)}} red papules.
First-line antibiotic treatment for Bacillary Angiomatosis is {{c1::erythromycin (or doxycycline)}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis (BA) is an infectious vascular proliferation.
Occurs in immunocompromised hosts.
Caused by GNRs of the genus Bartonella.
Histology: Lobular capillary proliferation with nuclear atypia and neutrophils.
Life-threatening if untreated, but highly responsive to antibiotics.
microReview: BA = AIDS + Bartonella + Neutrophils + Warthin-Starry stain + Antibiotic treatment.
examinerTraps: A 'friable red papule' in an HIV patient is more likely Bacillary Angiomatosis; a 'firm purple plaque' is more likely Kaposi Sarcoma.
sourceQuote: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts caused by opportunistic gram-negative bacilli of the Bartonella family.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A patient is diagnosed with a cavernous hemangioma of the liver. Which of the following describes the most likely histological appearance of this lesion?

options.a: Nests of uniform, round cells surrounding thin-walled vascular channels
options.b: Large, dilated vascular spaces filled with blood and separated by connective tissue stroma
options.c: Closely packed thin-walled capillaries with scant stroma
options.d: Irregular vascular slits lined by spindle-shaped cells with extravasated red blood cells
options.e: Sheet-like growth of pleomorphic endothelial cells with prominent hemorrhage

explanations.a: This describes a glomus tumor.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, cavernous blood-filled vascular spaces separated by connective tissue. They do not spontaneously regress.
explanations.c: This describes a capillary hemangioma.
explanations.d: This describes Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.e: This describes angiosarcoma.

ankiCards: The most common benign tumor of the liver is the {{c1::cavernous hemangioma}}.
Histologically, {{c1::cavernous}} hemangiomas have larger, more dilated vascular channels than capillary hemangiomas.
In the CNS, cavernous hemangiomas can occur in the {{c1::cerebellum/brainstem}} and may cause pressure symptoms.
Do cavernous hemangiomas usually regress? {{c1::No}}.
A complication of large hemangiomas involving platelet consumption is {{c1::Kasabach-Merritt}} syndrome.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are less common than capillary hemangiomas but larger.
Often involve deep structures (liver, CNS).
Grossly: Red-blue, soft spongy mass.
May be part of Von Hippel-Lindau disease if found in the CNS.
Clinically usually asymptomatic but can rupture or cause mass effect.
microReview: Cavernous Hemangioma = Large spaces + No regression + Liver (most common site).
examinerTraps: Clinically, a cavernous hemangioma in the liver is a 'don't touch' lesion because biopsy can lead to fatal hemorrhage.
sourceQuote: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, dilated vascular channels... they are more frequently involve deep structures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following conditions is characterized by autosomal dominant inheritance and multiple small aneurysmal telangiectasias of the skin and mucous membranes, often leading to recurrent epistaxis or gastrointestinal bleeding?

explanations.a: Sturge-Weber is sporadic, not autosomal dominant, and involves large port-wine stains.
explanations.b: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) is autosomal dominant and features telangiectasias of the skin, mouth, and GI tract.
explanations.c: VHL involves hemangioblastomas and visceral cysts/cancers.
explanations.d: NF1 involves café-au-lait spots and neurofibromas.
explanations.e: Tuberous sclerosis involves angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum) and hamartomas.

ankiCards: Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome is also known as {{c1::Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT)}}.
The inheritance pattern of Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome is {{c1::autosomal dominant}}.
Common clinical manifestations of HHT include {{c1::epistaxis}} and GI bleeding.
HHT is caused by mutations in genes that modulate {{c1::TGF-beta}} signaling.
In HHT, telangiectasias are found on the skin and the {{c1::mucous membranes (oral/GI)}}.
keyPoints: Osler-Weber-Rendu is a vascular dysplasia.
Characterized by malformed dilated capillaries and veins.
Present from birth.
Can cause iron deficiency anemia due to chronic blood loss.
AVMs in the lungs or brain are possible complications.
microReview: HHT (Osler-Weber-Rendu) = AD + Telangiectasia + Epistaxis + GI bleed.
examinerTraps: The primary symptom is often nosebleeds; don't overlook HHT in a differential for recurrent epistaxis in a patient with a family history.
sourceQuote: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome) is an autosomal dominant disorder... telangiectasias are present over the skin and oral mucous membranes.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old female presents with a rapidly growing, painful, pedunculated red nodule on her gingiva that bleeds easily with minor trauma. She is currently in her second trimester of pregnancy. Histology shows a lobular proliferation of capillaries with edema and an acute inflammatory infiltrate. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma is highly malignant and would show significant atypia; it is not typically associated with pregnancy.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis occurs in immunocompromised patients and is caused by Bartonella; this patient's pregnancy status suggests a different etiology.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a common benign lesion that often occurs on the gingiva, especially in pregnant women ('granuloma gravidarum').
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are usually subungual and involve specialized smooth muscle cells, not capillary proliferation.
explanations.e: Juvenile hemangiomas occur in infants, not adults.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granulomas are often associated with prior {{c1::trauma}}.
A pyogenic granuloma occurring on the gingiva of a pregnant woman is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Histologically, pyogenic granuloma is a {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
The clinical appearance of a pyogenic granuloma is a {{c1::pedunculated}} red nodule that bleeds easily.
Treatment for a pyogenic granuloma is usually {{c1::surgical excision/curettage}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is neither pyogenic (pus-producing) nor a granuloma.
Actually a lobular capillary hemangioma.
Commonly found on skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
Growth is rapid (weeks).
Regression is possible after pregnancy, but excision is often required.
microReview: Pyogenic Granuloma = Pregnancy/Trauma + Gingiva + Rapid growth + Bleeding + Lobular capillaries.
examinerTraps: Despite the name 'Pyogenic', the lesion does not necessarily contain pus, though it may be ulcerated.
sourceQuote: Pyogenic granulomas are capillary hemangiomas that manifest as rapidly growing red pedunculated nodules on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Two principal mechanisms underlie the development of vascular disease. Which of the following mechanisms is directly responsible for the formation of an aneurysm?

explanations.a: Lumen narrowing typically results from atherosclerosis and leads to ischemia rather than dilation or rupture.
explanations.b: Weakening of the vessel wall is the fundamental mechanism that leads to the dilation (aneurysm) or rupture of a vessel.
explanations.c: Complete obstruction usually occurs via thrombosis or embolism, causing acute infarction rather than aneurysm formation.
explanations.d: Intimal thickening is a stereotyped response to vascular injury that tends to narrow vessels rather than cause dilation.
explanations.e: Endothelial hyperreactivity is associated with conditions like Raynaud phenomenon, not the structural failure of the vessel wall.

ankiCards: The two principal mechanisms underlying vascular disease are narrowing/obstruction and {{c1::weakening}} of vessel walls.
Weakening of vessel walls leads to two primary complications: {{c1::dilation}} or {{c2::rupture}}.
Narrowing of vessel lumens can occur progressively through {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Precipitous obstruction of a vessel lumen is usually caused by {{c1::thrombosis}} or {{c2::embolism}}.
Arterial walls are thicker than veins to accommodate {{c1::pulsatile flow}} and {{c2::higher blood pressures}}.
keyPoints: Vascular disease is primarily driven by either narrowing/obstruction or wall weakening.
Aneurysms represent a structural failure of the vessel wall leading to dilation.
Atherosclerosis is a major progressive cause of lumen narrowing.
Arterial architecture reflects the need to handle high pressure compared to veins.
Weakening of the vessel wall is the prerequisite for both aneurysms and dissections.
microReview: Vascular pathology focuses on two main outcomes: ischemia (from narrowing/occlusion) and structural failure (aneurysms/rupture). Aneurysms are specifically the result of wall weakening.
examinerTraps: Atherosclerosis causes both narrowing and wall weakening (by inducing medial ischemia); however, the specific mechanism for 'aneurysm' is always wall weakening, not the narrowing itself.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following alterations in the extracellular matrix (ECM) of the aortic media is the most common pathogenetic feature shared by various types of aneurysms?

explanations.a: Lysyl oxidase is required for collagen cross-linking; its deficiency, not increased expression, would lead to wall weakening.
explanations.b: Aneurysms are associated with the activation (not inhibition) of MMPs, which degrade elastin and collagen.
explanations.c: Aneurysms occur when the balance of ECM is shifted, often due to inadequate synthesis of connective tissue (e.g., TGF-beta mutations or Vitamin C deficiency).
explanations.d: Increased TGF-beta signaling is often implicated in syndromic aneurysms like Marfan and Loeys-Dietz.
explanations.e: Smooth muscle cell loss (atrophy), rather than hypertrophy, is a classic feature of medial degeneration in aneurysms.

ankiCards: Aneurysms can occur when there is inadequate synthesis of {{c1::connective tissue}}.
Excessive connective tissue degradation in aneurysms is often mediated by {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
Cystic medial degeneration is characterized by the loss of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} and elastic fibers.
Mutations in the {{c1::TGF-beta}} signaling pathway are associated with certain familial aneurysms.
Tertiary syphilis causes aneurysms by causing obliterative endarteritis of the {{c1::vasa vasorum}}.
keyPoints: Aneurysm pathogenesis involves an imbalance in ECM metabolism.
Key factors include: defective ECM synthesis, excessive ECM degradation, and loss of smooth muscle cells.
MMPs are produced by inflammatory infiltrates (macrophages) in the vessel wall.
TGF-beta plays a dual role but is highly relevant in Marfan and related syndromes.
Structural integrity depends on the ratio of collagen synthesis to degradation.
microReview: Aneurysms are essentially 'wall failures.' This happens if the 'bricks' (collagen/elastin) aren't made well, are destroyed too fast (MMPs), or if the 'builders' (smooth muscle cells) die (medial ischemia/degeneration).
examinerTraps: Wait for 'TGF-beta'—while usually a growth factor, mutations leading to excessive signaling paradoxically cause wall weakness in specific syndromes.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male with a 40-pack-year smoking history and hypertension presents for a routine physical. On abdominal palpation, a non-tender, pulsatile mass is felt at the level of the umbilicus. Imaging reveals a 5.5 cm dilation of the infrarenal aorta. What is the most likely primary cause of the weakening in this patient’s vessel wall?

options.d: Congenital defect in the circle of Willis

explanations.a: Cystic medial necrosis (degeneration) is more characteristic of thoracic aortic aneurysms, often seen in Marfan syndrome.
explanations.b: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are primarily driven by atherosclerosis, which limits oxygen diffusion to the media, causing ischemia and wall weakening.
explanations.c: This describes the mechanism of syphilitic (luetic) aneurysms, which typically involve the thoracic aorta.
explanations.d: This refers to Berry aneurysms, which occur in the brain, not the infrarenal aorta.
explanations.e: Vasculitis (like Polyarteritis Nodosa) can cause aneurysms, but it is not the most common cause in an older smoker with a pulsatile abdominal mass.

ankiCards: The most common cause of an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
AAAs are usually located below the {{c1::renal}} arteries.
Atherosclerosis causes AAAs by inducing {{c1::ischemic}} atrophy of the media.
The classic clinical presentation of an AAA is a {{c1::pulsatile abdominal mass}}.
The risk of rupture for an AAA increases significantly when the diameter exceeds {{c1::5.0 to 5.5}} cm.
keyPoints: AAA is the most common form of aortic aneurysm.
Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for AAA.
Atherosclerotic plaques compromise nutrient/oxygen diffusion to the underlying media.
Loss of medial smooth muscle and elastic tissue leads to thinning and dilation.
AAA usually occurs between the renal arteries and the aortic bifurcation.
microReview: Older male + Smoker + Pulsatile mass = AAA. The pathology is atherosclerosis causing medial thinning because the 'gunk' in the intima prevents oxygen from reaching the media.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse AAA (atherosclerosis-driven, infrarenal) with TAA (thoracic, often hypertension or Marfan-driven).
sourceQuote: Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following descriptions best distinguishes a 'false aneurysm' (pseudoaneurysm) from a 'true aneurysm'?

options.a: A false aneurysm involves only the intimal layer
options.b: A false aneurysm is a result of cystic medial necrosis
options.c: A false aneurysm is a hematoma contained by extravascular connective tissue
options.d: A false aneurysm is specifically fusiform in shape
options.e: A false aneurysm always involves all three layers of the vessel wall

explanations.a: Dissections involve the intima; pseudoaneurysms involve a complete breach of the wall.
explanations.b: Cystic medial necrosis causes true aneurysms where the wall remains intact but thinned.
explanations.c: A false aneurysm occurs when a wall defect leads to an extravascular hematoma that freely communicates with the intravascular space (contained by perivascular tissue).
explanations.d: The shape (fusiform vs. saccular) does not define 'true' vs 'false' status.
explanations.e: A true aneurysm involves all three layers (intima, media, adventitia); a false aneurysm lacks these vessel wall layers in its boundary.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves an intact (but attenuated) arterial wall or thinned ventricular wall.
A {{c1::false}} aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) is a defect in the vascular wall leading to an extravascular hematoma.
The term 'pseudoaneurysm' is synonymous with {{c1::false aneurysm}}.
An aortic {{c1::dissection}} occurs when blood enters the wall of the artery through an intimal tear.
A {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm is a spherical outpouching involving only a portion of the vessel wall.
keyPoints: True aneurysms have all 3 layers of the vessel wall intact (though thinned).
False aneurysms are essentially 'leaks' contained by external connective tissue.
Common causes of false aneurysms include trauma or post-MI myocardial rupture contained by pericardium.
Saccular vs. Fusiform describes shape, not wall composition.
Dissection is distinct from an aneurysm as blood is within the wall, not just a dilated wall.
microReview: True = Wall is intact but stretched. False = Hole in the wall, blood held in by outside tissue. Dissection = Blood split the wall layers apart.
examinerTraps: An examiner might call a 'ventricular aneurysm' after an MI a 'true aneurysm' if the wall is intact (fibrotic), but a 'false aneurysm' if the wall ruptured and was contained by adhesions.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with sudden, severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back. Her blood pressure is 150/90 mmHg. Physical examination reveals long, slender fingers and a high-arched palate. Echocardiography shows a dilated aortic root. Which molecular defect is most likely present in this patient?

explanations.a: Type III Collagen deficiency is seen in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (Vascular type).
explanations.b: The clinical description (tearing pain, tall, long fingers) fits Marfan syndrome, which is caused by a defect in Fibrillin-1, leading to TGF-beta dysregulation and cystic medial degeneration.
explanations.c: Elastase overproduction is a mechanism in emphysema/AAAs but not the primary genetic defect in Marfan's.
explanations.d: VEGF is involved in angiogenesis, not the structural integrity of the aortic media.
explanations.e: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency leads to lung and liver disease; while it can increase elastase activity, it is not the cause of the described phenotype.

ankiCards: Marfan syndrome is caused by mutations in the {{c1::Fibrillin-1}} gene.
Fibrillin-1 mutations lead to abnormal {{c1::TGF-beta}} signaling.
The classic histological change in the aorta of Marfan patients is {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
Cystic medial degeneration involves the loss of {{c1::elastic}} fibers and their replacement by proteoglycans.
The most common cause of death in Marfan syndrome is {{c1::aortic dissection}} or rupture.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome is a leading cause of thoracic aortic aneurysms in young adults.
Cystic medial degeneration is the histological hallmark.
Structural weakness is due to defective scaffolding (fibrillin) and growth factor signaling.
Clinical signs: Arachnodactyly, lens ectopia, pectus excavatum.
Aortic root dilation often precedes dissection.
microReview: Marfan = Fibrillin-1 = High TGF-beta = Cystic Medial Degeneration = Weak thoracic aorta = Dissection/Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: A tearing chest pain indicates dissection, but the underlying 'dilation' mentioned is the aneurysm portion of the objective.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the classification of aneurysms by macroscopic shape, a spherical outpouching that involves only a portion of the vessel wall and often contains a thrombus is termed a:

explanations.a: Fusiform aneurysms are circumferential, symmetrical dilations of a long segment of the vessel.
explanations.b: Saccular aneurysms are discrete spherical outpouchings (5-20 cm) that involve only a portion of the wall and frequently contain thrombi.
explanations.c: A 'dissection' is not a shape-based classification of an aneurysm; it involves blood splitting the media.
explanations.d: Cylindrical is a synonym for fusiform, but 'Saccular' specifically matches the spherical description.
explanations.e: While a Berry aneurysm is saccular in shape, 'Saccular' is the general category used for this description in pathology texts.

ankiCards: A {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm is a spherical outpouching involving only a portion of the vessel wall.
A {{c1::fusiform}} aneurysm is a circumferential dilation of a long vascular segment.
Saccular aneurysms often contain {{c1::thrombi}} due to stagnant blood flow.
The diameter of a saccular aneurysm can range from {{c1::5}} to {{c2::20}} cm.
Berry aneurysms are a specific subtype of {{c1::saccular}} aneurysms found in the brain.
keyPoints: Aneurysms are classified by shape into saccular and fusiform.
Saccular: One-sided, 'sac' like, often thrombosed.
Fusiform: Entire circumference, spindle-shaped.
Shape does not necessarily determine the underlying etiology.
AAAs are more commonly fusiform, while Berry aneurysms are saccular.
microReview: Sac = Saccular (one side). Fuse = Fusiform (both sides/spindle).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'Saccular' with 'Berry.' All Berry aneurysms are saccular, but not all saccular aneurysms are Berry aneurysms (they can be in the aorta too).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Inflammatory cells, particularly macrophages, contribute to the expansion of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) primarily by which mechanism?

options.a: Secretion of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)
options.c: Direct phagocytosis of medial smooth muscle cells
options.e: Synthesis of defective type I collagen

explanations.a: VEGF stimulates angiogenesis, which may happen but is not the primary driver of wall weakening in AAA.
explanations.b: Macrophages in the inflammatory infiltrate of an AAA secrete MMPs (like collagenases and elastases) that degrade the ECM, weakening the wall.
explanations.c: Smooth muscle cell loss is largely due to ischemia or apoptosis, not direct phagocytosis by macrophages.
explanations.d: Coagulation occurs inside the aneurysm (mural thrombus), but the expansion of the wall itself is a proteolytic process.
explanations.e: Synthesis is done by fibroblasts/smooth muscle cells, not macrophages; macrophages are primarily degradative in this context.

ankiCards: In AAA, macrophages produce {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}} that degrade the ECM.
MMPs involved in aneurysm formation include {{c1::collagenases}} and {{c2::elastases}}.
Tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases ({{c1::TIMPs}}) normally regulate MMP activity.
An imbalance where {{c1::MMPs}} outweigh TIMPs leads to wall weakening.
Chronic inflammation in the {{c1::adventitia}} is a common finding in AAAs.
keyPoints: AAAs are characterized by chronic transmural inflammation.
Degradation of elastin and collagen is mediated by MMPs.
Smoking increases the inflammatory burden and MMP activity.
The 'balance' of the vessel wall depends on ECM synthesis vs. degradation.
Elastin loss is a particularly early and critical step in dilation.
microReview: Macrophages = MMPs = 'Eating' the wall proteins (elastin/collagen) = Weakness = Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: An examiner might ask if it's the 'intima' or 'media'—the inflammation is usually throughout, but the MMPs specifically destroy the structural media.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old female with a history of syphilis treated twenty years ago presents with a dry cough and difficulty swallowing. Imaging reveals a dilation of the ascending aortic arch with calcification. What is the most likely microscopic finding in the wall of this patient's aorta?

options.c: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.e: Fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel wall

explanations.a: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is a result of hypertension and affects small vessels, not the aorta.
explanations.b: This describes early atherosclerosis; while present, it isn't the specific mechanism for a syphilitic aneurysm.
explanations.c: Tertiary syphilis involves the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta, causing obliterative endarteritis. This leads to ischemic injury of the aortic media and 'tree-barking'.
explanations.d: Granulomatous inflammation of the aorta is seen in Takayasu or Giant Cell arteritis.
explanations.e: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in malignant hypertension or certain vasculitides, not chronic syphilis.

ankiCards: Syphilitic aneurysms occur during the {{c1::tertiary}} stage of syphilis.
Syphilis targets the {{c1::vasa vasorum}} of the ascending aorta.
The gross appearance of the aortic intima in syphilis is described as {{c1::tree-barking}}.
Ischemic injury to the media in syphilis leads to contraction of {{c1::fibrous}} scars.
Syphilitic aneurysms can lead to {{c1::aortic valve}} insufficiency (dilation of the ring).
keyPoints: Luetic (syphilitic) aneurysms are now rare due to antibiotics.
Mechanism: Endarteritis of vasa vasorum -> Medial ischemia -> Medial scarring.
Location: Exclusively the ascending aorta and arch.
Aortic tree-barking is due to irregular scarring of the media.
Complications include respiratory distress (compression) and heart failure.
microReview: Syphilis = Vasa Vasorum shut down = Media starves = Scars and dilates = Ascending aorta 'Tree-barking'.
examinerTraps: Tertiary syphilis causes *dilation* (aneurysm) of the ascending aorta, but *narrowing* of the vasa vasorum. Don't flip them.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes a 'mycotic aneurysm'?

options.a: An aneurysm caused by a fungal infection
options.b: An aneurysm arising from a congenital medial defect
options.c: An aneurysm caused by infection of the vessel wall
options.d: An aneurysm that has already ruptured
options.e: An aneurysm involving the pulmonary circulation

explanations.a: Despite the name 'mycotic' (suggesting fungi), most mycotic aneurysms are actually bacterial.
explanations.b: Congenital defects cause Berry aneurysms.
explanations.c: A mycotic aneurysm is an aneurysm resulting from the weakening of the vessel wall due to an infection (e.g., from an embolized vegetation in endocarditis).
explanations.d: Rupture is a complication, not a definition of a mycotic aneurysm.
explanations.e: Location does not define 'mycotic' status, though they can occur in various sites.

ankiCards: A {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm results from infection of a major artery.
Mycotic aneurysms can be caused by {{c1::septic emboli}} from infective endocarditis.
Extension of an adjacent {{c1::suppurative}} process (e.g., abscess) can cause mycotic aneurysms.
The most common organisms in mycotic aneurysms are {{c1::bacteria}} (despite the name).
Infection in a mycotic aneurysm induces a brisk {{c1::inflammatory}} response that destroys the media.
keyPoints: Mycotic aneurysms are infectious in origin.
They can arise from bacteremia, septic emboli, or direct extension.
Infection triggers rapid wall destruction compared to atherosclerosis.
The name is a historical misnomer; bacteria (Staph, Salmonella) are the usual culprits.
They carry a high risk of rupture and sepsis.
