microReview: Mycotic = Infection (usually bacteria, not fungi) -> Weakens wall -> Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: The word 'mycotic' often tricks students into picking 'fungal' (Option A).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Aneurysms that occur at branch points in the circle of Willis and are associated with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) are most commonly which type?

explanations.a: Fusiform aneurysms are common in the aorta, not the cerebral circulation.
explanations.b: Dissections in the brain are rare compared to the 'Berry' type dilations.
explanations.c: Berry aneurysms are small, saccular dilations in the cerebral vessels, classically associated with ADPKD and subarachnoid hemorrhage.
explanations.d: Mycotic aneurysms occur in the brain but are due to infection, not a congenital association with ADPKD.
explanations.e: Luetic (syphilitic) aneurysms affect the ascending aorta, not the brain.

ankiCards: {{c1::Berry}} aneurysms are the most common cause of non-traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage.
Berry aneurysms are associated with {{c1::Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD)}}.
The most common site for a Berry aneurysm is the {{c1::Circle of Willis}}.
Berry aneurysms lack a {{c1::internal elastic lamina}} and smooth muscle at the site of the sac.
Rupture of a Berry aneurysm typically presents as a '{{c1::worst headache of my life}}'.
keyPoints: Berry aneurysms are a specific type of saccular aneurysm.
They occur at vascular bifurcations (branch points).
The media is congenitally thin or absent at these points.
Risk factors include hypertension and smoking.
ADPKD is a major systemic association.
microReview: Berry = Circle of Willis = ADPKD association = Subarachnoid Hemorrhage.
examinerTraps: Berry aneurysms are *not* present at birth; the *predisposition* (medial weakness) is congenital, but the aneurysm develops over time.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular tumors are broadly classified based on their clinical behavior into benign, intermediate (borderline), and malignant categories. According to the standard classification of these lesions, which of the following is categorized as a malignant vascular tumor?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors are benign, exquisitely painful tumors arising from specialized smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, usually found in the distal digits.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign, rapidly growing capillary hemangioma that often occurs on the skin or gingival mucosa.
explanations.c: Angiosarcomas are highly malignant vascular neoplasms that exhibit aggressive clinical behavior and poor prognosis.
explanations.d: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is an intermediate-grade (borderline) vascular tumor, falling between benign hemangiomas and highly malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign vascular proliferation caused by opportunistic infection with Bartonella species in immunocompromised patients.

ankiCards: The most common malignant vascular tumor is {{c1::Angiosarcoma}}.
{{c1::Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma}} is considered an intermediate-grade (borderline) vascular tumor.
The glomus tumor is a {{c1::benign}} neoplasm arising from the glomus body.
{{c1::Angiosarcomas}} are often positive for the endothelial cell marker {{c2::CD31}}.
Vascular tumors are classified into three grades: {{c1::benign}}, {{c2::intermediate}}, and {{c3::malignant}}.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors are divided into benign, intermediate, and malignant categories.
Benign lesions include hemangiomas and glomus tumors.
Intermediate lesions include Kaposi sarcoma and hemangioendothelioma.
Malignant lesions are primarily angiosarcomas.
CD31 is a specific immunohistochemical marker for vascular differentiation.
Clinical behavior correlates with the degree of cellular atypia and architectural complexity.
microReview: Vascular tumors range from benign hemangiomas (common in infants) to intermediate Kaposi sarcomas (linked to HHV-8) and aggressive angiosarcomas (linked to radiation or chemical exposure).
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Kaposi sarcoma (intermediate/low-grade malignancy) with Angiosarcoma (high-grade malignancy). Bacillary angiomatosis is infectious/benign but mimics Kaposi sarcoma clinically.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors are categorized as benign tumors and tumor-like conditions, intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors, and malignant tumors.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old male former factory worker presents with abdominal pain and weight loss. Imaging reveals multiple hepatic masses. Biopsy shows malignant spindle cells forming irregular vascular channels that express CD31. This patient's condition is most strongly associated with chronic exposure to which of the following substances?

explanations.a: Beryllium exposure is associated with berylliosis (granulomatous lung disease) and lung cancer, not hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Asbestos is primarily associated with mesothelioma and bronchogenic carcinoma.
explanations.c: Vinyl chloride (used in PVC production), arsenic, and Thorotrast are classic risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: Benzene exposure is strongly linked to acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.e: Aflatoxin B1 is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
The vascular marker used to identify angiosarcoma cells is {{c1::CD31}}.
{{c1::Vinyl chloride}} is a chemical used in the manufacturing of polyvinyl chloride (PVC).
The morphology of angiosarcoma involves malignant {{c1::spindle cells}} forming vascular channels.
Angiosarcomas are most commonly found in the {{c1::skin}}, soft tissue, breast, and {{c2::liver}}.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare but aggressive malignant tumor.
Classic environmental triggers include vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
Malignant endothelial cells are identified by CD31 and vWF markers.
Tumors often present as multifocal masses within the liver.
Prognosis is generally poor due to late presentation and rapid growth.
microReview: Hepatic Angiosarcoma: Think 'VAT'—Vinyl chloride, Arsenic, Thorotrast. CD31+ spindle cells forming nasty vascular slits.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'vinyl chloride' for angiosarcoma; don't confuse it with 'aflatoxin' which causes hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
sourceQuote: Malignant tumors (angiosarcoma) are also associated with environmental exposures, including arsenic, Thorotrast, and vinyl chloride.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 2-week-old female infant is brought to the pediatrician by her mother, who noticed a bright red, raised 'strawberry-like' lesion on the infant's scalp. The mother states it was not present at birth but appeared shortly after. The lesion is soft, compressible, and measures 2 cm. Which of the following is the most likely clinical course for this lesion?

options.a: Progressive enlargement leading to local invasion
options.d: Permanent persistence without change in size
options.e: Immediate surgical excision required to prevent metastasis

explanations.a: Juvenile hemangiomas are benign and do not exhibit local invasion like malignant tumors.
explanations.b: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are extremely common in infants; they grow rapidly for a few months but then usually involute spontaneously by age 5 to 7.
explanations.c: Hemangiomas are benign lesions and do not transform into malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.d: Unlike port-wine stains (nevus flammeus), juvenile hemangiomas do not persist; they regress.
explanations.e: Surgical excision is rarely necessary because most lesions regress on their own.

ankiCards: A juvenile hemangioma is also known as a {{c1::strawberry}} hemangioma.
Juvenile hemangiomas typically appear {{c1::shortly after birth}} and regress by age {{c2::7}}.
The histological feature of hemangiomas is a proliferation of {{c1::capillaries}}.
Juvenile hemangiomas are categorized as {{c1::benign}} tumors.
Unlike juvenile hemangiomas, a {{c1::nevus flammeus (port-wine stain)}} does not regress spontaneously.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangioma is the most common vascular tumor of infancy.
They are 'strawberry' colored, raised, and lobulated.
Natural history involves rapid growth followed by gradual involution.
Majority (75-90%) completely regress by age 7.
Usually requires only observation rather than intervention.
microReview: Strawberry Hemangioma: Newborn, grows then shrinks, benign, don't touch (mostly).
examinerTraps: Distinguish between Juvenile Hemangioma (regresses) and Port-Wine Stain (grows with the child/stays).
sourceQuote: Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) are extremely common... these lesions grow rapidly for a few months but then fade and eventually regress.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm caused by Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8). While KS presents in several distinct clinical settings, the underlying pathology involves infection of which cell type by HHV-8, leading to dysfunctional proliferation and angiogenesis?

explanations.a: Fibroblasts may be present in the reactive stroma, but they are not the primary target of HHV-8 that defines the tumor.
explanations.b: Smooth muscle cells are not the cell of origin or the primary site of viral latency in KS.
explanations.c: HHV-8 (KSHV) infects endothelial cells, inducing a program of genes that lead to proliferation and recruitment of inflammatory cells.
explanations.d: Neutrophils are characteristically absent in KS; their presence would suggest bacillary angiomatosis.
explanations.e: Pericytes surround capillaries but are not the transformed cells in Kaposi sarcoma.

ankiCards: The infectious agent linked to all forms of Kaposi sarcoma is {{c1::HHV-8 (or KSHV)}}.
In Kaposi sarcoma, HHV-8 primarily infects {{c1::endothelial cells}}.
The four clinical forms of Kaposi sarcoma are {{c1::Classic}}, {{c2::Endemic (African)}}, {{c3::Transplant-associated}}, and {{c4::AIDS-associated}}.
The characteristic histopathologic feature of Kaposi sarcoma is the presence of {{c1::spindle}} cells.
The slits between spindle cells in Kaposi sarcoma contain {{c1::red blood cells (RBCs)}}.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
HHV-8 is the essential co-factor for development.
Morphology progress from patches to plaques to nodules.
Spindle cells with slit-like spaces containing extravasated RBCs are diagnostic.
AIDS-associated KS is the most common HIV-related malignancy.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma: HHV-8 + Endothelial cells + Spindle cells + RBC slits = KS.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse HHV-8 with HIV; HIV provides the immunosuppression, but HHV-8 is the oncogenic driver.
sourceQuote: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) and is most common in the setting of AIDS.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old male with HIV (CD4 count 150/mm³) presents with several friable, red-purple, dome-shaped skin papules. Histologic examination of a lesion biopsy reveals a vascular proliferation with an infiltrate of neutrophils and Warthin-Starry silver stain-positive organisms. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma lacks a prominent neutrophilic infiltrate and is not associated with bacteria on silver stain; it is caused by HHV-8.
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignancy with significant atypia, not a reactive-appearing bacterial-induced proliferation.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella species (B. henselae or B. quintana) in immunocompromised hosts, showing neutrophils and bacteria on silver stain.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are painful, subungual lesions unrelated to HIV or bacterial infection.
explanations.e: Cavernous hemangiomas are large, blood-filled vascular spaces without inflammatory infiltrates or infectious organisms.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by the bacteria {{c1::Bartonella henselae}} or {{c2::Bartonella quintana}}.
A key histologic difference between KS and Bacillary Angiomatosis is that the latter has {{c1::neutrophils}}.
The silver stain used to identify organisms in Bacillary Angiomatosis is {{c1::Warthin-Starry}}.
Bacillary angiomatosis typically occurs in {{c1::immunocompromised (HIV)}} patients.
The clinical appearance of Bacillary Angiomatosis is described as red-purple, {{c1::friable}} papules.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign vascular proliferation caused by Bartonella.
It mimics Kaposi Sarcoma clinically in AIDS patients.
Histology: Proliferation of capillaries with protuberant epithelioid endothelium.
Presence of neutrophils and 'dust-like' bacteria (seen on silver stain) is diagnostic.
It is treatable with antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin).
microReview: Bacillary Angiomatosis: AIDS + Red bumps + Neutrophils + Bartonella (Silver stain +) = Antibiotic treatment.
examinerTraps: The presence of neutrophils is the 'giveaway' for Bacillary Angiomatosis over Kaposi Sarcoma.
sourceQuote: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts caused by opportunistic gram-negative bacilli of the Bartonella family.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with an exquisitely painful, small (5 mm), blue-tinted nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. The lesion is extremely sensitive to cold and touch. This clinical presentation is most characteristic of which vascular tumor?

explanations.a: Cherry angiomas are benign, asymptomatic red papules that increase with age and are not painful.
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma is a malignant, often large, aggressive tumor, not typically a small subungual painful nodule.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, highly painful tumors arising from modified smooth muscle cells, frequently occurring in subungual locations.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granulomas are rapidly growing, often bleeding, red nodules but are not typically subungual or specifically painful to cold.
explanations.e: Lymphangiomas are benign proliferations of lymphatic vessels, usually larger and painless, often in the neck or axilla.

ankiCards: The most common location for a glomus tumor is {{c1::subungual (under the nail)}}.
Glomus tumors are derived from specialized {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} of the glomus body.
A clinical hallmark of glomus tumors is extreme {{c1::pain}} (often triggered by cold).
Histologically, glomus tumors show nests of uniform, round cells called {{c1::glomus cells}}.
Glomus tumors are categorized as {{c1::benign}} tumors.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign neoplasms of the glomus body.
The glomus body is involved in thermoregulation.
Classic site: distal digits, especially subungual.
Clinical triad: paroxysmal pain, point tenderness, and cold sensitivity.
Treatment is simple excision.
microReview: Glomus Tumor: Painful + Cold sensitive + Under the nail = Glomus cell (smooth muscle origin).
examinerTraps: The pain is the key. Most other vascular tumors (hemangiomas, lymphangiomas) are painless.
sourceQuote: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, exquisitely painful tumors arising from specialized smooth muscle cells of the glomus bodies.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A biopsy of a soft tissue mass shows a vascular neoplasm consisting of nests and cords of plump, 'epithelioid' endothelial cells with cytoplasmic vacuoles that occasionally contain red blood cells. The tumor is moderately aggressive, showing behavior intermediate between a benign hemangioma and a malignant angiosarcoma. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are benign and do not show epithelioid features or borderline aggressive behavior.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, thin-walled vascular spaces and are benign.
explanations.c: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor characterized by epithelioid endothelial cells and a borderline clinical course.
explanations.d: Stewart-Treves syndrome refers specifically to angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema, which is highly malignant, not intermediate.
explanations.e: Hemangiopericytoma is a historical term for tumors now largely classified as solitary fibrous tumors; they do not typically show these specific endothelial features.

ankiCards: {{c1::Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma}} is a vascular tumor with clinical behavior between benign and malignant.
The characteristic cell in Epithelioid Hemangioendothelioma is the {{c1::epithelioid endothelial cell}}.
In hemangioendothelioma, endothelial cells often contain {{c1::vacuoles}} that represent primitive vascular lumens.
Hemangioendotheliomas are considered {{c1::intermediate-grade (or borderline)}} tumors.
Malignant vascular tumors that are more aggressive than hemangioendotheliomas are called {{c1::angiosarcomas}}.
keyPoints: Hemangioendothelioma represents a diverse group of borderline vascular tumors.
Epithelioid type is well-described, appearing as cords of 'plump' cells.
Cytoplasmic vacuoles (blisters) in cells often contain RBCs.
Clinical course is unpredictable, ranging from benign to metastatic.
Excision is the primary treatment.
microReview: Epithelioid Hemangioendothelioma: Intermediate grade, epithelioid cells, 'blister' vacuoles with RBCs.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'epithelioid' cells with actual epithelium; they are endothelial cells that just look like epithelial cells.
sourceQuote: Intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors... include epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, a vascular tumor of adults occurring around medium-sized and large veins.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with a 4-month history of developing multiple enlarging, firm, purple skin nodules on her left arm. She has a history of radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer 10 years ago, complicated by chronic, severe lymphedema of that arm. What is the most likely diagnosis for the new skin lesions?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and usually occurs in HIV or specific elderly Mediterranean populations, not specifically in chronic lymphedema.
explanations.b: Lymphangioma circumscriptum is a benign lymphatic malformation, typically congenital or appearing early in life.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema (often post-mastectomy) is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome.
explanations.d: Basal cell carcinoma presents as pearly papules on sun-exposed skin, not purple nodules in lymphedematous limbs.
explanations.e: Stasis dermatitis is a skin change due to venous insufficiency, not a nodular neoplasm.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves}} syndrome.
The most common clinical scenario for Stewart-Treves syndrome is post-{{c1::mastectomy}} with axillary dissection.
Angiosarcoma presents as firm, {{c1::purple}} or red skin nodules.
Chronic lymphedema is a known risk factor for the development of {{c1::Angiosarcoma}}.
Angiosarcomas are highly {{c1::malignant}} neoplasms with a poor prognosis.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma can occur secondary to chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves).
Classic example: Arm edema after radical mastectomy.
Malignant endothelial cells form poorly defined vascular channels.
Prognosis is poor; 5-year survival is less than 30%.
Metastasis occurs early and widely.
microReview: Stewart-Treves: Old mastectomy + Chronic lymphedema + New purple nodules = Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Wait for the history of radical mastectomy and chronic edema; this is the classic 'clue' for secondary angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas can also occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema, classically in the ipsilateral arm several years after radical mastectomy.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old pregnant woman develops a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated nodule on her gingiva. It bleeds easily when she brushes her teeth. Histological examination shows a circumscribed proliferation of capillaries with associated edema and an inflammatory infiltrate. This lesion is best characterized as which of the following?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors are painful subungual lesions, not typically found on the gingiva during pregnancy.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a benign, rapid-growing, friable nodule often found on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, deep-seated vascular spaces and do not typically present as small pedunculated gingival masses.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis occurs in immunocompromised individuals and is caused by Bartonella, not typically associated with pregnancy.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a malignant, aggressive tumor with cellular atypia, not a benign reactive-appearing capillary proliferation.

ankiCards: A pyogenic granuloma found on the gingiva of a pregnant woman is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
The histology of a pyogenic granuloma resembles a {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized by being {{c1::friable (or bleed easily)}}.
True or False: Pyogenic granulomas are infectious in origin. {{c1::False}} (they are reactive/vascular).
The clinical course of a pyogenic granuloma often involves {{c1::rapid}} growth.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is neither pyogenic (pus-producing) nor a granuloma.
It is a lobular capillary hemangioma.
Common on skin, gingiva, and oral mucosa.
Frequent association with pregnancy (pregnancy tumor/granuloma gravidarum).
Often regresses after pregnancy or requires simple excision.
microReview: Pyogenic Granuloma: Pregnant woman + Bleeding gums + Red bump = Lobular capillary hemangioma.
examinerTraps: The name 'Pyogenic Granuloma' is a trick—it has nothing to do with infection or granulomatous inflammation.
sourceQuote: Pyogenic granulomas are capillary hemangiomas that manifest as rapidly growing red pedunculated lesions on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An infant girl born with features of Turner syndrome (45,X) is noted to have a large, fluctuant mass on the left side of her neck. Imaging shows a multiloculated cystic lesion without a clear blood supply. What is the most likely diagnosis for this neck mass?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are composed of small blood-filled vessels, not large cystic spaces filled with lymph.
explanations.b: Cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) is a common lymphatic malformation of the neck, frequently associated with Turner syndrome.
explanations.c: Thyroglossal duct cysts are midline neck masses that move with swallowing, not large multiloculated lateral cystic masses.
explanations.d: Branchial cleft cysts are usually found on the lateral neck but are typically unilocular and appear later in childhood/adolescence, not as massive congenital hygromas.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are small, painful, subungual lesions, not massive neck cysts.

ankiCards: A cystic hygroma is also known as a {{c1::cavernous lymphangioma}}.
Cystic hygromas are characteristically associated with {{c1::Turner}} syndrome.
The typical location for a cystic hygroma is the {{c1::neck}} (or axilla).
Unlike hemangiomas, lymphangiomas contain {{c1::lymph (or proteinaceous fluid)}} rather than blood.
Histologically, cystic hygromas show large spaces lined by {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
keyPoints: Lymphangiomas are benign counterparts to hemangiomas.
Simple (capillary) lymphangiomas are small; cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) are large.
Cystic hygromas are found in the neck or axilla of infants.
Classic association: Turner syndrome and Down syndrome.
Margins are often poorly defined, making surgical resection difficult.
microReview: Cystic Hygroma: Turner syndrome + Huge neck mass + Lymph-filled spaces = Cavernous lymphangioma.
examinerTraps: Identify the association with Turner syndrome—it's a classic USMLE 'link'.
sourceQuote: Cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) are typically found in the neck or axilla of children and are characteristically associated with Turner syndrome.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular disease is fundamentally categorized into two principal mechanisms. One involves the narrowing or complete obstruction of vessel lumens. Which of the following describes the second principal mechanism?

options.a: Increased elasticity of the internal elastic lamina
options.b: Weakening of vessel walls leading to dilation or rupture
options.c: Conversion of muscular arteries into elastic arteries
options.d: Decreased wall-to-lumen ratio in small arterioles
options.e: Preferential thickening of the adventitia in response to flow

explanations.a: Increased elasticity would theoretically strengthen a vessel's ability to handle pressure, rather than being a core mechanism of pathological dilation.
explanations.b: This is the primary mechanism underlying the formation of aneurysms and dissections, representing a failure of the structural integrity of the vessel wall.
explanations.c: Arterial types are determined by their function and location; conversion between these types is not a recognized pathological mechanism of major vascular disease.
explanations.d: In hypertensive states, the wall-to-lumen ratio typically increases to manage pressure, not decreases.
explanations.e: The intimal layer, not the adventitia, is the primary site of thickening in response to vascular injury.

ankiCards: The two principal mechanisms of vascular disease are narrowing/obstruction and {{c1::weakening of vessel walls}}.
Aneurysms occur when there is {{c1::dilation or rupture}} due to wall weakening.
Narrowing of vessel lumens can be progressive (e.g., atherosclerosis) or {{c1::precipitous}} (e.g., thrombosis).
Arterial walls are thicker than veins to accommodate {{c1::pulsatile flow}} and higher pressures.
The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}} as vessels become smaller.
keyPoints: Vascular pathology is a leading cause of global morbidity.
Stenosis and wall weakening are the two main drivers of vascular disease.
Aneurysms represent a loss of wall integrity.
Atherosclerosis and hypertension are major contributors to wall weakening.
Vessel structure (thick walls) is functionally adapted to high-pressure flow.
microReview: Vascular diseases generally follow two paths: blocking the pipe (stenosis/obstruction) or breaking the pipe (weakening/dilation). Aneurysms fall into the latter category.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse the response to injury (intimal thickening) with the primary failure mechanism of aneurysms (wall weakening).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An aneurysm is defined as a localized permanent dilation of a blood vessel or the heart. If the lesion is characterized by a wall that contains all three layers of the artery (intima, media, and adventitia), which of the following terms best describes this condition?

explanations.a: A pseudoaneurysm (or false aneurysm) occurs when blood leaks through a wall defect and is contained by extravascular connective tissue, not the original three layers.
explanations.b: A dissection occurs when blood enters the wall itself, separating the layers; it is not a dilation of all three layers.
explanations.c: A true aneurysm involves all three layers of the arterial wall (intima, media, and adventitia) or the attenuated wall of the heart.
explanations.d: A false aneurysm is a synonym for pseudoaneurysm; it lacks the three-layered arterial wall structure.
explanations.e: An arteriovenous fistula is an abnormal communication between an artery and a vein, not a localized dilation.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true aneurysm}} involves all three layers of the vessel wall.
The three layers of the arterial wall are the {{c1::intima, media, and adventitia}}.
A {{c1::false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm)}} is a wall defect leading to an extravascular hematoma.
Atherosclerotic and congenital aneurysms are typically classified as {{c1::true}} aneurysms.
A {{c1::dissection}} involves blood tracking between the layers of the vessel wall.
keyPoints: True aneurysms involve all three vascular layers.
False aneurysms are contained hematomas resulting from a wall breach.
Aneurysms can be saccular (spherical) or fusiform (circumferential).
The integrity of the media is crucial for preventing aneurysm formation.
Common sites for true aneurysms include the abdominal aorta and the brain (berry aneurysms).
microReview: If all 3 layers (intima, media, adventitia) are present in the dilated segment, it's a 'true' aneurysm. If the wall is just clotted blood and fibrous tissue (hematoma) outside the vessel, it's 'false'.
examinerTraps: Aortic dissection is often colloquially called an 'aneurysm' by patients, but pathologically, it is a separate entity where blood splits the media.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male with a 40-pack-year smoking history and long-standing hypertension presents for a routine physical examination. A pulsatile mass is palpated in the epigastric region. Ultrasound reveals a 5.5 cm dilation of the infrarenal aorta. What is the most likely primary pathological process responsible for the development of this lesion?

options.b: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.e: Mycotic infection of the vessel wall

explanations.a: Cystic medial degeneration is more commonly associated with thoracic aortic aneurysms and Marfan syndrome.
explanations.b: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum is characteristic of tertiary syphilis, which typically affects the ascending aorta.
explanations.c: Atherosclerosis is the dominant cause of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA), as plaque interferes with nutrient diffusion to the media, causing atrophy.
explanations.d: Congenital defects are associated with berry aneurysms in the Circle of Willis, not typically infrarenal AAAs.
explanations.e: Mycotic aneurysms are caused by infection; while possible, atherosclerosis is significantly more common in an elderly smoker.

ankiCards: The most common cause of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA) is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
AAAs are most frequently located in the {{c1::infrarenal}} portion of the aorta.
Atherosclerosis causes AAAs by causing {{c1::ischemic atrophy}} of the media.
The threshold for surgical intervention in AAA is typically {{c1::5 to 5.5}} cm.
Two major risk factors for AAA are {{c1::smoking}} and male gender.
keyPoints: AAA is primarily an atherosclerotic disease.
The infrarenal location is standard due to high turbulence and lower vasa vasorum density.
Media atrophy occurs because the intimal plaque blocks nutrient diffusion.
Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor.
Rupture risk increases significantly once the diameter exceeds 5 cm.
microReview: Old male smoker + pulsatile mass = AAA. Pathogenesis = Atherosclerosis. Location = Infrarenal. Risk = Rupture if >5cm.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse the location of Syphilitic aneurysms (ascending aorta) with Atherosclerotic aneurysms (abdominal aorta).
sourceQuote: Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the pathogenesis of aneurysms, particularly those associated with genetic syndromes like Marfan syndrome, there is a fundamental imbalance in the extracellular matrix of the media. Which of the following mechanisms best describes this imbalance?

options.a: Excessive production of Type I collagen
options.b: Increased degradation of elastin by matrix metalloproteinases
options.d: Overexpression of tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs)

explanations.a: Aneurysms are characterized by a loss of structural proteins like collagen and elastin, not an excess.
explanations.b: Aneurysm formation involves an imbalance where increased MMP activity (often from macrophages) degrades elastin and collagen faster than they can be replaced.
explanations.c: In Marfan syndrome, there is actually increased/aberrant TGF-beta signaling due to defective sequestering by fibrillin-1.
explanations.d: TIMPs inhibit MMPs; their down-regulation (not overexpression) would contribute to aneurysm formation.
explanations.e: Fibrin is involved in clotting; collagen and elastin are the key structural proteins of the vessel wall.

ankiCards: Aneurysm formation is often driven by an increased activity of {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
{{c1::Macrophages}} are a major source of MMPs in atherosclerotic aneurysms.
In Marfan syndrome, mutations in {{c1::Fibrillin-1}} lead to weakened elastic tissue.
Aberrant signaling of {{c1::TGF-beta}} is a key pathway in genetic thoracic aneurysms.
The loss of {{c1::elastin}} in the media leads to the loss of elastic recoil in aneurysms.
keyPoints: Aneurysms result from an imbalance between ECM synthesis and degradation.
MMPs degrade collagen and elastin in the media.
Genetic syndromes (Marfan, Loeys-Dietz) involve TGF-beta pathway mutations.
Inflammation (macrophages) accelerates wall degradation.
Cystic medial degeneration is the histological hallmark of these failures.
microReview: Aneurysm = Too much breakdown (MMPs), not enough buildup, or defective building blocks (Fibrillin). The result is a weak media that balloons under pressure.
examinerTraps: Wait for the specific gene mentioned. Fibrillin-1 is Marfan; TGF-beta receptor is Loeys-Dietz. Both cause thoracic aneurysms.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins... to accommodate pulsatile flow.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 52-year-old female presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset, excruciating, 'tearing' chest pain that radiates to her back. Her blood pressure is 210/110 mmHg. A chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum. Which of the following is the most significant risk factor for this patient's acute condition?

explanations.a: While a risk factor for atherosclerosis, hypertension is the much stronger driver for aortic dissection.
explanations.b: Diabetes is a vascular risk factor but is not specifically linked to the mechanical shearing of the media seen in dissection.
explanations.c: Hypertension is the most common risk factor for aortic dissection, as it causes degenerative changes in the media and increases wall stress.
explanations.d: COPD is not directly linked to aortic dissection pathology.
explanations.e: Alcohol abuse is not a primary risk factor for the development of aortic dissection.

ankiCards: The most common risk factor for aortic dissection is {{c1::hypertension}}.
Classic presentation of aortic dissection is {{c1::tearing or ripping}} chest pain.
Aortic dissection involves blood entering the {{c1::media}} layer of the vessel wall.
Radiographic finding of a widened {{c1::mediastinum}} is suggestive of aortic dissection.
The DeBakey and Stanford systems are used to classify {{c1::aortic dissections}}.
keyPoints: Aortic dissection is a medical emergency distinct from a true aneurysm.
Hypertension causes 'pressure-induced' medial hypertrophy and ischemia.
The 'tearing' sensation corresponds to the longitudinal cleavage of the media.
Type A dissections (ascending aorta) require urgent surgery.
Type B dissections (descending) are often managed with blood pressure control.
microReview: Sudden tearing pain + High BP = Aortic Dissection. Most important risk factor = Hypertension. Pathology = Medial cleavage.
examinerTraps: Aortic dissection is often triggered by hypertension, whereas Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms are triggered by atherosclerosis.
sourceQuote: Arterial wall thickness gradually diminishes as the vessels become smaller, but the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: What is the term used to describe an aneurysm that arises specifically when a circulating microorganism infects an existing arterial wall or a pre-existing aneurysm?

explanations.a: Berry aneurysms are congenital saccular dilations in the Circle of Willis.
explanations.b: Syphilitic aneurysms are caused by Treponema pallidum but have a specific name and location (ascending aorta).
explanations.c: A mycotic aneurysm is the standard term for any aneurysm resulting from an infection that weakens the vessel wall.
explanations.d: Fusiform refers to a shape (symmetrical dilation), not an etiology.
explanations.e: Saccular refers to a shape (asymmetrical bulge), not an etiology.

ankiCards: An aneurysm caused by infection of the vessel wall is called a {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm.
Common causes of mycotic aneurysms include {{c1::infective endocarditis}} or septic emboli.
A {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm is a spherical bulge involving only a portion of the vessel wall.
A {{c1::fusiform}} aneurysm is a circumferential dilation of a long vascular segment.
The term 'mycotic' is a misnomer; most of these infections are actually {{c1::bacterial}}.
keyPoints: Mycotic aneurysms result from infection (bacterial, fungal, etc.).
Common origins include septic emboli or direct extension from a nearby abscess.
They are highly prone to rupture due to rapid inflammatory destruction of the wall.
Saccular vs. Fusiform describes the shape, not the cause.
Atherosclerotic plaque can become seeded during a transient bacteremia.
microReview: Infection + Aneurysm = Mycotic Aneurysm. Most are bacterial (Salmonella, Staph) despite the name 'mycotic' suggesting fungi.
examinerTraps: Students often assume 'mycotic' only refers to fungi. In pathology, it refers broadly to any infection-induced aneurysm.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis)... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which structural specialization allows muscular arteries to exert the most significant control over blood flow and systemic blood pressure?

options.a: A high ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter
options.c: Abundant vasa vasorum in the inner third of the media
options.d: A thin tunica media relative to the adventitia
options.e: Large diameter to minimize resistance to flow

explanations.a: Small muscular arteries and arterioles have a high wall-to-lumen ratio, allowing their smooth muscle contraction to significantly alter resistance and pressure.
explanations.b: Fenestrated elastic laminae are more characteristic of large elastic arteries (like the aorta) to allow expansion during systole.
explanations.c: The inner media is usually nourished by diffusion from the lumen, not vasa vasorum.
explanations.d: A thick media is required for the contractile force needed to regulate flow.
explanations.e: Resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius; larger diameters minimize resistance but offer less control.

ankiCards: Resistance to blood flow is primarily controlled by {{c1::muscular arteries and arterioles}}.
The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}} as vessels get smaller.
Vessels that exert control over pressure are primarily {{c1::muscular}} vessels.
Arterial walls are {{c1::thicker}} than veins to handle high pressure.
Aneurysms are more common in {{c1::elastic}} and large muscular arteries.
keyPoints: Arterioles are the main resistance vessels.
Wall thickness/lumen ratio is the key metric for pressure control.
Elastic arteries (Aorta) dampen pulsatility; muscular arteries control distribution.
Vascular pathology often follows these anatomical specializations.
Aneurysms usually occur where the wall is subjected to high stress but lacks the muscular support of smaller vessels.
microReview: Large elastic pipes (Aorta) get aneurysms. Small muscular pipes (Arterioles) control the pressure. Small pipes have the highest wall-to-lumen ratio.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse the *function* of elastic arteries (recoil) with the *function* of muscular arteries (resistance/control).
sourceQuote: Arterial wall thickness gradually diminishes as the vessels become smaller, but the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing these muscular vessels to exert control over blood flow and pressure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 35-year-old male with tall stature, long fingers, and hypermobile joints is evaluated. His father died of a 'burst heart' at age 40. Echocardiography shows dilation of the aortic root. Histological examination of the aortic wall would most likely reveal which of the following?

explanations.a: Calcification is a feature of advanced atherosclerosis, not the primary genetic wall defect in Marfan syndrome.
explanations.b: Cystic medial degeneration (loss of smooth muscle and elastic fibers with mucoid material accumulation) is the hallmark of Marfan-associated aortic root dilation.
explanations.c: Granulomatous inflammation suggests Giant Cell or Takayasu arteritis.
explanations.d: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a small-vessel pathology.
explanations.e: Necrosis of the adventitia is not a primary feature of these connective tissue disorders; the defect is in the media.

ankiCards: {{c1::Cystic medial degeneration}} is the histologic hallmark of Marfan-related aneurysms.
Marfan syndrome involves a mutation in the {{c1::FBN1 (Fibrillin-1)}} gene.
Aortic root dilation in young patients should prompt evaluation for {{c1::Marfan syndrome}}.
Histologically, cystic medial degeneration shows accumulation of {{c1::glycosaminoglycans (mucoid material)}}.
Marfan syndrome patients are at high risk for aortic {{c1::dissection}}.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome = Fibrillin-1 mutation.
The result is weakened elastic tissue in the media.
Cystic medial degeneration is the descriptive term for this weakening.
Aortic root dilation leads to aortic insufficiency and risk of dissection.
This is a 'true' aneurysm involving all three layers.
microReview: Tall + long fingers (Marfan) + Aortic root dilation = Cystic Medial Degeneration. No inflammation, just a structural breakdown of the 'building blocks'.
examinerTraps: The term 'cystic' is a misnomer; there are no true epithelial-lined cysts, just pools of mucoid ground substance.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which anatomical location is the most common site for aneurysms associated with tertiary syphilis?

explanations.a: The infrarenal aorta is the most common site for atherosclerotic aneurysms.
explanations.b: Tertiary syphilis classically targets the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta, leading to medial ischemia and aneurysm.
explanations.c: Popliteal aneurysms are usually atherosclerotic.
explanations.d: Iliac aneurysms are typically associated with extensions of abdominal aortic aneurysms.
explanations.e: The Circle of Willis is the site for berry (congenital) aneurysms.

ankiCards: Syphilitic aneurysms typically occur in the {{c1::ascending thoracic aorta}}.
Syphilis causes inflammation of the {{c1::vasa vasorum}} (obliterative endarteritis).
Damage to the vasa vasorum leads to {{c1::ischemic}} injury of the aortic media.
A classic gross appearance of the syphilitic aorta is '{{c1::tree-barking}}'.
Syphilitic aneurysms can lead to dilation of the aortic {{c1::valve ring}}.
keyPoints: Tertiary syphilis causes obliterative endarteritis of vasa vasorum.
The ascending aorta is most affected because it relies heavily on vasa vasorum.
Media destruction leads to 'tree-bark' appearance due to scarring.
Can cause aortic valve insufficiency.
This is now rare due to effective antibiotic treatment of early syphilis.
microReview: Syphilis = Vasa vasorum destruction = Ascending Aorta = Tree-barking = Aortic Regurgitation.
examinerTraps: Atherosclerosis (AAA) = Abdominal. Syphilis (Thoracic) = Ascending. Dissection = Can be anywhere, but usually starts in the ascending (Stanford A).
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 40-year-old woman is found to have a saccular aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery during an evaluation for a persistent headache. Which of the following conditions is most strongly associated with this type of vascular lesion?

explanations.a: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is classically associated with berry (saccular) aneurysms in the Circle of Willis.
explanations.b: While hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension, it is not specifically associated with berry aneurysms in the same way ADPKD is.
explanations.c: Fibromuscular dysplasia usually affects renal or carotid arteries (string-of-beads), not the Circle of Willis.
explanations.d: SLE causes small vessel vasculitis, not large saccular berry aneurysms.
explanations.e: Takayasu arteritis affects the aortic arch and its major branches, not the intracranial circulation.

ankiCards: Saccular aneurysms in the Circle of Willis are commonly known as {{c1::berry}} aneurysms.
Berry aneurysms are associated with {{c1::ADPKD (Polycystic Kidney Disease)}}.
The most common site for a berry aneurysm is the {{c1::anterior communicating artery}}.
Rupture of a berry aneurysm causes a {{c1::subarachnoid}} hemorrhage.
The structural defect in berry aneurysms is usually a lack of {{c1::smooth muscle/internal elastic lamina}} at branch points.
keyPoints: Berry aneurysms are not present at birth but the defect is congenital.
ADPKD and Ehlers-Danlos are major associations.
Hypertension and smoking increase the risk of rupture.
Rupture presents as a 'worst headache of my life' (Subarachnoid hemorrhage).
They occur at vessel bifurcations.
microReview: Berry Aneurysm = Circle of Willis = ADPKD connection = Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the location; berry aneurysms are intracranial, while most other aneurysms discussed are aortic.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 34-year-old male with a history of advanced HIV (CD4 count 85 cells/mm³) presents with multiple painless, violaceous, raised skin plaques on his lower extremities and hard palate. Biopsy of a skin lesion reveals spindle-shaped cells forming slit-like vascular spaces containing red blood cells, with associated lymphocytic infiltration and extravasated erythrocytes. Which of the following infectious agents is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?

explanations.a: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of Kaposi sarcoma, which characteristically presents as spindle-cell proliferations forming slit-like spaces.
explanations.b: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can look similar clinically in HIV patients, but histologically it shows lobular capillary proliferation with neutrophils and nuclear dust, not slit-like spaces.
explanations.c: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with various lymphomas (e.g., Burkitt) and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, but not vascular tumors like Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.d: Human papillomavirus 16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx.
explanations.e: Cytomegalovirus causes retinitis and colitis in immunocompromised patients but is not oncogenic for vascular tissue.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is caused by {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
The histological hallmark of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::spindle-shaped cells forming slit-like vascular spaces}}.
The four clinical forms of Kaposi Sarcoma are {{c1::Classic (European), Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated}}.
Unlike bacillary angiomatosis, Kaposi Sarcoma histology lacks {{c1::neutrophils}}.
Vascular tumors can be classified as {{c1::benign, intermediate-grade, or malignant}}.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8.
Commonly presents as violaceous macules, plaques, or nodules in HIV/AIDS patients.
Microscopic findings include spindle cells, slit-like spaces, and extravasated RBCs.
HHV-8 infects endothelial cells and promotes oncogenesis via several viral proteins.
Extracutaneous involvement (GI tract, lungs) is common in the AIDS-associated form.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Slit-like spaces + RBCs. Bacillary Angiomatosis = Bartonella + Neutrophils.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Kaposi sarcoma with bacillary angiomatosis; the presence of neutrophils and Bartonella organisms (silver stain) points to bacillary angiomatosis, whereas slit-like spaces and spindle cells point to Kaposi.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old factory worker who has spent 20 years working in the production of polyvinyl chloride (PVC) is diagnosed with a highly aggressive hepatic malignancy. Biopsy of the liver shows malignant endothelial cells with significant pleomorphism and hyperchromatic nuclei forming irregular vascular channels. Immunohistochemical staining for CD31 is positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign tumor of the liver, characterized by large, blood-filled spaces, not malignant pleomorphic cells.
explanations.b: Hepatocellular carcinoma originates from hepatocytes, not endothelial cells, and would not typically be CD31 positive.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a malignant vascular tumor associated with exposures to vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast. CD31 is a specific marker for endothelial differentiation.
explanations.d: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor, but the association with vinyl chloride and the highly aggressive nature favors angiosarcoma.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are small, painful benign tumors arising from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, usually subungual.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride, arsenic, or Thorotrast}}.
The specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial cells is {{c1::CD31 (or vWF)}}.
Angiosarcoma of the skin is most commonly seen in the {{c1::scalp of elderly men}} or in areas of {{c2::chronic lymphedema}}.
The Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to angiosarcoma occurring after {{c1::radical mastectomy (chronic lymphedema)}}.
Histology of angiosarcoma shows {{c1::malignant endothelial cells forming irregular vascular channels}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant mesenchymal tumor of endothelial cells.
Chemical carcinogens (vinyl chloride) specifically target the liver for this tumor.
CD31 and von Willebrand factor (vWF) confirm endothelial origin.
Poor prognosis with a high rate of metastasis and recurrence.
Can also occur in the skin (post-radiation or lymphedema) and heart.
microReview: Vinyl Chloride + Liver + CD31(+) = Hepatic Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Often, examiners list hepatocellular carcinoma as a distractor for liver tumors; always look for the CD31 positivity or endothelial description to shift toward a vascular origin.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions. Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with an extremely painful, 5-mm diameter, red-blue nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. She notes that the pain is often triggered by exposure to cold. Histological examination reveals nests of uniform, specialized smooth muscle cells surrounding thin-walled vascular spaces. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma is a large, aggressive malignancy, not a small subungual nodule.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, exquisitely painful tumors that arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, frequently found under the nails.
explanations.c: Capillary hemangiomas are common benign vascular lesions but are not typically exquisitely painful or subungual.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a rapidly growing pedunculated red nodule on skin or gingiva, but lacks the specific glomus cell histology and temperature sensitivity.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts, not a painful subungual lesion.

ankiCards: The classic location for a glomus tumor is {{c1::subungual (under the nail)}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle cells}} of the glomus body.
A clinical hallmark of glomus tumors is {{c1::exquisite pain (often cold-induced)}}.
The glomus body is involved in {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors show {{c1::uniform cells in nests surrounding vascular spaces}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign neoplasms.
The distal digits, particularly the subungual region, are the most common sites.
Symptoms include paroxysmal pain and cold hypersensitivity.
Derived from the glomus body, a neuromyoarterial apparatus.
Surgical excision is curative.
microReview: Subungual + Very Painful + Cold sensitive = Glomus Tumor.
examinerTraps: Wait for the 'pain' descriptor—it is the distinguishing feature for glomus tumors among small vascular lesions.
sourceQuote: To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure and function.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 2-month-old infant is brought to the clinic with a bright red, raised, 'strawberry-like' lesion on the scalp. The parents state the lesion was not present at birth but appeared at 2 weeks of age and has grown rapidly since. Which of the following is the most likely natural history of this lesion?

options.d: Immediate need for surgical excision to prevent hemorrhage
options.e: Permanent persistence without change in size

explanations.a: The description fits a juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma. These are very common in infants, grow rapidly for a few months, and then typically regress spontaneously by age 5 to 7.
explanations.b: Benign hemangiomas do not transform into malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.c: Strawberry hemangiomas characteristically involute, unlike cherry hemangiomas which persist and increase in number with age.
explanations.d: Surgery is usually avoided because they regress naturally and surgery may cause more scarring than natural involution.
explanations.e: Regression is the rule for juvenile hemangiomas.

ankiCards: A 'strawberry hemangioma' is also known as a {{c1::juvenile hemangioma}}.
Juvenile hemangiomas are typically {{c1::absent}} at birth but appear in early weeks.
The natural history of juvenile hemangiomas involves {{c1::rapid growth followed by spontaneous regression}}.
Complete involution of strawberry hemangiomas occurs by age {{c1::7 (approx 75-90%)}}.
Histologically, hemangiomas are characterized by {{c1::increased numbers of normal or abnormal vessels filled with blood}}.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangiomas are the most common vascular tumor of childhood.
Appearance: Bright red, lobulated, raised.
Location: Skin, often head and neck.
Management: Mostly 'watch and wait' due to high regression rates.
Clinical course: Proliferative phase (first year) followed by involution phase.
microReview: Infant + Strawberry color + Regresses = Juvenile Hemangioma.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'Strawberry' (Juvenile) with 'Cherry' hemangiomas; Cherry hemangiomas occur in adults and do not regress.
sourceQuote: Vascular Structure and Function... Vascular Anomalies... Vascular Wall Response to Injury... Intimal Thickening: A Stereotyped Response to Vascular Injury
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 25-year-old female in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with a rapidly growing, 1-cm, red, pedunculated mass on her gingiva that bleeds easily with minor trauma. The lesion is soft and non-tender. Histology shows a highly vascular proliferation resembling granulation tissue. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas are deeper, larger, and not typically pedunculated or specifically associated with pregnancy or gingiva.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a common, rapidly growing vascular lesion of the skin or oral mucosa (especially gingiva in pregnant women, where it is called granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis presents similarly but is associated with Bartonella infection and HIV.
explanations.d: Kaposi sarcoma presents as flatter, violaceous lesions and usually occurs in different clinical contexts (e.g., HIV).
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are subungual and extremely painful, which does not fit this presentation.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is a {{c1::benign, pedunculated, red}} vascular lesion.
Pyogenic granulomas frequently occur on the {{c1::gingiva (gums)}} of {{c2::pregnant}} women.
The histological appearance of pyogenic granuloma resembles {{c1::granulation tissue}}.
The term 'pyogenic granuloma' is a misnomer because it is neither {{c1::pyogenic (pus-forming)}} nor a {{c2::granuloma}}.
When a pyogenic granuloma occurs in pregnancy, it is specifically called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a form of capillary hemangioma.
Often follows trauma and grows rapidly over weeks.
High vascularity leads to easy bleeding/ulceration.
Granuloma gravidarum may regress postpartum.
Treatment is usually surgical curettage or excision.
microReview: Pregnant + Gingiva + Rapid growth + Bleeds = Pyogenic Granuloma.
examinerTraps: The name 'Pyogenic Granuloma' is misleading (it has no pus and is not a granuloma); remember it's a vascular proliferation.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A newborn female is found to have a large, soft, fluctuant mass on the left side of her neck. Physical examination also reveals webbed neck and widely spaced nipples. Ultrasound of the mass shows multiple dilated cystic spaces without a clear capsule. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis of the neck mass?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are blood vessel tumors and usually present as solid red lesions, not large cystic spaces.
explanations.b: Cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) is a cystic vascular lesion typically found in the neck/axilla of infants, frequently associated with Turner syndrome (45,X).
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are small, painful, and subungual.
explanations.d: Simple lymphangiomas are smaller, more superficial lymphatic proliferations, while the large cystic variety is called cystic hygroma.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor that would not present in this neonatal, syndromic context.

ankiCards: A cystic hygroma is the common name for a {{c1::cavernous lymphangioma}}.
Cystic hygromas are frequently associated with {{c1::Turner syndrome (45,X)}} and {{c2::Down syndrome}}.
The typical location for a cystic hygroma is the {{c1::neck (or axilla)}}.
Histologically, cystic hygromas consist of large, dilated {{c1::lymphatic}} spaces.
Cystic hygromas are difficult to remove surgically because they lack a {{c1::capsule}} and infiltrate tissues.
keyPoints: Lymphangiomas are benign lymphatic counterparts of hemangiomas.
Cystic hygromas are the cavernous variant.
They are composed of endothelium-lined spaces filled with proteinaceous fluid.
Strong association with chromosomal aneuploidies.
May lead to hydrops fetalis if large and internal.
microReview: Turner Syndrome + Neck mass + Dilated lymphatic spaces = Cystic Hygroma.
examinerTraps: Focus on the association with Turner syndrome—this is the most common board-link for cystic hygromas.
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old female underwent a radical mastectomy for breast cancer 12 years ago, followed by axillary lymph node dissection. Since the surgery, she has had persistent, non-pitting edema of her right arm. Recently, she noticed several dark-red to purple nodules developing on the skin of her lymphedematous arm. Which of the following conditions is she most likely developing?

explanations.a: While dermatitis can occur in lymphedema, it does not explain the appearance of dark-red nodules which suggest a vascular neoplasm.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis requires Bartonella infection and is generally seen in immunocompromised states.
explanations.c: Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to the development of angiosarcoma in a limb with chronic lymphedema, most classically after mastectomy and lymph node dissection.
explanations.d: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 and usually presents in different distributions (legs, palate) and patient populations.
explanations.e: Sturge-Weber syndrome is a congenital disorder involving a port-wine stain in the V1/V2 distribution and leptomeningeal angiomas.

ankiCards: The development of angiosarcoma in a lymphedematous limb is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
Stewart-Treves syndrome typically occurs about {{c1::10 or more}} years after surgery.
The underlying cause of Stewart-Treves syndrome is {{c1::chronic lymphedema}}.
Angiosarcomas are tumors of {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
Histologically, angiosarcomas exhibit {{c1::vascular channels with malignant cells (CD31+)}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas can be induced by chronic lymphedema.
Classic board scenario: Post-mastectomy patient with arm swelling + new skin nodules.
These tumors are aggressive with poor 5-year survival.
May also be induced by therapeutic radiation.
Primary skin angiosarcoma (non-lymphedema) often affects the head/neck of elderly males.
microReview: Post-mastectomy + Lymphedema + New vascular nodules = Stewart-Treves (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: Wait for the long latent period (10+ years); if the lesion appears right after surgery, it's more likely a hematoma or infection.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular neoplasms is classified as an intermediate-grade (borderline) tumor, meaning it has biological behavior between benign hemangiomas and highly malignant angiosarcomas?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangioma is a benign vascular tumor.
explanations.b: Glomus tumor is a benign tumor of the glomus body.
explanations.c: Kaposi sarcoma is generally considered a low-grade malignancy or potentially reversible proliferation depending on the state of the immune system, but 'intermediate grade' is the classic category for hemangioendotheliomas.
explanations.d: Epithelioid hemangioendotheliomas and other hemangioendotheliomas are the classic 'intermediate grade' vascular tumors.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignant tumor.

ankiCards: Vascular tumors of {{c1::intermediate}} grade include Kaposi sarcoma and hemangioendothelioma.
Hemangioendotheliomas are characterized by behavior that is {{c1::between benign and malignant}}.
Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma occurs in {{c1::medium-sized and large veins}}.
Kaposi sarcoma is categorized as an {{c1::intermediate-grade (borderline)}} tumor.
Angiosarcoma is categorized as a {{c1::malignant}} tumor.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors span a spectrum from benign to malignant.
Benign: Hemangiomas, glomus tumors.
Intermediate: Kaposi sarcoma, hemangioendothelioma.
Malignant: Angiosarcoma.
Intermediate tumors are locally aggressive and have low metastatic potential.
microReview: Benign = Hemangioma. Intermediate = Kaposi/Hemangioendothelioma. Malignant = Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Kaposi sarcoma is often called 'cancer' in casual clinical settings, but for pathology boards, it is often grouped with intermediate-grade tumors due to its variable course.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... Malignant Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 4-year-old child presents with a large, flat, purple-red birthmark covering the right forehead and upper eyelid (port-wine stain). The child has also experienced recurrent focal seizures and developmental delay. Imaging of the brain reveals ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomatosis and cortical calcifications. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Von Hippel-Lindau disease involves hemangioblastomas (often in the cerebellum/retina) and renal cell carcinoma, not port-wine stains.
explanations.b: Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) is characterized by a port-wine stain in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve (V1/V2), leptomeningeal angiomas, and seizures.
explanations.c: Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome (hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia) involves multiple small telangiectasias and AVMs, not a large port-wine stain.
explanations.d: Neurofibromatosis type 1 features cafe-au-lait spots and neurofibromas, not port-wine stains.
explanations.e: Tuberous sclerosis features ash-leaf spots and angiofibromas, not port-wine stains.

ankiCards: Sturge-Weber syndrome is also called {{c1::encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis}}.
The facial lesion in Sturge-Weber syndrome is a {{c1::port-wine stain (nevus flammeus)}}.
The distribution of the port-wine stain in Sturge-Weber is usually in the {{c1::ophthalmic (V1)}} and {{c2::maxillary (V2)}} divisions of the trigeminal nerve.
The CNS finding in Sturge-Weber is {{c1::leptomeningeal angiomatosis}}.
Common clinical features of Sturge-Weber include {{c1::seizures, glaucoma, and intellectual disability}}.
keyPoints: Sturge-Weber syndrome is a sporadic congenital disorder.
Port-wine stains (nevus flammeus) are types of vascular ectasias.
The 'tram-track' calcification on CT is a classic sign of the leptomeningeal angioma.
Port-wine stains do not typically regress and grow as the child grows.
Mutations in the GNAQ gene are often implicated.
microReview: Port-wine stain (V1/V2) + Seizures + Leptomeningeal angioma = Sturge-Weber.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the port-wine stain with a strawberry hemangioma; port-wine stains are flat and do NOT regress.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular conditions is characterized by autosomal dominant inheritance, multiple small aneurysmal telangiectasias of the skin and mucous membranes, and frequent episodes of epistaxis or gastrointestinal bleeding?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious process, not inherited.
explanations.b: Cystic hygroma is a malformation of lymphatics, usually congenital/sporadic.
explanations.c: Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by telangiectasias on the skin, lips, and oral mucosa, which can bleed.
explanations.d: Spider telangiectasias are common in hyperestrogenic states (e.g., pregnancy, cirrhosis) and are not inherited in a mendelian pattern.
explanations.e: Nevus flammeus is an ordinary 'birthmark' or port-wine stain, usually sporadic.

ankiCards: Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome is also known as {{c1::Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT)}}.
HHT is inherited in an {{c1::autosomal dominant}} fashion.
Common clinical manifestations of HHT include {{c1::epistaxis (nosebleeds)}} and {{c2::GI bleeding}}.
HHT can lead to the formation of {{c1::arteriovenous malformations (AVMs)}} in the lungs, brain, or liver.
The basic lesion in HHT is a {{c1::telangiectasia (dilated small vessels)}}.
keyPoints: HHT involves mutations in genes of the TGF-beta signaling pathway.
Telangiectasias are present from birth and increase with age.
AVMs in the lungs can lead to paradoxical emboli (right-to-left shunt).
Diagnosis is clinical (Curacao criteria).
It is a benign but clinically problematic vascular anomaly.
microReview: AD inheritance + Telangiectasias + Epistaxis = Osler-Weber-Rendu.
examinerTraps: Key is the inheritance pattern (AD) and the recurring bleeding (epistaxis).
sourceQuote: VASCULAR STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION... The general architecture and cellular composition of blood vessels are comparable throughout the cardiovascular system.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 34-year-old male with a history of HIV infection and a CD4+ count of 180 cells/mm³ presents with multiple non-blanching, purple-to-red macules and plaques on his lower extremities. A punch biopsy of a lesion reveals proliferation of spindle-shaped cells, slit-like vascular spaces containing erythrocytes, and a prominent inflammatory infiltrate. Immunohistochemical staining is positive for a double-stranded DNA gamma-herpesvirus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis also occurs in HIV patients but is caused by Bartonella species and histologically shows neutrophilic infiltrates and lobular capillary proliferation.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 (KSHV). The clinical description of purple plaques in an HIV patient with spindle cells and slit-like spaces is classic.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor that occurs in older adults or in the setting of chronic lymphedema, showing more aggressive cytologic atypia.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a rapidly growing pedunculated red nodule that occurs on skin or oral mucosa, often following trauma or during pregnancy.
explanations.e: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated vascular channels and are usually deep-seated and not associated with HIV or spindle cell proliferation.

ankiCards: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with which virus? {{c1::Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}
What histological feature is characteristic of Kaposi Sarcoma? {{c1::Spindle cells and slit-like vascular spaces}}
Which vascular tumor presents as purple plaques in AIDS patients? {{c1::Kaposi Sarcoma}}
Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by {{c1::Bartonella}} and must be differentiated from Kaposi Sarcoma.
Kaposi sarcoma involves the proliferation of which cell type? {{c1::Endothelial cells}}
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor caused by HHV-8.
Four clinical types exist: Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
Histology shows spindle cells, extravasated RBCs, and slit-like spaces.
AIDS-associated KS is the most common HIV-related malignancy.
The lesions do not blanch because the blood is extravasated into the tissue/slits.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma is a low-grade malignancy of endothelial cells. In the US, it is most common in the setting of HIV/AIDS. Key differential is Bacillary Angiomatosis (neutrophils present).
examinerTraps: Confusing Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella) with Kaposi Sarcoma (HHV-8) is a common exam pitfall. Look for the presence of neutrophils (BA) vs spindle cells (KS).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A pathology resident is reviewing a slide of a small, exquisitely painful, red-blue nodule excised from under the fingernail of a 40-year-old patient. The lesion is composed of nests of uniform, round cells surrounding thin-walled vascular channels. These cells are specialized smooth muscle cells involved in thermoregulation. From which of the following structures did this tumor most likely originate?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) arise from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, an arteriovenous structure involved in thermoregulation, typically found in the subungual region.
explanations.b: Pericytes are found around vessels but characterize hemangiopericytomas, which are histologically distinct with 'staghorn' vessels.
explanations.c: Endothelial cells line all vessels, but the specific 'round cell' nests in a subungual location define the glomus tumor origin.
explanations.d: Lymphatic vessels give rise to lymphangiomas, which are painless and usually occur in the neck or axilla.
explanations.e: While glomus bodies are shunts, the specific cellular tumor originates from the neuromyoarterial glomus body itself.

ankiCards: A painful red-blue nodule under the fingernail suggests a {{c1::Glomus tumor}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle cells}} of the glomus body.
Which vascular tumor is exquisitely sensitive to cold? {{c1::Glomus tumor}}
Glomus bodies are involved in {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Describe the histology of a Glomus tumor: {{c1::Nests of uniform round cells around vessels}}
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign, highly painful tumors.
Most common location is subungual (under the nail).
Cells are derived from smooth muscle (SMA positive).
They are distinct from hemangiomas by their intense pain.
The glomus body regulates distal blood flow and heat.
microReview: Glomus tumor: Painful + Subungual + Smooth muscle origin. Don't confuse with subungual melanoma (pigmented) or hemangioma (painless).
examinerTraps: The examiner may focus on the 'painful' aspect; very few vascular tumors are painful except glomus tumors.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old female presents with several enlarging, dark-violet, indurated skin nodules on her right arm. Ten years ago, she underwent a radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection and radiotherapy for breast adenocarcinoma. Since then, she has had persistent, severe lymphedema of the right arm. Biopsy of a nodule shows highly atypical endothelial cells forming irregular, anastomosing vascular channels. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma can occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome), typically after radical mastectomy. Histology shows atypical endothelial cells.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious lesion in immunocompromised hosts, not associated with chronic lymphedema.
explanations.c: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and doesn't typically arise from post-surgical lymphedema sites.
explanations.d: Lymphangiomas are benign malformations, usually congenital, and do not show the malignancy/atypia described.
explanations.e: Pyogenic granulomas are benign 'pregnancy tumors' or reactive lesions, not malignant and not related to long-term lymphedema.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma occurring after radical mastectomy and chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
{{c1::Angiosarcoma}} is a malignant tumor of endothelial cells.
Common chemical risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma include {{c1::PVC, arsenic, and Thorotrast}}.
Histology of angiosarcoma shows {{c1::atypical endothelial cells}} and anastomosing channels.
The vascular marker {{c1::CD31}} is typically positive in angiosarcoma.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is highly aggressive with a poor prognosis.
Stewart-Treves syndrome: Angiosarcoma following chronic lymphedema.
Can be induced by radiation or chemicals (PVC, Arsenic).
Commonly found in skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Expresses endothelial markers like CD31 and von Willebrand factor.
microReview: Lymphedema + History of Mastectomy + Purple skin nodules = Angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves). High-yield for Step 1.
examinerTraps: Assuming any purple lesion in an older patient is Kaposi Sarcoma. Look for the specific history of lymphedema or chemical exposure.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following immunohistochemical markers is most specific for identifying tumors of endothelial cell origin, such as angiosarcomas or hemangiomas?

explanations.a: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells and carcinomas.
explanations.b: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (skeletal or smooth).
explanations.c: CD31 (platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule) is highly specific for endothelial cells and the tumors derived from them.
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells, such as melanocytes and Schwann cells.
explanations.e: Vimentin is a general marker for mesenchymal cells but lacks specificity for endothelial differentiation.

ankiCards: What is the most specific marker for endothelial cells in pathology? {{c1::CD31 (or vWF)}}
CD31 is used to diagnose which category of tumors? {{c1::Vascular tumors}}
Cytokeratin stains {{c1::epithelial}} cells.
Desmin stains {{c1::muscle}} cells.
S100 stains {{c1::melanocytes/Schwann cells}}.
keyPoints: CD31 is the 'gold standard' endothelial marker.
von Willebrand Factor (vWF) is also used but can be less sensitive.
Endothelial cells line all vascular spaces.
Markers help distinguish vascular tumors from poorly differentiated carcinomas or melanomas.
