The majority of juvenile hemangiomas {{c1::regress/involute}} by age 7.
Juvenile hemangiomas are histologically composed of thin-walled {{c1::capillaries}}.
A juvenile hemangioma that is present at birth and fails to regress is likely a {{c1::congenital}} hemangioma.
keyPoints: Capillary hemangiomas are the most common type of vascular tumor.
Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are extremely common in infants (1 in 200).
They are composed of small, thin-walled capillaries.
Total regression occurs in 75% to 90% of cases by age 7.
Management is usually observation unless the lesion obstructs vision or the airway.
microReview: Infant + Strawberry lesion + Rapid growth then regression = Juvenile Hemangioma. Histology: Closely packed capillaries.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'strawberry hemangioma' with 'port-wine stain'. Port-wine stains (nevus flammeus) do not regress and grow with the child.
sourceQuote: Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) of the newborn skin are very common... they grow rapidly for a few months but then fade and eventually regress.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old male who worked for 30 years in a chemical plant manufacturing polyvinyl chloride (PVC) presents with abdominal pain and weight loss. Imaging reveals multiple masses within the liver. A biopsy confirms hepatic angiosarcoma. In addition to vinyl chloride, exposure to which of the following substances is classically associated with this specific malignancy?

explanations.a: Benzene is primarily associated with leukemias (e.g., AML).
explanations.b: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and bronchogenic carcinoma.
explanations.c: Hepatic angiosarcoma is classically associated with exposure to vinyl chloride, arsenic (in pesticides), and Thorotrast (a radioactive contrast medium).
explanations.d: Aflatoxin B1 is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.
explanations.e: Beryllium exposure is associated with lung cancer and berylliosis.

ankiCards: The three classic carcinogens for hepatic angiosarcoma are {{c1::vinyl chloride}}, {{c2::arsenic}}, and {{c3::Thorotrast}}.
Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor of {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
Hepatic angiosarcomas carry a very {{c1::poor}} prognosis.
Vinyl chloride is used in the production of the plastic {{c1::polyvinyl chloride (PVC)}}.
Arsenic exposure typically occurs via {{c1::contaminated water}} or {{c2::pesticides}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma of the liver is rare but highly associated with specific chemical exposures.
Vinyl chloride monomer is a well-known occupational hazard in the plastics industry.
Arsenic and Thorotrast are the other two major risk factors.
The tumor involves malignant endothelial cells forming blood-filled channels.
It is often fatal within a year of diagnosis.
microReview: Hepatic Angiosarcoma: Vinyl chloride, Arsenic, Thorotrast. Marker: CD31.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse hepatic angiosarcoma (endothelial origin) with hepatocellular carcinoma (epithelial/hepatocyte origin). Vinyl chloride = Angiosarcoma; Aflatoxin/Hepatitis = HCC.
sourceQuote: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with distinct environmental carcinogens, including arsenic (pesticides), Thorotrast (radioactive contrast), and vinyl chloride (plastics).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An 8-year-old boy presents with a large, ill-defined, spongy mass on the left side of his neck. His mother notes it has been present since birth and has slowly increased in size. Physical examination reveals a soft, transilluminating mass. Histological examination shows large, dilated vascular spaces lined by a single layer of endothelial cells and filled with proteinaceous fluid but lacking red blood cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas contain large blood-filled spaces, not proteinaceous lymph fluid.
explanations.b: Cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) is a benign lymphatic malformation typically found in the neck or axilla of children, characterized by dilated lymphatic spaces.
explanations.c: Glomangioma is a variant of a glomus tumor with a prominent vascular component; it is usually painful and not a large neck mass.
explanations.d: Arteriovenous malformations are characterized by high-pressure shunting between arteries and veins.
explanations.e: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a flat, cutaneous ectasia, not a deep cystic mass.

ankiCards: Cystic hygromas are most commonly located in the {{c1::neck}} or {{c2::axilla}}.
Cystic hygroma is frequently associated with {{c1::Turner syndrome}} (45,X).
Histologically, lymphangiomas contain spaces filled with {{c1::lymph (proteinaceous fluid)}} and few RBCs.
Cavernous lymphangiomas are also known as {{c1::cystic hygromas}}.
A key physical exam finding for cystic hygroma is that it {{c1::transilluminates}}.
keyPoints: Lymphangiomas are the lymphatic counterpart to hemangiomas.
Capillary lymphangiomas are small; cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) are large.
Cystic hygromas are often associated with chromosomal abnormalities (Turner, Down syndrome).
They consist of large dilated spaces lined by endothelium.
Margins are often poorly defined, making surgical resection difficult.
microReview: Neck mass + Infant + Turner Syndrome + Transillumination = Cystic Hygroma. Histology: Lymph-filled dilated spaces.
examinerTraps: The presence of fluid in vascular spaces can be confusing; check if it's blood (hemangioma) or lymph (lymphangioma). Lymph-filled spaces lack red blood cells.
sourceQuote: Cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) are typically found in the neck or axilla of children and... can be up to 15 cm in size.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old pregnant woman in her third trimester presents with a rapidly growing, 1-cm, red, pedunculated nodule on her gingiva that bleeds easily with minor trauma. The lesion appeared three weeks ago. Biopsy reveals a circumscribed proliferation of capillaries with prominent overlying ulceration and edema. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis is seen in immunocompromised patients and contains bacteria; this patient is pregnant, a classic association for pyogenic granuloma.
explanations.b: While a pyogenic granuloma is a form of capillary hemangioma, the specific clinical presentation (pedunculated, bleeding, gingiva, pregnancy) defines it as a pyogenic granuloma.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a benign, fast-growing vascular lesion often occurring on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a malignant, poorly circumscribed lesion; pyogenic granulomas are benign and well-circumscribed.
explanations.e: Spider telangiectasia consists of a central arteriole with radiating vessels, usually on the skin of patients with high estrogen states, not a pedunculated mass.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is a subtype of {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma.
Pyogenic granulomas are frequently associated with {{c1::pregnancy}} (granuloma gravidarum).
The most common location for a pyogenic granuloma is the {{c1::skin}} or {{c2::gingival mucosa}}.
Despite the name, pyogenic granulomas are neither {{c1::pyogenic}} (pus-forming) nor {{c2::granulomatous}}.
Histologically, pyogenic granulomas appear as {{c1::lobular}} capillary proliferations with edema.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granulomas are misnamed; they are lobular capillary hemangiomas.
They are often triggered by trauma.
They occur frequently in the oral cavity.
In pregnancy, they are called granuloma gravidarum.
They can regress spontaneously or require simple excision.
microReview: Gingival nodule + Pregnant woman + Bleeds easily = Pyogenic Granuloma. Histology: Capillary proliferation.
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic granuloma' is a classic misnomer. It has nothing to do with infection (pyogenic) or chronic inflammation (granuloma). It is a vascular tumor.
sourceQuote: Pyogenic granulomas are capillary hemangiomas that manifest as rapidly growing red pedunculated lesions on the skin, gingival, or oral mucosa.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 10-year-old girl is brought to the clinic due to recurrent, severe nosebleeds (epistaxis). Physical exam reveals several small, blanching, ruby-red papules on her lips, tongue, and fingertips. Her father has a history of similar lesions and frequent gastrointestinal bleeds. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Von Hippel-Lindau disease involves hemangioblastomas of the cerebellum and retina, as well as renal cell carcinoma, but not telangiectasias of the lips.
explanations.b: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by telangiectasias on the skin and mucous membranes, leading to epistaxis and GI bleeding.
explanations.c: Sturge-Weber syndrome involves a facial port-wine stain and leptomeningeal angiomas, but not widespread mucosal telangiectasias.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts.
explanations.e: Kasabach-Merritt syndrome involves a large hemangioma that sequesters platelets, leading to consumptive coagulopathy.

ankiCards: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia is also known as {{c1::Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome}}.
The inheritance pattern of HHT is {{c1::autosomal dominant}}.
Telangiectasias in HHT are commonly found on the {{c1::lips}}, {{c2::tongue}}, and {{c3::fingertips}}.
Common complications of HHT include {{c1::epistaxis}} and {{c2::gastrointestinal bleeding}}.
HHT is caused by mutations in genes involved in the {{c1::TGF-beta}} signaling pathway.
keyPoints: HHT is a systemic vascular dysplasia.
Telangiectasias are dilated capillaries and venules.
Rupture of these vessels leads to bleeding (nose, gut).
Arteriovenous malformations can also occur in the lungs, brain, and liver.
TGF-beta pathway genes (ENG, ACVRL1) are mutated.
microReview: Telangiectasias (lips/tongue) + Epistaxis + GI bleed + Autosomal Dominant = HHT (Osler-Weber-Rendu).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse telangiectasias (dilated pre-existing vessels) with hemangiomas (new vessel growth/neoplasia).
sourceQuote: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome) is an autosomal dominant disorder... characteristically, telangiectasias are present over the skin and oral mucous membranes.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular tumors or ectasias is classically associated with port-wine stains in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve, ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomas, and glaucoma?

explanations.a: Osler-Weber-Rendu is HHT, characterized by telangiectasias and bleeding, not port-wine stains.
explanations.b: Von Hippel-Lindau is associated with cavernous hemangiomas and hemangioblastomas, but not trigeminal distribution ectasias.
explanations.c: Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) presents with a facial port-wine stain (nevus flammeus), seizures, and leptomeningeal angiomas.
explanations.d: Maffucci syndrome is characterized by multiple hemangiomas and enchondromas.
explanations.e: Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome involves limb overgrowth and vascular malformations.

ankiCards: Sturge-Weber syndrome is also called {{c1::encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis}}.
The classic skin finding in Sturge-Weber is a {{c1::port-wine stain}} (nevus flammeus).
The port-wine stain in Sturge-Weber follows the distribution of the {{c1::trigeminal nerve (CN V)}}.
Patients with Sturge-Weber are at risk for {{c1::seizures}}, {{c2::mental retardation}}, and {{c3::glaucoma}}.
The intracranial lesion in Sturge-Weber syndrome is a {{c1::leptomeningeal angioma}}.
keyPoints: Nevus flammeus is the most common form of ectasia (port-wine stain).
Sturge-Weber is a rare congenital disorder.
It is caused by a somatic mutation in the GNAQ gene.
Skull radiographs may show 'tram-track' calcifications of the gyri.
Glaucoma occurs due to increased venous pressure or anterior chamber angle anomalies.
microReview: Trigeminal Port-Wine Stain + Seizures + Glaucoma = Sturge-Weber Syndrome. Somatic GNAQ mutation.
examinerTraps: A 'simple' nevus flammeus (birthmark) is common and usually harmless; the combination with neurological symptoms is what defines Sturge-Weber syndrome.
sourceQuote: Sturge-Weber syndrome... is an uncommon congenital disorder... associated with facial port-wine stains, ipsilateral venous angiomatous masses in the leptomeninges, and seizures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male presents for a routine physical examination. He has a 40-pack-year smoking history and long-standing hypertension. On abdominal palpation, a non-tender, pulsatile mass is noted at the level of the umbilicus. Bedside ultrasound confirms a 4.5 cm dilation of the infrarenal abdominal aorta. Which of the following mechanisms is most central to the structural weakening of the vessel wall in this patient's condition?

options.a: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.b: Excessive proteolytic activity by matrix metalloproteinases
options.c: Cystic medial necrosis due to fibrillin-1 mutations
options.d: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis of the nutrient vessels
options.e: Congenital defect in the synthesis of type III collagen

explanations.a: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum is the hallmark of tertiary syphilis, which typically leads to thoracic aortic aneurysms rather than abdominal ones.
explanations.b: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are primarily driven by atherosclerosis and chronic inflammation, where macrophages and smooth muscle cells release matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) that degrade elastin and collagen in the media.
explanations.c: Cystic medial necrosis due to fibrillin-1 mutations describes Marfan syndrome, which typically presents with thoracic aortic aneurysms or dissections in younger patients.
explanations.d: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is a consequence of hypertension affecting small arterioles, not the large elastic/muscular abdominal aorta.
explanations.e: Defects in type III collagen synthesis are associated with Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, which can cause aneurysms but is much less common than atherosclerosis-related AAA.

ankiCards: The two principal mechanisms underlying vascular disease are {{c1::luminal narrowing/obstruction}} and {{c2::vessel wall weakening}}.
The primary driver of structural weakening in Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms (AAA) is {{c1::matrix metalloproteinase (MMP)}} activity.
In AAA, inflammation leads to the degradation of {{c1::elastin}} and {{c2::collagen}} in the tunica media.
The most common location for an atherosclerotic aneurysm is the {{c1::infrarenal abdominal aorta}}.
A significant modifiable risk factor for the development and expansion of AAA is {{c1::cigarette smoking}}.
keyPoints: Vascular disease pathology is divided into luminal narrowing and wall weakening.
AAA is most commonly associated with atherosclerosis and male smokers over age 65.
The pathophysiology involves chronic transmural inflammation and ECM degradation.
Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) derived from macrophages are critical for media weakening.
Clinical presentation often involves a pulsatile abdominal mass.
microReview: Aneurysms represent a failure of vascular wall integrity. In the abdominal aorta, this is usually an acquired defect driven by atherosclerosis and inflammation (MMP activity). In the thoracic aorta, it is more often related to hypertension or genetic connective tissue disorders (Marfan syndrome).
examinerTraps: Students often confuse the risk factors for AAA (smoking, atherosclerosis) with those for Aortic Dissection (hypertension). While hypertension contributes to AAA, smoking is a more potent risk factor for expansion.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism) • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the most significant difference between the structural specialization of arteries compared to veins at the same level of branching, as it relates to their ability to withstand hemodynamic stress?

options.a: Arteries possess a thicker tunica media to accommodate higher pressures
options.b: Veins lack an internal elastic lamina in all branches
options.c: Arteries have a larger lumen-to-wall thickness ratio
options.d: Veins rely on vasa vasorum only in the thoracic cavity
options.e: Arteries lack smooth muscle cells in the tunica adventitia

explanations.a: As stated in basic vascular architecture, arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
explanations.b: While veins have less distinct elastic layers, the defining feature related to hemodynamic stress in the source is wall thickness.
explanations.c: The opposite is true: the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter is higher in arteries than in veins.
explanations.d: Vasa vasorum are found in both large arteries and veins, though more prominent in veins due to lower oxygen content of venous blood.
explanations.e: Arteries typically lack smooth muscle in the adventitia (unlike large veins like the Vena Cava), but this is not the primary feature for accommodating pressure.

ankiCards: Arterial walls are {{c1::thicker}} than corresponding veins at the same branching level.
The structural specialization of arteries allows them to accommodate {{c1::pulsatile flow}} and {{c2::higher blood pressures}}.
The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}} as arteries become smaller (muscular vessels).
Vascular pathology is responsible for more {{c1::morbidity}} and {{c2::mortality}} than any other category of human disease.
Specific kinds of vessels are characterized by structural specializations that reflect distinct {{c1::functional roles}}.
keyPoints: Arterial walls are thicker than venous walls at matched branching levels.
Arterial structure is optimized for high-pressure, pulsatile flow.
Muscular arteries have a high wall-to-lumen ratio for pressure control.
Weakening of these structural components leads to aneurysmal dilation.
Vascular disease mechanisms include narrowing and wall weakening.
microReview: Arteries have evolved thick, muscular, and elastic walls to manage the high-pressure output of the heart. Any process that thins this wall or degrades its components (like atherosclerosis or medial necrosis) results in an aneurysm.
examinerTraps: A common trap is stating that veins have a higher wall-to-lumen ratio; in fact, arteries have much thicker walls relative to their lumen size to facilitate vasoconstriction and pressure regulation.
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular pathology is responsible for significant human disease. According to the two principal mechanisms underlying vascular disease, which of the following is classified as a consequence of wall weakening?

explanations.a: Atherosclerotic plaque progression is a mechanism of narrowing/obstruction.
explanations.b: Stenosis is a mechanism of narrowing/obstruction.
explanations.c: Dilation (aneurysm) and rupture are the two specific outcomes listed under 'weakening of vessel walls'.
explanations.d: Thrombosis causes precipitous obstruction, not weakening-related dilation.
explanations.e: Embolism is a mechanism of luminal obstruction.

ankiCards: The mechanism of vascular disease that leads to aneurysm is {{c1::weakening}} of vessel walls.
Narrowing or obstruction of vessel lumens can occur {{c1::progressively}} or {{c2::precipitously}}.
{{c1::Atherosclerosis}} is an example of progressive luminal narrowing.
{{c1::Thrombosis}} and {{c2::embolism}} are examples of precipitous luminal obstruction.
Vascular disease involves two main mechanisms: {{c1::obstruction}} and {{c2::weakening}}.
keyPoints: Vascular pathology is categorized into narrowing/obstruction and wall weakening.
Weakening leads to dilation (aneurysm) or rupture.
Narrowing leads to ischemia (stenosis or occlusion).
Atherosclerosis can contribute to both narrowing and (via media damage) weakening.
Vascular structure determines the characteristic anatomic distribution of diseases.
microReview: Vascular pathology causes morbidity via two paths: 1. Making the hole too small (stenosis/thrombosis) or 2. Making the wall too weak (aneurysm/rupture).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'cause' (atherosclerosis) with the 'mechanism' (narrowing vs weakening). Atherosclerosis can cause both, but the question asks specifically for the consequence of 'wall weakening'.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old female with a history of tall stature, arachnodactyly, and ectopia lentis presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset, severe 'tearing' chest pain radiating to the back. Her blood pressure is 110/60 mmHg. An urgent CT angiogram shows a longitudinal intimal tear and a false lumen in the ascending aorta. Which of the following describes the most likely cellular signaling abnormality in this patient?

options.a: Increased TGF-β signaling in the vessel wall
options.c: Inhibition of smooth muscle cell migration
options.d: Excessive deposition of mature collagen fibers

explanations.a: Marfan syndrome (suggested by phenotype) is caused by Fibrillin-1 mutations, which leads to increased bioavailability of TGF-β. Excessive TGF-β signaling causes cystic medial necrosis and aortic weakening.
explanations.b: In Marfan and other aneurysmal diseases, MMP activity is typically increased, not decreased.
explanations.c: The vascular response to injury involves increased migration of smooth muscle cells to the intima, but this patient's acute dissection is a wall weakness issue.
explanations.d: Aortic weakening in Marfan syndrome involves loss of elastic fibers and disorganized ECM, not excessive mature collagen.
explanations.e: Defective LDL receptors cause Familial Hypercholesterolemia, leading to premature atherosclerosis, not the classic Marfan dissection phenotype.

ankiCards: Marfan syndrome results from mutations in the {{c1::Fibrillin-1 (FBN1)}} gene.
Fibrillin-1 mutations in Marfan syndrome lead to increased {{c1::TGF-β}} signaling.
The pathological change in the media in Marfan-related aneurysms is called {{c1::cystic medial necrosis}}.
Aortic dissection is characterized by a {{c1::longitudinal tear}} in the intima followed by blood tracking into the media.
Excessive TGF-β signaling in the aortic wall leads to {{c1::weakening}} and dilation.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome is a major cause of thoracic aortic aneurysms/dissections in young people.
FBN1 mutation -> Loss of microfibril integrity -> TGF-β dysregulation.
TGF-β promotes matrix degradation and medial weakening.
Cystic medial necrosis involves loss of smooth muscle and elastic tissue fragmentation.
Dissection is a medical emergency often preceded by aneurysmal dilation.
microReview: In young patients with connective tissue signs, think Marfan/FBN1. The mechanism is a lack of Fibrillin-1 microfibrils to sequester TGF-β, leading to excessive TGF-β-mediated medial degradation (cystic medial necrosis).
examinerTraps: A common trap is assuming all aneurysms/dissections are due to atherosclerosis. In young patients with Marfan, it's a primary genetic medial weakness.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: While atherosclerosis affects many vessel types, its contribution to the development of aneurysms is most pronounced in elastic arteries. In the context of vascular wall structural response, why does intimal thickening often precede vessel wall weakening in atherosclerotic disease?

options.a: The intima lacks vasa vasorum, making it prone to ischemia
options.b: Intimal thickening is a stereotyped response to any vascular injury
options.c: The media cannot synthesize new collagen to repair defects
options.d: Smooth muscle cells only exist in the intima of large arteries
options.e: The internal elastic lamina prevents inflammatory cell migration

explanations.a: While the intima is avascular, this doesn't explain why thickening 'precedes' weakening in the stereotyped response to injury.
explanations.b: According to the source, intimal thickening is the 'stereotyped response to vascular injury'. This process often involves smooth muscle cell migration and matrix synthesis, which initially compensates but eventually leads to plaque and medial atrophy.
explanations.c: Smooth muscle cells in the media are capable of collagen synthesis.
explanations.d: Smooth muscle cells are the primary component of the tunica media, not the intima (normally).
explanations.e: Inflammatory cells easily cross the internal elastic lamina during atherogenesis.

ankiCards: The stereotyped response of the vascular wall to injury is {{c1::intimal thickening}}.
Atherosclerosis affects mainly {{c1::elastic}} and {{c2::muscular}} arteries.
During intimal thickening, smooth muscle cells migrate from the {{c1::media}} to the {{c2::intima}}.
Intimal thickening involves the synthesis of {{c1::extracellular matrix (ECM)}}.
The structural architecture of vessels is comparable, but specializations reflect {{c1::functional roles}}.
keyPoints: Intimal thickening is a universal response to vascular insult.
This process involves smooth muscle migration and ECM deposition.
In atherosclerosis, this response eventually compromises the media's integrity.
Weakening of the media under an atherosclerotic plaque leads to aneurysm.
Elastic arteries (like the aorta) are primary targets for this pathology.
microReview: When a vessel is hurt (high BP, toxins, cholesterol), it responds by thickening its intima. However, the presence of a thick atherosclerotic plaque interferes with the nutrition of the underlying media, causing it to thin and weaken, resulting in an aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'intimal response' (thickening) with the 'medial consequence' (thinning/weakening). They happen together in atherosclerosis-induced aneurysms.
sourceQuote: Intimal Thickening: A Stereotyped Response to Vascular Injury... atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which vessel layer is primarily responsible for the structural integrity and high-pressure tolerance of large elastic arteries, and whose degradation is the hallmark of aneurysmal disease?

explanations.a: The adventitia contains connective tissue and nerves but is not the primary pressure-bearing layer.
explanations.b: The intima is the thin innermost layer; its dysfunction starts atherosclerosis, but its thickness is not the primary pressure-bearing component.
explanations.c: The internal elastic lamina is a component of the vessel wall but is not a 'layer' that provides the bulk of structural integrity.
explanations.d: The tunica media, rich in smooth muscle cells and elastic fibers, is the primary layer providing structural strength; its weakening leads to aneurysms.
explanations.e: Vasa vasorum are small vessels that supply the outer layers of large vessels; they are not a structural layer themselves.

ankiCards: The {{c1::tunica media}} is the primary layer responsible for the structural integrity of large arteries.
The tunica media of elastic arteries is particularly rich in {{c1::elastic fibers}}.
Degradation of the tunica media leads to vessel wall {{c1::weakening}}.
The tunica media {{c1::thins}} in the presence of overlying atherosclerotic plaques.
Aneurysms occur when the wall's {{c1::integrity}} is compromised, leading to dilation.
keyPoints: Tunica media provides the structural 'backbone' of the arterial wall.
Elastic fibers in the media allow for recoil during the cardiac cycle.
Loss of medial smooth muscle cells results in wall thinning.
Media degradation is central to both AAA and TAA.
Inflammatory cytokines and MMPs are the agents of media destruction.
microReview: Media = Strength. Intima = Interface. Adventitia = Support. Aneurysm = Media failure.
examinerTraps: Watch for 'Internal elastic lamina' as a distractor; while it's important, the 'Tunica Media' is the comprehensive layer that contains the bulk of elastic tissue and muscle responsible for wall strength.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the pathogenesis of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA), the presence of atherosclerosis in the tunica intima is said to cause atrophy of the underlying tunica media. What is the most likely physiological mechanism for this medial atrophy?

options.a: Direct toxic effect of oxidized LDL on medial myocytes
options.b: Impaired diffusion of oxygen and nutrients from the lumen
options.c: Pressure necrosis from the high-velocity turbulent blood flow
options.d: Excessive production of nitric oxide by the dysfunctional endothelium
options.e: Mechanical stretching of the media by the expanding lipid core

explanations.a: While LDL is toxic, the primary structural reason for medial atrophy in AAA is nutrient deprivation.
explanations.b: The thick atherosclerotic plaque increases the diffusion distance for oxygen and nutrients from the lumen to the media, leading to ischemia and subsequent atrophy of the medial smooth muscle cells.
explanations.c: Turbulent flow causes endothelial damage, but it is not the primary cause of 'medial atrophy' under a plaque.
explanations.d: Dysfunctional endothelium in atherosclerosis actually shows *decreased* nitric oxide production.
explanations.e: The lipid core is within the intima; it doesn't mechanically 'stretch' the media into atrophy; rather, it starves it.

ankiCards: Medial atrophy in AAA is primarily caused by {{c1::impaired diffusion}} of nutrients from the lumen.
Atherosclerotic plaques in the intima increase the {{c1::diffusion distance}} to the tunica media.
Ischemia of the media leads to the loss of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}}.
Loss of medial cells and matrix leads to wall {{c1::thinning}}.
AAA usually occurs in the {{c1::infrarenal}} aorta because it has less vasa vasorum support for the media.
keyPoints: Large arteries receive some nutrients from the lumen via diffusion.
Thick plaques block this diffusion pathway.
The result is 'ischemic' atrophy of the tunica media.
Thinning of the media reduces the wall's ability to resist arterial pressure.
This process is a key step in the transition from atherosclerosis to aneurysm.
microReview: Plaque acts as a barrier. The media 'starves' of oxygen because it's too far from the blood in the lumen and (in the abdominal aorta) has poor vasa vasorum supply. Starved media = Weak wall = Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: A common distractor is 'pressure necrosis'. While pressure is the force that *dilates* the weak wall, the *reason* the wall is weak is nutrient-diffusion impairment.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: ... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old male with a history of untreated syphilis presents with a chronic cough and hoarseness. Imaging reveals a large aneurysm of the ascending aortic arch. The pathology of the aortic wall shows a 'tree-bark' appearance of the intima and significant scarring. Which of the following microscopic findings is most characteristic of this specific aneurysmal condition?

options.a: Hyaline deposition in the walls of small arterioles
options.b: Transmural granulomatous inflammation with giant cells
options.c: Plasma cell-rich infiltrate around the vasa vasorum
options.d: Disruption of the internal elastic lamina by neutrophils
options.e: Fibrinoid necrosis of the tunica media

explanations.a: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is associated with hypertension/diabetes, not syphilitic aneurysms.
explanations.b: Granulomatous inflammation is characteristic of Giant Cell or Takayasu arteritis.
explanations.c: Syphilitic (luetic) aneurysms are caused by obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum, often surrounded by a plasma cell-rich inflammatory infiltrate. This leads to medial ischemia and 'tree-barking'.
explanations.d: Neutrophilic disruption of the elastic lamina is more characteristic of acute infectious vasculitis.
explanations.e: Fibrinoid necrosis is typical of malignant hypertension or certain small-vessel vasculitides (like Polyarteritis Nodosa).

ankiCards: Syphilitic aneurysms typically involve the {{c1::ascending aorta / arch}}.
The characteristic microscopic finding in syphilitic aortitis is {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}} of the vasa vasorum.
The 'tree-bark' appearance of the aorta is due to {{c1::intimal scarring}} following medial ischemia.
The inflammatory infiltrate in syphilitic aortitis is predominantly composed of {{c1::plasma cells}}.
Obliteration of the vasa vasorum causes {{c1::ischemic}} injury to the aortic tunica media.
keyPoints: Tertiary syphilis causes 'luetic' aneurysms.
Target: Vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta.
Mechanism: Obliterative endarteritis -> Medial ischemia -> Weakness.
Gross appearance: 'Tree-barking' due to contraction of fibrous scars.
Complication: Aortic valve insufficiency (dilation of the aortic root).
microReview: Syphilis attacks the 'vessels of the vessels' (vasa vasorum). This starves the thick media of the thoracic aorta, leading to scarring and dilation. Remember: Syphilis = Thoracic/Ascending; Atherosclerosis = Abdominal/Infrarenal.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the location. AAA (Abdominal) is atherosclerosis; Syphilitic (Thoracic/Ascending) is vasa vasorum destruction.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old male smoker with poorly controlled hypertension presents with a 6-cm abdominal aortic aneurysm. Laboratory studies show elevated levels of circulating cytokines and increased activity of proteases in the aortic wall. Which of the following findings would most likely be observed on histopathological examination of the aneurysm wall?

options.b: Extensive loss of elastic fibers in the media
options.c: Acellular, hyaline thickening of the intima
options.e: Replacement of smooth muscle with organized thrombus

explanations.a: Onion-skinning is characteristic of hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis in malignant hypertension, not AAA.
explanations.b: Aneurysms are defined by the loss of structural integrity in the media; in AAA, this is visualized as the degradation and loss of elastic fibers due to MMP activity.
explanations.c: Hyaline thickening is seen in small vessel disease (hyaline arteriolosclerosis), not the large aortic wall of an aneurysm.
explanations.d: Granulomatous inflammation is seen in vasculitides like Giant Cell Arteritis, not typical atherosclerotic AAA.
explanations.e: Thrombus often lines an aneurysm (mural thrombus), but it does not 'replace' the smooth muscle of the wall; the wall itself is thinned and scarred.

ankiCards: A key histopathological feature of aneurysms is the loss of {{c1::elastic fibers}} in the media.
In AAA, {{c1::inflammation}} leads to the activation of proteases.
The primary proteases involved in AAA wall degradation are {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
Protease activity in the aortic wall leads to the breakdown of {{c1::collagen}} and elastin.
Loss of medial structural components results in {{c1::dilation}} of the vessel.
keyPoints: AAA wall histology shows chronic inflammation and matrix destruction.
Elastic fiber fragmentation is a hallmark of all true aneurysms.
The media becomes thin and is often replaced by fibrous tissue.
MMP-2 and MMP-9 (gelatinases) are often upregulated.
The resulting structural failure cannot withstand normal systolic pressures.
microReview: Histology of an aneurysm = Media in tatters. Specifically, the elastic fibers are broken (fragmented) and the smooth muscle cells are gone (atrophy).
examinerTraps: Watch for 'Mural Thrombus'. While mural thrombi are common *inside* the aneurysm, the question asks for the finding *in the wall* itself that explains the aneurysm's existence (loss of elastic fibers).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 34-year-old male with a history of HIV and a CD4+ count of 120 cells/mm³ presents with multiple non-blanching, violaceous macules and plaques on his lower extremities and oral mucosa. A biopsy of one skin lesion reveals spindle-shaped cells, slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells, and hyaline globules. Immunohistochemical staining is positive for a specific viral antigen. Which of the following is the most likely causative agent?

explanations.a: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of Kaposi sarcoma, which presents with spindle cells and slit-like vascular spaces.
explanations.b: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised patients, which also presents with vascular proliferations but features neutrophilic infiltrates and clusters of bacteria rather than spindle cells.
explanations.c: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with various lymphomas (e.g., Burkitt) and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not typically primary vascular tumors of the skin.
explanations.d: Human papillomavirus 16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx.
explanations.e: Cytomegalovirus can cause opportunistic infections in HIV patients (e.g., retinitis, colitis) but is not the primary driver of Kaposi sarcoma.

ankiCards: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by infection with {{c1::Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)}}.
The characteristic histology of Kaposi sarcoma includes {{c1::spindle cells}} and {{c2::slit-like vascular spaces}}.
Bacillary angiomatosis is differentiated from Kaposi sarcoma by the presence of {{c1::neutrophils}} and {{c2::Bartonella bacteria}}.
Kaposi sarcoma lesions in AIDS patients are frequently found on the {{c1::skin}}, {{c2::mucous membranes}}, and {{c3::gastrointestinal tract}}.
A common immunohistochemical marker for vascular endothelium used in tumor diagnosis is {{c1::CD31}}.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a low-grade malignant vascular tumor caused by HHV-8.
There are four forms: Classic, Endemic African, Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated (epidemic).
Histologically, it progresses from patches to plaques to nodules with characteristic spindle cells.
HHV-8 infects endothelial cells and induces a pro-inflammatory/angiogenic state.
Biopsy is essential to distinguish KS from bacillary angiomatosis.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma: HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Slit-like spaces + Extravasated RBCs. Common in HIV.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse Kaposi Sarcoma (HHV-8, spindle cells) with Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella henselae, neutrophils). Both appear as purple lesions in HIV patients.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old female presents with an intensely painful, 4-mm, blue-red nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. She notes that the pain is exacerbated by cold temperatures. Surgical excision is performed, and histology shows a well-circumscribed nest of specialized smooth muscle cells surrounding branch-like vascular channels. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, exquisitely painful tumors arising from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, typically found in the subungual region.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas are common benign vascular tumors but are usually painless and found on the skin of infants or children.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, blood-filled vascular spaces; they are usually deeper and not specifically associated with the subungual region or exquisite pain.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor with poorly formed vascular channels and significant cytologic atypia, unlike the well-circumscribed glomus tumor.
explanations.e: Pyogenic granuloma is a rapidly growing, pedunculated red nodule that bleeds easily, often occurring after minor trauma or during pregnancy.

ankiCards: A subungual, extremely painful, small red-blue nodule is characteristic of a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
Glomus tumors arise from the {{c1::glomus body}}, which is involved in {{c2::thermoregulation}}.
The cells in a glomus tumor are derived from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells.
Pain in a glomus tumor is often triggered by {{c1::cold}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors show nests of glomus cells surrounding {{c1::vascular channels}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign and classically subungual.
Clinical triad: paroxysmal pain, localized tenderness, and sensitivity to cold.
Derived from glomus bodies (arteriovenous shunts for temperature control).
Histology: Uniform, round cells with scant cytoplasm (glomus cells).
Treatment is simple surgical excision.
microReview: Glomus Tumor: Subungual + Pain + Cold Sensitivity + Modified Smooth Muscle cells.
examinerTraps: The word 'painful' is the strongest hint. Most other benign vascular tumors (hemangiomas) are asymptomatic and painless.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male who worked in a chemical plant for 30 years with chronic exposure to vinyl chloride presents with weight loss, abdominal pain, and hepatomegaly. Imaging reveals several large, poorly defined masses in the liver. A biopsy demonstrates malignant endothelial cells showing marked pleomorphism and positive staining for CD31. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare, highly malignant vascular tumor associated with exposures to vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
explanations.b: Hepatocellular carcinoma is the most common primary liver cancer, associated with cirrhosis and HBV/HCV, but it is of epithelial (hepatocyte) origin, not endothelial.
explanations.c: Hepatic hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor; it is typically asymptomatic and composed of cavernous vascular spaces without malignancy.
explanations.d: Kaposi sarcoma can involve the liver in AIDS patients but is specifically linked to HHV-8 rather than industrial chemical exposure.
explanations.e: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor, but it is less common than angiosarcoma in the context of vinyl chloride exposure.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}, {{c2::arsenic}}, and {{c3::Thorotrast}}.
Angiosarcomas are malignant tumors that stain positive for the endothelial marker {{c1::CD31}}.
The prognosis of angiosarcoma is generally {{c1::poor}} because they are often advanced at diagnosis.
Histologically, angiosarcomas exhibit highly pleomorphic {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
Angiosarcomas can also occur in the skin after {{c1::radiation therapy}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignant vascular neoplasm.
Environmental carcinogens (vinyl chloride) are specifically linked to the liver site.
CD31 (PECAM-1) is a definitive marker for endothelial origin.
They can occur in the skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Skin angiosarcomas often occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
microReview: Angiosarcoma: Malignant + CD31+ + Vinyl Chloride (Liver) or Radiation (Breast).
examinerTraps: Watch for the 'vinyl chloride' or 'Thorotrast' buzzwords; they almost exclusively point to Hepatic Angiosarcoma in board exams.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular tumors are classified as benign, intermediate (borderline), or malignant. Which of the following neoplasms is categorized as an intermediate-grade vascular tumor?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is considered an intermediate-grade (borderline) tumor because, while it can be locally aggressive and disseminate, it lacks the extreme pleomorphism and rapid lethality of high-grade angiosarcomas.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangioma is a benign vascular tumor.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignant vascular tumor.
explanations.d: Glomus tumor is a benign tumor of modified smooth muscle cells.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious/reactive vascular proliferation, not a neoplastic intermediate-grade tumor.

ankiCards: Kaposi sarcoma is classified as an {{c1::intermediate (borderline)}} grade vascular tumor.
Angiosarcoma is classified as a {{c1::malignant (high-grade)}} vascular tumor.
Hemangiomas (capillary/cavernous) are classified as {{c1::benign}} vascular tumors.
{{c1::Hemangioendothelioma}} is another example of an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
The marker {{c1::CD31}} is used to identify the endothelial origin of vascular tumors.
keyPoints: Classification is based on clinical behavior and histologic features.
Benign: Hemangioma, Glomus tumor.
Intermediate: Kaposi sarcoma, Hemangioendothelioma.
Malignant: Angiosarcoma.
Intermediate tumors are locally aggressive but have low metastatic potential compared to high-grade sarcomas.
microReview: Grades: Benign (Hemangioma), Intermediate (Kaposi, Hemangioendothelioma), Malignant (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: Students often misclassify Kaposi Sarcoma as fully malignant (high-grade) because of its association with AIDS and death, but pathologically it is intermediate/borderline.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 2-week-old female infant is brought to the pediatrician for a rapidly growing, bright red, raised lesion on her forehead. The parents state it was not present at birth. On examination, the lesion is soft, lobulated, and blanches partially with pressure. Which of the following is the most likely clinical course for this lesion?

explanations.a: The description fits a juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma, which typically grows rapidly in the first few months of life and then spontaneously regresses by age 7 in the majority of cases.
explanations.b: Juvenile hemangiomas are benign and do not transform into angiosarcomas.
explanations.c: Unlike port-wine stains (Nevus flammeus), strawberry hemangiomas usually regress rather than persist unchanged.
explanations.d: While some syndromes (like von Hippel-Lindau) involve multiple vascular lesions, a simple strawberry hemangioma does not 'spread' or metastasize.
explanations.e: Surgical excision is usually avoided as most lesions regress on their own, unless they obstruct vision or the airway.

ankiCards: The common name for a juvenile capillary hemangioma is a {{c1::strawberry hemangioma}}.
Strawberry hemangiomas typically appear {{c1::after birth (first weeks)}}.
The typical natural history of a strawberry hemangioma is growth followed by {{c1::spontaneous regression}}.
By age 7, approximately {{c1::75-90}}% of strawberry hemangiomas have regressed.
Strawberry hemangiomas are composed of {{c1::thin-walled capillaries}} with scant stroma.
keyPoints: Capillary hemangiomas are the most common type of hemangioma.
Juvenile (strawberry) type occurs in 1 in 200 live births.
They are often multiple.
Histology: closely packed capillaries lined by a single layer of endothelium.
Regression begins with fading color and softening of the nodule.
microReview: Strawberry Hemangioma: Infant + Rapid growth + Fades by age 7.
examinerTraps: Differentiate from Nevus Flammeus (Port-wine stain), which is present at birth, flat, and does not regress.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following histopathologic features most reliably distinguishes bacillary angiomatosis from Kaposi sarcoma in an immunocompromised patient?

options.c: Involvement of the skin and viscera
options.e: Presence of red blood cells in the lumen

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis is characterized by a prominent neutrophilic infiltrate and the presence of Warthin-Starry silver stain-positive bacteria. Kaposi sarcoma typically lacks neutrophils and instead features spindle cells and lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates.
explanations.b: Both conditions involve a proliferation of endothelial cells.
explanations.c: Both conditions can involve the skin and internal organs (viscera) in immunocompromised states.
explanations.d: CD31 is a marker for endothelium and will be positive in both vascular proliferations.
explanations.e: Both lesions involve vascular spaces that may contain red blood cells.

ankiCards: The inflammatory cell type characteristic of bacillary angiomatosis is the {{c1::neutrophil}}.
The silver stain used to identify Bartonella in bacillary angiomatosis is the {{c1::Warthin-Starry}} stain.
Unlike Kaposi sarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis is caused by {{c1::bacteria (Bartonella)}}.
Bacillary angiomatosis is treated with {{c1::antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin)}}.
Kaposi sarcoma is characterized by a {{c1::spindle cell}} morphology.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis (BA) is an opportunistic infection in AIDS.
BA is caused by Bartonella henselae (cats) or Bartonella quintana (lice).
Grossly, lesions are red papules or nodules.
Histology: Capillary proliferation with nuclear atypia and neutrophils.
BA can be fatal if not treated with antibiotics, whereas KS requires HAART and sometimes chemotherapy.
microReview: BA vs KS: BA = Neutrophils + Bartonella (Bacteria). KS = Spindle cells + HHV-8 (Virus).
examinerTraps: Both lesions look similar clinically (red/purple papules in HIV). The key is the 'neutrophil' in histology or 'Warthin-Starry' stain.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old female presents with multiple dark-purple, firm nodules on her left arm. She has a history of left-sided breast cancer treated with a radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection 12 years ago, which resulted in chronic, persistent lymphedema of the left upper extremity. A biopsy of a nodule confirms a malignant vascular tumor. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma is the diagnosis. When it arises in the setting of chronic lymphedema (classically post-mastectomy), it is referred to as Stewart-Treves syndrome, but the tumor type itself is angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Lymphangioma is a benign proliferation of lymphatic channels, usually appearing in children, not a malignant tumor in an adult.
explanations.c: Kaposi sarcoma is not typically associated with chronic lymphedema following mastectomy.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangioma is a benign vascular tumor.
explanations.e: Stewart-Treves syndrome is the name of the clinical scenario, but 'Angiosarcoma' is the specific name of the malignant tumor. In most standardized exams, if both are present, 'Angiosarcoma' is the pathological diagnosis.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema post-mastectomy is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
The latent period between mastectomy/lymphedema and the development of angiosarcoma is usually {{c1::10 or more}} years.
Histologically, angiosarcoma shows malignant cells of {{c1::endothelial}} origin.
Common sites for angiosarcoma include the skin, {{c1::breast}}, and {{c2::liver}}.
Angiosarcomas of the skin are most common on the {{c1::head and neck}} of elderly individuals.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are aggressive with a 5-year survival rate of ~30%.
They can be induced by radiation therapy.
Morphology ranges from well-formed vascular channels to solid sheets of cells.
CD31 and vWF (von Willebrand factor) are useful markers.
Chronic lymphedema promotes oncogenesis, likely due to local immune dysfunction.
microReview: Stewart-Treves: Post-Mastectomy + Lymphedema + Angiosarcoma (Malignant).
examinerTraps: Differentiating the syndrome (Stewart-Treves) from the tumor (Angiosarcoma). Always look for 'malignant' or 'pleomorphic' in the stem to confirm sarcoma.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old male undergoes a CT scan of the abdomen for unrelated trauma, which incidentally reveals a 3-cm, well-circumscribed, blood-filled cystic mass in the right lobe of the liver. The lesion shows peripheral nodular enhancement on arterial phase imaging. Which of the following best describes the expected histopathologic appearance of this lesion?

options.a: Large, dilated vascular channels separated by scanty connective tissue
options.b: Small, closely packed capillaries lined by a single layer of endothelium
options.c: Malignant spindle cells forming slit-like spaces with RBC extravasation
options.d: Nests of glomus cells surrounding small blood vessels
options.e: Thick-walled muscular arteries with fragmented internal elastic lamina

explanations.a: The clinical scenario describes a cavernous hemangioma of the liver, the most common benign liver tumor. Histologically, these consist of large, dilated (cavernous) blood-filled spaces.
explanations.b: This describes a capillary hemangioma, which is more common in the skin and consists of smaller vessels.
explanations.c: This describes Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.d: This describes a glomus tumor.
explanations.e: This describes findings related to vasculitis or arterial disorders, not a benign vascular tumor.

ankiCards: The most common benign tumor of the liver is the {{c1::cavernous hemangioma}}.
Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, {{c1::blood-filled}} vascular channels.
A potential complication of large cavernous hemangiomas is {{c1::thrombosis}} or {{c2::consumptive coagulopathy (Kasabach-Merritt syndrome)}}.
Histologically, cavernous hemangiomas are separated by {{c1::fibrous connective tissue (stroma)}}.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas {{c1::rarely}} regress.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are often incidental findings.
They are usually 1–2 cm but can be 'giant' (>5 cm).
They are well-circumscribed but not encapsulated.
Radiology: 'Filling in' of the lesion with contrast over time (centripetal enhancement).
They are usually asymptomatic and require no treatment.
microReview: Cavernous Hemangioma: Liver + Large spaces + Asymptomatic incidental finding.
examinerTraps: Do not biopsy suspected liver hemangiomas due to the risk of significant intraperitoneal hemorrhage; the diagnosis is usually made radiologically.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the pathogenesis of AIDS-associated Kaposi sarcoma, which of the following cytokines, induced by the Tat protein of HIV-1, is known to promote the growth of HHV-8 infected cells?

explanations.a: HHV-8 encodes a viral homolog of Interleukin-6 (vIL-6) that directly stimulates the proliferation of spindle cells. Additionally, HIV Tat protein promotes the production of inflammatory cytokines like IL-6 from infected cells.
explanations.b: Interferon-gamma is generally involved in Th1 immune responses and is not a primary growth factor for KS cells.
explanations.c: TNF-alpha is involved in inflammation but IL-6 is the specific growth factor emphasized in KS pathogenesis.
explanations.d: IL-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine.
explanations.e: TGF-beta is involved in fibrosis and immune suppression but is not the primary mitogen in the HHV-8/KS pathway.

ankiCards: HHV-8 encodes a viral version of the cytokine {{c1::IL-6}}.
The HIV protein {{c1::Tat}} promotes Kaposi sarcoma by stimulating cytokine production.
KS spindle cells produce {{c1::VEGF}}, which promotes angiogenesis.
HHV-8 remains in a {{c1::latent}} state in most infected cells within a KS lesion.
The viral protein {{c1::LANA}} (Latency-Associated Nuclear Antigen) is used as a diagnostic IHC marker for HHV-8.
keyPoints: KS is not a pure neoplasm early on; it is a reactive polyclonal proliferation.
Viral IL-6 (vIL-6) activates the JAK/STAT pathway.
VEGF and bFGF are also highly expressed.
The progression to a monoclonal malignancy occurs in the nodular stage.
HAART reduces KS incidence by lowering HIV viral load and cytokine levels.
microReview: KS Pathogenesis: HHV-8 + HIV Tat + IL-6 + VEGF = Spindle cell growth.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse vIL-6 with the markers used for diagnosis (CD31). vIL-6 is a mechanism of growth.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 22-year-old female in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with a rapidly enlarging, 1-cm, pedunculated, 'raw-meat' looking nodule on her gingiva. The lesion bleeds easily with minimal trauma. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a common, rapidly growing, pedunculated red lesion on the skin or oral mucosa (gingiva). It is often associated with pregnancy (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.b: While a pyogenic granuloma is histologically a form of capillary hemangioma, the term 'pyogenic granuloma' is the specific clinical designation for this rapidly growing, bleeding-prone lesion.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are usually subungual and painful; they are not typically pedunculated or associated with the gingiva.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor and would not typically present as a small, pedunculated gingival nodule in a pregnant woman.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis presents similarly but is associated with HIV/immunodeficiency, not pregnancy.

ankiCards: A pyogenic granuloma occurring on the gingiva during pregnancy is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized by being {{c1::pedunculated}} and {{c2::bleeding}} easily.
Despite the name, pyogenic granulomas are neither {{c1::pyogenic (pus-forming)}} nor {{c2::granulomas}}.
The histology of a pyogenic granuloma is a {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
The treatment for a bothersome pyogenic granuloma is {{c1::surgical excision}} (or waiting for post-partum regression).
keyPoints: Pyogenic granulomas are reactive, not truly neoplastic.
They can occur on the skin, lips, or gingiva.
Trauma is a common precipitating factor.
Extensive edema and acute/chronic inflammation are seen histologically.
Granuloma gravidarum often regresses spontaneously after delivery.
microReview: Pyogenic Granuloma: Pregnancy + Gingiva + Bleeds easily + Lobular capillaries.
examinerTraps: The name is a misnomer—it is not an infection and not a granuloma. It is a vascular proliferation.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular tumors are broadly categorized into three groups based on their clinical behavior. Which of the following is most accurately classified as an intermediate-grade (borderline) vascular neoplasm?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are common benign vascular tumors.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is the classic example of an intermediate-grade (borderline) vascular tumor, which is locally aggressive and has metastatic potential but is less aggressive than angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant vascular tumor with a very poor prognosis.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are benign, exquisitely painful tumors arising from specialized smooth muscle cells of glomus bodies.
explanations.e: Cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) is a benign lymphatic malformation, typically seen in the neck of infants.

ankiCards: Vascular tumors are categorized into {{c1::benign}}, {{c2::intermediate (borderline)}}, and {{c3::malignant}} groups.
{{c1::Kaposi sarcoma}} is the classic example of an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
{{c1::Angiosarcoma}} is a high-grade, highly malignant vascular neoplasm.
Glomus tumors are {{c1::benign}} vascular tumors arising from glomus bodies.
Benign vascular tumors typically form well-defined {{c1::vascular channels}} filled with blood.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors represent a spectrum from benign to highly malignant.
Intermediate-grade tumors are locally aggressive with low metastatic potential.
Kaposi sarcoma is the prototypical borderline vascular tumor.
Malignant tumors (e.g., angiosarcoma) are difficult to treat and have high mortality.
Benign tumors like hemangiomas often regress spontaneously in childhood.
microReview: Vascular tumors are divided by their biologic behavior: Benign (Hemangiomas), Intermediate (Kaposi Sarcoma, Hemangioendothelioma), and Malignant (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Kaposi sarcoma (intermediate) with angiosarcoma (malignant); though both involve endothelial cells, their clinical progression and grading differ.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... Malignant Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A specific subset of vascular tumors is strongly associated with viral infection and immunodeficiency. The pathogenesis of these lesions involves which of the following infectious agents?

explanations.a: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not primarily vascular tumors.
explanations.b: Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent for all forms of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.c: HPV-16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx.
explanations.d: CMV can cause opportunistic infections in immunocompromised patients but is not an oncogenic driver of vascular tumors.
explanations.e: HBV is primarily associated with hepatocellular carcinoma.

ankiCards: {{c1::HHV-8}} is the causative virus for Kaposi Sarcoma.
Kaposi sarcoma is often seen in patients with {{c1::AIDS/HIV}}.
HHV-8 is also known as {{c1::KSHV}} (Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus).
The clinical grades of vascular tumors are {{c1::benign}}, {{c2::intermediate}}, and {{c3::malignant}}.
{{c1::Kaposi sarcoma}} presents as purple or red skin plaques or nodules.
keyPoints: HHV-8 is essential for the development of Kaposi Sarcoma.
Kaposi sarcoma can present in four forms: Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
The tumor cells in Kaposi sarcoma are spindle-shaped.
Slit-like spaces containing red blood cells are a hallmark histological finding.
Treatment often involves HAART therapy in AIDS patients to restore immune function.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma is an intermediate-grade neoplasm caused by HHV-8, most commonly occurring in the setting of T-cell immunodeficiency.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse HHV-8 with HIV; HIV provides the immunosuppressive environment, but HHV-8 is the actual oncogenic virus for Kaposi Sarcoma.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... Malignant Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with several firm, violaceous nodules on her left arm. She has a history of a radical mastectomy followed by radiation therapy for breast cancer 10 years ago. Since the surgery, she has had persistent lymphedema in the same arm. A biopsy of a nodule reveals atypical endothelial cells forming irregular, anastomosing vascular channels. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella and seen in AIDS patients; it does not typically follow chronic lymphedema.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign and usually congenital or occurring in internal organs; they don't arise from chronic lymphedema.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma can occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome), often after radical mastectomy. Histology shows highly atypical cells.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign, rapidly growing red nodule, often on the skin or gingiva, associated with trauma or pregnancy.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are small, benign, and exquisitely painful subungual lesions.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
Angiosarcoma is characterized by highly {{c1::atypical}} endothelial cells.
Common risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma include {{c1::PVC}}, {{c2::Arsenic}}, and {{c3::Thorotrast}}.
Angiosarcomas often stain positive for the endothelial marker {{c1::CD31}}.
The prognosis for angiosarcoma is generally {{c1::poor}} (5-year survival <30%).
keyPoints: Stewart-Treves syndrome: Angiosarcoma + chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy).
Angiosarcomas are aggressive with high rates of metastasis.
They can occur in the skin, soft tissue, breast, or liver.
Histology shows pleomorphic cells and irregular vascular spaces.
Radiation is a known risk factor for subsequent angiosarcoma.
microReview: Angiosarcoma is a malignant vascular tumor. Key associations include chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy), radiation, and chemical exposures (PVC/arsenic in the liver).
examinerTraps: Wait for the history of chronic lymphedema or radiation to point toward angiosarcoma in a clinical vignette.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... Malignant Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular lesions is characterized histologically by a 'lobular' arrangement of capillary-sized vessels and is clinically known for rapid growth and a tendency to bleed after minor trauma?

explanations.a: Nevus flammeus (Port-wine stain) is a flat, permanent malformation that does not grow rapidly or bleed easily.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a benign, exophytic red nodule that grows rapidly and bleeds with minimal trauma.
explanations.c: Spider angiomas are small, central arterioles with radiating capillaries, often associated with hyperestrogenism.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is malignant and lacks a benign lobular capillary architecture.
explanations.e: Lymphangiomas are lymphatic malformations and do not typically present as rapidly growing, bleeding red nodules.

ankiCards: The histological name for pyogenic granuloma is {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are often associated with {{c1::pregnancy}} (granuloma gravidarum) or {{c2::trauma}}.
A common clinical feature of pyogenic granuloma is that it {{c1::bleeds}} easily.
{{c1::Spider angiomas}} are associated with high estrogen states like liver cirrhosis or pregnancy.
{{c1::Nevus flammeus}} is the medical term for a Port-wine stain.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer (it is neither pyogenic nor a granuloma).
It is a lobular capillary hemangioma.
Commonly found on gingiva (especially in pregnant women) or skin.
Surgical excision is usually curative.
It appears as a polypoid red mass.
microReview: Pyogenic granuloma = Lobular capillary hemangioma = Rapid growth + Easy bleeding + Pregnancy/Trauma association.
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic granuloma' is a trap; it has nothing to do with pus or granulomatous inflammation.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... Malignant Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 1-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for a bright red, raised 'strawberry-like' lesion on the scalp that has been increasing in size since birth. The parents are concerned about its appearance. What is the most likely natural history of this lesion?

options.b: Rapid growth followed by spontaneous regression
options.c: Permanent persistence without change in size
options.d: Spread to internal organs via the lymphatics

explanations.a: Juvenile hemangiomas are benign and do not undergo malignant transformation.
explanations.b: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas typically grow rapidly for a few months and then spontaneously involute by age 7 to 10.
explanations.c: Unlike Port-wine stains (Nevus flammeus), strawberry hemangiomas usually regress.
explanations.d: These are localized benign lesions and do not metastasize.
explanations.e: Strawberry (capillary) and cavernous hemangiomas are distinct entities; one does not turn into the other.

ankiCards: {{c1::Juvenile}} hemangioma is also known as a 'strawberry' hemangioma.
Strawberry hemangiomas usually appear {{c1::shortly after birth}}.
The typical natural history of a strawberry hemangioma is {{c1::spontaneous regression}}.
Spontaneous regression of strawberry hemangiomas usually occurs by age {{c1::7}} to {{c2::10}}.
Histologically, strawberry hemangiomas consist of {{c1::closely packed capillaries}}.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangioma is the most common tumor of infancy.
They are capillary hemangiomas.
Clinically appear as bright red, lobulated, and elevated.
Complete regression occurs in the majority of cases.
Intervention is only needed if they obstruct vision or the airway.
microReview: Strawberry Hemangioma = Infancy + Rapid growth + Spontaneous regression by childhood.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the regressing 'strawberry' hemangioma with the permanent 'Port-wine stain' (Nevus flammeus).
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... Malignant Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following benign vascular lesions is specifically characterized by extremely painful, small nodules, most frequently located under the fingernails?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis presents as red papules in immunocompromised hosts, caused by Bartonella, and is usually not subungual or specifically painful.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas are painless red nodules.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, highly painful tumors arising from glomus bodies, often located in the subungual region.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a large, malignant, often painless (initially) mass.
explanations.e: Lymphangiomas are benign lymphatic lesions, typically in the neck, and are not painful.

ankiCards: A {{c1::glomus tumor}} is a painful, subungual vascular tumor.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle cells}} of the glomus body.
The primary function of the glomus body is {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors show nests of {{c1::uniform round cells}} around vascular spaces.
The classic location for a glomus tumor is {{c1::under the fingernail}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are small (<1 cm).
They are exquisitely sensitive to cold and pressure.
Glomus bodies are arteriovenous shunts involved in thermoregulation.
Excision is the treatment of choice and is curative.
They are entirely benign.
microReview: Glomus Tumor = Painful + Subungual + Smooth muscle origin (glomus body).
examinerTraps: The pain is the defining clinical feature. If a subungual lesion is described as 'exquisitely painful,' think glomus tumor.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... Malignant Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 35-year-old male with advanced AIDS presents with multiple red, papular skin lesions and fever. A biopsy reveals proliferation of capillaries with prominent, protuberant endothelial cells and an infiltrate of neutrophils. Warthin-Starry silver stain demonstrates small bacilli. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8, shows spindle cells, and lacks a prominent neutrophilic infiltrate or bacilli on silver stain.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella species in immunocompromised patients; it shows capillary proliferation, neutrophils, and positive silver stains.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is malignant and lacks the neutrophilic infiltrate or bacterial association.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign lobular capillary hemangioma but lacks the bacterial association found in AIDS patients.
explanations.e: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, dilated blood-filled spaces, not small capillaries with bacilli.

ankiCards: {{c1::Bacillary angiomatosis}} is caused by Bartonella henselae or Bartonella quintana.
Bacillary angiomatosis is primarily seen in {{c1::immunocompromised}} patients (e.g., AIDS).
Histology of bacillary angiomatosis shows capillary proliferation with {{c1::neutrophils}}.
The silver stain used to identify Bartonella is {{c1::Warthin-Starry}} stain.
Treatment for bacillary angiomatosis involves {{c1::antibiotics}} (e.g., erythromycin).
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis mimics Kaposi sarcoma clinically.
It is an opportunistic infection, not a true primary neoplasm.
Caused by Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch) or B. quintana (trench fever).
Distinguished from KS by the presence of neutrophils and bacteria.
Responds well to antibiotic therapy.
microReview: Bacillary Angiomatosis = AIDS + Bartonella + Neutrophils + Capillary proliferation.
examinerTraps: The presence of neutrophils is a key histological clue to differentiate Bacillary Angiomatosis from Kaposi Sarcoma.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... Malignant Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 25-year-old male with a history of Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is found to have a large, deep-seated vascular mass in the cerebellum on MRI. If this lesion were located in the liver, it would most likely demonstrate which histological pattern?

options.e: Uniform round cells in glomus bodies

explanations.a: Lobular capillary proliferation describes a pyogenic granuloma.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated, blood-filled vascular spaces separated by connective tissue stroma; these are common in the liver and associated with VHL.
explanations.c: Spindle cells with slit-like spaces are characteristic of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.d: Atypical cells with anastomosing channels are characteristic of angiosarcoma.
explanations.e: Uniform round cells describe glomus tumors.

ankiCards: {{c1::Cavernous}} hemangiomas consist of large, blood-filled spaces.
Cavernous hemangiomas of the CNS are a feature of {{c1::Von Hippel-Lindau}} (VHL) disease.
The most common benign tumor of the liver is the {{c1::cavernous hemangioma}}.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas {{c1::do not}} regress.
Cavernous hemangiomas can be complicated by {{c1::thrombosis}} or calcification.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are often large and involve deep structures.
VHL disease is associated with hemangioblastomas of the cerebellum and retina.
Liver cavernous hemangiomas are usually asymptomatic and found incidentally.
They carry a risk of rupture if very large.
Histologically, they show thick-walled vessels with no cellular atypia.
microReview: Cavernous Hemangioma = Large vessels + Deep structures (Liver/Brain) + VHL association.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse cavernous (large spaces) with capillary (small spaces) hemangiomas; capillary ones regress, cavernous ones generally don't.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions... Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... Malignant Tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following markers is most useful for confirming the endothelial origin of a poorly differentiated malignant tumor suspected of being a vascular neoplasm?

explanations.a: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells (carcinomas).
explanations.b: Vimentin is a non-specific marker for mesenchymal cells.
explanations.c: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a highly specific marker for endothelial cells and is used to identify vascular tumors like angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells (melanoma, Schwann cells).
explanations.e: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells.

ankiCards: {{c1::CD31}} is a specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial cells.
Another name for CD31 is {{c1::PECAM-1}}.
{{c1::Von Willebrand factor}} is another marker used for endothelial identification.
Angiosarcomas are often poorly differentiated and require {{c1::immunohistochemistry}} for diagnosis.
Vascular tumors arise from {{c1::endothelial}} cells (or perivascular cells).
keyPoints: Immunohistochemistry is crucial for high-grade vascular tumors.
CD31 is the most commonly used marker.
