ankiCards: Glomus tumors typically occur in the {{c1::subungual (under nail)}} region.
The hallmark symptom of a glomus tumor is {{c1::exquisite pain}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::smooth muscle}} cells of the glomus body.
Glomus bodies are involved in the physiological process of {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Histology of a glomus tumor shows uniform round cells and {{c1::branching vascular channels}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign.
Extremely painful, often triggered by cold.
Most common in distal digits, especially subungual.
Derived from specialized perivascular thermoregulatory structures.
Cured by simple excision.
microReview: Painful + Subungual + Round cells = Glomus Tumor (Smooth muscle origin).
examinerTraps: The examiner may try to confuse 'Glomus tumor' with 'Glomus jugulare tumor' (a paraganglioma); the subungual location is the key for the vascular version.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign tumors and tumor-like conditions... Intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors... Malignant tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following immunohistochemical markers is the most specific for identifying a tumor as being of endothelial cell origin, such as an angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (smooth or skeletal).
explanations.b: Vimentin is a general marker for mesenchymal cells and is not specific to endothelium.
explanations.c: CD31 (also known as PECAM-1) is a specific marker for endothelial cells and is used to confirm the diagnosis of vascular tumors.
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells (e.g., melanoma, Schwann cells).
explanations.e: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells.

ankiCards: The most specific endothelial marker used in pathology is {{c1::CD31 (or von Willebrand factor)}}.
CD31 is also known as {{c1::PECAM-1}}.
Malignant vascular tumors like angiosarcoma will stain positive for {{c1::CD31}}.
Endothelial cells line the {{c1::tunica intima}} of blood vessels.
In poorly differentiated angiosarcomas, {{c1::CD31}} helps distinguish them from carcinomas.
keyPoints: Endothelial cells are the cells of origin for hemangiomas and angiosarcomas.
CD31 is the gold standard IHC marker for these cells.
Von Willebrand factor (Factor VIII-related antigen) is another marker but can be less sensitive.
Angiosarcomas may also express CD34.
IHC is critical for identifying poorly differentiated malignant tumors.
microReview: Endothelial marker = CD31.
examinerTraps: Vimentin is usually positive in vascular tumors because they are mesenchymal, but it is not specific. Always choose CD31 or CD34 for specificity.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign tumors and tumor-like conditions... Intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors... Malignant tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 2-week-old infant is brought to the pediatrician due to a bright red, raised, 'strawberry-like' lesion on the scalp. The parents report it was not present at birth but appeared recently and is growing. Which of the following is the most likely natural history of this lesion?

options.c: Persistent growth proportional to the child's height
options.d: Lifelong persistence with risk of rupture
options.e: Rapid expansion leading to consumptive coagulopathy

explanations.a: Infantile (strawberry) hemangiomas are benign and do not undergo malignant transformation.
explanations.b: Strawberry hemangiomas typically grow rapidly for a few months and then spontaneously involute (regress) by age 7 to 9 in the majority of cases.
explanations.c: Port-wine stains (Nevus flammeus) grow with the child, not strawberry hemangiomas.
explanations.d: They typically regress rather than persist for life.
explanations.e: While rare large hemangiomas can cause Kasabach-Merritt syndrome (consumptive coagulopathy), it is not the typical natural history for a standard scalp lesion.

ankiCards: Infantile hemangiomas are also known as {{c1::strawberry}} hemangiomas.
Strawberry hemangiomas are usually {{c1::absent}} at birth but appear in the first few weeks.
The majority of strawberry hemangiomas {{c1::regress/involute}} by age 7.
Histologically, strawberry hemangiomas are {{c1::capillary}} hemangiomas.
The peak growth phase for an infantile hemangioma is usually around {{c1::6-12 months}}.
keyPoints: Capillary hemangiomas are the most common type of vascular tumor.
Strawberry hemangiomas are extremely common in infants (1 in 200).
They are composed of thin-walled capillaries with scant stroma.
Complete involution occurs in 75-90% of cases by age 7.
Medical intervention is only needed if they obstruct vision or the airway.
microReview: Infant + Red/Strawberry lesion = Capillary Hemangioma -> Natural history is spontaneous regression.
examinerTraps: Distinguish between Strawberry Hemangioma (regresses) and Port-Wine Stain (persists and thickens).
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign tumors and tumor-like conditions... Intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors... Malignant tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Hepatic angiosarcomas have been strongly linked to occupational exposure to which of the following substances?

explanations.a: Aflatoxin B1 is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Vinyl chloride (used in the plastics industry) is a well-known carcinogen associated with hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Benzene is primarily associated with leukemia.
explanations.d: Beryllium is associated with lung disease (berylliosis) and lung cancer.
explanations.e: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and lung cancer.

ankiCards: The plastic industry chemical linked to hepatic angiosarcoma is {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
Besides vinyl chloride, hepatic angiosarcoma is linked to {{c1::arsenic}} exposure.
The historical radiocontrast agent linked to liver angiosarcoma is {{c1::Thorotrast}}.
Angiosarcoma is a malignancy of {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
Liver angiosarcomas are often diagnosed at a {{c1::late/advanced}} stage.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are rare but highly lethal.
Environmental toxins specifically target the liver for this malignancy.
Arsenic (pesticides) and Vinyl chloride (PVC pipes) are classic board associations.
Thorotrast (thorium dioxide) was a contrast agent used in the mid-20th century.
The latent period between exposure and tumor development is often decades.
microReview: Vinyl chloride + Arsenic + Thorotrast = Hepatic Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse hepatic angiosarcoma with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). HCC is associated with Hep B/C and Aflatoxin.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign tumors and tumor-like conditions... Intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors... Malignant tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following clinical features most accurately distinguishes Bacillary Angiomatosis from Kaposi Sarcoma in an HIV-positive patient?

options.a: The presence of spindle cells on histology
options.b: The presence of a neutrophilic infiltrate and bacterial clusters
options.c: A predilection for the lower extremities
options.d: The presence of HHV-8 DNA in the lesion

explanations.a: Spindle cells are characteristic of Kaposi Sarcoma, not Bacillary Angiomatosis.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis (caused by Bartonella) is characterized by a neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate and the presence of bacteria (visible on Warthin-Starry stain), whereas Kaposi Sarcoma lacks these.
explanations.c: Both can occur on the skin of the extremities.
explanations.d: HHV-8 is specific to Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.e: Both are vascular lesions and may stain for CD31, so this does not distinguish them.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by the bacteria {{c1::Bartonella (henselae or quintana)}}.
The stain used to visualize the bacteria in Bacillary Angiomatosis is {{c1::Warthin-Starry}}.
Unlike Kaposi Sarcoma, Bacillary Angiomatosis features an infiltrate of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
Bacillary Angiomatosis is treated with {{c1::antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin)}}.
Clinically, Bacillary Angiomatosis lesions are often {{c1::red/cranberry}} like papules.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign vascular proliferation, not a true neoplasm.
It occurs almost exclusively in immunocompromised patients.
It mimics Kaposi Sarcoma clinically.
Histology: Capillary proliferation with nuclear atypia and neutrophils.
Pathogen: Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch) or Bartonella quintana (trench fever).
microReview: Bacillary Angiomatosis = Bartonella + Neutrophils + Warthin-Starry stain + Antibiotic response.
examinerTraps: The examiner will provide a vignette of an AIDS patient and ask for the next step; if you suspect Bacillary Angiomatosis, the answer is often 'antibiotics' or 'Warthin-Starry stain'.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign tumors and tumor-like conditions... Intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors... Malignant tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 27-year-old female in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with a rapidly growing, pedunculated, red mass on her gingiva. It bleeds easily with minor trauma. The lesion is excised and shows a lobulated proliferation of capillaries with edema and an overlying ulcerated surface. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large dilated vascular spaces and are usually deep, not pedunculated gingival lesions.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors are subungual and extremely painful.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (Lobular capillary hemangioma) is common on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum) and follows trauma.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignancy, highly unlikely in a young pregnant woman with a small gingival lesion.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis occurs in immunocompromised individuals and is not associated with pregnancy.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer because it is neither {{c1::pyogenic (pus-forming)}} nor a {{c2::granuloma}}.
The 'pregnancy tumor' occurring on the gingiva is a {{c1::pyogenic granuloma}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are histologically {{c1::lobular capillary hemangiomas}}.
A key clinical feature of pyogenic granuloma is that it {{c1::bleeds easily}}.
The treatment for pyogenic granuloma is {{c1::surgical excision}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign, exophytic red nodule.
Common locations: Skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
Strong association with pregnancy (hormonal influence).
Can regress postpartum but often requires excision.
Histology: Proliferation of capillaries resembles granulation tissue.
microReview: Gingival mass + Pregnancy + Bleeding = Pyogenic Granuloma (Granuloma Gravidarum).
examinerTraps: Don't be fooled by the word 'pyogenic'; there is no infection or pus involved in the primary lesion.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign tumors and tumor-like conditions... Intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors... Malignant tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old male is found to have a large, 10-cm, poorly circumscribed mass in his liver during a routine ultrasound. Histology shows large, dilated vascular channels filled with blood and separated by a thin connective tissue stroma. These lesions are most commonly associated with which of the following genetic syndromes?

explanations.a: NF1 is associated with neurofibromas and optic gliomas, not typically cavernous hemangiomas.
explanations.b: Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is associated with cavernous hemangiomas of the cerebellum, brainstem, and retina, as well as hemangiomas in the liver and pancreas.
explanations.c: Sturge-Weber syndrome is associated with facial port-wine stains and leptomeningeal venous angiomas, not liver cavernous hemangiomas.
explanations.d: Tuberous sclerosis is associated with angiolipomas and facial angiofibromas.
explanations.e: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) features multiple small telangiectasias, not large cavernous hemangiomas.

ankiCards: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of {{c1::large, dilated}} vascular spaces.
The most common benign tumor of the liver is the {{c1::cavernous hemangioma}}.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas {{c1::do not}} spontaneously regress.
Von Hippel-Lindau disease is caused by a mutation in the {{c1::VHL}} gene on chromosome 3.
VHL syndrome includes hemangiomas and {{c1::renal cell carcinoma}}.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are less circumscribed than capillary types.
In the CNS, they are called cavernous malformations or hemangioblastomas (in VHL).
They may be clinically significant if they bleed or cause mass effect.
Liver cavernous hemangiomas are often incidental findings.
VHL association: VHL protein normally degrades Hypoxia-Inducible Factor (HIF).
microReview: Large blood-filled spaces = Cavernous Hemangioma. Associated with VHL if multiple/internal.
examinerTraps: The question might ask about the complication of a large liver hemangioma; the main risk is rupture and intraperitoneal hemorrhage.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign tumors and tumor-like conditions... Intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors... Malignant tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the most common clinical variant of Kaposi Sarcoma, which typically presents as indolent, reddish-purple skin plaques on the distal lower extremities of older men of Mediterranean or Eastern European descent?

explanations.a: AIDS-associated KS is aggressive and involves lymph nodes and viscera early.
explanations.b: Endemic African KS occurs in younger patients and is often very aggressive, especially in children (lymphadenopathic form).
explanations.c: Transplant-associated (Iatrogenic) KS occurs in patients on chronic immunosuppression and may regress if drugs are stopped.
explanations.d: Classic Kaposi Sarcoma fits the description: older men, Mediterranean/Eastern European (Ashkenazi Jewish), indolent course, restricted to the skin.
explanations.e: Iatrogenic is a synonym for transplant-associated in this context.

ankiCards: The four variants of Kaposi Sarcoma are {{c1::Classic, African, Transplant, and AIDS-associated}}.
The population group most associated with Classic Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::Mediterranean/Eastern European men}}.
Unlike the AIDS variant, Classic Kaposi Sarcoma is typically {{c1::indolent/slow-growing}}.
Endemic African Kaposi Sarcoma in children often affects the {{c1::lymph nodes}}.
In all variants, the common denominator is infection with {{c1::HHV-8}}.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma is a multicentric tumor of endothelial cells.
Classic KS: Not associated with HIV; stays cutaneous.
African Endemic KS: Prevalent in HIV-negative individuals in Africa.
Transplant-associated KS: Risk increases 100-fold post-organ transplant.
Treatment for AIDS-KS involves antiretroviral therapy (ART) to boost CD4 counts.
microReview: Elderly Mediterranean man + Leg plaques = Classic KS. HIV man + Disseminated plaques = AIDS-KS.
examinerTraps: Be careful with the term 'endemic.' While the virus is endemic in many places, 'Endemic African KS' refers to the specific aggressive clinical subtype found in Africa.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors... Benign tumors and tumor-like conditions... Intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors... Malignant tumors
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following cellular processes is the primary mechanism leading to the development of an aneurysm through the weakening of the arterial wall?

options.a: Increased synthesis of type I collagen in the adventitia
options.b: Degradation of the extracellular matrix by metalloproteinases
options.c: Proliferation of intimal smooth muscle cells
options.d: Deposition of hyaline material in the arteriolar wall
options.e: Activation of the extrinsic apoptotic pathway in endothelial cells

explanations.a: Synthesis of collagen actually strengthens the wall; it is the degradation or lack of synthesis that leads to weakening.
explanations.b: Aneurysms occur when the balance of collagen degradation and synthesis is tilted toward degradation, often mediated by matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) from macrophages.
explanations.c: Intimal thickening and smooth muscle proliferation are typically responses to injury or atherosclerosis that narrow the lumen rather than dilate it.
explanations.d: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is characteristic of hypertensive small vessel disease, not the weakening seen in large vessel aneurysms.
explanations.e: Endothelial apoptosis is a feature of early atherosclerosis but does not directly cause the structural wall failure required for aneurysm formation.

ankiCards: The two principal mechanisms of vascular disease are narrowing of the lumen and {{c1::weakening}} of vessel walls.
Aneurysms occur when the arterial wall is weakened, leading to {{c1::dilation or rupture}}.
Increased activity of {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}} is a key factor in the pathogenesis of aneurysms.
The structural integrity of the aorta is primarily maintained by the {{c1::tunica media}}.
A 'true' aneurysm involves all {{c1::three}} layers of the arterial wall.
keyPoints: Aneurysms are localized abnormal dilations of a blood vessel or the heart.
Pathogenesis involves an imbalance in extracellular matrix (ECM) metabolism.
Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) degrade collagen and elastin.
Weakening leads to progressive dilation according to the Law of Laplace.
Aneurysms can be classified as true (all wall layers) or false (extravascular hematoma).
microReview: Aneurysms represent a structural failure of the vessel wall. While atherosclerosis and hypertension are major risk factors, the common denominator is the degradation of the tunica media's structural proteins (elastin and collagen) by enzymes like MMPs, often released by inflammatory cells.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse 'intimal thickening' (a response to injury that narrows vessels) with the 'medial thinning' that occurs in aneurysms.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents for a routine physical examination. He is asymptomatic, but physical examination reveals a pulsatile, mid-abdominal mass. An ultrasound confirms a 5.2 cm dilation of the infrarenal abdominal aorta. Which of the following is the most significant contributing factor to the development of this condition?

explanations.a: Cystic medial degeneration is more commonly associated with thoracic aortic aneurysms and Marfan syndrome.
explanations.b: Endarteritis of the vasa vasorum is the hallmark of tertiary syphilis, which typically affects the ascending aorta.
explanations.c: Atherosclerosis is the leading cause of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA). It impairs nutrient diffusion to the media, causing wall weakening.
explanations.d: Congenital defects (e.g., in the Circle of Willis) lead to berry aneurysms, not infrarenal AAAs.
explanations.e: Mycotic aneurysms result from infection of the wall, usually following bacteremia, and are less common than atherosclerotic AAAs.

ankiCards: The most common cause of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA) is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
The classic clinical presentation of an AAA is a {{c1::pulsatile abdominal mass}}.
AAAs are most commonly located in the {{c1::infrarenal}} portion of the aorta.
Risk factors for AAA include male gender, age over 50, and {{c1::smoking}}.
Atherosclerosis causes AAA by limiting {{c1::nutrient and oxygen diffusion}} from the lumen to the media.
keyPoints: AAA is primarily a disease of older male smokers.
Atherosclerosis causes medial thinning and ischemia.
The infrarenal location is due to less vasa vasorum in that segment.
Rupture risk increases significantly once the diameter exceeds 5 cm.
Most AAAs are fusiform rather than saccular.
microReview: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms (AAA) are usually found between the renal arteries and the iliac bifurcation. Atherosclerosis induces an inflammatory response in the wall and thickens the intima, preventing oxygen from reaching the media, leading to atrophy and weakening.
examinerTraps: The examiner may use 'pulsatile mass' to lead you to AAA; always check if the question asks for the location (infrarenal) or the cause (atherosclerosis).
sourceQuote: Atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries... leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following best describes the structural difference between a 'true' aneurysm and a 'false' aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm)?

options.a: True aneurysms are always fusiform, while false aneurysms are saccular
options.b: True aneurysms involve an intact but attenuated arterial wall, while false aneurysms involve a wall defect
options.c: True aneurysms are caused by hypertension, while false aneurysms are caused by atherosclerosis
options.d: True aneurysms occur only in arteries, while false aneurysms occur only in veins
options.e: True aneurysms involve the intima only, while false aneurysms involve all three layers

explanations.a: The shape (fusiform vs. saccular) does not determine whether an aneurysm is true or false.
explanations.b: A true aneurysm involves all three layers (intima, media, and adventitia) of the wall, even if thinned. A false aneurysm is a breach in the wall leading to an extravascular hematoma.
explanations.c: Both types can have various etiologies, including trauma or infection.
explanations.d: Both can occur in the heart or vessels; they are not restricted by vessel type.
explanations.e: True aneurysms must involve all three layers; false aneurysms specifically lack the original vessel wall layers in their boundary.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the arterial wall (intima, media, and adventitia).
A {{c1::false}} aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) is a wall defect that leads to an extravascular hematoma.
An example of a false aneurysm is a {{c1::ventricular rupture}} contained by the pericardium.
A {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm is a spherical outpouching involving only a portion of the vessel wall.
A {{c1::fusiform}} aneurysm is a circumferential dilation of a long vascular segment.
keyPoints: True aneurysms: Intact but thinned wall (Atherosclerotic, Syphilitic, Congenital).
False aneurysms: Breach in the wall with a hematoma contained by connective tissue.
Dissection: Blood entering the wall itself through an intimal tear.
Saccular: 'Berry-like' outpouching.
Fusiform: Symmetric, spindle-shaped.
microReview: Understanding the layers involved is critical. If the wall is intact (even if weak), it is true. If the wall is broken and the 'vessel' is actually a blood clot held by surrounding tissue, it is a pseudoaneurysm.
examinerTraps: Aortic dissection is NOT an aneurysm; it is blood tracking within the media. However, a dissection can occur within an aneurysmal vessel.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old man with Marfan syndrome presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset, severe chest pain. Imaging reveals a significant dilation of the ascending aorta. Histological examination of the aortic wall would most likely show which of the following features?

options.b: Medial fragmentation and loss of elastic fibers
options.e: Foamy macrophage accumulation in the subendothelial space

explanations.a: Neutrophilic infiltration is seen in infectious or mycotic aneurysms, not Marfan syndrome.
explanations.b: Marfan syndrome leads to cystic medial degeneration, characterized by the fragmentation of elastic tissue and the accumulation of proteoglycans.
explanations.c: Granulomatous inflammation is characteristic of vasculitides like Giant Cell Arteritis.
explanations.d: Onion-skinning is seen in hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis associated with malignant hypertension.
explanations.e: Foamy macrophages are the hallmark of atherosclerotic plaques, which typically cause abdominal, not ascending thoracic, aneurysms.

ankiCards: The characteristic histological finding in Marfan-related thoracic aneurysms is {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
Cystic medial degeneration involves the loss of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} and elastic fibers.
In Marfan syndrome, mutations in the {{c1::fibrillin-1 (FBN1)}} gene lead to excessive TGF-β signaling.
{{c1::TGF-β}} signaling dysregulation leads to weakened elastic tissue in the aortic media.
Thoracic aortic aneurysms are most commonly associated with {{c1::hypertension}} and Marfan syndrome.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome: FBN1 mutation -> high TGF-beta -> weak ECM.
Cystic medial degeneration: Not actually 'cysts', but areas of proteoglycan accumulation.
Commonly affects the ascending aorta.
Risk of aortic dissection is extremely high in these patients.
Clinical signs: Tall stature, arachnodactyly, lens subluxation.
microReview: Marfan syndrome represents a genetic cause of medial weakening. Unlike atherosclerosis which causes secondary medial atrophy, Marfan involves a primary defect in the scaffolding (fibrillin) and regulatory signaling (TGF-β) of the media.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'Cystic Medial Degeneration' with 'Atherosclerosis'. AAAs = Atherosclerosis; Ascending TAAs = Hypertension or Marfan syndrome.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the pathogenesis of abdominal aortic aneurysms, which of the following best describes the role of the inflammatory infiltrate found in the vessel wall?

options.a: Production of antibodies against endothelial cells
options.b: Release of perforins causing smooth muscle necrosis
options.c: Secretions of matrix metalloproteinases that digest elastin
options.d: Formation of a protective fibrous cap over the media
options.e: Induction of angiogenesis to provide nutrients to the media

explanations.a: Anti-endothelial antibodies are associated with some vasculitides (e.g., Kawasaki), not typically AAA.
explanations.b: While smooth muscle loss occurs, it is generally due to ischemia or apoptosis, not primary perforin-mediated attack.
explanations.c: Macrophages in the inflammatory infiltrate secrete matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), which are essential for degrading the structural collagen and elastin.
explanations.d: A fibrous cap is a feature of an atherosclerotic plaque, not the media-weakening inflammatory process itself.
explanations.e: While neovascularization occurs, the primary pathologic role of the infiltrate is destruction of the ECM.

ankiCards: Inflammatory cells in an aneurysm wall secrete {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
MMPs primarily degrade two structural proteins in the aorta: {{c1::collagen and elastin}}.
Chronic inflammation in AAA is often triggered by {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Degradation of the {{c1::extracellular matrix}} is the final common pathway for wall weakening.
Genetic variants in {{c1::MMP-9}} have been associated with increased risk of AAA.
keyPoints: AAA pathogenesis is an active process of matrix remodeling.
Inflammatory cells (macrophages, T cells) are key players.
Tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs) are often decreased.
The loss of elastin is responsible for the initial dilation.
The loss of collagen is responsible for eventual rupture.
microReview: Think of the aneurysm wall as a battleground where degradative enzymes (MMPs) outpace the building/repair enzymes. This shifts the balance towards vessel wall thinning and outward expansion.
examinerTraps: The examiner might try to suggest the inflammation is 'infectious' (like a mycotic aneurysm). In the context of a typical AAA, the inflammation is a sterile response to atherosclerosis.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following locations is most characteristic for the development of a 'Berry' aneurysm?

explanations.a: The infrarenal aorta is the classic site for atherosclerotic AAAs.
explanations.b: The ascending aorta is the site for hypertensive or Marfan-related TAAs.
explanations.c: Berry aneurysms are small, saccular dilations occurring at branch points in the Circle of Willis (cerebral circulation).
explanations.d: Popliteal aneurysms are often associated with AAAs but are not called 'Berry' aneurysms.
explanations.e: Splenic artery aneurysms are the most common visceral aneurysms but are not 'Berry' aneurysms.

ankiCards: A 'Berry' aneurysm is a type of {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm.
The most common location for Berry aneurysms is the {{c1::Circle of Willis}}.
Rupture of a Berry aneurysm causes {{c1::subarachnoid}} hemorrhage.
Berry aneurysms are associated with {{c1::Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD)}}.
Berry aneurysms occur at vessel {{c1::branch points}} due to congenital media defects.
keyPoints: Berry aneurysms: Saccular, small, cerebral.
Site: Anterior communicating artery (most common).
Pathology: Absence of internal elastic lamina and smooth muscle at branch points.
Risk: Hypertension and smoking increase rupture risk.
Complication: 'Worst headache of my life' (subarachnoid hemorrhage).
microReview: Berry aneurysms are unique because they are often congenital (medial defects) rather than acquired through atherosclerosis, though hypertension plays a role in their expansion and rupture.
examinerTraps: Aneurysms in the Circle of Willis are Berry aneurysms; aneurysms in the small penetrating branches (Charcot-Bouchard) lead to intraparenchymal hemorrhage, not subarachnoid.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old man with untreated syphilis presents with a bark-like cough and difficulty swallowing. Chest X-ray reveals a dilated aortic arch. The pathology is driven by an obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum. Which layer of the aorta is most severely damaged as a direct consequence of this ischemia?

explanations.a: The intima actually thickens in response to the injury (tree-bark appearance), but it is not the site of the primary structural failure.
explanations.b: The vasa vasorum supply the outer two-thirds of the media. Obliteration leads to medial ischemia, loss of elastic fibers, and replacement with scar tissue.
explanations.c: The adventitia contains the vasa vasorum and shows inflammation, but the mechanical failure leading to the aneurysm occurs in the media.
explanations.d: Damage is widespread throughout the media, not localized solely to the internal elastic lamina.
explanations.e: The external elastic lamina is within the media/adventitia junction, but the entire media is the functional layer that fails.

ankiCards: Syphilitic aneurysms are caused by {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}} of the vasa vasorum.
Ischemia of the {{c1::tunica media}} leads to the 'tree-bark' appearance in syphilitic aortitis.
Syphilitic aneurysms typically involve the {{c1::ascending}} aorta.
Dilation of the aortic root in syphilis can lead to {{c1::aortic valve insufficiency}}.
Syphilitic aortitis is a manifestation of {{c1::tertiary}} syphilis.
keyPoints: Tertiary syphilis -> Vasa vasorum endarteritis -> Medial ischemia.
The resulting scarring causes 'tree-bark' intimal wrinkling.
The ascending aorta is preferentially affected.
Can cause 'Cor Bovinum' (massive heart) due to aortic regurgitation.
Now rare due to effective antibiotic treatment of early syphilis.
microReview: Syphilitic aneurysms are the classic example of 'obliterative endarteritis'. By choking off the blood supply to the vessel's own wall (the vasa vasorum), the strongest part of the vessel (the media) dies and is replaced by weak scar tissue.
examinerTraps: The 'tree-barking' is in the intima, but the 'weakness' is in the media. If asked what fails to cause the aneurysm, the answer is the media.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: According to the Law of Laplace, which of the following describes why an aneurysm is more likely to rupture as it increases in diameter?

options.a: The pressure inside the vessel decreases as the radius increases
options.b: The wall tension increases proportionally with the radius
options.c: The velocity of blood flow increases in the dilated segment
options.d: The thickness of the vessel wall increases to compensate for the dilation
options.e: The turbulence within the aneurysm decreases the wall stress

explanations.a: Pressure does not necessarily decrease; it is the tension on the wall that changes.
explanations.b: Wall Tension (T) = Pressure (P) × Radius (r). As the radius increases, the tension required to contain the same pressure increases, leading to rupture.
explanations.c: Velocity actually decreases in a dilated segment (Continuity Equation), which can lead to stasis and thrombosis.
explanations.d: The wall actually gets thinner (attenuated), not thicker, which further increases the risk of rupture.
explanations.e: Turbulence increases (high Reynolds number) in an aneurysm, which increases wall stress and risk of thrombus.

ankiCards: According to the Law of Laplace, Wall Tension is equal to {{c1::Pressure times Radius}}.
As an aneurysm's radius increases, the {{c1::wall tension}} increases.
The risk of AAA rupture increases significantly when the diameter exceeds {{c1::5.0 - 5.5}} cm.
{{c1::Stasis}} of blood within an aneurysm often leads to the formation of mural thrombi.
Laminar flow is replaced by {{c1::turbulent}} flow within the aneurysmal sac.
keyPoints: Law of Laplace: T = P x r.
Increasing diameter -> Exponentially increasing wall stress.
Stasis in the aneurysm sac predisposes to mural thrombi.
Mural thrombi can embolize (e.g., 'Blue Toe Syndrome').
Clinical management is based on diameter thresholds (e.g., surgery at 5.5cm).
microReview: Physics dictates the progression of aneurysms. Once a vessel starts dilating, the physics (Laplace) makes it harder and harder for the thinning wall to resist the internal pressure, creating a vicious cycle ending in rupture.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse velocity and pressure. In an aneurysm, the 'stretching' (tension) is the killer, governed by the radius.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old intravenous drug user presents with fever and a painful, rapidly enlarging mass in the right groin. Blood cultures are positive for Staphylococcus aureus. Imaging shows a 3 cm localized dilation of the femoral artery. This condition is most accurately termed which of the following?

explanations.a: While it may be saccular in shape, 'Mycotic' more accurately describes the infectious etiology.
explanations.b: Fusiform describes a long, symmetric dilation, which is less common in acute infections.
explanations.c: A mycotic aneurysm is an aneurysm arising from an infection (bacterial, fungal) that weakens the vessel wall.
explanations.d: Dissection involves blood entering the wall layers; it is not primarily an infectious dilation.
explanations.e: Berry aneurysms are specific to the cerebral circulation and are generally not infectious.

ankiCards: A {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm is caused by an infection of the arterial wall.
Common causes of mycotic aneurysms include {{c1::infective endocarditis}} and IV drug use.
The term 'mycotic' is a misnomer, as most of these aneurysms are caused by {{c1::bacteria}}.
Mycotic aneurysms are dangerous because they can rapidly {{c1::rupture}} due to suppuration.
Inflammatory destruction of the {{c1::tunica media}} is the hallmark of mycotic aneurysms.
keyPoints: Mycotic aneurysms can result from embolization of a septic thrombus.
They can also occur from direct extension of an adjacent infection.
Staphylococcus and Salmonella are frequent bacterial culprits.
They present with signs of infection (fever, leukocytosis) plus a pulsatile mass.
Treatment requires both antibiotics and often surgical intervention.
microReview: Mycotic aneurysms are the 'septic' version of wall weakening. Proteolytic enzymes from bacteria and neutrophils rapidly destroy the media, leading to high rupture risk compared to the slow progression of atherosclerotic aneurysms.
examinerTraps: The word 'mycotic' sounds like it refers only to fungi, but it refers to any infectious aneurysm (mostly bacterial).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Atherosclerotic plaques contribute to the formation of abdominal aortic aneurysms primarily by which of the following mechanisms?

options.a: Direct mechanical erosion of the tunica adventitia
options.b: Increasing the intraluminal pressure via stenosis
options.c: Inhibiting the release of nitric oxide from the endothelium
options.d: Obstructing diffusion of oxygen and nutrients to the media
options.e: Promoting the calcification of the internal elastic lamina

explanations.a: The plaque starts in the intima; it does not mechanically 'erode' from the outside (adventitia).
explanations.b: AAA usually occurs in large vessels where atherosclerosis does not cause significant stenosis; therefore, pressure does not increase significantly due to the plaque.
explanations.c: While NO release is impaired, this leads to vasoconstriction/hypertension, not the structural medial failure that defines an aneurysm.
explanations.d: A thick atherosclerotic plaque increases the diffusion distance for oxygen and nutrients from the lumen to the media, leading to medial ischemia and atrophy.
explanations.e: Calcification occurs but usually makes the vessel stiffer, not necessarily weaker in the way that leads to dilation.

ankiCards: Atherosclerosis causes AAA by creating a {{c1::diffusion barrier}} for nutrients.
Ischemia to the tunica media in AAA leads to {{c1::atrophy}} of smooth muscle cells.
The abdominal aorta is vulnerable to AAA because it has less {{c1::vasa vasorum}} than the thoracic aorta.
AAA is usually associated with {{c1::severe}} atherosclerosis.
Atherosclerotic plaques in AAA are often covered by a {{c1::mural thrombus}}.
keyPoints: Media depends on diffusion from the lumen (inner half) and vasa vasorum (outer half).
Atherosclerosis thickens the intima, blocking luminal diffusion.
Result: Medial 'starvation' and weakening.
This explains why AAA is infrarenal (where vasa vasorum are sparse).
Smoking exacerbates this by causing further vasoconstriction and hypoxia.
microReview: The vessel wall is a living tissue that needs food. Atherosclerosis acts like a 'blanket' over the intima, preventing the media from getting oxygen from the blood. This results in the death of the muscle cells that hold the vessel together.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'stenosis' of atherosclerosis in small vessels (like coronary arteries) with the 'dilation' it causes in the aorta.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 1-month-old male infant is brought to the clinic by his parents due to a rapidly enlarging red lesion on his right cheek. The lesion was not present at birth but appeared at 2 weeks of age. Physical examination reveals a 2-cm, bright red, lobulated, elevated mass that blanches slightly upon pressure. The lesion is soft and non-tender. Which of the following is the most likely clinical course for this lesion?

options.a: Progressive enlargement and eventual malignant transformation
options.c: Lifelong persistence with gradual darkening to a deep purple
options.d: Rapid invasion into local facial musculature and bone
options.e: Systemic dissemination to the lungs and liver

explanations.a: Vascular tumors like capillary hemangiomas are benign and do not undergo malignant transformation.
explanations.b: Capillary (strawberry) hemangiomas of infancy typically grow rapidly for a few months and then begin to involute, with most regressing completely by age 7 to 9.
explanations.c: Port-wine stains (nevus flammeus) tend to persist and darken, but strawberry hemangiomas regress.
explanations.d: This lesion is a benign capillary hemangioma, which is circumscribed and does not exhibit aggressive local invasion.
explanations.e: Benign hemangiomas do not metastasize; this behavior is characteristic of malignant angiosarcomas.

ankiCards: Infantile strawberry hemangiomas typically {{c1::regress}} by age 7.
The most common vascular tumor of infancy is the {{c1::capillary hemangioma}}.
{{c1::Capillary}} hemangiomas are composed of thin-walled capillaries with scanty stroma.
Unlike port-wine stains, strawberry hemangiomas {{c1::are not}} present at birth.
A strawberry hemangioma initially grows {{c1::rapidly}} before eventual involution.
keyPoints: Capillary hemangiomas are the most common vascular tumors of infancy.
They are often referred to as 'strawberry hemangiomas' due to their bright red appearance.
Lesions typically appear shortly after birth and grow rapidly for several months.
The vast majority (75-90%) undergo spontaneous involution by early childhood.
Histologically, they consist of packed, thin-walled capillaries lined by endothelial cells.
microReview: Juvenile capillary hemangiomas are benign, extremely common in neonates, and follow a predictable cycle of rapid growth followed by slow regression.
examinerTraps: Confusing strawberry hemangiomas (regress) with nevus flammeus/port-wine stains (persist and grow with the child).
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors are divided into three categories: (1) benign tumors, which are common and usually do not recur; (2) intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors; and (3) malignant tumors (angiosarcomas), which are rare but highly aggressive.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 34-year-old male with a history of HIV (CD4 count 150 cells/µL) presents with several painless, dark-purple, maculopapular lesions on his shins and hard palate. Biopsy of a lesion reveals spindle-shaped cells, poorly formed vascular spaces containing red blood cells, and extravasated erythrocytes with hemosiderin-laden macrophages. Which of the following pathogens is the causative agent of this condition?

explanations.a: HHV-6 causes Roseola infantum, not vascular tumors.
explanations.b: HHV-8 (also known as Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus, KSHV) is the definitive causative agent for all forms of Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.c: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.d: CMV causes retinitis and colitis in AIDS patients but is not the driver of Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.e: HPV-16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas (cervical, anal, oropharyngeal).

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is caused by {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
The classic histological feature of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells}} and slit-like vascular spaces.
In AIDS patients, Kaposi Sarcoma is categorized as {{c1::Epidemic}} KS.
HHV-8 induces Kaposi Sarcoma by promoting {{c1::endothelial}} cell proliferation.
The primary cells of origin in Kaposi Sarcoma are {{c1::endothelial}} cells (likely lymphatic).
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is an intermediate-grade vascular neoplasm.
HHV-8 is required for the development of all four clinical subtypes of KS.
Histology shows spindle cells, slit-like spaces, and extravasated RBCs.
Epidemic KS is the most common HIV-related malignancy.
Lesions progress through patch, plaque, and nodule stages.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma is a spindle cell tumor of endothelial origin strongly linked to HHV-8 infection, particularly in immunocompromised states.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Kaposi Sarcoma (HHV-8) with Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella), which presents similarly in AIDS patients but shows neutrophils and bacteria on Warthin-Starry stain.
sourceQuote: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a borderline vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8; it is most common in the setting of AIDS.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old female presents with multiple enlarging, ill-defined, violaceous skin nodules on her left upper arm. She has a history of a radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection and radiotherapy for breast cancer 12 years ago. Since the surgery, she has had persistent, severe lymphedema of the left arm. A biopsy of a skin nodule shows highly atypical endothelial cells forming irregular, anastomosing vascular channels. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors are small, painful benign tumors found under fingernails.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign proliferation seen in AIDS patients, caused by Bartonella.
explanations.c: Angiosarcomas are malignant vascular tumors that can arise in the setting of chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome), often following radical mastectomy and radiation.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign lesions that do not show cellular atypia or anastomosing channels.
explanations.e: Pyogenic granulomas are benign, rapidly growing red nodules, often on the gingiva or skin, with no association with chronic lymphedema.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves}} syndrome.
Histology of angiosarcoma shows highly {{c1::atypical}} endothelial cells.
A major risk factor for cutaneous angiosarcoma of the arm is previous {{c1::mastectomy with lymph node dissection}}.
Angiosarcoma is a {{c1::malignant}} vascular tumor.
Marker for identifying endothelial origin in angiosarcoma: {{c1::CD31}} (or vWF).
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are rare, highly malignant vascular neoplasms.
Risk factors include chronic lymphedema, radiation, and chemical exposures (vinyl chloride).
Stewart-Treves syndrome refers specifically to angiosarcoma following mastectomy-related lymphedema.
Histologically, they show irregular vascular channels lined by pleomorphic endothelial cells.
The 5-year survival rate is generally poor due to aggressive local invasion and metastasis.
microReview: Cutaneous angiosarcoma in the context of post-mastectomy lymphedema is the classic presentation of Stewart-Treves syndrome.
examinerTraps: Mistaking the 'violaceous' nodules for Kaposi Sarcoma. In a post-mastectomy patient with lymphedema, Angiosarcoma is the primary concern.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas are malignant vascular neoplasms that range from highly differentiated tumors with vascular channels... to wildly undifferentiated tumors.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with an intensely painful, 4-mm, blue-tinted nodule located under the nail bed of her right index finger. She notes that the pain is paroxysmal and exquisitely sensitive to cold temperatures. Excision of the lesion is performed. Histological examination reveals aggregates of specialized, uniform, round cells surrounding thin-walled vascular spaces. From which of the following cell types does this tumor originate?

explanations.a: Most vascular tumors arise from endothelial cells, but the glomus tumor is a specific exception.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors arise from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.c: Fibroblasts produce collagen; they are not the cell of origin for glomus tumors.
explanations.d: Pericytes are the origin for hemangiopericytomas (now often classified as solitary fibrous tumors), not glomus tumors.
explanations.e: Histiocytes are macrophage-lineage cells and are not involved in glomus tumor pathogenesis.

ankiCards: The classic location for a glomus tumor is {{c1::subungual}} (under the fingernail).
The key clinical symptom of a glomus tumor is {{c1::intense pain}} (often cold-sensitive).
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells.
The function of the normal glomus body is {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
On histology, glomus cells appear as {{c1::uniform round}} cells.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign, exquisitely painful tumors.
They are most commonly found in the distal portion of the fingers, particularly subungual.
They originate from the glomus body (an AV shunt for thermoregulation).
The tumor cells are modified smooth muscle cells, not endothelial cells.
Treatment is simple surgical excision, which is curative.
microReview: A painful, cold-sensitive subungual nodule is the pathognomonic presentation of a glomus tumor (modified smooth muscle cells).
examinerTraps: Assuming all vascular tumors are endothelial in origin. Glomus tumors are specifically from smooth muscle cells.
sourceQuote: Glomus tumors are benign, exquisitely painful tumors arising from specialized smooth muscle cells of the glomus bodies, arteriovenous structures involved in thermoregulation.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An immunocompromised patient presents with multiple red, friable, skin papules. Histology demonstrates a lobular proliferation of capillaries with prominent protuberant endothelial cells and an infiltrate of neutrophils. A Warthin-Starry silver stain reveals clusters of small, extracellular bacilli. Which of the following is the most likely pathogen responsible for these lesions?

explanations.a: Bartonella henselae (and B. quintana) causes bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised hosts, characterized by vascular proliferation and neutrophilic inflammation.
explanations.b: S. aureus causes pyogenic infections (abscesses, impetigo) but not organized vascular proliferative tumors.
explanations.c: MAC causes systemic infection in AIDS but does not typically present as vascular skin nodules.
explanations.d: HHV-8 causes Kaposi Sarcoma, which lacks the neutrophilic infiltrate and bacterial clusters seen here.
explanations.e: T. pallidum causes syphilis; while it involves blood vessels (endarteritis), it does not cause this specific angiomatous lesion.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
The histological stain used to identify Bartonella in bacillary angiomatosis is {{c1::Warthin-Starry}}.
Unlike Kaposi Sarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis contains an infiltrate of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
Bacillary angiomatosis occurs primarily in {{c1::immunocompromised}} patients.
Treatment for bacillary angiomatosis involves {{c1::erythromycin}} (or doxycycline).
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation caused by Bartonella bacteria.
It is an opportunistic infection in AIDS/immunocompromised patients.
Clinical presentation: Red skin papules or nodules.
Histology: Proliferating capillaries with nuclear atypia and neutrophils.
Silver stains (Warthin-Starry) are diagnostic, showing the bacilli.
microReview: Bacillary angiomatosis = AIDS + red papules + neutrophils + Bartonella (Warthin-Starry positive).
examinerTraps: Visually confusing this with Kaposi Sarcoma. Look for 'neutrophils' or 'silver stain' to distinguish Bartonella infection.
sourceQuote: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts... caused by opportunistic gram-negative bacilli of the Bartonella family.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with a rapidly growing, painless, pedunculated red nodule on her gingiva that bleeds easily with minor trauma. The lesion appeared two weeks ago. Physical exam shows a 1-cm, friable, ulcerated mass. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors are intensely painful and typically subungual, not gingival.
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor with significant atypia, not a common rapidly growing lesion in pregnancy.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a common, rapidly growing, pedunculated red lesion on skin or oral mucosa that often occurs in pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.d: Cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) are usually found in the neck of infants and are not pedunculated friable masses.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis occurs in immunocompromised individuals; this patient is pregnant but otherwise healthy.

ankiCards: A pyogenic granuloma occurring on the gingiva of a pregnant woman is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized by {{c1::rapid}} growth and frequent bleeding.
Histologically, pyogenic granuloma resembles {{c1::granulation tissue}}.
Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer because it is neither {{c1::pyogenic}} nor a true {{c1::granuloma}}.
The typical treatment for a pyogenic granuloma is {{c1::surgical excision}} (or curettage).
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a lobular capillary hemangioma.
It presents as a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated mass.
Commonly involves skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
Frequently associated with pregnancy (hormonal influence) or trauma.
Despite the name, it is not an infection and does not contain granulomas.
microReview: Pyogenic granuloma = 'Pregnancy tumor' of the gums; looks like red, bleeding granulation tissue.
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic granuloma' is a double misnomer; it is not induced by pus-forming bacteria and is not a granuloma histologically.
sourceQuote: Pyogenic granulomas are capillary hemangiomas that manifest as rapidly growing red pedunculated lesions on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A newborn is found to have a large, soft, fluctuant mass on the left side of the neck. Transillumination of the mass is positive. Chromosomal analysis reveals a 45,XO karyotype. The neck mass is most likely composed of which of the following?

options.d: Sheets of uniform round smooth muscle cells

explanations.a: The description (neck mass, transillumination, Turner syndrome) fits a cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma), which consists of massively dilated lymphatic spaces lined by endothelium.
explanations.b: This describes a capillary hemangioma, not usually associated with Turner syndrome or transillumination.
explanations.c: This describes a malignant tumor like angiosarcoma, which is not neonatal.
explanations.d: This describes a glomus tumor.
explanations.e: This describes a cavernous hemangioma, which contains blood, whereas cystic hygromas contain lymph (which transilluminates).

ankiCards: Cystic hygroma is the common name for a large {{c1::cavernous lymphangioma}}.
Cystic hygromas are frequently associated with {{c1::Turner}} syndrome (45,XO).
The classic location for a cystic hygroma is the {{c1::neck}} (or axilla).
Unlike hemangiomas, cystic hygromas contain {{c1::lymph}} rather than blood.
On examination, a cystic hygroma will {{c1::transilluminate}}.
keyPoints: Cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) are benign lymphatic malformations.
Commonly found in the neck or axilla of infants.
Strongly associated with Turner syndrome and Down syndrome.
They consist of large, dilated lymphatic spaces lined by endothelial cells.
They can be large and difficult to resect due to lack of distinct capsules.
microReview: Turner syndrome + neck mass that transilluminates = Cystic hygroma (lymphatic origin).
examinerTraps: Confusing lymphangiomas with hemangiomas. Key difference: Lymphangiomas have no RBCs in the spaces and transilluminate better.
sourceQuote: Cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) are typically found in the neck or axilla of children and are sometimes associated with Turner syndrome.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 62-year-old man who worked for 30 years in a factory producing polyvinyl chloride (PVC) presents with abdominal pain, weight loss, and jaundice. Imaging shows multiple hemorrhagic masses within the liver. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Hepatocellular carcinoma is associated with HBV/HCV and cirrhosis, not specifically vinyl chloride.
explanations.b: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare malignant tumor specifically associated with exposure to vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas are the most common benign liver tumors, but they are not linked to chemical carcinogens.
explanations.d: Hepatic adenomas are associated with oral contraceptive use.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis affects the liver (peliosis hepatis) but is caused by Bartonella in HIV patients, not industrial chemicals.

ankiCards: Exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}} is a known risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is also associated with exposure to {{c1::arsenic}}.
{{c1::Thorotrast}} (a former radiopaque contrast medium) is linked to hepatic angiosarcoma.
Angiosarcomas of the liver are highly {{c1::malignant/aggressive}}.
The cells of origin in hepatic angiosarcoma are {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare but classic 'environmental' cancer.
Associated with vinyl chloride (plastic industry), arsenic (pesticides), and Thorotrast.
It is a highly aggressive malignancy with a very poor prognosis.
Presents with non-specific symptoms like weight loss and abdominal pain.
Histology shows malignant endothelial cells lining vascular channels.
microReview: Vinyl chloride exposure + Liver masses = Hepatic Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Mistaking this for Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC). Vinyl chloride is the specific 'buzzword' for angiosarcoma of the liver.
sourceQuote: Hepatic angiosarcomas are associated with distinct carcinogens, including arsenic (used in pesticides), Thorotrast... and polyvinyl chloride (used in the plastics industry).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular tumors are pathologically classified based on their behavior. Into which of the following categories is a 'Hemangioendothelioma' placed?

explanations.a: Hemangiomas are benign. Hemangioendotheliomas have more aggressive potential.
explanations.b: Hemangioendotheliomas (e.g., epithelioid hemangioendothelioma) are classified as intermediate-grade/borderline tumors, meaning their behavior is between benign hemangiomas and malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.c: Angiosarcomas are fully malignant.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granulomas are often considered reactive, but hemangioendotheliomas are true neoplasms.
explanations.e: Vascular ectasias are hamartomatous-like, but hemangioendotheliomas are neoplastic.

ankiCards: Vascular tumors are classified as benign, {{c1::intermediate (borderline)}}, or malignant.
An example of an intermediate-grade vascular tumor is {{c1::hemangioendothelioma}}.
Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma typically occurs around {{c1::medium and large}} sized veins.
Borderline vascular tumors have a clinical course between {{c1::hemangiomas}} and {{c1::angiosarcomas}}.
Most hemangioendotheliomas are cured by {{c1::excision}}, but some can metastasize.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors follow a spectrum of biological behavior.
Hemangioendothelioma is the classic 'intermediate' category.
Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is a common subtype.
Clinical behavior is unpredictable but usually less aggressive than angiosarcoma.
Classification helps guide the aggressiveness of surgical and adjuvant therapy.
microReview: Tumor Spectrum: Hemangioma (Benign) -> Hemangioendothelioma (Borderline) -> Angiosarcoma (Malignant).
examinerTraps: Confusing the name 'Hemangioendothelioma' with 'Hemangioma' (benign) or 'Angiosarcoma' (malignant).
sourceQuote: Intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors: Hemangioendotheliomas represent a diverse group of vascular neoplasms with clinical behaviors that span the range between benign hemangiomas and highly malignant angiosarcomas.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Pathologists often use immunohistochemical markers to confirm the endothelial origin of poorly differentiated tumors. Which of the following markers is the most specific for identifying endothelial cells in a suspected angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: CD3 is a T-cell marker.
explanations.b: CD20 is a B-cell marker.
explanations.c: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a membrane glycoprotein highly expressed on endothelial cells and is used to confirm vascular differentiation.
explanations.d: CD45 is the common leukocyte antigen (CLA).
explanations.e: CD68 is a marker for macrophages/histiocytes.

ankiCards: The most common endothelial immunohistochemical marker is {{c1::CD31}}.
Another marker for endothelial cells is {{c1::von Willebrand factor (vWF)}}.
CD31 is also known as {{c1::PECAM-1}}.
Immunohistochemistry is vital for diagnosing poorly differentiated {{c1::angiosarcomas}}.
Markers like CD31 help distinguish vascular tumors from {{c1::carcinomas}} or lymphomas.
keyPoints: Endothelial markers are essential for diagnosing vascular neoplasms.
CD31 is highly sensitive and specific for endothelial differentiation.
Other markers include von Willebrand factor and CD34.
These markers help identify 'slit-like' spaces as vascular in origin.
In angiosarcoma, these markers may be the only evidence of the tumor's lineage.
microReview: Endothelial origin markers = CD31, CD34, vWF.
examinerTraps: CD34 is also an endothelial marker but is less specific than CD31 as it can be found in various fibroblastic tumors.
sourceQuote: Malignant endothelial cells can be identified by immunohistochemical staining for endothelial-specific markers such as CD31 or von Willebrand factor.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history presents to the emergency department with a deep, boring sensation in his lower back. On physical examination, a pulsatile mass is palpated in the mid-abdomen, superior to the umbilicus. Ultrasound reveals a 5.5-cm focal dilation of the infrarenal aorta. What is the most significant pathological mechanism contributing to the development of this lesion?

options.b: Cystic medial necrosis from TGF-beta signaling
options.c: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.e: Vessel wall thinning due to chronic hypertension

explanations.a: Atherosclerosis is the dominant risk factor and primary cause for Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms (AAA). The atherosclerotic plaque impairs nutrient diffusion from the lumen to the media, leading to smooth muscle cell death and extracellular matrix degradation (medial thinning).
explanations.b: Cystic medial necrosis is more commonly associated with Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms, often seen in genetic syndromes like Marfan syndrome.
explanations.c: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum is the hallmark of tertiary syphilis, which typically affects the ascending aorta (thoracic), not the abdominal aorta.
explanations.d: Polyarteritis nodosa causes necrotizing vasculitis and 'beading' in medium-sized muscular arteries, not large elastic arteries like the aorta.
explanations.e: While hypertension contributes to many vascular pathologies, atherosclerosis is specifically the most significant risk factor for the expansion and weakening of the abdominal aorta.

ankiCards: The most significant risk factor for the development of an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Abdominal aortic aneurysms typically occur {{c1::inferior}} to the renal arteries.
The primary pathological mechanism of AAA involves thinning of the {{c1::media}} layer of the vessel wall.
A clinical sign of an abdominal aortic aneurysm is a {{c1::pulsatile}} abdominal mass.
In AAA, atherosclerosis causes medial thinning by {{c1::impairing nutrient diffusion}} from the lumen.
keyPoints: AAA is primarily associated with atherosclerosis and smoking.
Most AAAs are located below the renal arteries and above the iliac bifurcation.
Medial weakening results from inflammation and matrix degradation within the wall.
AAA occurs more frequently in men and smokers older than age 50.
Clinical consequences include rupture, obstruction of branch vessels, and embolism.
microReview: Aneurysms involve a weakening of the vessel wall leading to dilation. Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are usually caused by atherosclerosis, while thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAA) are often caused by hypertension or connective tissue disorders. AAA presents as a pulsatile mass; rupture risk increases significantly when the diameter exceeds 5 cm.
examinerTraps: Students often confuse the primary cause of AAA (atherosclerosis) with the primary cause of Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (hypertension) or Syphilitic Aneurysms (obliterative endarteritis).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the two principal mechanisms that underlie the majority of clinically significant vascular diseases?

options.a: Endothelial hyperplasia and venous valve failure
options.b: Luminal narrowing and weakening of vessel walls
options.c: Lymphatic obstruction and smooth muscle atrophy
options.d: Pulsatile flow reduction and intimal calcification

explanations.a: While venous disorders are important, they are not the principal mechanism of the most morbid vascular diseases (like arterial ones).
explanations.b: Vascular disease morbidity and mortality are primarily driven by either stenosis/obstruction (narrowing) or wall weakening (dilation/rupture).
explanations.c: Lymphatic obstruction is a specific mechanism for lymphedema, not the broad underlying mechanism of vascular disease.
explanations.d: While intimal calcification occurs in atherosclerosis, it is a feature of the narrowing process, not a standalone principal category.
explanations.e: These are features of inflammation and shock, but not the primary structural mechanisms of chronic vascular pathology.

ankiCards: The two principal mechanisms of vascular disease are {{c1::narrowing (stenosis)}} and {{c2::weakening}} of vessel walls.
Narrowing of vessel lumens can occur progressively through {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Precipitous obstruction of a vessel lumen is usually caused by {{c1::thrombosis}} or {{c2::embolism}}.
Weakening of vessel walls typically leads to {{c1::dilation}} or {{c2::rupture}}.
Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity than any other category of {{c1::human disease}}.
keyPoints: Vascular disease is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality.
Pathology is divided into luminal obstruction and wall structural failure.
Stenosis can be slow (atherosclerosis) or sudden (embolism).
Structural failure leads to aneurysms and dissections.
Arterial lesions are generally more clinically significant than venous ones.
microReview: Vascular pathology focuses on two themes: Ischemia (due to narrowing/stenosis) and Hemorrhage/Aneurysm (due to weakening).
examinerTraps: Don't focus on just one mechanism like 'clots'; remember that structural weakening of the wall (aneurysm) is just as significant as narrowing.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which structural feature of the arterial system primarily allows muscular arteries to exert fine-tuned control over blood flow and systemic blood pressure?

options.a: A high ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter
options.b: An internal elastic lamina in the tunica adventitia
options.c: Extensive vasa vasorum in the intimal layer
options.d: Presence of valves to prevent retrograde flow
options.e: The absence of a smooth muscle media layer

explanations.a: As arteries become smaller, the absolute wall thickness decreases, but the ratio of wall thickness to the lumen diameter increases, facilitating better vasomotor control.
explanations.b: The internal elastic lamina is between the intima and media, not in the adventitia.
explanations.c: The vasa vasorum are found in the adventitia and outer media of large vessels, not the intima.
explanations.d: Valves are a characteristic of veins, not muscular arteries.
explanations.e: Muscular arteries have a prominent smooth muscle media layer by definition.

ankiCards: Arterial walls are {{c1::thicker}} than corresponding veins to accommodate higher pressures.
As arteries become smaller, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}}.
Control over blood flow and pressure is exerted by {{c1::muscular}} vessels.
Atherosclerosis primarily affects {{c1::elastic}} and {{c2::muscular}} arteries.
Structural specializations in vessels reflect their distinct {{c1::functional roles}}.
keyPoints: Arterial walls are thicker than venous walls at the same level.
Higher wall-to-lumen ratios in small vessels allow for pressure regulation.
The architectural design of vessels correlates with their physiological function.
Elastic arteries (aorta) handle high pressure; muscular arteries control flow.
Vascular disorders often show characteristic anatomic distributions based on vessel type.
microReview: Vessel structure dictates pathology. Elastic arteries (aorta) are prone to aneurysms due to pressure; muscular arteries are prone to narrowing; arterioles are prone to hypertensive changes.
examinerTraps: Avoid thinking that 'thickness' only refers to the absolute size; the ratio relative to the lumen is the key for resistance vessels.
sourceQuote: the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing these muscular vessels to exert control over blood flow and pressure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 58-year-old female with a history of long-standing hypertension and Marfan syndrome presents with sudden, excruciating pain that she describes as 'tearing' and 'radiating through to her back.' An imaging study shows a separation of the aortic layers with an accumulation of blood within the media. Which of the following is the most likely underlying histologic finding in this patient's aorta?

explanations.a: Aschoff bodies are seen in rheumatic heart disease, not aortic dissections.
explanations.b: Cystic medial degeneration, characterized by loss of smooth muscle cells and elastic tissue with accumulation of mucoid material, is the classic histological finding in aortic dissection, especially in those with Marfan syndrome.
explanations.c: Fibrinoid necrosis is typically seen in the arterioles of patients with malignant hypertension, not the large elastic arteries like the aorta.
explanations.d: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis occurs in small arteries and arterioles in response to benign hypertension or diabetes.
explanations.e: Transmural necrotizing vasculitis is characteristic of Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN).

ankiCards: The classic histological finding associated with aortic dissection and Marfan syndrome is {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
Aortic dissection is characterized by blood entering the {{c1::media}} layer of the vessel.
A major risk factor for aortic dissection is {{c1::hypertension}}.
The 'tearing' chest pain radiating to the back is highly suggestive of {{c1::aortic dissection}}.
Cystic medial degeneration involves the fragmentation of {{c1::elastic}} fibers.
keyPoints: Aortic dissection involves blood splitting the media layer.
Hypertension is the most common risk factor for dissection.
Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1 mutation) is a major genetic predisposition.
Cystic medial degeneration is the typical pathological change.
Dissections are medical emergencies requiring rapid management.
microReview: Sudden tearing pain = Aortic Dissection. HTN causes medial ischemia (vasa vasorum issues). Marfan causes defective elastic tissue (cystic medial degeneration).
examinerTraps: Aneurysm (dilation of all layers) vs. Dissection (blood between layers). They are different pathologies but often occur in similar patient populations.
sourceQuote: Aortic Dissection... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes a 'true' aneurysm from a 'false' aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm)?

options.a: A false aneurysm involves only the tunica adventitia and media.
options.b: A false aneurysm is a collection of blood that communicates with the lumen but is contained by extravascular tissue.
options.c: A true aneurysm is caused by a tear in the intima allowing blood to enter the media.
options.d: A true aneurysm involves only the tunica intima and the internal elastic lamina.
options.e: False aneurysms are always caused by congenital defects in the vessel wall.

explanations.a: A false aneurysm does not involve the vessel wall layers; it is contained by perivascular connective tissue.
explanations.b: This is the definition of a false aneurysm: a hematoma that forms outside the vessel wall but still communicates with the vessel lumen.
explanations.c: A tear in the intima that allows blood to enter the media defines a dissection, not necessarily a true aneurysm.
explanations.d: A true aneurysm must involve all three layers of the vessel wall (intima, media, and adventitia).
explanations.e: False aneurysms are usually acquired (e.g., following trauma or a femoral artery catheterization), not congenital.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the vessel wall.
A {{c1::false}} aneurysm is a wall defect leading to an extravascular hematoma that communicates with the lumen.
A dissection occurs when blood enters the {{c1::media}} and separates the wall layers.
An example of a true aneurysm is an {{c1::abdominal aortic aneurysm}}.
A common cause of a false aneurysm is {{c1::trauma}} or {{c2::iatrogenic (e.g., catheterization)}} injury.
keyPoints: True aneurysms include the intima, media, and adventitia.
False aneurysms are peri-vascular hematomas contained by connective tissue.
Saccular aneurysms are spherical outpouchings involving only a portion of the wall.
Fusiform aneurysms are circumferential dilations of a long vascular segment.
Aortic dissection is often mislabeled as an aneurysm but is a separate process.
microReview: True = 3 layers dilated. False = hematoma outside wall. Dissection = blood inside wall layers.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'Dissection' with 'Aneurysm'. A dissection is not always dilated, and an aneurysm is not always dissected.
sourceQuote: Aneurysms and Dissection... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the pathogenesis of abdominal aortic aneurysms, which of the following molecules is primarily responsible for the degradation of the extracellular matrix in the aortic media?

explanations.a: Alkaline phosphatase is a marker for bone turnover or biliary obstruction.
explanations.b: Creatine kinase is a marker of muscle damage.
explanations.c: Increased expression of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), especially by macrophages, leads to the degradation of elastin and collagen in the media, facilitating aneurysm expansion.
explanations.d: Myeloperoxidase is found in neutrophils and contributes to oxidative stress but is not the primary enzyme for matrix degradation.
explanations.e: Troponin I is a specific marker for myocardial injury.

ankiCards: The enzymes responsible for degrading the aortic media in AAA are {{c1::Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
MMPs in the aortic wall are primarily produced by {{c1::macrophages/inflammatory cells}}.
The two main structural proteins degraded in the media during aneurysm formation are {{c1::elastin}} and {{c2::collagen}}.
Genetic polymorphisms in {{c1::MMPs}} have been linked to increased risk of AAA.
Decreased levels of {{c1::TIMPs (Tissue Inhibitors of Metalloproteinases)}} also contribute to AAA pathogenesis.
keyPoints: Matrix remodeling is a balance between MMPs and TIMPs.
Chronic inflammation in the vessel wall recruits macrophages.
Degradation of elastin leads to loss of elastic recoil and wall expansion.
Collagen degradation reduces the tensile strength of the vessel.
Atherosclerosis provides the inflammatory stimulus for these changes.
microReview: Inflammation -> Macrophages -> MMPs -> Destruction of Elastin/Collagen -> Wall Weakening -> Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Beware of 'atherosclerosis' as the only answer; remember the biochemical mediators (MMPs) that actually do the structural damage.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with chronic hoarseness and a persistent cough. A chest radiograph reveals a large mass in the mediastinum, and a subsequent CT scan confirms a 6-cm aneurysm of the aortic arch. Physical examination shows no signs of Marfan syndrome, but his social history is notable for multiple untreated sexually transmitted infections in his youth. Which histological finding in the aorta would most support the suspected etiology?

options.d: Plasma cell-rich infiltrates in the vasa vasorum

explanations.a: Amyloid is not a standard finding in aortic aneurysms.
explanations.b: Giant cell granulomas are seen in Giant Cell Arteritis or Takayasu Arteritis, which are vasculitides, not the primary cause of arch aneurysms in this context.
explanations.c: Laminar medial necrosis is another term for cystic medial necrosis, common in Marfan's, but the patient's history suggests syphilis.
explanations.d: Syphilitic (Luetic) aortitis involves obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum with a characteristic plasma cell-rich infiltrate. This leads to ischemic injury of the media.
explanations.e: Verocay bodies are characteristic of Schwannomas, not vascular disease.

ankiCards: Syphilitic aneurysms classically affect the {{c1::ascending aorta/aortic arch}}.
The hallmark of syphilitic aortitis is obliterative endarteritis of the {{c1::vasa vasorum}}.
The inflammatory infiltrate in syphilitic aortitis is rich in {{c1::plasma cells}}.
Ischemia of the media in syphilitic aortitis leads to a '{{c1::tree-bark}}' appearance of the intima.
Tertiary syphilis can cause dilation of the aortic valve ring, leading to {{c1::aortic insufficiency}}.
keyPoints: Syphilitic aneurysms are now rare due to antibiotic treatment.
The aneurysm is a consequence of medial ischemia following vasa vasorum obstruction.
Clinical symptoms often involve compression of mediastinal structures (esophagus, recurrent laryngeal nerve).
Tree-barking results from contraction of fibrous scars in the wall.
Aortic root dilation can lead to heart failure.
microReview: Syphilis -> Vasa vasorum endarteritis -> Medial ischemia -> Weakness -> Arch Aneurysm (Tree-barking).
