options.e: The lack of smooth muscle cells in arterial walls

explanations.a: While veins have valves, this does not explain why atherosclerosis preferentially targets large arteries.
explanations.b: Elastic arteries actually have the largest absolute wall thickness, not the lowest ratio.
explanations.c: Different vessels have structural specializations for their roles (e.g., pressure vs. volume), which results in characteristic anatomic distributions for diseases.
explanations.d: Intimal thickening occurs in both, but atherosclerosis specifically targets certain arterial types.
explanations.e: Arterial walls have significant smooth muscle; it is their primary constituent in muscular arteries.

ankiCards: Many vascular disorders affect only particular types of vessels due to their {{c1::anatomic distributions}}.
Atherosclerosis affects mainly {{c1::elastic}} and {{c2::muscular}} arteries.
Arterial walls are thicker than veins because they must accommodate {{c1::pulsatile}} flow.
The general architecture of blood vessels is {{c1::comparable}} throughout the system, but structural specializations exist.
Structural specializations in vessels reflect their distinct {{c1::functional roles}}.
keyPoints: Diseases like atherosclerosis have characteristic anatomic distributions.
Vascular structure is tailored to functional roles (e.g., elastic recoil vs. resistance).
Elastic and muscular arteries are the main targets of atherosclerosis.
Venous disorders are 'not inconsequential' but clinically differ from arterial ones.
Vascular architecture is comparable but specialized across the system.
microReview: Pathology follows function. Atherosclerosis targets elastic/muscular arteries due to their specific structural and hemodynamic environment.
examinerTraps: Be careful to distinguish between 'general architecture' (which is comparable) and 'structural specializations' (which dictate disease patterns).
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions. Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Aneurysms and dissections are most specifically categorized under which chapter subsection of vascular pathology?

explanations.a: This section covers intimal thickening as a response to various injuries.
explanations.b: Hypertension is a risk factor for aneurysms but is a distinct subsection.
explanations.c: Arteriosclerosis includes atherosclerosis, which contributes to aneurysms, but 'Aneurysms and Dissection' is its own primary heading.
explanations.d: According to the chapter contents, Aneurysms and Dissection is a major heading starting on page 504.
explanations.e: Vasculitis involves inflammation of the vessel wall, which is a different category of pathology.

ankiCards: Aneurysms and Dissection are covered in Chapter {{c1::11}} of Robbins.
The subsection 'Aneurysms and Dissection' begins on page {{c1::504}}.
The major heading following 'Consequences of Atherosclerotic Disease' is {{c1::Aneurysms and Dissection}}.
Aortic dissection is categorized under the same major heading as {{c1::Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm}}.
The heading for 'Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm' is located under the {{c1::Aneurysms and Dissection}} section.
keyPoints: Aneurysms and dissections are grouped together in pathology textbooks.
AAAs and TAAs are the two primary types of aneurysms discussed.
They are distinct from vasculitis and hypertensive vascular disease.
The study of vascular disease starts with normal structure and function.
Aortic dissection is a critical differential for chest or back pain.
microReview: Aneurysms and dissections are primary vascular wall pathologies categorized together due to their shared mechanism of wall structural failure.
examinerTraps: Aneurysms are often *caused* by atherosclerosis, but in a classification task, they are their own entity.
sourceQuote: Aneurysms and Dissection... 504. Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm... 506. Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm... 507. Aortic Dissection... 507
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old female presents with acute onset of severe abdominal pain. An emergency CT scan shows a 6-cm dilation of the infrarenal aorta with evidence of extravasated blood. This presentation represents the end-stage failure of which vascular disease mechanism?

options.c: Weakening of vessel walls leading to rupture

explanations.a: Obstruction would cause ischemia (e.g., mesenteric ischemia), not a dilation with extravasated blood (rupture).
explanations.b: Progressive narrowing leads to stenosis; this patient has dilation and rupture.
explanations.c: The patient has a ruptured Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA). Aneurysms and their rupture are the result of the 'weakening of vessel walls' mechanism.
explanations.d: Intimal thickening is a protective or reparative response to injury, not the mechanism of terminal wall failure in an aneurysm.
explanations.e: Intimal thickening usually narrows the lumen and stabilizes the wall; weakening allows for the dilation seen here.

ankiCards: Extravasated blood near a dilated aorta on CT suggests {{c1::aneurysm rupture}}.
The two mechanisms of vascular disease are narrowing and {{c1::weakening}}.
Weakening of vessel walls leads to either {{c1::dilation}} or {{c2::rupture}}.
Vascular pathology is responsible for more {{c1::morbidity}} and {{c2::mortality}} than any other disease category.
The infrarenal aorta is a common site for {{c1::Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms}}.
keyPoints: Aneurysms involve permanent dilation of the vessel.
Rupture is the most feared complication of a weakened vessel wall.
Infrarenal location is classic for AAA.
Aneurysms are categorized under the 'weakening' mechanism of disease.
Imaging (CT) is used to diagnose the size and rupture status.
microReview: Aneurysm rupture is the clinical culmination of the 'weakening of vessel walls' mechanism, leading to life-threatening hemorrhage.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'progressive' nature of atherosclerosis with the 'precipitous' nature of a rupture.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Why are arterial walls structurally thicker than venous walls at the same level of branching?

options.b: To provide a larger surface area for nutrient exchange
options.c: To accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures
options.d: To facilitate the movement of deoxygenated blood
options.e: To allow for passive collapse during inactivity

explanations.a: Arteries accommodate higher, not lower, pressures.
explanations.b: Capillaries are responsible for nutrient exchange, not the thick-walled arteries.
explanations.c: Arterial walls must be thicker to withstand the high-pressure, pulsatile nature of cardiac output.
explanations.d: This is the function of the venous system, which has thinner walls.
explanations.e: Veins are more likely to collapse; arteries remain patent due to their thick, muscular/elastic walls.

ankiCards: Arterial walls are {{c1::thicker}} than corresponding veins at the same branching level.
Arteries are thicker to accommodate {{c1::pulsatile flow}}.
Arteries are thicker to accommodate {{c1::higher blood pressures}}.
The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}} as arteries become smaller.
Structural specializations in vessels reflect their distinct {{c1::functional roles}}.
keyPoints: Arterial vs. venous wall thickness is a key structural difference.
Pulsatile flow requires reinforced (thicker) walls.
Higher pressures in the arterial system necessitate structural support.
Structure-function correlation is fundamental in vascular pathology.
Thickness varies depending on the level of the vascular tree.
microReview: Arteries = High Pressure/Thick Walls. Veins = Low Pressure/Thin Walls. This explains why aneurysms (wall failures) are more clinically dramatic in the arterial system.
examinerTraps: A common distractor is 'nutrient exchange', which only applies to capillaries, not the muscular/elastic vessels mentioned in the text.
sourceQuote: For example, arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: According to the general architecture of the cardiovascular system, which vessel type is the main target of atherosclerosis?

options.b: Large veins and the vena cava

explanations.a: Capillaries are too small and lack the multi-layered wall structure required for atherosclerosis.
explanations.b: Veins are rarely affected by atherosclerosis due to low-pressure dynamics.
explanations.c: Atherosclerosis is explicitly noted to mainly affect elastic and muscular arteries.
explanations.d: Lymphatics are involved in fluid transport and do not develop atherosclerosis.
explanations.e: Small arterioles are typically affected by hyaline or hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis, not the classic atherosclerosis affecting larger vessels.

ankiCards: Atherosclerosis affects mainly {{c1::elastic}} and {{c2::muscular}} arteries.
The vessel structure that accommodates pulsatile flow is the {{c1::arterial}} wall.
Atherosclerosis involves the {{c1::intima}} of large vessels.
Vascular pathology is the leading cause of human {{c1::morbidity}}.
The anatomic distribution of atherosclerosis is described as {{c1::characteristic}}.
keyPoints: Atherosclerosis is an arterial disease.
It specifically targets elastic arteries (e.g., aorta) and muscular arteries (e.g., coronary).
It is a form of 'narrowing' (stenosis) and can lead to 'weakening' (aneurysm).
The location of vascular lesions is influenced by the type of vessel.
Elastic and muscular arteries have the specific architecture susceptible to plaque formation.
microReview: Atherosclerosis = Elastic/Muscular Arteries. It causes luminal narrowing or wall weakening (aneurysms).
examinerTraps: The exam may try to group all 'arteries' together, but the text specifically highlights elastic and muscular ones as the main targets.
sourceQuote: Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: If a patient's vascular disease progresses from a stable atherosclerotic plaque to a sudden vessel occlusion, which sub-mechanism of 'luminal narrowing' has most likely occurred?

explanations.a: Intimal thickening is a 'progressive' process, whereas the stem specifies 'sudden vessel occlusion'.
explanations.b: Dilation is the mechanism for aneurysms, which causes widening, not narrowing/occlusion.
explanations.c: The text states that obstruction can occur 'precipitously' via thrombosis or embolism.
explanations.d: Cystic medial degeneration is a mechanism of wall weakening (aneurysm), not acute occlusion.
explanations.e: This is a venous disorder and does not relate to the occlusion of atherosclerotic arteries.

ankiCards: Luminal obstruction can occur {{c1::progressively}} or {{c2::precipitously}}.
Precipitous vessel obstruction is typically caused by {{c1::thrombosis}} or {{c2::embolism}}.
Progressive vessel narrowing is typically caused by {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Narrowing of a vessel lumen is also called {{c1::stenosis}}.
The two mechanisms of vascular disease are {{c1::narrowing}} and {{c2::weakening}}.
keyPoints: Narrowing can be chronic (progressive) or acute (precipitous).
Atherosclerosis is the classic progressive narrowing process.
Thrombosis/embolism causes sudden, life-threatening obstruction.
Occlusion leads to distal ischemia and infarction.
These processes contrast with wall weakening (aneurysms).
microReview: Vascular narrowing has two speeds: progressive (atherosclerosis) or precipitous (thrombosis/embolism).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the underlying *disease* (atherosclerosis) with the *event* that causes sudden occlusion (thrombosis).
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism)
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the 'stereotyped response' of the vascular wall to injury?

explanations.a: Medial thinning is often seen in aneurysms, but it is not the universal stereotyped response to injury.
explanations.b: The text lists 'Intimal Thickening: A Stereotyped Response to Vascular Injury' as a specific subsection.
explanations.c: Rupture is a failure of the wall, not a standard reparative or reactive response to injury.
explanations.d: Fragmentation of the elastic lamina is a feature of specific diseases (like Marfan or Syphilis) rather than the universal response.
explanations.e: This refers to veins and is not the primary response to vascular injury discussed for arteries.

ankiCards: The stereotyped response to vascular injury is {{c1::intimal thickening}}.
Intimal thickening is a {{c1::stereotyped}} response to vascular injury.
Vascular structure is {{c1::comparable}} throughout the system.
Arterial wall thickness {{c1::diminishes}} as vessels become smaller.
Venous disorders are described as {{c1::not inconsequential}} in vascular pathology.
keyPoints: Intimal thickening is the universal response to any vascular insult.
It involves smooth muscle cell migration and ECM deposition.
It can contribute to luminal narrowing.
It is a 'stereotyped' process regardless of the nature of the injury.
This process is distinct from the primary mechanisms of weakening or narrowing.
microReview: Regardless of the insult (trauma, toxins, hypertension), the vessel wall responds by thickening the intima.
examinerTraps: Students often focus on the damage (like thinning) and forget the body's active response (thickening).
sourceQuote: Vascular Wall Response to Injury... Intimal Thickening: A Stereotyped Response to Vascular Injury... 488
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular tumors are categorized by their clinical behavior into benign, intermediate, and malignant. Which of the following neoplasms is classified specifically as a malignant vascular tumor?

explanations.a: Glomus tumors are benign neoplasms arising from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas are the most common type of benign vascular tumor, often occurring in skin or mucous membranes.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is a highly aggressive malignant tumor of endothelial cells with a poor prognosis.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign, often pedunculated, capillary hemangioma that frequently occurs on the gingiva.
explanations.e: Cystic hygroma is a benign cavernous lymphangioma typically found in the neck or axilla of children.

ankiCards: The most common benign vascular tumor of the skin is the {{c1::capillary hemangioma}}.
Angiosarcoma is classified as a {{c1::malignant}} vascular tumor.
Glomus tumors arise from modified {{c1::smooth muscle}} cells.
The benign vascular lesion often found in the neck of infants with Turner syndrome is a {{c1::cystic hygroma}}.
Vascular tumors are classified into three grades: benign, {{c1::intermediate (borderline)}}, and malignant.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors range from benign hemangiomas to highly malignant angiosarcomas.
Benign tumors (e.g., hemangiomas) are characterized by well-formed vascular channels.
Malignant tumors (e.g., angiosarcoma) show cytologic atypia and lack of organized vessel formation.
Intermediate tumors like Kaposi sarcoma show borderline behavior.
Classification is based on the degree of endothelial differentiation and mitotic activity.
microReview: Benign: Hemangioma (Capillary, Cavernous), Glomus tumor. Intermediate: Kaposi Sarcoma, Hemangioendothelioma. Malignant: Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse 'Intermediate' grade tumors like Kaposi sarcoma with purely malignant ones like Angiosarcoma. While Kaposi sarcoma is aggressive in AIDS patients, it is pathologically classified as intermediate.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors are classified as benign (e.g., hemangioma), intermediate (e.g., Kaposi sarcoma), or malignant (e.g., angiosarcoma).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old male with a history of HIV infection presents with multiple purple-to-red macules and plaques on his lower extremities. Histological examination reveals spindle-shaped cells and slit-like vascular spaces containing red blood cells. Which of the following pathogens is the primary driver of this neoplastic proliferation?

explanations.a: EBV is associated with lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not vascular tumors.
explanations.b: HHV-8 (also known as KSHV) is the causative agent of Kaposi sarcoma, characterized by spindle cells and slit-like spaces.
explanations.c: CMV causes opportunistic infections in HIV patients but is not oncogenic for vascular tissue.
explanations.d: HPV-16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas, specifically of the cervix and oropharynx.
explanations.e: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which mimics Kaposi sarcoma but is a bacterial infection, not a viral-driven spindle cell neoplasm.

ankiCards: The viral agent responsible for Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::HHV-8}}.
Microscopically, Kaposi Sarcoma shows {{c1::spindle}} cells and slit-like vascular spaces.
Kaposi Sarcoma is categorized as an {{c1::intermediate}} grade vascular tumor.
The most common clinical presentation of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::purple}} skin macules/plaques.
HHV-8 is also known as {{c1::Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV)}}.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
Four clinical types: Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
HHV-8 infection is necessary but not sufficient for KS development.
Histology: Spindle cells, slit-like spaces, and extravasated RBCs.
KS is the most common neoplasm in AIDS patients.
microReview: KS = HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Slit-like spaces + Purple plaques.
examinerTraps: Distinguish KS (HHV-8, spindle cells) from Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella, neutrophilic infiltrate). Both present as red/purple lesions in AIDS patients.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors... Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV8).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 58-year-old male who worked in a chemical plant for 30 years presents with weight loss, fatigue, and jaundice. Imaging reveals multiple ill-defined masses throughout the liver. Biopsy shows malignant endothelial cells with significant pleomorphism and positive staining for CD31. Exposure to which of the following substances most likely contributed to this condition?

explanations.a: Aflatoxin B1 is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Vinyl chloride exposure is specifically associated with hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Beryllium is associated with lung disease (berylliosis) and lung cancer.
explanations.d: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and bronchogenic carcinoma.
explanations.e: Benzene exposure is linked to acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
Besides vinyl chloride, exposure to {{c1::arsenic}} is a risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma.
The immunohistochemical marker {{c1::CD31}} is highly specific for endothelial differentiation.
Angiosarcomas are highly {{c1::aggressive}} malignant tumors.
Thorotrast, a former radioactive contrast medium, is associated with hepatic {{c1::angiosarcoma}}.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare but lethal malignancy.
Associated with vinyl chloride (PVC industry), arsenic (pesticides), and Thorotrast.
CD31 (PECAM-1) is a reliable marker for endothelial cells.
Angiosarcomas can occur in skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Late-stage presentation often involves liver failure or intra-abdominal hemorrhage.
microReview: Liver Angiosarcoma: Vinyl Chloride, Arsenic, Thorotrast. Marker: CD31.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Hepatic Angiosarcoma (Vinyl Chloride) with Hepatocellular Carcinoma (Aflatoxin, Hepatitis B/C).
sourceQuote: Malignant Tumors... Angiosarcoma... Hepatic angiosarcomas are associated with distinct carcinogens, including arsenic, Thorotrast, and vinyl chloride.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old female presents with a small, exquisitely painful, 5-mm bluish nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. The pain is triggered by cold temperatures. What is the most likely cellular origin of this lesion?

explanations.a: While this is a vascular-related tumor, the specific cells in a glomus tumor are not simple endothelial cells.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus bodies, which are thermoregulatory structures.
explanations.c: Pericytes are involved in hemangiopericytomas, not the classic subungual glomus tumor.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts are the origin of fibromas, not vascular glomus tumors.
explanations.e: Schwann cells are the origin of neuromas or schwannomas, which can be painful but lack the characteristic subungual vascular appearance.

ankiCards: Glomus tumors are most commonly found in the {{c1::subungual (under nail)}} region.
The classic symptom of a glomus tumor is pain triggered by {{c1::cold}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells.
The anatomical structure involved in glomus tumors is the {{c1::glomus body}}.
Glomus tumors are classified as {{c1::benign}} tumors.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign and exquisitely painful.
Subungual location is the classic clinical presentation.
Derived from glomus bodies (arteriovenous anastomoses involved in thermoregulation).
Histology shows nests of uniform round cells (glomus cells) surrounding vascular channels.
Surgical excision is typically curative.
microReview: Painful subungual nodule + Cold sensitivity = Glomus tumor (Modified smooth muscle).
examinerTraps: The pain is very specific; if cold sensitivity is mentioned in a subungual lesion, think glomus tumor immediately.
sourceQuote: Glomus Tumor (Glomangioma)... Benign, exquisitely painful tumors... most commonly found in the distal portion of the digits, especially under the fingernails.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Pathologists use various immunohistochemical markers to identify the endothelial origin of poorly differentiated tumors. Which of the following markers is considered the most specific for endothelial differentiation in the diagnosis of vascular neoplasms?

explanations.a: CD3 is a marker for T-lymphocytes.
explanations.b: CD20 is a marker for B-lymphocytes.
explanations.c: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a transmembrane glycoprotein expressed on endothelial cells and is a standard marker for vascular tumors.
explanations.d: CD45 is the leukocyte common antigen (LCA), used to identify hematopoietic cells.
explanations.e: CD68 is a marker for macrophages and histiocytes.

ankiCards: The most specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial cells is {{c1::CD31}}.
CD31 is also known as {{c1::PECAM-1}}.
In angiosarcoma, tumor cells typically stain positive for the marker {{c1::CD31}}.
Besides CD31, {{c1::CD34 (or Factor VIII)}} can also be used as a vascular marker, though it is less specific.
Immunohistochemistry is essential to distinguish {{c1::poorly differentiated}} angiosarcoma from carcinoma or melanoma.
keyPoints: CD31 is the 'gold standard' for identifying endothelial differentiation.
Vascular tumors often express von Willebrand factor (Factor VIII-related antigen).
CD34 is expressed by endothelium but also by various mesenchymal cells.
Marker expression helps differentiate angiosarcoma from other spindle cell malignancies.
Endothelial cells line the vascular spaces in benign tumors but form solid sheets in malignant ones.
microReview: Endothelial marker = CD31.
examinerTraps: Do not select CD45 or CD68 for vascular tumors; these identify inflammatory cells often found in the vicinity of tumors.
sourceQuote: The endothelial nature of the neoplastic cells can be demonstrated by staining with endothelial-specific markers such as CD31.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with several firm, violaceous nodules on her left arm. She has a history of a radical mastectomy followed by radiation and chronic lymphedema for 12 years. Biopsy of a nodule reveals a high-grade malignancy of endothelial origin. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious process seen in immunocompromised patients, not related to chronic lymphedema.
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy) is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome.
explanations.c: Kaposi sarcoma is HHV-8 related and usually presents as multiple lesions, not typically linked to post-mastectomy lymphedema.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangioma is a benign tumor and would not present as aggressive nodules in a lymphedematous limb.
explanations.e: Lymphangiomyomatosis is a rare lung disease involving smooth muscle proliferation, not a skin malignancy.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves}} syndrome.
Chronic {{c1::lymphedema}} is a major risk factor for cutaneous angiosarcoma.
Radiation therapy for breast cancer increases the risk of developing {{c1::angiosarcoma}} in the treated field.
Cutaneous angiosarcoma initially appears as small {{c1::sharply demarcated}} red papules or nodules.
The prognosis for Stewart-Treves syndrome is generally {{c1::poor}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma can occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves).
Commonly follows radical mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection.
Latency between lymphedema and tumor is usually 10+ years.
Can also be induced by therapeutic radiation.
Highly metastatic, usually to the lungs.
microReview: Mastectomy + Chronic Lymphedema + New skin nodules = Angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves).
examinerTraps: Wait for the history of chronic lymphedema; it's the classic 'trigger' for the Stewart-Treves variant of angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcoma... can also occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema, classically in the ipsilateral arm of women who have undergone radical mastectomy.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the characteristic histological feature of a 'cavernous hemangioma' compared to a 'capillary hemangioma'?

options.a: Presence of spindle cells and slit-like spaces
options.b: Infiltrative growth into adjacent skeletal muscle
options.c: Large, dilated vascular channels separated by connective tissue
options.d: Nests of uniform round cells around vessels
options.e: Massive neutrophilic infiltrate and bacterial clusters

explanations.a: Spindle cells and slit-like spaces are characteristic of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.b: Infiltrative growth is a feature of malignant tumors or occasionally hemangiomas, but not the defining feature of cavernous ones.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, thin-walled, dilated vascular spaces.
explanations.d: Nests of uniform cells around vessels are seen in glomus tumors.
explanations.e: Neutrophilic infiltrates and bacteria are seen in bacillary angiomatosis.

ankiCards: Cavernous hemangiomas are characterized by {{c1::large, dilated}} vascular spaces.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas are often {{c1::deeply}} seated.
Cavernous hemangiomas of the liver are usually {{c1::asymptomatic}}.
A cavernous hemangioma associated with the cerebellum is a feature of {{c1::von Hippel-Lindau}} disease.
Histologically, cavernous hemangiomas are separated by a {{c1::connective tissue}} stroma.
keyPoints: Capillary hemangiomas: small, thin-walled capillaries lined by endothelium.
Cavernous hemangiomas: large, dilated blood-filled spaces.
Cavernous types are more likely to involve internal organs (e.g., liver, brain).
They do not regress spontaneously, unlike some capillary (strawberry) hemangiomas.
Can be part of von Hippel-Lindau disease (specifically in the CNS/retina).
microReview: Capillary = Small vessels. Cavernous = Large vessels.
examinerTraps: Capillary hemangiomas (Strawberry) often regress; Cavernous ones usually do not.
sourceQuote: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, dilated vascular channels... They are more frequently involve deep structures than do capillary hemangiomas.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old pregnant woman presents with a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated nodule on her gingiva that bleeds easily. The lesion appeared during her second trimester. Biopsy shows a circumscribed proliferation of capillaries with associated edema and inflammatory cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma is malignant and would not typically present as a pedunculated gingival mass in pregnancy.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors are usually subungual and extremely painful.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) often occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis occurs in immunocompromised individuals and is caused by Bartonella.
explanations.e: Cystic hygroma is a lymphangioma of the neck in infants.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is a variant of {{c1::capillary hemangioma}}.
When occurring on the gingiva of a pregnant woman, pyogenic granuloma is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized by {{c1::rapid}} growth and easy bleeding.
The most common location for a pyogenic granuloma is the {{c1::skin or gingiva}}.
Histologically, pyogenic granuloma shows {{c1::capillary}} proliferation and edema.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is neither pyogenic nor a true granuloma.
It is a lobular capillary hemangioma.
Commonly follows trauma or occurs during pregnancy.
Often regresses spontaneously (especially post-partum) or requires simple excision.
Grossly appears as a 'red, mushroom-like' lesion.
microReview: Pregnancy + Gingiva + Red bleeding nodule = Pyogenic Granuloma.
examinerTraps: Despite the name 'pyogenic,' there is usually no infection or pus involved.
sourceQuote: Pyogenic granulomas are capillary hemangiomas that manifest as rapidly growing red pedunculated lesions on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation that can histologically mimic Kaposi sarcoma. This condition is caused by an infection with which of the following organisms?

explanations.a: S. aureus causes pyogenic infections but not vascular neoplastic-like proliferations.
explanations.b: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, not bacillary angiomatosis.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella henselae (from cats) or Bartonella quintana (from lice).
explanations.d: MAI causes disseminated respiratory/GI disease in AIDS, not vascular skin lesions.
explanations.e: Toxoplasma causes CNS lesions in AIDS.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by bacteria of the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
Bacillary angiomatosis is primarily seen in {{c1::immunocompromised/AIDS}} patients.
The histology of bacillary angiomatosis features {{c1::neutrophils}} and nuclear dust.
Bartonella species can be visualized using the {{c1::Warthin-Starry}} silver stain.
Treatment for bacillary angiomatosis involves {{c1::antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin)}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis: opportunistic infection in immunocompromised hosts.
Organisms: Bartonella henselae (cat scratch) or Bartonella quintana (trench fever).
Induces host HIF-1α, which stimulates VEGF and vascular growth.
Histology: Proliferation of capillaries with prominent 'epithelioid' endothelium and neutrophils.
Must be distinguished from Kaposi sarcoma as treatment (antibiotics) is curative.
microReview: Bartonella + AIDS + Vascular lesion = Bacillary Angiomatosis.
examinerTraps: The presence of neutrophils is a key histological clue that separates Bacillary Angiomatosis from Kaposi Sarcoma.
sourceQuote: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts caused by opportunistic gram-negative bacilli of the Bartonella family.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A neonate is born with a large, soft, fluctuant mass on the left side of the neck. Transillumination is positive. Chromosomal analysis reveals a 45,X karyotype. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for the mass?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are usually skin-based and don't typically present as large fluctuant neck masses in Turner syndrome.
explanations.b: Cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) is strongly associated with Turner syndrome (45,X) and presents as a neck mass.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are small, painful, and subungual.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a tumor of older adults, not neonates.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious process of the immunocompromised.

ankiCards: A cystic hygroma is a type of {{c1::cavernous lymphangioma}}.
Cystic hygroma is classically associated with {{c1::Turner}} syndrome.
The most common location for a cystic hygroma is the {{c1::neck (or axilla)}}.
On physical exam, cystic hygromas are positive for {{c1::transillumination}}.
Lymphangiomas differ from hemangiomas by the absence of {{c1::red blood cells}} in the lumina.
keyPoints: Cystic hygromas are benign lymphatic malformations.
Often found in the neck or axilla of infants.
Strong association with chromosomal abnormalities (Turner syndrome, Down syndrome).
Characterized by large, dilated lymphatic spaces lined by endothelium.
Can cause difficulty in swallowing or breathing if very large.
microReview: Neck mass + Turner syndrome (45,X) = Cystic Hygroma.
examinerTraps: Positive transillumination is a classic physical exam finding for cystic hygroma.
sourceQuote: Cystic hygromas (cavernous lymphangiomas) are typically found in the neck or axilla of children and are sometimes associated with Turner syndrome.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old female presents with multiple firm, violaceous nodules on her right upper extremity. Her medical history is significant for a radical mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection 12 years ago for breast adenocarcinoma, followed by chronic, non-pitting lymphedema of the right arm. A skin biopsy of a nodule shows malignant spindle cells forming irregular, anastomosing vascular channels. Which of the following is the most likely cellular origin of these lesions?

explanations.a: Fibroblasts are the origin of fibrosarcomas, which do not typically present as violaceous nodules in the setting of chronic lymphedema.
explanations.b: Pericytes are the origin of hemangiopericytomas, now classified as solitary fibrous tumors, which do not show the malignant anastomosing vascular channels seen here.
explanations.c: The patient has Stewart-Treves syndrome, which is angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema. Angiosarcomas are malignant tumors of endothelial cell origin, characterized by CD31 positivity.
explanations.d: Smooth muscle cells are the origin of leiomyosarcomas, which typically appear as bulky masses rather than cutaneous multifocal violaceous nodules.
explanations.e: Glomus cells are specialized smooth muscle cells involved in thermoregulation; glomus tumors are typically small, painful, subungual lesions, not large malignant nodules.

ankiCards: Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to {{c1::Angiosarcoma}} arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema.
The characteristic immunohistochemical marker for Angiosarcoma is {{c1::CD31 (or vWF)}}.
Malignant vascular tumors like angiosarcoma originate from {{c1::Endothelial}} cells.
Angiosarcoma commonly occurs in the {{c1::skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver}}.
Histologically, angiosarcoma shows malignant cells forming {{c1::anastomosing vascular channels}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor of endothelial cells.
Stewart-Treves syndrome occurs classically after radical mastectomy with lymph node dissection.
Chronic lymphedema is the primary risk factor for Stewart-Treves syndrome.
Lesions typically present as enlarging red/purple nodules or plaques.
Markers like CD31 and von Willebrand factor confirm endothelial origin.
microReview: Vascular malignancies range from the highly aggressive angiosarcoma to intermediate-grade lesions. Chronic lymphedema-associated angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves) is a classic board association.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Stewart-Treves (angiosarcoma) with lymphedema alone or cellulitis; the presence of purple nodules in a limb with long-standing swelling is highly suggestive of malignancy.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. ... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 34-year-old male with a history of HIV and a CD4+ T-cell count of 120/mm³ presents with multiple painless, dark purple plaques on his legs and trunk. Biopsy reveals a proliferation of spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces containing red blood cells, and a chronic inflammatory infiltrate. The pathogenesis of these lesions is most directly associated with infection by which of the following agents?

explanations.a: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent of all forms of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.b: HHV-6 is associated with Roseola infantum, not vascular malignancies.
explanations.c: HPV-16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas (cervical, anal, oropharyngeal), not vascular tumors.
explanations.d: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.e: CMV can cause retinitis or colitis in AIDS patients but does not cause Kaposi sarcoma.

ankiCards: The causative agent of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
Histologically, Kaposi Sarcoma shows spindle cells and {{c1::slit-like}} vascular spaces.
The most common clinical presentation of AIDS-associated KS is {{c1::cutaneous purple/violaceous plaques}}.
HHV-8 infects {{c1::endothelial cells}} and promotes their proliferation and survival.
Kaposi Sarcoma is classified as a {{c1::borderline/intermediate}} grade vascular tumor.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is an intermediate-grade vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8.
Four clinical types: Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
The spindle cell is the diagnostic cell type in the late stages of KS.
Slit-like spaces filled with extravasated RBCs are a hallmark feature.
HHV-8 encodes viral homologues of cyclin D and G-protein-coupled receptors.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma is the most common neoplasm in AIDS patients. It represents an opportunistic proliferation of endothelial cells driven by HHV-8 in the setting of immune deficiency.
examinerTraps: Distinguish KS from Bacillary Angiomatosis; KS has slit-like spaces and spindle cells, while BA has neutrophils and Warthin-Starry positive bacilli.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors: Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions, Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors, Malignant Tumors.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 29-year-old male presents with an exquisitely painful, 4-mm, blue-red nodule located under the fingernail of his left index finger. He notes that the pain is often triggered by exposure to cold temperatures. Histologic examination of the lesion shows aggregates of uniform, rounded cells surrounding small vascular spaces. These cells are most likely which of the following?

explanations.a: Fibroblasts form collagenous tissue; they are not the primary component of glomus tumors.
explanations.b: Endothelial cells line the vascular spaces but do not form the characteristic rounded cell nests of a glomus tumor.
explanations.c: Adipocytes are not found in vascular glomus tumors.
explanations.d: While glomus cells are related to perivascular cells, they are specifically defined as modified smooth muscle cells.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors arise from the specialized glomus bodies involved in thermoregulation and consist of nests of modified smooth muscle cells.

ankiCards: A glomus tumor is typically found in the {{c1::subungual (under fingernail)}} region.
The clinical hallmark of a glomus tumor is {{c1::exquisite pain (often to cold)}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors consist of {{c1::modified smooth muscle cells}}.
Glomus bodies are neuromyoarterial receptors involved in {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Glomus tumors are {{c1::benign}} vascular neoplasms.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are highly painful, small, benign tumors.
Commonly occur in the distal digits, especially subungual.
Arise from glomus bodies (arteriovenous anastomoses).
Composed of nests of uniform, round glomus cells.
Pain is a classic diagnostic clue, differentiating it from other hand nodules.
microReview: Glomus tumors = Small + Subungual + Painful + Modified smooth muscle cells.
examinerTraps: Wait for the 'cold sensitivity' or 'subungual' keyword; it is a pathognomonic clinical scenario for glomus tumor.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 27-year-old female who is currently 28 weeks pregnant presents with a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated mass on her gingiva that bleeds easily with minor trauma. The lesion appeared two weeks ago. Physical exam shows a 1-cm, friable, ulcerated nodule. If biopsied, the lesion would most likely demonstrate a proliferation of small capillaries organized in a lobular pattern. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas involve large, dilated blood-filled spaces and are usually deep-seated, not superficial gingival pedunculated masses.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a benign, rapidly growing vascular lesion often found on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis occurs in immunocompromised patients and is caused by Bartonella infection, not pregnancy.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a malignant, poorly circumscribed tumor, usually in older adults or post-radiation, not a pedunculated gingival mass in pregnancy.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are subungual and extremely painful, not friable gingival masses.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is actually a(n) {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
A common site for pyogenic granuloma in pregnant women is the {{c1::gingiva (gums)}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized by {{c1::rapid growth}} and {{c1::easy bleeding/friability}}.
Histologically, pyogenic granuloma resembles {{c1::granulation tissue}}.
Pregnancy-associated pyogenic granuloma is also called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is neither pyogenic nor a true granuloma.
It is a pedunculated red mass that often follows minor trauma.
Frequent occurrence in the oral cavity (gingiva).
Common in pregnancy due to hormonal influences.
Can regress spontaneously after delivery.
microReview: Pregnancy + gingival nodule + bleeds easily = Pyogenic granuloma (Lobular capillary hemangioma).
examinerTraps: The name 'pyogenic granuloma' is a trap; look for the capillary proliferation in the description to confirm it's a vascular tumor, not an infection or a granulomatous disease.
sourceQuote: Vascular Structure and Function ... Intimal Thickening: A Stereotyped Response to Vascular Injury
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 40-year-old male with untreated AIDS presents with several red-to-purple, skin-colored papules that resemble Kaposi sarcoma. However, histopathologic examination reveals a vascular proliferation with prominent neutrophils and nuclear dust. A Warthin-Starry silver stain demonstrates clusters of small, tangled bacilli. What is the most likely causative organism of these lesions?

explanations.a: Mycobacterium avium causes systemic infection in AIDS but does not cause angiomatous skin lesions with bacilli visible on silver stain.
explanations.b: Cryptococcus causes meningitis or pulmonary disease; it is a fungus (yeast), not a silver-stain positive bacillus in vascular lesions.
explanations.c: Staphylococcus aureus causes pyogenic infections (abscesses, impetigo) but not the specific angiomatous proliferation of bacillary angiomatosis.
explanations.d: Bartonella henselae (or B. quintana) causes bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised patients, mimicking Kaposi sarcoma clinically.
explanations.e: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, which does not contain bacterial bacilli or prominent neutrophilic infiltrates.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
The clinical appearance of Bacillary Angiomatosis mimics {{c1::Kaposi Sarcoma}}.
Unlike KS, Bacillary Angiomatosis features an infiltrate of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
{{c1::Warthin-Starry (silver)}} stain is used to identify the organisms in bacillary angiomatosis.
In immunocompromised patients, Bartonella henselae can cause {{c1::Bacillary angiomatosis}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in AIDS patients.
Caused by Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch) or B. quintana (trench fever).
Clinically mimics Kaposi sarcoma (red/purple papules).
Histology: Proliferation of capillaries with protuberant epithelioid endothelium.
Characterized by neutrophilic inflammation and bacteria on silver stain.
microReview: Vascular tumor in AIDS? If HHV-8 = Kaposi Sarcoma (Spindle cells). If Bartonella + Neutrophils = Bacillary Angiomatosis.
examinerTraps: Kaposi sarcoma and Bacillary angiomatosis look identical on physical exam; biopsy with silver stain is the tie-breaker.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors: Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions, Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors, Malignant Tumors.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 58-year-old male presents with weight loss, abdominal pain, and jaundice. He has worked in a factory for 35 years specializing in the polymerization of plastics, specifically involving vinyl chloride. Imaging reveals multiple masses in the liver. A biopsy confirms a high-grade malignancy composed of atypical endothelial cells. Which of the following exposures is most likely responsible for his condition?

explanations.a: Vinyl chloride exposure is a well-known risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma, a rare and aggressive malignant vascular tumor.
explanations.b: Aflatoxin B1 (from Aspergillus) is a major risk factor for Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC), not angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Carbon tetrachloride causes centrilobular liver necrosis and cirrhosis, but is not a classic carcinogen for angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: Benzene exposure is associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), not hepatic vascular tumors.
explanations.e: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and lung cancer, not liver angiosarcoma.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride, arsenic, or Thorotrast}}.
Vinyl chloride is used in the production of {{c1::polyvinyl chloride (PVC) plastics}}.
Angiosarcoma of the liver originates from {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
The prognosis of hepatic angiosarcoma is {{c1::poor (often fatal within a year)}}.
Aflatoxin B1 is to Hepatocellular Carcinoma as Vinyl Chloride is to {{c1::Hepatic Angiosarcoma}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor with atypical vascular channels.
Liver involvement is rare but linked to specific environmental toxins.
Classic toxins: Arsenic (pesticides), Thorotrast (old contrast), Vinyl chloride (PVC).
Presents with non-specific symptoms: pain, fatigue, weight loss.
Tumor cells express CD31, confirming vascular origin.
microReview: Toxin-induced liver cancer: Vinyl Chloride = Angiosarcoma. Aflatoxin = Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
examinerTraps: Watch for the specific industry (plastics/PVC) which points directly to vinyl chloride and angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism)
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 3-week-old female infant is brought to the pediatrician for a bright red, slightly raised 'strawberry-like' lesion on her scalp. The parents state the lesion was small at birth but has grown rapidly over the last week. The physician advises the parents that the lesion will likely continue to grow for several months and then spontaneously regress. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, dilated blood vessels and generally do not spontaneously regress; they may also be associated with deeper structures.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors are painful subungual lesions in adults, not strawberry birthmarks in infants.
explanations.c: Lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) are typically found on the neck or axilla and contain lymph, not bright red blood-filled capillaries.
explanations.d: Capillary hemangioma (juvenile or strawberry hemangioma) is the most common vascular tumor of infancy. It grows rapidly after birth and then regresses by age 7-9.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor of the elderly and would not show spontaneous regression.

ankiCards: The most common vascular tumor of infancy is the {{c1::capillary (juvenile/strawberry) hemangioma}}.
Juvenile hemangiomas usually {{c1::regress/involute}} spontaneously by age 7.
The clinical appearance of a juvenile hemangioma is often described as {{c1::strawberry-like}}.
Histologically, juvenile hemangiomas consist of {{c1::closely packed capillaries}} with thin walls.
Juvenile hemangiomas are most commonly found on the {{c1::skin (face/scalp)}}.
keyPoints: Capillary hemangiomas are benign proliferations of capillaries.
Extremely common in newborns (1 in 200 births).
Natural history involves a proliferative phase followed by involution.
Complete regression occurs in 75-90% of cases by age 7.
Treatment is usually conservative unless it obstructs vision or airway.
microReview: Infant + Strawberry skin mark + Rapid growth then regression = Juvenile Capillary Hemangioma.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse with a 'port-wine stain' (Nevus flammeus), which is a vascular malformation that does not regress and grows with the child.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors: Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions, Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors, Malignant Tumors.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An undifferentiated spindle cell tumor is identified in the retroperitoneum of a 60-year-old male. To determine the lineage of the tumor, immunohistochemistry is performed. The tumor cells show strong cytoplasmic staining for CD31. This finding is most characteristic of which of the following lineages?

explanations.a: Epithelial tumors (carcinomas) are characterized by Cytokeratin staining.
explanations.b: Myogenic tumors (leiomyosarcomas, rhabdomyosarcomas) stain for Desmin or SMA.
explanations.c: CD31 (Platelet Endothelial Cell Adhesion Molecule) is a highly specific and sensitive marker for endothelial cells and vascular tumors like angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: Neuroendocrine tumors stain for Chromogranin or Synaptophysin.
explanations.e: Melanocytic tumors stain for S100, HMB-45, or MART-1.

ankiCards: The IHC marker CD31 is specific for {{c1::endothelial}} cell lineage.
Vascular tumors (angiomas/angiosarcomas) typically stain positive for {{c1::CD31 or von Willebrand factor}}.
PECAM-1 is another name for the marker {{c1::CD31}}.
Undifferentiated malignant spindle cells staining for CD31 suggest a diagnosis of {{c1::Angiosarcoma}}.
Marker for Epithelial cells: Cytokeratin; Marker for Endothelial cells: {{c1::CD31}}.
keyPoints: CD31 is the standard IHC marker used to identify vascular tumors.
It marks the cell-cell junctions of endothelial cells.
Useful in distinguishing angiosarcoma from other spindle cell sarcomas.
Other vascular markers include Factor VIII (vWF) and CD34.
Endothelial cells form the inner lining of all blood vessels.
microReview: CD31 = Endothelial marker = Vascular tumor.
examinerTraps: CD34 is also positive in vascular tumors but is much less specific, as it also stains many other mesenchymal tumors.
sourceQuote: The general architecture and cellular composition of blood vessels are comparable throughout the cardiovascular system.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old woman undergoes an abdominal ultrasound for unrelated symptoms, which reveals a 2-cm, well-circumscribed, hyperechoic mass in the right lobe of the liver. Histologic examination of similar lesions shows large, dilated vascular spaces filled with blood and separated by a thin connective tissue stroma. Which of the following is the most characteristic feature of this specific tumor type?

options.a: Infiltration of the surrounding hepatic parenchyma
options.b: Large blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous stroma
options.e: Presence of a central stellate scar

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas are well-circumscribed and non-infiltrative.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are characterized by large, dilated vascular channels (caverns) filled with blood and separated by thin fibrous walls.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign and do not typically transform into angiosarcomas.
explanations.d: Hepatic adenomas, not hemangiomas, are strongly associated with oral contraceptive use.
explanations.e: A central stellate scar is the hallmark of Focal Nodular Hyperplasia (FNH), not hemangioma.

ankiCards: The most common benign tumor of the liver is the {{c1::cavernous hemangioma}}.
Histologically, cavernous hemangiomas show {{c1::large blood-filled spaces}} and fibrous stroma.
Percutaneous biopsy of a liver hemangioma is discouraged due to the risk of {{c1::hemorrhage}}.
Cavernous hemangiomas are usually {{c1::asymptomatic}} and found incidentally.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas involve {{c1::large, dilated}} vessels.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor.
Consists of large, thin-walled vascular channels.
Usually subcapsular and well-circumscribed.
Can cause symptoms if they are giant (>4 cm) and compress organs.
The risk of rupture is low, but biopsy is avoided if the diagnosis is clear on imaging.
microReview: Incidental liver mass + large blood spaces = Cavernous Hemangioma.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse with Hepatic Adenoma (O-Cpill link) or FNH (Stellate scar). Also, remember that biopsy is contraindicated due to bleeding risk.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 42-year-old male who recently underwent a renal transplant is receiving potent immunosuppressive therapy, including cyclosporine and corticosteroids. Three months post-transplant, he develops multiple red-purple skin macules on his trunk. Biopsy confirms Kaposi sarcoma. This specific clinical presentation is best classified as which of the following?

explanations.a: Chronic (Classic) Kaposi sarcoma occurs in older men of Mediterranean or Eastern European descent and is not associated with immunosuppression.
explanations.b: Lymphadenopathic (Endemic African) Kaposi sarcoma occurs in children in Africa and is very aggressive.
explanations.c: AIDS-associated (Epidemic) Kaposi sarcoma occurs in HIV-infected patients.
explanations.d: Classic Kaposi sarcoma is a synonym for Chronic KS, occurring in older Mediterranean men.
explanations.e: Transplant-associated (Iatrogenic) Kaposi sarcoma occurs in solid-organ transplant recipients on immunosuppressive therapy.

ankiCards: The four clinical types of Kaposi Sarcoma are {{c1::Classic, Endemic, Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated}}.
Transplant-associated Kaposi Sarcoma is also known as {{c1::Iatrogenic}} KS.
In Transplant-associated KS, the lesions may regress if {{c1::immunosuppression}} is reduced.
The 'Classic' form of KS usually affects the {{c1::lower extremities/distal limbs}}.
{{c1::HHV-8}} is the common factor across all four types of Kaposi Sarcoma.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma is an opportunistic neoplasm linked to T-cell immunity defects.
Iatrogenic KS is specifically linked to post-transplant immunosuppression.
It can be aggressive, involving internal organs.
Reducing immunosuppressive drugs is a primary treatment strategy.
Spindle cell proliferation and extravasated RBCs are seen in all KS types.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma Subtypes: Mediterranean/Elderly = Classic. Africa/Children = Endemic. HIV/AIDS = Epidemic. Transplant/Cyclosporine = Iatrogenic.
examinerTraps: Ensure you check the underlying cause (HIV vs Transplant) to distinguish between AIDS-associated and Transplant-associated KS.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors: Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions, Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors, Malignant Tumors.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 44-year-old male with a history of poorly controlled HIV infection presents with multiple firm, non-blanching, purple-to-red plaques on his lower extremities and hard palate. A biopsy of one lesion demonstrates a proliferation of spindle cells forming slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated erythrocytes and hemosiderin. Which of the following is the most likely causative agent responsible for this condition?

explanations.a: Human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8) is the primary oncogenic driver in all forms of Kaposi sarcoma, including the epidemic (AIDS-associated) form described here. It encodes viral homologs of cyclin D and other proteins that promote cell proliferation.
explanations.b: Human papillomavirus-16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx, not vascular tumors.
explanations.c: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and hairy leukoplakia, but not with vascular spindle cell tumors.
explanations.d: Cytomegalovirus causes opportunistic infections in HIV patients (retinitis, colitis) but is not the driver of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.e: Hepatitis B virus is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma and polyarteritis nodosa, not primary cutaneous vascular tumors.

ankiCards: The viral agent associated with Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::HHV-8 (Human Herpesvirus-8)}}.
The histological hallmark of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells forming slit-like vascular spaces}}.
Kaposi Sarcoma in AIDS patients typically presents as {{c1::purple/red plaques or nodules}}.
Extravasated {{c1::erythrocytes}} and hemosiderin are common histological findings in Kaposi Sarcoma.
HHV-8 belongs to the {{c1::Gammaherpesvirinae}} subfamily.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma is a low-grade vascular malignancy caused by HHV-8.
Histology shows spindle cells, slit-like spaces, and extravasated RBCs.
The 'epidemic' form is the most common HIV-associated malignancy.
Involvement can be cutaneous, mucosal (hard palate), or visceral.
HHV-8 infection is necessary but not sufficient for tumor development; immune status plays a major role.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) presents in four forms: Classic (elderly Mediterranean), Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and Epidemic (AIDS). All are linked to HHV-8.
examinerTraps: Distinguishing Kaposi Sarcoma from Bacillary Angiomatosis: KS has spindle cells and slits, while Bacillary Angiomatosis has neutrophils and Bartonella organisms.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: A 68-year-old female presents with several dark-red, firm nodules on her right arm. She underwent a radical mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection 10 years ago for breast cancer, which was followed by chronic, massive lymphedema of the ipsilateral extremity. A biopsy of a nodule reveals poorly differentiated endothelial cells with significant atypia and frequent mitotic figures. Which immunohistochemical marker would be most helpful in confirming the cell of origin for this malignancy?

explanations.a: Cytokeratin 7 is a marker for epithelial cells, used to identify carcinomas (like the patient's original breast cancer), not vascular tumors.
explanations.b: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a highly specific marker for endothelial cells and is used to identify vascular tumors like angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (smooth or skeletal), not endothelial cells.
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells like melanocytes and Schwann cells.
explanations.e: CD45 (Leukocyte Common Antigen) is used to identify hematopoietic/lymphoid cells.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema is known as {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
The most specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial differentiation is {{c1::CD31}}.
{{c1::Angiosarcoma}} is a malignant vascular tumor associated with radiation and chronic lymphedema.
Histologically, angiosarcomas show {{c1::atypical endothelial cells}} with frequent mitoses.
Angiosarcomas are often associated with high-dose {{c1::radiation}} exposure.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms.
Stewart-Treves syndrome describes angiosarcoma complicating chronic lymphedema.
They commonly occur in the skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
CD31 and vWF (von Willebrand factor) are the primary markers.
These tumors are aggressive with a poor 5-year survival rate.
microReview: Angiosarcoma: History of radiation/lymphedema + atypical endothelial cells + CD31/vWF positivity.
examinerTraps: Wait for the history: If the patient had a mastectomy, don't assume the new skin lesion is metastatic breast cancer (which would be Cytokeratin positive); consider Angiosarcoma if lymphedema is present.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: Vascular tumors are classified based on their biological behavior into benign, intermediate (borderline), and malignant. Which of the following is categorized as an intermediate-grade (borderline) vascular tumor?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignant tumor.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangioma is a common benign tumor.
explanations.c: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is an intermediate-grade tumor, meaning its behavior is between benign hemangiomas and highly malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.d: Glomus tumor is a benign, painful tumor of the distal digits.
explanations.e: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign capillary hemangioma variant often occurring on the gingiva.

ankiCards: {{c1::Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma}} is an example of an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
Benign vascular tumors are often called {{c1::hemangiomas}}.
Malignant vascular tumors are called {{c1::angiosarcomas}}.
Intermediate vascular tumors are also referred to as {{c1::borderline}} tumors.
A glomus tumor is classified as a {{c1::benign}} vascular-related tumor.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors reflect a spectrum of malignancy.
Hemangiomas (capillary/cavernous) are benign.
Kaposi Sarcoma and Epithelioid Hemangioendothelioma are intermediate.
Angiosarcoma is highly malignant.
Intermediate tumors are locally aggressive but have lower metastatic potential than angiosarcomas.
microReview: Classification: Benign (Hemangiomas), Intermediate (KS, Hemangioendothelioma), Malignant (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: Sometimes 'Hemangiopericytoma' is used in older texts; modern classification places it under Solitary Fibrous Tumor. Stick to Robbins classifications.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: A 31-year-old male presents with a 4-mm, exquisitely painful, small blue nodule located under the fingernail of his left index finger. The pain is triggered by cold exposure and pressure. Microscopic examination of the excised lesion shows nests of uniform, specialized smooth muscle cells surrounding branch-like vascular channels. What is the cell of origin for this tumor?

explanations.a: Endothelial cells line the vascular channels within the tumor, but the neoplastic 'glomus cells' are the primary component.
explanations.b: Pericytes are related but 'glomus cells' are specifically modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts are stromal cells and not the primary neoplastic component of glomus tumors.
explanations.e: Lymphatic endothelial cells form lymphangiomas, not glomus tumors.

ankiCards: The classic location for a glomus tumor is {{c1::subungual (under the nail)}}.
The key clinical symptom of a glomus tumor is {{c1::exquisite pain}} (often triggered by cold).
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells.
The glomus body's physiological function is {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Histologically, glomus cells appear as {{c1::nests of uniform round cells}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but extremely painful.
They are most commonly found in the distal digits, especially subungual.
Derived from the glomus body (a specialized thermoregulatory AV shunt).
The cells are modified smooth muscle cells.
Excision is curative.
microReview: Subungual + Pain + Cold Sensitivity = Glomus Tumor (Modified smooth muscle).
examinerTraps: Do not confuse this with a subungual melanoma, which is typically pigmented and not specifically sensitive to cold.
sourceQuote: To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure and function.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: A 24-year-old female in her second trimester of pregnancy develops a rapidly growing, pedunculated, red nodule on her gingiva that bleeds easily with minor trauma. If the lesion were to be biopsied, it would show a proliferation of capillaries with interspersed edema and an inflammatory infiltrate. Which of the following best describes the natural history or characteristic of this lesion?

options.a: It frequently undergoes malignant transformation to angiosarcoma
options.b: It is caused by infection with Bartonella henselae
options.c: It often regresses spontaneously or after pregnancy
options.d: It is associated with an inherited mutation in the VHL gene
options.e: It represents a true granulomatous inflammation

explanations.a: Pyogenic granulomas (lobular capillary hemangiomas) are entirely benign and do not transform into malignancy.
explanations.b: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which looks similar histologically but is infectious, not pregnancy-related.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granulomas are common in pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum) and often regress spontaneously after delivery.
explanations.d: VHL mutations are associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease and hemangioblastomas, not pyogenic granulomas.
explanations.e: Despite the name, 'pyogenic granuloma' is neither pyogenic (pus-forming) nor a granuloma histologically; it is a capillary hemangioma.

ankiCards: A 'pyogenic granuloma' appearing on the gingiva of a pregnant woman is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Histologically, a pyogenic granuloma is a {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
True/False: Pyogenic granulomas are composed of granulomatous inflammation. {{c1::False}}
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized by {{c1::rapid growth}} and easy bleeding.
The typical clinical course for granuloma gravidarum after delivery is {{c1::spontaneous regression}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it's a vascular proliferation.
Common on skin, gingiva, and oral mucosa.
Highly vascular, bleeds easily (friable).
Frequently associated with pregnancy (hormonal influence).
Histology shows exuberant granulation tissue-like appearance.
microReview: Pregnancy + Gingival nodule + Bleeding = Pyogenic Granuloma (Benign).
examinerTraps: The name is a trap! It's not a 'granuloma' (no epithelioid histiocytes) and not 'pyogenic' (not primarily an abscess).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: Exposure to certain environmental toxins is strongly associated with the development of hepatic angiosarcoma. Which of the following substances is a known risk factor for this specific malignant vascular tumor?

explanations.a: Aflatoxin B1 is a potent risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Vinyl chloride (used in PVC production), Arsenic, and Thorotrast are classic risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and bronchogenic carcinoma.
explanations.d: Benzene is associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.e: Beryllium exposure is associated with berylliosis (granulomatous lung disease) and lung cancer.

ankiCards: The environmental toxin associated with hepatic angiosarcoma in PVC workers is {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
Name three risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma: {{c1::Vinyl chloride, Arsenic, Thorotrast}}.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is a malignancy of the {{c1::endothelial}} cells in the liver.
Thorotrast, a radioactive contrast agent used historically, is linked to {{c1::angiosarcoma}} of the liver.
Hepatic angiosarcoma has a {{c1::long}} latent period between toxin exposure and tumor development.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is rare but lethal.
Strong association with specific chemical exposures.
Arsenic (pesticides) and Vinyl chloride (plastic industry) are key.
Thorotrast (radioactive thorium dioxide) was a historical cause.
Tumors are often multicentric and aggressive.
microReview: Vinyl Chloride/Arsenic/Thorotrast -> Hepatic Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the liver tumor: Vinyl chloride causes Angiosarcoma, while Aflatoxin/HBV/HCV cause Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: A 3-week-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for a bright red, raised 'strawberry-like' lesion on the scalp. The parents state it was not present at birth but has grown rapidly over the last two weeks. What is the most likely clinical course for this lesion?

options.b: Persistent growth requiring immediate surgical excision
options.c: Rapid growth followed by spontaneous involution by age 7
options.e: Life-long persistence without change in size

explanations.a: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are benign and never metastasize.
explanations.b: Surgery is usually avoided because most of these lesions regress on their own.
explanations.c: Juvenile hemangiomas are very common (1 in 200 births). They grow rapidly for a few months, then stabilize, and usually completely involute by age 7 in the vast majority of cases.
explanations.d: Juvenile hemangiomas do not 'transform' into cavernous hemangiomas; they are distinct entities.
explanations.e: Persistence is rare; involution is the hallmark of the 'strawberry' type.

ankiCards: The 'strawberry hemangioma' of infancy is histologically a {{c1::juvenile (capillary) hemangioma}}.
Juvenile hemangiomas typically appear {{c1::shortly after birth}} (within weeks).
Most juvenile hemangiomas will {{c1::spontaneously involute}} by age 7.
Histologically, juvenile hemangiomas are composed of {{c1::thin-walled capillaries}} with scant stroma.
The frequency of juvenile hemangiomas is approximately 1 in {{c1::200}} births.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangioma = Strawberry hemangioma.
Common in newborns, grows rapidly.
Usually regresses without treatment.
Histology: Proliferation of small, thin-walled capillaries.
Complete involution occurs in 90% by age 7.
microReview: Infant + Strawberry lesion + Rapid growth = Juvenile Hemangioma (Regresses).
examinerTraps: The rapid growth often scares parents (and students), but the correct management is usually observation as they regress.
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: Which of the following vascular conditions is characterized by a permanent dilation of small vessels, often forming a non-neoplastic 'birthmark' such as a nevus flammeus?

explanations.a: Ectasia is a general term for a permanent dilation of a pre-existing vessel (e.g., nevus flammeus or 'port-wine stain'). It is not a true neoplasm.
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma is a malignant neoplasm of endothelial cells.
explanations.c: Hemangioendothelioma is an intermediate-grade neoplasm.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation.
explanations.e: Glomus tumor is a benign neoplasm of specialized smooth muscle cells.

ankiCards: A 'port-wine stain' is a type of {{c1::nevus flammeus}}, which is a vascular ectasia.
{{c1::Ectasia}} refers to a permanent dilation of pre-existing vessels.
The association of a facial port-wine stain with leptomeningeal angiomas is {{c1::Sturge-Weber syndrome}}.
Unlike hemangiomas, ectasias are {{c1::not}} true neoplasms.
Telangiectasias are a form of {{c1::ectasia}}.
keyPoints: Ectasias are dilations of vessels, not true growths.
Nevus flammeus (birthmark) is the most common form.
Port-wine stains are a subset of nevus flammeus that thicken over time.
Sturge-Weber syndrome involves the distribution of the trigeminal nerve.
Spider telangiectasias are associated with high estrogen states (pregnancy, cirrhosis).
microReview: Ectasia = Dilation (e.g., Port-wine stain). Hemangioma = Neoplasm.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Ectasia (dilation) with Hemangioma (proliferation/neoplasm).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: A biopsy of a skin lesion in an immunocompromised patient shows a proliferation of capillaries with prominent 'epithelioid' endothelial cells, striking neutrophilic infiltrates, and nuclear dust. Warthin-Starry silver stain reveals clusters of tangled bacilli. What is the primary mechanism of vessel proliferation in this condition?

options.b: Bacterial induction of host hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF-1α)
options.c: MYC gene amplification following radiation injury
options.d: Loss of function mutation in the VHL tumor suppressor
options.e: Constitutive activation of the GNAQ gene

explanations.a: HHV-8 is the mechanism for Kaposi Sarcoma, which lacks neutrophils and silver-staining bacilli.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis (caused by Bartonella) stimulates vascular proliferation by inducing the host to produce VEGF through the HIF-1α pathway.
explanations.c: MYC amplification is seen in post-radiation angiosarcoma, not bacillary angiomatosis.
explanations.d: VHL mutations cause hemangioblastomas, not Bartonella-associated lesions.
explanations.e: GNAQ mutations are associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome and uveal melanoma.

ankiCards: The pathogen responsible for bacillary angiomatosis is {{c1::Bartonella (henselae or quintana)}}.
Bacillary angiomatosis histology features vascular proliferation and {{c1::neutrophils}}.
The special stain used to visualize Bartonella in tissues is {{c1::Warthin-Starry (silver stain)}}.
Unlike Kaposi Sarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis {{c1::is}} treatable with antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin).
Bartonella induces vascular growth by stimulating {{c1::VEGF}} production.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis occurs in immunocompromised (AIDS) patients.
Caused by Bartonella henselae (cats) or Bartonella quintana (lice).
Histology: Capillaries + Neutrophils + Nuclear dust.
Differential includes Kaposi Sarcoma (but KS lacks neutrophils/bacteria).
Treatment with antibiotics can lead to regression.
microReview: AIDS + Vascular lesion + Neutrophils + Silver stain (+) = Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella).
examinerTraps: The clinical presentation (purple nodules in AIDS) is identical to Kaposi Sarcoma. You MUST look for 'neutrophils' or 'silver stain' or 'bacilli' in the stem to choose Bacillary Angiomatosis.
sourceQuote: Infectious Vasculitis... can be caused by the direct invasion of vessel walls by infectious agents.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease

stem: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is a unique vascular tumor with a clinical course intermediate between benign hemangiomas and malignant angiosarcomas. It is most commonly characterized by which of the following molecular or histological features?

explanations.a: MYC amplification is characteristic of angiosarcomas arising in the setting of lymphedema or radiation.
explanations.b: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is frequently associated with a characteristic t(1;3) translocation resulting in a WWTR1-CAMTA1 fusion gene.
explanations.c: HHV-8 is specific to Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.d: GNAQ mutations are found in port-wine stains and Sturge-Weber syndrome.
explanations.e: VHL inactivation is found in hemangioblastomas (often in the CNS/retina) and renal cell carcinoma.

ankiCards: The characteristic translocation in Epithelioid Hemangioendothelioma is {{c1::t(1;3)}}.
The fusion gene associated with Epithelioid Hemangioendothelioma is {{c1::WWTR1-CAMTA1}}.
The behavior of Epithelioid Hemangioendothelioma is classified as {{c1::intermediate (borderline)}}.
Histologically, the cells in an epithelioid hemangioendothelioma appear {{c1::epithelioid or cuboidal}}.
Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma often occurs around medium and large {{c1::veins}}.
keyPoints: Epithelioid Hemangioendothelioma is a 'borderline' tumor.
Cells look like epithelial cells (plump/cuboidal) rather than flat endothelium.
Associated with t(1;3) WWTR1-CAMTA1 fusion.
Can occur in soft tissue, liver, or lung.
Clinical course is unpredictable; some are indolent, others behave more like angiosarcomas.
microReview: Borderline + Epithelioid cells + t(1;3) = Epithelioid Hemangioendothelioma.
examinerTraps: The name 'Epithelioid' might make you think of a carcinoma; always check for CD31/vWF markers to confirm vascular origin.
