examinerTraps: A common trap is thinking 'saccular' means it's less dangerous. Saccular aneurysms (like berry aneurysms) are highly prone to rupture.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 25-year-old female with a history of joint hypermobility and mitral valve prolapse presents with sudden onset of severe chest pain. CT angiography reveals a dilation of the ascending aorta. Histology shows 'cystic' spaces filled with basophilic mucoid material in the tunica media. Which of the following molecular pathways is most likely overactive in this patient?

explanations.a: VEGF is primarily involved in angiogenesis, not medial degeneration.
explanations.b: Overactivity of the TGF-β pathway is a hallmark of Marfan syndrome and Loeys-Dietz syndrome, leading to increased production of metalloproteinases and cystic medial necrosis.
explanations.c: NOTCH signaling is involved in cell fate but not classically the driver of cystic medial necrosis in aneurysms.
explanations.d: Wnt signaling is crucial in development and cancer but not the primary driver of Marfan-associated aneurysms.
explanations.e: Hedgehog is a developmental pathway not associated with the pathogenesis of aortic root dilation.

ankiCards: The histological hallmark of Marfan-associated aneurysms is {{c1::cystic medial necrosis}}.
Cystic medial necrosis involves the loss of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} and elastic fibers.
Marfan syndrome is caused by mutations in the {{c1::FBN1 (fibrillin-1)}} gene.
Excessive {{c1::TGF-β}} signaling is a key pathogenic mechanism in Marfan syndrome.
The mucoid material in cystic medial necrosis is composed of {{c1::glycosaminoglycans}}.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome involves a Fibrillin-1 mutation.
Fibrillin normally sequesters TGF-beta; its absence leads to TGF-beta overactivity.
Cystic medial necrosis is characterized by elastic fiber fragmentation.
This condition predisposes patients to Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (TAA).
TAA often leads to aortic root dilation and aortic valve insufficiency.
microReview: Thoracic aneurysms in young people should trigger thoughts of Marfan syndrome and 'cystic medial necrosis'. This isn't 'necrosis' in the standard sense, but rather a replacement of the healthy media with mucoid matrix.
examinerTraps: Wait for the age. Elderly + Aneurysm = Atherosclerosis/Hypertension. Young + Aneurysm = Genetic/Connective tissue disorder.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes a 'false aneurysm' (pseudoaneurysm), a critical differential in vascular trauma?

options.a: A focal dilation of all three layers of the arterial wall
options.b: An extravascular hematoma communicating with the intravascular space
options.c: A dissection of blood between the layers of the tunica media
options.d: A congenital thinning of the muscularis at arterial bifurcations
options.e: A circumferential dilation of the entire vessel diameter

explanations.a: This defines a true aneurysm.
explanations.b: A false aneurysm is a breach in the vascular wall leading to an extravascular hematoma that freely communicates with the lumen (e.g., following trauma or catheterization).
explanations.c: This defines an aortic dissection.
explanations.d: This describes the anatomy of a berry (saccular) aneurysm (true aneurysm).
explanations.e: This describes a fusiform (true) aneurysm.

ankiCards: A {{c1::false}} aneurysm occurs when a wall defect leads to an extravascular hematoma.
A pseudoaneurysm must {{c1::communicate}} with the intravascular space.
False aneurysms are often caused by {{c1::trauma}} or iatrogenic injury (e.g., catheterization).
Unlike a true aneurysm, a pseudoaneurysm is contained by {{c1::extravascular}} tissue/clot.
The risk of a pseudoaneurysm is primarily {{c1::rupture}} or infection.
keyPoints: Pseudoaneurysms involve a 'hole' in the wall.
The 'wall' of the pseudoaneurysm is often just clotted blood and fibrous tissue.
They frequently occur at the femoral artery site after cardiac cath.
They present as a pulsatile mass with a systolic bruit.
Treatment can involve ultrasound-guided thrombin injection.
microReview: True = All 3 layers dilated. False = Wall breached, hematoma held in by external tissue. Both can pulsate.
examinerTraps: An examiner might ask to differentiate a hematoma from a pseudoaneurysm. A pseudoaneurysm has a 'neck' and continuous blood flow into the sac, whereas a simple hematoma is clotted blood outside the vessel with no ongoing communication.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: The abdominal aorta is particularly susceptible to atherosclerotic aneurysms compared to the thoracic aorta. Which anatomical factor contributes most to this regional susceptibility?

options.a: Higher concentration of elastic fibers in the abdominal media
options.b: Lower density of vasa vasorum in the abdominal aortic wall
options.c: Absence of an adventitia in the abdominal segment
options.d: Increased presence of longitudinal smooth muscle
options.e: Lower mean arterial pressure in the abdominal region

explanations.a: The abdominal aorta actually has fewer elastic fibers than the thoracic aorta, making it less resilient.
explanations.b: The abdominal aorta has fewer vasa vasorum; thus, the media must rely on diffusion from the lumen. Atherosclerotic plaques block this diffusion, leading to medial ischemia and weakening.
explanations.c: The abdominal aorta has an adventitia like all large arteries.
explanations.d: The muscle arrangement does not explain the differential susceptibility to atherosclerosis-induced weakening.
explanations.e: Pressure is generally consistent or slightly higher due to wave reflection, but this isn't the primary anatomical susceptibility factor.

ankiCards: The abdominal aorta relies more on {{c1::diffusion}} for nutrients than the thoracic aorta.
The sparsity of {{c1::vasa vasorum}} in the infrarenal aorta predisposes it to aneurysms.
Atherosclerotic plaques cause medial {{c1::ischemia}} by increasing diffusion distance.
AAAs are mostly found between the {{c1::renal arteries}} and the aortic bifurcation.
The abdominal aorta has {{c1::fewer}} elastic lamellae than the thoracic aorta.
keyPoints: Vasa vasorum nourish the outer half of the media in large vessels.
The infrarenal aorta has the lowest vasa vasorum density.
Atherosclerosis creates a diffusion barrier for oxygen.
Medial cells die, and the matrix is replaced by weaker fibrous tissue.
This explains why AAA is much more common than TAA in atherosclerotic patients.
microReview: Infrarenal aorta = No vasa vasorum + Atherosclerosis = Medial starvation = Wall weakening = AAA.
examinerTraps: Don't say AAAs are caused by high pressure alone. While hypertension helps 'stretch' the wall, the underlying 'weakness' is usually atherosclerotic/ischemic in the abdomen.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions. Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 74-year-old male presents with deep, boring back pain. He has a history of tertiary syphilis. Imaging reveals a 'tree-bark' appearance of the ascending aortic intima and a 6 cm aneurysm of the aortic arch. What is the underlying mechanism of this vascular damage?

options.a: Lipid accumulation in the subendothelial space
options.b: Ischemic injury to the media via vasa vasorum endarteritis
options.c: Cystic medial necrosis due to fibrillin mutations
options.d: Direct bacterial invasion of the tunica adventitia
options.e: Autoimmune destruction of the internal elastic lamina

explanations.a: This describes atherosclerosis, which usually affects the abdominal aorta.
explanations.b: Tertiary syphilis causes obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum, leading to ischemia of the outer media and subsequent weakening/dilation (aneurysm).
explanations.c: This describes Marfan syndrome.
explanations.d: The damage is caused by the host inflammatory response to the spirochetes (endarteritis), not direct bacterial 'eating' of the wall.
explanations.e: This is more characteristic of Giant Cell Arteritis.

ankiCards: Syphilitic aneurysms typically involve the {{c1::ascending}} aorta.
The 'tree-bark' appearance in syphilis is caused by scarring of the {{c1::intima}}.
Syphilis causes ischemia of the media via obliterative {{c1::endarteritis}} of the vasa vasorum.
The specific stage of syphilis associated with aneurysms is {{c1::tertiary}} syphilis.
Dilation of the aortic root in syphilis can lead to {{c1::aortic valve}} insufficiency.
keyPoints: Syphilis = Obliterative endarteritis of vasa vasorum.
This causes 'luetic' mesaortitis (inflammation of the media).
The resulting scarring causes the 'tree-bark' appearance.
It favors the thoracic aorta because vasa vasorum are more abundant there.
Clinical signs: Respiratory distress (compression), cough, or aortic regurgitation.
microReview: Syphilis attacks the 'vessels of the vessels' (vasa vasorum). No blood to the media = weak wall = TAA.
examinerTraps: A common mistake is thinking syphilis causes AAAs. It almost exclusively causes Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (TAA).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Inflammation plays a dual role in vascular health. In the context of an enlarging abdominal aortic aneurysm, which cell type is the most significant source of the proteases that weaken the tunica media?

explanations.a: Endothelial cells produce some factors but are not the primary source of the MMPs that destroy the media in AAAs.
explanations.b: Macrophages within the atherosclerotic inflammatory infiltrate secrete matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) like collagenases and gelatinases that degrade the media.
explanations.c: Platelets are involved in thrombosis, not the primary enzymatic degradation of the vessel wall.
explanations.d: RBCs have no role in enzymatic medial degradation.
explanations.e: Fibroblasts typically attempt to repair the wall by producing collagen; the degradation is driven by the inflammatory cells (macrophages).

ankiCards: In AAA, the inflammatory infiltrate in the wall is primarily composed of {{c1::macrophages}} and T cells.
Macrophages secrete {{c1::MMPs (matrix metalloproteinases)}} which degrade elastin.
Degradation of {{c1::elastin}} and collagen leads to aneurysmal dilation.
MMP-2 and {{c1::MMP-9}} are specifically implicated in AAA pathogenesis.
The structural integrity of the aorta depends mostly on the tunica {{c1::media}}.
keyPoints: AAA is an inflammatory process as much as a hemodynamic one.
Infiltrating macrophages are the 'engine' of wall destruction.
They produce MMPs that outpace the inhibitory capacity of TIMPs.
Elastin degradation is the early step in dilation.
Collagen degradation is the final step leading to rupture.
microReview: Aneurysm = Macrophages + MMPs > TIMPs (Tissue Inhibitors of Metalloproteinases). The balance shifts to 'destroy' rather than 'maintain'.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'mural thrombus' (found inside the aneurysm) with the 'infiltrate' (found inside the wall). The thrombus is platelets/fibrin; the infiltrate is macrophages/T-cells.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 62-year-old female with long-standing, poorly controlled hypertension presents with a sudden, excruciating 'tearing' pain that radiates to her back. She is tachycardic, and there is a significant blood pressure difference between her right and left arms. While this condition is not a 'true aneurysm' by definition, it shares which of the following common underlying mechanisms with aneurysmal disease?

options.c: Obliteration of the lumen by plaque

explanations.a: Mural thrombi are common in aneurysms but are not the cause of the 'tearing' pain in dissection.
explanations.b: Aortic dissection is caused by an intimal tear followed by blood tracking through a weakened or degenerated tunica media, similar to how medial weakening allows for aneurysmal dilation.
explanations.c: Aneurysms and dissections actually involve lumen expansion or the creation of a 'false' lumen, rather than simple plaque obstruction.
explanations.d: In both aneurysms and dissections, the effective structural wall is thinned or compromised, decreasing the wall-to-lumen ratio.
explanations.e: This is a developmental/pathological process not central to the acute event of dissection or the structure of an aneurysm.

ankiCards: Aortic dissection is most commonly associated with {{c1::hypertension}}.
The 'tearing' pain of dissection often radiates to the {{c1::back}} (between the scapulae).
Dissection requires an {{c1::intimal}} tear and a weakened media.
Unlike an aneurysm, a dissection involves blood between the {{c1::layers}} of the media.
A BP discrepancy between arms suggests a dissection involving the {{c1::aortic arch}} or subclavian artery.
keyPoints: Aneurysms and Dissections both stem from medial failure.
Hypertension is the #1 risk factor for Aortic Dissection.
Dissection creates a 'false lumen' within the vessel wall.
It is a surgical emergency if the ascending aorta is involved (Stanford Type A).
The major cause of death in dissection is rupture into the pericardium (tamponade).
microReview: Aneurysm = Dilation of all layers. Dissection = Tear in the intima, blood 'dissects' the media. Both require a weak media to occur.
examinerTraps: The examiner might try to group dissection as a 'type' of aneurysm. It is not. It is a separate clinical entity listed under 'Aneurysms and Dissections' because they share the 'wall weakening' mechanism.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture... Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following human herpesviruses is the primary etiologic agent associated with the development of Kaposi sarcoma in patients with AIDS?

explanations.a: Human herpesvirus-1 (HSV-1) is primarily associated with orofacial lesions and encephalitis, not vascular tumors.
explanations.b: Human herpesvirus-4 (Epstein-Barr virus) is associated with lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, but not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.c: Human herpesvirus-5 (Cytomegalovirus) causes opportunistic infections in immunocompromised hosts but is not the driver of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.d: Human herpesvirus-6 is the causative agent of roseola infantum and is not linked to vascular malignancies.
explanations.e: Human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the definitive cause of all forms of Kaposi sarcoma.

ankiCards: Kaposi sarcoma is strongly associated with infection by {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
The four clinical forms of Kaposi sarcoma are {{c1::Classic, Endemic African, Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated}}.
HHV-8 is most likely transmitted via {{c1::sexual contact}} in the AIDS-associated form.
Histologically, Kaposi sarcoma is characterized by {{c1::spindle cells}} and slit-like vascular spaces.
The most common malignancy associated with AIDS is {{c1::Kaposi sarcoma}}.
keyPoints: HHV-8 is the essential cofactor for Kaposi sarcoma (KS).
KS is an intermediate-grade (borderline) vascular tumor.
AIDS-associated (epidemic) KS is the most common form in the United States.
Lesions progress through patch, plaque, and nodular stages.
Vascular tumors can be benign, intermediate, or malignant.
microReview: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a low-grade vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8. In the US, it is most frequent in HIV-positive individuals. It typically presents as purple/red skin macules or nodules and can involve internal organs.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse HHV-8 with HIV itself; HIV provides the immunosuppressive environment, but HHV-8 is the oncogenic driver of the vascular proliferation.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease. Although the most clinically significant lesions involve arteries, venous disorders are not inconsequential.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which immunohistochemical marker is most useful for confirming the endothelial origin of a poorly differentiated malignant tumor suspected of being an angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Vimentin is a marker for mesenchymal cells in general and is too non-specific to confirm endothelial origin.
explanations.b: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells and would be negative in most vascular tumors unless there is focal aberrant expression.
explanations.c: CD31 (PECAM-1) is a highly specific marker for endothelial cells and is used to identify vascular tumors including angiosarcomas.
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells, melanocytes, and chondrocytes, not endothelium.
explanations.e: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (skeletal, smooth, or cardiac) and is not expressed by endothelial cells.

ankiCards: The most specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial cells is {{c1::CD31}}.
Vascular tumors express {{c1::CD31 or von Willebrand factor (vWF)}}.
Angiosarcomas are malignant tumors of {{c1::endothelial}} origin.
{{c1::CD31}} (PECAM-1) is used to differentiate poorly differentiated angiosarcoma from carcinoma.
Vimentin is a marker for {{c1::mesenchymal}} cells.
keyPoints: Endothelial cells line the vascular spaces of all vascular tumors.
CD31 (Platelet Endothelial Cell Adhesion Molecule) is the gold standard marker.
CD34 and vWF (Factor VIII) are also used but may be less specific/sensitive.
Identification of endothelial origin is crucial for diagnosing vascular malignancies.
Vascular tumors range from benign hemangiomas to highly lethal angiosarcomas.
microReview: Vascular tumors are identified by endothelial markers. CD31 is the most specific, while CD34 and Factor VIII-related antigen are also commonly used. This helps distinguish them from other soft tissue sarcomas or carcinomas.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse CD31 with CD3; CD3 is a T-cell marker.
sourceQuote: To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure and function.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old male presents with severe, localized pain in his fingertip, specifically under the nail bed. The pain is exacerbated by cold temperatures. On physical examination, a small (3 mm), blue-red, exquisitely tender nodule is seen under the nail. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Subungual melanoma usually presents as a pigment stripe (melanonychia) and is typically not exquisitely painful or cold-sensitive.
explanations.b: Glomus tumor (glomangioma) is a benign, exquisitely painful tumor arising from the glomus bodies, often found in the subungual region and sensitive to cold.
explanations.c: Capillary hemangiomas are benign but are generally not painful or specifically localized to the subungual region with cold sensitivity.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a large, aggressive malignancy, not a small, localized, stable subungual nodule.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis presents as multiple skin lesions in HIV patients, not a single painful subungual lesion.

ankiCards: The classic triad of glomus tumor is {{c1::paroxysmal pain, pinpoint tenderness, and cold sensitivity}}.
Glomus tumors arise from {{c1::glomus bodies (thermoregulatory organs)}}.
The most common location for a glomus tumor is {{c1::subungual (under the nail bed)}}.
Glomus tumors are histologically characterized by {{c1::specialized smooth muscle cells}}.
Are glomus tumors benign or malignant? {{c1::Benign}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumor is a benign, extremely painful vascular neoplasm.
It arises from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
The subungual region of the fingers is the classic location.
Pain is often triggered by cold (paroxysmal).
Treatment is simple surgical excision.
microReview: The 'painful blue nodule under the nail' is the quintessential board presentation for a glomus tumor. It is a benign proliferation of glomus cells (modified smooth muscle) involved in thermoregulation.
examinerTraps: They may use 'paroxysmal pain' or 'cold sensitivity' to trigger the diagnosis. Don't pick melanoma just because it's under the nail.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An 8-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a large, soft, fluctuant mass on her neck. Her parents state it has been present since birth and has grown slowly. Imaging shows a poorly circumscribed, multicystic lesion. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) is a benign lymphatic malformation often found in the neck or axilla of children, frequently associated with Turner syndrome.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors are small, painful, and typically found in the extremities (fingertips), not as large congenital neck masses.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is an aggressive malignancy of adults, not a slow-growing congenital neck mass in a child.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a small, rapidly growing red nodule on the skin or mucosa, not a large cystic neck mass.
explanations.e: Sturge-Weber syndrome is characterized by a facial port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) and leptomeningeal angiomatosis, not a cystic neck mass.

ankiCards: Cystic hygroma is another name for {{c1::cavernous lymphangioma}}.
The most common site for a cystic hygroma is the {{c1::neck (or axilla)}}.
Cystic hygroma is classically associated with {{c1::Turner syndrome}}.
Lymphangiomas are composed of {{c1::lymphatic-filled}} spaces.
Are lymphangiomas benign or malignant? {{c1::Benign}}.
keyPoints: Cystic hygroma is a type of lymphangioma (benign).
Typically occurs in children and is often present at birth.
Found in the neck or axilla.
Consists of large, dilated lymphatic spaces lined by endothelium.
Associated with chromosomal abnormalities like Turner syndrome and Down syndrome.
microReview: Cystic hygroma is a benign lymphatic proliferation. If you see a large, soft, cystic mass in a child's neck or axilla, think cystic hygroma, and check for signs of Turner syndrome (45,X).
examinerTraps: Wait for 'neck mass since birth'—this is a key differentiator from other vascular or lymphatic lesions.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the biological behavior of Kaposi sarcoma, placing it between purely benign and highly malignant neoplasms?

explanations.a: While KS involves HHV-8 infection, it is a true neoplasm with clonal potential, not just a reactive proliferation.
explanations.b: Kaposi sarcoma is classified as an intermediate-grade (borderline) vascular tumor because it can be locally aggressive but rarely follows a traditional high-grade malignant course unless the patient is severely immunocompromised.
explanations.c: High-grade malignant vascular tumors are called angiosarcomas, which are much more aggressive than most forms of KS.
explanations.d: Hamartomas are disorganized tissues native to the site; KS is a neoplastic proliferation of spindle cells.
explanations.e: KS is a primary vascular tumor, not a metastatic carcinoma (which is epithelial in origin).

ankiCards: Kaposi sarcoma is categorized as an {{c1::intermediate-grade (borderline)}} tumor.
The spindle cells in Kaposi sarcoma are of {{c1::endothelial}} origin.
The classic form of Kaposi sarcoma usually occurs in {{c1::older men of Mediterranean or Ashkenazi descent}}.
The most aggressive form of Kaposi sarcoma is the {{c1::AIDS-associated (Epidemic)}} type.
The defining feature of Kaposi sarcoma histologically is the presence of {{c1::slit-like spaces containing red blood cells}}.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors are divided into benign (hemangioma), intermediate (KS), and malignant (angiosarcoma).
Intermediate-grade tumors are locally aggressive but have low metastatic potential.
KS is the prototype for intermediate-grade vascular tumors.
All forms of KS are associated with HHV-8.
Histology shows spindle cells and slit-like vascular channels.
microReview: Kaposi sarcoma occupies the 'intermediate' space in vascular tumor pathology. It's not benign like a hemangioma, but it doesn't usually kill as quickly as an angiosarcoma (unless in the context of advanced AIDS).
examinerTraps: Don't classify it as 'benign' just because it can be indolent; 'intermediate' or 'borderline' is the specific pathological classification.
sourceQuote: Vascular Tumors: Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Conditions; Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors; Malignant Tumors.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 65-year-old male former plastic factory worker presents with weight loss, abdominal pain, and hepatomegaly. He worked for 30 years with vinyl chloride exposure. Imaging reveals multiple hemorrhagic masses in the liver. A biopsy shows malignant spindle cells lining irregular vascular spaces. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Hepatocellular carcinoma is associated with HBV/HCV and cirrhosis, not specifically vinyl chloride, and does not show endothelial spindle cells.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are the most common benign liver tumors; they are not malignant and not associated with vinyl chloride.
explanations.c: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare, highly malignant tumor associated with exposure to vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast.
explanations.d: Hepatic adenomas are benign and associated with oral contraceptive use, not industrial toxins.
explanations.e: Metastatic colon cancer is common in the liver but would show glandular architecture (adenocarcinoma), not vascular spindle cells.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride, arsenic, or Thorotrast}}.
The cell of origin for angiosarcoma is the {{c1::endothelial cell}}.
Angiosarcoma is a {{c1::high-grade malignant}} vascular tumor.
Histology of angiosarcoma shows {{c1::atypical endothelial cells and irregular vascular channels}}.
Common sites for angiosarcoma include {{c1::skin, breast, and liver}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a highly aggressive malignant vascular tumor.
Liver angiosarcoma has specific environmental triggers (Vinyl Chloride).
It typically presents with vague symptoms and is often advanced at diagnosis.
Malignant cells express CD31.
Prognosis is generally poor with a high 5-year mortality rate.
microReview: Vinyl chloride + Liver mass + Vascular histology = Angiosarcoma. This is a classic USMLE association.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse vinyl chloride (angiosarcoma) with aflatoxin (hepatocellular carcinoma).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following conditions is characterized by a facial port-wine stain in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve and ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomatosis?

explanations.a: Von Hippel-Lindau disease involves hemangioblastomas of the cerebellum and retina, and renal cell carcinoma, not port-wine stains.
explanations.b: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) involves multiple small telangiectasias of the skin and mucous membranes.
explanations.c: Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) features a facial port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) and vascular malformations of the brain and eyes.
explanations.d: Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to angiosarcoma arising in a limb with chronic lymphedema.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation in HIV patients.

ankiCards: Sturge-Weber syndrome is characterized by a {{c1::port-wine stain (nevus flammeus)}} and leptomeningeal angiomatosis.
The port-wine stain in Sturge-Weber usually follows the distribution of the {{c1::trigeminal nerve (V1/V2 branches)}}.
Neurological complications of Sturge-Weber include {{c1::seizures and intellectual disability}}.
A port-wine stain is a type of {{c1::vascular malformation (ectasia)}}.
Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome is also known as {{c1::Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT)}}.
keyPoints: Sturge-Weber is a sporadic (non-inherited) phakomatosis.
It involves GNAQ gene mutations.
Classic triad: Port-wine stain, leptomeningeal angioma, and glaucoma.
Ipsilateral brain involvement leads to 'tram-track' calcifications on imaging.
Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a benign vascular ectasia.
microReview: Sturge-Weber = Face stain (CN V) + Brain angioma + Seizures. It is an association of vascular anomalies rather than a single 'tumor'.
examinerTraps: The port-wine stain must be in the trigeminal distribution. If the question mentions telangiectasias on the tongue and recurrent nosebleeds, think Osler-Weber-Rendu instead.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular lesions is most likely to be found as a result of an opportunistic infection in an AIDS patient, caused by a Gram-negative bacillus and presenting as red-purple skin nodules?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 (a virus), not a bacillus, though it also appears as red-purple nodules in AIDS patients.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation caused by Bartonella henselae or Bartonella quintana in immunocompromised patients.
explanations.c: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign reactive vascular lesion not specifically linked to AIDS or Gram-negative bacilli.
explanations.d: Glomus tumor is a benign painful tumor of the fingertips, unrelated to infection.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a malignant neoplasm, not an infectious-driven proliferation.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by the Gram-negative bacilli {{c1::Bartonella henselae or B. quintana}}.
The target population for bacillary angiomatosis is {{c1::immunocompromised (AIDS) patients}}.
Histologically, bacillary angiomatosis shows vascular proliferation and {{c1::neutrophilic}} infiltrates.
Bartonella organisms in bacillary angiomatosis are best visualized with {{c1::Warthin-Starry silver stain}}.
Does bacillary angiomatosis respond to antibiotics? {{c1::Yes (e.g., erythromycin)}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis can mimic Kaposi sarcoma clinically.
It is a reactive vascular proliferation, not a true malignancy.
Caused by Bartonella species (cat-scratch disease or trench fever agents).
Features characteristic 'clumps' of bacteria on silver stain.
Treatment with antibiotics (macrolides) is curative.
microReview: Bacillary angiomatosis = AIDS patient + Red nodules + Bartonella + Neutrophils. Kaposi sarcoma = AIDS patient + Red nodules + HHV-8 + Spindle cells/Lymphocytes. This is the crucial differential.
examinerTraps: The presence of neutrophils and the response to antibiotics favor Bacillary Angiomatosis over Kaposi Sarcoma.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old woman presents with several dark-purple, firm nodules on her left arm. She has a history of left-sided radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer 12 years ago, followed by chronic lymphedema of the arm. What is the most likely diagnosis of these new skin nodules?

explanations.a: While metastatic breast cancer can involve the skin, the history of chronic lymphedema and the appearance of vascular nodules strongly suggests a secondary vascular malignancy.
explanations.b: Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema, classically after mastectomy.
explanations.c: Lymphangiomas are benign congenital lesions, not new nodules arising in an elderly patient with chronic lymphedema.
explanations.d: Sturge-Weber is a congenital syndrome involving facial port-wine stains, not acquired nodules on a lymphedematous arm.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are small, painful subungual lesions, not multiple nodules on a lymphedematous limb.

ankiCards: The development of angiosarcoma in a limb with chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
Angiosarcoma can also occur as a complication of {{c1::radiation therapy}} for breast cancer.
Chronic lymphedema is a risk factor for {{c1::angiosarcoma}}.
Angiosarcomas are characterized by {{c1::aggressive local growth and high metastatic potential}}.
The clinical appearance of cutaneous angiosarcoma is usually {{c1::bruise-like or purple-red nodules}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are the most aggressive vascular tumors.
Stewart-Treves syndrome is a classic association (Post-mastectomy lymphedema -> Angiosarcoma).
Radiation is another major risk factor for cutaneous angiosarcoma.
These tumors have a very poor prognosis.
Diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy showing atypical endothelial cells.
microReview: Any time you see 'chronic lymphedema' or 'post-radiation' followed by new 'purple nodules', the diagnosis is Angiosarcoma. Stewart-Treves is the specific eponym for the lymphedema-associated version.
examinerTraps: They may try to lead you toward recurrent breast cancer, but the 'purple nodules' and 'vascular' description point toward angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old man presents to the clinic for a routine physical examination. He has a 45-pack-year smoking history and long-standing untreated hypertension. On abdominal palpation, a non-tender, pulsatile mass is noted at the level of the umbilicus. Imaging reveals a 5.2 cm focal dilation of the abdominal aorta. Which of the following is the most significant underlying contributor to the formation of this lesion?

options.a: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.b: Deficiency of vitamin C for collagen cross-linking
options.c: Atherosclerotic destruction of the vessel wall
options.d: Granulomatous inflammation of the tunica media
options.e: Congenital weakness of the muscularis layer

explanations.a: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum is the classic lesion of tertiary syphilis, which typically results in thoracic aortic aneurysms rather than abdominal ones.
explanations.b: Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) affects collagen synthesis but is not a primary driver of focal abdominal aortic aneurysms in elderly smokers.
explanations.c: Atherosclerosis is the major risk factor for abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA). It leads to intimal thickening, which compromises nutrient diffusion to the media, causing ischemia, atrophy, and wall weakening.
explanations.d: Granulomatous inflammation is characteristic of vasculitides like Giant Cell Arteritis or Takayasu Arteritis, not typically the cause of an infrarenal pulsatile mass in an older male smoker.
explanations.e: Congenital muscularis weakness is associated with berry aneurysms in the Circle of Willis, not abdominal aortic aneurysms.

ankiCards: The most common location for an atherosclerotic aneurysm is the {{c1::abdominal aorta}}.
Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are typically located {{c1::infrarenal (below the renal arteries)}}.
The major modifiable risk factor for the development of AAA is {{c1::cigarette smoking}}.
Atherosclerosis causes AAA by inducing {{c1::ischemic atrophy}} of the media due to diffusion limitations.
The diameter threshold for significantly increased rupture risk in AAA is generally {{c1::5.0 to 5.5 cm}}.
keyPoints: AAA is most common in male smokers over age 60.
Atherosclerosis is the primary pathogenic driver.
Most occur between the renal arteries and the iliac bifurcation.
Clinical presentation is often an asymptomatic pulsatile mass.
Complications include rupture, obstruction of branch vessels, and embolism from mural thrombi.
microReview: AAA is a disease of wall weakening. Atherosclerosis leads to a thickened intima, which prevents oxygen from reaching the media. This leads to medial necrosis and weakening of the elastic fibers.
examinerTraps: Students often confuse the site of Syphilitic aneurysms (Thoracic) with Atherosclerotic aneurysms (Abdominal). Remember: Syphilis is high (Thorax), Atherosclerosis is low (Abdomen).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: The pathogenesis of many aneurysms involves an imbalance between the synthesis and degradation of extracellular matrix components. In the context of abdominal aortic aneurysms, which group of enzymes is primarily responsible for the degradation of aortic connective tissue?

explanations.a: Caspases are involved in apoptosis, not the direct degradation of extracellular matrix fibers.
explanations.b: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), particularly MMP-2 and MMP-9 produced by macrophages, degrade elastin and collagen, leading to wall weakening.
explanations.c: Lysyl oxidase is required for cross-linking collagen and elastin; its inhibition (e.g., in lathyrism) weakens walls, but it is not the degrading enzyme in AAA.
explanations.d: Cyclooxygenases (COX) are involved in prostaglandin synthesis and inflammation, but they do not directly digest the matrix.
explanations.e: Tyrosine kinases are involved in cell signaling pathways and growth factors, not structural protein degradation.

ankiCards: Inflammatory cells in an aneurysm wall secrete {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
MMP-2 and {{c1::MMP-9}} are the specific enzymes most associated with AAA development.
Increased degradation of {{c1::elastin and collagen}} results in vessel wall dilation.
Tissue inhibitors of {{c1::metalloproteinases (TIMPs)}} usually balance MMP activity; a decrease leads to aneurysms.
Medial destruction in aneurysms is often called {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
keyPoints: MMPs are derived from macrophages and smooth muscle cells.
They degrade the structural integrity of the media.
Genetic variants in MMPs are linked to aneurysm risk.
Chronic inflammation is a key driver of MMP production in the vessel wall.
This process is a hallmark of 'remodeling' that goes awry.
microReview: Aneurysm = Weak wall. Weak wall = Loss of collagen/elastin. Enzyme responsible = MMP.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse TIMPs and MMPs. MMPs break down the wall; TIMPs protect it. An aneurysm involves high MMP and/or low TIMP.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 25-year-old male with a history of long limbs, spider-like fingers (arachnodactyly), and high-arched palate presents with sudden onset chest pain. Examination reveals a diastolic murmur at the right sternal border. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the Fibrillin-1 (FBN1) gene. Which of the following histologic findings is most likely present in his ascending aorta?

explanations.a: Obliterative endarteritis is seen in syphilis, not Marfan syndrome.
explanations.b: Marfan syndrome (FBN1 mutation) leads to defective fibrillin, which results in dysregulated TGF-beta signaling and subsequent cystic medial degeneration (loss of smooth muscle and elastic fibers with mucoid material accumulation).
explanations.c: Calcific intimal plaques describe atherosclerosis, which is not the primary mechanism of TAA in a 25-year-old with Marfan syndrome.
explanations.d: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in malignant hypertension or certain vasculitides, not Marfan-associated aneurysms.
explanations.e: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a small-vessel inflammation, often in the skin, and does not describe aortic medial changes.

ankiCards: The genetic defect in Marfan syndrome involves the {{c1::FBN1 (Fibrillin-1)}} gene.
Histologic 'cystic medial degeneration' is characterized by the loss of {{c1::elastic fibers}}.
Marfan syndrome causes a predisposition to {{c1::Thoracic}} aortic aneurysms.
Aortic root dilation in Marfan syndrome can lead to {{c1::Aortic valve insufficiency/regurgitation}}.
Defective Fibrillin-1 leads to excessive signaling of {{c1::TGF-beta}}.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder.
Medial degeneration results from failed elastic tissue scaffolding.
TGF-beta overactivity contributes to matrix loss.
TAA (Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm) in Marfan often involves the aortic root.
Rupture or dissection are the primary causes of death.
microReview: Marfan = Fibrillin-1 defect -> High TGF-beta -> Medial Weakening (Cystic Medial Degeneration) -> Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm/Dissection.
examinerTraps: Distinguish between AAA (Atherosclerosis) and TAA in Marfan (Cystic Medial Degeneration). They have different locations and different underlying biologies.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes a 'false aneurysm' (pseudoaneurysm)?

options.a: A focal dilation of the vessel wall involving all three layers
options.b: A tear in the intima allowing blood to enter the media
options.c: A hematoma that communicates with the intravascular space through a hole in the wall
options.d: A congenital thinning of the muscularis at arterial bifurcations
options.e: A diffuse, circumferential dilation of a long segment of a vessel

explanations.a: This describes a true aneurysm (e.g., saccular or fusiform).
explanations.b: This describes a dissection, where blood separates the layers of the wall.
explanations.c: A false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) is a wall defect leading to an extravascular hematoma that freely communicates with the intravascular space (contained by extravascular connective tissue).
explanations.d: This describes the pathogenesis of a berry aneurysm (which is a true aneurysm).
explanations.e: This describes a fusiform aneurysm, which is a type of true aneurysm.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the arterial wall (intima, media, adventitia).
A {{c1::false}} aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) is a wall defect that communicates with a hematoma.
In a(n) {{c1::aortic dissection}}, blood enters the wall itself and separates the layers.
A common cause of a pseudoaneurysm is {{c1::trauma}} or iatrogenic injury (e.g., catheterization).
A {{c1::saccular}} aneurysm is a spherical outpouching involving only a portion of the vessel wall.
keyPoints: True aneurysms have intact (though thinned) arterial wall layers.
False aneurysms are essentially pulsating hematomas.
Dissections are not technically aneurysms but involve blood within the wall.
Aneurysms are classified by shape into saccular and fusiform.
The distinction is critical for understanding clinical risk and treatment.
microReview: True = 3 layers dilated. False = Hole in wall + pocket of blood outside. Dissection = Blood between layers.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse a pseudoaneurysm with a dissection. A pseudoaneurysm has a complete breach of the wall, whereas a dissection involves blood tracking *within* the wall layers.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Syphilitic aneurysms are historically significant and specifically target the thoracic aorta. What is the fundamental mechanism by which Treponema pallidum infection causes the weakening of the aortic wall?

options.a: Direct lysis of elastic fibers by bacterial proteases
options.c: Inflammation and narrowing of the vasa vasorum
options.d: Deposition of type III hypersensitivity complexes

explanations.a: Treponema pallidum does not produce potent bacterial proteases that digest the wall directly.
explanations.b: Autoimmune cross-reactivity is a mechanism in rheumatic heart disease, not syphilitic aortitis.
explanations.c: Tertiary syphilis causes 'obliterative endarteritis' of the vasa vasorum. This results in ischemic injury to the outer media, leading to loss of smooth muscle and elastic tissue, and subsequent wall dilation.
explanations.d: This is a mechanism for certain vasculitides, but not for the specific medial weakening in syphilis.
explanations.e: While atherosclerosis may occur concurrently, it is not the mechanism of syphilitic aortitis.

ankiCards: Tertiary syphilis classically affects the {{c1::thoracic}} aorta.
The hallmark pathologic lesion of syphilitic aortitis is {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}} of the vasa vasorum.
Ischemic destruction of the media in syphilis leads to a {{c1::'tree-bark'}} appearance of the intima.
Syphilitic aneurysms can lead to dilation of the {{c1::aortic valve ring}}, causing regurgitation.
In contrast to syphilis, atherosclerotic aneurysms are mostly {{c1::abdominal}}.
keyPoints: Syphilis attacks the 'vessels of the vessels' (vasa vasorum).
This leads to medial ischemia and fibrosis.
The resulting scarring causes intimal wrinkling (tree-barking).
Patients often present with respiratory distress (compression) or heart failure (regurgitation).
Now rare due to effective antibiotic treatment of early syphilis.
microReview: Syphilis -> Endarteritis of vasa vasorum -> Medial Ischemia -> Weak Thoracic Aorta -> Tree-barking & Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'tree-barking' or 'vasa vasorum' as keywords for syphilis-related aortic questions.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old female presents with sudden onset of severe, 'tearing' back pain and a blood pressure of 200/110 mmHg. She has a history of poorly controlled hypertension. A CT scan shows a longitudinal intraluminal flap in the ascending aorta. Which of the following is the most likely underlying vascular pathology present prior to the acute event?

explanations.a: Aortic dissection is most commonly associated with hypertension and cystic medial degeneration (even in the absence of Marfan syndrome). Hypertension causes pressure hypertrophy of the vasa vasorum, leading to medial ischemia.
explanations.b: While atherosclerosis is common in the elderly, it is not the most frequent cause of 'tearing' dissection flaps; hypertension-related medial changes are more common.
explanations.c: Giant cell arteritis involves granulomatous inflammation and typically presents with temporal headaches, not acute aortic dissection.
explanations.d: Fibromuscular dysplasia typically affects the renal or carotid arteries in younger women, not the ascending aorta.
explanations.e: Berry aneurysm rupture causes subarachnoid hemorrhage, not chest/back pain with an aortic flap.

ankiCards: The most common risk factor for aortic dissection is {{c1::hypertension}}.
Aortic dissection is characterized by an intimal tear and blood tracking through the {{c1::media}}.
Type A dissections involve the {{c1::ascending}} aorta.
Type B dissections occur distal to the {{c1::left subclavian artery}}.
The classic clinical description of dissection pain is {{c1::tearing or ripping}}.
keyPoints: Hypertension is the #1 risk factor for dissection.
Dissection is NOT the same as an aneurysm, though they often coexist.
The tear usually occurs in the first 10cm of the aorta.
Can lead to cardiac tamponade (most common cause of death).
Medical emergency requiring rapid BP control or surgery.
microReview: High BP -> Vasa vasorum stress -> Medial Ischemia -> Cystic Medial Degeneration -> Intimal Tear -> Dissection.
examinerTraps: The examiner may describe the pain as 'tearing' to point to dissection. If the question asks for the 'most common cause,' it is almost always hypertension.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: What is the primary distinguishing feature of a 'mycotic' aneurysm?

options.a: It is caused by a primary fungal infection of the endothelium
options.b: It involves the destruction of the wall due to an infected thrombus or bacteremia
options.c: It is a type of aneurysm that specifically lacks an inflammatory infiltrate
options.d: It occurs only in patients with severe underlying cystic fibrosis
options.e: It refers to an aneurysm caused by heavy metal poisoning

explanations.a: Despite the name 'mycotic', most are bacterial, not fungal. The name was coined by Osler to describe the 'mushroom-like' appearance.
explanations.b: A mycotic aneurysm results from infection of the arterial wall, usually from a seeded bacterial embolus (e.g., infective endocarditis) or direct extension of an adjacent infection.
explanations.c: Mycotic aneurysms are highly inflammatory and destructive by definition.
explanations.d: There is no specific link between cystic fibrosis and mycotic aneurysms.
explanations.e: Heavy metal poisoning is not a cause of mycotic aneurysms.

ankiCards: A(n) {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm is an aneurysm resulting from an infection.
Most mycotic aneurysms are caused by {{c1::bacteria (e.g., Salmonella, Staph)}} rather than fungi.
Common sources of infection for mycotic aneurysms include {{c1::infective endocarditis}} or bacteremia.
The risk of {{c1::rupture}} is very high in mycotic aneurysms due to rapid wall destruction.
Mycotic aneurysms are characterized by a(n) {{c1::absent or destroyed}} internal elastic lamina.
keyPoints: The term 'mycotic' is a misnomer; most are bacterial.
Infection weakens the wall rapidly through suppuration.
Can occur in any artery, but often in the abdominal aorta or cerebral vessels.
Salmonella is a classic organism associated with infected atherosclerotic plaques.
Requires surgical intervention and long-term antibiotics.
microReview: Bacteremia/Endocarditis -> Wall infection -> Medial destruction -> Rapidly enlarging/rupturing aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Don't pick 'fungus' just because the name says 'mycotic'. It’s an old-fashioned term for 'infected'.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Mural thrombi are frequently found within the lumen of large aneurysms. Which of the following best explains why these thrombi form in an aneurysmal sac?

options.a: Increased laminar flow velocity in the dilated segment
options.b: Local deficiency of endothelial prostacyclin production
options.c: Stasis and turbulence in the area of widening
options.d: Direct activation of the extrinsic clotting cascade by elastin
options.e: Systemic hypercoagulability caused by the aneurysm

explanations.a: Flow velocity actually decreases as the cross-sectional area increases in an aneurysm.
explanations.b: While endothelial dysfunction may exist, it is not the primary driver compared to hemodynamic changes.
explanations.c: According to Virchow's triad, stasis and turbulence (which occur in the 'pocket' of an aneurysm) promote thrombus formation.
explanations.d: Elastin does not directly activate the extrinsic cascade; that is the role of Tissue Factor.
explanations.e: Aneurysms cause local, not systemic, hypercoagulability via local stasis.

ankiCards: The three components of Virchow's triad are stasis, hypercoagulability, and {{c1::endothelial injury}}.
In an aneurysm, thrombus formation is primarily due to {{c1::stasis and turbulence}}.
A thrombus found on the wall of a large vessel is called a {{c1::mural}} thrombus.
The danger of mural thrombi in AAA is distal {{c1::embolization}}.
Mural thrombi can occasionally obstruct the orifices of {{c1::branch}} vessels (e.g., renal arteries).
keyPoints: Aneurysms disrupt normal laminar flow.
The sac allows for stagnant blood, which clots.
Mural thrombi can be very thick, sometimes partially 'lining' the aneurysm.
Embolization can lead to 'blue toe syndrome' or intestinal ischemia.
Thrombus can hide the true size of the aneurysm on some imaging (like angiography).
microReview: Wide vessel = Slow flow = Stasis = Clot (Mural thrombus).
examinerTraps: Aneurysms don't just 'pop' (rupture); they also 'clot' (thrombose) and 'shoot' (embolize). Know all three complications.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... by thrombosis or embolism
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with the 'worst headache of her life.' CT imaging shows blood in the subarachnoid space. She has a history of hypertension and multiple family members with chronic kidney disease requiring dialysis. Which of the following is the most likely location of the vascular lesion responsible for her symptoms?

explanations.a: Infrarenal aorta is the site of AAA, which presents with abdominal/back pain, not headache.
explanations.b: Thoracic aorta is associated with TAA/dissection, presenting with chest pain.
explanations.c: This patient has symptoms of a ruptured berry aneurysm (subarachnoid hemorrhage). These typically occur at branch points in the Circle of Willis, with the anterior communicating artery being the most common site. There is a strong association with Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD).
explanations.d: Pulmonary artery aneurysms are extremely rare and don't cause subarachnoid hemorrhage.
explanations.e: Superior mesenteric artery aneurysms are rare and typically cause bowel ischemia if they complicate.

ankiCards: Berry aneurysms are most common in the {{c1::Circle of Willis}}.
The most common specific site for a berry aneurysm is the {{c1::anterior communicating}} artery.
Berry aneurysms are associated with the genetic condition {{c1::ADPKD}}.
Rupture of a berry aneurysm leads to {{c1::subarachnoid}} hemorrhage.
Berry aneurysms are caused by a lack of {{c1::internal elastic lamina and smooth muscle}} at branch points.
keyPoints: Berry aneurysms are small, saccular, and occur at arterial bifurcations.
Risk factors include hypertension, smoking, and ADPKD.
They are not atherosclerotic in origin.
The 'worst headache of life' is a classic 'red flag' clinical board clue.
Diagnosis is confirmed by CT without contrast or lumbar puncture (xanthochromia).
microReview: ADPKD + Headache = Berry Aneurysm = Circle of Willis = Subarachnoid Hemorrhage.
examinerTraps: The family history of kidney disease is the 'dead giveaway' for ADPKD, which links directly to berry aneurysms.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which layer of the arterial wall is most directly affected by the 'tree-barking' appearance seen in syphilitic aortitis?

explanations.a: While the adventitia is where the vasa vasorum reside and are inflamed, 'tree-barking' is an intimal surface description.
explanations.b: The media is where the destruction occurs (ischemia/scarring), but the 'tree-bark' appearance refers to the overlying surface.
explanations.c: The 'tree-barking' refers to the irregular, wrinkled surface of the tunica intima. This wrinkling occurs because the underlying media has been destroyed and replaced by fibrous scars that contract.
explanations.d: The internal elastic lamina is destroyed, but 'tree-barking' is a macroscopic intimal finding.
explanations.e: The external elastic lamina is also affected by ischemia, but not the site of the tree-bark description.

ankiCards: {{c1::Tree-barking}} is the macroscopic term for the intimal surface in syphilitic aortitis.
Tree-barking results from contraction of {{c1::medial scars}}.
Syphilitic aortitis involves the thoracic aorta and often leads to dilation of the {{c1::aortic root}}.
The specific inflammatory cells in the vasa vasorum in syphilis are {{c1::plasma cells}}.
The loss of medial support in syphilis leads to {{c1::aneurysmal}} dilation.
keyPoints: Tree-barking is a gross pathology term.
It indicates extensive medial scarring and secondary intimal changes.
It is a classic buzzword for tertiary syphilis.
Predisposes the aorta to both aneurysm and aortic valve insufficiency.
The 'bark' represents the puckered intima overlying fibrotic media.
microReview: Syphilis -> Vasa vasorum endarteritis -> Media dies/scars -> Scars pull on intima -> Tree-barking surface.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'tree-barking' (syphilis) with 'fatty streaks' (early atherosclerosis).
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 34-year-old male with a history of HIV (CD4+ count 140/µL) presents with multiple non-blanching, purplish-red macules and plaques on his lower extremities and hard palate. Biopsy of a skin lesion reveals a spindle cell proliferation with slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells. Which of the following infectious agents is the primary driver of this patient's pathology?

explanations.a: Human herpesvirus 6 causes roseola infantum and is not associated with vascular tumors.
explanations.b: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent for all forms of Kaposi sarcoma, including the AIDS-associated form described.
explanations.c: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not primary vascular tumors.
explanations.d: Cytomegalovirus causes retinitis or colitis in AIDS patients but does not induce spindle-cell vascular proliferation.
explanations.e: HTLV-1 is associated with adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, not endothelial cell neoplasia.

ankiCards: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by infection with {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
The histological hallmark of Kaposi sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells}} forming slit-like vascular spaces.
Kaposi sarcoma in AIDS patients typically presents on the {{c1::skin}} and {{c2::mucous membranes}}.
The red/purple color of Kaposi sarcoma lesions is due to {{c1::extravasated red blood cells}}.
Unlike most hemangiomas, Kaposi sarcoma lesions {{c1::do not}} blanch when pressed.
keyPoints: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a low-grade malignant vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8.
KS frequently occurs in immunocompromised individuals, particularly those with AIDS.
Classic KS involves the distal extremities in older men of Mediterranean or Eastern European descent.
Histology shows spindle-shaped endothelial cells and slit-like spaces.
HHV-8 encodes viral homologues of human genes that promote cell proliferation and inhibit apoptosis.
The AIDS-associated form is the most aggressive variant of KS.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma: HHV-8 + Spindle cells + HIV patient = AIDS-defining illness.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Kaposi sarcoma (spindle cells, lymphocytic infiltrate) with Bacillary angiomatosis (neutrophilic infiltrate, Bartonella), which both present as red-purple skin nodules in HIV patients.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An investigative pathologist is studying the differentiation of poorly formed vascular channels in a malignant soft tissue mass. Which of the following immunohistochemical markers is most specific for identifying the endothelial origin of these tumor cells?

explanations.a: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial cells and carcinomas.
explanations.b: Desmin is a marker for muscle cells (skeletal, smooth, or cardiac).
explanations.c: CD31 (platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule) is highly specific for endothelial cells and is used to diagnose vascular tumors.
explanations.d: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells, including melanocytes and Schwann cells.
explanations.e: Synaptophysin is a marker for neuroendocrine differentiation.

ankiCards: The specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial cells is {{c1::CD31}}.
CD31 is also known as {{c1::PECAM-1}}.
{{c1::vWF (von Willebrand Factor)}} is another marker sometimes used for endothelial cells but CD31 is more reliable.
Angiosarcomas are identified by their positive staining for {{c1::CD31}}.
Malignant vascular tumors that may appear poorly differentiated can be confirmed as endothelial using {{c1::CD31}}.
keyPoints: CD31 is a transmembrane glycoprotein expressed on endothelial cells.
Vascular tumors (benign or malignant) usually express CD31.
Immunohistochemistry is essential for differentiating angiosarcomas from undifferentiated carcinomas.
Angiosarcomas often have a very high grade, making CD31 staining crucial for diagnosis.
Endothelial markers help distinguish vascular spindle cell tumors from fibrosarcomas.
microReview: Endothelial marker = CD31.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'specific'—while CD34 is often positive in vascular tumors, it is less specific than CD31 as it stains many other mesenchymal cells.
sourceQuote: To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure and function.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 62-year-old male who worked for 30 years in a chemical plant manufacturing polyvinyl chloride (PVC) presents with weight loss, abdominal pain, and hepatomegaly. Imaging shows multiple hemorrhagic masses in the liver. Biopsy reveals malignant endothelial cells with significant nuclear atypia and large, irregular vascular channels. Which of the following substances is the most likely environmental trigger for this condition?

explanations.a: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and lung carcinoma, not hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Vinyl chloride exposure is a well-documented risk factor for hepatic angiosarcoma, a highly malignant vascular tumor.
explanations.c: Aflatoxin B1 is a risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: Benzene is associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.e: Beryllium is associated with lung disease (berylliosis) and lung cancer.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is classically associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
{{c1::Thorotrast (radioactive contrast)}} was historically associated with the development of hepatic angiosarcoma.
Angiosarcoma is a {{c1::malignant}} neoplasm of endothelial cells.
The prognosis for hepatic angiosarcoma is generally {{c1::poor}}.
Arsenic exposure is associated with {{c1::hepatic angiosarcoma}} as well as skin cancer.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare but highly aggressive tumor.
Environmental toxins (vinyl chloride, arsenic, Thorotrast) are known carcinogens for this tumor.
The tumor cells line irregular, slit-like, or cavernous vascular spaces.
Most patients present with advanced disease and poor survival rates.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is distinct from hepatocellular carcinoma (epithelial origin).
microReview: PVC/Vinyl Chloride + Liver mass + Endothelial atypia = Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse angiosarcoma (vascular) with hepatocellular carcinoma (epithelial) or cavernous hemangioma (benign).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An immunocompromised patient develops multiple red, friable skin papules. Histological examination shows a capillary proliferation with prominent swelling of the endothelial cells and an infiltrate of neutrophils and nuclear dust (leukocytoclasis). Silver stain reveals clusters of tangled bacilli. What is the most likely pathogen?

explanations.a: Bartonella henselae (and B. quintana) causes bacillary angiomatosis, a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised patients that mimics Kaposi sarcoma but contains neutrophils and bacteria.
explanations.b: Staphylococcus aureus causes pyogenic infections (abscesses, impetigo) but not vascular tumors.
explanations.c: Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare (MAI) causes granulomatous disease in AIDS patients, not vascular proliferation.
explanations.d: Treponema pallidum causes syphilis; while it affects vessels (endarteritis), it doesn't cause tumor-like angiomatosis.
explanations.e: Pseudomonas aeruginosa causes ecthyma gangrenosum in neutropenic patients, characterized by vessel wall necrosis, not benign proliferation.

ankiCards: The agent of bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised hosts is {{c1::Bartonella henselae}} or B. quintana.
Unlike Kaposi sarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis features an infiltrate of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
To visualize the bacteria in bacillary angiomatosis, a {{c1::Warthin-Starry (silver)}} stain is used.
Bacillary angiomatosis is treated with {{c1::antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin)}}.
Bartonella quintana is classically transmitted by {{c1::human body lice}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis is an opportunistic infection that mimics vascular tumors.
It is characterized by lobular proliferations of small capillaries.
Endothelial cells in this condition are often 'plump' or 'epithelioid'.
The presence of neutrophils and bacteria on silver stain differentiates it from Kaposi sarcoma.
Erythromycin or doxycycline are standard treatments.
Bartonella henselae is also the cause of Cat-scratch disease in immunocompetent hosts.
microReview: HIV + Red papule + Neutrophils + Silver stain (+) bacilli = Bartonella (Bacillary Angiomatosis).
examinerTraps: The word 'angiomatosis' sounds neoplastic, but the key is the silver stain positive for bacteria and the neutrophilic infiltrate, pointing to an infection.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 41-year-old woman presents with an extremely painful, small (5 mm), blue-tinted nodule located under the nail of her index finger. The pain is particularly severe when the finger is exposed to cold temperatures. Which cell type is the most likely origin for this tumor?

explanations.a: While it is a vascular-associated tumor, the glomus tumor does not arise from the endothelium itself.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors arise from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, which are specialized for thermoregulation.
explanations.c: Pericytes are the origin of hemangiopericytomas, not glomus tumors.
explanations.d: Schwann cells are the origin of neuromas or schwannomas, which can be painful but are not typically subungual and temperature-sensitive in this manner.
explanations.e: Fibroblasts produce collagen and form fibromas, which are not specifically painful or subungual.

ankiCards: A glomus tumor is a painful tumor classically found in the {{c1::subungual (under nail)}} region.
The cell of origin for a glomus tumor is the {{c1::modified smooth muscle cell}}.
The glomus body's physiological function is {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors show nests of small, uniform, round cells surrounding {{c1::vascular channels}}.
A key clinical trigger for pain in a glomus tumor is {{c1::cold exposure}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign and exquisitely painful.
They are most common in the distal digits, especially under the nails.
They originate from the specialized glomus bodies involved in temperature control.
Cells appear as uniform, round cells with scant cytoplasm ('monotonous' look).
Surgical excision is curative.
microReview: Painful + Subungual + Blue nodule = Glomus tumor (Smooth muscle origin).
examinerTraps: Wait for 'painful'—most vascular tumors like hemangiomas are painless; glomus tumors and angiolipomas are notable exceptions.
sourceQuote: To better appreciate the pathogenesis of vascular disorders, it is important to first understand the normal vessel structure and function.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A newborn is noted to have a bright red, raised 'strawberry-like' lesion on the scalp. It grows rapidly during the first few months of life. The parents are concerned about the cosmetic appearance. What is the most likely natural history of this lesion?

options.d: Requires immediate laser ablation to prevent ulceration

explanations.a: Infantile (strawberry) hemangiomas are common in newborns; they grow rapidly for a few months and then usually spontaneously regress by age 7 to 9.
explanations.b: Unlike port-wine stains, strawberry hemangiomas do not typically persist or grow throughout adulthood.
explanations.c: Hemangiomas are benign and do not transform into malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.d: While laser therapy is an option, it is not 'required' immediately in most cases as they regress on their own.
explanations.e: They undergo fibrous involution, not typically calcification or ossification.

ankiCards: The most common vascular tumor of infancy is the {{c1::infantile (strawberry) hemangioma}}.
Infantile hemangiomas typically undergo {{c1::spontaneous regression}} during childhood.
By age 7, approximately {{c1::75-90}}% of infantile hemangiomas have resolved.
The typical clinical appearance of an infantile hemangioma is a {{c1::bright red, raised}} lesion.
The 'juvenile' or strawberry hemangioma consists of {{c1::closely packed capillaries}}.
keyPoints: Infantile hemangiomas are benign capillary hemangiomas.
They occur in 1 in 200 births.
The 'strawberry' appearance comes from the high density of small vessels.
Regression begins with fading of the color followed by softening.
Reassurance is often the primary management.
They may be multiple or internal (e.g., in the liver).
microReview: Strawberry Hemangioma = Newborn + Rapid growth + Regresses by school age.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the natural history of a strawberry hemangioma (regresses) with a nevus flammeus/port-wine stain (persists/thickens).
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 5-year-old child presents with a large, port-wine stain covering the right side of the face in the distribution of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve. The child also has a history of seizures and mental retardation. Which genetic mutation is most strongly associated with this clinical triad?

explanations.a: Sturge-Weber syndrome is characterized by port-wine stains and leptomeningeal angiomas, caused by an activating somatic mutation in the GNAQ gene.
explanations.b: VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) mutations cause capillary hemangioblastomas and renal cell carcinoma, not Sturge-Weber syndrome.
explanations.c: NF1 is associated with neurofibromatosis type 1, featuring café-au-lait spots and neurofibromas.
explanations.d: TSC1 (tuberous sclerosis) causes hamartomas and angiofibromas, not port-wine stains.
explanations.e: PTEN mutations are associated with Cowden syndrome.

ankiCards: Sturge-Weber syndrome is associated with a {{c1::port-wine stain (nevus flammeus)}} in the V1/V2 distribution.
The triad of Sturge-Weber includes port-wine stain, {{c1::seizures (or intellectual disability)}}, and {{c2::leptomeningeal angiomas}}.
The genetic basis for Sturge-Weber syndrome is a somatic mutation in {{c1::GNAQ}}.
Port-wine stains in Sturge-Weber syndrome involve the distribution of the {{c1::trigeminal}} nerve.
Skull X-rays in Sturge-Weber may show 'tram-track' {{c1::calcifications}}.
keyPoints: Sturge-Weber syndrome is a congenital, non-hereditary vascular disorder.
Port-wine stains (Nevus flammeus) are permanent and do not regress.
The ipsilateral leptomeningeal angioma often leads to neurological deficits.
Somatic GNAQ mutations affect G-protein signaling.
Patients often develop glaucoma on the affected side.
microReview: Port-wine stain + Seizures + GNAQ = Sturge-Weber.
examinerTraps: Note that Sturge-Weber is a *somatic* mutation, not an inherited germline mutation like VHL or NF1.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following vascular tumors is characterized as a benign, large, cystic lymphatic space typically found in the neck or axilla of infants, often associated with Turner syndrome or Down syndrome?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are small blood vessel tumors, not lymphatic.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large blood-filled spaces, not lymphatic fluid.
explanations.c: Cystic hygroma (cystic lymphangioma) is a benign malformation of lymphatic vessels, classically found in the neck and associated with chromosomal abnormalities.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are small, painful smooth muscle-derived tumors of the digits.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignancy, not a benign cystic malformation.

ankiCards: A cystic hygroma is also known as a {{c1::cavernous lymphangioma}}.
Cystic hygromas are most commonly located in the {{c1::neck}} or axilla.
Turner syndrome (45, XO) is frequently associated with {{c1::cystic hygroma}}.
The fluid inside a cystic hygroma is {{c1::serous (lymphatic fluid)}}.
Histologically, cystic hygromas are composed of large spaces lined by {{c1::endothelial cells}}.
keyPoints: Lymphangiomas are the lymphatic counterparts of hemangiomas.
Simple (capillary) lymphangiomas are usually small and cutaneous.
Cystic hygromas can be large enough to cause breathing difficulties in infants.
They lack red blood cells in the lumina (distinguishes from hemangioma).
Often associated with trisomies and Turner syndrome.
microReview: Cystic Hygroma = Webbed neck + Turner Syndrome + Lymphatic mass.
examinerTraps: The presence or absence of RBCs in the vascular spaces is a major histological clue: RBCs = Hemangioma; No RBCs/Proteinaceous fluid = Lymphangioma.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 58-year-old woman presents with several dark, violaceous nodules on her left arm. She has a history of a radical mastectomy followed by radiation therapy for breast cancer 12 years ago, which resulted in chronic lymphedema of that arm. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is HHV-8 related and usually associated with immunosuppression, not chronic lymphedema.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is infectious and occurs in immunocompromised states.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma occurring in the setting of chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy) is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granuloma is a rapidly growing red nodule, often on the gums or skin, not associated with chronic lymphedema.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are small, painful subungual lesions.

ankiCards: Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to {{c1::angiosarcoma}} arising in a limb with chronic lymphedema.
The most common cause of Stewart-Treves syndrome is lymphedema following {{c1::radical mastectomy}}.
Angiosarcoma following radiation therapy typically has a latency of {{c1::several years (e.g., 10+)}}.
Cutaneous angiosarcoma often begins as small {{c1::red/purple}} nodules or plaques.
Angiosarcoma is a malignancy of {{c1::endothelial cells}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are aggressive, high-grade malignant tumors.
Risk factors include radiation, chronic lymphedema, and chemical toxins.
Stewart-Treves syndrome is a classic USMLE association.
Histology shows pleomorphic endothelial cells and poorly formed vessels.
They have a high rate of local recurrence and distant metastasis.
microReview: Post-mastectomy + Chronic lymphedema + New purple nodules = Angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves).
examinerTraps: Watch for the time delay; angiosarcomas usually appear a decade or more after the initial surgery/radiation.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 22-year-old pregnant woman presents with a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated lesion on her gingiva. The lesion bleeds easily with minor trauma. Histology shows a highly vascular proliferation resembling granulation tissue. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignancy with significant atypia, unlike the benign appearance here.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a common, benign, rapidly growing red lesion that often occurs on the skin or oral mucosa, especially during pregnancy (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, deep vascular channels and do not typically present as pedunculated oral lesions.
explanations.d: Kaposi sarcoma usually presents as multiple plaques in HIV patients, not a single pedunculated gingival mass.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is infectious and seen in immunocompromised patients; this patient is pregnant, which is the classic association for pyogenic granuloma.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer because it is neither {{c1::pyogenic (pus-forming)}} nor a {{c2::granuloma}}.
When a pyogenic granuloma occurs in a pregnant woman's gingiva, it is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum (pregnancy tumor)}}.
The histological appearance of pyogenic granuloma resembles {{c1::granulation tissue}}.
Pyogenic granulomas are characterized by {{c1::rapid growth}} and {{c2::easy bleeding}}.
The definitive treatment for a pyogenic granuloma is {{c1::surgical excision}}.
