explanations.e: Most are isolated and not markers of internal malignancy, unlike some syndromes (e.g., von Hippel-Lindau).

ankiCards: The common name for an infantile hemangioma is a {{c1::strawberry}} hemangioma.
Infantile hemangiomas usually {{c1::regress/involute}} by age 7 to 9.
Unlike port-wine stains, strawberry hemangiomas are {{c1::not}} present at birth.
Histologically, these consist of {{c1::closely packed capillaries}} lined by plump endothelium.
During the involution phase, the hemangioma is replaced by {{c1::fibrofatty}} tissue.
keyPoints: Infantile hemangioma is the most common tumor of infancy.
Characteristic 'strawberry' appearance (bright red, lobulated).
Clinical course: proliferation followed by slow involution.
Most do not require treatment unless they obstruct vision or airway.
GLUT-1 is a highly specific immunohistochemical marker for these.
Often absent or faint at birth, appearing in the first weeks.
microReview: Infantile Hemangioma: Grows fast, then goes away. Strawberry-like. GLUT-1 positive.
examinerTraps: Confusing Infantile Hemangiomas (strawberry) with Nevus Flammeus (port-wine stain). Port-wine stains are present at birth and do NOT regress; they grow with the child.
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which vascular lesion is characterized by large, dilated, thin-walled vascular spaces separated by a scan connective tissue stroma, often occurring in the liver or spleen, and may cause complications such as thrombosis or rupture?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas consist of small, thin-walled capillaries, not large dilated spaces.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, blood-filled vascular spaces and are the most common benign tumors of the liver and spleen.
explanations.c: Angiosarcomas are malignant with atypical cells, not thin-walled benign spaces.
explanations.d: Glomus tumors are small, painful, and arise from smooth muscle cells, not large cavernous spaces.
explanations.e: Spider angiomas are small, central arterioles with radiating capillaries, typically associated with hyperestrogenism.

ankiCards: {{c1::Cavernous hemangioma}} is the most common benign tumor of the liver.
Histology of cavernous hemangiomas shows {{c1::large, dilated blood-filled}} spaces.
A major risk of cavernous hemangiomas in internal organs is {{c1::rupture/hemorrhage}}.
In the CNS, cavernous hemangiomas are associated with {{c1::von Hippel-Lindau}} disease.
Cavernous hemangiomas are distinguished from capillary ones by their {{c1::larger}} vascular channels.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign but can be large.
Often found in the liver, spleen, and CNS.
They are well-circumscribed but not encapsulated.
Clinical significance: often an incidental finding on imaging.
Intravascular thrombosis and dystrophic calcification can occur.
They do not regress spontaneously (unlike infantile hemangiomas).
microReview: Cavernous = Big spaces. Capillary = Small spaces. Both are benign.
examinerTraps: Percutaneous needle biopsy is often contraindicated in suspected hepatic cavernous hemangioma due to the risk of significant hemorrhage.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 50-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer treated with radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection 12 years ago presents with multiple firm, violaceous nodules on her chronically swollen left arm. Biopsy reveals a high-grade malignancy with atypical endothelial cells. What is the most likely underlying mechanism for the development of this tumor?

options.d: Germline mutation in the VHL gene

explanations.a: The development of angiosarcoma in the setting of chronic lymphedema (following radical mastectomy) is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome.
explanations.b: HHV-8 is associated with Kaposi sarcoma, not post-mastectomy angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: BRAF mutations are common in melanomas, but not the primary driver for Stewart-Treves angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: VHL mutations cause von Hippel-Lindau disease (hemangioblastomas), not lymphangioma-associated angiosarcoma.
explanations.e: Stasis dermatitis leads to skin changes and ulcers, but not malignancy.

ankiCards: {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}} refers to angiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphedema.
The classic clinical scenario for Stewart-Treves is post-{{c1::mastectomy}} with lymph node dissection.
Angiosarcomas are tumors of the {{c1::endothelial}} cells.
The latency period for Stewart-Treves syndrome is typically {{c1::10 or more}} years.
The prognosis of cutaneous angiosarcoma is generally {{c1::poor}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma can occur in skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Stewart-Treves syndrome is a specific subtype.
Lymphedema is thought to impair local immune surveillance.
High-grade histology with pleomorphic cells and mitoses.
Often CD31 and Factor VIII-related antigen positive.
Highly infiltrative and difficult to excise completely.
microReview: Mastectomy + Chronic Arm Swelling + Purple Nodules = Stewart-Treves Syndrome (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse this with lymphangioma (which is benign). The high-grade atypical cells and violaceous nodules signify malignancy.
sourceQuote: Vascular pathology is responsible for more morbidity and mortality than any other category of human disease.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 5-year-old child presents with a large, ill-defined, soft tissue mass on the left side of the neck. The mass has been present since birth and is slowly increasing in size. Imaging shows a multi-loculated cystic mass. Histological examination shows large, dilated spaces lined by a single layer of flattened endothelium and containing proteinaceous fluid with occasional lymphocytes. What is the diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) typically occurs in the neck or axilla of children and is composed of large lymphatic spaces.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas contain blood, not lymph, and usually involve the skin, not deep cystic neck masses.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are small, painful subungual lesions, not large neck masses.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular lesion of immunocompromised adults.
explanations.e: Hemangioendothelioma is a borderline vascular tumor with more solid growth, not large cystic spaces.

ankiCards: Cystic hygroma is another name for {{c1::cavernous lymphangioma}}.
Cystic hygromas are frequently associated with {{c1::Turner}} syndrome (45,X).
The fluid inside a cystic hygroma is {{c1::lymph (proteinaceous)}} fluid.
The most common location for a cystic hygroma is the {{c1::neck}} or axilla.
Cystic hygromas are considered {{c1::benign}} lesions.
keyPoints: Lymphangiomas are the lymphatic equivalent of hemangiomas.
Cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) are large and cystic.
They lack a well-defined capsule, making excision difficult.
Histology: Dilated spaces with no RBCs in the lumen (usually).
Associated with chromosomal abnormalities (Turner and Down syndromes).
Can cause compression of local structures in the neck.
microReview: Cystic Hygroma = Neck Mass + Turner Syndrome + Lymph-filled spaces.
examinerTraps: Be careful to distinguish lymphangiomas from hemangiomas; the key difference is the absence of red blood cells in the lymphatic spaces.
sourceQuote: Structural specializations that reflect distinct functional roles characterize specific kinds of vessels.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular tumors are categorized into benign, intermediate (borderline), and malignant grades. Which of the following tumors is correctly categorized as an 'intermediate-grade' (borderline) vascular neoplasm?

explanations.a: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign capillary hemangioma.
explanations.b: Hemangioendotheliomas, specifically epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, are intermediate-grade tumors with clinical behavior between benign hemangiomas and malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.c: Cavernous lymphangioma is a benign lymphatic lesion.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a fully malignant vascular tumor.
explanations.e: Glomus tumor is a benign tumor of modified smooth muscle cells.

ankiCards: The classification of vascular tumors includes {{c1::benign}}, {{c2::intermediate}}, and malignant.
{{c1::Kaposi sarcoma}} and {{c2::hemangioendothelioma}} are intermediate-grade vascular tumors.
Intermediate-grade tumors are often locally {{c1::aggressive}} but have low metastatic potential compared to angiosarcomas.
Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma cells often resemble {{c1::epithelial}} cells.
Vascular tumors that are always malignant and aggressive are called {{c1::angiosarcomas}}.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors follow a spectrum of aggressiveness.
Intermediate-grade tumors can recur locally.
Hemangioendothelioma is a broad category of borderline tumors.
Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma often occurs around medium and large veins.
They contain vascular channels but also solid nests of cells.
Clinical behavior is unpredictable but generally better than angiosarcoma.
microReview: Benign = Hemangioma. Intermediate = Kaposi, Hemangioendothelioma. Malignant = Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Often, students classify Kaposi Sarcoma as purely malignant because of its association with AIDS, but it is technically 'intermediate' because of its variable and often indolent course.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors... Benign Tumors... Intermediate-Grade (Borderline) Tumors... Malignant Tumors.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following is considered one of the two principal mechanisms that underlie the majority of vascular diseases?

options.a: Increased vascular permeability leading to edema
options.b: Weakening of vessel walls leading to dilation or rupture
options.c: Upregulation of endothelial nitric oxide synthase
options.e: Reduction in the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter

explanations.a: While edema occurs in vascular disease, it is not one of the two primary mechanisms listed as the foundation of vascular pathology.
explanations.b: The text explicitly states that weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation (aneurysms) or rupture, is one of the two principal mechanisms of vascular disease.
explanations.c: Upregulation of eNOS is usually a physiological response; its downregulation is often associated with pathology, but it is not a primary mechanism of vessel structural failure.
explanations.d: Vascular pathology more commonly involve intimal thickening or medial changes rather than primary adventitial hyperplasia.
explanations.e: In muscular vessels, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter actually increases to exert control, and a decrease is not a primary underlying mechanism of systemic vascular disease.

ankiCards: Vascular pathology is responsible for more {{c1::morbidity and mortality}} than any other category of human disease.
The two principal mechanisms of vascular disease are {{c1::narrowing/obstruction}} and {{c2::weakening of vessel walls}}.
Narrowing of vessel lumens can occur progressively via {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Narrowing of vessel lumens can occur precipitously via {{c1::thrombosis or embolism}}.
Weakening of vessel walls typically leads to {{c1::dilation or rupture}}.
keyPoints: Vascular disease is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality.
Pathology generally involves either lumen obstruction or wall weakening.
Obstruction can be progressive (atherosclerosis) or acute (thrombosis).
Wall weakening leads to aneurysms or dissections.
The architecture of vessels is specialized to their specific functional roles.
microReview: Vascular disease is categorized into two main processes: luminal narrowing (e.g., atherosclerosis, thrombosis) and wall structural failure (e.g., aneurysms). Arteries have thicker walls than veins to handle higher pressures, and the wall-to-lumen ratio increases as vessels get smaller to allow for better pressure regulation.
examinerTraps: Students often focus only on atherosclerosis; remember that 'weakening of the wall' is a distinct primary mechanism leading to different clinical outcomes like rupture.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: As arterial vessels transition from large elastic arteries to smaller muscular arteries, which of the following structural changes occurs to allow for finer control over blood flow and pressure?

options.a: Total wall thickness increases as a percentage of body weight
options.b: The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases
options.c: The concentration of elastic fibers in the media increases
options.d: The lumen diameter increases relative to the vessel's length
options.e: The tunica adventitia becomes the primary pressure-bearing layer

explanations.a: Total wall thickness actually diminishes as vessels become smaller, even if the relative ratio increases.
explanations.b: The text states that although wall thickness diminishes in smaller vessels, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing muscular vessels to control blood flow and pressure.
explanations.c: Smaller muscular arteries have less elastic tissue and more smooth muscle compared to large elastic arteries like the aorta.
explanations.d: Lumen diameter decreases significantly as arteries become smaller (arterioles).
explanations.e: The tunica media, rich in smooth muscle, remains the primary layer for pressure control in muscular arteries.

ankiCards: As arteries become smaller, their wall thickness gradually {{c1::diminishes}}.
In smaller muscular vessels, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}}.
The increased wall-to-lumen ratio allows muscular vessels to control {{c1::blood flow and pressure}}.
Atherosclerosis mainly affects {{c1::elastic and muscular}} arteries.
Arterial walls are thicker than veins at the same level to accommodate {{c1::pulsatile flow/higher pressures}}.
keyPoints: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding venous walls.
Vessel structure reflects distinct functional roles.
Wall thickness decreases in smaller vessels, but the ratio to lumen diameter increases.
Muscular vessels exert control over systemic blood pressure.
Pathology often has characteristic anatomic distributions based on vessel type.
microReview: Functional specialization dictates vessel structure. Arteries handle high pressure with thicker walls; specifically, smaller muscular arteries have a higher wall-to-lumen ratio to regulate resistance and flow.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'absolute wall thickness' (which decreases in smaller vessels) with 'ratio of wall thickness to lumen' (which increases).
sourceQuote: Arterial wall thickness gradually diminishes as the vessels become smaller, but the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing these muscular vessels to exert control over blood flow and pressure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 66-year-old male with a history of long-standing hypertension and a 30-pack-year smoking history presents for a physical examination. The clinician notes a pulsatile mass in the umbilical region. An ultrasound reveals a 5.2 cm dilation of the infrarenal abdominal aorta. Which of the following pathological processes most likely initiated the wall weakening in this patient's vessel?

explanations.a: Cystic medial necrosis is more characteristically associated with thoracic aortic aneurysms and Marfan syndrome.
explanations.b: Atherosclerosis is the primary cause of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA), especially in older male smokers with hypertension.
explanations.c: Fibrinoid necrosis is typical of malignant hypertension or vasculitis, not the slow progressive weakening seen in AAA.
explanations.d: Giant cell arteritis affects smaller branches (like the temporal artery) or the aortic arch, not typically the infrarenal aorta.
explanations.e: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis affects small arterioles in the kidneys or other organs, not the large elastic/muscular arteries like the aorta.

ankiCards: The primary mechanism behind Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA) is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Atherosclerosis mainly affects {{c1::elastic}} and {{c2::muscular}} arteries.
Two principal mechanisms of vascular disease are narrowing and {{c1::weakening}} of walls.
Progressive narrowing of vessel lumens is exemplified by {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Vascular pathology is responsible for more {{c1::morbidity}} than any other disease category.
keyPoints: Atherosclerosis affects primarily elastic and muscular arteries.
Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms are often infrarenal.
Smoking and hypertension are major risk factors for vascular wall weakening.
Atherosclerosis causes progressive narrowing but also weakens the underlying media.
Diagnosis of AAA is often made by palpating a pulsatile mass or by ultrasound.
microReview: The most common cause of abdominal aortic aneurysms is atherosclerosis. While atherosclerosis causes luminal narrowing, it also leads to ischemia of the inner media, causing wall weakening and eventual dilation (the second primary mechanism of vascular disease).
examinerTraps: Atherosclerosis is often associated with 'narrowing', but in the context of aneurysms, its role in 'wall weakening' is the critical conceptual step.
sourceQuote: Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which vessel types are the primary site for the development of atherosclerosis, leading to both luminal narrowing and potential wall weakening?

explanations.a: Post-capillary venules are involved in inflammation and leukocyte trafficking, not atherosclerosis.
explanations.b: Veins and lymphatics are generally not affected by atherosclerosis.
explanations.c: The text explicitly states that atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries.
explanations.d: Arterioles are more associated with hyaline or hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis; capillaries are too small for atherosclerotic plaques.
explanations.e: Vasa vasorum are small vessels that supply the outer wall of large arteries; they are not the primary site of atherosclerotic plaque formation.

ankiCards: Atherosclerosis affects mainly {{c1::elastic}} and {{c2::muscular}} arteries.
The two mechanisms of vascular disease involve {{c1::narrowing}} and {{c2::weakening}}.
Vascular walls are thicker than veins to accommodate {{c1::higher blood pressures}}.
Specific vascular disorders have characteristic {{c1::anatomic distributions}}.
Arterial wall thickness diminishes as vessels become smaller, but the wall-to-lumen ratio {{c1::increases}}.
keyPoints: Atherosclerosis is a disease of elastic and muscular arteries.
Vascular diseases are often specific to vessel types.
Elastic arteries include the aorta; muscular arteries include coronary and renal arteries.
Pathology distribution is linked to vessel structural specialization.
Vascular structure corresponds to functional pressure requirements.
microReview: Atherosclerosis is localized to high-pressure, large-to-medium vessels (elastic and muscular arteries). It fits both primary mechanisms of vascular disease: it narrows the lumen and weakens the wall.
examinerTraps: Students sometimes think atherosclerosis can affect any blood vessel; it is actually restricted to specific arterial types.
sourceQuote: Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with sudden, severe chest pain. She has no significant medical history except for mild hypertension. A CT scan reveals a dissection of the ascending aorta. In contrast to an abdominal aortic aneurysm, this patient's condition is more likely primarily driven by which mechanism of wall weakening?

explanations.a: Atherosclerosis is the main driver of AAA, but less so for thoracic aortic dissections in younger patients.
explanations.b: Cystic medial degeneration (weakening of the media) is a common cause of thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections, distinct from the atherosclerotic etiology of AAA.
explanations.c: Infectious vasculitis (e.g., mycotic aneurysm) is a rare cause of wall weakening.
explanations.d: Intimal hyperplasia is a response to injury (like stenting) rather than a primary cause of dissection.
explanations.e: Venous hypertension leads to varicose veins, not aortic dissection.

ankiCards: Weakening of vessel walls leads to {{c1::dilation or rupture}}.
Structural specializations reflect distinct {{c1::functional roles}}.
Arterial walls are {{c1::thicker}} than veins to accommodate pulsatile flow.
Pathology in smaller muscular vessels is often related to control of {{c1::blood flow and pressure}}.
Two principal mechanisms of vascular disease involve narrowing and {{c1::weakening}}.
keyPoints: Thoracic aortic dissections involve medial wall weakening.
Cystic medial degeneration is a key pathology in the thoracic aorta.
Dissections and aneurysms both represent the 'wall weakening' mechanism.
Vascular architecture determines where specific diseases manifest.
Hypertension is a risk factor for both AAA and thoracic dissection.
microReview: While AAA is predominantly atherosclerotic, thoracic aortic issues like dissection often involve medial degeneration (e.g., in hypertension or Marfan syndrome). Both illustrate the 'weakening of vessel walls' mechanism.
examinerTraps: Students often assume all aortic dilations are atherosclerotic. The thoracic aorta often involves different medial pathologies.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following statements best explains why arterial walls are thicker than venous walls at the same level of branching?

options.a: Arteries contain more valves to prevent backflow
options.b: To accommodate pulsatile flow and higher pressures
options.c: To allow for more efficient gas exchange
options.d: Because they have a larger lumen diameter
options.e: To house larger amounts of vasa vasorum

explanations.a: Veins contain valves; arteries generally do not.
explanations.b: The text states arterial walls are thicker to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
explanations.c: Capillaries, not thick-walled arteries, are designed for gas exchange.
explanations.d: Arteries actually have smaller lumens relative to their wall thickness compared to veins.
explanations.e: Vasa vasorum are needed because the walls are thick, but the thickness itself is to withstand pressure, not to house the vessels.

ankiCards: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding {{c1::veins}} at the same level.
Thick arterial walls accommodate {{c1::pulsatile flow}} and {{c2::higher blood pressures}}.
The general architecture of vessels is {{c1::comparable}} throughout the cardiovascular system.
The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}} in muscular vessels.
Muscular vessels exert control over {{c1::blood flow and pressure}}.
keyPoints: Arterial thickness is a response to hemodynamic stress.
Pulsatile flow requires structural reinforcement.
Venous systems operate under much lower pressures.
Structure-function relationships are fundamental in vascular biology.
Muscular arteries regulate systemic resistance.
microReview: Vascular anatomy is a direct reflection of hemodynamics. Arteries must withstand high-pressure pulses from the heart, requiring a thicker, more muscular media than veins.
examinerTraps: A common mistake is thinking arteries are thicker to 'pump' blood; they are thicker primarily to 'withstand' and 'regulate' pressure and flow.
sourceQuote: Arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which specific vessels are primarily responsible for exerting control over systemic blood flow and pressure through changes in their wall-to-lumen ratio?

explanations.a: Elastic arteries (like the aorta) primarily dampen pulsatility rather than provide fine control of flow/resistance.
explanations.b: The text states that the increased ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter in muscular vessels allows them to exert control over flow and pressure.
explanations.c: Capillaries lack a muscular wall and cannot actively control pressure/flow themselves.
explanations.d: Venules are low-pressure collection vessels.
explanations.e: Large veins act as a reservoir but do not control systemic arterial pressure.

ankiCards: Vessels that exert control over flow and pressure are {{c1::muscular}} vessels.
In muscular vessels, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter is {{c1::increased}}.
Atherosclerosis affects mainly {{c1::elastic}} and {{c2::muscular}} arteries.
Vascular pathology in smaller vessels often has characteristic {{c1::anatomic distributions}}.
Normal vessel structure must be understood to appreciate {{c1::pathogenesis}}.
keyPoints: Muscular arteries are the resistance vessels of the body.
An increased wall-to-lumen ratio provides greater mechanical leverage for vasoconstriction.
Pressure regulation is a key function of the arterial tree distal to the aorta.
Vessel structural specialization defines its physiological role.
Elastic arteries transition into muscular ones as they branch.
microReview: While the aorta (elastic) handles the initial cardiac output, the muscular arteries and arterioles are the 'faucets' that regulate pressure and distribution, aided by their relatively thick walls compared to their lumens.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'elastic' (large/conducting) with 'muscular' (medium/distributing/regulating).
sourceQuote: the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter increases, allowing these muscular vessels to exert control over blood flow and pressure.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: If a vascular lesion is described as causing a 'progressive narrowing of the lumen,' which of the following clinical conditions is the most likely underlying cause based on the principal mechanisms of vascular disease?

explanations.a: Embolism is a precipitous (sudden) obstruction, not progressive.
explanations.b: Thrombosis is a precipitous (sudden) obstruction.
explanations.c: The text explicitly uses atherosclerosis as the example for progressive narrowing of vessel lumens.
explanations.d: Aneurysm rupture is a consequence of wall weakening, not luminal narrowing.
explanations.e: Dissection is a consequence of wall weakening and can lead to acute, not progressive, narrowing.

ankiCards: Progressive narrowing of vessel lumens is exemplified by {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Precipitous obstruction of vessel lumens is exemplified by {{c1::thrombosis/embolism}}.
Vascular pathology is responsible for more {{c1::morbidity and mortality}} than any other category.
The architectural composition of vessels is {{c1::comparable}} across the system.
Specific vascular disorders show characteristic {{c1::anatomic distributions}}.
keyPoints: Atherosclerosis is a chronic, progressive process.
Luminal narrowing leads to ischemia.
Acute events (thrombosis) often superimpose on progressive ones (atherosclerosis).
Wall weakening and luminal narrowing are the two 'rules' of vascular pathology.
Pathology is predictable based on vessel type.
microReview: The two ways to mess up a vessel: block the pipe (narrowing) or break the pipe (weakening). Atherosclerosis is the classic 'blocking' mechanism that happens slowly over decades.
examinerTraps: Ensure you distinguish between 'narrowing' (stenosis) and 'weakening' (aneurysm/rupture).
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis)
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old female presents with an extremely painful, 5-mm, firm, red-blue nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. Histologic examination reveals nests of uniform, round-to-oval cells surrounding thin-walled vascular spaces. From which of the following cell types do these neoplastic cells originate?

explanations.a: While present in the vascular spaces, endothelial cells are not the source of the painful 'glomus cells' that characterize this lesion.
explanations.b: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.c: Fibroblasts are part of the stroma but do not form the characteristic nests of uniform cells in a glomus tumor.
explanations.d: Pericytes are found around capillaries; while glomus cells are related to perivascular cells, they are specifically identified as modified smooth muscle cells.
explanations.e: Mast cells may be present in various inflammatory or neoplastic tissues but are not the primary neoplastic component of vascular tumors.

ankiCards: The glomus tumor arises from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells.
A painful, subungual, red-blue nodule is most likely a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
The glomus body is a specialized {{c1::arteriovenous anastomosis}} involved in thermoregulation.
Histologically, glomus tumors show nests of {{c1::uniform round cells}} around vascular channels.
The primary clinical symptom of a glomus tumor is {{c1::exquisite pain}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but extremely painful.
They typically occur in the distal portions of the fingers and toes, especially subungual.
Derived from glomus bodies involved in thermoregulation.
Excision is generally curative.
Histology shows characteristic round, uniform 'glomus cells'.
microReview: Glomus tumors are small, benign, yet exquisitely painful lesions of the distal digits. They originate from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, which regulates blood flow for temperature control.
examinerTraps: Students often confuse glomus tumors with subungual melanomas or hemangiomas. The hallmark is the extreme pain and the specific cell of origin (modified smooth muscle).
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors can be categorized into three broad groups: (1) benign tumors (e.g., hemangiomas), which usually form obvious vascular channels and have a regular endothelial monolayer; (2) intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors (e.g., Kaposi sarcoma); and (3) malignant tumors (e.g., angiosarcomas).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with several firm, violaceous nodules on her left arm. She has a history of a radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection and radiotherapy for breast cancer 12 years ago. Since that time, she has had persistent, non-pitting edema of the left arm. A biopsy of a nodule shows atypical endothelial cells forming irregular, anastomosing vascular channels. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and typically occurs in immunosuppressed patients or specific geographic populations, not specifically in lymphedematous limbs post-mastectomy.
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma can occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema, a phenomenon known as Stewart-Treves syndrome. It is a highly aggressive malignant vascular tumor.
explanations.c: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella henselae and occurs in immunocompromised patients, appearing as red papules, not in the setting of chronic lymphedema.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign lesions consisting of large blood-filled spaces; they do not show the cytologic atypia seen in this patient.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are small, painful subungual lesions, not large violaceous nodules on a lymphedematous limb.

ankiCards: Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to {{c1::angiosarcoma}} arising in a limb with chronic lymphedema.
Cutaneous angiosarcoma commonly occurs after {{c1::radical mastectomy}} and lymph node dissection.
Histology of angiosarcoma shows {{c1::atypical endothelial cells}} and irregular vascular channels.
Angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::arsenic}} or polyvinyl chloride (PVC) in the liver.
Radiation therapy is a known risk factor for the development of {{c1::angiosarcoma}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms.
Stewart-Treves syndrome: Angiosarcoma post-mastectomy lymphedema.
They can also be induced by radiation or chemicals (PVC, Thorotrast, arsenic).
Highly aggressive with poor 5-year survival.
Histology shows high mitotic rate and pleomorphic cells.
microReview: Angiosarcomas are aggressive malignancies of endothelial cells. In the clinical context of post-mastectomy lymphedema, the diagnosis is Stewart-Treves syndrome. Look for atypical vascular spaces and CD31 positivity.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse the purple/violaceous appearance with Kaposi sarcoma; look for the history of lymphedema or radiation.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors can be categorized into three broad groups: (1) benign tumors (e.g., hemangiomas), which usually form obvious vascular channels and have a regular endothelial monolayer; (2) intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors (e.g., Kaposi sarcoma); and (3) malignant tumors (e.g., angiosarcomas).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An 8-week-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for a rapidly growing, bright red, raised 'strawberry-like' lesion on the scalp. The parents state it was not present at birth but appeared at 2 weeks of age. Which of the following is the most likely clinical course for this lesion?

options.d: Progressive enlargement causing high-output heart failure

explanations.a: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are very common in newborns, grow rapidly for a few months, and then typically regress spontaneously by age 5 to 7 years.
explanations.b: Hemangiomas are benign and do not undergo malignant transformation into angiosarcomas.
explanations.c: Persistence is characteristic of port-wine stains (nevus flammeus), not juvenile hemangiomas.
explanations.d: While very large hemangiomas can theoretically cause high-output failure, it is not the typical clinical course for a small scalp lesion.
explanations.e: While they can bleed if traumatized, life-threatening hemorrhage is extremely rare for simple juvenile hemangiomas.

ankiCards: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas typically appear {{c1::shortly after birth}}.
The natural history of juvenile hemangiomas involves {{c1::spontaneous regression}}.
Most juvenile hemangiomas disappear by age {{c1::7}}.
Histologically, juvenile hemangiomas are {{c1::capillary}} hemangiomas.
Juvenile hemangiomas are most common on the {{c1::skin}} (location).
keyPoints: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are extremely common.
They grow rapidly initially and then involute.
1 in 200 births; often multi-focal.
Complete regression occurs in 75-90% of cases by age 7.
They are composed of thin-walled capillaries with scant stroma.
microReview: Juvenile hemangiomas are 'strawberry' lesions that grow then fade. They are benign capillary hemangiomas of infancy.
examinerTraps: Wait-and-see management is usually the answer; do not confuse with port-wine stains which do not regress.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors can be categorized into three broad groups: (1) benign tumors (e.g., hemangiomas), which usually form obvious vascular channels and have a regular endothelial monolayer; (2) intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors (e.g., Kaposi sarcoma); and (3) malignant tumors (e.g., angiosarcomas).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 40-year-old male with a history of HIV and a CD4 count of 150 cells/µL presents with multiple red-purple macules and plaques on his trunk and oral mucosa. A biopsy shows spindled stromal cells, slit-like vascular spaces, and extravasated red blood cells. Which of the following infectious agents is the primary driver of this pathology?

explanations.a: HIV causes the immunosuppression that allows the tumor to develop, but it is not the direct oncogenic driver.
explanations.b: Kaposi Sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), also known as HHV-8, is the etiologic agent of all forms of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.c: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can look similar clinically but has different histology (neutrophilic infiltrate, not spindled cells).
explanations.d: EBV is associated with lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.e: CMV causes retinitis and colitis in AIDS patients but is not oncogenic for vascular tumors.

ankiCards: The etiologic agent of Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
Histology of Kaposi Sarcoma features {{c1::slit-like}} vascular spaces.
Kaposi Sarcoma cells are typically {{c1::spindle-shaped}}.
AIDS-associated Kaposi Sarcoma is the most common {{c1::HIV-associated}} malignancy.
HHV-8 infects {{c1::endothelial cells}} and promotes their proliferation.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
Four types: Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
HHV-8 is found in all forms of KS.
Histology: Proliferating spindle cells and poorly formed vascular slits.
Extravasated RBCs and hemosiderin are common.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma is caused by HHV-8. In AIDS patients, it presents as purple lesions and is histologically characterized by spindle cells and slit-like spaces. It is considered an intermediate-grade neoplasm.
examinerTraps: Distinguishing KS from bacillary angiomatosis: KS has spindle cells/slits; Bacillary angiomatosis has neutrophils and pleomorphic bacteria visible on Warthin-Starry stain.

bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old man who has worked in a chemical manufacturing plant for 25 years presents with weight loss, abdominal pain, and hepatomegaly. Imaging shows multiple hemorrhagic masses within the liver. Biopsy reveals a malignant tumor composed of pleomorphic endothelial cells that are positive for CD31. To which of the following substances was this patient most likely exposed?

explanations.a: Aflatoxin B1 is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Exposure to vinyl chloride (used in PVC production), arsenic, and Thorotrast are well-documented risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Benzene is associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), not vascular tumors.
explanations.d: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and bronchogenic carcinoma.
explanations.e: Beryllium exposure is associated with berylliosis (granulomatous lung disease) and lung cancer.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
{{c1::CD31}} is a specific immunohistochemical marker for endothelial cells.
Other than vinyl chloride, {{c1::arsenic}} is a risk factor for liver angiosarcoma.
Angiosarcomas are characterized by {{c1::pleomorphic}} endothelial cells.
{{c1::Thorotrast}} is a radioactive contrast agent formerly linked to hepatic angiosarcoma.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a malignant neoplasm of endothelial origin.
Liver is a classic site for chemically-induced angiosarcoma.
Markers include CD31 and von Willebrand factor.
Very poor prognosis due to early metastasis.
Vinyl chloride exposure occurs in the plastics industry.
microReview: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare, fatal tumor of the liver's blood vessels. It is the classic example of an occupationally-induced cancer (vinyl chloride, arsenic). CD31 positivity confirms its endothelial origin.
examinerTraps: Aflatoxin B1 vs. Vinyl chloride: Aflatoxin causes Hepatocellular Carcinoma (epithelial); Vinyl chloride causes Angiosarcoma (vascular).

stem: Which of the following describes the histological appearance of a 'pyogenic granuloma' commonly found on the gingiva of pregnant women?

options.a: Large, dilated vascular spaces filled with blood and separated by a thin connective tissue stroma
options.b: A circumscribed, pedunculated mass of proliferating capillaries with edema and inflammatory cells
options.c: Poorly defined vascular slits lined by atypical spindle cells with frequent mitoses
options.d: Nests of uniform round cells surrounding thin-walled vascular channels
options.e: A mass of thick-walled vessels with prominent muscular layers and no atypia

explanations.a: This describes a cavernous hemangioma.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a rapidly growing red nodule that histologically resembles exuberant granulation tissue (capillaries and edema).
explanations.c: This describes Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.d: This describes a glomus tumor.
explanations.e: This describes an arteriovenous malformation or angiomyolipoma component, not a pyogenic granuloma.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is a variant of {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma.

Commonly occur on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
Associated with trauma or pregnancy.

They frequently ulcerate and bleed easily.

stem: A 5-year-old child presents with a large, flat, purple-red birthmark covering the left side of his face in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve. He has also had several seizures. Which of the following conditions is most likely associated with these findings?

explanations.a: Osler-Weber-Rendu (hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia) features multiple small telangiectasias of the skin and mucous membranes, not large facial marks.
explanations.b: Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) is characterized by a port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) in the V1/V2 distribution, ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomas, and seizures.
explanations.c: Von Hippel-Lindau is associated with hemangioblastomas of the cerebellum and retina, as well as renal cell carcinoma.
explanations.d: NF1 features café-au-lait spots and neurofibromas, not port-wine stains.
explanations.e: Tuberous sclerosis features ash-leaf spots and facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum), not port-wine stains.

ankiCards: Sturge-Weber syndrome is associated with a facial {{c1::port-wine stain (nevus flammeus)}}.
The facial lesion in Sturge-Weber syndrome usually follows the {{c1::trigeminal nerve}} distribution.
Sturge-Weber syndrome involves {{c1::leptomeningeal}} angiomas.
Clinically, patients with Sturge-Weber often present with {{c1::seizures}} and mental retardation.
Unlike juvenile hemangiomas, port-wine stains {{c1::do not regress}} with age.

Sturge-Weber syndrome: Port-wine stain + leptomeningeal angiomatosis.
Can cause glaucoma and seizures.
Associated with GNAQ gene mutations.
The skin lesion thickens and darkens over time.
microReview: Sturge-Weber syndrome is a sporadic phakomatosis. Remember the 'S's: Seizures, Stain (port-wine), and 'S'trigeminal nerve distribution.
examinerTraps: Confusion between Sturge-Weber and other neurocutaneous syndromes. The facial port-wine stain is the differentiator.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors can be categorized into three broad groups: (1) benign tumors (e.g., hemangiomas), which usually form obvious vascular channels and have a regular endothelial monolayer; (2) intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors (e.g., Kaposi sarcoma); and (3) malignant tumors (e.g., angiosarcomas).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 35-year-old male with advanced AIDS presents with several skin lesions that are bright red, dome-shaped, and bleed easily. Microscopic examination reveals a lobulated proliferation of capillaries with prominent, plump endothelial cells, mixed inflammatory infiltrates, and granular material that stains positive with a Warthin-Starry silver stain. What is the most likely causative organism?

explanations.a: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, which does not show granular bacterial clusters on silver stain.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella species (B. henselae or B. quintana) and features vascular proliferation with neutrophilic inflammation and bacteria visible on Warthin-Starry stain.
explanations.c: Treponema pallidum causes syphilis; while silver stains detect it, the lesions and histology (obliterative endarteritis) are different.
explanations.d: MAI causes systemic infection and granulomas in AIDS, not vascular skin lesions.
explanations.e: S. aureus causes pyogenic infections (abscesses, impetigo) but not this specific vascular tumor-like lesion.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
In bacillary angiomatosis, bacteria are visualized using the {{c1::Warthin-Starry}} silver stain.
The inflammatory infiltrate in bacillary angiomatosis is primarily {{c1::neutrophilic}}.
Bacillary angiomatosis occurs primarily in {{c1::immunocompromised/AIDS}} patients.
The clinical appearance of bacillary angiomatosis can mimic {{c1::Kaposi sarcoma}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis: opportunistic infection in AIDS.
Involves skin, bone, or liver (peliosis hepatis).
Driven by Bartonella-induced VEGF production.
Histology: Plump endothelial cells + neutrophils + bacterial clusters.
Responsive to antibiotic treatment (e.g., erythromycin).
microReview: Bacillary angiomatosis is a Bartonella infection in AIDS patients that mimics Kaposi Sarcoma clinically but is histologically distinct due to neutrophilic inflammation and the presence of bacilli (Warthin-Starry stain).
examinerTraps: The presence of neutrophils is a major histologic clue to distinguish Bacillary Angiomatosis from Kaposi Sarcoma (which usually lacks them).
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors can be categorized into three broad groups: (1) benign tumors (e.g., hemangiomas), which usually form obvious vascular channels and have a regular endothelial monolayer; (2) intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors (e.g., Kaposi sarcoma); and (3) malignant tumors (e.g., angiosarcomas).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the most common histological variant of hemangioma, typically found on the skin, subcutaneous tissues, or mucous membranes of the mouth?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas involve larger, deeper channels and are less common than capillary types in the skin.
explanations.b: Capillary hemangiomas are the most common type of hemangioma. They consist of thin-walled capillaries with scant stroma.
explanations.c: Arteriovenous malformations are structural anomalies involving larger vessels, not a tumor of capillaries.
explanations.d: Spider telangiectasia is a non-neoplastic vascular ectasia, not a true hemangioma.
explanations.e: Lymphangioma circumscriptum is a lymphatic malformation, not a blood vessel tumor.

ankiCards: The most common type of hemangioma is the {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma.
Capillary hemangiomas consist of {{c1::thin-walled}} capillaries.
Common locations for capillary hemangiomas include the {{c1::skin/mucous membranes}}.
Most hemangiomas are {{c1::benign}} (behavior).
A variant of capillary hemangioma that occurs in infants is the {{c1::juvenile (strawberry)}} hemangioma.
keyPoints: Hemangiomas are very common benign vascular tumors.
Capillary hemangiomas are composed of small, blood-filled vessels.
Most are present from birth or early childhood.
They can rarely occur internally (e.g., liver, though cavernous is more common there).
They are usually stable or regress.
microReview: Capillary hemangiomas are the 'garden variety' benign vascular tumor. They are made of capillaries and are very common on the skin.
examinerTraps: Ensure you distinguish between capillary (small vessels) and cavernous (large vessels).
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors can be categorized into three broad groups: (1) benign tumors (e.g., hemangiomas), which usually form obvious vascular channels and have a regular endothelial monolayer; (2) intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors (e.g., Kaposi sarcoma); and (3) malignant tumors (e.g., angiosarcomas).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 22-year-old male with a history of Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease undergoes an abdominal CT scan for routine surveillance. The scan reveals a well-circumscribed, 3-cm lesion in the liver. A biopsy shows large, dilated, blood-filled vascular spaces separated by connective tissue. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are made of small vessels and are less common in the liver than cavernous types.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas are the most common benign tumors of the liver and are characterized by large, dilated vascular spaces.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma is malignant and shows cytologic atypia, which is not described here.
explanations.d: Hepatocellular carcinoma is an epithelial malignancy, not a vascular lesion.
explanations.e: Hepatic adenoma is a benign epithelial tumor (hepatocytes), not a vascular lesion.

ankiCards: The most common benign tumor of the liver is the {{c1::cavernous hemangioma}}.
Cavernous hemangiomas histologically show {{c1::dilated}} vascular spaces.
Vascular spaces in cavernous hemangiomas are separated by {{c1::fibrous/connective}} tissue.
Clinically, cavernous hemangiomas are usually {{c1::asymptomatic}}.
Complications of large cavernous hemangiomas can include {{c1::thrombosis}} or rupture.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas involve large, blood-filled spaces.
They are frequently found in the liver and spleen.
Often discovered incidentally on imaging.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, they do not regress.
Von Hippel-Lindau disease is associated with various vascular tumors (hemangioblastomas).
microReview: Cavernous hemangiomas are large-vessel benign tumors. In the liver, they are the most common benign tumor and appear as blood-filled lakes on histology.
examinerTraps: Do not biopsy these if you suspect them clinically due to the risk of hemorrhage, although the question provides biopsy results for diagnostic confirmation.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors can be categorized into three broad groups: (1) benign tumors (e.g., hemangiomas), which usually form obvious vascular channels and have a regular endothelial monolayer; (2) intermediate-grade (borderline) tumors (e.g., Kaposi sarcoma); and (3) malignant tumors (e.g., angiosarcomas).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular pathology is categorized into two principal mechanisms that underlie disease. Which of the following describes the mechanism specifically responsible for the formation of an aneurysm?

explanations.a: Narrowing or stenosis leads to ischemia, but it is not the primary mechanism of aneurysm formation.
explanations.b: Obstruction, often caused by atherosclerosis or embolism, leads to downstream infarction rather than wall dilation.
explanations.c: Weakening of vessel walls is the fundamental mechanism that leads to the dilation or rupture characteristic of an aneurysm.
explanations.d: Thrombosis is a mechanism of luminal obstruction, which is distinct from the wall weakening that leads to aneurysms.
explanations.e: Intimal thickening is a stereotyped response to injury that typically narrows the lumen rather than dilating the wall.

ankiCards: The two principal mechanisms underlying vascular disease are narrowing/obstruction and {{c1::weakening}} of vessel walls.
Weakening of vessel walls typically leads to {{c1::dilation or rupture}}.
Aneurysms are categorized as a form of vascular disease driven by {{c1::wall weakening}}.
Progressive narrowing of vessel lumens is most commonly caused by {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Precipitous obstruction of vessel lumens is most commonly caused by {{c1::thrombosis or embolism}}.
keyPoints: Vascular disease morbidity/mortality is higher than any other disease category.
Stenosis and obstruction are primary mechanisms of luminal disease.
Wall weakening is the hallmark mechanism of aneurysms.
Atherosclerosis can cause both narrowing and wall weakening.
Different vessels show characteristic anatomic distributions for various disorders.
microReview: Aneurysms result from a loss of structural integrity in the vessel wall, whereas stenosis results from additive material (plaque) or thrombus within the lumen.
examinerTraps: Atherosclerosis is a risk factor for both mechanisms, but the question asks for the mechanism of the aneurysm itself (dilation), which is wall weakening.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: • Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens... • Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 69-year-old male presents with a dull, aching sensation in his lower back. He has a history of hypertension and a 40 pack-year history of cigarette smoking. Physical examination reveals a pulsatile mass in the periumbilical region. A CT scan confirms a 5.5 cm dilation of the infrarenal aorta. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: The classic presentation of a pulsatile abdominal mass in an older male smoker is an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA).
explanations.b: Thoracic aortic aneurysms usually present with chest pain, cough, or dysphagia and are located above the diaphragm.
explanations.c: Aortic dissection involves a tear in the intima and blood within the media; it typically presents with sharp, tearing chest or back pain.
explanations.d: A pseudoaneurysm is a hematoma that communicates with the intravascular space but is not bounded by the vessel wall layers.
explanations.e: AV malformations are direct connections between arteries and veins, not typically presenting as infrarenal aortic dilations.

ankiCards: A pulsatile abdominal mass in an elderly male smoker is most likely an {{c1::abdominal aortic aneurysm}}.
The most common location for an abdominal aortic aneurysm is {{c1::infrarenal}}.
The primary mechanism of AAA formation is the weakening of the {{c1::vessel wall}}.
Risk factors for AAA include {{c1::smoking}} and hypertension.
A diameter of >{{c1::5.0-5.5}} cm in an AAA usually indicates a high risk of rupture and a need for surgical intervention.
keyPoints: AAA is often asymptomatic until it ruptures or is found on exam.
Smoking is the most significant modifiable risk factor for AAA.
Infrarenal location is characteristic because of the lower density of vasa vasorum.
Aneurysms represent a permanent dilation of the vessel wall.
Pulsatile masses are a classic physical exam finding for large aneurysms.
microReview: Clinical triad for AAA: Elderly male, smoker, pulsatile abdominal mass. Mechanism: Atherosclerosis leading to medial thinning and wall weakening.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse AAA with dissection; dissection presents with acute, tearing pain, while AAA is often a slow, dull ache or asymptomatic.
sourceQuote: Aneurysms and Dissection... Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm... Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm... Aortic Dissection
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following best defines a 'true aneurysm' as opposed to a 'false aneurysm' (pseudoaneurysm)?

options.a: It involves only the intimal layer
options.b: It involves all three layers of the arterial wall
options.c: It is characterized by a wall composed of extravascular hematoma
options.d: It results from a tear in the intima allowing blood into the media
options.e: It only occurs in the venous system

explanations.a: Aneurysms that only involve the intima do not exist; true aneurysms involve all layers of the wall.
explanations.b: A true aneurysm involves an intact but attenuated arterial wall or thinned ventricular wall of the heart; it must involve all three layers (intima, media, adventitia).
explanations.c: This describes a false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm), where a wall defect leads to a hematoma bounded by extravascular tissue.
explanations.d: This describes an aortic dissection, which is distinct from a true aneurysm.
explanations.e: Aneurysms occur most significantly in the arterial system, particularly elastic and muscular arteries.

ankiCards: A {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the vessel wall (intima, media, and adventitia).
A {{c1::false}} aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) is a hematoma that communicates with the vascular space through a hole in the wall.
The layers of a vessel wall include the {{c1::intima}}, media, and adventitia.
An aortic dissection occurs when blood enters the {{c1::media}} through an intimal tear.
True aneurysms can be categorized morphologically as {{c1::saccular}} or fusiform.
keyPoints: True aneurysms: Wall is intact, involve all 3 layers.
Pseudoaneurysm: Wall is breached, hematoma is bounded by connective tissue.
Fusiform aneurysms: Symmetric dilations of the entire circumference.
Saccular aneurysms: Spherical out-pouchings involving only a portion of the wall.
Aortic dissection is often confused with but is distinct from true aneurysms.
microReview: Definition check: True = 3 layers intact. False = leak/hematoma contained by extravascular tissue.
examinerTraps: A common trap is defining a dissection as an aneurysm; they are related but distinct pathological entities.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular wall architecture dictates the response to hemodynamic stress. Which morphological change is most likely to occur in a vessel that experiences a chronic loss of medial structural integrity?

explanations.a: Stenosis is narrowing, usually due to additive pathology like plaque, not wall loss.
explanations.b: Loss of medial structural integrity (e.g., degradation of elastin) leads to the inability of the wall to resist pressure, resulting in an aneurysm.
explanations.c: Intimal hyperplasia is a proliferative response to injury, leading to wall thickening and lumen narrowing.
explanations.d: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is a thickening of small vessel walls associated with hypertension/diabetes, not dilation.
explanations.e: Thromboangiitis obliterans is an inflammatory, occlusive disease of small/medium arteries.

ankiCards: The loss of medial structural integrity in an artery leads to {{c1::aneurysm}} formation.
The two main structural components of the media that provide strength are {{c1::elastin and collagen}}.
In contrast to dilation, intimal thickening leads to {{c1::luminal narrowing}}.
Arterial walls are {{c1::thicker}} than venous walls to accommodate higher pressure.
Aneurysms represent the {{c1::weakening}} mechanism of vascular disease.
keyPoints: The media provides the structural strength of the arterial wall.
Elastic arteries (aorta) are prone to aneurysms when elastin is degraded.
Muscular arteries exert control over flow but can also dilate if the wall weakens.
Hemodynamic stress (hypertension) accelerates wall weakening.
Rupture is the most feared consequence of wall weakening.
microReview: Medial weakness = Dilation/Aneurysm. Intimal thickening = Narrowing/Stenosis.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'remodeling' (thickening) with 'weakening' (dilation).
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old female with a history of Marfan syndrome presents for a follow-up. Her echocardiogram shows a dilated aortic root and ascending aorta. Which of the following histological features is most likely to be present in her aortic media?

explanations.a: Marfan syndrome is associated with cystic medial degeneration (fragmentation of elastic fibers), which leads to thoracic aortic aneurysms.
explanations.b: Atherosclerosis is the primary cause of abdominal aortic aneurysms, not the genetic-related thoracic aneurysms in Marfan patients.
explanations.c: Granulomatous inflammation is characteristic of vasculitides like Giant Cell Arteritis.
explanations.d: Hyaline thickening is a feature of hypertensive small vessel disease (arteriolosclerosis).
explanations.e: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis affects small vessels (capillaries/venules), not the aorta.

ankiCards: Marfan syndrome is classically associated with {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}} of the aorta.
Thoracic aortic aneurysms in younger patients should prompt a search for {{c1::connective tissue}} disorders.
Cystic medial degeneration involves the fragmentation of {{c1::elastic}} fibers.
The dilated aortic root in Marfan syndrome can lead to {{c1::aortic regurgitation/insufficiency}}.
Aneurysms in the ascending aorta are more likely to be related to {{c1::hypertension or genetic disorders}} than atherosclerosis.
keyPoints: Thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAA) have different etiologies than AAA.
TAA is often associated with hypertension or Marfan syndrome (Fibrillin-1 mutation).
Cystic medial degeneration is the histological hallmark of Marfan-associated TAA.
Weakening of the wall in Marfan syndrome results from defective TGF-beta signaling.
Dilation of the aortic root is a precursor to TAA and potential dissection.
microReview: AAA = Atherosclerosis. TAA = Hypertension or Connective Tissue Disease (Marfan).
examinerTraps: Atherosclerosis is common, but it is *not* the primary cause of aneurysms in the ascending aorta (TAA).
sourceQuote: Aneurysms and Dissection... Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular disorders often show characteristic anatomic distributions. Atherosclerosis primarily affects which type of vessels, leading to potential aneurysm formation?

explanations.a: Capillaries are too small and lack the media required for atherosclerotic plaque formation.
explanations.b: Arterioles are affected by arteriolosclerosis, but atherosclerosis primarily targets larger vessels.
explanations.c: Venules are generally not affected by atherosclerosis because of low pressure.
explanations.d: Atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries, which are the sites where aneurysms typically develop.
explanations.e: Post-capillary venules are sites of inflammation and leukocyte extravasation, not atherosclerosis.

ankiCards: Atherosclerosis affects mainly {{c1::elastic and muscular}} arteries.
Anatomic distribution of vascular disease is determined by the {{c1::type}} of vessel involved.
Aneurysms occur in {{c1::arteries}} rather than veins because of higher pressure and wall structure.
Small muscular vessels exert control over blood {{c1::flow and pressure}}.
The ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}} as arteries become smaller.
keyPoints: Atherosclerosis is a disease of large and medium-sized arteries.
Elastic arteries include the aorta, carotid, and iliac arteries.
Muscular arteries include the coronary and renal arteries.
Aneurysms in the abdominal aorta are usually due to atherosclerosis weakening the wall.
The anatomy of the vessel dictates its susceptibility to specific pathologies.
microReview: Large/Medium arteries = Atherosclerosis & Aneurysms. Small arteries/Arterioles = Hypertension & Arteriolosclerosis.
examinerTraps: The text explicitly states atherosclerosis affects 'elastic and muscular' arteries; don't pick 'arterioles' even though they are small arteries.
sourceQuote: Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which principal mechanism of vascular disease is most likely to be caused precipitously by an embolism?

explanations.a: Weakening is usually a chronic process leading to aneurysms.
explanations.b: Dilation is the result of weakening, not embolism.
explanations.c: Embolism and thrombosis are the two primary causes of precipitous (sudden) obstruction of vessel lumens.
explanations.d: Rupture is a consequence of weakening, not typically a direct result of embolism.
explanations.e: Cystic medial necrosis is a chronic degenerative change in the wall.

ankiCards: Two ways the vessel lumen is blocked are {{c1::progressively}} or precipitously.
{{c1::Atherosclerosis}} causes progressive narrowing of the lumen.
{{c1::Thrombosis or embolism}} causes precipitous obstruction of the lumen.
Luminal obstruction leads to downstream {{c1::ischemia or infarction}}.
Unlike obstruction, weakening of the wall leads to {{c1::dilation}}.
keyPoints: Obstruction can be progressive (atherosclerosis) or sudden (embolism/thrombosis).
Vascular morbidity is often tied to luminal narrowing.
Precipitous events are medical emergencies.
Obstruction is distinct from dilation/aneurysm.
Normal vessel structure must be understood to appreciate these pathologies.
microReview: Slow blockage = Atherosclerosis. Fast blockage = Embolus. Wall break = Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Wait for keywords: 'Precipitous' indicates a sudden event like an embolus or thrombus.
sourceQuote: Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g., by atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g., by thrombosis or embolism)
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: In the context of arterial architecture, why are arterial walls thicker than corresponding venous walls?

options.c: To accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures
options.e: To store larger volumes of blood

explanations.a: Arteries carry higher oxygen levels (except the pulmonary artery).
explanations.b: Valves, primarily in veins, prevent backflow, not wall thickness.
explanations.c: The structural design of arteries allows them to handle the high-pressure, pulsatile output from the heart.
explanations.d: Capillaries, not arteries, are designed for gas exchange.
explanations.e: Veins are the primary reservoir (capacitance) vessels for blood volume.

ankiCards: Arterial walls are {{c1::thicker}} than venous walls at the same level of branching.
The structural difference in arterial walls accommodates {{c1::pulsatile flow}} and higher pressure.
As arteries become smaller, the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter {{c1::increases}}.
Smaller muscular vessels are the primary controllers of {{c1::blood pressure}}.
Vascular pathology in the aorta is often related to the {{c1::media}} layer's structural integrity.
keyPoints: Arterial thickness is a functional adaptation to pressure.
The 'capacitance' of the system resides in the veins.
Higher pressure in arteries makes them more prone to aneurysms than veins.
Wall/Lumen ratio increases in the periphery to control resistance.
Structural specialization reflects distinct functional roles.
microReview: Artery = High pressure/Thick wall. Vein = Low pressure/Thin wall. Aneurysms = Pressure overcoming a weak wall.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'volume' with 'pressure'. Veins hold more volume; arteries handle more pressure.
sourceQuote: For example, arterial walls are thicker than corresponding veins at the same level of branching to accommodate pulsatile flow and higher blood pressures.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old male with long-standing uncontrolled hypertension presents with sudden onset 'tearing' chest pain that radiates to his back. His blood pressure is 190/110 mmHg. Which of the following is the most likely pathological process occurring in his aorta?

explanations.a: AAA is usually asymptomatic and located below the diaphragm; it does not typically cause tearing chest pain.
explanations.b: Aortic dissection is characterized by 'tearing' chest pain radiating to the back, often in the setting of severe hypertension.
explanations.c: Giant cell arteritis causes headaches and jaw claudication in older patients, not acute tearing chest pain.
explanations.d: Kawasaki disease affects children and involves coronary artery aneurysms.
explanations.e: Thromboangiitis obliterans involves small/medium arteries in the extremities of smokers.

ankiCards: Sudden, 'tearing' chest pain radiating to the back is the hallmark of {{c1::aortic dissection}}.
The most common predisposing factor for aortic dissection is {{c1::hypertension}}.
Aortic dissection involves blood splitting the layers of the {{c1::media}}.
Aortic dissection is listed alongside {{c1::aneurysms}} as a major vascular wall disorder.
Unlike a true aneurysm, a dissection involves a {{c1::tear}} in the intimal layer.
keyPoints: Aortic dissection is a life-threatening emergency.
Hypertension is the number one risk factor.
It is distinct from an aneurysm but involves the same wall weakening mechanism.
The pain is typically described as 'tearing' or 'ripping'.
It can lead to cardiac tamponade or massive hemorrhage.
microReview: Dissection = Tearing pain + Hypertension + Intimal tear. Aneurysm = Pulsatile mass + Smoking + Wall dilation.
examinerTraps: Aneurysms and dissections are in the same chapter/section; the 'tearing' pain is the pathognomonic clinical clue for dissection.
sourceQuote: Aneurysms and Dissection... Aortic Dissection
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which morphological type of aneurysm is described as a spherical outpouching that involves only a portion of the vessel wall and often contains thrombus?

explanations.a: Fusiform aneurysms are circumferential and symmetric dilations of the vessel.
explanations.b: Saccular aneurysms are discrete, spherical outpouchings (ranging from 5 to 20 cm) that involve only a portion of the vessel wall.
explanations.c: A 'dissecting aneurysm' is a misnomer; the correct term is aortic dissection.
explanations.d: A Berry aneurysm is a specific type of saccular aneurysm in the Circle of Willis, but 'Saccular' is the broader morphological term.
explanations.e: Mycotic aneurysm refers to an infected aneurysm, regardless of its shape.

ankiCards: {{c1::Saccular}} aneurysms are spherical outpouchings involving only a part of the vessel wall.
{{c1::Fusiform}} aneurysms are circumferential dilations of the vessel wall.
Aneurysms often contain {{c1::thrombus}} because of turbulent blood flow.
Morphological classification of aneurysms includes {{c1::saccular and fusiform}}.
Small saccular aneurysms in the brain are called {{c1::Berry}} aneurysms.
keyPoints: Saccular: One-sided, spherical, like a 'sack'.
Fusiform: Both sides, spindle-shaped, long.
Morphology helps distinguish the likely cause and risk.
Aneurysms are often filled with laminated thrombi.
Aneurysm shape is used for clinical and radiologic description.
microReview: Saccular = Sack-like (part of wall). Fusiform = Spindle-like (entire circumference).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'Saccular' (the shape) with 'Berry' (the location-specific name).
sourceQuote: Aneurysms and Dissection
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 34-year-old male with a history of advanced HIV (CD4+ count 150 cells/mm³) presents with multiple raised, violaceous skin plaques on his lower extremities and hard palate. Biopsy of a lesion reveals a proliferation of spindle-shaped cells forming slit-like spaces containing extravasated red blood cells. Which of the following is the most likely cellular origin of this neoplasm?

options.c: Glomus cells of the thermoregulatory bodies
options.e: Smooth muscle cells of the tunica media

explanations.a: Pericytes are the cell of origin for hemangiopericytomas, not the lesion described.
explanations.b: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is the most likely diagnosis given the clinical setting of HIV and violaceous lesions. Histologically, KS is characterized by spindle cells and slit-like vascular spaces; immunohistochemical studies show these cells express markers of lymphatic endothelial cells (e.g., PROX1, podoplanin).
explanations.c: Glomus cells are specialized smooth muscle cells involved in thermoregulation and give rise to glomus tumors, which are typically painful subungual lesions.
explanations.d: While fibroblasts are present in many skin lesions, they do not form the characteristic vascular slits seen in Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.e: Smooth muscle cells are found in vascular walls but do not represent the primary neoplastic component of Kaposi sarcoma.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is associated with which human herpesvirus? {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}
The classic histopathological finding in Kaposi Sarcoma is {{c1::spindle cells with slit-like vascular spaces}}.
Kaposi Sarcoma spindle cells most closely resemble {{c1::lymphatic}} endothelial cells.
Besides the skin, Kaposi Sarcoma frequently involves the {{c1::gastrointestinal tract}} and {{c1::lymph nodes}}.
Vascular tumors in HIV patients with neutrophilic infiltrates are likely {{c1::Bacillary angiomatosis}} rather than Kaposi Sarcoma.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a malignant vascular neoplasm associated with HHV-8.
The four forms of KS are Classic (older Mediterranean men), Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated.
Spindle-shaped cells forming slit-like vascular spaces are the hallmark histological feature.
KS lesions are often violaceous because of extravasated red blood cells and hemosiderin deposition.
Immunohistochemistry usually reflects a lymphatic endothelial phenotype.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma = HIV/Immunosuppression + HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Vascular slits + Lymphatic origin.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse Kaposi Sarcoma with Bacillary Angiomatosis; both occur in HIV, but Bacillary Angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella and features neutrophilic inflammation, not spindle cells.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors are divided into three categories: (1) benign tumors (e.g., hemangiomas), which contain obvious vascular channels; (2) intermediate-grade tumors (e.g., Kaposi sarcoma), which are locally aggressive; and (3) malignant tumors (e.g., angiosarcoma).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with an exquisitely painful, 4-mm, blue-red nodule located under the fingernail of her right index finger. The pain is particularly severe when she is exposed to cold temperatures. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are typically painless and occur in infancy, often on the head or neck.
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor, usually occurring in the scalp of elderly patients or post-radiation, and is not typically small or subungual.
explanations.c: A glomus tumor (glomangioma) is a benign, exquisitely painful tumor arising from the specialized smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, frequently located in the subungual region.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granulomas are rapidly growing, pedunculated red nodules that bleed easily, often on the gingiva or fingers, but are not characteristically subungual or exquisitely painful to cold.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts, not a painful solitary subungual nodule.

ankiCards: The classic triad of a glomus tumor includes pain, tenderness, and {{c1::sensitivity to cold}}.
Glomus tumors arise from specialized smooth muscle cells of the {{c1::glomus body}}.
The most common location for a glomus tumor is the {{c1::subungual region (under the nail)}}.
Histology of a glomus tumor shows nests of uniform cells surrounding {{c1::vascular channels}}.
Unlike most vascular tumors, glomus tumors originate from {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} rather than endothelial cells.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but extremely painful.
They are derived from glomus bodies, which are thermoregulatory arteriovenous shunts.
Subungual location is the classic clinical presentation.
Pain is triggered by cold exposure.
Histologically, they consist of nests of uniform, round cells with scant cytoplasm.
microReview: Painful subungual nodule + cold sensitivity = Glomus Tumor (smooth muscle origin).
examinerTraps: Wait for the keyword 'painful' or 'cold sensitivity' to distinguish Glomus tumor from a simple subungual hematoma or hemangioma.
sourceQuote: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, exquisitely painful tumors that arise from specialized smooth muscle cells of the glomus bodies, arteriovenous structures involved in thermoregulation.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A biopsy of a red, friable skin lesion in a patient with HIV demonstrates a proliferation of capillaries with prominent, protuberant endothelial cells and an infiltrate consisting predominantly of neutrophils. Silver staining (Warthin-Starry) reveals clusters of bacilli within the tissue. What is the primary etiologic agent of this condition?

explanations.a: HHV-8 causes Kaposi Sarcoma, which shows spindle cells and minimal inflammation, not neutrophilic infiltrates or bacilli.
explanations.b: Bartonella henselae (or B. quintana) is the cause of Bacillary Angiomatosis, which presents in immunocompromised patients as vascular proliferations with neutrophilic inflammation and visible bacteria on silver stain.
explanations.c: Staphylococcus aureus causes pyogenic infections but not this specific form of vascular tumor-like proliferation.
explanations.d: HPV causes warts and some carcinomas, not vascular tumors.
explanations.e: CMV can cause systemic infection in HIV but is not associated with this histological pattern of vascular proliferation.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by bacteria of the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
The inflammatory infiltrate in Bacillary Angiomatosis is predominantly {{c1::neutrophilic}}.
The stain used to identify the bacilli in Bacillary Angiomatosis is the {{c1::Warthin-Starry (silver)}} stain.
Bacillary angiomatosis primarily affects patients with {{c1::immunodeficiency (HIV)}}.
The domestic cat is the reservoir for {{c1::Bartonella henselae}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary Angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation caused by Bartonella species.
It is a 'great mimicker' of Kaposi Sarcoma clinically but is distinct histologically.
Histology: Lobular proliferation of capillaries with plump endothelial cells and neutrophils.
Bacteria can be seen using silver stains.
It is curable with antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin).
microReview: HIV patient + vascular skin nodule + neutrophils + silver stain (+) = Bacillary Angiomatosis (Bartonella).
examinerTraps: The presence of neutrophils is the histological 'dead giveaway' to choose Bacillary Angiomatosis over Kaposi Sarcoma.
sourceQuote: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts (e.g., patients with AIDS) caused by opportunistic gram-negative bacilli of the Bartonella family.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 2-week-old infant is brought to the clinic due to a bright red, raised 'strawberry-like' lesion on the scalp that has been rapidly growing since birth. The parents are concerned about the cosmetic appearance. Which of the following is the most likely natural history of this lesion?

options.c: Lifelong persistence without change in size

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are benign and do not transform into malignant angiosarcomas.
