explanations.b: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas are very common in infants. They grow rapidly for several months but usually begin to regress by age 1–3 and disappear completely by age 7 in the vast majority of cases.
explanations.c: These lesions typically do not persist lifelong; they undergo involution.
explanations.d: Capillary hemangiomas do not metastasize.
explanations.e: Surgery is usually avoided because the lesion is benign and likely to regress spontaneously.

ankiCards: The most common form of vascular tumor is the {{c1::hemangioma}}.
A strawberry hemangioma of infancy is histologically classified as a {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma.
Most juvenile hemangiomas completely regress by age {{c1::7}}.
Hemangiomas that are present at birth and involve large cavernous spaces are called {{c1::cavernous}} hemangiomas.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas are often associated with the {{c1::von Hippel-Lindau}} disease.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangiomas are 'strawberry' lesions on the skin of newborns.
They are extremely common (1 in 200 births).
They are characterized by a 'growth phase' followed by an 'involution phase'.
Histologically, they are composed of thin-walled capillaries with scant stroma.
75% to 90% regress by age 7.
microReview: Newborn + red strawberry lesion + rapid growth = Juvenile Capillary Hemangioma (wait and watch for regression).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'strawberry' hemangioma (capillary) with the 'port-wine stain' (nevus flammeus), which does not regress and is associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome.
sourceQuote: Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) of the skin of newborns are very common (1 in 200 births); they can be multiple. They grow rapidly for a few months but then begin to fade and regress by 1 to 3 years of age.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old male presents with several enlarging, ill-defined, violaceous nodules on his scalp. Biopsy shows an infiltrative proliferation of pleomorphic, malignant cells forming irregular, communicating vascular channels. Immunohistochemical staining is positive for CD31. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma usually occurs in younger, immunocompromised patients and features spindle cells rather than highly pleomorphic cells forming irregular channels.
explanations.b: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign infectious process, not a malignant infiltrative neoplasm.
explanations.c: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms. In the elderly, they frequently occur on the scalp/face. CD31 is a specific marker for endothelial cells.
explanations.d: Cavernous hemangiomas are benign lesions with large, blood-filled spaces and lack cellular pleomorphism or infiltrative growth.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are small, benign, and derived from smooth muscle, not endothelial cells forming irregular channels.

ankiCards: The most common site for cutaneous angiosarcoma in the elderly is the {{c1::scalp}}.
{{c1::CD31}} is a highly specific immunohistochemical marker for vascular endothelial cells.
Angiosarcoma of the liver is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride (or arsenic/thorotrast)}}.
The 5-year survival rate for angiosarcoma is generally {{c1::poor (low)}}.
Angiosarcoma occurring years after radical mastectomy and chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves syndrome}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a high-grade malignant tumor of endothelial cells.
It can be induced by radiation, chronic lymphedema, or specific chemicals.
The scalp of elderly men is a classic location.
Histology ranges from well-formed vascular channels to solid sheets of undifferentiated cells.
Markers: CD31 and von Willebrand factor.
microReview: Elderly patient + scalp lesion + malignant vascular channels + CD31 positive = Angiosarcoma.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'atypical endothelial cells' or 'CD31' to confirm a diagnosis of angiosarcoma over a benign hemangioma.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms that range from highly differentiated tumors that resemble hemangiomas... to wildly anaplastic lesions.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 60-year-old woman, who underwent a radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection 12 years ago for breast cancer, presents with a new, rapidly enlarging, firm, purple-to-black nodule on her chronically swollen left arm. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: While recurrent cancer is possible, a purple/black nodule in the setting of chronic lymphedema strongly suggests a vascular malignancy.
explanations.b: Lymphangiomas are benign and usually present at birth; they do not appear as new aggressive nodules in adults.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema (post-mastectomy) is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granulomas are benign, small, and usually associated with trauma or pregnancy, not long-term lymphedema.
explanations.e: Capillary hemangiomas are benign infantile lesions.

ankiCards: Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to {{c1::angiosarcoma}} arising in chronic lymphedema.
The most common clinical scenario for Stewart-Treves syndrome is post-{{c1::mastectomy}}.
Angiosarcoma is also a known complication of previous {{c1::radiation}} therapy.
Unlike hemangiomas, angiosarcomas exhibit significant {{c1::cytologic atypia/mitoses}}.
Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a rare but aggressive malignancy.
Chronic lymphedema is a major risk factor (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
It typically presents as multiple small red papules or nodules that coalesce.
The prognosis is very poor due to early local invasion and metastasis.
Treatment usually requires radical surgery.
microReview: Mastectomy + chronic lymphedema + new purple nodule = Stewart-Treves (Angiosarcoma).
examinerTraps: The examiner might try to trick you into picking 'recurrent breast cancer', but the 'purple' color and 'lymphedema' history are classic for angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas can also occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema, classically in the ipsilateral arm of women several years after radical mastectomy.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following descriptions best characterizes the histological appearance of a pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma)?

options.a: Large, dilated vascular channels filled with blood and separated by a thin connective tissue stroma
options.b: A circumscribed lesion of proliferating capillaries with edema and an inflammatory infiltrate, often pedunculated
options.c: Interconnecting vascular channels lined by atypical, pleomorphic endothelial cells
options.d: Uniform, round cells in rows or clusters surrounding narrow vascular lumens
options.e: Nests of spindle cells with slit-like spaces and hemosiderin deposits

explanations.a: This describes a cavernous hemangioma.
explanations.b: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) presents as a rapidly growing, pedunculated, red lesion that bleeds easily; histologically it is a capillary hemangioma with surrounding edema and inflammation.
explanations.c: This describes angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: This describes a glomus tumor.
explanations.e: This describes Kaposi sarcoma.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer; it is neither {{c1::pyogenic (infectious)}} nor a {{c1::granuloma}}.
Pyogenic granuloma is histologically a version of a {{c1::capillary}} hemangioma.
A pyogenic granuloma that occurs in the gingiva of a pregnant woman is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
Clinical behavior of pyogenic granuloma is characterized by {{c1::rapid}} growth and frequent bleeding.
The preferred treatment for pyogenic granuloma is {{c1::surgical excision/curettage}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granuloma is a 'lobular capillary hemangioma'.
It often follows minor trauma.
It is commonly found on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
It is highly vascular and friable (bleeds easily).
Granuloma gravidarum is a specific subtype occurring in 1% of pregnant women.
microReview: Friable red nodule + oral/skin + rapid growth = Pyogenic Granuloma (benign capillary proliferation).
examinerTraps: Don't let the name 'pyogenic' fool you; there is usually no pus or primary bacterial infection involved in the pathogenesis.
sourceQuote: Pyogenic granulomas are capillary hemangiomas that manifest as rapidly growing red pedunculated nodules on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Cavernous hemangiomas of the cerebellum or retina are a diagnostic feature of which autosomal dominant hereditary syndrome?

explanations.a: Sturge-Weber is associated with port-wine stains (nevus flammeus) and leptomeningeal angiomas, not typically cavernous hemangiomas of the cerebellum.
explanations.b: Osler-Weber-Rendu (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) features multiple telangiectasias and AVMs.
explanations.c: Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is characterized by cavernous hemangiomas (hemangioblastomas) in the cerebellum and retina, as well as renal cell carcinomas and pheochromocytomas.
explanations.d: Tuberous sclerosis features angiofibromas and hamartomas, not vascular hemangiomas.
explanations.e: NF1 features neurofibromas and Lisch nodules, not vascular tumors.

ankiCards: Cavernous hemangiomas of the CNS are associated with {{c1::von Hippel-Lindau}} disease.
Unlike capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas show {{c1::large, dilated}} vascular channels.
Cavernous hemangiomas of the liver are usually found {{c1::incidentally}} on imaging.
Intravascular thrombosis and {{c1::dystrophic calcification}} are common in cavernous hemangiomas.
Cavernous hemangiomas are less well-{{c1::circumscribed}} than capillary hemangiomas.
keyPoints: Cavernous hemangiomas involve large, blood-filled vascular spaces.
They are more likely to involve deep structures (liver, CNS) than capillary types.
They do not regress spontaneously.
In the CNS, they can cause pressure symptoms or hemorrhage.
Associated with VHL disease (VHL gene mutation on chromosome 3).
microReview: Large blood spaces + deep organs (liver/brain) + VHL association = Cavernous Hemangioma.
examinerTraps: Ensure you distinguish between 'telangiectasias' (Osler-Weber-Rendu) and 'cavernous hemangiomas' (VHL).
sourceQuote: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, dilated vascular channels... They are more frequently involve deep structures than do capillary hemangiomas.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old plastic factory worker is diagnosed with a primary malignant tumor of the liver. Exposure to which of the following substances is the most likely risk factor for this specific malignancy?

explanations.a: Aflatoxin B1 is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), not angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Vinyl chloride (used in the plastics industry) is a well-known carcinogen specifically associated with hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and lung cancer.
explanations.d: Benzene is associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.e: While arsenic is associated with angiosarcoma, vinyl chloride is the specific substance linked to workers in the plastic manufacturing industry.

ankiCards: The specific industrial chemical linked to hepatic angiosarcoma is {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
Arsenic exposure, often via pesticides, is linked to which vascular malignancy? {{c1::Angiosarcoma}}.
Thorotrast, a formerly used radioactive contrast medium, is associated with {{c1::hepatic angiosarcoma}}.
The latent period between exposure to vinyl chloride and development of angiosarcoma is usually {{c1::long (decades)}}.
Angiosarcoma of the liver is a {{c1::highly}} aggressive tumor with a poor prognosis.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma of the liver is a rare but classic 'occupational' cancer.
Risk factors: Vinyl chloride, Arsenic, and Thorotrast.
Vinyl chloride is used in making polyvinyl chloride (PVC).
Histology: Malignant endothelial cells lining liver sinusoids.
It is often fatal within a year of diagnosis.
microReview: Plastic worker + Liver cancer = Hepatic Angiosarcoma (Vinyl Chloride).
examinerTraps: The examiner may include 'Aflatoxin' or 'Hepatitis B' as distractors; these cause Hepatocellular Carcinoma, which is a tumor of hepatocytes, not endothelial cells.
sourceQuote: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with distinct environmental carcinogens, including arsenic (e.g., in pesticides), Thorotrast (a radioactive contrast medium), and vinyl chloride (used in the plastics industry).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following clinical features is most characteristic of Osler-Weber-Rendu disease (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia)?

options.a: A single, large, port-wine stain following the distribution of the trigeminal nerve
options.b: Multiple small, dilated capillaries in the skin and mucous membranes that may bleed
options.d: A rapidly growing pedunculated gingival mass in a pregnant woman

explanations.a: This describes Nevus flammeus associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome.
explanations.b: Osler-Weber-Rendu disease is characterized by multiple aneurysmal telangiectasias of the skin and mucous membranes (e.g., mouth, GI tract) which are prone to rupture and bleeding (epistaxis/GI bleed).
explanations.c: This describes a glomus tumor.
explanations.d: This describes granuloma gravidarum (a pyogenic granuloma).
explanations.e: This describes von Hippel-Lindau disease.

ankiCards: Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT) is also known as {{c1::Osler-Weber-Rendu}} disease.
HHT is inherited in an {{c1::autosomal dominant}} pattern.
The primary clinical manifestation of HHT in the nose is {{c1::epistaxis (nosebleeds)}}.
Patients with HHT are at risk for {{c1::iron deficiency anemia}} due to chronic GI bleeding.
HHT involves mutations in genes that modulate {{c1::TGF-beta}} signaling.
keyPoints: HHT (Osler-Weber-Rendu) is an autosomal dominant vascular dysplasia.
It results in malformed, dilated capillaries (telangiectasias) and AVMs.
Commonly presents with nosebleeds (epistaxis).
Internal AVMs can occur in the lungs, liver, and brain.
Telangiectasias are visible on the tongue, lips, and fingers.
microReview: Recurrent nosebleeds + telangiectasias on tongue/lips + AD inheritance = Osler-Weber-Rendu.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse telangiectasias (tiny permanent dilations) with hemangiomas (actual neoplasms).
sourceQuote: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu disease) is an autosomal dominant disorder... characterized by multiple aneurysmal telangiectasias over the skin and oral mucous membranes.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 2-month-old female infant is brought to the pediatrician due to a bright red, raised, and lobulated lesion on her left temple. The mother reports the lesion appeared at 3 weeks of age and has grown rapidly since then. On examination, the lesion is soft and blanches partially with pressure. Which of the following is the most likely clinical course for this lesion?

explanations.a: This lesion is a juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma. These typically grow rapidly for several months and then spontaneously involute; approximately 90% regress by age 7.
explanations.b: Juvenile hemangiomas are benign lesions and do not transform into malignant angiosarcomas.
explanations.c: Unlike port-wine stains, which persist, juvenile hemangiomas are known for their characteristic regression phase.
explanations.d: Surgical excision is rarely indicated for infantile hemangiomas unless they obstruct vision or the airway, as most regress spontaneously.
explanations.e: While some syndromes like capillary malformation-arteriovenous malformation exist, a solitary strawberry hemangioma does not typically imply systemic visceral involvement.

ankiCards: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangiomas typically {{c1::regress}} by age 7.
The characteristic natural history of an infantile hemangioma involves rapid growth followed by {{c1::involution/regression}}.
True/False: Juvenile hemangiomas are present at birth. {{c1::False (they appear shortly after birth)}}.
Juvenile hemangiomas are histologically characterized by {{c1::capillary}} proliferation.
The most common vascular tumor of infancy is the {{c1::juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma}}.
keyPoints: Juvenile hemangiomas are extremely common in infancy.
They appear within the first few weeks of life, not at birth.
Rapid growth occurs during the first few months (proliferative phase).
Spontaneous involution occurs in the vast majority of cases by age 7.
Management is usually observational unless function (e.g., vision) is impaired.
microReview: Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) are benign capillary proliferations. They are distinct from nevus flammeus (port-wine stains) because they are raised and undergo a predictable cycle of growth and regression.
examinerTraps: A common trap is confusing strawberry hemangiomas with port-wine stains; remember that strawberry hemangiomas regress, whereas port-wine stains (associated with Sturge-Weber) grow with the child and do not regress.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions. Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 38-year-old man with a history of HIV infection and a CD4+ T-cell count of 150 cells/mm³ presents with several dark purple, non-blanching plaques on his shins. A biopsy of the lesion reveals a proliferation of spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells, and a lymphocytic infiltrate. Which of the following pathogens is the primary driver of this pathology?

explanations.a: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent in all forms of Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.b: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can look similar clinically but is characterized by a neutrophilic infiltrate and the presence of bacteria on silver stain.
explanations.c: CMV can cause retinitis or colitis in AIDS patients but does not cause vascular tumors.
explanations.d: EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not Kaposi sarcoma.
explanations.e: HPV-16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is caused by {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
The histological hallmark of Kaposi Sarcoma is the presence of {{c1::spindle cells}} and slit-like spaces.
Kaposi Sarcoma is most common in patients with {{c1::HIV/AIDS}}.
The skin lesions in Kaposi Sarcoma are typically {{c1::purple/red}} and do not blanch.
Bacillary angiomatosis is differentiated from Kaposi Sarcoma by a {{c1::neutrophilic}} infiltrate.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8.
There are four forms: Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated (Epidemic).
Spindle cells and slit-like spaces with RBCs are diagnostic features.
KS is an AIDS-defining illness.
Treatment involves highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) to restore immune function.
microReview: Kaposi Sarcoma involves endothelial cell infection by HHV-8, leading to oncogenic signaling. Distinguish it from Bacillary Angiomatosis, which is bacterial and treated with antibiotics.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the lymphocytic infiltrate of KS with the neutrophilic infiltrate of Bacillary Angiomatosis.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions. Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with an exquisitely painful, 4 mm, blue-red nodule located under the nail bed of her right ring finger. The pain is triggered by cold exposure and pressure. The lesion is composed of nests of uniform cells surrounding vascular channels. These cells likely originate from which of the following structures?

options.e: Endothelial cells of the lymphatic system

explanations.a: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) arise from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous anastomosis involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.b: Hemangiopericytomas arise from pericytes, but the subungual location and specific glomus cell morphology point to a glomus tumor.
explanations.c: While the tumor is painful, it does not arise from nerve endings; the pain is thought to be secondary to the lesion's structure or innervation.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts produce collagen; they are not the cell of origin for this vascular tumor.
explanations.e: The cells are not endothelial; they are the glomus cells that surround the endothelial-lined channels.

ankiCards: A glomus tumor is most commonly found in the {{c1::subungual (under nail)}} region.
The cells of a glomus tumor are derived from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells.
The classic triad for a glomus tumor is pain, localized tenderness, and sensitivity to {{c1::cold}}.
Histologically, glomus tumors show nests of {{c1::glomus}} cells around vascular spaces.
Glomus tumors are {{c1::benign}} (benign/malignant).
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are small, benign, but very painful neoplasms.
The subungual (under fingernails) location is highly characteristic.
They arise from the glomus body (thermoregulatory organ).
The cells are specialized smooth muscle cells.
Simple excision is usually curative.
microReview: Pain + Subungual + Cold sensitivity = Glomus Tumor. Originates from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
examinerTraps: The examiner may try to trick you with 'glomus jugulare' or 'paraganglioma'; focus on the subungual location and specialized smooth muscle origin.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions. Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with several firm, violaceous nodules on her left upper arm. She has a history of chronic lymphedema in the same arm following a radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection 12 years ago for breast cancer. Biopsy of a nodule reveals poorly formed vascular channels lined by highly pleomorphic, multilayered endothelial cells with frequent mitotic figures. Which of the following immunohistochemical markers would most likely be positive in these tumor cells?

explanations.a: The diagnosis is angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves syndrome). As a tumor of endothelial cells, it expresses the endothelial marker CD31 (PECAM-1) or von Willebrand factor.
explanations.b: Cytokeratin is a marker for epithelial tumors (carcinomas).
explanations.c: S100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells, such as melanoma or Schwann cells.
explanations.d: CD117 (c-kit) is a marker for gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) and mast cells.
explanations.e: HMB-45 is a marker for melanoma.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves}} syndrome.
A common endothelial marker used to identify angiosarcoma is {{c1::CD31 (or vWF)}}.
Angiosarcomas are {{c1::malignant}} (benign/malignant) vascular tumors.
Risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma include {{c1::vinyl chloride}} and Thorotrast.
Histology of angiosarcoma shows atypical endothelial cells forming {{c1::irregular vascular channels}}.
keyPoints: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant vascular tumor.
Common sites include skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
Chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves) is a major risk factor.
Radiotherapy is another known risk factor for cutaneous angiosarcoma.
CD31 is the most specific endothelial marker.
microReview: Stewart-Treves syndrome: Mastectomy -> Lymph node removal -> Chronic lymphedema -> Angiosarcoma. Look for CD31+ pleomorphic endothelial cells.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse this with recurrent breast cancer; the presence of vascular channels and CD31 positivity confirms a primary vascular malignancy.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions. Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An AIDS patient with cutaneous vascular lesions undergoes a biopsy. The pathology report notes the presence of 'Warthin-Starry stain positive bacilli' within the lesions. The lesion also demonstrates a prominent neutrophilic infiltrate. What is the most appropriate treatment for this specific condition?

explanations.a: The description (AIDS, vascular lesions, bacilli on silver stain, neutrophils) is diagnostic of Bacillary Angiomatosis caused by Bartonella. This is treated with antibiotics like erythromycin or doxycycline.
explanations.b: While HAART is important for AIDS, it is not the definitive treatment for an active Bartonella infection.
explanations.c: The lesions are often multifocal; systemic antibiotics are the treatment of choice.
explanations.d: Radiotherapy is used for Kaposi sarcoma, not bacillary angiomatosis.
explanations.e: Doxorubicin is a chemotherapy agent used for Kaposi sarcoma, not bacterial infections.

ankiCards: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by bacteria of the genus {{c1::Bartonella}}.
The silver stain used to identify Bartonella in tissue is the {{c1::Warthin-Starry}} stain.
Histologically, bacillary angiomatosis features a {{c1::neutrophilic}} infiltrate, unlike Kaposi Sarcoma.
Bacillary angiomatosis is primarily seen in patients who are {{c1::immunocompromised/AIDS}}.
The first-line treatment for bacillary angiomatosis is {{c1::erythromycin (or doxycycline)}}.
keyPoints: Bacillary angiomatosis mimics Kaposi Sarcoma clinically.
It is caused by Bartonella henselae or Bartonella quintana.
It occurs in immunocompromised individuals.
Key histology: Capillary proliferation with neutrophils and nuclear dust.
Bacteria are visible on silver (Warthin-Starry) stains.
microReview: Bacillary Angiomatosis = Bartonella + Neutrophils + Silver Stain + Antibiotics. Kaposi Sarcoma = HHV-8 + Spindle cells + Lymphocytes + Antivirals/Chemo.
examinerTraps: The presence of vascular proliferation in an AIDS patient can tempt you to pick Kaposi Sarcoma; look for 'bacilli' or 'neutrophils' to correctly identify Bacillary Angiomatosis.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions. Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with a rapidly growing, pedunculated, red mass on her gingiva. The lesion bleeds easily with minor trauma, such as tooth brushing. Histological examination shows a circumscribed proliferation of capillaries arranged in lobules, accompanied by edema and an inflammatory infiltrate. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: A pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a common, benign vascular lesion that often occurs on the gingiva of pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum).
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas consist of large, dilated vascular channels and are usually deeper and not pedunculated.
explanations.c: Glomus tumors are usually subungual and extremely painful, not typically gingival.
explanations.d: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor with significant cellular atypia, not seen here.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is associated with HIV and Bartonella infection, not pregnancy.

ankiCards: Pyogenic granuloma is also known as {{c1::lobular capillary hemangioma}}.
When a pyogenic granuloma occurs in a pregnant woman's gingiva, it is called {{c1::granuloma gravidarum}}.
A key clinical feature of pyogenic granuloma is that it {{c1::bleeds easily}}.
Histologically, pyogenic granuloma resembles {{c1::granulation tissue}}.
True/False: Pyogenic granulomas are associated with pus/infection. {{c1::False (the name is a misnomer)}}.
keyPoints: Pyogenic granulomas are neither pyogenic (pus-forming) nor true granulomas.
They are lobular capillary hemangiomas.
Common locations: skin, gingiva, and oral mucosa.
Frequently associated with trauma or pregnancy.
They may regress postpartum or require simple excision.
microReview: Pregnancy + Bleeding gingival mass = Pyogenic Granuloma. It is a benign proliferation of capillaries similar to granulation tissue.
examinerTraps: The term 'pyogenic' is a misnomer; there is no acute infection or pus, despite the name.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions. Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following environmental exposures is most strongly associated with the development of hepatic angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Vinyl chloride (used in PVC production), Thorotrast (radiocontrast agent), and arsenic are well-known risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and lung cancer.
explanations.c: Aflatoxin B1 is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.
explanations.d: Benzene is associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.e: Beryllium is associated with berylliosis and lung cancer.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
A now-obsolete radiocontrast agent associated with hepatic angiosarcoma is {{c1::Thorotrast}}.
Arsenic exposure is a risk factor for angiosarcoma of the {{c1::liver}}.
The prognosis for hepatic angiosarcoma is generally {{c1::poor}}.
Vinyl chloride is used in the manufacture of {{c1::polyvinyl chloride (PVC)}}.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is rare but highly lethal.
Associated with specific chemical/radiological carcinogens.
Latency between exposure and tumor development can be decades.
Presents with weight loss, abdominal pain, and jaundice.
Tumor cells are CD31+.
microReview: Hepatic Angiosarcoma triad of risk factors: Vinyl Chloride, Thorotrast, and Arsenic.
examinerTraps: Ensure you distinguish between Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HBV/HCV/Alcohol/Aflatoxin) and Hepatic Angiosarcoma (Vinyl Chloride/Thorotrast).
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions. Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A large, poorly circumscribed mass is found in the neck of a newborn with Turner syndrome. The mass is composed of large, dilated lymphatic spaces lined by endothelial cells and separated by an intervening connective tissue stroma containing lymphoid aggregates. What is this lesion called?

explanations.a: Cystic hygroma (cavernous lymphangioma) is a lymphatic malformation classically found in the neck or axilla of infants, frequently associated with Turner syndrome or Down syndrome.
explanations.b: Cavernous hemangiomas contain blood, not lymph, and are not typically associated with Turner syndrome.
explanations.c: Simple (capillary) lymphangiomas are smaller and located on the skin surface, unlike the large cystic masses of cystic hygroma.
explanations.d: Capillary hemangiomas are common skin lesions (strawberry hemangiomas) and do not form large cystic neck masses.
explanations.e: Glomangiomas are variants of glomus tumors and are not associated with Turner syndrome or large neck masses.

ankiCards: Cystic hygroma is a type of cavernous {{c1::lymphangioma}}.
Cystic hygromas are commonly found in the {{c1::neck (or axilla)}}.
Cystic hygromas are frequently associated with {{c1::Turner}} syndrome.
Histologically, cystic hygromas contain dilated spaces filled with {{c1::lymph (chylous fluid)}}.
Chromosomal abnormality often seen with cystic hygroma: {{c1::45,X}}.
keyPoints: Cystic hygromas are benign lymphatic malformations.
They are often present at birth.
Association with Turner syndrome (45,X) and Trisomy 21.
They can be large and difficult to resect due to poor circumscription.
They contain proteinaceous lymph fluid and small numbers of lymphocytes.
microReview: Turner Syndrome + Newborn Neck Mass = Cystic Hygroma. These are dilated lymphatic channels.
examinerTraps: If the question mentions 'blood-filled spaces', it is likely a cavernous hemangioma. If it says 'lymph-filled' or 'clear fluid', it is a lymphangioma/cystic hygroma.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions. Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Vascular tumors are generally categorized by their biological behavior. Which of the following tumors is classified as an 'intermediate-grade' (borderline) neoplasm, possessing features between benign hemangiomas and highly malignant angiosarcomas?

explanations.a: Kaposi sarcoma and hemangioendotheliomas are considered intermediate-grade vascular tumors because they are locally aggressive but have more variable metastatic potential than angiosarcomas.
explanations.b: Angiosarcoma is highly malignant and high-grade.
explanations.c: Cavernous hemangioma is a benign tumor.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious/reactive process, not a true neoplasm, though it appears tumor-like.
explanations.e: Glomus tumor is a benign neoplasm.

ankiCards: {{c1::Kaposi Sarcoma}} is an example of an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
Vascular tumors that are locally aggressive but rarely metastasize are termed {{c1::intermediate-grade (or borderline)}}.
Epithelioid {{c1::hemangioendothelioma}} is another example of an intermediate-grade vascular tumor.
Malignant vascular tumors are termed {{c1::angiosarcomas}}.
Benign vascular tumors are termed {{c1::hemangiomas}}.
keyPoints: Vascular tumors span a spectrum from benign to malignant.
Benign: Hemangiomas, Glomus tumors.
Intermediate: Kaposi Sarcoma, Hemangioendotheliomas.
Malignant: Angiosarcoma.
Intermediate tumors often have a predictable clinical course based on immune status (especially KS).
microReview: Vascular Tumor Spectrum: Hemangioma (Benign) -> Kaposi Sarcoma (Intermediate) -> Angiosarcoma (Malignant).
examinerTraps: Students often misclassify Kaposi Sarcoma as 'malignant' because of its association with AIDS, but biologically it is considered intermediate/borderline.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions. Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with recurrent epistaxis and multiple small, red, blanching macules on his lips, tongue, and fingertips. He mentions his father had similar lesions and frequent gastrointestinal bleeds. This patient most likely has a mutation in genes involving which of the following signaling pathways?

explanations.a: This is Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome), which is caused by mutations in genes (like endoglin or ALK-1) that modulate TGF-beta signaling in endothelial cells.
explanations.b: While VEGF is involved in angiogenesis, the primary defect in HHT is in the TGF-beta pathway.
explanations.c: Notch signaling is involved in vessel branching and arterial identity but is not the primary defect in HHT.
explanations.d: Wnt signaling is crucial in development and some cancers (like colon cancer) but not HHT.
explanations.e: MAPK signaling is involved in many growth factor responses but is not the specific pathway for HHT.

ankiCards: Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome is also known as {{c1::Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT)}}.
HHT is inherited in an {{c1::autosomal dominant}} pattern.
The clinical triad of HHT includes telangiectasias, recurrent {{c1::epistaxis}}, and AV malformations.
HHT is caused by mutations affecting the {{c1::TGF-beta}} signaling pathway.
Common complications of HHT include iron deficiency anemia and {{c1::GI bleeding}}.
keyPoints: HHT is an autosomal dominant disorder of blood vessel structure.
Telangiectasias are present on skin and mucous membranes.
Arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) can occur in the lungs, brain, and liver.
Rupture of AVMs can lead to life-threatening hemorrhage or paradoxical emboli.
Mutations involve genes like ENG (endoglin) or ACVRL1.
microReview: Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT) = Epistaxis + Telangiectasias + AVMs + TGF-beta mutations.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the blanching telangiectasias of HHT with the non-blanching purpura of vasculitis.
sourceQuote: Many disorders of the vasculature affect only particular types of vessels and thus have characteristic anatomic distributions. Thus atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 68-year-old male smoker with a history of hypertension presents for a routine physical examination. A pulsatile, non-tender abdominal mass is palpated at the level of the umbilicus. Imaging reveals a 5.2 cm dilation of the infrarenal abdominal aorta. Which of the following biochemical processes is most central to the weakening of the vessel wall in this patient?

options.a: Excessive production of tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases
options.b: Decreased production of transforming growth factor-beta
options.d: Deposition of amyloid-al proteins in the tunica media
options.e: Deficiency of vitamin C-dependent lysyl oxidase activity

explanations.a: Tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs) actually inhibit the breakdown of the extracellular matrix; a decrease in TIMPs, not an increase, contributes to aneurysm formation.
explanations.b: Transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) signaling is often paradoxically increased in certain familial aneurysms, leading to abnormal collagen/elastin synthesis, rather than simply decreased.
explanations.c: The pathogenesis of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) involves a chronic inflammatory infiltrate in the media and adventitia that releases matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), such as collagenases and gelatinases, which degrade the extracellular matrix.
explanations.d: Amyloid deposition is characteristic of cerebral amyloid angiopathy, not the typical pathogenesis of abdominal aortic aneurysms.
explanations.e: Vitamin C is a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase, and lysyl oxidase requires copper. While these are involved in collagen cross-linking, the primary mechanism in atherosclerotic AAA is inflammatory-driven degradation via MMPs.

ankiCards: The most common cause of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
The primary biochemical enzyme family responsible for extracellular matrix degradation in aneurysms is {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}}.
Risk factors for AAA include male sex, age over 65, and {{c1::smoking}}.
Abdominal aortic aneurysms are typically located {{c1::infrarenal}} (relative to the renal arteries).
A clinical sign of an abdominal aortic aneurysm is a {{c1::pulsatile}} abdominal mass.
keyPoints: Aneurysms represent a weakening of the vessel wall leading to dilation or rupture.
Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are more common in men and smokers.
MMP-2 and MMP-9 (gelatinases) play a major role in degrading elastic fibers in the media.
AAAs are usually located below the renal arteries and above the iliac bifurcation.
Rupture risk increases significantly once the diameter exceeds 5.0 cm to 5.5 cm.
microReview: AAA is primarily driven by chronic inflammation and degradation of the extracellular matrix (ECM) by matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs). It is most commonly associated with atherosclerosis.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the location; AAAs are usually infrarenal, while thoracic aortic aneurysms are often associated with hypertension or Marfan syndrome.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: ... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A patient is diagnosed with a 'false aneurysm' (pseudoaneurysm) following a femoral artery catheterization. Which of the following best describes the anatomical characteristic of this lesion?

options.a: Dilation of all three layers of the arterial wall
options.b: An out-pouching of the vessel involving only the tunica adventitia
options.c: A hematoma that communicates with the intravascular space through a wall defect
options.d: Blood entering the media and separating the vessel layers
options.e: A localized thinning of the tunica media without luminal communication

explanations.a: This describes a 'true aneurysm,' which involves all three layers (intima, media, and adventitia).
explanations.b: Pseudoaneurysms do not involve an intact layer of the vessel wall as the boundary; they are contained by extra-vascular tissue.
explanations.c: A false aneurysm is a wall defect that leads to an extravascular hematoma that freely communicates with the intravascular space.
explanations.d: This describes an aortic dissection, which is distinct from a pseudoaneurysm.
explanations.e: Thinning of the media without communication does not define a pseudoaneurysm, which specifically requires a breach in the wall.

ankiCards: A(n) {{c1::true}} aneurysm involves all three layers of the arterial wall.
A(n) {{c1::false (or pseudo)}} aneurysm is an extravascular hematoma communicating with the lumen.
An aortic {{c1::dissection}} occurs when blood enters the wall itself and separates the layers.
Common causes of pseudoaneurysms include {{c1::trauma}} or iatrogenic injury (e.g., catheterization).
The two shapes of true aneurysms are {{c1::saccular}} and fusiform.
keyPoints: True aneurysms: Intact (but thinned) arterial wall layers (intima, media, adventitia).
False aneurysms: Breach in the wall leading to a pulsatile hematoma contained by connective tissue.
Aortic dissection: Blood splays the media into two planes; not necessarily dilated.
Fusiform aneurysms: Symmetrical circumferential dilation.
Saccular aneurysms: Spherical out-pouching involving only a portion of the vessel wall.
microReview: Distinguishing true vs. false aneurysms depends on whether the vessel wall layers remain intact (though dilated) or are breached.
examinerTraps: Aortic dissection is often incorrectly called a 'dissecting aneurysm,' but it is not always associated with a pre-existing aneurysm.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: ... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following is the most common underlying cause for the development of abdominal aortic aneurysms?

explanations.a: Cystic medial degeneration is more commonly associated with thoracic aortic aneurysms and Marfan syndrome.
explanations.b: Tertiary syphilis causes obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum, typically affecting the ascending aorta (thoracic).
explanations.c: Atherosclerosis is the dominant cause of abdominal aortic aneurysms, as it compromises nutrient diffusion to the media.
explanations.d: Mycotic aneurysms are caused by infections (e.g., Salmonella, Bacteroides) and are less common than atherosclerotic AAAs.
explanations.e: Giant cell arteritis can lead to aneurysms, but it is a much rarer cause than atherosclerosis.

ankiCards: The dominant cause of abdominal aortic aneurysms is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
Syphilitic aneurysms typically involve the {{c1::ascending/thoracic}} aorta.
Aneurysms caused by infection are termed {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysms.
Cystic medial necrosis is associated with the genetic condition {{c1::Marfan syndrome}}.
The primary vessel layer weakened in an aneurysm is the {{c1::tunica media}}.
keyPoints: Atherosclerosis causes intimal thickening, which impairs oxygen diffusion to the media.
The resulting medial ischemia leads to muscle cell loss and wall weakening.
Syphilis targets the vasa vasorum in the thoracic aorta.
Mycotic aneurysms can result from septic emboli or direct bacterial seeding.
Smoking is the most important modifiable risk factor for atherosclerotic AAA.
microReview: Atherosclerosis is the #1 cause of AAA; Hypertension/Cystic medial necrosis is the #1 cause of Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the primary cause of AAA (atherosclerosis) with the primary cause of aortic dissection (hypertension).
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: ... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 24-year-old male with a history of long limbs and hypermobile joints dies suddenly while playing basketball. Autopsy reveals a massive hemopericardium and a tear in the ascending aorta. Histological examination of the aortic wall is most likely to show which of the following?

options.a: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
options.c: Fragmentation of elastic fibers and mucoid material accumulation

explanations.a: This is characteristic of syphilitic (luetic) aortitis, not Marfan syndrome.
explanations.b: This describes Giant Cell Arteritis, which typically affects older patients.
explanations.c: This describes 'cystic medial necrosis' (or cystic medial degeneration), the hallmark of Marfan syndrome and other connective tissue disorders leading to thoracic aortic dissection.
explanations.d: Atherosclerosis is rare in a 24-year-old unless there is severe familial hypercholesterolemia and usually affects the abdominal aorta.
explanations.e: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in vasculitides like polyarteritis nodosa or malignant hypertension, not typically in aortic dissection of this nature.

ankiCards: The histological hallmark of Marfan-associated aortic disease is {{c1::cystic medial necrosis}}.
Cystic medial necrosis is characterized by the accumulation of {{c1::glycosaminoglycans (or mucoid material)}}.
Marfan syndrome is caused by a mutation in the {{c1::fibrillin-1 (FBN1)}} gene.
Aortic dissection in the ascending aorta can lead to {{c1::cardiac tamponade (or hemopericardium)}}.
Aneurysms in young patients should trigger suspicion for {{c1::connective tissue disorders}}.
keyPoints: Marfan syndrome involves FBN1 mutations leading to TGF-β dysregulation.
Cystic medial necrosis is actually a misnomer; it is degeneration, not true necrosis.
Thoracic aortic aneurysms in Marfan patients are prone to dissection.
Dissection into the pericardial sac is a common cause of death (tamponade).
Loss of smooth muscle cells and elastic fiber fragmentation are key features.
microReview: Young patient + Tall stature + Sudden death + Aortic tear = Marfan Syndrome leading to Aortic Dissection/Aneurysm due to Cystic Medial Necrosis.
examinerTraps: The term 'cystic medial necrosis' is still used on exams even though it is technically an accumulation of mucoid ground substance and not 'cysts' or 'necrosis'.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which molecular signaling pathway, when overactive, is specifically implicated in the pathogenesis of aneurysms seen in Loeys-Dietz syndrome?

explanations.a: Wnt signaling is important in development and cancer, but not a primary driver of Loeys-Dietz aneurysms.
explanations.b: Loeys-Dietz syndrome is caused by mutations in TGF-β receptors, leading to increased TGF-β signaling and abnormal collagen/elastin synthesis.
explanations.c: Notch signaling is involved in CADASIL and other vascular pathologies, but not primarily Loeys-Dietz.
explanations.d: VEGF is central to angiogenesis, not the structural medial weakening of aneurysms.
explanations.e: EGF signaling is not the primary driver of this connective tissue disorder.

ankiCards: Loeys-Dietz syndrome is associated with mutations in {{c1::TGF-β receptors}}.
The signaling pathway overactive in Loeys-Dietz is the {{c1::TGF-β}} pathway.
Loeys-Dietz syndrome features include aneurysms, bifid uvula, and {{c1::hypertelorism}}.
Both Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes involve defects in the {{c1::extracellular matrix}}.
Increased TGF-β signaling leads to abnormal production of {{c1::collagen and elastin}}.
keyPoints: Loeys-Dietz syndrome mimics Marfan syndrome but has distinct features like bifid uvula.
It is caused by gain-of-function mutations in TGFBR1 or TGFBR2.
The increased TGF-β activity weakens the arterial wall.
This leads to aggressive aneurysm formation and rupture.
TGF-β signaling is a major therapeutic target being researched for these conditions.
microReview: Loeys-Dietz = TGF-β receptor mutations = Overactive TGF-β signaling = Aortic aneurysms.
examinerTraps: A common trap is thinking a receptor mutation always leads to 'decreased' signaling; in Loeys-Dietz, it leads to paradoxically increased TGF-β signaling in the vessel wall.
sourceQuote: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease: ... Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old female presents with severe back pain and hoarseness. A chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum. A CT scan confirms a large aneurysm of the aortic arch. What is the most likely mechanism causing her hoarseness?

options.a: Compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve
options.b: Invasion of the tumor into the vocal cords

explanations.a: Thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAAs) can expand and compress adjacent structures. Compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve as it loops under the aortic arch leads to vocal cord paralysis and hoarseness (Ortner's syndrome).
explanations.b: An aneurysm is a vascular dilation, not a malignant tumor, and does not 'invade' in the neoplastic sense.
explanations.c: Rupture would lead to acute shock and death, not localized hoarseness.
explanations.d: Brainstem ischemia would cause global neurological deficits, not isolated hoarseness.
explanations.e: While pneumonia can occur if the aneurysm compresses a bronchus, hoarseness is specifically a nerve compression symptom.

ankiCards: Thoracic aortic aneurysms can cause hoarseness by compressing the {{c1::left recurrent laryngeal nerve}}.
Symptoms of TAA due to compression of the esophagus include {{c1::dysphagia}}.
Symptoms of TAA due to compression of the trachea or bronchus include {{c1::cough/dyspnea}}.
A widened {{c1::mediastinum}} on CXR is a classic sign of thoracic aortic dilation.
The most common cause of thoracic aortic aneurysms is {{c1::hypertension}}.
keyPoints: TAAs can be asymptomatic or present with symptoms of 'mass effect'.
Left recurrent laryngeal nerve compression = Hoarseness.
Esophageal compression = Dysphagia.
Tracheal compression = Respiratory distress.
Erosion into bone (ribs/vertebrae) can cause localized pain.
microReview: Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm symptoms: Respiratory (trachea), Dysphagia (esophagus), Hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve), or Pain (bone erosion).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the left and right recurrent laryngeal nerves; only the left loops under the aortic arch.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which specific organism is historically associated with the development of aneurysms in the ascending aorta due to obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum?

explanations.a: S. aureus can cause mycotic aneurysms, but not specifically the obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum seen in syphilis.
explanations.b: Treponema pallidum (syphilis) causes endarteritis of the vasa vasorum in the tertiary stage, leading to medial ischemia of the ascending aorta.
explanations.c: Salmonella is a common cause of mycotic aneurysms, particularly in the abdominal aorta, but not the mechanism described.
explanations.d: TB can involve vessels by direct extension from a lymph node but is not the classic cause of luetic aortitis.
explanations.e: C. pneumoniae is found in atherosclerotic plaques but is not a primary cause of ascending aortic aneurysms via this mechanism.

ankiCards: Tertiary syphilis causes a(n) {{c1::obliterative endarteritis}} of the vasa vasorum.
The most common site for a syphilitic aneurysm is the {{c1::ascending aorta}}.
Medial ischemia in syphilitic aortitis leads to a '{{c1::tree-bark}}' appearance of the intima.
Syphilitic aortitis can cause dilation of the aortic valve ring, leading to {{c1::aortic insufficiency/regurgitation}}.
The vasa vasorum are located in the {{c1::tunica adventitia}} of large vessels.
keyPoints: Syphilitic (luetic) aortitis is a manifestation of tertiary syphilis.
Endarteritis causes narrowing of the vasa vasorum lumen.
Medial scarring (tree-barking) results from ischemia and loss of elastic fibers.
Dilation can involve the aortic root, leading to valvular incompetence.
Most patients die of heart failure due to aortic regurgitation, not rupture.
microReview: Syphilis -> Vasa Vasorum Endarteritis -> Medial Ischemia -> Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm + Aortic Regurgitation.
examinerTraps: The 'tree-barking' is an intimal finding, but the primary pathology starts in the vasa vasorum of the adventitia.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the most likely sequence of events in the formation of an atherosclerotic abdominal aortic aneurysm?

options.a: Primary medial calcification followed by intimal tear
options.b: Intimal plaque formation leading to impaired nutrient diffusion to the media
options.c: Direct bacterial infection of the tunica adventitia leading to wall thinning
options.d: Congenital absence of the internal elastic lamina
options.e: Autoimmune destruction of the endothelial glycocalyx

explanations.a: Medial calcification (Mönckeberg) usually does not lead to aneurysms as the lumen remains patent and the wall is not necessarily weakened in that manner.
explanations.b: Atherosclerotic plaques in the intima increase the diffusion distance for oxygen and nutrients traveling from the lumen to the media, causing medial ischemia and atrophy.
explanations.c: This describes a mycotic aneurysm, not the typical atherosclerotic pathway.
explanations.d: Congenital defects in the internal elastic lamina are associated with Berry aneurysms in the Circle of Willis, not AAA.
explanations.e: The glycocalyx is involved in many processes, but its destruction is not the primary mechanism of AAA formation.

ankiCards: In AAA, intimal plaques impair oxygen diffusion to the {{c1::tunica media}}.
Medial ischemia in AAA leads to the loss of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}}.
The inflammatory response in AAA is characterized by an infiltrate of {{c1::macrophages and lymphocytes}}.
Atherosclerosis typically affects mainly {{c1::elastic and muscular}} arteries.
Medial atrophy and {{c1::ECM (extracellular matrix)}} degradation are the final common pathways to AAA.
keyPoints: Aorta depends on diffusion from the lumen for its inner layers' nutrition.
Atherosclerosis acts as a physical barrier to this diffusion.
Medial ischemia results in smooth muscle cell death and fibrosis.
Inflammatory cells secrete MMPs that destroy elastin.
The result is a thinned, inelastic wall prone to dilation under arterial pressure.
microReview: Atherosclerosis -> Diffusion Barrier -> Medial Ischemia -> Medial Atrophy/ECM breakdown -> Aneurysm.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse the 'tree-barking' of syphilis (from vasa vasorum blockage) with the 'barrier effect' of atherosclerosis (from intimal plaque). Both cause medial ischemia but via different 'directions' of nutrient loss.
sourceQuote: Atherosclerosis affects mainly elastic and muscular arteries
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old man with a 30-year history of uncontrolled hypertension presents with sudden onset 'tearing' chest pain that radiates to his back. His blood pressure is 190/110 mmHg. A CT scan shows a longitudinal cleavage of the aortic media. Which of the following is the most likely pre-existing condition?

explanations.a: An AAA is a separate entity and not the primary 'pre-existing' histological state that usually leads to an acute dissection.
explanations.b: Syphilitic aortitis causes scarring, which actually makes the aorta *less* likely to dissect because the layers are fused by fibrosis.
explanations.c: Cystic medial degeneration (even if mild or age-related) is the most frequent pre-existing histological finding in patients who develop aortic dissection.
explanations.d: Atherosclerotic plaques can ulcerate (penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer), but 'cystic medial degeneration' is the more classic answer for the background of a dissection involving the media.
explanations.e: Kawasaki disease causes coronary artery aneurysms in children, not adult aortic dissections.

ankiCards: The most common risk factor for aortic dissection is {{c1::hypertension}}.
The classic clinical description of aortic dissection pain is {{c1::tearing or ripping}}.
Histologically, aortic dissection is associated with {{c1::cystic medial degeneration}}.
Aortic dissection involves a tear in the {{c1::tunica intima}}.
Blood in a dissection flows between the middle and outer thirds of the {{c1::tunica media}}.
keyPoints: Aortic dissection is not a 'true' aneurysm, though it may occur in one.
Hypertension is the leading cause of the medial changes that predispose to dissection.
Pressure-induced hypertrophy of the vasa vasorum reduces flow to the media.
The 'tearing' pain is a medical emergency.
Stanford Type A involves the ascending aorta; Type B does not.
microReview: Hypertension -> Medial Degeneration -> Intimal Tear -> Blood enters Media -> Dissection.
examinerTraps: Wait for the 'tearing' keyword. If 'tearing' is present, think Dissection. If 'pulsatile mass' is present, think Aneurysm.
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Mycotic aneurysms are caused by which of the following mechanisms?

options.a: Fungal infection of the vessel wall only
options.b: Infection of the vessel wall by any microbe
options.d: Congenital weakness in the Circle of Willis
options.e: Excessive accumulation of copper in the media

explanations.a: Despite the name 'mycotic,' these aneurysms are usually bacterial (e.g., from endocarditis), not strictly fungal.
explanations.b: The term 'mycotic' refers to any aneurysm caused by the weakening of a vessel wall due to an infection (bacterial, fungal, etc.).
explanations.c: This describes vasculitis, not a mycotic aneurysm.
explanations.d: This describes a Berry aneurysm.
explanations.e: Copper is a cofactor for lysyl oxidase; deficiency (e.g., Menkes disease) can cause aneurysms, but this is not the 'mycotic' mechanism.

ankiCards: A(n) {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm is caused by infection of the arterial wall.
The term 'mycotic' was coined by {{c1::William Osler}}.
Common causes of mycotic aneurysms include {{c1::septic emboli}} from infective endocarditis.
Mycotic aneurysms often lead to rapid {{c1::dilation and rupture}}.
Direct extension of a nearby {{c1::abscess (or infection)}} can cause a mycotic aneurysm.
keyPoints: Mycotic aneurysms are often the result of bacteremia (e.g., Salmonella).
They can also result from septic embolization (e.g., infective endocarditis).
The infection induces a vigorous inflammatory response.
Neutrophilic enzymes degrade the vessel wall rapidly.
They can occur anywhere, but the aorta and cerebral vessels are common sites.
microReview: Mycotic Aneurysm = Infected Aneurysm (regardless of whether the microbe is a fungus or bacteria).
examinerTraps: Don't be fooled by the word 'mycotic'—it usually means bacteria in a clinical setting!
sourceQuote: Weakening of vessel walls, leading to dilation or rupture
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 32-year-old female presents to the clinic complaining of an intensely painful lesion under the nail of her right ring finger. She mentions that the pain is sharp, paroxysmal, and often triggered by exposure to cold temperatures. Physical examination reveals a small, 4-mm, slightly blue-tinted nodule beneath the nail plate. Which of the following is the most likely cellular origin of this neoplasm?

options.b: Glial cells of the peripheral nerve
options.c: Endothelial cells of the lymphatic system

explanations.a: Glomus tumors (glomangiomas) are benign, extremely painful tumors arising from specialized smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, which are involved in thermoregulation.
explanations.b: Glial cells are not found in subungual vascular tumors; Schwann cells would be the nerve-related counterpart, but they do not form glomus tumors.
explanations.c: Endothelial cells line the vascular spaces in these tumors, but the characteristic painful component is derived from the modified smooth muscle cells.
explanations.d: Fibroblasts are not the primary neoplastic component of glomus tumors.
explanations.e: Pleomorphic mesenchymal cells are more characteristic of high-grade sarcomas, not benign glomus tumors.

ankiCards: The glomus tumor arises from {{c1::modified smooth muscle}} cells.
A painful subungual blue tumor sensitive to cold is a {{c1::glomus tumor}}.
The glomus body is an arteriovenous anastomosis involved in {{c1::thermoregulation}}.
Glomus tumors are most commonly found in the {{c1::distal digits (under nails)}}.
Unlike most vascular tumors, glomus tumors are characterized clinically by {{c1::intense pain}}.
keyPoints: Glomus tumors are benign but extremely painful.
Classic location is subungual (under the fingernail).
Derived from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body.
The glomus body regulates temperature via arteriovenous shunting.
Excision is usually curative.
microReview: Vascular tumors range from benign (hemangiomas, glomus tumors) to intermediate (Kaposi sarcoma) to malignant (angiosarcoma). Glomus tumors are unique due to their origin in thermoregulatory smooth muscle and their neurovascular-like pain profile.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse a glomus tumor with a subungual melanoma; the latter is usually pigmented (melanin) and painless, whereas the glomus tumor is vascular (blue-red) and exquisitely painful.
sourceQuote: Vascular tumors... include: Benign tumors and tumor-like conditions... Malignant tumors... Glomus tumor... Benign, exquisitely painful tumors... from specialized smooth muscle cells of glomus bodies.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: An 8-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician due to a bright red, raised, lobulated lesion on the scalp that has grown rapidly over the last 3 months. The mother reports the lesion was not present at birth. The physician explains that the lesion will likely regress spontaneously by age 7. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Cavernous hemangiomas involve larger vascular channels, are more deeply situated, and do not regress as frequently or completely as capillary hemangiomas.
explanations.b: Capillary (strawberry) hemangiomas are common in infants, grow rapidly after birth, and usually undergo spontaneous regression by early childhood.
explanations.c: Nevus flammeus (port-wine stain) is a vascular ectasia present at birth that does not regress; it typically grows with the child.
explanations.d: Pyogenic granulomas are rapidly growing pedunculated red nodules that often follow trauma and do not typically regress spontaneously.
explanations.e: Angiosarcoma is a highly malignant tumor, virtually never seen in infants as a bright red regressing lesion.

ankiCards: Juvenile hemangiomas are also known as {{c1::strawberry}} hemangiomas.
The natural history of a capillary hemangioma in an infant involves {{c1::spontaneous regression}}.
By age 7, approximately {{c1::75-90}}% of juvenile hemangiomas have disappeared.
Capillary hemangiomas are composed of {{c1::thin-walled capillaries}} with scant stroma.
Unlike nevus flammeus, strawberry hemangiomas usually {{c1::are not present}} at birth.
keyPoints: Capillary (strawberry) hemangiomas are the most common vascular tumor of infancy.
They typically appear shortly after birth and grow for several months.
Spontaneous involution occurs in the majority of cases by age 7.
Histologically, they consist of closely packed capillaries lined by endothelial cells.
Management is usually observation (watchful waiting).
microReview: Distinguishing pediatric vascular lesions depends on the presence at birth and the tendency to regress. Port-wine stains (Nevus flammeus) are present at birth and permanent. Strawberry hemangiomas appear post-birth and regress.
examinerTraps: Wait for the 'regression' keyword; if the lesion is permanent and associated with the trigeminal nerve, think Sturge-Weber syndrome (Nevus flammeus), not hemangioma.
sourceQuote: Juvenile hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) of the skin of newborns are very common... grow rapidly for a few months but then fade and disappear.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 48-year-old male with a history of poorly controlled HIV infection (CD4+ count 120 cells/mm³) presents with multiple painless, red-to-purple, plaque-like skin lesions on his lower extremities and trunk. Biopsy of a lesion reveals proliferating spindle cells forming slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells. Which of the following pathogens is the primary driver of this condition?

explanations.a: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus (KSHV), is the causative agent in all forms of Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.b: EBV is associated with various lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, but not Kaposi Sarcoma.
explanations.c: Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which can look similar clinically but has a neutrophilic infiltrate rather than spindle cells and slit-like spaces.
explanations.d: CMV is a common opportunistic infection in AIDS but does not cause vascular tumors.
explanations.e: HPV-16 is associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and oropharynx.

ankiCards: Kaposi Sarcoma is caused by {{c1::HHV-8 (KSHV)}}.
The characteristic histology of Kaposi Sarcoma includes {{c1::spindle cells}} and slit-like vascular spaces.
{{c1::Extravasated RBCs}} and hemosiderin are frequently seen in Kaposi Sarcoma lesions.
The four clinical forms of Kaposi Sarcoma are Classic, Endemic (African), Transplant-associated, and {{c1::AIDS-associated}}.
Kaposi Sarcoma is classified as an {{c1::intermediate/borderline}} grade vascular tumor.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a spindle-cell neoplasm caused by HHV-8.
AIDS-associated KS is the most common HIV-related malignancy.
Histology: Slit-like vascular spaces, spindle cells, and RBC extravasation.
Stages: Patch, Plaque, and Nodule.
HHV-8 is transmitted primarily through sexual contact or saliva.
microReview: KS is the quintessential AIDS-defining vascular tumor. It is functionally a low-grade malignancy driven by viral oncogenes that induce endothelial cell proliferation and an inflammatory milieu.
examinerTraps: Bacillary angiomatosis (Bartonella) is the 'great imitator' of KS in AIDS patients. Look for 'neutrophils' or 'Warthin-Starry stain' for Bartonella; look for 'spindle cells' and 'HHV-8' for KS.
sourceQuote: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm caused by HHV-8... widely recognized as an AIDS-defining illness.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 72-year-old male presents with several enlarging, ill-defined, purplish-red nodules on his scalp. He mentions they have appeared over the last few months and occasionally bleed. He has no history of radiation or significant chemical exposure. Biopsy shows highly atypical, pleomorphic endothelial cells forming irregular, anastomosing vascular channels that invade the dermis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Capillary hemangiomas are benign, lack cytologic atypia, and are most common in children.
explanations.b: Kaposi Sarcoma typically presents as plaques/nodules in HIV+ patients and features spindle cells rather than highly atypical, anastomosing vascular channels.
explanations.c: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms. Cutaneous angiosarcoma most often occurs on the head/scalp of elderly individuals and shows marked atypia.
explanations.d: Bacillary angiomatosis features lobular capillary proliferation and neutrophilic inflammation in response to Bartonella species.
explanations.e: Glomus tumors are small, benign, extremely painful, and occur subungually.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma of the skin most commonly occurs in the {{c1::scalp}} of {{c2::elderly}} individuals.
Histology of angiosarcoma shows {{c1::atypical/pleomorphic}} endothelial cells and anastomosing channels.
The 5-year survival rate for angiosarcoma is approximately {{c1::30}}%.
The endothelial marker used to identify angiosarcoma is {{c1::CD31 (or vWF)}}.
Cutaneous angiosarcoma can occur as a complication of {{c1::chronic lymphedema}} (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
keyPoints: Angiosarcomas are aggressive, high-grade malignant vascular tumors.
Elderly scalp is a classic site for the cutaneous form.
They express endothelial markers like CD31.
They can be induced by radiation or chronic lymphedema.
Microscopically, they show varying degrees of differentiation, from recognizable vessels to solid sheets of atypical cells.
microReview: Angiosarcoma is the 'worst-case scenario' for vascular tumors. It is highly invasive and metastasizes early. It is the malignant end of the spectrum where cells barely resemble normal endothelium.
examinerTraps: Often confused with bruising in the early stages because of the purplish color. Any 'bruise' on an elderly patient's scalp that doesn't resolve should be biopsied for angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas are malignant endothelial neoplasms... older adults... more often in the skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following chemical exposures is most strongly associated with the development of hepatic angiosarcoma?

explanations.a: Aflatoxin B1 is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, not angiosarcoma.
explanations.b: Vinyl chloride (used in PVC production), arsenic (pesticides), and Thorotrast (radiocontrast) are classic risk factors for hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanations.c: Benzene is primarily associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
explanations.d: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and lung carcinoma.
explanations.e: Carbon tetrachloride is a hepatotoxin causing centrilobular necrosis and cirrhosis, but not specifically angiosarcoma.

ankiCards: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to {{c1::vinyl chloride}}.
Besides vinyl chloride, exposure to {{c1::arsenic}} is linked to hepatic angiosarcoma.
{{c1::Thorotrast}} was a historical radiocontrast agent that caused hepatic angiosarcomas.
Angiosarcomas of the liver have a very {{c1::poor}} prognosis.
Angiosarcoma cells stain positive for the endothelial marker {{c1::CD31}}.
keyPoints: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare but highly fatal malignancy.
Environmental toxins play a significant role in its pathogenesis.
Vinyl chloride is the most cited industrial exposure (PVC workers).
Arsenic exposure can occur via contaminated well water or pesticides.
Latent periods between exposure and tumor development can be decades.
microReview: While most angiosarcomas are sporadic or radiation-induced, hepatic angiosarcoma is the classic 'occupational' cancer example for medical boards involving vinyl chloride.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse hepatic angiosarcoma (vascular) with hepatocellular carcinoma (epithelial). Vinyl chloride = Angiosarcoma. Aflatoxin/HBV = HCC.
sourceQuote: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with distinct environmental carcinogens, including... vinyl chloride, and arsenic.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 25-year-old male presents with a port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) on the left side of his face, following the distribution of the trigeminal nerve. Which of the following is a characteristic feature of this specific vascular lesion?

options.d: High risk of transformation to angiosarcoma
options.e: Infiltration of the dermis by neutrophils

explanations.a: Unlike strawberry hemangiomas, port-wine stains do not regress; they grow with the child and thicken the skin.
explanations.b: Nevus flammeus is considered a vascular ectasia (dilation of existing vessels) rather than a true neoplasm.
explanations.c: The primary pathology is the permanent dilation of dermal capillaries.
explanations.d: There is no significant risk of malignant transformation for nevus flammeus.
explanations.e: Neutrophilic infiltration is characteristic of bacillary angiomatosis, not nevus flammeus.

ankiCards: Nevus flammeus is classified as a vascular {{c1::ectasia}}.
A port-wine stain in the trigeminal distribution may indicate {{c1::Sturge-Weber}} syndrome.
Unlike hemangiomas, nevus flammeus lesions usually {{c1::do not}} regress.
Sturge-Weber syndrome involves port-wine stains and {{c1::leptomeningeal}} angiomas.
The clinical appearance of a port-wine stain is a {{c1::flat, pink-to-purple}} patch.
keyPoints: Nevus flammeus is a congenital vascular ectasia.
Port-wine stains are a common subset.
They are permanent and tend to darken and thicken over time.
Distribution in the trigeminal V1/V2 area suggests Sturge-Weber syndrome.
Sturge-Weber also includes glaucoma, seizures, and mental retardation.
microReview: Ectasias are not true tumors; they are dilations of pre-existing vessels. This is a crucial distinction from hemangiomas, which are true proliferations (neoplasms).
examinerTraps: Students often group all 'red marks' on infants together. Always check if it regresses (hemangioma) or stays/grows (ectasia/port-wine stain).
sourceQuote: Nevus flammeus (the ordinary 'birthmark') is the most common form of vascular ectasia... port-wine stains are a special form... grow along with the child.
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with several blue-black nodules on her right arm. She underwent a radical mastectomy followed by axillary lymph node dissection and radiation therapy for breast cancer 12 years ago. Since the surgery, she has had persistent, massive lymphedema of that arm. What is the most likely diagnosis for the new skin lesions?

explanations.a: While metastatic breast cancer can present in the skin, the history of chronic lymphedema strongly points toward a specific vascular malignancy.
explanations.b: Kaposi Sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and usually HIV, not post-mastectomy lymphedema.
explanations.c: Angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome.
explanations.d: Lymphangiomas are benign and usually present at birth, not as new nodules in an adult.
explanations.e: Bacillary angiomatosis is an infectious process in immunocompromised patients.

ankiCards: Angiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphedema is called {{c1::Stewart-Treves}} syndrome.
Stewart-Treves syndrome most commonly follows {{c1::radical mastectomy}} and lymph node dissection.
The latent period for Stewart-Treves syndrome is typically {{c1::10 or more}} years.
The appearance of Stewart-Treves syndrome is usually {{c1::bluish-red nodules}} on the edematous limb.
The prognosis for lymphedema-associated angiosarcoma is {{c1::poor}}.
keyPoints: Chronic lymphedema is a major risk factor for cutaneous angiosarcoma.
This association is classically seen after breast cancer treatment.
The malignancy arises from the lymphatic or vascular endothelium.
It is aggressive with high metastatic potential.
Biopsy is essential to distinguish it from hematoma or infection.
microReview: Stewart-Treves syndrome is a high-yield 'association' question. Chronic stasis of lymph seems to impair local immune surveillance or provide growth factors that eventually lead to malignant transformation of endothelium.
examinerTraps: Don't assume skin nodules on a breast cancer survivor are always recurrence of the adenocarcinoma. Chronic edema + purple nodules = Angiosarcoma.
sourceQuote: Angiosarcomas... can also occur in the setting of chronic lymphedema, classically in the ipsilateral arm... (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
bookReference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (10th Ed)

stem: Which of the following describes the 'patch' stage of Kaposi Sarcoma (KS)?

options.a: Nodular masses of spindle cells with mitotic figures
options.b: Macular lesions with dilated, jagged vascular spaces lined by thin endothelium
options.c: Raised, purple lesions with sheets of atypical, pleomorphic cells
options.d: Pedunculated red nodules with a surrounding 'collarette' of epithelium
options.e: Deep, large vascular channels filled with blood and separated by connective tissue

explanations.a: This describes the 'nodular' (late) stage of KS.
explanations.b: The patch stage consists of flat, maculopapular lesions with minimally atypical vascular spaces.
explanations.c: This describes a high-grade angiosarcoma, not the early patch stage of KS.
explanations.d: This describes a pyogenic granuloma.
explanations.e: This describes a cavernous hemangioma.

ankiCards: The three stages of Kaposi Sarcoma are {{c1::patch, plaque, and nodule}}.
The {{c1::patch}} stage of KS features flat macules with jagged vascular spaces.
{{c1::Spindle}} cells only become prominent in the plaque and nodule stages of KS.
Histologically, the early patch stage of KS can be difficult to distinguish from {{c1::granulation tissue}}.
KS lesions often contain {{c1::hemosiderin-laden}} macrophages.
keyPoints: Kaposi Sarcoma progresses through three distinct morphologic stages.
Patch: Earliest stage, flat, jagged vascular spaces.
Plaque: Intermediate, slightly raised, more spindle cells.
Nodule: Late, solid masses of spindle cells and slit-like spaces.
All stages are driven by HHV-8 and local cytokines.
microReview: Understanding the progression of KS is vital. It starts as a subtle vascular proliferation (patch) and matures into a cellular, spindle-cell tumor (nodule).
examinerTraps: The board often asks for the 'most characteristic' feature, which is spindle cells and slit-like spaces (nodule stage), but you must be able to recognize the early 'patch' stage as well.
